en: Śrīḥ.
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by the venerable sage Vidyāraṇya,
together with the commentary composed by Rāmakṛṣṇa and the commentary composed by the illustrious Acyutarāya Moḍak.
In this regard, the first chapter is titled *Tattvaviveka* (Discrimination of Reality).

Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa! Having bowed to the lords of sages, Śrī Bhāratītīrtha and Vidyāraṇya, I compose the *Padadīpikā* (Lamp on the Words) for the *Pratyaktattvaviveka* (Discrimination of the Nature of the Inner Self). [The author begins] with the performance of [the introductory verse], which is required by the tradition of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), for the sake of the unobstructed completion and widespread propagation of the work he intends to undertake.

He composes a verse to record the auspicious invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) characterized by salutation to his chosen deity and teacher—which he himself has performed—for the purpose of instructing his disciples; by implication, he also indicates the subject matter and the purpose:
*Homage to the lotus-feet of the venerable teacher Śaṅkarānanda.*
To him whose sole function is to swallow the great delusion with its playful charms, as if it were a fish by means of a hook. || 1 ||

Regarding the word *namaḥ*: He who brings about *śam*—that is, happiness—is *Śaṅkara*, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) who causes joy to the entire world, according to the Vedic scripture: "He indeed bestows bliss" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.1). *Ānanda* is the inner self (*pratyagātman*), whose nature is supreme bliss because it is the object of unsurpassed love. He who is both *Śaṅkara* and *Ānanda* is *Śaṅkarānanda*, the Supreme Self non-different from the inner self; he alone is the Guru.

According to the scripture: "He who, abiding in the form of the Ācārya, unites those lotuses with the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) for the purpose of their eradication into the supreme reality through initiation. The compound *Śrīmāñchaṃkarānandaguruḥ* is to be understood like *Gandhadvipa* (an elephant distinguished by its scent) and other such formations; by this, the Guru’s possession of sovereign powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth is indicated. Alternatively, he is *Śaṃkara* because he brings about peace (*śam*) through prosperity (*śrī*); as it is said: "The gift is the supreme refuge of the giver" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*).

Thus says the Śruti [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.9.28]. By this, the capacity of the venerable Guru to accomplish the desired objects of his devotees is indicated. To the feet of that Guru—which are indeed "ambujanma," meaning lotuses—let there be *namaḥ*, that is, prostration. Having done what? To him whose sole function is the swallowing of the crocodile of great delusion (*mahāmoha*) along with its playfulness (*savilāsa*).

"Playfulness" refers to the aggregate of effects; that which exists together with it is "with playfulness" (*savilāsa*). Such is the great delusion, which is root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*); that itself is the crocodile.

The meaning is: because it is an extreme cause of suffering for one who has fallen under its power—just like a crocodile or similar creature—the "grasping" (*grāsa*) refers to its devouring; that which has this as its sole, primary action or function is described thus, and [the mantra is] for that [Lord]. Furthermore, here, through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two terms *Śaṅkara* and *Ānanda*, the subject matter (*viṣaya*) characterized by the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is indicated;

and by the phrase beginning with *savilāsa*, the purpose (*prayojana*) characterized by the manifestation of unlimited bliss through the individual soul’s nature as the vast Brahman is also indicated.
The purpose, characterized by the cessation of all misfortunes without exception, has been stated explicitly at the very outset. || 1 ||
Now begins the commentary by Acyutarāya:

Salutations to the Supreme Brahman—the immutable form of non-dual bliss, existence, consciousness, and omnipresence, pure and free from taint; though it is the abode of the illusory spectacle of duality arising from delusion, it is the Tilaka-mark, self-luminous.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
titled *Tattvaviveka* (Discrimination of Reality).

I bow to all the preeminent teachers of the Vedas, to the true guru who is the ornament of Raghu’s lineage and established in Brahman, named Śrīmat Nārāyaṇa, and also to my own guru known as Mahādeva. || 1 ||

It is blissful (*ānanda*) precisely because it is devoid of the threefold limitation; for such is the meaning of scriptural passages as, "That which is the *bhūman* (the Infinite) is bliss," and "In the small there is no bliss. By this, its lack of being a human goal (*apuruṣārthatva*) is refuted. For this very reason, the remainder of the cited scripture states: "That which is the *bhūman* is immortal, whereas that which is small is mortal. For this very reason, it is "Being" (*sat*), meaning that which is not sublated throughout the three periods of time. Even with respect to that, when there is a requirement for a means of knowledge (*māna*), it is "Consciousness" (*cit*). Furthermore, even so, [the term *cit* is used] to avoid the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of [identifying it with] the nature of deep sleep (*sauṣupta-svarūpa*).

It pervades; for although it exists as such at that time, it is not perceived now because of its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*). Now, one might object: "Even regarding such an entity, since the superimposition of 'stainlessness upon the sky' is possible, if ignorance (*ajñāna*)—which is the root of that [superimposition]—exists, then effort [to remove it] would be futile. To refute this, he says "pure" (*vimala*). Furthermore, since the word "Brahman" (*brahman*) can denote the Vedas and so forth, he uses the word "supreme" (*para*) to exclude those meanings. Even for such a Brahman, if it were different from the individual soul (*jīva*), it would result in the doctrine of dualism (*bhedavāda*); therefore, he says "unchanging" (*kūṭastha*).

The meaning is that [the Self] is non-different from the inner witness (*pratyag-abhinna*). Now, if such is the reality of things, how is it that this phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is perceived? To this he says, beginning with "through delusion" (*mohāt*). By this, it is indicated that from one's own perspective, it indeed possesses the aforementioned nature. Furthermore, by the word "also" (*api*), it is suggested that since worldly perception is illusory, even the status of being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhānatva*) of the visible world does not exist there from the standpoint of ultimate reality. For this very reason, he says "the tilaka," and so on. According to Amara: "Tamāla-leaf, *tilaka*, *citraka*, and *viśeṣaka* [are synonyms for the forehead mark]."

The sense is this: just as it is well known that for auspicious women, a forehead mark (*tilaka*) made of saffron serves as an indicator of their good fortune, so too the aforementioned subject matter serves as an indicator of the supreme auspiciousness of the Śrutis. By this, it is suggested that even in the Advaita system, both sections (*kāṇḍa*) achieve their own respective purposes. Now, one might object that because of the aforementioned metaphors (*rūpaka*) and other figures, there is an element of artificiality; to this he says: "Sva... (His own...). Thus, having prostrated to the Supreme Lord according to the Śruti beginning with "yasya deve parā...", he likewise prostrates to his gurus.
Thus—by the words "all" and so forth. || 1 ||
The trustworthy Śrī Vidyāraṇya, together with the two delightful gurus, Bhāratītīrtha and Ānandagiri, thus dispelling the darkness, is beneficial to the lily groves, stainless, and free from blemish.

I, whose body is nectar, who am self-luminous, the lord of stars, free from fault, devoid of both waning and waxing, and known as Acyuta—the lord of the twice-born—compose this *Kaumudī* commentary upon the *Pañcadaśī*. 2.

Where there is knowledge— that is, true comprehension— of the splendor of either the spring or autumn season, such a forest or woodland is indeed like Sarasvatī, the goddess of speech. Furthermore, even a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) such as the Gaṅgā, which possesses a white color due to its natural form being revealed by the force of its turbulent current, is also [like her] because it is full of essence and weight, and is full of nectar.

The meaning is: by that "bhā" (splendor) which is distinguished (*saviśiṣṭā*), heavy (*gurvī*), and great (*mahatī*). Alternatively, there is a word-break as *ubhayā* (by both). The sense is: by a dark splendor similar to that of Śiva, who is denoted by the syllable *u*.

For this very reason, he is *sarasaguḥ*—one whose rays (*gāvaḥ*) are full of sap (*sarasāḥ*) and beautiful (*suṃdarāḥ*). Being such, he is *āptaḥ* (attained/reached). This is the meaning in the case of the Moon, which is denoted by the term *dvijeśa* (Lord of the Twice-born). However, in the case of the subject of comparison (*upameya*), the meaning is: by that splendor (*bhā*) which is the grace and sidelong glance (*kṛpākaṭākṣa*) of those *guravaḥ* (teachers) who reside within the self (*ātmaniṣṭha*) and are full of sap (*sarasāḥ*).

But regarding the previous [explanation] of the word *chēda* (cutting): "by Umā" means by the valid cognition (*pramā*) whose object is Brahman, which is denoted by the word *Śiva*. "Sarasagūḥ" means one whose speech (*gīḥ*) is "sarasā"—that is, eloquent in expounding Brahman;

being such, he reached Śrī Vidyāraṇya, and likewise Bhāratītīrtha, having attained them as the determiners of the intended meaning of their treatises. In this way, this third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) connects everywhere hereafter as well. However, in the case of the moon, which serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) suggested by the pun (*śleṣa*), it connects only with the qualifying attributes that indicate the distinction (*vaidharmya*) for the purpose of manifesting the figure of speech known as *vyatireka* (distinction).

*Dhvāntam* means primordial ignorance (*mūlājñāna*); in the alternative sense, it means nocturnal blindness (*timira*). *Vidhvaṃsayānaḥ* means that which destroys. *Kutsiteṣu śabdādiviṣayeṣu mutprītiryaiṣām* refers to those who take pleasure in contemptible objects such as sound and so forth;

their *avanam*—that is, protection through the discernment indicated by the composition of this very work—is itself his *hitam* (benefit). In the alternative sense, the meaning is "beloved by night-blooming lilies" (*kairava-kula*).

*Pañcadaśyām* refers to the treatise named *Pañcadaśī*; in the alternative sense, it means on the full moon day (*pūrṇamāsī*). *Nakṣatram* refers to a group of Brahmins subsisting on the profession of warriors (*kṣātra-vṛtti*); he whose lord (*īśa*) is [this group] because of its harmful nature is thus described.

Likewise; for this very reason. *Pradoṣa* means one who is free from the most excellent faults (*prakṛṣṭa-doṣa*). Such is he named *Acyuta*, whose renown as the author of the work belongs to him through *Acyuta*—the Supreme Self, the inner controller (*antaryāmin*). For this very reason, he is clearly the Lord and benefactor of the twice-born (*dvija*), those who subsist solely on the three [prescribed] modes of livelihood beginning with that of the Brāhmaṇas. || 2 ||
Having seen the commentary on the *Rāmakṛṣṇa*, let those twice-born ones who are connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor wander about during the *Kaumudī* festival for the sake of peace and satisfaction. 3.

In the moonlight denoted by the word *kaumudī*, those who are connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor (*rasajña*) are the *cakra* birds that savor its sweetness. Regarding the word "Rāma": here, due to its co-occurrence with the word "Kṛṣṇa," the white-colored Balarāma is indicated. Thus, just as the *baka* and the crow represent the low end of the scale, the swan and the cuckoo represent the high end; such are the two birds whose "narration"—the collection of sounds indicating the arrival of evening—is experienced intensely. Having perceived this...
And he wanders about for the sake of peace; thus it is. || 3 ||
The First Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.
If this fifteenth day— the moonlight of the full moon of fifteenfold bliss— did not exist, then even with the presence of lamps, the darkness of the lotuses would not be dispelled.

The two ends of the fortnights are the two fifteenth days; according to Amara, the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is characterized by extreme darkness—this is the meaning. As for "the lotus" (*puṣkara*), it refers metaphorically to the mind situated within your lotus-like heart; its "darkness" is ignorance. Alternatively, according to Amara’s definition of *puṣkara* as the sky or atmosphere, it means by not dispelling the darkness residing in that [sky]. || 4 ||

In this regard, it is said that first there is the purification of the meaning of the word *tat* (That) through five types of discernment (*viveka*). Then, by means of those same [five] lamps, the meaning of the word *tvam* (Thou) is to be known. (5) Through the treatise titled *Ānandapañcakātmabrahmānanda*, this work—which has non-dual unity as its very body—is intended to convey the meaning of the word *asi* (art). (6) Each group of five has been composed for the destruction of each of the five kinds of obstacles; thus should it be understood by the wise who seek the truth of "That Thou Art" (*tattvam asi*).

Regarding the categories [of existence]: || 7 || Just as those [errors] regarding the object, the latent impressions, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge are impossible, so too are the errors consisting of misconceptions regarding the means of attainment and their results; these should be understood according to their respective order. || 8 || In the scripture, they are destroyed by the excellence of qualification, systematic connection, and so forth, in due sequence; likewise here [in this system], they are destroyed by qualification, sacred revelation, reasoning, meditative absorption, and the realization of the fruit. || 9 ||

"Āsana" means "āsas," which signifies sitting firmly with the intellect; the meaning is that it is the state wherein one remains thus. Likewise, "phala" means liberation (mukti), and the meaning is the realization concerning that [liberation]. || 9 ||

Precisely because of its predominance, all this [teaching] exists there and there in a subtle form; therefore, no single section alone can establish those respective attributes. (10) If the fifteen obstacles are destroyed by these fifteen sections, then the understanding born of the spoken words shall be free from impediment. (11) Furthermore, devotion accompanied by the desire for union (*sāyojya*) and so forth, along with the contemplation of the qualified aspect (*saguṇa*) and the conviction in the truth therein—[this is devotion].

The first obstacle to the knowledge of the Lord is the notion that [the pursuit of] human goals is more significant. (12) The second obstacle to the knowledge of the Lord is the firm conviction that this entire scripture culminates in Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahman*). (13) The third obstacle to the knowledge of the Lord is the thought: "How could the attribute-less Self be the creator, sustainer, and destroyer of the world? Or how could it possibly be its controller? (14)

"Liberation arises only from the knowledge imparted by Īśvara, and never from anyone other than a Guru"—this fixed conviction is the fourth obstacle regarding the cognition of Īśvara. (15) "For one who is liberated, there is the manifestation of all things through being the Self of all; even the [desire] for universal controllership and so forth is the fifth obstacle regarding the cognition of Īśvara. (16) The desire to experience only those joys ending with the bliss of the *sūtrātmā*, and the excellence of [one's own] form and so forth—[these are further obstacles].

And this is the first obstacle here regarding the individual soul (jīva): how can scripture [be authoritative] concerning a soul that is accessible through perception and other means of knowledge, such as its being fair-complexioned and so forth? || 17 ||

The notion that the soul possesses the pride of having attained enlightenment is this second obstacle here in the living being. (18) If the self were pure consciousness alone, then all means of knowledge such as perception and the rest would be abolished; yet there is no such logical proof. This is the third obstacle here in the living being. (19) Liberation occurs through right meditation, action, and knowledge, or through meditation born of pure knowledge; such a conviction is the fourth obstacle here in the living being. (20)

If there were non-duality even in liberation, then the experience of the bliss of Brahman would not occur either. O Śiva, Śiva! How then could this fifth obstacle exist here in the living soul? (21) Where indeed are the objects of the senses, the teacher, the scriptures, the garden, the riverbank, and so forth, in the state of Kaivalya? Such agitation in the mind is the first obstacle, even regarding oneness. (22) Just as the goal of oneness is pursued by the proponents of non-duality according to their own view—

And by others: "Not believing thus, this second obstacle exists even regarding oneness: 'How could the individual soul (jīva) be the Lord (īśa) here at the end of the kalpa? And no reasoning is seen for this; this third obstacle exists even regarding oneness. (23-24)

Even in the case of one possessing knowledge (*jñānin*), liberation from non-duality exists only after the fall of the body, or else upon reaching the seventh stage (*bhūmi*); this is the fourth obstacle, even though oneness has been attained.

(25) Even in the state of singular flavor (*ekarasa*), there still exists the bliss of the couple within the nectar, by virtue of being a witness to one’s own nature; like the rays of the self-luminous sun, this is the fifth obstacle, even though oneness has been attained. (26) I shall explain how these [obstacles] are overcome through the *Tattvaviveka* and other treatises (*prakaraṇa*). Listen to that. (27)

Having understood that subtle secret through the grace of the Guru, [it is established that] in the first [chapter], there is primacy regarding the attainment of qualification for its sake, starting from the very beginning.

And because the passage beginning with "tat-pāda" and "śabda" has that [Brahman] as its purport; || 28 || thus, from the statement of concordance (*samanvaya*) through the investigation of the elements, the purport of the word "That" (*tat-pada*) regarding its meaning must be determined by the second [chapter] beginning with "sat" (Being). || 29 || This is in order to state the non-contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge.
[[page 4-to-4]]
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
titled *Tattvaviveka* (Discrimination of Reality).

In the third [chapter], the Brahman that has been discerned through the sheaths is honored as being "in the cave" (*guhā*) and so forth, which constitutes its essential meaning. (30) In the fourth [chapter] as well, by means of an inquiry into the duality fashioned primarily by the Lord (*Īśvara*), and by stating the absence of awakening during dissolution (*pralaya*) in the absence of a Guru, its primacy is established. (31) In the fifth [chapter], where it is stated that "Brahman is one;
thus, no duality whatsoever exists," its preeminence is to be understood even more clearly. (32)
By means of the illustration of the variegated cloth and so forth, detachment is expressed by the word "Self"; thus, the nature of the individual soul (jīva) is emphasized even in the sixth chapter.

33. This becomes clear from the explanation of the Śruti text, "If one [knows] the Self," in the seventh [chapter]. For those who know the essence (rasajñānām), the primary harmony (samanvaya) is established with reference to the individual soul (jīva). 34. Through the discernment of the purified soul and by means of various arguments, non-contradiction alone has been stated. Since there is no contradiction with other means of knowledge, why should there not be a focus on that [Self] even in the eighth chapter? 35. One whose obstacles have been destroyed by either meditation (dhyāna) or inquiry (vicāra) would indeed be enlightened.

By this statement, its being devoted to that [the Self] is clearly determined in the ninth chapter. In the tenth chapter, by stating the result—that the Self, like a lamp, is the illuminator of all and is of a single flavor, an ocean consisting solely of self-luminous bliss—its devotion to that is established. In the eleventh chapter, however, by teaching that the happiness derived from yoga is unsurpassed even when directed toward no external object, its status as a supreme human goal (puruṣārtha) must be determined as being devoted to that [the Self]. Its nature is non-duality.

In the twelfth [chapter] as well, the fact that the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa and other passages have that [oneness] as their purport should be understood from the statement of their perfect systematic connection (samanvaya) with it. || 39 ||

Moreover, in the thirteenth [chapter] as well, it was stated through various arguments that there is the possibility of the unity of non-duality; therefore, its predominance should be understood as equal [to that of the other chapters]. (40) And likewise, in the fourteenth [chapter], since liberation in the form of the non-dual Self is said to arise from knowledge alone, why should its orientation toward that [knowledge] not be even more evident? (41) In the fifteenth [chapter] too, there is indeed a statement regarding the non-dual, self-luminous, and abundant bliss, which is the illuminator of all parts of the illuminated.

The phrase "of the absence" indicates its orientation toward that [absence]. Thus ends [the section on] the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) concerning the distinction between the principles (tattva), the elements (bhūta), the sheaths (kośa), and duality.
Of the lamps known as the excellent drama of meditation, situated on the peak of manifold satisfaction. || 43 ||

The meaning is: "of those [disciples] who possess discrimination (*viveka*), whose names begin with syllables that transcend the words starting from *tattva* up to *mahāvākya*. This is indeed intended to indicate the skill in composing this play—a work consisting of a few verses, full of aesthetic flavor, and conducive to swift awakening—even for those attached to sense objects, provided they possess an extremely intense longing for liberation (*mumukṣā*). || 43 ||

Furthermore, the fifteenth [chapter] is indeed a small casket for the collection of those blisses which are exceedingly delightful due to their adjuncts being the objects of the knowledge of the non-duality of the self of Yoga. 44.
Because of the rule "optionally at the end of a word," there is heaviness for the letter *ta*. || 44 ||
Fifteen obstacles are dispelled by as many chapters; by this [work], the full-moon light of supreme bliss is attained by the foremost of the twice-born who are seekers of knowledge. 45.

The meaning is that there is a set of nine chapters beginning with the *Tṛptidīpa* and ending with the *Viṣayānanda*. For the "lords of the twice-born" (*dvijeṃdrāṇām*), who are knowers of Brahman, this refers to the *cakora* birds; for the *cakoras*, it means the full moonlight. The phrase "is accomplished" (*saṃpādyate*) is implied. In the alternative sense, it refers to the light of the moon. || 45 ||
But here, even the lamps of discernment and the joys do not shine in the absence of the moonlight [of the Guru], for they do not dispel the infinite darkness, even though they have arisen. || 46 ||
The meaning is that it consists of nine chapters beginning with the *Tṛptidīpa* and ending with the *Viṣayānanda*. || 46 ||
The five Vivekas composed by Śrī Vidyāraṇya, along with the Citradīpa, are [herein]; the remainder has been taught by the venerable Bhāratītīrtha. || 47 ||

The meaning is: that darkness which is ignorance (ajñāna) having as its locus and object the infinite Brahman; or alternatively, it refers to the darkness belonging to those infinite—that is, innumerable—individual souls (jīvas). And thus, because individual souls are infinite, this work may be beneficial for those among them whose doubts are dispelled by this very *Kaumudī* under discussion. In the alternative [interpretation], according to the *Amara-kośa*, "the sky (*kha*) is the path of the gods and is infinite," the meaning is the darkness situated in the ether. || 47 ||

O twice-born ones, even after propitiating [the deity] with incomparable efforts for fifteen or sixteen nights, there was neither the attainment of the desired nor the cessation of the undesired; such is the incomparable [state].
Thus ends the first chapter.

Accompanied by two commentaries, worship this [work]. (48) Having honored Jīvañjīva, Vidyāraṇya, and Bhāratītīrtha—who expound the true nature of reality—I illuminate the *Kaumudī* through the *Bhūmiprakāśa*. (49)

The meaning is: having reflected upon the subject matter of the intent of those respective treatises, considering them to be Vidyāraṇya and Bhāratītīrtha—the authors of the work at hand. Likewise, there is a word-break as *ajīvam*. The meaning is: having realized as one's own self (*ātmatvena*) that Brahman in which no individual soul (*jīva*) exists—that is, duality characterized by such a soul. Likewise, "having considered" (*matvā*) the transmigrating beings (*jīvān*) as being subject to suffering. This was the first illumination of the *Kaumudī* [commentary]. (49)

Then the venerable sage Vidyāraṇya, desiring to favor all seekers of liberation by extracting the essence of the purport of the entire collection of his major and minor works— beginning with the *Śrīmad-Brahmasūtra-Bhāṣya*— and wishing to compose a compendium consisting of fifteen chapters in the form of short treatises such as the *Tattvaviveka*, which would be beneficial for those possessing great intellect skilled in discerning the scriptures despite the defects prevalent in the Kali age, commenced this work with an auspicious invocation through various methods suited to their respective inclinations.

Having performed at the beginning of the work a benediction consisting of salutation to the Guru— who is non-different from the Supreme Lord according to the Śruti text beginning with "yasya deve"— which is prescribed by the Śruti inferred from the Mahābhāṣya tradition starting with "lādīni," which was practiced by the cultured elders such as the venerable Vālmīki and others, and whose sole fruit is the pacification of obstacles to the undertaking; and having composed this [salutation] even at the start of the book out of a desire to instruct his disciples, [the author now states] the subject matter and purpose for the sake of engaging those who possess discernment, since this is a treatise belonging to the Advaita system...

He also attaches [the name] to people, saying "by name. Now, by such Śruti and Smṛti passages as "He is attainable only by whom He chooses" and "I give that yoga of discernment by which they come unto Me," [it is shown that] through Śrī—the power of eternal sovereignty—He brings about the auspiciousness characterized by liberation for those who know. Thus, together with the pure Brahman, whose nature consists of Truth, Knowledge, and so forth, and which is indicated by the state of Lordship denoted by that word (tat-pada), [He acts].

"By the scriptural text beginning with ‘This is dearer than a son,’ the pure individual soul (*jīva*), which is the referent of the word *tat* (That) and is of the nature of bliss that is the object of unqualified love, is shown to be non-different from the referent of the word *tvam* (Thou) through a *karmadhāraya* compound. For the sake of realizing this, the scripture states: ‘He should approach a guru alone, carrying fuel in his hand—one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and firmly established in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭha*). Although the status of the guru as one who is most excellent and pre-eminent among those established in Brahman is established by the etymology of that very name, [the text continues] even when [he possesses]..."

By the qualifier *lāsayan* ("causing to dance"), it is understood that the "grasping" (*grāha*) is indeed ignorance along with its effects; that which has this as its "swallowing" (*grāsa*)—meaning its sole action or function—is [the state] from which, through the destruction of the entire visible world (*dṛśyadhvaṃsana*), the doctrine of immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*) is perceived. Thus, the doctrine of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) suggested by the first half of the verse is rejected.

If it is argued: "Is this verse not indeed improper, because of the doubt expressed by 'or' (*kiṃ vā... vā*) and because the meanings are mutually contradictory?"—we say no. This is because there is a metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*) of the Guru’s feet with lotuses.

By day, through the greatness of *saṃsāra*; by night, through the non-indication of the Sun (*sūra*); through its manifoldness, by accepting the various doctrines of ignorance (*anekadhā*) according to the manner to be described; and by means of the crocodile named *naka* situated within it—[the term *vilāsa*] being derived from the etymology "that which shines forth (*viśeṣeṇa lasati*) with this [ignorance]"—and by that which is characterized by pride (*mānitva*) and so forth, according to the Smṛti: "Ignorance is that which is otherwise than this," [he cuts] the heart-knot and all doubts.

This is because it is logical that the primary effect belongs precisely to that which is called accumulated karma (*saṃcita-karma*), gathered up until the moment immediately preceding knowledge—as evidenced by such scriptural texts as, "The knot of the heart is severed," and such traditional texts (*smṛti*) as, "The ignorant one, the faithless one, and the doubting soul perish. Thus, it should be understood that there is not even a scent of contradiction here. Nor, in this way, does the term *vilāsa* (manifestation) lose its natural fitness; for [the dissolution] applies only to those visible objects that exist as long as ignorance persists.

Since this contradiction has been resolved by restricting [the meaning] once comprehension is attained, and because the intention behind the singular form in the phrase "of the lotus-feet" (*pādāmbujanmanaḥ*)— namely, to indicate that the present venerable Guru, like Śrī Rāma, is a Supreme Person (*uttamapuruṣa*) whose limbs are equal and well-proportioned— is that this Guru possesses two powers in his feet:
one is to be given to those who are qualified for liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), and the other is for those who are qualified for immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*).

It should not be argued that the resolution of the aforementioned contradiction is appropriately achieved through a restrictive interpretation (*vyavasthayā*) based on the predominance of the primary sense; for if that were the case, there would be a sublation of the exclusion of all activities other than the destruction of duality—which is established by the natural force of the single word *ekakarmaṇaḥ*—within that context. Therefore, what has been stated [previously] alone is correct; this is the direction of the argument. Furthermore, although in common worldly usage there exists a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the lotus, the crocodile, and their effects, delimited by the lake...

Because the relationship of the eater and the eaten is not perceived there, and because, on the contrary, its very opposite is conceivable as occurring only occasionally; and because, even though a contradiction appears through the aforementioned metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*), the figure of *pariṇāma*—defined by such statements as "When the object (*viṣaya*) serves the purpose of the subject (*viṣayin*) for the sake of an action, it is *pariṇāma*"—must necessarily be expressed, it is therefore designated here as a mere semblance (*ābhāsa*). Thus, by stating the figure of the semblance of contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*), [the text says] "ā—" (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "ā-". The translation reflects this truncation.)
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 6]

It should be understood that, according to the method stated in such scriptural passages as "Someone beholds this [Self] as if it were a wonder" (*tattvaviveka*), the *śānta* (peaceful) sentiment alone is primarily suggested (*dhvani*) by the indication that the contradiction characterized by all suffering and duality is merely an appearance, being permeated by the sentiment of wonder (*adbhuta-rasa*). || 1 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, preceded by a statement of the intermediate purpose, he declares the commencement of the work:
"For those whose minds have been purified by service to the pair of his lotus feet..."
This analysis of reality is set forth for the sake of easy understanding. || 2 ||

Regarding the phrase *tatpāda* and so forth: those whose minds (*cetas*)—that is, their internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—are purified by service (*sevā*), characterized by attendance, praise, prostration, and the like, toward the pair of lotus-feet (*amburuha-dvandva*) of that Guru; for the sake of their easy understanding (*sukhabodha*), meaning for the effortless production of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), this following method is presented for the sake of [revealing] reality (*tattva*), which is the unimposed essential nature (*anāropita-svarūpa*), namely, "the indivisible Being-Consciousness-Bliss" (*akhaṇḍaṃ saccidānanda*).

By the great saying (mahāvākya), as will be stated in verse 46, "discrimination" (viveka)—meaning the discernment [of the Self] from the superimposed world characterized by the five sheaths—is enjoined; that is, it is performed. || 2 ||

Commentary (a0ṭī0): Now, one might object: "Granted that the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and so forth are established by means of *dhvani* and the rest; nevertheless, how is the stated purpose (*prayojana*) accomplished? Is it through the practice of meditation and other rituals—following the analogy of the worm in the dung (*bhramarakīṭanyāya*)—or by piercing [the heart] with the aforementioned subject matter as its form, either individually or in combination? In the first and last cases, since the knowledge of the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-veda*), which is required for ritual action and is otherwise beyond perception, can arise from that very [Vedic study] itself, what is the use of a fourfold definition (*caturlakṣaṇī*) that expounds it?"

If the treatise itself were not to be commenced, then by the principle of *kaimutika-siddhi* (establishment by implication), the same would necessarily follow for this present work which is rooted in it. Furthermore, in the intermediate stage, since the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) would otherwise result in futility, one must recognize the Self as distinct from the five sheaths and their causes—according to the method: "My body, my vital breath, my mind, my intellect, and my happiness are mine; who are you here?"—and even when there exists the realization of the Self as Truth, Knowledge, Infinity, and Bliss, [the following applies]... (Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated at the end.)

One might object: "Since no fruit is seen upon the mere exclusion of [lower] human states and so forth, and since even those who have studied the scriptures do not perceive liberation while living—and on the contrary, some of them are observed to behave exactly as they please"—anticipating this doubt, [the author cites] the Śruti: "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas and through sacrifice," and the Smṛti: "Knowledge arises in men from the destruction of sinful karma," and [the statement]: "The desire to know the Inner Self [arises] in the intellect..."

And from the Vārttika: "Having arisen from purity, once their purpose is fulfilled, they set like clouds at the end of the rainy season. Because of this, in the expression *vividiṣanti* ("they desire to know"), if one were to accept—just as in *aśvena jigamiṣati* ("he wishes to go by horse")—that the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), which is knowledge, is primary, then the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth would be untenable. Therefore, it is appropriate to apply figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to the very desire denoted by the primary suffix *san*, as indicated by the aforementioned Smṛti and the Vārttika. Thus, [the desire] belongs to the Lord who has enjoyed... [text fragment].

He provides the resolution that this work is meaningful because it serves as an aid for those seekers who possess pure minds—like a mirror—for the effortless realization of the non-dual reality of the Self, which is uncontradicted and unobstructed; this occurs by means of destroying the *durita* (demerits) that act as obstacles to the arising of knowledge, as described in the *Purāṇa* of Parāśara.

Thus, establishing its purpose and assigning it a name, he promises to compose the work with the words "tatpāda... (His feet...). The metaphor (*rūpaka*) and other figures are to be understood as before. || 2 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Desiring to demonstrate that the individual soul (jīva) possesses the nature of truth, knowledge, and so forth, in order to establish the possibility of the subject matter—namely, the identity between the jīva and Brahman—he first proves the eternity of consciousness by demonstrating its non-difference [from the Self]:
"In the waking state, objects such as sound and touch, being diverse, are perceived as distinct."
Therefore, though differentiated, it does not differ [from consciousness], because of its identity with that consciousness.

By the words "sound, touch, and so forth," he first establishes the non-difference of cognition within the waking state, which is characterized by clear empirical activity. The word "sound" [marks the beginning of this proof]. In the waking state, there is the perception of objects through the senses. In the specific state defined as "waking," the objects of consciousness—namely sound, touch, and so forth—are well known as the qualities of ether and the other elements; likewise, ether and the others are well known as their substrata.

Because they possess mutual diversity and distinctness from one another— like a cow, a horse, and so forth— they are individually differentiated from each other. Therefore, when they are separated by the intellect (*buddhi*) and discerned,
the cognition (*saṃvit*) of them— that is, the knowledge of those [objects] such as sound and the rest— manifests in a single form as "cognition, cognition" due to its uniform nature.
[The First Chapter] Accompanied by Two Commentaries.

It is not divided, like the sky. Herein is the formal argument (*prayoga*): consciousness, which is the subject of dispute, is devoid of intrinsic difference (*svābhāvikabheda*), because it is [devoid of] adventitious conditions (*upādhi*).

Because its difference is not perceived without a further act of conceptualization (*parāmarśa*), the cognition of sound is not distinct from the cognition of touch, just like space; for it is a cognition, like the cognition of touch.

Since the practical distinction between various cognitions can be accounted for through adventitious limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—just as in the case of space—the assumption of a real ontological difference should be understood as being refuted by the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). || 3 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection is raised: since it was promised that "this discrimination (*viveka*) of reality (*tattva*) is being enjoined," and because in our own system the word *tattva* denotes an unsublated entity—namely, non-dual Brahman alone—it is appropriate that the word *viveka* should convey a cognition of the distinctness of the unsublated dual [world], characterized as the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) consisting of the union of the real and the unreal, which has that [Brahman] as its sole object. [Thus, one might argue that the term *buddhi* here refers to the intellect: "Buddhi, manīṣā, dhiṣaṇā... [and so forth].

In the *Abhidharmakośa*, following the sequence of the names for cognition (*buddhi*), the term *saṃvit* is listed as "perception, apprehension, consciousness, and awareness. Through its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) as "awareness," and through its etymological derivation (*yoga*) as "one who correctly knows objects such as a jar," it denotes that [cognition] alone. Since, according to the doctrine of the creation of perception (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*), objects—due to their momentariness, perishability, plurality, and so forth—are not distinct from cognition and are merely its objects of knowledge (*vedyatva*), [the term refers to] that [cognition].

Anticipating the objection that it is improper to establish both difference and identity [simultaneously], [the author] maintains that the subject matter implied by the first verse—namely, the oneness of Brahman and the Self—is indeed nothing other than the inner reality (*pratyag-vastu*) which is of the nature of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and a single essence.

Since this very reality is of the nature of pure existence (*sanmātra*), free from sublation throughout the three periods of time, it is precisely that which, through the aforementioned etymological function (*yogavṛtti*), is stated in the present context:

“That consciousness (*saṃvit*) which is accepted as the fruit in the case of objects of knowledge directed toward external things—that same consciousness is here the object to be known, according to the authority of the Vedāntic teachings.”

Thus, because [the object] is intended by the word *saṃvit* according to the words of the venerable Sureśvarācārya’s lotus-feet, and because the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*) lacks scriptural authority and is refuted in the *Citradīpa*, even in the theory of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*), although objects are not distinct from knowledge in the form of mental modifications (*vṛtti*), they are nonetheless distinct from immutable knowledge (*kūṭasthajñāna*). Therefore, for all objects characterized as sound and so forth— all things that are of the nature of the visible— the aforementioned [reason] serves as the cause for their falsity.

Establishing that the nature of form (*rūpatva*) itself is characterized by diversity through its possession of various aspects, and by the impossibility of being divided into separate entities, [the author] implies its falsity.

Then, in order to preclude *vedyatva* (the state of being an object of cognition)—which follows as a constituent of falsity based on the divisibility of consciousness (*saṃvit*) from that [form]—he establishes its non-difference during the waking state by means of the reason of its eternal uniformity, beginning with the words "śabda... (verse 3).
Rāma’s Commentary: He extends the aforementioned principle to the dream state as well:
"In this way, what is perceived here in a dream is not stable, whereas in the waking state it is stable."
Therefore, because of that difference between those two, their consciousness, being of a single form, does not differ.

"So be it. Just as in the waking state there is a distinction between objects due to their variety and no distinction in consciousness due to its uniformity, so too—in that very same manner—when the instruments [of perception] have been withdrawn, the cognition born from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the waking state is the object; thus, even in the dream state, defined by the aforementioned characteristics, it is only the objects that are distinct, not the consciousness. Now, if the dream and waking states are of the same form regarding the objects...

Anticipating the question—"In that case, what is the basis for the conventional distinction between dream and waking, given the identity and difference between those [objects] and consciousness?"—he says:

"But here, the object of knowledge... Here, in the dream state, the collection of objects being perceived is not stable or enduring, because its body consists solely of cognition (*pratīti*). In the waking state, however, the collection of objects being perceived is stable and enduring, because they are capable of being seen even at a later time; therefore...

The meaning is that the distinction between those two—dream and waking—is due to the difference characterized by having stable or unstable objects. Anticipating the objection that if there is a distinction between dream and waking, there must also be a distinction between their respective cognitions (*saṃvit*), he says: "of those two. The qualifier "of a single form" contains the reason [for their non-distinction]. ||4||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Nor should it be argued that, once the visibility of all duality—exemplified by sound and so forth—is established, the qualification of "in the waking state" is redundant. Even if that were the case according to the aforementioned method, since the empirical usage of clear means of knowledge such as non-sublation occurs while the knower exists, and because that [waking state] alone possesses reality, it is therein that the truth of the first consciousness and the imagined nature of the objects of cognition are established.

With the intention that, according to this same principle, it is appropriate to extend that [analysis] elsewhere immediately thereafter, he states—beginning with "In the same way"—that there is no difference between the objects perceived in the waking and dreaming states in terms of their stability and so forth, and that there is no difference between the cognitions of those [objects], as previously established. || 4 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya [entitled Tattvaviveka]

Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus established the oneness of knowledge in the two states [of waking and dreaming], he now establishes that even the knowledge pertaining to the time of deep sleep is one with it; first, he proves the existence of knowledge therein:
"For one who has awakened from sleep, there occurs a memory consisting of the awareness of the darkness of deep sleep."
And that darkness, which had its objects previously unperceived, was then awakened.

Regarding the phrase "supta" (asleep): one who was previously asleep and subsequently awakened is "suptotthita. Alternatively, it means one who has arisen from sleep—that is, from deep sleep (*suṣupti*). His "awareness of the darkness of deep sleep" refers to the cognition or knowledge of the "darkness"—that is, ignorance—pertaining to the time of deep sleep, such as [the thought], "I did not know anything. That is merely a memory (*smṛti*) and not a direct experience (*anubhava*), because its causes—the contact of the senses with an object, pervasion, logical marks (*liṅga*), and so forth—are absent. This is the intended meaning. To the question "What follows from that?", he says:

"And that" means: that memory has an apprehended object—that is, it is so called because its object (*viṣaya*) has been apprehended, meaning experienced; the point is that in the world, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is observed that whatever is memory is preceded by experience. What follows from that? He says: "apprehended.

For that reason, it should be understood that this darkness of deep sleep was apprehended—meaning experienced—at that time during deep sleep. Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): the subject under dispute...
The cognition "I was not aware of anything" must be preceded by an experience, because it is a memory, just like the memory "that woman is my mother. (5)

A0 Ṭīkā: Even if the permanence of the pure witness-consciousness (*dṛṅmātra*)—which is about to be described as oneness—could be possible during states such as waking characterized by mental projection (*vikṣepa*), it would still have to exist in the state of concealment (*āvaraṇa*) known as deep sleep, which is experienced by everyone. Nor should it be argued that its existence there is necessary because of the impossibility of the memory of one who has awakened, namely, "I slept happily, I knew nothing. For even in your own view, that [memory]...

Because it is accepted [by all] that [the self] exists. For it is stated in the *Vārttika*: “There is no memory such as ‘I was not conscious’ regarding deep sleep; because there is no interval of time and so forth, [the self] does not possess a past state residing within itself. The meaning of this is: “There is no deep sleep” (*na suṣupta*). That which goes to deep sleep is “one who goes to deep sleep” (*suṣuptaga*);

his consciousness—of the nature described as “bliss” and so forth—is a cognition characterized by having as its object something not experienced during the waking state and so on. That is the memory...

The intended meaning is that one should not even entertain the suspicion that this [cognition] is a memory (*smṛti*), because it is a cognition whose object is a past fact—just as in the case of the thought, "In my childhood, there was the happiness of being nurtured by my mother," and so forth. He states the reason for this with the word "time" (*kāla*); by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), "place" (*deśa*) is included, since there is the experience, "I remember Kāśī at Pañcavaṭī. Although a memory involving spatial separation is indeed necessarily pervaded by temporal separation, nevertheless...

It should be understood that what is intended [by the opponent] is the primacy of the place and so forth, which serves as the cause for the distinctness (*vaijātya*) of the memory. And thus, since the self exists even at the time delimited by the memory, it alone is the experiencer; therefore, if one were to assert that the memory "I knew nothing"—which has the non-existence of everything as its object—is preceded by an experience of the non-existence of everything, then since the experience of the non-existence of both the cognition included therein and the self itself would be established by this very [memory], there would follow the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmyavāda*) and so forth.

The sense is that since the nature of the Self (*ātmatva*) follows the Self alone throughout all its states, it is eternal; and because it does not belong to past times such as the period characterized by the state of being a living being (*bhūta*), the recollection expressed as "I did not know then" cannot occur as a cognition lacking a subject (*akartṛ-vṛtti*), but is rather merely an error. Therefore, during deep sleep, because the mind has entered a specific channel called the *purītat*, [the Self is perceived] only through the limitation of what is other than that.

Anticipating the objection that there can be no suspicion of cognition there at all because the self-mind conjunction—which is the cause of cognition—is absent at that time—the author takes as the subject (pakṣa) the cognition (bodha), synonymous with knowledge, which consists of the thought "I was not aware of anything," etc., and which has as its object the *tamas* existing during deep sleep; this *tamas* has arisen from the state called deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and has been transformed into the form of the quality of *tamas*. This cognition is related to that state by a relation delimited by objectivity (*viṣayatā*). Thus, it is qualified as "pertaining to deep sleep" (*saupupta*).

Having established its status as memory (*smṛtitva*) by means of the reason characterized by its having as its object a meaning that is established in the past tense through a *taddhita* suffix, and having thereby proven— by the universal rule (*vyāpti*) that "whatever is memory is preceded by experience"— that it is preceded by a cognition whose object was the darkness at that time, [the author] establishes the existence of the consciousness under discussion even for that state. In the aforementioned Vārttika, by the term "residing in the Self" (*ātmastha*), [he refers to] the witnessing-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) residing in the living-consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*).

Since this very point— that it is precisely the negation of memory regarding the object of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) that is intended by the second quarter [of the verse]— was explained by Brahmānandācārya in the *Nyāyaratnāvalī*, [the author], suggesting that any contradiction [with that work] is due to a failure to understand its intended meaning, shows how, even though the cognition characterized as "witness" (*sākṣin*) may exist at that time, there can be no lack of causal conditions for the knowledge consisting of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), which is the cause of its being a memory.
The First Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

Having kept in mind that the venerable teacher Prakāśātman— the author of the *Vivaraṇa*— has accepted the view that even in deep sleep there exist three mental modifications (*vṛtti*) which are effects solely of the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), which consists of nescience transformed into the form of the quality of darkness (*tamas*) as testified by the witness-consciousness, and which have attained the form of bliss; [the author] states that, just as in waking and other states, in sleep too there exists the non-dual, partless, self-luminous, and uniform consciousness characterized by those respective modifications.
He provides the resolution, stating that the accomplishment [of the goal] for one who has awakened from sleep is indeed unimpeded: "Of one who has arisen from sleep," etc. (Verse 5).
Rāmānuja’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): He states that this experience is distinct from ignorance regarding its own object, yet non-different from other cognitions:
"That cognition is different from its object, but not from cognition itself, like the cognition of a dream."
In this way, there is a single consciousness even in these three locations, just as it is within the interior of the day.

"That consciousness" means that consciousness—the experience of deep sleep ignorance—is distinct and separate from the object, which is ignorance, because it is consciousness, like the consciousness of a jar. It is not different from other instances of consciousness because it is consciousness, like the consciousness of a dream. Stating the conclusion, he extends the aforementioned reasoning to other cases as well, beginning with the word "evam" (thus): "In the three states"—that is, in the three conditions such as waking and so forth occurring within a single day—consciousness...
How so? Because of the maxim that "every sentence is restrictive," it is like [the statement] "on another day. || 6 ||

A0 Commentary: Now, it may be argued that all this is well-established by the memory, "I attained happiness in sleep; I was not conscious of anything. Nevertheless, according to the Śruti: "When at the time of deep sleep everything has dissolved and he is overcome by darkness (tamas), he attains the nature of bliss; and again, due to the connection with the karma of another birth, that very same jīva sleeps and then awakens," it follows that at that time the jīva is dissolved into the state-knowledge which has transformed into the form of the aforementioned quality of *tamas*.

In the absence of an experiencer, however, the aforementioned state of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) remains exactly as it was— namely, the lack of being a memory. Nor can it be argued that, according to the *Vivaraṇa* school,

since the three aforementioned modifications belonging to the root ignorance— which take the forms of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), knowledge, and pleasure— are accepted there, the fragrance [of pleasure] would manifest upon the awakening of that which was experienced by the witness during the dissolution of the individual soul (*jīva*), just like the manifestation of fragrance in a camphor seed planted within a mango seed at the time of the ripening of its fruit.

It should not be argued that this is established solely through identity (*tādātmya*). For, rather than postulating that the memory of the soul—which was dissolved at that time and has now manifested in the waking state—is possible through identity with the Witness (*sākṣin*) who exists in both states, it is better, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*), to hold that such memory occurs through identity with the primordial ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) which exists in both states even without such a Witness; for as the Smṛti says, "From [the quality of] *sattva* arises knowledge," and [as the Śruti says], "The one unborn... (referring to the *ajāmekām*).

If it is argued that this is because the Śruti states, "red, white, and black," and thus the recollection of the individual soul (jīva) is possible when it has attained identity with the qualities such as *sattva* which cause knowledge, we say no. This is because the universal rule (*vyāpti*)—"whatever is cognition is distinct from its own object"—is accepted by all philosophical schools;

furthermore, since the experience of deep-sleep ignorance was established in the preceding verse precisely through the impossibility of explaining the aforementioned recollection otherwise, and since recollection and so forth arise... [text truncated].

By the natural force (*svārasya*) of the words beginning with "that" (*tyādi*), he indicates—through the half-verse beginning with "That consciousness" (*sa bodha*)—that the consciousness under discussion, which has deep-sleep darkness as its object, is distinct from the darkness that is its own object (since it is an object of a produced knowledge different from the immutable [kūṭastha] Self), yet non-different from any other cognition that is not of the nature of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) but is of the nature of the light of liberation; this is because it is immutable consciousness (*kūṭasthabodhatva*), just like the consciousness whose objects are dreams and so forth. Now, in the aforementioned inference, regarding the latter part of the probandum (*sādhya*), the primary qualification—

[Objection: Is the term "cognition" (*bodha*) in the phrase "the counter-correlative of the non-difference from the object to be proven (*sādhya*), which is pervaded by pervasion" intended to refer to all cognitions whatsoever as delimited by the property of being cognition (*bodhatva*), or does it refer only to the cognition that has been made the subject (*pakṣa*)? It cannot be the first, because the example would be unestablished. Nor can it be the second, because it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāpatti*). [Reply: This is not so, because there is a lack of understanding [of our position]. To explain:

just as a cognition whose object is a dream is non-different from the previously explained permanent cognition (*kūṭasthabodha*) of the waking state precisely because it is a permanent cognition, [so too is the case here].

Likewise, there is no fault whatsoever if one intends to express that even the darkness pertaining to the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is non-different from That (the Self) precisely because it is [of the nature of] reality (*tattva*). For a speaker does not perceive, nor does a listener understand, that just as the gold of an armlet (*keyūra*) is non-different from the gold of a bracelet (*kaṭaka*), so too the gold of an earring (*kuṇḍala*) must be non-different from it. Or, for example, just as reflections are distinct due to being reflected in waves that are gross, subtle, and subtler still.

Furthermore, even though there are many moons perceived—such as the moon reflected in water, the moon on Mount Kūṭastha, and so forth—they are all non-different from the moon itself by virtue of being "moon-ness. Just as an instructor establishes this for each case through three separate inferences in order to instruct a student, so it is intended here as well.

By this, whatever objection is raised by some—namely, that the non-difference between knowledge and its object can only be maintained by abandoning the doctrine of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi* (the view that creation is perception) within our own system, and by adopting the *vijñānavāda* (idealist school) as the opposing position—is also refuted.
2 I [pages 10–10]

Since that consciousness is not found anywhere else, it is distinct from its objects; thus, the attempt to prove that distinction is merely a case of proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhyatā*). Therefore, that too [is untenable].

This has been answered: in both cases, by taking only the appearance of cognition consisting of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), that which is excluded is established. Even in the doctrine of the non-difference between the object and its cognition, according to the first view, it is desired that [the Self] be distinct from that [cognition] in the case of immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-bodha*); and according to the other view, even though such distinction is absent, it is excluded by the very qualification of the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣaṇa*) as "other than the appearance of cognition consisting of a mental modification. This is the general direction. Thus, in all empirical transactions characterized by the three states beginning with waking— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)

The first half of the verse establishes the unity of consciousness on a single day, while the second half, beginning with the word *evam*, extends this to other days as well. According to the logical principle that "every sentence implies a restriction," the connection is as follows: just as there is only one consciousness in the three states—waking and so forth—on a single day, so too does it exist on other days. Here, the word *sthāna* refers to the states (*avasthā*). Thus, it is declared in the sacred tradition: "Of him, there are three abodes... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.9].
"Thāḥ," and so forth. || 6 ||
In months, years, yugas, and kalpas, in various ways, both those that have passed and those yet to come.
This single consciousness, self-luminous, neither rises nor sets.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (rā0 ṭī0): Just as there is non-difference of knowledge even across the three states in a single day, so too in other days—in various ways (anekadhā) and in many modes (anekaprakāreṇa)—through months that have passed or will come, through years such as Caitra and others, through Yugas beginning with Prabhava, through Ages beginning with Kṛta, and through Kalpas beginning with Brahma, there is indeed non-difference of knowledge; this is the meaning. He states the fruit of establishing the oneness of consciousness:

"It does not arise" means that because consciousness (*saṃvit*) is one, it does not arise—that is, it is not produced—and it does not set, nor does it perish. This is because production and destruction cannot be established in the absence of a witness; for it is impossible for that very consciousness to perceive its own production and destruction, and there is no other consciousness [to do so]. [Objection: But if there is no other consciousness, then due to the absence of a perceiver, this [consciousness] itself would not manifest, which would result in the blindness of the entire world. To this [it is replied]:

He says: "This [is the case]. Here, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Consciousness is self-luminous, because, while being non-objective (*avedyatve*), it is not non-manifest (*aparokṣatvāvyatireke*), unlike a jar. Nor is this reason unestablished (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*); for if consciousness were known by itself, there would be a contradiction between its being an object and its being a subject; if it were known by another, there would be an infinite regress. Therefore, since consciousness, appearing through its own luminosity, is capable of illuminating everything, the consequence of universal blindness does not follow—this is the sense. || 7 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭī0): Now, stating the conclusion, he suggests through implication that the aforementioned consciousness is self-luminous and devoid of temporal limitation by saying "māsa" and so forth. The units such as months and the like are indeed well-known from works such as the *Kālamādhava*. An objection may be raised: "Granted that this is so regarding the past and future divisions of time such as months and kalpas; however, since the consciousness under discussion is eternally immediate, it cannot be the counter-positive of its own prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) even within those divisions of time."

Raising the objection, "What follows from this regarding the subject at hand—namely, that eternality, which is synonymous with reality and consists in being non-subject-to-destruction? the author provides the answer:

the very establishment of the falsity of the duality manifested by that consciousness, characterized by its lack of self-luminosity. He specifies this [consciousness] with two qualifiers beginning with "eka" (one): because this consciousness does not arise—that is, is not produced—in any way whatsoever, even throughout months, years, yugas, and kalpas of the past and future.

It neither sets nor perishes; therefore, it is one and without a second, because both arising and destruction require a second factor for their accomplishment. Thus, the logical connection (*anvaya*) is that it exists as self-luminous and self-manifesting. By this, it has been established that even this immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-saṃvit*), which serves as the illuminator of its respective objects throughout the three states such as waking and so forth, cannot be the object of another consciousness—just as the objection might be raised through inference that "this [immutable] consciousness must be illumined by another consciousness because it is a form of knowledge, like knowledge in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti-jñāna*). This possibility is now addressed.

Thus, in this self-luminous consciousness (*saṃvit*), by the reasoning already established, the second [entity]—as delimited by the condition of being a second—is shown to be false, characterized by non-self-luminosity;

consequently, due to the absence of spatial limitation by any real entity through its absolute non-existence at all three times, its infinity is also indicated, characterized by the state of not being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the four kinds of non-existence. Now, if it is asked, "What is this self-luminosity? it is that which was [defined] by the ancient commentators.
It is defined by a purely negative (kevalavyatireki) reason, as follows—referring to the present consciousness: "In this regard, the formal argument (prayoga) is:

Consciousness is self-luminous (svayaṃprakāśā), because, while being unobjectifiable (avedyatve sati), it is immediate (aparokṣatvāt); for in the case of the opposite [of the reason], it is like a jar. Nor is this reason unestablished due to its qualification; for if consciousness were objectified by itself, there would be a contradiction between the status of object and agent, and if it were objectified by another, there would be an infinite regress. Therefore, it appears as self-luminous."

"But for knowledge, its self-luminosity is likewise [established] even without an objectivity induced by another cognition. The wise consider that very existence of its own nature—which is incapable of being an object primarily through doubt—to be self-luminosity. Thus, the definition is finalized as follows: self-luminosity is the existence of one's own nature which, while not being an object of cognition, is capable of being free from both doubt and concealment. In this regard, regarding the cognitive modification (*vṛtti-jñāna*) such as "this is a jar," the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*)—...

The term "truth" (*satyam*) is included in the definition to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the *bhāṣya*. When only that much is stated, there would be non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) with respect to Brahman itself—which is self-luminous—as an object of indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) produced by the words of an authoritative person (such as "Brahman exists as self-luminous"); therefore, the phrase "subject of doubt" (*saṃśaya*) and so forth is added. This is because [in that case], it is not an object of doubt and the like. Here, by the word "capable" (*yogya*) and so forth, even though Brahman is self-luminous and is the object of the aforementioned indirect knowledge, its status as self-luminous is [established].

It should be understood that because [the Self] is not an object of knowledge through [empirical] exclusion, even though it may be an object of doubt and the like, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) since its essential nature exists as something capable of being devoid of those [attributes]. If this is considered too cumbersome, let "not being dependent for its manifestation" (anadhīnabhānatva) alone be that [definition]. The detailed exposition, however, is to be found only in my commentary (*ṭīkā*); this is the direction [of the argument]. || 7 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Let it be so that consciousness is eternal and self-luminous; what follows from that? To this he says:
"This Self is supreme bliss, because it is the object of supreme love."
"May I not cease to be; may I indeed exist"—thus is love observed toward the Self.

"This" [refers to the following]: here is the formal argument (*prayoga*). This consciousness must be the Self, because while being eternal, it is self-luminous; for whatever is not so [i.e., not eternal and self-luminous] is not thus, like a jar. By establishing that the Self has the nature of eternal consciousness, its reality (*satyatva*) is also established, since there is no reality apart from eternity. Eternity is reality; that which possesses this [eternity] is eternal and real—so says the tradition.

The sense is that this is because it has been stated by those mixed with the *Spati* [the Sūta]. He establishes that the Self (*ātman*) is of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*) with the words "supreme bliss" (*parānanda*). The word "Self" (*ātma*) is to be supplied [from the previous context]. It is supreme and it is bliss; thus, it is "supreme bliss. The meaning is that its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is unsurpassed happiness. He states the reason for this with the word "supreme" (*para*): because it is the locus (*āspada*) of supreme—that is, unconditional and unsurpassed—love (*preman*), which is affection (*sneha*).

Therefore, the subject here is this inference: the Self is of the nature of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), because it is the object of supreme love (*parapremāspadatva*). That which is not of the nature of supreme bliss is not the object of supreme love, just like a jar. And since this [Self] is indeed the object of supreme love, it is not the case that it is not of the nature of supreme bliss. [Objection: But surely, since hatred such as "shame on me" is observed toward the Self, its being the object of love is unestablished.

Anticipating the objection as to why [the self] is the object of supreme love, he refutes it with the words "May I not cease to be," stating that this is not so because the [self's] being the cause of suffering is established otherwise, whereas love for the self is established by direct experience.
For (hi) because of this reason, regarding the self as the object, [one does not think] "May I not be" or "May I not exist";
let there never be my non-existence, but rather, "May I indeed exist"—may my existence always prevail.
The meaning is that since such love is seen and experienced by everyone, there is no lack of proof (asiddhi). || 8 ||
