[Commentary on the *Tattvaviveka*, Chapter 1, Verse 1] — Now, according to the view of the author of the *Vārttika*, based on such scriptural passages as "He who, dwelling within the self, is internal to the self," the individual soul (*jīva*)—

One might raise this objection: "Since the Lord Himself, who exists even within the self, is the witness—the illuminator of all states such as waking and so forth, and whose nature is the aforementioned consciousness—let Him alone be the Lord. In that case, because there would exist a second entity, namely the individual soul (jīva) distinct from Him, the absence of limitation by objects would not be established; thus, non-duality (advaita), which is signified by the term 'one' (eka), would not be proven. Anticipating this, [the author] addresses the consciousness characterized as the witness and defined as above, which consists of the five sheaths (pañcakośa)... [and its various states].

Although [Brahman] is distinct from the individual soul (jīva), which is a conscious entity characterized by the three [states], Brahman— defined by the characteristics of truth, knowledge, and infinity as established by the Taittirīya Śruti passage "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite"— is proven by the aforementioned reasoning to be devoid of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) consisting of the witnesshood caused by nescience (avidyā). Thus, for that which has become the purified referent of the term *tat* (*tattvampadārtha*), there exists, in that very form, the superimposition of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) and other such adjuncts caused by nescience.

He resolves that the true meaning of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) consists precisely in the real identity with the Self, which has been purified by the *tat-pada* and serves as the primary referent—expressing this as "This is the Self. This consciousness, characterized as described above, is the Self; for according to the statement of the learned, "Because it attains (*āpnoti*), because it takes up (*ādatte*), because it eats (*atti*) objects here, and because its existence is continuous (*saṃtata*), it is called 'Self' (*ātman*)," it is the Truth.

The meaning is that [the Self] exists as the innermost [reality], characterized by knowledge and so forth. Now, an objection: even if there is identity in their respective specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) such as "existence" and the like, or even if there is identity in their specific characteristic of being effects of gold—as in the case of a crown and a bracelet—there is no contradiction whatsoever regarding a real distinction between them. Nor is there any usage by the ancients [to the contrary]. For instance, the following inference for others (parārthānumāna) has been stated: "This consciousness ought to be the Self, because, while being eternal, it is self-luminous; whatever is not thus is not so, like a jar."

It cannot be said that inference itself constitutes a sublation [of the opponent's view], because the reason (hetu) lacks probative force (*aprayojakatva*) due to the absence of a sublation in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). If it is argued that an investigator does not perceive Caitra—who is fair-skinned, stout, young, and a learned Brahmin—to be non-different from such a Maitra, we reply: no; for there are positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) such as, "That which is the Plenum (*bhūman*) is bliss;
in the small there is no bliss," and "That which is the Plenum is immortal; that which is small is mortal."

Since it has been stated explicitly by the word "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) that the very entity denoted by the term "Bhūman"— which is devoid of the threefold limitation and is the non-counterpositive of the fourfold absence—

possesses the nature of supreme bliss and the nature of liberation (*kaivalya*), the absence of that [nature] would result in both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) being characterized by the limitation of objects (*vastu-pariccheda*) due to their distinctness, and thus be rendered insubstantial (*tuccha*). Furthermore, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the individual soul is a reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) in the intellect (*buddhi*), while the Lord is [the reflection] in ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, because there is no evidence for a plurality of distinct, immutable pure consciousnesses— given that [the world] is the witness whose nature is consciousness inseparable from its own internal reflection (*svacidābhāsa*), and given its falsity characterized by a lack of intrinsic existence (*svataḥ-sattā-śūnyatva*)— and because hundreds of scriptural passages such as "From duality, indeed, fear arises" actually condemn difference,
and because the presence of fear when difference exists in the waking state and its absence when it is absent in deep sleep are observed; [therefore, the world is not real].

[This is established] through the reasoning that supports the definition of that [Self], characterized by its connection with all the various means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and their respective objects (*prameya*). Now, one might ask: what is the reason for the meaning of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), which is the identity expressed as "This is the Self"? It is not correct to say that this [reason]—consisting in being devoid of the various forms of limitation (*pariccheda*)—has already been established previously.

For, in this way, by the word "one" (*eka*) in the context of the three states, the limitation of space is excluded; likewise, by the phrase "months and years" and so forth, and by the word "one" in the sense that "it neither rises nor sets," the limitation of time is excluded.

By the expression "devoid of limitation," the absence of limitation regarding the object is intended; since there is no means of knowledge other than the present scripture for the consciousness under discussion,

and because that [scripture]— in the form of great statements such as "That thou art"— has a meaning that may be subject to doubt, the scripture beginning with "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (Brahma-jijñāsā), as well as this very treatise, was composed by various teachers as an aid for different types of qualified aspirants, such as those of intense or moderate zeal, in order to remove obstacles and sublate misconceptions regarding its meaning.

And because [the self] is an agent (*kartṛ*). Nor should it be argued that if the individual soul (*jīva*) were distinct from the Lord (*īśvara*), who is the witness (*sākṣin*) whose nature is consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*), then it would be insentient (*jaḍa*) by virtue of being an object of perception—just like objects such as sound; for this would be an undesired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) for me, who follow the view of the Logicians (*tārkika*), and furthermore, no sublation (*bādhaka*) would arise even if there were a plurality of consciousnesses, as in the case of the Sāṃkhya and others. To this, it is replied: if the individual soul were distinct from the Lord, who is the witness whose nature is consciousness, as stated, then it could not be of the nature of bliss (*sukha-rūpa*).

Intending to show that reasoning (*tarka*) beginning with "it might be" (*syāt*) serves to refute duality by establishing the delimitation of the aforementioned reality, he states the nature of the Lord—characterized as the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi-saṃvit*)—as being unsurpassed bliss (*niratiśayānanda*), which proves His non-difference from the Self promised [in the opening statement]. By this, there is the exclusion of the petty bliss born of objects such as sound and so forth, which occurs during the limitations of waking and other states; for these are illusory (*māyika*) due to their coming and going. [Objection: But surely [this reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*)...

Since you establish that the aforementioned consciousness is of the nature of the Self even by means of its general form as "pleasure" (*nanda-rūpa*), let alone by that [form] qualified by "supremacy" (*paratva*), this [position] of yours is quite novel.

1. Accompanied by two commentaries.
To clarify the reason for this to an opponent who does not grasp his own intention— that [the Self] shines as the state of being a cognizer—

he states "pare" and so forth, with the remainder of the first half-verse: because this consciousness, denoted by the word *saṃvit*, which is the subject under discussion, is self-luminous by virtue of illuminating the three states of waking and so forth.

Consciousness (*citi*). It is the locus of supreme love because the means to happiness and so forth—the cognitions directed toward objects present in the waking state and other conditions—are dependent solely upon it; thus, for its sake, it becomes the substratum of unsurpassed love. Therefore, there is supreme bliss (*parānanda*). Since there is supreme bliss, the connection is made by supplying the words "therefore, it is the Self" (*ātma bhavati*). This is the intended meaning: if there were no cognition of a desired object such as a beloved woman, then [the cognition] regarding her being a means to happiness—

Consequently, there would be no status as something to be accepted (*upādeyatva*), nor would there be the enjoyment of pleasure; likewise, even undesirable things such as tigers would not possess that [status], and if that were the case, then because they would be objects to be rejected (*heyatva*) due to being means of suffering for you, the absence of the experience of suffering would also not be established. Therefore, since all living beings desire both [pleasure and the absence of pain], the aforementioned knowledge is necessary; thus, it is entirely appropriate that they possess unsurpassed love for that aforementioned consciousness which is the root of such knowledge.

In this manner, two inferences should be understood here in succession: 1. This consciousness must be supreme bliss (*parānanda*), because it is the object of supreme love (*parapremāspadatva*); otherwise, it would be like a jar. 2. Likewise, this consciousness is the Self (*ātman*), because it is supreme bliss; as before, [it would otherwise be like a jar]. By this, the scriptural passage is also supported: "This Self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than everything else—this Self which is more internal."

It is so. For it has been said by the venerable feet of the lordly sage Sarvajñātman in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*: "Whatever object exists here for the sake of something else, and whatever abandons its state of being for another simply by virtue of its own existence—those who know the definition of happiness describe that as happiness. Therefore, this [happiness] is equally present in the inner self (*pratyagātman*). Furthermore, love unconditioned by anything other than happiness is not observed in that which is not happiness; yet it is eternally found even in the inner self, even when it is obscured."

"It is established that even for the Naiyāyika, from the scriptural mention of 'what is dear' (preyas), there is an inference of its being pleasure; yet he does not maintain that this [pleasure] resides in the seer-self."

Therefore, since the delimitation of an object (vastu-pariccheda) as suspected by you is utterly impossible according to the method stated, the meaning of such sentences as "That thou art" (tattvamasi)—characterized by the non-duality of the inner self and Brahman in the form of Being-Consciousness-Bliss—is established as the secret of all scriptures. This meaning, which is the nature of absolute liberation (kaivalya), preceded by the sublation of all duality, is indeed free from obstacles, being supported by the six marks that indicate the intended purport (ṣaḍvidha-tātparya-liṅga). Now, [one might object]: "Do not [accept] this doctrine of non-duality..."
They utterly destroy [the opponent's position]. This has been stated by Śrī Mādhavācārya himself in the *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha*, concerning that system:
"In inference—"

Nor is difference determined [in this way]: that the Supreme Lord is different from the individual soul (jīva), because He is the object of service for him; for whoever is the object of service for someone else is different from that person, just as a king is different from his servant. Indeed, men who seek the human goal (*puruṣārtha*)—thinking, "May there be happiness for me, and may there not be even the slightest suffering for me"—would not become recipients of honor by desiring the status of a master builder (*sthapati*); on the contrary, they become vessels for all misfortune. Whoever [desires such things] for himself...

He who speaks of his own inferiority and the excellence of another's qualities, being pleased by that praise, grants the desired object to that praiser. As it is said: "Kings indeed humble him who says, 'I am a king,' but they bestow every desired thing upon one who proclaims the excellence of their own virtues. And thus, through the thirst for non-difference from the Supreme Lord, the excellence of Viṣṇu’s qualities is like a mirage, because of the assertion of equality.

"...the act of eating [the fruit] resembles the cutting off of one's tongue out of a desire for the fruit of a vast plantain tree," and so forth. To this, it is replied: This distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) which you seek to establish through inference—is it ultimate (*pāramārthika*), or is it merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*) for the sake of those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), intended to strengthen their devotion toward Him according to the maxim of the girl, the stone, and the child, due to an excess of devotion; or is it illusory (*prātibhāsika*)? Not the latter two. For the seeker of liberation—

For both the ordinary person (*jana*) and the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), this [consequence] is accepted. However, the first case is further examined. It is indeed beyond dispute that ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) consists in being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time.

Now, you have certainly already established this [reality] regarding difference; yet, out of a desire for victory over the proponent of non-difference (*abheda-vādin*), you must necessarily state that it is being proved by means of an inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
But that is simply not possible, because it would result in your identity with the Supreme Lord, who is omniscient, while you yourself are a person of limited knowledge (*kiñcijjña*).

Furthermore, one sees a dream such as, "I am indeed a servant, but the king must always be served by me"; this is because [the dream] deviates from the actual state of being a king. Nor should it be argued that citing a deviation in a dream is inappropriate because the discussion is taking place in the waking state alone; for even there, a long-lasting, practical dream is accepted [as valid]. Thus, it is recited in the *Aitareyaka*: "He has three abodes, three..."
"Like dreams," and so forth. Also in the *Bṛhad-Vāsiṣṭha*: "Know this to be a long dream, or a long delusion of the mind, or a long [delusion]...
[page 14]
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya.

"O descendant of Raghu, even the kingdom of the mind, known as the discernment of reality, is transmigratory existence. Furthermore, non-sublatability (abādhyatva) in the case of difference is simply the state of being free from sublation;

thus, there is indeed a very clear circularity (anyonyāśraya). Moreover, this is not a valid inference, because the reason (hetu) is either countered by an opposing argument (satpratipakṣa) or its pervasion (vyāpti) is unestablished (asiddha).

And because of its being established as such. For the Supreme Lord is, in an ultimate sense, non-different from the individual soul (*jīva*); for that [soul], which is a reflection in the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, has become the prototype (*bimba*) with respect to Him, just as the face situated on the neck is the prototype with respect to the reflection of the face in a mirror and the like. Thus it is said: "This self-luminous sun, though one, enters into many different waters; the Lord, though one, is made to appear as having diverse forms by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) within the field (*kṣetra*)."

For it is so stated in the scriptures: "Thus this Self is unborn," and "Indeed, the single Self of all beings dwells in every being; though one, it is seen as many, like the moon in water. And also: "It is a mere reflection," and "Therefore, the comparison [is appropriate]."

Furthermore, there is a state of counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣatā*) due to a powerful counter-inference supported by the two sūtras beginning with "like the sun and so forth" (*sūryakādivat*). Nor is it correct to argue that my inference is likewise supported by scripture, on the grounds that there exists the scriptural passage: "The Self is true, the individual soul (*jīva*) is true, difference is true, difference is true. This is because such a statement is not found in the currently extant recensions (*śākhās*), and thus its status as a fabrication is possible; for one may follow the maxim, "Let the wicked man be satisfied," regarding this conventional distinction.

Or rather, because it is due to its being a non-delusive cognition of an object not previously known. In fact, since the validity of that [scripture] regarding its own subject matter must be stated solely on the basis of its producing a cognition of an object that is uncontradicted and not already known, the scripture cannot have as its purport the teaching of that difference which—though established by means of valid cognitions such as perception possessing empirical validity—is sublated by well-known scriptural texts such as "There is no diversity whatsoever here.

Therefore, even one who speaks with tears must admit that the scripture has as its purport only the aforementioned empirical difference, as there is an absence of such a purport regarding the ultimate reality.

This must be considered by the Ānandatīrthīya [follower of Madhva]. Likewise, in the inference "The Supreme Lord is distinct from the individual soul because He is the object of service for it," and so forth, "being conditioned by Māyā" (māyopahitatva) is the *upādhi* (limiting condition).

Since the Supreme Lord, who is distinct as admitted by you, is the very subject (*pakṣa*) of this argument, the *upādhi* pervades the probandum (*sādhya*). In the example, namely the king, although he is the object of service for his servant, he lacks the property of being conditioned by Māyā; thus, the *upādhi* does not pervade the probans (*sādhana*). Therefore, because the reason is characterized by an *upādhi*, its invariable concomitance (*vyāpti*) is unestablished.

The increase [of merit] is indeed most evident. Likewise, sublation by hundreds of authorities such as the Śruti—beginning with, "For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another; but where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should one see?"—is also to be understood. Great effort has already been exerted here by the venerable ancient teachers, who are unsurpassed even by Brahmānanda Sarasvatī, in their thousands of works; however, fearing prolixity, I shall desist. Now, this...

The entire dualistic phenomenal world (*dvaitaprapañca*) is rooted solely in ignorance (*avidyā*), consisting as it does of that [ignorance] and its effects; and since its cessation occurs only through the immediate realization (*aparokṣajñāna*) of the identity of Brahman and the Self—arising from the mere inquiry into great statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*)—it follows that liberation is attained thereby. However, Rāmānuja does not accept this very ignorance as having a positive ontological nature (*bhāvarūpa*), as you [the Advaitins] maintain. This has also been demonstrated regarding his system in the *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha*.

This very point was summarized by the venerable Mādhavācārya: "The ignorance under discussion does not reside in Brahman, which is pure consciousness, because it is ignorance, like the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl. Now, if it is argued that the nature of the inner self—the substratum of the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl—is indeed nothing but pure consciousness, do not entertain such a doubt. For experience (anubhūti), by its very existence, renders some object fit for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

Because it is accepted that the nature of the self—which has other names such as *dakasvabhāva*, ignorance (*ajñāna*), realization (*avagati*), and consciousness (*saṃvit*)—is its being the knower of objects and its being knowledge itself, [it follows that it possesses knowledge as its quality].

If it is asked, "How can the self, whose very form is knowledge, have knowledge as its quality?", that is baseless. For just as a luminous substance such as a gem or the sun, while existing in the form of light (*prabhā*), is the substratum of the quality of light; and because that light exists elsewhere than its own substrate and possesses color, it is [considered] to have light as its form and quality.

Even though it is of the nature of a substance (*dravya*), it is designated as a quality (*guṇa*) on account of its being subordinate to that [consciousness]. In this way, this Self is indeed of the nature of self-luminous consciousness, and consciousness is its quality.

Thus says the Śruti: "Just as a lump of salt has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a mass of flavor, even so, my dear, this Self has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*). And: "In this state, this person becomes self-luminous. For indeed—
"There is no destruction of the knower’s consciousness" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.3.30); "Now, he who knows 'let me smell this,' he is the Self" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 8.12.4);
"This person consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart—He indeed is the seer, the hearer, the taster, the smeller, the thinker, the knower, the agent;

He is the person, the self of consciousness" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.3.7), and so forth. Nor does the scriptural text beginning with "For they are veiled by untruth" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 8.3.2) [contradict this].

It is not possible to maintain that [the term] refers to knowledge as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For the word *anṛta* has as its object that which is other than *ṛta*, and the word *ṛta* denotes ritual action (*karman*).
The First Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

Because of the statement, “The two who drink the *ṛta*,” *ṛta* refers to action (*karman*) performed without desire for its fruit, where the resulting reward is attained solely as a means of propitiating the Supreme Person.

In contrast, action other than that which yields the meager fruits of worldly existence is *anṛta*; it is opposed to the attainment of Brahman, as stated in the passage: “Those who do not know this world of Brahman are indeed held back by *anṛta*. Furthermore, in such passages as “One should know Māyā to be primordial nature (*prakṛti*),” the word *māyā* refers to the creation of manifold objects.

The term *prakṛti* denotes that which consists of the three *guṇas*, and it is not a designation for an indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) ignorance (*ajñāna*). This is because in passages such as, "By him, with his swift-moving [arrow], a thousand illusions (*māyā*) of Śambara were destroyed one by one as he protected the body of Vāla," we observe that the word *māyā* refers exclusively to that which is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*) and capable of producing a manifold creation. Therefore, there is never any teaching of an indeterminable ignorance in the Śruti.

To this, the following is said: First, let us examine that luminous substance such as a gem or the like, which you have employed as an example for your acceptance of the quality of knowledge (*jñāna-guṇakatva*) even in Brahman—which is the very basis of your inference. Is the light-substance (*prabhā-dravya*) of the gem and so forth a quality (*guṇa*) or not? It cannot be the first [option], because you yourself have stated that it is not a quality, since it is the substratum of the quality that is the form of light. Nor can it be the second. Its own...

It is not correct to say that light is of both forms—both as a substance and as possessing color—because it exists elsewhere than its substrate and because it possesses color, for this would contradict the statement you made subsequently;

nor is it correct to say it is of both forms on the grounds of being treated as a quality due to its being subordinate to that [substrate], for this would contradict the natural sense of the subsequent text. In that case, the very technical definitions of "substance" and so forth that you have stated would be abolished, since everything could potentially be a substance and so on. Likewise, what is this [light] to you regarding the gem and other such things?

Is light considered distinct from its source, or non-distinct, or perhaps both distinct and non-distinct? Or is it something other than these three positions? It cannot be the first, because through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth, its existence is dependent solely upon that [source]. Nor can it be the second, for you yourself have already provided the answer by stating that it exists elsewhere as well; indeed, a jar does not exist elsewhere than in itself. For this very reason, the third position is also untenable, as it would imply a single entity [possessing contradictory properties].

It is not [the first alternative], because of the confusion of all things arising from their being neither different nor non-different. Nor is it the fourth; for the question "What is that distinction? remains as it was, and since the causal relationship between the jewel and its radiance must necessarily be asserted, there would result the fallacy of the doctrine of the indefinable (*anirvacanīya*) regarding the radiance—which is the effect of the jewel—being distinct from its cause, the jewel, in accordance with the three positions concerning difference and so forth. Therefore, [this applies] to the conventionally real, self-luminous jewel and the sun...

By using the very example of the luster seen in luminous objects as a support for his livelihood, the Tridaṇḍin accepts that the Self—which is self-luminous and of the nature of consciousness—possesses the attribute of consciousness (*caitanyaguṇaka*). When that [position] is refuted, how could he not become one whose name is no longer meaningful? Furthermore, by the natural force of such Śrutis as "The Witness, the Knower, alone and devoid of qualities" (*sākṣī cetā kevalo nirguṇaśca*), which establish the reality of the Self as non-dual pure consciousness devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka-advaita-cinmātra-ātmatattva*), the [other] Śrutis cited by him, such as "as that... (*sa yathā...*), do not [contradict this]. For [the Self] is the Knower (*cetā*). Indeed, [it is not an object].

However, passages such as "of the knower" (*vijñātuḥ*) and so forth are more appropriately interpreted as being directed toward that [Brahman] alone, because there is no other possible destination for them and because of the maxim: "For those whose purposelessness has been refuted, the relative strength of their meanings is reversed. Furthermore, regarding Rāmānuja’s inference—"The ignorance under dispute does not reside in Brahman, which is pure consciousness, because it is ignorance, like the cognition of mother-of-pearl"—the cognition of mother-of-pearl cited as the example is also of the nature of pure consciousness.

Because it is dependent on [the subject], the example is indeed devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*). Nor should it be argued that, by the passage beginning with "For experience, by its very existence," although the inner self (*pratyagartha*) possesses the nature of knowledge, it has been established as having knowledge as a quality (*guṇa*); therefore, even in that case, it cannot be the locus of ignorance regarding an object such as a positive entity like mother-of-pearl, but must rather be the locus of the antecedent absence (*prāgabhāva*) of the knowledge regarding that object. For in that case as well, with respect to the knowledge-form, [it would have] the consciousness-knowledge as its quality...

This is because the analogy of the light of gems such as the *tvaṣṭṛsādhaka* and the sun (*maṇidyumaṇi*) has been immediately refuted by this [argument]. By this, in the scriptural passage, "Those who do not find this world of Brahman are indeed obstructed by untruth (*anṛta*)," the word "untruth" intends to refer to karma that acts as an obstacle to the arising of knowledge; thus, [it refers to] a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*).

The refutation of [the view that] knowledge is the destruction [of ignorance] has also been stated. For instance, from the simile of the buried treasure introduced in the preceding passage—"Just as those who do not know the field, though walking back and forth over a buried treasure of gold, would not find it; even so, all these creatures, going day after day to this world of Brahman, do not find it, for they are veiled by untruth (anṛta)"—it is evident that by the word *anṛta* the Śruti intends precisely positive ignorance (*bhāvarūpājñāna*). Likewise, [other passages confirm this].

For— just as men who are ignorant (*akṣetrajña*), being devoid of knowledge regarding that specific location designated by the term "field" (*kṣetra*) where a treasure of gold is buried (as will be described hereafter), even while walking repeatedly upon the ground above where that treasure of gold is buried, do not find— that is, they simply do not know— that place denoted by that word; in exactly the same way, all these creatures [do not know] this Brahman, which is directly perceived by the Witness (*sākṣin*) through the limitation of deep sleep.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 16]

These [verses] constitute the world known as *Tattvaviveka*, according to the words of the venerable author of the *Bhāṣya*: "Because it follows the meaning of the verbal root *bṛh* (to expand). It is that which is neither excluded from nor followed by anything else (*avyāvṛttānanugatam*).

"Reality is called Brahman; the meaning of Brahman would be difficult to attain here if there were a second entity," according to the statement of the venerable author of the Vārttika. This refers to the realization of the Self, which is self-luminous and the counter-positive of the fourfold absence. "Day after day" means every single day.

"Even as they go" means even though they reach [the state] by way of being veiled by root-ignorance, which has transformed into the form of the quality of *tamas* consisting of deep sleep. "This"—[refers to Him].

They do not find, nor indeed do they know, the world of Brahman, which is of the nature of Nirukti and the non-dual Self. Why? Because of the reason stated in the *Nṛsiṃha-Uttara-Tāpanīya Śruti*: "By untruth—that is, by Māyā, which consists of the experience of the form of darkness—this [world] is born; it is inert, delusive in nature, infinite, and worthless. This form, though its manifesting power has eternally ceased, is nevertheless seen by the deluded as if it were the Self. And as it is said: "It is both worthless and indefinable..."

And as it is said by the learned: "Māyā is to be known as threefold—Vedic, rational, and worldly"—the meaning is that [beings] are obscured and pervaded by ignorance (*ajñāna*), which, from the Vedic perspective, is insubstantial (*tuccha*), yet from the rational perspective is a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) that is indefinable (*anirvacanīya*) and has evolved from the nature of the quality of darkness (*tamas*). And thus, just as [one might say], "A treasure of gold exists in such-and-such a place,"...

First, the knowledge of that object, which is the word of a reliable authority, is required; thereafter, for one who desires it, there is the effort of digging to remove the earth covering it; following that, when all the obstructing earth and so forth have been entirely removed, its attainment occurs through the direct perception of it by means of the contact of the eye with the world; such is the initial indirect knowledge regarding Brahman.

"Day after day, all creatures go toward this world of Brahman, yet they do not find it"—this statement from the relevant Upaniṣadic passage implies that although all individual souls (*jīvas*) reach Brahman, the substratum of all phenomena during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), they do not realize it because they are enveloped by it. The required answer to this is: for one who desires that [realization], the obstacle is the experience of pleasure arising from the quality of intense darkness (*tamas*) which effects deep sleep, expressed as "I slept happily."

The effort of hearing [the scriptures] (*śravaṇa*) and so forth is intended to dispel that ignorance—which is established by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the memory of the waking state immediately after rising from sleep (in the form of the thought, "I knew nothing of anything"), which is established by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the obscuring power mentioned in the words of the Blessed Lord, "Knowledge is covered by ignorance; thereby living beings are deluded," which is understood as having a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*), and which has acquired such a character through the analogy of clay used in the aforementioned [scriptural] examples. Following that, there is the complete removal of all obstacles...

Through the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the identity of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikya*) arising from great statements (*mahāvākya*) such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), there occurs the destruction of the fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvaraṇabhāvarūpājñāna*) which consists in the sublation of duality;
and liberation (*mokṣa*)—characterized by the remaining of pure Being, consisting of self-luminous, supreme, indivisible, non-dual bliss—is thereby accomplished. Thus, the path is indeed simple.
Likewise, in passages such as "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti," the word *māyā* refers to reality (*satyārtha*), according to the Puranic statement cited above.

Thus, this [objection] is also refuted. By the very scriptural passage cited, beginning with "māyā is of the nature of *tamas*," the term is clearly explained through the etymology: that whose nature possesses two powers—*āvaraṇa* (concealment) and *vikṣepa* (projection)—just as a post has the power to conceal a thief and the power to distract him, and just as darkness has the form of *tamas*. Since its nature is knowledge, it is said: "The yogi, upon whose heart [the Lord] is established, crosses over the widespread ignorance (*avidyā*)."
Furthermore, because the Smṛti text—“Salutation to Him, the immeasurable Māyā, whose essence is knowledge”—explicitly states that it is *avidyā* (ignorance) in that context; [one might object]:

“But even in the illustration of the golden treasure, according to your own reasoning, first the covering that acts as an obstacle, such as the earth, is removed by actions like digging, and subsequently, through visual perception, the destruction of the ignorance consisting of the prior non-existence of the mentioned treasure is accomplished; exactly the same should apply in the present case as well.”

When, through the practice of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other means, specific karmas that obstruct the arising of knowledge—termed "unreal" (*anṛta*)—are destroyed, the destruction of ignorance (*ajñāna*), which consists of its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), occurs via the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman; and thus, where indeed could there be an indefinable positive entity (*anirvacanīya-bhāvarūpa*) as ignorance? Furthermore, even in the scriptural passage "Māyā is of the nature of darkness" (*māyā ca tamorūpā*), since darkness is of the nature of the absence of abundant light, it serves as the object of comparison precisely according to the etymological analysis (*vigraha*) you have stated.

If it is argued that even though there is an absence of reality in the illusion of the elements (*bhūtamāyā*), it must nonetheless be of the nature of non-existence, we say no. For, in the first statement, the removal of the veil and the direct realization [of the object] occur simultaneously. Although there is a certain internal distinction—namely, that in the illustrative example (the *dṛṣṭānta*) the earth covering the treasure remains elsewhere, whereas in the case under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*) there is only the destruction of the ignorance (*ajñāna*) that veils Brahman—the aforementioned [principle] remains valid.

Because there is no deviation from the state of equality. However, regarding the position that ignorance (*ajñāna*) is simply the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*), this has been refuted by Ācārya Vācaspati in the *Siddhāntabindu* and elsewhere.
[page 17]
The First Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

Furthermore, since even by me the category of non-existence (*abhāva*) has been generally refuted in the context of the manifestation of non-duality (*advaita*) and so forth; and since the second statement also has its answer provided by this very same reasoning; and because the former teachers have established that darkness (*tamas*) is a positive entity (*bhāva*); as for the claim that in the *Tattvamasi* and other such sentences, the "indirect indication" (*jahadajahallakṣaṇā*) is universally accepted in the Advaita scriptures as being illustrated by the sentence of recognition, "This is that Devadatta"—to that, we reply:

Thus, this presentation is flawed. For even in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), since there is an absence of contradiction, there is no possibility of even a trace of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). To begin with, the connection of a single entity with two times—the past and the present—is not contradictory. Furthermore, the contradiction regarding the connection with different locations—namely, that its residence in another place was past while its residence in the non-proximate place is present—is to be resolved by the difference in time. Even in the view that resorts to figurative indication, the contradiction is resolved by relying on figurative indication for only a single word.

The acceptance of both terms [of the proposition] as being figurative (lākṣaṇika) is not tenable; otherwise, if one does not admit the validity of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) because it apprehends a single object as qualified by both "that-ness" (*tattā*) and "this-ness" (*idaṃtā*), then the Buddhist, who maintains the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), would be victorious, as permanence could not be established. That is not so, because the absence of contradiction has not been proven. To explain: this authoritative statement (*āptavākya*) which generates recognition is intended for one who is in doubt. Thus—

It is indeed a matter of dispute. Thus, when you think, "This Devadatta whom you previously knew in Kāśī has now arrived here at Pañcavaṭī," you should not entertain any doubt such as "Who is this? regarding the person standing before you. Likewise, although the individual being perceived is grasped by direct perception (pratyakṣa) as a conscious entity delimited by the property of Brahminhood, it is apprehended in a general sense as "Who is this? through the latent impression (saṃskāra) of a forgotten acquaintance.

Since the doubt might arise as to whether [the object] is familiar or unfamiliar, the word *tat* (that) is employed to exclude that possibility; it serves as an indicator of prior familiarity and is placed in grammatical apposition with the word *idam* (this), which indicates the present location and so forth, for the purpose of awakening the knowledge of the true identity regarding that very individual perceived through direct perception. Thus, an authoritative person utters the statement, "This is that Devadatta. In that context, while the specific place and time are understood from the subject matter, their pastness and remoteness—

Similarly, even when this [object] and its space-time coordinates are cognized by means of "that" (*tat*) and so forth, because the speaker lacks the intention (*tātparya*) to convey them as objects of perception (*pratyakṣa*), and because the intention is directed solely toward the recognition of the individual (*piṇḍa*) whose identity was previously doubted, and because it is not impossible to employ words denoting past existence and so forth without [the use of "this"], the employment of the sentence of recognition— "This is that Devadatta"— which consists of both terms used in a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇika*), is indeed appropriate. And thus, in this case, regarding the two words "that" and "this":

It is universally agreed that the object capable of being denoted (*śakyārtha*) consists of two conscious entities: one delimited by past time and distant space, and the other delimited by present time and proximate space. The contradiction of their co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is quite evident. As for the claim that the relation of a single entity to both the past and the present times is not contradictory—that is indeed so, but only in terms of different substrates (*vaiyadhikaraṇyena*). However, in terms of co-referentiality, for a single [entity] to possess [both] the past and so forth—

The connection with two [different] times is indeed contradictory. Otherwise, the very existence of pastness and so forth in time would be unestablished; for it is experienced by everyone from children to Brahmā that "now there is no connection with the past time for me," and "when there was a connection with the past time, there was no connection with the present time for me. By this, the attempt to resolve the contradiction regarding the connection with different places through a distinction of time—such as by claiming that "residence in another place was past"—is also refuted. This is because it contradicts what is perceived from the sentence under discussion...
For the contradiction remains unavoidable, just as much as the coreferentiality with past time and so forth; for the coreferentiality with distant space and so forth is likewise incompatible.

As for the claim that the contradiction is resolved by resorting to *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) in only one word, and so on—that is trivial. Does that *lakṣaṇā* apply to that [past] word or to this [present] word? Not the first; for even if one grasps the mere body mentioned while abandoning the past time and so forth, there is still the present time which is denoted by the word "this" (*idam*).

Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; for if the sentence were to convey a coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that lump (*piṇḍa*) as delimited by both the inferior location and [the present time], it would result in partial invalidity (*aṃśikāprāmāṇya*), since the sentence would be indicating a present time and so forth already grasped by perception and other means of knowledge. Nor is the latter [alternative] possible either; because the sentence’s invalidity remains as it was, due to its conveying a lump qualified by a past time and so forth that contradicts perception and other means of knowledge. Even if there is a contradiction in one [entity] possessing the qualifications of both "thatness" (*tat-tva*) and "thisness" (*idam-tva*), if it is [merely] characterized (*upalakṣya*) by them—

This is because permanence is not established by the absence of that [momentary destruction], and because the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) cannot be refuted by the validity of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). By this, the inference that "the statement 'That thou art' (*tattvamasi*) and so forth does not sublate the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), because it is rooted in error, like a statement concerning a rope-snake produced by delusion," is also rendered ineffective; for the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*). For example, someone who, having seen a tiger in a dream, flees from it in accordance with its roar—therein...

This is an inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) directed against the Advaitin; therefore, it is appropriate to refute him according to his own system. The underlying intention is that since even the mere object of perception is rooted in illusion, the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) and other such sentences, being included therein, must likewise be so.
Vidyāraṇya’s *Pañcadaśī*, titled *Tattvaviveka*:
You are merely lying comfortably asleep on a bed of flowers, embracing your own beloved; therefore, you perceive only a dream characterized by tigers and the like—do not grieve for this.

It is well known that even Devadatta, upon being instructed by his own trusted friend, "Abandon [sleep] and arise; be vigilant," immediately becomes alert and free from grief due to the power of destiny. Therefore, the Tridaṇḍin doctrine—characterized by the atomicity of the individual soul (*jīva*), the manifold reality of the world, and so forth—is as worthless as the Mādhyamika view. A detailed exposition on this matter is to be found in the *Siddhāntasiddhāñjana*, the *Vedāntakalpalatā*, and other such works.

This is the general direction. By this, the proponents of nihilistic views (*nāstika*), the two types of Sāṃkhya, the two types of Jaiminīya, and others are also explained, since the status of being a proponent of difference (*bhedavāditva*) is the same in all cases. For that [difference], does difference reside in what is already different or in what is not different? Not the latter, because it would be contradictory. Not the first: does that difference reside in what is different by means of that very same difference, or by means of another difference? In the first case, there is a regressus ad infinitum in establishing its own existence.

In the first case, there would be self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) relative to itself. In the latter case, it must necessarily be stated that this difference (*bheda*), being a difference by its very nature, resides only in something already different.

Thus, if it were said that this difference resides in that which is made different by it, there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) through reciprocal reliance. Out of fear of that, if a third difference were introduced, there would be a circle (*cakraka*); and if yet another were required, there would be infinite regress (*anavasthā*). This swallowing of the multitude of such fallacies was performed by the Preceptor of the Gods (Brahmā).

This is indeed unavoidable. This has been explained in detail in the *Dvaitaratnarakṣaṇa*. We too shall explain it in our commentary on the *Muktimālālaṃkṛti*; so, enough of this digression—let us return to the subject at hand. Now, one might object: "Granted that the reality consists of pure consciousness (*dṛṅmātra*) preceded by the falsity of the visible world, nevertheless, the fact that the Self—which is the root of this [world]—is the locus of supreme love remains unproven. Fie upon me!

It is [known] as "deluded" because, through direct experience (*pratyakṣānubhūti*), hatred alone is perceived within the self; for instance, a virtuous wife becomes a hater of herself upon the death of her husband, since she has entered the fire. This is also established by inference (*anumāna*), such as: "In contrast, like one who possesses happiness," and so forth. Likewise, it is stated in the *Nautas*: "Where the white and black rivers meet, those who have bathed there fly up to heaven; indeed, those wise ones who cast off their bodies partake in immortality."

"Two persons in this world pierce the solar orb: the wandering mendicant absorbed in yoga, and he who is slain facing the enemy in battle. From this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and from the injunction (*vidhi*) inferred therefrom, as well as from the scriptural tradition which establishes the root principle—"One desiring immortality should cast off the body at Prayāga; one desiring to go to Satyaloka should cast off the body facing the enemy in battle"—it follows that even the status of being the object of ordinary affection is untenable in the case of the Self, let alone [the status of being the object of supreme love].

If it is argued that "that" [the Self] is defined by the quality of being unsurpassed (niratiśayatva), as expressed by the word *para*, we say no; for this would contradict experience. With this intention, he clarifies that very point with the latter half of the verse beginning with *me*. The meaning is: since I—the self, characterized by the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) and self-luminous—have existed, let there never be a destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) having me as its counter-correlative (i.e., let me not perish). Rather, may I always exist. My being...

"Vāstu" means "let there be. "In this manner" refers to the previously described way. The meaning is: within the Self—that is, the inner self (pratyagātman) which is non-different from Brahman, characterized as non-dual existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda) and indicated as the witness of the five sheaths (pañcakośa)—[Brahman] is perceived. This is a locative case used in the sense of the object (*viṣayasaptamī*). The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "That [Brahman] is perceived even by the ignorant as eternally established within the inner self";
thus, according to the words of the venerable Sarvajñātmamuni cited earlier, it is indeed experienced by all living beings. And so, fie on me—!

The sense is that [perceptions] such as "I" and so forth are established otherwise (anyathāsiddha) because they have as their objects limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as delusion, while inference and other means of knowledge have the body as their object.

Now, even if this is so, how can the falsity of duality perceived through direct perception be understood? It cannot be argued that [the falsity of duality is like] the moon appearing to be the size of a thumb due to an adjunct such as a finger, or its apparent duality, or like the mirage-water, the blueness of a conch shell, the appearance of gold in a conch, the sourness of molasses, or a reflection, and so forth.

It is not correct to say that [the non-dualist position] is sublated by those illustrations; for although they are deceptive due to a lack of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), the difference established by perception and other means—such as "a pot is not a cloth"—is not like that, because it is serviceable for causal functions such as carrying water.

Nor should it be said that this is not so because it was just stated that difference is not an object of perception and the like; for even if its distinctness were untenable, the subject of the inquiry—

If it is argued that there is no fault in accepting that difference (*bheda*) is simply the very nature of the object itself, we say no; for that is unproven. To explain: in the case of a jar or the like, its status as a "counter-correlate" (*anuyogitva*) and so forth is caused by difference, which results in a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*). Furthermore, in your own view, since non-existence (*abhāva*) is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*) and is real, and since difference is a specific variety of it, it is all the more untenable for difference to be the very nature of the jar and such objects. Therefore, its establishment must proceed solely through the doctrine of indeterminacy (*anirvacanīyatā*); enough of this prolixity.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Now, let it be granted that there is no lack of essential proof (*svarūpāsiddhi*) for love; however, because there is a lack of evidence for its being supreme, there is a lack of proof regarding the qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*).
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"That love is for the sake of the Self, not so for anything else; it is for the sake of another, but not so for the Self."
Therefore, that is supreme; by it, the Self attains the state of supreme bliss.

Regarding the phrase "that love": the love that exists elsewhere toward things other than oneself, such as a son and so forth, is solely for the sake of those [objects], caused by their being subordinate to the self, and is not natural. In the same way, the love existing toward the Self is not for the sake of another, nor is it caused by the Self being subordinate to something else; rather, it is caused solely by the fact of being the Self. Therefore, because it is free from limiting conditions (*nirupādhika*), it is supreme and unsurpassed. He states the resulting conclusion with the word "by that" (*tena*): by that unsurpassed...
Thus, by virtue of being the object of love, it is established that the Self is supreme bliss and consists of unsurpassed happiness. || 9 ||

Objection: Granted that, by the aforementioned experience, the self may be the object of mere love; nevertheless, in the inference—"The self, whose nature is consciousness as described, is supreme bliss because it is the object of supreme love, unlike a jar"—even if the fallacy of the reason (*hetu*) being unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*) is removed, the fallacy of the qualification being unestablished (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*) remains exactly as before.

Furthermore, even the love directed toward the self is, in reality, for the sake of dharma culminating in unsurpassed, non-conceptual *samādhi*, which serves as the means for the absolute destruction of suffering.

Fearing that there might also be a lack of essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*) in the reason [because it is not established that love is for its own sake], he provides a resolution by clarifying the meaning of the two verses from the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* cited earlier—"Everything is for the sake of that" and "Love is without further condition"—with the words: "That love... It must necessarily be the case that even the cessation of suffering mentioned by you is desired only as being connected to the Self; otherwise, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of desiring the cessation of another's suffering. Nor is there [such a desire] for the suffering of separation from Madalasa...

For the sake of the cessation of the suffering of his own son’s friend, Kuvalayāśva—celebrated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*—and for the attainment of that [friend] which serves as the cause of such cessation, he performed penance before the two serpent-kings named Kambala and Aśvatara. This was for the purpose of attaining the grace of Sarasvatī through the means of music, and through her, for the sake of obtaining the grace of Śrī Śaṅkara; thereafter, she too communicated it to him accordingly. Thus, at the beginning, there is another object of love, namely, his own subordinate...

It is not correct to claim that the reason (*hetu*) "like a pot" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For, according to the Smṛti statement, "compassion toward all beings," compassion—which consists essentially in the desire to remove the suffering of others in its primary sense—is a means of accomplishing the knowledge of one's own Self by way of nourishing divine endowments (*daivasaṃpat*). Thus, in that regard, it does not deviate from being subordinate to oneself (*svaśeṣatva*).
Therefore, it is revealed in the Upaniṣads: "Indeed, a husband is not dear for the sake of the husband; rather, he is dear for the sake of the Self."

"In the *Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa*, [the text] states through numerous synonyms, "The husband becomes dear," and so forth. For this very reason, it is not as [some might claim]. And thus, love directed toward the Self is supreme because it is non-metaphorical (*nirupacarita*), whereas love for sons and others is otherwise; therefore, there is no lack of proof regarding the qualification of the reason—that [the Self] is the object of supreme love. He concludes by stating the established result with the latter part of the verse beginning with "ataḥ" (therefore); the word "siddhā" (established) is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 9 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: He raises an objection regarding the nature of the Self as supreme bliss:
"If it does not manifest, there is no supreme love; if it manifests, there is no desire for sense objects."
Therefore, even while manifesting, this supreme bliss of the Self remains unmanifest.

Regarding the term "abhāna" (non-manifestation): does its nature as supreme bliss not manifest, or does it manifest? If there is non-manifestation—that is, if it is not perceived—then supreme love, meaning unsurpassed affection for the Self, would not exist, because affection is produced by the knowledge of the beauty of an object. On the other hand, if there is manifestation—that is, if it is perceived—then there would be no longing or desire for an object that is a means to happiness, such as a garland, or for the happiness produced by it; for when the fruit has already been attained, a desire for the means is logically untenable.

Furthermore, since there can be no longing for sensual pleasure—which is momentary, tainted by defects such as dependence on external means, and so forth—once one has attained eternal, unsurpassed bliss, it follows that the nature of the Self is not established as consisting of bliss. To this, he offers a rebuttal with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*):
because a defect exists in both positions—that [bliss] is manifest or unmanifest—for this reason, the supreme blissfulness of the Self remains even when it is manifest.
Even when there is cognition, that which has not appeared does not become cognized. || 11 ||

According to the Śruti, "One is born with three debts: to the sages by means of Vedic study, to the gods by means of sacrifice, and to the ancestors by means of progeny," it refers to the lineage of sons and so forth that must be produced for the sake of being free from debt to the ancestors. Now, if this is so, one might object that the liberation from the debt to the ancestors—which is accomplished solely through progeny as stated in the cited scripture, and which constitutes that very purpose—would be subverted. This is not the case. For that scripture [speaks of] the attainment of the world of Brahman by means of the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*), characterized by identity with those respective deities (such as the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas) attained sequentially by one's ancestors through the non-interruption of the lineage, and by the grace resulting therefrom.

Since even the *dāda* sacrifice has as its sole purpose the attainment of the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*) and so forth—and since, for that [sacrifice], which has the specific fruit of sensual pleasure, the inclusion of such sensual pleasures within the bliss of the Self is established by implication through the well-known *Taittirīyaka Upaniṣad*, which teaches the inclusion of all sensual pleasures from human bliss up to that of Hiraṇyagarbha within the bliss of one established in Brahman—he says "Of those for whom this... and so forth. Of those for whom this... his own—

Because it is luminous, it is eternally immediate. This very Self is the world, non-different from the aforementioned self-luminosity; since there exists this particular bliss, [the text] connects with the preceding [passage]: "What shall we do with offspring? For this very reason, the authors of the commentaries have also stated that [it] "as if conceals. And thus, since the aforementioned absence of longing for sense-objects is not at all perceived, this is a rope with snares on both ends—extremely perplexing.

Having understood this objection, the proponent reveals his own intention with the latter half of the verse beginning with "ataḥ" (therefore). The meaning is: because both positions have been refuted; that is, by what was stated previously, "This Self is supreme bliss," and so forth. [The point is] the supreme blissfulness of the Self.

Even though there is no distinction between generality and particularity in its manifestation, when the state of generality and particularity is imagined through ignorance, there is a supreme love for it in a general sense—other than...
The meaning is: even when the reason stated in the first position—characterized by the impossibility of [otherwise] accounting for [the facts]—is manifest. Regarding the non-appearance [of objects]:

"For the embodied one who does not take food, the objects turn away; but even that craving for them turns away, leaving behind its relish, once he has seen the Supreme" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.59). This refers specifically to the reason stated in the second position—characterized by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the absence of desire for sense objects—which is the result of the direct realization of the non-dual Self as taught by the Lord, and which is supported by specific scriptural authority and so forth.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: [the knower] appears as an indivisible whole (*akhaṇḍa*), which is the cause for the absence of desire for all objects that have become the fruit of that knowledge. Therefore, the intended meaning is this:

freedom from longing for sense-objects, pleasure, and the means thereto—such as wealth and women—is indeed the sign (*liṅga*) accepted by the Siddhāntin as the state of being free from obstacles to the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of reality. And thus, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: one who is established in reality is free from longing for all objects and so forth; having attained the supreme...
Because of [the Lord's] delight; "like a lover" in the case of the opposite [of non-delight]. We shall establish this very point further ahead as well. May there be auspiciousness! || 11 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, having raised the objection that "simultaneous appearance and non-appearance of one and the same thing are not tenable," [the author] asks: "Is this untenability due to being unobserved, or due to a lack of logical justification? It is not the first; thus he says:
"Like the sound of a son's recitation heard among a group of students."
Even when there is manifestation, the non-manifestation of that manifestation is possible due to an obstruction. || 12 ||

Regarding the phrase *adhyetṛvargastha*: one who stands in the midst of a group (*varga*)—that is, a collection—of students (*adhyetṛ*), namely those who recite the Vedas, is "standing in the midst of the group of students" (*adhyetṛvargamadhyastha*). Such a person is also a son; thus, [the compound means] "standing in the midst of the group of students and being a son. His study (*adhyayana*) is the recitation performed by him; the sound (*śabda*) or resonance (*dhvani*) of that [recitation], although appearing to a father standing outside, does not appear in its general form, nor specifically as "this is the sound of my son. In the same way, bliss (*ānanda*)— [Note: The provided source text appears to be an incomplete sentence. The translation reflects the available portion.]

The meaning is that even when there is manifestation (*bhāna*), non-manifestation occurs. He addresses the second [point] with the words "of manifestation" (*bhānasya*). Here too, the phrase "even when there is manifestation, there is non-manifestation" is to be supplied. The meaning is that by means of an obstruction to manifestation—that is, to the flashing forth (*sphuraṇa*) characterized as will be described—non-manifestation is logical; that is, it is established, in the sense that although there is a general cognition, there is no cognition in its specific form. || 12 ||

A0Ṭī0—Now, one might object: "Since the state of supreme bliss is established in the primary Self and has been previously described as existing at the same time [as its non-appearance], its manifestation and non-manifestation are both logically untenable. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that although there is manifestation of the self-luminous bliss of the Self—which is the reality of pure consciousness—it is like the word *adhyayana* (study) applied to a teacher’s son who belongs to a group of students (*māṇavaka*) characterized by the habit of reciting the Vedas and so forth; even though it is manifest, it is not perceived in its specific nature as the Sun, but only in a general way.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [page 22] 22.

In the *Tattvaviveka*, it is stated that even when there is a vivid cognition, there is a non-appearance; this is established as non-valid knowledge (*apramā*) by way of being an unbroken bliss in one view, as the sound of "one's own son" in another view,

and as a particular playful body (*līlā-vigraha*) of the Lord delimited by golden hair and beard in yet another view— functioning as a thing that fails to produce its effect despite the presence of the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) due to an obstruction.

He provides the resolution, stating that it is indeed logical and consistent—both in one case through its inclusion with the word "other students" (*anyādhyetṛśabda*) due to root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), and in the other case through the abundance of light (*prabhāprācurya*) and so forth—by saying: "the group of students" (*adhyetṛvarga*). Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): The state of unsurpassed bliss, which is non-different from the self-luminous Self, does not manifest in its specific detail despite manifesting in a general sense; this is because it is obstructed. [This is illustrated by] the son situated among the group of students...
Like the word "meditation" (dhyāna), it refers to one who possesses a golden beard and so forth while situated within the solar orb, and who likewise possesses a specific, graceful form. || 12 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question "What is this obstruction?", he says:
"The obstruction [occurs] regarding an object fit for the empirical usage of 'it exists' and 'it appears'."
Having rejected that [fault], the production of its opposite is stated. || 13 ||

Regarding the term *pratibandha* (obstruction): it refers to that which is fit for the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of "it exists" and "it shines. That is to say, it is fit for such usages as "it exists," "it is found," "it shines," and "it is manifest. Being both that [usage] and the object itself, it is expressed as such; in that regard, having set aside—that is, having rejected—the aforementioned usage, there is the production or generation of a contrary usage, namely, of the form "it does not exist" and "it does not shine."
It is called an obstruction. || 13 ||

A0 Commentary: Now, one might ask, "What is the definition of obstruction (*pratibandha*) at the outset? To this, he says: "Obstruction," etc., and "it exists," etc. The meaning is: having set aside—that is, having obstructed—the conventional usage such as "it exists" and so forth. [The phrase] "of that" refers to the conventional usage such as "it exists" and so forth; that is to say, of the aforementioned usage which is contradictory. By supplying the implicit sense—"obstruction is here defined by us as simply the production [of an obstacle]"—the connection is established.

[Objection: "Bondage" [is not established]. Furthermore, it is not correct to say that the general definition of that [obstructive factor] was stated by you yourself as being "the state of being an entity that does not produce an effect despite the presence of the causal complex in the preceding verse," for that is certainly not the intention of the author of the root-text (*mūlakṛt*). Since a definition is distinguished from another definition by its specific form, when the present obstruction is caused solely by ignorance of the root-text, even if such a definition were formulated in the root-text for the sake of a quick application of the definition to those of small intellect, I have nevertheless grasped its underlying intention.

Furthermore, this is because a much simpler definition has already been formulated. Nor should it be argued that even so, there is a clear contradiction in your definition, since "subject-hood" (*dharmitva*) is not perceived therein while at the root [of ignorance] there is only "attribute-hood" (*dharmatva*);

for in our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the relationship between attribute and subject ultimately resolves into non-difference in reality, being essentially identity (*tādātmya*). Nor is your definition too narrow (*avyāpta*) in the present context, because the root ignorance, being false, does not possess the nature of a real entity.

It must be said that [the definition] exists because of its manifestation. For by the very fact that it is manifested as being superimposed upon itself—through the etymology "ignorance exists" (astyajñānam) by means of Brahman alone, which is the uncontradicted reality (*vastu*) and pure existence (*sanmātra*), and which manifests it by bestowing its own existence—it does not lose its falsity (*mithyātva*), since it is devoid of intrinsic existence (*svataḥ sattā*).

[Objection: Even so, the definition stated in the root-text is under-extended (*avyāpta*) to the obstruction of effects such as burning caused by gems and the like, when performed by agents such as magicians; for the definition does not apply there.

If it is argued that [the reason] follows from positive concomitance (*anvaya*), we say no. For, with respect to fire—an object fit for such conventional usage where there is clearly the perception that "there is burning produced by fire"—one observes the production of a contrary convention, namely, "there is no burning produced by fire" and "it does not appear," thereby negating that very usage.

Now, it may be asked: even if the definition of the impediment (*pratibandha*) itself appears, its non-appearance is consistent with the impediment of its appearance; thus, as required by the preceding text—

If you argue: "Just as the original authors stated that very definition (*lak�ṣaṇa*), so too you should state that same, more concise definition in accordance with their intent, rather than a definition of an 'obstructor' (*pratibandhaka*), since the latter is not required," then in that very subsequent section, at the place where there is the letter *ka*, the letter *na* should indeed be read. And thus, the general definition (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) would be: "The nature of an obstructor is the state of being a thing which, despite the presence of the causal complex (*kāraṇa-sāmagrī*), does not produce its effect."

The point is that because [the cognition] culminates in a single moment, there is the conceptual burden (*kalpanā-gaurava*) of postulating a relationship of identity (*tādātmya*) between the property and the substratum (*dharmin-dharmibhāva*), and so forth. Nor should it be objected that the aforementioned definition is impossible because the absence of an obstructer (*pratibandhakābhāva*) is also included within the category of causes; for we do not accept that non-existence (*abhāva*) is a cause.

If that were the case, one might object that even antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) would not be a cause, and consequently, a jar that has already been produced would be produced again. However, this objection cannot be sustained.

Since the objection— that the jar would arise again simply because the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produced it has ceased to exist— is resolved by the possibility of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the first chapter is thus established.

This has been explained at great length by the venerable ancient teachers in their primary sources (*ākaras*) and elsewhere; therefore, we shall desist here. By this [explanation], the counter-positive of the absence that serves as the cause—

The definition of an obstructer (*pratibandhaka*) stated by the logicians—that it is "the state of being an obstructer" (*gitva*)—is also refuted. This is because, according to their own system, that definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*), as it applies even to the effect itself. Furthermore, in other systems, it is impossible [to define an obstructer] since non-existence (*abhāva*) is not considered a cause. Thus, the definition of an obstructer stated by me alone—namely, that it is the failure to produce an effect despite the presence of all prior causal conditions (*sāmagrī*)—is what should be accepted by discerning observers.
The summary. || 13 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary (rā0 ṭī0): He demonstrates the cause of the aforementioned obstruction through examples and their corresponding illustrations in sequence:
"The cause of that [obstruction] is the simultaneous occurrence [of similar sounds], as in the hearing of the word 'putra'."
In this world, beginningless ignorance alone is the sole cause of delusion.

Regarding the word "tasya" (of that): in the illustrative example characterized by hearing the sound of "son," the cause (*hetu*) or reason for that obstruction is "samānābhihāraḥ," which means reciting together with many others. Here, in the case of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), the single basis, the primary cause of delusions—that is, erroneous cognitions—is beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*), devoid of origination and possessing the characteristics to be described hereafter; this is the meaning of the phrase "the cause of the obstruction. || 14 ||

A0 Ṭīkā: Now, one might object: "Granted that such is the definition and so forth of *pratibandha* (obstruction/impediment), yet what is the cause for this established *pratibandha* to be characterized by the aforementioned definition of an obstructing factor (*pratibandhaka*) both in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*)? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the resolution with the words "tasya" (of that). The word "putra" (son) means the object characterized by the clear hearing of the word "suta. The phrase "of the father" implies "of the teacher. "Samāna" (equal)— ...a- [The sentence continues].

The meaning is that there is the utterance of sound together with young boys. Having thus stated the obstacle in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), he states it in the case under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "here" (*iha*).

Although the state of supreme bliss—which is the self-luminous Self—exists as a manifestation in its general aspect as the object of supreme love (which is the cause of supreme bliss), it does not manifest in its specific characteristic of being indivisible (*akhaṇḍatva*); this is the sense of the term "object" (*viṣaya*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "only ignorance (*avidyā*) exists."

Now, one might ask: what is the cause of this [avidyā] as well? To answer this, he qualifies it as "beginningless" (anādi). According to the Śruti: "When the individual soul (jīva), sleeping through beginningless māyā, awakens, then it realizes the unborn, sleepless, dreamless, non-dual [Reality]," it means that it is not the counter-positive of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva).
One might further ask: even so, is it of the nature of the absence of knowledge? To address that, he again qualifies it as "delusive" (vyāmoha). Specifically, [it is that which conceals] the truth...

It deludes (*mohayati*) from all sides (*āsamantāt*) in the form of "you" (*tvam*) and so forth—based on the root *muh* meaning "bewilderment"—and even regarding that which is not a means to one's welfare, it produces the notion that it is a means to one's welfare;

thus, the meaning is "as far as the entire phenomenal world (*dṛśya-prapañca*) beginning with 'you'. It thoroughly pervades that One (*ekam*), the Absolute (*kevalam*), and binds (*badhnāti*) it by fashioning it as an effect characterized by being a visible object other than the fourfold visible objects such as the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*); this is what is meant. Here, the word *nibandhana* retains its original gender (*ajahalliṅga*).

Even though it is neuter, its status as a qualifier of *avidyā* follows from the very statement: "Despite a difference in gender and number, there exists the relation of qualifier and qualified; however, the case-ending for both the qualifier and the qualified is one and the same. Thus, the sense is that because she (avidyā) is the transformative material cause (*pariṇāmy-upādāna-kāraṇa*) defined by the effects characterized as the visible world produced in the form of ether and so forth, she possesses the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpatva*). Here, by the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "avidyaiva" (only avidyā), [the author excludes other possibilities].

There is an exclusion of desire and action, which are respectively termed "prior" and "subsequent" latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and which take the form of mental dispositions (*saṃskāra*) and meritorious deeds (*sukṛta*), etc. For this very reason, the venerable Sureśvarācārya said: "The cessation of ignorance is liberation, and that [ignorance] is declared to be bondage. (14)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, in order to establish the knowledge of the Self which serves as the cause for removing obstacles, he explains *prakṛti*, which is its root cause:
"Endowed with the reflection of Brahman, which consists of consciousness and bliss..."
The qualities of tamas, rajas, and sattva constitute nature (prakṛti), and it is of two kinds.
"Cidānanda" means that which is endowed with, or joined to, the reflection—the shadow—of Brahman, whose nature is consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*).

*Tamaḥ*, *rajaḥ*, and *sattva* refer to the qualities of darkness, passion, and purity; the state of equilibrium among these qualities is called *prakṛti*. And that *prakṛti* is of two kinds, of two types. By the word "and" (*ca*), he indicates another type that will be described later. || 15 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 24]
[Commentary on the *Tattvaviveka*, Chapter 1]:

Now, one might object that there are scriptural passages such as, "Know Māyā to be Prakṛti and the Great Lord to be the wielder of Māyā"; "In the beginning, there was darkness, hidden by darkness"; "Remaining within the midst of ignorance"; and "This individual soul (jīva) has a limiting adjunct consisting of its effects."

The Lord (Īśvara) is indeed of eight forms— namely, one conditioned by Māyā, illumined by Māyā, reflected in Māyā, delimited by Māyā, conditioned by Avidyā, illumined by Avidyā, reflected in Avidyā, and delimited by Avidyā; likewise,

the individual soul (Jīva) is also of eight forms— namely, distinguished by the fourfold division beginning with "conditioned by Avidyā" and distinguished by the fourfold division beginning with "conditioned by the intellect" (Buddhi)— as has been described by the venerable ancient teachers according to their respective convictions.

In this regard, one might ask: what exactly are those two things denoted by the words *tat* (That) and *tvam* (Thou), which the author of the present work intends at the outset? Nor should it be said that he will explain them clearly immediately thereafter; for that would contradict the path of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth to be taught in the present treatise with the path of the *Citradīpa* as explained by that same author.
