Therefore, if one asks, "What then is the truth here?"—the answer is: it is precisely within the commentary on the *Citradīpa* that this is [clarified].

Having raised the objection that this contradicts the doctrine established by Thoktajīva regarding the nature of the Lord (Īśvara), and desiring to remove that contradiction, the author introduces the following [verse] because the very ignorance (avidyā) mentioned here as an obstacle is what is required: "cidānanda... etc. Since the suffix *mayaṭ* is seen in usages such as "a pot made of clay" (*mṛn-mayaḥ ghaṭaḥ*) or "a cloth made of threads" (*taṃtu-mayaḥ paṭaḥ*) even in its own primary sense, the meaning is: "that whose existence is dependent solely upon the reflection of one's own unconditioned bliss, which is non-different from self-luminous consciousness. By this, its...

By its being devoid of intrinsic existence (*svataḥ-sattā-śūnyatva*), its falsity (*mithyātva*) is stated. Otherwise, since that [Prakṛti]—which serves as the root of both [Māyā and Āvidyā] and is necessarily required for the purpose of describing the nature of Īśvara and others as merely reflections of Māyā and so forth according to the method to be explained later—would be described as possessing a reflection of Brahman consisting of *sac-cid-ānanda*, there would be no purpose [in such a description]. If, then, Īśvara and the rest were reflections of Brahman in Māyā and so forth, then their root...

Furthermore, the question arises: "What is this reflection of Brahman upon the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) which has become the substrate? Now, one might object: "Granted that the statement regarding [Prakṛti] being a reflection of Brahman is made to exclude its insignificance by establishing it as the foundational substrate for the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the individual soul (*jīva*); nevertheless, it is still improper for the followers of the Upaniṣads to describe it as possessing the three qualities (*traiguṇya*), just as the Sāṃkhyas do. We reply: No; for in the Śruti passage, "The unborn, one, red, white, and black," [the qualities] *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*... [are mentioned].

With the intention that the *Smṛti* passage, "Thus the qualities are born of *prakṛti*," describes the threefold nature (*vaiguṇya*) of that [nature] solely for the purpose of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the individual soul (*jīva*), he further qualifies it with the words beginning with "darkness" (*tamaḥ*). For this very reason, in order to establish its status as the root of the visible world known as the individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśvara*), and the universe (*jagat*), he also declares its division with the words "and twofold. That aforementioned *prakṛti* is twofold: [that consisting of] pure *sattva*...

The meaning is that there are two types: those in which *rajas* is predominant and those in which *tamas* is predominant. By this, their respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) as Īśa and so forth are established in sequence. From the word "and" (*ca*), it is understood that [the third type] is that in which *tamas* is predominant. (15)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He demonstrates that very twofold nature along with its cause:
"Māyā and Vidya are considered such by virtue of the purity and impurity of Sattva."
Having brought her under control through illusion, he would become the omniscient Lord. || 16 ||

Regarding the term *sattva*: the purity (*śuddhi*) of the quality (*guṇa*) *sattva*, which is luminous by nature, consists in its not being turbidified by another quality; [the compound refers] to those two, namely purity and impurity of *sattva*. These two are considered to be of two kinds: *māyā* and *avidyā*, as is accepted in the doctrine. The meaning is that *māyā* has pure *sattva* as its predominant element, whereas *avidyā* has impure *sattva* as its predominant element. He now demonstrates the purpose for which the distinction between *māyā* and *avidyā* was stated:

Regarding the phrase "the reflection in māyā" (māyābimba): the conscious self (cidātmā) reflected in māyā is the "reflection in māyā"; having brought that māyā under control—that is, having made it subject to its own will—it exists as the Lord (īśvara), who is omniscient and possesses attributes such as omniscience. || 16 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭī0): Now, it may be granted that there are these two kinds [of parts] due to the word "and" (ca) [in the verse], since Prakṛti—which undergoes transformation as the object of perception and serves as the material cause—is the material cause of the inert world; for it will be stated later: "By the command of the Lord, for the sake of His enjoyment, the elements—ether, air, fire, water, and earth—were born from Prakṛti, of which Tamas is predominant. Nevertheless, what is the relevance of this to the present context?

Anticipating the thought that, since the subject matter intended here is the entity called *avidyā*— proposed in the statement "In this context, it is indeed beginningless *avidyā*" and so forth— as being the obstacle to the manifestation of the Self’s own supreme bliss, and that one desiring to know its nature has arrived, [the author] first addresses it because of its importance as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the conscious principle.
The First Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

He provides the resolution by stating, in the first half of the verse beginning with *sattva*, the essential definition of the two primordial portions previously promised, along with their respective causes, and their two designations according to the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as Īśvara: "Thus, *māyā*-ness is the state of being the transforming material cause of duality—which is imagined through the reflection of one’s own consciousness within that [portion] where *sattva* predominates and is not overcome by *rajas* and *tamas*; while [the other] is the state of being the material cause of duality—which is imagined through the reflection of one’s own consciousness within that [portion] where [sattva] is overcome [by rajas and tamas] and where those [guṇas] predominate..."

The definitions of ignorance (*avidyā*) are thus established as: "being a transforming material cause" and "the state of being ignorance. Here, in the first definition, if only "being existent" (*sattva*) and so forth were stated, there would be an over-extension (*vyabhicāra*) to [other] ignorance; to exclude that, the term "unoverpowered" (*anabhibhūta*) is used. If only "transforming into duality" and so forth were stated, there would be an over-extension to cow-dung and the like, which serve as the material causes for transformations such as scorpions; to avoid this, the term "imagined" (*kalpita*) is added. Similarly, the phrase "inherent in itself" (*svagata*) and so forth is included to prevent the charge of impossibility (*asaṃbhava*). The same applies to the second definition.

One should understand that the function of each respective term [in the definition] is to exclude errors such as deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to *māyā* and other such entities. Now, an objection is raised: since the aforementioned dualistic nature is established by such scriptural texts as "the one unborn" (*ajāmekām*) and such traditional authorities (*smṛti*) as "know both Prakṛti and Puruṣa to be indeed beginningless," even though she (Prakṛti) is of an eternal nature, the capacity to transform the qualities of *sattva* and so forth—characterized by the aforementioned purity and other attributes—must be attributed to the Pure Brahman alone.

But that which was stated by the words "consisting of consciousness-bliss" (*cidānandamaya*) and so forth is restricted [to Brahman], because it is exhausted as being merely the cause of the existence and so on common to all; and because Īśvara and others, being reflections dependent upon Māyā and the like—which are established through the purity of attributes such as *sattva* that differentiate them—are pervaded by that [Brahman]. Therefore, it rests solely in the ultimate reality (*tattva*). Furthermore, due to the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), there is an absence of purity in the attribute of being a transformer (*pariṇāmayitṛtva*). Nor [does this apply] to being a reflection (*vivartatva*), witnesshood (*sākṣitva*), and so forth.

It must be said that this could also arise from the *vṛtti* (mental modification). If it is argued that this is possible even though those two [Māyā and Avidyā] are not inherently connected, that is true; the point is that since we accept that God alone is the transformer (*pariṇāmayitṛ*) of them, and because they are beginningless, there is no fallacy such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Regarding the statement "those two kinds of *prakṛti*," it was indeed stated by me myself in the *Bodhaikyasiddhi*: "This Māyā and Avidyā are born spontaneously; according to the Śruti, the individual soul (*jīva*)..."

"Where is the Lavaga [the opponent] who is averse? Thus, through the distinction between the purity of *sattva* and so forth, Vidyāraṇya taught in the *Tattvaviveka*: 'When *sattva* is overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*, it becomes *avidyā*; but *māyā* is not like that. The individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) are its two reflected forms, arising respectively from the pure consciousness of the Self, which is Brahman. Now, let it be as stated; however, regarding the attainment of the supreme bliss consisting of the nature of the Self as described—

Now, following the introduction concerning the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) which has become a source of bondage, the author summarizes both its essential nature and its function in the latter half of the verse with the word *māyā*. For the purpose of favoring living beings whose minds have been purified by service to the pair of lotus feet of that [Lord]—as promised in the passage beginning with "of those whose minds are purified by service to the pair of His lotus feet"—the grace bestowed upon the soul through a pure intellect attained by worshipping the Lord who is non-different from the true Guru would otherwise be impossible without knowledge of the essential nature of the Lord and other principles; therefore, he briefly describes that nature and its activity. Regarding *māyā*, which has been defined as above:
The meaning is that it reflects precisely because it is non-different from the original object (*bimba*). The definition of reflection and so forth has indeed been stated in my *Bodhaikyasiddhi*:

"Alternatively, reflection is considered to be the capacity for identity with the original object (*bimba*), brought about by its fitness [for such identity]. It is the proximity of a pure substrate (*upādhi*);

even in the view of those who desire that [identity], this is what constitutes being a reflection. Regarding the phrase *tadabhīpsat*: it refers to those who accept or acknowledge both the appearance of the original object (*ābhāsa*) and the reflection (*pratibimba*).

The meaning of the phrase "therein" (*tatra*) is that it refers to the opinion of those two teachers, namely the author of the *Vārttika* and the author of the *Vivaraṇa*. This is the explanation of the aforementioned text. As for the detailed exposition on this point, it should be made to amaze the mind right there; such is the direction. And thus, when there is an appearance of difference, reflection (*pratibimbatva*) is defined as that which conforms to their identity (*aikya*). By this, [the objection] regarding the mastery over Māyā and the omniscience produced by it is [refuted].
It is struck. || 16 ||
But another, being under the sway of ignorance, becomes manifold through the variety of that [ignorance].
That would be the causal body (kāraṇa-śarīra), and the Prājña is the one who possesses the conceit therein.

Regarding the term *avidyā*: the conscious self (*cidātman*), being under the sway of ignorance (*avidyā*) and existing as a reflection within it, is dependent upon that [ignorance] and is thus the individual soul (*jīva*). And because of its manifoldness—that is, because of the manifoldness of that limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) which is ignorance, and due to the gradations of impurity—it becomes "of many kinds," meaning it becomes diverse in various ways according to the distinctions of gods, animals, and so forth. Just as the pith [is extracted] from the *muñja* grass, so too is the Self [discerned].

"Extracted by reasoning from the triad of bodies, the wise become the Supreme Brahman itself"— thus, later on, he will state that the individual soul (*jīva*), having been distinguished from the triad of bodies, is indeed the Supreme Brahman. In that regard, what are those three bodies, or what is the nature of the individual soul when characterized by its respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)?
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
titled *Tattvaviveka* (Discrimination of Reality).
In response to the inquiry "What is it?", he explains all of that in sequence, beginning with the words "That is the causal body" (*sā kāraṇaśarīram*). That *avidyā* is the causal body;

because it is a particular state of *prakṛti* which serves as the cause for the gross and subtle bodies, it is metaphorically called the "cause. Furthermore, it is called a "body" (*śarīra*) because it perishes—that is, it is destroyed—through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). One who possesses the conceit of "I" (*aham-abhimānavān*) with respect to that causal body does so through the superimposition of identity (*tādātmyādhyāsa*).

The individual soul (jīva) is "the wise one" (prājña); that is, he whose nature consists in the experience of the imperishable consciousness is "wise" (prajña), and being wise, he is "the wise one" (prājña)—this is the meaning of his name. || 17 ||

A0ḍī0: Now, in connection with the description of the nature of the Lord as a reflection in *māyā*, the author explains—by means of the first quarter-verse beginning with "avidyā"—the subjection of the individual soul (*jīva*), whose characteristic is being a reflection in *avidyā*, which is established by implication; this is done for the sake of establishing the meaningfulness of the commencement of the scriptures and so forth. The word "tu" (but) serves to highlight the distinction between the Lord and [the individual soul]. By this, although there is equality between the two in terms of being reflected in an adjunct (*upādhi*) and so on, one [the Lord] possesses omniscience through His mastery over that [adjunct], while the other [the individual soul] is subject to it.

The objection—"How can there be some degree of omniscience through mere submissiveness (*vaśyatā*)?"—is refuted by the very definition of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) introduced by the passage beginning with "purity of being" (*sattvaśuddhi*). Now, even so, is this [submissiveness] one or many? If it is one, is the body associated with it one or many? And if it is one, is it delimited by the body of the listener (*śrotṛ*) or by the body of the teacher (*śāstṛ*)? There is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) [to choose between these].

Nor is it the second of the two [options] within either of the two groups mentioned above. Is that [being] the *sūtrātman*, also known as Hiraṇyagarbha, or is it someone else entirely, like a yogi who creates a multitude of bodies (*kāyavyūha*)? In the first case, since he—who identifies with the collective subtle body (*samaṣṭiliṅgaśarīra*)—is different in every kalpa and thus infinite, the proposition of his oneness is contradicted; furthermore, even if he were a collective entity, there would be no difference between him and the mere aggregate of individual appearances. In the latter case—

If there were the possibility of liberation at some other time even though non-liberation persists until the end of infinite kalpas, it would follow that [liberation] depends merely on the dullness of one’s faith. Furthermore, if the liberation of all apparent individual souls such as ourselves were possible through that very liberation occurring at a later time, then although our engagement in sinful karma—which causes suffering—would be impossible, our engagement in optional karma—which causes sensory pleasure—would still be possible; thus, [the path] leading to the purification of the mind would be undermined by desireless...

Nor is the first or second [alternative] tenable, because there would be the consequence of non-engagement even in the dharma of cessation—beginning with the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal regarding action and ending with *nididhyāsana*.

This very doctrine is the primary established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of Vedānta, known as the theory of the single soul (*ekajīvavāda*). This is because, in the *Siddhāntabindu*, the theory of manifold souls (*anekajīvavāda*) is shown to be inferior; and here too, by the force of the singular number in the phrase "another is under the sway of ignorance" (*avidyāvaśagastvanyaḥ*), the theory of the single soul alone is indicated as being more venerable.

Having indicated primacy by means of the word *mukhya* ("principal"), and having indicated subordination (*jaghanyatva*) precisely because it cannot otherwise be accounted for by the subsequent definition of the doctrine of manifold souls (*anekajīvavāda*) through the phrase "in many ways due to its variety" (*tadvaicitryādanekadhā*), one might ask: what is the intended meaning here of the venerable teacher Vidyāraṇya? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the resolution with the second quarter-verse beginning with *tat*. The underlying idea is as follows: by the word *tat*, [he refers to] that which is characterized primarily by *sattva*, though overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*.

The previously mentioned ignorance (*avidyā*)— which is essentially the world’s material cause, beginningless, indefinable, consisting of the second part of the aforementioned *prakṛti*, and whose sole sublation is the firm, immediate, and non-dual valid cognition of the identity of Brahman and the Self— is, due to its manifoldness— as stated in the scripture, "His supreme power is indeed heard to be diverse"—

and because it possesses thousands of specific divisions, causes even the single individual soul (*jīva*), though one in the present context, to become manifold in nature, like a face reflected in various mirrors.

Since this meaning must necessarily be stated, it is said there that although the individual soul (*jīva*) is one—being the mind reflected in *avidyā* just as a face is reflected [in a mirror]—it nevertheless becomes manifold in infinite ways due to the infinity of the distinctions consisting of *avidyā*, which are like the infinity of various reflections delimited by different dates such as the full moon or new moon. If it is asked, "Even so, what has been gained regarding the resolution of the aforementioned objection?", listen; hear what has been gained with careful attention. For instance: "Brahmavi..."

By hundreds of scriptural passages such as "He gives [the highest]," which state that liberation is attainable through knowledge alone, it is made known that bondage has as its material cause (*upādāna*) that very [ignorance] alone. And that [cause], being the root of the threefold duality consisting of the conscious (Īśvara), the individual soul (jīva), and the insentient (jagat)—characterized as spirit and matter—is denoted by the term *prakṛti*. It is an unbeginning positive entity, the sole adversary to the knowledge whose object is the non-dual identity with Brahman, and it is the fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) characterized by a predominance of *sattva* that is not overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*, [which brings about] differentiation.

That [liberation] occurs through various means such as *natya* (dance) and so forth has already been established above. In this context, since the scripture was commenced with the words "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*) solely for the sake of liberation— which consists in the destruction of ignorance that is the root of the suffering characterized by duality— and since that [liberation] is achievable only through the knowledge defined above,

and since that knowledge is produced very slowly in the doctrine of the plurality of souls (*jīvānānātva-vāda*) because it requires the purification of the referent of the term "That" (*tat-pada-artha*) by means of [understanding] the world beginning with ether as created by the Lord, [it follows that it is more easily attained in the doctrine of a single soul].
The First Chapter.
[Included in] the two commentaries:

In the *Vavāda*, however—it is said: "I am indeed Brahman; this entire universe is the expansion of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). All this, including the Lord (*seśa*), is [projected] by means of the three-fold ignorance (*avidyā*)."

By the statement beginning with "imagined by me" (*mayā kalpitam*), which negates the fivefold [superimpositions], it is stated that all visible phenomena other than ignorance (*avidyā*) are imagined solely by the individual soul (*jīva*).

Because this [realization] is produced quickly due to the absence of effort, *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living) is established at that very moment, even without the exertion of yoga practice and so forth. Thus, only one soul is to be enlightened by the scripture; as for others, because the aforementioned ignorance—and the manifold, diverse powers inherent in it—are extremely vast, [the scripture does not address them].

Speech itself is manifold, and living beings are merely its conceptual constructs. Keeping this secret truth in mind, it was said: "But another, under the sway of ignorance, appears as many due to its diversity. Furthermore, later on, in the concluding summary: "That [speech] would be the causal body, and the *prājña* is one who identifies with that reality," it is clear that even here the doctrine of a single body and a single soul (*ekaśarīraikajīvavāda*) is intended. This is because of the previously mentioned [doctrine of] the creator...

When it is established that the very absence of departure from this life constitutes the state of being a Lord (Īśvara) capable of fashioning the fivefold armor of the intellect for the living soul, then the possibility of Him fashioning a Guru and so forth is refuted by the principle of *kaimutya* (how much more so). Nor should it be asked: "How can the realization of non-duality arise from a Guru who is merely imagined?
For even an imagined Guru, by virtue of his omniscience, reveals the Truth; indeed, even an imagined [cause] leads to death.
This is because the matter has already been answered by the venerable teacher Saṃkṣepaśārīraka himself, who stated: "It may be like a serpent, but not like a lotus in the sky. Now, one might object:
"How do you determine that this alone is the intention of the original author, the venerable teacher Vidyāraṇya?

For the ancient commentators have explained this passage according to the literal text as supporting the doctrine of *nānājīvavāda* (the plurality of souls) alone. If this is argued, we reply: No; for [the text] contains both *sāvakāśa* (provisional) and *niravakāśa* (absolute)...

By the maxim that "between two [conflicting] rules, the one which leaves no room for application is stronger," it is observed that in these primary treatises, as well as in his own *Anubhūtiprakāśa*, only the doctrine of a single body and a single soul (ekajīva-vāda) known as *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi* is accepted; whereas the doctrine of multiple souls (*anekajīva-vāda*) known as *sṛṣṭadṛṣṭi*, though found extensively elsewhere, is intended only to signify the infinity of individual soul-manifestations (*jīvābhāsa*)—which are described as being manifold due to their diversity—as indicated by the aphorism. Thus, [the former alone is the final view].

Even in the case of the doctrine of the individual soul (*jīvavāda*) and others, since they produce *jīvanmukti* through rapid awakening, one might assume that very same intended meaning; yet, even so, it ultimately results in the primacy of this [Advaitic] view alone.

For example, it is stated in the third chapter, the *Kośaviveka*: "That which is Brahman—truth, knowledge, and infinite—that is the Reality; its states as Lord (*īśvara*) and as individual soul (*jīva*) are imagined by two limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). There exists a certain divine power (*aiśvarī śakti*) that governs all things, hidden from the *ānandamaya* [self] onwards."

When the powers (*śakti*) of all things are not restricted to their respective objective natures (*vastudharma*), then indeed the world would fall into disorder due to the mutual confusion of those natures. Through the penetration of the reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyāveśa*), that power shines as if it were conscious. By union with the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of those powers, Brahman itself attains the state of the Lord (*Īśvara*). When there is the intention to speak of the sheaths (*kośa*) as adjuncts, Brahman itself becomes the individual soul (*jīva*). Just as one and the same person is both father and grandfather in relation to his son and grandson, yet he is not so designated when the son and grandson are not intended to be expressed.

"The father is not the grandfather; likewise, neither the Lord (Īśa) nor the individual soul (jīva) [is the cause] when the sheath of power (śaktikośa) is not intended. Here, the word *jīva* is used in the singular, and not as *jīvāḥ*. Similarly, in the *Dvaitaviveka*, after asserting: "The duality created by both the Lord and the individual soul is distinguished; once there is this discrimination, the bondage to be abandoned by the individual soul will become clear," and having woven together scriptural passages such as *māyāṃ tu*, etc., [the author] says: "Having assumed a form... [and so on].
"The Lord entered the body as the individual soul (jīva)," so say those Śrutis; they declare that "jīvatva" [the state of being a soul] arises from the maintenance of the vital breaths (prāṇa).

Having thus described the general nature of the jīva, he defines it specifically: "That which is the substratum of consciousness, the subtle body (liṅgadeha), and the reflection of consciousness (cicchāyā) residing in the subtle body—the aggregate of these is called the jīva. Then, regarding the power of creation belonging to Māheśvarī Māyā...
"Indeed, there exists the power of delusion (*moha-śakti*), and it deludes that individual soul (*jīva*). Through delusion, having attained a state of helplessness, the mind grieves within the body.

All this duality created by the Lord has been briefly described. Thus, having summarized the visible world created by the Supreme Lord, and having introduced the duality imagined by the individual soul with the words beginning with "seven kinds of food" (*saptānna*), [the text continues]: "Rice and other grains, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, milk, as well as the mind, speech, and breath—these..."

"Let the truth regarding foodstuffs be understood"—having thus stated that even those things created by the Lord in His own form are also "created by the individual soul" (jīva) insofar as they are objects of its enjoyment, [the author] reconciles both [theories] without contradiction, stating: "The world, which is the work of the Lord and the object of enjoyment for the individual soul, is endowed with both; it should be understood just as a woman is born of her father yet is fit for her husband. Furthermore, [it is said]: "For the volition of the Lord, consisting of the function of Māyā, is the instrument for the individual soul; [the soul's volition], consisting of the function of the mind..."

What is this mental construction of a living being that serves as the means for experience? While the objects created by the Lord— such as gems and the like— remain uniform in nature, there arise various mental states in the experiencer.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya.

"Because it is the very essence of discrimination (*tattva-viveka*), its enjoyment is held to be manifold: one person rejoices upon finding the jewel, while another becomes angry at not having found it; the dispassionate one merely observes it here, neither rejoicing nor becoming angry. The three aspects pertaining to the jewel—'dear,' 'unpleasant,' and 'indifferent'—were created by living beings through the Lord."

"Form is common to the three [states]; the wife, the daughter-in-law, the sister-in-law, the mother-in-law, and the mother—though manifoldly so, the woman is differentiated only by the cognition of her relation, not by her own nature. By such passages, having clarified that the duality created by the individual soul (*jīva*) through the diversity of its volitions during creation is distinct from that created by the Lord (*Īśvara*), [the text continues]: "In this way, there are two objects, both being like water-pots: one made of clay and one made of cognition. The one made of clay is the object of measurement (*meya*); the witness (*sākṣin*)," and so forth.

The commentary (*bhāṣya*), however, consists of the intellect (*dhīmaya*). Having elaborated upon its nature as the cause of bondage through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—stating, for instance, "When this [intellect] exists, pleasure and pain exist;

when it is absent, neither of the two exists"—and having declared the fruit of the discrimination of the duality of the individual soul (*jīva-dvaita-vivecana*) with the words, "The supreme limit of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti) is attained through the abandonment of the duality of the individual soul; therefore, this discrimination between the Lord and the duality has been explained here," it concludes in this manner. Thus...

Furthermore, even in the doctrine of multiple souls (*nānājīvavāda*), it is established in the *Dvaitaviveka* that duality created by the soul alone is the cause of bondage; therefore, for the sake of its destruction, one must cultivate the yoga of firm renunciation. Consequently, it is illuminated that compared to that [doctrine], the present doctrine of a single soul in this single body (*prakṛtaikaśarīraikajīvavāda*) is superior, as it grants the swift realization of reality and the attainment of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). This very point has been stated explicitly by the authors of the root-text along with its supporting arguments in the *Kauṣītaky-upaniṣad-bhāṣya-vivaraṇa*.

In the eighth chapter of the *Anubhūtiprakāśa*, a commentary on the Upaniṣads, within the dialogue between Indra and Pratardana, it is stated: "The eleven organs and their objects indeed constitute the world; when one sleeps, the entire world is dissolved into the Self, which has the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as its limiting adjunct. If it be argued that only the organs dissolve and not the objects, that is not so. For the dissolution of the world is understood as the disappearance of its phenomenal appearance. That the world is merely phenomenal is clear in the established doctrine of Vedānta."

Therefore, when one is asleep, the world is dissolved; upon waking, it arises again. Let there be the perception of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as well; if that does not exist in deep sleep, then the mention of the *prāṇa* is merely from the perspective of another [state]. By means of the *prāṇa*, the Self is indicated. Upon awakening, the senses arise from the Self like sparks. From them come the presiding deities (*abhimānideva*), and from the deities, these objects. One who experiences Brahman highly values this "creation through perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*). From his own awakening—

"...therefore this entire cycle of transmigration dissolves like a dream," and so forth. Likewise, in the ninth chapter, in the dialogue between Bālāki and Ajātaśatru, observe this answer to the question "From where did [the person] come?": "From the Supreme Self, who is full and veiled by ignorance, [the person] comes; when the sleeper awakens, then from that Supreme Self the vital breaths (prāṇas) are born according to their respective natures, like sparks from a fire. The vital breaths—

From that [source], the birth of the deities presiding over the senses, such as Agni and others, occurs; through these senses (akṣas), objects are perceived, having emerged from those deities. There is one creation common to all, and another, the triadic creation. The former proceeds in the order of ether (ākāśa) and so forth; the latter proceeds in the order of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth. When the karma of all living beings is exhausted, there shall be a great dissolution (pralaya). Again, when karma arises for them, there shall be a great creation (mahāsṛṣṭi) from the Lord.

When the karma of one [individual] is exhausted, there is dissolution, which bears the name of sleep; when that karma arises again, there is creation, termed waking. For the sake of awakening to the reality of non-duality (advaita-tattva), creation is described everywhere—whether it be small or great; through it, the eternal non-duality is realized. Before the grand palace of a king, there may be a great gate, and behind it, the door to the inner apartments.

The small gate is called *radvāra*. Through the great gate, an audience with the King is suddenly difficult to obtain due to the great crowding of people and the abundance of guards. At the small gate, one devoted to his master forcibly beholds the King. Desiring the experience of what is created by vision, he likewise knows himself through force (*haṭha*). Having first understood the meaning of that state (*tatpadārtha*) through the Great Creation, and having then purified the meaning of "you" (*tvaṃpadārtha*), awakening arises from the Great Sentence.

It hangs down. Therefore, in this context, Ajātaśatru spoke of "creation through vision" (dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi) for the sake of awakening Bālāki, who was hanging [from the tree], to the realization that he was not Brahman.
For that ignorance which existed during sleep is indeed the dissolution of the ego (ahaṃkāra). That ego, having arisen again at the time of experiencing the fruits of karma, delimits the Self;
thus, as before, the Self becomes both agent and enjoyer. From the enjoying Self arises the sense organ, which is the instrument of enjoyment. [The one] who impels the sense organs...

The grace of the gods arises spontaneously; from the senses thus graced, the worlds shine forth as they emerge. This phenomenal creation is born from that [Self] and arises from it of its own accord. Even a child quickly understands that the creator of the world is the Supreme Self. However, the notion that "the Lord is endowed with majesty and is distinct [from the Self]" has long been ingrained in the minds of the wise; from this [notion] follows the sequence beginning with space (viyat) and so on. What is the use of much talk? Let it be as it is.
The First Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

"Any creation whatsoever is illusory (*māyikī*); therefore, the non-dual blissful Self is experienced in deep sleep. Thus, through the statements of the two chapters in this sequence, the doctrine of a single living being (*ekajīvavāda*)—characterized by the view that creation is a mere appearance (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭitva*) and delimited by a single body—is quickly produced as a means for attaining liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).

It is quite clear that [the scripture] favors those who already possess knowledge by generating the knowledge of the reality of *sattva*, and it favors those who desire to know (*vividiṣu*) by generating the knowledge of the truth regarding *sattva*. Therefore, according to their view, within the threefold division of the *prakṛti* consisting of the three *guṇas*—which is the material cause of duality and is otherwise known as root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*)—there is a single portion called "ignorance" (*avidyā*) which is the cause of the state of being an individual soul (*jīvatva*). Consequently, the individual soul, which is the reflection of that [portion], is also one alone.

However, the various perceived individual souls (*jīvas*)—which, due to that [one soul’s] manifoldness, appear in many ways according to the maxim of a face reflected in a hundred pieces of glass as indicated by the word "in many ways"—are merely semblances of souls (*jīvābhāsa*) imagined by Him. This is like the appearance of a world in the dream and waking states imagined by Him. Therefore, for each person to be instructed, there is the doctrine of the single soul with a single body known as the sheath consisting of deep-sleep bliss (*sauṣuptānandamayakośa*), which relies upon the teachings of the Upanishads and other scriptures on "creation through perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*). By taking recourse to this, the visible world immediately...

It follows that for one who possesses a false view (*mithyātva*), liberation known as *videhamukti*—characterized by the destruction of that ignorance through the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the non-dual Brahman-Ātman—and also *jīvanmukti*—characterized by the sublation of all phenomenal duality rooted in the subtle impressions of the sheaths consisting of bliss, which continue to appear until the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma—are both accomplished without effort; thus, this alone is the primary Vedāntic doctrine regarding such a person. And so it has been said concerning the sentient being to be addressed:

The intention is as follows: although the liberation of Śuka and others is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) based on the *ṣṭac* suffix, from the perspective of the scripture (*śāstradṛṣṭyā*), the individual soul (*jīva*) of Śuka and others is liberated because it possesses immediate realization of reality (*tattvāparokṣajñatvāt*), just like the insentient being addressed in the present context. Furthermore, from the perspective of an inference made by a bystander (*taṭasthānumitidṛṣṭyā*), the entire system—such as the distinction between the bound and the liberated and the doctrine of many souls (*anekajīvavāda*)—is perfectly well-established according to reality. Now, one might object: "Let it be that the system of the unity of the soul and so forth is accepted by the author of the root-text; nevertheless, even by the aforementioned method..."

It is indeed beyond dispute that the very ignorance of deep sleep, which consists of the sheath made of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*), is the primary body of the individual soul (*jīva*); and because it is the cause of the subtle and other bodies, it is designated as the "causal" (*kāraṇa*) body. However, regarding the nature of that very [ignorance]—which consists of both concealment (*āvaraṇa*) and projection (*vikṣepa*)—it will be stated in the root text to be seen upon the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma through the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*). Thus, [the ignorance] which consists of projection and brings about one's own experiences, such as the subtle body, [is what remains].

One must necessarily state the destruction of that duality which has been grasped, obstructed, and sublated; otherwise, one might suspect that for the knower of Brahman, there would be an absence of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Anticipating this objection, [the text cites] the Śruti: "He has three abodes, three states of dream," and "In the three stations, whatever is to be enjoyed, the enjoyer, and the act of enjoyment—distinct from these, I am the Witness, pure consciousness, the eternally auspicious (*sadāśiva*). Just as the stalk is extracted from the *muñja* grass, so too is the Self [extracted from the body].

"By means of reasoning, it is extracted from the three bodies; for the wise, the Supreme Brahman alone arises"—thus, according to the root text to be cited later, since the three bodies consisting of the cause and so forth, as established by the aforementioned scripture, serve as the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) supported by the individual soul (*jīva*) denoted by the term *tvaṃ*, even when the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*)—which has as its sole object the identity of the Self with the root Brahman—is destroyed, the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*), which is included among its effects, continues to exist as long as the *prārabdha* karma persists. Nevertheless, regarding that aforementioned material cause...

Even though a trace of the root ignorance that causes bondage persists, there is no contradiction [to its existence], because it has been stated in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* in exactly this way: "Jivanmukti exists as long as there is perception; and therein, the shadow of duality exists because of perception. To preserve the shadow of duality, there is a trace [of ignorance]; regarding that matter, one's own experience is the proof. Thus, that very aforementioned ignorance transforms itself into the form of the causal body (*kāraṇaśarīra*), which is dominated by the quality of darkness (*tamas*) as found in deep sleep.

He provides the resolution with the second half of the verse, beginning with "That [designation]," stating that the name "Prājña" (the Wise One) is also well-known from scripture for the individual soul (*jīva*) conditioned by that [unmanifest], on account of its being an intense experiencer of self-bliss and its ignorance regarding objects other than that; thus, it is called "Prājña" because it is an enjoyer of bliss, as in the scriptural passage: "The third quarter is Prājña, whose face is turned toward bliss. (17)

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In order to explain the subtle body (sūkṣmaśarīra) which follows in the sequence, and the individual soul (jīva) characterized by that [body], he describes the creation of ether and the other elements, which are its causes:
"By the command of the Lord, for the sake of the experience of that [soul], from Prakṛti in which Tamas predominates..."
From these, the elements—space, wind, fire, water, and earth—were born.

"Preponderant in *tamas*": for the sake of their enjoyment— that is, for the sake of the enjoyment of those wise ones (*prājña*), in order to accomplish the direct perception of pleasure and pain— from the aforementioned *prakṛti*, which is preponderant in *tamas* and serves as the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), [it arises] by the command of the Lord (*īśvara*).
[The Fifteenth Chapter, titled *Tattvaviveka*,
composed by Vidyāraṇya] of the *Pañcadaśī* (The Fifteen).

By the command of the presiding Lord of the universe—who is endowed with powers such as Īśana and whose command consists of the desire to create preceded by contemplation (īkṣā) and serves as the efficient cause—the five elements beginning with ether (viyat) and ending with earth were born; that is to say, they manifested and came into being. || 18 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Granted that the dualistic arrangement of consciousnesses (*cetanadvaitavyavasthā*) is thus established; nevertheless, ultimately, according to the view of the original author, since this rests upon the doctrine of many souls known as *sṛṣṭadṛṣṭi* (the view that the world is created [by the Lord]), how does the dualistic arrangement of the insentient (*jaḍadvaitavyavasthā*)—which is necessary for their experience—subsist? Having raised this doubt, [the author] first...

In the text, "Māyā and Vidya are considered [to arise] from the purity and impurity of *sattva*," the particle *ca* (and) indicates that, from the third constituent of *prakṛti* which is characterized by a predominance of *tamas*, and from that which is impelled by the Lord as the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*), there arise the five most subtle great elements (*mahābhūta*)— consisting of sound and the other qualities— as well-known from such scriptural passages as "From this very Self, space was produced," and so forth; these indeed serve as the cause of dissolution.
He provides the resolution: "Tamaḥ-pradhāna...
[and so forth]. Here, the ablative case in the word *prakṛteḥ* is intended to express the material cause (*upādāna*), just as in the expression "the cloth from the threads.

However, the status of being the efficient cause (*nimitta*) belongs solely to the Lord (*Īśvara*) as qualified by the will consisting of a modification of *māyā*, according to such scriptural passages as, "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate.'"
The state of being. || 18 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having described the creation of the primary elements (bhūtas), and now describing the creation of the derivative elements (bhautikas), he first states the creation of the five organs of perception:
"From the five portions of *sattva* of those [elements], the five sense-organs arise in sequence."
"The [five] known as the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose arise from the portions of *sattva*.

This means that from the five portions of *sattva*—the parts of the quality of *sattva* belonging to those [elements] starting with space (*viyat*), which serve as the material causes—the pentad of the organs of cognition, known as the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose, arises in sequence. These organs of cognition (*dhīndriyāṇi*) are the sense organs of knowledge (*jñānendriyāṇi*). Their pentad arises respectively.
The meaning is that each individual sense organ is produced from a portion of each of the elemental beings. || 19 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): To this he replies with the four verses beginning with "And the existent" (sacca). The phrase "by the command of the Lord" (īśvarājñayā) should be supplied and applied here as well, just as it was in the case of the creation of the elements. Here, the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth, which reside in *māyā*—the material cause of the elements—continue to persist even within the elements such as ether (*ākāśa*) that have resulted from their transformation; this is like the whiteness of milk persisting in curds, and not, as the logicians (*tārkika*) claim, a different set of qualities altogether.
Because there is no proof for that. "Dhī" means the faculty of cognition (jñānendriya). || 19 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having described the specific functions of each of the constituents of *sattva*, he now states their common function:
"By all of them, the internal organ [is formed], which is twofold according to its different modifications."
The mind (manas) would be of the nature of deliberation, while the intellect (buddhi) would consist of ascertainment.

Regarding the word "by them": the connection is that by all those constituent parts of *sattva* existing together, a substance—the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—which serves as the material cause for the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*), is produced. He states its internal subdivisions along with their causes, beginning with "functions" (*vṛtti*). That internal organ becomes twofold, of two kinds, through the distinction of functions, which is to say, the distinction of modifications (*pariṇāma*). He demonstrates this very distinction of functions with the words "the mind" (*manaḥ*). "Investigation" (*vimarśa*) is the nature of investigation.

That whose nature is doubt—that is, whose very essence consists of doubt—is the mind (*manas*). That whose nature is certainty—certainty being the act of determination (*adhyavasāya*)—is the intellect (*buddhi*), for it is that whose essence is such certainty. || 20 ||

Commentary (a0): By those [elements], namely the sattva-constituents of ether and so forth; as for mind (citta) and ego (ahaṃkāra), they are included within the very categories of mind (manas) and intellect (buddhi). ||20||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He now states the specific functions of each of the five portions of *rajas* that follow in sequence:
"By means of those five portions of *rajas*, their organs of action [arise] in order."
Those known as speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals were born.

"By the portions of rajas": from those very five portions of rajas—the rājasic constituents—of ether and the other elements, acting as the material cause (upādāna), there were born the organs of action (karmendriyas) known by these names: speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals, which are the instruments that produce activity. || 21 ||
The First Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Here too, by the word "that" (tat), it is the elements themselves that are meant. || 21 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He thus describes the common function of the portions of *rajas*:
"By all of them combined, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) becomes fivefold through its various functions."
Furthermore, they are prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna. || 22 ||

"By all these" means that by them acting together, having become causes through their combination, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is born—this is the ellipsis. He states its internal divisions: "due to the difference in functions. Due to the difference in functions—that is, due to the difference in activities such as breathing and so forth—the vital breath becomes fivefold, consisting of five modes.

He shows precisely the different modifications [of the breath] with the words "prāṇa" and so forth. The meaning is that those very modifications are denoted by such terms as "prāṇa" and the rest. || 22 ||
Commentary (a0): By those particles of dust from the ether and so forth; "vṛtti" means subsistence or existence. || 22 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He now demonstrates the purpose for which the creation of the elements beginning with space and ending with the vital breaths was described:
"By means of the five organs of perception, the five organs of action, the five vital breaths, the mind, and the intellect..."
The subtle body, composed of seventeen constituents, is called the *liṅga*. || 23 ||

"Buddhi" refers to cognitions, which are acts of knowledge; "karmāṇi" means activities; and the sense organs that produce those are the "buddhīndriyāṇi" (sense organs) and "karmendriyāṇi" (action organs)—this is the meaning. The "buddhikarmeṃdriyaprāṇāḥ" are the sense organs, action organs, and vital breaths; their "pañcakāni" are the five groups thereof.

Together with the mind (*manas*), which consists of deliberation, and the intellect (*buddhi*), which consists of determination—thus by these seventeen, numbering seventeen, the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*) [is formed].
It exists. He states another name for that very thing: "that is its mark" (talliṅgam). The meaning is that it is so described in the Vedāntas. || 23 ||
Commentary on Sūtra 1:

Having thus described the production of the causal complex of the *liṅga-śarīra*, which is also called "subtle," [the author] now states that it is indeed a collection of these [components], beginning with the word "buddhi. By the term "buddhi," only the valid cognitions (*pramā*) regarding objects such as sound, which are produced by the internal and external senses, are meant. Similarly, by the word "karma"...

Nor is it merely the activity of speech and so forth. Now, one might object: "This subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), consisting of a collection of seventeen elements including the organs of knowledge and the rest, is the effect of the unevolved (*apañcīkṛta*) elements; therefore, although it is not accessible through the means of perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), how can the vital breath (*prāṇa*) contained within it—which is likewise [imperceptible]—be perceived by touch through the delimitation of the mouth, nose, and other parts? This is true. Having raised this very doubt, it was resolved in my work, the *Advaitādhikaraṇacintāmaṇi*.

In the fourth cluster (*guccha*) of the second section (*kāṇḍa*) titled *Avirodha* within the *Mālāprabhā*, in the commentary on the sixth topical heading (*adhikaraṇa*) beginning with the words “And [the soul] is atomic” (*aṇuśca*), it is said:

“Now, while it may be granted that the sense organs—appearing as ‘mine,’ namely mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), thought (*citta*), ego (*abhimāna*), and the ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose, speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals—are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) and thus manifest solely to the Witness (*sākṣin*), how then is it with the vital breath (*prāṇa*)? As for its upward movement...”

Since that which consists of exhalation is experienced through tactile perception by means of the hand, fingers, and so forth, via the opening of the mouth and nostrils, it would—like external air—be manifest only to the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*). Nor should it be argued that this has already been answered in the previous section by the statement beginning with "by this [fact] of its being un-pañcīkṛta," for even there a question remains. To explain: is external air merely an auxiliary (*anugrāhaka*) to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), or rather...

The collective vital breath (*samaṣṭiprāṇa*) belongs to the collective individual soul (*samaṣṭijīva*), which is otherwise named *sūtrātman* and *Hiraṇyagarbha*. It is not the former [the external air]. This is because the individual vital breath (*vyaṣṭiprāṇa*) is an effect produced from a collection of the *rajas* portions of the five subtle great elements—sound and so forth—which have been quintuplicated (*pañcīkṛta*); thus, it is dependent solely upon that [collective soul]. On the other hand, the external air is produced by the quintuplication of the remaining fivefold portion of the subtlest (*tamas*) part of those aforementioned five subtle great elements; therefore, it consists of half a portion of the subtlest aerial *tamas* element and the other half consisting of similar elements.

[The first alternative is rejected] because, since [the individual vital breaths] consist of parts distinguished by being one-eighth of the eight [components of *tuṣṭi*], it is impossible for them to be its cause, and they lack the capacity to favor it. Nor is the second [alternative tenable]; for, while one must speak of the relationship between the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and collective (*samaṣṭi*) vital breaths as that of parts and whole (*avayava-avayavin-bhāva*), on the contrary, just as parts are the cause of the whole, it would follow that the internal (*ādhyātmika*) vital breath alone would be the cause of the cosmic (*adhidaivika*) vital breath. [This is untenable for the collective vital breath...]

Furthermore, because this [air] is produced from a specific aggregate of the rajasic portions of the five subtle elements— consisting of unevolved (apañcīkṛta) subtle sound and so forth— it lacks the capacity to be an object of tactile perception as defined above.
Therefore, if you argue that the system of the logicians alone is superior, namely that "prāṇa is the air moving within the body," and so forth—
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya.
In the chapter titled *Tattvaviveka*,

it is stated that according to the aforementioned method, although the vital breath (*prāṇa*)— being an effect of the five great elements in their unevolved state (*apañcīkṛta*) like the internal organs— is extremely subtle and possesses a middling dimension such that it is perceptible only to the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), it is nonetheless an object of tactile perception for all people through its delimitation by the mouth and nostrils.

Generally, although the gross body is an effect of the five great elements in their quintuplicated (*pañcīkṛta*) state, it consists predominantly of the earthly portion; yet, because even this earthly portion necessarily requires the specific integration of portions from the other four elements— ether and so forth— and because its aerial portion is quintuplicated and thus gross enough to be perceptible by touch, it possesses, along with the *prāṇa*, a similarity characterized by the aforementioned excellence of the power of action as long as it remains connected to the present body.

By virtue of the will of the Lord, past karma (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth, [the vital air] becomes identical with that [body], and thus has that very thing as its object. Since the air that serves as the cause of the gross body is *pañcīkṛta* (five-fold), it is entirely appropriate for it to be external. Just as in the view of other schools, terrestrial fire is not perceptible by the eye at the very moment of its production unless it has attained identity with wood and the like, so too in the Advaita view, the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—only when it has attained identity with the air that is the cause of the body—is capable of the aforementioned perceptibility.

Thus, what scent of contradiction could there be here? Just as, according to the view of others, smoke and the like are called a *liṅga* (probans) because they are "liṅgyate"—that is, they are made known or indicated by fire and so forth—so too this [object] is called a *liṅga* because it makes the Witness known by being directly manifested (*sākṣādbhāsya*) by Him. This is the meaning. || 23 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus described the subtle body, he now shows another state of the Prājña and Īśvara resulting from the identification with that [subtle body]:
"There, through identification, the Prājña attains the state of Taijasa."
The Lord [attains] the state of Hiraṇyagarbha; of those two, there is both individuality and totality.

Regarding the term "the wise one" (*prājña*): the "wise one" is the individual soul (*jīva*) whose limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is ignorance (*avidyā*) characterized by impure *sattva*. In that state, through the conceit of identity with the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*)—which is indicated by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and denoted by the word "light" (*tejas*)—he attains the state of being "Taijasa," that is, the name Taijasa.
The "Lord" (*īśa*) is the Supreme Lord whose limiting adjunct is *māyā* characterized by pure *sattva*. In that body, through the conceit "I am [this]," he attains the state of Hiraṇyagarbha.

The phrase "attains the designation of Hiraṇyagarbha" is to be supplied [to the verse]. Since the Taijasa and Hiraṇyagarbha are identical in their identification with the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra), one might ask:

what is the basis for the distinction between them? To this, he says: "Of those two. The meaning is that the distinction between the Taijasa and Hiraṇyagarbha arises precisely because one is the individual (vyaṣṭi) and the other is the collective (samaṣṭi). || 24 ||

I. Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, let it be granted that such things as the production of the subtle body—which serves as the instrument for the experience of the individual soul (jīva)—occur; nevertheless, even though there exists the state of being an individual soul (*jīvatva*), which consists of a reflection in the intellect (*vidyā*) dominated by impure *sattva* and delimited by root-nescience (*mūlāvidyā*) transformed into the form of the quality of *tamas*, [the following objection remains]... [previous argument].

With regard to this, the first half of the verse beginning with "Prājña" settles the question of whether or not there is a distinct designation for the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*)— just as there are other technical names like "Prājña," which are based on *yoga* (etymological derivation) and *rūḍhi* (conventional usage)— due to its having slightly more limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) than the causal body (*kāraṇaśarīra*). Here, "egoism" (*abhimāna*) is defined as a non-difference that tolerates difference, such as in the superimposition [of redness] upon a crystal, as in the expression "the crystal is red."

[The state of being] *sāttvika* is indeed identity (*tādātmya*) itself. Regarding "being *taijasa*": the meaning is that it possesses the designation *taijasa* because it arises through the conceit of the aforementioned identity with the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the predominance of *sattva*, which is the nature of light denoted by the word "fire" (*tejas*), and because of the Śruti stating, "The second foot is *taijasa*.

Now, one might object: "Granted that it has this other designation, nevertheless, its status as *taijasa* is due solely to the predominance of the fire known as bile (*pitta*), which generates delusion, and not due to what was stated [above]."
If it is argued that this is because the dream-state, which is characterized by delusion (*bhrama*), is seen to belong only to the *taijasa* [state], we say no.

For in the commentary on the eighth verse of the *Siddhāntabindu*, beginning with "Neither waking nor dream nor deep sleep for me," it is stated that the *taijasa*, who identifies with the dream, has the quality of *sattva* as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). As it says: "Thus, in the case of the self (*adhyātma*), there is the *taijasa*; in the case of the objective world (*adhibhūta*), Hiraṇyagarbha; and in the case of the divine (*adhidaiva*)..."

Viṣṇu; with respect to the self (*adhyātma*), he is the dream state; with respect to the divine (*adhidaiva*), he is protection; with respect to the elemental (*adhibhūta*), he is the quality of goodness (*sattvaguṇa*). The detailed exposition of this is to be found in the commentary *Nyāyaratnāvalī*; this is the direction [for further study]. Now, if it is argued that because the individual soul (*jīva*) possesses different designations due to its various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there must be external causes such as the ears and so forth, and internal organs such as the mind, intellect, and so forth—this is the meaning.
Not [the first chapter] [[page 33-to-33]]]

Regarding the point that the Lord must indeed be admitted to possess a single uniform nature because His limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is pure, the author states this in the second half of the verse beginning with "hiraṇya": [He is] like gold... [and so forth]. The detailed explanation follows.

The word "dyataḥ" (shining/manifesting) is to be supplied here as well and applied accordingly. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: through the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of identity with the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) in its entirety, even the Lord (*īśa*) attains the state of Hiraṇyagarbha.
When there is an expectation for a reason in this regard, he indicates it with the final quarter of the verse: "of those two" (*tayoḥ*). The meaning is:

because of that state [of being] which consists of the individual (*vyaṣṭi*), characterized by distinct limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and the collective (*samaṣṭi*), characterized by the aggregate of limiting adjuncts. This is because it was stated previously: "from which it is emitted."
The connection [is as follows]: thus, in this view, the point is that Hiraṇyagarbha and Virāj are merely limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the Lord (Īśvara). || 24 ||
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: He states the reason why the Lord is the totality (samaṣṭi) and individual souls (jīvas) are the partial manifestations (vyaṣṭi):
"The Lord is the totality because of His realization of identity with the Self of all."
Because of the absence of that [universal totality], those others are designated by the term "individual" (vyaṣṭi). || 25 ||

Regarding the term "universal aggregate" (*samaṣṭi*): Īśa, that is, Īśvara or Hiraṇyagarbha, becomes the universal aggregate through the realization of identity with his own self—that is, through the knowledge of oneness (*ekatva*) consisting in the realization of identity with himself—due to being the self of all *taijasa* beings who possess the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) as their limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Other individual souls (*jīva*) than that Īśvara, however, are designated by the term "individual aggregate" (*vyaṣṭi*) because of the absence of that state—the absence of such realization of identity. ||25||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: what is the basis for the aforementioned designations such as "individual" (*vyaṣṭi*) and so forth, as well as their etymological derivations? To this, he says:

"The aggregate" (*samaṣṭi*). The meaning is: the Lord (*īśa*), who is the conscious self reflected in the aforementioned *māyā*, as delimited by the state of Hiraṇyagarbha—characterized by the conceit of being the presiding deity over the entire collection of subtle bodies (*sūkṣmaśarīra*). [He is the one] reflected in all those respective individual ignorance-states (*avidyā*) delimited by all those respective subtle bodies (*liṅgaśarīra*).

The meaning is: "of those whose infinite conscious self is not distinct from [the Lord]. Regarding the word *sva* (one's own): here, the term *sva* is used for the purpose of excluding the pure [Self]. Even though only that much [the Self] is grasped, the truth is that the term is employed in its collective sense (*samuccita*) in order to avoid the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of the definition] to kinsmen and others, because one identifies with one's own kinsman as the Self. Thus, the meaning is: "due to the conceit of non-difference that tolerates difference with respect to such a qualified *sva*. The rest [is as follows]:...
But this is indeed clear. || 25 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus shown the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) and its presiding deities, Taijasa and Hiraṇyagarbha, he speaks as follows in order to establish the production of the gross body (sthūlaśarīra) and so forth, by describing the process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa):
"For the sake of that experience, and for the birth of the locus of experiencing destiny..."
The Blessed One quintuplicates each element, beginning with space.

For their enjoyment: the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, who is fully endowed with the qualities of sovereignty and the rest, again and again— for the sake of the enjoyment of those individual souls, that is,

for the very birth of objects of enjoyment and the bodies that serve as the locus of enjoyment— brings about the production of the five elements beginning with space (viyat), making each one of them fivefold (pañcīkaroti) for the arising of enjoyments such as food and drink, and for the birth of the four classes of bodies, such as the womb-born (*jarāyuja*).
That which consists of five elements makes [the body] consist of five elements as it is being produced. || 26 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, even if this were so, one might ask: "In the absence of objects of enjoyment and bodies for enjoyment, how can there be the establishment of those who enjoy? To this, he says: "For their enjoyment" (*tadbhogāya*). The meaning is that the Blessed Lord (*Bhagavān*), characterized by the sixfold attributes such as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and others, is the Supreme Lord (*Parameśvara*). He "five-folds" (*pañcīkaroti*) ether and the other elements—which consist of five remaining portions of *tamas* related to Him—impliedly. Although they are not five-fold in themselves, by virtue of being composed of those [portions], they become five-fold according to the method to be described.
That is to say, it extends [the universe] as that which appears as consisting of the five elements. The rest has a meaning that is not obscure. || 26 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question, "How can each one consist of five parts?", he says:
"Having first divided each one into two, and then again into four..."
Through their conjunction with their own and other secondary portions, they become five each.

"Dvidhā" (twofold): the word "dvidhā," uttered by way of *tantra* (repetition) for each individual element beginning with space (*viyat*), means having made it twofold, that is, having made it possessed of two parts. Furthermore, having again and again made each first part fourfold, that is, possessed of four parts—so it continues.
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
titled *Tattvaviveka*.

It is joined. By means of their respective second parts—namely, whichever is the gross second portion of each of the four other elements from among themselves—the first portions of the four [elements] are joined one by one with each of those [second parts]. Thus, ether and the others each become fivefold in nature. || 27 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "How can each of the five elements, such as space and the rest, possess a fivefold nature even while their own essential nature remains undestroyed?

Anticipating this doubt, he reveals the manner in which it occurs by saying, "dviveti" (as two). Here too, just as in the production of the subtle body and its constituent materials, the efficient cause is the volition of Īśvara, which consists of a modification of Māyā. And this being so, the Supreme Lord, whose will is true, [accomplishes the task] by mere volition as described.

Or rather: having divided each individual element, such as space and the rest, into two parts; and having further divided the first of those two parts into four; [then] "with their own respective [parts]" means together with the remaining second halves produced by that division from each respective distinct element denoted by the word "own. Through this conjunction—that is, through the merging—those five great elemental entities [become ten], from the half-parts of space and the others.
The connection is that it arises from the other eighth parts as well, such as space and so forth. || 27 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus explained the quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa), he shows the category of effects produced by those elements: "By them [is formed] the cosmic egg (aṇḍa); therein, the world, which arises as the locus for experience and the objects of enjoyment."
Hiraṇyagarbha becomes Vaiśvānara within this gross body.
Those consisting of fire (taijasa) have attained the state of the universe as gods, animals, humans, and so forth. || 28 ||

Regarding the term *tairaṇḍa*: from those five-fold compounded (*pañcīkṛta*) elements, which serve as the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), the Brahmāṇḍa, is produced. Within that Brahmāṇḍa, there are the worlds (*bhuvana*): the seven worlds beginning with Bhūmi situated in the upper portion, and the seven netherworlds (*pātāla*) beginning with Atala situated below the earth.
And within those worlds, there are foodstuffs such as grain suitable for consumption by various living beings, as well as bodies appropriate to each respective world.

By the command of the Lord (*Īśvara*), [the gross elements] arise from those very same five-fold compounded elements (*pañcīkṛta-bhūta*). Having thus described the production of the gross body (*sthūla-śarīra*), he states that for Hiraṇyagarbha—who possesses the conceit (*abhimāna*) of those gross bodies in his collective form (*samaṣṭi-rūpa*)—there is the designation *Vaiśvānara*; whereas for those who possess the conceit of each individual gross body in their distributive forms (*vyaṣṭi-rūpa*), known as the Taijasas, there is the designation *Viśva*. He says: "Hiraṇyagarbha. Abiding in this gross body, Hiraṇyagarbha...
The *nyagarbha* indeed becomes *vaiśvānara*; those very *taijasa*s existing therein become *viśva*. He states their internal subdivisions as "gods, animals," and so forth. || 28 ||

The commentary on verse 1 states its result with the half-verse beginning with "By them" (taih): "The egg" (aṇḍa) refers to the sphere of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍagolaka). Regarding "worlds" (bhuvana):

the meaning is that there occurs the production of bodies known as egg-born, womb-born, sweat-born, and soil-born, which have as their objects the fourteen worlds, sound, and so forth. Now, [one might object]: darkness—

[Objection: How can the five elements—which consist merely of the most subtle portions remaining from the primary *prakṛti* after the production of the five gross elements—be perceivable by the senses, given that they are merely products of the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*)? [Reply: This is not so. Just as there is power in the mantras recited by a magician, there is indeed such power in the quintuplication performed by the Lord (*Īśvara*). Thus, even though the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) and the like are not perceivable by the senses because they are not composed [of gross matter] in that way, there is no contradiction; everything is thus clarified. In this manner, with half [the verse], Brahmāṇḍa—

Having described the origin [of the individual], he states—by means of the first half of the verse beginning with "hiraṇya"—that the Lord, who has attained the state of Hiraṇyagarbha through the conceit of identity with the collective subtle body, also receives the name Vaiśvānara (also known as Virāj) by means of the conceit of identity with the aforementioned cosmic egg, which consists of the collective gross body, just as before. Here, the reading "abhavat" (became) is more appropriate; the reading "yātaḥ" (gone/attained) will likewise be explained immediately below.

[This is] because of the [word] *māṇatvāt* (due to being a vital breath), and because the reading *bhavet* (it would be) is the result of a scribe’s error. Now, if this is so, then even for those previously mentioned *taijasa*s—who identify with the subtle body known as the *vyaṣṭi-liṅga*—some other designation must indeed be assigned based on their identification with various gross individual bodies (*vyaṣṭi-sthūla-deha*). Therefore, he states this with the third quarter: "by the *taijasa*s. He describes their internal subdivisions with the fourth quarter, beginning with "the gods" (*deva*), etc. [The text continues with] *karma*...
"Vaiśvānara came into being"— this reading follows Acyutarāya’s commentary.
[Page 35] First Section.
Accompanied by two commentaries.

The mention of animals (*tiryak*) after the mention of gods is due solely to the equality of their lack of qualification [for yoga], and not due to a gradation based on *sāttvika* and other qualities. If that were the case, the reading would have necessarily been "gods, mortals, cows, and so forth" (*deva-martya-gavādayaḥ*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), those who are merged in the bodyless state (*videha*) and those merged in primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*) are included. The venerable Patañjali set forth these in the sūtra: "For those merged in the bodyless state and those merged in primordial nature, [samādhi] arises from the latent impression of [prior] existence" (*bhavapratyayo videhaprakṛtilayānām*). This was explained by Nārāyaṇatīrtha: "This too is *saṃprajñāta* [samādhi]."

The causal condition (*pratyaya*) is of two kinds: that which has means (*upāya*) as its cause and that which has existence (*bhava*) as its cause. Among these, he states that the one caused by existence is to be abandoned by those seeking liberation—beginning with the word "existence" (*bhava*). Those who have apprehended either the elements (*bhūta*) or the senses (*indriya*) as the Self, and whose internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are permeated by the meditation upon them, become merged into the elements and senses after the fall of the body; they are "bodiless" (*videha*), being devoid of the physical body composed of the seven constituents—flesh, blood, hair, fat, bone, marrow, and semen. In this same way, [they merge into] the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the Great Principle (*mahat*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and the five...

Having stated that those who have realized any one of the *tanmātras* as the Self and, through meditation upon them, become merged in the causal principles such as *prakṛti* are called "merged in nature" (*prakṛtilaya*), it is therefore said in the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "Those who contemplate the Unmanifest remain here for ten *manvantaras*; but having attained the attributeless *puruṣa*, no measure of time exists [for them]. (28)

66. Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Now, with two verses, he describes by means of an illustration the manner in which those living beings who have attained the designation of "the universe" fall into transmigratory existence due to their lack of knowledge of reality.
They look toward the external, being devoid of the realization of the reality that lies within.
They perform action for the sake of experience, and they experience in order to perform further action. || 29 ||

"Those [look] away. Those [beings], beginning with the gods, are perceivers of what is external; they perceive only external objects such as sound and so forth, but not the inward Self (pratyag-ātman). This is according to the Śruti: "The Self-existent pierced the openings outward; therefore one looks outward, and not at the inner Self" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 4.1). Now, one might object that the logicians and others do know the Self as distinct from the body; anticipating this, [the text continues]: even though they know the Self...
Thus, with the intention that [the individual soul] nevertheless does not know the reality established by the Śruti, he says: "The inner self" (*pratyak*), etc. Regarding "performing":

for this very reason, having presided over human and other bodies for the sake of enjoyment—the experience of pleasure and so forth—they perform actions appropriate to those respective bodies. (The word "action" [*karma*] is in the singular to denote the class. Furthermore, in order to perform action again, they enjoy the various fruits through divine and other bodies. As for the fruit—

Because in the absence of experience, there would be no possibility of desire for those respective things of the same class, and consequently, no possibility of performing the means to achieve them. || 29 ||
Commentary (a0ṭī0): Now, what follows from that? He says: "They [are] *parāg*. These refer to the gods and others. Regarding the term *parāg*:

according to the Śruti, "The Self-existent pierced the openings outward; therefore one looks outward, not at the inner self. Here, "Self-existent" (*svayaṃbhū*) means the Self itself is the source of existence (*bhūḥ* = *sattā*).

The meaning is: "He to whom [they belong] is the Supreme Self. *Khāni* refers to the sense organs (*indriyāṇi*). They are called *parāñci* because they extend (*añcanti*) or illuminate only toward the external (*parāṃsi*). He "separated" (*vyatṛṇat*) them; that is to say, he made them such that their nature is to perceive only what is directed outward (*parāk*), toward the external. The reason for this is stated as "the inward" (*pratyak*). Therefore, even though they are thus oriented toward the external, how does transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) come about? To this, he says with the second half of the verse: "of those acting... [and so on]. Regarding the word *śabda*— [End of provided fragment]

It is precisely out of a longing for the enjoyment of objects such as women and the like that they perform rituals such as the Agnihotra for the sake of worldly experience; likewise, they perform those very actions immediately and through their residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) in another birth, solely for the purpose of performing them again. The grammatical connection is that they enjoy those objects by means of their wives and others. (29)
Like insects in a river, they quickly moved from one whirlpool to another.
Moving from birth to birth, one never attains liberation.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Thus existing, those living beings—like insects fallen into the current of a river, quickly moving from one whirlpool to another—do not obtain relief or happiness; in the same way, quickly passing from birth to birth, they do not obtain happiness at all. || 30 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭī0): Thereafter, he clarifies the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra), which is the result of that [ignorance], by means of an illustration, beginning with the words "In a river" (nadyām). "Nirvṛti" refers to ultimate, absolute happiness. || 30 ||
