Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus described the occurrence of worldly existence, he first presents an illustration in order to show the means for its cessation.
The *Pañcadaśī*, composed by Vidyāraṇya,
has been extracted from it by that treasury of compassion, following the ripening of his virtuous deeds.
Having reached the shade of the tree on the shore called Tattvaviveka, they rest there at their ease. || 31 ||

Regarding the phrase "satkarma": those insects, through the ripening of their good deeds—that is, the ripening of merit previously acquired—were rescued by a certain compassionate and distinguished person; having been drawn out from the current of the river and reaching the shade of a tree on the bank, they rested as much as possible for their comfort. || 31 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might ask: "Since even gods and others cannot easily escape this, when will there be liberation from saṃsāra—which, like the example of the insect, results solely in the fruit of suffering born from the separation from the desired and union with the undesired, and is characterized by the endless cycle of birth and death, consisting of the delusion of duality? To this, he first clarifies that point through the illustration—starting with the words "satkarma" (good action). This [illustration] is also to be applied later to the subject of the analogy (*dārṣṭāntika*). Thus, here, regarding the epithet "by the treasure-house of compassion" (*karuṇānidhinā*):
The word "by some man" (kenacit puṃsā) is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 31 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, he applies the meaning established by the illustration to the subject of the illustration:
"Having thus received instruction from a teacher who perceives reality..."
Through the discernment of the five sheaths, one attains supreme liberation.

Regarding the phrase "the instruction": in the manner thus described, having obtained—that is, having accomplished—the instruction from a teacher who is a Guru and a seer of reality (tattvadarśin), one who possesses the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman as non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which serves as the means for knowing the meaning of statements such as "That Thou Art" (*tattvamasi*); and having accomplished this through the discrimination of the five sheaths (*pañcakośaviveka*), that is, through the discrimination of the five sheaths beginning with food (*anna*), as will be described—[one attains the goal].
Through discernment, they attain supreme bliss, which is the happiness of liberation. || 32 ||

Commentary (a0ṭī0): Now, he reveals that [instruction] regarding the subject at hand (*dāṣṭantika*) with the words "upadeśam" (the instruction). Just like the aforementioned insect, the first quarter of the previous verse also carries over here. "Those" refers to the living beings under discussion, such as gods and others. "Sad" (the True) refers to the collection of obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and expiatory (*prāyaścitta*) rites prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis, which are mixed with even a small portion of the Tantras performed with exclusive devotion to the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*), preceded by freedom from all desires for rewards and prohibitions accumulated over infinite births.

The meaning is: "by the grace of the Lord," which consists in being oriented toward the fruits of one's own specific duties (svadharma) appropriate to one's respective caste, stage of life (āśrama), and so forth. Regarding the word *tattva*: it refers to one who is superior and established in Brahman;

that is to say, from such a true guru whose characteristics were previously described in the passage beginning with "he gathers the meaning of the scriptures. "Having obtained instruction" means having heard the great sentences (*mahāvākya*) such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), which have been investigated. "Having attained"—this refers to the five [sheaths].

Because the gross body and so forth—denoted by terms such as "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and defined as individual manifestations (*vyaṣṭi*)—act as concealers of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is non-dual Brahman, just as the husk conceals the grain of rice;
and because these three bodies, like leather or chaff, must be separated from the Self whose nature is described as the bestower of existence and so on;
[the yogi] thereby attains—that is, reaches—the supreme, intense bliss of liberation, which is the state of the non-dual bliss of the Self.

The connection is as follows: regarding this, the venerable and eminent author of the Vārttika says: "Through the very path of the cognition that negates unreal objects and so forth—which arises from ignorance regarding the target characterized by 'Being' (Sat) and the rest—one attains what was to be attained solely through the destruction of ignorance. Thus, having known it, one knows it; being liberated, one is liberated; it ceases, and having ceased, it [remains ceased].
I swear this three times to you. (32)
Rāma’s Commentary: In response to the inquiry as to what those five sheaths beginning with food are, he teaches them:
"Food, vital breath, mind, intellect, and bliss—these are the five."
Enveloped by those sheaths, one's own self, through forgetfulness, enters into the cycle of worldly existence.

"Food is life. Food, life-force (*prāṇa*), mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and bliss (*ānanda*) are the five sheaths (*kośa*). "Intellect" here means discernment (*vijñāna*). He states the reason why these—food and the others—are designated by the term "sheath": "by them," etc. Enveloped—that is, covered—by those sheaths, the Self, which is one's own true nature, goes into *saṃsṛti*—the cycle of birth and so forth—due to forgetfulness, that is, through the forgetting of its own true nature.
The First Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

This is clear. Just as a sheath (kośa) is a cause of affliction for a silkworm by virtue of being its cover, so too food and the rest are called "sheaths" because they are causes of affliction for the Self by virtue of covering its non-dual bliss and other attributes; this is the meaning. 33.

Commentary (a0 ṭī0): Now, one might ask, "What are these five sheaths? To this, he points them out with the words beginning with "food" (*anna*). Furthermore, one might ask, "What is the reason for applying the term 'sheath' (*kośa*) to the gross body and so forth, which are denoted by the words 'food' and the rest? To this, he says with the words beginning with "by them" (*tair*). The intended meaning is that just as in common usage the word 'sheath' is applied to things like leather covers that enclose a sword, so too is it used here. Or, as in the case of a sheath...

The intention is as follows: just as a sheath produced by a *śakāra* insect becomes the cause of suffering for that [insect], so too, although food and other elements are produced from the Self through the sequence beginning with space (*ākāśa*) by the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), they become causes of suffering for that [Self] and are thus designated by the term "sheaths" (*kośa*). He states what follows from this in the passage beginning with "having forgotten" (*vismṛtya*).
Regarding this, the ancient commentator explained: "by forgetting one's own true nature. In that context, since memory pertains to what has been experienced—

Based on Patañjali’s statement, "Memory is the non-loss of what has been experienced," and the Logicians’ (Tārkika) statement, "Memory is knowledge produced by latent impressions (saṃskāra)," it is established in every respect that memory consists precisely in a mediate modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti) produced by impressions regarding an object previously experienced. Consequently, the category of "forgetfulness" (*vismiti*), which is the absence of such memory, refers to [the failure to recall] Śakuntalā’s marriage by the Gāndharva rite at Kaṇva’s hermitage, the subsequent conception of the fetus, and so forth.

Regarding the forgetting of objects, such as that of Duṣyanta resulting from the curse of Durvāsas as well-known in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts, it is utterly inappropriate to mention it in this context; for such forgetting is necessarily preceded by prior experience, whereas in the realization of Brahman as non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*), all duality is sublated, and thus the very conditions for forgetting do not exist. This is as established in the commentary on the first canto of the *Yogavāsiṣṭha*, concerning the [vision of] Viṣṇu bestowed upon Sanatkumāra.

Furthermore, this is because the acceptance of the curse following the promise, as well as the subsequent instruction regarding his birth in the form of Skanda, are not to be cited as examples, since they are merely the dramatic play (*nāṭya*) of the Lord’s divine sport (*īśvara-līlā*). Otherwise, even the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the non-dual Brahman-Self—which was achieved through such great effort—would result in futility due to the possibility of forgetting it during the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*); and thus, there would follow the consequence of the entire non-dualistic scripture (*advaita-śāstra*) being rendered useless.

Nor should it be argued that Arjuna’s very statement to Śrī Kṛṣṇa—“Delusion is destroyed, memory has been regained by me through Your grace, O Acyuta”—expresses that while *smṛti* (memory) pertains to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), its opposite, *avidyā* (ignorance), is characterized by forgetfulness (*vismṛti*). This is because, in that context, as in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad passage, “Upon the attainment of memory, there is the loosening of all knots,” the term *smṛti* is used figuratively to denote the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of non-duality itself. Thus, it is a matter of necessity (*agatyā*).

Even if one were to accept that [the Self] is the agent by virtue of its human-like nature—despite such a claim being impossible—according to the maxim "let the wicked man be satisfied," nevertheless, the root cause of the specific transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) characterized by birth, death, and so forth, as prescribed in the subsequent statement "he enters into transmigration" (*saṃsṛtiṃ vrajet*), resides exclusively in the fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) situated within the fifth sheath known as the *ānandamaya*, as established by the preceding statement: "The Self is covered by these sheaths. It is in this [ignorance] alone that [transmigration] is found to be indivisibly rooted.

Furthermore, since the phrase "obscured" (*āvṛta*) would result in a tautology— given that the obscuration which causes the concealment of limited bliss is already explicitly expressed by the word "obscured" itself— it is not tenable to argue that, just as Arjuna experienced a forgetfulness of Brahman described in the Bhīṣma-parvan, such a thing could also happen to us and others here, based on the fact that the *Anugītā* was taught in the Aśvamedha-parvan (which would otherwise be inexplicable). This is because that [account] intends merely to indicate the extreme rarity of the non-dual knowledge of Brahman (*advaita-brahmavidyā*), according to the aforementioned scripture.

Because it lacks the capacity to subvert a meaning established by such logical principles as "uselessness" (*vaiyarthyādi*), one might ask: what is the significance of the word "forgetting" (*vismṛti*) here? To this it is replied:

"In the ninth month, he becomes complete in all his limbs"—and [the text continues]: "I have died and been born again; I have been born and died again. Indeed, thousands of various wombs have been inhabited by me. Various foods have been eaten, and various breasts have been drunk from. Mothers..."

"Various fathers and friends are seen; and the creature, being afflicted while facing downward, is joined [with suffering]. One should practice Sāṃkhya and Yoga, or [meditate upon] the Puruṣa consisting of twenty-five principles. And then, in the tenth month, it is born—"And once born, touched by the wind, it does not remember that," so says the Nirukta. The word *jaṃtuḥ* means "by creatures" (*jaṃtubhiḥ*). Since it is "joined" (*samanvitaḥ*), it is therefore afflicted.

With my head bowed low, I am resolved that I shall be liberated from this [bondage] either by thoroughly practicing Sāṃkhya preceded by inquiry into Brahman, or Yoga which is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. The "Twenty-fifth" (Pañcaviṃśaka): In relation to the twenty-four principles (tattvas) superimposed as the intellect, the organs of action, the five vital breaths, the four groups of five beginning with sound, the internal organ, ignorance, desire, and karma—the Puruṣa who is their witness is the Twenty-fifth; from this...
[page 38-to-38]
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
titled Tattvaviveka (Discrimination of Reality).

The meaning is that one should promise, "I shall [attain liberation]. And thus, even if the collection of means such as discrimination (*viveka*) has arisen during a particular stay in the womb, the fact that the individual soul (*jīva*) might forget that promise due to the touch of external air, and that through such forgetfulness he would enter—that is, reach—the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), appears to be the intended view of the venerable Guru Vidyāraṇya. || 33 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He explains the natures of those sheaths (kośas) in their proper order:
"The gross body, known as the 'annamayakośa,' arises from the fivefold elements."
In the *liṅga*, however, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) exists along with the rajasic vital breaths and the organs of action.

By means of these one and a half verses beginning with "syātpaṃcīkṛta" and ending with "modāvṛttibhiḥ," [the following is explained]: the gross body produced from the five-fold elements (pañcīkṛtabhūtas), known as "food" (anna) and designated by the term "annamaya," constitutes the sheath (kośa). As for the vital breath (prāṇa), the "prāṇamaya" sheath consists of the five vital airs—prāṇa, apāna, and so forth—which exist within the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) and are characterized by activity (rājasa), being the effects of the quality of passion (rajo-guṇa), along with the organs of action such as speech and the rest.
It would be together with the ten sense organs. || 34 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭī0): Now, it may be granted that even for one born in such a specific state of gestation, through the power of destiny, there might arise the collection of means such as discrimination (*viveka*) and so forth;

and even if there were the undertaking of attaining Brahman through the practice of Sāṃkhya and Yoga performed therein, nevertheless, by the mere touch of the external air associated with worldly people, one might forget [that resolve] and experience the cycle of transmigratory existence characterized by grief and the like born of hunger and other needs. However, all this [occurs within] the five sheaths (*kośa*) described as beginning with the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*).

That it is indeed employed for the purpose of concealment is beyond dispute. Now, are these [states] other than the three gross bodies (sthūla-deha) and so forth previously mentioned as the causes of waking and the rest, or are they of the same nature as them? It cannot be the first, because they are not perceived [as such]. Nor can it be the latter, because there is no correspondence between the number three and the number five. Anticipating this objection, he provides the solution with the two and a half verses beginning with *syāt*. Regarding the word *anne*: "This very person consists of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*)."

This is because of the Vedic scripture: "Born from the semen produced by the food consumed by the ancestors, the body grows by means of food alone; that body is 'consisting of food' (annamaya). This refers to the first sheath, called "food," mentioned in the preceding verse, as explained in the subsequent analysis of the sheaths (*kośaviveka*). Now, with the half-verse beginning with "But in the subtle" (*liṅge tu*), he clarifies the inclusion of the three sheaths beginning with "consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*) within the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*). The word "but" (*tu*) is used to indicate its distinction from what preceded.

The meaning is: "by those consisting of *rajas*" refers to the effects of the aggregate of the quality of *rajas* (passion) previously mentioned, such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth. Likewise, the connection is that the vital breath (*prāṇa*), along with the organs of action which are the individual effects of *rajas*, exists within the *liṅga*—the subtle body known by that name—which is the sheath composed of vital breath (*prāṇamaya-kośa*). || 34 ||
Together with the sattvic sense organs, it consists of the mind and has the nature of reflection.
Together with those very [elements], the intellect (dhī), which consists of consciousness and is of the nature of determination, [arises]. || 35 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: That which was called the mind (*manas*), whose nature is deliberation and which consists of the effect of the *sattva* of the five elements, constitutes the "sheath consisting of mind" (*manomaya-kośa*) when joined with the five organs of knowledge—the ears and so forth—which are the individual effects of the *sattva* of each element.

This is how it connects with the preceding [verse]. Intellect (*dhī*), whose nature is certainty, is the *buddhi*, which is likewise of the form of the effect of that very *sattva*; [it is joined] with those same aforementioned organs of knowledge.
Together with those very [sheaths], being conjoined, there would be the sheath consisting of consciousness, which is called "consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya). || 35 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭī0): By such organs—that is, by the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*) which are the effects of the quality of *sattva* manifested individually as space and so forth, as previously described—the sheath consisting of mind (*manomaya-kośa*), whose nature is deliberation (*vimarśa*)—that is, whose essence is inquiry characterized by resolve and doubt—exists within the subtle body (*liṅga*). Likewise, by those very aforementioned organs of knowledge, along with the intellect (*dhī*) whose nature is determination, the sheath consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya-kośa*) also exists in the subtle body; this is the connection with the preceding [verse]. Here...

The point is that the presence of the organs of knowledge (jñānendriyas) within both the mental sheath (manomaya-kośa) and the intellectual sheath (vijñānamaya-kośa) is due solely to their being observed through the dual functions of doubt and certainty. || 35 ||
In its causal state, it is the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), characterized by functions such as joy and so forth.
Through identification with each respective sheath, the Self becomes composed of that very sheath. || 36 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Within *avidyā*, which constitutes the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*), there exists that which is impure *sattva*; this [is what] consists of *moha* and so forth.
[Page 39] First Chapter.

Accompanied by the two commentaries; [the self] consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is that which is joined with the specific types of happiness called *priya*, *moda*, and *pramoda*, which are produced by the sight of the beloved, the acquisition of what is desired, and the enjoyment thereof, along with their respective mental states (*vṛtti*). The one consisting of bliss—*ānandamaya*.

"It might be argued that the sheath (kośa) is what is meant. But if the gross body and so forth are indeed denoted by the terms "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and the rest, then how do we explain the sequence beginning with, "This person, verily,

consists of the essence of food" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1.1), followed by, "Different from this one consisting of the essence of food is the inner self consisting of breath" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.2.1), and "Different from that is the inner self consisting of mind" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.3.1)?

Having raised the objection—given that such [scriptural passages] exist, how can it be said that the Self is denoted by words such as *annamaya* (consisting of food)?—he replies with the word "tattat" (that respective). The inner Self (*pratyagātman*), because of its identity with each respective sheath (*kośa*) and because of the conceit of identity (*tādātmyābhimāna*) with each respective sheath, [is designated as such]. Thus he says: "tattat...
[and so forth]. The inner Self, through its identity with each respective sheath—that is, through the conceit of identity with each respective sheath—is [designated as such].

The meaning is that the Self may consist of this or that sheath at the time of empirical transaction (vyavahāra), being denoted by terms such as "consisting of food" (annamaya) due to the predominance of the sheath of food and so forth;
the word "but" (tu) is intended to highlight the distinction of the Self from these sheaths. || 36 ||

Commentary (a0ṭī0): He states that in the causal body (*kāraṇaśarīra*), there is only the sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*) by means of the half-verse beginning with "In the cause" (*kāraṇe*). Regarding "joy and so forth" (*modādi*):

along with the modifications (*vṛtti*) occurring during the waking state and others—such as *priya*, *moda*, and *pramoda*, which are produced by the sight of desired objects, the attainment [of them], and their enjoyment—the quality of *sattva* (the predominance of the *sattva-guṇa*) likewise exists in the cause; that is, in the causal body consisting of root-nescience (*mūlāvidyā*), which has transformed into the form of the *tamas-guṇa* during deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and serves as the cause for the waking state and other states.

It should be understood that even when [the world] is delimited by time, there exists the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss) through the modifications (*vṛtti*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) which have as their object the bliss of the Self (*ātman*) that is not known [by the intellect]. Now, let it be granted that the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*), beginning with the *annamaya*, are included within the three bodies characterized as gross (*sthūla*) and so forth; nevertheless, regarding the Self, [it is stated]: "This very person consists of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*).
Different from this one consisting of the essence of food is another inner self consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*). [Then come] the *manomaya*, the *vijñānamaya*, and the *ānandamaya*."

Having raised the objection as to how it is that they consist of those respective sheaths (*kośa*) and serve as their veils, as stated in the Śruti, he provides the resolution with the half-verse beginning "tattad... (36), showing that both facts are established solely through the superimposition of identity (*tādātmyādhyāsa*), which is indicated by the Vedic suffix *mayaṭ*.
Rāma’s Commentary: Raising the objection, "How then can such a Self become Brahman?", he states that it occurs through discrimination from the sheaths by means of positive and negative concomitance:
"Through the discrimination of the five sheaths by means of anvaya and vyatireka."
Then, having extracted his own self from that, he attains the Supreme Brahman. || 37 ||

Regarding the word *anvaya*: by means of the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that will be explained hereafter; or, by means of the discrimination (*viveka*) of the five sheaths (*pañca-kośa*), namely the sheaths beginning with the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*), through the discernment and separation of the inner self (*pratyagātman*); or rather, by separating the Self from the five sheaths beginning with the "consisting of food," having extracted one's own self—the inner self—from those sheaths by means of the intellect (*buddhi*).
Having ascertained the nature of consciousness-bliss, one attains—that is, reaches—the Supreme Brahman characterized as described above; the meaning is that one becomes Brahman itself. ||37||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, even though the cycle of transmigratory existence—characterized by the manifestation of endless duality in the form of a continuous flow of birth and death—is possible through the superimposition of identity with the Self based on the etymological lexicons (*nirukta-kośa*) and beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), [the Self remains] pure consciousness (*dṛṅmātra*) characterized as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) that sublates all objects of perception.

The established doctrine of the Advaita school is that liberation, which consists in the cessation of that [ignorance], has as its means the sublation of the duality of ignorance and its effects—such as its objects and substrates—which occurs simultaneously with the arising of unimpeded immediate valid knowledge (*aparokṣapramā*) produced solely by the great Vedāntic Mahāvākyas investigated within one's own respective branch of scripture, having as its object the identity of the individual self with Brahman (*ātmaikya*). Furthermore, that realization has already been indicated below in such passages as "This Self is supreme bliss" (*iyam ātmā parānandaḥ*); so what is the point of this [present] elaboration?

If it is argued that [this is unnecessary] because the same has already been established by the introductory text (*vyutpādana-grantha*), we reply: True. However, even if the purpose is accomplished for the highest class of practitioners (*uttama-adhikārin*) by that much alone, the subsequent text is meaningful as a grace (*anugrāhaka*) for those of intermediate capacity and others. This is according to the maxim that a scripture proceeds through both concise and detailed expositions.

With this intention, desiring to provide a detailed exposition (*vivaraṇa*) characterized by expansion upon the very realization previously indicated, [the author begins with] "Food is life" (*annaṃ prāṇaḥ*) and so forth, [describing] the *annamaya* and the rest.

Since it is stated that the very veil composed of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) is the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*), once the knowledge of the Self’s distinctness from that [sheath] arises through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that [veil] ceases.
Thus, for the sake of enabling those of middling and lower capacities to quickly engage in the discrimination of the Self according to that method, [the author says]: "ba...
