The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
titled Tattvaviveka (Discrimination of Reality).

By the very words of the venerable *Taittirīyaka* Śruti, which seeks unsurpassed welfare—“The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme”—the state of liberation, characterized by the non-dual Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*) and consisting of the dissolution of all duality, has been clearly revealed. Stating that this alone is the fruit of discrimination (*viveka*), he makes a formal promise (*pratijñā*) to such qualified seekers: “Anvaya... (verse 37).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now he demonstrates the intended positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka):
"In the absence of the gross body, there is the manifestation of the Self in dream."
That [cognition] is positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka); when that [object] appears, other things do not appear. (38)

Regarding the term "non-appearance": when there is the non-appearance—that is, the non-perception—of the gross body, which is the *annamaya-kośa*, during the state of dreaming (*svapna*), that which is the appearance of the Self (*ātman*), the inward-looking witness (*pratyak*), namely its manifestation as the witness of the dream, is the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the Self. In that very state of dreaming, while that [Self] appears—that is, while that Self manifests—there is the non-appearance of the other, meaning the non-perception of the gross body.

The phrase "the negative concomitance (vyatireka) of the gross body" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. In this context, by the words "positive concomitance" (anvaya) and "negative concomitance" (vyatireka), persistence (anuvṛtti) and exclusion (vyāvṛtti) are expressed. || 38 ||

A0 Commentary: Now, one might ask: what indeed are the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) here, by means of which the attainment of Brahman by the individual soul (jīva)—described as occurring in the very moment immediately following the soul’s extraction [from the body] due to the habitual identification with the five sheaths (pañcakośa), consisting of the gross body and so forth, which are the effects of the five great elements produced by beginningless ignorance—is explained? Anticipating this, [the author] first describes the waking state in order to dispel the superimposition (adhyāsa) upon the gross body.

Now, he states that in a dream, there is a persistence (*anvaya*) of the self—which is intended by the term "persistence"—and likewise a cessation (*vyāvartana*) of the gross body, which is intended by the term "exclusion" (*vyatireka*), using the words "amāna" and so forth. Thus, it follows that here, throughout all cases, what is intended by the general definition of "persistence and exclusion" is precisely the nature of persistence and cessation. But this is improper; for in the preceding verse, by the words "persistence" and so forth, [the author] described persistence and so forth as having the individual soul (*jīva*) as their agent.

Since the *yojaka* (the unifier) describes the attainment of Brahman in the moment immediately following the moment of separating the Self from that which is the material cause for the superimposition of identity—superimposition brought about by beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*) through the process of discriminating the five sheaths (*pañcakośaviveka*)—one must necessarily state that the Self possesses a definition of Brahman whose essential nature is neither deficient nor excessive.

However, that would not be possible at all; for, according to the methods already stated and those yet to be stated, it is declared that the Self persists even in states such as dreaming, whereas Brahman is pure.

Regarding this, the venerable author of the Vārttika has characterized [Brahman] as pure non-dual consciousness alone, devoid of all attributes such as exclusion and inclusion, stating: "That entity which is neither excluded nor inclusive is called Brahman; the true meaning of Brahman would be unattainable here if there were a second entity.
This is in accordance with the Śruti: "Just as pure water poured into pure water becomes exactly like that, so too, O Gautama, does the self of the sage who knows become."

Furthermore, identity is possible only when the purified individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman possess a nature that is neither deficient nor excessive. Now, one might object: according to the maxim that "even if one exists, the other two do not," just as the *āhavanīya* fire—though it may exist as a common fire ignited by food—is excluded from the oblation prescribed by the scripture "he offers in the *āhavanīya*" because it lacks the specific consecrations such as the formal establishment (*ādhāna*), so too, although persistence (*anuvṛtti*) exists in the Self, [identity] would be excluded due to the lack of persistence qualified by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).

If it is argued that by its very nature, the fitness for the state of Brahman is indeed appropriate, we say no; for in the aforementioned Vārttika, there is no intention to express a conjunction of both the absence of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and the absence of inclusion (*anugati*). If that were the case, then by the very use of the negative particle (*nañ*) in the expression "not excluded and not included" (*avyāvṛttānugatam*)—where "excluded and included" (*vyāvṛttānugatam*) refers to the combination of these two—the intended meaning would already be established. Thus, [the term] *avyāvṛttānanugata*...

It would not be employed [in that sense] at all; therefore, it must be said that in that context, the referent of the word *brahman* is precisely the non-dual reality of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) characterized by the absence of all attributes such as exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and persistence (*anuvṛtti*).

Likewise, for me too, let the referent of the word *ātman* be the immediate pure consciousness (*pratyak-cinmātra*) characterized by its persistence through all states from waking up to deep meditation (*samādhi*), as it is fit for identity with Brahman. If that were the case, then regarding the non-appearance of the gross body and so forth during the dissolution of states such as dreaming...

Why should it be necessary to state that the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of the Self from the three bodies— characterized by the non-perception of the gross body and the others— and likewise the inclusion (*anvaya*) of the Self therein— characterized by its perception— is for the purpose of subverting the superimposition of identity with the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) consisting of the three bodies? For, by the mere statement, "I am a Brāhmaṇa, possessed of waking and other states, possessed of vital breaths and so forth,
I am the Self," the reality of the innermost Self as pure consciousness, indicated by all attributes such as Brāhmaṇahood and the rest, [is established] in relation to all states and so forth.
The First Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

Because the accomplishment of the [thirty-two] characteristics is possible, one might ask: "What then is the intended meaning (*tātparya*) here of the venerable feet of the teacher Vidyāraṇya? Listen to the underlying intention (*ākūta*).
Previously, by the words "sound, touch, and so forth are objects of cognition," etc., the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) characterized as the witness of all was purified.

A specific means was employed— briefly stated as "this Self of the *tat* category is supreme bliss," and so forth— to express non-difference with the purified meaning of the *tvam* category; likewise, here, for the sake of bestowing the awakening to the inner Self of absolute non-duality through mutual exchange (*vyatihāra*), there is a mere discernment by means of the persistence of the purified *tvam*-category itself and its exclusion from the body and other such things that have attained identity with it through superimposition, which serves as a means consisting solely of discrimination toward the existence of infinite bliss.

It is stated that this is for the purpose of realizing the state of Brahman—which has become the referent of the word "That" (tat-pada)—within the reality of pure, non-dual consciousness; thus, everything is indeed full of aesthetic relish.
This is the direction [of the argument]. || 38 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus demonstrated the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that establish the gross body as not the Self, he now demonstrates those same concomitances for the purpose of understanding the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) in the same way:
"The positive concomitance (*anvaya*) would be the manifestation of the Self during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), when the subtle body is absent."
But "exclusion" (vyatireka) is said to be the non-appearance of the logical mark when that [object] appears. || 39 ||

Regarding the term "liṅga": in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), during the state of deep sleep, when there is the non-appearance of the *liṅga*—that is, the non-perception of the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*)—the appearance of the Self, its manifestation as the witness (*sākṣin*) of that state, constitutes the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the Self. When there is that appearance—that is, the appearance of the Self—the non-appearance of the *liṅga*, the non-manifestation of the subtle body, is called the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). || 39 ||

Commentary (a0): Thus, having described the persistence (*anvaya*) of the Self in the dream state—characterized by its manifestation as the witness—and the absence (*vyatireka*) of the gross body, which consists of the *annamaya-kośa* and is delimited by the waking state; and since it follows in due order, [the author] now briefly describes the persistence of the Self in deep sleep, characterized by its manifestation, and the absence of the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*), which consists of the triad of sheaths known as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), mind (*manas*), and intellect (*vijñāna*).
Thus, the three marks. || 39 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (rā0 ṭī0): Now, one might object: "Having commenced with the discrimination of the five sheaths (pañcakośa), the discrimination of the subtle body (liṅgadeha) is irrelevant to the subject at hand.
Anticipating this, he states that there is no such irrelevance because the triad of sheaths beginning with the vital-breath-sheath (prāṇamaya) is included within that very [subtle body]:
"Through the discrimination of that [subtle body], the sheaths of vital breath, mind, and intellect become discriminated."
For they are indeed distinguished there merely by the difference in the state of their qualities. || 40 ||

"From the discrimination of that": from the discrimination—that is, the discernment—of that subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), the sheaths (*kośa*) named *prāṇa*, *manas*, and *buddhi* become discriminated, meaning they are separated from the Self. Why is this so? To this he says: "For those... Because for that reason, in that subtle body, [the sheaths] exist merely as different states of the qualities (*guṇa*), that is, merely as different states of the qualities *sattva* and *rajas*, due to the predominance or subordination of the qualities.
The meaning is that they are distinguished and specified separately solely on account of their specific states. || 40 ||

The commentary (a0ṭī0) states its fruit with the word "tat" (that). The meaning is: through the discrimination (*viveka*) of that subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*)—by means of the previously mentioned positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth—the very definition of falsity (*mithyātva*), characterized by the absence of intrinsic existence (*svataḥ sattārāhitya*), is manifested through the delimitation (*avaccheda*) of the Self's distinctness from it. Regarding the phrase "prāṇa... and so on:

this means that the sheaths (*kośas*) named after these [elements] become discriminated, that is to say, they are brought to the aforementioned state of falsity. Now, [one might ask: of a single subtle body...

To the question, "How is it that those three [sheaths] are such merely by way of discernment?", he says: "For they... (*te hi*). The word "for" (*hi*) indicates the reason; because of which cause those three sheaths, beginning with the *prāṇamaya*, exist. In that regard, within the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*): regarding the phrase "the differentiation of the qualities" (*guṇāvasthābheda*). The previously mentioned differentiation of the two qualities—*rajas* and *sattva*—consists of the *prāṇamaya* sheath, which is formed from all the portions of *rajas* among the five subtle elements beginning with space, as well as the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and the organs of action (*karmendriyas*).

Likewise, from their combined *sāttvika* portions consisting of doubt, the mind (*manas*) is formed; and from those same portions when distributed, the five organs of perception (*jñānendriya*) arise—thus it is called "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*). Similarly, from those same portions when combined as determinative, the intellect (*buddhi*) is formed; and from those same portions when distributed, the organs of action (*karmendriya*) arise—thus it is called "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*). The meaning is that they exist as distinct entities for that very reason. The grammatical connection is: "they exist as separate. (40)
Udāna 6.1:
The Discourse on the Great Conflagration (Mahāpariḷāha Sutta)
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 42.

[From the commentary by Rāma on the *Tattvaviveka*: Now, he states the means for the discernment of the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*), which is intended to be described as the sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*):]
The manifestation [of the self] during deep sleep is its non-manifestation; however, its persistence during meditative absorption (samādhi) is its manifestation.
But the negative concomitance (vyatireka) regarding the manifestation of the Self is its non-manifestation in deep sleep. || 41 ||

Regarding the term "suṣupti" (deep sleep): in the state of *samādhi*, which will have its characteristics explained later, there is the non-appearance of deep sleep—that is, the non-perception of ignorance (*ajñāna*) in the form of the causal body, which is indicated by the word "suṣupti. However, as for the self (*ātman*), the particle "tu" is used for emphasis; that which exists as the appearance or manifestation of the self alone is the "inherence" (*anvaya*) of the self. When there is the appearance of the self—the manifestation of the self—there is the non-manifestation of deep sleep. Thus, [the self is present] even in deep sleep.

The very non-perception of ignorance, which is characterized by [the absence of] *pṛthaktva* (separateness), constitutes its *vyatireka* (exclusion). Herein is the formal argument (*prayoga*): The inner self (*pratyagātman*) is distinct from the *annamaya* and the other sheaths, because even while those [sheaths] are mutually excluded, it itself is not excluded. Whatever is not excluded even when these [others] are excluded is distinct from them; for example, a thread is distinct from flowers, or as the nature of "cowness" (*gotva*) is distinct from individual cows such as *khaṇḍa* and others. || 41 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, even while one is in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), he states the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the Self as being of the nature of manifestation, and the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of deep sleep as being of the nature of non-manifestation, with the words "In deep sleep... The point is that *samādhi* is well-established through such scriptures as: "When the previous conceptualization has dissolved and until another arises, the non-conceptual consciousness shines forth clearly. || 41 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: It has been stated that the attainment of Brahman occurs for the Self, which is distinct from the five sheaths through both positive and negative concomitance. He recites in substance the Kaṭha Śruti that establishes this, beginning with "The Person of the size of a thumb is the inner Self" (Kaṭha 6.17) and ending with "One should know Him as the bright, immortal" (Kaṭha 6.17): rā0 ṭīkā — anvayavyatirekābhyāṃ kośapañcakād viviktasyātmano brahmaprāptir bhavatīty uktam, tatpratipādikām "aṅguṣṭhamātraḥ puruṣo 'ntarātmā" [kaṭha0 6|17] ityādikāṃ "taṃ vidyāc chukram amṛtam" [kaṭha0 6|17] ityetāṃ kaṭhaśrutim arthataḥ paṭhati — Rāghavendra’s Commentary: It has been stated that the attainment of Brahman occurs for the Self, which is distinct from the five sheaths through both positive and negative concomitance. He recites in substance the Kaṭha Śruti that establishes this, beginning with "The Person of the size of a thumb is the inner Self" (Kaṭha 6.17) and ending with "One should know Him as the bright, immortal" (Kaṭha 6.17): rā0 ṭīkā — aṅguṣṭhamātro 'ṅguṣṭhaparimito yo 'ntarātmā hṛdayākāśe vartate tam antarātmānaṃ śukraṃ dīptimantam amṛtaṃ vināśarahitaṃ vidyāj jānīyāt | kathaṃbhūtam | īśānaṃ sarvasya jagataḥ prabhuṃ suvarṇajyotiḥ svayaṃprakāśam | punaḥ kathaṃbhūtam | yaḥ kaścid vijñānasārathir vijñānam ātmopāsanaṃ sārathiḥ sārathisthānīyaṃ yasya sa vijñānasārathiḥ | punaḥ kathaṃbhūtaḥ | manasā pāpmabhiḥ pāpācaraṇair asaṃspṛṣṭaḥ | evambhūto yaḥ puruṣaḥ sa taṃ vindatīti pūrveṇānvayaḥ || Rāghavendra’s Commentary: The inner Self, who exists in the space of the heart and is measured by the size of a thumb—one should know that inner Self to be bright, radiant, and immortal, free from destruction. Of what nature is He? The Lord, the Master of the entire universe, whose light is like gold, self-luminous. Furthermore, of what nature is the person? One who has discernment as his charioteer—meaning one for whom the practice of meditating on the Self stands in the place of a charioteer—and who is untouched by mental evils, that is, by sinful conduct. Such a person finds Him; thus is the connection with the preceding verse.
Just as the inner core of the muñja grass is extracted, so too is the self drawn out by means of reasoning.
By those who have conquered the three bodies, the supreme Brahman itself is born.

Regarding the word "yathā" (as): just as, in whatever manner, the *ipīkā*—the tender blade within the sheath of a specific grass called *muñja*—is extracted by means of the method characterized by separating it from the coarse leaves situated externally as its covering; even so, the Self is [extracted] by means of the method characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), from the threefold body previously mentioned, through the perfection of the means such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and the rest.

The intention is that if it is extracted and separated by those who hold the office [of officiants], it becomes the Supreme Brahman itself, because the characteristic of being of the nature of consciousness and bliss is common to both. || 42 ||

A0 Ṭīkā: Thus, in response to the inquiry as to what authority there is for the attainment of Brahman through the discrimination of the five sheaths (pañcakośa) consisting of the three bodies, he summarizes the meaning of the very Śruti passage—"The Person of the size of a thumb is the inner self, ever seated in the hearts of people; one should draw Him out from one's own body with fortitude, like a stalk from a reed; one should know Him as the bright and immortal"—with the words beginning with "yathā" (just as). From the *muñja* grass... [a specific kind of] grass... [the stalk is extracted].

*Ghāt*: The construction is as follows: just as a reed-stalk (*iṣīkā*)—so called because it is separated from its coarse sheath (*paṭa*)—is extracted by those who prepare *mauñjī* grass in the form of a delicate splinter, so [should one extract the self]. "The size of a thumb" means [the self is perceived] due to the limitation of the mind residing in the heart. "One should pull out" means one should discern [it] (*vivecayet*). || 42 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Fearing that since the complete knowledge of reality has been established by this much of the textual composition, there would be no occasion for the commencement of the subsequent portion of the work, he states the purport of the latter part of the text—preceded by a summary of what has already occurred—in order to justify its commencement:
"Thus, through reasoning, the identity of the higher and lower selves has been established."
That [reality] is indicated by sentences such as "That thou art" through the abandonment of their respective parts. (43)

Regarding the phrase "the higher and the lower": in the manner thus described, the oneness—the non-difference—of the higher and lower selves, that is, of the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam*, namely the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and the individual self (*jīvātman*), which has been rendered probable and accepted through means such as demonstrating the similarity of their defining characteristics by logical reasoning, is clearly indicated by sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).
This oneness is understood through the function of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) by means of the abandonment of parts—that is, by the discarding of the contradictory elements. || 43 ||
The First Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

43a. Commentary: Now, one might ask, "What does that have to do with the present subject? To this he says: "The higher and lower... This means by means of the ten verses beginning with "Food" and "Prāṇa. The meaning is: "of the higher and lower selves," that is, of the pure consciousness (cinmātra) characterized as the implied referents (lakṣya) of the terms *tat* and *tvam*. By means of reasoning... following...

This means by means of a specific reasoning (*yukti*) characterized by the fivefold positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*), namely those termed "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtta*). As it is stated in the *Siddhāntabindu*: "The positive and negative concomitance of the seer and the seen; the positive and negative concomitance of the witness (*sākṣin*) and the witnessed (*sākṣya*); the positive and negative concomitance of that which comes and goes (*āgamāpāyin*) and its substrate (*tad-adhiṣṭhāna*); and the positive and negative concomitance of the locus of suffering and the locus of supreme love. And: "The fifth is also the positive and negative concomitance of the persistent (*anuvṛtta*) and the excluded (*vyāvṛtta*). This is unity.

"Unity" (aikya) means non-difference (abheda). "Conceived" (saṃbhāvitā) means discarded, that is to say, rendered into the state of being merely a possibility. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "In reality" (tat-tve), etc. That is oneness (ekatā). || 43 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Since the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence "That thou art" (tattvamasi) is preceded by the knowledge of the meanings of the words "That" (tat) and so forth, he first states the primary denotation (vācyārtha) of the word "That" (tat).
That which is the material cause of the world, having taken up the darkness of illusion (māyā).
That sign, which is that pure being, is called "Brahman" by that word.

Regarding the phrase "of the world": that Brahman, whose characteristics are Being, Consciousness, and Bliss, having taken up *māyā*—which is characterized by *tamas* (the quality of darkness)—as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), becomes the material cause (*upādāna*) and the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the world consisting of the aggregate of effects, both moving and unmoving; and having taken up that same [māyā] when it is characterized by pure *sattva* (the quality of purity) as its limiting adjunct, it becomes the efficient cause (*nimitta*), the omniscient agent. Thus, that Brahman possesses the dual nature of both efficient and material cause.
That Brahman is Virāj, which is denoted by the word "That" (tat) in the sentence "That thou art" (tattvamasi). || 44 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭī0): Explaining that very process, he first states the primary meaning of the word "That" (tat) with the words "of the world" (jagataḥ).

The phrase "tāmasīm" means that which was previously described as being dominated by *tamas*, arising from *prakṛti* whose nature is primarily *tamas*. The word "having taken" (*ādāya*) is to be construed with what follows as well.

Thus, that Brahman—which is non-dual Being-Consciousness-Bliss, conditioned by the power of *māyā* dominated by *sattva* and *tamas*, and which is the non-distinct efficient and material cause of the universe—is precisely what is denoted by the word "That."
The meaning is that there is something to be expressed. || 44 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*) of the word "Thou" (*tvaṃ*):
"When that [intellect], which is of impure *sattva* and corrupted by desire, action, and so forth..."
That supreme Brahman is grasped; it is then expressed by the word "thou" (tvaṃpada). || 45 ||

Regarding the word "yadā" (when): that very Brahman, when—in a certain state—it takes up, that is, accepts as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), that *māyā* which is designated by the term "ignorance" (*avidyā*), because it consists primarily of impure *sattva* due to being mixed with a slight amount of *rajas* and *tamas*, and is therefore corrupted by desire, action, and so forth;
at that time, it is denoted by the term "thou" (*tvaṃpada*). || 45 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, he describes the denotation of the term *tvaṃ* (the "you" in *tat tvam asi*) as being like the Lord (*īśvara*), namely the individual soul (*jīva*), by the words "when... and so forth. [He refers to] that aforementioned *māyā*, which is also called *prakṛti*. The cause for the impurity of *sattva* is *kāma* (desire) and so on; by the word "etc.," latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are included. This is because of the statement of the venerable and worshipful Bhagavatpūjyapāda: "In this way, this beginningless and endless natural superimposition (*adhyāsa*) [is established]. Thus, it is of the nature of impurity as described.

One must avoid the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), wherein the existence of ignorance—characterized by the specific division between the primary nature (*pradhāna*) and the individual self (*prakṛti*)—depends on the existence of defects such as desire and karma, and the existence of those defects depends on the existence of that ignorance.

This is because it should be understood that, like the fivefold objects of perception (*dṛśyapañcaka*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), the entire phenomenal world superimposed in the form of a seed is itself beginningless. Likewise, its infinity follows precisely from the fact that it cannot be dispelled by anything other than the knowledge of Brahman. || 45 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus explained the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam*, he states the meaning of the sentence:
"Having abandoned even that triad which is mutually contradictory..."
The indivisible reality of existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda) is indicated by the Great Saying (mahāvākya). || 46 ||
Regarding the phrase *tatparam*, Acyutarāya reads it as *paramam*.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[the second part titled] Tattvaviveka.

Regarding the phrase "the triad": having abandoned—that is, having relinquished—that Māyā which is threefold, consisting of three types as described by the distinctions of being dominated by *tamas*, dominated by pure *sattva*, and dominated by impure *sattva*, and which is for that very reason mutually contradictory; [the text] states that the undivided (*akhaṇḍa*), differenceless Brahman, which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), is indicated by the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*). || 46 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭī0): Now, since the non-difference between these two is impossible due to their possessing contradictory attributes, he explains the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) through the figurative indication known as "partial abandonment" (*bhāgatyāga-lakṣaṇā*), saying: "the triad also," etc. That [triad] refers to Māyā. || 46 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might ask, "Where is it observed that the meaning of a sentence is communicated through the function of indication (lakṣaṇā) in this manner? Anticipating this, he says:
"In sentences such as 'This is that,' because of the contradiction between the two [terms]..."
Just as by the exclusion of two parts, a single locus is indicated. || 47 ||

Regarding the phrase "this is that": in sentences such as "This is Devadatta," because of the contradiction between the two attributes characterized by "that-ness" and "this-ness"—namely, their specific qualities of time and place—their identity is untenable. Therefore, by abandoning the contradictory portions of the two parts, the single substratum, the very nature of Devadatta, is indicated as being one and the same. || 47 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭī0): Now, an objection may be raised: "Granted that, because the two purified referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam* are both the Reality (*vastu*) characterized as Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), they are partless (*akhaṇḍa*) by virtue of being a single essence identical with the Self of all, and thus their status as the indicated meaning (*lakṣyatva*) may exist without contradiction; nevertheless, where in the world has this 'indication by abandoning parts' (*bhāgatyāgalakṣaṇā*), which you favor, ever been observed?
Anticipating this doubt, [the author] provides an illustration of its observation in sentences such as "This is that Devadatta," and thereby takes that very sentence as the example: "So'..."

Regarding the phrase "yam ityādi" (beginning with "yam"): the meaning is that the substratum is the conscious individual body named Devadatta, which serves as the locus for the notions of "that-ness" and "this-ness. || 47 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus stated the illustration, he states the illustrated application:
"Having thus abandoned Māyā and Vidya, which are the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the Supreme and the individual soul,"
The supreme Brahman alone, which is indivisible, being-consciousness-bliss, is perceived. || 48 ||

Regarding the phrase "māyā and avidyā": just as in a sentence such as "This is that Devadatta," one sets aside the two limiting adjuncts (upādhi)—namely, the previously mentioned *māyā* and *avidyā*—which serve as the conditions for the Supreme and the individual soul (*jīva*), the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) indicates nothing other than the Supreme Brahman itself, which is indivisible, free from difference, and of the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*). || 48 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) on verse a0 clarifies the point of application (dāṣṭāṃtika) with the words "māyā" etc. || 48 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might wonder whether the object indicated by the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) is with conceptual construction (savikalpa) or without conceptual construction (nirvikalpa).
Having raised this alternative, the proponent of the prima facie view states the defect in the first position:
"If that which is with conceptual construction were the indicated object, then the indicated object would be a non-entity."
The state of being an object of definition is neither observed nor possible for that which is free from conceptual construction. || 49 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the determinate" (*savikalpasya*): that which exists together with a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—namely, a form such as name, genus, and so forth, imagined through a distorted conceptualization—is "determinate. If this were the object of definition (*lakṣya*), to be understood by means of a sentence, then because it would be the meaning of the sentence as the defined object, the defined object would be a non-entity; it would be false. He states the fault in the second case [the indeterminate] with the words "of the indeterminate" (*nirvikalpasya*). Of the indeterminate...

In the world, the status of being a "defined object" (lakṣyatva) is never seen for that which is devoid of name, genus, and so forth; nor is it ever observed anywhere, nor is it even logically possible, because for that which possesses the property of being a defined object, its state of being free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpatva) would be contradicted—this is the meaning. || 49 ||

Commentary (a0): Thus, unable to endure the non-dual doctrine established by all the Vedāntas due to the accumulated sins of countless births, a proponent of duality such as a logician (tārkika) raises an objection at this very moment. Alternatively, some disciple desiring liberation might think: "After this instruction on the secret meaning of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya), there must be some extraordinary state, worthy of being tasted through the threefold division [of subject, object, and act], which is of the same nature as the bliss born from attaining my desired objects such as sound and so forth."
The First Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

Remaining with the hope that the supreme bliss known as Kaivalya would be attained, he perceives that the Supreme Brahman alone—which is partless Being-Consciousness-Bliss—is the object of perception;
yet, because that reality described [in the scriptures] is beyond the reach of speech and mind, his incomparable mind becomes agitated and he doubts, saying: "Of the conceptualized...
"Now, the statement that 'the Supreme Brahman alone, which is partless Being-Consciousness-Bliss, is perceived' appears to be inconsistent. For instance—"

To begin with, an entity that is devoid of the delimitations of space, time, and substance—which is what must be established by the term *khaṇḍapada*—is simply not possible in any way whatsoever. This is because, although Śuka was liberated, Vāmadeva was liberated, and so forth according to scripture, the existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is still perceived through direct perception by people such as ourselves; thus, since the delimitation by substance has not been eliminated, [the entity] is merely free from internal differences (*svagatabheda*). This is likewise the case for ether, atoms, and so on.

Since partless entities (niravayava-vastu) are devoid of internal difference, they possess indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*); indeed, they are simply the universal (*jāti*), because while being eternal and unitary, they inhere in many individuals. Thus, it is beyond dispute that [the word] "Being" (*sat*) and other such names are words denoting [such a universal]. And so, if the object is directly denotable (*śakya*) by that very [word], how can it be indicated (*lakṣya*), or how can it be indivisible? Furthermore, in this context, is the object indicated by the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) Brahman with attributes (*savikalpa*), as being pervaded by a limiting condition for indication (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka-dharma*)?

Or is it "non-conceptual" (nirvikalpa)? [The opponent might argue: "Because of such scriptural passages as, 'Having known that which is non-conceptual, infinite, devoid of cause and example, immeasurable, and beginningless, the wise one is liberated,' [the Brahman] is non-conceptual. [The author replies: Neither the first [option, being "existent"] nor the second [being "non-conceptual"] is correct. The intention is as follows: The first is not tenable because, since the object of definition (lakṣya) possesses conceptual content (savikalpatva), its nature as a real entity (vastutva) would be false.
Nor is the second tenable, because such a thing has never been observed before (adṛṣṭacaratvāt). || 49 ||
Rāghava’s Commentary: The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), stating that this objection is a futile rejoinder (jātyuttara), expresses the fault by means of an alternative analysis:
"The alternative [of the object] must belong either to the indeterminate (nirvikalpa) or to the determinate (savikalpa)."
In the first case there is contradiction; in the other cases, there is infinite regress, circularity, or self-dependence. (50)

77. Regarding the term "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*): Is this conceptualization—which you have formulated as to whether that which is characterized (*lakṣya*) is conceptual (*savikalpa*) or non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*)—itself non-conceptual or conceptual? In the first case, there is a contradiction; the contradiction stated by you [is as follows]:...

It is indeed *vāta* (the wind). Otherwise, in the second alternative, there would be infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and other faults. To explain: in the expression "the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of a conceptualized object (*savikalpa*)," where [one says] "it exists together with a conceptualization," both the instrumental case-ending term *vikalpena* and the nominative case-ending term *vikalpapadena* denote one and the same conceptualization. Or, if there were two [conceptualizations], and if that very one [conceptualization] were itself the locus (*āśraya*) as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the conceptualization that depends upon it—then [the fault follows].

If there are two [alternatives] involving self-dependence (*ātmāśrayatā*), then, since the alternative indicated by the word in the third case is itself of the nature of an alternative, its substratum would also be conceptual (*savikalpa*). Consequently, the alternative serving as its qualifier—whether it be the very alternative indicated by the word in the first case, or one other than those two—in the first instance there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatā*); and in the second instance as well, the alternative serving as the qualifier of the subject (the *dharmin*)—is it the alternative indicated by the word in the first case?

Furthermore, is [the proof] indicated as being other than those [means]? In the first case, there is the consequence of a circular argument; in the second case, there is the fallacy of infinite regress, as there would have to be yet another for that, and yet another for that as well.

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, let it be so; however, regarding the objection preceded by this conceptualization, there are two views in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the other [party], the Advaitin: that either the pure Brahman has no entry whatsoever into the discussion, or that it does have an entry. Since in both cases the aforementioned question is not possible, the proponent (*siddhāntin*), refuting the refutation of the aforementioned definition of the "object of characterization" (*lakṣya*), offers a conceptual alternative (*vikalpa*). This [which begins with] "sa—"...

"If the object of definition (*lakṣya*) were conceptual (*vikalpa*), the object of definition would be a non-entity; moreover, the state of being an object of definition for that which is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) has never been seen and is not possible. Thus, you have raised a conceptual dilemma regarding the question of whether the non-dual Brahman—of which I said, "the supreme Brahman, which is partless Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), alone is defined"—can be the object of definition. Since there is no entry at all for pure non-dual Brahman into the realm of discourse, Brahman is indeed conceptual (*savikalpa*).

Adopting the first view—that liberation arises from the knowledge of the variegated Brahman (*śabalabrahma*) alone, according to the maxim of testing a pure diamond as the target of the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*)—the first alternative is presented in the first half [of the work]. Likewise, adopting the second view—that even the pure non-dual Brahman (*śuddhabrahmādvaita*) is engaged in discourse—the second alternative is presented in the second half. Regarding that intended Brahman, whether it is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*) or with conceptual construction (*savikalpa*), the point situated in the first half is as follows:

This is the meaning of the two *ṭi*s. Therein, he first refutes [the opponent's view] with the words beginning "ādye" (in the first case): "Having aimed at Brahman as free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), by me this...
[page 46].
In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[in the chapter titled] *Tattvaviveka*,

by means of the verse beginning with "If the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) were the object of characterization" (*vikalpasya lakṣyatve*), a conceptual construction based on a question is formulated; thus, for one who asserts this, [the following] is the basis of reliance (*upajīvya*).

There would be a contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion, like saying "my mother is barren"; the meaning is that because [Brahman] is by nature free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*) and thus devoid of conceptualization across the three periods of time, it is impossible for it to be an object of conceptualization. Having thus refuted the first [position], he rejects the latter with the remainder of the passage beginning with "elsewhere" (*anyatra*). If you say that this very conceptualization which forms the basis of my question is directed toward Brahman as something possessing conceptual construction (*savikalpa*), then:

Regarding that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) directed toward Brahman which you have specified: is Brahman "with conceptual construction" (*savikalpa*) by means of that very conceptual construction produced by you, or by another conceptual construction? In the first case, since Brahman is the subject under discussion, there would be a dependence upon a conceptual construction produced by you for the sake of establishing Brahman’s state of being "with conceptual construction. This would constitute the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), characterized by a thing depending upon itself. It is just as in the first aphorism of the Nyāya school, where the sixteen categories beginning with the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) [are enumerated].

It has been stated that "the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). In this regard, it is beyond dispute that the word "reality" (*tat*) is intended to exclude error and the like. Consequently, in the present context, the knowledge of reality culminates in being of the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*). And it is universally agreed that such valid cognition has only the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as its instrument. Furthermore, that means of knowledge is not at all capable of producing valid cognition if it remains unknown itself; for, based on the experience "I know the sun by means of my eye," [the means of knowledge is understood] as qualified by the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

For it is only when the property of being a mountain-dweller (pakṣadharmatva) is known—as in the case of smoke on a mountain—that there arises the status of being the instrument for inferential cognition regarding that [fire]. And thus, if a knowledge of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇajñāna) requires another knowledge of a means of valid cognition, self-dependence (ātmāśraya)—defined as a thing depending upon itself—is clearly evident; the same applies here in the present case. If you say: "I have indeed formed this conceptual construction (vikalpa) concerning Brahman as the object to be defined, but the conceptual construction residing in the Brahman thus pointed out is the one under discussion..."

If you argue that the nature of Brahman, which serves as the *uddeśyatāvacchedaka-dharma* (the defining property of the subject), is indeed distinct from the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) [of it], and thus there is no self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), then we reply: here, for the sake of establishing the conceptual construction of the aforementioned *uddeśyatāvacchedaka*—namely, the nature of Brahman—one must first establish the conceptual construction of Brahman as being "with conceptual content" (*savikalpa*) by means of that very conceptual construction; and once the conceptual construction of the predicate (*vidheya*)—which consists in the conceptual construction of its being the object of the present definition—is established, then [the definition] is determined by that...

The establishment of its being conceptual (*savikalpatva*) by means of attributes such as "Brahman-hood" (*brahmatva*), which serve as the delimiters of the intended object (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), results in a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*) characterized by mutual dependence. For instance, in that very case, the establishment of the category of "means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*) depends upon the establishment of the category of "object of knowledge" (*prameya*)—which is the object of the valid cognition produced by that means—and conversely, the establishment of the category of "means of knowledge" depends upon its being the instrument for the valid cognition whose object is that [category of object]. Thus, the circularity is indeed evident.

[This] is the basis [of the objection]. This applies here as well. If, out of fear of this [consequence], you accept a third alternative for Brahman—namely, that it is characterized by being unknown (ajñātatva)—on the grounds that no other alternative is possible regarding an unknown Brahman, then, once the "being unknown" of Brahman is established, its status as the "subject of inquiry" (uddeśyatva) is established;

and once its status as the subject of inquiry is established, the establishment of the alternative of being the "object defined" (lakṣyatva) according to your own formulation follows; and once the alternative of being the object defined according to your formulation is established...

By the impossibility of that [cognition] otherwise, the establishment of "unknowability" (ajñātatva) therein would result in a circularity (*cakraka*) characterized by mutual interdependence among the three.

Or, for example, regarding the categories of substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence, when the question arises, "What is substance-ness (*dravyatva*)?", one might say, "Substance-ness is the possession of qualities and so forth. Thus, substance-ness is established through the possession of qualities and so forth. Then, when the expectation arises as to "by what relation is there the possession of qualities and so forth?"...

Regarding the phrase "by way of inherence" (*samavāyena*): once the possession of qualities and so forth is established, there arises a dependence upon the relation of inherence. To the question, "Why must that inherence itself be accepted? Viśvanātha Pañcānana states in his *Bhāṣāpariccheda* that "inherence-causality belongs to substance alone.

Thus, for the sake of inherence-causality within substance, there is a clear circularity (*cakraka*) dependent upon the establishment of substance. This would likewise apply here as well. If this were the case...
If you argue that the status of Brahman as the object of definition (*lakṣya*) and the object of conceptualization (*vikalpa-viṣayatva*) is not due to mere ignorance alone,

but rather— by resorting to the fourth alternative— that it is established through the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by hearing the scriptures hundreds of times, such as "Brahman with attributes" (*savikalpa-brahma*) and "Brahman without attributes" (*nirvikalpa-brahma*),
then [we reply]: even the state of being the object of the fourth alternative, namely the impression produced by hearing the aforementioned scriptures and so forth, must reside in Brahman.

It must be stated that [the cognition] arises through another conceptual construction (vikalpa) known as a latent impression (saṃskāra) from a previous birth, which serves as the cause for hearing the science of grammar; yet even that [impression] would have as its object yet another conceptual construction known as a latent impression from a further previous birth. Thus, in every way, an unavoidable infinite regress (anavasthā)—consisting in the absence of a finality in the chain of causes—would result. For example, in the general definition of a cause as "that which invariably precedes the effect," regarding the property of "invariably preceding":

Since, in the case of the pot, [properties] such as the shards are observed to be produced (*janya*) with respect to it, there is a necessity for its being an effect characterized by producibility (*janyatva*); therefore, [there must be] a cause for that which is necessarily [present].
[Page 47] First Section.
Accompanied by the two commentaries:

Since each of those [causes] also depends on its own prior existence, and that [prior existence] in turn depends on its being a necessary antecedent for its respective effect, the infinite regress (anavasthā) is well-established. It is the same here as well.

It is not as if everything has been shattered by the staff [of logic], for everything remains perfectly square [consistent]. Nor should it be said that the charge of the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) and so forth is impossible to avoid even for the Advaitins;

for in their conventional discourse, the Goddess Mahāmāyā—who is the crest-jewel of all defects—will simply take even those very defects and make them her crest-jewel, thereby adorning them. What then can be said of the mere specks of various intermediate defects? Therefore, whether by the opponent or by the proponent... [the truth]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical flow and philosophical argumentation present in the Sanskrit.)

Or rather, if you are a seeker of truth, you should not at all employ the maneuvers of the *Khaṇḍana* against the proponent of non-duality (*advaitavādin*), the sovereign emperor of those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta-cakravartin*), because he is the very source of this [truth]; instead, such maneuvers should be directed only toward the proponents of duality (*bhedavādin*). For the glow of a firefly does not shine even in a dream before the orb of the fierce sun.
Therefore, the intention is that by taking refuge at his feet alone, the obscuration of one's own knowledge must be dispelled. || 50 ||
Rāghava’s Commentary: This objection does not apply here alone; rather, such an objection preceded by similar dilemmas extends everywhere.
Thus he says:
"This [objection applies] to qualities, actions, universals, substances, relations, and entities."
Therefore, let it be accepted that all this is identical with its own essential nature. || 51 ||

"This" refers to this collection of objections regarding conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). It applies equally to the five categories of entities: quality, action, genus, substance, and relation. To illustrate: does a quality reside in that which is devoid of qualities, or in that which possesses qualities? Likewise, does an action reside in that which is devoid of action, or in that which possesses action? In the first case, there is a contradiction; in the other, there are fallacies such as self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). This should be understood in the same way for all cases. Now, this—

Anticipating the objection, "If [the alternative] is not a valid answer, then what is the valid answer?", he says: "By that" (tena). By that very fact of the incoherence of the alternative, let it be accepted that all these qualities and so forth belong to the essential nature (svarūpa);
the intention is that all qualities and the like reside in the essential nature of the entity. || 51 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Having thus raised the objection, [the author] states "this" (*idam*) to show that the refutation of the alternative you have proposed does not apply solely to it, but extends to all categories accepted by the proponents of difference (*bhedavādin*). Whether a quality (*guṇa*) resides in that which is devoid of qualities or in that which possesses qualities—the refutation of such alternatives should be understood as before. Furthermore, regarding the relation (*saṃbandha*), such as inherence (*samavāya*), does it reside in a substance (*dravya*) that is unrelated or in one that is related? This too was previously [discussed].

Just so; the term *vastu* refers precisely to the category known as *viśeṣa* (particularity) as accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas. Accordingly, one should consider whether this *viśeṣa* exists in an eternal substance that is itself devoid of particularity (*nirviśeṣa*) or in one that possesses particularity (*saviśeṣa*), and so forth. The point is that, in this manner, it is quite easy to apply the aforementioned method of refutation even to the six categories of existence (*ṣaḍbhāvapadārtha*) accepted by the logicians (*tārkika*). As for the refutation of non-existence (*abhāva*), however, it occurs through the manifestation of non-duality (*advaita*) upon the destruction of the two-fold manifestation [of existence and non-existence] in my work.

This has already been explained in detail in that commentary, so it is concluded here. He states the conclusion with the words "by that" (*tena*). The meaning is: one must accept—that is, acknowledge—that this entire web of the visible world is related solely to the nature of one's own self, which is the light of its own existence. The implication is that it possesses existence and so forth only through the light of existence that is non-different from one's own self; however, were it separate from that, it would be merely false. And thus, even within the totality of duality, there is an inherent lack of independent existence.
The intention is that you alone expand [as the universe]. || 51 ||
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Let it be so in other cases; what relevance does this have to the subject at hand? To this he says:
"In the reality of the Self, which is untouched by conceptual construction and its absence..."
But [properties] such as being conceptualized, being the object of definition, and relation, are indeed imagined (kalpita).

It conceptualizes. Regarding the reality of the supreme Self—which is untouched by both conceptualization and its absence, and which is devoid of contact with conceptualization or the absence of conceptualization—there exist [notions] such as "being conceptualized," "being indicated," and "relation.

Here, "being conceptualized" means being made an object by the previously mentioned [means], whether through determinate or indeterminate cognition; "being indicated" means being made known through the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*); and "relation" refers to the connection [between the two].

"Conjunction and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), substance (*dravya*) and the others are included. The particle "but" (*tu*) is used for emphasis. Among these, substance is defined by the logicians as "that which is the substratum of qualities," or "substance is the inherent cause," provided that it is distinct from action and possesses a genus (*jāti*).
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
titled *Tattvaviveka* (Discrimination of Reality).

The meaning is that all these—jāti (universal), which is defined as a quality residing in a substratum, eternal, unitary, and subsisting in many; and karma (action), which is defined as that which belongs to the same class as the non-inherent cause of conjunction and disjunction—are merely imagined within their own essential nature. || 52 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, if it is thus the case that the entire web of duality has its existence dependent solely on that which is to be illumined by the Light non-different from itself, then [one might ask]: is the relationship between the Seer and the seen—characterized as the state of the illuminator and the illuminated, and involving both real and unreal counter-correlates—[possible]?

Fearing that it might be argued that [the Self] must be described as having a dual nature—like the relationship between Ardhanārīśvara—and that this would result in the contingency of partial duality (*aṃśika-dvaita*), he provides the following resolution:

“*vikalpa*,” etc. Here, *vikalpa* means repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). Thus, the meaning is: “by means of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) and its destruction. Regarding the term “unaffected” (*asaṃspṛṣṭa*):
it has been stated in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*: “That upon which something is superimposed is not affected, even in the slightest degree, by any defect or quality produced by that [superimposed thing].”

Thus [it is said]. For this very reason, it is stated that [the Self] is "conceptualized" (*vikalpitatva*). By the first word [of the verse], its nature as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhānatva*) is indicated. Therefore, it is said in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*: "What need is there for much speaking here? I shall tell you; listen to the summary of the teaching on non-duality: Consciousness (*citi*), which transcends all speech and mind, yet participates in all verbal and mental transactions. (52)
Rāghava’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭī): In response to the inquiry as to what has been stated by this much of the textual exposition, he states the resulting conclusion:
"In this manner, the investigation of their meaning through these statements constitutes *śravaṇa* (hearing)."
But reflection (*manana*) is the contemplation of that which has been rendered plausible through reasoning. (53)

"Thus" (*ittham*) means: in the manner described by the collection of passages beginning with "That which is the material cause of the world," and so forth; through such sentences as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), there occurs *śravaṇa*, which is the contemplation of the meaning of those sentences—that is, the contemplation of the identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman.
Furthermore, through reasoning—such as that beginning with "Sound, touch, and the rest are objects of knowledge"—the oneness of the higher and lower selves is thus rendered probable.

The contemplation of what has been presented by this extensive composition in the manner described above—the realization that the meaning of what has been heard is logically consistent—is called *manana* (reflection). || 53 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, one might object that in this way, the realization of the Siddhānta cannot be accomplished without the internal means such as *śravaṇa* (hearing) and so forth.

Therefore, in response to the inquiry as to what the definitions of those [means]—prescribed by the Śruti in the passage, "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon"—are according to our own view, the author summarizes them in two verses in their proper order, beginning with the word *ittham*. *Ittham*... [and so on].

The meaning is: by means of sentences that convey the nature of things as expressed in etymology—that is, by the words of the Upaniṣads such as "Truth, Knowledge," and so forth, as well as the statements of their commentators, beginning with the venerable Bhagavatpāda Ācārya. Regarding the phrase "that" (tad) and so on: it refers to the constant contemplation of that which is to be established—the nature of non-dual, unattached pure consciousness. Reasoning (yukti) here means inference (anumāna), and it is based on existence (sattva). || 53 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now he describes *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation):
"That which [arises] for the mind established upon the object made free from doubt by those two..."
For this state of one-pointedness is called nididhyāsana (intense contemplation). || 54 ||

"By those two": by means of those two, hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), when one has become free from doubt—that is, when doubt or uncertainty has departed from it—one fixes the mind upon that object or subject. Since Patañjali has stated that "concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is the binding of the mind to a place," this state of one-pointedness—the possession of a continuous flow of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) in a single form—is called meditative cultivation (*nididhyāsana*). For indeed...
It is established in the Yogaśāstra that "meditation (dhyāna) is the one-pointed continuity of the mental faculty (pratyaya) upon that [object]. (54)

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on verse a0: “By those two” means by those two previously described [means], namely hearing (śravaṇa) and reflection (manana). Regarding the term *nirvicikitsa*, according to Amara’s lexicon—“*vicikitsā* is doubt”—it means that which is free from uncertainty (*asaṃdigdha*). || 54 ||
Rāmānanda’s Commentary: He describes *samādhi*, which is the state of the full maturation of that very *nididhyāsana*—[from page 49]:
Chapter One.
Accompanied by two commentaries:
having abandoned both the meditator and the meditation, one should gradually take as one's sole object of focus that which is beyond the reach of the intellect.
Concentration is defined as a mind like a lamp in a windless place. || 55 ||
Regarding "the meditator and meditation": in *nididhyāsana* (contemplative meditation), there first appear a triad—the meditator, the meditation, and the object of meditation.

Therein, when through the power of practice the mind, having gradually abandoned both the meditator and the meditation within the process of meditation, becomes focused solely upon the object of meditation—

When that [mind] becomes such that it has only one object as its sphere of activity, then it is called *samādhi*. Regarding this, there is an illustration: "in a windless place. The meaning is that just as a lamp situated in a place free from wind remains motionless, so too is it. || 15 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, if it is argued that since *śravaṇa*—characterized by the non-forgetting of the intended meaning of all Vedāntic statements through the indicative marks such as the opening context (*upakrama*) and so forth—and *manana*—characterized by the non-forgetting of the impossibility of that [non-duality] through reasoning (*yukti*) consisting of inference and other means assisted by various worldly and scriptural arguments favorable to it—have already been accomplished by those very [means], then what further [is required] regarding the non-doubtful identity of Brahman and the Self? [The text continues: ...some slight... (Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly).

If it is argued: "Since *nididhyāsana*—characterized by a continuous succession of transformations into the form of that [object] alone, preceded by the absence of transformation into any other form, with the mind firmly fixed upon an object possessing non-perceptibility (*aparokṣya*), and which removes contrary conceptions regarding the means and so forth—is already established, what is the purpose of subsequently mentioning *samprajñāta-samādhi* and the rest? This is true; however, in the present context, following the invocation of auspiciousness, [it is said]: "By the mind purified through service to the pair of lotus-feet of Him... and so on. This is intended to show that even for one who has attained the aforementioned *nididhyāsana*, there remains a further necessity for the practice of *samādhi*. Otherwise, how could the attainment of *aparokṣa-jñāna* (direct realization) arise from mere *nididhyāsana* alone? For it is stated in the *Yoga-bhāṣya*: "When the mind is restrained in this way, the seer abides in his own nature" (*yoga-sūtra* 1.3). And in the *Vivaraṇa* on that: "The mind, having been restrained through the previously mentioned means, becomes fit for *samādhi*. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Sūtra-bhāṣya*: "In the state of *samādhi*, the mind, being restrained, attains the highest purity and, becoming one with the Seer, perceives him directly" (*sūtra-bhāṣya* 1.41). Therefore, the mention of *samādhi* is necessary. Furthermore, the sequence of the means is as follows: first, the cultivation of the virtues of *yama* and *niyama*; then, the practice of *āsana*, *prāṇāyāma*, and *pratyāhāra*; thereafter, *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*; and finally, the attainment of *aparokṣa-jñāna*. Thus, the mention of *samādhi* is indeed appropriate. Moreover, since the term *samādhi* is used here to denote the state of the mind being absorbed in the object of meditation, it is not redundant. As it is said: "The mind, when its fluctuations are stilled, is called *samādhi*" (*yoga-sūtra* 1.2). Therefore, the mention of *samādhi* is justified. Finally, the mention of *samādhi* serves to indicate that even after the cessation of contrary conceptions, the mind must still be brought under control through the practice of *samādhi* until the final dissolution of all mental modifications. Thus, the purpose of mentioning *samādhi* is fully established. (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure and philosophical intent of the passage as it stands.)

By the statement, "This discrimination of reality (tattva-viveka) is set forth for their easy understanding," [the author] has undertaken this discrimination of reality out of compassion solely for those seekers of liberation whose minds have been purified by the performance of pure Vedic rites— such as the daily obligatory duties (*nityakarman*)— which are free from prohibited acts and dedicated exclusively to the Supreme Lord who is non-different from the Guru.

Therefore, for the sake of humans in this Kali age who possess short lifespans, [this work is not intended for those requiring] long-term practice preceded by all the equipment such as *haṭhayoga* and so forth.

Furthermore, because practices such as the worship of *kāla*, *phala*, *kāṣṭha*, *aṅga-yoga*, *karaṇaka*, *kada*, *hara*, and so forth are impossible [for one who has realized the truth], just as the reflection of a face or other objects cannot be correctly perceived even on a spotless mirror-surface or in water due to their inherent flickering nature, by that same logic, for the sake of experiencing the identity of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikya*), the purification of the internal organ (*svānta-śuddhi*) and its subsequent restraint are both necessary. Therefore, there must be a specific yearning for liberation (*viśiṣṭa-mumukṣā*) brought about by the three means beginning with the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities (*nityānitya-vastu-viveka*) and ending with meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, with the intention that since it was not mentioned previously, it is necessary to explain *samādhi* specifically in order to include it, [the author] states—after the hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other means have been accomplished as enjoined by the text, "The Self, indeed, my dear, should be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (*ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ*)—that *samādhi* alone is its fruit, beginning with the words "the meditator" (*dhyātṛ*). The meaning is that *samādhi* here refers to the *asaṃprajñāta* state. By this, the previously mentioned *nididhyāsana*...

In the statement "the state of meditation [arises] from the one-pointedness of the mind, and likewise through the sequence," the gradual process of practicing *samprajñāta-samādhi* is also implied. || 55 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that if mental modifications (*vṛtti*) are not perceived during samādhi, it is impossible even to ascertain that the mind has the object of meditation as its sole domain.
Anticipating this, he says "it is not so," because the existence of the modifications at that time is accessible through inference:
"But the modifications, though unknown at that time, have the Self as their object."
They are inferred from the memory that arises in one who has emerged from meditative absorption.

Regarding the phrase "the mental modifications (vṛttayaḥ) however": those modifications which have the self as their object—that is, for which the self is the range or domain—are at that time, during the period of meditative absorption (samādhi), inferred by one who has emerged from it through memory that has arisen. This inference takes the form: "For such a length of time I remained absorbed in meditation. The meaning is that this follows because the pervasion (vyāpti)—that whatever is remembered must have been experienced—is established in common worldly experience. || 16 ||
A0 Commentary: Now, raising the doubt as to whether mental modifications (vṛttis) exist at that time or not, he provides the resolution: "The modifications, however...
The word "arisen" (samutthitāt) is an adjective qualifying "recollection" (smaraṇa). || 56 ||

Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "In that case, since there is an absence of effort to produce a mental modification (*vṛtti*) at that time, how can there be a continuation of the modification?
Anticipating this doubt, he states that even in the absence of contemporaneous effort, it occurs due to the very first effort, aided by auxiliary factors such as unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Thus: "The continuation of modifications, however, arises from the first effort alone."
It would arise from the accompaniment of the latent impressions (saṃskāra) resulting from repeated practice, even though [the object] has not been seen before. || 27 ||

(Note: The commentary on this sūtra identifies the "neither-white-nor-black" as the merit of the yogi).

And that which is the impression produced by repeated practice—namely, the specific impression called *bhāvanā* generated through the repeated cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*)—arises from [the mind] existing together with those two auxiliary causes. || 57 ||
