It has been argued that even though transformation in the form of suppression (*rodha*) consists merely of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form of the pure Self, there is a distinction between *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi* and deep sleep because of the presence or absence of mental modifications, despite the fact that the non-perception of such modifications is the same in both cases. That is not correct, because it contradicts such scriptural passages as: "Liberation is remembered as being without an object when the five [senses] along with the mind come to rest," and "He should restrain them within the peaceful Self."

And it has been stated that this is because of the contradiction with those sūtras; therefore, this effort is indeed fruitless. If you say this, we reply: no, for you yourself have not understood their intended meaning (*tātparya*). To illustrate: first, regarding the position already mentioned, since the memory—"For so long a time I remained absorbed in the bliss of the non-conceptual samādhi"—is otherwise inexplicable for one who has emerged from the cessation-samādhi (*nirodha-samādhi*), according to the Vivaraṇa school, there [in that state] as well—as in deep sleep—[the self is present].

Because it is appropriate to conceive of the mental modification as being extremely subtle, having evolved solely from *sattva*, [the author], keeping in mind that this would be contradicted by the [scriptural] statement "of its own accord," proposes an alternative view with the words "or else" (*athavā*) and elaborates upon it. The scriptural passage beginning with "liberation is objectless" (*nirviṣaya*) teaches that the *asaṃprajñāta* samādhi has no object other than the Self (*ātman*). The *Yoga-sūtras* should also be understood in this same way. For this very reason, it was stated by the teacher of the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*: "Ā-..."

"The mind, which by its very nature abides in the form of both self and non-self, should be established through the practice of the view of non-self, having set aside the singular form of the self," and so forth. By this, it becomes clearly evident that the first position represents only the opinion of a partial school (ekadeśin). The details should be understood from that very source. || 57 ||

[Commentary by Rāmānanda]: Now, one might object that this form of *samādhi* has not been described or observed by previous teachers; anticipating this doubt, he says "it is not so," because it was indeed described by the supreme teacher, Śrī Puruṣottama.
As in the verse beginning "Like a lamp in a windless place," and so forth, in many ways.
The Blessed One explained this very same meaning to Arjuna.

"Āvṛta" means "contracted" (or obscured). The intended meaning, however, appears to be that prior to and subsequent to [the dawn of] knowledge, there is the manifestation of both the Brahman limited by ignorance (*avidyā*) and the pure (*śuddha*) Brahman.
Accompanied by Two Commentaries.
Chapter One. 51. [End of] the First Section.
Regarding the word *yathā*: through verses such as, "Just as a lamp placed in a windless spot does not flicker— this is the simile remembered" (Gītā 6.19),
the Blessed One, endowed with knowledge, sovereignty, and other qualities, has described this very *nirvikalpa-samādhi* in many ways and various manners.
He explained, that is, he demonstrated, form as the object to his disciple Arjuna. || 18 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Clarifying the point already stated with an illustration as well, he explains that which was previously set forth as the definition of non-conceptual absorption (*nirvikalpasamādhi*)—namely, "Absorption is said to be like a lamp in a windless place"—by citing authoritative scripture, beginning with the words "Just as a lamp...
and including the following: "Thus constantly engaging the self, the yogi, freed from impurity, easily attains the infinite bliss of contact with Brahman."

Thus the final section should be understood. And so, in a windless place such as a temple of Śiva where a lamp has been prepared, just as at the very beginning effort is disregarded for the sake of the abundance of all the necessary materials, yet thereafter that lamp burns with an unwavering flame until the completion of those materials—because the disappearance of the materials would otherwise be impossible—it appears that this is one and the same flame despite the differentiation of the flames within it at every moment; likewise, it is so in the present case as well.

The meaning is this: at the time of *saṃprajñāta-samādhi*, due to the perfection of the causal complex consisting of the initial effort, past impressions (*dṛṣṭa*), practice (*abhyāsa*), and so forth, even though there exist hundreds of mental modifications (*vṛtti*)—as evidenced by the impossibility otherwise of memory and other functions occurring during the intervals, much like in a continuous stream—the state appears as if it were of a single form because of extreme similarity. || 58 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the intermediate fruit of this samādhi:
"The millions of karmas accumulated here in this beginningless saṃsāra..."
By this, [impurities] go to dissolution, and pure dharma increases. || 59 ||

Regarding the phrase "beginningless" (*anādau*): it is clear that this refers to the beginningless. Here, in this saṃsāra, "accumulated"—meaning gathered—“crores of karmas” (*karmakoṭayaḥ*) refers to crores of actions characterized as meritorious and non-meritorious; this is an elliptical expression meaning "immeasurable karmas. By means of this samādhi, they "go to dissolution," that is, they perish. As it is said: "And his karmas are exhausted when He, the higher and the lower, is seen" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8).

Thus, according to the Śruti and the Smṛti passage, "The fire of knowledge [burns] all actions" (Gītā 4.37), it is clear that pure dharma—which serves as the means for the direct realization that removes avidyā along with its manifestations—increases. 19.
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Let it be so; what follows from that for the subject at hand? To this he says: "In the beginningless...

Here, since both the two positions—namely, liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*)—which were suggested by the first and second halves of the introductory verse beginning with "Salutation to Śrī Śaṅkara," are desired according to the distinction of the qualified aspirants (*adhikārī*), we take only those karmas that obstruct the arising of knowledge as being denoted by the word "accumulated" (*saṃcita*) in the present verse, specifically within the context of the position of *jīvanmukti*, which will be explained in the following verse.

But as for the accumulated *karmas* distinct from that [present one], according to that school's view, the intention is that they are destroyed solely by the arising of knowledge, based on the scriptural statement: "And his *karmas* are exhausted when He, the higher and the lower, is seen. By this, it is meant: by the aforementioned *nirvikalpa-samādhi*. || 59 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To the question "What is the proof for that?", he says:
"Those most skilled in yoga call this samādhi 'Dharmamegha' (the Cloud of Virtue)."
For from him he pours forth thousands of streams of the nectar of Dharma.

"Regarding the word *dharma*: those who know yoga best (*yogavittamāḥ*)—meaning those who possess the direct realization of Brahman through the excellence of their knowledge of yoga—have declared this nirvikalpa-samādhi to be *dharma* itself. He clarifies this by stating "it rains": for this reason, this samādhi rains down thousands of streams of the nectar of *dharma*, that is, streams characterized by *dharma*. [As it is said: "By abiding in this for even a single moment, one attains the fruit of a hundred sacrifices... [Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad 2.17]."
From the Śruti text "vaiśikhā," the connection with the preceding [verse] is: "Therefore, the ancients have declared dharma to be thus. || 60 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding this, he states the proof: "Dharma... and "Yoga...". [The latter refers to] Patañjali and others.

This is stated in the Yoga Sūtra, in the fourth chapter named Kaivalya: "Even for one who is not attached even to *prasaṃkhyāna*, when there is discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) in every respect, there is the *dharmamegha* samādhi.
*Prasaṃkhyāna* is the correct direct realization of the principles (*tattva*) through their similarities and differences; even for one who is not attached to that, the fruit is—
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 52]

The commentators on the Nārāyaṇa-vṛtti state that the word *psos* means "the discrimination of reality" (*tattvaviveka*). The reason for this is expressed by the word "it rains. This has been stated in the *Śivātharvaśikhopaniṣad*:
"Even of a hundred sacrifices, for a single moment... and so forth. (60)
Rāma’s Commentary: Now he states the supreme purpose of samādhi:
"When the web of latent impressions has been completely dissolved by this [samādhi]..."
When the accumulation of karma known as merit and demerit has been uprooted by its very roots.

"By this": by means of this samādhi, when the web of latent impressions (*vāsanājāla*)—which consists of the collection of mental traces (*saṃskārasamūha*) opposed to knowledge and which serves as the cause for the conceit of "I," "mine," agency, and so forth—is dissolved without remainder, that is, destroyed; and when the accumulation of karma known as merit and demerit is uprooted along with its root—that is, eradicated together with its foundation and destroyed—[the state described occurs]. || 61 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): What follows from that? To this he says with the following pair of verses: "By this" means by the white karma alone produced by the aforementioned samādhi; "when it has been dissolved" means when it has been destroyed. For this very reason, [he says] "she," and so forth. || 61 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the conclusion:
"The sentence, being unobstructed, [leads to realization] regarding that which was previously manifested as indirect."
Direct realization is produced, like [the knowledge of] a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand. || 62 ||

Regarding the term "sentence" (vākya): the sentence—such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) and others—being unobstructed, that is, being free from the hindrance posed by karma and latent impressions (vāsanā), produces—that is, generates—a realization (bodha), which is knowledge capable of manifesting reality in its immediate form (aparokṣa). This occurs with respect to the reality (tattva) which was previously manifested in a mediated way (parokṣa); it makes that reality manifest immediately, like a myrobalan fruit held in the palm of one's hand. || 62 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) on verse a0 states the result: "the sentence" (*vākyam*). This means the great sentences (*mahāvākya*) such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). Being unobstructed, it [removes] the aforementioned: the latent impressions regarding the object (*viṣaya-vāsanā*), doubt regarding the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-asambhāvanā*), doubt regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya-asambhāvanā*), contrary conceptions regarding the means (*sādhana-viparīta-bhāvanā*), and contrary conceptions regarding the fruit (*phala-viparīta-bhāvanā*).

The meaning is that [the mind] becomes void because it has been gradually eliminated by the fivefold obstacles known as *tabhāvanā*, as well as by the complete perfection of all means such as the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal (*nityānityaviveka*), and by the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) which accomplish the fruits such as hearing, reflection, meditation, and liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). Now, one might object: "But those five obstacles were mentioned in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* specifically in relation to the valid cognition produced by the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*): 'The intellect, though stained by human error, even when the faultless eye [of scripture] has arisen...'"

For example, it has been clearly stated with an illustration [in the *Brahmasūtrabhāṣya*] beginning with: "Just as a woman who is the object of desire does not become fruitful for her husband even though she is accessible through sacred scripture (*śruti*), so too [is the case] when [the Self] is in proximity" (*na phalāya bhartur viṣayā bhavati śrutisaṃbhavāpi tathātatsannidhau*). But here, since that [Self] is said to be "not fallen away" (*acyuta*) within the sentence itself, how is there no contradiction? To this he says: It is beyond dispute that the very realization "I am Brahman" arises from the inherent nature of sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), provided one has studied the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-svādhyāya*).

Likewise, for one who performs the practice, immediately after the vision [of the truth], there arises an appearance of the oneness of Brahman and the Self that is just like that which was previously indirect (*parokṣa*) due to the aforementioned obstruction; it does not, however, become eternally direct (*aparokṣa*). Therefore, because the aforementioned realization lasts for only three moments and—like fire obstructed by a barrier—it cannot persist for a long duration, he says that even in that case, it must be expressed by the sentence itself.
"Previously," etc. The implicit meaning is: "in the case of the subject matter, which is the non-dual unity of the Self with Brahman. "Is produced" means "is generated. || 62 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now he states the fruit of indirect knowledge:
"Indirect knowledge of Brahman is that which arises from the scriptures preceded by [the instruction of] a teacher."
It burns away all evil committed intentionally, just like fire. || 63 ||

Regarding the term "indirect" (*parokṣam*): the indirect realization of Brahman—verbal knowledge obtained through the mouth of a Guru preceded by a teacher, arising from scriptures such as "That thou art"—burns away every single sin committed intentionally, that is, performed with prior conscious intent, just like fire. || 63 ||

a0 Commentary: Thus, having raised the doubt that there must likewise be a difference in the fruits of indirect (parokṣa) and direct (aparokṣa) knowledge, [the author] proceeds by citing two passages from the second chapter of the *Yajñavaibhava-khaṇḍa* within the *Sūta-saṃhitā*, which are recited respectively according to their literal meaning.
The First Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

He explains this very point with two verses beginning with "parokṣam" (indirectly). The "deśika" is the venerable Guru. "Preceded by that" means produced by the Vedāntic statements taught by him, such as:
"If one knows that Brahman exists, then they know him as truly existing," and "I am the universe, the world... [and so forth].

The phrase "m" means that it is well-known through the Taittirīya Śruti in its sequential order. The term "evil" (pāpa) is also an elliptical designation for merit (puṇya), because both are alike in their capacity to grant birth. || 63 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the fruit of immediate knowledge (aparokṣajñāna):
"Immediate realization of the Self, preceded by verbal instruction from a teacher..."
He is the fierce sun for the darkness of ignorance, which is the cause of saṃsāra.

Regarding the term "immediate" (*aparokṣa*): verbal knowledge preceded by a teacher has already been explained. Immediate self-knowledge (*aparokṣātma-vijñāna*) is that knowledge of the immediate Self which is free from doubt and error. It is like the fierce sun at midday for the darkness of ignorance—the very ignorance that is the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Just as the fierce sun dispels the primordial darkness, it [dispels] the darkness of ignorance.
The meaning is "quail. || 64 ||
Commentary on verse 64: "Directly perceived" (aparokṣa), etc.
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the fruit of practicing this treatise:
"Having thus performed the discrimination of reality and having properly composed the mind..."
With the bonds of worldly existence dissolved, a person attains the supreme state before long. || 65 ||
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Discrimination of Reality" (*Tattvaviveka*), in the *Pañcadaśī* composed by the venerable sage Vidyāraṇya.
"In this manner": a person, having performed the discernment of reality (*tattva-viveka*)— the discrimination of reality characterized by the unity of Brahman and the Self,

which is the separation [of the Self] from the five sheaths (*kośa-pañcaka*)— and having fixed and stabilized the mind upon that reality according to the rules prescribed in the scriptures, becomes one whose bondage to transmigratory existence has dissolved through immediate realization (*aparokṣa-jñāna*), and thus attains the supreme state, which is of the nature of unsurpassed bliss.
The meaning is that one attains liberation without delay, without any postponement—that is, one becomes Brahman itself, characterized by truth, knowledge, and bliss. || 65 ||

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Discrimination of Reality" (*Tattvaviveka*), in the commentary on the *Pañcadaśī* known as the *Tātparyadīpikā*, composed by the scholar named Rāmakṛṣṇa, a servant of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, the illustrious Bhāratītīrtha Vidyāraṇya Muni. || 1 ||

A0 Ṭīkā: Thus, as stated in the fourth chapter of the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*: "The fire of the knowledge of Brahman—kindled by the wind of its own operation proceeding by the force of the reality itself—immediately and utterly consumes everything consisting of ignorance and its products; for it burns them without leaving a trace, and does not leave even the slightest vestige of another form of transmigratory existence. Therefore, for the knower, immediate liberation is certain. This occurs at the very same moment as the final valid cognition.

Having described immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*), which consists in the destruction of duality, for those qualified for it, he concludes the treatise by also describing liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) for those same qualified persons with the verse beginning "In this way" (*ittham*). By the phrase "here, before long" (*iha na cirāt*), he intends to refer to *jīvanmukti* as established in such scriptural passages as, "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released from the body. Now, an objection: was this not already discussed by you previously in the introduction to this treatise?

"Then, for one who desires union (*sāyojya*) and so forth, along with devotion toward the qualified [Lord] through the conviction that He is real, there is this first obstacle regarding the knowledge of the Lord's nature: 'the notion that He is a mere human goal'. Having thus introduced the initial obstacle called "objective latent impression" (*viṣayavāsanā*) concerning the knowledge of the Lord's essential form, [the author] subsequently introduces the text beginning with "In the first [stage], because of the attainment of qualification, there is primacy from the very outset," and "By the word 'tat-pāda' (His feet)," and so on.
If it is asked how the statement in another Āryā verse, “by being intent upon that,” which aphoristically indicates that the first [verse] sublates the aforementioned obstacles,

is to be understood, it is said in reply: Here, in this first chapter titled *Tattvaviveka*, there is, first of all, the presentation of the essential nature of the entire body of non-dual (Advaita) scriptures and their constituent treatises.
54. In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,

it is stated in general that for all treatises, the unknown identity of the meanings of the terms *tattva* and *padārtha* is the subject matter (*viṣaya*), while that same identity, once known, is the purpose (*prayojana*).

Although the subject matter and other elements are well-known, it appears that the attainment of qualification (*adhikāra-sampat*) alone is primarily expounded. The reason for this is that, from the very beginning, there is a primary focus on that goal, consisting precisely in the exposition of matters such as discernment (*viveka*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*). Furthermore, the reason for this is that at the commencement of the work—denoted by the word "beginning"—there is the verse: "For those whose minds have been purified by service to the pair of lotus feet... and so forth.

The connection with the preceding [sentence] is as follows: because this collection of verses—beginning with the passage starting "In that way, sound, touch, and so forth... and including "Sound, touch, and the rest are objects of cognition, distinct in their variety during the waking state; therefore, though differentiated [from one another], they do not differ from the consciousness of them due to its uniform nature," and ending with "Having thus performed the discrimination of the principles (tattva-viveka), having properly composed the mind in samādhi"—is devoted to that [liberation] and has the singular primary purpose of accomplishing the qualification [for liberation]. Therefore, [the word *asti*] is to be construed with what precedes.

Thus, in this context, within the very fulfillment of the qualification (*adhikāra*), the first indicator (*liṅga*) that reveals the intended meaning (*tātparya*)—characterized by predominance in both the introduction and the conclusion—is illuminated. Likewise: "There is no desire for objects while [the Self] shines forth"; and: "They perform action for the sake of enjoyment, and they enjoy in order to perform action;
like insects in a river, moving swiftly from one whirlpool to another, they go from birth to birth and never attain liberation."

And as for practice: "Having gradually abandoned both the meditator and the act of meditation, when the mind has the single object of meditation as its sole sphere—like a lamp in a windless place—that is called *samādhi*.

At that time, although the mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*) have the Self as their object, they remain unperceived; however, they are inferred from the memory that arises in one who has emerged from that state. Furthermore, the persistence of these fluctuations may occur even from the very first effort, aided by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) resulting from repeated practice performed without being seen [by the senses]."

This is its unprecedented nature: "When this web of latent impressions has been entirely dissolved, and when the accumulation of karma known as merit and demerit has been uprooted from its very foundation,
the sentence— being unimpeded and previously manifested as an indirect cognition— produces an immediate realization, like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand."
The Result: "Just as a lamp in a windless place," and so forth—in many ways, the Blessed One explained this very meaning to Arjuna;

thus say the exponents of the Arthavāda. "In this beginningless saṃsāra, tens of millions of accumulated karmas are dissolved by this [practice], and pure dharma increases. Those most skilled in yoga call this very dharma ‘samādhi,’ because from it flows a rain of the nectar-streams of dharma."

And there is the scriptural authority [of the word] *sraśaḥ*. Thus, when the subject matter of this section has been determined— by way of its unique primacy— to consist in the attainment of the qualification for *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi* through the sixfold signs beginning with the purification of the mind (*citta-śuddhi*), then, by virtue of that attainment,
the qualified seeker attains the fivefold states known as *sāyujya*, *sāṣṭi*, *sārūpya*, *sāmīpya*, and *sālokya* in union with the Saguna Brahman in the forms of Śiva, Viṣṇu, and so forth.

Even if among the various forms of liberation there is sequential liberation (*kramamukti*), how could devotion—characterized by love arising from the perception of it as the supreme human goal—possibly persist there? For that state lacks the conviction of its being true, due to the scriptural statement, "There is no happiness in the small," the experience established through the logic of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding the waking state and so forth, and the inference such as, "The subject under dispute is false because it is an object of perception, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. Thus, the introduction of this section is indeed well-founded.
In brief, the meaning is that when an object is investigated by an eligible person preceded by [the removal of] doubt, it possesses the capacity to sublate the aforementioned obstacles. || 65 ||

Thus [ends the work composed by] the lotus-feet of Śrī Nārāyaṇa Śāstri, who bears the name Paṣṭapa, the delighter of the lord of Advaita-vidyā, who sports in the milk-ocean of the Padas, Vākyas, and Pramāṇas, and who is the disciple of Śrīmad Dvaitasaccidānandendra Sarasvatī, the venerable wandering ascetic (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka) teacher.

Thus ends the first chapter, the *Tattvavivekaprakāśa*, in this commentary on the *Pañcadaśī* entitled *Pūrṇānandendukaumudī*, composed by Acyutaśarman, known as Moḍaka, whose mind acts like a swan. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter, titled "The Discrimination of the Great Elements" (Mahābhūtaviveka).
That non-dual reality which has been heard [in the scriptures] is [to be realized] through the discrimination of the five elements.
Therefore, the five elements, which are capable of being understood, are now analyzed in detail. || 1 ||
Rāma’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭī0): Having bowed to the lords of sages, Śrī Bhāratītīrtha and Vidyāraṇya, this commentary on the *Pañcabhūtaviveka* is composed by me. || 1 ||

"O Somya, in the beginning this was Being alone, one only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1). Since that Brahman, which is heard in scripture as the cause of the world existing prior to its manifestation— Being in nature and without a second— is by its very essence beyond the reach of speech and mind and thus cannot be understood on its own, it is taught through the method of discrimination (*viveka*) regarding the five elements (*bhūtapañcaka*), which constitute its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) as its effect.
He declares his discernment of the five elements through their state of being perishable: "The non-duality of Being" (sadadvaitam). || 1 ||
Commentary (a0): [I bow] to that which is the immutable form of the supreme Brahman—non-dual bliss, existence, consciousness, all-pervading, and stainless;
which, though the abode of the magician-like illusion of duality arising from delusion, is the forehead-mark of the Vedas and is self-luminous.
I bow to all the eminent teachers, to my true guru, the ornament of the lineage of Atri, who is established in Brahman, named Śrī Nārāyaṇa, and also to my own teacher named Mahādeva. || 1 ||
Having honored Jīvañjīva, Vidyāraṇya, and Bhāratītīrtha.
I illuminate the distinction between reality and the light of the eye by means of this moonlight. || 2 ||

Now, the venerable teacher Vidyāraṇya, commencing the second chapter of the *Pañcadaśī*, titled "Discrimination of the Elements" (*Bhūta-viveka*), performs an auspicious invocation characterized by the investigation of reality (*tattvānusaṃdhāna*)— which is well-known for its authority and purpose— and while intimating both the subject matter and the purpose of the present chapter, he [offers a salutation] for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the chapter described, consisting of the non-dual Pure Being (*advaita-sanmātra*) which is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the five elements as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

He promises an explanation: "The reality is non-dual" (*sadadvaitam*). It has been heard that the reality is non-dual. It was heard in the sixth chapter of the *Chāndogya*: "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed Being alone, one only without a second"; "All these creatures, my dear, have Being as their root, Being as their abode, Being as their support"; and so forth, regarding all distinctions.

The meaning is that the world is also traditionally taught as being non-different from emptiness (*śūnyatā*) by virtue of sharing the same efficient and material causes (*nimitta-upādāna*). By this, it is implied: if the means of valid cognition regarding the "wish-fulfilling jewel" of the non-dual Reality (*sadadvaita*), which is the ultimate goal of the Vedas, were to consist merely in the discernment of the five elements, then one might indeed propose the discernment of those elements as its cause; however, that is simply not possible. This is because there can be no connection between the elements and that non-dual Reality, as they are fundamentally unassociated.

Because they cannot be distinguished from one another due to their non-distinctness even when there is some degree of intermixture, and because such distinction is irrelevant to the aforementioned realization; for indeed,
that light which exists in the eyes during the cognition of the object is not the same as the light in the act of attaining Brahman.

"O dear, handsome Śvetaketu, my son, this world—which is presently perceived and consists of name and form, and which is produced—[existed] in the beginning, prior to its creation. As for time, it is indeed nescience (*avidyā*); this is well-established both by the *Siddhāntabindu* and because the seventh case-meaning of 'limitation' (*avacchedakatva*) is also well-known. Thus, the beginningless object of sight (*dṛśya*), which has attained identity with [Brahman] as characterized by nescience and is delimited by the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*), is therefore one alone and without a second, like one who is asleep, [free from] the threefold internal distinctions such as those of the self and so forth, and the distinctions of space and so forth."

The meaning is that there was only pure vision (*dṛṅmātra*), devoid of the threefold distinctions. He states the reason for this in the preceding section of the scripture, beginning with "O gentle one, all these have Being as their root" (*sanmūlāḥ somya*).

The sense is that just as this deer or water, when it turns back to its original state in the preceding moment, has that [original state] as its non-different efficient and material cause, so it is here. By this, the falsity (*mithyātva*) of duality is established.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 56]

[The objection] that "even when separating the great elements (mahābhūta) like sesame from rice, the reality of gold is perceived" has been refuted; for all duality indicated by the five elements is superimposed in that very manner by beginningless ignorance, and thus, just as in the case of a snake superimposed on a rope, when the superimposed is separated from its substratum, it is not cognized as such. || 1 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭī0): In that regard, first, in order to make known the distinction among the five elements beginning with space according to their qualities, he states those qualities:
"Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—these are the qualities of the elements."
One, two, three, four, and five qualities [belong] to ether and the other elements respectively.

[The author] says "Sound" (śabda). Now, one might inquire: "Are all these qualities present in all [of them], or is there one quality for each? Reflecting on this, he says "One... [verse 2], with the intention that neither of these two views is correct, but rather that there is another way.

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, it may be objected that *viveka* (discrimination) is indeed the separation of milk and water mixed together by means of conjunction, effected by the agent who separates them; and it is likewise the separation of mud and water effected by the agent who throws in the powder of *kataka* nut. Furthermore, in the case of gold and its bracelet, which are conjoined through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) due to their being cause and effect, and in the case of mother-of-pearl and silver, which have attained a state of illusory identity (*ādhyāsikaikatā*), their state of being distinct is of the nature of knowledge alone. Is this not so?

Anticipating the question, "Which one is intended in the present context?", he first analyzes and enumerates the specific, non-common attributes that differentiate the five elements, in order to awaken the listener to that very point at the end; he begins with the words "sound," etc. Based on the Vedic scripture stating "from ether comes air" and so forth, he declares the successive transfer of the qualities of each preceding causal element into each subsequent element, starting with "one," etc. (Verse 2).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He clarifies that very same point by means of another illustration:
"An echo is sound in the sky; in the air, it is the whistling sound."
There was a sensation of touch that was neither hot nor cold, and a crackling sound like "bhugubhugu" arose from the fire. || 3 ||

Regarding "echo" (*pratidhvani*): in space (*ākāśa*), sound alone is the quality (*guṇa*), and that [sound] takes the form of an echo. In air (*vāyu*), there are both sound and touch (*sparśa*). Therein, he demonstrates the sound of the air by means of an imitation—namely, the sound "vīsī. In the same way, the imitative sound should be understood in the subsequent cases as well. He states its touch: "having a touch that is neither hot nor cold. In fire (*vahni*), there are sound, touch, and form (*rūpa*).
These are the three qualities (guṇas), which are described in order; in the fire [of the breath], there is the sound *bhṛ-gu-bhu-gu-dhva-ni*. || 3 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might ask: does this established arrangement of the aforementioned qualities pertain to the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) in their un-compounded (*apañcīkṛta*) state, or to them in their compounded (*pañcīkṛta*) state? Since these [compounded elements] are to be known solely through scripture, their attributes must likewise be so. If the first case is intended, it is acceptable; but if the second, how can this be?
Anticipating this doubt, the author provides a resolution based on universal experience, beginning with the words "the echo" (*pratidhvani*), and so forth, [stating that] the qualities are truly...

This has been analyzed at the end by three and a half [verses]. It is well known that *pratidhvani* (echo) is another sound perceived from a sound produced in a portion of space delimited by a cave or similar object. Nor should it be asked: "Since it is stated in the Siddhānta and other treatises that this is a reflection (*prativimva*) of the sound, how can it have the nature of being a sound of the ether (*viyat*)? For, because it is not caused by anything other than the sound that has undergone reflection, it has that alone as its cause, just like the sounds of a drum and so forth.

And because it would not be so [if it were] caused by something else. The words "bīsa," etc., should be understood as imitations (*anukaraṇa*) of those respective sounds. Regarding the term "not hot":

the word "in air" (*vāyau*) is to be supplied. And thus, the intention is that touch is an inherent quality (*svābhāvika-guṇa*) in air, whereas sound belongs to the ether (*ākāśa*), which is its own material cause (*upādāna*). This should be understood in other cases as well. || 3 ||
The touch is warm, the form is light, and there is the sound of bubbling in the water.
Its touch is cold, its form is white, and its taste is said to be sweet. || 4 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Hot touch and light are its forms. In water, there are four qualities beginning with sound and ending with taste; he states them as follows: in water, there is the bubbling sound, cold touch, white color, and sweet taste. || 4 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): "Hot" and "radiant"—thus, fire possesses the three qualities (*traiguṇya*). "Water," and so forth; likewise, here [in water] there are four qualities (*cāturguṇya*). || 4 ||
The Second Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
On the earth-element, a clattering sound and a solid tactile sensation are recognized.
Blue and other colors constitute variegated form; sweet, sour, and other tastes constitute flavor. (5)

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He illustrates the five qualities beginning with sound and ending with smell that exist in earth, starting with the words "In earth, there is a clanging sound," and so forth. || 1 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding the phrase "on the ground" and "solidity": this is because it is experienced exactly in that way, and because the statement of the logicians is merely a technical convention (paribhāṣā). || 5 ||
The two qualities of fragrance and pleasant scent have been correctly distinguished.
The ear, the skin, the eyes, the tongue, and the nose constitute the five sense organs.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): With the words "the two fragrant scents," he concludes the matter stated thus far. Having thus described the distinction based on qualities (guṇataḥ), he now states the organs of perception (jñānendriyāṇi) as their effects, in order to make known the distinction based on their effects (kāryataḥ): "The ear... (verse 6).
The commentary on "a0" says: "Surabhi... [and so forth]. He concludes the exposition of the qualities with the words "guṇāḥ.

Having thus described the qualities of ether and the other elements, he states, in the manner taught in the *Tattvaviveka*, that the five sense organs are the effects of the *sattva* portion of those elements once they have been quintuplicated (*pañcīkṛta*), using half a verse beginning with "śrotraṃ... (verse 6).
The commentary on Rāmakaṇṭha shows their locations and functions: "That [faculty] situated in the spheres of the ears and so forth is, respectively, the perceiver of sound and the other [objects]."
Because of its subtlety, it is to be inferred from its effects; for the most part, it flows outward.

Regarding the phrase "from the ear, etc.": when there is the inquiry as to what proof exists for the existence of the sense organs (*indriya*), he states that it is inference based on the mark of an effect (*kāryaliṅgakānumāna*), saying: "due to subtlety" (*saukṣmyāt*). This [inference] should be understood as follows: "the perception of form is produced by an instrument, because it is an action, like the action of cutting," and so forth. "Due to subtlety" means that they are difficult to perceive because they are effects of the five unevolved elements (*apañcīkṛtapañcabhūta*). He describes their nature with the word "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*). Pa—
The meaning is that this is according to the Vedic revelation (śruti): "In the beginning, the Self-existent One pierced the openings" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 4.1). || 7 ||

The commentary on that [verse] states its function: "the ears and so forth. It describes its nature as being inferable from its effects and its subtle character: "due to subtlety," etc. Generally, it is manifold. || 7 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: By means of the word "mostly" (prāyaḥ), he shows that the sense organs sometimes perceive internal objects:
"Sometimes, when the ears are closed, an internal sound is heard."
In the vital breath, in the digestive fire, in the drinking of water, and in the eating of food.
For internal tactile sensations are manifested [in the absence of external objects], and when the eyes are closed, internal darkness is perceived.
In belching, there is the perception of taste and smell; such is the internal apprehension of the sense organs.

By means of two verses beginning with "kadācit": when the ears are occasionally covered, the internal sound existing within the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) and the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) is heard; during the drinking of water and the eating of food, internal tactile sensations are manifested—that is, they become manifest; when the eyes are closed, internal darkness is perceived; and upon belching, both taste and smell are apprehended. Thus—

In this manner, there is the grasping of the internal by the senses (*akṣa*). The genitive case in *akṣāṇām* is used in the sense of the agent. The meaning is that the grasping—that is, the apprehension—of the internal object occurs, with the senses as the agents; thus, it is the grasping of the internal object performed by the senses. || 8 || 9 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, an objection may be raised: since it is generally indicated by usage, one might argue that the internal objects of the senses must also sometimes be admitted as their objects. However, this is improper because it contradicts the scriptural text: "The Self-existent pierced the openings outward" (*parāñci khāni vyatṛṇat svayaṃbhūḥ*). Anticipating this, [the author] notes that since the word "only" (*eva*) is absent from the scripture, the maxim that "every sentence implies an emphasis" applies here provided there is no sublation; thus, regarding both internality and externality— [The text continues: ...there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the fact that the eyes and other senses perceive external objects is well-known in the world. Moreover, the statement "pierced the openings outward" is made with reference to the body, for it is observed that the eyes and so forth are situated externally relative to the body. Therefore, there is no conflict with the scripture. On the contrary, the scripture itself establishes the perception of internal objects through the passage: "But when he is in the state of deep sleep, being enveloped by consciousness, he does not know anything at all" (*svapnānta uccāvacamīyamāno rūpāṇi devaḥ kurute bahūni | uteva strībhiḥ saha modamāno jakṣadutevāpi bhayāni paśyan || tadeja-ti tannejati taddūre tadvantike | tadantarasya sarvasya tadu sarvasyāsya bāhyataḥ ||*); and also through the passage: "He who dwells within the earth, yet is other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, and who controls the earth from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (*yaḥ pṛthivyāṃ tiṣṭhan pṛthivyā antaro yaṃ pṛthivī na veda yasya pṛthivī śarīraṃ yaḥ pṛthivīmantaro yamayaty eṣa ta ātmāntaryāmy amṛtaḥ*), and so on. Since this is intended only with reference to the gross body, and because these spheres (the sense organs) are located at its lower part, [the opponent argues that] when the ears are covered, one experiences the hearing of the internal sound called *anāhata* produced by the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) within the body; to this he replies with the pair of verses beginning "kadācit": "Sometimes, when the ear is covered, being blocked by the fingers of the hand, while the vital air and the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) are present, the internal sound is heard."
The connection [of the sentence] is to be understood by supplying [the missing words] in this manner; likewise in the case of drinking water and eating food. || 8 ||
1.1.1 Commentary: "It is manifested" (*vyajyate*). The particle *hi* is used for emphasis. It means that only internal touches (*sparśa*) are manifested. Thus—

Bondage (*bandha*): likewise, in the case of the closing of the eyes—the ellipsis being "of the eyes"—the additional construction is that when concealment is effected, darkness itself is manifested internally. Similarly, in the case of emission (*udvāra*), the meaning is the upward movement of the wind residing in the stomach—consisting of the drinking of water, the eating of food, and the filling of the belly—which is of the nature of *udāna*.
Taste and fragrance (*rasagandhau*)—namely, sweet taste and fragrances such as saffron—are manifested, just as before. He concludes with the remainder of the verse beginning with "iti" and so forth.

If it is objected that this is not accepted by the ancient teachers, we say no; for the very root-author [Sureśvara], while revealing the intent of the *Pañcapādikā*, its commentary (*Vivaraṇa*), its sub-commentary (*Tattvadīpana*), and other works such as the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya-vākya-ṭīkā*, has established this very point in the *Vivaraṇasāra*. As follows: "But surely, in the analogy of darkness and light, the nature of being an entity and a non-entity is a limiting condition (*upādhi*)."

If it is argued that the Logicians (Tārkikas) maintain that darkness is the absence of light, while the Prābhākaras maintain that darkness is the absence of the perception of form, this is not so. For it is impossible for that which is perceived as possessing various states such as increase and decrease to be a mere non-existence; rather, it is a substance because it possesses the quality of blue color. [Objection: But if it were a positive entity (bhāva), how could there be a perception of it by one with eyes closed in a place filled with intense light? [For] by the intense light, its cessation would be admitted...

If it is argued that co-existence [of light and darkness] was previously stated to be possible only with dim light, we say no; for the perception of darkness existing within the eyeball is logically established. Nor is it impossible for the eye to grasp objects situated inside it, since we observe that one who has closed their ears perceives internal sounds. Furthermore, this does not entail the absurd consequence that collyrium and other substances situated inside the eyeball would also be perceived by one with eyes closed, because [the eye perceives] only those material things other than darkness that are accompanied by light.

"Because of the rule that it must be apprehended by an eye with applied ointment (*kṛtacakṣus*). This is its meaning: "limiting condition" (*upādhi*) refers here to heterogeneity (*vaiṣamya*), and not to the standard definition of a limiting condition as "that which pervades the probandum while not pervading the probans. For the latter is a specific fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) characterized by the "unestablished nature of being pervaded" (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*), and as such, it is a defect belonging solely to that particular reason, residing only in that specific reason. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one should understand the increase characterized by contraction. Regarding the phrase "of collyrium and so forth" (*añjanādeḥ*), by the word "etcetera" [the following is included].

[This is] a particle of camphor. Nor is it correct to object: "If that were so, then why is the collyrium and such residing in one's own eyes not perceived even by one whose eyes have opened with the assistance of light?
This is because there is no intervening space [between the eye and the collyrium]. Therefore, it is indeed logical that when the eyes are closed, the eyeball itself perceives the darkness within.
Furthermore, that darkness is of a positive nature (bhāvarūpa) has been stated even in the *Siddhāntabindu*. Thus, even darkness is indeed non-obstructive.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that *māyā* is indeed of the nature of a veil, an obstacle to visual cognition, and destructible by light; it manifests and disappears instantaneously, like lightning and the like. Furthermore, because it is not the material cause (*upādāna*) of the body—which is the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*)—the process of creation is not taught in the scriptures; thus, there is no contradiction.

Regarding this, the *Nyāyaratnāvalī* commentary states: "But [it may be argued]: 'In this way, [the world] is preceded by a reality characterized by being undestructible by valid cognitions and so forth, because it is luminous...'"

How can there be consistency with the statements in the *Vivaraṇa* and other texts, which—based on the inference beginning with "like the world"—accept that light is preceded by darkness that is destroyed by itself? For if darkness were a positive entity (*bhāva*) destructible by light, it would contradict the scriptural accounts of its creation; therefore, since it is of the nature of the absence of light, he says "In this way," etc. He clarifies its nature as an obscuration: "opposed to visual cognition" (*cākṣuṣajñānavirodhī*), meaning it is an obstacle to visual perception.

The meaning [is as follows]. Now, since light is the cause of visual perception based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), there is no evidence for darkness being its inhibitor; to this he says: "destroyed by light. If light were the cause of visual perception through the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga-sambandha*), then in the absence of light, visual perception would not arise. Therefore, with respect to visual perception, darkness is the inhibitor through the relation of delimitation (*avacchedakatā-sambandha*) with respect to the object. [This is] because of the light—

Because darkness arises in consciousness delimited by substances and so forth that are conjoined [with it], visual perception does not arise there; because darkness does not arise in consciousness delimited by light, visual perception arises there. The point is that since light destroys darkness, its positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) are exhausted in being useful for visual perception. [Objection: In that case, the creation of darkness should also be mentioned in the scriptures. To this, he says: "In the world... (saṃsāra...).
The Second Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.

"In the midst of the body, since there is no proof for the existence of *tamas* (darkness), *tamas* cannot be the material cause (*upādāna*) of the body; however, space (*ākāśa*) certainly exists within the body to provide room—this is the intended meaning. Now, if *tamas* is thus a positive entity (*bhāva*) and possesses parts (*sāvayava*), then according to the aforementioned reasoning, it would be directly [the cause], like space, of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because it is immaterial and formless, it must be admitted that it is perceived solely by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*); and since the *Mūla* states that "darkness is internal even when [the eyes] are closed," and because the *Vivaraṇasāra* clearly asserts its visibility by stating that there is a rule that light-assisted eyes perceive only that which possesses a form distinct from the body, [this is established].

Or rather, there is no contradiction. For it may be argued that what is an object of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) does not become an object of the eye, and what is an object of the eye does not become an object of the witness-consciousness; to this we say: "Certainly," because through reasoning the non-contradiction of both is possible. To explain: just as it is beyond dispute that the quality of sound, though manifested by the witness-consciousness, is nevertheless grasped by the auditory organ (*śrotra*), so too is the case for that which is not grasped by the senses but is directly perceived by the witness-consciousness.

This is because it has been stated in the *Siddhāntabindu* that the reflection of space is perceived in water and other such media. Likewise, since darkness is necessarily perceived by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), what obstacle is there to its blue color being visualized according to the aforementioned method? Nor is it correct to argue: "In your view, even in the absence of inherence (*samavāya*), identity (*tādātmya*) between substance and quality is necessary; therefore, if the color of darkness were visualized, it would follow that the darkness itself is visualized."

Otherwise, since sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa*) and is audible, it would follow that space itself must also be audible. If you argue that space is indeed intended to be audible precisely as delimited by sound, then one must likewise accept that darkness is intended to be visible precisely as delimited by its blue color. It is this very intention that underlies the argument stated in the root text and elsewhere; such is the secret. Now, regarding the subject at hand, there is a distinction between sound and color in terms of their being non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*) and pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*).

If it is argued that there is a disparity between the two cases, what does that matter? For the relation of identity (*tādātmya*) is equal in both instances. Nor should it be said that space (*ākāśa*) is manifest to the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi-bhāsya*) because the cognition "this is space" occurs even without a word, whereas darkness is not so because it is never perceived without the quality of blue color;
for such [blue color] is seen in deep darkness and in dim light. This is the direction of the argument. || 9 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus described the functions of the organs of perception, he now states their functions—which serve as the evidence for their existence—in order to establish their reality against one who denies the existence of the organs of action:
"The five activities are speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and experiencing pleasure."
Indeed, agriculture, trade, service, and so forth are included within these five.

"Five" (paṃca): [The compound] "speaking, taking, going, excreting, and pleasure" is a dvandva compound. The remainder [of the sense] is that the five well-known activities called speaking, taking, going, excreting, and pleasure are established. Now, raising the objection that since other activities such as agriculture and so forth also exist, how can it be said there are "five," he says: "Agriculture... (verse 10).

— Commentary (A0 Ṭīkā): Now, in order to describe the organs of action (*karmendriya*), he states the five activities that serve as their indicative marks, beginning with "five. An objection may be raised: since there exist hundreds of other activities such as agriculture and the like, how can there be a restriction to the number five? To this, he replies with "agriculture," etc. || 10 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question, "Which are those organs that produce action?", he says:
"The production of those actions occurs through the organs of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals."
That group of five organs of action resides in the spheres of the mouth and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "speech and hands": the remainder of the sense is that through the organs such as speech and so forth, the production of those actions occurs—that is, the arising of those activities comes about. Here too, one should observe an inference based on an effect, such as: "this [activity] is preceded by an instrument, because it is an action," and so forth. He states the locations of that pentad of organs of action: "the mouth and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the hands, feet, anus, and the opening of the genitals are included. || 11 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Next, he mentions the organs of action, beginning with speech, saying "vāk" (speech). Now, one might ask: where does this aforementioned pentad of organs of action reside? To this, he says: "mukhādi" (the mouth, etc.). An objection may be raised: by means of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), the existence of the organ of speech should be accepted as residing in the tongue itself, just like the organ of taste; therefore, why is the mouth—which serves as its general location—designated as the organ of speech instead of the tongue?

If it is argued that [the tongue] has been described as the locus (*sthāna*), that is true; for although the tongue— known as *vaikharī* speech— is the instrumental cause of the manifestation of those [sounds], it is nevertheless indicated by them.
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya [contains the section titled] "Discrimination of the Great Elements" (*mahābhūtaviveka*).

Even for those who do not hold [the specific] positions, the mention of "mouth" is consistent with the intended purpose of the speaker's intention. And those positions have been stated in the *Siddhānta-* [leaves].

In the Kaumudī: the throat is the place of articulation for the gutturals (ka-varga), the visarjanīya, and the sibilant *s*. The palate is for the palatals (*icuyaś*). The head is for the retroflexes (*ṛṭuraṣ*). The teeth are for the dentals (*ḷtulas*).
The lips are for the labials (*upūpadhmānīya*). For *ñamaṅaṇana*, it is also the nose. For *edait*, it is the throat and the palate. For *odaaut*, it is the throat and the back of the head.
The teeth and lips are for the letter *v*. The root of the tongue is for the jihvāmūlīya. The nose is for the anusvāra. Thus ends [the section]. 11.
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, he shows the function and the locus of the mind, which was introduced as the impeller of the ten senses mentioned above.
The mind is the presiding lord over the ten sense organs, situated within the sphere of the heart-lotus.
And that internal organ, due to its lack of independence regarding external objects, cannot function without the sense organs.
Regarding the word "mind" (mana): he states that its status as an internal organ is based on a specific reason—namely, "And that... (verse 12).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Hereafter, he states the internal sense organ (*antarendriya*)—the mind (*manas*)—which follows in sequence, as well as its location. He explains the reason for its status as an internal sense organ with the remainder of the verse beginning "In external... (bāhyeṣu), the word "objects" (*viṣayeṣu*) being understood by implication. || 12 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He clarifies the very fact that [the intellect] presides over the ten sense organs:
"When the objects have been presented to the senses, this [intellect] is the deliberator upon their merits and defects."
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are its qualities; for it is indeed modified by them.

Regarding the phrase "in the senses" (*akṣeṣu*): even when the senses (*indriyeṣu*) have been withdrawn and the objects have been established [within], this mind is that which investigates qualities and defects; the meaning is that it performs investigations such as "this is correct" or "this is incorrect. This is the underlying point: since the Self, by virtue of being the knower (*pramātṛ*), is common to all cognitions, whereas the eyes and other organs find their fulfillment merely in the production of the cognition of form and so forth, the investigation into their qualities and defects is [the function of] what is being perceived...

The mind must be accepted as its cause because it cannot otherwise be accounted for. To demonstrate that the mind possesses various functions such as detachment, desire, and so forth, he shows that it possesses the qualities of *sattva* and the rest, stating: "It consists of *sattva*," etc. He states the reason why these [qualities] are its attributes: "It is modified (*vikriyate*)," meaning that it undergoes transformation by means of those qualities. || 13 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, it may be argued that while the mind is indeed thus dependent on external objects, and the lotus of the heart is its location, what then is its specific function? To this, he says: "In the senses" (*akṣeṣu*). This means in the sense organs, such as the ear and so forth. "In the objects" (*artheṣu*) means in those characterized by sound and so on, which are sought after by them; that is, when they have been directed toward their respective objects for the purpose of grasping those objects. These—
"Mind. [The word] "guṇa" implies "it becomes [modified]. The reason for this is stated by the words beginning with "sattva.

Since the guṇas, as the primary material causes (upādāna) through their nature as *pradhāna* and so forth, exist within this mind, it is therefore modified by them; that is to say, it undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*) into the form of pleasure, pain, and delusion. || 13 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He elaborates upon the very fact that [the Self] undergoes modification through the qualities (guṇas):
"Dispassion, forbearance, magnanimity, and so forth, arise from Sattva."
Desire and anger, greed and effort—these and others arise from rajas.
Laziness, delusion, drowsiness, and other such distortions arise from tamas.
Regarding "dispassion" (vairāgya): because it is clear, it is not further explained. || 14 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might ask, "How are its Sāttvika and other modifications to be determined? Anticipating this, he explains them briefly and in sequence through three verses beginning with "Vairāgyam" (Dispassion). Dispassion is the firm lack of regard for anything other than the non-dual Self, produced by the realization that all objects of perception born of discrimination are essentially suffering, devoid of intrinsic existence, moment-to-moment changing, and perishable.
Thus it is.
[Page 61] Second Chapter.
Accompanied by two commentaries:
"If you feel anger toward one who has committed an offense, why do you not feel anger toward that anger itself?"
"Against that which forcibly stands as an obstacle to all human goals."

Thus, even when the capacity [to retaliate] exists—as implied by the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi*—patience (*kṣānti*) is the constant endurance of such [insults], through the discernment that pacifies anger born from the unsurpassed harm inflicted by others. This is achieved by contemplating the perishability of all that is perceived, regarding objects within one's own power.

Magnanimity (*audārya*) is precisely the enthusiasm for fulfilling the desires of supplicants at that very moment. Regarding the passage beginning with "desire" (*kāma*): desire is the longing for an object of affection that is perishable due to its connection with the falsity of all that is perceived. Anger is a mental state characterized by an internal burning produced by the obstruction of that [desire].
Greed is simply the intensification of that desire. Effort (*yatna*) here is the activity directed toward the means and the goal according to one's capacity. (14)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He demonstrates the respective effects of dispassion and the other qualities by dividing them:
"From the sāttvika [qualities] arises the accomplishment of merit; from the rājasa [qualities], the production of sin."
There is no fear from the tamasic state; rather, it would result only in the wasteful passing of one's life. || 15 ||
"By those characterized by sattva. || 15 ||

Commentary on verse a0: Regarding "indolence" (*ālasya*) and so forth—indolence is the aversion to the aforementioned effort even when one possesses the capacity. Delusion (*mūḍhatā*) is the mind being directed toward that [which is not the goal]. Drowsiness (*taṃdrā*) is the failure of the senses to grasp objects correctly due to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of sleep and the like, even while awake. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) applied to each of these three, one should respectively understand the host of divine natures such as tranquility (*śama*), self-restraint (*dama*), and supreme composure (*paramasamādhāna*), as well as the host of demonic natures such as hypocrisy (*dambha*), arrogance (*darpa*), and wickedness (*dauṣṭya*).

The group of demonic natures (rākṣasa-prakṛti), characterized by lack of illumination and lack of engagement, is also to be understood here. Now, he describes their results as well in two verses beginning with "By the sāttvika... The meaning is: by those which are *rājasa*—that is, non-scriptural, specific modifications of the mental states (*citta-vṛtti*) produced by the aforementioned *rajas*. By that [means], one obtains [the following]: approaching one's own wife during her fertile period;

teaching falsehoods; abstaining from the path [of dharma]; listening to the *Sāman* chants in the temple of the Lord and so forth; and [bathing in] the Gaṅgā during the moonlight of the month of Caitra...

There is the exclusion of touching [objects] such as wind and so forth, of beholding images of the Supreme Lord and the like, of tasting the flavor of His grace and so forth, of grasping the fragrance of His remains (nirmālya), and of the effort toward the path of renunciation. || 15 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Since these—the internal organ and all others—reside within the intellect, he declares their master:
"In this regard, the one who possesses the notion of 'I' is the agent; such is the established order of the world. (16)
Regarding this: the meaning is that the agent who possesses the cognition "I" is the Lord (*prabhu*). For in the world, one who performs action is indeed taught to be a lord. || 16 ||

Commentary on verse a0: Regarding the phrase "by those characterized by tamas," [the author] asks, "Of what? and replies, "I" (aham). This refers to the Self as qualified by the mental modification of egoity (ahaṃvṛtti). According to the etymology "that which is seen in the world" (lokyate), the meaning is "the entirety of the perceptible. || 16 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus described the constitution of the world, he now states the means for knowing its material nature:
"In those things endowed with manifest sound and so forth, materiality is extremely clear."
This should also be ascertained regarding the sense organs and so forth by means of scripture and reasoning. || 17 ||

"Clear" means that in objects such as jars, which are endowed with clear qualities like sound, touch, and so forth, their being effects of the elements is clearly understood. Anticipating the question of how the status of being an effect of the elements is determined in the case of the sense organs and the like, he says, "In the senses and so forth as well," [citing]: "For, my dear, the mind consists of food (earth), the vital breath consists of water, and speech consists of fire."

[Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4] and so forth; such scripture and inference establish that the disputed sense organs, such as the ear, must be effects of the elements, because they conform to the presence and absence of the elements. Whatever conforms to the presence and absence of something is seen to be its effect, just as...

A jar, which conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of clay, is seen to be the effect of clay; and since these [entities] are likewise [concomitant with Brahman], they are therefore [its effects]. Thus is the established rule in the world—this is the reading of Acyutarāya.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
titled "The Discrimination of the Great Elements" (Mahābhūtaviveka).

And the mind's conformity to the body is heard in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad in such passages as, "O dear one, the person consists of sixteen parts" (Chāndogya 6.7.1); this should be understood similarly in other instances as well. || 17 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Even so, why is the discernment of the five elements relevant here from the standpoint of non-dual reality? Anticipating this doubt, [the author replies]: Although the goal—characterized by the separation [of the elements]—is equally applicable to objects such as jars, which possess the qualities of the elements (sound, etc. perceived through perception and other means and which are effects of the elements, [this discernment is necessary] because the same reason for their being composed of the elements applies even to those things that constitute the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*), beginning with the auditory organ and extending to its limits.

He provides the resolution that accomplishment is understood through scripture (*āgama*) and inference (*anumāna*) alone, stating: "Clear," and so forth. In this regard, scripture is indeed the *Chāndogya* Upaniṣad passage: "For, my dear, the mind consists of food (*annamaya*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*) consists of water (*āpomaya*), and speech consists of fire (*tejomayī*). This has already been explained above in the *Tattvaviveka* by means of the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*). As for inference, it follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the mind and the vital breath with food and water respectively.

The proof for their being composed of the elements (*bhautikatva*) by virtue of being supports (*dhāyitva*) is well-known within that very scripture, beginning with the passage, "O dear one, a person consists of sixteen parts," and is even more well-known through common worldly experience. As for the sense organs, just as the ears and so forth, as well as the organs of speech and so forth,

are respectively the effects of ether and the other elements because they perceive the specific qualities (*tanmātra-guṇa*) such as sound and the rest, so too [are the internal organs] connected to channels identical to the spheres (*golaka*) that perceive those specific qualities of sound and the rest.

Because it is a sphere (*golaka*). Regarding the statement "in the case of the opposite, like the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*)," here, since deafness is perceived in the mouth, the nature of being a skin-sphere (*tvag-golaka*) in the hand, the integrity of the eye through metaphorical application to the feet, and the capacity to transform [substances] into odor in the anus and genitals are all perceptible, there is no lack of essential proof (*svarūpāsiddhi*) for the reason (*hetu*). A detailed exposition on this matter should be sought in the *Siddhāntabindu* and other such works. || 17 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Having thus distinguished between the primary elements and their derivatives, and while explaining the Vedic scripture that establishes the non-dual Brahman— beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1)— he states the meaning of the word "this" (idam) found in that passage:
It is understood through reasoning and also through scripture by means of the eleven faculties.
Whatever may exist here, this entire world denoted by the word "this" (idam). || 18 ||

Regarding the word "eleven": the meaning is that whatever is apprehended in the world by all means of knowledge (pramāṇas), such as perception and so forth, as well as by the cognitions arising from verbal testimony, presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), and others—all that is denoted by the word "this" (idam) found in the passage beginning with "All this is indeed Being" (sadeva). || 18 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Having thus established the nature of the individual and collective gross and subtle worlds, consisting of the elements and elemental objects, for the sake of the intended discrimination (*viveka*), and now desiring to explain the Vedic scripture beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second," which establishes the reality of non-dual existence (*sadadvaita*), he states the meaning of the words contained therein in the eleventh [verse]. Now, as for the internal organ and the external organs such as the ear...

If it is asked: "Granted that sound and the other [objects] can have the status of being instruments (*karaṇa*) in perception through [the sense organs], how is the status of being an instrument understood for the organs of action, such as speech?"—this is true. Even though they cannot be direct instruments, they can be causes of knowledge regarding their respective objects by means of actions such as the utterance of sound.

*Yukti* is inference (*anumāna*). By the word "also" (*api*), the object of the perception of the witness (*sākṣin*) other than the unevolved (*avyākṛta*), as well as the objects of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), are also included.
It is to be known. || 18 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus explained the meaning of the word "this" (idam), he now recites that very scripture according to its own meaning:
"All this, prior to creation, was indeed one alone, without a second."
"There was Being alone; name and form did not exist"—such is the statement of Āruṇi.

The meaning is as follows: the ear-organ (*śrotrendriya*) is that which perceives the quality of sound; its physical seat (*golaka*) is the ear-canal (*karṇa*). That whose [associated] channel (*nāḍī*) is identical to—that is, co-existent with—that [ear-channel], namely the physical seat called the tongue (*jihvā*), the state of being such [is the cause]. Thus, it is established by common experience among people that while there may be muteness in the case of deafness, deafness does not necessarily entail muteness—just as, for example, while the presence of smoke implies the presence of fire, the presence of fire does not imply the presence of smoke. And thus, regarding the physical seat associated with the same channel...
The former alone is the delimiting condition of the cause (*hetutāvacchedaka*), while the latter is merely indicative (*paricāyaka*).
[End of] the second section.
"Accompanied by two commentaries.
Regarding the word "this": it means the speech of Āruṇi—that is, Uddālaka, who is the offspring of Aruṇa. || 19 ||
Commentary on Verse 63:

Now, one might object: "Granted that this is what is intended by the word *idam* (this) in the aforementioned scripture—that is, duality other than the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*)—but what does that have to do with the present subject?

To this, the author recites that very scripture according to its meaning and expands upon the narrative of the instruction with the words "All this" (*idaṃ sarvam*). [This refers to] that which consists of the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*).
The meaning is "the entire web of the perceptible. Regarding the phrase "one alone," and so forth: this means being devoid of internal, homogeneous, or heterogeneous distinctions.

It refers to the words spoken by the great sage Uddālaka Āruṇi—born of the lineage of Aruṇa—to his own son Śvetaketu; the connection is made by supplying the word "exists" at the time of the instruction on Brahman. || 19 ||
The internal differentiation of a tree consists of its leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth.
From among trees, it is of the same class; from stone and so forth, it is of a different class.

Rāma’s Commentary: With the three words "one only, without a second," he seeks to preclude the three types of difference—namely, internal and so forth—which might otherwise be attributed to the Reality.
First, he demonstrates the three types of difference found in the world, beginning with internal difference, using the example: "of a tree... (verse 20).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, in order to explain the function of the words "one" and so forth found in the Śruti text, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second," [the author] generally elucidates the threefold division of differences—namely, those within itself and so forth—along with examples, beginning with the verse: "Of the tree... (20).

Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus demonstrated the threefold division in what is not the Self, [the author] states that the Śruti, by means of three words, precludes those same three divisions as they might erroneously apply even to the Reality: "In the same way, the threefold division that has accrued to the Reality is precluded."
By means of the three—namely, the determination of unity, the restriction [to that unity], and the negation of duality—in successive order. || 21 ||

"So be it. The meaning is that, because of the commonality of being a real entity (*vastutva*), the threefold internal distinctions—such as difference within itself and so forth—which would otherwise apply even to the reality whose nature is Being (*sad-rūpa-ātma-vastu*) just as they do to the non-self (*anātman*), are successively warded off by the three words "one only, without a second" (*ekam evādvitīyam*) from the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* (6.2.1), which express the determination of unity and the negation of duality. || 21 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, having shown these three types of difference, [the author] refutes them—even though they are possible within Brahman, which is of the nature of existence—because they are [merely] conceptual entities. He does so with the word "tathā" (so it is). Now, an objection may be raised: If this negation of the threefold difference is real (*sat*), then duality (*dvaita*) results; if it is unreal (*asat*), then all the more so duality results; and if it is both real and unreal, there is a contradiction due to the mutual exclusion of both; while if it is distinct from both real and unreal, then because it is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), duality results once again. [The author] replies: No. [This negation is] the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of duality consisting of the differentiator and the differentiated.

Because negation possesses the nature of being solely the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) by virtue of having the superimposed object as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*); because it is observed in cases such as "silver in mother-of-pearl" that the existence of both the positive and negative states of a superimposed object does not exceed the single existence of the pure substratum; and because the aforementioned duality must necessarily be superimposed upon Brahman in the form described, since its negation would otherwise be inexplicable. Nor [is there any contradiction] even so, on account of the scriptural statement "in the beginning" (*agre*) and the statement in the root-text "prior to creation" (*purā sṛṣṭeḥ*), which refer to time—

Now, regarding the section on "delimitation" (*pariccheda*): Time is indeed nescience (*avidyā*), according to the statement in the *Siddhāntabindu*: "O dear one, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support. This is because, in that context, it is intended that [time] is precisely that [nescience] which has attained identity with the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*)—the seed of the creation about to be described—as evidenced by the Śruti. || 21 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: First of all, it cannot even be suspected that there is any internal difference within the Real Entity (sadvastu), because it is partless; thus he says:
"Parts of the Real cannot be suspected, because no such constituent portion can be defined."
Name-and-form are not its two parts, because those two have not yet arisen.

Regarding the word "sat": having raised the doubt as to why name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) might not possess the quality of being a part of "Being" (*sat*), he states that they do not constitute a portion of Being because they did not exist prior to creation—thus: "name... (verse 22).

Commentary (a0): Now, an objection may be raised: "The statement that Brahman is devoid of internal difference due to its oneness is untenable; for even a single entity such as the sun or the moon is seen to possess internal distinctions through its rays and phases. Anticipating this, [the author] states that while the sun and others are thus [diverse] because they possess parts, [Brahman is not].
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[the section] titled "Discrimination of the Great Elements" (Mahābhūtaviveka).

Establishing that no internal differentiation can possibly exist in Brahman—which is of a single essence (ekarasa) and devoid of all attributes such as number, quality, and so forth—on account of its being partless (niravayavatva), the author proves that partlessness by the words beginning with "sataḥ" (of Being). The reason for this is given in the passage beginning with "tat" (that). Now, one might object: does not the Śruti state, "Having entered with this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms"?

And considering the Smṛti passage, "An eternal portion of Myself alone becomes the individual soul (jīva) in the world of living beings," one might suspect that the name-and-form manifested by the individual soul—which is itself a portion of Him—should indeed be considered His "limb" (avayava), which is another synonym for "portion" (aṃśa).
