Anticipating this objection, he provides the resolution with the words beginning with "name" (*nāma*), etc., on the grounds that such a relationship is impossible at the time delimited by the period prior to creation. || 22 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question, "From what [reason] is there an absence of name and form?", he says:
"Because creation consists precisely in the arising of name and form, prior to creation..."
Therefore, there is no arising of those two; it is partless, just like space.

Regarding "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), he states the conclusion: "Therefore," etc. Herein is the formal argument (*prayoga*): A real entity must be devoid of internal differentiation, because it is partless, like space. || 23 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭī0): Now, an objection may be raised: "If it is impossible for names and forms to arise prior to creation, then how can names such as 'Being' (sat), which are well-known from scriptures like *sadeva somyedamagra āsīt* and which consist in being free from sublation throughout the three periods of time, be possible even then, since Brahman is non-dual at that time? To this, the answer is: "Certainly. Since the aforementioned scripture speaks of that very nature [of Brahman] immediately following creation, it is not so [as you claim]. He states this with the verse beginning with "name" (*nāma*). He then states the conclusion: [The verse begins: *nāma...* [etc. He states the result:
"Therefore," and so forth. || 23 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Lest it be argued that while there may be no internal difference within Being itself, could there not be a difference from its own kind (sajātīya-bheda)?

Anticipating this, he states that one must claim that which is of the same class as Being would have to be another instance of Being; however, such a thing cannot be established because there is an absence of any distinction [between them].
He says: "There is no other Being of the same class, due to the absence of any distinguishing characteristic."
Without the distinction of the limiting adjuncts of name and form, there is no differentiation whatsoever for that which exists.

Regarding the phrase "always internal" (*sadaṃtaram*): one might object that a difference between the existent (*sat*) does indeed appear, as in the cases of "the existence of a jar" (*ghaṭasattā*) and "the existence of a cloth" (*paṭasattā*). Anticipating this, he states—referring to the difference in limiting adjuncts (*nāmarūpopādhibhedam*)—that such difference is merely conditional (*aupādhika*), like the space within a jar (*ghaṭākāśa*) and the space within a shed (*maṭhākāśa*), and does not appear by its own nature (*svataḥ*). Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*):

The reality that is the Existent must be devoid of difference from its own kind, because no difference is perceived in it apart from the reference to limiting adjuncts, just like the ether (*gagana*). ||24||

Having thus established the absence of internal difference through uniformity, he now establishes the exclusion of difference from those of the same class by means of an emphatic restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), using the sense of "exclusion of connection with another" (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), as in the expression "Pārtha alone is the archer. He does so with the words "sadaṃtaram" (distinct from the existent). The reason for this is stated as "vailakṣaṇya" (difference in nature).
He further substantiates that very point with the verse beginning "nāma" (name). || 24 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Let it be then that there is a difference from the dissimilar; anticipating this objection, he states that since the non-existent is the dissimilar of the existent, and because it is impossible for that which is non-existent to function as a counter-correlate (pratiyogin) precisely by virtue of its non-existence, even a difference having that as its counter-correlate does not exist:
"But the non-existent, being dissimilar, certainly does not exist, as is understood."
Therefore, it has no status as a counter-correlative; how then could there be a distinction from that which is of a different class? (25)
"Of a different class"—this refers to the following. || 25 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, by means of the negation of duality established through the term "non-dual" (advitīya), he further demonstrates its freedom from difference consisting of a dissimilar class (*vijātīya-bheda*)—namely, that it is devoid of anything of a different nature—by stating "dissimilar" (*vijātīyam*). Since it is not at all understood that there exists a non-existent reality (*asattattva*) which is dissimilar to the existent (*sat*), because by the very fact of saying "it exists," that [non-existent] would attain existence and thus lack non-existence; therefore, this non-existent thing has no dependence upon the existent regarding the object of difference consisting of a dissimilar class.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: since the state of being a yogin does not occur at all, how could there be a distinction from that which is of a different class? By this, [the second chapter, "That or One," is concluded].
Accompanied by two commentaries.

The doctrine of the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*), which is suspected based on such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," has been refuted. The detailed [exposition], however, is... [text continues].
This should be understood from the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* and other such works. || 25 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the conclusion:
"In this regard, however, some maintain that the Reality is one alone, without a second, and established."
Distraught, they described how this world was previously non-existent. || 26 ||

"Only one indeed. Now, in order to further solidify the non-duality of Being (sadadvaita) according to the maxim of "driving in a pillar," he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): "But here... (26).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, although the Madhyamika doctrine has already been demolished by way of [logical] resonance (*dhvani*), the author now raises an objection—beginning with the words "ekameva" and so forth—in order to refute it even directly, preceded by a restatement of what has transpired. Here, the meaning is: "when the reality (*sad-vastu*) devoid of the threefold delimitation (*pariccheda*) has been established. The word "tu" (but) carries the sense of "also" (*apy-arthaka*). By this, the impropriety of Akṣapāda and others is illuminated, precisely because [the truth] is established through scripture (*śruti*), reasoning (*yukti*), and so forth.

"Some" refers to certain specific Buddhists known as Mādhyamikas, proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*), and those who depend solely upon that [view]. Now, one might ask: "Even though the reality of Being (*sadvastu*) is established by the Vedas and other means of knowledge, how can there be a description of something contrary to it? To address this, the author qualifies them as "deprived" (*vihula*). The meaning is that they are of impaired intellect. For this very reason, this duality—which is not established by valid means of knowledge such as perception (*pratyakṣa*)—[exists] "in the beginning," that is, prior to creation.

The syntactical connection is that he described [the state] as being "only non-existent, indeed void. By this, the scriptural passage, "Now some say: 'In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent,'" becomes properly interpreted in its intended meaning. || 26 ||
Rāma’s commentary: He provides an illustration for the state of being overwhelmed:
"Just as the senses are overwhelmed when one is blindfolded in the dark, so too is his intellect."
Having heard of that which is indivisible and of a single essence, she becomes motionless and fears it.

Regarding the word "magnasya" (of the one immersed): he applies this to the subject at hand with the word "tathā" (so too). For this proponent of non-existence (*asadvādī*), the singular number is used in the sense of a class; having heard that the intellect—the internal organ—is a single, partless, and of uniform essence (*akhaṇḍaikarasa*) reality, it becomes "niṣpracārā," meaning it lacks movement toward a reality with form, or rather, it lacks movement toward a reality that is partless and of uniform essence. Consequently, it truly fears this reality. || 27 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "Even though non-duality (*advaita*) and Brahman are established by the Śruti and other authorities, what is the root cause of this agitation in the proponent of the aforementioned view? Anticipating this, the author clarifies that it is rooted solely in a lack of qualification (*anadhikāra*), illustrating it with an example: "Of one who is submerged... He applies the senses (*akṣāṇi*, i.e., *indriyāṇi*) to the subject at hand with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). "Of this proponent of Śūnyavāda," and so on; "indivisible," etc.; [and] the Śruti beginning with "Being alone, my dear... (*sadeva somyedam...*).
The meaning is that it has been stated thus; "Brahman is non-dual" is the implied sense. || 27 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He shows the agreement of the Teacher (Ācārya) regarding the meaning stated:
"The Gauḍācāryas [hold that] for other yogis, in the non-conceptual samādhi..."
They declared that those who are devoted to Brahman with forms experience extreme fear.
"The Gauḍa teachers," thus [it is said]. || 28 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Not only is this my own invention, but it is indeed traditional; saying this, he first introduces the consensus of the venerable Gauḍapāda Ācārya with the verse beginning "Gauḍa... (verse 28).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In response to the inquiry as to by which statement they spoke thus, he recites their very Vārtika:
"This so-called Asparśayoga is difficult to perceive for all yogis."
For yogis indeed fear this [ego], seeing fear where there is no fear. || 29 ||
*The reading "nirvikalpasamādhau" is that of Acyutarāya.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya.
[The section titled "Discrimination of the Great Elements"]

"Untouchable" (asparśa): this non-conceptual samādhi called "the yoga of the untouchable" is difficult to perceive for all yogis who are devoted to meditation with form; that is to say, it is hard to see and difficult to attain. He states the reason for this: "For the yogis... Because, for that reason, the yogis previously mentioned—who perceive duality—are like children in a fearful state within the fearless samādhi, which is devoid of fear, or in a solitary place.
Those who perceive it as a cause for fear, imagining it to be so, experience terror because of this yoga of non-contact. || 29 ||

He recites that very statement found in the section of the *Māṇḍūkya-kārikās* of the *Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad*: "Asparśa... etc. The meaning is: that in which there exists no contact—that is, no connection with the objectivity of the intellect—is thus [described]. This refers to the pure *tat-pada-artha* (the referent of the word "That") as characterized by *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*; in other words, it is the Self (*ātman*) which is the inward-facing pure consciousness (*pratyak-cinmātra*). || 29 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He states that this has also been declared by the venerable Ācāryas:
"And the venerable worshipful feet [of Śaṅkara] [have said this] regarding those whose minds are clever in dry logic..."
They call the Mādhyamikas deluded regarding this inconceivable, eternal Self.
"Bhagavat" [is explained as follows]. || 30 ||
A0 Commentary: Now, he introduces the consensus of the Vārtikakāra directly as well—“bhagavad... ||30||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He recites that Vārttika:
"Out of folly, these ignorant Buddhists disregard the Śruti."
Those whose only eye was inference attained the state of being selfless. || 31 ||
"Disregarding," thus [ends the commentary on verse] 31.
a0 Commentary: In that regard, he cites that very *Vārttika*: "anāhatya" || 31 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, having formulated the doctrine of non-existence (asadvāda), he refutes it:
"If you say that 'it was empty,' do you mean union with the existent, or identity with the existent?"
But for that which is empty, both [existence and non-existence] are not tenable, because they are contradictory. || 32 ||

Regarding the phrase "it was empty": the meaning of the alternative [presented] is that by the statement "it was empty," you either assert the connection of the void with the genus of existence (*sattājāti*) or its being of the nature of existence (*sadrūpatva*). Since both of these—characterized as the relation to existence and the state of being existent—are contradictory in the case of the void, they are not tenable; this is the meaning. || 32 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, following the maxim of "driving in a pillar," in order to strengthen the understanding that has been presented regarding the reality of non-duality (sadadvaita), [the author] restates and refutes the doctrine of non-existence (asadvāda) by means of a dilemma, beginning with the words "śūnyamāsīt" (it was void). O Mādhyamika, by the statement "śūnyamāsīt," which is rooted in the Śruti passage "taddhaika āhurasadevedamagra āsīt" (some indeed say that in the beginning this was non-existent alone), is it intended that "of the void there was existence" by virtue of the force of the verb (*āsīt*)?

Based on the traditional grammatical rule that *bhu* [is used] in the sense of existence (*sattā*) on earth, you either express some relation with "Being" (*sat*) delimited by past time, or—alternatively, since both the universal whose form is existence (*sattā-rūpa-jāti*) and the void (*śūnya*) are partless, devoid of qualities, and devoid of action—the first alternative being impossible—you express the state of being the Self of Reality (*sadātmatām*), that is, the nature of Being (*sadrūpatvam*). Thus is the connection. Both alternatives involve two mutually contradictory entities.

He refutes [the opponent's position] by means of a single reason called "contradiction" (vyāghāta), which consists in the impossibility of the same locus for [conflicting] properties, starting with the words "But not... (*na tu*). The word "but" (*tu*) serves to exclude the position stated by the opponent, or it has the sense of "also. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Because of being contradictory—that is, due to the contradiction consisting in the aforementioned definition—both of those [positions] are untenable. || 32 ||
Rāma’s Commentary (rāṭīkā): He confirms this very contradiction by means of an illustration—
[Second Chapter].
Accompanied by two commentaries:
It is not logical for the sun to be possessed of darkness, nor is it composed of darkness.
Since existence and emptiness are contradictory, tell me, how could there have been emptiness? (33)
It is not tenable. || 33 ||

In this regard, he clarifies the illustration with the words "it is not logical. He then applies it to the subject of the analogy with the words "of the existent and the void" (sacchūnyayoḥ). || 33 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, an objection may be raised: "In your view, the existence of ether and the other elements within the non-conceptual Brahman is contradictory.
Anticipating this, he says: "The name and form of ether and the rest are well-conceived through Māyā."
If name-and-form belong to that which is empty, then let it live for a long time! // 34 //

Regarding the phrase "of ether and so forth": if that is so, then the Buddhist—who asserts that name and form are merely imagined upon the existent reality even in the case of the void—would be contradicting his own tenet. With this intention, [the author] says: "of the void. (34)

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might raise the objection: "Just as in your view name and form (*nāmarūpa*) are merely imagined (*kalpita*) in the case of space and so forth, so too in the case of the Void (*śūnya*), those two must also be imagined by Māyā alone. Anticipating this doubt, he accepts it as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*) with the words "In the case of space and so forth," etc., and "Thus," etc. If the name and form of the Void are also indeed imagined by Māyā, then let that Void live long; let it remain.
The construction is "tv iti" (but [it is] so). The intention is that there is no fault because of the superimposition by means of what is imagined. || 34 ||

Rāmatīrtha’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "In that case, even for an existent reality (*sadvastu*), name and form must be admitted as merely imagined (*kalpita*) in your view, because, according to you, there is an absence of real name and form, just as there is for the void (*śūnya*)."
If it is argued that even though name-and-form exist, they are both merely imagined, then tell us this: [what is the basis for their imagination?]
Where indeed is an error observed that is without a substratum? || 35 ||
"Even if [it exists]"—with the intention that this position is untenable because it cannot withstand critical analysis, he refutes it with the words "then" (*tadā*).

This is the intended meaning: regarding the name and form of an existing thing (*sataḥ*), are they imagined upon something else that exists, or upon something non-existent, or upon the world? Not the first;

for we observe the superimposition of the name and form of one thing, such as silver, upon another, such as mother-of-pearl, and it is impossible for the name and form of an existing thing to be imagined upon that very same existing thing.

Not the second [alternative], because that which is non-existent and devoid of self-nature cannot serve as a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Not the third, because it is impossible for the world, having arisen from that which is existent, to have a substratum consisting of the conceptualization of existence, name, and form. Anticipating the objection, "Let there be no substratum for these two conceptualizations; why could they not exist? he says: "without a substratum" (*niradhiṣṭhāna*). || 35 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thereupon, the opponent raises a counter-objection (pratibandī) with the words "even though existing," and so forth. To refute that, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) asks with the words "then," and so forth. The reason for this is stated with the words "without a substratum," and so forth. || 35 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Just as a contradiction was stated in the passage, 'In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1), so too there is a defect in the passage, 'In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1). Thus he raises the doubt.
If there were a difference in the meaning of the words "was" and "is," a deficiency in the three qualities (guṇas) would result.
If there were no difference [between them], it would be a mere repetition; let it not be so, for it is observed to be thus in the world.

Regarding the phrase "it was existent" (*sadāsīt*): for instance, do these two distinct words have a difference in meaning or not? If they do, there is a loss of non-duality (*advaita*); if they do not, there would be a redundancy (*punarukti*). Therefore, taking up the second position—that "it was existent" is untenable—he refutes it with "not so. Anticipating the question, "What is the remedy for the fault of redundancy? he says: "In common usage... (verse 36).
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 68]

[The commentary on the section titled *Mahābhūtaviveka*: Now, even so, regarding the scriptural passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1), it is beyond dispute that the meaning of the verb is indeed existence, because the root *bhū* is traditionally remembered as signifying "existence" (*bhū sattāyām*). Thus, in the phrase "it was Being" (*sad āsīt*), [the sense is established].

Anticipating the objection that if *sattā* (existence) were distinct from the categories (*padārtha*), it would result in a doubling [of existence], whereas if it were not distinct, it would be a tautology, he provides the following resolution: "It was existent" (*sad āsīt*)—for such usage is observed in common worldly parlance. || 36 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question, "In what [other] instances in common usage is the absence of tautology observed in such constructions?", he says:
"The sentence performs what is to be done; it expresses the holding of that which is to be held."
To one who is permeated by such latent impressions (vāsanā), there arises the assertion that "it exists. || 37 ||
"1 It must be done. [Objection: "Let this be so in the world; what follows from it regarding the Śruti? To this he says: "ityādi" (beginning with 'thus'), etc. || 37 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He demonstrates those very same worldly usages with the words "it must be done" (*kartavyam iti*). Thus, he states that the declaration "Being existed" (*sad āsīt*) is indeed appropriate for one seeking liberation—exemplified by Śvetaketu—who is permeated by the aforementioned purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), using the words "and so forth" (*ityādi*). || 37 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, one might object that since there is no past time in a non-dual reality, the statement "in the beginning it existed" is untenable; anticipating this, he says: "The expression 'in the beginning' [is used] when there is an absence of time, due to the latent impression (vāsanā) of time."
Therefore, in this context, a second [teacher] is not even suspected with respect to the disciple. || 38 ||

Regarding the word "kāle" (at the time): one might suspect that prior to the origin of the world, Brahman was not accompanied by a second entity in the form of the world; however, this need not be doubted, because the scripture proceeds for the purpose of awakening the listener who is permeated by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of duality. Thus he says: "by that... (verse 38).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Even so, since the past time—which is the referent of the suffix in the word 'āsīt' (was)—exists, and since that same time is also conveyed by the word 'ayaṃ' (this), how can the real entity at that time be non-dual? Anticipating this objection, the author extends the previously stated reasoning to that case as well, stating: "kālābhāve... Here, the reading "agra ityuktiḥ" (the mention of 'before') is indeed correct, because the word "purā" does not occur in the Śruti text. Thus—
The sense is that this is merely an alternative reading (tyupapāṭha). || 38 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now he states the secret of the established doctrine:
"Whether an objection or a rebuttal be made, let it be done in the language of duality."
In the language of non-duality, there is neither the objection nor its reply. (39)

Regarding the term "objection" (*codyam*): the meaning is that during the state of conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*), objections and so forth must be raised; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), non-duality alone is the truth. || 39 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the second [objection] is not even suspected? Is this merely a command of kings? Anticipating this doubt, he provides a resolution by relying on the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that there is no entry at all into the discourse concerning non-dual reality (*advaita-vastu*), stating: "Or the objection" (*codyaṃ vā*). The meaning is: "the collection of objections. || 39 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In order to provide scriptural authority for the non-existence of duality from the perspective of ultimate reality, he says:
"Then it is motionless and profound; neither light nor pervasive darkness exists."
Something remains, which is indescribable and unmanifest. || 40 ||

"Then," [it is said]. "Stimite" means motionless; "gambhīram" means unfathomable, impossible for the mind to take as its object. It is not light (*tejas*), because it does not possess the nature of light; nor is it darkness (*tamas*), because it is distinct from darkness and is by nature unobstructed. "Tatam" means pervading. "Anākhyam" means incapable of being defined.
"Anābhivyaktam" means not made manifest even by the eyes and other senses. It is distinct from mere emptiness; therefore, it is "this something" (*kiñcit*).
The meaning is that there remains something which cannot be pointed out by her, and which persists as the ultimate limit for the negation of duality. || 40 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, what is the proof that the aforementioned scripture has as its purport the reality that is pure Being (*sanmātra*), devoid of the three divisions [of time]?
This is the second section.

Anticipating this objection, he states "it is indeed Smṛti" and recites that [text], beginning with "tadā": this is indeed Śrī Vasiṣṭha’s discourse to Śrī Rāma concerning the state of liberation while in the body (videhamukti).
It should be understood that the discourse concerning the resolution of questions regarding the objects of inquiry is indeed manifest in the *Bṛhadyogavāsiṣṭha* and other such works. || 40 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Granted that earth and the other elements may be non-existent because they are impermanent due to their having a beginning; but how can the existence of eternal space (ākāśa) be denied? Thus he raises the doubt:
"Granted that earth and the rest may not exist, since they perish down to the level of atoms..."
If it is asked: "How does the non-existence of space ascend to the intellect? (41)
"Is it not so? || 41 ||

Commentary on Sūtra 1.1.1: Regarding this, the logician (tārkika) raises an objection with the word "nanu" (but surely). "Te" means those Advaitins, you. "Prati buddhim" means with respect to the intellect. The meaning is: of the ether (ākāśa), whose destruction is rendered impossible even by thousands of means of valid cognition such as perception; its non-existence [is asserted] by the definition beginning with "tadā" and so forth.

In the *Smṛti* and in such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1), there is a lack of faith characterized by a literal acceptance of the meaning as it stands; that is to say, it is a non-existence caused merely by dullness. How can it be established in the intellect that even the ether—which possesses eternity defined as being neither the counter-positive of prior non-existence nor the counter-positive of destruction—is devoid of existence even during the period delimited by the time of dissolution? This is what [the opponent] asks.
The intention to revile. || 41 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He refutes [the objection] by means of an illustration:
"Just as you have resorted to the intellect [to explain] the sky, which is utterly devoid of the world..."
In that very same way, why does he not adopt a mind that is completely free from craving? 42.
"Entirely" (atyantam) means completely devoid of the world, that is, entirely free from the mere existence of the world. || 42 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), taking as his illustrative example the very ether (ākāśa) which has been accepted as eternal by the aforementioned logician, refutes him by relying upon that very point, stating: "Atyantam... (Verse 42).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Relying on the maxim that "what is actually perceived cannot be logically untenable," he raises an objection:
"If the sky devoid of the world is seen, even without light and darkness..."
What have you seen, and what in your position is not directly perceived? Indeed, space [is not so perceived]. (43)

Regarding the phrase "it has emerged": he refutes [the opponent's position] by stating that the very perception [of emergence] is unestablished—namely, "it shines. Furthermore, he states that this would also constitute an admission of a contradictory tenet (apasiddhānta)—namely, "moreover" (kiñca). || 43 ||

Anticipating the objection that this [criticism] is not a valid refutation because of the disparity between the illustration and the point at issue, he refutes— according to the opponent's own view— the perceptibility of space (*viyat*), which is devoid of light and other qualities, with the verse beginning "nirjagat" (verse 43).

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection that the absence of perception is equally applicable even to an existent entity, he says— refuting this on the grounds that the existence of the Real is established by universal experience—
"But the pure, existent reality is experienced by us who are certain [of its truth]."
Remaining silent does not constitute emptiness, because of the avoidance of even the cognition of emptiness. || 44 ||

Regarding the phrase "an existent reality" (*sad-vastu*): one might object that in the state of silence, there is only emptiness (*śūnya*) because nothing else whatsoever is perceived. Anticipating this doubt, he states, "nor is there emptiness," for even emptiness is not possible since there is no perception of emptiness itself. || 44 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, an objection might be raised: "The absence of perceptibility in the ether (*viyat*) is exactly the same as for any other existent entity (*sad-vastu*); just as you accept [the non-existence of the ether] solely on the basis of faith in the Vedas and so forth, I likewise accept the ether as eternal through the reasoning known as inference, which is supported by logic (*tarka*) and the like. Anticipating this, he resolves it by stating that such is not the case due to the difference between the two, and clarifies his own experience as the proof therein: [He continues: "Just as you accept [the ether's non-existence] based on the authority of scripture alone, I do not accept the ether as eternal merely through inference; rather, I accept it as non-eternal because it is perceived by my own direct experience (*anubhava*). Therefore, there is no parity between our positions. Thus, having established the distinction, he makes his own experience clear.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 70]

[The phrase] "called the discernment of the great elements" refers to the reality of sound. The word *tu* (but/however) serves to indicate a distinction. It is pure (*śuddham*) and non-dual (*nirdvaitam*). To exclude the possibility of error regarding this experience, he qualifies the Self with the word "by those who are certain" (*niścitaiḥ*). [This refers to] those beginning with the ancient teachers and ending with one's own guru—the knowers of Brahman who have expounded the Vedānta through faith and the reasoning that supports it.
The meaning is: by those who possess the determination beginning with [the word] *prabhṛti*. || 44 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "In that case, since the notion of existence is absent, even 'existence' (sattva) is not tenable. To this he replies:
"Even if the notion of existence does not exist, let it be so; for its self-luminosity [is sufficient]."
Because it is the witness to the state of being without a mind, true honor is easily attained by men. || 45 ||

Regarding the phrase "the cognition of existence" (*sadbuddhi*): since that [existence] is self-luminous, its non-cognition is not possible; thus he offers a rebuttal: "Let it not be so for this. [Objection:
If there is no cognition whose object is itself, how can the existent thing be apprehended? To this he replies: "In the state of being without mind" (*nirmanaskatve*). ||45||

Commentary (a0): Now, an objection may be raised: "What we have stated—that by virtue of the determination of the non-duality of the Self as Brahman, preceded by the falsity of the visible world as established through Vedānta as interpreted by the traditional lineage of teachers and supported by the logic of Vyāsa, one experiences pure non-duality as the true reality during the period of remaining silent, and that it is not experienced as a void because of the absence of the notion of a void—is incorrect; for just as [the experience of a void would follow] from the absence of the notion of a void..."

Anticipating the objection—"The experience of emptiness is not like that, because even the cognition of existence (*sadbuddhi*) is not perceived at the stated time; therefore, what proof is there for its experience?"—he provides the resolution: "Even the cognition of existence... [is self-evident]. He concludes by establishing that very point as it has been ascended upon by experience: "...in the state of *nirmanaska* (mindlessness)... Ma-... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "Ma-". The translation reflects the available portion.)

The meaning is as follows: because it was stated in the preceding section that there can be no form of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), there is an appearance of the nature of existence (*sadrūpabhāna*) whose object is the absence of all volitions (*saṃkalpa*), which is inferred by the retrospective reflection (*parāmarśa*)—"For this duration, I remained entirely free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*)"—occurring during the period of emergence (*vyutthāna*) characterized by the absence of the functions of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) consisting of volition and so forth. || 45 ||
Just as the witness remains undisturbed when the mind is free from expansion.
Prior to the manifestation of illusion, reality itself remains undisturbed.

— Rāma’s Commentary — Having thus demonstrated the manifestation of the witness, who is free from phenomenal expansion (niṣprapañca), while remaining in silence, he says "the mind" (verse 46) to show that by means of this illustration, the existence of the Reality even prior to creation can likewise be understood.
Yati-a0 ṭīkā: Thus, during the interval of remaining silent—
"When the previous conceptualization has dissolved, until the emergence of another..."
"Non-conceptual consciousness shines forth clearly for the time being."
The function of moving from one meaning to another meaning proceeds by moving within the interval.

And from the words of the venerable ancient teachers, "That which is without support and without modification is known as *sonmanī*," it is characterized by being the witness (*sākṣitva*) of the state of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa*), which is designated by the term "mindlessness" (*nirmanaskatva*).

Having caused that non-dual Pure Being (sanmātra) to ascend into the intellect of one seeking liberation, its suchness is established even by way of that analogy for the period preceding creation as well. The argument may also be inferred as follows: "In the time prior to creation, the Real Entity is devoid of the three kinds of limitation, because of the absence of manifested objects, like Pure Being characterized as the witness of the state of non-cognitive absorption (asaṃprajñāta). This is the general direction [of the reasoning]. || 46 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question, "What is the definition of Māyā?", he says:
"Māyā is His power, devoid of the principles (tattva), which is to be known through its effects, like the power of fire."
For a power is never perceived by anyone prior to its effect.

"Beyond reality" (*nistattva*) means that which is devoid of a separate reality from the entity that is the cause of the world; it is "comprehended through its effects," meaning it is known through the evidence of its effects such as space and so forth. This power (*śakti*) of this existent reality—the capacity to produce effects such as space and so forth—is called *māyā*. It is the very nature of the reality itself...
[page 71]... [end of fragment].
The Second Chapter, together with the two commentaries. 71.

He provides an illustration for the existence of a power distinct [from the substance] with the word "fire" (*agni*). The meaning is: just as there exists a capacity residing in fire and so forth, which is distinct from the essential nature of fire and the like, and is known through the evidence of effects such as the bursting of a seed-capsule (*sphoṭa*), so it is here. He confirms that power is known through the evidence of its effects by means of a negative formulation (*vyatireka*) with the words:
"For power is not... (verse 47).

Nā-ā-ṭīkā: Now, an objection is raised: In the Śruti text, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," nothing whatsoever other than Brahman is mentioned with reference to the time prior to creation; yet, in the preceding verse, it was stated, "due to the expansion of Māyā," and so forth.

By means of the illustration of the witness (sākṣin) being undisturbed—characterized by the absence of testimony due to the lack of mental modification—it was stated that even for an existent reality (sad-vastu), non-duality is caused precisely by the absence of the expansion of *māyā*. In response to one who objects, "What is the proof for *māyā*? And what is its definition that distinguishes it from everything else?", he answers by explaining it with the words "nistattvā" (devoid of reality). Thus, this is indeed an inference based on the mark of the effect (*kāryaliṅgaka-anumāna*).

In this regard, conventional means of valid cognition (*vyāvahārika-pramāṇa*) and their corresponding definitions are likewise stated in brief. For instance—beginning with "Being only, my dear," and so forth—the world is established as the effect of the non-dual Brahman that is Being, based on the otherwise inexplicability of such scriptural passages as "It emitted heat," and so forth; and it is established by scripture as being the effect of His power called *māyā*, according to the texts: "One should know *māyā* to be His material cause" and "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold."

The root [text] says: "Because it is an effect, like burning. This means that just as in the world, having observed an effect characterized by the burning of grass and so forth originating from fire residing in a heated iron ball or similar object, one infers a certain power inherent in that [fire] alone which is conducive to that [effect], so too it is in the present case. By this, its falsity—characterized by being devoid of intrinsic existence (svataḥ-sattā) and designated by the term *nistattva*—is implied. Therefore, [regarding] every effect...

Furthermore, the definition of *māyā* as "that which is inaccessible to valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) while possessing a power whose existence is non-different from that of Being" also follows logically. Now, if *māyā* is thus inaccessible to valid means of knowledge, how can it be sublated by the knowledge of the oneness of the non-dual Brahman and the Self? For that which is established by valid means of knowledge is never sublated anywhere. Consequently, the presentation of the aforementioned inference is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhīvāda*). To this we say: no, for there is a lack of understanding of the matter. Ta- [text fragment]

Stay! By the statement defining [the world] as "devoid of reality" (*nistattva*) and so forth, what is intended is precisely that [the world] is cognizable through inference possessing empirical validity (*vyāvahārikaprāmāṇya*).

And thus, just as objects such as a jar—which are cognizable through means of knowledge like perception that possess empirical validity—are nonetheless sublated by the final valid cognition, so too would it be for *māyā*. Nor does this imply that the venerable author of the *Vārttika* [would have to admit] that ignorance (*avidyā*) lacks the nature of ignorance.

However, this very definition must be stated: that which is intended as the unique characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) is the inability to withstand valid cognition (*pramāṇāsahiṣṇutva*). It should not be argued that there is a contradiction between this and the definition under discussion, because in that context, by the term "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), what is intended is exclusively the great Vedāntic mahāvākya resulting from inquiry into the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-artha*).
Otherwise, by those very [authorities]:
"This is called ignorance only by remaining within ignorance itself;
however, from the perspective of Brahman, this so-called ignorance is not in any way tenable."

Thus, the statement in the *Vārttika*—"it is postulated"—suggests that the ignorance (*avidyā*) designated as "Māyā-pura" is to be understood through an inference based on the mark (*liṅga*) of its effects; this [suggestion] would otherwise be contradicted. Therefore, it is indeed appropriate that its definition and other characteristics are as stated above. Now, one might object: if it follows from this that Māyā is a power whose existence is not distinct from its effects and their relations, then the qualifier "effect" (*kārya*) is redundant. Anticipating this objection, [the author] addresses that very subject...

Even though its purposefulness has been stated by way of its not indicating what is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the author] demonstrates the necessity of that [indication] through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—on the grounds that it would otherwise be impossible—for one who insists that it should not be included in the definition due to the resulting prolixity, with the latter half of the verse beginning "For not... (na hi). || 47 ||
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Having thus established that power (śakti) is inferable from its effects, he now establishes its nature as being beyond the categories (nistattvarūpa):
"Power is not an entity distinct from the existent; for fire is not [separate] from its own power."
But if it is distinct from the six categories, what could be said to be the true nature of this capacity? (48)
"It is not a real entity. This is the intended meaning: Is the power of a real entity existent or non-existent? It cannot be existent; for if it were so, [page 72] 72...

In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya, in the section titled *Mahābhūtaviveka*, [it is argued that] because it is non-different from Being (*sat*), it is impossible for it to be its power (*śakti*). Regarding this stated point, he provides an illustration: "Indeed, not [from] fire... In the second case as well, what...?

With the intention of raising the alternative that [the object] is either equal to a human horn or distinct from existence, he asks: "In the case of being distinct from existence" (sadvilakṣaṇatāyām). || 48 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Even if power (*śakti*) is non-different from its effect, as is established in the case of the power of a magnet, its distinctness must necessarily be asserted for the sake of establishing that the Existent (*sat*) is devoid of connection [with anything else]. If that were so, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural passages introduced with 'Being alone, my dear... (*sad eva somyedam...*), because by that very [power], the Existent would possess a second. Anticipating this objection, [the author asks]: "Is this power of the Existent identical to the Existent, or is it different from the Existent? It cannot be the first," and so on.
"No," he says. Illuminating the reason for this, he clarifies the example by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "For not... The underlying intention is as follows:

if fire itself were that power, then how could it be obstructed by a magnet-stone (*maṇi*) and the like? Yet it is directly perceived by everyone in the world that its power—which is distinct from it yet dependent upon it—is indeed obstructed. Otherwise, even the Vaiśvānara fire mounted upon a khadira-wood coal would be [obstructed] by a magnet-stone.

If there were contact with the hand, the non-perception of a blister or similar effect would be contradicted; therefore, the claim that "the power of an existent entity is itself of the nature of existence" is merely the prattle of a child.

This point is to be seen in detail in my own *Muktiramālaṃkriyā*, which is a commentary on the *Advaitaratnarakṣaṇa*. He indicates that the second [alternative] is not tenable because it is logically inconsistent by saying "existent" (*sat*). And thus, this [text] is intended precisely to establish what was previously promised regarding that which is devoid of reality (*nistattva*).
The intention is that this is a formal presentation (upanyāsa). || 48 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Therein, having restated the first position, he refutes it:
"If [you say] it is emptiness, then that which is empty is said to be the effect of Māyā."
Neither empty nor existent—let suchness (tattva) be understood here as being just so.

Regarding the term "emptiness" (*śūnyatva*): the meaning is that if [the opponent] intends for both name and form to be empty, then let them live long in that state. Therefore, he says "not empty" (*na śūnyam*), indicating that the second alternative remains; the intention is that the nature of *māyā* is indefinable in terms of being either existent or non-existent. || 49 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Why do you thus rebuke [us], since it is possible to say that emptiness (*śūnyatva*) itself is the reality?

Anticipating this doubt, he says, "If [you say] 'emptiness'," etc., because that emptiness, along with name and form, has already been refuted in the passage beginning with "If so, may you live long," and so forth; therefore, it is not so. He states the conclusion: "Not emptiness. And thus, of that [emptiness], existence and non-existence—

The intended meaning is that even while you are weeping, you must necessarily accept the very nature of indeterminability (anirvacanīyatva), which consists of falsity characterized by the possession of two contradictory characteristics. || 49 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: To provide scriptural authority for this point, he cites the Śruti:
"At that time, there was neither non-existence nor existence; rather, there was only darkness."
Through association with darkness (tamas), it [becomes] goodness (sattva), not by itself, because that [goodness] is excluded from its own nature.

"Not non-existent" (nāsat). The meaning is that the scriptural passage beginning with "In the beginning, there was darkness hidden by darkness" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.7.17.1) is the authority. To the question, "If so, how can 'darkness was' be said to be existence?", he says: "Because of its connection with being" (sadyogāt). To the question, "Why? he says: "Because of the negation of that [non-existence]" (tanniṣedhāt). || 10 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): To show that this meaning is not merely our own invention, but is indeed stated by the Śruti itself, he recites that very passage in its sense: "nāsadāsīt" (There was neither non-existence...). Non-existence (*asattva*) consists in being devoid of identity with existence (*sattādātmya*), while simultaneously being the counter-correlative of absolute non-existence in respect of all space and time. Now, [one might object]: how can there be a creation of non-existence—otherwise known as the Void—which is the exclusive object of conceptual construction?

If it is argued that the negation may apply to the prior time-limit (*prākālāvacchedena*), we say: "Certainly. However, because that which is characterized as being non-opposed to existence (*bhāvāpratiyogilakṣaṇa*) possesses the aforementioned nature, this negation does not apply to it at all; rather, it applies only to the effects of the primordial ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) to be described hereafter—namely, to ether and so forth, which are fit for cognition as "existent ether" and the like, and which have attained identity with existence (*sattādātmyāpanna*). With this intention, based on the scriptural passage, "In the beginning there was darkness, hidden by darkness," he indicates: "It was not existent" (*no sadāsīt*).
The Second Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
[This is] by [the verse beginning with] "73.

...dityādinā" (and so forth). If that is so, what was there at that time? To this he says: "But what... And thus, the falsity—characterized by being neither existent nor non-existent—rests ultimately upon the root ignorance denoted by the word *tamas*. Now, even if this is so, one might object based on the traditional rule (*smṛti*) that the root *bhū* means "existence" (*sattā*), [as expressed in the phrase] "by the word *abhūt*..."
In that very case, existence is perceived; thus, how can the aforementioned falsity (mithyātva) apply there? To this he says: "Because of its connection with Being" (sadyogāt).
By this, the falsity intended by me—the absence of intrinsic existence—is also illuminated therein. || 50 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary—He states the conclusion:
"For this very reason, its status as a second [entity] is not reckoned, just like a void."
In the world, the life of Caitra and his power are not recorded as separate things.

"For this very reason" means that since Māyā possesses no inherent existence (*svataḥ-sattva*), its status as a "second" entity is not even reckoned—meaning it is not at all taken into account—just as in the case of the void (*śūnya*). To illustrate the non-acceptance of a second entity for that which is unreal, he provides the example: "Not in the world," etc. (Verse 51).

The commentary (ṭīkā) states the conclusion: "For this very reason" (*ata eva*). Just as in the Śruti text "one only, without a second," the existence of a second is reckoned by the opponent (the Śaṅkara school) as being merely an absence relative to a second counter-correlative within Brahman, so too [in our view], it is not reckoned by that aforementioned power whose existence is entirely dependent upon that [Brahman]. He establishes this very point through a negative example: "Not in the world... (verse 51).

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Since it is observed that when there is an increase in power (*śakti*), life increases, therefore power itself must possess a separate life. To this, he replies:
"If life increases when power increases, then [power] is the cause of that increase."
It is not power, but rather its effects, such as warfare, agriculture, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "excess of power": he refutes [the objection] by stating that "in that case," [showing] that power is not the cause for prolonging life, but rather its effect, such as war, agriculture, and so forth; he then applies this to the subject of the illustration with "likewise. || 52 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might object: "In the world, even though there is no written record of the separation between Caitra’s life and his power, it is indeed observed that when power increases, the duration of life increases—as seen in the case of elephants and others. Therefore, this [separation] is merely to be inferred through inference based on the mark of the effect (*kāryaliṅgaka-anumāna*). Anticipating this, [the author] replies: By means of the inference, "Caitra possesses greater power because he has a longer life, like an elephant," one establishes the distinction between the property (*dharma*) of power and the substratum (*dharmin*) of life; thus, in the proof of the distinction between the property and the subject, the cause and the probandum are related as effect and...

He provides the resolution that the reason—namely, the presence or absence of the state of being a warrior—is indeed non-conclusive, by means of the passage beginning with "in case of superior power" (*śaktyādhikye*). Furthermore, does the word "living" (*jīvita*) refer to longevity or to strength? It cannot be the first, because even long-lived creatures such as crows lack superior power. Nor can it be the second, because the individual (*vyakti*) indicated by the verb "is written by me" under the term "living" remains undetermined; having this in mind, [the author] speaks of "power" (*śakti*).

The increase in the individual [denoted] by the word *jīvita* (life) does not infer an increase in the capacity [of the individual], but rather it is the very activity—such as fighting or agriculture—expressed by the term "capacity" (*śakti*) that infers an increase in capacity; for such activities as fighting are observed only when there is an increase in capacity, and not in its absence. Thus, because of the causal relationship between these two alone, there exists a relationship of reason and consequence (*hetu-sādhya-bhāva*). Therefore, the increase in the individual denoted by the word *jīvita* is otherwise [than an increase in capacity].
The construction is: "The proof of the greatness of power is indeed established. || 52 ||
In no way whatsoever is there a separate enumeration of mere capacity.
But since there is no effect of power at all, how can a second [power] be suspected? || 53 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Regarding the phrase "in every way" (*sarvathā*): one might suspect that although the Existent (*sat*) does not possess a second entity by way of its own power (*śakti*), it nevertheless becomes accompanied by a second through its effect (*kārya*).

Anticipating this objection, he states: "But the effect of the power... (verse 53), meaning that because the effect is non-existent at that time, the Existent is not accompanied by a second even by way of that effect.

The commentary (ṭīkā) concludes with "sarvathā" (in every way). Now, one might object: even so, let the Brahman's state of having a second (sadvitīyatva) at the beginning of creation after the dissolution be accounted for solely by that effect; to this he replies—"śakti... (by its power). || 53 ||
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya [the commentary by Rāma, titled *Mahābhūtaviveka*:
Now, does the power of Being (*sacchakti*) exist everywhere in Being, or in only one part? Not the first, because it would be attained by those who are liberated...]

Fearing that [if the power were to reside in the whole] it would result in the non-existence of Brahman, and that [if it resided in a part] there would be a contradiction due to its being partless, he says— with the intention of stating that the first [possibility] is not accepted and the resolution for the second will be stated later:
"That power does not reside in the entirety of Brahman, but rather occupies only a single part."
Just as the potentiality of a jar exists in the earth, specifically in moist clay. || 54 ||
"Not in its entirety. He provides an illustration for [the case of] partial occurrence with the word "pot" (ghaṭa) and so forth. || 54 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "In this case, like speech and other such powers, does this power reside in the entirety of Brahman through an illusory identity (*ādhyāsika-tādātmya*), or does it reside in only a portion of it? Neither is possible, because [in either case] there would be the consequence of [Brahman] being limited by measure. If this is argued, we say no. For, in the very sky delimited by the rays of the eye directed upwards and aided by light, the locus of the error of blueness (*nīlimabhrama*) is found. Thus, [the power resides in that specific delimited space].
Just as a distinction distinguishes both the thing to be distinguished and [itself], without requiring another distinction;

In accordance with the method stated in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*: "Delusion manifests both its own effect and another delusion, even without [the mediation of] a further delusion," it follows that this [power] is but a specific portion of Brahman delimited by the aforementioned superimposed power; this is illustrated by an example.
He clarifies this with the words: "Not in its entirety" (na kṛtsnā). || 54 ||
All beings constitute one foot of Him; His three-footed self-luminous nature abides in its own glory.
Thus, the Śruti declares that Māyā exists as a partial manifestation.
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the proof for the fact that power (*śakti*) exists in only one part [of Brahman], citing *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 3.12.6: "A foot of this... (95).

66. Commentary on the Verse (Pā-a0 ṭīkā): Regarding the requirement for a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in this context, he cites the Śruti: "A quarter belongs to him" (*pādo'sya*). It is intended that the conceptualization of "quarters," however, is in accordance with the Śruti solely with the aim of [facilitating] the understanding of disciples who possess the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) arising from reflection upon the four-footed Dharma (*catuṣpāddharma*). The actual Vedic reading (*śrauta-pāṭha*), however, is as follows:
"Of this, all beings constitute one quarter; his three quarters are the immortal in heaven"—this is indeed well-known. || 59 ||
Pervading this entire universe with but a single portion, I remain as the world.
Thus Kṛṣṇa spoke to Arjuna regarding the fact that [the world] is but a single part of the whole.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Not only is there Śruti, but there is also Smṛti; thus he says: "Having pervaded... (56).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "What is the proof that the scriptural passage cited, 'A foot of Him are all beings,' etc., has its own literal meaning as its intended purport?
Anticipating this doubt, he states that the very Smṛti which corroborates it is the proof: "Having pervaded," etc. (Verse 16).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, he states the proof for the actual existence of the nature of the Nirguṇa (the Devoid of Attributes) [Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.90.1]:
"Having encompassed the earth on all sides, He transcends it by ten fingers' breadth."
And here, in the Vikārāvati, there is the statement of the authors of the Śruti and the Sūtras. || 57 ||

Regarding the phrase "that [Self] is the ground": the meaning is that this refers to the statement of the author of the Sūtras, "And [the Self] does not abide in modifications, for thus it declares its state" (Brahma-sūtra 4.4.19). || 57 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might object that even the cited Smṛti does not have the meaning stated above, because it is possible to interpret its sense as follows: "I am the Lord of Lakṣmī; this entire, complete world—consisting of the aggregate of things both stationary and moving—is pervaded and restrained by a single portion of my will in the form of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpa*); and thus, standing apart from all activities other than those assigned to each [being] by my own decree, I remain distinct. Anticipating this doubt, the Śruti...
It is also stated in the Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad that Brahman has three quarters.

Accompanied by the two commentaries.

[The author] says "sa" and so forth, stating that it is not so, because there would be a contradiction with the other two Brahma-sūtras. "Sa" refers to the aforementioned Supreme Self (paramātman). Vi-...

"From white, from everywhere. "The earth" refers to the *pṛthivī*; this is an illustration [extending] as far as the entire web of duality (*vaitajāla*). "Having encompassed"—the meaning is that he pervaded the entire web of the visible world, including both the internal and external, just as space pervades the blueness superimposed upon itself. The syllable *hi* is for the purpose of establishing the connection with the *Puruṣasūkta*. "Ten," and so forth; it means in such a way that his form remains beyond what is indicated by ten fingers. "He transcended" (*atyatiṣṭhat*) means he existed beyond. Thus is the syntactical connection.

Regarding the phrase "vikāra" (modification): this is the nineteenth sūtra of the fourth pāda of the final section of the *Uttaramīmāṃsā*, which reads: “And [the Lord] does not abide in modification, for thus He declares His state. Herein is the commentary (*bhāṣya*) by the venerable Śrīmad-Bhagavatpāda:

“Moreover, the supreme form of the Lord, which is eternally liberated, does not abide in modification; it is not merely within the scope of modifications, such as the solar orb and other substrates. For thus [the scripture] declares of Him...”
The traditional teaching (āmnāya) declares the abiding of form: "Such is His greatness; yet the Puruṣa is greater than that. All beings constitute one quarter of Him;
His three quarters are the immortal in heaven," and so forth. || 57 ||
Even though [the object] is partless, one who asks "in the whole" or "in a part" superimposes parts upon it.
The Śruti, desiring the welfare of the listener, speaks the reply in that very language.

Rāma’s Commentary: Then, raising the objection as to what the resolution is for the contradiction regarding partlessness, he states the intent of the cited scripture with the view that there is no contradiction because partlessness is accepted as being real: "Even though partless," etc. (Verse 18).

Commentary (a0): Now, one might object: "If this is so, then there is a contradiction with the partlessness (*niraṃśatva*) of Brahman, which is indicated by such scriptural texts as 'In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second,' and which is also implied by the inference favored by the venerable Citsukhācārya—who understood the purport of those scriptures—namely: 'This cloth is the counter-correlative of an absolute non-existence residing in these threads, because it possesses parts, like other objects that possess parts. Anticipating this objection, [the author] states *dvai-*...

To the one who asks, "Is this [superimposition] placed upon the entirety of Brahman, or only upon a portion of it?"—whether that questioner is a seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) adhering to the doctrine of a single soul (ekajīvavāda), or whether it is addressed to seekers of liberation according to the doctrine of manifold souls (nānājīvavāda)—the Śruti, desiring the welfare of its listeners and wishing to bring about their auspiciousness by making them intent on hearing its own instruction, provides an answer by superimposing a "portion" upon Brahman, which is indeed partless, using that very terminology. Therefore, there is not even a scent of the aforementioned contradiction; thus he resolves [the objection]: "ni-" [etc.].
"Even in the case of a ray," [it is said]. || 58 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He now states that for which purpose Māyā was established in Brahman:
"The Power, resting upon the reality of Being (sattattva), may conceive modifications within that which exists."
Just as various colors applied to a wall produce a manifold painting upon that wall. || 59 ||

Regarding the phrase "the seven principles" (*sattattvam*): "transformations" (*vikriyā*) refers to specific effects produced through various modes of modification; this is the meaning. He provides an illustration for this with the word "colors" (*varṇā*); colors such as red, yellow, and so forth are specific modifications of the constituent elements (*dhātu*). || 59 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) on verse a0 states the conclusion: "The true reality" (sattattvam). It refers to modifications (vikriyāḥ), namely the transformations such as creation and so forth. To facilitate understanding for those of immature intellect, he clarifies the intended illustration with the word "colors" (varṇāḥ). Here, by the term "color," one must understand specifically pigments such as vermilion and the like that cause red, yellow, and other hues. Even these, upon investigation of the object, are found to be nothing but clay, just as the wall serving as their substratum is essentially clay alone.

The intention is that they are like illustrations of the power of Māyā, which produces the world by producing various forms. By the use of the plural number, the essence of the Śruti—"His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold"—is indicated as being summarized. || 59 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Therein, he first demonstrates a specific effect—the ether (ākāśa) is the first modification (vikāra), and it possesses the nature of providing space (avakāśa).
The reality of existence, namely that "space exists," likewise follows through into space itself.
Regarding the word "first": he states its essential nature as "that space. He provides the reason for space being an effect of Brahman with the words "space" || 60 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 76]

[In the commentary on the section titled "Discrimination of the Great Elements" (Mahābhūtaviveka), having raised the doubt as to what the intermediate modifications are among those modifications such as creation and so forth, and desiring to state that there are exactly five in accordance with the proposition "discrimination of the five elements," and in response to the inquiry as to which one is the first among them, from that...]

Based on the Vedic scripture, "From this Self, space was produced," he describes that [Self] whose nature is Being (sat), and therein explains the persistence of the existence that serves as the substrate, along with its experience, stating: "The primordial... (verse 60).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"The reality of existence (sattattva) has a single nature; space (ākāśa) possesses a dual nature."
There is no space when the sky exists; thus, both of these remain as a duality.
"One" (eketi): He clarifies the meaning already stated with the words "there is no space" (nāvakāśaḥ). When there is an existent reality (sad-vastu), there is no space;

rather, there is only the single nature of existence (sat-svabhāva). But in the case of space (ākāśa), both are present—namely, that nature of existence and this nature of space. This is the meaning. || 61 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, it may be argued that "space" (*avakāśa*) is indeed the mere absence of parts; for in a composite object such as a wall, no space is perceived at all.

Thus, the category of "space" is simply the absence of obstruction consisting of the atoms of the four elements—earth and so forth—and this is understood by the verb "is" (*asti*), which contains the suffix *laṭ* denoting the present tense, as the locus of such an absence at that very time. Therefore, it is not [the case that space is a positive entity].

Anticipating the objection that Brahman is the existent reality (*sad-vastu*), yet there exists some first modification called "space" (*ākāśa*) imagined by its power, [the author] replies: even in the present time and so forth, because space acquires its own nature only through the permeation of existence (*sadanuvedha*), the terms "absence of obstruction" (*avakāśāvaraṇābhāva*) and "space" (*ākāśa*) are not synonyms; for they differ in their grounds for application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*), namely the delimiters of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), and in their conventional usage. With this intention, he explains the difference in the essential natures (*svabhāva-bheda*) between the principle of existence (*sattattva*) and space.

He explains: "One" (ekā). That is the nature of the existent reality (sad-vastu-svabhāva), characterized by being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time. This is the "space" (avakāśa). || 61 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He explains the nature of existence and space as being respectively singular and dual through another method:
"Or, that which is the quality of the echo is not perceived as existent."
In the sky there are two with sound; by that, one with sound doubled makes the sky sixfold.

Alternatively: it has been established above that an echo is a quality of space (*vyoman*). This echo is not seen—that is, it is not perceived—in a real entity (*sad-vastu*), yet both the dense [matter] and the sound "sat" (being) are perceived in space.
For that reason, space, which is of the nature of "Being," is "twice-featured" (*dviguṇa*); the meaning is that it possesses two natures. || 62 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Previously, it was stated that sound is the specific quality of space, as in the phrase 'the echo is a sound in the sky'; thus, sound alone was declared to be the unique attribute of ether. To this, he says: "Or else" (*yadvā*). But even so, what relevance does this have to the present topic? To this, he says: "In the sky" (*vyomni*). Furthermore, why is that? He states the resulting conclusion with the remainder of the verse beginning with "by that" (*tena*). The meaning is: "one" (*ekam*) refers to the very nature of non-duality (*advaita*). It is "twofold" (*dviguṇam*).

The second quality is that which has the common property called "sound" (śabda); that [space] is thus. And so, the meaning is this: space becomes possessed of the subtle quality of sound through the very existence of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), which is the object of the ignorance that is the material cause of the error. || 62 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If space is an effect of Being (Sat) along with Brahman, then how can it appear that 'the existence of space' is an attribute of Being?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The power which conceives of space brings about the non-difference between Being and space."
Having established the status of property and its owner, one should conceive of them as being reversed. || 63 ||

Regarding the phrase "that power": that *māyā* which conceives space within the real entity first conceives the non-difference between the real and space, and subsequently conceives their relationship as property and property-possessor in reverse order; thus, the appearance of space as having existence is established—this is the meaning. || 63 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): [Objection] If that is so, then one would perceive only the word "existence" (sat), and not the existence of space (ākāśa) as the word "existence.
[End of] the second section.

And [the word] "existence" (*sattā*). Anticipating the objection that it is generally perceived as being so, he provides the resolution with the word "yet" (*tu*). "Reversal" (*vyatyaya*) means the opposite. And thus—avi- (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on a philosophical work, likely Advaita Vedānta, discussing the nature of existence and perception.)

The meaning is as follows: the very existence (*sattā*) of the non-dual Brahman—which serves as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) by having attained identity with the primordial manifestation (*vivarta*) known as space (*ākāśa*), which consists of the single quality of sound (*śabda*) and the nature of ether (*avakāśa*)—is itself capable of being perceived as "the existence of space" (*ākāśasya sattā*) and so forth. This is because, although it has itself assumed the status of a property (*dharma*) such as space within its own substratum, it remains fit for such cognition, just as in the cases of "this is silver" (*idaṃ rajatam*) and "silver is this" (*rajatam idam*). Thus, even while being the substrate, it appears as the property of space and so on. || 63 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question of how this inversion was brought about by Māyā, he says:
"Ordinary people perceive that which has attained the state of space as being existent, yet they perceive the existence of space itself [as non-existent]."
For that is indeed appropriate for the logicians regarding Māyā.

Regarding the word "existent" (*sat*): when the investigation into the true nature of reality is conducted, just as clay attains the form of a jar, the existent (*sat*) has attained the state of being space;
that is, the real entity has reached the form of the ether. Yet worldly beings and, among them, the logicians within the scriptures, perceive the opposite:

they understand the existence (*sattā*) of the substratum (*dharmin*), namely the sky or ether, as well as its generic property (*jāti*) of being "existent" (*sad-rūpa*). Now, one might object: "Is it not illogical for one thing to be perceived as another?"
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Of Māyā. The meaning is that it is logical for Māyā to be the cause of a perception contrary to reality. || 64 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): That very point—the conceptualization of the reversal of the relationship between the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the superimposed (*adhyasta*), which are respectively the real (*sat*) and the void (*vyoman*)—is clarified by the verse beginning with "sataḥ. That which, through *māyā*, has attained or reached the state of being the void, that is to say, the nature of space (*ākāśatva*), is what all worldly beings who are unrefined perceive; likewise, even among those who are refined, the logicians (*tārkika*)—those who follow the systems of Gautama and Kaṇāda, which prioritize reasoning (*tarka*)—perceive it in that same way.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: even for those who have abandoned all doctrines of duality, they understand and conceive of an "intense universal" (*utkaṭajāti*)—namely, the existence (*sattā*) which is the property (*dharma*) of the substratum (*dharmī*) that is space (*vyoman*), known as the "highest universal" (*parasāmānya*), whose occurrence is distinct from substance (*dravya*) and the other categories—on the basis of the statement of Viśvanātha Pañcānana: "Existence is called 'higher' because its occurrence is distinct from substance and so forth.
Now, one might ask: why do even these non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) have such an error? To this he replies with the remainder of the verse, beginning with "māyāyāḥ" (of Māyā). || 64 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He clarifies that Māyā is the cause of erroneous cognition by demonstrating a worldly maxim:
"In whatever manner a thing exists, its being so appears through a means of valid knowledge."
"The alteration [of perception] occurs through delusion"—this is a principle common to all the world. (65)

Regarding the phrase "yadyathā" (as it is): the meaning is that this principle is well-known to all the world. That which exists as a mother-of-pearl shell and so forth, in whatever manner—that is, by way of its form as a mother-of-pearl shell and so on—its being such, its nature as a mother-of-pearl shell and so forth, shines forth through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); whereas its being otherwise, its nature as silver and so forth, appears through delusion (*bhrānti*) by way of error. This is the sense. || 65 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) on verse a0 clarifies that very point through worldly logic: "That which... || 65 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus shown the erroneous perception resulting from delusion, he states the means for its cessation:
"In this way, whatever object appears prior to the inquiry into the Śruti..."
Through investigation it is found to be otherwise; therefore, let the sky be contemplated.

"Thus" means: in the manner described, prior to the investigation of the meaning of the Śruti—that is, before the inquiry into the subject matter of the Vedas—whatever entity, which is Brahman in the form of Pure Being (*sad-rūpa*), exists through delusion in the form of the ether (*gagana*) and so forth; that very thing, by means of reflecting upon the meaning of the Śruti, undergoes a reversal:

it abandons its state as ether and the like, and becomes Brahman alone in the form of Pure Being. Therefore, since the perception of the true nature of reality (*vastu-yāthātmya*) is possible through the investigation of the Śruti, let that [Brahman] be considered as the ether and consciousness (*cit*).
The meaning is: "let it be considered. || 66 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Applying the aforementioned logic to the present context, [the author] establishes the necessity of the inquiry regarding space according to the method previously stated, beginning with the words "evam" (thus). Regarding the phrase "śruti" and so forth: whatever object—that is, the entire collection of entities included within duality—appears or manifests in what manner prior to the inquiry into Vedānta; however, by means of inquiry, that is, by means of the aforementioned discrimination...
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 78] 261.

[The phrase] "called the discrimination of the great elements" (mahābhūtaviveka) follows from the manner of explanation previously stated. For whatever reason something is perceived erroneously—that is, understood in a contrary way—for that reason, one should investigate *viyat*, the subject at hand, namely space (*ākāśa*), in accordance with the conclusions of the Upanishads; this is the connection, supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhṛtya*). || 66 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He demonstrates the very nature of the inquiry:
"The ether and existence are distinct because of the difference in their words and because of the difference in their locations."
The cognition of difference arises because [the quality of sound] persists in air and the other elements, but not in space. || 67 ||

Regarding the word "bhinne" (in the case of difference): this refers to the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*). He states the reason—namely, "because of the word"—meaning that the words *viyat* (ether) and *sat* (being) are not synonyms. He states another reason—"and because of cognition"—and clarifies that very reason with the words "in air, etc.": that cognition which appears as persisting (*anuvṛtta*) among the elements such as air in the form "air exists," "fire exists," and so on, but which does not appear in that way [with respect to others], is the distinction (*bheda*).
The meaning is that the cognition of difference arises from the curds. || 67 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Demonstrating the nature of the aforementioned inquiry into space (*viyat*), he makes his formal proposition: "In the case of *bhinne*. The meaning is that space and Brahman (*ākāśabrahmaṇī*) are distinct, possessing empirical difference (*vyāvahārikabhedavatī*). The reason for this is stated by the words beginning with "śabda" and so on. [The opponent objects:

"In cases such as 'ghaṭaḥ' and 'kalaśaḥ,' although there is a difference in words, there is no difference in meaning; therefore, there is the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), characterized by the presence [of the reason] where the probandum is absent. Thus, [the argument] is not [valid]."

The author states this through the words "buddheśca" and so forth. Thus, the meaning is that there is only one reason, namely: "because of the difference in being the object of cognitions produced by non-synonymous words. This is to be understood as being like the case of a pot, a cloth, and so on. In that regard, if there were non-difference between space (*viyat*) and [the other elements], then, just as space does not persist in air and the others, existence (*sat*) would likewise fail to persist; thus, he supports the argument with the words "in air and the others" (*vāyvādiṣu*), etc. It is not [the case].

Nor is it correct to say that space (vyoman) is also perceived as pervading air and the other elements by way of its own nature as sound; for although space is the transformative material cause (pariṇāmy-upādāna) of air, it is only the quality of space—namely, sound—that persists [in air], just as the white color persists in a cloth produced from white threads, whereas the designation "thread" does not apply to the cloth. In contrast, Brahman is merely the illusory material cause (vivartopādāna) therein, and thus it persists only through its own generic aspect as the reality of Being (sadrūpa).
The sense is that the distinction between those two is indeed clear. He concludes with the remainder of the verse, beginning with "iti" (thus). || 67 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus established the difference between existence and space, he demonstrates the reversal of the relationship between the substratum and its attribute—which was perceived through the delusion that space possesses existence—by means of inquiry:
"Existence is the attribute [of space] because it subsists in more [entities] than space."
