When the existent is distinguished by the intellect, tell me: what is the nature of space?

"An existent entity (sad-vastu)" means that just as there is a substance (dravya) which persists through color, taste, and so forth, so too there is Being (sat) which persists through ether, air, and so forth; this is its nature as the substratum (dharmin). Just as color, which is excluded from taste and the like, is a property (dharma), so too is ether, which is excluded from air and the like, a property. Now, one might object: "In that case, just as the form (rūpa) distinct from a jar is real, so too would ether, being distinct from Being, be real. Anticipating this, [the author] states "distinct from Being" (sadvayatirikta)—
He says "not so" because the sky, which has been mentioned, is difficult to define: "by the intellect" (dhiyā) || 68 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): For this very reason, he states that only that which exists possesses the status of a subject (*dharmin*), saying "the existent thing" (*sadvastu*). He states the conclusion, saying "by the intellect" (*dhīyā*); the intended meaning is that [the object] is insubstantial (*tuccha*). || 68 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He raises the objection that its being difficult to define is unproven:
"If it is of the nature of space, then consider it to be non-existent."
If you say that what exists is divided into "being" and "non-being," then there is a contradiction for you. (69)

Regarding the phrase "consisting of space" (avakāśātmaka): [the opponent objects that] in that case, because it is distinct from existence (sat), it would simply be non-existent (asat). To this, he provides the rebuttal: "not non-existent" (na asat).
He states the fault for one who claims that there is no non-existence for that which is distinct from existence: "distinct" (bhinnam) || 69 ||
[On the matter of] having made a formal proposition.
[Page 79] Second Chapter.
Accompanied by two commentaries.
Commentary on verse 79: Now, was it not stated by you yourself in such passages as "The first modification is space (ākāśa); it possesses the nature of providing room" and so forth?

Thus, immediately following [the previous verse], their difference was established by the words "When [space] is divided, space exists," and so forth. Now, however, with the intention of asking how its insubstantiality (*tucchatva*) is implied by the words beginning with "by the intellect" (*dhiyā*), he restates that doubt and replies: "By the very fact of being separated from that existent (*sat*) by the intellect, its insubstantiality is to be understood by you yourself"—this is stated in the verse beginning with "avakāśa. But surely, let there be a difference from the existent; nevertheless, the definition of non-existence (*asattva*)— [The opponent objects: "But surely, let there be a difference from the existent; nevertheless, the definition of non-existence—"

He reveals the contradiction against one who says, "Let there not be the emptiness of space": "It is distinct. And thus, regarding the statement "space and existence are distinct," I have stated in the commentary that they possess a conventional distinction; therefore, there is no contradiction. || 69 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that there could be no manifestation if [the object] were non-existent, he states that manifestation is not contradictory because it is distinct from the void:
"If it appears, let it appear; that is indeed an ornament for that which is illusory."
That which appears as non-existent is false, like a dream-elephant and so forth. (70)

"If it is argued that [the world] appears," he says "yadasat" (that which is non-existent) in order to show the lack of contradiction by stating the definition of a false object along with an illustration.
The meaning is: that object which, though non-existent in its own nature, yet appears, is false—just like an elephant in a dream and so forth. || 70 ||

— Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "If it is thus insubstantial (*tuccha*), how can it appear as 'this'? Anticipating this doubt, he resolves it by stating that its appearance is not contradictory precisely because it is *anirvacanīya* (indefinable), characterized by being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent, beginning with the words "it appears" (*bhāti*) and so forth. || 70 ||
Just as genus and individuality, the embodied and the body, and quality and substance are distinct from one another.
In the same way, let there be a distinction between space and existence; what is there to wonder at in this? (71)
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection that a difference between two things invariably perceived together has never been observed, he says: "jāti... (Verse 71).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might argue that there is indeed a difference between space (*vyoman*) and existence (*sat*), just as there is between a genus (*jāti*) and an individual (*vyakti*). To this, he says: "Genus," etc. (Verse 71).
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: He raises a doubt, suggesting that although difference is indeed perceived, it does not yet become firmly established:
"Even if difference is understood, if it does not become deeply rooted in the mind..."
Tell me: is this [term] lacking conventional usage because of its lack of exclusivity or because of doubt? (72)
Regarding the phrase "the Buddha as well": in order to state the rebuttal to that, he asks for the reason why there is no certainty, [answering] "due to lack of one-pointedness. ||72||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Even so, one might suspect that its falsity—like that of a dream—is simply unbearable. Anticipating this, [the author] asks by way of an alternative inquiry: "Even though you are enlightened... (verse 72). The question is: regarding this well-established firmness of the falsity of the ether (*viyat*)—which is distinct from Being—and of the difference relative to it, which is like an elephant in a dream, does your consciousness lack consistency (*anaikāgya*), or is there doubt? What is the cause [of your failure to grasp this]? Thus he asks.
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the resolution for the first [objection]:
"Be vigilant; in the first [stage], there is meditation; in the other, discernment."
Establish it through authoritative testimony and reasoning; thereby, it shall become most firmly rooted.

"Be vigilant" means: regarding the first alternative, be vigilant—that is, be attentive in mind—because of the previously stated definition of meditation (*dhyāna*) as "the one-pointedness of the mental state (*pratyaya*) therein. Regarding the second [alternative], he states the refutation: "In the other.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "From that... (verse 73).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Even though this question has been asked, without waiting for an answer, out of the excellence of His supreme compassion, He Himself teaches the means for both cases in succession, beginning with the word "apramatta" (vigilant). Regarding the first case, the meaning is: in the object consisting of lack of one-pointedness (*anaikāgrya*), which acts as an obstacle to the arising of the certainty that takes as its object the difference between the Real Entity and Its illusory manifestation (the ether) and the falsity of that difference—thereby destroying the identity (*tādātmya*) with the ether. [This refers to] meditation...
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya, [the section] titled "Discrimination of the Great Elements" (*Mahābhūtaviveka*).

This means: by the construction of a continuous flow of uniform cognition in the form "I am Brahman," characterized by the mind's state as a witness (*sākṣitva*). In other words, this refers to the object of the aforementioned obstacle known as doubt regarding something else. And thus, it is indicated that one should investigate the inherent consistency of the three chapters [of the Brahma-sūtras] according to their four characteristics (*lakṣaṇya*) in reverse order. || 73 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"When the distinction between space and existence has become firmly established through meditation, through reasoning, and even through scriptural authority..."
The sky is never real, nor does it possess any substance like a hollow space.

"From meditation" (*dhyānāt*): Meditation has the characteristics previously described; "measure" (*māna*) refers to what was stated in the passage, "The ether and existence are distinct because of the difference in sound and the difference in cognition," while the reasoning was stated in the passage beginning with, "Because the existent reality functions as something additional. When, through these means such as meditation, the distinction between the ether and existence becomes firmly established in the mind, the ether never appears as real, but rather always appears as purely false; and the existent reality (*sadvastu*), too, does not appear as having holes or spatial openings.
The remainder of the sentence is "it does not exist at all. || 74 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: what is the fruit of such great effort? To this, he says: "From meditation" (dhyānāt). || 74 ||
To the knower, the void always appears as being devoid of any conceptual delineation of objective categories.
This [light] of his also shines forth, preceded by its flawlessness. (75)
— Rāma’s Commentary — He states the result of the discrimination between space and existence: "of the knower," etc. (verse 75).
Commentary (a0): Now, to the question "Of whom is this fruit, which is obtained even today in the Kali age?", he says in two verses beginning with "jñasya" (of the knower). || 75 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To the question of what happens for one who constantly contemplates the falsity of the sky (ākāśa) and the reality of that which exists, he says:
"When the latent impression has increased, [one perceives] the proponent of the reality of the sky..."
And seeing it endowed with the awakening of the six measures, the wise man is filled with wonder.

Regarding the phrase "in the latent impression" (vāsanāyām): the meaning is that the wise man, the knower of reality who perceives the sky as existent, feels astonishment upon seeing someone asserting the reality of the ether while being devoid of the realization of the non-existent nature of that which lacks any objective basis. || 76 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): "In the latent impression" (vāsanāyām) means in the continuous succession of impressions resulting from the contemplation of the falsity of the world and so forth. "The wise one" (budhaḥ) refers to one who is established in Brahman. || 76 ||
Thus, when the falsity of space and the reality of existence have been impressed [upon the mind],...
By this reasoning, let the existence of air and the other elements be discerned. || 77 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He extends the stated principle to other cases as well with the words "evam" (thus). || 77 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on A0: He extends the stated principle to other cases as well with the word "evam" (thus). The meaning is: when [the mind] has been perfumed—that is, when it is continuously attended by the limit of firmly produced latent impressions (saṃskāra). || 77 ||
Illusion resides in one part of an existing entity; it operates within that very part.
In that case as well, the wind situated in one part [of the body] is postulated as being discerning.

Rāmānuja’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that since it is impossible for air—which is an effect of space—to have identity with the Real Entity (sadvastu), which is not its cause, the discernment of the Real from air is purposeless.
Anticipating this, he states "by the Real Entity" (sad-vastunā) to show that even in the absence of a direct connection, there is an indirect connection. || 78 ||
a0 ṭī0—Therein, he first elucidates the method of discerning air with the three verses beginning with "In the real entity" (sadvastuni). ||78||
The Second Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

Rāja-Ṭīkā: Having thus demonstrated the relationship between the two winds, he states the attributes perceived in the wind in order to provide knowledge of their distinction based on those attributes.
Dryness, touch, motion, and velocity—these are considered the properties of air.
The three natures—Being, Māyā, and Space—are also contained within the Wind. (79)
"Exhaustion and touch. Having thus stated the specific attributes, he states those that are obtained by way of their cause: "The three.
The meaning is that those three natures—the specific qualities or attributes of *sat* (Being), *māyā*, and *vyoman* (Space)—are also "wind-going," meaning they exist within the wind. || 79 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding the word "drying" (*śoṣa*): although it has been established previously that touch alone is the primary attribute of air, nevertheless—based on the Smṛti statement, "The wind does not dry," as well as from direct perception of the drying of garments moistened by mere wind and the observation of movement and so forth residing therein—it is not contradictory to hold that drying, movement, and velocity are also intermediate attributes of that [air]. Nor is it the case that...

It should not be argued that this statement introducing the perception of its motion and so forth is improper, because it is impossible for properties such as motion to be objects of perception prior to the perception of the substratum (the air), according to the maxim "there can be no painting when there is no wall," and because, in the Nyāya system, that [substratum] alone is initially the object of inference.
For if air were not perceptible, the universal experience of everyone— "I am touching cold air"— would be contradicted.
Therefore, since it is more reasonable that there be many benefits [from this], the statement of the logicians—that air is to be inferred from touch—must be rejected.
The details, however, should be understood from the original sources; this is the direction [of the argument]. || 79 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question "What are those properties?", he says:
"The existence [of the property] 'the wind exists' is [perceived] when the existent wind is distinguished [from its qualities]."
The nature of Māyā is the state of being devoid of essential reality; it is like a sound moving through space. || 80 ||

Regarding the term "wind": the first property of the existent reality (*sadvastu*) is its nature as existence (*sad-rūpatva*), which serves as the basis for the conventional usage that "wind exists. When the existent reality is distinguished from the wind, that which is its lack of ultimate reality (*nistattva-rūpatva*) is the second property, belonging to *māyā*. The third property is sound, which has come from the ether (*vyoman*); such is the meaning. || 80 ||
Commentary on verse a0: "Vāyu" means air; "sadbhāvaḥ" means existence (sattvam). || 80 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "In the discussion concerning the discernment of space (*vyoma*), it was stated that while existence (*sat*) persists through air and the other elements, it does not persist in space; thus, the cognition of difference was established by precluding the persistence of space in air and the rest. Yet now, the persistence of space is being asserted. Therefore, there is a contradiction between what preceded and what follows. Thus he objects.
It was previously stated that the persistence of existence occurs everywhere, whereas that of space does not.
How then is it that your speech, which conforms to the sky, is not contradicted? (81)
Regarding the word "sataḥ": the ellipsis is that the persistence [of the self] in space is now being described. || 81 ||

Commentary (a0): Regarding that, he raises an objection against the previously stated contradiction—that while [existence] persists in air and the other elements, it does not persist in space—by stating:
"Of the existent... (sataḥ) || 81 ||
The previously mentioned statement was "following after a flaw," but this one now is as follows:
Since it is merely the persistence of words that has been described, how could there be a contradiction in speech? (82)

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Previously, the persistence of the essential nature (svarūpa) characterized as "space" was refuted. Now, it is stated that there is only the persistence of attributes (dharma), not the persistence of the essential nature; therefore, there is no contradiction. He resolves this with the verse beginning with "chidra. || 82 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya— [the section titled Mahābhūtaviveka]

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He resolves [the objection] by stating that the two statements are purposeful due to a difference in their subject matter—“chidra” (the gap), etc. It should be understood that I have already raised this doubt and resolved it within my own commentary on that very point. || 82 ||
If it is argued that [the effect] is non-existent because of its distinctness from the cause, then how [is this so]?
Due to the irregularity of unmanifest māyā, there is also a state that is not composed of māyā.

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "If it is argued that because the wind is distinct from Brahman, it possesses the characteristic of non-existence—that is, being composed of Māyā—then why should it not also be non-composed of Māyā, given its distinction from Māyā whose nature is the Unmanifest (avyakta)? Thus he asks: "nanu" (now, if...). ||83||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Again, the disciple raises this doubt: "Now, [the word] 'nanu'—this word 'how' (katham) is also to be construed after the word 'śabda'. Thus, the intent of the doubt is as follows: if air (vāyu) were non-real (atattva) because of its distinctness from real entities, then why would the unmanifest Māyā not also be composed of non-Māyā (amāyāmaya) due to its difference from the unmanifest? Such is the nature of the doubt. || 83 ||
In this context, it is precisely the state of lacking the nature of reality that constitutes the defining characteristic of illusion.
That [power] is equal in both the capacity and its effect, despite the distinction between the manifest and the unmanifest. ||84||
Rāma’s Commentary: It is not "unmanifestness" (*avyaktatva*) that is the cause for being composed of *māyā*, but rather the state of being devoid of the categories (*nistattvarūpatva*).

Since this [state] exists in air and so forth just as it does in *māyā*, there is no loss of the quality of being composed of *māyā*; thus he resolves [the objection] with the verse beginning "nistattva... (84).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He provides the resolution that non-existence (*asattva*) indeed does not mean the triviality (*tucchatva*) under discussion, but rather the state of being devoid of any ontological principle (*nistattvarūpatva*). Thus he says: "Devoid of principles" (*nistattva*), etc. (84).

Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Since both the power (śakti) and its effect (kārya) are equally devoid of the nature of the principles (nistattvarūpatā), from what source does the distinction characterized by being manifest (vyakta) or unmanifest (avyakta) arise?
Anticipating this, he dismisses the inquiry as irrelevant to the present context:
"Since the discrimination between existence and non-existence is the subject at hand, let that be considered."
Let there be an internal distinction among non-existent things; what is the use of such a consideration here? (85)

Regarding the phrase "existence and non-existence": the meaning is that for that which is non-existent—namely, the form of illusion (māyā) and its effects—there is an internal distinction consisting of being manifest or unmanifest. || 85 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, if the nature of being a reality (*tattvarūpatva*) is identical for both power (*śakti*) and its effect (*kārya*), then what is the basis for the effect being manifest (*vyakta*) while the power remains unmanifest (*avyakta*)? Having raised this doubt and intending to show that such differentiation is based solely on the state of being an effect and so forth, [the author] considers that since there is no fruit in investigating the internal subdivisions of unreal entities (*asadvastu*), and because there is the possibility of delay in grasping the primary, all-encompassing real entity (*sadvastu*), it is better simply to disregard them in that regard.
He provides the resolution [to this objection] with the words "because it is always existent" (sadāsatvāt). || 85 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the conclusion:
"The existent reality is Brahman; the remaining portion is Vāyu; and the ether is false."
Having caused him to dwell for a long time in the air, one should abandon the wind of false belief.

"Along with its substance. That which is similar to Vāyu is the form of Brahman; the remaining portion is devoid of *tattva* (reality), and thus the true nature of Vāyu is that he is devoid of *tattva*.

Because he is of a nature devoid of *tattva*, like space (*ākāśa*), he is illusory (*mithyā*). Having thus caused the illusoriness of Vāyu to dwell [in the mind] for a long time, one should abandon Marut; the meaning is that one should abandon the notion that "Marut is real. || 86 ||
Commentary (a0): Then, he states what is established in the present context: "The real entity... (verse 86).
Rāghavabhaṭṭa’s Commentary: One should likewise contemplate the fire as being subordinate to the wind, just as was stated regarding the wind.
This consideration regarding deficiency or excess applies to these coverings of the cosmic egg.
The Second Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

83. "One should contemplate" [is the instruction]. Now, one might object: "By the passage beginning with 'māyā situated in one part of the real entity' (tatra...), the state of being less or more (nyūnādhika-bhāva) regarding space and the other elements was stated; however, that is not seen anywhere in the world. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The cosmic egg... (brahmāṇḍa...). 87.

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on A0: He extends the aforementioned principle to fire as well—“one should contemplate” (ciṃtayet). Now, one might ask: how is it to be determined that fire exists in a lesser degree than air? To this he says: “the cosmic egg” (brahmāṇḍa). || 87 ||
Rāghavabhaṭṭa’s Commentary: To the question of by how much portion fire is less than air, he says:
"Fire is conceived as being one-tenth part less than air."
The gradation described in the Purāṇas [is established] by tenfold increments among the five elements.

Regarding the word "of air" (*vāyoḥ*): he dispels the suspicion that this [air] might be merely real by saying "in air" (*vāyau*). Anticipating the objection that "this state of deficiency and excess is merely a fabrication of one's own imagination," he says: "as stated in the Purāṇas. || 88 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): To the question of how much smaller that portion is, he says: "of the air" (*vāyoḥ*). This means in the air, that is, in consciousness delimited by the air; in other words, it is superimposed by imagined *māyā*. Now, what is the proof for such a restriction? To this he says: "by the Purāṇas. This is stated in the twenty-sixth chapter of the third book of the *Bhāgavata*:
This is the egg known as the "Specific" (viśeṣa), consisting of [elements] increased in sequence by multiples of ten.
"Surrounded by water and the other elements, it is covered on the outside by the Pradhāna."

In this context, with respect to the terrestrial cosmic egg (*pārthivabrahmāṇḍa*), the water that serves as its covering is ten times greater; beyond that, fire is greater than water, wind is greater than fire, and space is greater than wind—this is quite clear. Therefore, it is entirely consistent that wind is ten times less than space, fire is ten times less than wind, and so forth. Here, the primary principle (*pradhāna*) is indeed *māyā*, which consists of the three qualities (*triguṇā*). || 88 ||
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: He states the essential nature of fire: "Fire is hot, its essence is light, and it moves forward."
That fire exists, though devoid of substantial reality, yet it possesses sound and touch.

Regarding the word "fire" (*vahnir iti*): here too, he states that the properties of the cause persist [in the effect] just as they do in the case of air—by the words "preceding," etc. When there is the inquiry as to what those properties are, he says: "it exists," etc. (89).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might ask, "What is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of fire? To this he says: "Fire. Here too, he clarifies the aforementioned sequence from the preceding [verse] with the words: "It exists. The meaning is that when it is separated from "Being" (*sat*), it becomes devoid of reality (*nistattva*). || 89 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Thus, having first restated the conformity with the qualities of its cause, he shows its own inherent quality:
"The innate quality of fire, which is joined with the portions of Being (sat), Māyā, Space, and Wind..."
In that regard, let all form belonging to an existent being be analyzed by means of the cognition of "otherness. (90)

Regarding the phrase "sanmāya": having thus explained the nature of fire along with its qualifiers, he now distinguishes fire from the existent reality (*sadvastu*)—in the words "tatra" (therein). The meaning is: "among those [factors], having distinguished through the intellect all other collections of attributes (*dharmajāta*) from the existent reality (*sat*), let that [reality] be separated. || 90 ||

Commentary (a0): To the question, "What is the inherent quality (*nija-guṇa*) of fire, which possesses the persistence of 'being' (*sat*) and so forth? he says: "Being" (*sad*). Therein, as before, he effects the differentiation of "being" by means of the remainder of the verse beginning with "Therein" (*tatra*). || 90 ||
When the fire has been discerned by mindfulness, and false views have been perfumed [by it].
One should contemplate that the waters have been prepared as being reduced by one-tenth. ||91||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 84]
[The commentary by Rāma, titled *Mahābhūtaviveka*: Having thus ascertained the falsity of fire, one should contemplate the falsity of water; this is stated in the verse beginning with "sataḥ" (91).]

Commentary (a0 ṭī0): Since that fruit [of the previous practice] consists in the realization of its own falsity, he prescribes this same contemplation even for waters, stating: "The waters... (verse 91).
These waters exist as the principle of emptiness, conjoined with sound and touch.
Possessing form through the conformity to other attributes, their own essence is their quality. || 92 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He further demonstrates the causal attributes and its own inherent attributes by distinguishing them, beginning with "There is heat" (saṃtyāpa).
The meaning is that they are joined with "sound-touch," which refers to touch accompanied by sound (saśabda). || 92 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, he explains the persistence of existence and other qualities in water, as well as its primary attribute, with the verse beginning "saṃti" (they exist).

Regarding the word "sā" (she/it): the analysis of the compound is "that which is joined with touch accompanied by sound" (*saśabda-sparśa-saṃyutā*). The word "svīya" (their own) is to be supplied, referring to these [qualities]. The sense of "asti" (exists) is implied. || 92 ||
When the water has been separated from it while one is mindful, and its falsity has been impressed upon the mind.
One should visualize that the earth is conceived as being present in the waters, diminished by one-tenth.

Rāma’s Commentary: Having ascertained the unreality of water through the practice of discernment and meditation, he states that the unreality of earth must thereafter be contemplated, beginning with the verse "sataḥ" (93).
Commentary (a0): Here too, as before, when the destruction of false views has occurred, he enjoins the contemplation of the earth with the words "of the existent" (sataḥ).
The remainder, however, is exactly as previously explained. || 93 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To contemplate its falsity, he also analyzes its attributes:
"The element earth exists, yet it is empty of reality; in it, sound and touch possess form."
Taste is distinct from smell; let one's own true nature be discerned. || 94 ||
Regarding the statement "there is being" (*asti bhūḥ*), he says "being" (*sattā*) because existence-in-itself must be distinguished from those [entities]. || 94 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, here too, while stating the persistence of other attributes and its own primary quality, [the author] says "it exists" and "it has become," indicating that even there, existence (*sattā*) must be discriminated. And as for "that": the meaning is that it is false (*mithyā*), being devoid of existence in itself. || 94 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the result of the separation from being:
"When being has been separated, the ground of falsehood remains."
The cosmic egg, situated within the earth, is less than one-tenth the size of the earth.
"Separately. Now, in order to distinguish the existent from the elemental products such as the cosmic egg and so forth, he shows the manner of its location with the words "of the earth," etc. (95).
The commentary on the result states this with three verses beginning with "pṛthu": "bhūmi" etc. The word "asti" (is) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 95 ||
Within the cosmic egg reside the fourteen worlds.
While these worlds exist, the bodies of living beings abide in them according to their respective natures.
Rāma’s Commentary: "The cosmic egg," etc. This is clear. || 96 ||
Commentary on verse 96: "Brahmāṇḍa" etc. The meaning is: "respective[ly]," that is to say, without transgressing the established order of the scriptures as they are. ||96||
When the worlds, bodies, and material objects within the cosmic egg are separated [from their source], [the Self remains].
Let the non-existent shine as if they were existent; even if they appear so here, what harm is there in that? || 97 ||
The Second Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the fruit of the discernment of those [categories] in the verse beginning with "brahmāṇḍa" (verse 97).

Commentary on verse 85: Regarding the phrase "the world of the Brahmāṇḍa," here the word *deha* (body) should be understood as referring to the gross body accompanied by the subtle body, which is characterized by the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) along with the external sense organs described previously. By this, it is intended that the purification of the referent of the term *tvaṃ* (the "thou") is also achieved. || 97 ||
Rāma’s Commentary—He clarifies the very point already stated—that there is no harm in their manifestation—with the verse:
"When the non-existence of the elements, their derivatives, and Māyā has been thoroughly cultivated..."
This cognition that "all this is non-dual" never undergoes subversion.

Regarding the word *bhūta*: when the falsity of the elements (*bhūta*) such as space and so forth, of elemental products (*bhautika*) such as the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and so forth, and of Māyā which is their cause, has been firmly impressed upon the mind through discernment and meditation, the realization of the non-duality of the Real Entity (*sad-vastu*) is never again obstructed; this is the meaning. || 98 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, even if this were so, it might be argued that the statement—"let the cosmic egg, the worlds, and the body, being separated from the real entity which is the purified meaning of the word *tat*, appear as merely false due to their lack of existence"—is improper; for liberation is not established by that much alone. Indeed, liberation characterized by the destruction of that ignorance which is experienced in the form "I do not know Brahman" cannot be [attained] through what is denoted by the word *sat*...

If it is argued that everything distinct from Brahman is established as false by the very fact of its being borrowed [from Brahman], because knowledge and ignorance are opposed only when they share the same locus and object—this is not so, due to a lack of understanding. To explain: since the ego (ahaṃkāra), which falls within the subtle body (liṅgadeha), is distinct from the real entity that is Brahman, its falsity is established; and thus, the ignorance regarding Brahman—which resides in the individual soul (jīva) whose nature is consciousness delimited by that [ego]—is [itself] a non-dual real entity.

Intending to show that liberation while living (jīvanmukti) occurs immediately because [the world] is destroyed both by the knowledge of the identity of the Self with the Brahman of Form (rūpabrahman) and by the destruction of its limiting substratum (āśraya), he says: "consisting of elements and elemental products" (bhūtabhautika). This very point—that this much alone constitutes duality—is also stated in the *Siddhāntabindu*: "The phenomenal world (prapañca), consisting of ignorance (avidyā), that which is pervaded by it, and its effects, is the object of perception (dṛśya-padārtha). Although it lacks ultimate reality (apāramārthikatva), since its empirical existence (vyāvahārikasattva) is admitted, it is not like a dream-object."

The definition [of the unmanifest] is as useless as the definition of a category (*padārtha*). Yet, it is also threefold because of its utility in meditation (*upāsanā*) and so forth, due to the distinction between the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), the formed (*mūrta*), and the formless (*amūrta*).

Among these, *avidyā* accompanied by the semblance of consciousness (*sābhāsāvidyā*)—which exists in the form of the seed-potency for the manifest world of both the formed and the formless—is called "unmanifest" (*avyākṛta*). This is because, although it is not produced by that [Brahman], it ceases upon the cessation of that [Brahman]; and because, being pervaded by it, it is beginningless together with the consciousness, the relation [between them], the division of the individual soul and the Lord (*jīveśavibhāga*), and the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*). Now, [an objection]: in the root text...

The statement that duality consists precisely of the three categories known as the elements (*bhūta*), their derivatives (*bhautika*), and *māyā* is an implicit conclusion derived from the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the latter half of the verse. However, in the *Siddhāntabindu*, it is stated that this [duality] consists of ignorance (*avidyā*), its object (*tad-viṣaya*), and its effects; furthermore, it is described as being of three kinds, namely the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), the embodied (*mūrta*), and the unembodied (*amūrta*). If one asks how these two works can be considered consistent, the answer is: true. In the root text (*Mūla*), by the term *māyā*, the unmanifest itself—which consists of ignorance and its object—is intended. This is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

This is because, according to the interpretation in the *Tabinduvyākhyā*, such a specific intention is necessary; otherwise, even if "ignorance" (*avidyā*) were understood by the term "māyā," there would be the undesirable consequence of failing to include the other four types of objects—beginningless and so forth—mentioned in the root text. Likewise, it is clear that in the root text, by the terms "elements" (*bhūta*) and "elemental" (*bhautika*), the author intends to express exactly what the proponents of the Siddhānta have explained: that the effects of ignorance consist of both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*). Thus, there is complete agreement [between the two works]. Nor can it be argued that even so, in the *Siddhāntabindu*... [the term] "ignorance" and so forth... *(Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragmentary commentary on the relationship between the *Siddhāntabindu* and the *Vedāntasiddhāntamuktāvalī*. The translation reflects the logical arguments regarding the necessity of specific terminology and the consistency of philosophical intent.)*
Now, one might ask: why has there been this repetition by stating that "that [perceptible object] is also of three kinds," after having already defined the perceptible object?

This is because what was previously stated in the aphorism has simply been explained further by the subsequent sentence. [Objection: Even so, it is beyond dispute that the perceptible object consists of only this much.
And if that is so, where is the *prātibhāsika* (illusory) perceptible object included? Nor should it be said that it is merely an effect of *avidyā* (ignorance), for [it has already been] defined...

It is not correct to argue that this [dream object] need not be mentioned here because it is already included within the "empirical" (*vyāvahārika*) reality by virtue of accepting the empirical existence of objects such as knowledge, since this [dream object] is merely "illusory" (*prātibhāsika*); nor is it correct to say that it should not be cited because its falsity is accepted by both parties—as seen in the inference from the *Advaitasiddhi* and other texts, "The subject of dispute is false, because it is visible, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. This is because the present treatise—
I am neither the waking state nor the dreamer, nor deep sleep; I am neither the Viśva, nor the Taijasa, nor the Prājña.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 86]
"Because the three [elements] consist of ignorance, that which is called the discernment of the great elements—the Fourth—is the one remaining; I am Śiva, the absolute."

Thus, having introduced the commentary on the eighth verse: "In this context, the designation of sequence is according to the order of dissolution (*layakrama*). For, in our view, categories (*padārtha*) are of two kinds: the Seer (*dṛk*) and the Seen (*dṛśya*). This is because the categories postulated by other proponents are included within these very two," and so forth, [the author discusses] the Self (*ātman*).

Since this is presented specifically for one who desires to know (*jijñāsu*), and because it is necessary to state that even an object of appearance (*prātibhāsika*)—just like the denial of dreams and the like in the root verse—is a visible entity (*dṛśya-padārtha*) for that seeker, we do not at all understand what the intention of the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī is here. Consider attentively: in this very same work, he has also well-stated that such a visible entity is indeed illusory (*prātibhāsika*).

With reference to the objects of perception as defined by etymology (*nirukta-dṛśya-padārtha*), it has been stated that even though such objects lack ultimate reality (*apāramārthikatva*), their investigation is not futile because they are admitted to possess empirical existence (*vyāvahārika-sattva*), unlike dream-objects. Consequently, one must necessarily admit that there exist even illusory (*prātibhāsika*) objects of perception—such as those in dreams—which are considered by them [the opponents] to have futile investigations; otherwise, the integrity of the text's internal consistency (*grantha-svārasya*) would be irretrievably compromised.

Because of this [reason], for it is not the case that anyone would—by virtue of being like a firefly in the darkness or being like a sun—a firefly, or by virtue of being unworthy of salutation, maintain that the Blessed One is unworthy of salutation; nor would anyone consider a conscious being to be incapable of the term "firefly. This is something even children can believe.

And thus, in the statement "that too is threefold," the word "that" (tat) refers back to the empirical objects of perception suitable for meditation and the like, and then proceeds to the unmanifested (*avyākṛta*) and so forth.

Even though a threefold division is established, by the word "api" (also/even) used in conjunction with it, it must be stated that the phenomenal object (*dṛśyapadārtha*), including even the illusory (*prātibhāsika*), is indeed threefold according to the distinction between the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), the subtle (*mūrta*), and the gross (*amūrta*). This is because it accords with the natural sense of the subsequent text. For instance, in this very work, later on, regarding the waking state (*jāgradavasthā*), it is said: "Since cognitions such as that of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell lack epistemic validity (*aprāmāṇikatva*), although their objects are not empirical (*avyāvahārika*), [they still involve] the operation of the senses..."

Because it occurs at that time, its status as "waking" is established. Likewise, further on in this very [text], having introduced the threefold nature of each of the three states beginning with waking, it is stated regarding the threefold nature of dreaming: thus, the attainment of mantras and so forth within a dream is "dream-waking";
the cognition "I have seen a dream even within a dream" is "dream-dream"; and whatever is experienced during the state of dreaming that cannot be recounted in the waking state is [the third type].

That is what is meant by "dream-sleep. Thus, this dream-sleep characterized as above, as well as the delusion experienced even during the waking state—such as when, in dense darkness, one sees something in a forest but is unable to say whether it was a wild beast or a ghost—is the unmanifested phenomenal (prātibhāsika) [level of reality]. Likewise, the aforementioned delusions of the waking state, such as mother-of-pearl appearing as silver, are concrete (mūrta). Similarly, that which has been stated...

Just as a dream is so in the waking state, and a mental kingdom (*manorājya*) is likewise purely immaterial, it is entirely logical that there is a diversity of illusory appearances (*prātibhāsika-dṛśya*). The uncommon characteristics constitutive of the unmanifested (*avyākṛta*) and other states—namely, being indistinct, distinct, or slightly distinct—are certainly not barred here any more than they are in the case of the empirical (*vyāvahārika*) and unmanifested levels. Nevertheless, the distinction between the empirical and the illusory is established by their respective sublation: the former being unsublated by anything other than the knowledge of Brahman, while the latter is sublated by it.

The arising of the day [of creation] is thus entirely clear. But surely, even if the established system of the learned masters has been demonstrated in this way, how is the fundamental arrangement of the primary source—the elements (*bhūta*), elemental derivatives (*bhautika*), and *māyā*—to be understood? In that regard, even if the term *māyā* intends the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), and even if the terms "elements" and so forth intend the effects of ignorance (*avidyā*) consisting of form and so on as appropriate, where does the illusory duality (*prātibhāsika-dvaita*)—which is other than the real (*satya*) and the empirical (*vyāvahārika*) dualities—reside?

It would be included [in the definition]. Nor should it be argued that because its falsity—characterized by the absence of intrinsic existence (*asattva-lakṣaṇa*)—is already established and accepted by everyone, stating it again would result in a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), and therefore its non-inclusion is actually desired; for the falsity characterized by the lack of self-existent being (*svataḥ-sattā-śūnyatva*) and so forth, though accepted by ourselves, is not accepted by any of those non-Buddhist outsiders (*tairthika*) who maintain theories other than the theory of indeterminable manifestation (*anirvacanīya-khyāti*), such as the theory of misapprehension (*anyathā-khyāti*). Therefore, its elucidation...

If you argue that its necessity lies solely in its being for the sake of charity (*dāna*), then listen: the word *māyā* may mean "the magic of Śambara" (*śāṃbarī-kṛpā*). This is supported by Hemacandra’s lexicon (*Anekārthasaṃgraha*) stating "deceit (*dambha*) and intellect (*buddhi*"), and by Medinī’s lexicon stating "*māyā* may mean the magic of Śambara or intellect. Since the word *māyā* denotes not only the specific illusions created by magicians such as Śambara, but also the elements—space and so forth—as well as their derivatives, such as the intellect and other mental faculties, both of these are *māyās*.

And by the etymological derivation *vyākṛta-aindrajāla-ādi-bhrānti* (delusions such as manifested magic, etc. and *tathā tāsām* (and likewise those [others]), it is indeed possible that even in the present context, illusory (*prātibhāsika*) objects of perception are included; may those whose hearts are most tender and compassionate take note of this—this is the summary. || 98 ||
The Second Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
When duality, consisting of the earth and other elements, exists as something distinct from the ever-present non-duality;
In the world, that causal efficiency occurs exactly as it has been observed.
Rāghava’s Commentary (Rā0ṭī0): Now, one might object: "If earth and the other elements do not exist, would this not lead to the collapse of the wise person's worldly activity?

Anticipating this, he says—beginning with "From the non-duality of Being"—that even when the falsity of earth and so forth is ascertained through discrimination, worldly activity is not lost, because there is no destruction of their conventional form. || 99 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "If, upon the exclusion of the entire duality of earth and so forth from the Reality that is Being (*sad-vastu*), the realization 'I am indeed Brahman, the non-dual Reality' arises, and even if at no time or place should there be any misconception characterized by such notions as 'I am a Brāhmaṇa' or 'the visible world is real,' nevertheless, for the knower of Brahman, the cessation of the empirical usage of duality—which persists until the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma—would still occur through the interaction of knowledge and ignorance."

Anticipating the objection that, since simultaneity is impossible, how could even *prārabdha* karma bring about experience (*bhoga*) characterized by the direct perception of either pleasure or pain and so forth under such conditions, he provides the following resolution: "It exists" (*sat*). Even though duality in the form of the earth and other elements is illusory, the specific causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) produced by them remains as it was before; thus, because the non-dual Self can function at times other than those occupied by mental states such as pleasure, there is the possibility of experiencing *prārabdha* karma and attaining liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).

The intended meaning is that there is no inconsistency whatsoever, since [the experience of] union with one's own young woman is also possible. For this very reason, the venerable feet of the illustrious master Śrī Sarvajñātmamuni said:
I see all this as if it were a painting; I abide in the infinite, partless, singular body of consciousness.
I behold the Self as non-dual, whose sole nature is infinite bliss, and I behold the phenomenal world like a burnt rope.
"I experience non-duality as clearly as a wood-apple fruit held in the palm of my hand; I perceive the body as if it were a mere illusion.
Thus, both my manifestation in this world and my attainment of the supreme good are well-established for me."

The traditional teachers [hold that] *ahiniyanī* means "the sloughed skin of a snake. The source for this is the Śruti itself, which, concerning the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), states: "Just as the sloughed skin of a snake might lie dead and cast away upon an anthill, even so does this body lie. This is the general direction [of the argument]. 99.
In whatever manner the Sāṃkhyas, Kāṇādas, and Vaiśeṣikas [describe] the diversity of the world, [it is refuted].
It is conceived through manifold reasoning that it may be so and so. (100)
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary (rā0ṭī0): Now, one might object: "If the reality of existence (*sattattva*) is of a non-dual nature, why is the duality propounded by the Sāṃkhyas and others not refuted?
Anticipating this doubt, he states—beginning with the verse *sāṃkhya*—that we do not strive to refute it because we accept that duality as being merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*). || 100 ||

But [the author of] the *Tu-a* commentary [objects]: "Granted that, by this much, there may be a conclusion regarding the duality appearing [in experience] as being as negligible as the blackness of the sky; nevertheless, for the purpose of refuting the difference (*bheda*) propounded as real by the authors of the Sāṃkhya and other systems..."
Having raised the objection that one must strive for liberation and that this consequently leads to great distraction, he resolves it with the words "Sāṃkhya," etc.
The sense is that there is no contradiction at all, because even in our own system (siddhānta), conventional difference is accepted. || 110 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection that it is improper to disregard the distinctions among existent things established by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), he says:
"The reality of non-duality has been disregarded by other disputants who are free from doubt."
Thus, what loss is there for us who disregard that Veda? (101)

Regarding the phrase "despised": just as the Sāṃkhyas and other proponents of different doctrines disregard non-duality—which is established by the Vedas and other means—without hesitation, so too, when we disregard their duality by relying on scripture, reasoning, and experience, what is lost for us? This is the meaning. || 101 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if it is argued that even so, this ultimately results in mere contempt for duality, [the author] clarifies that this is indeed acceptable according to the perspective of those who maintain the reality of difference, by means of an illustration from their own view: "It is disregarded," etc. (101).
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 88]
If the disregard for duality, known as the discernment of the great elements, is well-established, the intellect will become firm in non-duality.
When that [state] is stable, this person is called "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta). || 102 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (rā0ṭī0): Now, one might object: "But surely this disregard for duality is purposeless. Anticipating this, he says "dvaita... [verse 102], asserting that this is not so, because there exists a purpose characterized by the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that this disregard for duality is merely a bold assertion, as it yields no fruit; to this he says: "Disregard for duality" (dvaitāvajñā). To the question "What follows from that?", he replies: "Steadfastness" (sthairye). Thus, the essential point is established: the definition of being a *jīvanmukta* is precisely the state of having firm, unwavering vision whose sole object is the non-dual Self. This is the truth. || 102 ||
—This is the state of Brahman, O Pārtha; having attained this, one is no longer deluded.
Abiding in this, even at the time of death, one attains the Brahman-nirvāṇa.

Rāghavendra Ṭīkā: With the intention that the goal is not merely liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), but also liberation after death (*videhamukti*), he cites the words of Kṛṣṇa from the *Bhagavad Gītā* (2.72): "This... (verse 103).
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): If it is asked, "What is the proof for this?", one replies, "The Bhagavad Gītā itself," and recites its very words:

"This... The meaning is: "pertaining to the Brāhmī [state]," that is, related to the non-dual identity of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikya*). "Stability" (*sthiti*) means the steadiness of the intellect regarding that [identity]. || 103 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To dispel the doubt that the word "at the time of death" (antakāla) refers to the falling away of the present body, he states the intended meaning:
"The perception of mutual identity between real non-duality and unreal duality..."
Its "time of end" is nothing other than the very cognition of its dissolution. || 104 ||

Regarding the phrase "sadadvaita" (non-duality of the Real): the "end of that delusion of unity"—which consists of the knowledge of oneness characterized by mutual superimposition upon non-duality in the form of the Real and duality in the form of the unreal—is precisely the cognition of the distinction between those two, non-duality and duality, as being real and unreal respectively; the meaning is that there is no other [end] than the falling away of the present body. || 104 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might object: "Granted that there may be an absence of delusion due to the attainment of the aforementioned stability of the intellect, since ignorance—which is the very root of that [delusion]—has been destroyed;

however, if it persists therein even until the time of death, then disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*) would result, and not otherwise. This is precisely what is understood from the natural force (*svārasya*) of the second half of the verse.
And this is entirely appropriate.
"And at the time of death, whoever departs casting off the body while remembering Me alone,
attains My state; there is no doubt about this."

Anticipating the objection that this is so because of such supplementary statements (*vākyaśeṣa*) as those beginning with "thus," [the author] provides the resolution while explaining the meaning of the term *antakāla* (time of end) as accepted in the present context: "In the non-duality of Being" (*sadadvaita*). The meaning of the two locative endings is precisely that of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*). And thus, the experience of mutual superimposition (*aikyādhyāsa*) delimited by the state of being non-dual Being and delimited by the state of being unreal duality—that is "non-duality of Being. This means that within duality, the real entity (*sadvastu*) is perceived as conjoined, and within the real entity, duality is [perceived].
That is to say, it is the superimposition [of one thing] by way of identity. Regarding the word "tasya" (of that): the remainder is indeed clear. || 104 ||
Let there be separation from life here for as long as time permits, according to what is well known.
Even at that time, there is no returning again for delusion once it has departed. || 105 ||
Rāghavendra Ṭīkā: Now, with the intention that there is no fault even in accepting the meaning as it is commonly known in the world, he says "Or else" (yadvā). || 105 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, it may be argued that the aforementioned "time of culmination" (antakāla) results in nothing other than the valid knowledge (*pramā*) concerning the identity of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikya*), which—preceded by a firm disregard for duality—causes the stabilization of the intellect regarding non-duality. How then can that stabilization of the intellect, occurring subsequently, be delimited by that [time]?
The Second Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

Because it has already been established that it is appropriate for that [knowledge] to bestow liberation upon one who possesses the contemplation of its own witness-nature regarding its own object, [the author], due to a lack of satisfaction with that [previous explanation], says: "Or else" (*yadvā*). Regarding the phrase "in that": thus, for one who possesses the stability of a cognition whose object is non-duality—preceded by the firmness of the contempt for duality arising from the previously mentioned delusion—even at the time delimited by the end characterized by the separation of the vital breaths (*prāṇaviyoga*), there may be a recurrence [of delusion] through fainting and so forth.

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that [liberation] occurs through attainment alone. Furthermore, it should be understood that the intended meaning of the *Gītā* passage is that by remaining in this aforementioned state of abiding in Brahman (*brāhmasthiti*), and having performed the most firm practice, one certainly attains the Nirvāṇa of Brahman at the time of death, even if there is a state of unconsciousness (*mūrchā*) or the like during the moment of dying. || 105 ||
Whether healthy and seated, or sick and wallowing on the ground.
Or let him faint, or let him give up his life; there is no doubt whatsoever. || 106 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He elaborates upon the very meaning already stated in the verse beginning with "free from disease" (106).

Commentary (a0): Now, as for the objection beginning with "even at that time," let it be granted that this refers solely to immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*). Thus, by virtue of the practice of the "I-am-Brahman" meditation—which is characterized by the eightfold yoga assisted by the ripening of previously practiced hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth—there arises, at the very moment of death marked by the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma, a direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) produced by the repeatedly studied Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), "I am Brahman," which has as its object the non-dual identity of Brahman and the Self. Even for one who has [passed away]...

If it is argued that there can be no recurrence of the delusion of non-duality due to fate—that is, its attainment at another time does not occur—and therefore this [verse] must be explained as referring to *jīvanmukti* according to the method previously stated, we reply: True. For it is beyond dispute that this statement, beginning with "This is the state of Brahman" (*eṣā brāhmī*), is intended to explain the "time of end" mentioned in the previously cited verse from the Bhagavad Gītā. And thus, when explained in this manner, the meaning of the passage there—"This is the state of Brahman..."—is established.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the statement, "O Pārtha, having attained this, one is not deluded," which refers to liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). Nor should it be argued that the first half-verse refers to *jīvanmukti*, while the second half-verse beginning with "sthitvā" (having remained) refers to immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*), so that the word "api" (also), which indicates the acceptance of both scripturally established positions, would be consistent. [For Arjuna asks: "Arjuna said: What is the state of one whose wisdom is steady?"... [and so on].

Since the introduction begins with the words "bhāṣā" and so forth by presenting the case of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), it must be stated that the conclusion likewise refers to such a person. Therefore, this alone is the established doctrine of the Bhāṣya and other works; thus the author of the root-text clarifies his own intention with the words "nīroga" (free from disease). The phrase "it may arise again" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 106 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that at the time of separation from life, since knowledge is destroyed by fainting and the like, error would surely arise.
Anticipating this, he provides an illustration regarding the absence of the destruction of knowledge:
"Day after day, even when what was studied in dreams or deep sleep is forgotten..."
Just as one would not be unlearned on the following day, in that same way, knowledge does not perish.

Regarding the word "dina" (day): just as when one has studied the Veda every day, even if it is forgotten during states such as dreaming or deep sleep, there is no lack of Vedic study on the following day; likewise, at the time of death, even in the absence of contemplation upon reality, there is no destruction of knowledge—this is the meaning. || 107 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, one might object that a return [to worldly life] is indeed possible through forgetfulness; therefore, he says: "Day by day" (dine dine). || 107 ||
Knowledge produced by a means of valid cognition does not [remain] without a powerful means of valid cognition [to support it].
It is not destroyed, nor is any means of knowledge stronger than the Vedānta observed. || 108 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He establishes the very non-existence of the destruction of knowledge with the verse beginning "pramāṇa" (108).
Commentary (a0): He states another reason for the non-destruction of the fruits of knowledge: "pramāṇa... (verse 108).
Therefore, the true non-duality established by the Vedānta is not sublated.
Therefore, even at the time of death, liberation remains established through the discernment of the elements.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Discrimination of the Great Elements" (*mahābhūtaviveka*), in the *Pañcadaśī* composed by the venerable sage Vidyāraṇya. 2.
