Rāma’s Commentary: He concludes the point thus established with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). || 109 ||
Thus ends the *Mahābhūtavivekadīpikā*, composed by the scholar named Śrī Rāmakṛṣṇa, a servant of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Bhāratītīrtha Vidyāraṇya Muni. 2.
11.11 Commentary on Verse 11—Stating the conclusion, he summarizes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*): even at the time of death, one is not obstructed; thus...

Dhaḥ. And thus, the entire non-dualistic scripture culminates only in that true reality of non-duality which is the state of liberation (*kaivalya*) characterized by the identity of Brahman and the Self, devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*). By this, [the following objection is addressed]: "This scripture reaches its final conclusion in the qualified (*saguṇa*) Brahman"—this firm conviction constitutes the second obstacle to the realization of the Lord.
Thus, regarding the understanding of the meaning of the word *tat* as purified, the second obstacle has been stated; likewise:

"In this way, through the investigation of the elements based on the teaching of *samanvaya*, the second [obstacle] is also [removed] by determining that the word *tat* has that [Brahman] as its primary purport, through such [statements] as 'from that [arose] the *rasa*,' and so forth."

By this, that which was stated regarding the second section’s capacity to sublate [the first] is indeed consistent. For instance: having begun with "the non-duality of Being" (*sadadvaita*), it concludes by stating, "therefore, the non-duality of Being, established by the Vedāntas, is not sublated. Thus, the concordance of the Vedāntas regarding Brahman is singular:
"All this was, prior to creation, one alone, without a second."
"In the beginning there was Being alone; name and form did not exist," so says the speech of the Āruṇis.

"Thus, the threefold division of an existent entity (*sad-vastu*) that has been proposed is refuted. Therefore, the repetition [of the argument] begins with "therefore, there are no parts," and so forth.
"This is called the 'untouchable yoga' (*asparśa-yoga*), difficult to perceive by all yogis"—this constitutes its novelty (*apūrvatā*).
If disregard for duality is well-established, the intellect will become firm in non-duality.
"When that [state] is stable, this person is called 'liberated while living' (jīvanmukta)"—this is the fruit.
“Pervading this entire universe with but a single fraction of myself, I stand as the world.”
"Thus Kṛṣṇa said to Arjuna that [the world] is but a single part [of himself]"— this is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda).
The Power, resting upon the seven principles, brings about transformations within the existent.
Just as various kinds of paintings exist upon a wall, situated within the surface of the wall.

Thus, by means of these sixfold logical arguments, the *samanvaya*— defined as the culminating convergence of the intent of all Vedāntas, including those exemplified by the Chāndogya Upaniṣad— has been established primarily upon non-dual Brahman alone. Consequently, for the qualified seeker who, through service to a venerable Guru, seeks to dispel the aforementioned obstacle characterized by the stubborn conviction that the entire scripture culminates in Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahman*), this present treatise is provided as a commentary.
"How might it not be obstructed while being performed?"—thus all is auspicious. (109)

Thus ends [the work] titled *Pūrṇānandadukaumudī*, composed by the student Acyuta Śarman, whose mind sports like a royal swan at the lotus-feet of the venerable Nārāyaṇa Śāstri— whose name is also Modaka— and who bears the sixth surname Advaitavidyadiramaṇa; he who roams the milky ocean of the venerable Padavākya-pramāṇa, and who is a disciple of the venerable Dvaitasaccidānandendra Sarasvatī, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya*).
In the commentary on the Dhāyā, the second chapter, the Illumination of the Discrimination of the Elements, is complete. || 2 ||
May there be constant and supreme dedication to the lotus feet of the illustrious Śaṅkara, the best of gurus.
May there always be incomparable prosperity for cows, eminent Brāhmaṇas, the Vedas, and the scriptures that are favorable to them.
Now begins the third chapter, titled "The Discrimination of the Five Elements.
Rāma’s Commentary: Having bowed to the venerable Bhāratītīrtha and Vidyāraṇya, the lords among sages.
I shall provide a concise commentary on the discrimination of the five sheaths.

Commencing this treatise entitled *Pañcakośaviveka*, which takes the form of a commentary on the *Taittirīyopaniṣad-bhāṣya*, the Teacher first declares his intended work while indicating its subject matter along with its purpose, so as to ensure the engagement of the listeners:
"That Brahman which is hidden in the cave [of the heart] shall be [revealed] through the discrimination of the five sheaths (*pañcakośaviveka*)."
Therefore, the five sheaths, which can be understood [from that], are now analyzed in detail. || 1 ||

Regarding the phrase "hidden in the cave": according to the Śruti text, "He who knows it as hidden in the cave, in the supreme ether" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), that Brahman which is described as being hidden in the cave can be known through the discernment of the five sheaths (kośas) denoted by the word "cave. Therefore, the pentad of those sheaths is now clearly distinguished and demonstrated from the perspective of the innermost Self (pratyagātman).
This is the meaning. || 1 ||
A0 Commentary: [I bow to] that which is the immutable form of the non-dual bliss, existence, consciousness, and all-pervading, stainless Supreme Brahman;
which, though causing the dissolution of the Indra’s net of delusion, is itself self-luminous and the crest-jewel of the Vedas.
I bow to all the most excellent teachers, to the ornament of the Raghu dynasty, to my true guru established in Brahman named Śrī Nārāyaṇa, and also to my own teacher known as Mahādeva. || 1 ||
Having honored Jīvañjīva, Vidyāraṇya, and Bhāratītīrtha;
I illuminate the distinction between the treasury [of the *Abhidharmakośa*] and its commentary (*bhāṣya*) by means of the moonlight of the *Rāmaprakāśa*. || 2 ||
Now, the venerable sage Vidyāraṇya, desiring to compose the treatise titled *Kośaviveka*,

performs an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) consisting of the contemplation of the reality of Brahman as the Self— which has the fruit of pacifying all anticipated obstacles and is established by renowned means of valid knowledge— and announces this work while indicating its subject matter and purpose, beginning with the verse "guhā... from the *Taittirīya Upaniṣad*.

Having first promised liberation— characterized by the sublation of the duality existing through ignorance and having as its sole instrument the valid knowledge regarding Brahman— for one desiring liberation in the words, “The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme,” and having briefly defined the nature of that which is to be known with the words, “That is Truth, That is Knowledge,” etc., the scripture then declares, in response to the inquiry as to where that [Brahman] is located, “He who knows It hidden in the cave,” etc.; this refers to the Supreme Being who is to be described by the term ‘cave’ and is situated beyond the five sheaths (kośas) beginning with the physical body.

The meaning is as follows: the reality of the Self, which is Brahman, serves as the substratum for the duality superimposed by beginningless ignorance; since its existence and manifestation depend solely upon that [Brahman], it can only be known through self-luminosity by means of subverting the duality characterized by a separation from it—wherein all perceived objects such as the sheaths (kośas) are merely counter-correlates. Therefore, it is to be understood through inquiry preceded by excellence in scripture, reasoning, and experience. || 1 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: what is this "cave" (guhā) in which Brahman is deposited and realized through the discernment of the five sheaths?
Anticipating this doubt, the author states the meaning intended by the word "cave" according to the Śruti: "The vital breath (prāṇa) is within the body; the mind (manas) is within the vital breath."
From that [comes] the agent, from that the enjoyer; such is this succession within the cave.

"From the body," etc. From the body consisting of food (*annamaya*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—the one consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*)—is internal, more interior; from the vital breath (*prāṇa*), i.e., from that consisting of breath, the mind (*manas*) [is more interior].
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya;
[the section] titled "Discrimination of the Five Elements" (*Pañcabhūtaviveka*).

From that, the internal one is the *manomaya*; from that, the *vijñānamaya* is more internal—thus the word "internal" (*āntara*) is supplied [from the previous sentence]. From that, the *vijñānamaya*—O [disciple]...

The meaning is that this "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) is also internal, just like the preceding ones. The meaning is that this series, beginning with that which consists of food (annamaya) and ending with that which consists of bliss (ānandamaya), is denoted by the word "cave" (guhā). || 2 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): To the question "What is that cave?", he says: "From the body... The agent is the sheath consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya-kośa*);

the enjoyer is the sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). Nor should it be argued that there is an impropriety due to the lack of common locus (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between agency and enjoyership; for although those respective designations exist by virtue of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of each particular sheath, there is still a unity in all five sheaths through their identity with the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*). || 2 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now he demonstrates the nature of that which consists of food (*annamaya*) and its non-selfhood: "Born from the semen produced by the food consumed by the father, it grows by means of food alone."
That body, consisting of food, is not the Self, because it existed prior [to birth] and perishes afterward.

Regarding the phrase "pitṛbhukta" (consumed by the father): that body which is produced from the semen born of the food consumed by the father—consisting of rice, barley, and other grains—and which, after birth, grows solely through food such as milk, is the "annamaya" (composed of food), being a modification (*vikāra*) of food.
That [body] is not the Self (*ātman*). Why? To this he says: "māg" (before). Because of its absence before birth and after death.
The meaning is: because of the absence of such a body. The intended sense is: the body under dispute is not the self, because it is an effect, like a jar or similar objects. ||3||

Commentary (a0): Therein, first, regarding the gross body, it is established as being composed of food (*annamaya*) through its connection with food and so forth, based on the scriptural text: "This very person consists of the essence of food" (*sa eṣa puruṣo'nnarasamayaḥ*). It is not the Self. He proves its non-selfhood through reasoning formulated from experience—namely, that it is like a pot because of its possession of causal properties such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)—in the verse beginning with "pitṛbhukta" (consumed by the father). The meaning is: "prior" refers to before the infusion of semen; "subsequent" refers to after death (*pañcatva*). ||3||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that "let there be a reason, but let there be no probandum; since there is no subverting argument (bādhaka) against the contrary position, this reason is inconclusive," he refutes it by stating that such is not the case because there do exist subverting arguments known as "the acquisition of what was not done" (akṛtābhyāgama) and "the loss of what was done" (kṛtavipraṇāśa):
"How could that which did not exist in a previous birth produce that birth?"
One does not experience here the accumulated evil karma from a future birth.

Regarding the phrase "in a previous birth": since this self, which consists of this present body, did not exist in a prior birth, even if the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) that causes this birth were absent, this birth would nonetheless have to be accepted; thus, the fallacy of "attaining what was not earned" (akṛtābhyāgama) would follow. Likewise, since this self, consisting of the body, will not exist in a future birth—due to its non-existence or absence—there would be no enjoyer of the fruits of the merit and demerit performed here [in this life], and consequently, karma would be destroyed even without being experienced.

[If that were so,] there would follow the consequence of [the result's] destruction; this is the "loss of what was done" (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*). Thus, because of the existence of such subverting factors consisting of the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done, the sense is that the self's status as an effect must not be accepted. || 4 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that the reason [in the argument] is "unproven" (*aprayojaka*) due to the absence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*). Anticipating this, he states—beginning with "pūrva"—that the absence of a subverting proof is itself unestablished. If the gross body (*sthūladeha*) alone were the self (*ātman*), then it would be beyond dispute that such a self did not exist in a previous birth. Consequently, in the absence of an agent to perform the actions that produce this present birth, how could this self, in the form of the body, bring about this birth? It could not be established in any way whatsoever.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is with the word *knuyāt* (he would destroy). Thus, the intention is that there would indeed be the well-known fault of "the acquisition of what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*). In the same way, he reveals the "destruction of what was done" (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*) by the word *bhāvī*: "In that same manner, even in a future birth, this self in the form of a body, being non-existent [at that time], would not experience the karma accumulated here during the period prior to its own destruction; for even in the interval before enjoyment, its destruction would occur. This is the sense. || 4 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus demonstrated that the sheath consisting of food (annamaya-kośa) is not the Self, he now shows the nature of the sheath consisting of vital breath (prāṇamaya-kośa) and its non-selfhood:
"That which is full within the body, bestowing strength and setting the senses in motion..."
The vital air consisting of breath is not the Self, because it is devoid of consciousness. || 5 ||
The Third Chapter 1
Accompanied by two commentaries.

Regarding the word "pūrṇa" (full): that wind which, being full—meaning pervading the body from the feet up to the head—bestows strength, providing capacity in the form of *vyāna*, and exists as the activator and impeller of the senses such as sight and the rest; that wind is the *prāṇamaya* (consisting of vital breath).

It is said: that [prāṇa] also is not the self. He states the reason for this: "because it is insentient" (caitanyeti). The meaning is: the vital breath (prāṇa), which is the subject of dispute, is not the self because it is insentient, like a jar (ghaṭavat). || 5 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Having thus refuted the Cārvāka who maintains that the body is the self, [the author] refutes those followers of Hiraṇyagarbha who maintain that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the self, by means of an analysis of the sheath consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya-kośa*), based on the statement from the *Citradīpa*: "Thus they spoke. He says: "Full" (*pūrṇa*). That wind which, bestowing strength upon the body, is full and therefore the activator of the senses (*akṣāṇām*); even this, being devoid of consciousness, is insentient (*jaḍa*).
The construction is: "the self does not consist of you. As before, the Śruti and other authorities are to be inferred here as well. || 5 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, preceded by a demonstration of the nature of the mind-made [self], he declares that this too is not the Self:
"That which creates the sense of 'I' and 'mine' with respect to the body, the home, and so forth..."
Deluded by states such as desire and the like, he is not that self consisting of mind.

Regarding the phrase "the sense of 'I'": he who conceives the sense of "I" (ahambhāva) in the body and the notion of "mine" (mamatā)—the conceit of ownership—regarding the house and so forth, is "consisting of mind" (manomaya); such a one is not the Self. Why is this? To this he says: "due to desire and so forth. This is a qualifying attribute containing a reason; the meaning is that because it possesses fluctuations such as desire and anger, its nature is unstable. [The Self] is not the one consisting of mind, because it is subject to modification, like the body.
Such is the intended meaning. || 6 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, while refuting the doctrine that the mind is the Self, [the author] analyzes the sheath composed of mind (manomaya-kośa) with the words "I-ness" (ahaṃtā). [The term] "subject to delusive modification" (bhrāntavikārī) indicates, by this very fact, the reason for its being non-Self: namely, its nature as something subject to transformation (pariṇāmitva). || 6 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Immediately following this, demonstrating the true nature of the *vijñānamaya*—which is denoted by the term "agent"—the text shows that it is not the Self:
"During deep sleep, it remains dissolved; during the destruction of the body, it pervades [it] as far as the tips of the nails."
The intellect, being endowed with the reflection of the Self, is not the Self; it merely bears the designation "consisting of consciousness."

Regarding the word *līnā*: that intellect (*dhī*), which is endowed with the reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyopetā*) and joined with the manifestation of consciousness (*cidābhāsayuktā*), being dissolved (*vilīnā*) during sleep (*suptau*), i.e., at the time of slumber, and then existing pervading the body (*vapuḥ*)—that is, extending as far as the tips of the nails—at the time of waking (*bodhe*), is what is designated by the term "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*). Even this is not the Self, because it exists in states such as dissolution (*vilaya*).
The meaning is: "because it is subject to change, like a jar and so forth. || 7 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, while refuting the Buddhist position, he also analyzes the sheath consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya-kośa) with the verse beginning "līna" (merged). "Cicchāyā" means the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa). Here, the state of being merged during deep sleep is the reason for its not being the Self. || 7 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that since the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*) are indistinguishable in their nature as internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the conceptualization of two distinct sheaths in the form of "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) is untenable.

Anticipating this, he states that because of the actual existence of a distinction based on their respective functions as agent and instrument, the differentiation into "consisting of mind" and so forth is indeed logical:
"The internal organ undergoes modification through its roles as agent and instrument."
These two, consciousness and the mind, are both internal and external to one another.

Regarding the phrase "as agent" (*kartṛtva*): the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), being both the agent and the instrument, undergoes modification—that is, it transforms—into the form of an agent and the form of an instrument. These two, the agent and the instrument, are designated by the terms "intellect" (*vijñāna*) and "mind" (*manas*).
Since these two exist in a relationship of internal and external relative to one another, the existence of two sheaths (*kośa*) is established. || 8 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, titled "The Discrimination of the Five Elements" (Pañcabhūtaviveka). [Page 94]

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask, "What is the distinction between the mental sheath (manomaya-kośa) and the intellectual sheath (vijñānamaya-kośa)? To this, he says: "By the state of being an agent," and so forth. "Internal organ" (antaḥkaraṇa) refers to the internal sense-faculty. The phrase "mutually" (parasparam) implies the relationship of the defined and the definer. Regarding "by the state of being an agent": thus, the state of being an instrument (karaṇatva) residing in a particular modification of that [other] internal organ is indeed defined by the state of being an agent residing in a particular modification of the internal organ. This is defined by the state of being an instrument residing therein...
The truth is that agency belongs solely to the Primal One (Pitāmaha). When he undergoes transformation, then consciousness and the mind come to exist internally and externally;
such is the logical connection. || 8 ||

Rāma’s Commentary (rā॰ ṭīkā): Now, in order to demonstrate that the one denoted by the term "the enjoyer" (bhoktṛ), namely the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), is not the Self, he states its essential nature:
"A certain inward-turned mental modification (vṛtti) bears the reflection of bliss."
During the enjoyment of merit and during the cessation of enjoyment, it dissolves in the form of sleep.

Regarding the phrase "a certain [mental state]": at the time of enjoying merit—that is, during the experience of the fruits of meritorious actions—a certain modification of the intellect (*dhīvṛtti*), being turned inward, partakes of the reflection of bliss, which is the nature of the Self consisting of the three parts of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. That very same mental state, upon the cessation of enjoyment—the end of the experience of the fruits of meritorious actions—merges into the form of sleep;
that mental state becomes dissolved. This is the intended meaning: that [state] consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*). || 9 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Having thus discarded the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) consisting of the three sheaths (*kośa*), he explains the sheath of bliss (*ānandamayakośa*), known as the causal body (*kāraṇadeha*), in order to refute it: "A certain... [verse 9]. The mental modification (*vṛtti*) occurs in the waking state and so forth, while in deep sleep (*supti*), it belongs to ignorance (*avidyā*).
Rāma’s Commentary: He states its non-selfhood:
"Because it is occasional, even this one consisting of bliss cannot be the Self."
That Self which is manifest, O Ānanda, is eternally established.

"Because of its occasional nature" (*kādācitkatvataḥ*): the meaning is that even this "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) would not be the Self because it is occasional, like objects such as joy (*prīti*) and so forth. Anticipating the objection that if the selfhood of all existing things beginning with the "consisting of bliss" is denied, the consequence of total non-selfhood (*nairātmya*) would follow, he says: "being the prototype" (*vimbabhūta*). This refers to the bliss consisting of the terms "dear" (*priya*) and so forth, which exists as a reflection within the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties.
That bliss which has become manifest—that is, which has become the cause—is indeed the Self (*ātman*). Why? To this he says: "Always" (*sarvadā*). The meaning is:

because of its eternity (*nityatvāt*). The intended sense is as follows: the bliss under discussion must be the Self because of its eternity; for whatever is not the Self is not eternal, such as the body and so forth, since they are non-eternal due to having an origin, like the ether (*ākāśa*) and other such things. Thus, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) [in the reason]. || 10 ||
Having refuted that [position], he states his own view through reasoning: "Because of its occasional nature" (kādācitkatvataḥ). || 10 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He raises an objection: "But surely, having begun with the body, [the inquiry] concerns things ending with the bliss of sleep..."
Let it not be that there is selfhood; yet no other [self] whatsoever is experienced. || 11 ||

Regarding the word "nanu": if, for the reasons already stated, it is not possible for the sheaths (kośas) beginning with the *annamaya* and ending with the *ānandamaya* to be the Self, let them not be;
however, another Self does not exist at all, because no such thing is perceived. || 11 ||

Commentary (a0): [The opponent] objects with the intention that the reason "always" (*sarvadā*) is indeed unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), because no bliss distinct from the bliss at the end of sleep is ever perceived. With this thought, he raises the objection: "Now... (11).
Commentary (rā0): [The author] refutes it.
"Certainly, all [states] such as sleep are experienced, but not the others."
Nevertheless, who can prevent that by which these are experienced? || 12 ||
The Third Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

'Certainly. Here, by the word 'sleep' (nidrā), the bliss of sleep (nidrānanda) is indicated. What was stated—that from sleep up to the body, only these are perceived and nothing else is experienced—is true. How, then, is the existence of a Self distinct from those admitted? To this, he says:"

"Even so" (tathā'pi): the meaning is this—how can that experience not be accepted, by the power of which these [sheaths] beginning with the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) are perceived, even though nothing else is being perceived? || 12 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) resolves [the objection] with "Certainly" (vāḍham). Thus, the sense is that the Self does not experience at all the objects consisting of sleep, bliss, and the end [of those states], nor anything other than them. || 12 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If there exists a Self other than those already mentioned, then it ought to be perceived; since it is not perceived, it does not exist.
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Because it is itself the very nature of experience, it exists as that which is never an object of experience."
Because there is no other knower or knowledge [besides itself], it is unknowable, not due to its non-existence.

Regarding the word "itself" (*svayam*): because the Witness of the [sheaths] beginning with the *ānandamaya* is of the nature of experience itself, it cannot be an object of experience. Now, one might ask: even if it is of the nature of experience, why should it not be an object of experience? Anticipating this objection, he says: "the knower" (*jñātṛ*). There is the knower and there is knowledge; these two—the knower and knowledge—are distinct from any other knower or knowledge. Since they do not exist [as objects] within that [Witness], it is unknowable; that is, it does not become an object of the knower, because of the absence of the knower and so forth.
Is it because it is not known, or because of its own non-existence? To the question, "What is the reason for this conclusion? he replies: "But not by way of non-existence.
The meaning is that non-existence has already been refuted previously, since [the Self] is the witness of sleep, bliss, and so forth. || 13 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if the nature of the Self belongs only to the one who experiences the aforementioned objects, then its establishment must be asserted by an experience dependent upon that very experiencer. Consequently, just as sleep, bliss, and so forth were experienced by me—the experiencer—through an experience residing within myself, there would arise the cognition: "I too have been experienced by that very same [experience]. Therefore, according to the analogy of the fire produced by the friction of bamboo, the experience extends only as far as the object to be experienced.

If it is argued that in the absence of the sentient being (*vitṛ-sattva*), because of the non-existence of that [experience] as well, there would follow the state of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), we say no. This objection might indeed hold if there were an experiencer of the object at the end of the bliss of sleep and a substratum for that experience; however, that very thing does not exist. As it is said: "That which is to be enjoyed, the enjoyer, and the act of enjoyment—whichsoever may exist—in the three abodes..."
"I am Sadāśiva, the witness, pure consciousness alone, distinct from them."

Thus, by means of the scriptural statement and the reasoning that the world would fall into blindness in the absence of a self-luminous Self, he says "by itself" (*svayameva*) with the intention of establishing that this very [Self] is of the nature of experience. The implicit meaning is "of the witness of the aforementioned reality at the end of sleep and bliss. Having thus dispelled the contingency of the world's blindness by revealing the witness-self as self-luminous, he also refutes the consequence of nihilism (*śūnyavāda*) by saying "the knower" (*jñātṛ*). The aforementioned...

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: distinct from that which has perished, there is some other knower who is the substratum for the cognition of those objects; likewise, there is the cognition—that is, the awareness—having those as its object.

Precisely because of the absence of such [external] objects, this Self, which is the self-luminous witness (*sākṣin*), is "unknowable" (*ajñeya*); however, it is not unknowable due to non-existence. || 13 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To illustrate the impossibility of the Self, which is of the nature of experience, being itself an object of experience, he provides an example:
"Just as sweetness and other inherent qualities do not transfer their own attributes to other things..."
There is no need for it to be reflected upon itself, nor is there anything else that could reflect it.

Regarding the phrase "because of sweetness" (*mādhuryāt*): by the word "etc. (*ādi*), sourness and so forth are included. Those whose inherent natures (*svabhāva*) are specific qualities born together, such as sweetness and the rest, are "those whose nature is sweetness and so forth," namely molasses and the like. Among them, those that "bestow their own qualities" (*svaguṇārpiṇām*)—meaning they bestow their own qualities such as sweetness—upon other substances with which they are mixed, such as chickpeas and the like; for them, there is no requirement for bestowing those [qualities] upon themselves, that is, upon their own essential nature characterized as molasses and so forth. This is the meaning.
There is no expectation—that is, no desire—regarding the imparting or producing of sweetness and so forth, in the form of thinking that "sweetness and the like must be produced by someone.
Furthermore, there is nothing else that imparts [these qualities]; the meaning is that there is no other substance apart from molasses and such that bestows sweetness and its like. || 14 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 96]

[In the commentary on the fifth chapter titled "Discrimination of the Five Elements" (Pañcabhūtaviveka), he clarifies the illustration with the verse beginning "mādhuryādi" and its half-verse. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), sourness and other tastes are included;
the meaning is "of such things as sugar-candy, granulated sugar, and the like. 14.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the conclusion with an illustration:
"Even in the absence of another donor, these [qualities] possess that very nature."
Let it not be so that [the self] is an object of experience; however, its nature as consciousness is never lost. || 15 ||

Regarding the phrase "in the absence of another bestower": the meaning is that just as certain things like molasses possess the nature of sweetness even in the absence of another substance that bestows sweetness, so too, although the Self may not be an object of experience, it certainly possesses the nature of being experience itself. || 15 ||

Commentary on verse a0: "In another instance of bestowal" (arpakāntareti) refers to these [categories] such as the *khaṇḍa* and so forth. He applies this to the subject at hand: "Lest it be so" (mā bhūt tatheti). || 15 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To provide proof for the stated meaning, he says:
"He becomes self-luminous; he shines forth before everything else."
Following that very one as he shines, the world is illumined by his light.

Regarding the word "himself" (*svayam*): there are scriptural passages such as, "In this state, this person becomes self-luminous" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.9); "He shines forth brilliantly before all this" (Nṛsiṃhapūrvatāpanīya Upaniṣad 2); and "Everything shines after Him alone as He shines; by His light all this is illumined" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.10; Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.14; Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.14). These and other such scriptures [establish this].
The meaning is that they make known the self-luminosity of the Self. || 16 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, if it is asked what proof there is for the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of the Self in this way, [the author] strings together those very scriptural passages (*śruti*) in three verses beginning with "svayam" (itself). Here, in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, it is said: "In this state, this person becomes self-luminous. In the *Nṛsiṃha-Uttara-Tāpanīya*, it is said: "It shines forth more brilliantly than all this. And: "Everything shines after Him as He shines; by His light, everything..."
The meaning is that the very Śruti texts themselves, appearing in sequence in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad, are the authority for this matter. || 16 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He recites the meaning of the passage, "By what should one know that by which one knows all this? O, by what should one know the knower? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14):
"That by which one knows all this—by what other means could one know it?"
By what means could one know the knower? For the object of knowledge, there must be a means.

"By which this... means: by which Self, whose nature is witnessing-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), all living beings know this entire collection of objects; how could men understand that witnessing Self through anything else—a witnessless, insentient thing? This is the sense of the remaining words. He states the purport of this very statement: "The knower..."—by what object of perception (*dṛśyabhūta*) could one know the knower of the collection of objects?

"One should know" means that no one knows [it]. Now, anticipating the objection that "one will know it by means of the mind," he says: "capable. The instrument—the mind, which is the means for knowledge—is capable and competent with respect to the object of knowledge (*vedya*), that is, the thing to be known; but it is not so with respect to the Self, the knower (*jñātṛ*), according to such scriptural passages as, "Neither by speech nor by mind" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 6.12). Furthermore, if the Self were itself an object of knowledge, there would be a contradiction between its being the object (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*).
The state of being. || 17 ||
Commentary on verse a0: "By which one knows all this—by what could one know that?
"O, by what could one know the knower? Thus it is said in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. Living beings (jīvas) know; they perceive. Let those who know come to know. || 17 ||
"One should consider that as its manifestation"— this is the reading of Acyutarāya.

97. Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Only when the Self is self-luminous does it know the object of knowledge, and for it there exists no knower.

Considering both of these two scriptural statements—“That is indeed other than the known, and furthermore, above the unknown” (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19) and “It is other than that which is known” (Kena Upaniṣad 3)—to be authoritative, he recites them according to their meaning:
“He knows all that is to be known; there is no other knower of Him.”
Its nature is that of a consciousness distinct from both the known and the unknown.

"He knows"—that Self knows every single object that is knowable. There is no other knower or perceiver of that Self. That Brahman, whose very nature is consciousness, is distinct from both the known and the unknown; "known" means made an object by knowledge, and "unknown" means veiled by ignorance—it is different from both because its essential nature is pure consciousness. This is the meaning. || 18 ||
"He knows that which is to be known, yet there is no knower of him"—thus it is stated in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*.
"It is indeed other than the known, and likewise above the unknown"—thus it is stated in the *Talavakāra Upaniṣad*. || 18 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that a consciousness distinct from both the known and the unknown is not experienced.

Anticipating this, he says with irony: since consciousness itself is the very nature of the act of knowing—which is characterized as "knowing"—if there were no experience of that [consciousness], it would follow that even the known object could not be experienced; therefore, the experience of consciousness must necessarily be admitted.
For whom no experience whatsoever arises even regarding awakening.
How can a scripture awaken him? He is like a clod of earth fashioned in human form. (19)

Regarding the phrase "even regarding awakening": for that dull-witted person (*manda*) in whom no experience—that is, no direct realization—of even awakening, which consists in the manifestation of jars and other objects, arises in any way whatsoever, how could the scripture awaken him? The meaning is that it could not awaken him at all, for he is merely a human-shaped clod of earth, as insentient as a clod. || 19 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Even though the eternally unchanging consciousness (*kūṭasthabodha*), which is distinct from knowledge consisting of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) and is self-luminous as declared by the sacred scriptures, has been taught, I do not experience it. To such a person, the author mocks this very doubt with the words "Even in [the case of] cognition" (*bodhe’pi*). This is indeed a locative of object (*viṣayasaptamī*). "Experience" (*anubhava*) here means the awareness of its own self-luminosity. || 19 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: The statement "consciousness is not perceived" is itself contradictory; therefore, he states this with an illustration:
"Just as the statement 'Do I have a tongue or not? leads only to shame."
I do not perceive awakening with the thought, "Awakening is to be realized"—such is that state.

The statement "I have a tongue" or "I do not have a tongue"—such speech serves only for the sake of shame, that is, solely to produce embarrassment, and not to demonstrate intelligence, because speech is impossible without a tongue. Similarly, the statement "I am not understood by you" or "I must be understood from now on" is likewise merely a cause for shame; the meaning is that such usage cannot be established without actual understanding. || 20 ||
a0 Commentary: Therein, he clarifies the illustration with the verse beginning "jiva" (like a living being). || 20 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: One might object, "Let such an awakening be as you describe; nevertheless, what relevance does this have to the realization of Brahman under discussion?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In whatever thing there is an awakening in the world, upon the neglect of each of those..."
The realization that "that which is pure consciousness is Brahman" is the certain conviction regarding Brahman.

Regarding the phrase "in which": in this world, in whatever object characterized by a jar or the like cognition—that is, knowledge—exists, when there is disregard for each of those objects, such as the jar and so forth, meaning when they are treated with indifference, that which remains as pure cognition (*bodhamātra*) pervades everything, including the jar and the rest.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [the section] titled "Discrimination of the Five Elements" (Pañcabhūtaviveka).

The meaning is that the intellect (*dhī*), the understanding (*buddhi*), the certainty regarding Brahman (*brahmaniścaya*), or the realization of Brahman (*brahmāvagati*) consists in the conviction that "that very vibration which exists as the sewn-together [universe] is indeed Brahman. || 21 ||

"That consciousness which is accepted as the fruit in the case of external objects of knowledge is itself the object to be known here, according to the authority of the statements of the Vedānta."
The remainder, however, is indeed clear. || 21 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If Brahman is understood as the experience of objects such as jars by means of disregarding those objects themselves, then this discrimination of the five sheaths (kośapañcaka) would be purposeless. Anticipating this doubt, he states that it is not useless, because the cycle of transmigration does not cease without the knowledge of Brahman as the inner self (pratyagrūpatā), and thus [the discrimination] is useful for realizing that nature.
Upon the abandonment of the five sheaths, through the awakening of the witness-consciousness, [only that remains].
That alone would be its own true nature; for it to be emptiness is difficult to establish.

Regarding the phrase "in the five sheaths": when one has abandoned the five sheaths—beginning with the *annamaya* (consisting of food)—and, through the intellect, has reached the certainty that they are not the Self (*anātman*), because the consciousness that is their witness (*sākṣin*) remains as a residue, that very consciousness in the form of the witness is one's own true nature; it is indeed Brahman itself. An objection might be raised: "If the sheaths beginning with the *annamaya*, which are established by experience, are abandoned, would there not be a residue of mere emptiness (*śūnya*)? Anticipating this, he says: "Emptiness... [and so forth].
The meaning is that the emptiness of that witnessing consciousness is difficult to establish and hard to accomplish. || 22 ||

Commentary (a0): If this is so, then there is a contradiction with your initial proposition (*pratijñā*). For you have proposed that Brahman, being hidden within the cave of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*), is attainable through the discrimination of them; yet now it is being presented as being of the nature of consciousness characterized by the jar and other objects. This is true. However, although that [Brahman], which is the purified referent of the word *tat* (*tatpadārtha*), possesses the aforementioned nature of consciousness characterized by the jar and so forth, it is nevertheless [distinct from] that which is characterized by the five sheaths.

Without the valid knowledge (*pramā*) of the non-difference between the Self and the pure consciousness that is the witness of the form of renunciation (*tyāga*), there can be no cessation of the fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*)—which is of the nature of a beginningless positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), resides in the Self, and has the Self as its object, and which serves as the cause for the immediate delusion of duality (*dvaitabhrama*). With the intention that the discrimination of the five sheaths (*pañcakośaviveka*) is therefore truly fruitful for that purpose, he provides the answer with the word "five.

[He does so] because, despite having been refuted in the passage, "It is unknowable due to the absence of another knower and knowledge, not due to non-existence," the Madhyamika view might still arise through the possibility of forgetfulness.

He refutes this again with the final quarter [of the verse]: "emptiness" (śūnyatvam). The connection is to be understood by supplying the words: "Since even the existence and manifestation of emptiness depend solely upon that [consciousness], its emptiness is indeed impossible. || 22 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He demonstrates the very difficulty [of this position] as follows:
"First of all, that which is called 'self' (ātman) exists, because it is not a subject of dispute."
If there were dispute even with oneself, who would be the opponent in that case? (23)

"It exists. The nature of the self (*svasvarūpa*), which is denoted by the word "self," certainly exists according to the views of both the worldly and the Vedic; why is this so? To this he says: "Because of dispute," etc. This means that the nature of the self is not an object of disagreement. He states the refutation for the opposite case: "In the self," etc. If there were disagreement even regarding one's own self, then who would be the opponent in this present dispute?
The meaning is that there might not be anyone at all. || 23 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) explains that very point: "It exists" (*asti*). "Self" (*svayam*) means the Self (*ātman*), which is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*) as denoted by the word "self. The reason for this is given as "in dispute" (*vivāda*). He removes the objection regarding the unestablished nature of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*) with the words "even in itself" (*svasminnapi*). "In dispute" (*vivāde*) means a formal debate (*vāda*) characterized by specific features such as *jalpa* and so forth. Indeed, its definition and other details are stated in the *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha*, while treating the Nyāya system.

By the authors themselves [it is stated]: "Vāda (debate) is a specific type of discourse whose fruit is the determination of truth. Jalpa (wrangling) is a discourse between those desiring victory, characterized by the employment of arguments for both sides.

Vitaṇḍā (cavil) is a specific type of discourse devoid of the establishment of one's own position. Thus, "discourse" (kathā) is defined as the adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis by the proponent and the opponent.
The Third Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

And thus, the ownership of [the subject] must indeed be stated without doubt by both the proponent and the opponent, since the engagement in the debate would otherwise be impossible. The point is that if that very [subject] were the locus of dispute, then the absence of an opponent would be easily established. || 23 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, anticipating the objection that there might be an opponent who himself maintains the non-existence of the self, he states that no such person exists:
"But the non-existence of one's own self is not pleasing to anyone, except through delusion."
For this very reason, the Śruti declares the sublation of the proponent of non-existence.
"Regarding *svāsattvam* (one's own non-existence)": the meaning is that, setting aside the single state of delusion, no one accepts the non-existence of oneself in any other state.

Anticipating the question, "How is this determined?", he says, "Therefore (*ataḥ*). Since this [doctrine] is not pleasing to anyone, for that very reason even the Śruti declares the refutation of those who maintain such non-existence. || 24 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): For this very reason, [it says] "his own" (*sva*). The word *tu* has the sense of *api* (even/also). The meaning is: "to anyone at all. He states that this is also in accordance with the Śruti by saying, "For this very reason" (*ata eva*). || 24 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In response to the inquiry, "What is this scriptural passage?", he recites that scripture beginning with "Non-existent indeed" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1) according to its meaning:
"If one knows Brahman as non-existent, he himself would become non-existent."
Therefore, let there be no effort for this [object], but rather its own existence should be admitted. (25)

"Non-existent" (asat): if one were to know that Brahman is non-existent, then one would oneself become non-existent by knowing the non-existence of Brahman, because of one's own very nature being that of Brahman; this is the meaning. He states the conclusion: "Therefore" (ataḥ) || 25 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) reads that very Śruti in its sense: “It is non-existent,” and so forth. Thus the Taittirīyas record: “He becomes non-existent indeed, if he knows Brahman as non-existent. He states the conclusion: “Therefore,” meaning: of this Self consisting of pure consciousness, which is the ultimate limit remaining after the sublation of the five sheaths (pañcakośa). || 29 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, desiring to state that the Self is self-luminous, he raises the question regarding what its nature would be if it were not an object of knowledge:
"If one should ask, 'What then is it like?', [the answer is] 'For in that case, there is no "being like this" (īdṛktā) at all.'"
Determine its true nature to be that which is neither like this nor unlike this. 26.

"What is its nature?"—this is the intended meaning: if one accepts that the Self is qualified by some form such as "being like this" (*īdṛktva*) and so forth, then it would be an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) precisely by that form; if that is not accepted, then [the Self] would be a mere void. It is true that if "being like this" and so forth were accepted, it would be known in that very way. However, that is not accepted; thus he says: "What is its nature? (*īdṛk*). This is also an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for "being like that" (*tādṛktva*). He states the absence of both: "That which... (*ya-*)...
"Thus it was never seen before. || 26 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, [the opponent] asks with a hidden intention, "If the Self is indeed real even though it is unknowable, what wrong has the son of a barren woman done?
Thus, he inquires about the nature of its essence: "Of what kind? In this way, the proponent himself addresses that question: "O disciple, or rather, O disputant, you should ask:
'In what manner does that Brahman, the nature of the Self, exist—being accepted as real even though it is unknowable? This refers to the object of the inquiry.

Having restated the objection with "if one were to do so," he provides the resolution that there is no such manner at all in that case, using the words "īdṛktā" (the state of being like this). Therefore, he states the conclusion with "yat" (that which):

"O disciple, O disputant, that object which is not 'like this'—meaning it is not directly perceptible—and likewise 'not like that'—meaning it is not other than that [perceptible], is [the reality]. This is the reading of Acyutarāya.
1. One should ask, "Is it like this?"—this is the reading of Acyutarāya.
In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[in the section titled] "Discrimination of the Five Elements" (*pañcabhūtaviveka*),
determine with certainty that the very nature which is like space is the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), characterized by being preceded by the support of the Vedas and other authorities.
The syntactical connection is: "Make it the object of a specific determination. || 26 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that the meaning is not established by mere assertion, he explains the meanings of the words *īdṛk* (such) and *tādṛk* (so) and establishes their applicability here: "That which is an object of the senses is called *īdṛk* (this-like); that which is beyond the senses is called *tādṛk* (that-like)."
The subject is not an object of the senses because it is self-evident; therefore, it is not beyond perception.

Regarding the phrase "of the senses" (*akṣāṇām*): it is observed that objects such as a jar, which are perceptible (*pratyakṣa*), possess the nature of being denotable by words like "this-like" (*īdṛk*); whereas things like *dharma*, which are imperceptible (*parokṣa*), possess the nature of being denotable by words like "that-like" (*tādṛk*). However, the Self (*ātman*), the seer, lacks the status of being "this-like" because it is not an object of knowledge produced by the sense organs; nor does it have the status of being "that-like," because it is not imperceptible by virtue of its very own nature.
This is the meaning. || 27 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Illuminating the reason therein, he explains the meaning of such terms as "akṣāṇām" (of the senses) and so forth—namely, "akṣāṇām iti.

Therein, he states the non-existence of the first [category] along with its reason: "viṣayīti. The construction is as follows: since the subject (*viṣayī*) is of the nature of pure illumination, it is not at all an object of the senses. Likewise, he refutes the last [category] as well: "svatvāditi" (because of self-nature). || 27 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Then, under the guise of demonstrating the result, he refutes the second position—that it is void—stating:
"Therefore, although this [Self] is not an object of cognition, it is immediate; thus, it is self-luminous."
"Truth, knowledge, and infinity—this is the definition of Brahman here. (28)

"Unknowable" (avedya) means that although it is not an object of knowledge produced by the senses, it is self-luminous (svaprakāśa) because it is immediate (aparokṣa). Here is the formal argument (prayoga): The Self is self-luminous, because it is immediate even without being the object of consciousness, just like consciousness itself. Nor is the reason unestablished regarding the qualification, for if the Self were the object of consciousness, there would arise the contradiction of the status of both object and agent [in a single entity]. Its agency exists by virtue of its own essential nature.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because [the same entity] possesses the status of an object (*karmatva*) by virtue of its specific form (*viśiṣṭarūpeṇa*), then by the same logic, even in the act of going (*gamana-kriyā*), one and the same thing would have the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*) by its own nature and the status of an object by its specific form; this leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, the example is not devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*), because if consciousness were to require another consciousness for its own manifestation, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). According to the Tarka school, a jar is manifested by the cognition of the jar, and the cognition of the jar is manifested by a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*); thus, like consciousness itself, it serves as an example for self-luminosity (*svaprakāśa*).

If it is argued that [the Self] lacks a means of proof (*sādhanavikala*), we say no; for knowledge does not manifest through another knowledge, and thus it is not lacking a means of proof. Now, one might object: even if the Self is established as self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), its status as Brahman is not established because it lacks the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman. Anticipating this, he applies those characteristics to it, beginning with "Truth" (*satyam*). According to the Śruti, "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1.1), that which is the characteristic of Brahman—
The meaning is that what was [previously] described as momentary exists within the Self. || 28 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): In this case, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), perceiving the hidden intention of the opponent—that if the self is not an object of perception and so forth, it must be non-existent like the son of a barren woman—refutes that non-existence by demonstrating its self-luminosity along with its defining characteristics: "Ave... [etc.]

"Even the sky," etc. By the word "even" (api), its distinction from objects such as a jar is indicated. By this, the definition of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) is established as being "immediacy while being an object of knowledge. Thus, what I previously stated—namely, that [self-luminosity] consists in not depending on another for its manifestation—is precisely what results here. Now, one might ask: even so, how can there be non-difference between this [self-luminous entity] and Brahman? To this, he says: "It is true," etc. (28).
— Rāghavendra’s Commentary — To establish the reality of the Self, he first states the definition of reality:
"Reality is the absence of sublation; [it belongs] to that which is the sole witness to the sublation of the world."
Tell me, what witnesses does sublation have? For it is not accepted as being without witnesses.

Regarding "the nature of truth": truth consists in being devoid of sublation (*bādha*). That which is not subject to sublation is true; that which is subject to sublation is false—this is the distinction between them, according to the former teachers.
[End of] the third section. [page 101]
[This work] is accompanied by two commentaries.

[It is so] because it has been stated by those [authorities]. To the question, "Let that be; what is the relevance to the present topic? he says: "The world," meaning that which is characterized by the gross and subtle bodies and so forth.

As for the sublation (*bādha*) consisting in the non-existence [of the self] during sleep, fainting, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*): since the Self exists precisely as the witness (*sākṣin*) of that [state], what witness could there be for this sublation of the Self? What is the witness of that sublation which is itself the object of sublation? The meaning is that no witness exists at all. Anticipating the objection, "Could the sublation of the Self not be without a witness? he says: "But not... A sublation devoid of a witness must not be admitted; otherwise—
The meaning is: "lest there be an over-extension [of the principle]. || 29 ||
Commentary (a0): Therein, he establishes its reality—“satyatvam” and so forth. The rest is quite simple. ||29||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He clarifies the aforementioned point by means of an illustration:
"When all material forms have been removed, indeed, the immaterial ether remains."
When all possible [alternatives] have been refuted, that which remains is indeed that very thing.

Regarding the phrase "when they have been removed": when material objects such as jars and the like, which are located within a house or similar space, have been removed— that is, when they have been taken out from the house and so forth— then, just as only the sky remains, which is impossible to remove, even so, when all things distinct from oneself— whether material or immaterial, such as the body, senses, and so forth— which are capable of being rejected, have been rejected by the Śruti through the words "not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6), at the end, in that final state where everything has been rejected...
The meaning is that the awareness which remains as the nature of consciousness (kṣitva) is precisely that self (ātman) which is free from sublation. || 30 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Therein, he clarifies the illustration with the words "when [the objects] have been removed. He applies this to the subject of the illustration with the words "in the case of the possible [objects]. The phrase "to sublate by means of their being objects of perception" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Alternatively, the connection is as follows: that pure consciousness (*dṛṅmātra*) which remains as the residual substratum—being impossible to sublate by virtue of its being the illuminator—is precisely that which is the True Brahman, uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time. || 30 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "If everything that is perceived is negated, nothing at all remains; therefore, how can it be said that 'that which remains' is the Self? For what is it that remains? To this, he replies: "That which remains when everything is sublated is neither something nor nothing; that alone is That."
In this case, it is only the linguistic expressions that differ; for there is indeed no contradiction whatsoever. (31)

Regarding the phrase "negating everything": even by one who says that nothing whatsoever remains, a cognition whose object is the non-existence of all things must necessarily be admitted for the sake of establishing such a practice. With the intention of stating that this very [cognition] is the nature of the Self (ātman) as we maintain it, he replies with the words "that which is not. The meaning is: that consciousness which is expressed by the word "nothing" is itself that Brahman. Now, [an objection is raised]: since the word "nothing" denotes non-existence—how can it be Brahman?

Anticipating the objection as to how consciousness (*caitanya*) can be expressed by the word "I" (*aham*), he provides the following rebuttal with the verse beginning "bhāṣā": since the witness of sublation (*bādhasākṣin*) must necessarily be admitted, the disagreement concerns only the expressive words and not the thing expressed. Here, regarding the inner self which is the witness of sublation, only the linguistic expressions—such as "the witness," "consciousness," and so forth—are differentiated; however, the witnessing consciousness itself exists as unassailable, meaning it is free from sublation. || 31 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): To further solidify the very point already stated, following the maxim of "driving in a pillar," he elucidates it with confidence, beginning with the words "sarva" (all). The meaning is that that very Consciousness which manifests as the non-existence of everything—that which is "nothing at all"—is indeed Brahman. Thus, while you, being undiscriminating, employ the word "na kiṃcit" (nothing) according to your own intention to denote the absence of all objects of perception, in reality, this [Consciousness]— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)

When an investigation is conducted, since even non-existence (abhāva) is no different from other things in being perceptible, one must admit—even if weeping—that [the word] does not denote that [non-existence], but rather denotes the Consciousness (caitanya) which serves as the witness to its sublation (bādha). However, for me, when all objects of perception are sublated, only that Consciousness which illumines them remains;
thus, I employ a word that directly denotes that [Consciousness]. Therefore, the connection [of the argument] is that our modes of expression alone differ here. He states the conclusion:
"Without contradiction" means that it exists in its entirety; such is the construction of the sentence. || 31 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He establishes the aforementioned point on the basis of scripture:
Therefore, the Śruti, having sublated that which is to be sublated, leaves this [reality] remaining; thus was the Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya.
This very Self, known as the discernment of the five elements, is of the nature of the exclusion of what it is not, expressed as "not this, not this" (neti neti). || 32 ||

"For this very reason": because the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) is indestructible, for this very reason the Śruti text, "This Self is 'not this, not this'" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.9.26), by means of negating non-self entities through the form of exclusion, having sublated and discarded the entire collection of non-self things that are fit for negation, leaves over and remains as the direct nature (*pratyaksvarūpa*) which is impossible to negate. || 32 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on verse a0: He corroborates the stated point with scripture, [beginning with] "ata eva" ("for this very reason"). The scriptural text, "This Self is 'not this, not this'," having sublated the duality consisting of cause and effect—which is to be sublated—[states] "atad" ("not that"), meaning by way of its non-differentiation from the visible world. Therefore, the connection is that it leaves as a remainder only the non-dual Brahman-consciousness, which is the inner self (pratyagātman) as previously described. || 32 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: It has been stated that the scriptural text "not this, not this" (neti neti) sublates that which is capable of being sublated while leaving behind that which cannot be sublated.
With a view toward explaining what kind of thing is capable of being sublated and what kind is incapable, he demonstrates both by distinguishing them:
"Whatever form there may be, as long as it can all be abandoned..."
For that Self is impossible to perceive, formless, and free from all affliction.

"This has such a form" (*idaṃrūpam*). "This has such a form" means that the body and so forth, whose nature (*svarūpa*) is a form being experienced as an object of sight, are "this-formed. The word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis. The two words *yadyāvat* (as much as) are intended to include all objects of sight.

This being the case, the meaning is that whatever is an object of sight can indeed be entirely abandoned. One becomes "not this-formed," meaning unfit to be apprehended as "this" by way of objective identity (*idantā*) through the realization of the inner self (*pratyak*).

The meaning is that [the witness] is impossible to abandon. By means of the particle *hi*, which indicates what is well-known, he suggests that because the witness is one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), it is unfit for abandonment.

He states the conclusion: "The Self. The meaning is that the witness who is free from sublation is indeed the Self, and not the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) or other objects of perception (*dṛśya*). || 33 ||
Commentary on the verse (a0 ṭīkā): In that regard, he sets forth the reasons with the two half-verses beginning with "This form, however" (idaṃ rūpaṃ tu). || 33 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Let it be that the Self is subject to sublation; what relevance does this have to the present topic? To this he says:
"The reality of Brahman is established, while its nature as knowledge has been stated previously."
This is clearly stated by such statements as "because it is self-experienced" (svayamevānubhūtitvāt). || 34 ||

"Siddham" (established). That which was stated as truth (*satyatva*) regarding Brahman, characterized by Brahman, is established in the Self (*ātman*). To the inquiry, "Granted that there is truth, how is there knowledge (*jñānatva*)?", he says—having already demonstrated it previously—"knowledge-ness": "Because it is itself the very experience (*anubhūti*), it does not possess the state of being an object of experience (*anubhāvyatā*)" (Śloka-vārttika 1.1.2, verse 13). By such statements, its nature as knowledge has already been correctly established.
The meaning is that it has been stated. || 34 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, in order to establish the nature of [the Self] as knowledge, the author recalls what was already established previously by way of restating the context—beginning with the words "It is established" (*siddham*). Here, since the subject at hand is the demonstration of the application of the definition of Brahman for the purpose of establishing its non-difference from the Self—the pure consciousness that is the Witness and the ultimate limit of the sublation of the five sheaths—it would have been more appropriate to say "it is established in the Self" (*ātmani siddham*); nevertheless, the statement "in Brahman" (*brahmaṇi*) is used because of its absolute...
The intended meaning is that it is precisely with the intention of [establishing] difference. || 34 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even if reality (*satyatva*) and knowledge (*jñānatva*) are established in the Self, infinity (*anantya*) is not possible, because it is not established even in Brahman.
Anticipating this doubt, he first establishes that [infinity] in Brahman:
"Therefore, it is not limited by space due to its all-pervasiveness, nor is it limited by time due to its eternity."
Nor is there infinity in Brahman even in terms of its substantial reality, because it possesses the nature of all things; thus, [infinity] is threefold in Brahman.
The Third Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
103. Not because of all-pervasiveness; for it is said: "Eternal, omnipresent, all-reaching, and extremely subtle" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.6).
"Omnipresent and eternal like space"; "The eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious" (Kaṭha 5.13; Śvetāśvatara 6.13);
"All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.5.7); "For all this is Brahman" (Māṇḍūkya 2);
"Brahman alone is all this" (Nṛsiṃhottaratāpanīya 7)—in such scriptural passages, [the attributes of] pervasiveness, eternity, and being the self of all [are established].
The meaning is that, because Brahman is taught [as such], its threefold infinity—consisting in the absence of limitation by space, time, and substance—must be accepted. || 35 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): In this very way, he establishes here also the infinity characterized by the absence of limitation in space, time, and substance—expressed as "not because of being all-pervasive" (na vyāpitvāt). The meaning is that this is also established by such scriptural passages as, "And like space, He is omnipresent and eternal," "All this is what this Self is," and "For all this is Brahman. || 35 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states that this is not only from scripture but also from reasoning:
"And because space, time, and other objects are imagined through Māyā."
Therefore, there is no distinction made by place and so forth; hence, the infinity of Brahman is manifest.

Regarding "place and time": because the causes of delimitation—namely, objects other than [Brahman] in terms of place and time—are themselves imagined through *māyā*, no ultimate delimitation by place and so forth is possible in Brahman, just as there is none in the sky with respect to a city of the *gandharvas* and the like. Therefore, infinity (*ānantya*) in Brahman is indeed manifest; for it is said: "This is the Truth: the Self is Brahman itself" (*Nṛsiṃha Upaniṣad*, Tāpinī 9), and "Brahman is the Self alone here. Thus, it is so.
"There is no doubt; Om, Truth! The Self alone is the Lord Nṛsiṃha, who is Brahman" (Nṛsiṃha Upaniṣad 1.9);

"This Self is Brahman" (Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 2)—since the non-difference of the Self from Brahman is established by such scriptural passages, the intended meaning is that its infinity is likewise proven. || 36 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He establishes that very point through reasoning as well, beginning with the words "deśa" (space). Thus, just as the sky—being imagined by means of things such as a city of Gandharvas—possesses the threefold limitation of space and so forth, in the same way, the reality of the Self that is Brahman has no limitation caused by space and the like, because it is not imagined by Māyā. This is the meaning. He states the conclusion: "Brahman... Accordingly, the followers of the Atharva Veda declare the identity of Brahman and the Self.

In the *Nṛsiṃhottaratāpanīya*: “This is the truth: the Self is indeed Brahman, and Brahman is indeed the Self; for in this matter there should be no doubt. Thus, *Oṃ*, the truth is that the Self alone is the divine Nṛsiṃha, who is Brahman. || 36 ||

Rāma’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Granted that because the insentient universe is superimposed upon Brahman, it lacks the capacity to limit Brahman; however, since this is not impossible for the two sentient beings—the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)—Brahman's infinity would be untenable due to its being subject to limitations caused by them.

Anticipating this doubt, [the author] intends to show that since even those two possess forms conditioned by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and thus lack ultimate reality, they too cannot serve as causes for actual limitation.
"That Brahman which is truth, knowledge, and infinite—that is the Reality; that [Self] belongs to it."
And both lordship and the state of being a living soul (jīvatva) are imagined through two limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

"It is the Truth. That Brahman whose nature is Truth and so forth is the Reality; that alone is the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*). As for the lordship and the state of being an individual soul (*jīvatva*) of that Brahman which are well-known in the world, those are superimposed (*kalpita*) by means of the two adjuncts (*upādhi*) to be described hereafter. Therefore, because they are merely superimposed, like an insentient object, the sense is that the individual soul and the Lord likewise lack the capacity to delimit that [Brahman]. || 37 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection may be raised: "Granted that insentient things such as space (*deśa*) do not limit Brahman because they are merely imagined within it by *māyā*; however, how is it that sentient beings—the individual souls (*jīvas*)—and the Lord (*Īśvara*) do not limit Brahman as real entities? If that were the case, the infinity of Brahman would be difficult to maintain. Anticipating this doubt, he says, "It is true," etc., meaning that this is not so, because both the soul and the Lord are likewise imagined through the two limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) which are about to be described. || 37 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 104.
[The commentary by Rāghavānanda on the *Pañcabhūtaviveka*—

In response to the inquiry as to what those two limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are, and desiring to demonstrate both of them in succession, he first defines the power (*śakti*) which constitutes the limiting adjunct of the Lord (*īśvara*):]
There exists a certain divine power that governs all things.
Beginning with that which consists of bliss, she is hidden within all things.

Regarding the term "power" (*śakti*): there exists a certain power belonging to Īśvara—which serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for Īśvara—and which cannot be defined by such forms as existence or non-existence; it is the regulator of all things and the capacity for governing all those objects subject to regulation mentioned in the *Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa* [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7], beginning with the earth. Anticipating the question of where this power resides or why it is not perceived, he says:
"Ānandeti. The meaning is that [the Self] exists hidden within all things, from those consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) up to the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and therefore it is not perceived. || 38 ||

Commentary on the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā*: In order to illuminate these two aforementioned limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and wishing here to briefly present his own accepted system regarding the individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśvara*), and so forth—which was elaborated upon in the two preceding chapters—he [the author] states: "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold... (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8).

He explains that power (*śakti*), which is well-known from such scriptural passages as those cited above, as being superimposed from the perspective of people like us upon pure Brahman itself as an beginningless entity—stating, "Power. Now, one might object: even if it be granted that this [power] is imagined within pure Brahman as its substratum, does it nevertheless favor the Lord (*īśvara*) in the form of the consciousness reflected in itself, or rather [the consciousness] reflected in its own specific [limiting adjuncts]?

Is she partial toward the living body (*drūpajīva*), or is she partial toward pure consciousness alone (*śuddhacinmātra*)? It is not the first [option], because [the Lord] is impartial toward the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

Nor is it the middle [option], because since that [pure consciousness] lacks omniscience and the status of being the cause of all, it is impossible for it to be the regulator of all things as will be described later. Nor is it the first [option after all], because since its status as a regulator must be predicated even with respect to ignorance—which is included within "all things"—its omniscience [would be compromised].

If it is argued that this leads to a contradiction, we say no; for since she is the regulator of all things, her inclusion within the definition of omniscience is precisely what is intended in the first position.

Furthermore, because ignorance regarding any object included within "all things" would contradict the omniscience of Īśvara, it must necessarily be stated that she regulates [ignorance] as residing in the *jīva*, like dullness (*jāḍya*) and other such qualities.
With this intention, he qualifies her as "belonging to Īśvara" (*aiśvarī*). This distinguishes her from the *pradhāna* accepted by the followers of the Sāṃkhya who acknowledge Īśvara.

"Something" (kācit) means "indescribable" (anirvacanīya), because it cannot be defined as being existent or otherwise. To the question, "Why must this be accepted? he says: "All... [sarva...]. To the question, "Why is it not perceived? he says: "Bliss... [ānanda...]. || 38 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection—"Why should that [power], which is invariably unperceived, not simply be non-existent?"—he states that it must necessarily be accepted because the regularity of the world would otherwise be inexplicable:
"When things could not be regulated by their inherent powers, then [the power] would indeed not exist."
Indeed, through the mutual confusion of their respective properties, the world would surely fall into disorder.

Regarding the phrase "the properties of things" (*vastudharmā*): if the solidity, fluidity, and so forth of things such as earth were not established by means of their respective capacities (*śakti*), then, due to the confusion (*sāṃkarya*)—that is, the commingling and coexistence in one place—of those properties, the world would collapse; the meaning is that it would fall into a state where conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) becomes indeterminate. The particle *khalu* indicates what is well-known. (39)
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Lest it be argued that there should be no restriction regarding all things, he says: "The properties of objects" (vastudharmāḥ). || 39 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection that it is not logical for this [Māyā], being insentient, to be the regulator of the universe, he says:
"Through the entry of the reflection of consciousness, that Power shines as if it were sentient."
Through union with the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of that power, Brahman attains the state of Īśvara. || 40 ||

Regarding the phrase *cicchāyā*: that power (*śakti*), by virtue of receiving the shadow of consciousness—that is, through the entry of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*)—shines forth as if conscious, having attained a state of consciousness as it were; therefore, its status as a regulator is logically established. This is the meaning. [To the objection: "Let that be so, but what relevance does this have to the present topic?
