The Third Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

He says: "By its power" (*tacchakti*). This is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is the power. That very thing is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); through conjunction with it—that is, through connection with it—Brahman itself, characterized by truth and so forth, attains or reaches the state of being the Lord (*īśvaratām*), which is the possession of attributes such as omniscience. || 40 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection is raised: "But surely, the regulation of all things, as stated by the Inner Controller Brahman in such passages as 'He who dwells in all,' belongs to the Lord alone, and not to His insentient power (śakti). To this, he says: "By the will of Consciousness" (cicchāyā). This means: "by virtue of contact with one's own reflection of consciousness" (cidābhāsa). An objection is raised: "In that case, who is this Lord? To this, he says: "That" (tat). That which is characterized by such a reflection of one's own consciousness...

"Power" (śakti) is beginningless ignorance; that itself is the limiting adjunct (upādhi). The meaning is: "due to its conjunction with that [Self], because of the superimposition of identity with it. By this, it is indicated that even in their doctrine, these [teachers] ultimately arrive at the theory of reflection (ābhāsavāda). || 40 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Since the sheaths (kośas) that constitute the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) of the state of being a living soul (jīvatva) have already been described, he now states that the state of being a living soul is caused by them:
"When there is the intention to describe the sheaths as limiting adjuncts, Brahman itself attains the state of being a living soul."
The father and grandfather are each established in relation to their respective son and grandson.

Regarding the phrase "the sheath as a limiting adjunct" (*kośopādhi*): when one considers the intention behind the term "sheath as a limiting adjunct," it means that Brahman itself—characterized by truth and so forth—becomes the object of the empirical usage of "living being" (*jīva*) when there is a living being. Now, one might object: "It has never been observed anywhere that a single entity can simultaneously possess two contradictory attributes. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Just as [a single] Devadatta... [one person]. Just as a single Devadatta... [is seen in different ways].

Just as a father becomes a grandfather with respect to his grandson, so too Brahmā becomes the individual soul (jīva) when the limiting adjunct of the "sheath" (kośa) is intended, and he becomes the Lord (īśvara) when the limiting adjunct of "power" (śakti) is intended; such is the meaning. || 41 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Having thus described the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of Īśvara and His essential nature, he now describes the limiting adjuncts of the individual soul (jīva) and so forth, beginning with the word "kośa" (sheath).
He clarifies the illustration for both cases with the words "like a father. This is also indicative of the entire world. || 41 ||
When sons and others are not intended to be expressed, there is neither "father" nor "grandfather."
Therefore, neither Īśvara nor the individual soul [is the agent] when the sheath of power (śaktikośa) is not intended to be expressed. || 42 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: In reality, however, neither the state of being a living soul (jīvatva) nor the state of being the Lord (īśvaratva) exists in Brahman; he states this with an illustration: "Of a son, etc. (verse 42).

Commentary (a0): Having thus stated the superimposition (*adhyāropa*), he now clarifies its negation (*apavāda*) by means of an illustration, beginning with the words "of the son, etc. The intended meaning is this: just as in the absence of a son and so forth, the non-existence of the duality imagined therein—which is denoted by the term "world"—is established precisely because it is inseparable from the absence of the one who imagines it. || 42 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now he states the fruit of the knowledge thus described:
"He who knows Brahman in this way becomes Brahman himself."
Because Brahmā has no birth, he is not born again. || 43 ||
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Discrimination of the Five Sheaths," in the *Pañcadaśī* composed by the venerable sage Vidyāraṇya. || 3 ||

Commentary: Now, one might ask: since the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the Lord, namely *śakti*, and the five sheaths (*kośa*) that constitute the limiting adjunct of the individual soul (*jīva*), have not been negated by a subverting cognition (*bādhadhī*) at the outset, how could there be a non-intentional treatment of them? Consequently, how could there be the absence of the duality consisting of the world of ether and so forth, as well as the duality characterized by the notions of "I" (*ahaṃtā*) and "mine" (*mamatā*), both of which are imagined by those [adjuncts]?

If it be argued that the objective reality (*vastu*) has already been cast far away [by the previous arguments], we say no. This is because the potency (*śakti*), the series of sheaths (*kośa-paṅkti*) which constitute its effects, the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) as conditioned by those sheaths, and the entire expanse of duality imagined by them, are all sublated solely by the single valid cognition of the non-duality of the Self's true nature (*ātma-svarūpa-advaita-pramā*). Furthermore, the means for this—characterized by the discrimination of the aforementioned sheaths and so forth—has already been understood from what was stated previously. Indicating this, he concludes with a statement of the result: "He who... Thus says the Śruti: "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed."

"He who is liberated from the knots of the heart-cave becomes immortal," and "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," and so forth. The Smṛti passage, "He is not born again," etc., should also be understood in this context. By this, that which was stated in the introduction—"How indeed can the attributeless Self be the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer of the world?"—is addressed.
Or rather, this third type of restriction, namely the "Lord," is possible as a means of cognition;
thus, the statement regarding the third restriction refers to the referent of that term.
Likewise: "Brahman, discerning the sheaths, speaks so as not to contradict perception and the other means of valid knowledge."

It considers that in the third [chapter], beginning with "the cave is its essential meaning" (*guhā tadarthabhūtam*), this third section called *Kośaviveka* constitutes a contradiction to that [previous position], and that is indeed appropriate. For instance, there, even though the Self is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), regarding its being the non-different efficient and material cause of the world, the opening statement is "Brahman hidden in the cave" (*guhāhitam brahma*); likewise, for one who is thus...

The concluding statement, "This is Brahman, [known through] the Vedas," constitutes a single sign of the identity between the two, because liberation is granted by knowing that the very Brahman characterized as the cause of the universe is the true nature of the individual soul (jīva). As it is said: "That Bliss which is the prototype (bimba), the Self, remains forever. And: "In whatever object there is no awareness in this world, upon the neglect of that [object...]"
The conviction that "that which is pure consciousness is Brahman" constitutes the determination of Brahman (*brahmaniścaya*);

such [statements] constitute *abhyāsa* (repetition). "Ascertain its true nature as being neither like this nor like that" constitutes *apūrvatā* (novelty). "Since there is no birth for Brahman, therefore he is not born again" constitutes the *phala* (fruit/result). "'This is the supreme lineage within the cave' constitutes the *arthavāda* (eulogy)."

The reasoning [for this] begins with the words "of those whose nature is sweetness and so forth," and continues with "the father and grandfather are one, just as the son and grandson are distinct. Thus, although Brahman is devoid of attributes (nirguṇa), it is characterized as the cause of the universe by its sixfold marks; yet, through its own power, upon the sublation of that [causal state], it is indeed possible for it to exist in the form of the individual soul (jīva) and in the form of liberation (kaivalya), which is non-dual existence, consciousness, and bliss. Therefore, there is not even a trace of doubt regarding the impossibility of this object of knowledge (prameya). This is the general direction [of the argument]. || 43 ||
Thus ends the third chapter, the Illumination of the Discrimination of the Sheaths (*kośavivekaprakāśa*), in the commentary on the *Pañcadaśī* by the venerable Paramahaṃsa. 3.
Now begins the fourth chapter, titled "Discrimination between Duality" (Dvaitaviveka).
Rāma’s Commentary: Having bowed to the venerable masters Bhāratītīrtha and Vidyāraṇya, [I shall compose this work].
I shall provide a word-by-word commentary on the *Dvaitaviveka*. || 1 ||

Performing the auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) characterized by the recollection of the reality of the desired deity for the sake of completing the work he intends to compose without obstacle, and taking for granted the fourfold preliminary requirements (*anubandhacatuṣṭaya*) pertaining to this treatise on Vedānta, he announces the commencement of the book:
"The duality created by both the Lord and the individual soul (*jīva*) is here being discerned."
When discernment exists, bondage becomes clearly manifest as something to be abandoned by the individual soul. || 1 ||

"By Īśvara": by Īśvara, who has the cause (*kāraṇa*) as his limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), acting as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*); and by the *jīva*, who likewise has the effect (*kārya*) as his limiting adjunct and is characterized by the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyayin*). The duality—the world—is created and produced, and is then analyzed, that is, demonstrated through differentiation. He prevents this analysis of duality from being rendered purposeless—like an examination of a crow's teeth—by stating: "In the analysis. When the analysis is performed—that is, when the differentiation between the two dualities created by the *jīva* and the *Īśvara* is accomplished—[the purpose is achieved].

When there is a living self (jīva) as previously described, bondage—which is the duality that is the cause of bondage—must be abandoned and relinquished; it becomes manifest, meaning it reaches clarity. The sense is that it is thus determined: "this much is to be abandoned by the living self. || 1 ||

A0 Commentary: [I bow to] that which is the immutable form of the supreme Brahman—non-dual bliss, existence, consciousness, all-pervading, and stainless—which, though the abode of the illusory net of duality arising from delusion, is the self-luminous crest-jewel of the Vedas.

I bow to my own guru, the most excellent of all teachers, the ornament of the lineage of Atri, the true preceptor established in Brahman, known by the name Śrī Nārāyaṇa, and also to the one named Mahādeva. || 1 ||
Having honored Jīvañjīvā, Vidyāraṇya, and Bhāratītīrtha.
I illuminate the discernment of duality through the light of the Fourth state, as if by moonlight. || 2 ||

Now, the venerable teacher Vidyāraṇya, desiring to compose the fourth chapter of the *Pañcadaśī*, titled "Discrimination of Duality" (*Dvaitaviveka*), explicitly states its subject matter and purpose for the sake of engaging those who are discerning; by doing so, he also implies the corresponding real and scriptural [purposes] regarding the Lord.

He performs an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*), which is well-known as the purpose of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and characterized by its connection to the subject matter (*raṇa-lakṣaṇa*), with the words "By the Lord" (*īśvareṇa*). This is the intended meaning: here, since the discrimination between the duality created by the Lord (*īśvara*) and the individual soul (*jīva*) is an inseparable prerequisite, their respective attributes and their corresponding conformable forms, as well as their true nature, must be stated. Thus, the subject matter (*viṣaya*) of this scripture consisting of four chapters (*caturlakṣaṇī*) is characterized by pure identity with That; and the fruit (*phala*) consists of liberation in the form of the destruction of ignorance regarding that subject matter.
Or rather, the purpose itself might be real. || 1 ||

[Commentary on the *Dvaitaviveka*, Chapter 1]—Regarding the duality created by the Lord (*īśvara*), there are those who do not accept the Vedas as the word of God even among the branches of the four Vedas; those who, while accepting them, maintain that the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is the creator through the medium of karma; and those who accept His status as creator in a different manner, such as the Mādhyamikas and the Kāpilas.

Intending to refute, in effect, the Digambara Jains, Rāmānuja, the Jain logicians (Ārhata-tārkika), and others, he summarizes their positions through eight verses beginning with "māyāṃ tu... (II.1). Thus, the connection is as follows: having taken as the subject consciousness conditioned by Māyā, the followers of the Śvetāśvatara branch of the Yajurveda say, "From this [consciousness], the Lord of Māyā creates this universe. (II.2)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: The statement from the Aitareya Upaniṣad follows in meaning:
"In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone; He thought, 'Let me create.'"
"By his mere volition he created these worlds," so say the Bahvṛcas. || 3 ||

Regarding the word "Self" (*ātman*): by this sentence, "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever, not even what one might desire. He thought, 'Let me create the worlds,' and he created these worlds" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.1), the students of the *Ṛgveda* branch declare that the non-dual Supreme Self alone is the creator of the universe. || 3 ||

Commentary (a0): Regarding the word "Self" (ātman): "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever that blinked. He thought, 'Shall I now create the worlds? He created these worlds. Thus it is recorded in the Aitareya Upaniṣad. || 3 ||
These, in order, are space, air, fire, water, earth, the six [tastes], and the body.
From that Self, this Brahmā, all beings have come into existence.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Intending to show that the Taittirīya Śruti is also an authority for the Lord being the cause of the universe, he recites its passage according to its meaning in two verses, beginning with "kham" (the ether). || 4 ||
Commentary on verse a0: "From this very Self, indeed, space was produced," and so forth. || 4 ||
"May I become many; may I procreate"—thus [He thought] out of desire.
"Tittiri says that having performed austerity, he created the entire world. || 5 ||
"Rāma-Ṭīkā: Having begun with 'Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite,' [it continues] 'from this very Self...'"

By the passage beginning with "ether was produced" and ending with "from food, the person," it is stated that the entire world, from ether down to the body, has arisen from Brahman—which is non-different from the inner self—by way of being hidden in the cave of the heart; and subsequently, by the passage, "He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate,' He performed austerity; having performed austerity, He created all this, whatever exists here," [it is shown] of that same [Brahman].
The meaning is that Tittiri declares Brahman’s authorship of the world through His prior deliberation preceded by the desire to create the universe. || 1 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding the phrase *bahu syām* ("May I become many"): the meaning is that this is also recorded in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, which states: "He desired: 'May I be many; may I procreate. He performed austerity. Having performed austerity, he created all this, whatever exists here. Here, "austerity" (*tapas*) refers specifically to the contemplation of the karma of individual souls (*jīvas*) concerning the world about to be created—for him, austerity consists of knowledge (*jñānamayaṃ tapa*).
Such is the intention [of the author], based on another scriptural passage (śrutyantara). || 5 ||
In the Rāmatīrtha commentary, he states that even in the Chāndogya [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2], it is heard that Brahman alone is the creator of the world:
In the beginning, this was Being alone; then it thought unto itself for the sake of becoming many.
And the Sāma-singers declare that he creates fire, water, food, and beings born from eggs and so forth.
"This [is it]" refers to Brahman in the form of Being, devoid of a second, as stated in the passage: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second.
This is the fourth section.
Accompanied by the two commentaries, [page] 109:

Having proceeded [from the previous context], [the text continues] with "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and "It created fire," and so forth, [showing] that very [Brahman] preceded by such reflection (*īkṣaṇa*).

The meaning is that after describing [the Self's] status as the creator of fire, water, and food, the followers of the Sāmaveda describe its role as the fashioner of bodies such as those born from eggs and so forth, by means of the passage beginning with: "Of these beings, there are indeed only three seeds: the egg-born, the living-born, and the soil-born" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.3.1). ||6||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Regarding the phrase "this was in the beginning" (*idamagra*): having begun with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* records that [the Being] thought, "May I become many, may I procreate," and subsequently emitted fire, water, food, and the egg-born beings, and so forth; such is the meaning. || 6 ||
Just as sparks arise from a fire, so do they arise from the Imperishable.
"Various indeed are the sentient and insentient entities," so says the Atharvaṇa Śruti.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Even in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad, the origin of the world from Brahman—denoted by the term *akṣara* (the Imperishable)—is heard in the scripture: "Just as from a well-kindled fire sparks of the same nature fly forth by the thousands, even so, O gentle one, various beings are born from the Imperishable and into that very same [Imperishable] they enter" (Muṇḍaka 2.1.1). Thus he says: "Like sparks... (verse 7).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding the word *visphuliṅgāḥ* ("sparks"): "Just as from a well-kindled fire sparks arise by the thousands, similar in form [to the fire], even so, O gentle one, various beings are born from the Imperishable (*akṣara*), and into that very same [source] they also dissolve. Thus [says] the Atharvaṇa Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
It is heard in the Ḍākopaniṣad: || 7 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Thus, he states in two verses that even in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad it is heard that the world, consisting of name and form, arose from Brahman which is denoted by the term "undifferentiated" (avyākṛta): "The world was previously undifferentiated; now it is being differentiated."
Through the two visible factors, name and form, those [distinctions] are manifest in Virāṭ and the others.

Regarding the word "jagat" (the world): By the scriptural passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed unmanifest; it was then manifested by name and form, as 'He is such-and-such a name' and 'This is such-and-such a form'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7), the creation—characterized by the manifestation of name and form—is said to proceed from Brahman, which is denoted by the term "unmanifest" prior to creation and which has Māyā as its limiting adjunct (upādhi). Of those two, name and form, [the manifestation occurs] within gross effects such as Virāṭ and the rest.

And this clarity is expressed by the statement: "Even now, this very world is differentiated by name and form, as 'He is of such a name' and 'This is of such a form'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7). And those [entities] beginning with Virāj are shown by the passage starting from "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self, in the form of a person" and ending with "In this very way, he created everything that exists here, whatever has a pair, down to the ants" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1); such is the meaning. || 8 ||

Commentary on verse a0: Regarding the word "jagat" (the world), it is recited in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "In the beginning, this was indeed unmanifest; it was then manifested through name and form, as 'this one has such a name' and 'this one has such a form. || 8 ||
After a long time, Manu, humans, cattle, donkeys, horses, goats, and sheep [were produced].
The Vājasaneyins state that the pair [of opposites] ends with ants.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary—9.
[The text provided consists of two vertical bars (||), which in classical Indic scripts typically mark the end of a section or verse. [End of Section]

Commentary on verse 9: Regarding the term *virāṭ*—it means that this has been demonstrated in that very same [text], beginning with "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, in the form of a person" (*ātmaivedamagra āsītpuruṣavidhaḥ*) and ending with "In this very way, he created everything here, whatever exists as a pair, even down to the ants" (*evameva yadidaṃ kiṃca mithunamā pipīlikābhyastatsarvamasṛjata*). ||9||

Rāma’s Commentary: Following the description of the creation of duality by the scriptural citations just mentioned, he states that the Lord’s entry into that [creation] in the form of the individual soul (jīva) has also been declared:
"Having assumed another form—that of the individual soul—the Lord entered the body."
Thus those Śrutis declare that "living-ness" (jīvatva) arises from the maintenance of the vital breaths (prāṇa).
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 110.

[Having composed the commentary known as *Dvaitaviveka*—Rāghavaṭīkā: "Having made... means that the Śrutis [declare] the non-transient Brahman to be distinct from the *jainva*, which is another form related to the individual soul (*jīva*), a form characterized by modification.

To the question, "Why is there the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) within the body or the collection of bodies? he says: "The state of being a living soul... [This occurs] through being the master and impeller of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth.
Having thus maintained its vital breaths, it entered [the body] after assuming that form; so it has been said. || 10 ||
Commentary on Sūtra 1.1.1: Thus, [the texts state]: "Having pierced this very aperture, he entered by this door"; "Having created that, he entered it";
and "Entering by means of this very living self (jīva), he manifested names and forms"—such is the sequence.

He states that entry into the aforementioned bodies of Virāṭ and others has also been described by means of His own essential nature, which has attained connection with the individual soul (jīva) through well-known Vedic texts such as "Gāyatrī" and so on—thus he says: "Having done... Now, one might ask: "How can even the Lord possess the state of being a jīva? To this he replies: "The state of being a jīva... The meaning is: due to the superimposition of identity with the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra), which is characterized by the vital breaths (prāṇa). In this way, even the verbal root *jīv* (to live), meaning "the maintenance of the vital breaths," becomes consistent. || 10 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In response to the inquiry "What is that?", he says:
"That which is the substratum of consciousness, and furthermore, that which is the subtle body (liṅgadeha)."
The reflection of consciousness residing in the subtle body (liṅgadeha) and its aggregate is called the individual soul (jīva). || 11 ||

Regarding the term *caitanya*: the meaning is that the aggregate of these three—the consciousness (*caitanya*) which is the substrate and the basis for the conceptualization of the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*), the subtle body itself which is imagined therein, and the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) residing within that subtle body—is designated by the word "jīva. || 11 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) explains that very point: "Consciousness" (caitanya). "Reflection" (chāyā) means a reflected image (pratibimba). || 11 ||

Rāghava’s Commentary (rā0ṭī0): Now, one might ask: "If the Lord Himself has entered in the form of the individual soul (jīva), how can He possess contradictory attributes such as ignorance and suffering?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
But that which is the Māyā of Maheśvara is like his power of creative manifestation.
And the power of delusion exists; it deludes that living being.

Regarding the phrase "but the Māheśvarī": the Māheśvarī is that Māyā belonging to Maheśvara, which is mentioned in the Śruti, "But [He created] Maheśvara, the possessor of Māyā" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10). Just as that Māyā possesses the power of manifestation (*nirmāṇa-śakti*), meaning the capacity for the creation of the world, it also possesses the power of delusion (*moha-śakti*), meaning the capacity for causing bewilderment; for the Śruti states, "This [world] is insentient and consists of delusion" (Nṛsiṃha Upaniṣad Tātparya 9).

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "That [power] deludes the individual soul (jīva). This power of delusion (mohana-śakti) deludes that aforementioned individual soul, making it devoid of knowledge of its own true nature, such as consciousness and bliss. || 12 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, one might ask, "Even so, why is he ignorant? To this, he says: "Because she belongs to Maheśvara. || 12 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"Due to delusion, having attained a state of powerlessness, the mind grieves within the body."
This entire duality has been created; thus it has been explained in brief.

"Out of delusion" (mohāt) means: having attained a state of powerlessness regarding the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired due to the aforementioned delusion, one becomes immersed in the body—having fallen into the conceit of identity with the physical form—and grieves, meaning one assumes the conceit of being a sufferer and so forth. This is the meaning based on the Śruti: "On the same tree, the person is immersed and grieves, deluded by powerlessness" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.1.2). This will be explained further...
He concludes the section on conduct (*vṛtta*) in order to avoid confusion with the mental [discipline], beginning with the word "Īśa": "In brief" means concisely. || 13 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): "Precisely because of this delusion" means that he is submerged [in it], identifying with it. He concludes: "The Lord," etc. || 13 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection—"What is the proof for the individual soul (jīva) being the creator of duality?"—he says:
[Chapter Four]
Accompanied by two commentaries;
in the Saptānnabrāhmaṇa, duality created by the individual soul (jīva) is elaborated.
The Father produced the food-grains through the action of the sevenfold knowledge.

Regarding the phrase "from the sevenfold food": anticipating the question of how this is elaborated there, he summarizes in substance the statement—"The Father produced the seven foods by means of intelligence and austerity" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.1)—which establishes the creation of duality denoted by the term "sevenfold food."
"Annas" (foods) means the individual soul (jīva), which is the protector of all worlds by producing the universe through its own unseen merit (adṛṣṭa); this is the meaning. || 14 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Having thus established the duality created by Īśvara for the sake of explaining the discrimination (*viveka*) thereof, [the author], now reaching the occasion to speak of the duality of the individual soul (*jīva*), dispels the doubt regarding its lack of foundation with the words: "Of seven kinds of food" (*saptānnāt*). The meaning is: "In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka. While describing that method, he strings together the very words of that passage according to their sense: "Of seven kinds of food" (*annāni*). And thus it is recorded in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka: "That which [consists of] seven kinds of food through wisdom... (*yatsaptānnāni medhayā*).

"By means of austerity, the Father generated [them]. The meaning is that the "Father"—the collective soul (*samaṣṭijīva*) who, through the medium of his own unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), is the generator of the seven [worlds] to be described hereafter. || 14 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, one might ask for what purpose the creation of the sevenfold food was intended; anticipating this doubt, its specific application is also stated: "One part he made common to all, two he assigned to the gods, three he made for himself, and one he gave to animals" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.1).
Thus, one part is the food of mortals, two are the foods of the gods, and the fourth is the food of animals.
The other triad is for one's own sake, consisting of the distribution of food. || 15 ||
He says that it is stated by means of a sentence:
"The food of mortals. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "the application has been stated. || 15 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, he states its purpose and its classification with the words "Of mortals... The followers of the Kāṇva recension record: "One [portion] of it was common; two he assigned to the gods; three he made for himself; one he gave to the cattle. (15)
Rice and other grains, the new- and full-moon sacrifices, milk, and likewise the mind.
By this [verse], let it be understood that there are seven kinds of food, consisting of speech and vital breath. || 16 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: And those seven kinds of food are described by the passage beginning with, “One part of it is common;
this is that common food of his which is eaten here,” and continuing through, “This self consists of speech, consists of mind, and consists of breath.”
He states that these have been shown through a sequence of sentences in the form of two slightly incomplete sections: "vrīhyādikam" (beginning with rice), etc. || 16 ||

In response to the question of what their forms are, the author summarizes that form—which has been elaborated in the third Brāhmaṇa of the third Prapāṭhaka of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad itself, beginning from the section "One is common to all" up to the end of the third Kaṇḍikā, "consisting of mind" and "consisting of vital breath"—in the phrase "rice and so forth. Thus, rice and so forth are for mortals; the New and Full Moon sacrifices are for the gods; and milk is for animals.
Thus, the division of the seven types of food for the living being—consisting of speech, mind, breath, and the four elements—is established. || 16 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that since the seven kinds of food mentioned are included within the universe and were therefore created by the Lord (Īśvara), it is improper to say they were created by the individual soul (jīva). Anticipating this doubt, he says:

"Even though these were created by the Lord in their essential nature (svarūpataḥ)... [This implies that while their underlying substance was fashioned by God, their form as objects of experience was fashioned by the soul; thus, the objection does not hold.]
Nevertheless, through knowledge and action, the individual soul attained the state of being that food. (17)
"By Īśa" means by both knowledge and action. Knowledge refers to that which is enjoined and that which is prohibited;

action refers to enjoined forms such as sacrifice and prohibited forms such as violence. "The state of being their food" means that those beings, from rice and other grains up to living creatures, serve as the instruments for his own enjoyment. || 17 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, since all seven of these are included within the world, they must be created by the Lord according to the previously cited scriptural authority.
[The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya, titled *Dvaitaviveka*.

If it is argued that [the self] must be enveloped, that is true; nevertheless, according to the Śruti, "Knowledge and action, as well as prior experience, accompany him," [it follows] from knowledge and action...
He states that even by means of the individual soul (jīva), those [objects] are indeed created for the sake of the soul's own enjoyment, because it is their enjoyer: "By the Lord," [verse 17].
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question "What is meant by this?", he says:
"The world, which is the work of the Lord and the object of experience for the individual soul, is endowed with both."
Just as a woman belongs to her father and is to be enjoyed by her husband, so should this be understood. || 18 ||

Regarding the phrase "the work of the Lord": the meaning is that the world, described as consisting of seven kinds of food in the form of rice and so forth, is connected to two things—namely, being the work of the Lord and being the object of enjoyment for the individual soul (jīva).
To provide an illustration for one thing being related to both, he says: "born of the father... (18).

Commentary (a0): Now, one might object that it is illogical for one [the Lord] to be the creator of an object while another [the individual soul] must be its enjoyer. Anticipating this doubt, he says "by the Lord" (*īśena*), asserting that such a thing is indeed possible; therefore, it is not so [illogical]. The sense is this: although the Lord is the creator of the world by virtue of being the bestower of the fruits of the individual soul's karma and so forth, He is not an enjoyer because His desires are eternally fulfilled. However, for the individual soul, since it brings about those results through karma and the like, it is entirely logical that it be the enjoyer. In that regard:
The illustration is "the father," etc. || 18 ||
For the Lord’s volition, whose nature consists of the function of *māyā*, is the means for the birth of living beings.
The volition of the individual soul, consisting of mental activity, is the means for experience.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question, "What is the instrument for the Lord and the individual soul in the creation of the universe? he says: "Māyā... (verse 19).

Commentary (a0): Now, in response to the inquiry—"What is the means by which the Lord and the individual soul create the world, respectively for the purpose of bestowing the fruits of karma and for their own enjoyment?"—he says: "Māyā" (verse 19).

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Apart from the essential nature of an object created by the Lord, there is no separate aspect of 'being an object of enjoyment' (bhogyatva); what, then, is created by the individual soul (jīva)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"While an object such as a gem, fashioned by the Lord, remains uniform in its nature..."
Due to the multiplicity of the mental modifications of the experiencer, its experience is held to be manifold. || 20 ||

Regarding the phrase "created by a lord" (*īśanirmita*): the meaning is that the manifold enjoyment perceived with respect to a single object implies a corresponding diversity in the form of the object of experience (*bhogya*) which serves as its cause. || 20 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "If there were some object created by the individual soul (*jīva*) that was distinct from the nature of things created by God, and if that were the form of the object of experience (*bhogya*), then the hypothesis of the soul's creatorship might be plausible. However, we do not perceive such a thing. Anticipating this doubt, he demonstrates it [the existence of such an object] with the verse beginning with *īśa*. (20)

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If there were a difference in experience, then a difference in the objects of experience could be postulated; however, that very difference does not exist.
Anticipating this, he says, "It is not so, because it is actually perceived":
"One rejoices upon obtaining a jewel, while another indeed becomes angry due to its non-acquisition."
Seeing this very [world], the dispassionate one neither rejoices nor becomes angry. || 21 ||
"He rejoices" means this: one person desiring a jewel, having obtained it, rejoices; another, likewise desiring it, becomes angry because of not obtaining it.
But one who is detached from the object—the jewel—does not even perceive that jewel, and thus does not experience the joy and anger caused by gain and loss. This is the meaning. ||21||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): To the question "How is there an abundance of enjoyment?", he says: "He rejoices," etc. By this, the effects of the Asura, Rākṣasa, and Daiva natures—consisting of the qualities of Rajas, Tamas, and Sattva respectively—are illuminated. || 21 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question, "What are those various forms created by the individual soul (jīva) that are colored by the distinctions of enjoyment?", he says:
[Page 113] Fourth Section.
Accompanied by the two commentaries:
"The beloved, the unloved, and the indifferent— these are the three forms residing in the jewel."
Created by living beings, the form created by the Lord is common to all three.

Regarding the word "dear" (*priya*): the specific forms characterized as being dear, not dear, or indifferent, which reside in the gems and are created by individual souls (*jīva*), are superimposed upon that form of the gem which is common to all three and permeates them; that [common form] is fashioned by the Lord (*īśvara*). This is the meaning. || 22 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Granted that there may be a distinction in the effects such as joy produced by gain and so forth, nevertheless, there is certainly no distinction in the underlying reality.
To this, he says, "The beloved," etc., [verse 22], stating that such an objection is not valid because it is actually observed.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He clarifies the aforementioned distinctions in the forms created by the individual soul through another illustration:
"She is a wife, a daughter-in-law, a sister-in-law, a mother-in-law, a mother—thus in many ways."
A woman is distinguished by the cognition of her counter-correlate, not by her own essential nature.

Regarding the term "wife" (*bhāryā*): the sister-in-law (*nanāndā*) is the husband’s sister; the wife of the brother-in-law (*yātā*) is so called by way of a correlative cognition—that is, a cognition directed toward correlates such as the husband’s father-in-law and so forth—with respect to each respective correlate. || 23 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): To strengthen that point, he provides another example, beginning with "bhāryā" (wife). *Nanāndā* is the husband’s sister; *yātā* is the wife of the husband’s younger brother. || 23 ||
Surely, let the cognitions be distinct, but the form is not distinct.
No such excellence has ever been seen in a female form created by the Creator. || 24 ||

Rāma’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Indeed, while distinct cognitions such as 'wife,' 'daughter-in-law,' and so forth, which have a woman as their object, are indeed perceived, no difference is seen in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the woman who is the object of those cognitions. Therefore, the statement that 'the woman is differentiated by the cognition of her correlates' is untenable. Thus he raises the objection with the words "nanu" (now, [one might object]). || 24 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): He raises an objection once more with the words "nanu" (but surely). || 24 ||
Let it not be so; there is no woman composed of flesh, but another who is composed of mind.
For although the body made of flesh is not divided, the one made of mind is indeed divided.
Rāma’s Commentary: Since the distinctness of knowledge is invariably concomitant with the distinctness of the object of knowledge, one must certainly accept a difference in the forms of the objects;
with this intention, he offers the following rebuttal: "Not so. (29)
The commentary resolves this by stating, "Not so. The reason for this is given in the passage beginning with "māṃsa" (flesh).

The phrase "some other [body]" is also connected to the term "consisting of mind" (*manomayī*) by way of the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣigolakanyāya*). To the question "What follows from that?", he replies with "māṃsa," etc.; here, the particle *hi* indicates the reason.

Otherwise, there would be no distinction at all between the words, cognitions, and linguistic usages such as "wife" and so forth. Therefore, the essential point is that one must necessarily accept that the various mental women (manomayī yoṣit) imagined through the respective perceptions of living beings are indeed distinct from one another. || 25 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "In cases such as error and the like, since there is an absence of external objects, let the object therein be composed of the mind; however, in the case of valid cognition, that is untenable because the external object exists. To this he replies:
"Let it be composed of the mind in the cases of error, dream, mental construction, and memory."
If it is argued that the object of measurement is not composed of mind according to the measure of the waking state; || 26 ||

Regarding the word "bhrānti" (error): it means that by means of *māna*, i.e., by means of the instruments of knowledge such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, [there is no error] with respect to the *meya*, i.e., the object of knowledge (*prameya*). || 26 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on a0: Again, he raises an objection with the words "bhrānti" (error). Regarding "jāgrat" (waking): the meaning is "by means of the empirical instruments of knowledge such as perception that occur during the waking state. || 26 ||

The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya [the commentary by Rāma called *Dvaitaviveka* states regarding the locus of valid cognition (*pramiti-sthala*) that one accepts the existence of external objects]:
Indeed, if there were a real measure, it would take on the form of the object through its connection with that which is to be measured.
This meaning has been declared by both the author of the Bhāṣya and the author of the Vārttika. || 27 ||
"Certainly. But how, then, is the mind-made nature (*manomayatva*) of that object stated? To this he says: "But in the case of manifestation" (*bhāne tu*).

In the case of manifestation, the appearance in the form of the object would arise from its connection—that is, its relation—with the object of cognition (*meyena*). Lest one should suspect that this is merely a fabrication of one's own imagination, he says: "According to the Bhāṣya. (27)

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Even within the realm of empirical means and objects of knowledge (*vyāvahārika-pramāṇa-prameya*), there certainly exists another entity called "cognition" (*pramiti*) consisting of the mind.

Otherwise, how could there be a cognition in the form of the consciousness delimited by the object—the jar—which is defined by the consciousness delimited by the internal organ's modification (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) that has reached as far as the jar through the eye aided by light—[a cognition] which is denoted by the term "means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*) and [results in] the form of the consciousness delimited by the jar, the object of knowledge (*prameya*)? Without such a cognition, ignorance (*ajñāna*) in the form of the cause regarding that object would not cease.

With the intention that the valid cognition (*pramā*) residing in a portion of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) pervading the body itself should not perish as a single unit, he provides the resolution: "Certainly" (*bāḍham*). The word "intellect" (*buddhiḥ*) is to be supplied [to complete the sentence]. Now, one might object: "In cases such as error (*bhrānti*), let it be granted that the object consists of the mind (*manomaya*) because of the absence of an external object; however, even when an external object established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exists, to again accept an object consisting of the mind is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhīvāda*) and is indeed contrary to tradition. He dispels this doubt:
"Having spoken thus," [he said]. || 27 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: In that regard, he first cites the words of the author of the Bhāṣya:
"Just as copper poured into a crucible becomes like it, so too [is the soul]."
The mind, pervading form and the other [objects], is certainly seen as resembling them. || 28 ||

"Like a mold (mūṣā)": just as molten copper poured into a mold takes on its likeness—that is, becomes identical in form to it—so too the mind, pervading and taking as its object the sense-objects such as visible forms, certainly and necessarily appears in their likeness; this means it is perceived as such. || 28 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): At the outset, he cites two statements from the venerable Bhāṣyakāra found in the *Upadeśasāhasrī*, beginning with the word "sūpa" and so forth. A *sūpa* is well known as a specific kind of vessel made of clay, coated with honey and molasses, used for the purpose of preparing medicinal substances (*dhātu*), images (*mūrti*), and the like. Copper sprinkled [with mercury] therein—this is an illustration that includes gold and other metals—is indeed the supreme...

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: just as that which is called "water" (*ūpa*), when melted by contact with a blazing fire, certainly becomes similar to it and takes on its very form upon contact with a solid substance;
so too, the mind, when reaching objects such as forms (*rūpa*) and so forth, is certainly seen to become similar to them and take on their very form. || 28 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection may be raised: "In the case of copper and other metals, when they have been melted through contact with fire and poured into a crucible, they assume the shape of the crucible upon cooling due to the impact of the hard mold; however, since the intellect is formless and distinct from copper and such substances, how can it assume their form even when pervading the objects?
Anticipating this doubt, he states another illustration:
Or, just as a lamp, which is the manifestor, may take on the form of that which it manifests.
Because it manifests all objects, cognition appears as having the form of the object. (29)

Regarding the term "manifestor" (*vyañjaka*): just as a manifestor, such as light or sunlight, which illuminates, would attain—that is, assume—the form, that is, the possession of form, of the manifested object, such as a jar; in the same way, cognition (*dhī*) also, because it is a manifestor of all objects and because it illuminates all things, appears—that is, is perceived—to possess the form of the object, meaning its form is like the form of the object itself. (29)
Commentary (a0): Now, one might object that while it is possible for a material substance such as copper to take the form of the mold, it is inappropriate for the immaterial mind to do so;

anticipating this objection, the author clarifies the point with another illustration: "Or like a manifester... (*vyañjako vā*). "Manifester" (*vyañjaka*) means that which illuminates. The word "light" (*āloka*) is to be understood as a separate term. "Of the manifested" (*vyaṅgyasya*) means of that which is to be illuminated. || 29 ||
The Fourth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now he states the words of the author of the Vārttika:
"The production of the means of knowledge from the knower proceeds toward the object of knowledge once it has been produced."
And that [consciousness], being conjoined with the object of cognition, attains the appearance of the object of cognition. || 30 ||

Regarding the word "of the mother" (*mātuḥ*): from the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), who is the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) residing within the intellect (*buddhi*) together with its substratum (*sādhiṣṭhāna*), there occurs the "accomplishment of the means of knowledge" (*mānābhiniṣpatti*). The remainder of the sense is that the accomplishment—that is, the arising—of the means of knowledge, which consists of a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) accompanied by a manifestation (*sābhāsa*), takes place. Once that means of knowledge has been accomplished—that is, once it has arisen—the object of knowledge (*meyam*), such as a jar, [is manifested].

It "assumes that form," meaning it attains it. Furthermore, what is that? That means [the cognition], being conjoined with—that is, connected to—the object of knowledge (*meyena*), becomes "resembling the object of knowledge" (*meyābham*).

Its state of being so—namely, the fact that its appearance (*ābhā*) is like the appearance of the object of knowledge—is its "having the same form as the object of knowledge" (*meyasamānākāratvam*); the meaning is that it attains or reaches that state. || 30 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) thus cites the Vārtika as well: "From the mother," which means from the knower (*pramātṛ*). "Of the means" (*māna*); the connection is that the production of the aforementioned means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) occurs. To the question "What follows from that?", it says: "Having come into being," and so forth. That is, the means of knowledge characterized as previously described approaches—that is, reaches—the object of knowledge (*prameya*) characterized by its connection with the object. To the question "What follows from that too?", it says:
"Me" and so forth. || 30 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Let it be so; what follows from this in the present context? To this he says:
"In this way, there are two kinds of objects: those made of clay and those made of cognition."
That which consists of clay is to be measured by a means of knowledge; however, that which consists of intellect is to be manifested by the witness-consciousness.

"Even so," [it may be argued]. Now, one might object: "Just as a clay pot cannot be perceived by that very same clay, so too a pot made of mind (manomaya) cannot be grasped by that very mind; and since there is no other perceiver, its existence is unproven. Anticipating this, he states—beginning with "mṛnmaya"—that the absence of another perceiver is unproven. The meaning is: just as the clay [pot] is both the means of knowledge (māna) and the object of knowledge (meyya), so too the mental [pot] is illumined by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin). || 31 ||
The commentary on the aphorism states the conclusion: "This being so," etc. But the other [method] is indeed straightforward. || 31 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that "let it be so; however, it is not known which of these two kinds of duality is to be abandoned and which is not," he states, intending to show that only that created by the individual soul (jīva) is to be abandoned, that it is the cause of bondage:
"Through positive and negative concomitance, the intellect-based [duality] is the cause of the individual soul's bondage."
When this [self] exists, pleasure and pain exist; when it does not exist, the duality does not exist. || 32 ||

Regarding the term *anvaya*: he demonstrates positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) itself with the words "when this exists" (*asmin sati*). When this mental manifold created by the living being (*jīva*) exists—that is, while it is present—pleasure and pain exist; but when that [manifold] is absent, the pair—pleasure and pain—does not exist.
This is the meaning. || 32 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Granted that the object consisting of the intellect (*dhīmaya*) is manifest to the witness because it is mental—just like error and so forth—but what about the subject under discussion? To this he says: "Anvaya" (concomitance). The meaning is that these two—namely, the existence of bondage when the object consisting of the intellect exists during waking and dreaming, and the absence of bondage when that is absent during deep sleep and meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—are indeed well-established facts. But [one may ask]: "Is not liberation the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), and is that [ignorance] not bondage? [The text continues: ...is declared to be bondage. Thus, since the cessation of ignorance is liberation, its presence constitutes bondage. Therefore, the existence of the object consisting of the intellect is established as the cause of bondage. Consequently, the statement that the Self is not an object is not contradicted by the fact that the object consisting of the intellect is manifest to the witness. This is the sense. Furthermore, the object consisting of the intellect is not the Self; rather, it is the reflection of the Self within the intellect. And since that reflection is non-different from the Self, it is said to be "manifest to the witness. However, the reflection is not the Self, for the Self is consciousness alone, whereas the reflection is insentient. Moreover, the reflection is not the witness, for the witness is the seer, while the reflection is the seen. Nor is the reflection the intellect, for the intellect is the instrument of seeing, while the reflection is the object seen. Therefore, the reflection is neither the Self, nor the witness, nor the intellect. What then is it? It is the appearance (*pratibhāsa*) of the Self within the intellect. And since that appearance is non-different from the Self, it is said to be "manifest to the witness. Yet, the appearance is not the Self, for the Self is consciousness alone, while the appearance is insentient. Furthermore, the appearance is not the witness, for the witness is the seer, while the appearance is the seen. Nor is the appearance the intellect, for the intellect is the instrument of seeing, while the appearance is the object seen. Therefore, the appearance is neither the Self, nor the witness, nor the intellect. What then is it? It is the manifestation (*avabhāsa*) of the Self within the intellect. And since that manifestation is non-different from the Self, it is said to be "manifest to the witness. However, the manifestation is not the Self, for the Self is consciousness alone, while the manifestation is insentient. Moreover, the manifestation is not the witness, for the witness is the seer, while the manifestation is the seen. Nor is the manifestation the intellect, for the intellect is the instrument of seeing, while the manifestation is the object seen. Therefore, the manifestation is neither the Self, nor the witness, nor the intellect. What then is it? It is the perception (*upalabdhi*) of the Self within the intellect. And since that perception is non-different from the Self, it is said to be "manifest to the witness. But the perception is not the Self, for the Self is consciousness alone, while the perception is insentient. Furthermore, the perception is not the witness, for the witness is the seer, while the perception is the seen. Nor is the perception the intellect, for the intellect is the instrument of seeing, while the perception is the object seen. Therefore, the perception is neither the Self, nor the witness, nor the intellect. What then is it? It is the cognition (*vijñapti*) of the Self within the intellect. And since that cognition is non-different from the Self, it is said to be "manifest to the witness. However, the cognition is not the Self, for the Self is consciousness alone, while the cognition is insentient. Moreover, the cognition is not the witness, for the witness is the seer, while the cognition is the seen. Nor is the cognition the intellect, for the intellect is the instrument of seeing, while the cognition is the object seen. Therefore, the cognition is neither the Self, nor the witness, nor the intellect. What then is it? It is the experience (*anubhava*) of the Self within the intellect. And since that experience is non-different from the Self, it is said to be "manifest to the witness. But the experience is not the Self, for the Self is consciousness alone, while the experience is insentient. Furthermore, the experience is not the witness, for the witness is the seer, while the experience is the seen. Nor is the experience the intellect, for the intellect is the instrument of seeing, while the experience is the object seen. Therefore, the experience is neither the Self, nor the witness, nor the intellect. What then is it? It is the realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the Self within the intellect. And since that realization is non-different from the Self, it is said to be "manifest to the witness. However, the realization is not the Self, for the Self is consciousness alone, while the realization is insentient. Moreover, the realization is not the witness, for the witness is the seer, while the realization is the seen. Nor is the realization the intellect, for the intellect is the instrument of seeing, while the realization is the object seen. Therefore, the realization is neither the Self, nor the witness, nor the intellect. What then is it? It is the self-luminous nature (*svaprakāśatva*) of the Self within the intellect. And since that self-luminosity is non-different from the Self, it is said to be "manifest to the witness. But self-luminosity is not the Self, for the Self is consciousness alone, while self-luminosity is a property. Furthermore, self-luminosity is not the witness, for the witness is the seer, while self-luminosity is the state of being seen. Nor is self-luminosity the intellect, for the intellect is the instrument of seeing, while self-luminosity is the object seen. Therefore, self-luminosity is neither the Self, nor the witness, nor the intellect. What then is it? It is the very essence (*svarūpa*) of the Self within the intellect. And since that essence is non-different from the Self, it is said to be "manifest to the witness. However, the essence is not the Self, for the Self is consciousness alone, while the essence is a substrate. Moreover, the essence is not the witness, for the witness is the seer, while the essence is the seen. Nor is the essence the intellect, for the intellect is the instrument of seeing, while the essence is the object seen. Therefore, the essence is neither the Self, nor the witness, nor the intellect. What then is it? It is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the Self within the intellect. And since that reality is non-different from the Self, it is said to be "manifest to the witness. But the reality is not the Self, for the Self is consciousness alone, while the reality is an ontological status. Furthermore, the reality is not the witness, for the witness is the seer, while the reality is the seen. Nor is the reality the intellect, for the intellect is the instrument of seeing, while the reality is the object seen. Therefore, the reality is neither the Self, nor the witness, nor the intellect. What then is it? It is the absolute non-duality (*advaita*) of the Self within the intellect. And since that non-duality is non-different from the Self, it is said to be "manifest to the witness. However, non-duality is not the Self, for the Self is consciousness alone, while non-duality is a relation. Moreover, non-duality is not the witness, for the witness is the seer, while non-duality is the seen. Nor is non-duality the intellect, for the intellect is the instrument of seeing, while non-duality is the object seen. Therefore, non-duality is neither the Self, nor the witness, nor the intellect. What then is it? It is the pure, unconditioned Self (*kevala-nirupādhika-ātman*) within the intellect. And since that pure Self is non-different from the Self, it is said to be "manifest to the witness. But the pure Self is not the Self, for the Self is consciousness alone, while the pure Self is a state of liberation. Furthermore, the pure Self is not the witness, for the witness is the seer, while the pure Self is the seen. Nor is the pure Self the intellect, for the intellect is the instrument of seeing, while the pure Self is the object seen. Therefore, the pure Self is neither the Self, nor the witness, nor the intellect. What then is it? It is the final cessation (*nivṛtti*) of all objects within the intellect. And since that cessation is non-different from the Self, it is said to be "manifest to the witness. However, the cessation is not the Self, for the Self is consciousness alone, while the cessation is an absence. Moreover, the cessation is not the witness, for the witness is the seer, while the cessation is the seen. Nor is the cessation the intellect, for the intellect is the instrument of seeing, while the cessation is the object seen. Therefore, the cessation is neither the Self, nor the witness, nor the intellect. What then is it? It is the supreme peace

If it is argued that, based on the words of the venerable Vārtikācārya, "He is taken away" (*hṛtaḥ*), bondage exists precisely when fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) exists even during deep sleep and so forth, whereas in its absence there is an absence of bondage even during the waking state and so forth—and thus the stated positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are indeed untenable—this is true. Nevertheless, even though that is the case in reality, what is intended here is that the absence of bondage consists specifically in the dissolution of the mental objects that yield pleasure and pain, even after the destruction of fundamental ignorance. [The soul...]

Since it will be stated later in the very same way that "the supreme limit of liberation [is attained] through the abandonment of the duality of the individual soul," and because in its absence there would be no liberation while living even after the destruction of ignorance, he says with this intention: "While this exists" (satyasmin). || 32 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: "Why could the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) not have external objects as their domain? To this, he says:
From the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
titled "Discrimination between Duality" (*Dvaitaviveka*):
"And even though external objects do not exist, a person is bound in dreams and similar states."
Even when this [mind] exists during states of meditative absorption, sleep, or fainting, it is not bound. || 33 ||

"Even when it is non-existent": a person—that is, a human being (this being an illustration for others as well)—is bound by pleasure and pain, meaning he is joined with them, even though the external object is unreal and non-existent, such as a woman who is favorable [to him] or a tiger who is unfavorable, during the time of dreams, recollections of dreams, and so forth; however, in meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) and the like, he is not bound and does not become a partaker of pleasure, pain, and so on, even though this external object is real.
Thus, the meaning is that positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) do not exist with respect to that [object]. || 33 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Even so, let it be that the external object alone provides pleasure and the like; what is the use of an internal mental state (dhīmaya), since that [external object] suffices?
To this, he says: "And even when non-existent... The meaning is that pleasure and the like are bound—that is, experienced—[by the mind]. || 33 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He clarifies, through an illustration, the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the mental world as being the cause of bondage:
"Even while his son has gone to a distant land, the father remains here alive."
Having thought him dead because of the deceptive words [of the messenger], she weeps aloud.

Regarding the phrase "to a distant land": when a son has reached another country and is indeed still living there, his father, remaining here in his own home, imagines his son to be dead due to the deceptive and false words of a fraudster—one who deceives others—such as the statement, "Your son is dead," and consequently weeps excessively. || 34 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) on verse a explains that very point through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) by means of the two verses beginning with "dūradeśam":
"A *vipralambhaka* is a deceiver. || 34 ||
Even when he has died, she does not weep as long as news of it has not been heard.
Therefore, for every living being, the world is a mental construct that creates bondage.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (rā0 ṭī0): Even though that very son has died right there, as long as the news of his death has not been heard, one does not weep. He states the conclusion with the words "ataḥ" (therefore). || 35 ||
Commentary on verse a0: Regarding the phrase "even when dead," he states the conclusion: "Therefore... (verse 35).

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He raises an objection, fearing that if one accepts that the world consisting of intellect alone is the cause of bondage, it would result in the fallacy of an apasiddhānta (a deviation from established doctrine) due to the denial of external objects.
If it is argued that the doctrine of consciousness-only (vijñānavāda) must stand because external objects are useless;
For it is not possible to establish a form within the heart, because of the necessity of depending upon something external. || 36 ||

Regarding the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*): although it is indeed the mental proliferation alone that serves as the cause of bondage, nevertheless, because external objects are also accepted as being the cause of that [proliferation], there is no undesirable consequence of falling into the position of Vijñānavāda (Idealism). This is the intended meaning. || 36 ||
In that regard, he raises an objection with the words "vijñāna" (consciousness). He provides the resolution with "no. [The term] "hṛdi" means in the mind (citta). || 36 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Indeed, an external object need not be required to provide the form within the mind, since it is established that the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of preceding mental manifestations alone serve as the cause for subsequent mental manifestations. Anticipating this, he accepts [the position] by way of a bold argument (*prauḍhavāda*):
"Or let there be the uselessness of the external; we are not able to prevent it."
For it is an established principle that means of valid cognition do not depend upon a purpose. || 37 ||

"Uselessness. If that is so, what is the difference from the Vijñānavāda? To this he says: "External. The meaning is that the difference lies in this alone: the Vijñānavādins deny the external object itself, whereas we do not; thus, because it is devoid of purpose, even the acceptance [of such a position] is improper.
The Fourth Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "The purpose. The meaning is that the establishment of a thing depends upon the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), not upon its purpose;
for neither common people nor disputants admit that something established by a means of valid cognition could be non-existent merely on account of being devoid of a purpose. || 37 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Since the transformation of the mind into the form of an object could occur solely through preceding latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and so forth, what would be the use of an external object? Anticipating this objection, he establishes that external object by another method, stating "futility" (*vaiyarthyam*). The sense is that even without a specific purpose, cognitions such as those of grass and the like occur; therefore, means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not depend upon a purpose. || 37 ||
If bondage is the duality of the mind, it is pacified by the obstruction of that [dualistic] cognition.
Therefore, one should practice yoga alone; tell me, what is the use of knowledge of Brahman? (38)

Rāmānuja’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): He raises an objection, [asking]: "If bondage... (38). [The objection is: If mental duality alone is the cause of bondage, then since its cessation would be possible through yoga—which consists of the restraint of the mind—the acceptance that the knowledge of Brahman is what removes bondage would be contradicted.
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Again, he raises an objection: "baṃdhavā" (by bondage). || 38 ||
Rāma’s Commentary — Having raised the alternative as to whether the cessation of duality through yoga is said to be merely temporary or absolute,
and having accepted the first, he refutes the second:
Even when duality is momentarily stilled, there is the destruction of future births.
"Without the knowledge of Brahman, [liberation] would not exist"—this is the proclamation of the Vedānta drum. (39)
Regarding the term *tātkālikī* (occurring at that very moment): "Knowing God, one is released from all fetters" [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.8;

2.12–13]; "Having known Śiva, one attains ultimate peace" [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.14]; "When men shall roll up space like a piece of leather, then, without having known God, there will be an end to suffering" [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.20]. Thus...

The sense is that, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) in the scriptural texts, it is declared that the cessation of bondage occurs solely from the knowledge of Brahman. || 39 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) resolves [the objection] by partially accepting [the point]: "tātkālika... (momentary), etc. || 39 ||
Even though the duality created by the Lord has not yet ceased, its nature is false.
Having realized non-dual Brahman, it is possible for one who asserts the oneness of reality to understand [all things]. || 40 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that without the removal of external duality, the knowledge of non-dual Brahman simply cannot arise.

Anticipating this, he states—beginning with "Even though not removed"—that even in the absence of such removal, the ultimate non-duality can be understood through the mere knowledge of its falsity. || 40 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on Verse 40: Now, one might object: "Without the cessation of external duality, the knowledge of non-dual Brahman itself is impossible, because that [duality] acts as its obstruction.

Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it with the words "anivṛtte’pi" (even when not ceased), for since the falsity of that [duality] is realized, it cannot act as an obstruction; moreover, this is observed to be exactly so in the case of Devadatta and others situated within a house containing a mirror. Thus, it is not so. || 40 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To counter the insistence that it is not the knowledge of the falsity of duality that causes the realization of non-duality, but rather its cessation itself, he says:
"But upon its cessation at the time of dissolution, [realization would not occur] due to the absence of the teacher, the scriptures, and so forth."
Even in the absence of dualistic opposition, it is not possible to realize non-duality.

Regarding the word "malaya": it means in the state of dissolution (*pralaya*), that is, when there is the cessation of that duality; however, Acyutarāya reads the text as "even in the non-appearance of non-duality" (*advaitābhāne 'pi*).
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
titled "Discrimination between Duality" (Dvaitaviveka).

The sense is this: even if duality—which you maintain to be an obstacle to non-dual knowledge—is removed despite the absence of obstructive duality, the non-dual reality cannot be understood because of the absence of the means for knowledge, namely the teacher, the scriptures, and so forth; therefore, the removal of that [obstructive] duality is ineffective. || 41 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): To one who is excessively attached to the very destruction of duality, he cites an instance of deviation [from the rule], saying "in dissolution" (pralaye).
The intention is that this is an illustration by implication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and other such states as well. || 41 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Nevertheless, raising the objection as to how non-dual knowledge can arise when duality exists, he says:
"The duality created by the Lord is neither subverting nor establishing [of non-duality]."
And since it is impossible to remove [it], let that be; from where could it possibly exist? || 42 ||

"Non-sublating" (avādhakam): The duality created by Īśvara is non-sublating, because it has been stated that the knowledge of non-duality arises precisely through the knowledge of its falsity; furthermore, it is a means of realization (*sādhaka*) because it serves as an instrument for knowledge in the form of the Guru, the scriptures, and so forth. Since duality in the form of space and such cannot be removed by us, the meaning is:
let that duality remain; for what reason should it be rejected? || 42 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) states the conclusion: "It is non-sublating" (avādhakam). Because it does not obstruct the realization of non-dual Brahman through its own realization of falsity, it is non-sublating therein; yet, because it produces that [realization] in the form of the Guru, the scriptures, and so forth, it is also a means of accomplishment (sādhaka)—this is the truth.

Furthermore, since it was created by the Lord in this manner, it can be removed only by Him and not by the individual soul (jīva); therefore, he says, "to remove," that penance is indeed improper. || 42 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, he classifies the duality of the individual soul (jīva):
"The duality of the individual soul is twofold: scriptural and non-scriptural."
One should adopt that which is scriptural for the sake of awakening to reality. || 43 ||

"Live," he says. Is both of these always to be abandoned? No; he says, "one should adopt. This means until the realization of reality—that is, up to the point of attaining the knowledge of reality. || 43 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on verse a0: Now, one might ask: "Just as the duality created by the Lord—consisting of the Guru, the scriptures, and so forth—is useful for the knowledge of Brahman, is there likewise some duality created by the individual soul (jīva) that serves that purpose, or not? To resolve this doubt, he analyzes it with the words "But the duality of the jīva" (jīvadvaitaṃ tu).
The word "but" (tu) is intended to distinguish it from the former [divine] duality. What follows from that? He says: "One should accept... (upādadīta). || 43 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In response to the inquiry as to what that scriptural duality is, he says:
"The scriptural mental world is known as the inquiry into the Self and Brahman."
"That reality is to be abandoned in the Buddha"—this is the instruction of the Śruti. (44)

Regarding the term *ātman*: the meaning is that the scriptural mental activity consisting of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth—which is called inquiry (*vicāra*)—concerning Brahman in its immediate form, constitutes the world. An objection is raised: "The statement [in verse 17] that [the world exists] 'until the realization of reality' is untenable, because it has been said [in verse 18]: 'One should spend the time from sleep until death in reflection on Vedānta. Anticipating this, he says: *buddhe*. This means: when reality—characterized by the identity of Brahman and the Self—has been realized, that is, directly perceived.

If it is asked, "What then is the interpretation of the statement 'therefore, because there is no sleep'? we reply that its purpose is precisely that, because the first half of the verse—“One should not grant even the slightest opportunity for desire and the like”—prohibits the granting of any occasion for desire and so forth. Thus, the sense is that there is no inconsistency whatsoever. || 44 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, it may be granted that although the duality of the living self (*jīvadvaita*) is twofold—distinguished as scriptural and so forth—the scriptural variety is indeed to be adopted until the direct realization of reality (*ātattvasākṣātkāra*). Nevertheless, in response to the inquiry as to what its actual nature is, he says: "The Self" (*ātmeti*). By this, the referent of the term *tvam* (the individual soul) and the referent of the term *tat* (Brahman) have been stated in succession; and the investigation (*vicāra*) of these two consists of the mental activity characterized previously by the triad of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the rest.
The Fourth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

The meaning is that it is called "Stada" (the giver). Now, one might object: "Let that [state] continue even after direct realization; let him not give even the slightest opportunity for desire and the like, and let him spend his time from sleep until death in the contemplation of Vedanta. If this is argued, we say no, because it contradicts the scripture to be cited later, which shows that the aforementioned statement regarding the non-opportunity for desire and so forth—

He says "Buddhe" (when awakened) because the purport lies precisely in renunciation; the meaning is that in reality, there is the oneness of Brahman and the Self, preceded by the falsity of the visible world.
"When awakened" means when [the truth] has been unimpededly realized as immediate. || 44 ||
Having studied the treatises and having practiced them again and again, the wise man...
Having realized the Supreme Brahman, one should cast those [other things] aside like a firebrand.
Rāma’s Commentary: Beginning with the words "The scriptures," he cites the Śruti texts intended to demonstrate that [the Self] is to be abandoned after the realization of truth has occurred. || 45 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): In response to the inquiry as to which scriptures speak thus, [the author] recites those very passages from the two types of Amṛtabindu and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣads, beginning with "Having studied the scriptures... and so forth. The meaning is: like a firebrand, that is, like a piece of wood burning [at one end]. ||45||
Having studied the scripture, the wise person should be devoted to knowledge and higher realization.
One who seeks grain should discard the straw entirely; likewise, one should abandon the knot of worldly attachment without remainder.
Rāma’s Commentary—verse 46.
Commentary on verse a0: "The book" (grantham) refers to the straw (palālam), which is the chaff (tupam). || 46 ||
Having understood that very [Self], the wise Brahmin should practice wisdom.
One should not meditate on many words, for that is a weariness of speech.
Rāma’s Commentary—verse 47.
Commentary on verse a0: "Tameva" means precisely the non-dual Self. || 47 ||
Know Him alone as the One; indeed, abandon all other words.
The scriptural passages beginning with "A wise man should restrain his speech" are clear [on this point]. (48)

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: By the verse beginning with "Know Him alone as one" (tamevaikaṃ vijānītha), the Śruti passage—"Know Him alone as the Self; abandon other words"—(Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.5) and "He is the bridge to immortality"—(Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.9) is cited according to their meaning. || 48 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, he cites the *Muṇḍaka* Śruti—"Know that very One alone as the Self; abandon other words"—as corroborative evidence for this stated meaning, saying "tamevaikam" (that very one). The purport is that, in this way, at all times, the contemplation of the non-dual Self alone is to be enjoined, and not any other collection of activities whatsoever. Similarly, he recites the passage from the *Kaṭhavallī*: "One should restrain speech... and so forth. Ya—

The meaning is that one should suppress [the breath] by cutting it off. He concludes with the words "and so forth.
