By the word "etcetera," one should understand the very passage from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad which follows the statement "Having known this very thing, one becomes a sage," and which enjoins solely the contemplation of the identity of Brahman and the Self, preceded by the renunciation of the knower (vidvatsaṃnyāsa). || 48 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the internal subdivisions of non-scriptural duality as well:
"Non-scriptural duality is also of two kinds: intense and mild."
Intense passion, anger, and the like, as well as other forms of mental ideation (manorājya). || 49 ||
1 [Amṛtabindūpaniṣad 1] 2 [Brahmabindūpaniṣad 18] 3 [Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad 4.4.21] [page 120–120] 120

The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya, titled *Dvaitaviveka*, states that [the other] is unscriptural. He provides two examples of the twofold [nature] in sequence, beginning with "kāma": the meaning is that the other is inferior. ||49||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, he states that this non-scriptural duality imagined by the individual soul (*jīva*) exists in two forms according to the distinction of "intense" (*tīvra*) and so forth—namely, "even that which is non-scriptural" (*aśāstrīyamapi*). To the question of what its characteristics are, he says: "desire" (*kāma*), etc. (Verse 49).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: One might ask: "Are these two to be abandoned only after the realization of truth, as is the case with scriptural duality? To this he says:
"Both must be discarded prior to the realization of truth for the sake of achieving that realization."
For tranquility and concentration are heard [taught] among the means of accomplishment. || 50 ||

Regarding the phrase "both": to the question "For what purpose is the warding off of the senses [mentioned] first?", he says, "for the sake of attaining awakening" (*bodhasiddhaye*). He provides the reason for this:

"tranquility" (*śama*). Since those two [the senses and their objects] are to be abandoned prior to the realization of reality (*tattvabodha*), it is for that very reason that tranquility (*śānti*) and concentration (*samādhi*) are heard of among the means to the knowledge of Brahman—such as the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities—by means of the words "tranquil" (*śāntaḥ*) and "composed" (*samāhitaḥ*). This is the meaning. || 50 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Both. When there is an expectation as to what the proof for this is, he states it: "Tranquility" (śama). The intention is that this is well-known from the Kaṇva recension of the Śruti: "Having become tranquil, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, one should see the Self in the very Self. || 50 ||

Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Now, one might object that since it was stated that [the body] must be discarded prior to the awakening to reality, it would follow that it should be accepted after that time;
anticipating this doubt, he says:
"And after awakening, that [body] is to be abandoned for the sake of attaining liberation while living (jīvanmukti)."
For one who is bound by the afflictions of desire and the like, there is indeed no liberation.

Regarding the phrase "from awakening": he reinforces the aforementioned point by way of its contrapositive with the words "desire and so forth. The meaning is that for one who is bound—possessed of that very affliction consisting of desire and the like—liberation, namely the state of being liberated while living (*jīvanmuktatva*), is certainly not non-existent. || 51 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might object: "Granted that desires and the like, which are imagined by the individual soul (*jīva*) and constitute an intense, non-scriptural duality, must be abandoned through the perfection of means such as tranquility (*śama*) even prior to the realization of reality (*tattvabodha*); however, what is the obstacle to their continued existence after the realization of reality? Anticipating this doubt, it is replied that since that [duality] has been sublated along with its root by the realization of reality, its persistence thereafter must be described as existing only in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). That too, [is not possible for the soul...]

He provides the resolution, stating "from awakening," because [the afflictions] are obstacles to liberation and must therefore be destroyed even after awakening. The reason for this is given as "desire and so forth.
The meaning is that the very suffering or exhaustion caused by desire and the like constitutes bondage. || 51 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "For one who is distressed by the cycle of birth and so forth, what is the use of this temporary liberation while living (jīvanmukti), when there is the ultimate human goal consisting in the absolute cessation of birth? To this, he raises the following doubt:
"Let this liberation while living not exist; however, in the absence of birth, there would be no sense of 'I'."
Therefore, let there even be rebirth for you for the sake of liberation while in the disembodied state (videhamukti); you would be satisfied with mere heaven alone. || 52 ||

Regarding the term "liberation while living" (*jīvanmukti*): he refutes [the objection] by means of a counter-argument (*pratibandī*), stating that if one were to abandon liberation while living out of fear of the cessation of worldly enjoyments, then liberation after death (*videhamukti*) would likewise have to be abandoned out of fear of the cessation of enjoyments in the hereafter. Thus: "In that case... (verse 52).

Commentary (a0): Now, one might object: "Granted that all this may be possible if there is such a thing as liberation while living (jīvanmukti)—following the maxim 'there can be no painting without a wall'—yet we do not perceive any proof for its existence in the state beyond death (paratva) and so forth. Nor is it correct to say that scripture itself, such as 'For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged,' is the proof for that. For the venerable Sarvajñātma-munīśvara has stated in his own works that such passages are merely arthavāda (laudatory or explanatory statements)."

This has been stated in the fourth chapter of the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*: "The entire collection of scriptures concerning the conviction of liberation while living is to be applied to the liberated-while-living as a conceptual construct."

"Since its purposefulness is established by that much alone, there is immediate liberation (sadyomukti) from this very cause"— thus [it is said]. This is the fourth chapter, accompanied by the two commentaries.
And this verse has been explained by the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī: "But surely, when one who knows the Truth attains immediate disembodied liberation, [it is said]:
'For him there is delay only so long as he is not released from the body; then he shall be merged [in Brahman].'"
“When one abandons all desires that have entered the mind,
O Pārtha, and is satisfied in the self alone by means of the self, then one is said to be of steady wisdom.”

Anticipating the objection that scriptures establishing *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living) would otherwise be devoid of subject matter (*nirviṣaya*), [the author] states: "Regarding *jīvanmukti*... He intends to show that there is no contradiction, because such texts—like those concerning the liberation of Śuka, Vāmadeva, and others—are *arthavāda* (eulogistic statements); they are devoted to the glorification of the knowledge of Brahman by way of restating a *jīvanmukti* conceived as a possibility for one of superior intelligence.
It is so described because it serves as a means of conviction regarding *jīvanmukti*. This is established because its purposefulness (*arthavattva*) is logically consistent.

Because it is established that its purpose consists in the form of praise; for this reason, for this cause—that is to say, because the scripture concerning liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) has a different subject matter. This very same view is also stated in the *Siddhāntaleśasaṃgraha* in the fourth chapter itself:
"Since the remaining [means] are impossible once the contradictory [knowledge] has arisen, [the scripture] is a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*)."
The teacher Sarvajñātman clearly stated this based on the scriptural teaching of *jīvanmukti*.

This point has also been refuted in that very commentary (*ṭīkā*) of his: "Since not even a trace of ignorance can remain when a contrary cognition arises, it would be necessary to postulate another cognition for the destruction of that trace; however, by parsimony (*lāghava*), it is more appropriate that this [contrary cognition] itself is the destroyer of ignorance.

Furthermore, since such scriptural passages as 'For him there is delay only so long' are intended merely to praise the knowledge of the Self and do not have *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living) as their primary purport, they are nothing more than explanatory eulogies (*arthavāda*). This is another opinion.

"Ha! It is contradictory. Therefore, fearing that such [a state] might not belong to him, he raises the objection: "Liberation while living" (*jīvanmukti*). Keeping in mind that this objection is rooted solely in a failure to understand the purport of what preceded and followed it, [the author replies]: If you do not accept *jīvanmukti* itself on the grounds that its establishment would require the abandonment of desires and the like, resulting in the loss of worldly enjoyments, then [you must face the consequence] out of fear of the cessation of enjoyments in the afterlife.

He reveals the *pratibandī* (the counter-argument) itself with the second half of the verse, implying that even liberation while living (*videhamukti*) would thus become unworthy of regard. For in that context [it is said]:
"The fire of perfect knowledge, ignited by the activity of the wind of the true nature of reality, immediately consumes everything consisting of ignorance and its products."
"It does not burn that which is untainted, nor does it leave even the slightest trace of another form of saṃsāra; therefore, for the wise, immediate liberation is certain."

Thus, since the doctrine of immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*) was established in the preceding verse, this subsequent verse is intended for that very purpose. Accordingly, it has been stated here explicitly as well: "Immediate liberation [is attained] correctly for this reason. Alternatively, having introduced the doctrine of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) through the subsequent verses beginning with "within the range of the wise,"...
"First, there is liberation while living (jīvanmukti) because of its perception; and therein, because of its perception, there is the shadow of duality.
There is a slight remnant for the preservation of that shadow of duality; in that matter, one's own experience is the authority.
Having established this with the final portion of the text:
“I see all this as if it were a painting; I abide as the partless one in the infinite body of pure consciousness.
I behold myself as non-dual, whose sole form is infinite bliss, and I view the phenomenal world as if it were a burnt rope.
Though non-dual, I experience it as clearly as a bilva fruit in the palm of my hand, and I look upon the body as if it were a mere blade of grass.”

Thus, he has also demonstrated his own experience by saying, "In this way, my manifestation as if living and the attainment of the supreme good are well-established for me"; therefore, it is not the case that she [the Śruti] is not in agreement with that—this is the general direction of the argument. || 12 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He raises an objection to release the counter-implication (pratibandī).

When heaven is to be abandoned because of the defects of decay and excess, as set forth by Vidyāraṇya in the *Pañcadaśī*: [The verse continues: When even heaven is to be discarded due to the faults of diminution and excess, then what need is there to mention other [worldly] pleasures? // 122 //
Why is this self, which is the very essence of the darkness of defects such as desire and so forth, not itself abandoned through the discernment of duality? (53)

Regarding the word "kṣaye" (in destruction): since heaven and the like are to be abandoned because they are associated with defects, it is stated that desire and the like—which are themselves of the nature of extreme defect because they obstruct all human goals—are all the more to be abandoned; thus he says, "tadā" (then). || 53 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Anticipating the objection regarding the refutation of the counter-argument (*pratibandī*) already stated, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) further confirms it precisely because of that superiority—beginning with the word "kṣaya. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Does he not fall away? means "Is he not one fit for the supreme renunciation denoted by the word 'fallen'? The answer is: "He does not; rather, something [superior] certainly comes to pass. || 53 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Since desire and the like—which are the cause of extreme misfortune—have been abandoned through the cultivation of dispassion and other means, what fault is there in accepting desires that serve only for worldly enjoyment? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Even after realizing the Truth, if you do not abandon desire and the rest entirely..."
For you, who transgress the scriptures, there shall be the practice of acting according to your own whims. (54)

Regarding the word "tattvam" (the truth): the meaning is that by the conceit of being a knower of reality, you would transgress the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions and, being subject to desire and other such impulses, act according to your own whims. || 54 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might raise the objection: "For the yogi who is satiated by the nectar of knowledge and has accomplished all that was to be done, there remains nothing whatsoever to be performed; if there were anything left to do, he would not be a knower of reality.
Based on such a statement, one might wonder where even the renunciation of my desires remains as a duty to be performed. To counter this with a demonstration of the resulting calamity:

He rejects [this view], saying "the truth is as follows. Here, by the word "without remainder" (niḥśeṣa), it is indicated that even a mere trace of the latent impression (saṃskāra) of those [actions] is indeed destructive of the bliss of liberation while living (jīvanmukti). This is the reason for acting according to one's own desire: namely, "karma" [as the cause]. || 54 ||
Rāmānanda’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection, "Let it be so; what is the harm?", he cites the words of Sureśvarācārya, which are intended to demonstrate that such a position is undesirable:
"If one who has realized the true nature of non-duality were to act according to his own whims..."
What difference is there between dogs and those who see the truth regarding the consumption of impurity? (55)

Regarding the phrase *buddhādvaita*: one who has realized the non-dual true nature (*svatattva*)—that is, Brahman whose very essence is non-duality—is called *buddhādvaitasvatattva*. If such a knower of reality were to engage in acting according to his own whims (*yatheṣṭācaraṇa*), then even the eating of impure things and the like would be permissible. If that were the case, there would be no distinction whatsoever between dogs and those who perceive the ultimate reality. This is the meaning. || 55 ||
— Commentary (A0):

Anticipating the objection that this might be an acceptance of an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), [the author] states: This statement of an "acceptance of the desired" is not made by one who experiences the non-dual reality of the Self according to the tradition (*saṃpradāya*) through the falsity of the visible world; rather, it is uttered by a master-deceiver of people who possesses some refinement from scriptural study but lacks the light of the tradition (*saṃpradāya-sūrya*).
Suggesting that this applies to some lustful person indeed, he pacifies the wickedness of acting according to one's whims by means of the very words of the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi*:

"By whom [the Truth] was realized" (*buddhena*). The meaning is: "of him who possesses that [realization]," namely, the non-dual Brahman-Atman unity which has been directly perceived (*aparokṣīkṛta*) as the true reality, together with the principle characterized by the falsity of duality. If there were such a thing as acting according to one's whims, then what difference would there be between dogs and those who perceive the Truth regarding the consumption of impure things?

The connection is that there would be a distinction [between them]. Therefore, the implication is that for those who possess the knowledge of the real Brahman, there is no such thing as acting according to one's own whims. This very point has been stated by the author of the *Mūla* in the *Anubhūtiprakāśa*:
"Furthermore, one who was previously devoted to merit attains knowledge, and not otherwise."
"And subsequently, through that latent impression (vāsanā), he performs only meritorious deeds. || 55 ||
The Fourth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
— Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection, "What undesirable consequence has been brought about by this much?", he offers a reply with a touch of irony:
"Previously, due solely to the defects of the mind, you were afflicted; now [you are afflicted] because of awakening."
And yet, there is the censure of the entire world— oh, how great is the majesty of your awakening!

Regarding the phrase "from awakening": the sense is that prior to the dawning of the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), you experienced affliction due to mental defects such as desire and anger; however, now you must endure even the censure of the entire world—thus, there is a doubling of your suffering. || 56 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Even there, out of compassion, he mocks him who is excessively attached to that very [view] expressed in the aforementioned words, in order to set him on the true path—beginning with the words "bodhāt" (from enlightenment). Here, by the use of the present tense in the phrase "kliśyasi" (you suffer), it is implied that even now you have no enlightenment at all. || 56 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: If so, what should be done? To this he says:
"O knower of reality, do not desire equality with those such as dogs and pigs."
By abandoning all defects of intellect, may you be worshipped by the people like a god.

"Be free from desire": Do not long for equality with those who are the lowest of all, such as Virāha, by virtue of being unable to renounce desire, even though you possess the knowledge that is the cause of supreme excellence; rather, by abandoning all defects of the mind characterized by desire and the like, become worthy of worship by all people, like a god—this is the meaning. || 57 ||

Commentary (a0): Even so, out of compassion, he teaches while proclaiming to the world that his status as a knower of reality (*tattvavit*) must indeed be accepted—by means of the two verses beginning with "viḍvarāha" [5.58–59]. The underlying intention is that this statement regarding his assumed status as a knower of reality is made solely for the purpose of gaining acceptance of his own instruction. || 57 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the means for abandoning that [desire]:
"The perception of defects such as desire for rewards, and so forth, are the causes for the abandonment of desire and the rest."
They are well-known in the treatises on liberation; seek them out and be happy.

One desires. "Desirable things" (*kāmyāḥ*) refers to objects of desire such as heaven and so forth; those [objects] for which undesirable things like hatred and so forth are primary are called "desirable and so forth" (*kāmyādayaḥ*).

Regarding their defects—such as impermanence, the state of having a superior [object], and so forth—their "vision" (*dṛṣṭiḥ*), meaning observation, is the first among [the sequence beginning with] the investigation of the nature of anger and so forth. He states the authoritative proof (*pramāṇa*) for these being the cause for the renunciation of desire and so forth: "It is well-known" (*prasiddhaḥ*). Even if that be so, what follows from it?
To this he says: "Having searched for them" (tānanviṣya). || 58 ||

Commentary on verse a0: Regarding the phrase "kāmyādi" (desire, etc.), the word "ādi" (etcetera) includes the "kāma" (desirous one) and "kāmuka" (lustful one). By the first term [of the compound], the investigation into their essential nature is intended. Regarding "mokṣa" (liberation): this means in the scriptural works of the sages that establish liberation, such as the *Bṛhadvāsiṣṭha*, the *Mokṣadharma*, and the *Sūtasaṃhitā*. Thus it has been stated in the *Bṛhadyogavāsiṣṭha*:
“Bearing hair like soot, difficult to touch yet pleasing to the eye—
women, like the flames of the fire of evil deeds, burn a man like straw,” and so forth. To me, wealth, which is a wheel of accumulated anxieties, does not lead to bliss.
"And houses with wives who have recently given birth, like the homes of those in dire calamity," and so forth. This should be understood in other instances as well. ||18||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Granted that desire and the like should be abandoned because they are causes of misfortune; however, since the 'kingdom of the mind' (manorājya) is not such a cause, its abandonment is not required. Thus he raises this doubt.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[the section titled] "Discrimination between Duality" (Dvaitaviveka).
Let this desire and the like be abandoned; for what loss is there in [allowing them to remain] within the realm of the imagination?
Because it is the seed of all faults without exception, injury is said by the Blessed One [to be the root of non-restraint]. (59)

"Let it be abandoned. Anticipating the objection that although it is not a cause of harm directly, it must nevertheless be abandoned because it is a cause of it indirectly, he replies with the verse beginning "aśeṣa... (59).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Granted that desire and the like are to be abandoned because they are direct causes of misfortune, yet mental longing (*manorājya*) is not so. To this he replies with the verse beginning "tyajyatām" (let it be abandoned). Although it is not so directly, it is not as you say, because it is so through a succession of causes; thus he says "aśeṣa... (all...). 59.
In a person who dwells upon sense-objects, attachment to them arises.
From attachment arises desire; from desire, anger is born. (60)

Rāghava’s Commentary: He cites the words of the Blessed Lord (Bhagavad Gītā 2.62), which are intended to demonstrate how [the mind] becomes a cause of misfortune through a succession of stages: "Dhyāyataḥ" (meditating...). 60.

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He recites a portion of that very statement of the Blessed One: "Dhyāyata" (meditate), etc. Attachment (*saṅga*) is the superimposition [of the idea] that something is a means for achieving one's own welfare. Desire (*kāma*) is the longing for its attainment and so forth. Anger (*krodha*) is a modification of the mind characterized by a blazing intensity, produced by the frustration of that desire. || 60 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: If so, what is the means for abandoning this kingdom of the mind? To this he says:
"The kingdom of the mind can be conquered through non-conceptual samādhi."
That [state] is also well-attained through gradual savikalpa-samādhi. || 61 ||
Regarding the word "possible": he asks, "How is that established? and replies with the words "easily accomplished. || 61 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, even if this were so, one might still ask how that pride can be abandoned; therefore, he says: "It is possible to conquer.

To address the fact that this [conquest] itself is difficult to achieve, he says: "It is easily accomplished. This means according to the sequence stated by Patañjali, namely: yama, niyama, āsana, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi—these are the eight limbs. || 61 ||
— Rāghavānanda’s Commentary — Now, one might object: "Let it be so for one endowed with the eight-limbed yoga; but what is the destiny of one who lacks it? To this, he says:
"By means of the reality of the Buddha, which is free from defects of the intellect and characterized by dwelling in solitude..."
By uttering the long Praṇava, the kingdom of one's desires is conquered.

"Buddhatattvena" means: by that person who has realized the truth (*tattva*)—namely, the reality characterized by the identity of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikya*); who is free from the defects of the intellect such as desire, anger, and so forth; who is a solitary dweller (*ekāntavāsī*) whose habit is to reside in a secluded place; [by such a person], having uttered the long *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) consisting of twelve or more *mātrās*, the kingdom of the mind (*manorājya*) is conquered, which is to say, it is warded off. || 62 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, [an objection is raised]: "But this means is not easily accessible. To this, he says: "buddhā—" etc. The defects of the intellect (*dhīdoṣāḥ*) are desire and the like. || 62 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To the question, "What happens when the kingdom of the mind is conquered? he says:
When that [mind] is conquered, the mind remains devoid of mental fluctuations (vṛtti), like a mute person.
This state was extensively taught by Vasiṣṭha to Rāma.
Regarding the phrase "when that [mind] is conquered": just as a mute person remains devoid of all verbal activity, so too the mind, when completely [withdrawn], remains [in that state].
[Page 125] Fourth Section.

The meaning is that [the mind] remains devoid of external objects. He states the authority for the fact that the state of the mind being without mental modifications (*avṛttika*) constitutes the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*): "This state," and so forth.
The meaning is that this state is this very stage. || 63 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Conquered" (jita). The meaning is that the "state" (pada) is the condition of the mind free from conceptualization (niḥsaṃkalpa), which is to be attained by the practitioner. || 63 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He cites two verses by Vasiṣṭha:
"The cleansing of the mind of the visible world occurs through the realization that the visible does not exist."
If that is perfected, then the supreme bliss of nirvāṇa has arisen. || 64 ||

Regarding the phrase "the visible" (*dṛśya*): the meaning is that if, through the knowledge that the world does not exist apart from the non-dual Brahman—based on such scriptural passages as "There is no diversity whatsoever here" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.4.19; *Kaṭha Śruti* 4.11)—the removal of the visible from the mind has been accomplished, then one should know that the unsurpassed bliss of liberation (*mokṣasukha*) has been realized. || 64 ||

Commentary (a0): In response to the inquiry, "How was it stated by the venerable Vasiṣṭha regarding the state of the mind's freedom from conceptualization (*niḥsaṃkalpatva*)?", [the author] cites two verses from the *Bṛhadyogavāsiṣṭha* for the sake of savoring the essence, according to the maxim of the "sample grain" (*sthālīpulākanyāya*). "The visible object... and "...as the visible object...":
the meaning is the removal of the superimposition of the visible world upon the mind. If this is accomplished, then that very state is reached; for here there is no diversity whatsoever.

The connection is as follows: by the sublation of all duality as taught by the Śruti, there arises the manifestation of self-luminous bliss—the nature of liberation which is non-different from the Self—characterized by the supreme, intense, and unsurpassed bliss of Nirvāṇa. And thus, at that time, the mind becomes entirely devoid of volitional thought (saṃkalpa); this is the intended meaning. || 64 ||
The scripture has been thoroughly investigated and long debated among one another.
Apart from the silence resulting from the abandonment of latent impressions, there is no higher state.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Furthermore, the non-dualistic scripture (*advaita-śāstra*) has been thoroughly investigated, and likewise, through mutual dialogues between teachers and disciples, it has been made understood over a long period of time. Having done this, what has been concluded? To this he says: "Having completely abandoned...

The meaning is that it has been concluded that for the mind from which the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of desire and so forth have been perfectly cast off, there is no higher human goal (*puruṣārtha*) than its state of silence (*tūṣṇīṃbhāva*). || 65 ||

Commentary on verse a0: "It has been investigated. The *śāstra* refers to the collection of non-dualistic texts (*advaita-grantha-jāta*). Although this has been investigated and analyzed by me, having first attended upon my guru, and although it has been debated and demonstrated to one another over a long period of time among fellow students and disciples—even so—"it has been completely abandoned" means that the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of desire and other passions have been entirely uprooted.

This is the meaning. From such *mauna* (silence/contemplation), one attains the state where "having become weary of both non-*mauna* and *mauna*, one then becomes a *brāhmaṇa*" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad). Furthermore, based on the etymology that a *muni* is one whose nature is reflection (*manana*), and *mauna* is his action, it refers to the state of the mind being devoid of volition—produced either by the sublation of duality or by the opposition of the mind [to duality]—preceded by immediate knowledge equal in rank to *nididhyāsana* (meditative absorption). This is the sense. The construction is: "Without (*ṛte*) this, there is no higher place (*pada*). || 65 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Thus, when the mind that has attained cessation is distracted by *prārabdha* karma, in response to the inquiry as to what the means for countering that distraction may be, he says:
"Sometimes the intellect is distracted by karma that yields experience."
Furthermore, she would become concentrated at that very moment through the proficiency gained from practice.

Regarding the phrase "it is distracted": if the intellect (buddhi) is occasionally distracted by the karma that has begun to bear fruit (prārabdha-karma), which bestows worldly enjoyments, then that intellect shall, by virtue of the firmness of its practice, become concentrated once again at that very moment; this is the meaning. || 66 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, one might ask: even when in the aforementioned state, if the mind is distracted for the sake of experiencing the fruits of past actions (*prārabdha*), what is the remedy?
To this he says: "It is distracted... Therefore, the essential point is that only the strengthening of practice (*abhyāsa*) must be cultivated. || 66 ||

He who has no mental distraction does not consider himself a knower of Brahman.
"The sages who have seen the further shore declare: 'This one is indeed Brahman. (67)

[In the commentary by Rāmānanda on the work titled *Dvaitaviveka*, he states that even for one who is always free from mental distraction, the status of being a knower of Brahman is merely figurative—thus he says: "Distraction...

Commentary (Ṭīkā): For this very reason, it is said—"distraction" (vikṣepa). Thus it has been stated by the venerable and worshipful Śrīmad Bhagavatpūjyapāda in his *Manīṣāpañcaka* (5.66):
From even a tiny fraction of a fraction of that ocean of bliss, these [gods] such as Śakra attain their satisfaction;
yet, having attained that state in which the mind is utterly tranquilized, the Sage is truly liberated.

"In that eternal ocean of bliss, there is only Brahman itself with its attributes dissolved; surely this is my conviction: that there is no knower of Brahman whatsoever whose feet are not worshipped by the lords of gods and asuras. || 67 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Here too, he cites the words of Vasiṣṭha:
"Having abandoned both seeing and not seeing, [the Self] remains by itself in its absolute form."
O Brahmin, he who merely remains [in that state] is not himself a knower of Brahman.

Regarding "seeing and not seeing": he who, having abandoned the two-fold worldly discourse of "I know Brahman" and "I do not know [Brahman]," abides as the non-dual consciousness itself, is Brahman itself and not a knower of Brahman—this is the meaning. || 68 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding the matter stated, he cites the very words of Vasiṣṭha—beginning with "darśana"—as an illustration. "O Brahmin" is an address directed specifically toward that crest-jewel among brāhmaṇas who had arrived in the course of that conversation. "Darśana" means knowledge and ignorance. The word "hi" signifies that one should sublate the superimposition of identity in both cases—that is, the notions "I am the knower" and "I am ignorant. The rest, however, is quite straightforward. || 68 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He concludes the entire analysis of duality:

Therefore, this [distinction] has been analyzed here through the differentiation between the Lord and duality. || 69 ||

Regarding the phrase "of liberation while living" (*jīvanmukteḥ*): this aforementioned type of one liberated while living attains—that is, reaches—the supreme pinnacle, the unsurpassed state of ultimate consummation, through the avoidance or abandonment of the duality of living beings, which is the mental world (*manomaya-prapañca*). For this reason, this duality of living beings has been distinguished—that is, clearly demonstrated by being separated—from the duality of the Lord (*īśvara-dvaita*), meaning from the duality created by the Lord. || 69 ||

Thus ends the *Dvaitaviveka-pañjikā* (Commentary on the Discrimination of Duality), composed by the scholar named Rāmakṛṣṇa, a servant of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, Śrī Bhāratītīrtha Vidyāraṇya Muni. 4 || 11 || || ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, while stating the result, he concludes the section with the words "of liberation while living" (*jīvanmukteḥ*). And thus, that which was stated here previously in the introduction (upodghāta)—85—[is now confirmed].
"Liberation arises only from the knowledge imparted by Īśa, and not from any other teacher whatsoever"—
this fixed conviction constitutes the fourth obstacle to the realization of Īśa.
Thus, this is the fourth obstacle, known as the cultivation of ideas contrary to the means for realizing the meaning of that [supreme] state.
Likewise: "In the dissolution [of duality], through inquiry into the duality fashioned by the Lord as primary, [one attains it] without a guru.
"In the fourth [chapter] as well, its primacy is established by the statement regarding the absence of awakening."

Thus, in this fourth section titled "Discrimination of Duality" (Dvaitaviveka), the fact that all of this constitutes its sublation is indeed consistent with the introductory indicators and other such signs. For instance, as follows herein:
"The duality created by the Lord through the individual soul (jīva) is discerned;
when discernment occurs, bondage, which is to be abandoned by the soul, becomes manifest"—
thus begins [the work].
Likewise, the concluding summary states: "The supreme limit of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) is attained through the abandonment of the duality of the individual soul;
therefore, here [in this work], such a discrimination between the Lord and the duality has been discerned.

Thus, the bondage to be abandoned by the individual soul becomes clearly manifest only through the means of discriminating between the duality of the creation of the Lord and the individual soul as taught by the Guru.

The first indication of the primary purport [of the Upanishads] is this characteristic of unity established by the introduction and other criteria, because it is well known from the Smṛtis and other sources that even the Lord, through his playful incarnations as Hari, Hara, Caturānana, and others, awakened the non-dual nature of the Self in seekers such as Arjuna; nevertheless, [Arjuna said], "I am your disciple; teach me who have taken refuge in you."

The secret is this: since his status as a disciple is well-known to be centered on Arjuna, his status as a teacher ultimately culminates in that very same [Arjuna] even within that [Advaita] position; thus, it comes down to that alone. "Even though the duality created by the Lord has not ceased, one who asserts the identity of reality is able to understand non-dual Brahman by realizing the illusory nature of that duality."

Furthermore, there is the following scriptural passage regarding practice: "But at the time of dissolution, when that [duality] has ceased, because of the absence of teachers, scriptures, and so forth—even though opposing duality does not appear, the non-dual cannot be understood. And so on.

"There is no such thing as a woman made of flesh; rather, there is another, consisting of mind"—this is the unprecedented nature [of the teaching]. Since a woman consisting of mind, distinct from the woman perceived through direct perception and other means as being made of flesh, was taught by the Guru himself, this meaning was articulated by both the author of the Bhāṣya and the author of the Vārtika. Thus, the fruit is the Guru’s greatness and the reverence for the tradition. This—

The state of being a *tīrtha* (sacred authority) has been extolled in many ways by Vasiṣṭha in the *Rāmāyaṇa*; thus, in that very context, there is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Furthermore, there is a logical justification (*upapatti*) beginning with the words, "But upon the cessation [of the world] at the time of dissolution, due to the absence of gurus, scriptures, and so forth. Therefore, among all six types of evidentiary marks (*ṣaḍvidhaliṅga*), the greatness of the Guru alone is paramount;
may all be most auspicious! || 69 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the *Śrī-Pūrṇānandendukaumudī*. 4.

Rāma’s Commentary: Having bowed to the venerable Bhāratītīrtha and Vidyāraṇya, the lords of sages...

66. For the sake of establishing the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self—the means to liberation for one desiring liberation—the supremely compassionate Teacher, while sequentially determining the meaning of the four well-known Mahāvākyas, first addresses the statement found in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka: "Prajñānam Brahma" [Ait. 5.3].
In the great statement (mahāvākya), "The knower of the Self," he explains the meaning of the word *prajñāna*: "That by which one sees this, hears it, smells it, and articulates it."
That which discerns its own various tastes is declared to be *prajñāna*. || 1 ||

"By which one sees": by means of that [consciousness]—the consciousness conditioned by the modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) that has issued forth through the door of the eyes—the person sees or perceives this visible form and so forth; likewise, by means of that [consciousness] conditioned by the modification of the internal organ that has issued forth through the door of the ears, one hears the collection of sounds;

similarly, by means of that [consciousness] conditioned by the modification of the internal organ that has issued forth through the door of the nose, one smells the collection of odors; or by means of that [consciousness] delimited by the organ of speech...

By this [consciousness], one explains; one utters the collection of sounds by which, through the medium of the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) emerging via the faculty of taste, one perceives the two tastes—the sweet and the non-sweet. And the word "ca" (and) has the sense of including what has not been mentioned; thus, the meaning is that the Consciousness which exists, characterized by all the faculties and the various modifications of the internal organ—both those already mentioned and those not mentioned—is here called "prajñāna. By this [it is explained] the passage beginning with "by which one sees," etc.
The meaning of this entire intermediate textual passage—that "all these are indeed names of consciousness"—has been shown here in summary. || 1 ||
A0 Commentary: [I bow to] that which is the immutable form of the supreme Brahman—non-dual bliss, consciousness, all-pervading, and stainless;
though it is the abode of the magician’s trickery of delusion regarding duality, it is the forehead-mark of the self-luminous Vedas.
I bow to all the most excellent teachers, to my own guru named Śrī Nārāyaṇa—the ornament of the lineage of Atri and a true teacher established in Brahman—and also to him known as Mahādeva. || 1 ||
Having honored Jīvañjīva, Vidyāraṇya, and Bhāratītīrtha.
I shall illuminate the discernment of sentences through the manifestation of their objects by means of this "Kaumudī" (Moonlight).

Now, the Blessed One, the Guru Vidyāraṇya, desiring to compose the fifth chapter of the *Pañcadaśī*, titled "The Discrimination of the Great Sayings" (*Mahāvākya-viveka*), performs an auspicious invocation characterized by the contemplation of the non-dual Self—the well-established means of knowledge—and simultaneously indicates the subject matter and other elements. He proceeds to briefly explain the four great sayings found in the various branches of the Vedas, which are extremely concise, for the sake of one who possesses the most intense desire to know, using the four verses beginning with "By which... (*yeneti*).

Regarding the word *gmaiḥ*: The great sentence (*mahāvākya*) found in the Aitareya Upaniṣad, "Brahman is consciousness" (*prajñānaṃ brahma*), has as its referent for the term *prajñāna* the pure consciousness of the individual soul (*jīva-caitanya*) itself, because of the introductory statement, "by which one sees, by which one hears," and so forth; thus he says, "by which one perceives. By this, it is shown that the intention of the concluding Śruti is that the names of consciousness are merely designations for the consciousness characterized as the witness (*sākṣin*) of all internal and external mental modifications (*vṛtti*) along with their appearances (*sābhāsa*). ||1||
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus explained the meaning of the word *prajñāna*, he states the meaning of the word *brahma*:
"In the four-faced [Brahmā], Indra, and the gods, as well as in humans, horses, cows, and so forth..."
Therefore, consciousness is the one Brahman; thus, even in that which consists of Brahman, it is pure intelligence.

Regarding the term "four-faced": among those who possess bodies—whether superior, such as gods and others; intermediate, such as humans; or inferior, such as horses, cattle, and so forth—the fifth chapter [concerns] space and the other elements.
Accompanied by the two commentaries.
This...
"This Brahmā is Indra.
The meaning is that the single consciousness which exists as the cause of the birth and so forth of the world within all beings is Brahmā. And by this—
The meaning of this intermediate passage, beginning with "Thus, wisdom is the foundation" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 5.3;

Ātmabodha 1) and ending there, has been shown in brief. Having thus stated the meaning of the individual words, he states the meaning of the sentence: "Therefore" (ataḥ). Since Brahman, which is consciousness (*prajñāna*), is situated everywhere, therefore the consciousness situated even in me is indeed Brahman; the meaning is that there is no distinction in their nature as consciousness. || 2 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, he states the meaning of the term "Brahman" with the words "caturmukha" (four-faced). The phrase "this is Brahman," and so forth, up to "the foundation of wisdom"—this is the remainder [of the scriptural citation]. Therefore, for the reason of oneness (*ekatva*), the connection is as follows: even in me—that is, in the consciousness (*caitanya*) characterized by being delimited by the aggregate of the body and so forth denoted by the word "I"—there exists only the non-duality of Brahman. || 2 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus determined the meaning of the Great Saying (mahāvākya) found in the Ṛgveda branch, he now states the meaning of the word "I" (*ahaṃ*) in order to reveal the meaning of the Great Saying "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*) located in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad among the Yajurveda branches.
The supreme Self is fully present within this body, which is qualified for the knowledge [of Brahman].
Abiding as a witness within the intellect, it is called the "I" as it flashes forth. || 3 ||

"Complete" (*paripūrṇa*) means: the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is complete by its very nature and undivided by space, time, or substance, exists as the witness (*sākṣin*)—and thus not subject to modification—within this body, such as that of a human being, which is a product of *māyā* and serves as the locus for the acquisition of knowledge (*vidyā*). This body is endowed with the means for knowledge such as tranquility (*śama*) and is fit for the attainment of knowledge through the practice of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth; therein, it exists as the witness of the intellect (*buddhi*) and, by extension, of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*).

The meaning is that, by abiding as the illuminator and remaining as such, while vibrating and manifesting, it is perceived as "I" and is expressed by the word "I" through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). ||3||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, he explains the great maxim (*mahāvākya*) "I am Brahman" found in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* with the words "paripūrṇa" (perfectly full). The meaning is that, by virtue of being devoid of the three-fold limitations such as space and so forth, It is not the counter-positive (*apratiyogin*) of the four kinds of non-existence (*abhāva*). That is to say: by the absence of spatial limitation, It is not the counter-positive of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*); by the absence of temporal limitation, It is not the counter-positive of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or emergent non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*); and by the absence of substantial limitation, It is not the counter-positive of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).

Furthermore, the fact that non-existence has no counter-correlate (pratiyogin) within the Self is implied. For this very reason, it is said to be "other" (*para*). As it is said: "That which one attains, that which one takes, and that which one eats of the objects here..."

Because of the statement of the learned, "That which exists as its continuous state is therefore called the Self (ātman)," and because of the etymological derivation that this Self is the Supreme (para), it is the supreme bliss of inward illumination. By this, its status as the unsurpassed goal of human life is illuminated. That [Self] is also indicated in this body of the qualified seeker of knowledge through the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal, and so forth.
The meaning is: "one whose body is perfected by the ultimate means of meditation. It signifies that [the Self] shines forth while remaining as the witness of the intellect (buddhi).

The intention is that, in reality, within that very expanse of pure consciousness (cinmātra), there is the locus of the activity of manifestation. It is "expressed" as "I"; the meaning is that it is characterized as such. || 3 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the meaning of the word *brahman*:
"The Supreme Self, which is inherently full, is described here by the word *brahman*.
Through the reflective awareness of oneness in the form 'I am,' I become Brahman. (4)

"From itself" (*svataḥ*): the meaning is that the previously mentioned Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is self-perfect by its own nature and unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, is described—i.e., indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*)—by the word "Brahman" (*brahma*) in this Great Saying (*mahāvākya*).

He states that the identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, which is obtained through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words, is referred to by the word "I am" (*asmi*) contained within this sentence: "I am" (*asmīti*).
He states the conclusion: "By that," [verse 4].
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding the word "svataḥ" (by itself). Thus, the meaning of the term *brahman* is exactly as stated in the Vārttika beginning with "avyāvṛtta" (unrestricted), and so forth.

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, in order to illuminate the meaning of the sentence "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7) found in the Chāndogya Śruti, he states the indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha) of the word "That":

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He explains the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), which belongs to the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* of the same Vedic branch as that [text], with the words "One alone," etc. The meaning is: that Reality, which is devoid of the threefold internal and other distinctions, which is uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time, and which is free from name and form—non-dual (advaita) and existing even now prior to the creation of the superimposed duality—is the referent (*lakṣya*) of the word "That" (*tat*). || 5 ||
In this context, the word "thou" (tvaṃ) denotes that reality which transcends the body and senses of the listener.

"that oneness" (*tadaikyam*). The meaning is: let those seeking liberation experience the oneness—the identity of those two, the referents of the words *tat* and *tvam*, which is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). ||6||

Commentary on verse a0: "Of the listener" means of the disciple who performs the means such as hearing [the scriptures]. Rāmānuja’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Desiring to explain the meaning of the sentence "This Self is Brahman" [Māṇḍūkya 2], which belongs to the Atharvaveda and follows in the sequence of topics, he first demonstrates the intended meaning of the two words "this" (ayam) and "Self" (ātmā) in their respective order:
"The state of being self-luminous and immediate is understood from the word 'this'."

Since the word "Self" (*ātman*) is seen to be applied even to the body and other such things, in response to the inquiry as to what is intended by the word "Self" here, he says:

Thus, "ahaṃkārādi-dehānta" refers to that [aggregate] which begins with the ego and ends with the body. Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now he states the meaning of the term *brahman*: "That which is seen," etc. The meaning is that it is the reality which serves as the ultimate limit for the sublation of duality due to its falsity. He states the conclusion with the remainder of the verse beginning with "that": thus, what was previously established here in the introduction—that for the liberated one, there is the manifestation of all things everywhere by virtue of being the Self of all—is [confirmed].

Having thus described the five obstacles— characterized by contrary mental impressions regarding the fruit [of knowledge] and having as their object the cognition of the nature of the Lord who constitutes the referent of the term *tat*— with the words, "Even the [Lord's] being the controller of all and so forth is this fifth obstacle in the cognition of the Lord," [the author concludes that] liberation is indeed oneness with Brahman, wherein no duality whatsoever exists.
Thus, it should be understood that the preeminence of that [non-duality] is even more clearly evident in the fifth chapter.

Consequently, the capacity of this fifteenth chapter of the *Pañcaprakaraṇa*, titled *Mahāvākyaviveka* (Discernment of the Great Sayings), to subvert the aforementioned obstacles is entirely consistent with its exclusive focus on liberation characterized by the non-dual identity of the Self and Brahman. This applies equally to the great sayings of the four Vedas, beginning with the *Ṛgveda*.

According to the statement in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*, "The essence of liberation is said to be unsurpassed bliss and the cessation of the entire mass of suffering, because it consists solely in Brahman, whose nature is self-luminous and bliss"; since liberation is of that singular nature, all the ancient teachers have refuted in their various treatises those proponents of duality who teach meanings contrary to the sense of the aforementioned Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*). Therefore, this is the Fivefold Discrimination (*vivekapañcaka*).

It is auspicious that [this work] culminates solely in the great purport (*mahātātparya*) directed toward the Pure Lord known as the referent of the term "That" (*tatpadārtha*), which has been purified by its capacity to sublate the five successive obstacles known as: doubt regarding the etymology, doubt regarding the object, latent impressions regarding the object, impossibility regarding the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), impossibility regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the cultivation of the opposite of the means, and the cultivation of the opposite of the result. || 8 ||

Thus [ends] the work titled *Pūrṇānandendukaumudī*, composed by the student Acyuta Śarmā, whose surname is Moḍaka and whose mind moves like a royal swan among the lotus-feet of the venerable Nārāyaṇa Śāstrī— whose secondary name is Paṣṭupaṇa, who is the mountain of the non-dual knowledge, who sports in the milk-ocean of the venerable Padavākya-pramāṇa, and who is a disciple of the illustrious Advaitasaccidānandendra Sarasvatī, the teacher of the wandering mendicants (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka*) of the most exalted order.
The fifth chapter, the Mahāvākya-viveka-prakāśa, in the commentary on the Pañcadaśī, is complete. || 5 ||
Now begins the sixteenth chapter, titled *Citradīpa*, the fifteenth [chapter] of the work.
Rāma’s Commentary: [I salute] Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, who is moon-colored, and who has four arms.
One should meditate upon the one with a serene countenance for the pacification of all obstacles. || 1 ||
By the mere remembrance of whom, obstacles indeed depart to a great distance.
I bow to that Elephant-faced One, the bestower of desired objects. || 2 ||
Having bowed to the two lords of sages, Śrī Bhāratītīrtha and Vidyāraṇya.
An exposition of the Citradīpa, which brings about an understanding of its essential meaning, is now composed.

In order to ensure the unimpeded completion of the work he intends to compose, the author performs an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) consisting of the contemplation of the reality of his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) by means of the term "Supreme Self" (*paramātman*). Keeping in mind that this work is a treatise on Vedānta and that its status as such is established by the very subject matter and other elements belonging to that [Vedānta], and following the maxim that "the worldless [Brahman] is manifested through superimposition (*adhyāropa*) and negation (*apavāda*"), [he proceeds to describe] that which has been superimposed upon the Supreme Self...
He declares the manner of the world's existence along with an illustration:
"Just as the fourfold state of things is seen upon a painted canvas."
In the same way, the fourfold state is to be understood within the Supreme Self. || 1 ||

Regarding the word "yathā" (just as): just as there is a fourfold state of those [entities] to be described in the case of a painted cloth, so too should the fourfold state to be described be understood in the case of the Supreme Self. || 1 ||
I bow to the Supreme Brahman, who is non-dual bliss, existence, consciousness, all-pervading, and eternally pure;
who, though appearing as the illusory net of duality through delusion, is the Tilaka (foremost ornament) that dissolves it; who is self-luminous and the ultimate goal of the Vedas;

and who is the crest-jewel of the Raghu dynasty, the true Guru established in Brahman, along with all the most excellent teachers. *Note: This is the opening verse of the *Advaitānandabhāṣya* by Ānandagiri.*
I bow to my own guru, known as Śrīmannārāyaṇa, who is also named Mahādeva. || 1 ||
Having honored Jīvañjīvaka, Vidyāraṇya, and Bhāratītīrtha,
I shall clearly elucidate the *Citradīpa* by means of the illumination of the essence of the *Kaumudī*.

Now, the venerable Vidyāraṇyācārya, composing the sixth chapter of the *Pañcadaśī*, titled "The Lamp of the Multicolored" (*Citradīpa*), first establishes the subject matter and purpose according to the Advaita scriptures for the sake of engaging those proficient in internal science (*antarvāṇi*). He also performs an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) characterized by the inquiry into the true nature of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which is well-known as having both authority and a specific purpose, by citing the *Maitrāyaṇī* [Upaniṣad]: "Like a painting, it is false yet pleasing to the mind."

He elucidates this through the very example of a famous painted cloth, based on the Śruti and the Smṛti known as the Bṛhadyogavāsiṣṭha which states, "An uncreated, colorless painting has arisen in the sky," using the word "yathā" (just as). || 1 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In response to the inquiry "What is that?", he sequentially points out the four states for both the illustration and the illustrated object:
"Just as a cloth is washed, rubbed, marked, and dyed."
The inner controller (antaryāmī) of consciousness, the soul of the creator (sūtrātman), and likewise the cosmic soul (virāḍ-ātman) are thus impelled.
Regarding the word "yathā" (as): there are four stages, such as being washed, rubbed, marked, and colored, just as in the case of a painted cloth.
This concludes the sixth chapter.
Accompanied by two commentaries:

||| 133 || Just as [these states are found in the individual soul], so too in the Supreme Self (paramātman), one should understand that there are four states—namely, the inner ruler of consciousness (cid-antaryāmī), the thread-self (sūtrātman), and the cosmic body (virāṭ). This is the meaning. ||| 2 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): In response to the inquiry as to how those four states exist in both the illustration and the illustrated, he clarifies this with the words "Just as" (yathā). || 2 ||
— Rāghava’s Commentary: He explains in sequence the nature of the states exemplified by the illustrations:
"In this context, that which is naturally white is called 'washed' (dhauta), while that which has been smeared with food is called 'stained' (dhvasta)."
It should be smeared with ink and freed from defects by filling in the gaps in the letters.
Regarding the term "inherently" (*svataḥ*): among its own states, it is said to be "white" or "washed" when it exists inherently, that is, without connection to any other substance.
It may be "smeared with food," "rubbed," "endowed with forms made of ink," "marked," "filled with colors as appropriate," or "colored. || 3 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) clarifies the very nature of being "washed" (dhauta) and so forth with the words: "svataḥ" (by itself). || 3 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He explains those [terms] in relation to the subject at hand:
"The inner controller, however, is the Lord of Māyā, who by means of subtle creation [manifests] from Himself."
The supreme one, whose essence is the Sūtra, is called Virāṭ by virtue of the gross creation alone.

Regarding the term "from itself" (*svataḥ*): the Supreme Self (*paraḥ paramātmā*), when devoid of *māyā* and its effects, is called "Consciousness" (*cit*). Through association with *māyā*, He is the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*). Through association with the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*), which is the aggregate of the effects of the unquintuplicated elements (*apañcīkṛtabhūta*), He is the Thread-Self (*sūtrātmā*). Through association with the gross body (*sthūlaśarīra*), which is the aggregate of the effects of the quintuplicated elements (*pañcīkṛtabhūta*), He is Virāṭ. || 4 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) applies this [analogy] to the subject at hand as well: "Cognition by itself" (*svataścit*). Now, an objection may be raised: "In a cloth woven from threads, 'being washed' (*dhautatva*) consists precisely in a specific refinement (*saṃskāra*) produced by the washerman through washing; whereas here, no such refinement is mentioned for cognition. Thus, there is a disparity. This is not so, because in that case, by the word "washed," what is intended is simply the possession of a natural white color residing in the cotton threads themselves.

Furthermore, regarding the activity of the aforementioned washerman, it is because he is employed there for the purpose of removing the refinement applied by the visiting weaver. It is with this very intention that the word *svataḥ* (by itself) is used as a factor establishing the commonality of purity in both cases. The phrase beginning with "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) connects with the subsequent term "sūtra" (thread). || 4 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, if the Supreme Self is the locus of the canvas, then the paintings supported by it must be specified;
therefore, he says:
"Living beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, as well as insentient objects..."
It exists through the relationship of superior and inferior, like a painting on a cloth. || 5 ||

Regarding the phrase "Brahmā and the others": the meaning here is that within this Supreme Self, all things—from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—whether sentient beings such as gods and so forth, or the collection of insentient things such as mountains and rivers existing in the relationship of superior and inferior, are like figures in a painting. || 5 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might object: "Granted that this Supreme Self, designated as 'Para,' is indeed Virāṭ through the specific limiting adjunct known as the gross creation; yet, where are the individual souls (vyaṣṭi-jīvas) imagined to reside, which are pervaded by the collective soul (samaṣṭi-jīva) denoted by the term Sūtrātman—that which is delimited by the adjuncts consisting of the subtle creation characterized by the five unquintuplicated great elements and their effects? Anticipating this doubt, the author provides a solution with an illustration, stating: "Brahmā and the others... [in this very place].

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is: "those for whom Brahmā, the four-faced one, is the first (ādya) or primary (prathama)"—this is according to the *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* type of *bahuvrīhi* compound, as in the example "bring the long-eared one" (*laṃbakarṇam ānaya*). He is indeed the first embodied being; he is indeed called the Puruṣa.
"He was the first creator of beings; Brahmā appeared in the beginning.

According to this Smṛti, even the Four-faced One (Brahmā) is merely a particular individual soul (*jīva-viśeṣa*). However, in the case of the *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* interpretation—just as in the expression "bring Citragu" and so forth—[the term refers to the one who possesses those qualities]. *The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, titled Citradīpa.* [End of fragment]

"Now, that which is indeed its *rājasa* (passionate) portion is this *brahman* who is the religious student (*brahmacārin*)," according to the Maitrāyaṇīya Śruti. The sense is that since he is the Lord (*īśvara*) by virtue of being a specific *līlā-vigraha* (sportive form) of the Illusory Lord (*māyī-īśvara*), it is precisely his exclusion [from the category of *brahman*] that is intended.
Now, if it is asked, "Even so, who can quell the doubt as to which of these two positions is superior?"—the answer is: "Brahman, indeed, is this... [and so forth].

The truth is this: in accordance with the unity of the Śruti passage, "In the beginning this was non-existent; then it knew only itself: 'I am Brahman. Therefore, it became all," the Smṛti usage of the word *brahman* as referring to the collective individual soul (*samaṣṭijīva*) and so forth is indeed the superior position. Otherwise, there would be a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*) in passages such as "the pillar" (*staṃba*) and others.
[Regarding the phrase] "living beings" and so on: this includes not only living beings but also insentient things like mountains. [Regarding the words] "excellent" and "cloth": here...
The syntactical connection is "it exists. || 5 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To state the reason for the world, beginning with Brahmā, being situated within consciousness, he provides an illustration:
"The various appearances of garments belonging to the figures depicted in a painting [are distinct from one another]."
They were fashioned as if from a cloth bearing a variegated pattern.
Regarding the word "citra" (in a painting): just as in a painting, the bodies of humans and others are depicted along with various types of garments endowed with diverse colors;
yet, because they do not ward off cold and so forth, they are merely semblances of garments. || 6 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, in response to the inquiry as to what the nature of living beings (*jīva*) is in this context, he provides an illustration in order to elaborate upon the theory of appearance (*ābhāsavāda*) which is about to be explained, in the two verses beginning with "citra" (verse 6). The phrase "by a painter" is to be understood as implicit.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the application to the subject at hand:
"The individual manifestations of consciousness (cidābhāsas) belong to those embodied beings who are superimposed upon consciousness."
These beings, designated by the name "living souls," transmigrate in many ways.

"Separately": thus, it is only for the bodies of gods and others superimposed upon the Supreme Self that individual reflections of consciousness (acidābhāsas) are postulated as the so-called living beings (jīvas), and not for mountains and such things. He states the reason for postulating them [for the former] with the word "in many ways" (bahudhā). The intention is that these living beings transmigrate in many ways through the acquisition of bodies as gods, animals, humans, and so forth, whereas the Supreme Self does not, because It is changeless (nirvikāritva). ||7||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): "Separately, separately" means that they are superimposed upon the consciousness of Brahman, which serves as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
"Of those possessing bodies" is the meaning. The ellipsis to be supplied is "is imagined through *māyā*. || 7 ||
Just as one perceives colors situated in the appearance of a cloth, even though they reside in the cloth that serves as their support.
Thus the ignorant speak; they consider the transmigratory existence of the individual soul (jīva) to be eternal.
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "Indeed, all disputants, both worldly and philosophical, maintain that transmigratory existence belongs to the Self alone;
what then is the cause of this? Suspecting that ignorance itself is the cause, he states it with an illustration: "Like the appearance of a cloth," etc. (Verse 8).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): What follows from this? He says—“vastrābhāsa” (the appearance of clothing). Just as ignorant and deluded people attribute the blue, yellow, and other colors residing in the mere appearance of clothing worn by gods, humans, and others depicted in a painted cloth to the underlying garment itself;

in exactly the same way, only fools perceive the agency and so forth residing in the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) within the transmigrating individual soul (jīva) as belonging to the pure Consciousness itself. || 8 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, he explains the absence of the conceptualization of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) in the case of mountain rivers and the like, supported by an illustration:
"In the case of mountains and such depicted in a painting, no reflection of cloth is drawn."
For the reflection of consciousness does not likewise exist in the clay and other elements situated within the creation. || 9 ||
Regarding the phrase "in the case of a painting": the sense is that there is no purpose [for such a distinction]. || 9 ||
The Sixth Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.

Commentary: Now, one might object: "Granted that this is so, do these individual souls (*jīvas*), which are of the nature of reflections of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), exist in insentient things such as clay and stone, or not? He dispels this doubt with an illustration, beginning with the words "In a painting" (*citrastha*). Nor, in that case, [is it the case that] trees and so forth situated in a painting...

It is not correct [to argue] that even names and the appearance of clothing would result in being lifeless like clay and so forth because they are merely written down; for by the word "etcetera," what is intended is only those things whose possession of life is not established by scripture and the like—such as clay and so on—whereas the fact that trees and such possess life is established by scriptures such as the *Mokṣadharma*, which states: "Therefore, trees smell [fragrance]," and so forth. This is the general direction of the argument. 9.
This saṃsāra is the ultimate reality, firmly attached to the substance of one's own self.
Thus, this delusion is ignorance; it is removed by knowledge.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Thus, in order to establish that transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), which is superimposed upon the Self, is to be removed by knowledge, he states its root cause, ignorance (avidyā), in the verse beginning with "saṃsāra. || 10 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, it was stated in the preceding verse that only the ignorant claim that transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) resides in the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), while it actually resides in the Self whose nature is pure Brahman.
To address the inquiry as to what kind of ignorance this is and to explain its essential nature, he says: "Transmigratory existence... (verse 10).
Rāma’s Commentary: In response to the inquiry as to what this knowledge is and what the means to its attainment are, he demonstrates the nature of that knowledge and the means to its attainment:
"Transmigration belongs to the individual soul (jīva), which is a reflection of the Self, and not to the reality of the Self."
Thus, awakening becomes knowledge; it is obtained through inquiry. || 11 ||
"Of the appearance of the self" means "of the appearance of consciousness. || 11 ||

What is that knowledge (vidyā)? To this he replies: "The Self" (ātma). Transmigration (saṃsāra) is the appearance of duality as if it were real. To the question of how that knowledge is obtained, he says: "It is obtained" (labhyate). || 11 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: It has been stated that knowledge is obtained through inquiry; anticipating the question of whose inquiry leads to the attainment of knowledge, he says:
"Therefore, one should always inquire into the world, the individual soul, and the Supreme Self."
When the states of being as a living soul and the states of the world are sublated, only one's own Self remains. || 12 ||

Regarding the word "sadā" (always): one might object, "Let the Supreme Self be investigated; since He abides as the fruit in the state of liberation, what use is there for an investigation of the individual soul and the world?

Anticipating this doubt, he says "jīvabhāva... [verse 12], explaining that the Supreme Self remains as the residue after the sublation (*apavāda*) of those two, and thus their investigation is indeed useful.

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "By investigating what object is this aforementioned form of knowledge attained? Anticipating this doubt, he states [the objects] with the words "sadā" (always). Just as in the delusion "this is a snake," it is precisely the rope, the object, and their mutual relation that must be investigated; there, when the snake and its relation are sublated by the light of a lamp through the destruction of the dense darkness, only the rope—which was the actual object—remains. In the same way, in the investigation...

The sense is that it is entirely appropriate to say that when the states of being an individual soul and the state of the world are sublated by means of the destruction of the aforementioned ignorance, one's own Self alone remains. || 12 ||
There is no sublation of those two due to non-apprehension; rather, there is the ascertainment of their falsity.
Otherwise, people would be liberated without effort during states such as deep sleep or fainting. || 13 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "If, through inquiry, the notions of the individual self (*jīva*) and the world (*jagat*) are sublated, then only one's own Self remains. One might then fear that if the individual self and the world are sublated by such inquiry, their non-perception would lead to the cessation of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Anticipating this, the author states "not non-perception" (*nāpratītiḥ*), explaining the intended meaning of the word "sublation" (*bādha*) and providing a refutation against the opposing view. [This is because] in states such as deep sleep or fainting, there is an absence of the perception of duality even on its own, without the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
The meaning is that there would be liberation. || 13 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, what is the meaning of the term "sublation" (*bādha*) here? To this, he says: "Not non-apprehension. Nor is this [the case].
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya [entitled *Citradīpa*]:

It is now argued that [the definition] is too narrow (*avyāpta*) because it does not apply to delusions such as nacre-silver or the rope-snake; for in those cases, although there is no perception of them as being delusions devoid of a substrate (*nirupādhi*),—

The intention is that [the practice] would not be free from the possibility of falling into the lower realms due to uncertainty regarding meditation. He states the refutation for the opposing view with the words "no cet" (if not); by the word "etc. (*ādi*), death and so forth are also included. || 13 ||
Even when only the Supreme Self remains, that is the ascertainment of its reality.
If there were no forgetting of the world, liberation while living (jīvanmukti) would not be possible.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: By the statement "only one's own Self remains," it is intended that the very knowledge of the reality of the Supreme Self is meant, and not the forgetting of the world as something distinct from It; for if the latter were the case, it would result in the undesirable consequence of there being no liberation while living (jīvanmukti). Thus he says: "The Supreme Self... (verse 14).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): [Objection: "If this is so, then since only one's own self remains, there is a contradiction with the non-duality (advaita) implied by the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) in the previous verse through its own words. [Reply: True. Even there, it is because a technical (pāribhāṣika) meaning is intended in exactly this way;
thus he says: "The Supreme Self" (*paramātman*). Furthermore, he states the sublation of the opposing view (vipakṣabādhaka) with the words beginning "If not" (*no cet*). || 14 ||
Knowledge born of inquiry is twofold: indirect and direct.
In that regard, this inquiry is concluded upon the attainment of direct knowledge. || 15 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Since it was stated that one should "always reflect," and given that this reflection might continue until the fall of the body, he states its limit with the verse beginning "parokṣa... (verse 15).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, it may be argued that since the root *jīv* is traditionally remembered as meaning "to sustain life" (*prāṇadhāraṇe*), and based on the etymology "the living one (*jīva*) is he who lives," liberation (*mukti*) for such a being is established; yet, even after this [realization], because it is a qualified illusion—like a mirage—and because all superimpositions are false, there remains the state characterized by the continuous contemplation of the non-dual Self, which precedes all visible phenomena utilized for the enjoyment of *prārabdha-karma* other than the root ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*). This [state] belongs to the *jīvanmukta*. [The text continues: ...of the *jīvanmukta*, which consists in the constant realization of the non-dual Self prior to all visible objects employed for the experience of the remaining *prārabdha* karma, distinct from the root ignorance, while all superimpositions are being sublated. [The text continues: ...is not contradicted by the fact that the body and so forth continue to appear due to the momentum of past impressions (*saṃskāra*). For it is well known that even after the cessation of the cause, the effect persists for some time due to residual momentum, as in the case of a potter’s wheel or a potter’s rod. Furthermore, the cessation of the body and its adjuncts occurs only when the momentum of the *prārabdha* karma is exhausted, not merely through the dawn of knowledge. Therefore, the state of the *jīvanmukta* is logically consistent. [The text continues: ...therefore, the state of the *jīvanmukta* is established. Moreover, the cessation of the body and its adjuncts does not occur simply upon the dawning of knowledge, but rather when the momentum of the *prārabdha* karma is spent. Consequently, the status of the *jīvanmukta* is free from contradiction. [The text continues: ...and thus the status of the *jīvanmukta* is proven. Furthermore, the dissolution of the body and its adjuncts does not happen immediately upon the rise of knowledge, but only when the force of the *prārabdha* karma has run its course. Hence, the condition of the *jīvanmukta* is entirely consistent with reason. [The text continues: ...and so the condition of the *jīvanmukta* is firmly established. Moreover, the falling away of the body and its accessories does not take place at the very moment of the awakening of knowledge, but rather when the impetus of the *prārabdha* karma is fully spent. Therefore, the state of the *jīvanmukta* is perfectly logical. [The text continues: ...thus the state of the *jīvanmukta* is demonstrated. Furthermore, the disintegration of the body and its adjuncts does not occur precisely at the onset of knowledge, but only once the momentum of the *prārabdha* karma has been exhausted. Consequently, the condition of the *jīvanmukta* is beyond reproach. [The text continues: ...and thus the status of the *jīvanmukta* is confirmed. Also, the destruction of the body and its accessories does not happen at the first flash of realization, but rather when the force of the *prārabdha* karma has come to an end. Moreover, the cessation of the body and its adjuncts does not occur simply upon the dawn of knowledge, but rather when the momentum of the *prārabdha* karma is spent. Consequently, the condition of the *jīvanmukta* is free from contradiction. [The text continues: ...and thus the status of the *jīvanmukta* is confirmed. Also, the destruction of the body and its accessories does not happen at the first flash of realization, but rather when the force of the *prārabdha* karma has come to an end. Therefore, the state of the *jīvanmukta* is perfectly sound. [The text continues: ...and so the status of the *jīvanmukta* is settled.
