Since there is no possibility of liberation being established otherwise, the determination of the reality of pure consciousness alone is the remaining of the Supreme Self; nevertheless, as enjoined in the preceding verse beginning with "one should always investigate," the investigation of the world and so forth is prescribed at all times.
However, that [investigation]—known as the scriptural mental inquiry into the Self and Brahman—is as follows: [The mental world consisting of the inquiry into the Self and Brahman...]

To resolve the doubt that this contradicts the statement in the *Dvaitaviveka*, "The teaching of the Śruti is that even that [knowledge] regarding the reality of the Buddha is to be abandoned," he establishes the twofold nature of the previously defined *vidyā* in general: "And it is indirect (*parokṣā*). He then states what follows from that: "Among those, the direct (*aparokṣā*)," etc. (15).
If one should say, "Brahman exists," that is merely indirect knowledge (parokṣajñāna).
If one cuts through [ignorance] with the realization "I am Brahman," that is called direct realization (sākṣātkāra). || 16 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: It has been stated that the knowledge born of inquiry is twofold, distinguished by being either indirect (parokṣa) or direct (aparokṣa). He now demonstrates the nature of both of these in succession, beginning with: "Brahman exists" (16).

Now, the commentary on that [verse] defines those two knowledges: "It exists," and so forth. And thus it is traditionally taught in sequence in the *Brahmavallī* and the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*: "If one knows that 'Brahman exists,' then they know him as truly existing."
And [it says]: "He knew only himself as 'I am Brahman'; therefore, he became all that. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10) || 16 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Thus, he promises the investigation into the true nature of the Self, which is the unique cause for the direct realization of the Self:
"For the sake of accomplishing that direct realization, the true nature of the Self is investigated."
By which he is immediately liberated from the entire cycle of existence. || 17 ||

Regarding the phrase "its direct realization": the connection with the preceding [verse] is that it is for the sake of accomplishing that direct realization by which a person is liberated immediately. || 17 ||

Commentary: Anticipating the objection, "How can the aforementioned direct realization (sākṣātkāra) come about?", [the author] indicates that it arises precisely from the discernment of the reality of the Self (ātmatattva-vivecana) and makes this formal declaration: "That direct realization... This refers to the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu). "By which direct realization" means by that realization through which... "All... means as many as there are—

The meaning is "due to that superimposition. According to the statement in the *Kalpataru*, the mental modification (*vṛtti*) which takes as its object the pure Brahman immediately brings about the cessation of itself and its other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). This means it occurs at the very same time as the final mental modification produced by the great Vedantic Mahāvākyas, which have been well-reflected upon according to one's own Vedic school and taught by a true Guru known as a Sākṣātkāra. One is liberated—that is, one becomes a *jīvanmukta*—in the manner previously described. Regarding the word "that" (*tat*): [it refers to the aforementioned state].

The meaning is: "for the sake of accomplishing such direct realization. Regarding the word *ātman*: this refers to the nature of the Self (*ātman*) which is uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time.

The syntactical connection is as follows: "it is distinguished" (*vivicyate*), meaning it is made known as being preceded by the falsity of duality superimposed upon it, by way of its separation from that superimposed duality. By supplying the word *na* ("not"), the natural state of being free from pride (*amānitva*) is illuminated. || 17 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: In order to ascertain the ultimate oneness of the conscious Self (cidātman), he points out the divisions of consciousness as they appear during the state of empirical transaction: "The immutable, Brahman, the individual soul (jīva), and the Lord (īśa)—thus consciousness is fourfold."
Just as the space within a jar and the great space [are one], so too are the space within water and the space within clouds.
Regarding the term "immutable" (kūṭastha): he provides an illustration for the fourfold nature of the one who is dependent on the Lord—namely, "the space within a jar," and so forth. || 18 ||

a0 Commentary—In this scripture, a statement that reveals the identity of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is called a "Great Statement" (*mahāvākya*). This is because the subject matter of the scripture consists solely of that [identity]. However, since it is impossible for those two—the individual soul and the Lord—to be one with their respective meanings (which are characterized by consciousness and are mutually contradictory as qualified entities) without accepting the function of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) known as *jahadajahatsvārthā* (partially abandoning and partially retaining the primary meaning), both their indicated (*lakṣya*) and expressed (*vācya*) meanings must be considered.

He indicates the two meanings of the word *dāra* in sequence with the words "kūṭastha" and so forth. Thus, here is the description of the author of this work, the teacher named Mādhava, during his earlier stage of life:
"He whose lineage is Bhāradvāja and whose Vedic branch is that of the Yajurveda."
He whose Sūtra is that of Bodhāyana is indeed the omniscient Mādhava;
for, based on the words of praise for him found within his own texts, [he is known] as a follower of the principal Yajurvedic branch called Taittirīya, according to the Sūtra of Bodhāyana.

It is precisely the Mahāvākya found in the Upaniṣads— namely, "He who is this person and he who is yonder in the sun, he is one"— that is intended to be analyzed here. This is because the word denoting the individual soul (jīva) is first encountered in that very passage, even though other Mahāvākyas from different recensions, such as "I am Brahman," also exist.
"Recited according to the dharma of one's own Vedic study, situated within the Vedānta of one's own Vedic branch, and protected by the tradition;
taught by a teacher who is a renunciant and a seer of the Supreme—that alone is the Great Saying (mahāvākya) which is the direct cause of liberation.
Since, according to these words of the venerable Sarvajñātmamuni, it is precisely that [Saying] belonging to one's own branch which effects liberation, in this present verse—

And because the sequence beginning with the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed what is perceived. Now, having raised the objection—"But how can the one, non-dual, self-luminous, infinite Consciousness be fourfold?"—the Teacher clarifies this by means of an illustration, stating "the space within a jar" (*ghaṭākāśa*), etc. The nature of the "space in water" (*jalākāśa*) and so forth, however, the Teacher will explain immediately hereafter. But [one might object]: "In the *Tattvaviveka*, the very nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) was already established in this way by these same [terms]:"
Endowed with the reflection of Brahman, which consists of consciousness and bliss,
that Prakṛti is twofold according to the qualities of Tamas, Rajas, and Sattva;
and through the purity or impurity of Sattva, these two are considered to be Māyā and Avidyā.
"Having brought that [māyā] under control by means of the reflection of māyā, one becomes the omniscient Lord;
but another, being subject to ignorance (avidyā), is manifold due to its various diversities.
Thus, the final meaning here is exactly as I have stated while treating this very doctrine in the *Bodhaikyasiddhi*:
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya states: "Avidyā is that in which the quality of sattva is overwhelmed by rajas and tamas; Māyā is not so.
The individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) are respectively the forms of its reflections upon the pure consciousness of Brahman-Ātman."
[This is called the *Citradīpa*.

Therein, the meaning is that [the Self] possesses the nature of a reflection within ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth. The words "Brahman" and so on are merely qualifiers of pure consciousness (*śuddhacit*).
Here, moreover, at the commencement of the composition—]

"Just as a cloth is washed, beaten, marked, and dyed, so too is the Inner Controller (antaryāmī), the Thread-Self (sūtrātman), and the Virāṭ-Self described. Having begun thus, [it continues]: "But the Inner Controller is inherently the possessor of Māyā due to his subtle creation."
It was stated [previously]: "This Supreme One, whose essence is the Sūtra, is called Virāṭ for the sake of gross creation.
Now, however, He is described as "the Immutable" (kūṭastha) and so forth. How is it that these three systems of exposition are not mutually contradictory?

If it is argued that this is also the view of the Ācārya, it is replied as follows: In the *Tattvaviveka*, the venerable Vidyāraṇyācārya described the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) according to his own conviction;

that very same [view] has been set forth by me in the *Bodhaikyasiddhi* following the tradition of the ancient teachers. According to that, the Brahman-consciousness reflected in *prakṛti*—which is another name for root-ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) and is characterized by the quality of *sattva* overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*—is the individual soul (*jīva*). That same [Brahman-consciousness] reflected in the portion of that [ignorance] characterized by *sattva* that is not so overwhelmed is the [Lord].

The term "Lord" (*īśvara*) is indeed so. In this context, it refers to the Supreme Lord Śrī Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda and his disciple Śrī Sureśvarācārya—known as the author of the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārtika* on the Sūtras—who are incarnations of Hari, Hara, and Caturānana (Brahmā). Since this non-dualistic (*advaita*) system is composed by these three sages, who are like the three grammatical systems (*trimuni-vyākaraṇa*), it follows the maxim: "Among the sages, authority increases in descending order. Thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) as taught by him [Sureśvara] is the most authoritative. Śrī...

In order to indicate his agreement with the *Ābhāsa-vāda* (the theory of reflection) favored by the author of the *Carama-muni-vārtika*, and for the sake of making it easy for those desiring to know (*bubhutsu*) to ascend the path of understanding through two distinct methods using examples such as the painted cloth and the space within a jar, this exposition was composed out of incomparable compassion. Among these, the *Ābhāsa-vāda* favored by the venerable author of the *Vārtika* has been stated in the *Siddhāntabindu*: "The Self conditioned by ignorance (*ajñāna*), having attained identity with that ignorance..."

The venerable Vārttikakāra [Sureśvara] states that, due to the non-discrimination (*aviveka*) from the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), the inner controller (*antaryāmī*), the witness (*sākṣī*), and the cause of the world are so designated; and because the intellect (*buddhi*) is superimposed upon it, through the non-discrimination from its own reflection of consciousness which has attained identity with that [intellect], it is called the individual soul (*jīva*), the agent, the enjoyer, and the knower.
This very position is termed the "Theory of Reflection" (*ābhāsavāda*). Furthermore, the definition of "reflection" (*ābhāsa*) has been stated by me in the *Bodhaikyasiddhi* itself.

Right at the beginning of the *Pratibimbavāda* (the theory of reflection), the author of the *Prakaṭārthavivaraṇa* presents his own view regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). This is consistent even with scriptural statements such as "which creates the two—[the soul and the Lord]—from the appearance of heaven" (*svargāvabhāsa*), and so forth. Furthermore, "being a reflection" (*ābhāsatva*) means that while its existence is dependent (*nighnasattve*), it is merely a semblance equal to that [original].

According to Amarasimha’s lexicon, "dependent" (*nighna*) is synonymous with "subordinate" (*adhīna*) and "subject to" (*āyatta*); thus, the meaning is "while its existence is subject to [another]. In this way, the status of being a reflection and the status of being a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) are also [established].

In that very context it is observed: that which does not sublate the error induced by its own cognition is an *upādhi* (limiting adjunct) by virtue of its remoteness. For its essential nature (*tattva*) consists in being a superimposer of its own attributes;

this is seen in the case of the face and so forth, with respect to the mirror and other such objects. "Its essential nature" means, in short, its status as an *upādhi*. And thus, according to the view of the author of the *Vārttika*, it is beyond dispute that the intellect (*buddhi*) alone is accepted as the *upādhi* of the individual soul (*jīva*). Furthermore, in the *Tattvaviveka*, that [intellect] is described as both pure and impure—

It has been stated that [the subtle body] is produced from the fivefold sattva-portion of the five gross elements—such as ether and sound—which have not yet undergone quintuplication (*apañcīkṛta*), and which are the transformations of the third portion known as *tamas*; this third portion is itself distinguished from the two portions of *prakṛti* called *māyā* and *avidyā*, which consist of the pairs of *sattva*-predominant and *mūla-avidyā* (also named *māyā-avidyā*).
Thus it is said: "But another [individual soul], subject to *avidyā*, becomes manifold through its various diversities."

Regarding the first half of the verse, "That [state] would be the causal body; therein the Prājña possesses self-conceit," it must necessarily be stated that the nature of the individual soul (jīva) described there refers only to the period of dissolution during which the collective unmanifest (samaṣṭy-avyākṛta) is designated as the individual deep sleep (suṣupti). This is because it is understood exactly so from the second half of the verse beginning with "sā" (that), which follows immediately thereafter.
"By the command of the Lord, for the sake of his enjoyment, the elements— space, air, fire, water, and earth— were born from primordial nature (prakṛti) in which darkness (tamas) predominates."

accompanied by the two commentaries.

This is because of such passages as these, and because of the logic of the aforementioned creation. Therefore, since in the state of unmanifestedness (*avyākṛta-daśā*) the three parts of *prakṛti*—known as the root ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) and so forth—exist only in a state of unified identity, and since the individual soul (*jīva*) is not produced [by them], knowledge must necessarily exist even at that time; thus, [the process of] creation...

In the state of manifestation (*vyaktadaśā*), that *sattva* which has evolved into the form of the intellect (*buddhi*) according to the aforementioned method is likewise overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*, because it is an effect of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) dominated by *tamas* and because it has entered the state of creation. Thus, such a nature of ignorance (*avidyātva*) exists even in the manifest intellect; and in that ignorance which has entered the unmanifest state (*avyākṛtadaśā*), there exists the intellect in the form of an extremely subtle latent impression (*saṃskāra*), the existence of which is established by the fact that otherwise the beginninglessness of the individual soul (*jīva*) would be untenable.

Since the nature of *rūpa* (form) is also logical, the uniformity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is established according to both the views of the *Vārttika* and the *Tattvaviveka*. Thus, even in the *Vārttika* school, although the *Siddhāntabindu* describes the theory of reflection (*ābhāsavāda*) as involving "exclusive indication" (*jahallakṣaṇā*), it subsequently mentions "inclusive-exclusive indication" (*jahadajahallakṣaṇā*), which is accepted by all.

Consequently, the theory of reflection (*pratibimbavāda*) favored by the *Tattvaviveka* also ultimately culminates in that aforementioned *ābhāsavāda*, because the portion consisting of the limiting adjuncts is false (*mithyātva*).

Even in the theory of reflection (*pratibimbavāda*), it ultimately results in the theory of non-appearance (*abhāsavāda*); thus, the identity of the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) as a superimposed entity has already been stated, and that [identity] of the two is indeed logical. Similarly, although in the *Tattvaviveka* it appears as if there is a difference—since Māyā alone is said to be the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of Īśvara according to the Vārtika school, whereas Avidyā is stated [to be so]—nevertheless, when investigation is conducted, [the conclusion follows] from the scriptural text: "And Māyā is of the nature of darkness."
"Salutation to that one whose nature is knowledge, the immeasurable, by fixing the mind upon whom the yogi crosses over the vast expanse of ignorance and illusion."

And because of this traditional teaching (*smṛti*), since *māyā* is sublated by knowledge, it is established as *avidyā*; and since *avidyā* serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the Lord (*īśvara*) and consists primarily of pure *sattva*, it is also established as *māyā*. Thus, in both systems, the limiting adjunct of the Lord being of one and the same nature, the Lord—the Witness (*sākṣin*) conditioned by that adjunct—is indeed one and the same. Where, then, is there even a scent of contradiction between the *Tattvaviveka* and the *Citradīpa*? Likewise, in the *Kośaviveka*:
“Through the entry of its own reflection, that power shines as if it were conscious.
Through union with the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of that power, Brahman itself attains the state of the Lord (Īśvara).
When the sheath (kośa) is intended as the limiting adjunct, Brahman itself becomes the individual soul (jīva).”
"Father and grandfather are one, just as son and grandson are [one] in relation to each other. Also, in the *Dvaitaviveka*:
"That which is consciousness as the substrate, and that which is the subtle body (liṅgadeha)..."

The reflection of consciousness (cicchāyā) residing in the subtle body (liṅgadeha), together with its [mental] aggregate, is called the individual soul (jīva). Just as Māheśvarī possesses the power of manifestation (nirmāṇa-śakti), she also possesses the power of delusion (moha-śakti); she deludes that very soul.

Furthermore, it should be understood that those statements which set forth the true nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth ultimately culminate in the theory of appearance (*ābhāsa-vāda*), as intended by their purport; this is the secret, owing to the natural force of the term *cicchāyā* (the reflection of consciousness). Moreover, the two methods presented for clarifying the theory of appearance through analogies such as the painted cloth and the space within a jar are likewise entirely consistent. To explain: therein, first, that which corresponds to pure Brahman is the *dhauta-* [cloth].

The cloth and the great space are indeed joined; however, the doubt as to how the water-space— which corresponds to the Lord— is like a struck cloth will be refuted right here at the outset, even with censure.

"Predominated by *tamas* among the fields (*kṣetra*), and predominated by consciousness among the conscious selves (*citātman*), it becomes the supreme cause through [the cultivation of] meditation, knowledge, and action"— thus did the author of the *Vārttika* [state] the causality of both the insentient and the sentient.
If it is argued that these [attributes] are stated of the *paramātman* alone and not of the *īśvara*, we say no;
for here too there is mutual superimposition (*anyonyādhyāsa*), just as between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the immutable witness (*kūṭastha*).
Sureśvara, having taken for granted the identity of Īśvara and Brahman, declares this in the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya: [verse 140]
"Truth, knowledge, and infinite—that Brahman from which [the world] has arisen:
ether, air, fire, water, earth, herbs, food, and the body," so says the Śruti.
From the perspective of superficial observation, the causality of Brahman appears therein.
Because the cause is real, a mutual superimposition (adhyāsa) is therefore accepted;

this [superimposition] consists of mutual superimposition, just like a cloth smeared with turmeric [appears as red]. Through friction it attains oneness, and in that same way, through delusion, it has attained oneness.
"The cloud and the sky, as well as the great sky, are not distinguished by the ignorant;
likewise, those who perceive only the surface see the identity of Brahman and Īśvara."
In this way, just as the illustration of the Lord was clarified, so too is the illustration of the living being and the world clarified:
"Just as a cloth, though marked on all sides, might be rubbed [to remove the marks],
so too is the body of the Lord marked everywhere with subtle forms."
Just as grain or a variety of vegetables sprout forth from every side,
so too is this delicate sprout of the world;
it is like a cloth filled with colors, or like a world where the light of the sun has not yet appeared.
"Just as a crop when it has borne fruit, so too does Virāṭ shine forth with a manifest form.
Regarding the phrase "with subtle forms," the meaning is "with subtle *liṅga*-bodies. [This concludes the section from the work titled] *Citradīpa*.

By this, the superimposition of the *sūtrātman*, who identifies with the collective subtle body (*samaṣṭiliṅgaśarīra*), is indicated. And thus it is said: "The Self is like the reflection of a cloth. "Just as the space within a jar is entirely concealed by the space of the water, so too is the immutable (*kūṭastha*) [Self] [concealed] by the individual soul (*jīva*); this is called mutual superimposition."
Thus, it should be understood that both the superimposition of the individual soul (*vyaṣṭijīva*) and the superimposition of the entire world (*jagadadhyāsa*) have been illuminated.
This has also been explained by me, along with inquiries, in the *Bodhaikyasiddhi* under the section titled "Refuting the Contradiction Between the Two Methods of the *Citradīpa*."

In the *Citradīpa*, Vidyāraṇya speaks— conforming to the Vedas and cherished by the Vārtikācārya— to instruct those of fragmented intellect as to whether the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) is the Lord or not; for if it were the former, there would be a loss of its being the Self, and if the latter, there would be no experience of reality.
The doctrine of manifestation (*ābhāsavāda*) is clearly explained through two types of reasoning, joined with fourfold arguments; first,
by means of the illustration of a variegated cloth, and subsequently through examples such as the space within a jar, reflections in water, and the shadow of that [jar] cast upon the sky.

The fourfold nature of consciousness has been declared through the distinctions of the immutable (kūṭastha), the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśa), and pure Brahman; yet the unreality of these two—the jīva and the īśa—is established in every way.
Here, when the cloth is washed, it is the Brahman that is clearly revealed, even as it is joined together.
In an instant, the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī) is again depicted along with the Sūtra;
the Virāṭ is filled with syllables, and above that, the individual soul (Jīva) is considered to resemble the appearance of a cloth. Therefore, there is no fivefold nature of consciousness (Cit).
Listen to the unity of these two auspicious paths, which is proclaimed as the "markedness" (*lāñchitatva*) by the *Citraśāyyā*.
[Page 141] The Sixth Chapter.
Accompanied by two commentaries: "Therefore, where in the thread could there be an appearance of a cloth? That which is here, in its own state of equilibrium, is the very life-force (jīva).
The appearance of the cloth is merely the arrangement of lines; there is no disagreement on this point."

Likewise, how indeed can the individual soul (jīva) be superior even to the collective totality (sūtra), which is like a cloth filled with colors? This Virāj is said to occupy the place of the world; yet even that must be investigated, for it is as follows:
Let it be so; this resolution is appropriate regarding the individual soul and the world.
Nevertheless, what would it be for the Lord? For He too is entirely equal [to them].
However, there is this much distinction from the nature of the Lord as previously described:
In the second [state], that form appears as if supreme to the ignorant mind;

this one who was previously described as "the Illusionist" (māyī), like a garment being shaken out, is here the Great Lord known as the Inner Ruler (antaryāmī), reflected within the impressions of the intellect.

It has been said that this [intellect] is like the sky reflected in a dense cloud; even there, if it is contemplated, not even a particle of difference exists between the two. Indeed, the distinction is merely a matter of perspective.
For the intellect is considered to be nothing but lines, and thus the collection of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) resides upon the canvas of the mind.
Those who are born when [the intellect] is thoroughly churned—does he not discern them by means of them?

Thus, they too reside within the single Māyā which is the nature of the collective intellect; therefore, what distinction could there be between that [Māyā] and the reflected [objects], once they are defined as being delimited?

Surely the *Bhāmatī*-author has declared the individual soul (*jīva*) to be delimited, and this same "reflected self" (*praticchāyātman*) has been stated by the *Vivaraṇa*-author and others as well; therefore, how could there not be a difference [between them]?
It is not so, for it arises from a failure to grasp the heart of both positions. Thus, this path has been set forth here by our teachers for the sake of being accepted by both.
It must be stated: how could that which is immutable (kūṭastha) ever be established as being like a jar or a potsherd on the path of transmigration?
For when a cloth appears upon a painting or the like, is that cloth not merely that [appearance], even if it is pure?
When a teacher says, "This is a thief; he is indeed a post," the notion of a thief arises through the cognition of a post.
"Just as in this world [the snake] is sublated by the [rope-]vision, so too is that which is highly esteemed [as the self] sublated by the sentence 'That thou art' and others.
Only when such sublation occurs can there be a common substratum for the two;
thus, through the association of the reflection with the Pure [Self], there arises the calculation of worldly existence, and from this follows the distinction between the bound and the liberated."
The detailed exposition on this point should be understood from my own commentary titled *Advaitātmaprabodha*; this is the direction [for further study].

Thus, here the immutable (*kūṭastha*) conscious Self (*cidātmā*), characterized by witnesshood (*sākṣitva*), is the purified referent of the term "thou" (*tvaṃpadārtha*). The individual soul (*jīva*), which is the literal meaning of the term "thou," is merely the reflection of that consciousness in the intellect (*buddhi*)—which is itself a construction of root ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*)—and is therefore entirely false. It has been cited as an illustration for the immutable Self.

The space within a jar (*ghaṭākāśa*) is delimited by the appearance of a cloth, as is the pure cloth itself. In the case of the individual soul (*jīva*), however, it is precisely like the great space reflected in water filled with the space of a jar, and likewise like the appearance of a cloth. Similarly, Brahman is indeed pure non-dual consciousness alone; it is the purified referent of the word *tat*. In this regard, the analogies are the great space and the washed cloth. The Lord (*Īśvara*), on the other hand, is in every respect merely that reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) reflected in the root-ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) superimposed upon that [Brahman].

The meaning denoted by that term is indeed false. In this regard, the illustrations are the great space reflected in water limited by clouds, and a cloth that has been folded. The *sūtrātman*, the collective individual soul (*samaṣṭijīva*), the cosmic person (*virāṭ*), and the gross world and so forth—therein the illustration is simply a cloth that has been marked and dyed. Just as in such expressions as "He who is a thief is a post," where there is no thief at all but only a post exists, so too, in the case of sublation (*bādhā*), while the individual soul and the rest truly exist, there is a co-referentiality with Brahman.

The locus of the objection: In another view, the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of Īśvara, designated as *māyā* and so forth, is indeed the sheath of bliss and fear; [this is established] through the definition of partial exclusion (*bhāgatyāga-lakṣaṇā*).

The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya [the chapter titled *Citradīpa*] has already been discussed above. To summarize: the theories of the "delimited reflection" (*avacchinna-pratibimba-vāda*) and the "reflected reflection" (*pratibimba-pratibimba-vāda*) are also included within this very [theory]. || 18 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Since the space delimited by a jar (*ghaṭākāśa*) and the great space not so delimited (*mahākāśa*) are well known, he sets those aside and explains the less familiar "space of water" (*jalākāśa*):
"The water within the space delimited by a jar is that in which [the sun] is reflected."
The sky with its clouds and stars is called the "water-sky. || 19 ||

Regarding the phrase "delimited by a jar" (*ghaṭāvacchinna*): the water that exists within the space delimited by a jar reflects the sky along with its clouds and stars; this reflected sky within the water is called "the space of the water" (*jalākāśa*). || 19 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "In the illustrations provided for the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), what are these 'water-space' and 'cloud-space'? Therefore, he explains those two according to his own view with the following two verses beginning with "ghaṭāvacchinna... (19).
Rāghavabhaṭṭa’s Commentary: He explains the ether of clouds (abhra-ākāśa):
"That which is seen as a circle of clouds in the midst of the great ether (mahākāśa)..."
By way of being a reflection, the cloud and the sky are situated there in the water.
"Of the great space" means: in that circle of clouds, within the water that is there—this is the meaning. || 20 ||
Commentary on verse 20: Regarding the phrase "of the great space" and so forth, the connection is that [the reflection] exists there in the water as a reflection. ||20||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Since the water of the clouds is not perceived, how can there be knowledge of the sky being reflected therein?
Anticipating this, he says: "The water, which is a portion of the cloud, exists in the form of frost."
In that case, this reflection in the sky is inferred from its lack of wateriness. || 21 ||

Regarding the phrase "meghāṃśa" (a portion of the cloud): although the water residing in the cloud is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), its existence as a subtle constituent form of water is inferred from the effect characterized by rain. Furthermore, by the very mark (*liṅga*) of being water, its state of possessing a reflection is also established. Through the inference: "The subject under dispute is water that must possess the reflection of the sky, because it is water, like water contained in a jar," the presence of the reflection of the sky is established even in the water that constitutes a portion of the cloud.
The meaning is that this is understood by you. || 21 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, what is the proof for this? To address this, he says: "meghāṃśeti" (by the rays of the clouds). The intention is that whatever is water possesses a reflection of the sky, because of its nature as water; this pervasion (vyāpti) is observed in the case of the sky reflected in water. || 21 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus explained the fourfold ether as the illustrative example, he now explains the *kūṭastha* (the immutable), which was mentioned first among the subjects of illustration:
"The consciousness delimited by the two bodies [as their] substrate."
He who remains unchanging like a mountain peak is called "kūṭastha" (the immovable). || 22 ||

Regarding the term "substratum" (*adhiṣṭhāna*): because it exists as the support for the two bodies—the gross and the subtle—which are effects of the fivefold and non-fivefold elements and are imagined by ignorance (*avidyā*), the Self delimited by those two is called the "immutable" (*kūṭastha*). He states the reason for applying the word "immutable" in this context: "like a peak" (*kūṭavat*) || 22 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, even if this is so, the object designated as *kūṭastha* (the immutable), which was mentioned first in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), is likewise non-worldly (*alaukika*).

Therefore, he explains that very term according to his own intended meaning: "The substratum" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and "immutable" (*kūṭa*). Regarding "immutable" (*kūṭa*): [it is used] in the sense of a battle, a mountain peak, or the pole of a plow.
[Page 143]
The Sixth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
According to Amara’s lexicon, “*kūṭa* is not feminine,” the meaning is that like a solid mass of gold or similar material, one remains without change even when subjected to a hundred blows. || 22 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus established the immutable (kūṭastha), he now establishes the individual soul (jīva) by means of its being a reflection of consciousness superimposed upon that immutable, since it follows the nature of the intellect reflected therein: "The intellect is superimposed upon the immutable; therein lies the reflection of consciousness."
Through the maintenance of the vital breaths, that living being is joined with saṃsāra. || 23 ||

Regarding the term "immutable" (*kūṭastha*): he states the reason for its being designated by the word "living being" (*jīva*) with the words "of the vital breaths" (*prāṇānām*). Anticipating the objection that postulating a living being distinct from the immutable is unnecessary, he says "by transmigratory existence" (*saṃsāreṇa*), meaning that such a being must be admitted for the sake of explaining how transmigratory existence—which is impossible for the immutable—is possible for one who undergoes modification. || 23 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, he also explains the *jīva* as he himself intends it—starting with the words "kūṭa" and "cit. The term "cit" means a contemptible reflection, that is, one that is entirely illusory (*mithyā*). Regarding the phrase "of the vital breaths" (*prāṇānām*), there is indeed a traditional rule (*smaraṇam*) stating: "The *jīva* is so called because it sustains the vital breaths (*prāṇa-dhāraṇa*). || 23 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "If there exists an immutable reality distinct from the individual soul (jīva), why does it not manifest?
Anticipating this doubt, he states—with an illustration—that it is because [the immutable] is concealed by the individual soul.
Just as the space within a jar is entirely concealed by the water and the outer sky.
In the same way, that which is immutable [is superimposed] upon the individual soul; this is called mutual superimposition. || 24 ||

[The opponent] objects: "But surely this concealment (tirodhāna) is not propounded anywhere in the scriptures. Anticipating this doubt, he says, "That is mutual superimposition (anyonyādhyāsa)," meaning that it is not so, because it is designated by that term [in the scriptures]. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "It is stated in the Bhāṣya and other works. ||24||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Therein, he makes known the reason for their mutual superimposition by saying "jala" (water). The meaning is: "the aforementioned water and space. || 24 ||
This individual soul never distinguishes [itself from] the immutable.
Let it be understood that this beginningless non-discrimination is root-ignorance (mūlāvidyā). || 25 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that this very non-perception of difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the immutable self (kūṭastha) during the state of worldly existence must be stated as the cause of the ignorance (avidyā) that constitutes bondage.
Anticipating this, he says "This" (verse 25), asserting that the very failure to perceive the distinction between the jīva and the kūṭastha is indeed ignorance.

The reason for this is stated as "this" (ayam). The syntactical connection is: "Let it be understood that this beginningless non-discrimination is indeed root-ignorance (mūlāvidyā). By this, the Sāṃkhyas and others are refuted; such is the truth. || 25 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To clarify that the previously mentioned individual soul (jīva) is a conceptual construction of ignorance (avidyā), he analyzes ignorance as follows:
Ignorance is established as twofold, consisting of the forms of projection (vikṣepa) and concealment (āvṛti).
The superimposition that "the immutable does not shine" or "does not exist" is concealment (āvṛti). || 26 ||

Regarding "distraction" (vikṣepa): because it is more important as a cause of distraction, he defines obscuration (āvaraṇa) first. "It does not appear" means that obscuration is the cause for the conventional usage [of the thought] that "the immutable [Self] does not appear," "it is not manifest," or "it does not exist. || 26 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "But mutual superimposition is well-established everywhere as the relation between the substrate and the object superposed, and its identity with that [substrate] therein; how then can it be ignorance? To this he says: "Vikṣepa... Thus, the meaning is that the aforementioned superimposition is indeed of the nature of *vikṣepa* (projection). He states the concealment (*āvṛtti*): "Not... (26).
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 144.

[From the *Citradīpa*, Rāma’s Commentary:]— Now, raising the objection, "What is the proof for the existence of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the veil created by it?", he states that it is simply the experience of the world: *nanvavidyāyāstatkṛtāvaraṇasya ca sadbhāve kiṃ pramāṇamityāśaṅkya lokānubhava evetyāha-* (Rāma’s Commentary) — Now, raising the objection, "What is the proof for the existence of ignorance and the veil created by it?",
he states that it is simply the experience of the world.
An ignorant person, when questioned by a wise one, does not awaken to the immutable reality.
Having realized that the immutable does not shine and does not exist, one speaks even while [knowing this]. || 27 ||

"An ignorant person": when a learned man asks an ignorant person, "Do you know the immutable (kūṭastha)?", the ignorant person, having experienced ignorance, says, "I do not know it. This is the experience of avidyā (ignorance). Not only does he express the experience of ignorance itself, but he also says, "The immutable neither exists nor appears," having experienced both the non-existence and the non-appearance of the immutable. This is the experience of āvaraṇa (veiling). Therefore, the meaning is that in both cases, direct experience is the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). ||27||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, raising the objection that the attainment of the Veda is observed [in the world], the author provides the resolution—that it is indeed based on worldly experience—and clarifies this with the verse beginning "The ignorant one" (ajñānī). The construction is as follows: when an ignorant person is asked by a learned man, "O Devadatta, do you know the Immutable One (kūṭastha)? and he replies "No," it means that he does not perceive, nor indeed knows, the Immutable One. For this very reason, it is said that the Immutable One neither exists nor appears [to him].

And even though one has understood that [object] in a general way through its self-luminosity, one speaks of the two kinds of obscuration regarding it—namely, those consisting of the distinction between the unreal and so forth;
such is the logical connection. || 27 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection may be raised: according to your view, since the Self is self-luminous, ignorance (avidyā) cannot logically exist within it; for, like light and darkness, their natures are mutually contradictory, and thus a relationship between them is untenable. In the absence of ignorance, the obscuration caused by it would be impossible to define. In its absence, the projection (vikṣepa) rooted in that obscuration could not occur. And in the absence of projection, there would be no evil to be removed by knowledge (jñāna), and thus [knowledge would be purposeless].
Fearing that, consequently, the scriptural authority establishing that [Self] would be rendered useless, he says—showing that all this is sublated by the previously mentioned experience:
"How can there be ignorance regarding that which is self-luminous? Without it, how could there be concealment?"
This direct self-experience devours such webs of reasoning as these. || 28 ||
"Self-luminous" (svaprakāśa): the sense is that, according to the maxim "for what is actually perceived, nothing is impossible," there can be no contradiction. || 28 ||

Commentary (a0): [The opponent] objects, "But this contradicts your own established doctrine," with the words "sva" (one's own). [The author] replies that this objection does not arise because it contradicts experience, with the words "ityādi" (and so forth); the meaning is that this [objection] was already refuted previously. || 28 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that since experience is fallacious due to its contradiction by the aforementioned reasoning, reality cannot be ascertained through it.

Anticipating this, [the author] states that if the validity of experience is not accepted, then because the logician himself has admitted that mere reasoning is non-conclusive, there could never be an ascertainment of reality for a logician anywhere.
If there is no confidence in one's own experience, then even reasoning would lack a firm foundation.
Or how could one who considers himself a logician attain certainty regarding reality? || 29 ||
"In one's own experience," [it is said]. || 29 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that since experience—like dreams and the like—can be illusory, it cannot serve as a subverter of reasoning that supports valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Anticipating this, the author provides a rebuttal by way of a counter-argument, based on the Sūtra "Because reasoning is not established" (*tarkāpratiṣṭhānāt*), stating: "In one's own experience... The sense is that even in the position of the logicians (*tārkika*), the lack of certainty regarding reality remains exactly as it was. ||29||

Rāma’s Commentary (rā॰ ṭīkā): Now, one might raise the objection: "Surely experience alone is the determiner of reality; nevertheless, reasoning (tarka) must also be accepted for the sake of knowing the possibility of the object being experienced. Having restated this doubt, he says: "In that case, reasoning should be described only in accordance with experience, and not in contradiction with it."
The Sixth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
If reasoning were required for the ascent to awakening, then that being the case—
Let it be reasoned according to one's own direct experience; let it not be subjected to fallacious reasoning.
"For the sake of ascending to the intellect. || 30 ||

Commentary on 145a: Now, he [the opponent] releases the counter-objection with the words "buddhi" (intellect). The proponent, by accepting that [point], instructs him with the word "tathā" (so it is). || 30 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: In response to the inquiry, "What is this experience (anubhava) in accordance with which reasoning (tarka) is to be described?", he recalls the previously mentioned experience concerning the domain of ignorance (avidyā) and so forth:
"One's own experience regarding ignorance and concealment has been demonstrated."
Therefore, let it be reasoned that immutable consciousness is not contradictory [to the self]. || 31 ||
Regarding "one's own experience": he states the conclusion with the words "therefore" (ataḥ). || 31 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): If this is so, then what is one's own experience (*svānubhūti*) in this regard? To this he says: "One's own" (*sva*). He states the conclusion: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). || 31 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He demonstrates that very argument by means of dramatic representation:
"If that is so, let this veil indeed be experienced as being sublated by its contradictory."
Discernment, however, is its opposite; let it be observed in one who possesses the knowledge of reality. || 32 ||

Regarding the phrase "tacced" (if that [consciousness]): the point is that if consciousness alone—which is the very agent that effects the veiling by ignorance—were the opponent of that [ignorance], then the manifestation of ignorance itself would not occur.
If one asks, "In that case, what is the opponent of ignorance?", he says: "viveka" (discrimination). Discrimination is the knowledge produced by the inquiry into the Upaniṣads.
To the question, "Where is the opposition of discrimination to ignorance observed?", he says: "tattvajñānini" (in the knower of reality). || 32 ||

Commentary (a0): He states the logical necessity—that it cannot be otherwise—for the non-contradiction of ignorance with the immutable consciousness (*kūṭasthacaitanya*): "If that [consciousness]... Then, he asks what its opposite is and answers: "Discrimination (*viveka*), however... || 32 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus shown the concealment by ignorance (avidyā), he now describes the superimposition of projection (vikṣepādhyāsa):
"In the immutable consciousness concealed by ignorance, there is the consciousness associated with the two bodies."
For it is indeed a superimposition of projection (vikṣepādhyāsa) that silver is superimposed upon mother-of-pearl.

Regarding the term *avidyā*: the meaning is that the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), accompanied by the grossly characterized subtle body, which is superimposed upon the immutable inner self (*pratyagātman*) that possesses the previously mentioned veil of ignorance (*avidyāvaraṇa*), is the superimposition of projection (*vikṣepādhyāsa*). || 33 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, regarding this beginningless non-discrimination (*aviveka*), which was introduced as "root ignorance" (*mūlāvidyā*), it has been stated that this root ignorance is established in two forms by way of distraction (*vikṣepa*) and concealment (*āvaraṇa*). Between these two aforementioned states, distraction [is preceded] by concealment.

Having first established that [the Self is] the Witness, he now defines *vikṣepa* (projection) with the words "ignorance" (*avidyā*). Since it will be stated later that "there is no difference between the immutable [Self] and Brahman except in name," here, in the context of ignorance, its concealment, and the projection caused by them, the substrate is understood by the term "immutable" (*kūṭastha*) to be Brahman itself.
*Citi* is the reflection of consciousness in the intellect, i.e., the semblance of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*). The word "indeed" (*hi*) means that this is well-known in the scriptures. || 33 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: To establish that this mental projection (vikṣepa) is indeed a superimposition (adhyāsa), he demonstrates its similarity to the superimposition of silver upon mother-of-pearl:
"The 'this'-aspect possesses reality, while the silver is perceived as residing in the mother-of-pearl."
Thus, both its own nature and its substantiality are seen to be distinct from the state of distraction.

And as for the "this" portion: just as the quality of being situated in the front region and so forth, as well as non-sublatability, which reside in the mother-of-pearl, [are present] in the superimposed object.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[the chapter] titled Citradīpa (The Lamp of the Painting).

The meaning is that, although the selfhood and substantiality reside eternally in the immutable [Self], they appear as if inherent in the superimposed reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa). || 34 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, raising the objection, "How can this be superimposition? and having analyzed its causal factors in the illustrative example, the author reveals them in the case under discussion as well—beginning with the words "And the 'this'-portion. [The reflection] belongs to another [the mirror], while [the consciousness] resides in the immutable (Kūṭastha). || 34 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus demonstrated the perception of the common aspect in both cases, he shows the equality of the perception of the specific aspect:
"Just as the blueness, back-surface, and triangularity are concealed in mother-of-pearl."
Thus, even in the immutable (kūṭastha), non-attachment, bliss, and so forth are concealed.
"Blue," [it is said]. || 35 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭī0): He states another set of conditions for that equanimity in two verses beginning with "nīla" (blue). By the word "ādi" (and so forth), Brahmanhood is included. ||35||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He shows another example of similarity: "Just as in the illustration, that which is superimposed is called 'silver' (rūpya), so it is here."
The conviction "I am" is the name for the superimposition of fluctuations upon the immutable [Self]. (36)

Regarding the phrase "of that which is superimposed": just as in the illustrative example of mother-of-pearl, there is the name "silver" for the object superimposed upon it—namely, the name *rūpya* meaning "silver"—so too, in the case of the immutable reality (*kūṭastha*), there is the name "I" (*aham*) for the previously mentioned mental modification (*vikṣepa*) in the form of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) which is imagined thereon. This is the meaning. || 36 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā) on the phrase "of that which is superimposed": In both instances, the term *nāma* refers specifically to a name or designation (*saṃjñā*). The meaning is that "ascertainment" (*niścaya*) is indeed a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*). || 36 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection may be raised: "In the illustrative example, when sensory contact occurs with the mother-of-pearl fragment present before one, the misconception of silver—thinking 'this is silver,' which is distinct from that [shell]—is indeed possible; however, such is not the case with the subject of the illustration, namely, the misconception of a reality distinct from the Self.

Anticipating this, [the author] replies: "Even here, while the conscious Self shines forth by its own self-luminosity, the misconception 'I am' is perceived as something distinct from it; therefore, [it is not the case that no such misconception exists]."
Intending to address this inconsistency, he says:
"Perceiving this aspect [of the shell] by itself, one conceives it to be silver."
Likewise, perceiving itself by itself, it conceives the notion "I am."
"This is the portion" (idamaṃśa). || 37 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "If there exists a *kūṭastha* (the immutable witness) distinct from the *ahaṃkāra*, then it would be equivalent to the silver in the mother-of-pearl; what is the proof for that very point? To this, he says: "The 'this'-aspect" (*idamaṃśam*). "By itself" means by the Witness (*sākṣin*). "Beholding" means perceiving through the eyes, making it directly manifest (*aparokṣīkurvan*) as delimited by light. "Itself" refers to the *kūṭastha* denoted by the word "this. "By itself" means precisely by its own self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*). "Beholding" means experiencing it even without the mediation of a mental modification (*vṛtti*).
Thus, up to this point. || 37 ||
But this [distinction] is described as being distinct; likewise, let it be accepted that "mine-ness" (svatva) and "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) are also distinct.
For both the universal and the particular are indeed understood in both cases. || 38 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Since the words *svayam* (self) and *aham* (I) have the same meaning, how can there be a similarity between the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dāṣṭantika*)?

Anticipating this doubt, he says "idam" [verse 38], asserting that this is not so, because in both cases there is a similarity in the nature of the general and the particular regarding the meanings of the words *idam* and *rūpya*, as well as the words *svayam* and *aham*.
Commentary (Ṭīkā): For this very reason—it is said, "But this..."—the reason for that is stated: "And it is universal" (sāmānyam). || 38 ||
Devadatta will go himself; you likewise should observe it yourself.
"I am not able myself"—thus it is used in the world. (39)
The Sixth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): In order to clarify that the meaning of the word *svayam* (self) is of a general nature, he first demonstrates a common worldly usage: "Devadatta," etc. (Verse 39).
The commentary (ṭīkā) explains that very point through the two verses beginning with "Devadatta": || 39 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Let it be so; however, one might ask, "How does this much establish that the meaning of the word *svayam* (self) is of a generic nature?
Anticipating this, he says: "Just as [in the expressions] 'this is silver' or 'this is cloth,' so too is the case with *idam* (this)."
Among these—“that,” “you,” and “I”—it conceives of itself as “I.”

The meaning is as follows: just as in cases such as "this silver" (*idaṃ rūpyam*)—wherever [it occurs] in reference to silver, cloth, and so forth—the word *idam* ("this") is employed, and thus its referent is understood to have a universal form;
likewise, because the word *svayam* ("self") is employed everywhere in expressions such as "that," "you," and "I," the referent of that word is also understood to possess a universal form. || 40 ||
Commentary (a0): "This is silver"—this is the conceit (*abhimāna*), which is the [illusory] conjunction (*saṃsarga*). || 40 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Let it be that in common worldly usage there is a distinction between the words "I" (aham) and "mine" (sva); however, he asks what relevance this has for the immutable Self (kūṭasthātman):
"Let 'mineness' be distinct from 'I-ness'; what does that matter to you regarding the immutable Self?"
It would occur to me that this very meaning of the word "self" (svayam) is the immutable (kūṭastha). || 41 ||

Regarding the phrase "because of the nature of 'I'" (ahaṃtva): it follows that the very meaning of the word "self" (svayam), which is of the nature of a universal (sāmānya-rūpa), is the immutable (kūṭastha). Thus he says: "the meaning of the word 'self'. (41)

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, having established the difference between "mineness" (svatva) and "I-ness" (ahaṃtva), the opponent raises an objection even while accepting that difference, beginning with the words "because of I-ness" (ahaṃtvāt). The proponent (siddhāntin) provides the resolution, beginning with the words "the word 'self'" (svayaṃśabda). || 41 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "The property of 'selfhood' (svatva) precludes otherness, but it does not reveal immutability (kūṭasthatva). To this, he says:
"If it is argued that selfhood excludes otherness, then [let there be] the exclusion of otherness."
For that would indeed be exactly what the speaker intends to assert regarding the immutability of the Self. (42)

Regarding the phrase "the exclusion of otherness": since the meaning of the word "self" (*svayam*) is precisely the immutable (*kūṭastha*) Self, the exclusion of otherness by way of selfhood is indeed intended;
thus he resolves [the objection] with: "The exclusion of otherness belongs to the immutable. (42)

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "In this way, the meaning of the word *svayam*—which is a synonym for the word *sva*—would be merely the exclusion of others (*anyavāraṇa*), and not 'the immutable' (*kūṭastha*). Thus he raises the objection again with the words "anyatve" (if it were otherness). He answers by accepting the objection as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*) with the words beginning "anyavāraṇam" (the exclusion of others).
For in our established doctrine, it is intended that the immutable [Self] alone is non-dual Brahman. || 42 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Since the two words *svayam* and *ātman* have different grounds for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*), they cannot have the same referent—just as the words 'cow' and 'horse' do not; therefore, how can that which is denoted by the word *svayam*, namely the immutable (*kūṭastha*), be the Self? Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it by showing that they can indeed have the same referent, just like the words 'hand', 'palm', and so on:
"It is not so."
"Self" (svayaṃ) and "soul" (ātman) are synonyms; therefore, they are used together in common worldly usage.
Therefore, there is no application [of the term]; thus, "selfhood" (svatva) and "soulhood" (ātmatva) are what exclude others. || 43 ||

Regarding the phrase "itself is the self": he states the reason why these two terms cannot be used together as synonyms—that is, they lack simultaneous application—in the words "therefore, in common usage. He states the resulting conclusion in the words "hence, ownership. || 43 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [page 148] 148.

[Commentary on the *Citradīpa*, Chapter 1] — Now, raising the objection that there is a difference between the meanings of the words "self" (*ātman*) and "itself" (*svayam*), just as there is between the meanings of the words "pot" (*ghaṭa*) and "cloth" (*paṭa*), the author provides the resolution with the verse beginning "itself" (*svayam*). He states the conclusion with the remainder of the verse beginning "therefore" (*ataḥ*). || 43 ||
"A pot does not know by itself"—thus is selfhood [denied] in the case of pots and the like.
If it is observed even in insentient things, let it be seen from the perspective of the existence of the Self.

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that since the word "self" (svayam) is observed to be used even for insentient objects such as jars, the identity of "selfhood" and "consciousness" is untenable; thus he raises this doubt with the verse beginning "the jar. He replies with "let it be seen," stating that because the consciousness of the Self exists even in jars and other such things in the form of manifestation (sphuraṇa), the use of the word "self" for them is not contradictory. || 44 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He raises the objection of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the state of being a synonym for "etymological derivation" (*nirukta-paryāyatva*) with the words "the pot itself. He refutes that as well by accepting the consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), with the remainder of the verse beginning "let it be seen," and so forth. || 44 ||
The distinction between sentient and insentient is certainly not created by the immutable Self.
However, let it be understood that this is produced by the intellect and is indeed produced by the manifestor alone. || 45 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (rā0 ṭī0): Now, one might object: "If the consciousness of the Self were present even in jars and other such objects, then the distinction between the sentient and the insentient would be without a cause.

Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it by showing that the distinction between the sentient and the insentient exists because of the presence or absence of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), stating: "The sentient... (verse 45).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "If even jars and other objects possess the nature of the Self, what is the root cause of the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious?

Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that this distinction is rooted solely in the presence or absence of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) mirrored in the intellect (buddhi): "The conscious... (verse 45).
Just as the appearance of consciousness is imagined through delusion within the immutable.
And likewise, insentient things such as jars and the like are imagined in that very same [consciousness]. || 46 ||

Rāmatīrtha’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious is accepted as being caused by the presence or absence of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), then the acceptance of the Self's existence within unconscious objects would be purposeless. Anticipating this, and with the intention that although the immutable (kūṭastha) cannot be accepted as the cause of the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious, it must nevertheless be accepted as the substratum for the conceptualization of the unconscious, [the author states] regarding the jar and so forth therein:
He states the nature of being imagined along with an illustration: "Just as the conscious [self]," etc. (46).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): If that is so, then what is the root cause for the notion of "Self" in objects such as jars? To this he says: "Just as... This means: in the case of the immutable reality of Brahman, which is the Self. "Delusion" refers to beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*) itself. || 46 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He raises an objection regarding the over-extension [of the argument] if "mineness" (svatva) and "selfhood" (ātmatva) were identical: "In that case, those two [mineness and selfhood] would also [be present] in 'you,' 'I,' and so forth, just like mineness."
If it is argued that because [the universal] is present everywhere, those two [particulars] also have it as their self-nature; || 47 ||

"Regarding 'these two, thatness and thisness' as well": the sense is that, just as "mineness" (svatva)—which is pervasive everywhere in instances such as "you" and "I"—is the very nature of the Self, why should "thatness" and "thisness," which are likewise pervasive everywhere, not also be the nature of the Self? || 47 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): There, he raises the objection of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)—namely, that "the 'that-ness' and 'this-ness' [are also like this]"—meaning that they would be like "ownership" and "one who possesses ownership. || 47 ||
Rāghava’s Commentary: Since the nature of being "that" and "this" occurs more extensively than the nature of being the Self, he states that the nature of being the Self is not possible for them:
"Even though those two—the nature of being 'that' and the nature of being 'this'—are pervasive, they [do not constitute the Self]."
Just as it is impossible for rightness and the like [to be the self], so too the nature of being a self is not at all conceivable.
The Sixth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

"Even though those two [thatness and thisness] are in the nature of the Self (ātmatva)": although thatness (*tat-tva*) and thisness (*idaṃ-tva*) are pervasive in "you," "I," and so forth—just as selfhood (*svatva*) is pervasive in them—even so, since the nature of the Self (*ātmatva*) is also pervasive within them, the conventional usage of "this is the Self" (*idam-ātmatvam*) and "that is the Self" (*tad-ātmatvam*) is possible; therefore, those two [thatness and thisness] do not exceed the nature of the Self.

Because it is a function (*vṛtti*), its being the very nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpatā*) is not possible; the illustration for this is "of rightness (*samyaktva*) and so forth. The meaning is: just as in the case of rightness and wrongness, which persist within the state of selfhood (*ātmatva*) due to the conventional usage of "right selfhood" and "wrong selfhood," [so too is the case here]. (48)

Commentary (Ṭīkā): [The author] replies that even though those two—*tat-tva* (thatness) and *idam-tva* (thisness)—are included within the nature of the Self (*ātmatva*), as evidenced by such conventional usages as "the nature of the Self accepted by the proponent" and "this nature of the Self accepted by the opponent," it is not possible for them to possess properties such as correctness of the Self (*ātmasamyaktva*) and so forth; thus he says: "Even though those two are the nature of the Self... (Verse 48).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus concluded the incidental discussion, he restates a matter established by worldly convention in order to demonstrate the resulting implication:
"The notions of 'that' and 'this,' 'self' and 'other,' 'you' and 'I' are mutually [relative]."
There is no doubt that these are well-known in the world as being mutually opposed. || 49 ||

Regarding the phrase "thatness and thisness" (*tattedaṃte*): the meaning is that it is well-known from common worldly usage that these function as opposites, as seen in such expressions as "that and this" (*tad idam*), where "thisness" (*idaṃtā*) is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of "thatness" (*tattā*); "otherness" (*anyatva*) is the counter-correlate of "selfhood" (*svatva*) in the expression "I am other than myself" (*svayam anyaḥ*); and "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) is the counter-correlate of "thou-ness" (*tvantā*) in the expression "you and I" (*tvam aham*).
This is the intended sense. || 49 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): One might ask, "Let this be so; however, what is the relevance to the subject at hand? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] provides examples of pairs of opposing attributes in general, in order to demonstrate that "selfhood" (*svayaṃtvam*) is indeed the direct opposite of "otherness" (*anyatvam*), and that this [selfhood] exists only in the immutable (*kūṭastha*). He states: "That-ness and this-ness" (*tattedante*);
thus ends verse 49.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Let it be so; what follows from this regarding the subject at hand? To this he says:
"Let the Self be accepted as the immutable (kūṭastha), the direct opposite of change."
This "I" is imagined within the self as the counter-correlative of that fear. || 50 ||

Regarding the phrase "of otherness": the meaning is that the referent of the word "you" (tvam), which is the counter-correlative of otherness, and the referent of the word "I" (aham), which is the counter-correlative of selfhood, are superimposed upon the immutable reality (kūṭastha) as a semblance of duality. || 50 ||
Commentary on verse a0: He states the conclusion with the words "of otherness" (anyatāyāḥ). To what follows from that, he replies with the words "of selfhood" (tvaṃtāyāḥ) || 50 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection—"Even though the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the immutable witness (kūṭastha) exists in the manner described, why do all people not know it thus?"—he says:
"The difference between 'I-ness' (ahaṃtā) and 'mineness' (svatva) is manifested as if they were two distinct things."
Even though it was clear, they fell into delusion and asserted its oneness.

Regarding the term "I-ness" (ahaṃtā): since the immutable witness of the intellect cannot be perceived directly by the intellect itself, the meaning is that they have apprehended the identity between the individual soul (jīva) and the immutable witness (kūṭastha), both of whom appear as the "I. || 51 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, even though the distinction between "I-ness" (ahantva) and "mine-ness" (svatva) is established, their mutual superimposition occurs due to delusion; this is stated in the verse beginning with "ahaṃtve" (51).
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, in response to the inquiry as to what the cause of this delusion regarding the identity between the individual soul (jīva) and the immutable witness (kūṭastha) is, he says:
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya:
[In this chapter titled] *Citradīpa*, it is precisely this superimposition of identity (*tādātmyādhyāsa*) that has been produced here by the previously mentioned ignorance (*avidyā*).
When ignorance has ceased, its effect ceases as well. || 52 ||

Regarding the term *tādātmya*: here, in this treatise, it means "by means of that ignorance" which was described in the passage, "this beginningless non-discrimination. Since this [superimposition] is an effect of ignorance, its cessation occurs only through the knowledge that sublates ignorance; thus he says: "in ignorance" (avidyāyām). || 52 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, let it be granted that this superimposition of the ego (ahaṃkāra) occurs upon the immutable Self (kūṭasthātman); nevertheless, is this [superimposition] of the nature of identity (tādātmya) or of the nature of conjunction (saṃsarga)? He settles this point with the words "tādātmya" (identity). The reason for this is stated as "pūrva" (prior). To the question "What follows from that?", he replies: "avidyāyām" (in ignorance). Unity is indeed the primary effect; it ceases because of the absence of its material cause (upādāna).
The meaning is "he sees. || 52 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, it might be argued that since superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is an effect of ignorance (*avidyā*), its cessation should follow from the cessation of that ignorance; however, this is untenable because the body and other such effects of ignorance are still perceived even when the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self has arisen. To this, he says:
"In the state of identification with the functions of ignorance, they perish by knowledge alone."
But the true nature of distraction is that it perceives the exhaustion of prārabdha karma. || 53 ||

Regarding the phrase "the functions of ignorance" (*avidyāvṛttīti*): the cessation of both concealment (*āvaraṇa*) and identification (*tādātmya*), which have ignorance as their sole cause, occurs through knowledge (*vidyā*) alone.

However, there is no contradiction in the fact that the nature of projection (*vikṣepa*), which is produced by ignorance conjoined with karma, persists until the exhaustion of that karma. This is the intended meaning. ||53||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that if this were so, there would be no liberation while living (jīvanmukti); to this he says: "Because it is produced solely by ignorance" (avidyā). This means because it is generated only by nescience. However, as for the distraction involving the body, senses, objects, and so forth, since it is produced by prārabdha-karma, it perishes only upon the destruction of that karma;
thus he says: "Of the distraction... (vikṣepasya) || 53 ||
Even when the appropriation has perished, it awaits its effect for a moment.
Thus say the logicians; why should that not be possible for us as well? (54)

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Since the prārabdha karma is merely the efficient cause (nimitta), how can the effect continue even when the material cause (upādāna) has been destroyed by its mere existence?
Anticipating this doubt, he establishes the possibility of that continuation through an example well-known from other scriptures: "When the material cause...
(verse 54).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection is raised: since even *prārabdha* karma shares the same material cause (*upādāna*) as ignorance (*avidyā*)—by way of the beginningless impressions of desire (*saṃskāra*), like the seed and the sprout—how can it persist when that [ignorance] is destroyed? To this, he says: "When the material cause... The implied meaning is: because of the cognition that "the cloth has been destroyed. || 54 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, anticipating the objection that logicians maintain an effect exists for only a single moment and not for a long duration, he says:
"By those [logicians], such a moment is declared to consist of a number of days of threads."
Let this moment here be regarded as worthy of an incalculable cycle of delusion. || 55 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the threads": the sense is that because saṃsāra has continued from beginningless time, it is not contradictory for its momentum (saṃskāra) to cause it to persist for a long duration, like the whirling of a potter’s wheel. || 95 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "How can there be an equality between that imagined moment and the duration of time sufficient for the experience of the *prārabdha* (commenced karma)?

To this, he says: "Of the threads" (*tantūnām*). This means: of the threads which are the material cause (*upādāna*) of the cloth. "In days" (*dinaiḥ*): [meaning] those well-known to last for only a few days, from their beginning until their destruction. || 55 ||
The Sixth Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.

151 Rāghavānanda’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, having raised the objection that "the logician has stated this according to reason, and you have likewise," he demonstrates the difference between his own statement and that of the logicians:
Without a measure that withstands scrutiny, they conceptualize things in vain;
for those who speak on the basis of scripture, reasoning, and experience, what indeed is difficult to accomplish? (56)

[The author] refutes [the objection]: the meaning is that there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) apart from a measure that is capable of withstanding scrutiny and able to endure investigation. The scriptural authority (śruti) is: "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged [in the Absolute]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2). The logical argument (yukti) is the illustration of the whirling wheel and so forth. The experiential testimony (anubhūti) is the experience of the realized ones (vidvats). The intention is: what is impossible to state on the basis of these means of valid cognition? || 56 ||

Commentary (a0): In reality, for the logicians who maintain the theory of production (*ārambhavāda*), it is precisely improper for the effect to persist for even a single moment after the destruction of its material cause, as there is no stronger evidence for such a thing. For us Advaitins, however, who maintain the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*), [the situation is explained] by the Śruti: "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall attain [Brahman]," just as in the case of one who approaches a mirage with the intention of drinking water because of the perception of water therein.

Even though there is sublation by the direct perception of the saline earth delimited by the midday sunlight which serves as its substrate, there is still the occurrence of the cognition of that [salt] through delimitation by its adjacent space for as long as there is conjunction with light and so forth;
likewise, liberation while living (jīvanmukti) exists because of such cognition, and therein the shadow of duality exists because of such cognition.
"There is a slight trace [of duality] for the sake of preserving the shadow of duality; in that matter, one's own experience (*svānubhūti*) is the authority"—
thus, for those who speak of the experience revealed in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*, there remains some effect for a short time even after the destruction of the material cause (*upādāna*).
He says that there is no obstacle to its persistence with the words "without" (vinā). || 56 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Let the dispute with wicked logicians rest; I shall now speak of the subject at hand.
Obeisance! The oneness of the immutable and the transforming has been established. (57)
"Let it be so. Through delusion, the identity between the immutable (kūṭastha) and the transforming (pariṇāmin)—the referents of the words "self" and "I"—is established. 17.

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Therefore, setting those aside, we follow the subject at hand; thus he says, "Let it be. He explains that with the words "His own," etc.; the word "through superimposition" (*adhyāsāt*) is to be supplied as the remainder. The reason for this is stated: "Because [the Self] is immutable" (*kūṭastha*). || 57 ||
All those who consider themselves wise— both worldly people and non-Buddhist outsiders— are wandering in delusion.
Out of folly, they disregarded the sacred scripture and relied solely upon mere reasoning. || 58 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If the identity between the immutable (kūṭastha) and the individual soul (jīva) is established through delusion, why do some not realize that this is a delusion?
Anticipating this, he says "bhrāmyantaḥ" (they wander), [implying] it is because they lack a thorough investigation into the intended meaning of the scriptures. || 58 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask, "Why are the Tārtikas being ignored? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the answer by means of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) logic: "They wander," etc. (Verse 18).
In that regard, some are devoid of the reflective awareness of the preceding and the succeeding.
They shamelessly apply fallacious arguments to their respective positions.
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: "Why do even some expounders of the meaning of the Vedas not know this?
Anticipating this doubt, he states that it is because they lack a comprehensive reflection upon the meaning of the Vedas, saying: "pūrvāpara... (verse 19).
Commentary (a0): Now, as to the question of what the reason is for even the non-Buddhists (*tairthika*) disregarding the scriptures, he says: "pūrvāpara... (verse 19).
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 152.
[The commentary by Rāma on the *Citradīpa*: First, by accepting perception as the sole means of valid knowledge, he restates the position of the Lokāyata and others, which is extremely crude.]
They asserted that the selfhood belongs to the aggregate beginning with the immutable [primordial matter] and ending with the body.
The Lokāyatas and the vulgar rely upon what merely appears to be direct perception. || 60 ||

Regarding the phrase "beginning with the immutable" (kūṭasthādi): anticipating the objection that the body and so forth might possess ultimate selfhood because it is established by perception, it is stated that [such perception] is a semblance of perception (pratyakṣābhāsa). || 60 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): In order to refute all those proponents of duality, [the author] first restates the extremely crude Lokāyata doctrine, beginning with "kūṭasthādi" (the immutable, etc.). The word "pāmarāḥ" (the common folk) means even all worldly people. By the use of the word "ābhāsa" (appearance), the fact that it is unexamined is indicated therein. || 60 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Although they maintain that perception alone is the means of valid knowledge, he says that they also cite scriptural statements in order to show that their own doctrine is established by the Vedas, so as to delude others:
"Just as [the proponents of the Self as a mere aggregate] cite the sheath made of food (annamaya-kośa) to make their own position conform to the Śruti..."
They accepted the established doctrine of Virocana as their authority. || 61 ||
