"To make scriptural" (*śrautīkartum*): by the word "sheath consisting of food" (*annamaya*), the passage beginning with "This very person consists of the essence of food" (*sa vā eṣa puruṣo 'nnarasamayaḥ*) [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1], which establishes the sheath of food, is indicated as Virocana’s established doctrine (*siddhānta*). By that, the passage beginning with "The self alone consists of the body" (*ātmaiva dehamayaḥ*), which sets forth his doctrine, is indicated. They propose these two passages as their authority.
The meaning is that they are not capable of being established in this way because it would contradict the context. || 61 ||

Regarding this, the commentary on verse 61 (a0 ṭīkā) states: "Those who maintain that perception alone is the sole means of valid cognition are deceivers; thus he says: 'In order to make [the Veda] authoritative through hearing' (śrautīkartum). || 61 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having first pointed out the defects in this view, he introduces another perspective:
"Because in this [system] the death of the body is observed to occur upon the departure of the individual soul (jīvātman)."
The Lokāyatas and others say that the self is indeed distinct from the body.
The individual self (jīvātman). || 62 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, while refuting the aforementioned doctrine, he states the internal view of the Lokāyatas: "jīva... (verse 62).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the inquiry, "Of what nature is the self as distinct from the body, and by what means of valid cognition is it apprehended? [the author replies]:
"The notion of 'I', which is regarded as being perceptible, [apprehends] that which is distinct from the body."
One should cause the self of the senses to depart through such applications as "I speak," and so forth. || 63 ||

Regarding the phrase "as being perceptible": the meaning is that, because we observe such usages as "I speak" and "I see," the self is that which is accessible to the notion of "I" (ahambuddhi) as distinct from the body. || 63 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Let it be so; however, even for me, inference is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in our system. Therefore, how can that [Self] be established, or what is its nature? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the answer: the very cognition "I am" (which you accept as perceptual) takes as its object something distinct from the body because it lacks any mention of the body; furthermore, through such usages as "I speak," he establishes that it is indeed of the nature of the sense-faculties (*indriya*). He says: "Perceptual... (pratyakṣa-).
"By the state of being wounded," [it is said]. || 63 ||
The Sixth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

153 Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection as to how the sense organs, being insentient, can possess the nature of the Self, [the author] states that their insentiency is unproven because the dialogue among the senses is heard in the Śrutis.
The quarrel among the sense organs, beginning with speech, is heard in the Vedas.
And therefore, their selfhood consists in consciousness; for it is from that very [consciousness] that it arises.

Regarding the phrase "of speech and so forth": since consciousness alone is the defining characteristic of the Self (*ātman*), he states that it is appropriate for the conscious sense organs to possess the nature of the Self—thus:
"the nature of the Self. (64)
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, since the sense organs are insentient (*jaḍa*), how can they possess the nature of the Self? To this he says: "Of speech and the rest.
And thus it is recorded by the Kaṇvas: "They said to Speech, 'Sing the Udgītha for us. 'So be it,' she replied; then Speech sang the Udgītha for them," and so forth. || 64 ||
But those who follow Hiranyagarbha, the proponents of the doctrine that the vital breath (prāṇa) is the self, have spoken thus.
Even when the sense organs such as the eyes are lost, one lives as long as the vital breath (prāṇa) exists. || 65 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In order to set forth another school of thought, he says: "The followers of Hiraṇyagarbha. (65)
Commentary (a0): Now, he states the view of those who maintain that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the self, in a pair of verses beginning with "the followers of Hiraṇyagarbha" (65).
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He shows that there are scriptural indications for the view that the vital breath (prāṇa) is the Self:
"The vital breath remains awake even when [the others] are asleep; the excellence of the vital breath and so forth are heard in scripture."
The sheath consisting of vital breath (prāṇamaya-kośa) has been thus fully explained in detail. || 66 ||

Regarding the term *prāṇa*: the awakening of the *prāṇa* is heard in such passages as, "In this city, the fires indeed remain awake through the *prāṇa*" (Praśna Upaniṣad 4.3). Furthermore, the preeminence and other qualities of the *prāṇa* are heard in, "When he had entered into that *prāṇa*, he arose; that became the *uktha*; that is this very *uktha*. And the sheath consisting of *prāṇa* (*prāṇamaya-kośa*) is elaborated upon in such passages as, "Another inner self consists of *prāṇa*."
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the dialogue of the vital breaths (prāṇasaṃvāda), the entry [into the body], and so forth are to be understood. || 66 ||

Commentary on verse a0: "The vital breath (prāṇa)"—this implies "Devadatta even while asleep. And thus, with reference to deep sleep, the Śruti says: "In this city, the fires of the vital breaths alone remain awake"; and also in the Praśna Upaniṣad: "All this is under the control of the vital breath. || 66 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He presents the view of those who hold that the mind, which is even more internal than the vital breath (prāṇa), is the Self:
"Those people devoted to meditation consider the mind to be the Self."
The non-enjoyership of the vital breath (prāṇa) is evident; therefore, the quality of being an enjoyer belongs to the mind.
"Mind is the Self," he says. He states the reasoning for the fact that vital breath (prāṇa) is not the Self with the words: "of the vital breath... (sūtra 67).

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on a0: Now he states the view of the Upāsaka—“The mind,” etc. He refutes the doctrine that the vital breath (prāṇa) is the self with the words “of the vital breath,” etc.; the remainder of the argument is “because it is not the substratum of pleasure and so forth. || 67 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He cites a scriptural passage establishing the reasoning for the mind being the self:
"The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings."
The mind, which is described in scripture as the "sheath made of mind," is therefore called the Self.

"It is the mind alone. He shows another scriptural passage—“From this very self consisting of breath (prāṇamaya), there is another inner self consisting of mind (manomaya)” (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.2)—by saying "it is heard. He states the conclusion by saying "therefore. || 68 ||

In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya, in the commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the chapter titled *Citradīpa*, verse 68, he cites scripture as well to establish his own position: "The mind alone... (mana eva).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He presents the view of the Buddhist, who maintains that even the internal consciousness (vijñāna) is the Self:
"The proponents of momentariness say that consciousness is the Self."
For it is clearly understood that the mind has consciousness as its root. || 69 ||
Regarding "consciousness": he states the reasoning for consciousness being internal with the words "since" (yataḥ). || 69 ||
— Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, he establishes the Buddhist doctrine with five verses beginning with "Consciousness" (vijñāna). Therein, the reason [is as follows]:
"Because" [is said]; the remainder of the sentence is "because the intellect (buddhi) is internal. || 69 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Raising the objection—since the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is denoted by the terms "intellect" (vijñāna) and "mind" (manas), is one, how can there be a relationship of cause and effect between the mind and the intellect?—the author first demonstrates their distinction in order to establish that relationship:
"The internal organ is twofold: the function of 'I' (ahaṃvṛtti) and the function of 'this' (idaṃvṛtti)."
Consciousness would be the "I-function," and the mind would be the "this-function. || 70 ||
"The functioning of the 'I' (ahaṃvṛtti). || 70 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): To demonstrate that the intellect (*buddhi*) is indeed more internal than the mind (*manas*), he briefly describes the nature of both: "The function of 'I'... (verse 70).
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: He states the relationship of cause and effect between the two:
"It is clear that this modification [of the mind] has the notion of 'I' as its seed."
Without knowing one's own self, no one at all perceives anything external.

"It is the seed-nature of the notion of 'I'. He establishes this very point with the words "not having known," etc. The meaning is that the absence of the arising of the mental modification (vṛtti) of "I" follows from the non-arising of the modification of "this"; thus, there is a relationship of cause and effect between these two. || 71 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): What follows from that? He states it thus: "The notion of 'I'... The reason for this is given: "...without having known... ||71||
Rāma’s Commentary: He provides experiential proof for the momentariness of that consciousness:
"Since birth and destruction are perceived in every moment within the measure of the activity of the 'I'-notion."
Consciousness is momentary; therefore, it is self-luminous because it is known by itself.

Regarding the term "moment" (*kṣaṇa*): having established momentariness, he establishes self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) with the words "self-luminous. The meaning is that it is cognized by itself alone. || 72 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) states its momentariness with the words "in every moment. It also states its self-luminosity with the final quarter of the verse beginning with "self" (sva). || 72 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He states that scripture is the authority for the selfhood of consciousness:
"The scriptures declare that this sheath consisting of consciousness is the individual soul (jīva)."
All of saṃsāra consists of this: birth, destruction, pleasure, and so forth. || 73 ||

Regarding the phrase "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*): the sense is that statements such as, "Different from this self consisting of mind (*manomaya*) is another inner self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*)," and "Consciousness performs the sacrifice," establish that consciousness is the Self. || 73 ||
Commentary (a0): In that regard, he also cites scripture as authority for the followers of the Taittirīya school: "consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya). || 73 ||
The Sixth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
Consciousness is momentary and not the self, like a flash of lightning or the blinking of an eye.
Because nothing else is perceived, the Mādhyamikas have declared that [all things] are empty. || 74 ||
155 Rāghava’s Commentary: He presents the view of the Śūnyavādin, a sub-sect of the Buddhists, with the verse beginning "Consciousness" (vijñānam). ||74||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, refuting the doctrine of consciousness-only (vijñānavāda), he states the view of the Yogācāra school with the two verses beginning with "vijñānam" (verse 74).
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He states the scriptural authority for your view: "In such passages as 'this was indeed non-existent,' this very [non-existence] is heard."
The entire world, consisting of both knowledge and the object of knowledge, appears as a mere mental construction.

Regarding the statement "this was indeed non-existent," one might ask: if the void alone possesses that nature, what becomes of the world as it is perceived? To this, he says: "Through knowledge... (verse 75).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): "Asadeva" etc. This refers to the Chāndogya Upaniṣad passage beginning with, "Regarding this, some say that in the beginning this was indeed non-existent," and so forth. || 75 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He refutes this view as follows:
"The existence of the Self [is established] because there can be no error without a substratum."
Even for that which is empty, there must be a witness; otherwise, you could not have made this statement regarding it. (76)

Regarding the term "without a substratum" (*niradhiṣṭhāna*): since that which is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvarūpa*)—namely, the void (*śūnya*)—cannot logically function as a substratum, and since an error (*bhrama*) cannot occur without a substratum, the existence of the Self (*ātman*), which serves as the substratum for the conceptualization of the world, must be admitted. Furthermore, even for the proponent of the Void (*śūnyavādin*), the Self must necessarily be admitted as the witness (*sākṣin*) of the void; otherwise, if it were not admitted, the statement "this void is the void"—that very designation of yours—would be impossible.
The sense is that, in your Buddhist view, [the self] would not be established. || 76 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) refutes this view with the words "niradhiṣṭhāna" (without a substratum). Since it is impossible for that which is called "void" (*śūnya*)—namely, a non-existent thing such as a hare's horn, which is the counter-positive of an absolute absence of existence delimited by all space and time—to serve as a substratum, the intended meaning is that only that which has the nature of existence (*sat-rūpa*) can be the substratum of all error.
Stating the reason for this, he also declares the consciousness-nature (*cid-rūpatā*) of the Self, which is that very existent nature serving as the substratum: "of the void... [etc.]

The word *pīti* (joy) connects here with the phrase "this self exists. In that regard, he establishes the proof through the principle of "otherwise it would be inexplicable" (*anyathānupapatti*), [saying] "otherwise":

the connection is that for this Mādhyamika, who maintains emptiness, there could not even be the employment of words such as "emptiness exists" and so forth without an experience having that [emptiness] as its object. || 76 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: What, then, is this Self? To this he says:
"The blissful one (ānandamaya) is other than the one consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya) and is more internal."
"It must be apprehended as 'it exists'—this is the Vedic perspective. (77)

"Another" refers to the fact that because of the existence of such scriptural passages as, "Different indeed from this self consisting of consciousness is another inner self consisting of bliss," and "It should be apprehended as truly existing by means of its essential nature," it must be accepted that the self consists of bliss; this is the Vedic vision, the Vedic established doctrine. || 77 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): If this is so, then who is your self? To this he says: "Another" (anya). The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: there exists the Vedic perspective in the form of scripture, stating, "Different from this self consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya) is another, higher self, the self consisting of bliss (ānandamaya)," and "He is to be perceived as truly existing by way of His essential nature. || 77 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 156.
"Is it minute, large, or middling?"—thus do the disputants argue even in that case.
Indeed, they dispute in many ways regarding that which is called the "Lamp of Consciousness," relying upon scripture and reasoning. (78)

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus demonstrated the disagreement regarding the essential nature of the self, he now shows the disagreement among disputants concerning its specific dimension: "It is atomic" (verse 78).
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Having thus determined its nature, he states the dispute regarding its dimension: "The atom... (78).
Rāma’s Commentary: Here, he first presents the view of those who maintain that [the self] is atomic:
"Those who hold to the intermediate state (antarālāḥ) declare it to be atomic, on account of its movement through subtle channels."
He moves among those who are equal to even a thousandth part of a single hair. || 79 ||
"Minute" (aṇu). He states the reason for designating it as minute: "subtle" (sūkṣma). He explains this: "of the hair" (romṇaḥ).
The word "in the channels" (nāḍīṣu) is to be supplied. The intention is that movement within the subtle channels would not be possible without minuteness. || 79 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Since they were mentioned first, [the author] now speaks of the proponents of the atomic theory (*aṇuvādinaḥ*), beginning with the words "the atom" (*aṇum*). Those who take—that is, accept—the internal movement within the extremely subtle channels (*sūkṣmatamanāḍīpracāra*) as the basis for their doctrine of atoms are thus called Rāmānujas and Mādhvas. This was stated by the author himself at the beginning of the section on the Mādhva school in the *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha*: "This very... [and so forth].

Although there is a similarity [between our view] and that of the followers of Manu regarding the atomicity of the soul, its subservience, the non-human authorship of the Vedas, the capacity of established facts to convey meaning, the self-validity of knowledge, the threefold nature of the means of valid cognition, the dependence upon the Pāñcarātra, and the reality of the diversity of the phenomenal world, he— disregarding them as being relegated to the camp of the Kṣapaṇakas by accepting three mutually contradictory positions such as dualism and so forth— established, by way of a different approach, that the collection of Vedāntic statements beginning with "That thou art" has another intended meaning.
Under the guise of a commentary on the Brahma-mīmāṃsā, Ānandatīrtha established a distinct system. || 79 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question, "What is the proof for its atomicity?", he says:
"This one is subtler than the subtle; this one is indeed more minute than the minute."
The Śrutis declare its atomic nature by the hundreds and thousands.

Regarding the word *aṇoḥ*: the meaning is that such scriptural passages as “Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great,” “This atomic Self is to be known by the mind,” and “Eternal, subtler than the subtle” [are the authorities]. || 80 ||
Commentary (a0): He also corroborates this with the scriptures by means of two verses beginning with "aṇoḥ" (of the subtle). || 80 ||
Of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair, further divided into a hundred parts;
And another Śruti says: "That Jīva is to be known as a portion. (81)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary (rā0 ṭī0): He cites another scriptural passage—“vālāgra” etc.—[verse 81].
Commentary (Ṭīkā): "Vāla" means that which is imagined or conjectured. || 81 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He presents the view of those who maintain that the self has a medium size:
"The Digambaras assert its medium size from the feet to the head."
Because consciousness is observed to pervade [the body] even up to the tips of the nails, as stated in the scriptures. || 82 ||

Regarding the term "naked ones" (digaṃbara), he states the justification for it: "from the feet," etc. He further states that the scriptural authority for this is the passage, "This very [Self] has entered here up to the tips of the nails," by saying "up to the tips of the nails. || 82 ||
There are three positions: difference, non-difference, and both difference and non-difference.
[End of] the sixth chapter.
Accompanied by two commentaries.
Commentary on the Verse—Now, because it is equally subject to refutation, he states the final doctrine of the Ārhata school immediately after the discussion of the atomic theory (aṇuvāda): di-
By the words "the ether," and so forth; and by the phrase "up to the tips of the nails": "This very [Self] has entered here up to the tips of the nails. || 82 ||

Rāghava’s Commentary: Now, one might object that if [the body] possessed a middling dimension, the movement through the channels (nāḍī) established by scripture would not be possible; anticipating this, he says:
"But the movement through the subtle channels occurs by means of subtle constituent parts."
As if putting on a cloak with both hands, [one puts on] the gross body. || 83 ||

Regarding the phrase "subtle channels" (sūkṣmanāḍī): just as when the two hands, which are parts of the body, enter a garment, the body itself is said to have entered the garment, so too, by means of the movement of the subtle constituents of the self within the channels, the movement of the self itself is figuratively attributed [to it]. This is the meaning. || 83 ||

Commentary on verse a0: Regarding the words "subtle" (sūkṣma) and "sheath" (kañcuka), according to Amara’s lexicon, "kañcuka means armor (vāravāṇa), not feminine," the meaning is that it is like wearing a suit of mail. || 83 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that if the self possesses a fixed intermediate size, its entry into bodies that are smaller or larger due to the influence of karma would be impossible.

Anticipating this, he states that because the self’s fixed intermediate size is maintained through the addition and subtraction of parts, both [the entry into various bodies and the fixed size] are not contradictory, just as in the case of the body itself.
There is also entry into bodies that are smaller or larger through coming and going.
By that, the intermediate status of the portions of the self is determined. || 84 ||
Regarding the phrase "deficient or excessive": he states the conclusion with the words "by that" (tena). || 84 ||
Commentary on verse 84: Regarding the word "deficiency" (*nyūna*): it refers to coming and going, which are [respectively] destruction and origination.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He refutes this by pointing out that if the self were composed of parts, it would follow that it is non-eternal, like a jar;
for in that case, its destruction would necessarily occur, just as that of a jar.
Who could be the preventer of the loss of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done? (85)

Regarding the phrase "of that which has parts": let it be so; what is the fault in that? To this he replies: "If that were the case. [The fault would be] the destruction of merit and demerit already performed without their being experienced, and the "accrual of the unperformed" (*akṛtābhyāgama*), which is the granting of fruit for those not yet performed. The sense is that these two faults would arise if one were to admit the impermanence of the self. || 85 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Refuting both the theories of the atom (aṇu) and so forth, [the author] first refutes the doctrine of the Ārhata (Jaina) school itself with the words "sāṃśasya" (of that which has parts).
This is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for [the refutation of] their theory of falsity (mithyātva). || 85 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Therefore, by the method of elimination, the all-pervasiveness of the Self is established; thus he says:
"Therefore, the Self is indeed great; it is neither atomic nor of intermediate size."
Like space, it is all-pervading and partless, as is agreed upon by the Vedas.

"Therefore" [is said]. Regarding this, he states the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa): "like space. The meaning is that the scripture beginning with "And like space, all-pervading and eternal," and "Partless and actionless," is the authority. || 86 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, having presented the refutation of both [positions], he establishes his own conclusion with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). The reason for this is given as "like space" (*ākāśavat*). This is because of the scriptural texts such as "He is omnipresent and eternal like space" and "Partless, actionless, and tranquil," as well as because the two scriptural passages concerning the "atom" and the "tip of a fingernail" intend to convey that [the Self] is imperceptible to the senses due to its extreme subtlety, and that it is conditioned by the intellect (*buddhi*), and so forth.
Such is the meaning. || 86 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. Page 158.
Having spoken thus, they fell into a great dispute regarding its specific details.
Furthermore, he is of the nature of acid (the non-conscious), of the nature of cit (consciousness), and also of the nature of both cit and acid. || 87 ||

[The commentary by Rāma on the *Citradīpa*: Having thus established the all-pervasiveness of the Self, he now demonstrates the disagreement among disputants in order to ascertain its nature as consciousness—beginning with the words "Having said this" (ityuktvā). || 87 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Having thus generally determined the omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of the Self, the author begins the determination of its specific nature with the words "ity uktvā" (having spoken thus). The term "of the disputants" (*vādinām*) is implied. The meaning is: having spoken in the aforementioned manner, they set forth their respective doctrines, arguments, and so forth. The phrase "its specific nature" (*tad-viśeṣa*) and so on is straightforward. He formulates that very method in the aphorism (*sūtra*): "acid... (87).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He presents the view of those who maintain that [the self] is insentient in nature:
"The Prābhākaras and the Tārkikas declare its insentient character."
The self is a substance like space, and consciousness is its quality, like sound.

Regarding the Prābhākaras: he restates their system as follows—"Substance is like space. This indicates the inference: "The self ought to be a substance because it possesses qualities, like space. He shows the specific quality that establishes the distinction of the self from earth and the other elements: "Like sound. The self is distinct from earth and the others because it has the quality of cognition (jñāna). That which [is not the self], such as earth...
One should observe the following inference: that which does not differ from [other] substances does not possess the quality of cognition, just like earth and so forth. || 88 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Among those mentioned there, he first states the proponents of the doctrine that [the self] is of the nature of consciousness (acidrūpa), namely the Prābhākaras. Regarding that, he states the reasoning accepted by them: "Like space" (ākāśavat) || 88 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states its other specific qualities: desire, aversion, effort, merit and demerit, pleasure and pain.
And these impressions (saṃskāras) of that [consciousness] are declared to be its qualities, like consciousness itself. || 89 ||
"Desire" refers to the formative forces (saṃskāra) that constitute cultivation (bhāvanā). || 89 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Anticipating the objection that consciousness (*cit*) alone might be the only quality of the self (*ātman*), he states its other qualities as well—beginning with "desire" (*icchā*). Thus, according to their doctrine, the individual soul (*jīva*) possesses fourteen qualities, consisting of these [nine] together with knowledge (*jñāna*), and the pentad beginning with number (*saṃkhyā*); this is the essential point. || 89 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the cause for the production and destruction of these qualities:
"When the self is joined with the mind, the qualities [arise] for one who possesses his own unseen merit (adṛṣṭa)."
They are born and then they dissolve in deep sleep due to the exhaustion of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa). || 90 ||
Regarding the word "ātmanaḥ" (of the self): the syntactical connection is that there is a conjunction of the self, who possesses his own unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), with the mind. || 90 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, he describes the manner in which the aforementioned qualities arise and so forth, beginning with the words "of the self" (ātmanaḥ). || 90 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection—"If the self is of the nature of insentience (acidrūpa), how can its status as a conscious entity be accepted?"—he states that it is so because it possesses consciousness:
"Because it possesses consciousness, this [self] is sentient, endowed with desire, aversion, and effort."
He must be the agent and the enjoyer of dharma and adharma, because he possesses suffering and other such qualities. (91)
"Because of possessing consciousness. He states another reason for the self's nature as consciousness: "desire," etc. He describes its distinction from God: "it would be," etc. || 91 ||
The Sixth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

159 a0 Commentary: Thus, stating the reason for the consciousness of the Self even though it is non-conscious by nature, [the author] says "because it possesses consciousness" (citimattvāt), implying that from that very fact, agency and so forth also follow. || 91 ||
Just as in this world, pleasure and so forth occur occasionally due to the power of karma.
Likewise, in another world, desire and so forth are produced in the body by means of karma.

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If the Self is all-pervading, how can its movement to other worlds and so forth be possible? Anticipating this, [the author] explains that just as there is the conventional usage of the Self's "abiding" and so forth when desire and the like arise in this body due to the power of karma, so too, when another body arises in another world due to the power of karma, there is the conventional usage of the Self's "movement" and so forth in that location because of the arising of pleasure and the like within the portion of the Self delimited by that new body; thus, [such movement] is merely figurative.
Intending to show that [the self] possesses movement and so forth, he says: "Just as here, by the power of karma... (92).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "How can there be movement to another world and so forth for one who is all-pervading? To this he says: "Just as... He applies this to the subject at hand: "In the same way... The construction is as follows: when a body is produced in another world by means of karma, it is by that very karma that desire and the rest are generated therein. || 92 ||
And in this way, going and coming would be possible even for that which is omnipresent.
"The entire section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa) is the authority here," they said. || 93 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Regarding the phrase "Thus," he asks: what is the proof for the self possessing attributes such as agency?
To this, he says: "In the Karma-kāṇḍa. || 93 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): What follows from this? He says: "In this way" (*evam ca*). In response to the inquiry as to what the proof for this is, he says:
"The section on ritual action" (*karmakāṇḍa*). He concludes the views of the two aforementioned schools with the word "thus" (*iti*). Those Prābhākaras and the logicians (*tārkika*) say...
The grammatical connection is that they should not speak thus. || 93 ||

— Rāma’s Commentary — Now, an objection is raised: "But was it not stated here that the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss) is internal to the *vijñānamaya* (consisting of consciousness), and thus the *ānandamaya* is the Self?
Yet now another entity possessing desire and so forth is being presented; therefore, there is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows. Anticipating this, he says:
That which remains in deep sleep is the sheath consisting of bliss (ānandamaya-kośa).
That Self of theirs, whose consciousness is unmanifest, is the first sheath; these [elements] are its qualities. || 94 ||

Regarding the phrase "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya): during deep sleep, when the indistinct consciousness remains, the sheath consisting of bliss (ānandamaya-kośa) is what is left over; that is the first of these sheaths. Among the five sheaths mentioned in the Śruti, this is the self (ātman) according to the Prābhākara school and others. The meaning is that knowledge and the other qualities previously mentioned belong to this self. || 94 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "What is the distinction between these [sheaths] and the Self (ātman) accepted by you? To this, he says: "Consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*). "Of these" refers to the Prābhākaras and others. "The preceding sheath" is the sheath consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya-kośa*). "Of this" refers to the Self accepted by them, whose consciousness is indistinct.
"Those" refers to the previously mentioned intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. (94)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states that the Bhāṭṭas describe this very Self as having the nature of both consciousness and insentience, by saying:
"Having postulated that consciousness is latent, [they maintain] the nature of being both insentient and conscious."
The followers of Bhaṭṭa maintain that memory arises from the self through the emergence of a mental conception.

Regarding the word "hidden" (*gūḍham*): the followers of Bhaṭṭa (the Bhāṭṭas), having postulated—that is, having attributed—a hidden and indistinct consciousness (*caitanya*) to the self, describe it as being of a dual nature, consisting of both the conscious and the insentient.

He states the reason for this attribution of consciousness: "the attribution of consciousness" (*cidutprekṣā*). The construction is: "the attribution of consciousness arises from memory that has arisen.
The meaning is that for one who has awakened from sleep, an attribution of the consciousness of deep sleep occurs based on the memory produced [upon waking]. || 95 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 160.

[Commentary on the *Citradīpa*, Chapter 1]—Now, he states the Bhaṭṭa school’s view concerning the very subject matter already mentioned: "Hidden," etc. The reason for the creative imagination (*utprekṣā*) of consciousness is given as "having arisen": namely, the memory of Devadatta who has awakened from deep sleep, such as "I slept happily, I was not aware of anything..."
The meaning is that its form is "diṣam" and so forth. || 95 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He clarifies the very manner of the conscious imagination:
"Having become inert, [he thinks] 'then there was sleep'; thus, at that time, there is the memory of inertia."
Without the experience of dullness, it is in no way possible. || 96 ||

"Having become insentient": the meaning is that at the time of deep sleep, the memory of insentience in the form "I slept" arises in the person who has awakened; since this memory would be inexplicable without an experience of insentience during the time of deep sleep, it leads one to infer an experience of insentience at that time. || 96 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Having restated that very [point], he establishes his own nature as both insentient and conscious by means of that indicative mark (*liṅga*), using the verse beginning with "jaḍo bhūtvā" (having become insentient).

"I" refers to the self at that time, during the period of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). "Having become insentient, I slept"—this is the form of the recollection. "Then" refers to the time of rising from sleep.
The word "jāḍyena" (by means of insentience) is to be construed with the phrase beginning with "vinā" (without). || 96 ||
Furthermore, the non-cessation of the seer's vision is heard [in scripture] during sleep; therefore, this [seer exists].
The Self shines like a firefly by means of both non-luminosity and luminosity. || 97 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭī0): He states the proof for the absence of the loss of consciousness during deep sleep: "Of the seer... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23]. For it is said in the Śruti: "Indeed, there is no loss of the vision of the seer, because of its indestructibility. This means that for the Self, who is the seer, there is no loss of the vision that constitutes its very nature, because its essential character is free from destruction. Otherwise, even for one who asserts such a loss, it would be impossible to speak of it without a witness; therefore, consciousness exists in deep sleep.
Because the absence of dissolution is heard [in scripture], for that reason as well, this Self is endowed with both non-manifestation and manifestation, like a firefly; such is the meaning. || 97 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): In this regard, he also cites scripture as authority—“of the seer” and so forth. The meaning is that the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad itself, with reference to deep sleep, declares: “Indeed, there is no loss of the vision of the seer, because of its imperishability; but there is nothing second to it, nothing else distinct from it, which it might see. This is joined with what follows: “joined” (yuktaḥ). || 97 ||
If it is not accepted that a partless entity can possess a dual nature in any way whatsoever.
Therefore, the discerning followers of Sāṃkhya say that the Self is indeed of the nature of consciousness alone. || 98 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary (rā0 ṭī0): Having stated the refutation of this Bhāṭṭa view, he sets forth the Sāṃkhya position with the words "niraṃśasya" (of that which is partless). || 98 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, having refuted this [position], he states the Sāṃkhya doctrine: "Of that which is partless," etc. (98).
The portion of inertia (jāḍya) is the nature of Prakṛti; it is subject to transformation and consists of the three qualities (triguṇa).
Prakṛti proceeds for the sake of the Puruṣa's experience and liberation. || 99 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question, "What then is the status of the memory of insentience (*jāḍya*)," he says: "The portion of insentience" (*jāḍyāṃśa*).

He states the purpose for postulating *prakṛti*—which is of the nature of that [insentience] and consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—with the words: "Of consciousness" (*citaḥ*).
This means "of the Puruṣa. || 99 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): If this is so, then what is the fate of the portion of dullness (jāḍya) inferred from the etymological tradition (nirukta-smṛti)? To this, he says:
[Page 161] The Sixth Chapter.
[This is] accompanied by two commentaries.

Regarding the phrase "the portion of insentience" (jāḍyāṃśa): that is the nature [of the object] under discussion. Now, one might ask: why should such a nature be postulated? To this he says: "of consciousness" (citaḥ).
The meaning is: of the Self, whose nature is consciousness. || 99 ||

Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Now, one might object: since the conscious principle (cit) is unattached and Prakṛti and Puruṣa are therefore utterly distinct, how can the experience of enjoyment and liberation belong to the Puruṣa through the activity of Prakṛti?
Anticipating this doubt, he states that enjoyment and liberation are attributed to the Puruṣa because of the non-apprehension of their distinction.
Bondage and liberation are considered to belong to unattached consciousness due to the non-apprehension of its distinctions.
For the sake of establishing the distinction between bondage and liberation, there is a differentiation of consciousness, as in the case of the ancients.
Regarding the phrase "of the unattached one": he states that the Sāṃkhyas, like the logicians and others, accept a plurality of selves, saying "bondage and liberation. || 100 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, [an objection is raised]: "In your view, how can there be bondage and so forth for the Self, which is unattached? To this, he says: "Of the unattached" (*asaṅgāyāḥ*). The implicit meaning is: "from the Self, which is established as beginningless, and from nature (*prakṛti*) and its effects. From such [a Self]. "Bhedeti" means: "as in the case of the aforementioned proponents, such as the Bhāṭṭas and others. "Cit" connects with the phrase: "there is no plurality of selves" (*nānātmatvamasti*). || 100 ||
That which is beyond the Great (mahat) is called the Unmanifest (avyakta), which is primordial nature (prakṛti).
Just as non-attachment is heard [in scripture], so too is it clear from the statement "for he is unattached. (101)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He cites scripture regarding the existence of *prakṛti* and the disjoined nature (*asaṅgatva*) of the *puruṣa*: "Of the Great [One]... (101).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): In this regard, he cites scripture as authority with the words "of the Great" (mahataḥ). The meaning is that it is heard in the Śruti: "For this Puruṣa is indeed unattached. || 101 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus demonstrated the disagreements among disputants regarding the individual soul (jīva), he now establishes the nature of God (Īśvara) in order to demonstrate the disagreements concerning Him: "For [God] is indeed the regulator of Prakṛti, which is active in proximity to Consciousness."
The followers of Yoga call him Īśvara; he is heard in scripture to be superior to the individual souls (jīvas).

Regarding the phrase "in the proximity of consciousness": one might object that the postulation of a Lord distinct from primordial matter (prakṛti) and the individual soul (puruṣa) lacks authoritative evidence; anticipating this, he says: "He [is distinct] from the individual souls. || 2 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Having thus presented the conflicting views of various disputants regarding the individual soul (jīva), which is the denotation of the term *tvam*, he now demonstrates those same views concerning the Lord (Īśvara), the denotation of the term *tat*, and states the system of Patañjali: "In the proximity of consciousness" (*citsaṃnidhau*), etc. "The regulator" (*niyāmaka*) means the controller.
By this, it is indicated that the flaw in the earlier [Sāṅkhya] view is the impropriety of insentient primordial matter (*prakṛti*) acting independently. || 102 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He cites that very scripture which establishes the existence of the Lord:
"The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas"—thus says the Śruti.
For in the Āraṇyaka, the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) has been established through non-agitation.

Regarding the term "Pradhāna": Pradhāna is the state of equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas); the kṣetrajñas are the individual souls (jīvas); their lords are the qualities such as sattva and the rest;
the meaning is that [the Lord] is the controller of those. He states that not only this scripture teaches the Lord, but also the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa, by saying:
"In the Āraṇyaka. || 3 ||

Commentary on A0: Here too, he cites scripture as authority—namely, the verse beginning with "pradhāna. The meaning is that He is the Lord (pati) of both *pradhāna*—which is *prakṛti* existing in a state of equilibrium of the *guṇas*—and the *kṣetrajñas*, which are the individual souls (*jīvas*). Alternatively, it means He is the Lord (*īśa*) of the *guṇas*, such as *sattva* and the others, that is to say, their controller.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 162.
[Regarding the title *Citradīpa*:
he states that not only this Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad is the authority here, but also the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa located in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad—thus: "In the Āraṇyaka" (verse 103).]
Even here, disputants quarrel with their respective arguments.
For they indeed cite scriptural passages according to their own understanding.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He announces that very disagreement among disputants with the words "even here" (anāpi). "According to their wisdom" means according to their respective levels of intelligence. || 4 ||
Commentary (a0): Even there, he announces the disagreements among disputants with the words "atrāpi" (even here). || 104 ||

Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Now, he recites in substance the aphorism propounding the Lord as stated by Patañjali: "The Lord is a particular Puruṣa untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, and the latent impressions thereof"—"Untouched even by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, and their latent impressions."
The Lord would be a particular kind of male being, like a living soul (jīva), yet he too would be devoid of attachment.

Regarding the term *kleśa*: the afflictions (*kleśa*) are the five beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*). Actions (*karma*) are those aphorized as: "The karma of the yogi is neither white nor black; for others, it is of three kinds. When the root exists, its maturation consists of birth, lifespan, and experience; these are called the maturations of action (*karmavipāka*). The specific fruits are their latent dispositions (*āśaya*); the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by them constitute the Lord (*īśvara*), a particular person who remains untouched by those afflictions and the like. He too is a living being (*jīva*).
The meaning is that it is of the nature of consciousness, free from the eighteen adjuncts. || 5 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Therein, first, he demonstrates this very point according to the Pātañjala system: "By afflictions, actions, fruitions, and latent impressions... This is indeed the Pātañjala Sūtra: "The Lord is a specific Puruṣa untouched by afflictions, actions, fruitions, and latent impressions. The same applies to the other sūtras concerning afflictions and so forth. Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are the five afflictions. Action is white, black, or neither for the yogi; it is of three kinds for others. When [action exists]...
At the root, their maturation consists of birth, lifespan, and experience; the meaning is that the latent dispositions (*āśaya*) of these three are the formative forces (*saṃskāra*). || 105 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: "If [the Self] is of the nature of unattached consciousness, how can it be a controller?
To this, he says: "Nevertheless, because it is a specific kind of Person (puṃviśeṣa), its status as a controller is proclaimed."
Otherwise, in this case, bondage and liberation would both fall into a state of instability.
"Even so," he says. He states the fault that would arise if one does not accept God as the controller: "there would be a lack of order. (6)
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "How can this [Self], whose nature is unattached consciousness, possess the quality of being a controller? To this, he says: "Even so" (tathāpi). || 106 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that the Lordship of the unattached Supreme Self lacks any basis of proof, he says:
"From fear of Him," and so forth, [referring to] the unattached Supreme Self.
That which has been heard is logical for him as well, because of his lack of connection with afflictions, karma, and so forth.

"Bhīṣeti" (He terrifies). His status as the controller is heard in scripture. Now, one might ask: "Even if it is heard in scripture, how can that which is illogical be accepted? To this he says: "It is also logical. The meaning is that it is appropriate because the afflictions and other such qualities belonging to the individual soul (jīva) are absent [in Him]. || 7 ||

Commentary: For this very reason, he states that even what was said in such passages as "From fear of Him the wind blows," regarding the fact that the Unattached [Brahman] generates fear in the wind and other elements, is indeed logical: "bhīṣā'smāditi" (from fear of Him...). || 107 ||
And because living beings are also unattached, afflictions and the like do not arise for them, just as [it does not arise] in the case of space.
Due to the non-apprehension of discernment (viveka), the afflictions (kleśa), karma, and so forth previously mentioned [arise]. (8)
The Sixth Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.

163 Rāghavānanda’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "But are not individual souls (*jīva*) also of the nature of unattached consciousness and likewise devoid of afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth? If that is so, what is the distinction between them and the Lord (*īśvara*)? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that although souls are inherently devoid of afflictions and the like, afflictions and so forth do exist for them due to the failure to grasp their distinction from the intellect (*buddhi*).
He recalls what was stated previously with the words: "Of living beings" (jīvānām) || 8 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): In reality, although even for living beings there is indeed an absence of afflictions and the like, it is nevertheless based solely on the failure to grasp their distinction [from the Self]; thus he says: "Even for living beings... (108).
They consider eternal knowledge, effort, and desire to be the qualities of the Lord.
Logicians maintain that it is illogical for that which is unattached to be a controller.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: However, the logicians (tārkikas), unable to accept that the Unattached One (the Lord) can be a controller, maintain that He possesses a triad of qualities such as knowledge which are eternal, in order to establish His distinction from the individual soul (jīva). Thus he says: "Eternal," etc. (9).
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, preceded by this refutation, he states the view of the logicians (tārkika) with the words "nityajñāna" (eternal knowledge), etc. || 109 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection—"How can that [Pradhāna], which possesses qualities such as desire, be distinct from the individual soul (jīva)?"—he resolves it by stating that it is precisely because of the eternality of those qualities:
"Its status as a specific type of spirit (puṃviśeṣatva) is due to its qualities alone, and not otherwise."
The Śruti has proclaimed: "He whose desires are true and whose resolve is true," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the state of being a specific male": he states the proof for the eternality of the qualities (guṇas) with the words "satya" [and so forth]. || 110 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, the Lord’s status as a "distinguished person" (puṃviśeṣatva) is indeed justified by His attributes such as eternal knowledge, as stated in the Śruti passage, "He whose desires are true, whose resolves are true," and so forth; this is what he says with the words, "puṃviśeṣatvamapi" (even His status as a distinguished person). || 110 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Since that [position] also possesses defects, he states another alternative:
"If He possessed eternal knowledge and so forth, creation would indeed occur at all times."
Therefore, Hiraṇyagarbha is the Lord, joined with a subtle body (liṅgadeha).

Regarding the word "eternal": to the question of what the form of that Hiraṇyagarbha is, he says—“by means of the subtle body” (liṅgadehena). The meaning is that the Supreme Self, having Māyā as its limiting adjunct, is called Hiraṇyagarbha through the conceit of being the aggregate of subtle bodies. || 11 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, refuting even this view, [the author] introduces the position of the Hiraṇyagarbhas, who maintain that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the self, stating that they have spoken thus; he presents the previously mentioned doctrine of Hiraṇyagarbha regarding the determination of the Lord as being like that of the individual soul (*jīvātman*). [He says: "Eternal... and "By the *liṅga*... The meaning is: "by the aggregate subtle body (*samaṣṭiliṅgaśarīra*). || 111 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: What is the proof for Hiraṇyagarbha’s status as the Lord? To this he says:
"The greatness of him [Hiraṇyagarbha] is described in great detail in the Udgītha Brāhmaṇa."

Even though the existence of the *liṅga* (the subtle body) persists, this [liberated soul] does not possess the state of being a living being (*jīvatva*) due to the absence of karma and other such factors.

Regarding the term "udgītha": one might raise the objection that the living being (jīva) would exist due to its connection with the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra). Anticipating this, he states—"even though the subtle body exists"—to show that it is not the jīva because of the absence of ignorance (avidyā), desire (kāma), and action (karman). || 12 ||
Commentary (ṭīkā): Regarding that, he states the proof: "udgītha... || 112 ||
Without the gross body, the subtle body is not perceived anywhere.
Therefore, the body of Vairāja is the Lord, possessing a head and other limbs on all sides.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 164]

[From the commentary by Rāma on the *Citradīpa*: Because the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) alone is not perceived apart from the gross body (*sthūladeha*), the Lord says—“without the gross body”—that the Virāj, who identifies with the aggregate of gross bodies, is indeed the Lord. 13.
Commentary (a0): Here too, he states the view of those who worship the Universal Form (viśvarūpa), preceded by its refutation: "sthūla... (Verse 113).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the proof for its existence:
"And thus, 'thousand-headed' and also 'having eyes on all sides'."
Those who contemplate the Universal Form say, "It has been heard," incessantly.
The phrase "sahasraśīrṣā" refers to the Vedic passage [Rigveda 10.90.1]; this is the understood meaning. Those who contemplate the Universal Form (viśvarūpa) are the worshippers of Virāj. ||14||

a0 Commentary—Regarding that, he states the proof: "sahasra... etc. The Taittirīya Śruti itself also includes such passages as, "He whose eyes are on all sides and whose faces are on all sides. || 114 ||
If [the Lord] possessed hands and feet everywhere, then even worms and the like would possess lordship.
Therefore, the four-faced god alone is the Lord, and no other person.
Rāma’s Commentary: Here too, he says "from all sides" (sarvataḥ) to show that one should take refuge in another deity by perceiving faults [in the current practice]. ||115||
Commentary (a0): Since a fault would likewise arise here, he states the view of the worshipers of the Four-faced One (Brahmā) with the two verses beginning with "sarvataḥ" [verse 115].
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question "By whom was this said?", he replies: "The Prajāpati, being approached by them for the sake of a son, spoke thus."
They also cite such scriptural passages as, "He created living beings," and so forth. || 16 ||

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of a son," he states—beginning with "Prajāpati created offspring"—that such scriptural passages serve as the authority for that [position], saying: "Prajāpati... (verse 16).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding the phrase "for the sake of a son," he provides the scriptural authority for that as well: "Prajāpati... This Śruti passage also belongs specifically to the Taittirīya branch. || 116 ||
From the navel of Viṣṇu arose the Creator, who was born from the lotus.
Some people, the devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas), say that Viṣṇu alone is the Lord. || 17 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the Bhāgavata doctrine—“Of Viṣṇu,” etc.—[verse 17].
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, he summarizes the Vaiṣṇava position with the verse beginning "Of Viṣṇu" (viṣṇoḥ). || 117 ||
Because he was unable to seek out the feet of Śiva, Śiva [bestowed grace] upon him.
Those who follow the Śaiva Āgamas claim that the Lord is Śiva, not Viṣṇu.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the doctrine of the Śaivas with the words "of Śiva" (śivasya). || 18 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, by association with Mādhva, Rāmānuja, and others—who are primarily followers of the Pāñcarātra and Bhāgavata systems—the author introduces the Tantric Śaiva doctrine as well, beginning with the words "of Śiva. For this very reason, the meaning is that the Tantrikas consider themselves to be followers of the Āgamas. || 118 ||
He also worshipped Vighneśa in order to destroy the three cities.
Those devoted to the Gāṇapatya doctrine declare Vināyaka to be the Lord.
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He states the Gāṇapatya doctrine: "The three cities," etc. (Verse 19).
The Sixth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

165a0 Commentary: Since it is well-known in the Purāṇas and other texts that he (Iśvara) was the one who performed the worship of Gaṇapati for the sake of achieving the defeat of the demon Tripura, the author states the view of the Gāṇapatyas— that he alone is the Lord— with the verse beginning with "pure" (119).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He extends the aforementioned principle to other cases as well:
"In this same way, others [speak] differently and differently, out of attachment to their respective positions."
They established [their views] by relying on mantras, explanatory passages (arthavādas), ritual manuals (kalpas), and so forth. || 20 ||

"Thus" [means]: there are others who are worshippers of Bhairava, Mairāla, and so forth. He states the reason for describing [the matter] in various ways with the words "their own" (*svasva*). He shows that there are authoritative sources (*pramāṇa*) for each of those cases with the word "mantra. || 20 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, indicating that the views of the Sauras and others may likewise be inferred by oneself through the method of illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), he concludes the disagreements among those who propound the doctrine of a non-existent God (*anukteśvaravāda*) with the words "evam" (thus). Regarding the term "mantra": the meaning is that *mantratva* (the nature of being a mantra) is the status of being a statement of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇavākya*) designated by the word "mantra," which is distinct from injunctions (*vidhi*)—characterized as consisting of any one of the *liṅ*, *loṭ*, or *tavya* suffixes—as well as from explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) that praise [such injunctions]. Thus.

The meaning is that "Kalpatva" (the nature of being a Kalpa) consists precisely in being a statement containing the sense of an agent (*ārṣa*) regarding what ought to be done (*kartavyatā*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth are included. Having relied [upon these], that is, through the pride of their respective partisan views, they propounded the Lord in various ways; such is the connection of the sentence. || 120 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question of how many such doctrines there are, he states that they are innumerable:
"Starting from those who maintain the Lord is the inner controller (antaryāmī) down to those who maintain the Lord is the immobile objects (sthāvara)."
This is because of the observation of the family deities of the Aśvattha, Arka, Vaṃśa, and other lineages. || 21 ||

Regarding the phrase "the Inner Controller" (*antaryāmin*): anticipating the objection that the doctrine of the Lord as the presiding deity of stationary objects (*sthāvara*) has never been observed anywhere, he says: "Aśvattha, Arka," etc. (Chapter 21). **Commentary:** Now, even so, one might ask: how many doctrines exist regarding the Lord as the source of nature (*prakṛti*)? To this he replies: "The Inner Controller," etc. The ellipsis is to be completed by adding "are innumerable. The reason for this is stated by the words beginning with "Aśvattha," etc. (Verse 121).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, in response to the inquiry as to which of these differing views is to be accepted and which is to be rejected when there is such a diversity of opinions, he says:
"By one desiring the ascertainment of reality, who investigates through logic and scripture..."
There is but one single practice, and that too is clearly explained here. || 22 ||

Regarding the phrase "tattvaniścaye" (in the determination of reality): for those persons who, desiring the determination of reality—that is, with the wish for the determination of reality—are habituated to investigating both logic (*nyāya*) and scripture (*āgama*), their understanding should be one and the same. To the question of what that [understanding] is like, he says: "That too is here" (*sāpyatra*). || 22 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if this were so, would it not follow that there would be a lack of confidence everywhere? To this he says: "tattva... (regarding reality). This means: by the desire for a definitive conclusion (nirṇaya) concerning an object that is not sublated. Logic (nyāya) is scripture rooted in reasoning; whereas tradition (āgama) is that which is rooted in authoritative command (ājñā).
It should be understood that within this very [category], all verbal Brahman—from the Vedas up to poetry—is included. || 122 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To demonstrate that very realization, he cites the corresponding scriptural passage:
"One should know Māyā as Prakṛti, and the wielder of Māyā as Maheśvara."
By its constituent parts, this entire world is pervaded.

"Know Māyā alone... etc. One should know Māyā alone to be *prakṛti*, the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the world; but one should know the Possessor of Māyā (*māyin*), who has Māyā as his limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), namely the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), to be the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). The meaning of this scripture is that this entire world is pervaded by the individual souls (*jīvas*), which are mobile in nature and constitute the limbs or portions (*aṃśas*) of this Possessor of Māyā, the Great Lord. || 23 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): In order to produce that very cognition (pramiti) designated as the realization of the one form, [the author] first cites the Śruti as an introductory statement (upoddhāta): "But [He created] Māyā... (123).
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [page 166] 166.
Rāma’s Commentary: He states that a determination regarding the Lord is appropriate in accordance with this scripture:
"Thus, in accordance with scripture, the determination regarding the Lord is logical."
Furthermore, according to the Citradīpa,
there would likewise be no contradiction for those who maintain that the Lord is the ruler even of stationary beings.

Regarding the word "iti": having raised the doubt as to why this is logical, he says "tathā" (so it is), because it is not contradicted anywhere. The sense is that since everyone accepts [the existence of] God, there is no contradiction with anyone. || 24 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Thus" (iti). He states the logical justification for that: "That being so" (tathā sati) || 124 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might ask, "What is the nature of this Māyā, which is the material cause of the universe? To this he says:
"And this Māyā is of the nature of darkness (tamas), because of its description as such in the Tāpanīya [Upaniṣad]."
Regarding that, the Śruti itself declared direct experience to be the means of valid knowledge.

"And this is Māyā. From what [source] is this known? To this he says: "In the Tāpanīya. The meaning is that because the nature of Māyā as being of the form of darkness (*tamas*) is declared in the *Tāpanīya Upaniṣad*. When there is the inquiry, "What is the proof for Māyā being of the form of darkness?", he states:
"Anubhūti" (Experience). He asserts that here the scripture itself, as "experience," is the proof. || 125 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, raising the doubt as to what the very substance of *māyā* is, [the author] provides the resolution by summarizing the meaning of the scripture—namely the *Nṛsiṃhottaratāpanīya*, which is well-known for stating "And *māyā* is of the nature of darkness, distinct from experience; this is inert, delusive, infinite, and void, such is its form"—in two verses beginning with "And *māyā*... (129).

Rāma’s Commentary: In that regard, when the inquiry arises as to what the experience is regarding Māyā’s nature as darkness (tamas), he states that the Śruti itself clarifies the experience here by saying, "That is insentient and of the nature of delusion.
Thus, the Śruti makes this experience manifest: "It is insentient and of the nature of delusion."
She declared its infinity because it is clear even to children and cowherds.

Regarding the term "insentient" (jaḍam): he states "from childhood" (āvāla) to show that its status as established by all experience is declared by the Śruti through the word "infinite" (anaṃtam). The meaning is that the fact that the insentient and delusion are the effects of Prakṛti is the experience of everyone, from children and cowherds on up. || 26 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): "Inert" (jaḍam) and "down to children" (āvālam). The meaning is "starting from a child cowherd.
And thus, the intention is that the infinity of ignorance is due precisely to its being well-known to all conscious beings, and not because of its indestructibility. || 126 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the meaning of the word "jaḍa" (insentient):
"Indeed, that which is the very nature of insentient things such as jars and the like, which are non-conscious by essence—that is 'jaḍa'."
"That wherein the intellect becomes blunted—that, worldly people call delusion. || 27 ||
Regarding the phrase "of an acidic nature," he explains the meaning of the word *moha* (delusion) with the words "where... (verse 27).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Even so, how is it that you possess dullness? To this he says: "acid" (non-conscious). He likewise explains the nature of delusion (moha) as follows:
"yatna" (effort), etc. There is also the traditional rule (smṛti): "the root *muh* means bewilderment. || 127 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states that infinity, characterized by being established through universal experience in the manner described, is thus proven:
"In this way, even by all people, this is experienced from the perspective of worldly perception."
But from the perspective of reasoning, it is inexpressible, according to the Vedic scripture: "Non-being did not exist. (28)

"Thus" means: this nature of being characterized by darkness (*tamas*), which consists of dullness and delusion. Now, if *māyā* is established through the experience of all people, [then] regarding jars and so forth—[this is] the sixth chapter.

Accompanied by two commentaries. 167. Anticipating the objection that [ignorance] might not be removable by knowledge like a jar, he says: "By reasoning" (yukti). The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of setting aside the doubt. [The text continues: "anirvā... [incomplete].
Since it cannot be defined as either existent or non-existent, what is the proof for that? To this he says: "It is not non-existent" (nāsat). || 28 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): This form of his is indeed common even to the ignorant; thus he says, "In this way" (ittham). If so, how is it viewed from the perspective of the wise? He says, "By reasoning" (yukti). Even there, due to the lack of satisfaction arising from the principle that "reasoning is not firmly established" (tarkāpratiṣṭhāna), he cites scripture itself as the authority, saying, "Not so" (na). || 128 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the intended meaning of this Śruti:
"It was neither non-existent, because it was manifest; nor was it existent, because that would be contradicted."
From the perspective of true knowledge, what has been heard is trivial, because it ceases to exist through impermanence. || 29 ||

The meaning is that [this form] is negated by the scriptural text, "Non-being was not," and by the text, "There is nothing whatsoever here that is manifold. However, its being both existent and non-existent is illogical due to contradiction; thus, it is disregarded by scripture. Having thus demonstrated indeterminability from the perspective of reasoning, he says "by knowledge" to show that scripture—through the experience of the wise—reveals the insubstantiality (*tucchatva*) of this form, stating, "This form of his is insubstantial. The reason for its insubstantiality is...
"Of Māhātasya. || 29 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) on *a* summarizes that very scripture according to its meaning: "Not non-existent" (*nāsat*). Then, it asks how that is so from the perspective of knowledge (*jñāna-dṛṣṭi*), and answers: "Vidyā" (*vidyā*). The meaning is that this form has been declared in the sacred tradition (*śruta*) to be insubstantial (*tuccha*). As it is stated in the *Vārttika*: "But from the perspective of Brahman, this ignorance (*avidyā*) is not in any way tenable. (129)
The commentary on Rāmānuja concludes the established point:
"This [ignorance] is threefold: unreal (tuccha), indeterminable (nirvacanīya), and real (vāstavī)."
Māyā is to be known through three types of knowledge: that derived from scripture, that derived from reasoning, and that derived from common worldly experience. || 130 ||

"Empty" (tucchā): the meaning is that Māyā is to be known as threefold—empty because it is non-existent even in the three periods of time according to scriptural knowledge (śrauta-bodha), indeterminable (anirvacanīyā) according to logical knowledge (yauktika-bodha), and real (vāstavī) according to worldly knowledge (laukika-bodha). || 130 ||
And thus, as a result, he states the three views concerning that [object] in the verse beginning with "tucchā" (130).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the purpose of this Śruti, which demonstrates the existence and non-existence of this world:
"It demonstrates the existence and non-existence of this world."
And just as a painted cloth [is displayed] through its expansion and contraction, so too is it [the case here]. || 31 ||

Regarding this: he provides an illustration for how a single illusion alone can manifest both the existence and non-existence of the world—starting with the words "from expansion" (prasāraṇāt). || 31 ||

— Commentary (A0 Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Granted that such is Māyā, what does it do? Anticipating this doubt, the author provides the answer while explaining the meaning of the *Tāpanīya Śruti*, which states that it "shows both its existence and non-existence. He begins with the word "asya" (of this). In this regard, he provides an illustration from the *Prakṛti*...

It brings forward precisely what is situated in that context: "And because of expansion" (*prasāraṇāt*). Just as a painted cloth, through its expansion, demonstrates the existence of the collection of colors and their non-existence through its contraction, so too this Māyā demonstrates the existence of this world through its production and maintenance, and its non-existence through its dissolution; such is the meaning. || 131 ||
For illusion would indeed be independent [of anything else] if it were not perceived without consciousness.
Even if it were independent, it would be exactly the same, because that which is unattached cannot undergo alteration. (32)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: By the scriptural statement, "by way of independence and lack of independence," the independence and lack of independence of Māyā are demonstrated.
Vidyāraṇya’s *Pañcadaśī*, titled *Citradīpa*.

[The author] states the justification for both [theories] in the verse beginning with "asvatantra": "Being dependent" (*asvatantra*) means that it does not shine forth apart from the consciousness that illuminates it. It is non-independent (*asaṃ-*)...
The meaning is that she is independent because she effects a transformation of her own self. || 32 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, by the phrase "not [by] independence or non-independence," he also reveals that Māyā possesses both independence and non-independence, exactly as stated in the *Uttaratāpanīya-śruti*—namely, "for [Māyā] is non-independent" (*asvatantrā hi*). The word "otherwise" (*anyathā*) means: [if it were otherwise], there would be the consequence of [the Self] being associated with adjuncts (*saṃga*), and so forth. || 132 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He clarifies this very act of transformation: "She makes the immutable and unattached Self into the world."
By means of the nature of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), he also created both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa).

Regarding the phrase "unchanging and unattached": he states that it effects the division between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), as declared by the Śruti in the passage, "It creates [the distinction] through its reflection," by using the term "consciousness-reflection" (cidābhāsa). || 33 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) clarifies that very point with the words "kūṭastha" and so on. Thus, based on the scriptural statement, "He creates the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) by means of reflection," it is said that [the Self] manifests both the individual soul and the Lord through the nature of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa): "cidābhāsa... (verse 133).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that "if the Self were to undergo change, its immutability (kūṭasthatva) would be lost," he says:
"Without disturbing the immutable [Self], it creates the world and so forth."
What wonder is there in Māyā, which brings about that which is difficult to accomplish? || 34 ||

Regarding the term "immutable" (*kūṭastha*): one might object that it is difficult to conceive how the immutable nature [of Brahman] can be maintained while simultaneously bringing about the manifestation of the world and so forth. Anticipating this doubt, he says "difficult to accomplish" (*durdhaṭa*) to show that this is not a cause for wonder, because Māyā is precisely that which makes even the impossible possible. The underlying sense is that otherwise, its very status as *māyā* would be forfeited. || 34 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, [an objection is raised]: "But if the Self undergoes transformation, its immutability (*kūṭasthatva*) would be lost. To this, he says: "The immutable" (*kūṭastham*). [An objection: "But how is this logically possible? To this, he says: "The sole difficult-to-accomplish" (*durghaṭaikā*) || 134 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To illustrate that the nature of Māyā is to accomplish the impossible, he says:
"Fluidity in water, heat in fire, and hardness in stone."
And the fact that illusion is difficult to reconcile is established by itself, not from anything else. || 135 ||
"Fluidity," etc.: the meaning is that just as fluidity and other qualities of water and so forth are natural, in the same way, Māyā possesses the power to accomplish the impossible. || 139 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, raising the doubt as to how it is that He performs such difficult feats, [the author] states that this is indeed His innate nature: "As long as the world does not directly perceive that wonder... (135).
But later, when he reflects upon it in his mind, he realizes, "This was an illusion," and he becomes tranquil.

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "It has been stated that the power of Māyā to perform the impossible is not a cause for wonder; this is untenable, because we observe in the world that Māyā is indeed a cause of amazement.
Anticipating this doubt, he says, "He does not know," [verse 36], to show that Māyā is a cause for wonder only as long as its employment remains unperceived by the user, and not thereafter.

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that it is indeed a marvel that Māyā performs such impossible feats; to this, he says: "He does not know. The meaning is: He [the Lord] does not know that controller of Māyā, who is the non-dual Self. || 136 ||
The Sixth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
For objections indeed proliferate against those who assert that the world is a real entity.
Nor is it to be questioned as an illusion, because that [illusion] has questioning as its sole nature. || 37 ||

169 Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Furthermore, such objections should be directed against the Naiyāyikas and others who maintain the reality of the world, but not against the proponent of Māyā; thus he says: "It spreads forth" (prasaratīti). || 37 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "Without destroying the immutable nature of the Self (*kūṭasthātmatva*), how can Māyā manifest [it] as the world and so forth? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that the scope for questioning the relationship between cause and effect belongs only to the logicians (*tārkika*) and others who maintain doctrines such as *ārambha* (aggregation) and *pariṇāma* (transformation), but not to the proponent of *vivarta* (illusory manifestation). He says: "For they proceed... and so on. That which is to be questioned is that which is to be challenged. The reason for this is stated by the words beginning with "of that" (*tasyāḥ*). [This concludes the section on] the challenge.
The meaning is: because it consists solely of the fundamental form of ignorance. || 137 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) that would follow if one were to raise an objection against the proponent of Māyā-vāda:
"If there were an objection even to an objection, then I am raising an objection to your objection."
Therefore, the objection must be refuted; it should not be further challenged.
Regarding the phrase "even when challenged": if one asks, "What then should be done?", he says: "It must be avoided. || 38 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Even in that case, regarding the objection characterized by your own critique, some cause must be stated for the effect, simply because it is an effect. Since causality consists precisely in being invariably antecedent to the effect, it is dependent upon the effect; thus, there would be a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*) and so forth.

Consequently, the objection against you alone would remain, and its refutation would be extremely difficult to achieve. Therefore, no further objection can be raised against the proponent of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavādin*).
He says "even when there is an objection" (codye 'pi) to show that you must act as one who asserts a distinction. || 138 ||
Because Māyā, whose sole body is wonder, takes the form of an inquiry.
The wise should diligently seek a solution to this. || 39 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He elaborates upon the very point already stated in the verse beginning with "wonder" (vismaya). || 39 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Granted that this may be the resolution for the proponent through the logic of refutation (*khaṇḍanayukti*), how then is there a resolution for me, who am merely desirous of knowledge (*jijñāsu*)? To this, he says: "Whose sole body is wonder" (*vismayaikadehāyāḥ*). This means: she whose very form is the marvelous alone, due to her skill in bringing about the occurrence of the impossible. By such *māyā*, [is meant] that ignorance (*ajñāna*) by which the nature of this objection—the form of the object to be challenged, which has become the subject of doubt—is [concealed].

Therefore, while ignorance persists, doubt regarding the object appears, such as "Is this a post or not? This means, in short, that it consists solely of ignorance. For this very reason, it is said by those possessing wisdom—meaning those who possess indirect (parokṣa) knowledge, according to the Smṛti passage, "Having known this, one becomes wise"—that [the Self] is to be sought after. Alternatively, because of the supplementary statement in the Smṛti, "and having done what was to be done," it is direct (aparokṣa) knowledge alone that is the cause of being wise in this context.

"By those desiring liberation who are constant and spontaneous" means, in short, by those desiring liberation who are the fourfold universal monarchs (*caturcakravartin*). "There too, with effort" means by exerting oneself even to the point of risking one's life.
By this, it is implied that [this practice] is not to be neglected under any circumstances. || 139 ||

He raises an objection—Rāghavendra’s commentary states: "It is appropriate to seek a means of avoiding [the world] once its illusory nature is ascertained; however, that very ascertainment is not established at present."
If you say that its very nature as illusion must be determined, then determine it!
Let that characteristic of illusion which is well-known in the world be observed. (140)

Regarding the phrase "the state of being an illusion" (*māyātvam*): with the intention that its status as an illusion should be determined because the defining characteristics of an illusion are present, he says "then" (*tarhi*).
