To the question "What is the definition?", he says "in the world" (*loke*) [verse 140].
Commentary (Ṭīkā): If this is so, then in that case— [page 170]
From the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya:
"As long as the world does not know Him directly, so long does it experience wonder."
"But later, when he holds in his mind that 'this was an illusion,' he becomes pacified."

To the disciple who says, "Regarding that which is called the *Citradīpa*, one must take refuge in the very experience of the wise as previously taught by the venerable masters," he [the teacher] expresses his assent with a restatement: "It is indeed the nature of *māyā*. He states the means for that [realization]: "In the world... (verse 140). The words "by you here" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question, "What is the characteristic of that [state] as well?", he says:
"That which cannot be defined, yet shines with perfect clarity."
People understood that [the world] is illusion (māyā), as in the case of Indra’s net and similar phenomena. || 41 ||
"It cannot be defined. (41)

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): To the question, "What is the definition of *māyā* as it is commonly known in the world? he says: "Not [so]. Thus, the general definition of *māyā* is established as: being that which appears most clearly while being unfit for such a definitive description. The pair of syllables (*da* and *la*) are included respectively to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to Brahman and to the void (*tuccha*). || 141 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He applies the definition established in the illustration to the subject of the illustration: "If this world appears clearly, its [ultimate] determination is impossible."
Therefore, behold the world as consisting of illusion, without partiality.
It is clear. || 42 ||
The commentary applies that [definition] to the object of definition (lakṣya), stating: "It is clear. || 142 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question of how the world is impossible to define, he demonstrates this:
"When it is attempted to be defined by all the learned scholars..."
Ignorance appears before them in certain stages.
"In order to determine. || 43 ||

A0 Commentary: Now, [an objection is raised]: "But surely the world is defined by modern logicians and others. To this, he says: "To define... (verse 143). Rā0 Commentary: He clarifies the impossibility of definition through an illustration:
"The body, senses, and so forth... (verse 143).
How are phenomena produced by vigor?
Or, when it is asked, "How is your consciousness?", what is your answer? (44)
"The body, the sense organs, and so forth. (44)
The commentary (ṭīkā) on verse a0 clarifies those very stages (kakṣā): "deha" etc. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the vital breaths, the internal organs, and so on are included.

Furthermore, the third stage—namely, "what connection can there be between the Self, whose nature is consciousness, and the body and other such things?"—is also to be understood from the use of the plural number at the beginning of the section on the stages. || 144 ||
The proponent of the doctrine of inherent nature (svabhāvavādī) raises an objection:
"If this is the inherent nature of valor, how was it known by you?"
Those positive and negative concomitances which are broken are [rendered] impotent by their lack of efficacy. || 145 ||

Regarding the word "of virility" (*vīryasya*), the proponent asks: "How is that so? Anticipating the objection that one knows this through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), he replies, "Not so," because there is no universal pervasion (*vyāpti*). He explains: "Through positive and negative concomitance. Since virility is futile in the case of a barren woman, the attainment [of offspring] does not occur; nor is there any other rule such as "wherever there is virility, there is a body and so forth. (145)
The Sixth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
171a0 Commentary: Having raised the objection regarding the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*), he refutes it with the words "of energy" (*vīryasya*). Now, one might ask:

why is the intrinsic nature of energy being disparaged, given that its determination is possible through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) alone? If this is asked, the answer is no; for there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*), as he states:
"By way of positive concomitance," [it is said]. || 145 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Since he has been asked thus again and again, the conclusion is that one should give the answer, "I do not know anything of this. He states the final resort [of such a person]:
"I do not know anything of this; at the end, I am your refuge."
For this very reason, the great ones proclaim its nature to be like a magician’s trick (indrajāla).
"I do not know," [he said]. || 46 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Therefore, he states "I do not know" to show that the matter culminates in fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) alone. [The phrase] "of you," refers to the dualist logician and others. He states the conclusion with the words "for this very reason. || 146 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He shows the consensus of the elders regarding the aforementioned indeterminability (anirvacanīyatva):
"What else is this sorcery (indrajāla) like, wherein the semen situated within the womb perceives the various sprouts produced from the lotuses that are its hands and head?"
In succession, he sees himself endowed with many appearances— infancy, youth, and old age— and likewise he eats, hears, smells, goes forth, and returns.
"From this," [it is said]. || 47 ||
Commentary (a0): How do the great ones describe this duality as being like a magician’s trick? To this, he cites their very words: "From this... I too have said in the *Akalpitacidambaryā*:
"For a moment she is my beloved upon my head; for a moment she is the river right here; for a moment she is the young woman in my lap; and for a moment she occupies half of my own body."
“One moment Madanasundarī, another moment Vikaṭapañcavaktra; what more of this other sorcery (indrajāla) is to be seen within the conscious self? || 147 ||
Having thoroughly investigated and observed it, like a body or a banyan seed, let it be seen.
Where are the grains, and where is the tree? Therefore, conclude that this is mere illusion (māyā). || 48 ||
Rāghava’s Commentary: He states that it is not only the body that is difficult to define, but even the banyan tree and so forth, with the words "like the body" (dehavat). || 48 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Indicating that even the Śruti corroborates the stated meaning, he clarifies the illustration of the banyan seed mentioned therein with the words "dehavad" (like the body). This has indeed been elaborated in the twelfth section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, beginning with "Bring a fruit from this banyan tree. He states the conclusion: "tasmāt" (therefore). Ascertain that the entirety of duality is like a magical illusion, consisting of nothing but Māyā.
The meaning is: "ascertain it as being indeed false. || 148 ||
Those logicians and others who harbor pride in their etymological interpretations.
But they were well-trained by Harṣamiśra and others in the Khaṇḍana and other such works.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that "even if it cannot be defined by us, it is nevertheless defined by teachers such as Udayana," he says: "In the case of definition" (niruktau). || 49 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Even if we lack the capacity to define the world, nevertheless, ancient thinkers such as the logicians (tārkika) and others have already provided definitions of the world—including its nature as cause and effect—in their respective treatises. To this, he replies with the words: "In the definition" (niruktāv iti).
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 172]

[The work] named *Citradīpa* by the venerable Śrī Harṣamiśra, the author of the *Khaṇḍana*; by the word "etcetera," other ancient scholars who were experts in shattering the proponents of duality are also to be understood. || 149 ||
Indeed, those entities which are inconceivable—one should not apply them to speculative reasoning.
Indeed, the world, whose form consists of an inconceivable arrangement, is [unfathomable] even by the mind.
Rāma’s Commentary: He corroborates the stated meaning with the words of the traditional authorities: "Inconceivable," etc. (Verse 150).

The commentary on verse a0 states that the traditional saying is likewise: "Inconceivable indeed are those entities. What is that [entity] in the present context? He says: "Inconceivable... (verse 150).

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Granted that the world possesses such inconceivable construction, what relevance does this have for Māyā? To this he says: "Know that Māyā is the seed of the power of inconceivable construction."
That very same single seed of Māyā is experienced during deep sleep. || 51 ||

"Of inconceivable arrangement" means that the seed, which is the cause possessing the power of inconceivable arrangement, is itself Māyā. To the question, "Where has such a cause been seen?", he says: "Māyā. || 11 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Granted that the world consists of an inconceivable arrangement, yet what relevance does this have to *māyā* in the present context? To this, he says: "inconceivable" (*aciṃtya*). This means possessing the power of inconceivable arrangement. Such a "seed" (*bīja*)—according to Amara’s lexicon, where "seed" (*vīja*), "cause" (*hetu*), and "source" (*kāraṇa*) are synonymous—means the cause. To the question "Where is that?", he replies: "*māyā*"—meaning that which has the form of *māyā*.
The logical connection is that the seed is that very one which is experienced during deep sleep; "by all living beings" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. || 151 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To the question, "How is it the seed of the universe?", he says: "The world of waking and dreaming is dissolved therein, as a tree is contained within its seed."
Therefore, the latent impressions of the entire world abide within you.

Regarding the word "jāgrat" (awake): to the question "What follows from that?", he says "tasmāt" (therefore). Since Māyā is the cause of the world, the meaning is that all the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the entire world reside therein, in that Māyā. || 52 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): He states the reason for this with the words "jāgrad" (while awake), etc. Regarding that:
"Having reflected well upon the destruction of the body and so forth, let it be observed."

"Where are the grains, or where is the tree? Therefore, conclude that this is *māyā*. Thus, he clarifies the very example established on the basis of the illustration of the banyan seed and so forth mentioned below in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*: "the seed..."

By these and other such statements: just as a tree [resides] in its seed, so too within that state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) which is being experienced—within the seed consisting of *māyā*, which is the very nature of the waking world and possesses the characteristic of being its cause—the entire universe (*viśva*), including the waking and dreaming worlds and their respective times such as the waking period, is dissolved. Therefore, the connection is that the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the entire universe reside therein. By this, the view of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭipakṣa*), which was elucidated in works such as the *Tattvaviveka*, is also established right here.
The inclusion of that is manifested. || 152 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: What follows from that? He says:
"In those [impressions], consciousness is reflected."
Let the indistinct reflection of consciousness be inferred as being like a cloud in the sky. || 53 ||

Regarding the phrase "that which is cognition": one might object, "If there is indeed a reflection within those [cognitions], why is it not experienced? Anticipating this, he says "cloud-like," meaning it is because it is indistinct. Then, if so, how is its existence established? To this he replies: "Let it be inferred. || 13 ||
The Sixth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

173a0 Commentary: Now, even so, what is it there? He says: "That mental impression which is the intellect" (*yā buddhivāsanā*). Therein, the reflection of consciousness called the *cidābhāsa*, which was previously presented as the proof for the state of being the Lord (*īśvaratva*), is recalled by means of the analogy of the cloud and the sky; it does not indicate an inference.
The *yati* is at the word "megha. || 153 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "While the water of the clouds may indeed possess an indistinct reflection of the sky, there exists water in a jar of the same kind that possesses a distinct reflection of the sky; therefore, the inference of the cloud-sky is possible. But here, since there is no such illustrative example, how can an inference arise?
Anticipating this doubt, the author states the following in order to provide a similar illustrative example for this case as well:
That very seed, together with its appearance, sprouts in the form of cognition.
Therefore, the reflection of consciousness appears very clearly within the intellect. || 54 ||

"With appearance" (sābhāsam): the meaning is that this very ignorance, when transformed into the form of the intellect (buddhi) as characterized by the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), becomes clearly possessed of the reflection of consciousness. If this is so, then an inference is indicated here: "The mental impressions (vāsanās) within the intellect under dispute must possess the reflection of consciousness, because they are specific states of the intellect, just like the modifications (vṛtti) of the intellect. || 54 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Having thus defined Īśvara—whose nature is a subtle reflection of all mental impressions (*buddhi-saṃskāra*) residing in the ignorance (*ajñāna*) of the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) according to the aforementioned method—the author now defines the *jīva* as well: "sābhāsameva" (only with its reflection). The meaning is that it [the *jīva*] is precisely that which was described as the ignorance of the time of sleep, characterized by the reflection of consciousness called the aforementioned Īśvara. The portion beginning with "dhī" (intellect) is straightforward. A-...

The intention is that, in relation to [pure] knowledge, the very grossness of the intellect—which has become one with that body—is the cause for the clear manifestation of the individual soul (jīva), which is called the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa). || 154 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Thus, having established through reasoning the fact that both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) are products of Māyā as stated in the Śruti, he concludes:
"By means of the reflection of Māyā, He creates the individual soul and the Lord"—so it is heard in the Śruti.
Those two are well-established, like the space within a cloud and the space within water. || 155 ||

Regarding the phrase "by means of the appearance of Māyā": one might object that since the Jīva and the Īśvara are equally products of Māyā, how can a distinction between them be established? Anticipating this doubt, he states—comparing them to the space within a cloud and the space reflected in water—that the distinction is established by the presence of an indistinct and a distinct limiting adjunct (upādhi) respectively. Thus he says: "The space within a cloud... (verse 155).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, he concludes the determination of the nature of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), along with their supporting consensus and illustrative examples, with the verse beginning "māyā. The claim that this is "heard in the Śruti" is merely a result of negligence (*prāmādika*). For the construction is more elegant if interpreted as follows: "The individual soul and the Lord, who have been made objects of hearing in the various Śrutis, are well-established like the space within a cloud and the space within the water [of a cloud]. || 155 ||
Illusion exists within the cloud, like frost situated within a cloud.
The reflection of consciousness within the latent impressions of the intellect remains like the sky situated within frost. || 56 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He clarifies the similarity between the Lord and the cloud and the sky with the verse beginning "like a cloud" (meghavat). || 56 ||

a0 Commentary—Therein, he clarifies the illustration of the cloud and the sky in relation to the subject of the analogy with the words "like a cloud. The meaning is that the "reflection of consciousness" (cidābhāsa)—the reflection of consciousness within the aforementioned latent impressions—is the Lord (Īśvara). || 156 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Anticipating the question, "What is the proof that the reflection in Māyā is Īśvara?", he states that it is indeed Śruti:
"The reflection of consciousness dependent on Māyā is heard in scripture as the Lord of Māyā (Māyī), the Great Īśvara."
For he alone is indeed the inner controller, the omniscient source of the universe.

Regarding the phrase "dependent on Māyā": it is stated that not only is his status as the Lord (Īśvara) heard in scripture, but a whole range of attributes such as being the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) is also heard; thus he says: "the Inner Ruler. || 57 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 174]
Commentary on the *Citradīpa*, Chapter 1:

Now, it may be objected that the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) as the possessor of *māyā* is heard in scripture, such as: "Know *māyā* to be nature (*prakṛti*), but know the Great Lord to be the possessor of *māyā*," and likewise by the passage beginning with "He who dwells in the earth... up to "This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal."

Regarding the question of who is that one heard of in scripture as the inner controller (*antaryāmī*), the omniscient (*sarvajña*), the all-knowing (*sarvavit*), and the source of the world (*jagadyoni*)—as in the scriptural texts, "He who is omniscient," and "From whom the Illusionist (*māyī*) creates this universe"—the author says: "Illusion" (*māyā*). (157)

Rāmānanda’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "How is it established by the Śruti that the reflection of the latent impressions of the intellect (dhīvāsanā) possesses the nature of Īśvara and so forth?
Anticipating this doubt, he shows the Śruti passage that establishes this:
Having introduced the state consisting of bliss pertaining to deep sleep, the Śruti spoke thus:
"This one is the Lord of all"—this is that very Lord spoken of in the Vedas. || 58 ||

Regarding the term "pertaining to deep sleep" (*sauṣuptam*): the meaning is that the scripture, beginning with "In the state of deep sleep, [the self] has become one, a mass of pure consciousness," establishes that the Lord-hood and other attributes belong to the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss), which is of the nature of a reflection of the mental impressions (*dhīvāsanā*). || 58 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: if the nature of Īśvara is the reflection of the consciousness-manifestation (*cidābhāsa*) within the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the intellect (*buddhi*) established in the aforementioned state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), what [is the purpose of this]?

Regarding this, he states the authoritative source: "That of deep sleep" (*sauṣuptam*). This qualification is intended to exclude those portions of the *ānandamaya-kośa* (the sheath consisting of bliss) which consist of mental modifications produced by the sight of desired objects and so forth during the waking state and other stages, as per such scriptural passages as: "His very pleasure is the head; joy is the right wing; delight is the left wing," and so on. The phrase "according to the Māṇḍūkya Śruti" is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence. || 158 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection that the omniscience and other attributes of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) contradict direct experience, he says:
"One should not at all dispute his omniscience and so forth."
Because the meaning of the Vedic revelation is unimpeded, and because everything is possible within māyā. || 59 ||

Regarding the phrase "beginning with omniscience" (*sarvajñatvādika*): why is this so? To this he says, "based on scripture" (*śrauta*). Furthermore, he states, "in [the case of] māyā," to show that there is no contradiction regarding the effect (*kārya*) for this reason as well. || 19 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: even if this is so, how can he possess omniscience and other such qualities? To this, he says: "All... In that regard, the reason is: "Vedic... [and so on]. If that were the case, then statements such as "the stones float" would not be figurative descriptions (guṇavāda); anticipating this objection, he says the remainder of the verse beginning with "In [the realm of] Māyā... (verse 159).

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that in the absence of supporting reasoning, even the Śruti would be a mere *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), like the passage concerning stones floating on water, he establishes the Lord's sovereignty and other attributes in order to prove the authority of the Śruti:
"Whatever this [Lord] creates as the universe, no person is able to alter that."
No one is capable [of such power]; therefore, he is called the Lord of All (Sarveśvara). || 60 ||

"This" means: that which this one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) creates—the universe beginning with the waking state—cannot be made otherwise by anyone; therefore, the meaning is that he is the Lord of all (sarveśvara). || 60 ||

— Commentary (Ṭīkā): If this were so, then Māyā would likewise produce the state of being a living soul (jīvatva) and the state of being the world (jagattva) for Īśvara, as well as the state of being Īśvara for those two [the soul and the world]. To this, he says: "This... (verse 160).
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now he establishes His omniscience:
"The latent impressions (vāsanās) of the minds of all living beings reside therein."
Everything is embraced by them; therefore, he is called the Omniscient One.
The Sixth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

175. Regarding the word "without remainder" (*aśeṣa*): therein, within that ignorance (*ajñāna*) which serves as the cause during deep sleep (*sauṣupta*), reside the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of all the cognitions (*buddhi*) of all living beings, which are its effects.

By those latent impressions, the entire universe is encompassed and made an object; therefore, since [the individual soul] has as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that ignorance which possesses the latent impressions of all cognitions—
The meaning is that he is not called "omniscient. || 61 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): In this way, he also establishes His omniscience—[with the verse beginning] "aśeṣa...
The meaning is that "embraced" (kroḍīkṛta) signifies "made an object" (viṣayīkṛta). || 161 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If omniscience exists, why is it not experienced?
Anticipating this doubt, he states that it is not experienced because its limiting conditions—the latent impressions (vāsanās)—are imperceptible:
"Because the latent impressions are imperceptible, omniscience is indeed not perceived."
Having observed that in all cognitions, let it be inferred from their latent impressions (vāsanās). || 62 ||
Regarding the phrase "of the latent impressions" (vāsanānām): anticipating the question, "How then is that [omniscience] understood?", he says, "residing in all cognitions.

The meaning is as follows: omniscience residing in all cognitions must be preceded by omniscience existing within the latent impressions that constitute its own cause, because it is a specific attribute residing in an effect, just like the color and other qualities residing in a cloth. || 62 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): If this were so, then it would follow that everyone would have direct perception of all objects during deep sleep; therefore, he says: "of the latent impressions" (*vāsanānām*). The meaning is: because they are eternally immediate (*nityapārokṣya*), unlike merit (*dharma*) and the like. However, their manifestation to the Witness (*sākṣin*) occurs precisely as being unknown (*ajñātatvena*). For this very reason, the conclusion of the *Vivaraṇa* is that everything is manifested by the Witness through both the states of being known and being unknown. || 162 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Having established His omniscience, He now establishes His status as the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmī*), as declared by the Śruti:
"Indeed, [He resides] within the sheaths consisting primarily of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) and elsewhere."
Abiding within, it governs; therefore, it attains the state of being the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin).
Vijñāna says: The logical connection is that it impels while abiding elsewhere, such as in earth and so forth; therefore, [it is the self]. || 63 ||
Commentary (a0): Thus, he establishes its nature as the inner controller (antaryāmin) through two verses beginning with "vijñānamaya.
Elsewhere means in the earth and so forth. || 163 ||
Abiding within the intellect, he is its inner controller; though his form is the intellect itself, he cannot be perceived by it.
"He restrains the intellect from within"—thus it is proclaimed by the Veda.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To show that the entire Aitareya Brāhmaṇa is the authority on this point, he sequentially cites in substance the passage "He who dwells in the intellect" (Yo vijñāne tiṣṭhan...), which constitutes a portion of it, beginning with the words "In the intellect" (Buddhau). || 64 ||
Commentary (a0): Therein, he summarizes the meaning of the scriptural passage, "He who, dwelling in consciousness... as follows: "In the intellect" (buddhau) || 164 ||
Just as a thread resides in a cloth by way of being its material cause, so too [is it with the self].
Because it has the nature of all appropriation, this [Self] is situated everywhere. || 165 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, for fear of excessive length in explaining each successive section (*paryāya*) of the *Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa*, and in order to establish that this commentary applies to all sections, the author explains the section beginning with "He who [dwells] in all beings" (*yaḥ sarveṣu bhūteṣu*).
While explaining the meaning of the phrase "He who dwells in all beings," he states the following by means of an illustration: "The thread... (verse 165).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): In that regard, he reveals the underlying reasoning along with an illustrative example: "The thread," etc. (Verse 165).
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 176.

[The commentary by Rāma on the *Citradīpa*— Now, raising the objection: "If this [Self] exists everywhere as the material cause (*upādāna*), why is it not perceived everywhere?"— he says "because it is within all" (*sarvāntaratvāt*):]
The thread is distinct from the cloth, and the fiber is likewise distinct from the thread.
Let that state be inferred wherein there is the repose of internality.
"Even from a cloth," it is said. Herein lies this inference: "The gradation of internality must rest upon something somewhere, because it is a gradation, like the gradation of atomicity. (66)

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection may be raised: "If the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) is the material cause (*upādāna*) of all things, then, like clay in the case of jars and other objects, He would necessarily be perceptible everywhere. This is true; however, is it on the basis of being the material cause that perceptibility is being attributed, or on the basis of the aspect of the common substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-sāmānyāṃśa*)? It cannot be the first, because this Lord—who is of the nature of a reflection of Consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) within the impressions of the intellect residing in deep-sleep ignorance (*sauṣuptāvidyā*), like a cloth folded upon a stone—is concealed by His own limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

Because it was just stated [in the previous passage] beginning with "due to the imperceptibility of its latent impressions" (*vāsanānām parokṣatvāt*), that which is superposed upon it must likewise be so. Nor is the last alternative [the object of perception] possible, because this [pure consciousness] lacks the nature of being a substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). For it is only that which is pure, like a washed cloth, that serves as the substrate for the illusion of all objects of perception;

and since its aspect of generality—the light whose essence is existence—is self-luminous, its perceptibility is accepted everywhere precisely for the sake of providing the specific form (*svarūpa*) for the illusions of name and form.
Therefore, he says "even from a cloth" (paṭādapi) to show that this [self] is to be understood through inference and scripture alone. || 166 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even though he is internal, why is the Inner Controller not seen, as is the case with horses and other such things?
Anticipating this doubt, the author says—with the intention that he is not seen because, unlike those [external objects], he lacks externality:
"Even when two or three intermediate stages are perceived, this one remains internal."
Therefore, it is not perceived; thus, the determination is made through reasoning and scripture alone.

Regarding the phrase "at intervals of two or three": from what, then, does its determination arise? To this he says: "From that. The reasoning is that the activity of an insentient entity is untenable without the superintendence of a sentient being; as for scripture, it has already been cited. || 67 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection is raised: "Just as the threads and other components within a cloth are perceived, why is there no such perception of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), who is likewise the material cause? Since He is veiled by ignorance (*ajñāna*) and other factors, there can be no such seeing; therefore, what is the proof for His existence? Anticipating this doubt, the author provides the following resolution: "dvitryāntaratva... The meaning is: "of those two or three *antaratva*-levels," that is, the stages of intermediate positions. || 167 ||
Because it exists in the form of cloth, it is therefore called "cloth," just as a city exists within its fortifications.
Because he exists in every form, his entire body is likewise composed of all things.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the meaning of the verse "for whom all beings are the body" as follows: "In the form of a cloth," etc.
Just as a cloth is the body of the thread existing in the form of a cloth, so too, the meaning is that everything is the body of [the Self] existing in the form of everything. || 68 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, as to how its state of being the body of all—which is declared in such scriptural passages as "He who dwells in all," and so forth—comes about, he says:
"In the form of a cloth. (168)
Therefore, the cloth likewise undergoes contraction, expansion, movement, and so forth.
It necessarily exists; there is not even the slightest independence in the cloth. (69)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: With two verses beginning with "Of the thread," he states the purport of the statement "He who, from within, restrains all beings," using an illustration. || 69 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): For this very reason, he states that "this alone is independent" in the two verses beginning with "taṃtoḥ" (169).
The Sixth Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.
Likewise, this inner controller (antaryāmin), by whatever latent impression (vāsanā) and in whatever manner [he acts] therein—
It will certainly undergo transformation; of this there is no doubt. || 170 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Just as the contraction of a cloth occurs through the contraction of its threads and so forth, even so, the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī), abiding as the material cause within the earth and other elements, necessarily brings about that entire collection of effects in whatever manner it undergoes modification into the form of effects such as jars, according to whichever latent impression (vāsanā) is operative.
That which comes into being is "existence" (bhāva). || 170 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): "In that manner" (tathā)—the ellipsis is to be supplied as "as long as there is anything visible" (yāvaddṛśyam). || 170 ||
The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, O Arjuna.
Causing all beings to revolve, mounted upon a machine by means of his illusory power.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus cited the Śruti that establishes the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin), he also cites Smṛti—beginning with the words "The Lord" (īśvara). || 71 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): In that regard, he cites Smṛti as an authority: "The Lord" (īśvara) || 171 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the meaning of the phrase "of all beings":
"All beings consist of consciousness; they abide in the heart."
Indeed, the Lord, who has become the material cause of that [universe], undergoes transformation therein. || 72 ||
"All beings" refers to those who reside within the heart-lotus. Anticipating the question, "How is it that they are situated in the heart?

he states, "Because of its being their material cause," meaning that they exist in the heart because the inner controller (antaryāmin) undergoes transformation into the form of the intellect (vijñānamaya). || 72 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He explains the cited statement with the three verses beginning with "sarvabhūtāni" (all beings). "In the heart" means in the collective internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). "Is modified" means that it undergoes various transformations for the sake of bestowing the fruits of respective karmas, by being conditioned by latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth;
the sense is that within individual souls (*jīva*), there occur modifications of the internal organ consisting of the operations of various desires and the like. || 172 ||

In the commentary on the verse beginning with "yaṃtrārūḍhāni," he explains the meaning of the two words *yaṃtra* and *āroha*: "The cage of the body and so forth is the *yaṃtra*; 'ascending' (*āroha*) it is the state of identifying with it."
There may arise the delusion of engaging in what is prescribed and prohibited.
Regarding the phrase "dehādi" (the body, etc.), he states the meaning of the verbal root in the word "bhrāmayan" (causing to wander): "vihita" (ordained), etc. || 73 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now he explains the meaning of the term "ascending the machine" (*yaṃtrāroha*), beginning with the words "body, etc. (*dehādi*). Regarding the phrase "thus causing to revolve" (*bhrāmayan*), he explains the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) with the words "prescribed," etc. For the rule of the verbal root is: *bhramu* (to wander) means "not remaining in one place" (*anavasthāna*). And thus, it certainly exists in the case of [the soul's] active engagement (*pravṛtti*). || 173 ||
In the form of consciousness, by virtue of its nature as the activity of that [consciousness].
The Lord is transformed by His own power through Māyā; for that is indeed a delusion.
Rāma’s Commentary: Now he explains the meaning of the suffix *ṇic* and the word *māyā*: "vijñānamaya" (consisting of consciousness), etc. || 74 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, he explains the meanings of the words *pratyaya* and *māyā* with the verse beginning "vijñānamayeti. Regarding the word *tat* (that):

it refers to the continuous succession of activities within the body, senses, and mind directed toward enjoined objects and the like. By its own power—that is, by the aggregate of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) residing in the ignorance of deep sleep—it undergoes modification (*vikriyate*). This means that for the sake of bestowing the fruits of various actions upon the aforementioned individual souls, [Māyā] manifests as volition within their respective internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
The meaning is that it becomes favorable to one's birth. || 174 ||
This very point is heard in the Śruti through the statement, "He who dwells within as the inner controller" (*antaryāmī*). Thus ends the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya.
This principle known as the "Lamp of Consciousness" (Citradīpa) should be applied by the intellect everywhere, including the elements such as earth and the rest. || 175 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states that this very meaning applies to the Vedic term *yamayati* as well—namely, "He controls from within"—and extends the aforementioned explanation to other synonymous terms with the words "in the earth and so forth. || 175 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) states that this very meaning also applies to the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa Śruti, which is the source for the etymological tradition (niruktasmṛti): "He causes [the earth] to move from within" (antaryamayati).
He extends this stated meaning to the other successive passages concerning the earth and so forth, saying: "In the case of the earth and the others. || 175 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He cites another scriptural statement to show that all activity is dependent upon the Lord of All:
"I know dharma, yet I have no inclination toward it; I know adharma, yet I have no aversion to it."
Whatever I am commanded by some god residing in my heart, that I shall do. ||76||
"I know the Dharma," [he said]. || 76 ||
Commentary (a0): Regarding the point stated, he cites another scriptural passage as well: "I know," etc. (176).
Do not entertain the doubt that there is no purpose served by human effort, for [it is not so].
The Lord manifests even in the form of human effort.

Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Now, one might object that if activity were dependent upon God, human effort would be useless; anticipating this, he refutes it by stating that such is not the case, because human effort is also of the nature of God—“Not so, for there is a purpose. Here, “purpose” (artha) means the objective, and “human exertion” (puruṣakāra) means human effort. || 77 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "If this is so, then human effort would be entirely futile in all cases; consequently, the entire body of scriptures consisting of injunctions and prohibitions concerning such effort would be useless. Anticipating this doubt, the author provides the following resolution: "Not so" (nārthaḥ). || 177 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If human effort is also of the nature of the Lord, then the impelling by the Inner Controller (antaryāmipreraṇa)—described as 'He restrains' and 'He causes to wander'—would be redundant.
Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it, stating that this is not so because the fruit characterized by the knowledge of one's own self as unattached exists through the realization of that [Lord].
The activity of the Lord through such a warrior must certainly not be obstructed.
Nevertheless, through the awakening of the Lord, there arises the cognition that one's own self is unattached.

"Such as this": by means of such an awakening—namely, the knowledge of the Lord's abiding even in the form of human effort (puruṣakāra) and so forth—there occurs activity, which is the impelling [of beings] in the form of an inner ruler (antaryāmin). || 78 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "If human effort is also essentially of the nature of the Lord, then even when such knowledge exists, the Lord's activity in directing those like us toward the bestowal of the fruits of karma would not cease; and if that is so, what is the fruit of the aforementioned awakening? To this, he says: "In this manner" (*īdṛg*). This activity of mine in acquiring merit is indeed of the very nature of the Lord, and thus the arising of the realization "I am truly unattached" (*asaṅga*) is the fruit.
This is the intended meaning. || 178 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question, "What is the purpose even of knowing the soul's state of non-attachment?", he says:
"By that much alone, liberation is attained"—so say the Śrutis and likewise the Smṛtis.
"Śruti and Smṛti are my very commands"—this too was spoken by the Lord. (79)
Regarding the word "tāvasā" (the two): he cites a Smṛti text to show that what is declared in Śruti and Smṛti is not to be transgressed—namely, "Śruti and Smṛti. || 79 ||
The Sixth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

179. Commentary: To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "To that extent" (*tāvatā*). That even those two [the Vedas] possess the nature of being the command of the Lord—on this point as well, he cites a Smṛti:
"The Śruti and the Smṛti... (179).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states that even according to the Śruti, the Lord is the cause of fear:
"The fact that His command is the cause of fear is indeed heard in the Śruti: 'From fear of Him...'"
This would constitute universal sovereignty, distinct from the state of being the inner controller.

Regarding the phrase "ājñāyāḥ" (of the command): having raised the doubt as to why the Lord's being the cause of fear was stated, he says "sarveśvara" (the Lord of all), thinking that it is intended to establish the distinctness of His status as the Lord of all from His role as the Inner Controller (antaryāmitva). || 180 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): To demonstrate that this [command] is not to be transgressed, he cites scripture: "Of the command," etc. Thus, the meaning is as follows:

since He is the Lord of All, as previously stated in the cited scripture, this quality of being the Governor of All—which is characterized by the impelling of all things through His nature as the Inner Controller—is simply another such attribute residing in Him, distinct from the previously elaborated attribute of being the Lord of All which arises from His illusory (māyika) nature. || 180 ||
"Indeed, by the command of this Imperishable," so says the Śruti.
And there is a sacred tradition (śruti) that says: "This Teacher has entered within. || 81 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Regarding the point that the Lord alone is the regulator both externally and internally, he cites two scriptural passages, beginning with "etasya" (of this). || 81 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Right here, he cites two other scriptural passages—one from the Kaṇvas and one from the Taittirīyakas—in their respective order, beginning with "etasya vā" (Of this, indeed...). 181.
Rāghava’s Commentary: He states the meaning of this [verse] as it follows in sequence: "This is the source of the world, because he effects its origin and dissolution."
Manifestation and disappearance are considered to be origination and dissolution. || 82 ||

Regarding the phrase "the source of the world" (*jagadyoni*): he connects the statement "for [Brahman is] the origin and dissolution of beings" with the proposition as its logical reason, using the words "origin and dissolution. The meaning is that because it is the agent of origin and dissolution—that is, of creation and destruction—it is the source of the world. He states the intended meaning of the terms "creation" and "destruction" with the words "manifestation and disappearance": the construction is that "creation and destruction are understood as manifestation and disappearance. (82)
Commentary on Verse 1: Thus, he establishes the status of the Lord—of the nature previously promised—as the cause of the universe by stating "the world" (*jagat*).
The reason for this is given as "origination" (*prabhava*). He explains those two [terms] according to his own view with the words "manifestation" (*āvirbhāva*) and so forth. || 182 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He establishes, with an illustration, the quality of causing manifestation:
"It manifests the entire universe that was dissolved within itself."
Just as this cloth is spread out by the power of the karma of living beings. || 83 ||
"It makes manifest" means that just as a rolled-up painted cloth makes its own paintings manifest by being unrolled, so too does the Lord; this is the meaning. || 83 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, to the question "How does this [Brahman] manifest the universe?", he says: "It manifests...
He clarifies the illustration for that with the words: "Just as a cloth... (183).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He demonstrates that very [Lord] is the cause of dissolution:
"Furthermore, He causes the entire universe to disappear into His own self."
Just as a cloth is contracted by virtue of the exhaustion of the karma of living beings. || 84 ||
"Again" means: just as that very same cloth, when folded, causes the various patterns to disappear, so it is here. || 84 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 180]
[In the commentary on the chapter titled *Citradīpa*, verse 184: In this very manner, he also describes the process of concealment (*tirobhāva*), beginning with the word "again" (*punar*).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He shows other illustrations for manifestation and disappearance:
night and day, sleep and waking, and the opening and closing [of the eyes].
These two, creation and dissolution, are like the kingdom of dreams within the state of silence.
Regarding the term *rātrighasrau*: *ghastra* means "day. (185)
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Even there, for the sake of providing further illustrations, he says: "Night and day," etc. (185).
By virtue of possessing the power of manifestation and concealment.
In this case, objections concerning initiation, transformation, and so forth, have no place. || 86 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: Is God the source of the world by way of being its material cause (*ārambhakatva*), or by way of undergoing transformation into that form (*tadākārapariṇāmatva*)? It cannot be the first, because it is impossible for the non-dual [Brahman] to be a material cause. Nor can it be the second, because transformation is impossible for that which is partless.
Anticipating this objection, he refutes it by resorting to the doctrine of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*): "Āvirbhāva... (verse 86).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): In our Siddhānta, which maintains the doctrine of illusory manifestation (vivartavāda), all effects such as appearance and so forth are logically established solely through the nature of Māyā; therefore, there is no room for the suspicion of other doctrines such as the theory of material aggregation (ārambhavāda). Thus he says: "Appearance and disappearance... (verse 186).
The Lord cannot likewise be the cause of insentient things in their aspect of being subject to decay.
However, by virtue of a portion of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), this [intellect] becomes the cause of the individual souls (jīvas). || 87 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If there is only one Lord, how can He be the material cause of both the sentient and the insentient universe?

Anticipating this doubt, he states—beginning with the words "of the insentient"—that by virtue of the predominance of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi), He becomes the material cause of the insentient, and by virtue of the predominance of consciousness (cit), He becomes the material cause of the sentient.

Commentary (a0): Now, let it be granted that the Lord is thus the cause of the insentient world, such as space and so forth; nevertheless—“The individual soul, the Lord, the pure mind, and likewise the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord.
[Thus it is said.]

Ignorance (avidyā), that [Māyā], and the union with the intellect (citi)—these six are beginningless for us, according to the words of the ancient teachers. However, this is not the cause for individual souls (jīvas) who are themselves beginningless; thus, the status of being the source of the universe (jagadyonitva) has been affirmed.

[An objection is raised: "In that case, [the cause] would necessarily be contracted. To this, he says: "of insentient things" (*acetanānām*). The intention is as follows: just as the sun is the cause for the manifestation of a mirage through its own rays, and is likewise the cause for the manifestation of their shimmering reflections through its own inherent, imagined aspect of being a cause—that is, its aspect of luminosity (*vitratva*)—so it is here.
And thus, there is not even a scent of contradiction in this; such is the direction of the argument. || 187 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that it is untenable to establish the illusory Lord (māyāvin) as the cause of the universe, since Sureśvarācārya has declared that the Supreme Self alone is such; thus he raises this doubt in two verses:
"The one in whom darkness (tamas) predominates is the cause of the fields (kṣetra), while the one in whom consciousness (cit) predominates is the cause of the conscious selves (cidātman)."
The Supreme attains the state of being the cause through meditative cultivation, knowledge, and action. || 88 ||

"Predominantly *tamas*": this means having as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) *māyā* in which the quality of *tamas* predominates; "by the dispositions, knowledge, and actions of the fields"—that is, of the bodies and so forth—where "disposition" refers to mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), "knowledge" to meditation on deities and the like, and "actions" to those characterized by merit and demerit; the meaning is that these serve as the instrumental causes. || 88 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Even there, anticipating a contradiction with the Vārtika school's view, he first cites their words and then promises to resolve it by means of two verses beginning with "tamaḥpradhāna. || 188 ||
The Sixth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
Thus, the author of the Vārttika [has established] that both the insentient and the sentient are causes.
If it is argued that these were spoken of the Supreme Self alone and not of the Lord (Īśvara), then listen.
Rāma’s Commentary— || 89 ||
Commentary on 181a:

Regarding the word "iti" (thus): it refers to the Supreme Self, which is indeed the pure Brahman. In reality, however, this very doubt belongs only to someone like me, whose intellect is unrefined and who is ignorant of the internal consistency of what precedes and follows; it was merely cited here by the Teacher and refuted for the sake of clarifying the understanding of such a person—this is the truth. Furthermore—
Because, when the pure [nature] is grasped by means of the word, darkness and so forth cannot possibly exist as predominant. || 189 ||
Here too, there is a mutual superimposition, just as between the individual soul (jīva) and the immutable witness (kūṭastha).
Having established the existence of both Īśvara and Brahmā, Sureśvara says: || 190 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Since it is intended that, just as in the case of the referent of the word *tvam* (the individual self), there is a mutual superimposition (*anyonyādhyāsa*) between the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the object superimposed (*āropya*) even in the case of the referent of the word *tat* (Brahman), he refutes [the objection] with the words "mutual superimposition" (verse 190).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): He indicates the reason for what was asserted with the words "anyonya" (mutually). || 190 ||
They have arisen from that Brahman which is truth, knowledge, and infinite.
"Space, air, fire, water, earth, herbs, food, and the body"—thus says the Śruti.

Rāmatīrtha’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: "How is it known that Sureśvarācārya proceeded by taking for granted the mutual superimposition (*anyonyādhyāsa*) of Īśvara and Brahman? Anticipating this, he cites the scripture according to its meaning to show that it is established through a careful consideration of the scriptural sense: "Truth... (verse 91).
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "How is it that the mutual superimposition (*anyonyādhyāsa*) of Brahman and Īśvara is accepted by the venerable feet of the teacher Sureśvarācārya?

Anticipating this doubt and in order to establish it, he summarizes in substance the very Vedic scripture which is the root of the doctrine of the pure Brahman as the cause, as found in the *Vārtika* verses cited by the opponent: "It is true," etc. (191).
Rāma’s Commentary: Let it be that this is a scriptural text; how, then, is the mutual superimposition understood through it?
To this, he says: "From the perspective of superficial observation, the causality of Brahman appears therein."
And because of the reality of that cause, another superimposition (adhyāsa) is admitted. || 92 ||

"Āpāteti" (In the phrase "at first glance"): the meaning is that in that scripture (*śruti*), the causality of the world with respect to Brahman—which is characterized by truth and so forth and is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*)—and the reality of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) which is dependent on *māyā* and is the cause of the world, as they appear at first glance, would not be possible without mutual superimposition (*anyonyādhyāsa*). || 92 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, by means of the very secret of the scripture thus proclaimed, [the author] establishes mutual superimposition (*anyonyādhyāsa*). He says: "Āpātataḥ" and so on. The word *āpātam* means that which has the destruction of ignorance as its limit; therefore, the meaning is "of that vision which arises prior to that [destruction]," namely, the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) consisting of doubt and the like. Of Brahman—of the Brahman characterized by existence (*satya*) and so forth, which is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*). Its "causality" (*hetutā*), that is, its being the cause of the world, appears.

The meaning is that it is *tīyate* (crossed over) and not *pramīyate* (measured/cognized). The reason for this is given by the word "hetoh" (from the cause): the logical connection (*anvaya*) is that since the reality (*satyatā*) of the cause is perceived, therefore mutual superimposition (*anyonyādhyāsa*) is accepted. For, according to other scriptural passages such as, "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is real," causality belongs only to that which possesses the attribute of reality, and not to the qualityless Brahman. Therefore, [the cause] possesses attributes such as being real...

The intended meaning is that when Īśvara is excluded, one must necessarily admit a mutual superimposition (adhyāsa) between him and the attributeless Brahman indicated by that [term]. And thus, the scriptural statement from another source, "From this, the Māyin creates this universe," is also supported in this way, as it defines Īśvara as having the causal adjunct (upādhi). || 992 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 182.
This consists of mutual superimposition, like a cloth smeared with food.
Through contact it attains oneness; through that delusion, it has reached a state of unity.

[From the *Citradīpa*, Rāma’s Commentary: Thus, having established the identity of Īśvara and Brahman through mutual superimposition (*anyonyādhyāsa*), he reinforces it by recalling the previously cited analogy of the "beaten cloth" (*ghaṭṭitapaṭa*): "Mutual... (verse 93).
Commentary (a0): Thus, reminding us of the previously mentioned illustration, he defines the nature of the Lord as established through mutual superimposition: "anyonyābhyāsa... (193).
Rāma’s Commentary: To illustrate the aforementioned point regarding common perception, he provides another example:
"The cloud and the great sky are not distinguished by the ignorant."
In the same way, those who perceive only the superficial appearance see the identity of Brahmā and Īśvara.
"Like the cloud and the sky"—the meaning is that they perceive the identity of Brahmā and Īśvara, not their difference. || 194 ||

Commentary (a0): Having thus stated the illustration for the superimposition of identity between Īśvara and Brahman, he now describes that [superimposition] even when their difference is not perceived: "megha... (verse 194).
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: From what, then, does the perception of difference between Brahmā and Īśvara arise? To this he says:
"From the investigation of the intended meaning by means of indicators such as the opening statement (upakrama) and so forth."
This Great Lord, the master of illusion, creates the unattached Brahman.

Regarding the word "upakrama" (beginning): once the purport of the Śruti has been ascertained through the sixfold marks—namely, beginning, conclusion, repetition, novelty, fruit, and corroborative statement—as stated in the principle that "the marks for determining purport are these six," it follows that Brahman is understood to be unattached and emitted by Māyā;
this is the remainder of the sense. || 195 ||
a0 Commentary: He states the conclusion: "By means of the introductory statements and so forth. || 195 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: By demonstrating the uniformity of the opening and the conclusion in the Śruti, he clarifies the stated non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*) of Brahman:
"Beginning with 'Truth, Knowledge, Infinite,' [the text] concludes [with the same]."
The determination of its lack of connection [with speech] is expressed by the words, "from which words turn back. || 96 ||
"It is true. The remainder of the sense is that, therefore, the determination of its being unattached follows. || 96 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): In that regard, he states the indicative mark for Brahman’s state of non-attachment: "Truth," etc. (196).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He demonstrates the meaning of the scripture that establishes the Lord as the creator of the world through His power of illusion (māyā):
"The Illusionist creates the universe, and He is confined therein by His own illusion."
Another Śruti says "another," by which the Lord would create. (97)

Regarding the word "māyī" (the wielder of māyā): the meaning is that the scriptural passage, "From him, the wielder of māyā, creates this entire universe; and another, bound by māyā, is confined within it," demonstrates the Lord's nature as the creator and the individual soul's state of bondage within that world. || 97 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Regarding the fact that the Māyin is the creator, he cites scripture itself—namely, "asmānmāyī sṛjate viśvametattasmiṃścānyo māyayā saṃniruddhaḥ" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad). || 197 ||
Rāmatīrtha’s Commentary: Having thus established that the Lord consisting of bliss is the cause of the world, he now describes the manner in which the world originates from Him.
The sixth chapter,
together with the two commentaries:
This Lord, consisting of bliss, reflected, "May I become many."
He became the form of Hiraṇyagarbha, like a sound in deep sleep. || 98 ||
"Consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya): the grammatical connection is that, having looked [upon it], he became the form of Hiraṇyagarbha. Regarding this, he states an illustration:
"asleep" (supti). || 98 ||

Commentary (a0): Having thus determined Īśvara as the consciousness delimited by the sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*), he clarifies His creative activity with the verse beginning "ānandamaya. The connection is that when He "beheld," He then became Hiraṇyagarbha.
In this regard, the illustration is indeed clear. || 198 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Since the creation is heard of as occurring sequentially in passages such as, "From that very Self, space was produced," and yet it is also heard of as occurring simultaneously in the statement, "He created all this," there arises the inquiry as to which [account] is to be accepted and which is to be rejected.
In response, he states that both are to be accepted because they are supported by scripture and reasoning:
This creation should be understood as occurring either sequentially or simultaneously, according to the scriptures;
for there exist two kinds of scriptural authority, and because two kinds of dream-visions are observed. (99)

Regarding the phrase "in succession": the construction is that this creation of the world—since there exist two kinds of scriptural statements—is to be understood as occurring either successively or simultaneously, according to the scriptures.

The reasoning for this is "because of the observation of two kinds of dreams"; the sense is that in the world, one observes a multitude of dream-objects both arranged in succession and not arranged in succession. || 99 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: is creation gradual or otherwise? To this he says: "In succession" (*krameṇa*).

For there is the scriptural hearing of a sequence in the passage, "From that very Self, space was produced" (*tasmād vā etasmād ātmana ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ*); whereas there is the scriptural hearing of simultaneity in the passage, "He created all this" (*idaṃ sarvam asṛjata*). || 199 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He describes the true nature of Hiraṇyagarbha:
"The Sūtrātman, known as the subtle body, consists of the collective essence of all individual souls."
Because he maintains all forms of ego-consciousness (ahaṃmāna), he possesses the powers of action, knowledge, and so forth. || 200 ||

"Sūtrātman" means: he whose self (ātman), which is his essential nature (svarūpa), is woven through the world like a thread in a cloth; he who is thus designated as the subtle body (sūkṣmadeha). He consists of the aggregate of all individual souls (jīva)—that is, he is the collective form (samaṣṭisvarūpa) of all those limited by their subtle bodies (liṅgaśarīra). The reason for this is stated: "consisting of the 'I-notion' (ahaṃmāna) in all [individuals]. This refers to the presence of the "I-notion" within all the individual subtle bodies (vyaṣṭiliṅgaśarīra).
The intended meaning is "because of reality. And [He] possesses the powers of will, knowledge, and action. || 200 ||
— A0 Ṭī0 — Now, one might object: "Granted that the Lord himself becomes Hiraṇyagarbha due to a certain preponderance of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), what then is his nature in that state?
To this he replies: "mūrteti" (as embodied). || 200 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He provides an illustration for the perception of the world during the state of Hiraṇyagarbha:
"Whether at dawn or at twilight, this person is immersed in dense darkness."
Just as the world shines [in that state], so too is the universe perceived indistinctly. || 1 ||
Regarding "pratyūṣa": *pratyūṣa* refers to the time of dawn. || 1 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭī0): In response to the inquiry as to how the world is perceived at that time as being purely volitional (*sāṃkalpika*), he clarifies this by means of an illustration: "Or like at dawn," etc. (201).
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 184.

[The commentary by Rāma, titled *Citradīpa*: Having thus stated the examples well-known in the world, he illustrates the "stained cloth" mentioned in the previously cited verse beginning with "yathā dhautaḥ" (as a washed [cloth]).]
Just as a cloth might be marked all over with ink by a stain.
Likewise, the body of the Lord is marked everywhere with subtle forms.

"From all sides" means that just as a cloth, when rubbed, becomes marked with various forms consisting of ink, so too the body of the illusory Lord (māyin) is marked by subtle bodies (liṅgaśarīra), which are the effects of the unquintuplicated elements (apañcīkṛtabhūta). This is the meaning. || 2 ||
Now, he applies the previous illustration to that point as well: "From all sides," etc.
Just as a woven cloth is marked everywhere with subtle patterns, so too the body of the Lord must be marked everywhere by subtle forms; such is the construction of the verse. || 202 ||
Just as grain or various kinds of vegetables are covered on all sides by sprouts.
In that very same way, this sprout of the world is tender and delicate. || 3 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To facilitate comprehension through its grandeur, he states another illustration: "Or like a crop," etc. (3).
Commentary (a0 ṭī0): Again, for the sake of illustration, he reveals another example with the words "or as grain. According to Amara, "pelava" means soft, tender, or thin. || 203 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus clarified the nature of the Sūtrātman, he elucidates its differentiated states—Virāj, which has as its limiting adjuncts the effects of the five-fold elemental evolution—by means of three examples:
"Or like sunlight and the sky, or a cloth filled with colors."
Just like a crop that has borne fruit, so did Virāṭ shine with a radiant form.
—Regarding "ātapeti": after the rising of the sun, the world illuminated by the heat is the "world of heat-light" (ātapābhātaloka). || 4 ||

A0 Commentary: Having thus elaborated upon the nature of Hiraṇyagarbha, his effects, and the nature of the world as it exists in those states, he now reveals the state of Virāj for that same entity when possessed of a slightly different specific limiting adjunct (upādhi), by means of three similes beginning with "ātapena" (by heat). || 204 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the proof for its existence:
"This has been declared in the Viśvarūpa chapter and also in the Puruṣasūkta."
They know his limbs to extend from Dhātṛ to Vapu.

Regarding the term "Viśvarūpa" (the Universal Form): in response to the inquiry as to what kind of form was described in the chapter on the Universal Form and elsewhere, he states—beginning with "Dhātṛ" and so forth—that the form of the entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, was described. || 205 ||
He establishes that [truth] with authoritative evidence: "viśvarūpa... and so on. *Staṃtra* is a particular type of extremely minute insect.
One should supply the word "śrutyādayaḥ" (the Vedas and so forth) as the subject and connect it with the verb "viduḥ" (they know). || 205 ||
Īśa, Sūtra, Virāṭ, Vedhas, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Vahni.
The Vināyakas, Bhairavas, Mairālas, Mārikās, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas; || 6 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question, "What relevance does this have to the present subject? he says, with the three verses beginning with "The Lord" (īśa), that every category of entity—from the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) down to the plowman (Kuddālaka)—should be worshipped as being the Lord himself. || 6 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): What follows from this regarding the subject at hand? To this he replies with the triad beginning with "īśa" (verse 206).
The reading "viralam" occurs.
[Page 185] Sixth Chapter.
Accompanied by two commentaries:
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; cows, horses, deer, and birds.
The aśvattha, vaṭa, āmra, and so forth; barley, rice, grass, and so forth. || 7 ||
Rāma’s Commentary—verse 7.
a0 ṭī0—The word *vipra* [is explained as follows]: according to Amarasimha, *āmraśbhūta* means "become a Brahmin" (*vipra*). || 207 ||
Water, stones, clay, wood, axes, spades, and so forth.
All these lords, when worshipped, are bestowers of fruits.
Rāma’s commentary—verse 8.
Commentary on verse 185: Regarding the word *vāsya*, it is well known as the tool of a carpenter for cutting wood; in the Mahārāṣṭrī language, it is called *vāṃkaśa*. || 208 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: The scripture stating, "In whatever way they worship Him, that very thing they become," is the authority for the existence of those respective fruits resulting from those various modes of worship; thus he says:
"In whatever way they worship Him, they attain the fruit accordingly."
But the excellence or deficiency of the fruit follows from the excellence or deficiency of the worship of the object of veneration. || 9 ||

Regarding the phrase "in whatever manner": one might ask, "If all are indeed lords (īśvara), from where does the disparity in results arise? Anticipating this doubt, he states that the disparity arises from the distinction between the objects of worship—such as the presiding deities (adhiṣṭhāna) and the modes of worship—whether they be images (arcā) and so forth, according to their classification as *sāttvika* and the like; thus he says: "due to the excellence of the result" (verse 9).

In that regard, for one who seeks the authority [for this], he summarizes the meaning of the Śruti—"In whatever way they meditate upon Him, that very thing they become"—in the words "yathā yathā" (in whatever way). If that is so, then how is there a gradation of results? To that he says: "phala... (the result...). 209.

Rāma’s Commentary: Having raised the doubt as to whose worship leads to liberation—given that the attainment of worldly fruits occurs in this manner—he states that it does not occur through anything other than knowledge:
"Liberation, however, arises only from the knowledge of the reality of Brahman, and not otherwise."
Just as the sound of one's own voice does not cease without one's own awareness of it. || 210 ||

—Regarding "liberation": he provides an illustration for this with the words "one's own awakening. Just as a dream imagined during one's own sleep does not cease without one's own waking, so too the cycle of one's own transmigratory existence, imagined through ignorance of Brahman, does not cease without the knowledge of the reality of Brahman.
The state of being. || 210 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Let it be so; nevertheless, to the question "From the worship of whom does liberation arise?", he says: "But liberation...
For this very reason, the venerable feet of the author of the Vārtika have said:
"One should understand that whatever fruit may arise from meditative cultivation, and whatever fruit may arise from ritual action, those do not endure, just like a union with a courtesan."
Therein, he clarifies the illustration with the word "sva" (one's own). Therefore, a discerning person should strive solely for the sake of the knowledge that bestows liberation. ||210||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "The statement that liberation, characterized by the cessation of duality, is to be accomplished through the realization of reality (tattva-bodha) by means of the analogy of a dream is untenable, because the duality to be negated cannot be equal to a dream. Anticipating this, he says: "It is not so; for it is indeed equal to a dream insofar as it consists of erroneous perception, since the scripture declares:
'These three—deep sleep, the dream state, and [the waking state]—are mere illusion (māyāmātra). Thus, there is indeed equality with a dream.
This entire world is a dream within the non-dual reality of Brahman.
It consists of both the conscious and the unconscious, appearing in the forms of the Lord (Īśa), the individual soul (Jīva), and so forth. || 11 ||

The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya, titled *Citradīpa*: "As non-dual"— that which exists as the entire world in the form of the Lord (*Īśvara*), the individual soul (*jīva*), and so forth, consisting of consciousness, is this non-dual [Brahman].
The construction is: "that which is a dream in the reality of Brahman. || 11 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "The illustration of a dream for bondage (*bandha*), which is to be removed, is indeed inappropriate. For while a dream, being merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*), is sublated as long as the knower exists, bondage—consisting of the duality of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) and so forth—is admitted to have empirical reality (*vyāvahārikasattva*) because it is not sublated as long as the knower exists. Anticipating this doubt, [the text says]: "He has three abodes and three dreams; these three... and so on.

He provides the resolution [to the objection] with the words "non-dual" (advitīya), based on the scriptural statement, "Deep sleep, dream, and mere illusion," and the statement from the *Māṇḍūkya-kārikā*, "It is a dream for one who perceives otherwise. Since the entire duality beginning with the waking state is generally characterized by being perceived erroneously, it possesses the status of being merely phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*); thus, even though there are internal distinctions such as the specific nature of a dream, its character as a dream does not depart. Therefore, he resolves [the issue]. || 211 ||
The one consisting of bliss and the one consisting of consciousness are the Lord and the individual soul.
These two are fashioned by Māyā; by them everything is fashioned.

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection—“How can the Lord (Īśvara) and the individual soul (jīva), who are non-different from Brahman, be included within the world?”—he states that they are included within the world because they are fashioned by Māyā: "Consisting of bliss," etc. (Verse 12).

A0 Commentary: Now, raising the objection, "Who is the creator of this dream, which consists of visible forms? [the author] states that it is primordial *māyā* itself that fashions the Lord and the individual soul—known as the sheaths consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) and consciousness (*vijñānamaya*)—as the witnessing seers, and through them, fashions the entire universe. Thus he says: "The sheath of bliss... (verse 212).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: It has been stated that everything was imagined by those two; now, in response to the inquiry as to which of them imagined what, he says:
"The creation, beginning with the act of seeing and ending with the entry [into the body], was imagined by Īśvara."
The cycle of worldly existence, beginning with the waking state and ending with liberation, is imagined by the individual soul.

Regarding the phrase "from seeing, etc.": the meaning is that the creation, established by the scriptural passage beginning with "He thought, 'Let me create the worlds'" and ending with "he entered through this door," has the Lord (Īśvara) as its agent; whereas the transmigratory existence, established by the scriptural passage beginning with "He has three abodes" and ending with "he saw this very person as Brahman, the most real," has the individual soul (jīva) as its agent. || 13 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, even so, one might ask: "How much of this duality is imagined by the Lord (Īśvara), and how much by the individual soul (Jīva)? To this, he says: "From the act of seeing," and so forth. || 213 ||
They do not know that non-dual reality of Brahman, which is free from attachment.
They engaged in a futile quarrel between the individual soul and the Lord, both of whom were products of Māyā.

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: "If Brahman alone is the ultimate reality, why is there this disagreement among disputants regarding the nature of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)?
Anticipating this doubt, he states that it is due to their lack of knowledge of the truth established by the scriptures, saying: "Non-dual" (advitīyam). || 14 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) are thus equally imagined (kalpita), then why is there a dispute among all disputants regarding their very nature? To this, he says: "The non-dual" (advitīyam). || 214 ||
Having understood this, we always rejoice in those who are established in reality.
We indeed lament for others; we do not dispute out of delusion.

Rāma’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): Anticipating the objection that since the disagreements among disputants regarding the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) are rooted in ignorance, they should be enlightened by means of such reality, he says "Having known... (jñātvā), [implying] "no," because such effort would be in vain. || 215 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if this is so, then all these proponents of duality (bhedavādins) must be instructed by you, the Siddhāntin;
thus begins the sixth chapter.
[The commentary] accompanied by two explanations.
[Verse 187] says:

"Having known... The word *sat* (the Real) also applies to the subsequent [verse], like a lamp placed on a threshold (*dehalī-dīpa*). [It refers to] others who are devoid of the refinement of scriptural study (*śāstra-saṃskāra*). [Verse 215]
Those beginning with the worshipers of grass and ending with the practitioners of yoga have resorted to delusion regarding the Lord.
Those beginning with the Lokāyatas and ending with the Sāṃkhyas have resorted to delusion regarding the individual soul (jīva). || 16 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He shows, by way of classification, the disputants who are confused regarding both God and the individual soul due to delusion—beginning with "ṇa" (no). || 16 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, as to who these deluded ones are, he says: "tṛṇa... etc. The sense is that all of these have indeed been set forth below. || 216 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question, "From what cause do they possess such delusion? he says:
"When they do not know the reality of Brahman as non-dual..."
All of them are indeed deluded; for them, where is liberation, or where is happiness? (17)

Regarding the word "without a second": what follows from that? To this he says—“of them. Because there is no rest of the mind due to the obsession with establishing the position they have adopted, they possess not even worldly happiness; thus he says—“what [happiness] here? || 17 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, one might ask, "From what [source] does the error of even Sāṃkhya and Yoga arise? To this, he says: "Brahman is non-dual. (217)
If there were a state of superior and inferior among them, let it be so; what does that matter?
Indeed, the awakened one is not touched by the kingdom of dreams or by begging for alms. || 18 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even in the absence of the knowledge of Brahman among them, a distinction of high and low is seen due to other forms of knowledge;

thus, some may experience happiness resulting from their superior status. Anticipating this doubt, he states with an illustration that such [happiness] is to be disregarded by those seeking liberation: "High and low... (18).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that even there, a gradation exists based on the degree of being "internal" (*antaraṅga*) and so forth; therefore, he says: "The highest," etc.
Therein, he provides a justification by means of an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a corroborative instance), stating: "In a dream," etc. (218).
Therefore, those seeking liberation should never direct their minds toward the doctrines of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa).
However, one must investigate the reality of Brahman and realize it.

Rāma’s Commentary: He concludes that since the doctrines of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) lack the cause for liberation, seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*) should not fix their minds upon them—thus, "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Then, raising the doubt as to what should be done instead, he states that through the inquiry into the Vedas (*śruti-vicāra*), the realization of Brahman alone must be achieved—thus, "But rather" (*kiṃtu*). || 19 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) states the conclusion: "Therefore" (tasmāt). It is not only that one should spend time in inquiry alone;

rather, having examined what obstacle exists for oneself regarding the realization that is the fruit of that inquiry, and having removed it by means of the methods taught in the scriptures, one must also immediately achieve the realization of the reality of one's own non-duality (advaita-tattva). This is stated by the remainder of the verse: "and let [it] be realized. || 219 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "In order to ascertain the reality of Brahman, the true nature of those two [the individual soul and the Lord] must be known as things to be abandoned.
Anticipating this, he says that if that were the case, the intellect would not reach its completion regarding the doctrines of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) alone;
rather, he states that those two serve as the cause for the ascertainment of reality by way of being the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).
Let them both attain [their goal]; plunge into them yourself, for you are not under their compulsion by that much alone.
188 [The Lamp of Citra]

"Vidyāraṇya’s *Pañcadaśī* [is presented] as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
