By this much—namely, by the possibility that these two, the doctrines of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), serve as the cause for determining the truth through their role as the prima facie view—the construction is: "O you who are helpless and devoid of discriminative knowledge, do not sink into those very doctrines of the *jīva* and the *īśvara*. || 220 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Even though the views regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) as stated above are accepted by other schools of thought, they are indeed useful for determining the ultimate truth (*tattva-nirṇaya*) as the prima facie positions (*pūrvapakṣa*). Therefore, why is it appropriate to disregard them? To this, he says: "As the prima facie position" (*pūrvapakṣatayā*). Those two—the Sāṃkhya and other doctrines concerning the *jīva* and *īśvara*—are "prior" (*pūrva*). Regarding the word "ultimate truth" (*tattva*): if they were to reach that status [as the final conclusion], then let it be so. Nevertheless, even to this extent, the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) is helpless and lacks independent control.

The connection is that one should not sink into those two aforementioned [faults] of speech and action. By this, it is indicated that they are as boundless as the ocean and are the cause of misfortune. || 220 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "Since both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), as described in the Sāṃkhya and Yoga scriptures, are of the nature of pure consciousness (śuddhacidrūpa), they too must be accepted by you; therefore, they cannot be treated as the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
To this he replies: "The jīva spoken of in Sāṃkhya is an unattached, all-pervading consciousness; such is the Lord."
If you say that those two meanings of "tat" and "tvam" taught in Yoga are pure, then listen. || 21 ||

Regarding the phrase "asaṃgacid" (unattached consciousness): although the followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga maintain that both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) are pure consciousness (*śuddhacidrūpa*), they nevertheless accept a real distinction between them. Therefore, [the author] states "Listen," indicating that this is not our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*). || 21 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Regarding that, having restated the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) as propounded by the Sāṃkhyas and others, he raises an objection with the words "asaṅga" (unattached). Thereupon, he promises to provide a resolution with the word "nanu" (but surely). || 229 ||
These two meanings, namely *tattva* (reality) and *maurubhāva* (the state of being great), have attained the status of our established doctrine (*siddhānta*).
That particular stage is intended solely for the purpose of awakening one to non-duality.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: “*na tattvamor iti*. The construction is: “The two meanings of the words *tat* and *tvam* have not reached our established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

Now, one might object: “But even by you, the pure meanings of the words *tat* and *tvam* have been described as distinct through the terms *kūṭastha* (the immutable) and *brahman* (the absolute). Anticipating this, he says: “*advaitabodhanāyaiveti*. It is precisely for the sake of awakening to non-duality—that is, for the purpose of establishing their identity by means of dispelling the distinctions well-known in the world—that those two [words] are used in distinction.
The intention is that although the two are not restated, their difference is nevertheless established. || 22 ||
The commentary says this: "Not so. *Kakṣā* means reasoning. || 222 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: If that is so, for what purpose is the purification of categories? To this he says:
"Deluded by beginningless Māyā, the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) appear to be very distinct."
They consider that purification alone is intended for the exclusion of those two.

Regarding the word "beginningless" (*anādi*): here, by the term *māyā*, ignorance (*avidyā*) which deludes its own substratum is indicated. Having attained erroneous cognition through that [ignorance], people consider the possession of agency and so forth on the part of the individual soul (*jīva*), and the possession of qualities such as omniscience on the part of the Lord (*īśvara*), to be ultimately real.
Therefore, the meaning is that purification is performed precisely for the sake of removing that [erroneous cognition]. || 23 ||
Regarding this, he states the reason: "beginningless," etc. The phrase "is desired by us" is implied. || 223 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Desiring to demonstrate the very method for purifying the meaning of the words, he recalls the previously mentioned illustration as a means to that end:
"Therefore, the appropriate illustration was correctly set forth earlier."
Consisting of the space within a jar, the great space, the space in water, and the space of the clouds.
(24) "For this very reason" means: for this very reason that the purification of categories (*padārtha*) must be performed. (24)
Regarding the question "Why is it so?", he says: "For this very reason" (ata eva). || 224 ||
The Sixth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): He states the method for purifying the categories of existence:
"Those two—water and the sky—are dependent respectively upon water and the ether; [the ether] is in those two."
The two substrates, however, are the jar-space and the great space, both perfectly pure.
Regarding the phrase "water and clouds": those which are the water, the sky, and the clouds are not ultimately real because they are dependent upon the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of water and clouds.

The space within a jar and the great space (mahākāśa), which serve as their substrates, are perfectly pure; the meaning is that they consist solely of space, independent of limiting adjuncts such as water and the like. || 225 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) clarifies that very point with the words "jala" and "jalākāśa. "Jalākāśa" refers to the great space reflected in the water of a full pitcher. "Abhrākāśa" is precisely the great space reflected in the water in the form of frost contained within the belly of a cloud;
the sense is that this has already been explained in the root text itself. || 229 ||
Thus, bliss and consciousness consist of Māyā, being under the control of the two powers (adhi).
But in the utterly pure Brahman, which is the immutable substrate of that [universe], [there is no such change].
The commentary on Rāmānuja’s gloss explains the application to the subject at hand with the words "evam" (thus). || 26 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) applies this to the illustration at hand with the words "evam" (thus). Now, an objection may be raised: this illustration is inconsistent. For it is beyond dispute that the water-sky and the cloud-sky are indeed reflections of the great sky (mahākāśa) according to the principle stated above. However, in your own understanding, the individual soul (jīva) is accepted as the reflection of the immutable witness-self (kūṭastha), who is its substrate; it is not held to be the reflection of Brahman in Māyā, which would be the Lord (īśvara).

If it is argued that there would be a correspondence between the illustration and the illustrated only if [the individual soul] is intended to be a reflection of Brahman—just as the great ether (mahākāśa) is the locus for Brahman itself—it is true; however, it was stated in that way precisely with the intention of expressing the non-difference of the immutable (kūṭastha) from Brahman. The authors of the root-text will state this very point further on:
"There is no difference between the immutable [Self] and Brahman except in name alone;
for the space within a jar and the great space (the universal ether) are never separated from one another. || 226 ||
If Sāṃkhya and Yoga are considered to be applicable to this very category;
The body should be accepted as the self because it is characterized by being composed of food (annamaya). || 27 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, if it is argued that both the Sāṃkhya and Yoga systems must be accepted because they are useful for the stage of purifying the two categories [of self and non-self], we reply that this is to understate the matter; for we must also accept other scriptures as being useful for that same stage. Thus he says: "This... (verse 27).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might raise the objection: "In that case, let the utility of Sāṃkhya and other systems be precisely for the sake of establishing the purified soul (jīva) and so forth.
Anticipating this, he replies by means of a counter-objection: "This... (verse 227).
If it is argued that these three—the diversity of selves, the reality of the world, and the Lord as distinct—are [real], [then...]
At that time, they abandon the consensus of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and Vedānta.

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Raising the objection, "From where, then, does Sāṃkhya and Yoga derive their opposition to Vedānta?", he states that it lies in the aspect characterized by the difference of the individual soul, the reality of the world, and the neutrality of the Lord, saying: "The difference of the Self," etc. (Verse 28).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if this is so, then in what respect do Sāṃkhya and Yoga contradict Vedānta? To that he says: "The Self... (verse 228).
If it is argued that the individual soul has accomplished its purpose merely by attaining non-attachment, then—
One’s purpose is fulfilled even by the mere permanence of [the worship] with incense, sandalwood, and so forth. || 29 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [pages 190–190]

—[The commentary on the *Citradīpa* by Rāma: Now, one might object: "Since liberation is established simply through the knowledge of the soul's (*jīva*) state of non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*), what is the use of the realization of non-duality (*advaita*)? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states the non-duality...
Keeping in mind the intention that qualities such as non-attachment cannot be conceived without that knowledge, he states the answer: "The individual soul (jīva). (29)

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might raise the objection that the individual soul (jīva) would have its purpose fulfilled merely by the realization of the non-attachment taught therein; this doubt is refuted by means of a counter-argument: "The soul... (verse 229).
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He reveals his underlying intention:
"Just as the permanence of garlands and such things is difficult to establish, so too is that of the Self."
It is not possible for the two Lords of the World to exist together without being joined. || 230 ||
"Yathā" means: appearing in the form of qualifiers for two [parents] who are alive. || 230 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, if it is argued that the permanence of things such as a garland is difficult to establish, then one might say that the non-conjunction of the Self [with the body] according to the Sāṃkhya and other systems is likewise so; to this he says: "Just as... The meaning is: while both are living and existing. || 230 ||
Rāghava’s Commentary — He clarifies the very impossibility [of liberation]:
"In that case, Nature would inevitably bring about attachment just as before."
Even the Lord restrains this [mind]; if that is so, what liberation can there be for it? (31)
"Indeed, it must be so. He states the conclusion: "Who is this? || 31 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) on verse a0 explains that very point: "Necessarily," etc. "As before" means as previously stated. "This" refers to the individual soul (jīva). ||231||

Rāghava’s Commentary: Since attachment and restriction are effects of non-discrimination, one might raise the objection: "If attachment and restriction are caused by non-discrimination, then once non-discrimination has ceased through discriminative knowledge, how could attachment and the like ever arise again?
To this, he says: "If it is argued that attachment and restriction are caused by non-discrimination..."
The doctrine of illusion has been forced upon the evil-minded Sāṃkhya by sheer force.

Regarding the term "non-discrimination" (*aviveka*): [the opponent] objects that if this were so, it would result in the fallacy of an unestablished position (*apasiddhānta*), and [the author] refutes this with the words "by force" (*balāt*). This is because it is impossible for mere non-existence (*abhāvamātra*) to produce an effect that is a positive entity (*bhāvakārya*). Nor is the second alternative [tenable], because one does not observe anything other than discrimination (*viveka*), such as a jar (*ghaṭa*), to be a cause of conjunction.
As for the third [alternative], since that would be a positive ignorance (*bhāvarūpājñāna*), it follows that the doctrine of Māyā (*māyāvāda*) is being accepted. || 32 ||

Commentary (a0): Anticipating the objection that this attachment to *prakṛti* and so forth is rooted in non-discrimination (*aviveka*), [the author] says "non-discrimination" (*aviveka*) to show that such a view would lead to the doctrine of *māyā* (illusionism), and thus it is not so. For non-discrimination is indeed the absence of discrimination; therefore, how could there be the effect consisting of attachment and so forth? Consequently, even if the Sāṃkhya were to cry out with the word "non-discrimination," he must nevertheless accept primordial ignorance (*ajñāna*) as having a positive ontological form (*bhāvarūpa*). Thus it follows.
This is the intended meaning. || 232 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: One might object that since the distinction between bondage and liberation cannot be established if non-duality is accepted, the plurality of selves must be admitted; thus he says:
"For the sake of establishing the distinction between bondage and liberation, let the multiplicity of selves be accepted."
If this is argued, it is not so, because Māyā is capable of establishing [the distinctions].

Regarding the phrase "bondage and liberation": he refutes [the objection] with "Not so, because... (na yataḥ), on the grounds that the distinction between bondage and liberation is possible for even a single self through the power of māyā. || 33 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "In that case, according to your view, the systematic arrangement of bondage and so forth would be impossible without a plurality of selves; therefore, the Sāṃkhya doctrine must be accepted.
Anticipating this doubt, he provides the following resolution: "Bondage... (verse 233). It is Māyā alone that will establish all such systematic arrangements.
The Sixth Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.
191 Rāghava’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Anticipating the objection as to how even Māyā could establish [the world], he says that it is because her very nature is to accomplish the impossible.
Do you not see the contradiction in saying, "I shall bring about that which is difficult to accomplish"?
But the Śruti does not at all tolerate the notion that bondage and liberation are real.

Regarding the phrase "durghaṭam" (difficult to establish): having raised the objection that even if bondage is illusory (*avidyaka*), liberation must be accepted as real, he says "vāstavau" (both are real) to show that this is not so, because it contradicts scripture. The meaning of "na sahatetarām" is "it does not tolerate it at all. The sense is that [the Śruti] does not tolerate liberation as real any more than it tolerates bondage as real. || 34 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "How could she even do this? Anticipating this doubt, he says "durghaṭam" (the difficult-to-accomplish) to show that it is not so, because it is observed in cases such as magicians that even what is difficult to accomplish is brought about through the power of *māyā* alone, based on the vow: "I shall accomplish this. If it is argued that "this is merely imagined," he replies with "vāstavau" (they are real). || 234 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He cites the scripture that negates the reality of liberation and so forth:
"There is no cessation and no origination; there is no bound soul and no seeker."
Neither one who desires liberation nor one who is liberated—this is the ultimate reality.

"Not cessation" means that there is no cessation, which is destruction; no origination, which is connection with a body; no bound soul, which possesses attributes such as pleasure and pain; no seeker, who is one who practices hearing and so forth; no one desiring liberation, who is endowed with the fourfold qualifications; and no liberated one, whose ignorance has ceased—all this does not exist from the perspective of the ultimate reality. || 235 ||
Commentary (a0): He recites that very Vedic revelation concerning the knower of immortality: "Not... (235).
Both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) are the two calves of the wish-fulfilling cow known as Māyā.
For those who drink [the nectar] according to their desire, duality is indeed non-duality alone as the ultimate reality.

Rāma’s Commentary: Thus, having established that the distinction between the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), and so forth, consists of Māyā, he concludes [the argument] with the verse beginning "māyākhyāyāḥ" (36).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, having established through reasoning that the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) and so forth is illusory—like a magical trick—he concludes its falsity by means of a metaphor: "Māyā... (verse 236).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary:

Now, one might raise the objection: "Granted that the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is illusory because they are both products of māyā, yet since the immutable Brahman and the individual soul are ultimately real, their distinction must also be ultimately real. Anticipating this, [the author] addresses the nature of the difference that serves as the basis for such a distinction.
He refutes this by means of the following reasoning: "There is no difference between the immutable [Self] and Brahman except for a mere name."
The space within a jar and the great space are never, indeed, separated from one another. (37)

Regarding the term "immutable" (kūṭastha): although a distinction is perceived merely through names, he recalls the previously mentioned illustration to show that in reality no distinction exists—namely, "the space within a jar" (ghaṭākāśa). || 37 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, even if this is so, the distinction between the immutable (kūṭastha) and Brahman remains just as it was; therefore, how can non-duality (advaita) and liberation (kaivalya) be established?
To this, he says: "The immutable... (237).
Rāma’s Commentary: He states what the result is of thus establishing the falsity of difference:
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya:
that very non-duality which was heard prior to creation is the same as it is now and even higher than that.
Even in liberation, this illusion called the "variegated lamp" pointlessly deludes all people. (38)

Regarding the phrase "that which is non-dual" (*yadadvaitam*): the meaning is that the very Brahman which is established as "without a second" (*advitīya*) in the Śruti passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," is the reality because it is unsublated throughout the three periods of time; duality is not real. [Objection: Why, then, is there an insistence on all these distinctions? To this he says: "Māyā in vain" (*vṛthā māyā*). The meaning is that people persist in such insistence because they are devoid of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). || 38 ||
And so, he says—“That which is non-duality”—to show that the attainment of the non-dual Self, characterized by its existence across the three periods of time, is indeed accomplished.
This is based on the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*: “In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second.

Now, if this is so, then whose is transmigratory existence? To this he replies with the remainder of the verse, beginning with “in vain” (*vṛthā*): [transmigratory existence is] in vain, being devoid of intrinsic reality.

That *māyā*, which is the root ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) and is false by its very nature, causes this entire multitude of living beings in the world to wander in vain—that is, pointlessly—by means of the notion that duality is real even within the non-dual Self, causing them to revolve through heaven, hell, and so forth; this too is "in vain. This should be construed by repeating the word "vain" (*vṛthā*). Therefore, there is not even a trace of room for doubt regarding the non-duality that has been asserted. Such is the direction [of the argument]. Otherwise, *māyā*—
Because if that [universe] were produced by that [creator], it would follow that the world is not false. || 238 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Indeed, those who describe the world as consisting of illusion (māyā) and reality as non-dual are themselves seen to be subject to transmigratory existence; therefore, what is the purpose of the knowledge of reality? To this, he raises the doubt: "What is the use here of saying that even these [who speak thus] are deluded by ignorance?"
Not as before, because no error is observed here in their case. || 39 ||

Regarding those who say "it is so": although there is worldly activity for some due to the power of karma, because they lack the aforementioned clinging (*abhiniveśa*), he refutes them by saying "not as [you think]" (*na yathā*). || 39 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, raising the objection that even the proponents of the Siddhānta are merely deluded by *māyā*, and therefore asking what is the use of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), he provides the resolution with the verse beginning "He who... (yaḥ). The reason for this is given by the remainder of the verse, beginning with "as before" (*yathāpūrvam*). Here, [the context concerns] the falsity of the visible world (*dṛśyamithyātva*) and the non-dual nature of the Self (*advaitātmatva*). || 239 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To demonstrate the absence of delusion in the wise, he first states the conviction of the ignorant:
"Therefore, the entire cycle of worldly existence, pertaining to both this world and the next, is real."
"It neither shines nor exists"—such is the conviction of the ignorant regarding non-duality.

Regarding the term *aihika*: that which exists in this world (*iha*) is *aihika*, consisting of the nourishment of sons, wife, and so forth; that which exists in yonder world (*amuṣmin*) is *āmuṣmika*, consisting of the experience of the bliss of heaven and the like. || 240 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, in order to clarify the aforementioned observation of the absence of delusion in the knower, [the author] restates the delusion of the ignorant: "aihiketi" || 240 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: He shows the distinction of this from the ascertainment of reality (tattvaviniścaya): "The certainty of the knower is seen to be the opposite of this [ascertainment], and it is rightly perceived."
Bound by their own respective convictions, they each think, "I am liberated. || 41 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the knowers": the meaning is that there is the certainty that non-duality (*advaita*) is the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*), whereas transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is not ultimate. Having raised the doubt as to what follows from this, he says—referring to the verse beginning with *svasva*—"the fruit arises according to one's own respective certainty. || 41 ||
The Sixth Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.
193 - Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): However, the certainty of the knowers, being of the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*), is indeed the opposite of the aforementioned certainty; thus he says:

Regarding the phrase "of the knowers": the meaning is that the entire cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), appearing in the form of duality, is indeed false like a mirage; rather, its nature is the realization in the form of "I am indeed Brahman, which is non-dual Being-Consciousness-Bliss" (*advaita-saccidānanda*).
What follows from that? He says: "each his own," etc. (241).
He raises an objection—the *Rāma-tīkā* states: "The statement that 'non-duality appears' is based solely on scripture and not on experience; therefore, there is no certainty regarding it.
If non-duality is not immediate (*aparokṣa*), then [how can it be known] since it appears as the very nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*)?"
If duality does not appear in its entirety, how can everything else appear? (42)

Regarding the phrase "not non-duality": he refutes the objection that its being beyond the scope of experience is unproven by stating, "not by way of the nature of consciousness. The meaning is that it appears as the form of a pervasive luminosity (*sphuraṇa*) running through jars and other objects, such that one says, "the jar shines," "the cloth shines," and so forth. Now, an objection is raised: "Even if its nature as consciousness appears, it is not perceived in its entirety"—this is expressed by the word "in its totality" (*aśeṣeṇa*). [The response is: The absence of appearance in its completeness is common even to the case of duality.
Thus he asks: "What is duality? (42)

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that even though verbal knowledge exists, liberation is not possible because they lack direct (aparokṣa) realization; to this he says: "No" (na). Anticipating the doubt that there might still be partiality even in that case, he resolves it through a counter-argument: "In its entirety" (aśeṣeṇa). || 242 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus stated the equality of the defects, he now states the equality of the remedies:
"Indeed, the manifestation [of the defects] in both cases is equal in its general outline."
Just as the proof of duality [is established], so too is the proof of non-duality; what more is there to say by that? (43)

"By way of a mere direction" (*diṅmātreṇa*) means by way of a single part (*ekadeśena*) of the two, namely duality and non-duality; such is the meaning. Anticipating the question, "How is there parity of refutation by this much?", he says: "Just like the establishment of duality" (*dvaitasiddhivat*). The meaning is: in your position (*pakṣe*), by the existence of the cognition of that single part to that extent, why does the establishment of non-duality—the certainty of non-duality—not occur just as the establishment of duality—the certainty of duality—does? Rather, it certainly does occur. || 43 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), while still maintaining his hidden intention, states that there is an equality of solutions corresponding to the equality of defects: "By way of mere direction," etc. (243).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: The proponent of the prima facie view raises a doubt regarding the non-establishment of non-duality by way of another argument:
"How indeed can this non-duality, which is devoid of duality, exist when there is the cognition of duality?"
But the manifestation of consciousness is not in contradiction with this duality; therefore, both are unequal.

Regarding the phrase "by means of duality": non-duality (*advaita*) is that which is devoid of duality; because these two are mutually contradictory, when duality is perceived, non-duality cannot possibly exist—this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "In that case, since duality is also opposed to non-duality, it follows equally that when non-duality appears, duality is unestablished. Anticipating this objection, the proponent of the prima facie view says: "But the manifestation of consciousness... In your own system, the very perception of the nature of consciousness is what constitutes the perception of non-duality.
And since that [non-duality] lacks opposition to duality, the sense is that there is no equality between the two. || 44 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Again, the proponent (pūrvavādī) raises an objection in another manner: "By means of duality" (*dvaitena*). For you, the knower, it is indeed beyond dispute that non-dual Brahman is devoid of duality. Therefore, while there exists knowledge regarding duality in the form of opponents such as ourselves, how can this aforementioned non-dual Brahman be established? It cannot be established at all; such is the logical connection (*anvaya*). If that is so, then duality too, being of the nature of the manifestation of consciousness (*cidbhāna*), is non-dual.
Anticipating the objection, "But how can there be such a manifestation? he says, "However, the manifestation of consciousness...
[and so forth]. Therefore, the meaning is that both manifestations—of duality and non-duality—are not equal; they are by no means the same. || 244 ||
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya [the commentary by Rāma called *Citradīpa*]:
"Because even though duality is perceived, it lacks reality, it does not subvert real non-duality."
To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) replies:
"In that case, listen: duality is unreal because it consists of māyā."
Therefore, by process of elimination, real non-duality shines forth. || 245 ||

Thus: "Presumption by elimination" (pariśeṣa) is the comprehension [of a meaning] when, upon the negation of what is possible, there is no possibility elsewhere, leaving only that which remains. || 245 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), awakening his own hidden intention, provides the resolution: "If that is so, then...

The meaning is as follows: by the method of elimination (pariśeṣāt), when the unreal (asat) and illusory (mithyābhūta) duality is sublated because it consists of māyā, that which remains is characterized as the foundational substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) serving as the limit (avadhi). || 245 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He demonstrates the very method of elimination:
"The entire world is indeed Māyā, consisting of an inconceivable arrangement."
Having thus determined this, let the reality of things be established as residing in non-duality alone. (46)

"Unthinkable" (aciṃtya) means that which cannot be thought of; "unthinkable arrangement" refers to that whose form is such. By this manner—namely, that the entire world is merely illusion (*māyā*) and thus false—the falsity of duality is ascertained because it is indefinable; the meaning is that non-duality (*advaita*) alone remains as the reality. || 46 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) on verse a0 reveals that very manner: "Inconceivable," etc. || 246 ||
If duality again appears as a reality to you, then [you must act] accordingly once more.
Examine this; what effort is required for that? Tell me.
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even if non-duality has been ascertained in this way, the reality of duality continues to appear again and again due to prior latent impressions (vāsanā).

Anticipating this doubt, he says, "Again, of duality," etc., to effect its cessation—that one should repeatedly contemplate its falsity. The intention is that Vyāsa has prescribed the repetition of hearing and so forth regarding the Self in the fourth chapter [of the Brahma-sūtras] with the rule: "Repetition [is required], because of the instruction being given more than once" (*āvṛttirasakṛdupadeśāt*). || 47 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Even though the method for subverting duality and leaving non-duality as the remainder has thus been taught to the disciple seeking liberation, if the reality of non-duality still flashes forth due to past latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), he says "again" [in verse 247] to address what loss there could be for you if one were to further pursue that very subversion.
If it is asked, "For how long?"—let this weariness be regarded as duality.
But in non-duality (advaita), this [dualistic distinction] is not tenable, because it wards off all misfortune. || 48 ||

Rāma’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Anticipating the question of for how long one must investigate in this manner, he states [verse 48]: "For how long... Since it has been stated that this investigation is concluded upon the attainment of immediate knowledge (*aparokṣavidyā*), which serves as the limit for the duration of inquiry, such weariness regarding the investigation into non-duality (*advaita*) is not appropriate; rather, weariness is appropriate only toward the appearance of duality (*dvaitapratibhāsa*).
Thus he says: "For how long... (48).
Commentary (Ṭīkā) on A0: To address the question of how long this continuous practice (*anusaṃdhāna*) should be maintained, he says: "How long? (248).
[Objection: "If it is argued that hunger, thirst, and so forth are observed in me just as they were before," [the reply follows].
Who could say that the "I-sense" (ahaṃkāra), which is denoted by the word "self," is not an object of perception? (49)

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even for Māyā, who possesses direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) of the non-dual reality of the Self, hunger, thirst, and other afflictions are not yet eliminated; therefore, the power of self-knowledge to remove suffering remains unproven. Thus he raises this doubt with the words: "Hunger, thirst, and so forth... [page 195] What then? My...
The Sixth Chapter, together with the two commentaries. 195.

—Having raised the dilemma as to whether [the ego] is seen in the *ahaṃkāra* denoted by the word "self" (*bdavācya*), or rather in the conscious self (*cidātman*) characterized by the word "I" (*macchanda*), he accepts the first alternative, stating: "denoted by the word 'I'. The second is not [acceptable], because that [conscious self] is unattached (*asaṅga*) and is not an object; this should be understood from the external [commentary]. || 49 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Again, he raises an objection based on contradiction with experience, stating "hunger" (*kṣut*). He resolves it by distinguishing between the objects [of the experiences], stating "the word 'I'" (*macchabda*). || 249 ||
If it were argued that these [limitations] would also apply to the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa) due to the superimposition of identity (tādātmyādhyāsa), [we reply: no.
Therefore, maintain the superimposition, but always exercise discernment.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: One might raise the objection that even though such [superimposition] does not exist in reality, it may nonetheless appear through delusion;

thus he says, "Even in the nature of consciousness" (cidrūpe’pi). If this is so, then for the sake of removing superimposition, which is the cause of misfortune, one should always practice discrimination; thus he says, "Let there be no superimposition" (mā’dhyāsam) || 250 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, even so, they appear in the Self as well due to the power of superimposition; therefore, he says: "Even in that which is of the nature of consciousness. || 250 ||
If it is argued that superimposition occurs instantaneously through the force of firm latent impressions (*vāsanā*), [we reply:]
And one should cultivate discernment in order to firmly establish it at all times. || 51 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Since superimposition may recur due to the power of beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā), he states that for its cessation, discrimination alone must be repeatedly practiced and no other means; thus he says: "Suddenly," etc. (Verse 51).
Commentary (ṭīkā): Anticipating the objection that [the realization] might occur quickly due to the firmness of the mental impression (saṃskāra), he says: "Instantly" (jhaṭiti). || 251 ||
One should not say that the falsity of duality in solitude is established by reasoning alone.
For the experience of the very nature of the construction of the city is witnessed by oneself.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "The illusory nature of duality is established by reasoning alone through inquiry, not by experience.

Anticipating this, he refutes it with the words "Discrimination" (verse 52), asserting that such an objection is not valid because the experience of falsity—characterized by its inconceivable construction—is witnessed by one's own self-evident consciousness.
Commentary (a0): Anticipating the objection that even there [in the case of the Self] there is an absence of experience, he refutes it with the words "Viveka" (Discrimination). || 252 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "If the definition of the category of falsity (mithyātva) as 'having an inconceivable structure' is stated, it would be over-extensive (ativyāpti), applying even to the conscious Self (cidātman).
To this, he replies:
"If the conscious Self were of inconceivable structure, then let it be so; we have no objection."
We call the funeral pyre "well-piled" because of its eternal nature.

Regarding the phrase "cidapi": intending to state that the definition of falsity consists in being of inconceivable construction while being associated with antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), [the opponent] might first concede that the Self possesses inconceivable construction, saying, "Let it be so. Anticipating the objection that such a concession would result in a contradiction of one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), he refutes it by saying, "We do not," and provides the reason therein: "because of eternality. The construction is: "We do not say that consciousness (*cit*) is of inconceivable construction. || 53 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Even there, the opponent again raises a doubt regarding the invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*), saying "ciddhi" [consciousness indeed]. With a hidden intention (*gūḍhābhisaṃdhi*), the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) accepts this with the words "tarhi" and so forth. Revealing that very intention, he makes manifest the reason for his acceptance with the words "nityatva" and so forth; the meaning is: "from the reason consisting of eternity. || 253 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Anticipating the question, "From what [source] does the eternity of consciousness arise?", he states that it is because there is no experience of its prior non-existence (prāgabhāva).
In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya:
"Prior non-existence has not been experienced by consciousness, and therefore consciousness is eternal."
The prior non-existence of duality, however, is experienced by consciousness. || 54 ||

Regarding the statement "the prior non-existence of consciousness" (*citprāgabhāva*) in the *Citradīpa*: since the prior non-existence of consciousness has never been experienced, it follows that consciousness is eternal. This is the intended meaning here: one who asserts that there is a prior non-existence of consciousness must be asked whether that prior non-existence of consciousness is experienced by consciousness itself or by something else. It cannot be by something else.

Because anything other than that [consciousness] is insentient (*jaḍa*), it is impossible for it to be an experiencer. Even in the position that "it is experienced by consciousness," does it occur through another consciousness or through itself? Not the first, because in the doctrine of non-duality (*advaitavāda*), there is no other consciousness at all. Even if such another were admitted, since an absence whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is consciousness cannot be apprehended without the apprehension of that consciousness, if that [absence] were also being apprehended, it would follow that it is insentient like a jar or other objects. Nor is the second [option] tenable.

"Because it is impossible for an intrinsic nature to be grasped by itself. Now, one might object: since duality consists of distinctions such as the subject (*pramātṛ*) and so forth, and since that absence [of duality] cannot be experienced by that very same subject, and because there is no other experiencer of it, duality—like consciousness itself—would necessarily be eternal. Anticipating this, he refutes it by stating that the absence of another experiencer is unproven, saying: "Of duality... [The absence of duality during waking and other states is experienced by the witness (*sākṣin*) in deep sleep.]
The meaning is that because darkness is being measured [observed], He is the witness; for there is a scriptural statement: "He is the witness of all. || 54 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): If it is argued that, because its structure is inconceivable, duality (*dvaita*) must likewise be eternal, he says "prāk" [etc.].

He states the non-establishment of the reason for duality with the words "dvaitasya. This means "of duality which is distinct from the beginningless," or alternatively, "of the manifestation of duality. The secret point is that, by this, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding that which is beginningless. || 54 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: And thus, since the definition of falsity—consisting in being possessed of a prior absence and having an inconceivable construction—is present in duality, the falsity of duality is established; so he says:
"For duality, being joined with a prior absence, is constructed like a jar and so forth."
Nevertheless, this inconceivable construction is false, like a magician's trick.

"Prāgabhāva... [means] "endowed with antecedent non-existence. This is a qualifying attribute containing a reason: duality is said to be like a water-pot and so forth because it is endowed with antecedent non-existence. Even though that duality is being constructed, its construction is inconceivable; therefore, while it is being constructed, by virtue of having an inconceivable construction, it is false—like a palace created by a magician. || 255 ||
The commentary on verse a0 states the conclusion: "By the prior non-existence," etc. (255).
Consciousness is directly perceived, and the falsity of that which is other than it is experienced.
How is it that "non-duality" and "being directly perceived" are not contradictory? || 56 ||

Rāma’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Consciousness (*cit*), being self-luminous, shines as eternally immediate; furthermore, it has already been shown that the falsity of whatever is distinct from consciousness is experienced by that very consciousness. This being so, for one who asserts that non-duality (*advaita*) lacks immediacy, there would be a contradiction; thus he says: "Because [non-duality] is perceived by consciousness" (*cit-pratyakṣa*). The phrase "because it shines in the form of consciousness" is intended to include the previously stated reasoning.
The word "śva" (dog) [is used]. How is it that the statement "non-duality is not immediate" is not contradictory? Such is the construction [of the sentence]. || 56 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might object: "In this way, the falsity of duality is established by reasoning alone—such as 'the subject of dispute is false because it is an arrangement of the inconceivable, like a magical illusion'—and not by experience. To this, he says: "Consciousness" (cid). Thus, the meaning is: of the entire web of duality consisting of name and form, which is other than—that is, distinct from—consciousness. By means of the cognition of its falsity, there is a separation [from consciousness], characterized by a lack of existence and illumination.

The meaning is that non-existence in terms of its own intrinsic being (*svataḥ-sattā-śūnyatva*) is not experienced through the destruction of its own nature; rather, it is made an object precisely by self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśa-cit*). He asks what follows from this and says: "not non-duality" (*nādvaitam*). Thus, the connection is: how could the claim made by the proponents of duality—that non-duality is not directly perceived (*aparokṣa*)—fail to be refuted? || 256 ||
The Sixth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Thus, he asks why faith does not arise in some persons, even though they understand the meaning of the Vedānta.
Having understood this, why are some still dissatisfied? Let this be explained.
Tell me, why is it that even for an enlightened Cārvāka and others, the self is the body? (57)
Regarding the word "thus" (*ittham*): wishing to state that [the opponent's position] is devoid of correct investigation, he takes up a counter-argument with the words "of the Cārvāka and others.
By the word "others," common folk are included, whereas one who is awakened is skilled in reasoning through inclusion and exclusion (*ūhāpoha*). || 17 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Even though some here possess knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures through indirect means (*parokṣataḥ*), why are they still dissatisfied? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the resolution with the word "ittham" (thus). The intended meaning is that, in this case, the very obstacle of being far-sighted (*dūradṛṣṭa-pratibandha*) is the cause [of their dissatisfaction]. || 257 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He raises an objection regarding the release from the counter-argument:
"If it be argued that there is no correct inquiry on his part due to a defect in his intellect, so be it."
But being dissatisfied, they did not examine the meaning of the treatise in particular. || 58 ||

Regarding the word "correctly" (*samyak*): he establishes it through equanimity with the words "so it is" (*tathā*). The particle *tu* connects back to "due to a defect in the intellect" (*dhīdoṣāt*), and it carries the sense of the word *eva* (only/indeed). || 58 ||

Commentary (a0): He reveals the counter-argument (*pratibandī*) with the words "samyak" (properly). He states that even in the present case, the situation is exactly the same, with the verse beginning "asaṃtuṣṭās tu... (But those who are dissatisfied...). || 258 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus reflected upon reality, he recites the scriptural passage that establishes the fruit of the knowledge of reality born from such reflection:
"When all desires that dwell within his heart are released..."
If it is argued that the Vedic fruit is not seen [in this way], it is indeed seen. || 59 ||

Regarding the phrase "when": the second half of the mantra, "Then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains Brahman," means that when—at which time—all those desires and so forth, rooted in the superimposition of identity with the body, which exist in the heart of this seeker of liberation, are liberated—that is, they cease upon the cessation of superimposition through the knowledge of reality—then at that very moment, the mortal [who was previously] subject to death due to the superimposition of identity with the former body...

The person (*puruṣa*) becomes immortal and free from superimposition (*adhyāsa*) due to its absence. He states the reason for this: "In this very state, one attains Brahman. The meaning of this scriptural passage is that "in this very body" (*atra*), one "attains" (*samaśnute*)—that is, fully reaches—Brahman, which is characterized by truth and other such qualities. An objection is raised: "Is this result taught by scripture, such as the cessation of desires and so forth, established through experience, or is it merely verbal? [The author] replies: "Thus, it is scriptural... *sama-*... [text continues].

With the intention that its status as something perceived is established by examining the purport of the immediately preceding scriptural statement, he offers the rebuttal: "That is indeed perceived. (59)

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that even so, the fruit of the knowledge of reality as declared by the Śruti is not seen in the knower of reality; anticipating this doubt, he provides the resolution with the verse beginning "yadā" (when). || 259 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To clarify that [Self] has been seen, he cites the relevant verse and states its meaning:
"When all the knots of the heart are rent asunder..."
Desires are explained as being of the nature of a knot, according to the remainder of the statement. || 260 ||
The meaning is as follows: by the supplementary statement "when all [this]," the release from desire is explained as the breaking of the knot (*granthibheda*).

Since this breaking of the knot—characterized by the cessation of the superimposition of identity between the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) and the conscious self (*cidātman*)—is established through direct experience (*anubhava*), it is not something imperceptible.
The phrase "by the supplementary statement" means "by this sentence. || 260 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [pages 198–198]
The commentary (ṭīkā) explains that [point] with the verse beginning "When all... (yadā sarve). || 260 ||
Through lack of discrimination, one unifies the ego-sense with the conscious self.
The desires expressed by the word "kāma" are the thoughts, "May this be mine," and "May that be mine. (61)
Rāghava’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "In common usage, the word *kāma* denotes only a particular kind of desire; therefore, how can it be explained as a 'knot' (*granthi*)?

Anticipating this doubt, he states that it is only a specific type of desire rooted in superimposition (*adhyāsa*) that is denoted by the word *kāma*, and not desire in general—thus: "Ahaṃkāra... (Verse 61).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, even if this is so, one might ask what the nature of the treatise itself is at its very beginning; therefore, he says: "Egoism," etc. This means the Consciousness-reflection (cidābhāsa) and the Immutable One (kūṭastha). "Due to non-discrimination" means through mutual superimposition (parasparādhyāsa). Having thus stated the "knot" (granthi), he states the meaning of the word "desire" (kāma), which is rooted in that: "May this be mine," etc. (261).
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If it is only desire rooted in superimposition (*adhyāsa*) that must be abandoned, then some other [desire] must be accepted.
Anticipating this, he says that because it lacks the quality of being a sublater (*bādhaka*), it is indeed accepted:
"Without allowing the conscious Self (*cidātman*) to enter [into it], perceiving the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛti*) as separate..."
Even if one desires ten million objects, there is no further affliction once the knot [of ignorance] is severed.

"Without causing to enter": the meaning is that one should not cause the conscious self (cidātman) to enter into the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) by means of the practice of identifying with it (tādātmyābhyāsa), nor incorporate it therein. || 62 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Without causing [it] to enter" (*apraveśya*). This means without causing the ego (*ahaṃkāra*)—which is the reflection of consciousness delimited by that [ego]—to enter the immutable Self (*kūṭastha-cidātman*), and thus not unifying it through mutual superimposition (*anyonyādhyāsa*) based on the identity induced by root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*).
For this very reason, seeing it as distinct—that is, different—from the immutable Self, and perceiving it as false due to its lack of existence and other attributes, he...

Furthermore, the connection [of the verse] is as follows: even though one who desires the ten million objects—such as conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and so forth—because of their desirability, for that knower of reality, there is no affliction whatsoever due to the breaking of the aforementioned knots. || 262 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection that in the absence of superimposition (adhyāsa) there would be no arising of desires at all, he says— anticipating that their emergence may still be possible due to the force of commenced karma (prārabdha-karma)— that even when the knot [of ignorance] has been severed, desires may still arise from the defect of prārabdha.
Even after growing up, because of the abundance of your sins, you remain as dissatisfied as you are now.
"Even the breaking of the knot"—regarding this, he provides an illustration: "even having understood," etc. (63).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that if this were so, desire itself would not exist; anticipating this, he says: "Even upon the breaking of the knot" (granthibhede 'pi).
In that regard, he provides the opponent himself as an illustration by saying: "Even having understood" (buddhvāpi) || 263 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He clarifies that in the absence of superimposition (adhyāsa), the desire and other states residing in the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) do not obstruct [the perception of the Self] by demonstrating two examples:
"Likewise, by the desires and so forth residing in the ego-sense, as well as by the diseases of the body and so forth..."
Or what would the birth and destruction of trees and such have to do with the Self, whose nature is consciousness? (64)

Regarding the term "I-consciousness" (ahaṃkāra): the meaning is that just as there is no affliction of the witness of the I-consciousness by diseases and so forth residing in the body—because it is devoid of connection with the body—and just as [there is none] by birth and so forth residing in trees and the like, even so, upon the cessation of superimposition, there is no affliction by desire and so forth residing in the I-consciousness. || 64 ||
Objection: Even so, the immutable Self (kūṭastha) would still be subject to desire and other qualities belonging to the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) mirrored in the ego (ahaṃkāra).
[Page 199] Chapter Six.

Anticipating the objection that "the state of being earth (kṣititva) must indeed exist," [the author] clarifies with two examples that there is no contradiction whatsoever by this much alone—[beginning with] "ahaṃkāra"— *Vyākhyādvayasametā* | 199. Anticipating the objection that "the state of being earth (kṣititva) must indeed exist," [the author] clarifies with two examples that there is no contradiction whatsoever by this much alone—[beginning with] "ahaṃkāra"— (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary (*vyākhyā*) on a philosophical work, likely Advaita Vedānta. The phrase *vyākhyādvayasametā* indicates it is accompanied by two commentaries. The numbering "199" likely refers to a verse or section number.)
Thus it is said. || 264 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: One might object that since the non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*) of the conscious Self (*cidātman*) is uniform, there was no obstruction by desire and the like even prior [to the breaking of the knot]; to this he replies:
"If you say it was thus even before the breaking of the knot, do not forget that [it is not so]."
This very breaking of the knot has been accomplished by you; therefore, you have become successful. || 265 ||

Regarding the phrase "due to the breaking of the knot" (*granthibhedāt*): since we define such an awakening itself as the "breaking of the knot," this objection is actually in our favor; thus he says, "do not forget that. (265)
Commentary (a0): If it is argued that "this [state] occurs even before the breaking of the knot," he satisfies [the objection] by stating that this very state is indeed the breaking of the knot—thus:
"The knot... (verse 265).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states that the very absence of such knowledge is the knot:
"If the deluded do not know in this way, this indeed is the knot, and nothing else."
The difference between those of deluded intellect lies solely in their being bound by knots and their subsequent breaking of them.
"Not so. Now, one might object: "If desire is admitted even in the case of the knower (jñānin), then on what basis is there a distinction between the knower and the ignorant?
Anticipating this, he says—referring to the verse beginning with *granthitadbheda*—"there is no distinction whatsoever other than the breaking or not breaking of the knot. (66)

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): "It is truly marvelous that fools do not understand at all that the entire range of desires and so forth resides solely in the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), and not in the immutable Self characterized as its witness! Thus, out of encouragement, the disciple says "Not so" to the venerable Guru. Thereupon, the venerable Guru, in order to further strengthen the disciple's understanding, establishes the state of being bound within that very [reflection] by means of the aforementioned lack of discrimination (aviveka), saying: "This is that."
He states the conclusion: "The knot and its dissolution," etc. (verse 266).
Whether in the engagement or the withdrawal of the body, senses, mind, and intellect, [one remains as a witness].
Indeed, there is not the slightest difference between one who is ignorant and one who is awakened.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He clarifies the very absence of any other cause [for bondage] with the words "In activity... (verse 67).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, it may be asked: "How is it possible that the suffix *mātra* excludes other attributes (*dharmāntara*), given that there is a difference in attributes between engagement and withdrawal as they occur in the world and so forth? To this, he says: "Or, in the case of engagement... (267).

The distinction between a Vratya and a Śrotriya is based on whether they recite the Vedas or not; there is no difference between them regarding food and other such matters. This same principle should be applied here.
Rāma’s Commentary: He provides an illustration for the stated point with the verse beginning "vātyā" (68).
a0 Commentary: Therein, he clarifies the illustration with the verse beginning "vātyā" (68).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He cites a statement from the Gītā as proof for the fact that the man of knowledge is free from the "knot" (of ignorance):
"He does not loathe actions undertaken, nor does he long for those desisting."
"He who sits like one indifferent" is said to be the "breaker of the knot. || 69 ||

"He does not hate" means that he does not feel aversion toward arisen sufferings that have been encountered, nor does he long for ceased pleasures; the meaning is that he conducts himself like one who is indifferent. "The breaking of the knot" (granthibhidā) refers to the severing of the knot (granthibheda). || 69 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, what is the proof for this? To this he says: "He does not hate," etc., by means of this very statement of the Blessed One as explained above. || 269 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 200.

[From the *Citradīpa*, Rāma’s Commentary: He raises an objection, suggesting that this statement is intended to enjoin indifference (*audāsīnya*) and is not an authority for the severing of the knot (*granthibheda*):
"If indifference is what is to be enjoined, then the word 'desiring' (*rat*) would be redundant."
If it is argued that his body and so forth are incapable [of acting], that is simply a disease. || 270 ||

Regarding the term "indifference" (*audāsīnya*): he offers a rebuttal, stating "the word 'vac' [is redundant]," on the grounds that if the passage were intent upon an injunction (*vidhi*), the word "vac" would be superfluous.

Anticipating the objection that the knower's body and so forth lack the capacity for action and thus do not engage in activity—not because of the severing of the knot (*granthibheda*)—he mocks this by saying, "they are not capable. ||270||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Even so, a state of perpetual indifference must indeed be maintained even after the realization of the non-dual Self. Anticipating this doubt, he provides the following resolution: "Indifference... Having raised the objection that for those who know the non-dual Brahman, there should arise a state of rigidity regarding the body and so forth—just as there is an absence of activity in the body toward embracing a woman with variegated and restless eyes due to the realization of the falsity of all objects perceived—he replies with a touch of irony: The meaning is as follows: Just as a person who knows a rope to be a snake does not act toward it out of fear, so too, because of the realization of the falsity of everything perceived, there is an absence of activity in the body and so forth toward things such as embracing a woman with variegated and restless eyes. Thus, for those who know the non-dual Brahman, let there be a state of rigidity regarding the body and so forth. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Indifference... etc. This is the sense. The word *audāsīnyam* (indifference) means the absence of activity. The phrase *sarvadṛśye'pi* (even toward everything perceived) means even toward the entire aggregate of objects of perception. The term *mithyātvabodhāt* (from the realization of falsity) refers to the knowledge that the world is illusory. The expression *citracañcalavilocanāliṅganādau* (toward embracing a woman with variegated and restless eyes and so forth) indicates the various objects of desire. The phrase *dehādeḥ pravṛttyabhāva iva* (like the absence of activity in the body and so forth) serves as an illustration. The word *advaitabrahmavidām* (of those who know the non-dual Brahman) refers to those who have realized the non-dual Absolute. The term *dehādistabdhibhāva eva* (a state of rigidity regarding the body and so forth) means a state of being like a log of wood. The word *bhūyāt* (let there be) expresses a wish. The particle *iti* marks the end of the objection. The word *sopahāsam* (with a touch of irony) indicates that the following statement is made with derision. The word *samādhatte* (he resolves) means he provides the answer. The word *āha* (he says) introduces the verse. The particle *hi* (indeed) is used for emphasis. The word *na* (not) is a particle of negation. The word *ca* (and) is a conjunction. The word *kiṃcit* (anything) means something. The word *kurvanti* (they do) means they perform. The word *kecit* (some) refers to certain people. The word *jñāninaḥ* (the wise ones) refers to those possessed of knowledge. The word *svayam* (themselves) means by their own accord. He explains this with the half-verse beginning "They are not capable" (*na śaktāḥ*). Regarding this demonstration—that there is an absence of engagement in embracing the variegated moon-faced one—there is a certain distinction to be made. The absence of engagement occurs simply because there is no gross form beyond the form depicted in the painting, and not because of a realization of its falsity. Otherwise, there would likewise be no engagement in gazing at her again with passion; for that [passion] belongs to the same class as that [engagement].
The secret is that because it serves as a reminder of the beloved who has been experienced, [the cognition] indeed exists there, even though it is false in nature. || 270 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Let it be; what is the fault therein? To this he says:
"Those of great intelligence consider the realization of truth to be a disease that leads to destruction."
Their wisdom is exceedingly clear; tell me, what is difficult for them to accomplish? (71)
"Tattvabodham" means that which is difficult to accomplish and impossible to achieve. || 71 ||
Commentary on verse 71: Regarding the word "tattva" (reality), the term "kṣaya" (decay) is an adjective qualifying the disease.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "This is an ill-placed jest, for it is established in the Purāṇas that those possessed of knowledge do not engage in worldly activity. To this he replies:
"If you say that the non-engagement of Bharata and others is so stated in the Purāṇas..."
While eating, playing, and experiencing pleasure, did you never hear this sacred tradition? 72.

Regarding the phrase "of Bharata and others": not knowing the Vedic scripture (*śruti*), you object; he refutes this with the words "eating" (*jakṣan*). The meaning is that you have not heard the Vedic statement: "Eating, playing, rejoicing—whether with women, or vehicles, or kinsmen, or friends—not remembering this body, which is subject to rebirth. The verbal root *jakṣ* (from which *jakṣan* is derived) signifies both eating and laughing. "Playing" (*krīḍan*) means wandering about according to one's own will and taking delight with women.

"Not remembering this body as a new acquisition" (nopajanaṃ smaran) means not recollecting or connecting with this own body which exists in the vicinity of people; "not remembering this body as a new acquisition" is the meaning. In the verse, "finding delight" (ratim vidan) is the explanation of the Vedic word "rejoicing" (ramamāṇa). || 72 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, if you object—"Since the absence of worldly activity among those who know reality, such as Jaḍabharata and others, is well-known in the Purāṇas and other texts, how can the aforementioned ridicule be appropriate?"—we reply: that is not so, because you yourself have failed to understand their true intent. With this hidden intention, he offers a counter-argument by saying "of Bharata and others. The word "others" (ādi) includes Ṛṣabha-deva and the rest. Regarding the word "jakṣat" (eating/joying), it is stated thus in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad [8.12.3]: [The text continues with the citation from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. ...so too in the Chāndogya [Upaniṣad]. (Note: The provided source text ends mid-citation; the translation reflects the available portion.)

In the Mādhyandina recension, within the Prajāpati-vidyā, it is recorded: "Eating, playing, and delighting with women, or with vehicles, or with kinsmen, he does not remember this body, thinking, 'This is the place of procreation. The meaning of this has been stated by the author of the root-text himself in the *Anubhūtiprakāśa*:
"Consuming various kinds of food and the like in the bodies of Indra, kings, and others..."
Sometimes he laughs with children and sometimes he sports with women.
Indeed, accompanied by vehicles and kinsmen, he rejoices somewhere.
[Sixth Chapter]
Accompanied by two commentaries:
"He shall never again remember this body having come into the presence of people."
Formerly, suffering arose through the delusion of identity with this body;
now that the delusion has vanished through discernment, that suffering is no longer perceived today.
Even in former times, there was no identity with the bodies of Indra, kings, and others;
therefore, not even the slightest suspicion of suffering from such bodies exists for him.
The witness observes all the pleasures residing in that body;
yet, through the conceit of identifying with the witness-self, the knower (the individual soul) falsely appropriates them as its own.
Even though the witness perceives sufferings,
the knower of reality does not take up pride regarding them, because those sufferings are illusory in nature.
The pleasures arising from sense objects are but mere fragments of the bliss of Brahman;
therefore, it is only in those who know reality that a partiality for these [objects] is found.
"He attains only merit, not sin; he does not encounter the gods"—thus another Vedic text declares the happiness of one who perceives the Self in all.
Whatever the subjects grieve for, that should belong to them alone;
"there is no one who regards all as his own self"—this too the Śruti has declared.
Even though I am the self of all, I am indeed not tainted by the defects of the body and so forth;
for just as the nature of the sun remains untainted even when it touches outcasts and the like.
All living beings, from Brahmā down to the immovable plants, are known to be my city;
how then could defects such as desire, anger, and the like arise in me from any other source?
Thus spoke the teachers, skilled in the awakening to Brahman, in ancient times;
for there are numerous examples here that grasp only at pleasure.
The honeybee takes the nectar from the flower and nothing else;
the ascetic accepts alms, but not the impurity found in anyone's house.
If it is argued that even a fool possesses partiality toward happiness,
then let him too understand the truth for the sake of his own well-being.
"When reality is realized, he no longer remembers identity with his own body;
consequently, when suffering has perished, he perceives only eternal bliss. (201)

Nor should it be said that, even by this much, the accomplishment of the means for activity is not established for one who knows reality; for the very activity consisting in the conceit of all pleasure is indeed established. Therefore, equality with the indifferent is entirely appropriate. || 272 ||
For Bharata and others never remained anywhere after completely renouncing food and other necessities.
But those who fear attachment remain indifferent, like wood or stone. || 73 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "In that case, what is the status of the Purāṇas? Anticipating this doubt, and intending to show that even the Purāṇas are primarily concerned with teaching equanimity rather than advocating for the absence of worldly activity, he says: "For [the Purāṇas] do not [teach] the avoidance of food and so forth... (73).
The commentary (ṭīkā) on that very point says: "Indeed not," [verse 73].
In this world, one who is attached is indeed afflicted, while one who is free from attachment enjoys happiness— thus it is stated in the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya.
Therefore, association with such people must always be abandoned by one who desires happiness—this is the lamp of consciousness. (74)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question, "From where does even attachment arise? he says: "For one who has attachment... (74).

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on verse a0: He states the reason for this: "For attachment indeed... The meaning is that one is "afflicted," which is to say, tormented. "Bliss" refers to the bliss of liberation-in-life (*jīvanmukti*) produced by the contemplation of universal identity (*sārvātmya*). || 74 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If it is only mental attachment that must be abandoned, then how is it that people describe those who act externally while being devoid of internal attachment as being ignorant and so forth?
Anticipating this doubt, he says that it is because they lack knowledge of the essential purport of the scriptures:
"Not knowing the heart of the scripture, the fool speaks in various ways."
Let the decision regarding fools be set aside; our established doctrine is now being stated. || 275 ||
"Having understood this... Therefore, he says "of the fools," meaning that the conduct of the deluded need not be investigated here.
Then, in response to the expectation of what should be pursued instead, he says "our established doctrine," meaning the heart of the scripture. || 75 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "In this context, the word *saṅga* (attachment) refers only to the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the body and so forth, and that is purely mental.

Therefore, if internal attachment is abandoned, what harm is there even if one moves about externally as one pleases? Accordingly, it is said in the *Vāsiṣṭhasāra*: 'O Rāghava, abandon internally but move about externally with attachments in the world. If you say this, we reply: No, because such arbitrary conduct (*yatheṣṭācaraṇa*) has already been refuted in the very section on the discrimination of duality (*dvaitaviveka*).

Regarding the statement "in the spoken words," he says "without knowing" (ajñātvā) [verse 275], with the intention that by the term *bahiḥ-saṅga* (external attachment), it is established— through the principle of the impossibility of otherwise— that the instruction for Rāghava’s wandering there was solely for the sake of gathering the external world and for the performance of the conduct appropriate to his own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*).
Dispassion, awakening, and cessation are their mutual companions.
They generally exist together, though they are occasionally separated.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question "Who is this?", he says: "By means of dispassion," etc. (76).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, in response to the inquiry, "What is your established doctrine? he states it: "Vairāgya... etc. This refers to a certain place and time, and to a particular knower of reality. As it is stated in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: this was Yājñavalkya’s reply to those [sages] at the time they were provoked by the Munis upon the taking of a thousand cows in Janaka’s assembly, where [Yājñavalkya] said, "We are indeed seekers of cows. || 76 ||
The causes, essential natures, and effects of these [categories] are distinct; there is no confusion among them.
The meaning of the treatise should be understood correctly by one who investigates it thoroughly. || 77 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Since detachment and the other qualities are observed to exist through mutual exclusion, there may be a doubt regarding their non-difference; therefore, he states that their difference must be understood from the difference in their causes and natures: "hetusvarūpa... (Verse 77).

Regarding the commentary on the phrase *taddhetvādi*: what follows from that? He says—*hetu* etc. Since these [qualities], such as detachment (*vairāgya*) and the rest, have distinct causes, there is no confusion among them; this is the logical connection (*anvaya*). That, however, is the meaning of the scripture. *Vra-*...

The secret of the non-dual (advaita) scriptures: by one who "praticinvatā"—meaning by such a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) who thoroughly investigates (*pravicinvatā*), that is, who sifts, purifies, or gathers [the truth] with excellence, characterized by the favor of signs such as the opening statements (*upakrama*) and so forth, and by the superiority consisting in the tradition of the experience of those who know Brahman. The reading *prativivicyatā* is a corruption. Likewise, although *praticinvatā* is grammatically correct, it must be disregarded because it lacks the reinforcement of the intended meaning; it should be understood exactly as stated.
The connection is with the word "vya" (it is so). || 77 ||
The desire to abandon the vision of faults, and again, lack of dejection regarding enjoyments.
These three—the uncommon cause and so forth—are also [the causes] of dispassion. (78)
The Sixth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
203 Rāghavānanda’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): He shows the triad of causes and so forth for that dispassion (*vairāgya*) in the verse beginning with "doṣadṛṣṭiḥ" || 78 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He states those very [qualities] for each of them respectively in order with the three verses beginning with "dopa" (78).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now he shows the causes and so forth for the awakening to reality:
"Likewise, the triad beginning with hearing, as well as the discrimination between reality and falsehood."
Furthermore, these three are considered to be the non-arising of awakening. || 79 ||

Regarding the phrase "from hearing and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are included. This is because hearing and the others are enjoined as means for the vision of the Self in such passages as, "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. Thus, hearing and the rest are causes of knowledge.

[This results in] the discrimination between reality and falsehood, the knowledge of the difference between the immutable [Self] and the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth, the non-arising of the [false] text [of superimposition], and the non-production of mutual superimposition (*anyonyādhyāsa*). (79)

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Regarding the phrase "from hearing and so forth" (śravaṇādīti), it refers to the non-arising—that is, the non-manifestation—of the superimposition of consciousness (cit) upon the unconscious (acid) within the text. ||79||
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: He shows those [means] for cessation:
"The restraints and so forth, the cessation of the intellect, and the complete destruction of worldly activity."
The causes and so forth of cessation are thus stated to be without confusion. || 280 ||

Regarding the phrase "Yama and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (ādi), Niyama and the others are included; and "the restraint of the intellect" (dhīnirodha) is Yoga, characterized by the restraint of the fluctuations of the mind (cittavṛttinirodha). || 280 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding the phrase "Yama, etc."—the term *saṃkṣaya* means complete destruction, which is a state of forgetfulness like deep sleep; for it will be stated later that "this is indeed the limit of cessation," meaning absolute annihilation (*ātyantikadhvaṃsa*). Nor is there, in this way, any worldly activity whatsoever arising from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) for one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) who is established in the non-discursive concentration (*asaṃprajñātasamādhi*), also known as "nirvikalpa"—just as in the case of Devahūtī, who, though her body was nourished by another, remained free from the nourishment of another.

It should not be argued that because the practices of Payogila and others, as well as the movements and worldly activities of the divine Ṛṣabha, are described in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*, it is therefore improper to describe the total absence of such activity [in this context]. For, with reference to the sage Uddālaka—who is renowned in the *Śrīmad Bṛhad-yogavāsiṣṭha* as being seated in *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*—no worldly activity whatsoever is mentioned even from the perspective of the world until the exhaustion of his *aprārabdha* karma; it is precisely with that intention that [the present text] speaks here.

Since total destruction (*saṃkṣaya*) has already been mentioned, and because Devahūti’s [destruction] is slightly less than that, while R̥ṣabha’s is also slightly less than hers, it must necessarily be stated that his state is merely secondary (*gauṇa*). We shall explain this in detail in the sixteenth chapter of this work, which consists of a commentary on the *Jīvanmuktiviveka* section; this is the summary. || 280 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question of whether these [factors] possess equal importance or not, he says:
"The realization of reality (tattvabodha) would be the primary [factor], because it directly bestows liberation."
Both dispassion and cessation are these two aids to awakening. || 81 ||

Regarding the phrase "realization of truth" (*tattvabodha*): the meaning is that this is based on the Vedic scripture which states, "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey. As for the other two [stages], they serve as aids, according to the scripture: "A Brahmin should attain detachment; nothing unaccomplished is gained by what is done. For the sake of realizing That, he should approach a Guru alone—being calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and composed—and seeing the Self within the self."
This is understood from these two [verses]. || 81 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might ask: "Even so, which among these is the primary one? To this he says: "Tattva... (The Reality). If it is then argued that [qualities] such as detachment (*vairāgya*) are therefore useless, he says: "Bodha... (Awakening). || 81 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: It was stated that [the qualities] generally exist together but are occasionally separated; regarding that, he states the reason:
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya:
if even these three [chapters] are fully matured, they are the fruit of great austerity.
This [treatise] called the *Citradīpa* is, in some places, obstructed here and there by some obstacle at some time. || 82 ||

"Even all three" means that when the accumulation of merit acquired over many lifetimes reaches its full maturity, the coexistence of these three occurs; otherwise, however, according to the obstructing sins, there may be an obstruction for a particular person at a particular time—this is the sense. || 82 ||
