Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask, "How is it that all three of these possess completeness? To this, he says, "All three [are complete] by means of great austerity alone. Now, regarding the doubt as to whether their deficiency arises solely from the absence of the aforementioned austerity or from some other cause as well, he accepts the latter possibility. He says, "By evil (duritena). This occurs in certain instances, such as at the very assembly of Janaka, where there was a partial lack of certain objects like cows that had become specific subjects of focus.

The meaning is that it occurs only at the time when the members [of the assembly] have been mentioned as required; however, it does not occur with respect to all locations and so forth—this is the sense. || 82 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Even in that case, he states that if the realization of reality is obstructed, there is no liberation:
"When dispassion and cessation are complete, yet enlightenment is obstructed..."
For whomever [this occurs], there is no liberation; rather, through the power of austerity, there is only a world of merit.
Regarding the word "vairāgya" (detachment): anticipating the objection that the cultivation of detachment and so forth would then be fruitless, [the author says]:
"Having reached the worlds of the meritorious and having dwelt there for countless years..."
One who has fallen from yoga is born into the house of the pure and the prosperous.
Based on these words of the Blessed One, he states that the attainment of the world of merit occurs: "The world of merit [is attained] by the power of austerity. (83)
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding that, [the author] asks, "What occurs when what is obstructed? and answers with the two verses beginning with "vairāgya" (verse 83).
When enlightenment is complete, the other two are then bound to it.
Liberation is certain, yet the suffering that is currently perceived does not cease.

Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: He states that if detachment (*vairāgya*) and cessation (*uparati*) are obstructed, the bliss of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) is not accomplished—“When awakening is complete,” etc. (84).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): "Full" (pūrṇa) means that which has become the fruit of prārabdha-karma; "seen" (dṛṣṭa) means suffering. || 84 ||
The disregard for even the world of Brahmā is considered the ultimate limit of dispassion.
The realization culminates in the understanding that the Supreme Self is identical to one's own self, just as the body is considered one's self [in common parlance]. || 85 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now he shows the limit of dispassion and the other stages—“In the world of Brahmā,” etc. (85).
Commentary (a0): Therein, he describes the ultimate limit of all three with the verse beginning "Brahman" and continuing for one and a half verses (285).
For forgetfulness, like sleep, indeed constitutes the limit of cessation.
By this method, the internal gradations [of intensity] should be determined. (86)

Rāma’s Commentary: Regarding the phrase "like one who has fallen asleep," he says "diśā" (by direction) to indicate that the internal gradations [of experience] are to be determined by one's own intellect. || 86 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on verse a0: "Like one who has fallen asleep" is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should be understood as including other states such as middling detachment (*madhyama-vairāgya*) and so forth. Thus he says:
"In this manner. || 86 ||
Because of the diversity of the karmas they have undertaken, the Buddhas appear in various different ways.
Therefore, the meaning of the scriptures should not be confused by the wise.
The Sixth Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.

205 Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Since even those possessing the realization of reality (tattvabodha) are observed to possess passion and other afflictions, and thus exhibit inequality, it is impossible to determine that knowledge alone is the cause of liberation.
Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that passion and the like are obstacles to liberation because, like diseases and so forth, they are the fruits of prārabdha-karma (commenced karma).
Therefore, since this [objection] is unestablished, one must not dissent from the meaning of the scripture; thus he says: "Because of the diversity of commenced karma" (sūtra 87).

Commentary (a0): Now, even among those who possess the realization of the primary reality of non-duality (advaita-tattva), some are devoted to the conduct of their caste and stage of life (varṇāśramācāra), while others are like deluded children or intoxicated persons;
some are full of passion and enjoyers, and others are practitioners of yoga—the state of the wise is observed not to be uniform.

Based on the statement from the *Svārājyasiddhi* that there are indeed various kinds of conduct (*śīla*), one might ask: "If knowledge (*jñāna*) also possesses the demonic wealth (*asurasaṃpat*) of passion and so forth, is it a semblance of knowledge or is it real? Even if it is the latter, just as fire is prevented from burning its fuel by a magnet and the like, how can it be determined whether or not liberation—consisting in the destruction of ignorance—is manifested through such passion and the rest? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the following resolution:
"Initiated" (ārabdhā) || 87 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: What, then, should be practiced? To this he says:
"Let them act in whatever way they do, according to their respective duties."
All awakening is undifferentiated; liberation is equal—this is the established conclusion. || 88 ||

"Each for themselves": the meaning is that for all [liberated ones], the knowledge "I am Brahman" is of a single form, and their abiding in the nature of the faultless Brahman is likewise identical. || 88 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, even so, what is the point regarding the subject at hand? To this he says: "One's own... (svasva...), verse 88.
The world-picture is projected upon one's own consciousness, like a painting on a canvas.
Having disregarded that [world] through illusion, let consciousness alone remain as the residue. || 89 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He shows the purport of this treatise in brief: "The world," etc. (89).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, he summarizes the meaning of the treatise by means of the very example already introduced—“the world,” etc.

The meaning is that one should bring about the final resolution (*paryavasāna*) in the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which is pure consciousness alone (*cinmātra*), serving as the limit of sublation (*bādhāvadhi*). For the sublation of silver and the like does not occur anywhere other than in the fragment of mother-of-pearl. This is because the existence and non-existence of superimposed things have their sole reality in the substrate.
"Because reality is fixed; this is the reality. (89)
Those wise ones who constantly contemplate this "Lamp of Consciousness" (Citradīpa).
Even while beholding the variegated world, they do not become deluded as they did before. || 290 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Citradīpa, in the Śrī Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. || 6 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the fruit of studying this work: "The Citradīpa" (The Lamp of Citations), etc. || 290 ||

Thus ends the commentary on the *Citradīpa*, titled *Tātparyabodhinī*, composed by the scholar named Rāmakṛṣṇa, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Bhāratītīrtha Vidyāraṇya. 6.

Commentary (a0): He states the fruit of practicing this treatise: "The Citradīpa. They "contemplate" it, and not merely recite it. By this, it is indicated that the fruit of contemplating the intended meaning of this work is the absence of delusion as previously described, and not mere vocal recitation and the like. Now, an objection: was it not stated by you earlier in the introduction?
"The soul of the Sūtra has an excessive desire to enjoy only those who are self-controlled and blissful;
and the possession of beauty and other such qualities is the very first obstacle here for the individual soul."
206. *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya, [The Sixth Chapter titled *Citradīpa*].

Having thus described the first obstacle, known as "desire for objects" (*viṣayavāsanā*), which concerns the understanding of the meaning of the term *tattvamasi*—specifically the purity denoted by the word *jīva*—[the author now addresses] *citra*-...

By means of the illustration of the cloth and so forth, detachment (*vairāgya*) is indicated by the word "self" (*ātman*); thus, even in the sixth [chapter], the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) is primary. Therefore, this sixth chapter, titled *Citradīpa*, which is primarily concerned with determining the nature of the individual soul preceded by an emphasis on detachment, serves as a refutation of the aforementioned obstacles. If it is asked how that is so, it is explained as follows:
For instance, the introduction states: "Just as the fourfold state is seen in a painted cloth, so too should the fourfold state be understood in the Supreme Self."
"The variegated world is projected upon one's own consciousness, like a painting on a canvas;

having disregarded that [world] through Māyā, let only consciousness remain. This concluding verse, using the analogy of a painted canvas, describes the state of the jīva known as the immutable Self (kūṭasthātman) when there is a sense of distaste for all objects of perception, including pleasure.
And in the case of the pure essential nature (*śuddhasvarūpa*), the first indicative mark (*liṅga*) is clearly the one that conveys the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*):
"From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, all living beings here, even the insentient..."

"It exists in the manner of superior and inferior [states], like a painted cloth"; "He neither hates those things that have arisen nor desires those that have ceased; sitting like one indifferent, he is called a 'piercer of the knot'"; such is the practice.

If it is argued that the non-engagement of Bharata and others [in ritual acts] is stated in the Purāṇas, then did you not hear the Śruti which says, "Eating, playing, and enjoying pleasures"? Thus, there is both the fruit of novelty and an explanatory passage (arthavāda).
"One who is attached is oppressed by the world; one free from attachment enjoys happiness.
Therefore, attachment must always be abandoned by one who desires happiness.

Such is the logical justification. Consequently, by means of the sixfold indicators (liṅgas) mentioned above, this section [establishes] the complete collection of all the means, such as discrimination and dispassion.

Since the primary focus is on the singular nature of the purified *jīva*—known as the immutable (*kūṭastha*) and characterized by witnesshood—the capacity of the aforementioned [scriptural statements] to sublate obstacles is indeed beyond dispute; such is the direction of the argument. || 290 ||

Thus ends [the work] titled *Pūrṇānandendukaumudī*, composed by Acyuta Śarman, known by the surname Moḍaka, a student of the illustrious Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrīmad Dvaitasaccidānandendra Sarasvatī; one whose mind resembles a royal swan dwelling in the lotus-feet of Śrī Nārāyaṇa Śāstri— whose secondary name is Paṣṭhaputra— and who sports in the milk-ocean of the illustrious Padavākyapramāṇa and is a jewel in the lap of the Goddess of Advaita-Vidyā.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Citradīpaprakāśa, of the commentary on the Pañcadaśī. 6.
Now begins the seventh chapter, titled *Tṛptidīpa*, on the fifteenth [day].
Rāma’s Commentary: Salutations to the Guru, who is Śiva, whose nature is indivisible bliss.
Salutations to the one whose form is the fire of wisdom, which is skillful in destroying the darkness of ignorance of disciples. || 1 ||
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas, he dispels the darkness of ignorance.
May Vidyātīrthamaheśvara grant the four aims of human life. || 2 ||
Having bowed to the two lords of sages, Śrī Bhāratītīrtha and Vidyāraṇya;
This commentary on the *Tṛptidīpa* is composed through the grace of my guru.
If a person were to know the Self, realizing "This is I."
Desiring what, or for the sake of what desire, would one cause this body to suffer? || 1 ||

Commencing the treatise titled *Tṛptidīpa*, the venerable teacher Bhāratītīrtha first recites the scriptural passage (*śruti*) that is to be explained, since this work consists of an exposition upon that scripture: "If one [knows] the Self... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2). || 1 ||
Commentary (a0): Non-duality is Brahman—the form of existence, consciousness, omnipresence, stainlessness, supreme bliss, and immutability;
though it is the abode of the illusory spectacle of duality arising from delusion, it is the self-luminous crest-jewel of the Vedas.

I bow to all the eminent teachers, to my true guru, the ornament of the lineage of Atri who is established in Brahman, known by the name Śrī Nārāyaṇa, and also to my own teacher named Mahādeva. || 1 ||
In my exposition of the words of the ancients— that spiritual practice proceeds from exclusive reliance on devotion—
I have thoroughly milked the cow of Vidyāraṇya’s thought, which yields a most rare flavor, as far as my intellect extends.

I compose this commentary, adorned with explanations, upon the *Pañcadaśī* consisting of nine chapters, which is the very speech of my most venerable guru, the world-renowned Śrī Bhāratītīrtha. || 2 ||
Having honored Jīvajīva, Vidyāraṇya, and Bhāratītīrtha.
I shall indeed clarify the *Tṛptidīpa* by means of the light of the Sage [Śaṅkara], just as one clarifies the moonlight.

Then the Blessed One, the eminent sage Bhāratītīrtha— who is ever solely devoted to the inquiry into the non-dual reality of the Self (*advaitātmatattva*), which is either discursive (*vācārika*) or practical (*yaugika*) as will be described hereafter— out of supreme compassion [composed this work] based on the *Citradīpa*, one of the fifteen extremely simple treatises (*prakaraṇa*) on non-duality initiated by his own disciple, the omniscient Mādhavācārya (famous in his previous stage of life as Śrī Vidyāraṇyācārya), for the singular benefit of the best among those seeking liberation.

Having thoroughly examined the complete *Tattvaprakaraṇī*, he was satisfied; then, reflecting upon the meaning of the final quarter-verse of its concluding stanza, he spontaneously commenced the remaining nine chapters as if in play. Among these, beginning with the seventh chapter—which is titled *Tṛptidīpa* because it arises solely from the satisfaction mentioned at the outset—he composed it so that it is situated within the single seventh stage of the analytical inquiry (*vicāra*) to be described hereafter. Furthermore, revealing even the subject matter and other details of that [seventh stage], he, who is renowned for his authoritative...
Even while disregarding other auspicious rites, he recites only the mantra from the Kaṇva recension of the Upaniṣad: "If one [knows] the Self... (1).
Rāma’s Commentary: Now he shows the inquiry he intends to undertake and its fruit:
"The intention of this Śruti is here properly investigated."
That contentment which belongs to one liberated while living is made manifest by him. || 2 ||
The Pañcadaśī, composed by Vidyāraṇya; page 208.

"Regarding the name *Tṛptidīpa* (The Lamp of Contentment): here, in this work called *Tṛptidīpa*, the intended meaning—the purport—of this Śruti passage beginning with "If one [sees] the Self," is thoroughly investigated. By means of that investigation of the intended meaning, the contentment of the living-liberated (*jīvanmukta*) well-known from the Śruti becomes clear."
It becomes clear as one strives. || 2 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, in accordance with all the ancient masters such as the authors of the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika*, the intended purport of the present treatise is described according to the aforementioned scripture (*śruti*). This consists in the nature of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)—characterized as the witness of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa-sākṣitva*)—which is common to all the sections of the non-dualistic scriptures (*advaita-śāstra*) intimated by the recited scripture; and [the nature of] that which is denoted by the word *tat*, characterized as pure consciousness, which is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the entire phenomenal world (*dṛśya*) as indicated by the word *tvaṃ*.

He declares his promise by means of the first and second halves of the verse respectively, stating the unique subject matter and purpose for the sake of engaging wise seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*), which consist of the destruction of root ignorance— characterized as beginningless, positive in nature, and consisting of the object [of knowledge] whose form is the unity of the meaning of the word "That" (tat) and the word "Thou" (tvam), which has that same unity as its locus, and which is to be dispelled solely by the aforementioned valid cognition (*pramā*) regarding the object— and which is called liberation. By this description of the intention of the cited scripture, it becomes clear and manifests of its own accord.
This is the meaning. || 2 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: "The division of words, the statement of their meanings, the analysis of compounds, the syntactical connection, and the resolution of objections—this is the fivefold characteristic of a commentary."

Since the characteristics of the method of exposition have thus been stated, he briefly demonstrates creation as a subordinate means for explaining the meaning of the word "Puruṣa," on the basis of the scriptural statement: "By the appearance of Māyā, He makes [the two], the Jīva and the Īśvara."
The individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) are indeed merely imagined; everything is imagined by them.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the appearance of *māyā*": an *upoddhāta* (introduction) is the description of another matter for the sake of the subject matter to be established, having first grasped that subject matter in the intellect. Here, by the word *māyā*, *prakṛti*—which consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, is endowed with the reflection of Brahman who is composed of consciousness and bliss (*cidānandamaya*), and serves as the material cause of the universe—is denoted.
And that *prakṛti*, being divided into two types according to the purity or impurity of the *sattva* quality, is respectively called *māyā* and *avidyā*.

The very consciousness of Brahman reflected in those two—māyā and avidyā—is called the Lord (Īśvara) and the individual soul (jīva); this has been explained by the venerable Guru Vidyāraṇya in the work titled *Tattvaviveka*:
"Endowed with the reflection of the Brahman consisting of consciousness and bliss..."
The qualities of tamas, rajas, and sattva constitute Nature (prakṛti), which is twofold;
through the purity and impurity of sattva, these two are considered to be Māyā and Vidya.
Having brought that illusory power under control, the Lord would become omniscient.
But another, under the sway of ignorance, is manifold due to its various diversities.
"That would be the causal body (kāraṇa-śarīra), and the Prājña is the one who possesses self-conceit therein."

Keeping this very point in mind, the Śruti also proceeds with the statement: "Māyā and Avidyā themselves become [the cause] through the reflection (ābhāsa) of the Jīva and the Īśvara. Therefore, the Jīva and the Īśvara are both imagined by Māyā; the entire rest of the world is imagined by those two alone. || 3 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Having thus declared the subject matter and purpose of this [work], and because the declaration of the inquiry cannot be established without its explanation due to the urgency of the zeal to demonstrate it—
“Word-separation, statement of word-meanings, grammatical analysis, connection of the sentence,
and the resolution of objections— this is the fivefold characteristic of exposition.”
The Seventh Chapter [pages 209–209]
[This work] is accompanied by two commentaries.

(209) Since the definition stated in the *Pārāśara Purāṇa* consists of the exposition of the meanings of words (*padārtha*) and so forth, [this section serves as] an introduction (*upodghāta*) for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the word "Person" (*puruṣa*) contained therein.

This is precisely what is stated in the two verses from the *Cidvibhāga-prakaraṇa* (the "Lamp of Consciousness"): that in order to teach the process of emanation in brief according to ultimate reality (*tattva*), [the Lord] creates the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) through the appearance of *māyā*, and that everything is thus projected by those two.
"It is heard in the Śruti that [the Lord] creates the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) by means of the appearance of Māyā."
"Īśvara and the individual soul (jīva) are the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) and the one consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya);

these two are imagined through Māyā, and by them everything is imagined. Having thus grasped the portions of these two [from the Upaniṣads], [the author] intends his own specific point: that Īśvara and the jīva are indeed merely imagined, because they are so stated in scripture.

Having thus completed the first verse, he wrote the second verse from that same work—beginning with "īkṣaṇādi" and so forth—as well as the word "māyā," for the purpose of explaining the division [of the topics], such as: "How much is the creation? By whom was it conceived? || 3 ||
The creation, beginning with the act of seeing and ending with the entry [into the body], was fashioned by the Lord;
the cycle of worldly existence, beginning with the waking state and ending with liberation, is fashioned by the individual soul (jīva). || 4 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Regarding that, [the author] states by what and how much was projected: "Beginning with the act of seeing" (*īkṣaṇādi*). That which has "seeing"—as heard in the scripture, "It thought:

'May I be many, may I procreate'"—as its beginning is "beginning with seeing. That which has "entry"—as heard in the scripture, "Having entered with this living self (*jīva* as the *ātman*)"—as its end is "ending with entry. It is a subsequent *karmadhāraya* compound: that which both begins with seeing and ends with entry.

[The word] *rayaḥ* [means "king" or "swift"]. This creation (*sṛṣṭi*) was fashioned by the Lord (*īśvara*). That cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) which begins with the waking state (*jāgradādi*) is "that which begins with the waking state. Liberation (*vimokṣa*) is the end (*anta*) of that which;

thus, "that which ends in liberation" is the cycle of worldly existence imagined by the individual soul (*jīva*). The meaning is that this is because the soul possesses the conceit (*abhimāna*) of being that [cycle]. And those states beginning with the waking state are heard [in scripture] as follows:
This very one, his self deluded by māyā, having assumed a body, performs all actions.
That very same person, while awake, attains complete satisfaction through various enjoyments such as women, food, drink, and so forth.
Even in a dream, the individual soul is the experiencer of pleasure and pain within the world of the universe imagined by its own māyā.
At the time of deep sleep, when everything has dissolved, one overcome by darkness attains the nature of bliss.
And again, through the connection with the karma of another birth, that very same living being sleeps and then awakens.
The individual soul (jīva) who sports within the three cities—from him, indeed, has arisen this entire manifold universe.
That by which the manifold world of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth, is illumined.
"Having realized 'I am that Brahman,' one is liberated from all bonds. || 4 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding "īkṣaṇa" (contemplation), the meaning is that it is well-known from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "He contemplated; He created fire... having entered through this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms. Regarding "vimokṣa" (liberation), [it refers to] neither one who desires liberation nor... [text fragment].

The scripture states that "liberated" (mukta) is the ultimate reality; thus, even liberation, which consists in the destruction of ignorance, possesses that same status [of being the ultimate reality] precisely because its counter-correlative (pratiyogin) is merely conceptual. ||4||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus explained the creation that is useful for understanding the meaning of the word *puruṣa*, he now states the meaning of the word *puruṣa*:
"The Self, which is the substratum of the delusion, is of the nature of immutable, unattached consciousness."
Due to mutual superimposition, the individual soul (jīva) residing in the intellect (buddhi), which is otherwise unattached, is here called the person (puruṣa).

Regarding the phrase "the locus of delusion" (*bhramādhiṣṭhāna*): That Supreme Self who exists as the locus of delusion—the immutable, unattached, conscious embodiment, whose nature is changeless and unattached consciousness, and who stands as the substratum for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the body, senses, and so forth—is indeed unattached.
Through mutual superimposition, having superimposed upon each other the nature of the other and the attributes of the other, one becomes the participant in all worldly transactions.
In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[in the chapter titled] *Tṛptidīpa*, it is stated:

"By means of the superimposition of identity (*tādātmyādhyāsa*) as described by the noble teachers, the individual soul (*jīva*), residing in the intellect which is free from attachment, exists within that intellect which is devoid of any ultimate relationship with itself."

In this scripture, that which exists as the *jīva* is not what is called "the person" (*puruṣa*). For the word "person" is etymologically derived by the scripture in the passage: "This person indeed lies within all cities (bodies)" (*sa vā ayaṃ puruṣaḥ sarvāsu pūrṣu puriśayaḥ*). Since the state of being a "person" belongs to the [Supreme] Person alone, it is the immutable Consciousness itself—the very Person—which serves as the substratum for the conceptualization of the intellect and so forth, and which, having attained the status of a *jīva* by being reflected in the intellect, is denoted by the term "person. Thus it is said:
This is the intended meaning. || 5 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Having thus introduced the topics of creation (*sṛṣṭi*) and transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), which are fashioned by the Lord (*Īśvara*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), he now explains the meaning of the word "Person" (*puruṣa*). [The verse begins with] "Delusion" (*bhrama*). Thus, it is clear here that the intended method is precisely the doctrine of the reflection of the Lord as the manifestor (*īśvarībhūtābhāsavāda-prakriyā*), which is stated in the *Cidvilāsa* and approved by the venerable feet of the author of the *Bhagavad-vārttika*. As for the literal meaning of the words, of the delusion—
As stated in the *Citradīpa*: "The intellect (buddhi) is superimposed upon the immutable [Self]; therein, the reflection of consciousness is the individual soul (jīva).
Through the maintenance of the vital breaths (prāṇas), it becomes joined with transmigratory existence.

Thus, by means of ignorance (avidyā), the superimposition of the intellect—accompanied by its own luminosity—is established upon that which serves as its substratum (adhiṣṭhāna). This is well-established.

This is because the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* states that the term "substratum" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) refers to an object characterized by the delusion of manifestation (*savilāsamoha*). The meaning is that the Self (*ātman*), which is the object of ignorance (*avidyā*) together with its effects, is such a thing, namely the "inner self" (*pratyak*). Regarding the word "immutable" (*kūṭastha*): it means one whose nature is exclusively consciousness (*cit*), free from modification and non-associated (*asaṅga*). "Even though such [a Self]"—regarding the word "non-associated": it means the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) manifested in a cognition that is not itself connected [to the Self]. "Both these two"—regarding the word "mutually" (*anyonya*): [they are] mutually...

This refers to the mutual superimposition characterized by conjunction and identity, as stated in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya* ("having superimposed the nature of one upon the other, and the attributes of one upon the other," etc.). Here, in the context of the present scripture, [the term] "Puruṣa" is used because of the Vedic text: "He is indeed that Puruṣa; he is the one who lies within all cities (bodies). Furthermore, according to the Vedic text: "The Jīva who sports in the three cities," the Puruṣa is indeed the Pūruṣa. Thus, [it refers to] the five sheaths together with their substrate.
The connection is that there exists the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) which has been severed. || 9 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "In this context, let the word 'puruṣa' refer only to the individual soul (jīva) in the form of a mere reflection of consciousness; what is the use of this underlying substratum (adhiṣṭhāna), the immutable consciousness (kūṭastha-caitanya)? Anticipating this doubt, he states that even this [immutable consciousness] must be accepted in order to establish its role as the participant in liberation and so forth: "The individual soul, together with its substratum, is the qualified agent in liberation and other such states, but not [the jīva] alone."
It is absolute, because no error exists without a substratum, and because it is in some way unestablished.

"Accompanied by the substrate" (sādhiṣṭhānaḥ): The individual soul (jīva), accompanied by the substrate—that is, associated with the immutable consciousness (kūṭastha-caitanya)—is qualified for, or becomes an eligible agent for, the performance of the means to liberation, heaven, and so forth, such as liberation itself. It is not the mere reflection alone that is so; why? To this he says: "Without a substrate" (niradhiṣṭhāna). The sense is that in the world, a superimposed object is never seen to exist devoid of a substrate. || 6 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: since the preceding verse beginning with "from waking up to liberation" [describes] what appears to be a lack of logical connection, why is the term *puruṣa* introduced as entering into the substrate, the immutable Self (*kūṭasthātman*)? To this he says: "With its substrate" (*sādhiṣṭhāna*). The reason for this is given in the words: "Without a substrate" (*niradhiṣṭhāna*).
Thus, the venerable author of the Vārttika has said: "This alone is our misfortune—that the Self is perceived as a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*)."
"Namaḥ" [is the mantra]. || 6 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, by means of two verses, he demonstrates how that very [intellect], when conjoined with its substrate, is the agent of involvement in transmigratory existence, analyzing it as follows:
"Conjoined with the portion that is the substrate, it takes hold of the portion that is delusion."
At that time, the individual soul conceives the notion, "I am a transmigrating being."

Regarding the phrase "the substrate-portion" (*adhiṣṭhānāṃśa*): when the individual soul (*jīva*) takes as its own nature—that is, accepts as its very self—the two bodies (the subtle and the gross), which are joined with the substrate-portion, accompanied by the immutable witness (*kūṭastha*), and endowed with the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), it then conceives the egoistic notion, "I am a transmigrating being. || 7 ||
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
Commentary on 211a:

Now, even if this be so, regarding the phrase "from the waking state up to liberation for this person denoted by the term *jīva*," one must necessarily accept an *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi* compound—just as in the case of the word *citragu* (possessor of brindled cows)—in order to distinguish "liberation" (*vimokṣa*) from transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Consequently, [the sequence]...

In response to the inquiry as to when and how the experience of being drawn forth (*sāritva-anubhava*) and the experience of being liberated (*muktatva-anubhava*) occur, he says the following in two verses beginning with "adhiṣṭhānāṃśa": || 7 ||
Through the sublation of the illusory element, there arises the predominance of the substrate.
Whenever that occurs, one realizes: "I am the conscious self, free from attachment. || 8 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Furthermore, when—due to the disregard for the illusory portion consisting of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) together with the two bodies, arising from the knowledge of its falsity—the state of being dominated by the substrate occurs, such that the individual soul (jīva) accepts the true nature of the immutable substrate itself as its own essence, then it realizes and knows: "I am the conscious Self, and I am unattached. || 8 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā) on "of the delusive portion": When, through the excellence of practice in hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, and through the grace of the lotus feet of the venerable Guru, there arises—by means of the dawning of the final light known as the direct realization of Brahman, preceded by the falsity of duality regarding the subject matter of the identity of the individual self and Brahman produced by the great Mahāvākyas such as "That Thou Art"—then [this occurs]; such is the connection. || 8 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "If it is accepted that the consciousness which is the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna-caitanya) is the very nature of the individual soul (jīva), then the statement that 'the conscious Self realizes, "I am unattached"' would be untenable; for that which is of the nature of unattached, immutable consciousness cannot be the object of the notion of 'I' (ahaṃpratyaya). Thus he objects.
If you ask how egoity is not appropriate in that which is without attachment, listen to this.
The meaning of "I" (aham) is threefold: one is primary, and two are secondary.

"Not non-attached" (nāsaṅga): the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) is not possible with respect to the non-attached object that is the conscious self (cidātman), because how could it know "I am" from anything else? The meaning is: not in any way at all. Although, in its primary sense (mukhyayā vṛttyā), the conscious self lacks the status of being the object of the notion of "I," the author, wishing to show that this [status] exists through secondary indication (lakṣaṇayā), first analyzes the meaning of the word "I"—"Listen," etc. "Of 'I'" (ahamaḥ) means of the word "I" (ahaṃśabdasya). || 9 ||

Commentary on Sūtra 1: Regarding this, he raises an objection with "No" (na). The word "ahaṃkṛtiḥ" (the act of "I-making") from the phrase "How [can there be] 'I'? (asmītyahaṃkṛtiḥ) is to be supplied here as well. [The objection is: Since the word "I" (ahaṃpada) functions through the power of manifestation (vṛtti) in that which is unattached (asaṅga), there can be no mental modification (cittavṛtti) having as its object the Consciousness qualified by the body and so forth produced thereby.

To provide a solution— showing that this [state] is indeed possible by means of a final, valid cognitive modification (vṛtti) in the form of pure consciousness alone, which arises by abandoning the qualified aspect through the function of indication (lakṣaṇā-vṛtti) based on the Taittirīya Śruti, "I am Brahman," and the Kāṇva Śruti, "I am Brahman"— the author addresses the disciple, saying: "Listen."
In space and so forth, there is one kind of reality;

in the pure internal subject alone, there is another kind of reality; and through their conjunction, there is yet another reality therein—this is how the word "real" (satya) is understood in that context.

Thus, while illuminating the very mode of indication known as *ajahadajahatsvārthā* (non-abandoning-and-non-abandoning of its own meaning) at the feet of the lordly sage Sarvajñātman, he divides the meaning of a word itself into three types, beginning with "one": The primary [meaning] is the denotable (*śakya*); the two non-primary [meanings] are the indicated (*lakṣya*). (9)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In response to the inquiry as to what the primary meaning is, he shows it:
"The body [of the Self] consists of the superimposition of one upon the other between the immutable and the reflection."
Having become one, it becomes the primary [principle]; therein it is employed by the deluded.

Regarding the phrase "mutually": the essential natures of the immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-cit*) and the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) attain identity through mutual superimposition (*anyonyādhyāsa*), and this becomes the primary meaning denoted by the word "I" (*ahaṃ*).
To the question, "Why is this its primary meaning? he says: "In that regard, by the deluded... [and so on]. Since... [page 212]...
[the text continues].
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[the section titled] *Tṛptidīpa*.

[The word] *dhyāhāraḥ* [is supplied]. The meaning is that since the word "I" (*ahaṃ-śabda*) is employed by everyone—even those devoid of the knowledge of discrimination—regarding that very nature consisting of the undifferentiated, immutable reflection of consciousness (*kūṭastha-cidābhāsa*), it follows that this [usage] is primary (*mukhyatva*). || 10 ||

In that regard, in response to the inquiry as to which [of the two] is primary, he says: "mutually" (*anyonya*). This means: by way of mutual superimposition (*adhyāsa*), as previously established. "The immutable" (*kūṭastha*) refers to the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) within the intellect (*buddhi*), characterized by witness-consciousness (*sākṣitva*) and devoid of modification. "Body" (*vapuḥ*) means its essential nature (*svarūpa*). "Becoming one," that is, having become as if one, "the primary *ahamartha* (the referent of 'I') comes into being"—this is the syntactic connection. Now, an objection:
To the question "Where has this been seen?", he provides the illustration with the word "tatra" (there). It refers precisely to such a primary meaning (*śakyārtha*). All who are deluded are ignorant;
they employ the word "I," as in "I am a Brāhmaṇa"—this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. || 10 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now he shows the two secondary [kinds of liberation]:
"In that regard, the knower of reality knows the two secondary [liberations] as the separately-manifesting and the immutable."
I employ the word "I" interchangeably in both worldly and Vedic usage.
"Separately": when the reflection (*ābhāsa*) and the immutable (*kūṭastha*) are each intended as the meaning of the word "I," then they become non-primary meanings.
He states the reason for their being non-primary: "In that regard, the knower of reality... Here too, the word *yataḥ* ("since") is to be supplied.

Since the knower of reality [uses] the word "I" there—in common worldly usage and in Vedic usage—with respect to those two, the immutable and the reflection of consciousness—[they are thus secondary].

The construction is: "he employs [the term] in its secondary sense. This is the intended meaning: because the undifferentiated form of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) and the immutable witness (*kūṭastha*) is the object of universal worldly usage, it possesses primary significance; however, because the differentiated form is used for discourse only occasionally by a few people, it possesses secondary significance. || 11 ||

Commentary on Verse 1: Now he states the two non-primary [meanings] with the words "separately" (*pṛthak*). If they are intended as distinct objects of the word "I," then they are both non-primary and merely indicated (lakṣya) meanings of the word "we" (*asmad*); this is the meaning. He clarifies the examples for those two as before with the word "therein" (*tatra*). That reality—

The knower is established in Brahman. In that regard, "alternately" means successively for those two, the reflection and the immutable. The meaning is that there is worldly usage such as, "I am going today toward the Gaṅgā to bathe. Likewise, in Vedic usage, this refers to the time of *saṃprajñāta-samādhi*—such as when one thinks "I am Brahman"—and to the time of investigating reality at will; the construction is that the word "I" (*ahaṃ*) is employed in these instances. || 11 ||
Rāghava’s Commentary (rā0 ṭī0): He elaborates upon the very point already stated—that [the Lord] employs [these names] by way of succession—for the sake of ease of understanding, in two verses:
"In worldly transaction, such as 'I am going,' etc., the wise man..."
Having distinguished the reflection of consciousness from the immutable [Self], he intends to speak of that [reflection]. || 12 ||

Regarding the term "worldly": in worldly transactions such as "I, the wise one, am going," the learned person, having distinguished the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) from the immutable (kūṭastha), intends—that is, desires—to express that very reflection by means of the word "I. || 12 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) on verse a0 explains the two aforementioned types of worldly usage by itself through the sequence beginning with "laukika" and so forth, in two verses:
"I am unattached; I am the conscious Self"—this is from the perspective of scriptural vision.
The wise man employs the word "I" with reference to the immutable and absolute Self alone.

Regarding the term "unattached" (*asaṅga*): this very wise person, from the perspective of the scriptures, through the knowledge born of hearing the Vedānta, applies the word "I" by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to the immutable Self—which is distinct from the mere reflection of consciousness—thinking, "I am unattached," or "I am the conscious Self. Therefore, the intention is that since the status of being the object of the notion of "I" is possible for the immutable Self as the referent of the word "I" through secondary indication, the knowledge "I am unattached" is logically established. || 13 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): "I am unattached"—this is to be connected with the word "this wise one" (*budha*). This refers to the subject under discussion; "wise one" means one who is established in reality (*tattvaniṣṭha*). Thus, the sense is that even though [the Self] is unattached, the use of the expression "I" is entirely appropriate through the functions of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and pervasion (*vṛttivyāpti*). || 13 ||
The Seventh Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.
But knowledge and ignorance belong only to the reflection of the Self, and not to the Self itself.
And so, how can the reflection perceive, "I am immutable"? (14)
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, it was stated that the individual reflection (*pṛthagābhāsa*) and the immutable witness (*kūṭastha*) are not the primary meanings of the word "I" (*ahaṃ*).

Between these two, does the immutable witness know "I am unattached" for the sake of removing ignorance, or is it the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*)? It cannot be the immutable witness, because, being of the nature of unattached consciousness, the states of being a knower or an ignorant person are impossible for it; therefore, the state of being a knower and so forth must be attributed to the reflection of consciousness. And this being the case—

He raises the objection that the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), being distinct from the immutable (kūṭastha), cannot know "I am the immutable"—this is expressed in the verse beginning with "jñānitājñānitā" (14).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding this, he raises an objection with the words "jñānitā" (the state of being a knower). The intended meaning is that the reason—namely, that the relationship between the sublated and the sublator is observed everywhere to occur only when knowledge and ignorance share the same locus and object—is indeed implicit. To the question "What follows from that?", he replies with "tathā ca" (and so it is). The implication is that, under such circumstances, the established doctrine previously stated—that [the Self] is unattached (*asaṅga*) and so forth—is indeed untenable. || 14 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He refutes [the objection] by stating that its difference from the immutable (kūṭastha) is indeed unestablished:
"This defect does not apply, for the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) possesses the singular nature of the immutable."
Because appearance is false, there remains only the immutable. || 15 ||

"It is not this. He states the reasoning for that: "Because it is a mere appearance (ābhāsatva). The sense is that just as the reality of the reflection of a face perceived in a mirror is the very face located on one's own neck, so it is here. || 15 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on A0: Therein, he promises to provide a resolution, saying "This is not [the case]," etc. The reason for this is stated by the words beginning with "cidābhāsa" (the reflection of consciousness).

The meaning is that its existence and other attributes depend solely upon the immutable (kūṭastha) Self. To the question "Why is that so?", he replies with the second half of the verse: "Of the reflection," and so forth.
And thus, just as the son of Kuntī was previously capable of understanding "I am the son of Kuntī" based solely on the mother’s word, which provided the basis for his existence and other attributes—
Likewise, even the reflection (the individual soul) ought indeed to realize "I am [Brahman]" through the word of the Śruti; this is the truth. || 15 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) is false, then the knowledge that 'I am the immutable' (kūṭastha), which is based upon it, must also be false.
To this he replies: "If even the realization 'I am the immutable' were false, who would say 'no'?"
For the spreading of a snake upon a rope is not accepted as being real.

Regarding the phrase "I am the immutable" (*kūṭastha*): since it is accepted that everything other than the nature of the immutable is illusory, he dismisses [the objection] by stating that such illusoriness is precisely what we desire, saying, "Who would say 'no'? He clarifies the stated point with an illustration, beginning with "for not... (*na hi*).
The meaning is that just as the movement and other attributes of a snake imagined upon a rope, though perceived, are not accepted as real, so it is in this case as well. || 16 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that even so, the attribute called "the state of being a knower" (jñānitā), which resides in a false appearance, must likewise be unreal.

To this he raises the doubt: "I am the immutable" (*kūṭastho'smi iti*). He refutes it by granting the point: "No" (*na iti*). The sense is this: just as the common expression "the rope-snake has disappeared," though observed, is not real, so too is this case. || 16 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that if knowledge were false, it could not bring about the cessation of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), [the author] states—

with the intention that such cessation is indeed possible because the transmigratory existence to be ceased is likewise of that same nature, just as the cessation of sleep occurs through the vision of a tiger in a dream—
that "transmigratory existence is indeed brought to an end by such an awakening."
"For the offering should be commensurate with the yakṣa," so say the people of the world. || 17 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 214.
"By such a one, [the work] named *Tṛptidīpa*. Therein, he corroborates the worldly proverb, "As is the Yakṣa, so is the Bali," with the verse beginning "yakṣa... (verse 17).

Commentary (a0): Now, if even the realization of reality (*tattvāvabodha*) is false, then how can transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) be brought to an end? If this is asked, [the answer is] that transmigratory existence, which is to be ceased, is likewise of such a nature; for according to the maxim "as is the Yakṣa, so is the Bali," we observe the cessation of a dream-tiger through a means that makes known its falsity by means of an instruction from one's own self, even though that instruction is not authoritative. Thus, by such a realization, transmigratory existence—which consists of the entirety of duality—[is ceased].
He states that it indeed turns back: "Even by such [a person]," etc. (17).
Rāma’s Commentary: He summarizes the point thus established:
"Therefore, having distinguished that reflected person from the immutable Self,"
"The Śruti declared that one ought to realize: 'I am the immutable (kūṭastha). (18)

"Therefore" means: since the immutable (kūṭastha) alone is the innate nature of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), therefore the reflection of consciousness, which is denoted by the word "Person" (puruṣa) when conjoined with the immutable, is able—by means of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā)—to discern that immutable from its own false nature and realize, "I am the immutable. It is with this intention that the Śruti said "I am" (asmi). This is the meaning. || 18 ||

The commentary concludes with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). Since the true nature of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) is indeed the immutable (*kūṭastha*), therefore that immutable one—qualified as the immutable—is the "reflection" (*ābhāsa*). The meaning is that in the relevant scriptural passage, the term "person" (*puruṣa*) denotes the individual soul (*jīva*), which is merely a reflection. Having distinguished that immutable one from the superimposition of identity with oneself caused by beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*), [one realizes: *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.*

The connection of the words is as follows: the Śruti, beginning with "If [one] should [know]," declared—that is, spoke—that one ought to know, that is, to realize, "I am the immutable (kūṭastha). || 18 ||
The Rāma-Ṭīkā states regarding *prāya*: having thus explained the intended meaning of the employment of the two words "puruṣa" and "asmi," [it now explains] the employment of the word "ayam."
An unambiguous and non-erroneous cognition of the body as the self is observed.
In order to determine that it is "just like that," this [word] "this" (ayam) is employed. || 19 ||

Regarding the phrase "without doubt": Just as among worldly people, a cognition such as "I am this" is perceived with respect to the self in the form of the body—a cognition free from doubt and error—so too, with regard to the subject matter here, the inner self (*pratyagātman*), it is stated by the Śruti that "this [self]" is to be understood; the ellipsis being that it is so designated in order to determine that such a knowledge must be accomplished for the attainment of liberation. || 19 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Having thus described the intended meaning through the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) of the verb "I am" (*asmi*) with the category of the person (*puruṣa*) previously mentioned, he indicates the intention behind the use of the scriptural term "this" (*ayam*) by stating "asaṃdigdha" (free from doubt). Doubt, which is synonymous with uncertainty, consists of two immediate cognitions regarding the existence and non-existence of a state within a common substratum and object, such as: "Is this a pot, or is it not? Therefore—

The notion of "this" regarding that [Self] is an error, as in the thought, "This is silver. The intention here is that, just as the cognition "I am fair-complexioned, a Brahmin"—which is not sublated by either [of those two notions]—is constantly experienced with respect to the Self characterized as the body, so too must there be a cognition regarding the object, the eternally immediate Self which is the immutable (kūṭastha). || 19 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To corroborate that such knowledge alone is the means to liberation, he cites the words of the Teacher:
"Knowledge [of the Self] sublates the notion of the body being the Self, just as the notion of the body being the Self is sublated [by the knowledge of the Self]."
He in whom this [realization] exists within his very self is liberated, even if he does not desire it. || 20 ||

Regarding "the body as the Self": just as there is a firm conviction concerning the body as the Self, such as "I am a human being," so too [is there a similar error] regarding the inner Self itself as the body.
This concludes the seventh chapter.
Accompanied by the two commentaries:
He in whom the knowledge "I am Brahman" arises through the sublation of the cognition that the body is the self—such a wise person, even if not desiring [action],...
The meaning is that even one devoid of the desire for liberation is liberated, because ignorance—the cause of saṃsāra—has been sublated by knowledge. || 20 ||

Commentary (a0): In this regard, he cites the words of the venerable author of the Bhāṣya found in the *Upadeśasāhasrī* as authoritative evidence: "deha... [etc.]. The phrase "the sublater of the knowledge of the body as the Self" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); by it, the meaning is that it is the sublater of the entire world of objects (*akhiladṛśya*). By the use of the particle *eva* ("only"), there is an exclusion of any object other than the oneness of Brahman and the Self. || 20 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Another intention for the use of the word "this" (ayam) can be proposed—if it is said that "this" denotes immediacy, then let that be stated.
For self-luminous consciousness is always directly manifest. || 21 ||

"This" (*ayam*): the sense is that just as in expressions such as "this jar," the immediacy (*aparokṣya*) of the object indicated by the word "this" is observed, so too is it in the case of "I am this. He says, "Let that be stated," meaning that this is indeed acceptable to us as well. Why? To this he says, "By itself" (*svayam*). Consciousness (*caitanya*), which manifests independently of any other means of proof, is eternally immediate because there is no intervening obstacle.
The meaning is: because it has been accepted by us. || 21 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Anticipating the objection that this object is perceptible and present because of the rule—"the word *idam* denotes what is near, while *etad* denotes what is closer"—and thus this thing under discussion is directly perceived, [the author] accepts this as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), since the Self is pure consciousness that is self-luminous. He states:

"This... Self-luminosity is defined precisely as the state of not being dependent on another for its cognition. A detailed exposition of this may be found in my works, *Bodhaikyasiddhi* and *Advaitātmaprabodha*.
And it should be seen in the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā; this is the summary. || 21 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If the self is admitted to be eternally immediate because its nature is self-luminous consciousness, then by accepting the description of the intention behind the use of the word 'this' (ayam), the previously stated views—that the self is an object of mediate cognition, that it is an object of immediate cognition, or that it is both the substrate and the object of knowledge and ignorance—would become untenable.
Anticipating this objection, he says that everything will be consistent, just as in the case of the "tenth man."
This knowledge and ignorance are respectively indirect and direct.
Even though its nature is eternally immediate, the duality may still exist, as in the case of the tenth stage.

Regarding the term "indirect" (*parokṣam*): the meaning is that this pair—consisting of the indirect and the direct (*aparokṣa*), and the other pair consisting of knowledge and ignorance—might appear as if it were the tenth [unknown] thing, even though the Self is by nature eternally direct. || 22 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, by the phrase "this [is] immediate" (*ayam ity aparokṣatvam*), the immediacy of the Self is accepted as being indeed threefold, due to its eternal self-luminosity. By the phrase "free from doubt" (*asaṃdigdha*), the immediate cognition regarding that [Self] is also admitted; consequently, by implication, both mediate cognition regarding that same object and beginningless ignorance (*anādyajñāna*) are established. These two types of cognition—mediate and so forth—as well as ignorance, are self-luminous...

If it is argued that [ignorance] is indeed contradictory to the non-dual Self, which by its very nature is eternally immediate (*nityāparokṣa*), we say no; for such a thing is observed in the world. To explain: the two cognitions under dispute—the two cognitions regarding the beginningless ignorance—have as their object and locus the eternally immediate Self alone. This is because, while being superimposed, they possess an object, like the ignorance produced by the forgetting of the two cognitions regarding the tenth man. With this intention, he provides the resolution: "It is indirect" (*parokṣam*). || 22 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He explains the illustration:
"At that time, his knowledge of the number nine was lost due to the confusion regarding the tenth."
Even while looking at those nine, the tenth does not know, "I am the tenth."

Regarding the phrase "the number nine": at that time, the tenth person— whose discriminative knowledge has been stolen away by the number nine residing in the persons to be counted— is [thus described].
Vidyāraṇya’s *Pañcadaśī*,
titled *Tṛptidīpa*:
even while observing those nine items to be counted and seeing them correctly, one perceives oneself— the agent of the counting— through delusion.
The meaning is that he does not know, "I am the tenth. || 23 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He clarifies the aforementioned illustration with five verses beginning with "na vā" (not so). Ten Brāhmaṇas, having set out to visit all the holy places (tīrthas) of Bharata-varṣa for the purpose of circumambulating the earth, crossed a certain river of vast waters at some point in the evening and reached the opposite bank during the night; there, one among them—[the river] being any one of those possible according to the aforementioned place and time— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)

Death himself proceeded to count those who were to be counted. [The word] *nava* means "nine. One whose knowledge—that is, the cognition in the form "I am the tenth"—has been taken away or removed by that number nine, is such as this.

Therefore, for the reason of that delusion (*vibhrama*), even though he was himself the tenth at that time, although he was looking at those nine Brāhmaṇas who had been counted, he did not know, indeed he did not realize at all, "I am the tenth. This is the syntactical connection.

And thus, even though [the Self] is manifest to oneself through direct perception, the intention is that the "ignorance of the sprout" (pallavājñāna) had approached—like darkness when a lamp is removed—due to the latent impression (saṃskāra) of the absence of the memory of being the tenth, which has as its object oneself and is ignited by the counting of nine other persons distinct from oneself. ||23||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus demonstrated knowledge in the tenth verse, he now shows its effect, which is concealment:
"It does not shine; the tenth does not exist"—then one regards oneself as the tenth.
Having understood this, he speaks; the wise know that the obscuration is produced by ignorance (ajñāna). || 24 ||
"He does not appear. At that time, the tenth person, though being the tenth himself, thinks "the tenth does not appear" or "he does not exist," and says so.
The wise know that the cause of this empirical usage is produced by ignorance (ajñāna); it is an effect of ignorance, namely, concealment (āvaraṇa). This is the remainder [of the thought]. || 24 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Having thus illustrated the tenth [person] as an example—showing that even while ignorance is being experienced, it appears as eternally immediate—the two veils (*āvaraṇa*) caused by that [ignorance], which are to be destroyed by the subsequent parokṣa and aparokṣa cognitions, are treated collectively as one and stated: "It does not appear. Even when the count of you nine is performed, the tenth does not appear; he is not manifested.

This is the meaning. The intention is that this obscuration of non-manifestation (*abhānāvaraṇa*) is to be destroyed solely by immediate valid cognition (*aparokṣapramā*). For this very reason, the meaning is "it does not exist" or "it is not found at all. It should be understood that this obscuration of non-existence (*asadāvaraṇa*) is to be sublated solely by mediate valid cognition (*parokṣapramā*). Thus, in the manner described; "then," at the time of counting nine persons other than oneself; "oneself" (*svam*), which is the self (*ātmā*); as the "tenth"—one who counts himself as the tenth according to the previously stated method.

"Though he is such—that is, though he is one engaged in counting up to ten, meaning one occupied with the aforementioned calculation of ten—and though they know him as such, meaning they perceive him through their own constant direct experience, he speaks; that is, he declares. The connection is: 'the wise (paṇḍitāḥ)—this word being understood—know that which is the veil caused by ignorance. But the ancient commentators [explain]: "When it does not appear, then the tenth [person] himself [does not recognize] his own tenth state."

The wise have explained that one says "he does not shine" and "he does not exist," thinking that the tenth [person] exists; they further state that the cause of this conventional usage is known by the learned to be *avidyā* (ignorance), which is its effect and an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*). In this context, they have analyzed whether the word ending in the absolutive suffix (*ktvā*), namely "having thought" (*matvā*), connects only with the phrase "the tenth does not shine, he does not exist," or whether it connects with both: "having thought that his own tenth [person] exists, [one says] 'the tenth does not shine' and 'he does not exist.'"

The word "matvā" (having thought) connects with each of the two [clauses] individually. Alternatively, it connects with both the subject and the predicate—as they appear in the written text—in the relationship of qualifier and qualified, as follows: "having thought that one's own self, though being the tenth, does not shine forth [or] does not exist. It is not the first case, because it would result in the lack of syntactic connection for the three accusative endings in the phrase "svaṃ daśamaṃ santam" (one's own self, being the tenth). Nor is it the second case, because if one thinks [of oneself] as the tenth, there can be no such thought as "it does not shine forth" or "it does not exist" regarding one's own self.

Not even the third [alternative] is possible. For although it might be argued that one says "the tenth does not appear" or "he does not exist"—taking these as referring to the two types of concealment (*āvaraṇa*) regarding one's own self who actually exists as the tenth—since the verb "says" (*vakti*) requires an object, and since the connection must somehow be stated even if it is merely implied (that "the tenth does not appear, he does not exist"), this would result in a violation of the rule that "verbal expectancy is fulfilled only by words. Therefore, [the sentence must be understood] through repetition (*āvṛtti*).

Furthermore, because it would entail the fault of excessive prolixity, whether my [version] of one *yojana* is better or that of the ancients is for those at the forefront of aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*) alone to discern.
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.
"Mmy tenth son has died in the river," he wails, weeping aloud in grief.
The wise know that crying and so forth are distractions caused by ignorance.
— 217 Rāghavendra’s Commentary — He demonstrates the specific distraction that is the effect of ignorance alone: "In the river," etc. || 25 ||
Commentary (a0): Having thus described the obscuration regarding the tenth object, he speaks of distraction (vikṣepa): "In a river," etc. (25).
Then, having heard the words of the trustworthy person that "the tenth is not dead," [he was relieved].
One knows the tenth [state] as being beyond the senses, like the heavenly worlds and so forth. || 26 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the indirect knowledge which removes the aspect of non-existence regarding the tenth [state]: "He is not dead," etc. (26).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, he states the indirect knowledge concerning this [matter] with the words "not dead" (*na mṛta*). Regarding the word "trustworthy" (*āpta*): it means the speech of someone previously acquainted with him, who has arrived there by chance—according to the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit (*kākatālīya*)—due to an excess of compassion born from hearing the sound of the aforementioned weeping at that time; a person whose great reliability has been personally experienced and who is non-deceptive. || 26 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He now demonstrates the immediate knowledge that removes the aspect of non-appearance of that very [Self], saying:
"You yourself are the tenth," thus pointed out after counting.
Having known [the Self] through direct perception, one rejoices indeed and does not weep. || 27 ||

"‘It is you indeed. Having counted himself together with the nine previously enumerated by him, and having realized through direct perception—knowing ‘I am the tenth’ as demonstrated by the words ‘you are indeed the tenth’—he attains joy and abandons his weeping. || 27 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, when he asked, "Where is the tenth?", [the teacher] tells what occurred in response: "It is you yourself. || 27 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus restated the seven states as demonstrated in the tenth chapter by means of an illustration, he says that they should likewise be applied to the subject, the Self:
"Ignorance, veiling, projection, the two kinds of knowledge, and contentment."
The departure of sorrow—these [qualities] are to be applied to the conscious self (cidātman). || 28 ||

Regarding the term "ajñāna": it is a dvandva compound consisting of ignorance (ajñāna), obscuration (āvṛti), projection (vikṣepa), the two kinds of knowledge (dvividhajñāna), and contentment (tṛpti). ||28||

Commentary (a0): Let it be so in the case of the ten illustrations; however, one might ask, "Even if this group of seven states beginning with ignorance has been explained through the illustrations, what relevance does it have to the present subject—the non-dual Self? In response to this expectation, he says, "Ignorance... etc., to show that these seven states are likewise to be applied there as well. Regarding the word *tṛptayaḥ*, some manuscripts read *hṛṣṭayaḥ*. The meaning is that these are specific superimposed states. || 28 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: In that regard, he demonstrates ignorance and so forth concerning the Self in successive order:
"That reflection of consciousness, whose mind is attached to worldly existence, at some time..."
This [individual] does not know its own true nature, which is self-luminous and immutable.

By the four verses beginning with "attached to saṃsāra," [it is said]: this reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), its mind being attached to meditation for the sake of acquiring sense objects and so forth, never—at any time prior to the inquiry into the scriptures—knows its own true nature (svatattva), that is, its own innate form (nija-rūpa), which is the self-luminous consciousness (svaprakāśa-cid-rūpa), the immutable (kūṭastha) inner Self (pratyagātman). That which is thus unknown is ignorance (ajñāna). || 29 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Demonstrating that very method of applying the seven aforementioned states, he first clarifies the state of ignorance (*ajñānāvasthā*) with the verse beginning "saṃsāra..."— one whose mind is attached to the phenomenal world of duality (*dvaitaprapañca*), which possesses only the semblance of essence consisting of the momentary pleasure born of sexual union, according to the etymological derivation "that in which the true essence (*sāra*) exists completely" and the Vedic scripture stating, "The organ of generation is the sole abode of all pleasures."
This is the meaning. || 29 ||
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya states incidentally that the immutable (*kūṭastha*) neither shines nor exists.
The author of this work, titled *Tṛptidīpa*, states:
"One falls into the distraction of thinking, 'I am the doer and the enjoyer. (30)
Rāma’s Commentary: "It does not appear" (na bhāti). When the context of the conscious Self (cidātman) arises, the immutable one (kūṭastha), thinking "I do not exist, I do not appear," speaks thus.

This concealment (āvaraṇa), which is an effect of ignorance, superimposes upon the Self agency and other attributes—just like the designation of the non-existence and non-appearance of the immutable one.
The cause of this superimposition is the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) associated with the two bodies; this is the projection (vikṣepa). || 30 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, he reveals the two veils (āvaraṇa) in sequence—the one characterized by non-manifestation and the one characterized by non-existence—by means of the first half-verse beginning with "na bhāti" (it does not shine). Then, he speaks of the distraction (vikṣepa) as well, by means of the second half-verse beginning with "kartā" (the agent). || 30 ||
In such cases as "there exists a changeless one," he knows the object indirectly through hearsay.
Thereafter, through inquiry, one knows: "I am indeed the immutable. || 31 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: "The immutable exists. Being instructed by another, one knows that the immutable exists;
this is indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*). By virtue of the ripening of hearing and other means, one knows, "I myself am the immutable"; this is direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*). ||31||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, he demonstrates his indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) by means of the first half of the verse beginning with "asti" ("it exists"). The meaning is: by hearing the significance of the *Taittirīyaka* scripture, which states, "If one knows that Brahman exists, then they know him as truly existing. Then, regarding direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), he speaks by means of the second half of the verse beginning with "paścāt" ("afterwards"), [referring to] the ripening of hearing and other practices through qualification, and from the deliberation upon the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*). || 31 ||
One thus casts off the entire mass of sorrows, such as "I am the doer" and "I am the enjoyer."
He is contented, thinking, "What was to be done has been done; what was to be attained has been attained. || 32 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Regarding the word "agent" (kartā): after the knowledge of the immutable and unattached Self, one abandons the entire mass of sorrows such as agency and so forth;

this is the "departure of sorrow. Furthermore, one rejoices, thinking, "The multitude of duties to be performed has been done—accomplished—and the multitude of fruits to be attained has been reached—obtained. This is the meaning of "contentment" (tṛpti). || 32 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, he describes sorrow, liberation, unrestrainedness, and contentment in succession by means of two half-verses beginning with "kartā" (the agent). || 32 ||
Ignorance is veiling, and likewise, distraction is indirect cognition.
Direct intuition is liberation from sorrow and unbounded contentment.
Rāghava’s Commentary: He restates the seven stages, which have also been mentioned in the illustrative example, with the words "ignorance" (ajñāna) and so forth. || 33 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): In the tenth illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), the previously mentioned seven states beginning with ignorance (*ajñāna*) were already shown in relation to the illustrated subject (*dārṣṭāntika*).
Now, he reiterates them for the purpose of establishing another specific point: "Ignorance... (verse 33).
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that if these seven states are admitted to be attributes of the Self (ātman), its immutability (kūṭasthatva) would be contradicted.
Anticipating this, he states that these seven states belong only to the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) and not to the immutable Self:
"These seven states belong to the reflection of consciousness; within them, these two..."
Bondage and liberation reside therein; three are known as the causes of bondage.

Regarding the phrase "seven states": according to the maxim that "every sentence implies restriction," it is understood that these belong to the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) alone, and not to the immutable witness (*kūṭastha*). Anticipating the objection that the presentation of these seven states here might be useless, [the author] says, "Among these, these two," with the intention that the presentation is not useless, as its purpose is to illuminate their role in producing bondage and liberation. [The question arises: Is there bondage or liberation for all seven of these without distinction?
He says "no" regarding their being caused by karma: "therein. This means that there are three [karmas] consisting of the obscuration of ignorance and the distraction of the mind. || 34 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Therein, while establishing that very distinction, he also establishes that their sole property is the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa)—
[Page 219] Seventh Chapter.
Accompanied by two commentaries.
"Seven," and so forth. By this, the quality-less nature (*nirdharmakatva*) of the immutable self (*kūṭastha-ātman*) is implied. Among those [qualities], how many are the producers of bondage?

Therefore he says "therein," ending with the final quarter-verse; the meaning is that there are three [impurities] characterized by ignorance (ajñāna), concealment (āvṛti), and distraction (vikṣepa). || 34 ||

Rāma’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Desiring to clarify the nature of all three by demonstrating their respective functions in order to show how they cause bondage, he first demonstrates the nature of ignorance (ajñāna):
"I do not know" is the cause of the indifferent person's worldly discourse.
Ignorance is said to be conjoined with the prior non-existence of deliberation (vicāra). || 35 ||

"I do not know. The meaning is that the ignorance being experienced as "I do not know" is said to be the cause of indifferent worldly activity, accompanied by the prior absence of inquiry into the true nature of the Self. || 35 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, in response to the inquiry as to what the definition of ignorance (*ajñāna*) itself is at the outset, he summarizes it: "I do not know. And thus, even the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*), such as the body and so forth, are perceived through the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamatva*) by one who thinks, according to the verse composed by me: "He who perceives, 'My body, my vital breath, my mind, my intellect, my happiness'—who is he? There is no answer here. In this manner, they are experienced as belonging to the self.

Just as one who is not directly perceiving a horse does not know "Who am I?", so too, although Brahman is established through indirect means such as the scriptures in passages like "From which [all this arises]"— as the non-different material and efficient cause of the birth and so forth of the produced universe— one still does not know Brahman through direct perception. Thus, it is concluded that ignorance is indeed a positive entity (*bhāva-rūpa*) that cannot withstand critical inquiry, and is known through the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of its effects, characterized by the behavior of indifference and so forth.

By this, the definition of ignorance (*ajñāna*) is established as follows: it is a positive entity (*bhāva*) that consists solely of an unobstructed immediate cognition, which has as its object and locus a single, self-luminous, infinite Pure Being (*sanmātra*). Here, if one were to state merely "being a positive entity subject to sublation" (*bādhyabhāvatva*), there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the effects of ignorance such as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; therefore, the qualification "pure" (*satyam*) is included to exclude those. Furthermore, this excludes the "shoot-like" (*pallava*) ignorance regarding objects such as pots during states like deep sleep, as well as the ignorance regarding the Self.

Regarding the phrase "sanāyānādi" (beginningless and eternal): even there, if one were to substitute the term "dhvaṃsi" (perishable) for the word "bādhyapada" (the locus of sublation), there would be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding the ignorance of Śuka and others under the view of liberation-in-life (*jīvanmukti*); therefore, the term "bādhyapada" is used. Similarly, in the absence of the word "bhāva" (existence), there would be over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*) even in the case of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the aforementioned cognition; that is why it is included. By this, the logicians (*tārkika*) and others who claim that ignorance is merely the non-existence of knowledge are refuted. Likewise, [it excludes] yoga, devotion, ritual action, and meditation—any one of which...

The theories of cumulative [causality] have also been refuted. Similarly, the term "immediate" (*aparokṣa*) is used to exclude the obscuration that obstructs the realization of the transcendental. Likewise, the term "unobstructed" (*apratibaddha*) is used to avoid the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of ignorance which possesses an obstruction such as any one of the past, future, or present. The term "of such a kind" (*tādṛk*) is employed to prevent the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the ignorance that is a mere sprout produced by the cognition of a jar or similar objects. In the same way, regarding the preceding member [of the definition], the word "that" (*tat*) serves to eliminate the transcendence (*pārokṣya*) of Brahman, which is the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) of that term.

"Self-luminous" (*svaprakāśa*): [This is stated] to exclude the notion that the Self, which is the referent of the term *tvam*, possesses a second entity. "Infinite" (*ananta*): This is to ward off the consciousness (*saṃvit*) accepted by the Buddhists and the Prābhākaras. "Being" (*sat*): This is for the purpose of intending the absence of difference in the form of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), which is known as the delimitation of an object (*vastu-pariccheda*). "One" (*eka*): This is to indicate its quality-less nature (*nirguṇatva*). "Only" (*mātra*): This is to show the non-difference between the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam*. "The locus," etc.: This is for the sake of [establishing] the identity of the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam*. Such is the direction [of the argument]. (39)
Rāma’s Commentary: He now demonstrates the nature of the veil (āvṛti) and its effect:
"Having deliberated by way of the wrong path, one thinks, 'This [world] does not exist, nor does it shine.'"
The effect is held to be that which arises from the exclusion of what is contrary [to it]. || 36 ||

"By my path" means that after investigating solely through logic, bypassing the method prescribed in the scriptures, there arises a contrary empirical usage (vyavahāra) of the form "the immutable one does not exist" or "does not appear"; this is the meaning of the "effect of obscuration" (āvaraṇakārya). || 36 ||
