Commentary (a0): Having thus defined ignorance (*ajñāna*), he now describes the two types of obscuration (*āvṛti*)—which follows in the sequence of topics—as being grounded in the object and the self respectively, and as having the nature of producing the non-existence of ignorance through its various forms, by means of the half-verse beginning with "by the wrong path" (*amārgeṇa*). This refers to the investigation into scriptures that propound duality, other than the investigation into the Upaniṣads as enjoined by the scriptural texts of positive and negative concomitance, such as: "But I ask about that Person taught in the Upaniṣads," and "One who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One."

The meaning is "by way of the moment. Now, one might object: even when such an investigation has been conducted by this path, what [happens] when even those scholars who maintain the doctrine of difference [encounter] Brahman—[[page 220-to-220]] 220?

The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya—[specifically the chapter titled] *Tṛptidīpa*—concerning the non-existence of the manifestation of the reality of the identity of the Self, indeed constitutes an obscuration in the form of a veil; for this [obscuration] is established by implication (*kaimutya-siddha*) for other living beings as well. Now—

Just as previously, at the occasion of establishing the definition of ignorance (*ajñāna*), its effect was described as being of the nature of the behavior of one who is indifferent—specifically, the form "I do not know myself even as non-dual Brahman through direct perception"—so too must the effect of the aforementioned concealment (*āvṛti*) be stated here. To this, he says [the following] by way of the remainder, namely the word "contrary" (*viparīta*). The first half-verse is also to be supplied here by repetition. After investigating by means of the wrong path—that is, by means of the scriptures and so forth of those who propound duality—one [realizes] the reality of Brahman and the Self...

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: that which is characterized as "it does not exist" and "likewise it does not shine"—being merely a contrary empirical usage consisting of the modes of speaking and so forth regarding the manifestation of the non-dual Self which is pure Being and self-luminous—is held to be the effect of the state of concealment (*āvaraṇāvasthā*), whose definition has been stated above. || 36 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He shows the nature of distraction (vikṣepa) and its effect: "Distraction is said to consist of the two bodies and the reflection of consciousness."
All sorrow, beginning with the sense of agency, known as saṃsāra, is his bondage. || 37 ||

Regarding the phrase "dehadvaya" (the two bodies): the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) itself, accompanied by the two bodies known as the gross and the subtle, is *vikṣepa* (projection). It is the cause of bondage; all sorrows such as agency and so forth, termed "transmigration," are the effects of this reflection of consciousness—this is the remainder [of the sense]. By the word "ādi" (and so forth) in the term "kartṛtvādi" (agency and so forth), the states of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) and others are included. || 37 ||

— Commentary (A0 Ṭīkā) — Now, he defines *vikṣepa* (distraction), which follows in the order of enumeration, with the words "dehadvaya" and so forth. The gross body (*sthūladeha*), consisting of the five elements, is indeed perceptible. [The subtle body consists of] the pentad of organs of knowledge such as hearing, the pentad of organs of action such as speech, the pentad of vital breaths beginning with *prāṇa*, as well as the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*). These constitute—

The subtle body consists of the fifteen kalās, and that which is qualified by both of these is the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa)—meaning the manifestation of the self’s consciousness reflected in the intellect.

Thus, he describes its function as well: "due to agency" and so forth. The entire, complete cycle of transmigratory existence known as *saṃsāra*—including even the bondage of the silkworm—is the effect of this reflection of consciousness, the individual soul (*jīva*), characterized by the aforementioned distractions; just as there is agency and so on, so too [is there bondage].
The connection is made by supplying the word "is" (asti). || 37 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection may be raised: "It is untenable to say that there are seven states of the *cidābhāsa* (the reflection of consciousness), because the manifestation of the *cidābhāsa* occurs prior to the emergence of the *vikṣepa* (projection) from ignorance (*ajñāna*) and concealment (*āvṛti*), and since the *cidābhāsa* is included within the *vikṣepa*, it cannot logically be a state of its own. Anticipating this, he says: "Ignorance and concealment—these two are established prior to the *vikṣepa*."
Even so, these two states belong only to the distraction itself, not to the Self.

Regarding the term "ignorance" (ajñāna): although these two forms of the veil of ignorance existed prior to the emergence of mental projection (vikṣepa), they do not constitute states of the Self, because it is impossible for the Self—which is by nature unconditioned—to possess states. Therefore, by process of elimination, the sense is that these two must be described as states of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa). ||38||

Commentary (a0): Now, an objection is raised: "Since the reflection of the conscious effulgence (*cidābhāsa*) occurs in the intellect—which is an effect of the *sattva* aspect of the five unevolved great elements such as space, produced by the self-consciousness delimited by ignorance (*ajñāna*)—how can ignorance and concealment (*āvaraṇa*) be states of that [effulgence]? For it was stated that there are these seven states of the conscious effulgence. Anticipating this doubt, he provides the resolution: "Ignorance... (verse 38).

Rāma’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that it is untenable to designate [the mind] as being in a state of distraction because the actual distraction of the one possessing that state is absent at that time, he says—despite the absence of the distraction itself—the designation as being in a state of distraction is not contradictory, since the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that distraction exists at that time:
"Even prior to the arising of distraction, there is the latent impression of distraction."
Therefore, that state of being [of the two] is indeed non-contradictory. || 39 ||
Regarding the term "distraction" (vikṣepa): the construction of the sentence is that, for that reason, the description of those two as being in that state is not contradictory. || 39 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Since distraction (*vikṣepa*), according to the manner just described, is indeed the effect of ignorance (*ajñāna*) and its veil (*āvaraṇa*), how could those two [ignorance and the veil], which exist prior to it, remain in that state? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the resolution: "Distraction... By this, it is shown that this individual soul (*jīva*) has as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) its effects.
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

Thus, the contradiction between the two scriptural passages—"For the one unborn [Self] lies near, enjoying [the body]" and "The one unborn [Self] lies near"—which speak respectively of the soul's being produced and its being unproduced, has been raised. For the first scripture intends to refer to the intellect (*buddhi*), which serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the soul, as being an effect; whereas the second scripture intends to refer to the beginningless continuity of that soul’s subtle impressions (*saṃskṛti*), which reside in root-nescience (*mūlāvidyā*) and proceed according to the analogy of the seed and the sprout. Thus, these two have distinct objects of reference.

This is the secret. In this very manner, those statements found in the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, the Bṛhad-vāsiṣṭha-rāmāyaṇa, and so forth, which maintain that the individual soul (jīva) is born, are to be explained. This is the direction [of the argument]. || 39 ||
Because they have been superimposed upon Brahman, these two abide in Brahman.
One should not entertain such doubts, for [the power] of all [these goddesses] is deposited in Brahmā alone.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): An objection is raised: "Rather than describing this state as a state of *vikṣepa* (distraction) by way of accepting an unestablished latent impression (*saṃskāra*), it would be better to describe it as a state of Brahman, which is well-known as the underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Anticipating this, he refutes it with the words "In Brahman," etc., on the grounds that such an argument would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). ||40||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "What is the use of this postulation of the beginninglessness of *saṃskāras*? Since ignorance (*ajñāna*) and concealment (*āvṛtti*) are superimposed upon Brahman by a false view, it is far more logically established that they are indeed states of Brahman. Anticipating this doubt, he provides the resolution with the words "In Brahman" (*brahmaṇi*).

Because even the subsequent fivefold set of states, such as projection (*vikṣepa*), is superimposed precisely upon Brahman as qualified by root-ignorance (*mūlāvidyopahita-brahmaṇi*), there is no state whatsoever that belongs exclusively to the individual soul (*jīva*).
The intended meaning is that this would lead to the fallacy of over-extension (atiprasaṅga), such that [the consequence] would not hold at all. || 40 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even though there is no difference in their being superimposed upon Brahman, states such as being a transmigratory being (saṃsāritva) cannot be the states of Brahman, because they are experienced as residing in the individual soul (jīva), occurring after the emergence of mental distraction (vikṣepa).
Thus he raises the doubt: "I am a transmigrator; I am awakened; I am free from sorrow; I am content."
If the higher states pertaining to the individual soul do not appear when one has gone to Brahman. || 41 ||

Regarding the term "saṃsārī" (the transmigrating soul): the state of being a transmigrator consists of possessing attributes such as agency; the awakened one is one who possesses the direct realization of reality (tattva-sākṣātkāra) and is free from sorrow (niḥśoka), meaning devoid of grief due to the contentment born of having accomplished all that was to be done, as will be described later. The meaning is that this subsequent state—characterized by "I am [this]"—resides in the individual soul (jīva);
it appears as dependent upon the individual soul, not as dependent upon Brahman. || 41 ||

The opponent raises the objection that this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) does not occur because it contradicts the experience of reality (*tattvānubhava*); the proponent restates this doubt as follows: "I am a transmigrating being" (verse 41).

Rāma’s Commentary: If this is so, then since ignorance and the veil (āvaraṇa) are also experienced as residing in the individual soul (jīva), they too must simply be states of the soul; thus he offers the following rebuttal:
In that case, I am ignorant, for from my perspective, the manifestation of the reality of Brahman does not exist.
Thus, these two previous states indeed appear when [the planet] is situated in the Jīva [Navāṃśa]. || 42 ||
"In that case, 'I am ignorant'—the meaning is: from my own perspective, according to my own experience. || 42 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He refutes that [position] with the words "tathā" (so too). Just as you have established the refutation of the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of my argument by relying solely on experience, so too I shall state that the status of being a *jīva* (individual soul) belongs to both the states of ignorance and manifestation (*āvṛtti*) respectively; thus, the distinction between the unawakened and the one possessing indirect or direct knowledge must necessarily be accepted. This is the intended meaning (*tātparya*). By the word "Brahman," [it is implied that] even for a single [entity], the state of manifestation...

The intention is that this twofold nature [of ignorance] is due to its being destructible by two types of knowledge—mediate (*parokṣa*) and immediate (*aparokṣa*)—based on the perspective of the absence of the veil of non-existence (*asadāvaraṇa*) and the presence of the veil of existence (*sadāvaraṇa*), and not otherwise.

For if it were otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the statement of their identity made both previously—in the earlier text stating that "in reality, ignorance is the veil" (*tattve tvajñānamāvṛtiḥ*)—and later, regarding the prior state (*pūrvāvasthā*).

Nor should it be argued: "In that case, let there be only one state even for the two types of knowledge such as mediate and so forth, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*)," because mediate knowledge [is different from immediate knowledge].
The sense is that, because it is necessary for the performance of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), the existence of a distinct state is indeed indispensable. || 42 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 222.

[From the commentary by Rāmānanda on the *Tṛptidīpa*: Now, one might ask, "In that case, how did the former teachers state that Brahman is the locus of ignorance? Anticipating this doubt, he shows their intended meaning:]
They declare that Brahman is the substratum of ignorance by virtue of being its locus.
I spoke thus because of the state of being a living soul and because of the conceit arising from ignorance. || 43 ||

Regarding the phrase "of ignorance": the meaning is that its being the locus (*āśraya*) [of ignorance] was stated with the intention (*vivakṣayā*) of expressing that Brahman is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of ignorance. Anticipating the objection—"What intention did you have in stating that it is the state of the individual soul (*jīvāvasthātva*)?"—he reveals his own intention: "the state of the individual soul. (43)

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, if ignorance is indeed resident in the individual soul (jīva) based on such experiences as "I am ignorant," then how can the venerable Śrī Sarvajñātmamuni have stated in his *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* that "the undivided Consciousness alone is the Kalā [ignorance], partaking of both the status of locus and object," thereby asserting that its locus and object are Brahman alone? Anticipating this doubt, the statement in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* is made with the sole intention of emphasizing that Consciousness is the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) for the beginningless positive error (bhrama) consisting of ignorance.

"In that case, our own [position] is that ignorance belongs to the individual soul (jīva). As for the statement beginning with 'I am ignorant, for [ignorance] does not exist from my perspective when the reality of Brahman shines,' that is intended to mean that such a state exists in the soul because it identifies with that [ignorance] in the manner described. Thus, since the subject matter differs, there is not even a scent of contradiction here," he says: "of ignorance...
[The word] "jaguḥ" means that the teachers of the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* and others have so declared. || 43 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus demonstrated the three states that are causes of bondage, he now shows the two remaining states which are the causes of liberation by means of the cessation of the previously mentioned ignorance-obscuration (ajñānāvaraṇa): "When this ignorance has been destroyed by the two kinds of knowledge, the concealment caused by it [is likewise destroyed]."
Both of these two views—that "it shines" and that "it does not exist"—perish.

"By means of the two kinds of knowledge": when ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is the cause of obscuration, has been destroyed by the two kinds of knowledge characterized as mediate (*parokṣa*) and immediate (*aparokṣa*), both types of obscuration—which were produced by that ignorance and serve as the cause for the empirical usage "it does not shine" and "it does not exist"—perish due to the absence of their cause. || 44 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Granted that ignorance (*ajñāna*), though single, resides in Brahman as delimited by its status as the substrate (*adhiṣṭheya*) and exists as a state of the individual soul (*jīva*) as delimited by its status as the object of cognition (*abhimeya*); nevertheless, how can there be the destruction of this [ignorance] along with its effects? To this, he says: "By means of two kinds of knowledge.

[The word] *tatkṛtā* [is to be understood as follows]: the word *āvṛtiḥ* (obscuration) is to be supplied. By this, it is demonstrated that non-existence, obscuration, and the obscuration of manifestation are indeed the effects of ignorance.

It is abandoned. And if this is not the case, then one should not say: "In that instance, since the definition of being the counter-positive of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva-pratiyogitva) is [present], it follows by virtue of being produced (janyatva) that there would be an absence of obscuration delimited by that prior time;

and if that were so, there would be the consequence of perceiving unobscured knowledge. This is because, in the present context, what is intended by "being an effect" (kāryatva) is precisely that which is sublated by its own sublation and is common to all other visible objects. And that [effect-nature] exists in the two kinds of obscuration—dense darkness and [the like]—which accompany it.

It is entirely appropriate that this [ignorance] is common to all, for it exists not only in the fourfold beginningless visible objects such as the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)—which are pervaded by the state of possessing blue color and are like darkness—but also in the phenomenal world (prapañca) consisting of ether and so forth, which is produced by the aforementioned ignorance and functions like the perception of a snake in the dark or the nature of being a venomous serpent resulting from that cataract-like timira.
Thus, the rejection of the sixfold enumeration of beginningless categories, such as "the individual soul is not the Lord," is also established; this is the general direction of the argument. || 44 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In response to the inquiry as to which part is removed by which means, he shows both by dividing them:
"Through indirect knowledge (parokṣajñāna), the state of being a cause for the veil of unreality (asattvāvṛti) perishes."
For the state of being the cause of the non-manifestation [of reality] is indeed destroyed by immediate (aparokṣa) knowledge. || 45 ||

Regarding "indirect knowledge" (*parokṣajñāna*): through indirect knowledge in the form "the immutable Self exists," ignorance's status as the cause of the veil of non-existence (*asattvāvaraṇa*) is removed. Through direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) in the form "I am the immutable Self," however, ignorance's status as the cause of the veil in the form "the immutable Self does not appear" is removed. ||45||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Regarding that, he states the classification of its destruction: "parokṣa" (indirect) and so on; "asattva" (non-existence) and so on. The meaning is: being the material cause of the veil residing in the root ignorance (mūlājñāna). || 45 ||
The Seventh Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, regarding the two states that constitute the fruit of knowledge, he describes the first state:
"When the obscuration of non-manifestation has perished, due to the cessation of the superimposition of being a finite soul (jīvatva)."
All sorrow, including the sense of being an agent and so forth, which is called "saṃsāra," ceases. || 46 ||
Regarding the phrase "the veil of non-shining" (*abhānāvaraṇa*): when the veil of non-shining has ceased, the state of being a *jīva*—which was perceived through delusion (*bhrānti*)—also ceases.
Consequently, all sorrow known as *saṃsāra*, characterized by agency and so forth, which is caused by that [state of being a *jīva*], comes to an end; this is the meaning. || 46 ||

Commentary (a0): Thus, having stated that among the seven states of the individual soul (*jīva*) previously promised in the verse beginning with "In this way, ignorance is the veil" (*evamajñānamāvṛtiḥ*), only three states ending with "projection" (*vikṣepa*) constitute bondage by the statement "three are remembered as causes of bondage," and having described the two states consisting of the very nature of knowledge which removes that [bondage], there are now described, in sequence according to their respective prior and subsequent causes, the two states resulting from that [knowledge]: liberation from sorrow and so forth.

He makes [the truth] understood through the state of "Thou" by means of two verses beginning with "abhāna" (non-shining). In the phrase "kartṛtvādi" (agency and so forth), the word "ādi" (and so forth) includes the states of being an enjoyer, a knower, and the like. || 46 ||
Because all of saṃsāra has ceased, there is the manifestation of the state of being eternally liberated.
Furthermore, satisfaction would be unrestrained because of the non-arising of sorrow. (47)

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus demonstrated the state characterized by the departure of sorrow, he shows the second state, characterized by unrestrained satisfaction, with the words: "When all worldly existence has ceased" (47).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): "Nivṛtta" (withdrawn) and "nitya" (eternal). The meaning is that when the superimposition of fire upon gems such as a self-luminous ruby is sublated, its [the gem's] true nature shines forth; likewise, when all duality is sublated, one immediately experiences the state of being eternally liberated, which consists in abiding in the non-dual Brahman that is one's own substrate. || 47 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that—since the work has proceeded with the explanation of the mantra, "If one should know the Self"—to introduce here a description of the seven states beginning with ignorance (ajñāna) in the middle of the discourse is irrelevant to the subject at hand—the author intends to show that it is not irrelevant because it was stated as a supplement to the determination of the purport of the scriptural text, "If one should know the Self. With this in mind, he states the purport of the scripture:
These two—namely, immediate knowledge and the cessation of sorrow—are both [attained].
"If [the breath] should reside in the state of the living, it declares 'I am the Self,'" so says the Śruti. || 48 ||

Regarding the phrase "aparokṣajñāne" (in direct knowledge): the intention is that this mantra is set forth to explain two of the seven states that exist within the sphere of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), characterized respectively by direct knowledge and the cessation of sorrow. || 48 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Having thus established the meaning of the scripture, he now connects it with the mantra previously promised: "Aparokṣa... and so forth. Thus, the mantra beginning with "If one knows the Self" (*ātmānaṃ cet*) is intent upon propounding two specific states—namely, the state consisting of immediate knowledge and the state consisting of the cessation of sorrow—among the multitude of states such as ignorance that reside in the individual soul (*jīva*), which is termed the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*). These two are designated as the fifth and sixth [states]. Thus it is said.
The reclining one. || 48 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Regarding the statement "this" (*ayam*) signifying immediacy (*aparokṣatva*), it was said that by the word "this," the immediacy of the Self is expressed.

Anticipating the objection that if this were so, the Self would be merely the object of immediate knowledge and not the object of mediate knowledge, he analyzes immediate knowledge in order to explain that point:
"This" refers to immediacy, and that [immediacy] is of two kinds.
Because the object is self-luminous, it is perceived in this very manner even by the intellect. || 49 ||
Regarding the phrase "this is [it]," he states the reason for its twofold nature: "of the object," etc. [The object] is the Self, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*).
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
titled *Tṛptidīpa*:

Because it is self-luminous (*kāśatvāt*), because it does not depend on any other means for its own empirical functioning, and because that object is perceived by the intellect (*dhī*) alone through its self-manifesting nature— of that [object]...
The meaning is: "from the observation of the self. || 49 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Since the nature of Brahman is directly and immediately perceived—as established by the Śruti text, 'Brahman is that which is immediate and direct'—its immediacy, consisting in self-luminosity characterized by natural and independent manifestation, is inherently established. Therefore, how could the Mantra teach that this [Brahman], being of the nature of unattached and immutable consciousness and thus unproduced, possesses the state of being a modification? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] cites the aforementioned Śruti: "Only by knowing Him... and so forth.

Since there exist hundreds of scriptural passages such as, "Death comes; no other path exists for proceeding," [the author] provides a resolution by stating that what is intended in the aforementioned mantra as "ignorance regarding states" (avasthājñāna) is precisely the state of being the object of immediate valid cognition (aparokṣapramā) known as the final mental modification (caramavṛtti) arising from the inquiry into "That thou art" (tattvamasi).

To explain this immediacy mentioned in the mantra with its restatement, he divides it into two types, beginning with the words "This... and so forth. In that regard, the reasons are also given in sequence—
[This is explained] by the verse beginning with "ha-viṣaya" and so forth. || 49 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Let this twofold nature be granted; however, one might ask, "What follows from this regarding the status of being an object of indirect (parokṣa) knowledge?
Anticipating this doubt, he states that the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of the object is not incompatible with its being an object of indirect knowledge:
"Even at the time of indirect knowledge, there is the self-luminosity of the object."
Because of the awakening that "Brahman exists as equal and self-luminous. (50)

Regarding the phrase "in the case of indirect knowledge" (*parokṣajñāne*): just as at the time of direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), even at the time of indirect knowledge, the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*) of the object, Brahman, certainly exists. He states the justification for this: "Brahman is self-luminous. || 50 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "If the immediate nature (*aparokṣatva*) of Brahman is twofold—consisting of its being the very essence (*svarūpa*) and the objectivity (*viṣayatva*) of a valid cognition (*pramā*) that functions within it—then there could be no mediate knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) concerning Brahman at all, since, by virtue of its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), it is eternally immediate. Anticipating this doubt, he provides the resolution with the verse beginning "parokṣa... (verse 50).

Rāma’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection as to how knowledge whose object is Brahman non-different from the inner self (pratyagātman) can be indirect (parokṣa), he states that it is because the aspect of the inner self is not grasped:
"Without delineating 'I am Brahman,' one might instead delineate 'Brahman exists.'"
This is knowledge of an object beyond the senses; it is not erroneous, because no sublation is perceived.

"I am Brahman. Now, one might suspect that this is an error. Is its erroneous nature due to (1) sublation, or (2) because it lacks the manifestation of "being so," or (3) because it is grasped as something remote when it ought to be grasped as immediate, or (4) because some part [of the object] is not grasped? Having thus proposed these four alternatives, he first refutes the first with the words "This... (verse 51).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Let it be so; since the Śruti states, 'If one knows that Brahman exists, then they know him as truly existing,' it is possible to have the cognition that Brahman exists as self-luminous. Thus, let there be no contradiction in Brahman’s self-luminosity even regarding its indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*). However, according to the statement of the learned, 'The aforementioned indirect knowledge is valid as a true experience because it is independent,' how can it be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) at all, given that it apprehends [the object] incorrectly?"

If you say, "It may be so," that is true; however, is the invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) of knowledge intended on account of its being sublated (*bādhita*), or even on account of its non-apprehension of some particular aspect residing in the object that has become its own content? It is not the first, because immediately following this in the present context, that [invalidity] will be refuted with the words, "If there were a means of knowledge [saying] 'Brahman does not exist,'" and so forth. Nor is it the second, because that will be resolved immediately thereafter with the words, "merely by the non-mention of its manifestation," and so forth.

Having thus intended [to demonstrate this], he first enacts the perception of the transcendent (parokṣajñāna) itself, including the mention of its counter-correlate, and asserts its non-erroneousness with the passage beginning "I... and ending with "...not erroneous. Therein, he makes known the reason for this with the word "vādha" (sublation). || 51 ||
If there were the conceit that "Brahman does not exist," it would certainly be sublated.
And we do not perceive such a powerful pride [in them] as would cause them to be obstructed. || 52 ||
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): He explains the reason [for this] with the words "Brahman does not exist. || 92 ||
Commentary—Explaining that very point, he reveals the intended meaning (abhisaṃdhi) with the words "Brahman does not exist," and so forth. || 52 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He refutes the second view by means of an over-extension:
"If [the cognition] were erroneous merely because it does not mention the individual, then even the cognition of heaven would be erroneous."
There would be error because there is no mention of the individual instance and because one observes the mention of the universal. ||53||

The meaning is as follows: since there is no apprehension of heaven in the specific form "this is heaven," but rather because it is cognized in a general form such as "it exists in heaven," it follows that even the cognition of heaven would be subject to the status of being an error. || 53 ||
In the commentary on verse 53, he addresses the second objection as well by means of a counter-argument (prati-bandī), stating: "The individual... and so forth.
Rāma’s Commentary: He refutes the third [position]:
"There can be no delusion regarding that which is capable of being directly perceived as being indirect."
It is "indirect" (parokṣa) because it lacks direct mental representation; thus, by implication, indirectness is possible [in that case]. || 54 ||

Regarding the phrase "by way of immediacy" (*aparokṣatvena*): it is impossible for a mediate cognition (*parokṣajñāna*) whose object is Brahman—which is non-different from the inner self (*pratyak*) and capable of being grasped as immediate—to be an error. Why is this so? To this he says: "mediate" (*parokṣam*). Since there is no apprehension of Brahman in the form "Brahman is mediate," one might ask: "From where, then, does its mediacy derive? Anticipating this, he says: "by implication" (*arthāt*). This is because there is no such distinct mental projection (*vyatyullekha*) as "this is Brahman."
The sense is that its imperceptibility is established by implication. || 54 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection might be raised: "The aforementioned counter-argument is indeed improper. Since heaven is perceptible, it is possible for the cognition of heaven—which has as its object the universal 'heaven-ness' (svargatva) composed of both genus and individual—to be valid even if it is indirect (parokṣa), provided it does not explicitly mention the individual. However, since non-dual Brahman is pure consciousness (dṛṅmātra) and thus not like that, a parokṣa cognition of something that is eternally capable of being directly perceived must necessarily be an error. Anticipating this, he says "not so" (maivam): apa-
Regarding the word "rokṣatva" (the state of being hidden): he indicates the reason for that with the latter half of the verse beginning with "parokṣamiti. || 54 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He raises a final objection:
"If the cognition of the jar were an error because it apprehends only a portion [of the whole], then..."
Even that which is partless possesses parts through the differentiation of its excluded portions. (55)

"Partially" (aṃśa): the meaning is that even when a part of Brahman is grasped, it is an error because the internal (pratyak) part is not grasped. [The opponent objects: "In that case, the cognition of a jar and so forth would also result in being an error. He refutes this with the words "the cognition of a jar," the intention being that [in the case of a jar] there is no grasping of its internal parts.

[The opponent asks: "But since a jar has parts, it is possible for some parts to be grasped while others are not; however, since Brahman is partless, how can there be the possibility of grasping a part?"

Anticipating this objection—that its possession of parts might arise from the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) which are the objects to be excluded—he says: "of that which is partless" (*niraṃśasya*). ||55||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection is raised: From the Śruti passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it knew only itself, thinking 'I am Brahman'; therefore, it became all," it appears that in immediate (aparokṣa) cognition, the aspects of Brahman, Self, and Existence (sat) are perceived. However, in the Śruti passage beginning with "If one knows that Brahman exists," which teaches mediate (parokṣa) cognition, only the aspects of Brahman and Existence are within the range of perception, excluding the aspect of the Self. Therefore, because of the non-apprehension of these [three] aspects, mediate valid cognition would be an error.

Anticipating this objection, he again refutes it by means of the argument beginning with "parts" (*aṃśa*). For in the cognition of a jar, that very portion delimited by its parts where there is contact between light and the eye is what appears; thus, since even there there is no apprehension of [all] parts, the consequence is that it would be an error—this is the intended meaning. Nor should it be said that even so, the admission of parts is improper, because [the Self] possesses a nature opposed to the unreal, the insentient, and the finite, and is free from the three bonds and suffering.
In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[in the chapter titled] *Tṛptidīpa*,
the intention is clarified as follows: since it is desired here that the matter be determined exactly as it was established by the venerable ancient teachers in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*.
The commentator [explains] with the very half-verse beginning "even though it is partless" (niraṃśasyāpi). || 55 ||
Likewise, the aspect of non-existence would be removed by means of indirect knowledge.
The cessation of the non-manifesting parts would be brought about by direct cognition. || 56 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In response to the inquiry as to which two are the lineages to be excluded, he says: "The aspect of non-existence," etc. (16).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection might be raised: "In the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*, the aspects such as 'unreality' (*anṛta*) and so forth, which are to be excluded from all objects of perception, were indeed stated explicitly. Likewise, here, what are the two aspects well-known in duality that are to be destroyed by indirect and direct knowledge, and what are the two aspects to be rejected in non-dual Brahman? Anticipating this, he explains them in sequence, beginning with the verse starting "asat" and continuing through the entire section on the phenomenal world (*saprapañca*). This very [work] has been expanded by me...

In the first chapter of the *Vodhaikyasiddhi*, within the section on the "Establishment of the Restriction According to Each Object" (*pratikarmavyavasthā*) during the discussion on the nature of cognition, it is stated:

"Let this delusion regarding the locus of objects remain as it is; what is lost by this much? If, immediately following that, the distinction between the immediate (*aparokṣa*) and the mediate (*parokṣa*) is maintained..."

"Therefore, the object [of knowledge] should be feared as if it were one's own self; for that reason, the venerable Bhāratītīrtha-pāda stated in the *Śabdādau* (and other works) that 'the [nature of] sound and so forth is directly [perceived]'—thus, having introduced the system of the indirect (*parokṣa*) and so forth according to the view of Bhāratītīrtha:

'The obscuration of the non-existent (*asad-āvaraṇa*) would exist, as well as the obscuration of the appearance of things as they truly are (*yathāvad-bhāna-āvaraṇa*), within the range of the object.'"
The destruction of the first [knot] occurs through indirect means, while that of the last indeed occurs through direct perception;
in the object, it attains its state solely through the relationship designated as "object."

And because it exists as the very substratum within the self, like a cataract in the eye, this has already been established by the initiated in the *Siddhāntaleśa*; however, that was done only by way of illustration. Therefore, having now examined the *Tṛptidīpa*, I have described it here precisely according to its actual nature.
Its detailed exposition is clear in works such as the *Advaitasiddhi*; therefore, this is not outside the tradition (*asāṃpradāyika*).

Furthermore, the state of being counter-correlates (*pratiyogitā*) for existence (*sat*) and manifestation (*bhāna*) belongs only to the qualified [entities], so there is no contradiction between them. For that which is the Supreme Self—consisting of existence and luminosity—is never obscured, precisely because it is the foundational support (*upajīvya*).

"May it be auspicious that Māyā seems to veil Ānanda, even according to the words of the mirror"—thus [ends the verse]. For further details, one should consult my own commentary on this very work, titled *Advaitātmaprabodha*; this is the direction [for further study]. || 56 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He further strengthens the point that indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) regarding an object capable of being grasped through direct perception (*aparokṣa*) does not constitute an error by demonstrating an illustrative example:
"The indirect cognition, 'There is a tenth person,' is seen to be erroneous."
In the same way, even the notion that "Brahman exists" would be equally [an obstacle], due to the veil of ignorance.

Regarding the phrase "the tenth": the non-erroneous indirect knowledge produced by the authoritative statement "there is a tenth" would likewise be erroneous, just like the knowledge produced by the statement "Brahman exists. The point is that both are equal insofar as they involve the aspect of veiling non-existence (asattvāvaraṇa) caused by ignorance (ajñāna). ||57||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might raise the objection: "How can the indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) consisting of the use of the first-person verb 'there is Brahman'—which refers to the non-dual reality of the Self as Brahman that is fit to be perceived through the use of the second-person verb 'I am Brahman' in its aspect as the Self—be valid? To dispel this doubt by means of the illustration of the tenth man, he says:
"The statement 'the tenth exists' is not erroneous. (Verse 17)
The tenth [chapter] is "It Exists," which is read as "without error.
[End of page 227] Seventh Section.
Accompanied by Two Commentaries.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Now, if it is argued that only indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) arises from the sentence, from what does direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) arise? Thus, the doubt is raised.
He states that [this occurs] precisely from a sentence accompanied by inquiry:
"When the meaning of the sentence 'The Self is Brahman' has been investigated exhaustively..."
Just as an individual is pointed out by the statement, "You are the tenth. || 58 ||

Regarding the word "Self" (*ātman*): when the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*), "This Self is Brahman," is properly investigated, the identity of Brahman—which was previously understood as existing in a remote manner—as being non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is directly realized. In this regard, there is the illustration "just as":
the meaning is that just as the state of being the tenth person is directly realized in one's own self from the sentence "You are the tenth," so it is here. || 58 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Just as from the words of a reliable person one may have a mediate (parokṣa) cognition that 'the tenth man exists,' so too from the Vedic statement there may be a mediate cognition of Brahman, which is indeed of the nature of valid knowledge (pramā). Nevertheless, how can there be immediate (aparokṣa) [knowledge] regarding the non-dual, qualityless Brahman, when such immediate perception—like the visual perception of a conscious being in the case of the 'tenth man' or the form of a cow—is possible? [The author] refutes this objection with an illustration, beginning with the word *ātma*. (Verse 18)
Rāma’s Commentary: He describes the manner in which immediate realization arises through a statement accompanied by inquiry, using an illustration:
"When the question 'Who is the tenth? is answered with 'It is you yourself'..."
Having counted them together with oneself, one should remember oneself as the tenth. || 59 ||

Regarding the word "the tenth": when the question "Who is this tenth whom you have identified as existing? is asked, and the answer "It is you yourself" is given, one counts the other nine together with one's own self and remembers oneself alone as the tenth; such is the meaning. || 59 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, if the direct perception of the tenth person were not indeed verbal (*śābda*), but rather visual (*cākṣuṣa*) like the form of a fair-complexioned person or the like, then there might be room for the suspicion of a disparity between the illustration and the illustrated—the attributeless Brahman. Since we do not see that very thing at the outset, he clarifies this by explaining the manner of the direct perception of the tenth person, beginning with the words "The tenth," etc. (verse 59).
Rāma’s Commentary: Since this cognition—"I am the tenth"—is produced by a statement accompanied by inquiry, it is not of the nature of error and so forth; thus he says:
"The cognition arising from the statement 'I am the tenth' is not sublated for such a person."
There is no doubt regarding its novelty in the beginning, middle, and end. || 60 ||

Regarding the phrase "the tenth": the cognition "I am the tenth," which arises from the sentence "You yourself are the tenth" accompanied by the investigation characterized by counting, is not destroyed—that is, it is not sublated by any other knowledge. Furthermore, during the act of counting, even when the nine [others] are counted at the beginning, middle, and end, no doubt arises as to whether "I am the tenth or not. Therefore, that [cognition]...
The meaning is that it is of the nature of firm immediate perception. || 60 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭī0): Previously, due to the delusion of counting his own group, he failed to include himself; thus, the distraction arose in the form of [the thought], "The tenth died in the river," and so forth.

Now, however, a certain compassionate person, having promised, "There is a tenth among you; do not grieve," and having been asked by him, "Where is he? Who is he? and so on, was instructed, "You yourself are the tenth.
Then, having counted those nine along with himself, he realized that he himself was indeed the tenth, as [the teacher] said, "You are the tenth."

Because the calculation performed in the aforementioned manner is free from obstruction, one who contemplates from that pure cognition the thought "I am the tenth," the cognition arising from the sentence "You are the tenth" is a valid knowledge (*pramā*). This cognition is not sublated even at the beginning, middle, or conclusion of the counting of the nine others in the aforementioned manner;
likewise, no doubt arises within oneself regarding being the ninth. Thus, he states the resulting conclusion: "I am the tenth."
"Arising from the sentence," [it is said]. || 60 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 228.
[In the commentary on the *Tṛptidīpa* by Rāma: He applies all of this to the subject at hand (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "Existence as Brahman" (*sadeva*),
etc., [stating] that the existence of Brahman is [established] through indirect means (*parokṣataḥ*).
Having grasped it, one should manifest the individual self through such statements as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi).

Regarding the phrase "beginning with 'sadeva'": having first ascertained the existence of Brahman through such statements as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second," and having contemplated the logical reasoning concerning its entry into the form of the individual soul (jīva) to conceive of it as the inner self (pratyag-rūpa), one should directly realize the Self as non-dual Brahman—thinking "I am Brahman"—by means of such statements as "That thou art. || 61 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He clarifies the aforementioned point by applying it to the subject at hand (*dārṣṭantika*) with the words "sadeva... and so on. This means: by that which was taught by the father named Uddālaka to his own son named Śvetaketu in the sixth chapter of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*—namely, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second.

Therein, having grasped the existence of Brahman through that [teaching] as something indirect (*parokṣataḥ*), [the Lord], having entered by means of this living self (*jīva-ātman*), [differentiated] name and form.

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: just as [the ancient sage], when faced with obstacles such as doubt arising from the logical arguments set forth in Vedic texts like "I shall explain," attained a realization born from the investigated sentence "That thou art" (tattvamasi) which—preceded by the falsity of duality—manifests the non-dual identity of Brahman and the Self, so too should the qualified seeker of today manifest that same kind of manifestation. || 61 ||
This realization of one's own identity as Brahman [should be maintained] in the beginning, middle, and end.
Therefore, it never deviates; thus, direct perception is firmly established.

Rāma’s Commentary: "In the beginning, middle, and end" etc. Therefore, this realization of the Self as Brahman does not change at all, even during the empirical dealings of the Self throughout the beginning, middle, and end of the five sheaths (kośas). Thus, the meaning is that the status of this realization as immediate, direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) is firmly established. || 62 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, stating the conclusion, he summarizes the doctrine of the "immediacy of words" (*śabdāparokṣavāda*) which has been discussed: "At the beginning, middle, [and end]," etc. This refers to the Vedic scripture: "O gentle one, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support. Thus, it means "even at the times of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. "Immediacy" (*āparokṣyam*) means the immediacy of the word (*śabdāparokṣatvam*). || 62 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: "How is it known that first only indirect knowledge arises from the sentence alone, and subsequently direct knowledge arises from it when accompanied by inquiry? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In ancient times, Bhṛgu [attained it] through the definition known as the causality of birth and so forth..."
Then, having grasped it through indirect means, he beheld its manifestation through investigation.

Regarding the phrase "origin and so forth" (*janmādi*): long ago, a certain sage named Bhṛgu, having understood that Brahman is the cause of the world through the definition known as being the cause of the world's origin and so forth—as heard in the scriptural passage, "That from which these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter at death; desire to know That, for That is Brahman"—then attained a clear realization of it through an inquiry into the five sheaths, beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*).
The meaning is that he has perceived Brahman, whose nature is the inner self. || 63 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): It is not only in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad that, first, a mediate knowledge of Brahman arises from a statement establishing the mere existence of Brahman—which serves as the motive for engaging in inquiry—and subsequently, once inquiry has commenced, immediate knowledge also arises through the grace of that very inquiry from the Upaniṣadic statements that establish the identity of Brahman and the Self; rather, he demonstrates that this is certain even in the Taittirīya and other Upaniṣads—beginning with the words "janmā... (the birth...).

Thus it is recited by the Taittirīyas in the Bhṛguvallī Upaniṣad: "Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa, approached his father Varuṇa and said, 'Sir, teach me Brahman. He said this to him: 'Food, breath, eye, ear, mind, and speech.
[The reading "parokṣeṇa" (indirectly) is found in the text of Acyutarāya.]
The Seventh Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.

He said to him: "That from which indeed these beings are born, that by which, once born, they live, and that into which they enter at death—desire to know that; that is Brahman," and so forth. In this context, there was a renowned great seer named Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa, who desired to know Brahman.

Having approached his father, [the son] first understood *Brahman* indirectly through the "tāṭasthya-lakṣaṇa" (indirect definition) of *Brahman*—namely, its being the non-different efficient and material cause of the birth and so forth of the produced universe—as made known by the statement beginning with "Do you know... (*vettha*). [The son then reasons: "The substrate of the illusion of fire must be a self-luminous jewel.
Why? Because it is the non-different efficient and material cause of that [illusion]. Whatever is the non-different efficient and material cause of something is the substrate of that [illusion]."

The meaning is: by means of indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) consisting of inference—just as one might say that a necklace is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for a snake due to the non-differentiation of its cause and material basis (*nimittopādāna*), even though there is an error regarding a venomous serpent. "Having grasped" means having accomplished the removal of the veil (*āvaraṇa*) that brings about the non-existence of that [snake] with respect to its object. "Then, immediately after," means from inquiry (*vicāra*). This is because of the discernment of the locus of its perception, known as the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) such as "food is life" (*annaṃ prāṇam*), and so forth.
The construction is: he "beheld" (aikṣata), that is, he made manifest through direct perception, the "individual manifestation" which is the state of the identity of Brahman and the self. || 63 ||
Although the father of Bhṛgu did not utter the sentence "Thou art That" (tattvamasi) for the sake of the direct realization of the Self;
Nevertheless, having reflected that food is indeed life-force, he spoke of the physical body.
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "In this section, since there is an absence of instructional statements such as 'You are Brahman,' how can Bhṛgu [attain realization]?
Anticipating this doubt, he says "Even though" (yadyapi), because he demonstrates the locus suitable for inquiry, which is the cause for the direct realization of the Self. || 64 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Varuṇa did not actually utter the sentence 'Thou art Brahman' to Bhṛgu as a means of producing direct realization; so how can that [realization] arise? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the resolution with the words "Even though" (*yadyapi*). Here, in this *Bhṛguvalli*, [the realization arises]. || 64 ||
Having investigated again and again within the sheaths of food, vital breath, and the rest.
Having perceived the manifestation of bliss, he also joined it with the characteristic of Brahman.

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Granted that the realization of the inner self (*pratīc*) occurs once the sheaths beginning with the *annamaya* have been investigated, how can there be realization of Brahman?

Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that since the inner self is indeed Brahman, by investigating the five sheaths and realizing the manifestation of the Self as Bliss (*ānanda*), one perceives the definition of Brahman:
"From Bliss alone, indeed, these beings are born; by Bliss they live; into Bliss they enter at their passing. Thus, the definition of Brahman—|||
He says that he has joined [the breath] toward the west alone, in the verse beginning with "food, life-breath, etc. (65).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "In the aforementioned context of inquiry, how did Bhṛgu, having performed his investigation, subsequently achieve the immediate valid knowledge (*aparokṣapramā*) whose object is the non-duality of Brahman and the Self as pure consciousness? To this, he says: "Food, vital breath, etc. By the word "etc.," the sheaths consisting of mind (*manomaya*), intellect (*vijñānamaya*), and bliss (*ānandamaya*) are included. Through the excellence and repetition of such inquiry, [he realized] Brahman, which is characterized as the non-distinct efficient and material cause (*nimittopādānatva*) of the birth and so forth of the produced universe.

The meaning is: it is precisely through the perfection of practice in presenting various types of reasoning, such as those concerning definitions, their application, and their supporting factors, including both worldly and other forms of logic. || 65 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that the application of the definition of Brahman—consisting of bliss and the nature of the Self—to the inner self (pratīc) would not be possible, because Brahman, being "transcendental" (taṭastha), is distinct from the inner self.
Anticipating this doubt, he says that there is no such difference, because scripture declares that Brahman, whose characteristics are truth and so forth, exists in the form of the inner self.
"Truth, knowledge, and infinite"—such is the defining characteristic of Brahman.
Having stated this, it is demonstrated in the treasuries by way of being deposited in a cave. || 66 ||

"Truth," etc. Having thus stated the defining characteristic (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) of Brahman through the words "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānamanantaṃ brahma*), the meaning is that by the subsequent sentence, "He who knows [Him] hidden in the cave, in the highest heaven" (*yo veda nihitaṃ guhāyāṃ parame vyoman*), its very nature as the inner self (*pratyagrūpatva*) is declared by virtue of its abiding within the cave of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*). || 66 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, an objection may be raised: since the sheath consisting of bliss (ānandamaya-kośa), like the four sheaths beginning with that consisting of food (annamaya), is equally an object of perception (dṛśyatva), [how can it be the Self?
On this point— [page 230] 230.
In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[in the chapter titled] *Tṛptidīpa*,

having raised the doubt as to how the definition of Brahman— as described as being ultimately nothing but pure consciousness (*dṛṅmātra*)— can possibly be applied [to the world], he provides the resolution: "It is true" (*satyam*).

In the *Brahmavallī*, by means of the first sūtra-like statement, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," the means— characterized by knowledge whose object is non-duality— and its result— liberation (*kaivalya*) consisting in the destruction of that very knowledge which has as its sole locus and object [Brahman]— are presented. Then, in response to the inquiry, "What is the nature of that reality, Brahman, through ignorance of which liberation of the aforementioned character occurs?", its essential nature is established by the statement, "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite."

Having thus summarized the abundant characteristics, when the inquiry arises as to what the means of knowing that [Self] is, [the answer is: "He who knows [Him] hidden in the cave, in the highest heaven. This refers to that very uncontradicted, eternally immediate consciousness, characterized by being the substratum of the five sheaths—beginning with the *annamaya* and ending with the *ānandamaya*—which are intended by the word "cave. It is established by scripture that "Where there is plenitude (*bhūman*), there is bliss; in the small there is no bliss," and it is designated by the term "infinite" (*ananta*) according to the threefold [distinctions] such as space and so forth.

By supplying the ellipsis, the connection is as follows: it has been demonstrated by the aforementioned scripture that the Reality itself—which is devoid of all distinctions, which serves as the substratum for the entire delusion of duality characterized by the five sheaths (kośas), and which is of the nature of non-conceptual, inward bliss—is precisely this. Therefore, although the bliss characterized by a specific mental modification (*manovṛtti*) produced by the enjoyment of a desired object called "joy" is indeed an object of sight (*dṛśya*), the bliss of the Self, which is Brahman non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*) and is characterized as the witness (*sākṣin*) of that [mental state], is pure seeing (*dṛṅmātra*) alone.
The meaning is that it is indeed consciousness alone. || 66 ||
With these words,

Rāma’s Commentary (*Rā0 Ṭīkā*) states: Having thus demonstrated, through an examination of the *Taittirīya* Śruti, that direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) arises from inquiry preceded by indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), he now demonstrates the same by examining the *Chāndogya* Śruti as well:
Indra understood [the Self] indirectly through such definitions as "That which is the Self."
Desiring to realize it directly, he went to his teacher four times.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the indirect": it is heard in the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad that Indra, having understood the Self indirectly through the defining characteristics taught in such passages as, "The Self which is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, and free from sorrow," approached the teacher Brahmā four times for the sake of realizing that Self directly by means of inquiry and the negation of the three bodies. || 67 ||

Commentary (a0): Having thus demonstrated that for both Śvetaketu and Bhṛgu, there was first indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) produced by the single act of hearing the initiating statement, and subsequently, through the ripening of that inquiry and by His grace alone, even direct realization (*aparokṣajñāna*) occurred; and having done so, now—in order to enrich the faith of modern seekers of liberation through the abundance of traditional accounts—the author cites the well-known instance of Indra as recorded in the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

"By means of the indirect" (*ti-parokṣeṇa*) refers to the statement beginning with "That which is the Self" (*ya ātmā*). The meaning is: from the sentence spoken by Prajāpati, characterized by [attributes] such as "the Self that is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow," and so forth. "Indirectly" means by means of a specific modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) characterized as knowledge, which merely removes the veil that causes the non-existence [of the truth]. The phrase "having awakened to non-dual Brahman" is to be supplied [as the object]. That very veil concerning that [Brahman] is what is meant.
The word "nivartya" (having turned back) refers to this; the remainder, however, is clearly explained in that very same place. || 67 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now he shows that this is also demonstrated in the Aitareya Śruti:
"In the passage beginning with 'The Self, indeed, this [was]...', Brahman is defined as something beyond perception."
Through superimposition and negation, Brahman has been revealed as pure consciousness.

"Or, [it is] the Self. By the statement, "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking," the definition of Brahman is set forth. Then, beginning with, "He thought, 'Let me create the worlds,'" and continuing with, "Of him, three... [the text proceeds].

Having described the manner of superimposing the world upon the Supreme Self by means of the passage, "There are three abodes: this is an abode, this is an abode, this is an abode," and having described the negation (*apavāda*) of that which was superimposed by means of the passage, "Once born, he looked toward all beings: 'What else could I possibly speak of here?

[the text continues] with the passage, "He saw this very Person as the most extensive Brahman, thinking, 'I have seen this,'" [thereby establishing] the identity of the nature of Brahman with the inner self (*pratyagātman*).

Furthermore, you have stated that, beginning with the words "In truth, in the person... and so forth, the seventh chapter demonstrates the suffering of dwelling in the womb and other such states in order to generate detachment, which is a means to knowledge.
Accompanied by the two commentaries, [it states]:

"By means of the inquiry beginning with 'What is this Self? Thus we meditate,' and so forth, preceded by the purification of the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam*, [one realizes] that 'Brahman is consciousness' (*prajñānam brahma*)."
The meaning is that the Brahman-hood of the Self, whose nature is pure consciousness, has been demonstrated. || 68 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, even in the Aitareya Śruti, it is shown that first there is indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) from an intermediate sentence, and subsequently, direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) arises from the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) once it has been investigated. He states this with the words "The Self, indeed" (*ātmā vā iti*). For it is thus recorded there: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking," and so forth. In this way, by means of this sentence defining the essential nature (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*), [the indirect knowledge is established].

The meaning is that, having stated the definition of the Self's own nature, and once indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) has arisen through that, the manner of superimposing the world upon it is elaborated in detail by passages such as "Then he thought: 'Let me create the worlds,'" and finally, by means of the great sentence "Brahman is consciousness" (*prajñānaṃ brahma*), even direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) of it is made clear through the process of negation (*apavāda*). || 68 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: By means of an intermediate statement, he extends the aforementioned principle to other scriptural passages as well:
"Through an indirect statement, the knowledge of Brahman may arise."
In every case, through the inquiry into the Great Sayings (mahāvākya), there arises immediate intuitive knowledge (aparokṣadhī).
"In the interval" means in all cases, that is, in all the Śrutis. || 69 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) clarifies that this rule is to be seen even in other Upaniṣads with the words: "By means of an intermediate [text]," || 69 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that the claim that inquiry into the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) produces immediate realization (aparokṣajñāna) is merely a fabrication of one's own imagination.
Anticipating this, he says "not so," because the teachers have established this very point in the Vākyavṛtti:
"The Great Saying is declared for the sake of achieving the immediate realization of Brahman."
Therefore, regarding the direct realization of Brahman through the function of the sentence, there is no disagreement.
Regarding the phrase "the direct realization of Brahman": the meaning is that there is no disagreement concerning the direct knowledge of Brahman arising from this statement. || 70 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, in the discussion regarding the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa-vidhi*), the authors of the *Siddhāntaleśa* and the *Siddhāntasūktimañjarī*, having presented the view of the *Vivaraṇa*, state: "Likewise, those words previously produced indirect knowledge; when conjoined with reflection (*manana*) and so forth, they produce direct perception, like the mind of one who is free from defects."

Having raised the objection that this [view] is non-traditional because it has been stated thus, he says "Brahman" to show that it is not so, since the venerable commentators themselves have explicitly established this in their *Bṛhadvākyavṛtti*. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "In the direct realization of Brahman, [it arises] from the great sentence characterized by 'That thou art' (*tattvamasi*), etc., once it has been investigated. (70)
Rāma’s Commentary: He demonstrates the method of exposition in the Vākyavṛtti:
"That which shines as the objective support for the notions of 'I' and the word [‘I’]..."
That consciousness which is inseparable from the internal organ is designated by the term "thou" (tvaṃpada). || 71 ||

"By way of being the objective support (ālambanatayā)": that conscious self (cidātman), which—within the consciousness conjoined with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and conditioned by the internal organ—shines forth as the objective support, that is, as the object, of the notion "I" and the word "I"; such a consciousness is designated by the term *tvam*.
The meaning is that it is the referent of the term *tvam*, or rather, that for which the word *tvam* is the designator (*abhidhā*) or denoter (*vācaka*). || 71 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, he writes the very eight verses found therein that establish this [point], beginning with "By being the object" (ālambanatayā) and so forth. The meaning is: the referent expressed by the word *tvaṃ* (thou) within the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). || 71 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus explained the meaning denoted by the term *tvaṃ* (you), he now states the meaning denoted by the term *tat* (that).
In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya:
"The source of the world, characterized by omniscience and other attributes, has *māyā* as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)."
That which is called the *Tṛptidīpa* is the "Thou" (*tvaṃ-pada*), consisting of the essence of Truth and so forth, characterized by indirect knowledge and a mixture of the manifest. || 72 ||

"Having *māyā* as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)" means being variegated by mediacy, that is, characterized by the attribute of being remote. Having thus stated the extrinsic definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*), he states the intrinsic definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*)—namely, "consisting of reality and so forth. Those things beginning with reality, such as knowledge and the rest, are "reality and so forth" (*satyādayaḥ*). That whose essence (*ātman*) or nature (*svarūpa*) consists of these is "of such a kind. That which has the word "That" (*tatpada*) as its designation (*abhidhā*)—that is, the word "That" is its designator (*abhidhā*) or denoter (*vācaka*)—is "designated by the word 'That'" (*tatpadābhidha*). That [is Brahman].
The meaning is that it is "inexpressible. || 72 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, because it is the most venerable as being the recipient of the fruit of liberation, he has first explained the meaning of the referent (*vācyārtha*) of the term *tvaṃ* (you).

Now, since the occasion has arrived, he also explains the meaning of the referent of the term *tat* (that), beginning with the word "māyā. *Māyā* is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), in which pure *sattva* predominates. According to the definition of an adjunct—that which attributes its own qualities [to another]—it is like the confusion that "the crystal is red," where [the redness] belongs to the saffron in close proximity to it. In this way, [Māyā] [projects] all duality...

The meaning is: "one for whom there is a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) regarding delusion (*bhrama*). For this very reason, it says "the world" (*jagat*). This refers to that which is the non-different instrumental and material cause (*nimittopādāna*) of the birth and so forth of the produced world.

For this very reason, it says "omniscience and so forth" (*sarvajñatvādi*). By "and so forth" (*ādi*), omnipotence and other qualities are included. For this very reason, it says "through mediacy" (*pārokṣyeṇa*).

That is to say, it is "variegated" (*śabala*)—meaning possessed of a mixture—with mediacy, insofar as it is distinct from the immediate, self-luminous inner self (*pratyagātman*). Thus, [it is] the extrinsic...

Having briefly summarized that which pertains to the meaning of the word *tat*, he also expresses its essential definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) with the words "satyādi" (truth, etc.). By the word "ādi" (etcetera), knowledge, infinity, bliss, and so forth are included. "Of such a kind" refers to the word *tat*. The meaning is: that which possesses the denotative function (*abhidhā-śakti-vṛtti*) of the nominative form "that" (*tat*), which is connected to the word *tat* in the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). || 72 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus explained the meanings of the individual words, he states that the figurative function (lakṣaṇā) must be resorted to in order to convey the meaning of the sentence as a whole:
"The directness and indirectness of the One, its being accompanied by a second, and its fullness..."
Since these two would otherwise be contradictory, therefore figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) proceeds.

Regarding the phrase "perceptibility and imperceptibility": the compound *pratyakparokṣatā* is a *madhyamapadalopa* (elision of the middle term) meaning "perceptibility and imperceptibility together with being accompanied by having a second. Since perceptibility and imperceptibility, as well as having a second and being complete, are mutually contradictory in a single entity, the meaning is that one must resort to the function of *lakṣaṇā* (indication). || 73 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might object: "Granted that the meanings of the referents of the terms *tvam* and so forth have been stated in this way, what is the relevance to the subject at hand? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] explains: Since for the single, non-dual Self (*ātman*) indicated by the word *asi*, its being both immediate (*pratyak*) and remote (*parokṣa*), its being eternally immediate and yet distant, as well as its having a second (*sadvitīyatva*) and its being complete (*pūrṇatā*), and its being qualified by the visible (*dṛśyavaiśiṣṭya*) and its being an indivisible, uniform essence (*akhaṇḍaikarasatā*), are contradictory and thus untenable, [the author proceeds] to show their lack of contradiction through natural consistency (*svārasi*).

He provides the resolution: "The term *pratyak* [etc.]. He explains that figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—defined by the learned as "the operation [of a word] proceeding through an inseparable connection with its primary denotation"—is indeed a secondary function of words (*jaghanyā śabdavṛttiḥ*), yet it is employed here by seekers of liberation who must necessarily accept it because the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) with words such as "inner self" (*pratyak*) and so forth would otherwise be untenable; likewise, the same applies to the single word in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second."
The inapplicability of the intended meaning (tātparya) of scriptural passages such as "beginning with day" is also manifested as a basis for figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). || 73 ||
And as to what that [function] is like, he says:
"In sentences such as 'That thou art,' the function is indication (lakṣaṇā), specifically partial indication (bhāga-lakṣaṇā)."
There is no other [distinction] between these two words in a sentence such as "this is that" (so'yam), etc. (74).

"—*tattvamasi* (That thou art). This means [the use of] *bhāga-lakṣaṇā* (partial indication), which is to say *bhāga-tyāga-lakṣaṇā* (indication by abandoning a part). In this regard, the example is "*so 'yam*" (This is that).

Just as in the sentence "This is that Devadatta," the function of *jahad-ajahat-lakṣaṇā* (indication by abandoning and not abandoning) is resorted to for the two words "that" and "this," and no other [function], such as *na-jahat-lakṣaṇā* (non-abandoning indication), is employed.
The meaning is that, just as there, here too it is neither a primary sense (kṣaṇā) nor a secondary indication without abandoning the primary sense (ajahallakṣaṇā). || 74 ||
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

233a0 Commentary: Now, even if this is so, one might raise the objection: Is this [the sentence] *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning), like "The hamlet is on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) and so forth;

or is it *ajahatsvārthā* (not abandoning its own meaning), like "A white [dog] is running" (*śveto dhāvati*) and so forth; or is it *jahadajahatsvārthā* (partially abandoning and partially not abandoning its own meaning), like "This is that Devadatta" (*so 'yaṃ devadattaḥ*) and so forth? To this objection—

He says "that very [statement]," namely "That thou art" (tattvamasi) and so forth. Regarding the term "partially": the meaning is that it is called "partial renunciation" (bhāgatyāga), which is known as the "renunciation-retention of its own primary sense" (jahadajahatsvārthā). ||74||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "In sentences such as 'Bring the cow,' the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is observed even without the function of indication (lakṣaṇā);
why then should it not be the same here? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Neither a mere relation nor a qualified entity is accepted here as the sentence-meaning."
The meaning of the sentence is held by the wise to be an indivisible single essence.

Regarding "relation" (*saṃsarga*): in common worldly usage, in sentences such as "bring the cow," the relation of the word-meanings—such as "cow" and so forth—which are recalled by the words and possess mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other conditions, is accepted as the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). Just as in examples like "the blue, large, fragrant lotus," the lotus qualified by qualities such as blueness is accepted as the sentence-meaning, it is not so here in these great sentences (*mahāvākya*), where neither the relation nor that which is qualified by it is accepted as the sentence-meaning.

However, the meaning of the sentence is accepted by the learned as being of an undivided, single flavor, or as a mere reality devoid of internal distinctions such as subject and object; therefore, the meaning is that one must resort to *lakṣaṇā* (indication). || 75 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection may be raised: in sentences such as "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), it is observed that the sentence-meaning—characterized by a relation otherwise known as "conjunction" (*saṃsarga*)—of the objects such as the cow, which are recalled through the power (*śakti*) previously grasped for words like "cow" by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*āsatti*), occurs even without *lakṣaṇā* (indication). Likewise, in sentences such as "The blue, large, fragrant lotus," the object qualified by the color blue and so forth is understood through the very function of denotation (*śakti-vṛtti*).

If it is argued that "let it be as it has been seen in other cases, so too in the present instance," we say no; for there is no consensus among the ancient teachers such as the venerable Bādarāyaṇa, who knew the meaning of all the Vedas. Thus he says: "Or [it is] a relation (*saṃsarga*)," and so forth. What, then, is the sentence-meaning accepted here in the great statements (*mahāvākya*) such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*)? To this he replies: "An indivisible unity (*akhaṇḍaika*)," etc. The meaning is: by way of being Brahman, which is non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*) and is devoid of the threefold internal and other distinctions. And thus it is stated in the aphorism of the Great Sage (Bādarāyaṇa): [the following sūtra].

"The non-difference from that [cause] is established on account of words such as 'originating' (ārambhaṇa) and others," and "But that [Brahman is the cause] because of the harmony [of the texts]" (tattu samanvayāt). A detailed exposition of this should be sought in the commentary on these very sūtras; this is the direction [for further study]. || 75 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He demonstrates the meaning of the sentence as an indivisible single essence:
"That inner consciousness which shines forth is characterized by non-dual bliss."
And its nature is non-dual bliss, characterized solely by the consciousness of the inner self. || 76 ||

Regarding the term *pratyagbodha*: the inner consciousness (*pratyagbodha*) is the all-pervading conscious Self (*cidātman*) that shines forth; it manifests as the witness (*sākṣin*) of the intellect and other faculties.

Its meaning is that it is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), characterized by non-dual bliss (*advayānanda*), being secondless and of the nature of bliss. Furthermore, such a Supreme Self, whose sole characteristic is inner consciousness and whose essence is pure consciousness (*cidekarasa*), is indeed the very same as the inner Self (*pratyagātman*). || 76 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, in response to the inquiry as to what kind of sentence-meaning this indivisible, single-flavored reality of yours is, he summarizes it with the words "the inward" (pratyak). The meaning is that it manifests solely as non-dual inwardness, shining forth in opposition to duality.

Such is the realization: the Self, which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) characterized as the witness of deep sleep and so forth, and which is the purified referent of the term "thou" (*tvaṃpadārtha*).

It shines forth—that is, it manifests—as the illuminator of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*). Regarding the phrase "non-dual": "This Self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than everything else; it is the innermost of the inner.
