Of this very bliss, other beings partake only as a fraction.

"He lives"—"He understood that bliss is Brahman"—and "For he alone causes bliss," according to these scriptural passages, the meaning is that [the Self] is indeed of the nature of Brahman, characterized as non-dual existence-consciousness-bliss (*advaita-saccidānanda*). The word "is" (*asti*) is to be supplied. Thus, he states the mutual exchange [of attributes] with the words beginning "non-dual bliss. In this way, the Supreme Self, whose characteristic is non-dual Brahman, is also the inner self (*pratyak*). That is to say, it exists solely as the single form of consciousness within all. By this, the sorrow—
The actual identity of the meanings of the words *dhī* and *tat* is indicated. || 76 ||
When, in this manner, there arises through the work composed by Vidyāraṇya, the Pañcadaśī, the realization of mutual identity;
Indeed, at that very moment, the non-Brahmanhood of the referent "thou" (tvaṃpadārtha), which is called the Lamp of Satisfaction (Tṛptidīpa), would be sublated. || 77 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To the question, "What would result from such an understanding of the indivisible reality (akhaṇḍārtha)? he says: "In this way" (ittham). || 77 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, he describes this fruit with two verses beginning with "ittham" (thus). Regarding the word "anyonya" (mutual):
it means the valid cognition (*pramā*) whose object is the mutual, real identity (*aikya*). Here, "identity" (*tādātmya*) refers exclusively to ultimate non-difference;

it is not the conventional definition of identity as "non-difference that tolerates difference" residing in attributes and their substrata (*dharma-dharmin*), etc. By the word "yat" (which), [he refers to] the aforementioned valid cognition [extending through] infinite births.

By this, its extreme rarity as the fruit of merit is implied. "Thou" refers to the meaning of the *tvam*-portion—the inner self (*pratyagātman*) characterized as the witness of the five sheaths. "Non-Brahmanhood" means being distinct from Brahman, who is the purified meaning of the *tat*-portion—consisting of truth, knowledge, infinity, and bliss, and characterized as the substratum of all that is perceivable. This [non-Brahmanhood] exists only at the very moment of the aforementioned realization; it does not persist in subsequent moments. Thus it has been said.

For the authors of the *Kalpataru* [state]: "The mental modification (*vṛtti*) which takes pure Brahman as its object arises as the cessation of itself and all other adjuncts (*upādhi*). Indeed, the word "hi" (for/indeed) serves to establish what is well-known through the experience of the wise. The connection is: "it would be excluded," meaning it would cease. || 77 ||
And if the object itself is thus remote, then what follows? Listen.
The inner consciousness abides as the singular form of full bliss.

Rāma’s Commentary on "tadarthasya": Regarding the phrase "of its meaning," the non-Brahmanhood of the *tvamartha*—the inner self—is established through delusion, while the nature of Brahman as being Brahman belongs to the *tadartha*. Furthermore, the remoteness of Brahman—that it is an object of knowledge accessible only through indirect (parokṣa) cognition—is also removed. To the question, "What follows from that?", he asks, "If this is so? and provides the answer: "Listen. || 78 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on verse a0: Regarding the phrase "and of its meaning" (*tadarthasya ca*). The particle *ca* (and) has the sense of "also. It should be construed by supplying the words: "even the remoteness (*parokṣatva*) of the meaning of that word (*tatpadārtha*), as defined above, would be removed; it would be destroyed at that very moment. He summarizes the result of that [realization], which still involves expectation, with the remainder of the verse beginning "If it were thus," etc. (verse 78).

— Rāma’s Commentary — Now, an objection is raised: "Since the definition of scripture (āgama) is that it is a means for correctly attaining indirect experience through the power of convention, how can it be said that a sentence produces direct knowledge? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that this person is devoid of a thorough understanding of the established doctrine (siddhānta).
Having set down the rice, he mocks [the opponent]:
"If this were so, then it would follow that parokṣajñāna (indirect knowledge) is derived from a mahāvākya (great sentence)."
By those [means], their knowledge of the established tenets of the scriptures shines forth most brilliantly. (79)
"Such being the case" means that those who speak thus do not know the secret of the established doctrine (siddhānta). || 79 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, if it is the case that the immediate realization (*aparokṣa-anubhava*) whose object is the non-duality of Brahman and the Self arises solely from the great sentences (*mahāvākya*) when they are investigated, then for what purpose was the injunction of hearing and so forth established by the Śruti: "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon"? Therefore, the scripture (*āgama*) is the means for the correct indirect experience (*parokṣānubhava*) through the power of its conventional meaning.

Thus, in accordance with the definition of *āgama* (scriptural authority) written by Rāmakṛṣṇa— and based on the Amarakośa’s statement that *samaya* refers to "vows, customs, time, established doctrine, and agreement"— by the power of the knowledge of word-potency (*padaśaktigraha*) regarding the objects denoted by the term *samaya*, [the Veda] is designated by the word *āgama* because it generates valid indirect experience (*parokṣānubhava*) arising from both the Vedic source, such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," and the worldly source, such as "Bring the cow."

He dispels the doubt that knowledge derived from the words of a reliable person (āptavākya) must necessarily be indirect (parokṣa) by means of a derisive remark: "If this were so. This is the seed of the derision here: namely, the scriptural passage cited, such as "The Self, indeed, should be seen," has been explained by the venerable Vidyāraṇya-svāmin himself in his *Anubhūtiprakāśa*.
The Seventh Chapter [of the *Guhya-garbha*]
Accompanied by two commentaries:
By the statement "the Self is to be seen," the knowledge of reality is indicated; however, by the statement "it is to be heard" and so forth, inquiry is [indicated].

It is shown: The logic (*nyāya*) consisting of direct statement, indicative mark, and so forth—which effects a discrimination of the power of words—is declared as the cause for the manifestation of the meaning of the sacred text (*śruti*); therefore, [the text says] "it is to be heard" (*śrotavya*). Reasoning (*tarka*) that eliminates doubt regarding the possibility of the meaning is called reflection (*manana*). Here, only that reasoning which does not contradict the Vedic scriptures is to be accepted, and no other. Concentrated meditation (*nididhyāsana*) is said to be the understanding that is independent of anything else, because the word "by means of realization" (*vijñānena*) is uttered in order to exclude the suspicion that it might be mere meditative visualization (*dhyāna*).
"Having prescribed that 'it is to be seen,' and likewise hearing and reflection with reference to consciousness (*vijñāna*), [the scripture] then declared consciousness to be the limit. Thus,
having prescribed this, and here aiming at the unimpeded direct realization of the non-dual Brahman-Self, [the author] identifies hearing and reflection as the most intimate means for that end.

Since it has been stated that the very knowledge of the Self (*ātma-jñāna*), characterized as described above and constituting the fruit [of practice], is the ultimate ground of attainment, what occasion indeed is there for the doctrine of the immediacy (*aparokṣa*) of meditation (*dhyāna*), which is denoted by the term "reflective contemplation" (*nididhyāsana*)? Likewise, regarding this definition of scripture (*āgama-lakṣaṇa*) provided here by the ancient commentator named Rāmakṛṣṇa in the passage beginning with "by the force of convention" (*samaya-balena*), is it of divine origin or human? Not the first; for [scripture is defined as] perception, inference, and tradition (*pratyakṣa-anumāna-āgama*).

Regarding the term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), the word *āgama* is indeed employed in the context of verbal testimony within the *Yogasūtra* itself, and likewise in its commentary by Vyāsa. However, in the definition provided there—namely, "An object perceived or inferred by a reliable person (*āpta*) is taught through words for the sake of transferring one's own knowledge to another; the resulting mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the listener concerning that object arising from those words is *āgama*"—the specific characteristics [of verbal testimony] are not observed here. Nor is the latter [definition] tenable, as it cannot withstand scrutiny. For instance, it is devoid of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) and other such defects.

It is generally agreed by all that *dharma* alone is the defining characteristic [of scripture]. However, even though words such as "You are the tenth," "O son of Kuntī, you are that," and so forth, possess the status of *āgama* (scripture) by virtue of being the speech of a reliable person (*āpta*), they lack the capacity to produce a correct indirect experience (*parokṣānubhava*) through the force of convention (*samaya*); thus, there is no over-extension (*vyāpti*). Likewise, because the *Tarkasaṃgraha* states that "the cognition of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) as qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*) is *parāmarśa*," and "inference (*anumāna*) is the *parāmarśa* of the mark (*liṅga*)," it follows that the recollection of pervasion (*vyāptismṛti*) is the means.

Furthermore, the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition] to inference—which is a means for producing a correct indirect experience (*samyak-parokṣānubhava*)—by the force of the cognition of smoke on the mountain and so forth, which serves as the subject (*pakṣadharmin*) and is denoted by the word "time" (*samaya*), is also quite evident. Therefore, the sense is that the ridicule directed by the authors of the *Mūla* (the *Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya*) against those who maintain that verbal testimony cannot produce direct perception (*aparokṣa*) and who insist on the necessity of generating only indirect knowledge (*parokṣa-jñāna*) is entirely appropriate. A detailed discussion of this point, however, [is provided elsewhere].
The manner in which the identity of my own consciousness is established should be observed at the very beginning; this is the general direction. || 79 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, let the established conclusion of the scripture stand for a moment; however, one might object that the production of indirect knowledge from a sentence is proven by inference.
To this, he raises the following doubt: "Let the conclusion of the scripture rest; by reasoning, it is established that cognition from a sentence is indirect."
"It is not like the sentences concerning heaven and so forth, because there is a deviation in the tenth [chapter]. (80)

"Let it be so. The meaning is that the status of producing indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) is established by the inference: "The subject under discussion (the Vedic sentence) must be capable of producing indirect knowledge, because it is a sentence, like a sentence describing the beginning of creation (*sarga*)," etc. He refutes this, saying "it is not so," on the grounds that in the sentence "You are the tenth," despite its being a sentence, the production of immediate (*aparokṣa*) knowledge is observed.
The state of being. || 80 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, even so, the proponent establishes by the force of inference that verbal testimony (*śabda*) is a means of knowledge for objects beyond the senses (*parokṣa*) alone, beginning with the words "Let it be," and so forth. Thus, the formal argument (*prayoga*) in the debate is as follows: "A sentence is a means of knowledge for objects beyond the senses alone; because it is a sentence; like sentences such as 'One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. Thereupon, the opponent [the Siddhāntin] points out the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) of the aforementioned reason.
He refutes that [position] by means of a threefold argument, stating "it is not so. He makes known the reason for this with the words beginning "the tenth," and so forth. || 80 ||
For one who desires the Brahman-hood of the self-evidently immediate jīva.
"The perfected state would vanish into invisibility"—oh, what a great argument this is! (81)

Furthermore, since it would follow that the individual soul (jīva), which is the referent of the term "thou" (tvaṃpadārtha), lacks immediacy, one must accept that the Great Sentence (mahāvākya) does not produce mediate knowledge; thus he says: "By itself," etc. (81).
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 236.
[Commentary on the *Tṛptidīpa*:

Thus, even regarding the excessive consequence (*atiprasaṅga*) in the etymological view, he says "svataḥ" (by itself). The connection is as follows: "Aho! (Oh! expresses that the reasoning is great; it is a sarcastic remark. 81.
"Desiring growth, even the root has been destroyed"—such is the saying.
By your grace, this worldly speech has become meaningful and perfected.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that this might be an acceptable consequence (iṣṭāpatti), he says: "Vṛddhim" (verse 82).
— Commentary (a0 ṭīkā):
Regarding the aforementioned mockery, worldly people also favor the reciter, saying, "He has grown old. || 82 ||
The individual soul (jīva) is consciousness inseparable from the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which constitutes its state of immediate perception.
The state of being an Arhat exists due to the presence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), but not for Brahman, which is devoid of adjuncts. || 83 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary:

Now, one might object: "It is appropriate for the individual soul (jīva) to be directly perceived because it possesses adjuncts (upādhi); however, since Brahman is devoid of adjuncts, such direct perception is not tenable. To this, he raises the following doubt: "The internal organ... (verse 83).

Commentary (a0): Furthermore, regarding that point, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvavādī) raises an objection: "The internal organ" (antaḥkaraṇa), etc. According to the scriptural statement that "this individual soul (jīva) has its limiting adjunct (upādhi) as its effect," the meaning is that the soul is consciousness delimited by the intellect (buddhi). || 83 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He refutes the objection that the attributelessness of Brahman is unestablished by stating:
"It is not so, because the cognition of Brahman-hood has for its object that which is possessed of limiting adjuncts."
This continues until liberation in the Videha state, because the limiting adjunct has not yet been removed. (84)

"It is not so regarding Brahman. The meaning is this: since the knowledge that the individual soul (jīva) possesses of its own nature as Brahman has for its object an entity characterized by limiting adjuncts (sopādhika), the Brahman that is its object must also be characterized by limiting adjuncts; and the fact that a cognition has an object characterized by limiting adjuncts is not possible without the object of knowledge itself being characterized by limiting adjuncts. Why is this so? To this he says: "As long as... (verse 84).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), asserting the lack of essential proof (*svarūpāsiddhi*) for the reason of "being devoid of limiting adjuncts" (*anupādhikatva*) with respect to Brahman as the object of realization, offers a resolution: "Not so. For this very reason, it has been stated by me in the *Siddhāntaratnaśuddhānta*: "By this, the contradiction between the two views—that liberation arises from the knowledge of the variegated [Brahman] and that liberation arises from the knowledge of the pure [Brahman]—is also refuted. [This is because] the final [knowledge] has as its object non-dual pure consciousness (*advaitacinmātra*)."

Even though there is a multiplicity of objectivities (viṣayatā) conditioned by the knowledge whose form is the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*), that [object] is not there superimposed by other visible things; for indeed, for an examiner looking at a pure diamond or other gem, there is no valid cognition (*pramā*) of it as such [i.e., as being superimposed] without the reflection in the eye. || 84 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that two distinct limiting adjuncts (upādhis) must then be stated for the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman; anticipating this, he says:
"It is distinguished by the presence or absence of association with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)."
The state of being a living soul (jīva) is due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and the state of being Brahman is not otherwise.

Regarding the phrase "the internal organ" (antaḥkaraṇa): the meaning is that the association with and the dissociation from the internal organ are themselves the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) for the states of being a living soul (jīva-bhāva) and being Brahman (brahma-bhāva), respectively. || 85 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if the realization of Brahmanhood has only that which is characterized by limiting adjuncts (sopādhika) as its object, then it would contradict the following statement:
"Brahman is said to be that reality which is neither excluded from anything nor inclusive of anything else;
the meaning of 'Brahman' would be unattainable here if there were a second entity."

Anticipating the objection that this contradicts the *Vārttika*, he says—"the internal organ," etc.—to show that such is not the case, since you yourself have failed to understand its intended meaning.

Thus, for those who claim that if a second entity exists, the meaning of Brahman would be unattainable here in the non-dualistic scripture (*advaita-śāstra*), [he replies as follows]... the venerable *Vārttika*...

The intended meaning is that since it is clearly accepted by the venerable teachers that Brahman-hood consists precisely in consciousness delimited by the absence of duality, there is not even a scent of contradiction with that view. || 85 ||
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

237 Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Let the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), being positive in nature, be an adjunct (*upādhi*) due to its connection [with the self]; however, its absence—the lack thereof—being negative in nature, it is not appropriate for that.

Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states the definition of an adjunct as previously mentioned: "An adjunct is that which persists as long as the effect and is the cause of differentiation. The [absence of the internal organ] possesses this characteristic...
With the intention that the status of being a limiting adjunct (upādhi) is indeed appropriate because both presence and absence exist, he replies:
"Just as affirmation may be a limiting adjunct, why should negation not be likewise?"
The nature of being a chain is not differentiated by the distinction between gold and iron.

Regarding the word "yathā" (just as): just as a positive entity (*bhāva*) consisting of a connection with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) may serve as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), so too why should a negation (*pratiṣedha*) consisting of the absence of the internal organ (*abhāva*)—namely, its disjunction—not likewise be an adjunct? The meaning is that it certainly would be. Nevertheless, one might object that a distinction characterized by being positive or negative is indeed observed; anticipating this, and intending to show that such a distinction is irrelevant and thus to be disregarded, he provides an illustration:

"Like gold," etc. The meaning is: just as the distinction between being gold, iron, and so forth—which is useless regarding the aspect of obstructing human movement—is to be disregarded, so it is here. || 86 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection: in the world, it is observed that only a positive entity (*bhāva-padārtha*), such as saffron placed near a crystal, serves as an adjunct (*upādhi*) for the illusion that "the crystal is red. As it has been stated in the *Advaitasiddhi*: "For this very reason, the established doctrine of the Vedāntins is that ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth are adjuncts with respect to [the Self's] being the Witness (*sākṣitva*). And so, how can the absence of duality (*dvaitarāhitya*), which is of the nature of a negation (*abhāva*) and characterized by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), [be an adjunct]?

Anticipating the objection that Brahmanhood itself might serve as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), he provides the following resolution: "Just as... Here, "prescriptiveness" (*vidhitva*) is simply the state of being a positive entity (*bhāvatva*), and not the status of being conveyed by a sentence composed of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. Likewise, "prohibitiveness" (*niṣedhatva*) is simply the state of being either a relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*) or a mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), and not the status of being cognized by a sentence that makes known the means to an undesirable end (*aniṣṭasādhanatā*). And thus, even according to the view that the superimposed existence and non-existence have as their sole nature the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) alone—

The essential point is this: even if negation (*pratiṣedha*) is not a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), according to the view that destruction is indeed a modification of existence based on the words of Yāska such as "it is born, it exists," etc., its status as an adjunct is entirely logical. He confirms this very meaning through a specific instance of corroboration (*arthāntaranyāsa*)—namely, "gold" and so forth.
Alternatively, this should be understood as a negative example (*vyatirekadṛṣṭānta*) intended to strengthen the stated argument. || 86 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: To firmly establish that negation, like affirmation, serves as a means for the realization of Brahman and thus functions as an adjunct (*upādhi*) to Brahman, [the author] shows that the teachers have demonstrated that both affirmation and negation are means for the realization of Brahman:
"By way of the exclusion of the non-Brahman (*atadvyāvṛtti*), and directly by way of affirmation (*vidhimukha*)."
"The engagement with the Vedāntas would be by way of injunction," so it was stated by the Teacher. (87)

Regarding the term *atat*: by the word *tat*, Brahman is denoted; by the word *atat*, that which is other than it—such as ignorance (*ajñāna*) and so forth—is meant. The negation or exclusion expressed by "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) and similar formulations is the removal of that which is not-Brahman. That very exclusion or removal of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is its form, which serves as the means (*upāya*). Through that, there is both a direct injunction (*vidhi*) and an injunction by way of exclusion. Direct injunction consists in the employment of words that directly denote [Brahman], such as "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānam anantam*), and so forth; and through that, the injunction [is established].
The meaning is: "even by way of that mouth. The remainder [of the sentence] is: "the activity, the engagement, the exposition of the Vedāntas—that is, the Upaniṣads—is directed toward Brahman. ||87||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that it is contrary to tradition for negation to serve as a means [of knowledge]. Anticipating this, and desiring to resolve it by pointing out that the venerable author of the Bhāṣya himself stated in the *Bṛhadvākyavṛtti* that both injunction and negation are equally means for the realization of Brahman, the author writes the first half-verse from that very work and completes the remainder with the words "atad" and so forth. For it was stated there in the preceding section as follows: [The original verse: *Atadbhāve 'tadātmatve tadabhāve ca darśitam | Vidhinā pratiṣedhena dvārābhyām brahma bodhyate ||* [Translation: When it is not that [i.e., when it is other than the world], when it is not of the nature of that [i.e., when it is not the Self], and when that [the world] is absent—through these two doors, namely injunction and negation, Brahman is made known. Thus, in that context, the preceding... [text continues].
The composition of the commentary:

"Having thus ascertained the meaning of 'Thou' (tvam), one should then contemplate the meaning of 'That' (tad) both by way of the exclusion of what it is not (atad-vyāvṛtti) and directly through positive affirmation (vidhi-mukhena).

[It is] characterized by the absence of all defects of transmigratory existence, defined by such attributes as 'not gross' (asthūla) and so forth; possessing qualities such as invisibility (adṛśyatva) and the like; with the impurity of darkness (tamas) cast away; and with all excellence removed..."
"Ānanda is the embodiment of truth and wisdom; he whose characteristic is pure existence, who is full, is celebrated as the Supreme Self," and so forth.
In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya—

specifically in the verse titled "The Lamp of Contentment" (*Tṛptidīpa*)— that which is imagined upon Brahman, namely the unreal, insentient, and painful (the non-Brahman), is refuted here, just as silver is imagined upon a mother-of-pearl shell.

The visible object is seen as having its form severed; that exclusion—such as "this is not silver" or "there is no silver here"—is precisely the sublation (*bādha*) by means of such scriptural passages as "neither gross nor subtle," and so forth. This is the meaning of "in that manner. Thus, in the subsequent verse beginning with *nirastātiśaya*, it is that which is taught by such scriptures as "For who indeed could breathe, or who live, if this Ākāśa were not bliss? and "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite."

"By him" refers to that which is the direct method characterized by the mouth of Brahmā (the Creator), meaning it is the means for the realization of the non-dual inner Self (*pratyagadvaitabodha*). "Of the Vedāntas" means of the Upaniṣads.

"Twofold" means of two kinds, according to the manner explained above. "Activity" (*pravṛtti*) means the longing through the medium of a venerable true Guru for the awakening of those who desire to know the non-dual Brahman, the king of all twice-born; this is the sense. "It may be," or "it should be spoken"—this refers to the aforementioned manner. "Ācārya" refers to the venerable [Guru] known as Bhagavatpāda.

The implication is that the collection of explanations regarding prohibitions exists within the *Vṛhadvākyavṛtti* as spoken by the Jagadguru. Therefore, the intended meaning is that the status of being an adjunct (*upādhitva*) is exactly the same for prohibition as it is for injunction, insofar as both serve as means to the realization of Brahman. || 87 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "If it is accepted that the Vedāntas bring about the knowledge of Brahman through the exclusion of what is not-Brahman (atad-vyāvṛtti), then there arises the undesirable consequence of having to abandon even the meaning of the word 'I', which is the immutable self (kūṭastha). Consequently, the knowledge expressed by the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) 'I am Brahman' cannot arise. Thus he asks:
"How can there be the cognition 'I am Brahman' if the referent of 'I' is abandoned?"
For in this way, the abandonment of a part is declared through the indication of a portion (bhāgalakṣaṇā). || 88 ||
Regarding the phrase "the referent of 'I'" (*ahamartha*): since the entire referent of the word "I" has not been abandoned, he refutes [the objection] with "it is not so.

For the reason that, by means of *bhāga-lakṣaṇā*—that is, *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (indication by partial exclusion)—only the inert portion (*jaḍāṃśa*), which is one part of the referent of the word "I," is set aside, and not the immutable witness (*kūṭastha*). Therefore, the knowledge "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*) is logically established; this is the meaning. || 88 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection is raised: "If it is indeed the case that, according to the established doctrine (siddhānta), the Upaniṣads (vedāntas) convey non-dual Brahman solely by means of the exclusion of what is not that reality (atadvastu-vyāvṛtti), then since the referent of the word 'I' (aham-padārtha) must necessarily be abandoned, how can there be an experience born from the inquiry into sentences such as 'That thou art' (tat tvam asi) through the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of 'I am Brahman' (ahaṃ brahmāsmi)? Thus he asks: "The referent of 'I'... By accepting the previously mentioned figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) characterized by the abandonment of a portion [of the primary meaning], the denoted object of the referent 'I'— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical flow of the argument up to the point where the solution to the objection is being introduced.)

With the intention that this objection is itself improper—given that while the consciousness qualified by the five sheaths (pañcakośa) is false because it is an object of perception and non-self, and thus may be abandoned, there is no abandonment of pure vision (dṛṅmātra), the consciousness indicated by those sheaths, or the referent indicated by them, and therefore there is no forgetting of that [consciousness]—he provides the resolution:
"Not so" (naivam). For this very reason, he uses the past-tense form *udita* (was stated), meaning "for it has just now been established by us immediately prior. ||88||
Upon the complete relinquishing of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), that which remains is the conscious self (cidātman).
By the statement "I am Brahman," the state of being Brahman is perceived by the witness-consciousness.
Rāma’s Commentary: By means of acting out the method of awakening through the relinquishment of partiality, he demonstrates it with the verse beginning "antaḥkaraṇa" (verse 89).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): And thus, by the principle that a negation applies only to the qualified object of an injunction, when the internal organ—which serves as the substrate for the appearance [of the world] and constitutes a qualification of the referent of the word "I"—is completely sublated through inquiry preceded by scripture, reasoning, and experience, characterized by such sublation; and when the indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha), which remains as the limit of that sublation, is the conscious Self (cidātman) characterized by witness-consciousness (sākṣitva); then, by means of the experiential sentence "I am Brahman" and so forth, non-dual Brahman— (Note: The provided text appears to be an incomplete fragment of a commentary on Advaita Vedānta, specifically discussing the sublation of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and the realization of the non-dual Self.)

He states—beginning with "the internal organ"—that you are indeed experienced by the wise as that final mental modification known as the knowledge of the indivisible Brahman (*akhaṇḍabrahmavidyā*), which, by means of the destruction of ignorance, serves as the root cause for the appearance of difference and the concealment of its nature as non-dual Brahman. || 89 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, one might object that since the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), it cannot logically be an object of a mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*).
Anticipating this, he says:
"Though self-luminous, the witness (*sākṣin*) is indeed made an object by a mental modification, just like anything else."
The fact that this [consciousness] is pervaded by its fruit has been refuted by the authors of the treatises. || 90 ||
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.
"Self-luminous" (*svaprakāśa*) means like other [entities] such as a pot; the sense is that a mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) arises in the form "I am self-luminous.

Anticipating the objection that this would entail the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), [the author replies: this is not a contradiction of tenets, because even the former teachers have accepted that [the Self] is pervaded by a mental modification (*vṛtti-vyāpyatva*).

Thus he refutes [the objection] with the words "being pervaded by the fruit" (*phalavyāpyatvam*). The "fruit" (*phala*) is the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) mirrored in the mental modification (*vṛtti*); the sense is that being pervaded by that [fruit] has already been rejected for this inner self (*pratyagātman*), because its nature is that of self-luminous manifestation (*sphuraṇa*). || 90 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) explains this: "Even though it is self-luminous" (*svaprakāśo’pi*). By the word "even" (*api*), it is indicated that although there is no need for a mental modification (*vṛtti*) for its manifestation, its utility is nonetheless necessary for the purpose of removing the veil over the non-dual bliss caused by the aforementioned root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*).

The phrase "by a mental modification" means by the final mental state produced by the great sentences (*mahāvākya*) such as *Tattvamasi* when they have been investigated. [It is not like other objects] which are manifested to the witness-consciousness (*sākṣibhāsya*) as distinct from it.

This refers to the example "like a bell-metal vessel" (*ṭapaṭa*) and so forth. Now, an objection is raised: if the witness (*sākṣin*), though self-luminous, is pervaded by the modification of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇavṛtti*) just like a jar or other objects, then it must also be pervaded by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) cast upon it; and in that case, it would follow that it is insentient (*jaḍa*), just like those objects. To this, the author provides a resolution, indicating the agreement of the venerable ancient teachers, beginning with the word "phala": Brahman itself, characterized as the witness, is eternally self-luminous by its very nature.

Because it is obstructed and because it has been approached, this is the meaning of the word "this" (idam). And thus, the meaning is: of this very subject at hand, namely Brahman characterized as the Witness.

By the authors of the scriptures—meaning by the ancient teachers, such as the authors of the Sūtras and so forth—it is only the state of being pervaded by the fruit, that is, only the state of being the object of consciousness, and not—CG.

Transcending delusion and purified, he is described by the sages as one whose form has passed beyond delusion; he is the witness within his own heart, and when his body is reflected in that which arises therein, he is called the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).
When ascended upon a mental modification (*vṛtti*), it is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); then, having fully pervaded the modification of the intellect, the object of cognition—
"The locus [of error] is the Supreme Self, which consists of objects beginning with sound arising from delusion; it is the object of knowledge.

Thus it has been stated by the traditional teachers that consciousness delimited by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by a means of valid cognition, having attained identity with the consciousness delimited by the object, is designated by the term "fruit" (*phala*). That [consciousness] is the object [of the fruit]. However, such a state is untenable. For instance, regarding Brahman—

One who asserts that there is no pervasion by the result characterized as "manifestation" (*phala-vyāpti*) in that which has been defined [as Brahman] must be asked: Is the non-acceptance of such pervasion because you hold that wherever there is pervasion by the result, there is insentience (*jaḍatva*), and thus—by the pervasion that insentience applies to Brahman as well, like a jar—you do not accept it; or is it because you hold that wherever there is insentience, like a jar, there is pervasion by the result, and thus—since Brahman lacks insentience due to its being consciousness (*cit*)—you do not accept it? It is not the former.

The first [alternative] is accepted, as it leads to a desired conclusion. The last is not tenable, because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of ignorance (*avidyā*) and other such things which are manifested by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣibhāsya*).

For in those cases, although they possess insentience (*jaḍatva*) due to being different from consciousness (*cidbhinnatva*), the absence of being "objectified by the fruit" (*phalavyāpyatvābhāva*) is universally admitted. This has been elaborated upon by Madhusūdana Sarasvatī in the *Vedāntakalpalatikā*: "Or, let it be granted that even Brahman possesses a superimposed objectivity (*kalpitaviṣayatā*); yet it should not be said that this results in the undesirable consequence of its being insentient (*jaḍatva*) by virtue of being an object of action (*karmatva*)."

Only an objectivity (*viṣayatā*) that possesses the same level of reality as the subject itself can constitute "objectness" (*karmatva*). And this is possible in the case of a jar and the like, because both are equal in being of a conventional nature (*vyāvahārika*). But in the case of Brahman, even though there is a conventional objectivity, it is not equivalent [to the subject] due to the absence of ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*); so what is untenable here? By this, the scriptural text, "Him who is to be known through the Upaniṣads," is also vindicated. Or else, [the consciousness of] Caitra—

It is precisely being the object of the *nyaya* (logical inference) that brings about insentience (*jaḍatva*), and not even being the object of a mental modification (*vṛtti*). This is because [the scriptures] state: "From which words turn back," "It is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech; I ask you about that Person whose secret essence is the Upaniṣads," "One who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One," and "That which is to be known is known only through the Veda.

Such a conclusion is reached in accordance with both types of scriptural testimony. As for the fact that the authors of the treatises have rejected the idea that Brahman is the object of the fruit [of knowledge], [they did so] because— [The passage ends abruptly here.]

They say that for the destruction of ignorance, the pervasion by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) is required because it is logical; however, it is only the "pervasion by the fruit" (*phala-vyāpyatva*) that brings about insentience (*jaḍatva*). To this, [the author] replies: since the scriptures designate as the "fruit" only the consciousness manifested by the internal organ's modification produced by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), if being pervaded by that [consciousness] were the cause of insentience, then even objects revealed by the Witness (*sākṣin*)—just like Brahman—would not be insentient. On the other hand, the status of being an object of consciousness (*caitanya-karmatā*) applies to everything [else], conditioned by its difference from consciousness.

In this regard, that very [ignorance] is the cause of insentience. Furthermore, it should be understood that even in the cited kārikā, the word "fruit" (*phala*) refers exclusively to pure consciousness (*caitanyamātra*).

Now, an objection may be raised: since the mental modification (*vṛtti*) has that [object] as its content, it is necessarily the case that consciousness colored by that [modification] also has it as its content, because a mental modification arises only when it contains the form of consciousness within itself.
This has been stated by Vidyāraṇya in the *Pañcadaśī*: “The entity of space [arises] solely from the conformity to its own nature, not from a causal agent.”
"Just as the filling of space occurs in the case of a jar through visual perception,
so too do the cognitions [of objects] such as a gourd or suffering take on those forms due to causes like merit (dharma) and the like;
yet, the pervasive awareness of the self-established object occurs in accordance with the nature of the thing itself."

Likewise, in the work titled *Tṛptidīpa*, it is argued that insentience (*jaḍatva*) is unavoidable because consciousness is the object [of the mental modification]. However, consciousness as qualified by a mental modification (*vṛttyuparaktacaitanya*) does not itself require being pervaded [by another consciousness], because it is consciousness by its very nature; for there can be no further fruit within a fruit. As for those things distinct from it, which lack self-luminosity, their pervasion [by consciousness] is necessary.
It must certainly be resorted to; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

As it has been said: "That very consciousness which is accepted as the fruit in the case of objects of knowledge external [to the self] is itself the object of knowledge here, according to the authority of the statements of the Vedānta."

If it be argued that, "Surely here, by those who explain the word *phala* (fruit) occurring in the aforementioned *kārikā*s as referring solely to pure consciousness (*caitanya-mātra*), the doctrine of both the authors and the commentators [of the *Brahmasūtras*] is refuted"—if you think thus, you are certainly mistaken; for these [authors] have, on the contrary, clarified that very intended meaning (*tātparya*) in accordance with the consensus of the *Sūtrakāra* and the *Bhāṣyakāra*. It is for this very reason that, having accepted the position that the qualified [Self] (*viśiṣṭa*) is not distinct from the pure [Self] (*śuddha*), [the author] here...

Furthermore, because the *Vārttika* beginning with "garthaprameyeṣu" has also been cited [as an authority], one should not ask: "In that case, where does the aforementioned refutation apply? For although the authors of the treatises have accepted the inclusion of the function (*vṛtti*) and the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by taking the particle *eva* in the aforementioned *kārikā* to mean the exclusion of connection with anything else (*itarayogavyavaccheda*), they nevertheless rejected its being pervaded by the fruit (*phalavyāpyatva*) because it would entail insentience (*jaḍatva*). Thus, the intent is to explain [the verse] by supplying the word "only" (*eva*)—that is, [to show that] it is only the being pervaded by the fruit that is prohibited.

For it has been stated quite explicitly that "you alone [are the cause] of the induction of insentience. Likewise, it was said by the venerable author of the *Bhāṣya* in the section on Right Conduct (*Sadācāra-prakaraṇa*):
"Let there be only the being pervaded by the mental mode (*vṛtti-vyāpyatva*); how could there be pervasion by the fruit (*phala-vyāpti*)?"
"Because the Supreme Self is of the nature of self-luminosity and because it is established [as such]. || 90 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: To demonstrate that the Self is not pervaded by the result, he shows that it is the non-Self which is pervaded by both the mental modification and its result: "Both the intellect and the reflection of consciousness residing therein pervade the jar."
Therein, ignorance is destroyed by the intellect, and the jar manifests through its appearance.

"Buddhitaditi" [means "the intellect and that"]. He states the purpose of the pervasion of both with the word "tatra" (therein). Therein, between those two—the intellect and the reflection of consciousness—ignorance perishes by means of the intellect, that is, through its modification (*buddhivṛtti*) acting as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because of the opposition between knowledge and ignorance. By the reflection, that is, the reflection of consciousness, the jar manifests, since it is insentient and thus incapable of manifesting by itself; this is the sense. || 91 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might object: "Let there be no pervasion by the fruit (*phala-vyāpti*) in the self; however, in the case of the non-self alone, two things are indeed perceived from the very beginning—the first being the pervasion by the operation (*vṛtti-vyāpti*), and the second being the pervasion by the fruit. For all forms of valid cognition (*pramā*) are experienced as follows: knowledge produced by the mere contact of sense-organ and object is perception (*pratyakṣa*), while knowledge produced by subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*) is inference (*anumiti*), and so forth. Anticipating this objection, [the author states that] even if such were the case in the view of the Logicians (*tārkika*), [their position remains untenable].

Considering that, because this is a general principle, it will become perfectly clear through a more subtle investigation conducted according to his own system, he clarifies it with the words "buddhi" (intellect). That the appearance of consciousness occurs precisely at the moment of the emergence of a mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) has already been indicated immediately following [the previous verse] by the statement of the *Vārttika*: "The reality of space [arises] solely from its own nature, not from a causal agent," and so forth. Thus, although there is no disagreement regarding the fact that the cognition of a jar possesses both natures (the form of the object and the form of the cognition), nevertheless—

To further strengthen that point, he also reveals there an inference having that as its mark (*liṅga*), based on a distinction in the effect—namely, "therein": the destruction of the ignorance regarding a jar is produced solely by a cognition having that [jar] as its object. This is because it is the destruction of the ignorance regarding a jar. By way of contrast (*vyatireka*), it is like the destruction of the ignorance regarding a cloth. The same applies to the manifestation (*sphūrti*) of the jar.
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

It is produced by pure consciousness (cinmātra), which is the pervader of the jar, because it is the manifestation (sphūrti) of the jar; this should also be understood through the counter-example that what is not so produced is like the manifestation of a cloth.

Therefore, it should be understood that there is not even a scent of dispute regarding the fact that the valid cognition (pramā) of a jar and the like possesses both forms—namely, the modification (vṛtti) and the pervasion (vyāpti). || 91 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now he demonstrates the difference [of the Self] from that [intellect]:
"In the case of Brahman, for the destruction of ignorance, the pervasion by a mental modification (vṛtti) is required."
Because its nature is that of self-manifestation, no external appearance is required. || 92 ||

Regarding the term "in Brahman": because the identity of the individual self (*pratyak*) and Brahman is veiled by ignorance (*ajñāna*), an expansion [of consciousness] through a mental modification (*dhīvṛtti*) produced by the Great Sentence—taking the form "I am Brahman"—is required for the cessation of that ignorance. Since the Self itself is of the nature of luminosity (*sphuraṇa-rūpa*), no reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) is required for its manifestation; therefore, the meaning is that even though a reflection of consciousness might be logically possible, it is of no use. || 92 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might object: "Granted that this may be so regarding the valid cognition of a jar and the like; however, even though the status of being a valid cognition (*pramātva*) is the same for the valid cognition of Brahman, why is it not accepted that it likewise possesses both natures? To this he replies, "In Brahman," [stating] that it is precisely because there is no purpose [for such an acceptance]. || 92 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He clarifies the aforementioned point by means of an illustration:
"Just as the eye and a lamp are required for the perception of a jar or similar objects,"
It is not the seeing of the lamp that is required, but rather the eye alone. || 93 ||

Regarding the word "eye": in the perception of a jar or similar object shrouded in darkness, both the eye and the lamp are required; however, in the case of perceiving the lamp itself, it is not so. Rather, only the eye alone is required. Just as that is the case, the connection with the preceding [verse] is that [the same applies] for the destruction of ignorance regarding Brahman. || 93 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He clarifies the very point already stated by means of the empirical example of self-luminosity, beginning with "the eye and the lamp. This is an illustrative instance; it also applies to the sun and so forth. Thus, for the perception of a jar or similar object, both the eye and the lamp are required by Devadatta; however, for the perception of the lamp itself, those two are not required at all, but rather only the single eye is required. Just as that [eye] is required, so too [is the Self] in the case of Brahman for the destruction of ignorance, and so forth—as previously stated.
The connection with the verse should be understood. || 93 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that because it is the very nature of the intellect and its modifications to be characterized by the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), there must necessarily be a pervasion of the result [of knowledge] even in Brahman, just as it occurs in objects such as pots.
Anticipating this, he says: "Even though this reflection of consciousness remains, it becomes one with the Supreme Brahman."
But it cannot produce an extraordinary result in Brahman, unlike [the case of] a seed and so forth. || 94 ||

"Even though it is present" means that although there is a reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) in the mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward Brahman—just as there is in a modification taking the form of a jar or the like—nevertheless, this reflection does not appear as distinct from Brahman; rather, like the light of a lamp situated in the midst of a blazing sun, it becomes as if one with it.
Therefore, the meaning is that it does not produce any excellence characterized by a new manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) in Brahman. || 94 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, even so, one might argue that according to the reasoning stated in the cited Vārttika—namely, "merely by virtue of the nature of the object, space" and so forth—even when there is a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of non-dual Brahman, as in the case of a jar, the pervasion of the fruit (*phalavyāpti*) is unavoidable because of the inherent nature of the presence of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*). To this, he says: "Even though situated... Just as the reflection of the sun reflected in a mirror, while illuminating jars and other objects inside a house, [remains facing itself] when its own orientation is directed inward...

Just as when facing the sun alone, one attains identity with it and does not project even a blade of grass as a distinct attribute, so too, within the mental modification (vṛtti) taking the form of Brahman, the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa)—though present by its very nature—attains identity with Brahman alone; it should be understood that it does not establish even an atom’s worth of any separate quality therein. || 94 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "It has been stated that there is no pervasion by the fruit (*phala-vyāpti*) in Brahman, yet there is pervasion by the mental modification (*vṛtti-vyāpti*); what is the proof for this?
Anticipating this, he states that scripture (*āgama*) is the proof:
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 242.
And that it is immeasurable and without beginning—this has been declared here by the Śruti.
[In the work titled *Tṛptidīpa*, it is heard that this [Brahman] is to be attained by the mind alone; thus, its state of being pervaded by the intellect is declared. (95)

Regarding the term "immeasurable" (*aprameya*): in this mantra from the *Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad*, "That which is free from conceptual construction, infinite, devoid of cause and example, immeasurable, and beginningless—by knowing which the wise man is liberated," the word "immeasurable" expresses the state of being beyond the reach of results. Furthermore, in the *Kaṭhavallī*, the state of being pervaded by the intellect is heard [in the verse]: "By the mind alone this is to be attained; here there is no diversity whatsoever."
The meaning is that it is heard [in scripture] that [the object] is pervaded by the mental modification (vṛtti). || 95 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, he states "It is immeasurable" (aprameyam) [verse 95], explaining that the two mutually contradictory scriptural statements— "immeasurable and beginningless," etc., and "this is to be measured by the mind alone," etc.— are consistent only when intended respectively to mean the absence of pervasion by the result (phala-vyāpty-abhāva) and the presence of pervasion by the mental function (vṛtti-vyāpti-sadbhāva).

Rāma’s Commentary: It was stated that by the mantra "If one should know the Self," two states pertaining to the individual soul (jīva)—namely, immediate realization (aparokṣajñāna) and the cessation of sorrow—are designated. With this verse beginning with "If one should know the Self," the scripture declares to what extent immediate realization is expressed through these two states pertaining to the individual soul, namely immediate realization and the cessation of sorrow.
In response to this inquiry, he says: "If one should know the Self from the statement 'I am this'..."
That awakening which delineates the manifestation of the Self as Brahman is what is called [knowledge]. || 93 ||

Regarding the phrase "the Self": the meaning is that this sentence expresses the realization that arises when one delineates—that is, makes the object of cognition—the manifestation of the Self as Brahman, whose nature is a distinct Self non-different from Brahman characterized by truth and other such qualities, [in the form] "I am Brahman. || 96 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "Granted that this is so, what relevance does this have to the explanation of the specific scriptural passage promised at the commencement of the present treatise? In response to this expectation, [the author] states: "If [one knows] the Self... This indicates that direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) alone is the meaning of the first half of that verse; through this much of the textual composition, it has been determined that this alone constitutes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the doctrine of verbal directness (*śabdāparokṣavāda*). The word "iti" marks the end of the citation (*pratīka*).
The meaning is: "from the statement," that is, from the great sentences (mahāvākya) such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) which have been investigated for their true reality. || 96 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "In that case, since immediate knowledge is established through a single inquiry into the statement according to the method previously described, the repeated practice of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth—which is enjoined in passages such as 'repetition because of the teaching being given more than once'—would not need to be performed.
Anticipating this doubt, he states that it must indeed be performed, for the Teachers have declared that its repetition is to be practiced for the sake of strengthening knowledge.
Let it be that direct realization arises here from the Great Sentence; nevertheless, this [realization]—
It is not firm because the teachers urge [the student] toward hearing and the other [limbs of yoga] once again. || 97 ||

"Let there be awakening. Here, let there be immediate (aparokṣa) awakening regarding the subject of Brahman-Ātman from the Great Saying (mahāvākya), heard once and accompanied by inquiry. Even if this be so, it is not yet firm; therefore, hearing (śravaṇa) and the rest must be repeated. This is the meaning, because the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarācārya has stated that one should repeat hearing and the other means even after the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence has arisen. From this, the phrase "for the sake of strengthening knowledge" (jñānadārḍhyāya) is obtained as the sense. || 97 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Even there, an objection is raised: "Let it be so. However, for Devadatta—who has grasped the power (*śakti*) of words and their meanings—the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) arising from the authoritative statement (*āptavākya*) qualified by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors certainly arises as a firm valid knowledge (*pramā*). Since this is so in cases such as "O son of Kuntī, you are the tenth" or "You are That," where is the need for firmness in that instance? To this, he says: "Of hearing and the rest," etc.
By the remainder. || 97 ||
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
Until the realization of the meaning of the statement "I am Brahman" becomes firmly established.
One should practice hearing and the other [limbs of yoga], accompanied by tranquility and the rest. || 98 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Anticipating the question of by which statement this was declared by the Teachers, he recites that statement: "I am Brahman. || 98 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, in response to the inquiry as to what that statement of the Teacher is, he recites that very sentence found in the *Bṛhadvākyavṛtti*: "I am Brahman. This word "iti" connects with the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence, and not with the sentence itself; otherwise, even if "ahaṃ brahmāsmi" were taken as a mere representative of the sentence, there would be the undesirable consequence of failing to include sentences such as "tat tvam asi. This is the intended sense. [The text continues: "udaraṃbharya-"...
To exclude [the notion that it is] practice, he says "it pacifies" (*śameti*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), reflection (*manana*) and so forth are included. || 98 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might ask, "Why is the knowledge produced by the means of valid verbal testimony not firm? Anticipating this, he says:
"Certainly, there are causes for its firmness; [one such cause is] the multiplicity of scriptural texts."
The impossibility of the matter and its contrary mental cultivation. || 99 ||
"Certainly. For indeed, there are certainly many causes for firmness; they exist in every way. These are: first, the multiplicity of scriptural texts (*śruti*), which is the diversity of the Vedas;

second, the impossibility of the object itself—the non-dual Brahman, which is of an undivided, single-flavored nature—due to its being beyond the world of ordinary experience; and third, contrary mental impressions (*viparīta-bhāvanā*) in the form of the egoistic conceit of agency. Therefore, because these causes are present, [the firmness of conviction arises] through direct experience (*aparokṣānubhava*).
The sense is that the recitation of the *śravaṇa* and other rites must be repeated for each deity. || 99 ||

A0. Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even according to the Teachers, once the verbal cognition in the form of valid knowledge has arisen from the sentence and has destroyed the ignorance regarding that same object, why was the practice of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth enjoined in the manner described for the sake of further strengthening it? What is the reason for this?
Anticipating this doubt, he provides the resolution: "Certainly" (*bāḍham*). This has been stated by the venerable feet of the lordly sage Sarvajñātmamuni: [The verse follows...]

Just as an intellect, though it may arise from flawless eyes, does not result in its fruit when it is defiled by human error and does not have a straight object, so too is the cognition regarding the Self, even though it arises from the Vedas.
But when human error has ceased, it becomes fruitful again through the removal of obstacles;
just as, for example, when a gem or a mantra is removed, a column of smoke arises from fire.

Thus, by both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is established that the causes for the lack of firmness in the aforementioned valid knowledge (*pramā*) are, in order, as stated by the words "multiplicity of scriptures" (*śruti-anekatā*) and so forth: (1) doubt regarding the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-asaṃbhāvanā*), (2) doubt regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya-asaṃbhāvanā*), (3) contrary contemplation regarding the means (*sādhana-viparīta-bhāvanā*), and—by the force of the word "and" (*ca*)—contrary contemplation regarding the result (*phala-viparīta-bhāvanā*).

These are the four obstacles [to be removed] through the study of the *Catur-lakṣaṇī*, the latter part of the *Mīmāṃsā*, under the grace of the feet of a teacher who is both learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman (*brahma-niṣṭha*).

In this [work], those things to be refuted are indicated by the four chapters—named *Samanvaya*, *Avirodha*, *Sādhana*, and *Phala*—which have been elucidated in the commentaries of Śrīmad-Bhagavatpāda and others, and which take as their objects the processes of hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), and samādhi. || 99 ||

Rāma’s Commentary — Having thus set forth the three causes for a lack of firm conviction, he states that repeated hearing (*śravaṇāvṛtti*) must be performed to remove the lack of firm conviction caused by the diversity of scriptural texts (*śrutinānātva*):
Due to the differences in Vedic branches and the differences in desires, the ritual action heard [in scripture] varies from one case to another.
Therefore, one should practice listening so that no such doubt arises here as well.

Regarding the term "branch" (*śākhā*): just as a difference in ritual action is heard [in scripture] due to a difference in branches, as in, "That which is performed by the *Ṛgveda* is the office of the *Hotṛ*, that by the *Yajurveda* is the office of the *Adhvaryu*, and that by the *Sāmaveda* is the *Udgītha*"; or just as there is a difference due to a difference in desire, as in, "One desiring rain should sacrifice with the *Kārīrī*, one desiring long life [should sacrifice] with the *Śatakṛṣṇala*."
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 244.

[The distinction between various ritual acts, such as that known as the *Tṛptidīpa*, has been heard. Thus, even regarding the Upaniṣads, when there arises a doubt concerning a difference in the reality being propounded, the meaning is that one must listen again and again in order to dispel that doubt. (100)

Commentary (Ṭīkā): In this context, in order to dispel the doubt regarding the impossibility of valid means of knowledge caused by the multiplicity of scriptural texts (*śruti*), he prescribes that hearing (*śravaṇa*) itself must be performed, using a negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*) from the previous system [of Mīmāṃsā]: "Due to the difference of branches... It is recorded in scripture that there is a difference in ritual action due to the difference of branches, as in: "The office of the Hotṛ priest is performed with the Ṛgveda, the office of the Adhvaryu with the Yajurveda, and the Udgītha with the Sāmaveda. "One desiring rain should sacrifice... [and so forth].

The passage beginning with “One desiring cattle [should sacrifice] with three” and so forth arises from the distinction of desires; thus, the meaning is that here in this section on Brahman (*brahmakāṇḍa*), just as in the previous section (*pūrvakāṇḍa*), there is likewise a distinction of Brahman—this is the implicit sense. Therefore, one should not entertain any doubt regarding the distinctions within Brahman; hence, the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) should practice hearing (*śravaṇa*). This is the completion of the thought. || 100 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In response to the inquiry as to what that "hearing" (śravaṇa) is, he states its definition:
"Of all the Vedāntas, from the beginning, middle, and end..."
The understanding that the purport [of the scriptures] lies solely in Brahman as the Self constitutes "hearing" (śravaṇa). || 1 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the Vedāntas": upon a thorough examination of the beginning, conclusion, and other criteria of all the Upaniṣads, it is determined that their purport lies solely in the inner self (pratyagātman) whose nature is Brahman. This certainty—that this is the ultimate, indirect goal—is what is meant by "hearing" (śravaṇa). || 1 ||
Commentary (a0): Let it be so; nevertheless, in response to the inquiry as to what the definition of "hearing" (śravaṇa) is, he summarizes it with the words: "Of the Vedāntas" (vedāntānām). || 101 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: To the question, "Where is such hearing (śravaṇa) described?", he says: "This has been well-stated in the Chapter on Concordance (Samanvayādhyāya) by those who bring about the stability of the intellect."
In the second chapter, the possibility of the object [of knowledge] was explained through logical arguments.

Regarding the phrase "the chapter on concordance" (*samanvayādhyāya*): the ellipsis is that this hearing (*śravaṇa*) was well-expounded by Vyāsa and others in the chapter on concordance. He states "mental composure" (*dhīsvāsthya*) to indicate that reflection (*manana*), which is the cause for removing doubts regarding the impossibility of the meaning, has been described in the second chapter. Through arguments denoted by the word "reasoning" (*yukti*)—which produce mental composure by means of resolving inconsistencies concerning the object of knowledge—the possibility of the meaning is established. Once the meaning has been rendered possible...
The meaning is that reflection (*manana*), which consists of the continuous pursuit of [the truth] regarding you, has been described in the second chapter. || 2 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that the purport (*tātparya*), which is difficult for those who are not omniscient to discern, is determined by means such as the introductory context (*upakrama*). To this, he says: "Samanvaya" [etc.].

This refers to the aforementioned definition of purport. The implicit meaning is that this was well-stated by the venerable teacher Bādarāyaṇa. Thus, he states that reflection (*manana*), which has the result of removing doubt regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*), is also taught in that very same *Brahmasūtra*, in the second chapter titled "Non-contradiction" (*avirodha*)—beginning with the word "dhi" [etc.].
Day by day. || 102 ||
Due to firm habituation over many births, the notion of a self arises instantaneously with respect to the body and so forth.
In this way, even the cognition of the reality of the world arises again and again.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now he shows the contrary conception and the means for its cessation: "bahujanma... (verse 3).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Granted that this is so; nevertheless, what is this previously mentioned twofold contrary conception (*viparītabhāvanā*) that is to be removed by the meditation (*nididhyāsana*) prescribed in the Śruti passage, 'The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon'? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the answer with the verse beginning with "bahujanma" and its quarter-line. Thus, in this context, the referent of the word "Self" (*ātmapadārtha*) would be nothing other than the first body and so forth, and not [the true Self].

The first is the meditation on [the Self] as pure consciousness characterized by being the witness of that [world], which constitutes a meditation contrary to the means (*sādhanaviparītabhāvanā*). The second, however, is the meditation contrary to the result (*phalaviparītabhāvanā*), which holds that duality alone is real, and not liberation characterized by the bliss of the self-luminous Brahman—the result consisting in the falsity of duality brought about by the cessation of ignorance through the knowledge of reality. This is the distinction. || 103 ||
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
This cultivation is contrary [to reality]; it ceases through one-pointedness of mind.
This occurs even before the instruction on the reality, through the practice of this very [meditation].

245. Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Regarding the phrase "viparīta" (contrary), one might ask from what source this one-pointedness (*aikāgya*) arises, which turns back contrary mental impressions (*bhāvanā*).

Anticipating this, he says: "tattva... (from the reality...). This one-pointedness occurs even before the instruction on Brahman, through the meditation (*upāsanā*) upon Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahman*).
The meaning is "having known. || 4 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask, "How is this [distracted state] not removed? To this he says: "From one-pointedness" (*aikāgyāt*). By the second quarter [of the verse], the meaning is: from the cessation of mental modifications (*cittavṛtti-nirodha*) produced by reflecting upon the aforementioned established conclusions (*siddhānta*) declared in the third and fourth chapters of the *Uttara-mīmāṃsā*. [Objection: But is not one-pointedness, as defined above, [attained only after] becoming "calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated" (*śānto dānta uparatastitikṣuḥ samāhito bhūtvā*), and [as stated in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, 1.2.24]: "Not for one who is not detached from evil deeds..."?

If [the opponent] with firm intent accepts [the following], saying: "One who does not eat the truth (ritānna), who is not tranquil, who is not concentrated, or whose mind is not peaceful, cannot attain this through wisdom"—thus, by both positive and negative scriptural statements (*anvaya-vyatireka-śruti*) and from his own experience prior to that, [he argues] that this [wisdom] is already established by means of the *nirodha-samādhi* prescribed as a qualification for the seeker—[the author replies]: "Because of meditation" (*upāsanāt*). [This refers to] meditation on the qualified (*saguṇa*) or unqualified (*nirguṇa*) Brahman, or on a symbol (*pratīka*), or on the "I-grasping" (*ahaṃgraha*).

The meaning is: "From the extensive practice of bhāvanā, characterized by the production of uninterrupted mental modifications (cittavṛtti) in the form of that [object] alone, which is denoted by the term 'worship' (mopāsti). || 104 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, raising the question "How is this known?", he states that because the investigation of meditations has been conducted within the Vedānta scriptures:
"Therefore, the meditations have also been considered here in this treatise on Brahman."
For one who has not practiced previously, that state may be attained through the subsequent practice of Brahman.
Regarding the phrase "meditations" (upāstayah): since one who has not performed meditation could not have such a birth, he says "previously" (prāk). || 105 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He states the reasoning for that with the words "meditations" (upāstayah). Here, in this work titled *Prakṛta-Uttara-Mīmāṃsā*, they have been "considered," meaning they have been investigated at the beginning of the third chapter. He reveals that very hidden intention with the word "previously" (prāk).

As it has been stated in the *Jīvanmuktiviveka*: "For this very reason, the one qualified for knowledge (*vidyā*) is of two kinds: one who has performed meditation (*kṛtopāsti*) and one who has not performed meditation (*akṛtopāsti*). Among these—"

If, after performing upāsanā (meditative worship) until it culminates in the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the Self, one proceeds toward knowledge (*jñāna*), then—due to the firmness of the reality of the dissolution of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) and the destruction of the mind (*manonāśa*)—the renunciation of the knower (*vidvatsaṃnyāsa*) and liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) are accomplished spontaneously after that knowledge. Such a person alone is the primary qualified candidate intended by the scriptures. Therefore, although the renunciation of the knower and the renunciation of the seeker (*vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa*) are distinct in their essential nature, they are presented together in the scriptures with reference to such a person.

The two appear as if they were confused. However, those of the present day, for the most part having performed no prior spiritual discipline (*upāsti*), suddenly engage in knowledge (*vidyā*) out of mere eagerness.

They then bring about the temporary destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) and the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*). By that much, they accomplish hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana*);
and through these, when firmly practiced, true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) duly arises by means of the removal of ignorance, doubt, and error. Of that [knowledge], the subverting cognition—

Since ignorance has ceased due to its non-existence, and because there is no further cause for its arising, there is no possibility of its weakening. However, the dissolution of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) and the destruction of the mind (*manonāśa*) quickly recede—like a lamp in a windy place—because of the absence of firm practice and because they are repeatedly obstructed by *prārabdha* karma, which brings about the experience of yoga. Thus says Vasiṣṭha:

"Indeed, this abandonment of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) is considered more difficult than all previous efforts; it is harder to accomplish even than uprooting Mount Sumeru. Arjuna also said: "O Kṛṣṇa, the mind is indeed restless, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate; its restraint—I [find it]..."
"Or like the wind, it is extremely difficult to achieve.

Therefore, for the learned renunciants (*vidvatsaṃnyāsins*) of the present day, there is merely the persistence of knowledge; however, the dissolution of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) and the destruction of the mind (*manonāśa*) require effort.

"...it is established that [these] are not to be accomplished. Now, one might object: even for a qualified seeker who has performed the meditations (*upāsti*), although the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) duly arises through the gradual removal of ignorance, doubt, and error by means of hearing, reflection, and meditation (*nididhyāsana*) practiced with firm intensity, nevertheless—[due to] the lack of the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*)—...
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 246.

It has been stated in the *Tṛptidīpa* that because of the absence of firm practice regarding the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*) and the realization of the Self (*ātma-darśana*), those two alone must be accomplished through effort. However, you have here introduced this "desire-based" (*aikāmya*) *nididhyāsana*, which serves to remove contrary impressions (*viparīta-bhāvanā*). Although the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*) rooted in that [practice] indeed arises even prior to the instruction of reality (*tattva-upadeśa*) through meditation, nevertheless—

If it is asked: "What is the connection between this and what precedes it?"—namely, that in the absence of prior practice in meditation (*upāsanā*), one-pointedness toward That [Brahman] may arise through the practice of Brahman—itself, we reply: there is none, because of a lack of understanding of the matter. To explain: here, beginning with the passage "this arises from the meditation on It even before the instruction of reality," and ending with the section stating that for one who has not practiced previously, it may come about later through the practice of Brahman, [the author] establishes that prior to the instruction of Brahman...

For one who has performed *upāsanā*, one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgyra*) is indeed established by nature; thus, it becomes firm merely through the arising of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). However, for one who has not performed *upāsanā*, this one-pointedness does not arise; therefore, it must be achieved through the practice of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) to uproot doubts (*asaṃbhāvanā*), and through the repeated meditation on Brahman (*brahmābhyāsa*) known as *nididhyāsana* to destroy contrary notions (*viparītabhāvanā*). This has been stated, and it is likewise [explained] in the aforementioned *Jīvanmuktiviveka*.

Is it not so? What inconsistency is there here? As for the fact that in that [other] context it was stated that even for one whose ignorance has ceased (*nivṛttāvidya*), liberation through the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*) and so forth must be accomplished for the sake of *jīvanmukti*, whereas here it is stated that for one who is not yet such [a person], one-pointedness is to be accomplished through the practice of Brahman for the sake of removing contrary conceptions (*viparītabhāvanā*);
this collection of internal differences does not undermine the agreement regarding the primary point previously mentioned. This is the direction of the argument. || 105 ||
Reflecting upon that, speaking of that, and mutually awakening one another to that.
And the wise know that single-minded devotion to this is the practice of Brahman.
— Rāma’s Commentary — In response to the inquiry as to what kind of practice constitutes the cultivation of Brahman, he says: "That [practice] consists of concentration... (verse 6).

The commentary (ṭīkā) explains the very practice of Brahman that was promised: "That meditation" (*taccintanam*). The word "in solitude" (*ekānte*) is to be understood as implied. Thus, in the absence of disciples who are inferior or equal to oneself, there is the teaching of that [Brahman] and so forth in due order. The word "alone" (*eka*) is for the purpose of excluding others while one is awake. || 106 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To clarify this exclusive devotion to Him alone, he cites the Śruti:
"Having known that very [Self], the wise Brāhmaṇa should cultivate wisdom."
One should not meditate on many words, for that is a weariness of speech.

"Regarding that very [Self]": the wise *brāhmaṇa*—endowed with the means such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and desiring to become Brahman, that is, seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*)—should, having realized that very Supreme Self which is the innermost form, and having known it in such a way that doubt and the like cease to exist, cultivate—that is, accomplish—*prajñā*, which consists of a continuous stream of knowledge regarding the unity of Brahman and the Self. He should not meditate upon nor recollect the many words whose objects are the non-Self (*anātman*).

By the term "meditation" (dhyāna), verbal expression is also indicated; for otherwise, one could not express [anything], since the exhaustion of speech would be impossible through meditation on words. To the question "Why?", he says: "Of speech" (vācaḥ). For that is its expression. By this, remembrance is also indicated. "Of speech" is an elliptical expression for "of the mind" as well. "Exhaustion" (viglāpana) means that which causes exhaustion (*viglāpayati*); it is the cause of fatigue. This is the intended meaning: other than...
In the continuous application of giving, there is fatigue of the mind; but in the verbal expression thereof, there is fatigue of speech. || 7 ||

— Commentary (a0 ṭīkā) — He cites scripture as authority for the practice of meditation on Brahman characterized as described above: "Tameva...
