[The text continues: "The wise one" (*dhīraḥ*) is one who possesses celibacy and other such virtues. "Having known that very one"—that is, having realized the non-dual Self (*advaitātman*) without doubt and through direct perception (*aparokṣīkṛtya*). "A Brāhmaṇa" refers to...

This refers to the intention of being established in Brahman as an inevitable necessity. And thus it is recorded by the Kāṇvas: "Having finished with scholarship, one should desire to abide in childlike simplicity; having finished with both scholarship and childlike simplicity, one becomes a sage; and having finished with both non-sagehood and sagehood, one becomes a Brāhmaṇa. The meaning of this Śruti has been explained by the venerable Vidyāraṇya-svāmī in the *Anubhūtiprakāśa*:

“Scholarship, childhood, and silence—these are hearing [the scriptures] and so forth; by means of these one becomes a Brāhmaṇa. In this context, ‘Brāhmaṇahood’ is the state of being Brahman. The detailed explanation of the meaning of the individual components and so forth should be understood from that very source. For this reason, it says “prajñām” (wisdom) and so on. This means a continuous flow of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) whose object is the identity of Brahman and the Self. By this, *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) is implied. He states the fault in not performing it with the words beginning with “na” (not). Hearing...
The Seventh Chapter.

This includes even those [words] established by the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) such as *praṇava* and so forth; this is the implied meaning (*ārthika*). It is intended to indicate the inclusion of a limited number of words suitable for the continuous contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*) of the Self, beginning with the *praṇava*.

"Many" means that one should not contemplate, nor reflect upon, nor even remember them. The reason for this is given by the words "of speech," etc., based on the Vedic scripture: "Whatever one contemplates with the mind, that very thing one speaks with speech. || 107 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Having thus cited the Śruti that establishes one-pointedness, he also cites the Smṛti:
"Those people who worship Me, thinking of no other..."
For those who are constantly devoted to Me, I provide for their well-being and security.

"Those who are non-different": those persons who, being non-different through the knowledge "I am Brahman," are identical with Me, and thus meditating on Me in that very way, worship Me—worship Me constantly at all times—remaining as My very form; for them, who are eternally disciplined and whose minds are always fixed on Me, I, being realized as their own Self, provide *yoga-kṣema*, which consists of the attainment of what has not been obtained and the preservation of what has been obtained.
"I carry out and accomplish *yogakṣema*"; this is the meaning. || 8 ||

In the commentary on verse 1, he corroborates the stated meaning with Smṛti: "Ananyāḥ" (non-different). This means those people who have performed the hearing and reflection (*śravaṇa* and *manana*) upon the Vedāntas as previously described, and who desire to know the reality of the Supreme Self. "Mām" refers to Me, the non-dual Supreme Self. "Ananyāḥ" [means] "I am Brahman."

"Endowed with the meditation on non-difference from 'Smī'" means being joined with that very thought. "They contemplate" means they are meditating; the sense is that they remain as if they have attained identity with Me. "I" refers to the Supreme Self contemplated in the manner described. "Of them"—meaning of those practitioners of the aforementioned form—"I carry their yoga and kṣema," which means the attainment of stages not yet reached, preceded by the preservation of stages already attained. I do this precisely through their having ascended to the aforementioned meditation.
The connection is: "I shall accomplish. || 108 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the purport of the cited Śruti and Smṛti passages:
"Thus, the Śruti and Smṛti [enjoin] constant one-pointedness of the intellect upon the Self."
For they are prescribed for the destruction of contrary mental cultivation.

Regarding the word "iti": the meaning is that these two, Śruti and Smṛti, establish constant one-pointedness of mind upon the Self for the purpose of removing contrary mental impressions (viparīta-bhāvanā). || 9 ||

The commentary on verse a0 states the purport of the aforementioned scripture and so forth: "Thus" (iti). The particle "hi" is used for emphasis. That is to say, it is solely for the purpose of destroying contrary mental impressions (viparītabhāvanā). || 109 ||
The cognition of something as being otherwise, having abandoned its true nature as it actually exists.
It would be a perverted cultivation, just like the notion of an enemy toward one's father and so forth. || 110 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: "From what cause do the notions of the body and so forth being the Self, and the notion of the world being real, constitute erroneous conceptions (*viparītabhāvanā*)? Anticipating this, he states their definition in order to show that they possess the characteristics of such conceptions, beginning with the words "Whatever... as it is. Whatever object—such as mother-of-pearl—exists in a certain way, namely, in the form of mother-of-pearl and so on; its reality is its nature as mother-of-pearl. To abandon that and to have a cognition of it as something else—that is "being otherwise" (*anyathātva*).

The cognition—that is, the knowledge—of this [object] having the form of silver and so forth would be a "perverse mental impression" (viparītabhāvanā). This means, in short, the cognition of something as being what it is not. He provides an illustration of this: "in the case of a father and so forth. || 110 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, in response to the inquiry as to what the characteristics of this very "perverse contemplation" (viparīta-bhāvanā) are, the author defines it with the words "That which...

He illustrates it with the passage beginning "In [the case of] one's father, etc. The phrase "delimited by dim darkness, etc. is to be understood as implied. Furthermore, since the nature of that [contemplation] was already described previously by the words "through many births," there is no tautology. || 110 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 248.
[In the commentary on the *Tṛptidīpa* by Rāma: He applies the previously stated definition to the present subject:
"This Self is distinct from the body and so forth, and this world is false; these two..."
The notion that the body and so forth are the self, and the conviction in their reality, is the cultivation of error. (11)

"Self" (ātman): this self is in reality distinct from the body and so forth; and this world is false. Even though this is so, the notion that these two—the self and the world—respectively take the form of the body and so forth, and the notion that they are real, is what is meant by "perverse conceptualization" (viparīta-bhāvanā). || 11 ||

Commentary (ṭīkā): He applies the previously stated definition of erroneous mental impression (*viparītabhāvanā*)—beginning with "due to firm practice over many births" and so forth—to its essential nature as well, stating: "The Self... (verse 111).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having previously stated the matter in general terms—that it ceases through one-pointedness—he now states it in a specific form:
"Through the contemplation of reality, that [ignorance] perishes; therefore, [one should contemplate] the state of being distinct from the body."
One should constantly cultivate within oneself that the world is entirely false.

Regarding the phrase "by the contemplation of reality" (*tattvabhāvanayā*): that [contemplation] is the contrary notion consisting of the ideas of the body and so forth being the self and the world being real. It would perish through the contemplation of reality—that is, through the continuous meditation on the self’s transcendence of the body and the world’s falsity.
Therefore, it is said that one should always contemplate the self’s transcendence of the body and so forth, as well as the falsity of the world consisting of the body and so forth. || 12 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Let this be so; however, for one who is distressed by the question, "Even if this be the case, how might this [mind] be pacified?", the author states its specific means—characterized by one-pointedness of mind achievable through the previously mentioned practice of Brahman—by way of its general nature, saying, "By the contemplation of reality" (*tattvabhāvanayā*). Furthermore, when there is a need to distinguish the objects therein, he summarizes that with the words beginning "Therefore" (*ataḥ*) along with their supporting reasons. Now, as for the fruit that arises from contemplation...

And if there were a fruit of action, it should not remain [permanently], just as in the case of union with a courtesan; for the *Vārttika* states that fruits produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—whether born of ritual action or otherwise—are perishable. If it is asked: "How can there be no further arising of the contrary cultivation once the cultivation of reality has been destroyed?"—the answer is no, because the aforementioned *Vārttika* refers to the cultivation existing prior to the attainment of the knowledge of reality, whereas the cultivation in question here is...

This is for the sake of strengthening that [knowledge], because it consists merely in the subsequent investigation of reality, and because it yields a fruit identical to the knowledge of reality; this is indeed clear further on as well. || 112 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In this regard, he asks whether there is a requirement for observances (niyama), as there is in the case of mantra-recitation and the like, or not—namely, whether the cognition of non-difference from the Self [is achieved] like the recitation of mantras or like the meditation on the Form (mūrti).
And here, should the cognition of the world's falsity be what is to be excluded, or otherwise? (13)

"What is meant by 'like the recitation of mantras'? [The question is: Is the cognition of the self's distinctness—the knowledge that the self is separate from the body and so forth, as well as the contemplation on the falsity of the world—to be practiced according to fixed rules like the recitation of mantras, meditation on deities, and so on; or can it be performed even without such rules, like ordinary worldly activity? || 13 ||

Commentary (a0): In this regard, it is beyond dispute that *bhāvanā* (meditative cultivation) is indeed a continuous succession of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) taking on the form of the object to be cultivated (*bhāvya*), according to both of the aforementioned definitions.

Nevertheless, based on such Smṛti texts as "The Goddess whose limit is a thousand," should one, during the morning twilight worship (*prātaḥ-saṃdhyopāsana*), necessarily repeat with a fixed number—like the daily recitation of a thousand [mantras]—both the mental modification whose object is the identity of Brahman and the Self, and the mental modification whose object is the falsity of duality? Or...

Or, based on the *Pātañjala Sūtra*—“Dhyāna is the one-pointedness of the mind upon that object”—one should contemplate by establishing a continuous flow of mental modifications of the same kind as the object of meditation, unassailed by modifications of a different kind.

One might then ask, having raised the alternative: "Should the meditation on Viṣṇu and others prescribed in the *Bhāgavata* and other texts—such as 'one should meditate on the lotus-feet of the Blessed Lord'—be performed every day at the *brāhma-muhūrta* and so forth, or is it rather indefinite according to another method? Thus he asks: "What?"
Thus it is said in the mantra. 113.
The Seventh Chapter: Equality of the Two Commentaries.
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: He says that because it yields visible results, there is no fixed rule here:
"Know it otherwise," meaning that due to its having a visible purpose, it is like eating.
One who desires to eat eats like one who recites prayers; no one is ever truly restrained.

"Otherwise" means without a restrictive rule (*niyama*). He states the reason for this: "because it has a visible purpose" (*dṛṣṭārthatvena*). Regarding that, he provides an illustration: "like eating" (*bhuktivat*). Anticipating the objection that even in the case of eating—which serves a visible purpose—restrictions are observed in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, he replies:
"one who is hungry. A person desiring to eat in order to remove hunger does not eat according to a restrictive rule, just as one performing a recitation (*japa*) does not.
Rather, the meaning is that he takes food in such a way that the affliction of hunger may be pacified. || 14 ||
Commentary (a0): Therein, he provides a resolution by relying on the final limit [of the argument] through two verses beginning with "Otherwise" (anyathā). || 114 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He elaborates on this very point:
"He eats or does not eat; he enjoys [pleasures] according to his own will or otherwise."
By whatever means possible, he desires to dispel his hunger. || 115 ||

"He eats" means: when food is available, he sometimes eats, or he does not eat; when it is not available, he passes his time without eating at all due to activities such as gambling that distract from the affliction of hunger. Or else, whether standing, walking, or lying down, he eats according to his own whim. In this way, by whatever means possible, he desires to remove the immediate pangs of hunger. This is the underlying intention regarding hunger.

One should perform eating itself for the sake of the visible fruit characterized by the cessation of the two [extremes]; however, the restrictive rules (niyamas) are for the sake of the next world. || 115 ||
a0 Commentary: "Otherwise" means in the manner described previously, such as by eating only at night (naktādi). || 115 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He shows the distinction between recitation and eating:
"One should perform the recitation as a mandatory rule, because its non-performance results in spiritual transgression."
If it is performed otherwise, there is misfortune due to the inversion of accents and phonemes. || 16 ||

Regarding the term "niyamanā" (restraint), he states the reason for it: "in the case of non-performance. One might object: "Let it be so that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in not performing [the rite]; however, there is no such transgression in performing it otherwise. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "anyathā" (otherwise). For it has been stated: "A mantra deficient in accent or phoneme, if wrongly employed, does not convey its intended meaning. That is a thunderbolt of speech (*vāgvajra*) which destroys the sacrificer, just as Indra’s enemy [was destroyed] due to a fault in the accent."
This is the intended meaning. || 16 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) clarifies the distinction between recitation (*japa*) and eating by means of the word "necessarily" (*niyamena*). This means by a fixed rule regarding the daily number of repetitions, such as one thousand. It indicates the reason for this with the phrase "if not performed": the meaning is that scriptural tradition (*smṛti*) reveals a transgression (*pratyavāya*), as in the passage, "One who neglects the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) is eternally impure and unfit for all ritual acts. Not only is there this much restriction, but there is another as well—
He says "otherwise" (anyathā); the reason for this is given as "in terms of accent" (svarataḥ). [As it is said:
"A mantra that is deficient in accent or phoneme, if incorrectly employed, does not convey its intended meaning."

That thunderbolt of speech destroys the sacrificer, just as Indra’s enemy [was destroyed] due to an error in accent; the point is that it is well known in the *Śikṣā* that the inversion of accents and so forth produces fault. || 16 ||
And cultivation that is contrary [to reality] causes affliction upon being perceived, just like hunger.
By whatever means it may be, there is no sequence of performance here once this has been accomplished.
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, since hunger is a cause of perceived suffering, one must certainly eat even irregularly in order to alleviate it.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [the section titled] Tṛptidīpa (The Lamp of Contentment) 250.

Anticipating the objection that since false contemplation (*parītabhāvanā*) lacks such reality, the meditation that removes it must necessarily be practiced for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭaphala*), he says:
"Just as hunger... The sense is that the fact that false contemplation is a cause of suffering is established by experience. || 17 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, even if this is so, one might ask: "What relevance does this have to the present subject, which is the investigation of reality that shatters contrary conceptions?
To this, he says: "Just as by hunger... (verse 17).
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that the means [to liberation] should therefore be demonstrated, he states that it has already been shown:
"The means was stated previously, consisting of the discourse on the nature of that [Self] and so forth."
Even when one is solely intent upon this, there is indeed no compulsion, just as in the case of meditation.

Regarding the term "means" (upāya): one might object that, unlike recitation (japa), there need not be a fixed rule such as facing the east; however, just as in meditation, there must be a requirement for one-pointedness characterized by exclusive devotion.
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "This... (verse 18).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, what is that means? To this he says: "The means" (upāya). By the word "etc. (ādi), the mutual awakening to that [truth] is included. Nor should it be argued that, even so, since the mental state (cittavṛtti) in the fourth stage—called "exclusive devotion to That"—is devoid of objects other than the Supreme Self and always has That alone as its object, it would entail a great bondage because it is to be accomplished through the eight limbs beginning with restraint (yama); for that [state] is merely a continuous reflection (anusaṃdhāna).
He says that this is because of the distinction [of this] from [ordinary] meditation: "Even when there is single-minded devotion to this... (18).
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Since meditation consists merely of contemplating the object of meditation, what necessity is there for it?
Anticipating this doubt, he first states the nature of meditation in order to demonstrate the necessity for it:
"The continuous flow of the intellect's cognition of the form, uninterrupted by anything else..."
In that state, meditation is the intense application of the mind whose nature is fickle. || 19 ||

Regarding the word "mūrti": the continuity (*sāṃtatyam*) of cognitions related to a form—that is, of those cognitions whose object is the form of a deity and so forth, which exist as an uninterrupted flow—is called "meditation" (*dhyāna*) when it is not interrupted by another, namely, when it is not interposed by a cognition of a different kind (*vijātīya-pratyaya*). Having thus defined the nature of meditation, he shows the necessity for it with the word "tatra" (therein). [He describes one] whose nature is to wander constantly...
The meaning is that it is just as there is an obstruction when an elephant, a horse, or other such animals are tied together at a single post or similar location. || 19 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, raising the doubt as to what the distinction is between *anusaṃdhāna* (contemplative pursuit) and *dhyāna* (meditation), the author briefly defines them with the verse beginning "mūrti" and so forth. The word "mūrti" (form) refers to the qualified (saguṇa) aspect [of the deity]. The word "dhiyaḥ" (of the intellect) should be construed with that very term [mūrti] earlier. Nevertheless, he states what [the distinction] is therein with the remainder of the verse beginning "tatra" and so forth. "Nirbandhaḥ" means restraint (*nirodhaḥ*). || 19 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He cites a statement from the Gītā as authority regarding the restlessness of the mind:
"For the mind, O Kṛṣṇa, is restless, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate."
I consider his restraint to be as difficult to achieve as that of the wind.
"Indeed, it is restless," etc. "Distracting" (*pramāthi*) means having the nature of agitating; the meaning is that it is the cause of a person's agitation, powerful, capable, and uncontrollable.

"Firm" (*dṛḍha*) means that whether an object is present or absent, once it has become attached to it, it is impossible to extract [the mind] from there. Therefore, the restraint of that mind is as extremely difficult as the restraint of the wind. (120)

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): In this regard, he supports Arjuna’s statement with the words "For it is restless" (cañcalam hi). He says "disturbing" (pramāthī) and so forth because even a restless animal and the like can be killed; the meaning is that [the mind] has the nature of disturbing discrimination through desire, is difficult to restrain due to powerful obsession, and cannot be drawn away from firm objects such as women. || 120 ||
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.
Even from drinking a great quantity of poison, or even from uprooting Mount Sumeru.
Moreover, O virtuous one, the restraint of the mind is difficult even for one who has conquered hunger.
16.1 Rāghavānanda’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): He also cites a statement from the Vāsiṣṭha as authority for the mind's difficulty in being restrained—beginning with "api" (even). ||21||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): In this very manner, the venerable Vasiṣṭha also spoke thus, beginning with the word "api" (even). The term "of the great" (*mahataḥ*) is used for the sake of signifying the period of the single ocean (*ekārṇava*). Since the drinking of the seven oceans was performed by Agastya, [the phrase] "well indeed" (*sumeva*) is used because that [drinking] was also performed by the Creator (*vidhātṛ*) at the time of creation. Furthermore, since that [creation] was limited by the bow of Hara and performed by Rāma, [the phrase] "also" (*api*) is used; and since even that was performed by Kṛṣṇa... [the phrase] "also" (*api*) is used.
"Like a horse," [it is said]. || 21 ||
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: In the present context, he shows the distinction from that [previous case]:
"There is no compulsion at the beginning of the narration, like a body made of adamant bound by chains."
However, those whose intellects are enriched by diversion through the ancient histories and other such works [are not so affected]. || 22 ||

Regarding the phrase "in narration and so forth": the meaning is that for one whose body is bound by chains, there is no such restriction in narration and so forth as there is in other circumstances. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), activities such as thinking about those [topics] are included. He states with "but rather" (*kiṃtu*) that not only is there an absence of restriction, but on the contrary, it is a diversion for the intellect: "Itihāsa" refers to the stories of the ancients; those things beginning with them—such as the presentation of worldly narratives, supporting arguments, and illustrative examples—are [the means]. They are *asaṃ-* [i.e., *asaṃyama* or lack of restraint].
Those histories and so forth are known to be infinite; thus, "infinite histories and so forth" refers to those [works]. The intellect's diversion—that is, its sphere of play—consists of them.
Regarding this, there is an illustration: "like a drama. This means like the observation of a dance performance. || 22 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Granted that there may be such great difficulty regarding meditation (*dhyāna*) due to the manifold defects of the mind's restless nature;

however, how can that absence [of difficulty] exist in the present case of *anusandhāna*—which is characterized by the continuity of memory whose object is the non-dual identity of Brahman and the Self, realized through the prior sublation of the falsity of duality?
In response to this expectation, the author elaborates upon that very point with the words beginning "In the narration, etc. The word "etc. (*ādi*) includes mutual instruction regarding that [truth].
"Infinite" means that it is a number well-known from the *Bṛhad-vāsiṣṭha*, the *Mokṣadharma*, the *Sūta-saṃhitā*, and so forth, as established by the Itihāsas and other sources. || 122 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that through discourses and other means, one could also achieve single-minded devotion to That through knowledge; anticipating this, he says:
"Consciousness alone is the Self, and the world is illusory"—in this [knowledge] one reaches the final conclusion.
The distraction of nididhyāsana cannot be caused by the Itihāsas and other such works. || 23 ||

"Only consciousness (cideva)," etc. The meaning is that since the purport of the *itihāsas* and other such texts culminates in this point—that the Self is of the nature of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and not of the nature of the body and so forth, and that the world is illusory—there is no distraction from *nididhyāsana*, which is designated by the term "exclusive devotion" (*ekaparatva*), caused by them. || 23 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that even through discourse and other such means, there could indeed be an obstruction to those two specific parts of the aforementioned means—namely, the contemplation of That (taccintanā) and exclusive devotion to That (tadekaparatva). To this, he says: "Consciousness alone" (cideva). || 23 ||
In agriculture, commerce, service, and so forth, as well as in poetry, logic, and the like.
The intellect is distracted by their activity because of the impossibility of recollecting reality.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection that if it were accepted that the Itihāsas are authoritative, then agriculture and other such activities would also follow as being so, he says: "Agriculture... (verse 24).

The commentary (ṭīkā) on verse a0 confirms the very point already stated by providing a counter-example: "kṛṣi" etc. By the word "ādi," Vedic ritualistic acts performed for specific desires (kāmya-karma) are to be understood. Having thus described the distraction of the intellect regarding physical activities, he speaks of it regarding verbal activities as well—those concerning objects other than Brahman—starting with "kāvyā" etc. By the word "ādi," all the compositions of those who propound duality are included. The reason for this is given in the final quarter of the verse: "tair... and so forth. || 24 ||
The Pañcadaśī, composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 252]
[Commentary by Rāmānanda on the *Tṛptidīpa*:
Now, one might object that since agriculture and similar activities obstruct the investigation into reality (*tattvānusaṃdhāna*), they must be abandoned;
and if that is so, then even eating and other such acts, being of the same nature, should also be abandoned. Anticipating this doubt, he says:]
One should indeed apply oneself here to engaging in eating and other such activities.
It is possible [to do so] because of the absence of extreme distraction and because of the swift recovery of mindfulness. || 125 ||
"It is precisely by one who is connecting [the thoughts]. Why? To this he says: "Because of the absolute... Why is there also an absence of distraction? To this he says:
"...because of the swift recollection again. (125)
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that since even eating and other such acts, like agriculture and the like, cause one to forget the ultimate reality (tattva), they too ought to be abandoned.

To this, he says: "by one who is indeed maintaining [the connection]," and so forth. By the word "etc. (ādi), the entire daily routine (āhnika) is intended. The reason for this is given by the words "extremely" (atyanta). The reason for that, in turn, is given by the words "swiftly" (āśu) and so on. In the section on Right Conduct (sadācāra-prakaraṇa), the venerable author of the Bhāṣya [Śrī Madhvācārya] stated that the duality (dvaita) of the entire daily routine...

The sense is that since [the practice] is prescribed as being of the nature of contemplating the non-duality of Brahman and the Self—which is preceded by [the removal of] false belief—and since I have also explained it exactly in that way in my commentary on that [text], the recollection arises again for one who has quickly engaged in eating and so forth after reflecting upon that [commentary]. || 125 ||
Misfortune arises not from the mere forgetting of reality, but rather from its perversion.
There is no time for error at any point for one who recollects [the Lord] instantaneously. || 26 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even if there is an absence of distraction at that time, since forgetfulness of reality still exists, there would be a loss of the purpose of human life.
Anticipating this, he says: "Forgetfulness of reality... Why, then, does misfortune arise? To this he replies: "But from error...
Anticipating the objection that "if forgetfulness occurs, error will also occur," he says: "In order to err... (26)

— Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Even so, there could still be a forgetting of reality during the intervals occupied by necessary activities such as eating. To this, he says: "tattva... (verse 26).

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Just as for one engaged in eating and so forth, why should the recollection of reality not also occur for one engaged in the practice of reasoning and the like?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "There is no opportunity for the recollection of reality for one who is occupied with other practices."
On the contrary, because it is struck down by repeated practice, reality is forcibly disregarded. || 27 ||

Regarding the phrase "from the memory of reality": it is not merely that there is an absence of opportunity for the contemplation of reality; rather, because the semblance of poetry, logic, and so forth is contrary to the practice of reality, even if reality is remembered at that time, it is forcibly set aside. Thus he says: "On the contrary... (verse 27).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "In that case, just as with eating and other such acts, let there be a swift recollection of reality for one who practices reasoning and the like. Anticipating this, he provides the resolution: "Of the recollection of reality... It is not merely that there is no opportunity for it there; rather, there is even opposition. Thus he says: "On the contrary... [The term] *upekṣyate* means it is abandoned. || 27 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: As proof for the necessity of abandoning verbal discourse that contradicts the investigation into reality, he recites the meaning of the scriptural passage, "Know Him alone; abandon other words; He is the bridge to immortality," as follows:
"Know Him alone as the One; indeed, abandon other words."
Thus it has been heard elsewhere: "But [this] is merely a weariness of speech. (28)
Regarding the phrase "only that," he says "likewise" (tathā), because this sentence is also heard in scripture: "One should not meditate on many words, for that is a weariness of speech. || 28 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, it has been established and accepted that worldly activities such as eating are not in conflict with the inquiry into reality;
[this concludes] the seventh chapter.

Anticipating the objection that "if the study of the Vedas and other scriptures is disregarded because it is opposed [to non-duality] due to its dualistic nature, then the scholarship of the Advaitins is poorly adorned," [the author] states: "accompanied by the two commentaries. (253)

"Having understood through the Veda alone that very [Self] which was previously taught, the wise Brāhmaṇa should cultivate wisdom; he should not meditate on many words, for that is a weariness of speech. Even though this has been established, for one who is prone to forgetting it, the author recollects that same Vedic passage by reading another such scripture in substance: "Know that One alone as the Self; other [words]... Thus it is chanted by the followers of the Atharva Veda: "Know that One alone as the Self; other [words]... (Note: The final sentence is incomplete in the source text, but the translation reflects the structure and intent of the provided fragment.)
"Release both [ends]; this is the bridge to immortality. The remainder, however, is quite clear. || 28 ||
One should not live by abandoning food and such, nor by abandoning other scriptures.
Why do you not live? For what reason do you maintain such a stubborn persistence in this matter?

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, to one who insists that just as food and other necessities are not abandoned, so too the study of other scriptures and the like should be pursued—apart from the investigation of reality—he says: "Food and so forth... (29).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, he again clearly rebuts the one who is thus intent upon the doctrine of difference (bhedavāda)—beginning with the words "food and so forth" (āhārādi). By the word "and so forth" (ādi), sleep and other such states are included. || 29 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "In that case, how is it that even those who know the truth, such as Janaka and others, engage in activities like governing a kingdom?
To this he replies: "If it is asked how Janaka and others governed their kingdoms, it was due to their firm realization."
Likewise, O Tarka, if it is so for you as well, then either study or practice agriculture.

Regarding the phrase "of Janaka and others": he offers a rebuttal with the intention that, because they possessed firm immediate realization (*dṛḍhāparokṣajñāna*), that [scriptural authority] does not sublate [their experience].
To one who says, "In that case, I too possess firm awakening," he replies: "So be it" (*tathā*). || 130 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Even there, one who is attached to the scriptures of the proponents of difference (bhedavādin) again raises an objection with an illustrative example, beginning with "janakādeḥ.
To that, the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) replies with "dṛḍha. The limit of its firmness has indeed been shown by the venerable author of the Bhāṣya himself in the *Upadeśasāhasrī*:

“Just as the knowledge that the body is the self is sublated by the knowledge that the self is not the body, so too for one in whom [the knowledge] arises regarding the Self alone—he is liberated even against his will. Now, an objection: from the previously cited verse in the *Bṛhadvākyavṛtti*, “As long as the realization of the meaning of the sentence ‘I am Brahman’ does not become firm, one should practice hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, accompanied by tranquility (*śama*) and other qualities,” it follows that according to the stated method, there must be practice of hearing and so forth in order to remove doubts such as improbability (*asaṃbhāvanā*).

Fearing that even as he practices, his own realization might now become firm, he approves—even though they cause great distraction, and even though they consist of both scriptural and worldly activities, as well as the study of logic and the practice of agriculture—of those very activities, saying "So be it. || 130 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "How can those who know the truth and perceive the worthlessness of worldly existence engage in such [actions]?
Anticipating this doubt, he states that because the fruit of *prārabdha* (commenced karma) is inevitable, they engage in action for the sake of exhausting it through experience:
"By the force of the latent impression of falsity..."
Out of a desire for the exhaustion of prārabdha karma.
They proceed without affliction, according to their respective karmas. || 31 ||
Regarding "falsehood" (mithyātva), etc.: 31.

Commentary (a0): Now, one might ask: "How could the initial engagement in the aforementioned two types of worldly discourse even be possible for those who experience the entire range of the perceptible as being unreal, insentient, and of the nature of suffering, and as being illusory? To this, he says: "mithyātve... (regarding its falsity). This has also been stated in the *Svārājyasiddhi*:
“Some are devoted to the conduct of their caste and stage of life, while others are like deluded children or intoxicated men.”
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya [in the chapter titled *Tṛptidīpa*] states:
"The state of the passionate enjoyer, the yogi, and others who possess knowledge is observed to be not of a single form."
Regarding the word "mugdha" (the deluded): these include Jaḍabharata, Cyavana, Datta, Ātreya, and others; as well as the passionate enjoyers such as Saubhari and others. || 131 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that there might then be engagement even in improper conduct, he says:
"One should not fear such an over-extension [of the argument] regarding those who are subject to the power of their own karma."
Or rather, tell me: by whom could karma be prevented?

Regarding the phrase "an over-extension" (atiprasaṅga): suspecting that an over-extension might also follow simply by the force of what has already begun, he accepts it, saying "let it be so. || 32 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if this were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (atiprasaṅga) of engaging even in improper action (vikarman); to this he replies with the word "atiprasaṅga.

The reason for that is given by the word "sva" (one's own). This is the intended meaning: for those who know Brahman, the activity of the body, senses, and so forth—maintained by prārabdha-karma—is like their own blackness established in the view of the world; even in the absence of the causal complex [for new karma], because of the destruction of root-ignorance (mūlāvidyā), it proceeds according to the analogy of a wheel spinning in a counter-clockwise direction.

Therefore, it must necessarily be stated that [the seeker] is engaged solely in *saṃskāra* (purificatory action). Accordingly, both from the *Smṛti* passage beginning, "A man, devoted to his own respective duty (*svakarma*), attains perfection," and from the *Aparokṣānubhūti*: "Through the performance of the duties of one's own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*), through austerity (*tapas*), and by pleasing Lord Hari, the fourfold means beginning with detachment (*vairāgya*) shall arise for men"—it follows that [perfection arises] from the diligent fulfillment of the command of the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*), which consists in the observance of all actions designated as *svakarma*, excluding those that are optional (*kāmya*) or prohibited (*niṣiddha*).

Since it is certain that they are solely governed by the purification of their rites— consisting of the obligatory and occasional *śrauta* and *smārta* actions, penances, and sacraments, performed according to the rules appropriate to their respective caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), free from the desire for fruits and the conceit of agency accumulated over countless births—

it is not at all to be feared that there will be the undesirable consequence (*atiprasaṅga*) characterized by the engagement in improper conduct or arbitrary behavior. Thus it has been stated in the *Anubhūtiprakāśa* as well:

"Furthermore, one who is previously devoted to merit attains knowledge, and not otherwise; subsequently, through that latent impression (*vāsanā*), he performs only meritorious acts. Also, in the *Svānubhavadarśa*: "Although there is no attachment to the performance of meritorious or sinful deeds when this is so, because it is caused by pure impressions, the knower of reality generally possesses faith in merit and no inclination toward sin; this is his natural disposition (*nisarga*). And this has been elaborated by me in works such as the *Dvaitajalajāta*.

This direction may be further established at length in the respective sections ahead; such is the general point. Now, one might object: "If this is so, then by the statement 'or let it be,' the acceptance of the improper conduct known as *atiprasaṅga* (excessive license) is perceived. Anticipating the doubt that even *atiprasaṅga* might occur solely due to the force of *prārabdha* (commenced karma), the author accepts it, saying: "Or let it be. If it is asked how this accords with the commentary of the ancient [teacher], we reply: "Or rather (*yadvā*): if it be so, then after the dawn of knowledge, there is no longer any sin whatsoever."

If it is argued that this contradicts the [Brahma-sūtra] section stating, "When there is suchness (tathātva), upon its realization, there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior [sins], because of the designation thereof," we say no. For, in accordance with the opening statement (*upakrama*), that [sūtra] intends to refer to sins committed while ignorance persists. Therefore, it is said in the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi*:
"From unrighteousness (*adharma*) arises ignorance; from that comes acting according to one's whims."
"How could that [renunciation] exist in a religious act where even dharma is not desired?
Thus it is said;
and in the *Ādarśa* as well: "Having seen the essence of the Supreme Brahman, Hari, the compassionate one, declared in the *Gītā* that there is renunciation."
Therefore, acting according to one's own whims does not belong to him, provided that [his state] is the ripening of knowledge.
Having this in mind, he says: "Or let it be so. The reason for this is stated by the words beginning with "by whom" (keneti). || 32 ||
In this regard, both the knower and the ignorant are equal with respect to their prārabdha-karma.
Affliction does not overcome the man of knowledge due to his fortitude; the fool suffers because of his lack of fortitude.

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Since both the knower and the ignorant person must necessarily experience their *prārabdha* karma, how can their distinctness be established? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of the knower... (verse 33).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if this is so, what is the distinction of the knower? To this he says: "Of the knower" (jñāninaḥ). || 33 ||
The Seventh Chapter.
Accompanied by two commentaries.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): In this regard, he states an illustration:
"Even when the fatigue of two travelers on a path is equal, [one perceives] the proximity [of the destination]."
One who understands should proceed with wonderful fortitude; another remains behind, dejected in mind.
"The path," [it is said]. || 34 ||
In this regard, he clarifies the illustration with the verse beginning "The path" (mārga). ||34||

255. Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus established the meaning of the first half of the mantra beginning with "If [one knows] the Self," he introduces the second half, which is intended to demonstrate the fruit [of such knowledge], by restating its sense:
One who has directly realized the nature of the self is correctly established and is not subverted by error.
Desiring what, or for the sake of what desire, should one burn with affliction for the body? || 135 ||

"Directly" (*sākṣāt*): one whose intellect has correctly realized the self; that by which the self is directly realized is "directly realized self," and such is his intellect. "Unsublated by error" (*aviparyayabādhita*): it is not sublated by error—that is, by the notion of identifying the self with the body and so forth—thus it is "unsublated by error. Both of these are qualifying attributes containing a reason. (135)

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Having thus restated the meaning of the first half of the verse, which was established as the subject of the Śruti to be explained, he introduces the second half with the words "sākṣāt" (directly). The word "samyak" (properly) connects with both [the preceding and following terms] according to the maxim of the central gem (*madhyamaṇinyāya*). Thus, the meaning is: one who possesses valid knowledge (*pramā*) regarding the immediate Self, characterized by non-sublation. For the sake of that [non-sublation], he says "aviparyaya" (free from error); [meaning] never afflicted by the mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) born of erroneous cognition.

"Devoid"—this is the meaning. Such a person, desiring what purpose—whether happiness or the destruction of suffering—would, following after the triad of bodies beginning with the gross (sthūla), undergo intense distress (saṃjvaret) and even experience great misery? Rather, because both the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer are illusory (mithyātva), he would not be miserable at all; such is the connection [of the verse]. || 135 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the essential meaning of this half-verse:
"Because of the realization of the world's falsity, the seeker of desire and the object of desire are both excluded."
In the absence of those two, the torment would subside like an oilless lamp.

"Because the world is illusory. Both the object of desire (*kāmya*) and the desirer (*kāmuka*) are implied and thereby refuted. He states the reason for their refutation: "because the world is illusory. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Of those two. The meaning is that in the absence of those two—the object of desire and the desirer—the torment caused by longing would subside due to the absence of its cause, like a lamp without oil. || 36 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, in order to explain the remaining second half of the mantra which is to be interpreted, the author provides a sutra indicating its purport with the words "jagat" etc. The meaning is: as long as there exists the state of a sublated cognition regarding the sphere of duality. According to Medinī, the term *ākṣiptau* means "reproached," "threatened," "dragged," or "ornamented"; here it means "disregarded. || 36 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question, "Where is the absence of desire seen in the absence of objects of desire?", he says: "In a city of Gandharvas, there is nothing created by a magician."
Knowing this, he desires it, yet smilingly seeks to abandon it.

Regarding the term "gandharva": one who knows that even a certain object situated in a city created by illusion is merely produced by a magician does not desire it; not only is there an absence of desire, but rather, thinking "this is false," he laughs and wishes to abandon it. || 37 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object that even though it is illusory, a most beautiful painting of a beloved woman and so forth is indeed gazed upon with love;
to this, he says: "Gandharva... This means: in a city created by an illusionist through the power of Māyā, which is agitated by mantras pertaining to the Gandharva deities.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[the chapter] titled Tṛptidīpa (The Lamp of Contentment).

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: one who knows that this object, such as a jar, is created by a magician, does not desire anything at all, nor does he wish to enjoy it; rather, on the contrary, while laughing, he wishes to abandon it—to relinquish and cast it away. And thus, the sense is that even when there is a desire to see such a painted picture, no desire to eat (*bubhukṣā*) arises at all. || 37 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He applies this to the subject of the illustration:
"One who possesses such discernment regarding enjoyments that are pleasant only at first sight..."
He does not take delight in them, but rather desires to abandon them by viewing them as defects. || 38 ||

"Āpāteti. Thus, regarding enjoyments (*bhoga*)—which are called "enjoyments" because they are being enjoyed—which are delightful only at first sight and pleasing merely to the perception, such as garlands, sandalwood paste, women, and so forth; one who possesses such discernment, who reflects upon their being delightful only at first sight, does not become enamored with them nor does he form an attachment.
Rather, by seeing their defects, he desires to abandon them. || 38 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He applies this to the subject of the illustration (dārṣṭāntika) with the verse beginning "āpāta... etc. "Āpāta" means taking destruction (pāta), that is, ruin, or sublation born of inquiry as the limit; thus, "āpātaramaṇīya" means those things which are beautiful only at first sight—that is the meaning. || 38 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question, "What are these defects of sense objects? he says:
"There is suffering in the acquisition of wealth, and likewise in its preservation."
There is suffering in loss and suffering in expenditure; fie upon these things that cause such affliction! (39)
"Of objects," [it is said]. || 39 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, in response to the inquiry as to what those defects of sense-objects (*viṣayadoṣa*) are, [the author] cites two verses from the *Bṛhadvāsiṣṭha* by way of illustration to demonstrate these defects, because—based on the ancient saying, "The Creator created delusion in two ways: toward women and toward gold"—among all objects of sense, gold and women are the most powerful causes of great infatuation. Starting with the verse beginning "Of objects" (*arthānām*), he proceeds in order to discuss wealth and so forth.
[The lords of] Nīta and Avinindaka; regarding expenditure, the example of suffering is well known indeed in the case of Nṛga. || 39 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus demonstrated that sense objects are causes of suffering, he now shows their occasional attractiveness:
"But in this mechanical puppet made of flesh, within the cage of limbs moving like a machine..."
What indeed can be beautiful in a woman who is characterized by sinews, bones, and joints? (140)

By means of the two verses beginning with "māṃsa" (flesh), [the author explains]: sinews, veins, and bones are well known. "Knots" (granthayaḥ) refer to the testicles, breasts, and so forth, which consist of accumulations of flesh. In this body—which is like a mechanical puppet made of flesh, a doll accompanied by these [parts], and whose cage of limbs is as fickle as a machine (yantra)—what is there that is beautiful? The meaning is: nothing at all. || 140 ||
Commentary on verse a0: Regarding "māṃsa" (flesh), Amara states that *pāñcālikā* refers to a doll made of cloth, ivory, and so forth.

Regarding "yantra," the meaning is "moving like a mechanical device," that is, like a puppet on a string. In such a [body]—regarding "aṅga": the word "cage" (*pañjara*) is employed as part of a metaphorical figure (*rūpaka*) to illustrate that just as a cage is a binder for parrots and other birds, so too is this body of a young woman a binder of the minds of men. While such [a body] exists...

Up to the word "flesh" (*māṃsa*): this refers to the puppet (*puttalikā*) composed of the seven constituent elements (*dhātu*), beginning with flesh. For this very reason, it says "sinews" (*snāyu*). According to the Vedic text, "May my skin, hide, flesh, blood, fat, marrow, sinews, and bones be purified; I am light," and so forth, the term *vasnasā* is used. Furthermore, according to Amara’s lexicon, *snāyuḥ* (sinew) is a feminine noun; thus, *snāyavaḥ* (sinews) refers specifically to that particular tissue located near the bones. Therefore, the "knots" (*granthi*) are those belonging to the bones characterized by such sinews.

The meaning is: "of that woman who is distinguished by that [very nature]," namely, by being composed of flesh and so forth. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "What indeed is beautiful—what lovely collection of limbs such as the face—is there in such a woman? And thus, the intention is that because of her extreme loathsomeness due to the flesh and other parts, there is not even a trace of beauty therein. 140.
The Seventh Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.
In such treatises as these, the faults have been thoroughly explained.
Constantly reflecting upon those [truths], how could one sink into sufferings? (41)

257. Rāghava’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): By the word “and so forth” (*ityādi*) in the phrase “in such [verses] as,” verses beginning with—“Having separated the skin, flesh, blood, and tears, look closely at the two eyes; if they are beautiful, why do you delude yourself in vain?”—are included. || 41 ||

This is an illustrative example of such scriptures; therefore, by constantly studying them, one will not remain submerged in the ocean of suffering—thus he says: "In such [texts] as these. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), those texts which are the source of this [work] are included, such as the Śākala-śruti: "Friendships with women do not truly exist; they are the hearts of hyenas," and likewise: "She is called 'wife' (jāyā) because she is born (jāyate)... [and so forth].

And as for the statement, "Whatever is born again from this [body]," that is indeed the Śruti. Likewise, in the Yajurveda—the Maitrāyaṇīya Śruti also says here: "O Blessed One, what is the use of the enjoyment of desires in this body, which is a foul-smelling, worthless aggregate of bone, skin, sinew, marrow, flesh, semen, blood, phlegm, tears, pus, feces, urine, bile, and kapha? Similarly: "For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain."
Statements such as these from the Smṛtis and other sources are also to be understood in this way. || 41 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: When the defects of sense objects are perceived and the desire for enjoyment ceases, he provides an illustration supported by reasoning:
"Even when tormented by hunger, one does not wish to eat poison."
One whose thirst has been quenched by sweet food, knowing this, does not foolishly desire it again.

Regarding the word "by hunger": one who is himself undeluded and possessed of discrimination, whose thirst—that is, craving or longing—is destroyed and eliminated by the eating of sweet food; such a person, knowing "this is poison," does not wish to swallow it, meaning he does not desire to eat it. || 42 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Therein, he indicates the underlying cause by means of an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration through a related instance), beginning with "nudhye" and "mṛṣṭa. The meaning of "mṛṣṭa" is as follows: one whose desire for food—that is, hunger—is destroyed (*dhvasta*) by that which is "mṛṣṭa," meaning prepared or refined food such as boiled rice (*odana*). Furthermore, the word "knowing" (*jānan*) is used to exclude the possibility that this is due to ignorance. Even so, the word "unconfused" (*amūḍha*) is used to rule out the delusion of being possessed by a planet or similar influence. He does not wish to eat (*jighatsati*), that is, to consume it.
The syntactical connection is "he desires. || 42 ||
If, due to the predominance of prārabdha karma, a desire for [the cessation of] diseases should arise;
Even then, being afflicted, he experiences [suffering] like one held in forced labor. || 43 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection that even for a knower of Truth (jñānin), desire might arise due to the power of prārabdha-karma, he says—beginning with "prārabdha"—that even when such desire exists, one does not eat with relish. || 43 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, one might ask, "How then can Saubhari and others have a desire for enjoyment? To this he says: "Prārabdha...
The meaning is that it is like the *viṣṭi*—the term *veṭha*, well-known in Maharashtra, which refers to a fixed obligation—that has been grasped and maintained by them. || 43 ||
Or even wise householders, full of faith, while partaking [of the meal].
"Even now our karma is not destroyed," they say, and thus they suffer incessantly.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question, "How is this to be understood?", he says, "Those who eat," based on what is observed in the world. || 44 ||

He illustrates this with the verse beginning "yuñjānāḥ. The meaning is: even those enjoyments brought about by the power of *prārabdha* (commenced karma). "Full of faith" refers to those such as Jaratkāru and others, who possessed the conviction that there was a hell like a well at the root of a blade of *dūrvā* grass, based on the words of their ancestors. || 44 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that for those who know the truth, suffering caused by worldly existence is untenable, as it would result in the futility of knowledge;
anticipating this, he says—*The reading follows Acyutarāya’s commentary as "mṛṣṭānnam" (delicious food).
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya:
[The chapter titled] *Tṛptidīpa*.
This is not a hardship here, nor is it the heat of worldly existence; rather, it is detachment.
For it is taught that the suffering of worldly existence has its cause in deluded cognition.
"This is not [the case]" means that this heat of saṃsāra, which consists of remorse—thinking, "This affliction has not yet been severed by our karma"—does not exist.
Rather, there is detachment from saṃsāra, which is the state of being free from attachment. He states the reasoning for the absence of its capacity to cause heat: "Because of delusion," etc.
For, as the former teachers have declared, the heat of saṃsāra has its source in deluded cognition (*bhrāntijñāna*) and is produced by deluded cognition.
But this [other type] is not of such a kind because its root is discriminative knowledge; this is the meaning. || 45 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): If this is so, then there is no distinction from saṃsāra; to this he says: "No. The reason for that is: "Because of delusion" (bhrānti). || 145 ||
Distressed by solitude, he finds satisfaction in meager enjoyments.
Otherwise, even with infinite enjoyments, one is never satisfied at any time.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Raising the doubt as to how it is known whether this affliction is rooted in discernment (*viveka*) or rooted in non-discernment (*aviveka*), he states that it is rooted in discernment because it brings about the cessation of desire: "By means of discernment" (verse 46).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, if it is asked, "How is it determined that the aforementioned affliction (*kleśa*) is rooted solely in non-discrimination (*aviveka*)?", [the author] replies, "By means of discrimination" (*vivekena*), indicating that this is known precisely through inference based on the effect (*kāryaliṅgakānumāna*). The intention is that this is observed to be so in cases such as Jaratkāru and others. The point of contention (*vimataḥ*) is that affliction is rooted in non-discrimination, because it resides in those who are satisfied with meager enjoyments (*alpabhogatuṣṭaniṣṭhatvāt*). This is established by the method of difference (*vyatireka*): [where there is no non-discrimination], there is no affliction, as in the case of one who possesses discrimination (*vivekikaleśavat*). Thus, it is by way of difference.
He clarifies the illustration with the words "otherwise" (anyathā). || 46 ||
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of the objects of desire.
Like a fire fed with oblations, it increases all the more. || 47 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that even for one who lacks discrimination, satisfaction might arise through enjoyment alone—and therefore discrimination is not a necessary factor—he cites a scriptural text demonstrating that enjoyment is not a cause of satisfaction: "Never, indeed, does desire... (47).

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on verse a0: Therein, he cites the Purāṇa as authority with the words "na jātu" (never). "Jātu" means at any time whatsoever. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that desire—the longing for sense objects—by no means subsides through the enjoyment of desired objects (*kāmānām*). He clarifies the illustration for this with the word "haviṣā" (with oblation): "like fire," meaning like Agni, according to the Amarakośa definition "kṛṣṇavartman" as fire. || 47 ||
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: He states that it is established by experience that enjoyment rooted in discernment (*viveka*) is a cause of satisfaction:
"For enjoyment, when consumed after full comprehension, leads to contentment."
A thief who has been recognized and then served develops friendliness and no longer acts as a thief.

"Having fully understood" (parijñāya) means that when one has the prior experience that "this enjoyment is only this much and is to be achieved through such effort," it is observed to be the cause of the sense of sufficiency (*alam-buddhi*). Now, one might object: how can enjoyment, which is the cause of craving, produce contentment merely by being associated with discrimination? Anticipating this doubt, he says—"having recognized"—pointing out that in common worldly experience, it is seen that a thing produces an opposite effect due to the influence of a particular associate, as in the case of "This is a thief."
The meaning is that once this is known, a person who associates with him does not become a thief, but rather attains the state of friendship. || 48 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might object that contentment with little enjoyment is unproven in this world because it is never observed. Anticipating this, he provides the following resolution: even limited enjoyment, when preceded by discernment (*viveka*), can produce the opposite result due to the power of its constituent factors, much like a specific type of poison. This is expressed in the verse beginning with "parijñāya. The meaning is: having understood through discernment the entire apparatus of enjoyment, as well as the efforts required for its accomplishment and so forth. He provides an illustration for this:
"Having understood," [it is said]. || 48 ||
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
259 Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Since the mind is by nature inclined toward desire, how can it be satisfied by a mere trifling enjoyment?
Anticipating this doubt, he states that satisfaction indeed occurs because the mind, once grasped through *nididhyāsana* (repeated contemplation), is no longer such [by nature].
Even that slight enjoyment of play which belongs to the mind when it is restrained—
One highly values that very [state] which has not yet attained expansion, because it is afflicted. || 49 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the mind": even a slight experience of play—that is, a slight experience of enjoyment—of the mind that has been restrained and brought under control through the practice of yoga, if it has not attained expansion (alabdhavistāra) and has not reached abundance (aprāptavāhulya), he considers that very experience to be great; the meaning is that, because it is afflicted (kliṣṭa)—that is, possessed of defects—he regards it as superior. || 49 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Furthermore, he states another reason for the contentment of the discerning person with even a small amount of enjoyment—beginning with the words "of the mind" (*manasaḥ*). Following the immediate realization (*aparokṣapramā*) concerning the non-difference between the non-dual Brahman and the Self as previously described, there is the contemplation of that unity (*aikyānusaṃdhāna*), which is preceded by the understanding of the falsity of duality and the practice of hearing, reflection, and meditation (*śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana*) characterized by the fourfold marks, resulting in the removal of doubts and other obstacles for the sake of strengthening that realization; this is the sense. [The mind] is "restrained" (*nigṛhītasya*), meaning it is blocked. Regarding the word "absorption" (*līlā*): [it refers to the state where the mind is dissolved].

The meaning is that there is the enjoyment of some desired object produced by effort, as in the case of Saubhari and others. Even that which is very slight—referring to the mind characterized as described above—it is implied that [the mind] is restrained by the aforementioned method of cessation. The construction is: "being afflicted, it has not attained expansion; not having reached infinite resolve, it is satisfied with much" (or rather, "it is satisfied with even a little"). Just as a bound king who has been released is content with a mere village.
He is neither bound by others nor overcome; he does not hold his kingdom in high esteem. || 50 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To show that even a subdued mind finds satisfaction through even a slight enjoyment, he provides an illustration: "Like one released from bonds" (verse 50).

— A0 Commentary: Therein, he clarifies the illustration with the words "baddha" (bound), etc. This means that one who was previously bound, confined in prison, is later released or liberated. "Ākrānta" means pervaded. || 150 ||
When discernment is awake, characterized by the perception of faults [in worldly objects].
How can one who has already begun an action generate a desire for enjoyment? || 51 ||

Rāma’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "If it is said that desire for enjoyments may arise due to the predominance of prārabdha-karma, then it is illogical to say that desire arises by the power of karma; for when discriminative knowledge (viveka-jñāna), which obstructs desire, is present, the arising of such desire is impossible. Thus he raises this doubt with the verse beginning "viveke" (verse 51).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Even there, he raises an objection: "Viveka" [verse 51].
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Even though faults have been perceived, the arising of desire may still occur because the *prārabdha* (the karma that has already begun to bear fruit) is of various kinds;
thus he offers this rebuttal: "This is not a fault, since *prārabdha* is seen to be of many varieties."
Desire, lack of desire, and the desire of another—these are remembered as the threefold *prārabdha*. ||52||
"Not so," he says. He demonstrates its very manifold nature with the words "desire" and so forth.
The meaning is that it is threefold: that which produces desire, that which bestows enjoyment through lack of desire, and that which bestows enjoyment through the desire of another. || 52 ||
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) resolves [the objection] with the words "This is not so. The reason for this is given by "since" (yataḥ).

He summarizes those very [objections] as "desire" (icchā) and so forth; that is to say, they are rooted in desire and the like. For a detailed exposition on this point, one should consult my own work, *Prārabdhadhvāntadīdhiti*; it is not elaborated here for fear of making the treatise too voluminous. || 52 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 260]
Thieves who indulge in indolence, even those who take pleasure in the king's wives;
Even while knowing the lamp of contentment, they desire their own misfortune through the force of prārabdha-karma. || 53 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He shows the *prārabdha* (karmic momentum) initiated by desire with the verse beginning "apathya" (verse 53).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Therein, at the outset, he illustrates that which is commenced by desire (*icchā-prārabdha*) with the verse beginning "apathya... [The phrase] "of one who is ill" is implied; this follows the maxim: "Everything is wholesome for those who possess strength. Regarding the word "commenced" (*ārabdha*): it refers to the instigation of various actions at that time, as evidenced by the examples of Bhīmasena consuming sugar-cane juice mixed with poison, Śrī Kṛṣṇa's destruction of the butter and other items, and Candra’s act of approaching the wife of his preceptor (*guru-dāra-gamana*).
This means: by the force of karma whose fruit has already begun to manifest. || 53 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question, "How is it known that the desire to indulge in unwholesome things is the fruit of *prārabdha* (commenced karma)? and intending to show that it is unavoidable, he says:
"And even by the Lord, this cannot be prevented here."
For the Lord himself said this to Arjuna in the Gītā.
"Not so," he says. To the question, "Why is it that they desire what is unwholesome and so forth in this world? he replies with the words "Because... (54).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the aforementioned examples are otherwise established through extensive deliberation, the only thing that ought to be done is the total eradication of the desire for activities such as indulging in unwholesome things. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And not here" (*na cātra*). "Here" means in this world; the meaning is that *prārabdha* (the momentum of past karma) is the root of this intensity of desire. By the word "also" (*api*), it is indicated that its absence elsewhere is established by the principle of "how much more so" (*kaimutya*)—that is, in the other state [liberation]. In that case—
The reason is: "since" (yataḥ). || 54 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He cites a verse from the Gītā:
"Even one who possesses knowledge acts in accordance with his own nature."
All beings follow their own nature; what can restraint accomplish?

"According to his nature": even a person possessing discriminative knowledge acts in conformity with, that is, in accordance with, his own *prakṛti*. *Prakṛti* refers to the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of previously performed merit, demerit, and so forth, which become manifest at the beginning of the present birth. If this is true for one who possesses knowledge, how much more so for a fool? Therefore, "beings follow their nature. Can any restraint—whether by me or by anyone else—effect a cessation of their engagement in activity or withdrawal from it? No.
The meaning is that it does not suffer at all. || 55 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He cites that very statement: "similarly" (*sadṛśam*). Here, the meaning is as follows: setting aside the distinction well-known from scripture—that "both knowledge and action, along with past experience (*pūrvaprajñā*), follow him"—it is these three alone—knowledge, action, and the impressions (*saṃskāra*) denoted by the term *pūrvaprajñā*—that constitute the material cause (*upādāna*) of the body and so forth. By the word "also" (*api*), there is here, as before, an argument *a fortiori* (*kaimutya*). [The text continues: "beings" (*bhūtāni*) refers to those characterized by the nature of becoming, such as those born from a womb...

The meaning is that [the souls] are simply the consciousnesses of living beings delimited by bodies of such-and-such a kind. The rest is indeed clear. Here, because of the qualifiers such as "discrimination" and so forth applied to the collection of impressions (saṃskāra) known as "prior cognition," it is intended that the entirety of the scriptures achieves its purpose through the removal of those impressions by means of effort.
We shall establish this in detail when we have the opportunity in the sixteenth [chapter]; this is the direction [of the argument]. || 155 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To support the inevitability of powerful *prārabdha* karma, he cites another scriptural statement:
"If there were a remedy for events that are destined to occur..."
Then Nala, Rāma, and Yudhiṣṭhira would not have been defiled by sufferings.
"Unavoidably" means of those states that are necessarily destined to occur, such as suffering and so forth. || 56 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might raise the objection that there may indeed be some other underlying intention behind the aforementioned Smṛti; this doubt is refuted by means of a counter-argument:
[Page 261] Seventh Section.
[This is] accompanied by two commentaries.

Regarding the word "inevitably" (*avaśyam*): the author [Śaṅkara], however, states that there is agreement from other scriptural passages regarding the inevitability of *tīvra-prārabdha* (intense *prārabdha-karma*), saying "inevitably."

The meaning is that [this refers to] the inevitability of states such as suffering, as has been explained. "Remedy" means avoidance. Regarding the word "na" (not): the meaning is "successively in the Kṛta and other ages. Here, although there was the perception of a fault—namely, that gambling between Nala and Yudhiṣṭhira is censured by the Dharmaśāstras—their engagement in it occurred solely due to an inevitable prior impulse, because of the traditional law (smṛti) which states: "One who is challenged shall not withdraw, even from gambling or even from battle."

But this is not correct; for just as the injunction "A king should sacrifice with the Rājasūya" implies that even though it is obligatory, it must be abandoned when one is afflicted by a twelve-year drought, so too its abandonment is possible in the present case. In the same way, Rāma’s engagement in killing the golden deer must be explained as occurring despite his knowledge of its impossibility.
This will be elaborated upon in the *Bodhaikyasiddhi*. || 56 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that if prārabdha karma is unavoidable, then the Lord—who is incapable of avoiding it—would lose His status as the Lord, he says:
"The Lordship of the Lord is not lost by that much, because..."
Even their inevitability was created by Īśvara alone. || 57 ||

"And yet there is no lack of lordship. Why is this? To this he says: "Because" (yataḥ). "Necessarily" (avaśyam): because the very necessity of the occurrence of these things, such as suffering and so forth, was created by the Lord himself; therefore, there is no consequence of His being non-lordly—this is the meaning. || 57 ||

Commentary on Verse 1: Now, one might object: although Nala and Yudhiṣṭhira, being included among the class of individual souls (jīva-koṭi), are capable of experiencing the unavoidable suffering resulting from their own past actions (prārabdha-karma) due to their dependence on karma, and are thus fit to serve as examples; Śrī Rāma, however, being the Lord (Īśvara), acts like the world merely as a sport (līlā).

If it is argued that—since the state of isolation (*kaivalya*) has been determined by the aphorisms of the Great Sage (Patañjali) and others to be merely illusory for human beings—it is impossible for Śrī Rāma, who desires to favor all living beings by manifesting the drama of a human being and thereby communicating the meaning of the Vedas as established by the Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsās, to be subject to the bondage of karma; and furthermore, since he is incapable of remedying the suffering produced by such karma (following the maxim of a painting on a wall), his case cannot serve as an illustration [of the rule]; this is true. Nevertheless, because Śrī Rāma is the Lord (*īśvara*), he is indeed independent of karma.

Nevertheless, because His volition is true, it must undoubtedly be accepted that He is subject to His own illusory will (*māyika-svecchā*). Thus, in the *Siddhāntabindu*, regarding the Lord (*īśvara*), it is stated: "According to the view of the author of the *Vārttika*, however, the Lord alone is the Witness; thus, the 'seen' (*dṛś*) is twofold, distinguished as the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). Among these, the Lord is also threefold, due to the distinction between Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Rudra, based on the differentiation of the three qualities (*guṇa*) of the ignorance (*avidyā*) that constitutes His own limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). [The text continues with: *kāra-*...

Viṣṇu, conditioned by the quality of *sattva* which has become the cause [of preservation], is the protector; Brahmā, conjoined with *rajas* which has become the cause [of creation], is the creator. However, Hiraṇyagarbha is not Brahmā because he lacks the status of being the cause of the gross elements (*mahābhūta*). Nevertheless, because he is the creator of the gross elements, he is metaphorically designated as "Brahmā" in some contexts. Rudra, conjoined with *tamas* which has become the cause [of dissolution], is the destroyer. Thus, the forms of the four-armed, four-faced, five-faced, and so forth, are the male manifestations of that very One. Śrī Bhāra... [text ends]

The forms beginning with those of the Fish, the Tortoise, and others, as well as the infinite other incarnations such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and so forth, manifest through mere divine play (*līlā*) for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees;

this also should be meditated upon. Thus, Viṣṇu—whose primary function is protection, whose manifested *līlā*-form is displayed by that [Māyā] alone, and who is delimited by the predominance of the *sattva* quality associated with Māyā—manifests by His own will. From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the *Ṛg* and *Sāman* verses were born; the meters... [chaṃdāṃsi]... were born.
From the Śruti passages such as "From Him [Brahman] the Ṛgveda was born; from Him the Yajurveda was born," and from the Sūtra "Because He is the source of the scriptures" (*śāstrayonitvāt*),

as well as from Smṛti texts such as "The Vedas, the scriptures, and this entire body of knowledge— all these arise from Janārdana," it follows that merit and demerit— consisting of the satisfaction and frustration produced by the performance of injunctions such as the *saṃdhyopāsana* and prohibitions such as the drinking of liquor, which reside within the entirety of the *Śabdabrahman* characterized by the Vedas manifested by Himself— [result in] pleasure and pain.

It is also entirely agreed upon by all who maintain the existence of the external world (*sarvāstika*) that He conceived, according to the very method of the succession of beginningless saṃsāra, the power of the necessity of giving.

Therefore, it must necessarily be accepted that He, through His own will, endowed His devotees—who are characterized by the predominance of the practice of merit alone—with the capacity for the power of both cursing and favoring; and that He likewise established in them the capacity for proficiency in bestowing mental purity, heaven, and so forth, within the context of meritorious action during their state of unwavering meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*).
[It is] thus: by him, due to the power of the curse pronounced by Sanatkumāra, there occurred the attainment of ignorance preceded by the dissolution of his omniscience;

and for some time, while Bhṛgu remained in meditative absorption, his wife herself [protected] the Asuras, who were her own disciples and had come to her for refuge, while they stayed at the hermitage.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 262.

Because he constantly protected him from the weapons and other missiles of the celestial armies that had followed upon his back through the power of his ascetic penances such as the Vratya-vrata, Viṣṇu, who is partial to the side of the gods,
severed his head with his own unfailing discus named Sudarśana; thereafter, having emerged from his meditative absorption, Bhṛgu cursed him as well.

Due to the power of a curse most famous in the *Padma Purāṇa* that "separation from his wife shall occur," when the Brāhmaṇa Devadattaśarman beheld the incarnation of Nṛsiṃha on the banks of the Payoṣṇī, his wife died at that very moment out of sheer terror; because of the curse likewise pronounced by him, as well as the well-known curse of Vṛndā, he experienced separation from Jānakī three times during the incarnation of Śrī Rāma— all of this is found in the very first canto of the *Bṛhad-Yogavāsiṣṭha*.
It is thus related: therein, having perceived the defects in the pleasures of objects such as heaven, a certain king named Āgniveśya became supremely dispassionate.

At the command of the king, Vālmīki—intent on awakening him to the non-dual knowledge of Brahman under the guise of narrating the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Rāma—was addressed by that king through a messenger sent by the gods.
