The king said: "Who is Rāma? Of what nature is he? To whom does he belong? Is he bound or indeed liberated? This I wish to know with certainty."
"Speak, O best among those who know reality!
[The commentary: 'Knowledge' (jñāna) means that by which something is known; the meaning is that it is the cause of certainty."

Vālmīki said: "By the very pretext of a curse, Hari, assuming the guise of a king, was deprived of his omniscience; thus your lord became possessed of only limited knowledge. Commentary: *bhavat* [became]. *abhavat*. The absence of the augment *aṭ* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

The King spoke regarding the cause of the curse: "Tell me, who was cursed by Rāma, whose nature is consciousness-bliss and whose very form is pure awareness? Speak to me. Vālmīki said: "Sanatkumāra, being free from..."

I too resided in the abode of Brahmā. Viṣṇu, the Lord and Sovereign of the three worlds, arrived from Vaikuṇṭha; he was honored there by Brahmā and the inhabitants of Satyaloka. Seeing him there without Kumāra, the Lord Īśvara said: "Sanatkumāra, you have become paralyzed by pride through your haughty behavior and lack of desire; therefore, become afflicted by passion, known by the name Śarajanman. By him, Viṣṇu was also cursed.

"You possess omniscience; yet, for a short time, having abandoned that, you shall become ignorant. Having seen his wife killed, Bhṛgu, overwhelmed with anger, said: 'O Viṣṇu, there shall indeed be separation from your wife as well, because you deceived Vṛndā by means of a stratagem. Therefore, by my word, you shall undergo separation from a woman. [The wife] of Devadatta was indeed..."
Standing on the bank of the Yoṣṇī, she beheld Viṣṇu wearing the guise of Nṛsiṃha and met her death. Afflicted by the sorrow of separation from his wife, Nṛhari was indeed cursed by her.

*Commentary:* Although Nṛhari was directly perceived (*ṛta*) through meritorious deeds that were difficult to accomplish (*duḥkhaiḥ*), he was cursed by her. He was [afflicted] by... *bhṛ-*... [sufferings].

"Thus was Guṇa cursed by Prince Devaśarman; Viṣṇu was cursed by Vṛndā, and by that [curse] he attained the state of a human being. Therefore, although Śrī Rāma, as the Supreme Lord (Īśvara), is not subject to the bondage of karma, according to the aforementioned reasoning: by the performance of acts enjoined by the Vedas—which are His own word and constitute His command—there arises merit (sukṛta) characterized by the voice of bliss (*svar*), which is the cause of happiness; and by the performance of prohibited acts, there arises demerit (*duṣkṛta*) characterized by the voice of suffering (*svar*), which is the cause of misery. Thus...

In this beginningless cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*), that which is determined solely by one’s own will is designated here by such terms as "destiny" (*niyati*) and "inevitability" (*avaśyambhāvitā*). Therefore, even the power to bestow curses and so forth upon Sanatkumāra—the sovereign of supreme merit—and upon Bhṛgu and others, arose precisely from the necessity of their own will; thus, the preservation of that [will] is absolutely necessary for oneself. This is the sense: that the inevitability of objects such as suffering and its causes, as expressed by the term "intention" (*bhāva*), is in every respect unavoidable.

On the basis of the mere similarity of being remediable, it is quite easy to include Śrī Rāma among Rahūgaṇa, Anubhāvana, and Yudhiṣṭhira. However, there is this further distinction: for those two who are situated within the category of individual souls (*jīva*), the inevitability of suffering and so forth is produced by karma; but for the Lord Śrī Rāma, who is situated within the category of the Supreme Lord (*īśvara*), it is produced solely by His own will, as He possesses the power of true resolve (*satyasaṃkalpa*) according to the aforementioned principle. For this very reason, this example of Śrī Rāma [is cited].

The teachers have applied the term *prārabdha* (commenced) exclusively to the consideration of [karma] performed with desire, and not even to the consideration of that performed without desire. Even so, it is certainly not the case that the Lord’s will cannot be designated by the term *prārabdha* in the same way as karma; and thus, the inclusion of it within that specific section of the inquiry remains equally inappropriate.
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

It must be stated that it is indeed *sthāyī* (the stable). Even though its usage there [in the sense of "beginning"] is impossible through conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) or through etymological-conventional meaning (*yogarūḍhi*), the term *prārabdha*—meaning "that which has been extensively begun" (*pracuram ārabdham*), "that which has been firmly begun" (*pragalbham ārabdham*), or "that which has been commenced" (*prārabdham*)—is applied even to the Will of the Lord (*īśvarecchā*) in such forms as: "The state of necessity consisting of suffering and so forth, produced by evil deeds and the like, which is of the nature of a *māyika-vṛtti* (illusory mental modification), has necessarily been brought about (*ārabdham*) with excellence (*prakarṣeṇa*) by means of the Will (*yogaiḥ*). Thus, the application of the word *prārabdha* occurs even in the case of the Lord's Will.

Because [such] activity is possible. Therefore, although there exist thousands of sufferings according to the worldly perspective, the Supreme Lord’s failure to provide a remedy—being directed toward the preservation of His own fixed boundaries through an beginningless succession—does not at all diminish His supreme sovereignty; on the contrary, just like a king, even though He possesses the power to do so, the fact that the Blessed One endures thousands of sufferings for the sake of preserving the boundaries ordained by Himself results only in great glory.

He clarifies that intention with the words, "And not lordship," etc. The reason for this is given by the passage beginning with "since," etc. The meaning is: of these [beings], who experience the arising of suffering and so forth due to their evil deeds and the like, as delimited by specific places, times, and objects. || 57 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus described *icchā-prārabdha* (voluntary *prārabdha*) with its full elaboration, he begins to speak of *anicchā-prārabdha* (involuntary *prārabdha*).
This is understood precisely through the questions and answers between Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa.
And there is also that which has begun without prior desire; listen to that. || 58 ||

"—By means of question and answer. The construction is as follows: that there exists a *prārabdha* (commenced karma) even without prior desire is understood and known precisely through the questions and answers of Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa. To state that, he addresses the disciple: "Listen to that. (18)

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "By the reasoning already stated, you have merely inferred that the inevitability of the fruits of actions depends solely upon the will of God; however, such a thing is generally not found stated explicitly by him anywhere. Anticipating this doubt, the author provides a resolution by reciting a single meaning that is suitable for sequential application to both the preceding and following passages—according to the maxim of the eye-ball in a crow's eye—beginning with the words "praśna" (the question). This [inevitability] of the fruits of these actions...

The meaning is that the necessity of existence depends solely upon the will of Īśvara. Regarding Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa: although the word *Kṛṣṇa* should logically come first because it is more venerable and has fewer syllables, the usage in the *Gītā-bhāṣya*—"taking Arjuna as the cause" (*arjunam nimittīkṛtya*)—indicates that the word denoting him (Arjuna) comes first. This is because his status as the sole sufficient cause for the manifestation of the scripture of the *Bhagavad-gītā* makes him even more venerable than the other. Thus, the word [denoting] him is placed first.
It is clear from the very questions and answers. At the beginning of the third chapter of the Bhagavad Gītā:

Arjuna said: "If you consider knowledge to be superior to action, O Janārdana, then why do you urge me toward this terrible action, O Keśava? With these seemingly contradictory words, you are, as it were, confusing my intellect. Therefore, tell me one thing with certainty."

"By which means may I attain the highest good? The Blessed Lord said: "O sinless one, in this world a twofold path has been declared by me from of old: the path of knowledge for the Sāṅkhyas and the path of action for the Yogins."
The meaning is: "by those very two [verses] just presented. Here, only a mere indication of Madhusūdana Ācārya’s commentary is cited:

"Now, in that case, since knowledge and action are as contradictory as light and darkness, their combination is impossible; therefore, let it be that they pertain to different types of qualified practitioners (*adhikārins*). True, this is indeed possible. However, it is not proper to instruct both [knowledge and action] to a single person, such as Arjuna. For one does not [instruct] knowledge to one who is a qualified practitioner of action..."

The thought that one must teach steadfastness in action (*karma-niṣṭhā*) is not tenable; nor is it the case that steadfastness in action is intended for one qualified for knowledge (*jñāna*). If it is argued that the teaching is given as an option (*vikalpa*) with respect to a single person, we say no, because an option between the superior and the inferior is logically impossible. Furthermore, since liberation consists in the essential nature of the Self characterized by the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), there can be no gradation (*tāratamya*) therein. Therefore, since it is impossible to give a single teaching to one person if steadfastness in knowledge and steadfastness in action have different qualifications (*adhikāra*), they must share a single qualification.

Furthermore, because two contradictory things cannot be combined and because it is illogical to praise knowledge with respect to action, one whose intellect becomes bewildered—thinking that if an option between them is accepted, it would be improper to abandon the superior knowledge (which is achieved without effort) in order to perform the inferior action (which involves much exertion)—says:
"Arjuna said: What then, O Janārdana? [For] by all people, You are 'ardita'—that is, entreated for their desired objects."
The intention behind the address "O Siddha" is this: since you are such a person, it is not at all improper that I should also entreat you for the sake of determining what is most beneficial.
If you consider the intellect directed toward the reality of the Self to be superior—that is, more praiseworthy—even than action performed without desire (niṣkāma-karma).
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[the section titled] Tṛptidīpa.

Why then, at such a time, do you urge me—who am devoted to You—toward a terrible action involving manifold hardships such as violence, specifically impelling me with words such as "Your right is to action alone"? O Keśava, Lord of All, it is not fitting for You, the Sovereign of All who grants all desires, to practice deception toward me, Your devotee and disciple, who has approached You as Your sole refuge with words such as "Instruct me. This is the intended meaning.

[Arjuna says: "Is it not true that I do not deceive anyone, much less you, who are so dear to me? If you ask, 'Why then do you see a sign of deception in me?', he replies with the verse beginning, 'As if by a confused [speech]' (vyāmiśreṇeva). Your words are certainly not confused;

however, because of my doubt regarding whether [the teaching] pertains to a single office or different offices, your speech—which concerns the duty of a vow toward me—appears to me as if its meaning were confused and intermingled."

It establishes two distinct conclusions. By that statement, you—out of extreme compassion—seem to delude, or rather, seem to involve me, who am of dull intellect, in a confusion arising from my failure to understand the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of your words; however, the sense of the word "seem" (*iva*) is that you do not actually delude me, for it is only due to the defect of my own disposition that such delusion occurs. Furthermore, since it is impossible for two contradictory things to be combined under a single authority, and because there is no single unified purpose [in the two statements], [the conclusion follows].

Since the aforementioned conceptual alternatives are untenable, if you consider there to be a distinction between those qualified [for each], then—because it is impossible to give instruction in two contradictory paths to a single person like me—tell me which one is it: that knowledge or that action? Having ascertained my qualification, speak; so that, by means of either that knowledge or that action alone, preceded by the ascertainment of my qualification, and being practiced by you and by me, I may attain the highest good, liberation—that is, I may become fit to obtain it. Thus, regarding knowledge and action—

Since both [the paths] have a single eligible person (*adhikārin*), and because neither an option (*vikalpa*) nor a combination (*samuccaya*) is possible, it is established that Arjuna’s question was intended to ascertain the difference between their respective eligible persons.

Here, all the erroneous views of others have been refuted by the force of *śruti*, *smṛti*, and logic; since the author of the Commentary has already exerted great effort on this repeatedly, I have not set out to do so again.
“By me, who perceives the essence of the Bhāṣyakāra’s doctrine, only the text itself is here joined together.
The intention of the Blessed One is revealed solely for the sake of purifying his own speech.
When Arjuna had thus asked regarding the distinction between the types of qualified aspirants, the Blessed Lord spoke this reply in accordance with that: "In the world... (loke).

In this world, which is considered to consist of those qualified [for spiritual practice], there are two kinds of people distinguished by their pure and impure internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*). For them, there are two kinds of steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*), that is, two modes of abiding: devotion to knowledge (*jñāna*) and devotion to action (*karman*). This was previously stated by me—acting for your ultimate benefit—in the preceding chapter, explained with clarity and excellence. Thus, the intention is: "Do not be despondent due to the suspicion that the qualified persons might be one and the same. O sinless one!

By awakening [Arjuna], He brings him to the state of being fit for instruction and indicates Arjuna’s readiness. There is only one *niṣṭhā* (steadfastness), which is of two kinds due to the distinction between the states of the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*);

however, to show that there are not two independent *niṣṭhās*, the word is used in the singular as "*niṣṭhā*. Thus He will say: "He who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one, he truly sees. He demonstrates that very *niṣṭhā* in its twofold nature. Saṃ-...

The term *sāṃkhya* refers to those who have attained the correct realization of the Self (*samyag-ātmabuddhi*), who have practiced celibacy (*brahmacarya*) from the very beginning, who have renounced the world, whose purpose is firmly established through the specialized knowledge of Vedānta, who have ascended to the plane of wisdom, whose internal organs are purified, and who are the *sāṃkhyas*. [The word *jñānayoga* is derived as follows: that by which knowledge itself is joined with Brahman; thus it is called *jñāna-yoga*.

The steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*) in that [practice] has been stated through the etymological derivation of "yoga" as that by which one is joined (*yujyate*). This was taught in such passages as, "Restraining all those [senses], let him sit disciplined, with Me as his supreme goal. However, for those yogins whose internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are impure and who have not yet ascended to the plane of knowledge (*jñānabhūmi*), steadfastness is taught through *karmayoga*—that is, through action itself. For those engaged in the discipline of action, "yoga" is so called because action is joined to the purification of the internal organ by means of this [practice]. Through the door of purifying the internal organ, they ascend to the plane of knowledge.

"For there exists nothing better for a Kṣatriya than a righteous war" (Gītā 2.31), and so forth. Therefore, there is neither a combination nor an option between knowledge and action; rather, for those whose internal organs are purified by desireless action, knowledge arises only through the renunciation of all actions. However, due to the difference in states consisting of the purity or impurity of the mind, two types of steadfastness have been taught to you. This [steadfastness] has been declared to you in the context of Sāṃkhya...

"But for one who hears this in the context of yoga..."—the intention [of this statement] is that because this single [instruction] is useful for both [paths] according to the distinction of the stages (*bhūmikā*), there is no futility in the teaching even though there is a difference in qualification (*adhikāra*). Such is the meaning. Thus, following precisely the questions posed by Arjuna and the answers given by the Blessed One as determined by the former teachers regarding the Bhagavad Gītā, it is clearly understood and known that the necessity of the certainty regarding the results connected with action depends solely upon the will of the Lord (*īśvarecchā-mātra*). This is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*).
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

265. But here, it appears that the Blessed One has merely addressed Arjuna’s doubt regarding the combination of the two— namely, the steadfastness in knowledge and the steadfastness in action, which were introduced as the subject matter of the Veda in the preceding chapter— by stating simply that they share a single agent through their relationship of means and end.

If you argue that the necessity and certainty of the inevitable ripening of karma is not established as being dependent on the mere will of Īśvara simply by this much—because it is established as beginningless—you have missed the point. The divinity of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is indeed beyond dispute, as determined by the *Siddhāntabindu*, which ascertains the intent of all the aforementioned teachers.

Thus, within the succession of beginningless transmigrations, by virtue of His power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpa*), He has willed by His own will that the fruits of both [types of] steadfastness mentioned above shall necessarily come to pass.

Since the necessity of cultivation (*bhāvanaiyatya*) has been explicitly revealed in the present context, there is not even a scent of dispute here; such is the direction [of the argument]. Thus, it has been explained that the meaning of this [verse]—which is consistent with the preceding texts—is understood through the very questions and answers between Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa. Now, following the same method as before, it is being explained along with its connection to the second half of that [verse], which provides the required answer. Let it be so: desire, non-desire, and the desire of another constitute the threefold *prārabdha* (commenced karma).

Regarding the statement "it is remembered," among the three types of *prārabdha* previously promised, [the author] now addresses the question: "What is the proof for the existence of *anicchā-prārabdha* (unwillingly commenced karma)?

He answers this with the verse beginning with "praśna" (question), etc. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "also. The connection is as follows: that there exists even an *anicchā-pūrvaka-prārabdha* is understood precisely from the question and answer about to be spoken by Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa, beginning with "atha kena" (then by what?). How was that [established] through the aforementioned question and so forth?
Observing the disciple who asks thus, he directs him toward the subject with the remainder of the verse beginning with "That" (tat). || 158 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Therein, he first shows Arjuna’s question:
"Now, by what impelled does this person commit sin?"
O descendant of Vṛṣṇi, even though he did not desire it, he was as if compelled by force. || 59 ||

Now, as for the question "By whom?": O Vārṣṇeya, O kinsman of the Vṛṣṇis, by what impelled or prompted does this person perform a sinful act—even against his will, even while not desiring it—as if forcibly commanded by a king? || 59 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Therein, he first recites the question, beginning with "Now" (*atha*). Here too, the commentary of Madhusūdana Ācārya himself is written as appropriate: "In this way, for those who accept the doctrine of the Blessed One, there is the attainment of the highest good (*śreyas*)."

And it has been stated that those who do not accept this have fallen from the path to the highest good (*śreyomārga*). Regarding the falling away from the path to the highest good—both in the performance of optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) preceded by a desire for fruits and in the performance of mere sin—it has been described through many reasons, beginning with the words, "But those who find fault with this... and so forth.
In this regard, there is this summary verse:
— I I

Loss of faith, as well as malice, a corrupted mind, delusion, being under the sway of one’s own nature, abundant passion and hatred, and a fondness for the dharma of others— these are said to be the carriers onto the evil path.

In this regard, having set aside the causes for engaging in optional (*kāmya*) and prohibited (*pratiṣiddha*) actions, Arjuna spoke in order to follow the Blessed One’s teaching and to ascertain those very causes: "Then, by what... (2.62). Previously, the root of evil was stated in such passages as "When a man dwells on sense objects" (2.62); and now, it has been explained at great length in such passages as "Deluded by the qualities of *prakṛti*" (3.29). Among these, are all [the causes] equally predominant?

Now, regarding the causes: is there only one primary cause, while the others are merely its auxiliaries? In the first case, there would be great effort required to ward off each of them individually. In the latter case, however, once that single [cause] is refuted, the task would be accomplished. Therefore, tell me: by what reason was this man—who does not follow your doctrine and is deluded regarding all knowledge—prompted and impelled toward sin and misfortune?

Driven by a desire for results, he performs all kinds of actions—whether optional rites preceded by a motive for fruit, such as the Citrā sacrifice; or means for achieving ends like the killing of enemies, such as the Śyena rite; or prohibited acts, such as eating *kalañja*—even though he himself does not wish to do them. Yet, even though he desires it, he does not perform the action characterized by renunciation (*nivṛtti*), which has been taught because it leads to the supreme goal of man. And this state of affairs is not possible without dependence on another; therefore, by whom [is he constrained] by force?

Just as a servant, though knowing that an action contrary to his master’s will leads to all manner of misfortune, nevertheless performs such a deed when commanded by the king, so too [is Arjuna acting]. Tell me of that person who sets one on the path of ruin, so that having learned of him, I may strive to utterly destroy him—this is the meaning. O Vārṣṇeya, [descendant] of the Vṛṣṇi clan.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [pages 266–266]

By addressing her as one who has graciously descended into the family of his maternal grandfather— known as the *Tṛptidīpa*— he suggests that he, the son of a Vārṣṇeyī, should not be neglected by her. || 159 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s reply:
"This is desire, this is anger, born of the quality of rajas."
A great eater and a great sinner—let him crush this enemy here.

Regarding the word "kāma" (desire): this desire, which is well-known as arising from the quality of passion (*rajo-guṇa*)—that is, having its origin (*samudbhava*) in the quality of passion—is that which impels a person toward action. At times, this very desire also transforms into the form of anger (*krodha*). What, then, is that anger like? It is "mahāśana," meaning it has a vast appetite for the multitude of sense objects. It is called "mahāpāpmā" (the great sinner) because it is metaphorically so designated due to being the cause of great sin.

Therefore, its nature as a great evil is established. Consequently, in this context of *saṃsāra*, know this enemy—which takes the form of desire (*kāma*) and anger (*krodha*)—to be such. The intended meaning is this:

by the force of *prārabdha* (commenced karma), it is either desire or anger—both of which are effects of the intensified quality of *rajas*—that impels a person to action, and not the mere inclination or will (*pravṛtti-icchā*). || 160 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): When Arjuna had thus questioned, [the Lord replied by citing the following Vedic text]: "Now, indeed, they say: 'This person consists entirely of desire. In the beginning, this was only the Self, one alone. He desired: 'May I have a wife; may I procreate; may I have wealth...'"

The answer established by the Śruti, beginning with "Perform your duty," is as follows: Śrī Bhagavān says, "This is desire. That which you asked about—the cause that forcibly impels one toward the path of misfortune—is this very desire, the great enemy. It is because of this that all calamities befall living beings. Now, one might object: "Is it not seen that anger also impels one toward malevolent rites (abhicāra) and the like? To this he replies: "This is anger. Anger is indeed nothing but desire arising from some particular cause.

When obstructed, it transforms into anger; therefore, this anger is also that very same thing. The meaning is that when this great enemy alone is warded off, all human goals (puruṣārtha) are attained. To explain the means for warding it off, he states its cause: "arising from the quality of rajas. Since the quality of rajas—characterized by pain, activity, and force—is its source or cause, the effect conforms to its cause; therefore, it too is of that same nature.

Although the quality of *tamas* is also a cause of that [desire], nevertheless, because *rajas* alone is predominant in the inclination toward suffering, it is *rajas* alone that is specified. By this it is stated that when *rajas* is diminished by a *sāttvika* mental state, *tamas* is also diminished. Alternatively, to the question of how it acts as an impeller toward the path of misfortune, he says: "For desire is the source from which the quality of *rajas*, characterized by activity and the like, arises."

Consisting of a longing for sense objects, arising spontaneously and setting *rajas* in motion, it impels the person toward action characterized by suffering; therefore, the intention is that this [desire] must necessarily be destroyed. Now, one might object: "There are four means—conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and punishment—and when the first three are impossible, the fourth, punishment, should be employed, but not by mere force. Anticipating this, he specifies [the nature of desire] in order to state the impossibility of those three: "It is a great eater, a great sinner... [and so forth].

"PM" means this: he is a "great eater" (*mahāśana*) because his appetite is vast, according to the *Smṛti*: "One should attain tranquility, realizing that all the rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women on earth are not enough for even one person. Therefore, he cannot be won over by gifts. Nor can he be subdued by conciliation or sowing dissension, because he is a great sinner and extremely fierce; for, impelled by him, one commits sin even while knowing it leads to undesirable results. Therefore—

Know— that is, understand— that this very desire is the enemy here in this worldly existence; for all of this has been explained by the author of the Vārttika in his commentary on the Śruti text, "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone."

Since the aforementioned qualified person possesses autonomy with respect to both engagement (*pravṛtti*) and cessation (*nivṛtti*), why does he engage in the process of saṃsāra rather than on the path characterized by cessation, which completely destroys the misfortunes of saṃsāra? It must be explained by whom he is impelled [to do so].

Even knowing that there is the ripening of misfortune, he still engages [in action]. Such engagement is never observed anywhere except under the influence of dependence on another. Therefore, for a person seeking the highest good (*śreyas*), one must state the impeller toward undesirable actions; for the sake of removing that [impulsion], the subsequent scripture (*parā śruti*) would have this purpose: "This [world] is devoid of the goals of man (*puruṣārtha*) and is crowded with every kind of misfortune. Thus, the dull-witted person desires unattained human goals through means, and likewise seeks to abandon misfortunes.
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

The ignorant person is not certain about the Self; for the Śruti says, "Being one whose desire has arisen from ignorance, [he acts]. Indeed, no action whatsoever is seen here belonging to anyone that is performed without desire. Whatever a living being does, all that is the movement of desire. This desire is indeed anger.

"The statement beginning with 'this' [is] from the Smṛti: 'Therefore, nothing other than desire is perceived as the motivator. The phrase 'without desire' is from the words of Manu. The rest is clear. || 160 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "In this context, it is observed that only desire and anger act as the motivators of a person, not the *anicchā-prārabdha* (unwillingly commenced *prārabdha-karma*).
Anticipating this doubt, he cites that very statement which establishes its status as a motivator:
"O son of Kuntī, bound by one's own action born of one's own nature..."
That which you do not wish to do out of delusion, you will nevertheless do against your will.

Regarding the phrase "born of its own nature" (*svabhāvajena*): O son of Kuntī, being bound by one's own performed action—which is precisely one's own *prārabdha* karma—you will, even if you do not wish to do so, perform that which you do not desire to do out of delusion and lack of discrimination, being helpless and subject to another's power. Therefore, the sense is that one must accept the existence of *prārabdha* karma that occurs against one's will. || 61 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "According to the statement of Madhusūdana Ācārya that 'desire (kāma) consists of longing for sense objects,' it is understood that only desire—characterized by a craving for desired objects such as sound and so forth—is the motivator for the acquisition of those respective objects. Thus, what relevance does this have to the promise to state the authoritative means regarding objects undertaken without prior conscious desire? To this, we reply: "Quite true. This [objection] arises from Arjuna’s question here.

Although the question concerns the very object that serves as the cause for activity preceded by a lack of desire—implied by the word "anicchan" (not desiring)—and since it is impossible for that unseen [cause] to be clearly manifested without its visible form, the Lord’s answer culminates in His intent being directed toward that very point through the aforementioned form of desire;

nevertheless, bearing in mind that there exists a specific statement of His own from the eighteenth chapter to make that [unseen cause] even more clearly understood for you, [the author] says: "Assuming... and so forth.
The Teacher recites this: "Born of one's own nature" (*svabhāvajena*). Here too, the commentary of the venerable Madhusūdana is written: He explains *prakṛti* (nature).
"Bound by action born of one's own nature"—that is, by one's own innate, non-acquired action such as valor and so forth, which arises from the previously mentioned *kṣatriya* nature;

you, O Kaunteya, are constrained and brought under control. That battle, which has the slaughter of kinsmen and so forth as its cause—[you engage in it] out of delusion, thinking, "I am independent; I shall act exactly as I desire."

Thinking "I shall cause [it] to fall," you do not wish to act out of delusion; nevertheless, even against your will and though you do not desire it, being dependent upon natural karma and dependent upon the Supreme Lord, you will certainly act. || 161 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now he states that there exists what is begun by the will of another:
"Neither unwilling nor willing, they are joined with the courtesy of others."
They experience pleasure and pain; for this is indeed the result of actions preceded by the will of another.

"Nor those who do not desire": even those who do not desire do not experience [the results], and even those who do desire do not experience them. Rather, being joined with courtesy toward others, they experience pleasure and pain solely for the sake of pleasing them. Therefore, the meaning is that this well-known *prārabdha* (commenced karma), which serves as the cause for the enjoyment of such pleasure and so forth, is preceded by the will of another. For this very reason, since *prārabdha* cannot be avoided even when its defects are perceived, there is the will of that [other].
The meaning is that one cannot prevent its being a cause. || 62 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Having thus established the two types of *prārabdha* among the three promised—namely, those consisting of desire (*iccha*) and lack of desire (*aniccha*)—the author now briefly summarizes the third, *parēcchā-prārabdha*, with the words "Not unwillingly" (*nānicchanto*). The term "others" (*pare*) refers to those who are clever, skillful, dexterous, capable, enterprising, and energetic—according to Amara’s lexicon—as well as those impelled by the power of other people; this is the meaning. The word "living beings" (*jīvāḥ*) is to be understood as implicit. [They experience] pleasure and pain.

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: they experience [the results] through the medium of the well-known favors and restraints performed by Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra, just like Hariścandra. The word "hi" is used for emphasis. The construction is that this alone is action preceded by the will of another. || 162 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 268]

[From the commentary by Rāmānanda on the *Tṛptidīpa*: Now, one might object that if even a knower of reality (*tattvavit*) is admitted to have desire, it would contradict the scriptural text, "Desiring what? (*kim icchan*). Thus, he raises the doubt: "How then is desire denied in such a way as 'desiring what'? ]
It is not a negation of desire, but rather a sublation of desire, like a roasted seed.

"How then?"—the meaning of this question is: by the sentence "What does he desire?", how is the absence of desire described? He provides the answer: "It is not a negation of desire. He explains that it is not by this [sentence] that the absence of desire is being stated; rather, what is made known is that even though desire exists, it lacks the capacity to produce purposeful activity. To illustrate its lack of efficacy despite existing in its own nature, he states an example:
"Roasted," thus [it is said]. || 63 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "In that case, the possibility of the aforementioned various types of *prārabdha* karma must be asserted even for those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), precisely because liberation while living would otherwise be inexplicable. Consequently, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as 'If he [should desire]... (*ātmānaṃ cet...*) which begin with 'What desiring... (*kim icchan...*). Anticipating this objection, the author provides the following resolution: "How then? (verse 163).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He elaborates upon the meaning briefly stated:
"But seeds that have been roasted are incapable of producing their effects."
The desire of the wise should be regarded as such; because it lacks substantial reality, it does not produce an effect.

Regarding the phrase "roasted": just as roasted seeds, although existing in their own nature, do not produce effects such as sprouts, so too the desire of the wise person, though existing in itself, is incapable of producing effects such as addiction because it is sublated by the knowledge of the non-existence of the object desired. This is the meaning. || 64 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He clarifies the aforementioned illustration with the words "But roasted... (*bharjitāni tu*). He applies this to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "The wise one... (*vidvaditi*). Just as roasted seeds of rice and the like, though capable of production, do not at all produce sprouts and so forth, so too the will (*icchā*) of the knowers of Brahman such as Saubhari and others—even while characterized by non-existence due to the realization of the unreality [of the world]—is [directed toward] the direct perception of the oneness of the non-dual Brahman and the Self, which is indicated by the falsity of duality.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: because [the knowledge] effects its result through the production of merit and so forth, it must be accepted that after the completion of *prārabdha* karma, it no longer brings about the experience of duality. || 164 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "In that case, the will of the knower should not even be admitted, since there is an absence of fruit.
Anticipating this, he states—with an illustration—that the absence of fruit is unproven because the fruit characterized as experience does indeed exist:
"Even though a burnt seed does not sprout, it is still utilized for eating."
Even the desire of the wise would result in meager enjoyment and not in great calamity. || 165 ||
"Burnt seed" means roasted, so to speak. "Calamity" (*vyasana*) is of many kinds, such as misfortune and the like;
for the lexicon states: "Calamity (*vyasana*) occurs in the sense of misfortune, ruin, fault, or that which arises from passion or anger. (65)

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, regarding the statement that both the example and the illustrated case are incapable of producing their respective effects due respectively to being burnt and to being wise—is this incapacity for some particular effect, or is it absolute? It cannot be the first, because even in the case of seeds that have not been burnt, there is generally an absence of the production of some particular effect—such as sprouts and the like—due to their not having been sown, or even when sown, due to being damaged by drought and so forth; this occurs despite their being delimited by the nature of "seed-ness."

Nor is it the case that [the reason] is observed everywhere, because in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the state of being burnt is not a relevant factor (*aprayojaka*). Likewise, even though ignorant people possess the desire for sexual union with Rambhā and so forth, one observes that they do not perform such actions in the mortal world, nor even in the heavenly world (*svarloka*) without such merit (*puṇya*); therefore, in the subject of the argument (*dārṣṭāntika*) as well, the state of being a knower (*vidvattva*) is not a relevant factor. Nor is the last [alternative] correct, because the action of eating and so forth, as well as the action of experiencing the fruits of *prārabdha* karma, occur sequentially.

Wishing to resolve this doubt by demonstrating that it is based solely on a failure to understand the nature of existence, the proponent clarifies his own position regarding both cases: "When [the seed] is burnt...
[Page 269] — Seventh Chapter.
[This is] accompanied by two commentaries.

Regarding the word "alpa" (small): it refers to [a state] like that of Jaratkāru and others, where there is merely some slight enjoyment, but not [a state] like that of Bharata and others which brings about identity with another birth.
The meaning is "the application of [one's] self. Regarding the word *vyasana*, Amara states: "It refers to misfortune, ruin, or a fault born of desire or anger. Likewise, Viśva states:

"*Vyasana* refers to an inauspicious addiction such as drinking, women, hunting, and so forth; it refers to a sinful act resulting in undesirable divine retribution, poison, or a fruitless effort. || 165 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that it is karma alone which, by means of experience, produces even calamity; anticipating this, he says:
"Because its purpose has been fulfilled through experience, the prārabdha-karma is exhausted."
The reality of what is to be enjoyed is perceived through delusion, and therein arises calamity.

"By experience" (bhogena): the meaning is that since prārabdha-karma is a cause for mere experience, it does not produce affliction (vyasana). From what, then, does the birth of affliction arise? To this he says: "That which is to be experienced" (bhoktavya). In that regard, in that context. || 66 ||

A0. Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even for the wise man, if enjoyment exists by his own will, there would surely be many calamities characterized by misfortune and the like, caused by separation from those enjoyments and so forth. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] replies: Since the *prārabdha* (commenced karma) that impels enjoyment is restricted solely to granting the body and other factors that produce pleasure and pain to the individual soul, it achieves its purpose through that alone; therefore, as in the case of Bharata and others, it is not able to cause the aforementioned calamities. Thus ends the response.

"He maintains it as an object of enjoyment" (*bhogena*). One should not ask: "If that is so, then how did the aforementioned calamity come to pass for Bharata and others? [The answer is: It was due solely to the delusion regarding the reality of his own body and so forth, which serves as the cause for compassion toward the deer fawn that was to be enjoyed, and which is rooted in ignorance. Thus he says: "That which is to be enjoyed... (verse 166).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He shows the delusion that is the cause of this calamity:
"May this enjoyment not perish; may it increase further and further."
"May obstacles not hinder me; I am fortunate because of this"—such is the delusion. (67)

"May it not perish"—meaning, "may this enjoyment not perish; may it increase further and further; may obstacles not hinder it, may they not create an obstruction to it; through this very enjoyment, I am fortunate and have achieved my life's purpose"—such is the delusion that arises.
And from that, there comes "addiction" (vyasana); such is the meaning. || 67 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, it may be objected: "While everyone generally says that the entire phenomenal world, consisting of the body and so forth, is real, why is it that nowadays in the Kali age, many who consider themselves learned—though they are actually commoners who take refuge in the Vedānta scriptures—mostly cover their mouths [with secrecy], being solely intent on acting as they please within, while even thousands of them constantly proclaim its unreality? [The text continues: ...even though there are thousands... [of such people].

Anticipating the question of how one who desires to know [the truth] may obtain it—and that for the sake of one's own awakening and the instruction of others, a definitive conclusion must be reached after thorough examination—it is said, "It arises from delusion alone.
To clarify this, the author vividly demonstrates the specific nature of delusion as it falls within the scope of one's own experience and so forth, saying: "May it not perish! (167).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In this context, he states the means for its remedy:
"That which is not to be, will not be; and that which is to be, cannot be otherwise."
Thus, this realization, which destroys the poison of anxiety, brings an end to delusion.

"Yadabhāvi" means that which is incapable of coming to be will certainly not come to be; and that which is capable of coming to be will certainly not be otherwise. This is the "poison-destroyer of anxiety" (*cintā-viṣaghna*). Thoughts such as "When will this auspicious thing of mine happen? or "When will this undesirable thing cease? are like poison because they cause the destruction of the person with whom they are associated; thus, it is called the "poison-destroyer of anxiety" because it destroys this poison of anxiety. In this way—
That awakening which is real is the remover of delusion; the meaning is that it is the remover of the aforementioned delusion. || 68 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, let it be granted that for them this determination of the final delusion is indeed inferable from their respective empirical transactions; nevertheless, even for the wise, as long as there exists the desire for enjoyment produced by *prārabdha* karma, there remains the possibility of calamities such as separation from desired objects of enjoyment.
Thus, the state [of suffering] persists.
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[the section] titled *Tṛptidīpa*.

If it is argued that this is not so, we say no; for they possess the great mantra of firmest discrimination (*viveka*), which neutralizes the *kālakūṭa* poison produced by the ocean of *saṃsāra*—including all conceivable sufferings and the like.

With this intention, he reveals their resolve with the words "That which... (*yad iti*). The phrase "by the appointment of the Lord, whose will is true and who bestows the fruits of *prārabdha-karma*" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The remainder, however, is quite clear. || 168 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Since both the wise man and the ignorant man are alike in being enjoyers of experience, why is it that one suffers from addiction while the other does not?
Anticipating this doubt, he states that this distinction is established by the presence or absence of erroneous cognition:
"Even when the enjoyment is the same, the deluded man falls into addiction, whereas the awakened man does not."
For one who is exhausted by the pursuit of an impossible goal, there is great calamity.
"Even one who is the same" means one who has awakened, possessed of knowledge, a wise person. To the question, "How is delusion a cause of calamity?", he says:
"Of an impossible object. (69)

Commentary (a0): If it is argued that, even though there is equality between both the wise and the ignorant in the enjoyment of the fruits such as pleasure produced by *prārabdha* karma, the resulting benefit and harm occur respectively because they are rooted in discrimination (*viveka*) and non-discrimination (*aviveka*), then—intending to say, "May you live long"—the Teacher repeats those words and states the cause of the many calamities for the deluded person through the two halves of the verse beginning with "Even though equal" (*same’pi*). He says: "By intellect" (*buddheti*).

"Buddham" means that which is the object of the final valid cognition (*pramā*) produced by the great Mahāvākyas such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), wherein non-dual Brahman and the Self are realized as one, preceded by the falsity of duality; it exists always, and thus is "tathā" (thus). Regarding "aśakya" (impossible): this refers to the previously mentioned impossible things, such as "May this enjoyment not perish, may it increase further and further. || 169 ||
Having realized that enjoyment consists of illusion, one should withdraw attachment from it.
Even while eating, he forms no mental construction; how then could there be any calamity?
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He shows the absence of that [delusion] for the discerning person with the words "the state of being composed of māyā" (māyāmayatvam). || 70 ||
Commentary on Verse 1:

Now, if this is so, one may ask how a knower of reality (tattvavit) experiences the enjoyment of *prārabdha* karma; in response to this expectation, he summarizes [the answer] with the word "prāya" (mostly).
Regarding the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*), such as garlands, sandalwood, women, and so forth—"āsthām" means an excessive degree of attachment (*premātiśaya*). He [then] summarizes...

The meaning is that there should be no obstacles, that they should not hinder [the practice], and that one should have such specific mental dispositions as thinking, "I am blessed by this. By the word *api* ("even"), it is suggested through implication (*dhvani*) that if even the aforementioned resolve were absent, the absence of addiction would be established *a fortiori*. He clarifies that very point through a rhetorical question: "Whence could there be addiction? (170).
It is like a dream or a magical illusion, consisting of an inconceivable arrangement.
Seeing the world as something seen and then lost, how could one take delight in it? (71)

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even when the illusory nature [of the world] is understood, since enjoyment at that time serves as a cause for pleasure, why should there be a cessation of worldly activity?
Anticipating this doubt, he states—beginning with the word *svadram*—"because of the perception of manifold defects. (71)

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, even if duality is illusory, according to the maxim of the eyes of a variegated hundred-petaled lotus, [the world] consists of forms such as the moon and the moon-faced one...

Anticipating the objection as to how the withdrawal of attention from that [worldly object] is easily accomplished given its extreme pleasantness at that moment, the author briefly summarizes with an illustration and a challenge in the verse beginning with *svapne* (in a dream). For in the Advaita system, there are indeed two views: the theory of creation upon perception (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*) and the theory of perception of the created (*sṛṣṭadṛṣṭivāda*). [The verse: "In a dream, a hundred-petaled lotus made of gold, possessing a thousand rays, shines; yet when one awakens, that very same thing is not seen. Therefore, the wise man should withdraw his mind from the objects of the world, which are like a dream. [Commentary: Even compared to the previously mentioned hundred-petaled lotus of variegated colors, this desired object existing within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is experienced as having an inferior reality. Therefore, the withdrawal of the mind from such an object is entirely appropriate. This is stated with an illustration and a challenge. For in the non-dualist doctrine, there are indeed the theories of "creation upon seeing" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*) and "seeing what has been created" (*sṛṣṭadṛṣṭivāda*). [The verse continues: "The waking state is like a dream; the dream is like the waking state. The difference between them is merely a matter of time. Thus, the wise man should withdraw his mind from the objects of the world, which are like a dream. [Commentary: The waking state is similar to a dream, and a dream is similar to the waking state. The distinction between the two is simply a difference in duration. Consequently, the wise person should withdraw their mind from worldly objects, which are comparable to a dream. By this, the author indicates that the waking state is unreal, just like a dream, and thus the withdrawal of the mind from it is easily achieved. Furthermore, he suggests that the dream state is also real, just like the waking state, thereby refuting the view that the dream is unreal while the waking state is real. This is because, according to the *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*, both states are equally unreal, being mere appearances. Therefore, the withdrawal of the mind from the waking state is easily accomplished through the practice of contemplation (*upāsanā*). Thus, the author concludes that the withdrawal of the mind from the waking state is indeed possible. [The verse continues: "The waking state is like a dream; the dream is like the waking state. Therefore, the wise person should withdraw their mind from worldly objects

Thus, there are two views based on the distinction of qualified authorities (*adhikāri-bheda*), both of which are indeed accepted by all the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*). In the former view, there is a twofold nature of existence (*sattā-dvaividhya*): the existence of the visible world (*dṛśya-sattā*) is merely apparent (*prātibhāsikī*), whereas the existence of the Seer (*dṛk-sattā*) is exclusively ultimate (*pāramārthikī*). In the latter view, however, there is a threefold nature of existence (*sattā-traividhya*): in addition to the ultimate existence of Brahman, the empirical existence (*vyāvahārikī*) of ether and so forth is distinct from the apparent existence of things like nacre-silver; for although they are equal in their falsity (*mithyātva*) regarding the visible world, the latter is distinct from the former.

Acceptance [of this view]: The distinction between phenomenal (prātibhāsika) and empirical (vyāvahārika) existence is established solely by their being sublated or unsublated by knowledge other than that of Brahman.
[End of] the seventh chapter.
We shall elaborate upon this in works such as the *Bodhaikyasiddhi*. Thus, here, for the sake of a beginner who is not yet qualified [for higher teachings], the analogy of the dream is presented.

The intention is that the final illustration is presented for one who still harbors attachment to the world. For it is well known that a magician’s trick (indrajāla)—such as a city manifested by māyā agitated by mantras and the like—has its existence dependent upon the magician.

In reality, although even that is merely phenomenal (prātibhāsika), because it is an error conditioned by an adjunct (sopādhika-bhrama) like a painting and so forth, it possesses a slightly higher degree of existence than dreams and the like; thus, it serves as an illustration for the empirical (vyāvahārika) world.

The intended meaning is "you. The reason for this is given by the terms "inconceivable" and "seen," which are placed in reverse order. The meaning is that what is seen due to its momentary power exists only to perish; it is fragile as a moment. || 171 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If there is knowledge of the similarity [of the world] to a dream or a magician's illusion, then attachment would not arise; but how does that very [attachment] come into being?
Anticipating this doubt, he states the means for its arising:
"Having seen one's own waking state through the direct perception of one's own dream..."
Being vigilant, one should meditate upon both of them repeatedly every day.

"His own dream": having perceived his own dream as if it were directly present through these two verses, and experiencing his own waking state, he—remaining vigilant regarding both the dream and the waking state—should repeatedly reflect that "this waking state is equal to a dream. (72)
Commentary (Ṭīkā): In that regard, for the sake of the first type of qualified seeker, he prescribes the contemplation upon those examples, beginning with "one's own" (svasva-).
"By means of direct perception" (āparokṣyeṇa) means by the direct perception of the witness-consciousness (sākṣipratyakṣeṇa). || 172 ||
Having long contemplated the complete equality of those two while awake, [he attains liberation].
Having completely abandoned the notion of its reality, one no longer feels attachment as before. (73)

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): Having thus long reflected upon the complete similarity between those two states—dream and waking—characterized by being causes of temporary enjoyment, by transformation, by insipidity, and by perishability; and having abandoned the notion of reality even regarding the waking state, he does not feel attachment (*anurajyati*), meaning he does not become enamored with waking objects either, just as in the previous state of knowing the world to be real. || 73 ||
The commentary on the result states: "For a long time," etc. (173).

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: since there is a mutual contradiction between the knowledge of the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—which depends on the unreality of its objects—and enjoyment (*bhoga*), which depends on the reality of its objects, how can enjoyment be established when such knowledge of falsity exists?
Anticipating this doubt, he resolves it by showing that there is no contradiction, because enjoyment does not depend upon the reality of its objects.
This duality is a magical illusion (indrajāla), because its arrangement is inconceivable.
For one who does not forget this, what loss can there be from the experience of *prārabdha* karma? (74)

Regarding the phrase "it is a magician's trick" (*indrajāla*): having reflected through reasoning that this duality—the entire collection of objects of enjoyment—is false, like a magician's trick because its construction is inconceivable, for the wise person who does not forget this [realization], what loss is there to the contemplation of falsity due to the experience of pleasure and pain, which are the fruits of *prārabdha* karma?
By the word "or" (*vā*), it is implied: what loss is there to enjoyment due to the contemplation of falsity? For their objects are distinct.
Such is the meaning. || 74 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, while providing for the practitioner of the final stage an investigation into the experience of those very examples, [the author] also pacifies the doubt as to how the enjoyment of *prārabdha*—characterized by the direct perception of either pleasure or pain—could possibly occur when that [realization] exists, given the impossibility of two mental modifications (*vṛtti*) existing simultaneously. He does so with the words "It is a magical illusion" (*iṃdrajālam*). This [world] possesses the nature of being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*), as characterized by the direct perception of the Witness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*).

The duality delimited by its own boundaries—the entire collection of the phenomenal world (prapañca) composed of the fivefold distinctions such as the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)—possesses falsity, like a magical illusion (indrajāla), which is universally accepted as being false. It is "inconceivable" because its construction is beyond the reach of thought; for, by contrast, it would be like Brahman [if it were not so].
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[the section titled] Tṛptidīpa (The Lamp of Contentment).

The intention is that since duality alone is the subject (*pakṣa*), this formulation is indeed a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*). Now, one might object: "Let this be a formal application of the inference for the falsity of duality; nevertheless, what relevance does it have to the present context? To this he says: "Thus" (*iti*). The meaning is: "of one who possesses an absence of loss of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) brought about by the continuous flow of memory produced by the aforementioned inference. This implies "of the knower of reality" (*tattvavit*). And thus, there is an absence of the aforementioned memory and its latent impressions.

The point is that in the absence of *ahantā* (the sense of "I"), the witness-consciousness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*) can indeed perceive the mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) which has been transformed into one of the forms—such as pleasure—produced by *prārabdha-karma*. Furthermore, there is no simultaneous occurrence of two such modifications either. In fact, according to the view of the Logicians (*tārkika*), who maintain that a cognition such as "the jar and the cloth" is a single cognition consisting of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*), the simultaneous occurrence of two cognitions is impossible. This is even more so in the view of the Advaitins, who possess subtle vision.

However, just as the light of a lamp, though being one and the same, appears divided by the differences of its respective delimiters (avacchedaka) when it simultaneously illuminates various objects such as jars and cloths situated nearby, so too it must be admitted that the single consciousness, when ignited as the intellect (*buddhi*), emerges outward through the various sense organs at once, assumes the form of each respective object, and becomes divided precisely by the differences among those respective mental modifications (*vṛtti*) delimited by those objects serving as their delimiters. These—

Nor has it been explained that its manifold transformation occurs simultaneously with an internal nature consisting of pleasure and so forth; for experience is exactly like this: "In my foot there is the pleasure born from the touch of the lotus-hands of a young woman; in my eyes, the pleasure born from gazing upon her smiling face; and likewise within me, the pleasure arising from the remembrance of the feet of Śrī Guru Hara. Therefore, the wise should reflect that not even a trace of contradiction exists here. || 174 ||
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: He demonstrates the very difference in their subject matter:
"The persistent effort [is directed] toward the recollection of the illusory nature of the knowledge of reality."
The persistence of the soul in experiencing the fruits of its commenced karma consists of pleasure and pain. (175)

Regarding the term *nirbandha*: it means persistence in the contemplation of the world's falsity—like a magician’s illusion—with respect to the knowledge of reality that has the principles of the universe as its object; it does not mean the denial of experience.

Furthermore, it refers to the insistence on the soul’s experiencing pleasure and pain resulting from *prārabdha* karma, but not to the imposition of reality upon that which is being experienced. This is the intended meaning. || 175 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Generally, contradiction is observed only between two things that have the same object, such as light and darkness. However, in the present case, since there is an absence of identity of object itself, such contradiction does not exist. To indicate this, the author clarifies the difference in the effects of the knowledge of reality (tattvavidyā) and prārabdha-karma with the words "nirbandha" (insistence). The phrase "dvaitaviṣaye" (regarding the object of duality) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 175 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus demonstrated that they have different objects, he states the authoritative scripture:
"Knowledge and the [karmic] undertaking do not contradict each other because their objects are distinct."
Indeed, even by those who know [the truth], a magical illusion is seen as a mere diversion. || 76 ||

Regarding the term "vidyā" (knowledge): the meaning is that knowledge (*vidyā*) and the karma that has begun to bear fruit (*prārabdha-karma*) do not contradict each other because they have different objects, just like the simultaneous cognition of form and taste. Anticipating the objection—"Where has it been seen that the knowledge of the illusory nature of an object of experience does not obstruct that experience?"—he says:
"by those who know," etc. Even by those who know the magic trick (*aindrajāla*), that is, by those who understand the specific wonder associated with a magician's illusion...
The meaning is that it is well known that [it] is perceived. || 76 ||
The commentary on verse a0 states the conclusion: "Vidyā" (knowledge). Therein, he provides experiential evidence: "Even by those who know.
This means even by those persons who have reached the certain conclusion that these mango trees and other objects produced by magic are indeed false. || 176 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Furthermore, one who asserts that there is a contradiction between knowledge (*vidyā*) and the commenced karma (*prārabdha-karma*) must be questioned: Is it said that the commenced karma is opposed to knowledge, or that knowledge is opposed to the commenced karma? It is not the first case; thus he says:
"If [the commenced karma] were to feed [the agent] by establishing the reality of the world..."
It is always opposed to knowledge; its reality does not arise from mere enjoyment. || 77 ||
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

Regarding the word "jagat" (the world): if the *prārabdha* karma, having established and brought about the reality and non-sublatability (*abādhyatva*) of the world—that is, of the entire range of objects of experience—were to cause the individual soul (*jīva*) to experience [them], namely, were to grant him pleasure and pain, then it would contradict knowledge (*vidyā*), because it would remove the falsity (*mithyātva*) that is the object of knowledge. It would not [contradict knowledge].

The meaning is that [the prārabdha] does not act in that manner, but rather bestows experience alone; therefore, the prārabdha is not opposed to knowledge. Anticipating the objection that the reality of the object of experience might follow from the force of that very experience, he says: "From mere experience" (bhogamātrāt). The sense is that there is no corroborative instance for the argument that "the disputed world is real because it is an object of experience. || 77 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): If this is so, then at what time would there be a contradiction between these two? To this, he says: "The world... (verse 177).
Enjoyment arises undiminished through imagined things that are one's own property.
In the same way, let enjoyment be accepted as occurring even through waking objects that are unreal. (78)
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that there is no illustrative example for the claim that enjoyment occurs through illusory objects; anticipating this, he says:
"anūna" (not deficient), etc. || 78 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might object: "How can one bring about the experience of *prārabdha* karma in this world without establishing some degree of reality for it? Nor is it correct to say—just as was stated immediately before—that 'even by those who know the truth, a magical illusion (*aindrajālika*) is seen as a diversion,' because even in the aforementioned example, since the verb 'to see' (*dṛś*) is used, there is no possibility of enjoyment in the form of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, what follows from this?"

Anticipating the objection that this might be mere intentional rhetoric (*tātparya*), he provides a resolution by clarifying it through an example that is experienced daily by almost everyone and is consistent in all its aspects; for in the world, when witnessing a magical illusion (*indrajāla*), the experience of satisfaction resulting from eating the fruits or other objects produced therein is always uncertain due to their occasional nature.
Thus he says: "not deficient" (*anyūna*). || 178 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; thus he says:
"If knowledge were to destroy the world of prārabdha-karma..."
Then it would exist; however, its denial does not occur through the realization of its illusory nature. || 79 ||

"If it were knowledge" (*yadi vidyā*): If knowledge were to negate the entire collection of worldly fortune, dissolving the very nature of the object of experience as it appears—just like the negating cognition "this is not silver"—then it would obstruct the *prārabdha-karma* by removing the means for the experience of pleasure and pain that constitutes the enjoyment of *prārabdha-karma*. But it does not do that; rather, it only makes known its falsity (*mithyātva*). Therefore, it does not [obstruct] *prārabdha-karma*.

The sense is that it is not contradictory to reality. Now, one might object: "Does it not follow that by the very cognition of falsity, the thing's own nature (svarūpa) would also be dissolved? Anticipating this, he says: "But not... [as in] illusion" (na tu-māyā).
The sense is that in cases such as a magician’s trick (indrajāla), the cognition of falsity is observed even without the dissolution of the thing's own nature. || 79 ||

Commentary (a0): Let it be so that the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is in every way non-opposed to *prārabdha* karma; nevertheless, because it is perceived through Śruti and Smṛti—such as "His actions perish when He, the higher and the lower, is seen," and "The fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes"—as being opposed to action in general, its opposition to *prārabdha* is established by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). In that regard—
To address the objection that this might not be so, he says: "If.

"The fire of the knowledge of Brahman—kindled by the operation of the wind that proceeds from the power of the true reality—completely and utterly consumes ignorance along with everything arising from it;

for it burns them away without leaving a trace, and it does not leave behind even the slightest vestige of the nature of transmigratory existence. Therefore, liberation is certain for the knower immediately."

Thus, even for someone who— following the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* and the well-known account of the sage Uddālaka in the *Bṛhadvāsiṣṭha*— has now taken refuge with single-minded devotion in a preeminent teacher established in Brahman after first cultivating the fourfold qualifications (*sādhana-catuṣṭaya*), and who continues to practice the hearing, reflection, and so forth of the Vedānta scriptures, [liberation] has not yet arisen because of the direct realization of the non-dual identity of Brahman and the Self; therefore, preceded by renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*)...
*The reading "anyūna" is that of Acyutarāya.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
titled Tṛptidīpa (The Lamp of Contentment).

By means of the practice of the attributeless *ahaṃgraha* meditation— instructed as previously described, characterized by the contemplation of the identity between the meanings of the words "I" (*ahaṃ*) and "Brahman" (*brahma*), purified through the utterance of the *praṇava*— at the time of death:
"He for whom there is no ripened meditation here, [must attain it] in the next world."

Based on the statement, "One is liberated upon realizing the Truth, whether at the time of death or in the world of Brahmā," if liberation— consisting in the destruction of the duality of *prārabdha* karma— should occur through the arising of the knowledge of Truth at the very moment of death when the maturation of meditation has reached its peak, then that person's knowledge (*vidyā*) regarding Brahman would negate the entire visible world for them.
The connection is that [the practice] would then destroy it, becoming a destroyer of the *prārabdha* (the karma already set in motion). || 179 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He elaborates on this very point:
"Without denying that this is a magical illusion, people [perceive it as such]."
Knowing it for what it is and not denying the experience, one likewise possesses the understanding that it is an illusion (māyā).

"Without denying" (anapahnutya): just as people, without denying that its nature is like a magical illusion (indrajāla), know it for what it is, saying, "This is a magical illusion," so too, without denying or dissolving enjoyment—that which is to be enjoyed—the realization of its being Māyā arises; the meaning is that there occurs the knowledge of the world's falsity. ||80||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, he clarifies with an example from the previously introduced position of *jīvanmukti*—that it is like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*), consisting of *māyā*—by means of a scriptural passage from the *Taittirīya Upaniṣad*, stating "without denying" (*anapahnutyā*) and so forth. Just as there is no denial of the aforementioned magical illusion, so too one does not deny or reject the experience (*bhoga*)—the direct perception of pleasure and so on produced by *prārabdha* karma—nor the duality (*dvaita*) regarding the objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*) and the rest, which is of the nature of *māyā*.

The logical connection is that [the world] is easily established as being dependent on you; therefore, even though it cannot be denied, the intended meaning is that the very understanding of its illusory nature (māyātva) is illustrated by the aforementioned example. || 180 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Since the scripture beginning with "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should one see? teaches the non-existence of the seer, the act of seeing, and the object seen, it follows that knowledge, upon arising, must dissolve the world. This being so, he raises an objection based on scripture as to how the experience of enjoyment could possibly belong to the knower, using two verses:
But where one perceives this world as one's own self, what [perceiver] would there be, by what [means], and of what [object]?
"What should one smell? What should one speak?"—thus it has been proclaimed extensively in the Śruti.

With the words "But where," etc.: in which state of knowledge (*vidyāvasthā*), for this wise one, the entire world has become his very self—where, through the realization that "all this is what this Self is," everything becomes his own essential nature (*svarūpa*)—in that state, who is the seer? By what instrument, such as the eye, could he see what object, such as a form, is to be seen? Likewise, by what characterized as the sense of smell could he smell what, such as a flower, or what speech could he speak by what [organ]?

Or he might speak by means of the tongue; the word "or" (vā) is used here to indicate the absence of activity in the other sense organs. The meaning is that this has been stated many times in the Śruti in such a manner. || 81 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection may be raised: according to the aforementioned method, in the view that liberation is attained while living (jīvanmukti), the knowledge of reality merely makes one understand the falsity of duality;
it does not effect its destruction. And thus, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the experience of the fruits of past actions (prārabdha-bhoga) remains perfectly possible for the knower.

One might object that [the view] is indeed untenable because it contradicts such scriptural passages as, "But where for him everything has become the Self alone, by what and whom should he see? and so forth;

this is raised by the pair of verses beginning with "yatra tv asya. The word "tu" (but) is intended to indicate a distinction from the meaning of the preceding scripture, namely, "For where there is duality as it were, there one sees another," etc., following the valid cognition produced by the scripture, "All this is what this Self is," and so forth. This is implied by the context.
"By what would one smell that? By what would one taste that? By what would one speak to that? By what would one hear that?

By what would one think of that? By what would one touch that? By what would one perceive that?"—the meaning is "in many such ways. The word *vā* (or) is used precisely to indicate the cessation of all the organs of action. || 181 ||
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.
Rāma’s Commentary: To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"By that [means], having negated duality, knowledge arises; and not otherwise."
And if you ask how enjoyment can exist for the wise one in such a state, listen: || 82 ||

Therefore, regarding the claim that there is duality: in the sūtra, "It refers to either deep sleep or liberation, for [the scripture] has made this clear," the scriptural passage beginning with "But where for him... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1) was explained as referring to either the state of deep sleep or liberation; consequently, the negation of the world does not occur through knowledge.
Thus he responds: "Listen. (82)

— Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "By that," and so forth. Since this objection has been raised, the answer has already been determined by the venerable teacher Vādarāyaṇa himself in the fourth pāda of the fourth chapter of the Uttara-mīmāṃsā; therefore...

He turns the questioner toward himself solely for the purpose of hearing the hidden meaning of the oral tradition of the Seers, by means of the remainder of the verse beginning with "iti" and so forth. || 182 ||
"Or rather, the scripture concerns the state of deep sleep or the state of liberation."
For this has been stated very clearly in the sūtra beginning with "svāpyayasampatyoḥ" (Sūtra 4.4.16). || 83 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: "Dissolution" (svāpyaya) means deep sleep; "attainment" (saṃpatti) means liberation. || 82 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He explains that very same point by first citing the relevant portion of the Sūtra—namely, "suṣupti" (deep sleep). For one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*), this refers to the state of deep sleep, because that alone is experienced by him every day at all times. But for one who is liberated (*mukta*), this [Sūtra] refers only to the state of liberation, as in the present Śruti passage beginning with, "But where for him everything has become the Self alone. Thus, regarding the state of one seeking liberation, he speaks to his beloved wife Maitreyī concerning *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living).

The intention is that this is because [Yājñavalkya], having entered such a state, spoke thus from his own experience during nirvikalpa-samādhi and so forth. The word "vā" (or) serves precisely to indicate the alternative based on the differences in those respective experiences. To the question, "What is the authority for the meaning of the aforementioned Śruti? he says: "It has been stated. Regarding "sva": the meaning is that it is found in the final quarter of the fourth chapter (*catur-lakṣaṇī*) of the *Brahma-sūtra*, specifically in the sūtra: "It is made manifest as depending on either deep sleep (*svāpyaya*) or union (*saṃpatti*). Indeed (*hi*).

The word *eva* (only) is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). The construction is as follows: it has been stated that in such a Sūtra alone, the collection of meanings already mentioned is expressed with extreme clarity. As for the meaning of the Sūtra:

"deep sleep" (*svāpyaya*) is "sleep" (*supti*), based on the Śruti passage, "For he has gone to his own (*sva*), for he has merged (*apīta*). "Attainment" (*saṃpatti*) means liberation (*mukti*). The phrase "of those two" refers to deep sleep and liberation.
The term "either one" (*anyatarat*) signifies being the subject of an optional alternative (*icchika-vikalpa*), as in the injunction, "One should sacrifice with either rice or barley."

That which exists there according to such dependence—namely, depending on those seeking liberation and depending on those already liberated, respectively—is this collection of objects consisting of the absence of duality. The particle *hi* is used for emphasis. This is because it has been revealed and made manifest by the very scripture beginning with "But when for him... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23). || 183 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He states the objection against not accepting that this scripture has deep sleep and so forth as its subject matter:
"Otherwise, the status of Yājñavalkya and others as teachers would not be possible."
Scholarly wisdom is seen through duality; when duality is not seen, speech does not speak.
