"Otherwise"—he states the reasoning for this with the words "duality," etc. If Yājñavalkya and others were to perceive duality, then, due to the absence of the knowledge of non-duality, they would not be teachers (*ācāryas*). On the other hand, if they do not perceive duality, then, because of the non-perception of those to be taught—the disciples and so forth—the teacher's speech would not proceed toward the disciple for the purpose of instruction. Therefore, the implication is that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the interruption of the tradition of knowledge (*vidyā-saṃpradāya*). || 84 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, this scripture, which illuminates direct experience, states: "But in that state of knowledge wherein the world became the Self alone for him, then who could smell what, by what means, in the non-dual Supreme Reality?"

If it is argued that this has been explained as referring solely to the state of having just attained liberation, that is true; however, in the present context, the primary focus is on the state of that knowledge.
Vidyāraṇya’s *Pañcadaśī*, titled *Tṛptidīpa*.

He states "otherwise" (*anyathā*) because that [scriptural statement] cannot be explained otherwise than as having the intention of conveying the state of reality (*tathātva*). The reason for this is given: "duality," etc. Ta-...
Therefore, the aforementioned method alone is the correct one; such is the direction [of the argument]. || 184 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "Granted that the knowledge possessed by Yājñavalkya and others during their state as teachers is indeed 'vidyā' (knowledge); nevertheless, it does not possess the status of *aparokṣa-vidyā* (immediate, direct knowledge) because of the continued existence of the perception of duality. However, since there is an absence of the perception of duality in *nirvikalpaka-samādhi* (non-conceptual absorption), that alone is *aparokṣa-vidyā*. Thus he [the opponent] questions:
But in non-conceptual samādhi, it is because of the non-perception of duality.
If it is argued that this very state is direct knowledge (aparokṣavidyā), then why is deep sleep not likewise so? (185)

Regarding the term "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*): he refutes [the objection] by stating, "Why is deep sleep not likewise so?", because even the non-perception of duality leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). || 185 ||
— Commentary (A0 Ṭīkā):

Now, one might object: let the status of Yājñavalkya and others as teachers be established by means of indirect knowledge (*parokṣavidyā*) alone; however, the non-perception of duality is possible only in non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpasamādhi*), for it is said: "When the five faculties of knowledge, along with the mind, and the intellect cease from their activity... [Yājñavalkya Upaniṣad 1.50].
"Having attained which, one considers no other gain to be superior to it; established in which, one is not shaken even by heavy suffering"— so says the Śruti, "They call this the supreme goal."

"One should know that as the disjunction from the conjunction with suffering, designated as yoga"—from this *smṛti* (traditional authority), it follows that at that time the seer abides in its own nature. Fearing that the state of *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi* alone might be considered immediate knowledge (*aparokṣavidyā*) based on the sequence of *Yogasūtra* aphorisms beginning with "the wisdom there is truth-bearing" (*ṛtaṃbharā tatra prajñā*), he provides a resolution to avoid such an over-extension: "nirvikalpa... (verse 185).
Rāma’s Commentary: He raises an objection to avoid an over-extension [of the argument]:
"If you say that one does not know the reality of the Self during sleep..."
It should be stated that knowledge is simply the cognition of the Self, not the forgetting of duality. (86)

Regarding the phrase "the reality of the Self" (*ātmatattvam*): if it is argued that deep sleep cannot be considered knowledge (*vidyā*) because, although there is an absence of the perception of duality, there is also an absence of knowledge directed toward the Self, then it follows that only discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñāna*) possesses the nature of knowledge, and not the mere absence of the perception of duality. To this, he says: "Then... (verse 86).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "the reality of the Self" (ātmatattva). || 186 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "If it is argued that knowledge (*vidyā*) consists only of the combination of the non-perception of duality and the realization of the Self, and not of each individually—" then [it follows that] jars and other such objects [would also be knowledge].
They would be partakers of half-knowledge, due to their forgetting all duality. (87)

Regarding the phrase "both": he refutes [the objection] that if even the forgetting of duality were admitted as a constituent part of knowledge (*vidyā*), then inert matter (*jaḍa*) would also follow as being half-knowledge, by saying "then jars and so forth. He states the justification for this here: "all... (verse 87).

Commentary (a0): Now, anticipating the objection that—on the basis of the cited scriptures and other authorities—the nature of immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) consists precisely in the union of both the vision of reality and the non-vision of the visible world—he rebukes this with a mocking counter-argument in the two verses beginning with "ubhayam" (both). || 187 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Within this very same position, he states with derision that even those persons possessing meditative absorption (samādhi) would not possess even partial knowledge:
"Because of the multiplicity of distractions, such as the sound of mosquitoes and the like..."
Your knowledge would not be as firm as that of Vādī and the others. || 88 ||
The Seventh Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.

Regarding the phrase "the sound of mosquitoes": just as the forgetting of duality is firm in the case of [meditating on] jars and the like, such forgetting of duality is not possible for you in your samādhi. The meaning is that this is because of the presence of many distractions, such as the sound of mosquitoes and so forth. || 88 ||

Commentary on verse a0: Regarding the word *maśaka* (mosquito), [it is said]: "Holding the body steady with the three parts erect, having withdrawn the senses into the heart by means of the mind, the wise man should cross over all terrifying currents by means of the raft of Brahman. Restraining the vital breaths here while his movements are disciplined, he should breathe out through the nostrils when the breath has become thin. A wise man should hold the mind without distraction, like a chariot yoked to vicious horses."

"Therefore, one should apply oneself to a practice in a place that is level, pure, free from pebbles, fire, and sand, devoid of noise, water-reservoirs, and the like; it should be agreeable to the mind and not painful to the eyes, situated in a cave or a windless shelter. This implies, as stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, that the practice of yoga is beset by many obstacles, such as the pain to the eyes and the sound of gnats. || 188 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that only the knowledge of the Self constitutes true wisdom (vidyā), and not the forgetting of duality; to this, he replies:
"If you maintain that the cognition of the Self alone is wisdom, then be happy."
If you wish to restrain a wicked mind, then restrain it as you please. || 89 ||

"It is the very cognition of the Self"—with the intention that "this is what we desire," he offers a blessing: "Then may you be happy. Now, one might raise the objection: "But if the cognition of the Self alone is knowledge (*vidyā*), and that does not arise in a defiled mind, then the cessation of mental fluctuations must be practiced in order to eliminate the defects of the mind. He restates this doubt with the words, "The defiled mind," and then accepts it with, "Restrain it. (89)

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus ridiculed and refuted, the opponent or the disciple accepts the established doctrine (siddhānta) with the words beginning "The Self" (ātma). Then, having repeated his statement, the proponent of the established doctrine greets him with a blessing, using the words beginning "Thus" (iti).

Observing him who is doubting whether the cessation of the mind (cittanirodha) should be practiced through discernment (viveka), dispassion (vairāgya), and so forth for the sake of the bliss of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), he says:
"Corrupt," so it is said. || 189 ||
Therefore, that which is desired must be sought, because of the observation of its illusory nature.
"Even if he should desire, he should not desire like an ignorant person; for it is heard in the Śruti: 'What is there to desire? (190)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: "That is desired"—the words "to us as well" are to be supplied. Why? To this he says: "Because it is to be sought.

The meaning is that since the illusory nature of the world is properly perceived when the defects of the mind have been removed—this being what is sought for the sake of knowing the non-dual Self—it is therefore "desired. Thus, he concludes the intended meaning of the portion of the mantra beginning with "desiring what? (kim icchan).

Regarding the phrase "desiring": even though he desires, he would not desire like an ignorant person; therefore, the scriptural text asks, "Desiring what?"—this is the construction of the meaning. || 190 ||

The commentary on *a0* states: "The reason for that is 'that' (*tad*). Regarding "it is to be desired" (*eṣṭavyā*): the meaning is that duality (*dvaita*) is what is to be desired or longed for; the sense is that no one is ever fully satiated by the splendor of a beloved's locks of hair. The conclusion is stated as: "Even though desiring" (*icchan api*). Since duality itself is sublated, even the desire of the knower, as well as its agent, object, and instrument, are likewise [sublated]; therefore, it does not exist for the ignorant.
This is the intended meaning. Now, he states the consistency with the present mantra by saying "Desiring what? and so forth. || 190 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the reason for describing the intention in this way:
"Attachment is the mark of ignorance; let attachment and the rest remain in the wise man."
Thus, these two treatises are indeed meaningful, as there is no contradiction between them in this way. (91)

"Passion is the mark [of ignorance]"—this refers to the scriptural teaching aimed at negating passion for one who knows reality, as in: "Passion is the mark of non-awakening on the grounds of mental exertion; how can there be verdant growth for that tree which has fire in its hollow? On the other hand, there is a teaching aimed at accepting passion for that very same person, as in: "Since the purpose of the scripture is fully accomplished, liberation occurs by that much alone according to the measure [of knowledge];
let passion and the like exist as they may, for the absence of them does not cause any fault. Thus, it is for that very person that passion is accepted.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 278.

And thus, when this is the case, both treatises— the one titled *Tṛptidīpa* and the other— become meaningful and purposeful for the knower of reality (*tattvavid*), provided there is an absence of intense attachment (*dṛḍharāga*). This is because, without contradiction,

the treatise intended to prohibit attachment has as its object those with intense attachment, while the treatise intended to accept it has as its object those with a semblance of attachment (*rāgābhāsa*).
The state of being. || 91 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Not only is the consistency of the meaning of the Śruti—“Desiring what, for the sake of what, would one suffer for the body?”—established by the aforementioned determination of the desire of one who knows reality, but the contradiction between two statements of the Vārtikakāra is also resolved;
thus he says: “Rāga” (attachment).
"Passion is the mark of ignorance in the fields of mental exertion;
how can there be straightness in that tree which has fire within its hollow?
This statement, found in the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi*, indeed prohibits the state of being a knower (*vidvat-bhāga*). Its essential meaning, however, is as follows: in the mind—

This means: it has as its objects those things called sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, which have become the ground for the movement of the mind. Attachment (*rāga*) is the longing for a desirable object;

it is the mark (*liṅga*)—that is, the indicator by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*)—of ignorance (*abodha*), which is the pervasive [cause]. The logical connection (*anvaya*) is: "The pervaded (*vyāpya*) exists. That is to say, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is as follows:
wherever in a person a longing directed toward a desirable object is observed, there is ignorance. That very [pervasion]...

He confirms this by means of an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroborative illustration) with the words beginning "kutaḥ" (why?). Regarding the phrase "of that tree in whose hollow there is fire": the term *śādvala* refers to grassy ground; according to Amara’s lexicon (*śyādo haritaḥ śādvalaḥ*), it means possessing a green color. The connection is: "Why [would it be so]? It could not be so under any circumstances. Now, he reveals a certain portion of a statement by the author of the *Vārttika* itself, which is contrary to this, using its opening words: "Let them be... (*saṃtu*).
For this very point is contained within the *Vārttika* on the *Bṛhadāraṇyakabhāṣya*:
"Since the purpose of the scripture is accomplished, liberation occurs by that much alone according to the means of knowledge;
let passion and the like remain as they may, for their presence does not invalidate [the attainment of that state]."

The meaning of this [phrase] "of the subject matter of the scripture" (*śāstrārthasya*) is as follows: that which instructs—that is, teaches what is beneficial to the living being—is the *śāstra*, namely the Veda.

Its "subject matter" (*artha*) is that which is to be established, characterized by the identity of the supreme Brahman and the Self, a specific reality uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time; it means, in other words, of the instruction concerning that [reality].
The sense is that [this instruction] is complete and leaves nothing further to be taught. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Liberation," and so forth.

By that alone—meaning by the very fact that there is no remainder of the objects to be taught—liberation in the form of *kaivalya* (isolation) occurs for the qualified seeker; it is the destruction of beginningless duality such as ignorance (*avidyā*). "From the means of knowledge" (*miteḥ*) means from the cause, which is the valid cognition (*pramā*) of identity with Brahman as previously described. "It may indeed be so" (*syād bhūyād eva*) is the reason why the word "knower of Brahman" (*brahmavit*) is implied there. "Kāma" means absolutely; "rāga" and so forth include hatred and the rest, according to the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "because there is no distinction [of them] from beasts and the like. Let them remain (*santu tiṣṭhantu*).

Because their existence—that is, the presence of passion (*rāga*) and the rest—is contingent upon that [ignorance], the connection is as follows: it does not offend [the truth], for it cannot once again establish the reality of duality which has already been sublated by the non-dual knowledge (*advaita-vidyā*). "Thus," and so forth: "thus" refers to the manner previously described. "The two treatises" refers to the pair of *Vārtikas*.

This being the case, even when the direct knowledge (*aparokṣa-brahma-vidyā*) of Brahman has arisen from the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) investigated according to the method stated above, [objections such as] impossibility and the like do not indeed [apply].

When [the knowledge] has become firm through the practice of hearing and so forth, then because attachment and other passions— which coexist with the lack of such inquiry— act as signs of ignorance by strengthening that ignorance, once that [knowledge] has reached maturity through the complete removal of all doubts and the like, those same passions, now coexisting with inquiry, appear merely as semblances (ābhāsa).

The meaning is: "And when that [non-contradiction] is established. The ellipsis is: "Because there is no presentation of mutually contradictory meanings according to the aforementioned systematic arrangement, it is meaningful—that is, it becomes effective in its own purpose. || 191 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus described the intended meaning of the portion "desiring what," he states the intended meaning of the portion "for whose sake":
"Because of the perception of one's own self as being unattached, just like the falsity of the world."
The statement "for whose sake [are] desires? is intended to express the non-existence of an enjoyer.
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

Regarding the word "jagat" (the world): just as it was stated, "desiring what? (*kim icchan*) with the intention of expressing the absence of any real object of desire through the realization that the world is illusory (*mithyātva*), so too has the Śruti declared, "for whose sake [are desires]? (*kasya kāmāya*) with the intention of expressing the absence of any real state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) through the realization that the Self is unattached (*asaṅga*).
This is the meaning. || 92 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if it is argued that only those passions such as attachment (*rāga*) which manifest while being co-extensive with the inquiry into reality (*tattvānusaṃdhāna*) possess the status of being mere appearances (*ābhāsa*), then it follows that the entirety of duality consisting of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) and the enjoyed (*bhogya*) must also have its reality investigated. In that case, although the falsity of the enjoyed object—such as the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) and so forth—has already been established through examples like dreams and magical illusions (*indrajāla*), the falsity of the enjoyer must also necessarily be stated. To this, he says:
Like the falsity of the world. || 992 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "The negation of the self's status as an enjoyer must be preceded by an assertion of that possibility; however, such possibility does not exist because the self is unattached.

Anticipating this doubt and intending to show that this is not so because such [enjoyment] is established by one's own experience, he cites the scripture that restates this fact, following its meaning:
He does not desire his wife, husband, or anything else for the sake of their respective enjoyments.
However, it has been proclaimed extensively in the scriptures that [this world] exists for the sake of one's own enjoyment.

Regarding the phrase "He thinks, 'She is mine'" (*patijāyā iti*): by means of this textual sequence beginning with "Indeed, it is not for the sake of the husband that the husband is dear" and ending with "But it is for the sake of the Self that everything is dear," it is established that the phenomenal world, consisting of husband, wife, and so forth, serves as a means for the enjoyment of the Self. Therefore, the meaning is that there arises the contingency of the Self being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). || 93 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "How can this intention to deny the existence of an enjoyer be easily established? For there are scriptural texts concerning the enjoyership of the Self, just as there are texts concerning its lack of connection (asaṃgatva). Indeed, there are many such passages, such as: 'Verily, it is not for the sake of the husband that the husband is dear, but for the sake of the Self that the husband is dear,' and so forth. Anticipating this, the author summarizes that [scriptural] meaning in brief: "The husband, wife, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi),...
"Verily, it is not for the sake of all that everything becomes dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that everything becomes dear"—this much of the text is to be taken up. || 193 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus demonstrated the self's status as an enjoyer, he now analyzes that enjoyer in order to refute it:
"Is it the immutable consciousness-reflection, or rather, is it of the nature of both?"
In that case, the immutable Self does not become an enjoyer, for it would attain the state of being an enjoyer only through its association [with the intellect]. || 94 ||

"What is meant by 'immutable'?"—this question intends to present an alternative: does the status of being an enjoyer belong to the immutable [Self], or to the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), or to that which consists of both?
Regarding this, he first answers the first alternative: "The enjoyer is therein. (94)

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, in order to resolve the aforementioned doubt, he questions [the opponent] by postulating the Self—which is generally accepted as the enjoyer—through the words "Is it the immutable one? and so forth. Among the aforementioned alternatives, he first offers a rebuttal with the words "In that case, no," and so on. To the question "Why?", he replies with the remainder of the verse beginning "Because of its being unattached" (*asaṃgatvāt*). The meaning is: because of what is stated in the Śruti, "For this Puruṣa is indeed unattached. || 194 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection, "Let there be non-attachment, yet let there also be the state of being an enjoyer; what is the harm?", he says:
"Experience is defined as the modification known as the conceit of pleasure and pain."
How is it that being both immutable and subject to transformation is not a contradiction? || 95 ||

"Bliss" (sukha) [is explained as follows]: enjoyment (*bhoga*) is characterized by the conceit of being happy or unhappy; that is not possible for one who is unattached and immutable (*kūṭastha*), because it is impossible for immutability and changeability to coexist in a single locus—this is the meaning. || 195 ||
*Sukhiduḥkhī* is the reading of Acyutarāya.
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya:
[The commentary on the chapter titled] *Tṛptidīpa*.

[Objection: Since both scriptural passages—one establishing non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*) and the other establishing the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*)—are authoritative, both [must be accepted].

Anticipating the objection that [the self] might be so, he says "sukhiduḥkhī" etc., [stating] that it cannot be so because of the resulting contradiction (*vyāghāta*). The reading "sukhaduḥkhābhimāna" is indeed merely a scribal error; for superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is never observed by way of presenting a property (*dharma*), such as "I am happiness. Furthermore, according to Amara’s lexicon—"garva, abhimāna, ahaṃkāra"—it is stated that the term *abhimāna* refers specifically to that *ahaṃkāra* characterized by identity with the substrate (*dharmitādātmya*). Nor is it the case that [one thinks] "happiness has arisen for me," and so forth.

It is not correct to say that even the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of pleasure and so forth must be called "enjoyment" (*bhoga*), and thus the definition established in the present context—that enjoyment is the superimposition of identity with either pleasurefulness and so on—would be over-narrow (*avyāpti*) because it does not apply there; for upon the final conclusion of inquiry, that [perception] also culminates in this very [superimposition].
This is the truth. 195.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that the enjoyership would then belong to the appearance of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), which is subject to modification.
Anticipating this, he refutes it by stating that even if modification were present, such an entity cannot exist without a substratum; therefore, this is not so.
Because it is dependent upon the fluctuating intellect, even when there is a modification in the reflection.
For a delusion devoid of a substratum does not persist as something absolute. || 96 ||

Regarding the term "subject to modification" (*vikārī*): since the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) is dependent upon the modifying adjunct of the intellect (*buddhi*), even though modification is possible within itself, it cannot exist independently—setting aside the immutable substratum (*kūṭastha*) which serves as its locus—because that reflection is merely superimposed and possesses only a superimposed nature. Thus, the point is that even for the mere reflection of consciousness, the status of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) is not possible. || 96 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): If it is argued that, in that case, let the enjoyer be merely a reflection—like the moon in water—subject to modification because it depends upon the modifying intellect, and thus let it be as stated in the second alternative, we say no. For that which lacks a substratum is like a flower in the sky; thus he says: "The subject of modification... (Verse 196).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Therefore, the third alternative remains; thus he says:
"For this reason, in the world, the enjoyer is said to be of the nature of both."
Beginning with such a Self, the immutable one is declared as the remainder in the Śruti.

Regarding the term "consisting of both": since the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) is not possible for either [the Self or the intellect] individually, that which consists of both—the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) together with its substrate (*sādhiṣṭhāna*)—is designated as the "enjoyer" during the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). The point is that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), even this dual nature is not tenable. Now, one might object: just as non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*) is taught in such passages as "for this Puruṣa is indeed unattached," [so too is the nature of the enjoyer taught] in such passages as "this one who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths."

Anticipating the objection that since the state of being a witness is also heard [in scripture], the nature of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), which consists of both [the witness and the agent], must also be ultimately real and not merely established by worldly convention, he says "tādṛg" (such) to show that this is not so, because the scripture has no such intention there: "Having referred to such a self—the enjoyer conditioned by the intellect (*buddhi*)—the immutable conscious self (*cidātmā*), which is the substratum for the conceptualization of the intellect and so forth, remains as the remainder. [This excludes] the non-self, such as the intellect and so on.
The meaning is that [the Self] is established by elimination in the Śruti, such as the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and other texts. || 97 ||

1376a0 Commentary: If it is argued that, by process of elimination, let the third position alone be the case, [the author] replies with the words "both" (*ubhaya*), stating that even if such were the case during the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no enjoyer whatsoever. This refers to the Śruti passage beginning with "He is not this, he is not that" (*sa eṣa neti netyādi*). || 197 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Therein, he first briefly demonstrates the meaning of the passage from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad:
"When asked, 'Which is the Self?', Yājñavalkya, awakening [his interlocutor], [spoke as follows]."
Beginning with that which consists of consciousness, he left nothing remaining of that attachment.
Regarding the term "Self": when Janaka asked, "Which one is the Self? thus inquiring about the Self, Yājñavalkya, awakening him to that truth, [proceeds as follows].
This is the seventh section.
Accompanied by two commentaries:

[the text] begins with "consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths" (*vijñānamayaḥ prāṇeṣu*) and so forth, and concludes by isolating the unattached, immutable (*kūṭastha*) Person through the statement, "for this person is indeed unattached" (*asaṅgo hyayaṃ puruṣaḥ*).
Or rather, the meaning is "non-eternal. || 98 ||

Commentary (A0): Therein, first introducing the variegated (śabala) [Brahman] characterized by the dialogue between Janaka and Yājñavalkya, he briefly cites the Śruti—which aims at the remainder that is the pure Self—in its actual meaning: "The Self," and "consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya). This which is "consisting of consciousness"— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)

The meaning is that, having begun with the variegated [Self] by means of the passage beginning with "Maya is among the vital breaths," [the scripture] has made known the pure Self alone as the limit of sublation through the statement, "For this Person is unattached. || 198 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Having thus demonstrated the method of remaining as the non-attached Self in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, he now shows that same method in other Vedic texts such as the Aitareya, beginning with the inquiry "Who is this Self? and so forth.
Beginning with that which possesses both natures, the immutable one remains as the residue in the scripture. || 99 ||

"What is this Self? "What is this Self that we worship? Which one is that Self?"—in such investigations into the Self, beginning with the Self as conditioned by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), it is the immutable (*kūṭastha*) Self consisting of pure consciousness alone that remains as the residue; thus it should be understood in other instances as well.

Upon reflecting on the scriptures thus stated, the falsity of the enjoyer who possesses both natures [the conditioned and the unconditioned] is established, while the ultimate reality is the immutable, non-associated Self who is not an enjoyer.
The status of being an agent is established. || 99 ||
Commentary (a0): Thus, he cites the Aitareya Śruti as well, by way of illustration for all the Upaniṣads, beginning with "Who is this? (199).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: "If the enjoyer is false according to the method stated above, how does the notion of his reality arise in living beings?
Anticipating this, he says:
"Due to a lack of discrimination, the Self superimposes the reality of the immutable [Self] upon itself."
Considering this to be real agency as an enjoyer, one never desires to abandon it. || 200 ||

Regarding the term *kūṭastha*: the Self (*ātman*), which is commonly known in the world as the enjoyer, due to a lack of discrimination—specifically, the absence of knowledge that distinguishes itself from the immutable (*kūṭastha*)—superimposes upon itself the reality that resides in the immutable.
Through that [superimposition], it regards even its own inherent state of being an enjoyer as real, and thus does not wish to relinquish its connection [to that state] at any time. || 200 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if this is so, then why do all living beings, believing their own state of being enjoyers to be real, engage in activity for the sake of that enjoyment?
To this, he says: "The immutable" (kūṭastha). [The word] "desires to abandon" (jihāsati) means desires to give up; the word "enjoyment" (bhoga) is to be supplied as the object. || 200 ||

— Rāghavendra’s Commentary — Now, one might object: "In that case, how is it established that the object of enjoyment is subordinate to the Self, as stated in the passage, 'But for the sake of the Self, everything becomes dear'?

Anticipating this doubt, [the author] replies: It is not the subordination to the immutable (kūṭastha) Self that is being established; rather, it is the subordination to the Self as it is well-known in the world...
He states that the scripture merely reiterates the fact that both [the husband and wife] are essentially subordinate to the enjoyer:
"The enjoyer desires a wife, a husband, and so forth, solely for his own enjoyment."
This worldly account has been correctly recounted by the Śruti.

Regarding the word "enjoyer" (bhoktā): the meaning is that this worldly circumstance—that whoever is an enjoyer in the world desires the instruments of enjoyment, such as a wife and so forth, for his own enjoyment—has been correctly restated by the Śruti; no other matter is being propounded. || 1 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, if it is thus the case that the enjoyer—the individual soul (jīva) known as the reflection of consciousness—is likewise entirely false, just like the objects of enjoyment, then how is it that the Śruti declares that all things have the Self as their ultimate end, stating: "But for the sake of the Self, everything becomes dear"? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5). How can the entire range of objects of enjoyment be said to exist for the sake of the Self?
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 282.

To this, he says "the enjoyer" (*bhoktā*) from the passage beginning with "Tṛptidīpa. The meaning is: by means of the Śruti in the form of "O, indeed, not for the sake of the husband's desires," and so forth. || 201 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary—Translation: Anticipating the question, "For what purpose [is this said]?", he states that it is for the sake of directing love toward the enjoyer alone:
"Since objects of enjoyment are subordinate to the enjoyer, let there be no attachment to the objects of enjoyment."
Therefore, he desires to instill that attachment toward the Pradhāna itself as the enjoyer. || 2 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the objects of enjoyment": since the husband, wife, and so forth—being objects of enjoyment—are merely instruments for the enjoyment of the enjoyer (the self), one should not cultivate attachment toward those objects of enjoyment. Rather, the meaning is that this is taught as an injunction that one should instead cultivate attachment toward the enjoyer alone, who is the primary entity. || 2 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Just as the statement 'Fire is the remedy for cold' and others are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) that serve as supplements to injunctions such as 'One offers oblations in the Āhavanīya fire,' it must likewise be admitted that the present scriptural passage is a supplement to some injunction. This is true; however, it concerns the Blessed Yājñavalkya, who—desiring to instruct Maitreyī, his inquisitive wife, on the identity of Brahman and the Self, while saying "As I explain [this], meditate upon it"—[spoke these words].

Intending to show that its status as an auxiliary to the injunction for *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) is established by this very statement, he resolves [the objection] with the words: "Of the objects of enjoyment" (*bhogyānām*). This has been stated in the *Anubhūtiprakāśa*:

"From the word 'one who meditates' (*nididhyāsaka*), [the scripture] proclaimed the fruit to be the renunciation of everything; for one does not meditate while not having abandoned thoughts of other things."
You are worthy [of this]. That continuous reflection upon the meaning heard from the mouth of the Guru is called *nididhyāsana*, and that is attained through one-pointedness (*aikāgrya*).

When a lack of interest in the non-Self arises in the mind and interest in the Self emerges, that mind—purified by a mass of merit—is fit for one-pointedness. Once one-pointedness has been established in the pure [mind], one should increase it through discrimination (*viveka*). Therefore, the discrimination between the pleasant and the unpleasant is taught to Maitreyī.
Thus; "he desires to enjoin," meaning he wishes to establish [the rule], as is understood from the etymological scripture (*nirukta-śruti*). || 202 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Preceded by the renunciation of affection for objects of enjoyment, he cites a Puranic verse as an illustration of the duty to direct one's own love toward the Self, following a prayer for love toward the Lord:
"That unswerving love which the undiscriminating have for sense-objects..."
As I remember you, may she never depart from my heart. || 3 ||

Regarding the phrase "that joy": O Lord of Lakṣmī (Māpa), may that firm and unswerving joy which exists among the undiscriminating—those devoid of self-knowledge—with respect to sense objects, depart from my heart, that is, from my mind, as I remember you and constantly contemplate you.
The meaning is: may my mind abandon attachment to sense objects and remain forever fixed upon you alone. Or else, [it refers to] the undiscriminating...

Whatever firm attachment exists toward sense objects—may that same attachment existing toward sense objects not depart from my heart as I remember you; may it not go away, but remain forever—this is the meaning. || 3 ||
Commentary (a0): To further elaborate upon that, he also cites the Purāṇa with the words "yet" and so on. O Māpa, O Lord of Lakṣmī!

That unswerving, uninterrupted affection which exists among the undiscriminating—those lacking in wisdom—for sense objects such as pleasant sounds and the like; may that same kind of affection for sense objects [be withdrawn] from my heart as I remember You, the attributeless Self, by reflecting according to the practice of hearing and the other limbs of yoga. From such a heart...

"May she not depart"—that is to say, may she go away; [rather,] may the meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) on the identity of Brahman and the Self be free from obstacles. However, some, instead of taking *mā* as a vocative, interpret it as having an implied sense, saying: "O *Yā* (She), etc.—may that non-dual love of the same nature as her not depart from the heart of me who remembers you; may such [love], having you as its sole object, remain forever. || 203 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: "Let it be so; what relevance does this have for the Purāṇa or the Śruti? To this he says:
"By this reasoning, one whose intellect is detached from all fortune..."
Having withdrawn that pleasure, he desires to know this enjoyer.
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

"By this principle" means: by this principle stated in the Purāṇas, a person whose intellect is dispassionate— that is, one whose mind is detached from the entire range of objects of enjoyment characterized as husband, wife, and so forth— having withdrawn that pleasure directed toward objects of enjoyment into the Self, which is the enjoyer;...
He desires to know himself; he wishes to understand it. || 4 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) on the result states: "Thus" (iti). When the enjoyer has been established in a general sense as the substratum of the notion of "I," the meaning is that he is of a dual nature, consisting of both the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) and the immutable witness (kūṭastha). "Desires to know this enjoyer" means, in other words, he wishes to understand him in his true reality. || 204 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Thus, having concluded the discussion on love for the Self alone, he states the resulting fruit along with an illustration:
"A common person [finds pleasure] in garlands, sandalwood, wives, garments, gold, and so forth..."
Just as one who is heedful does not become negligent toward a consumer of that food. || 205 ||

Regarding the verse beginning with *srakcandana*: just as an ordinary person (*pāmara*) remains vigilant and attentive toward objects such as garlands and sandalwood paste, so too the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) does not become negligent—that is, he does not exercise lack of attention—toward the Self; rather, the meaning is that he remains established in the contemplation of that [Self] alone. || 205 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, what is the nature of the love that has been withdrawn from objects of enjoyment toward the enjoyer? To this he says: "A garland," etc. He does not become negligent; the meaning is that he remains constantly attentive through uninterrupted contemplation focused solely upon that [object]. || 205 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He clarifies the absence of inattention itself through many illustrations:
"He practices poetry, drama, logic, and so forth, continuously."
Just as one desiring victory [examines his own strength], so should one desiring liberation examine oneself.

Regarding the word "kāvya": just as a seeker of victory—a preeminent person in this world desiring to defeat his opponent—constantly practices poetry and the like, so too should one who desires liberation always investigate one's own Self. || 6 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Having clarified that very method through illustrations, he now prescribes the inquiry into the Self—which consists of the practice of the Self—just as was previously prescribed for the practice of Brahman, by means of the three verses beginning with "kāvyam" and so forth. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), Sāṃkhya and other systems are included. [The term] "svam" refers to one's own Self.
The meaning is that it is well-known from such scriptural passages as, "Space was not produced," and so forth. || 206 ||
Just as one performs recitation, sacrifice, meditation, and so forth with faith;
Just as one might have faith [in the scriptures] out of a desire for heaven and the like, so too should one have faith out of a desire for liberation from one's own [bondage].

Rāma’s Commentary: Regarding the word *japa* (recitation): just as one who seeks heaven and other such goals according to the Vedas performs their respective means, such as recitation and so forth, preceded by faith (*śraddhā*), so too the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) should, out of a desire for liberation, place his trust in his own Self as revealed in the Śrutis. || 7 ||
Commentary on verse a0: "Japa" refers to the recitation of mantras such as the Gāyatrī, which is well known. "Yāga" refers to sacrifices such as the Cāturmāsya.

"Upāsanā" is meditation characterized by the Sandhyā-vandana and other rites; by the word "ādi" (and so forth), long-term sacrificial sessions (*satra*) and the like are included. Regarding "heaven and so forth": according to the scriptural texts, "By action one attains the world of the ancestors" (*karmaṇā pitṛlokaḥ*) and "The Brahmins seek to know Him through the study of the Vedas and sacrifice" (*tam etaṃ vedānuvacanena brāhmaṇā vividiṣanti yajñena*), [one attains] the world of the ancestors and mental purity.
"By the will of [the Lord] and so forth" means, in short, within one's own non-dual Self as the object. || 207 ||
Just as a yogi might achieve one-pointedness of mind with great effort, so too [should it be accomplished].
Thus, one should distinguish one's own self through the desire for liberation, and not merely through the desire to attain powers such as atomization (aṇimā).

Rāma’s Commentary: Regarding the phrase "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittaikāgyam*): just as a yogi who practices yoga might achieve one-pointedness of mind with great effort out of a desire to obtain powers such as *aṇimā* (atomicity) and so forth, in that same way, this person too should always discern the Self—that is, know it by distinguishing it from the body and other such things. || 8 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 284.
[The commentary on the *Tṛptidīpa* titled *Aṣṭama*:

"One-pointedness of mind" (*cittaikāgryam*). The meaning is: one's own purified referent of the term *tattvam* (the Self), characterized as the Witness and called the Immutable (*kūṭastha*). Here, by means of the three similes beginning with "the poet," all verbal, physical, and mental activities are respectively—]

By means of this illustration for those who disregard both self and others, it is illuminated that—according to the principle that the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) is stronger than the sequence of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*)—a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) should abandon all activities such as bodily ones and remain devoted solely to the non-dual Self (*advaitātman*) for the sake of strengthening the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). || 208 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might ask, "What is the fruit of their constant practice? To this he says:
"Their skills increase through proficiency in practice."
Just as that [perception] does, so too its discrimination becomes clear through practice.

Regarding "skills" (*kauśalāni*): just as for those who practice poetry and the like, their skills increase in various subjects through proficiency in practice, so too for this seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), through practice, discrimination—the knowledge of the Self's distinction from the body and so forth—becomes clear and manifest. || 9 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, having raised the doubt as to how firmness in the knowledge of reality (*tattvavidyā*) might be achieved, he resolves it by means of that very illustration—“*kauśalāni*. This refers to those persons mentioned previously, such as the seeker of victory (*vijigīṣu*) and others. It becomes clear—that even throughout the three periods of time, it does not become stained at all by the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the reality of duality and so forth, just as the sky is not darkened by the appearance of blueness. || 209 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the fruit of the clarity of discernment:
"Discernment is the true nature of the enjoyer, remaining unattached throughout the states of waking and the rest."
Through positive and negative concomitance, [the nature of] the witness is determined. || 210 ||

"Vivincatā" means: by the person who, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), discriminates—that is, knows by way of distinction from the insentient objects of enjoyment—the true nature of the enjoyer, which is the enjoyer's ultimate reality; by such a person, the unattached witness (*sākṣin*) is determined or ascertained throughout the states of waking and so forth, namely waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. This is the meaning. || 210 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "How can the absence of the superimposition of duality (*dvaitādhyāsa*) be recognized as having reached full maturity through the practice of the aforementioned discrimination?
To this, he says: "Viviñcata" (discriminating). This means in the states of waking and so forth—namely, waking, dreaming, deep sleep, fainting, death, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
This is also an illustration that includes creation, maintenance, and dissolution (*sṛṣṭi-sthiti-pralaya*). || 210 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He demonstrates positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka):
"In whatever state one is seen—the waking, dreaming, or deep sleep—that is the seer."
For it is universally accepted that experience occurs only there and not elsewhere. (11)

Regarding the phrase "yatreti": among the states of waking and so forth, in whichever state—whether waking, dreaming, or deep sleep—that threefold object of experience (bhogya), namely the gross, the subtle, and bliss, is seen and experienced by the witness (sākṣin) as the seer; that which is seen remains only there, in that very state, and not elsewhere. It does not exist in other states; however, the witness exists as the underlying continuity everywhere—this is the universal experience.
For it is well-known that he is authorized; such is the meaning. || 11 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "What kind of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are these, which are established by the witness (*sākṣin*) and are incapable of proving [anything]? In response to this doubt, he defines the positive and negative concomitances as established by one's own experience, beginning with the words "where. By the "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*), meaning the witness (*sākṣin*). "Waking," etc., means within the midst of the three states beginning with waking. "Where" means in that state characterized as waking, or characterized as dreaming, or characterized as deep sleep. Within the state...

The word "śeṣa" (the remainder) is implied here. It is seen—that is, manifested—such as the gross body, pots, cloths, and so forth, through the doors of the sense organs like the eyes; that is to say, it is directly made an object [of perception] in dreams and the like. However, those very things—the gross body, pots, cloths, and so forth—experienced during the waking state exist only in the waking state, and not in dreams and the like.
The Seventh Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.

In this way, there is the experience that the ignorance and so forth—which are the causes of the gross and subtle phenomenal world—experienced in dreams and the like, do not exist in the waking state, but only in those very states such as dreaming. The particle *hi* indicates what is well-known; the construction is that this [experience] is "consented to" (*saṃmatā*), meaning it is universally accepted by all. And thus, the "concomitance" (*anvaya*) denoted by the word "continuity" (*anusyūtatvena*) belongs to the Seer, the Witness, because He persists through all states. This is distinct from the [concomitance] of the object of perception (*dṛśya*), which, being delimited by states such as waking, possesses the gross and other [attributes] that serve as its delimiters.

The intention is that in states other than those [specific ones], because the visible object—though qualified by the delimiting conditions (avacchedaka) designated by the names of those respective states—is absent, the negative concomitance (vyatireka), expressed as exclusion (vyāvṛtti), becomes manifest. Now, one might object: "When A exists, B exists" is positive concomitance (anvaya); "when A is absent, B is absent" is negative concomitance (vyatireka). This is the consensus of the logicians (tārkika) and others. In all such examples, such as 'when the threads (tantu) exist, the cloth (paṭa) exists' and 'when the threads are absent, the cloth is absent,' [the relationship is established]. [The text continues: ...in all such examples... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the logical structure and philosophical intent of the preceding portion.)

If it is asked, "Why are the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding the elements (*bhūta*) not stated here?", the answer is no. For even though those two were indicated right here by the Teacher for the purpose of establishing that the Self—characterized as the Witness—is unattached throughout the three periods of time, you yourself have failed to grasp their intended meaning. To illustrate:

when the existence of the visible objects, such as the gross body which serves as a limiting adjunct, is present through the delimitation of various states like waking and so forth, [the Self remains] in the non-dual Self, the direct Seer... [in the Witness].

According to Pāṇini’s rule "jñāyām" (Pāṇini 5.2.91), there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) such that the existence of witnesshood, characterized by being the seer of that [knowledge], follows from knowledge; whereas, when knowledge is negated, there is an absence of witnesshood defined by the aforementioned characteristic—this is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). This is the summary. || 211 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: With the intention of showing that there is not only direct experience but also scriptural authority, he recites two passages from the text according to their meaning: "Whatever he sees there, he does not carry over with him, for this person is unattached; having rejoiced and wandered about in that state of serene clarity, and having seen both merit and sin, he returns again according to the rule, according to his source" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3). And so forth.
Whatever he perceives there, he remains untouched by it.
"Upon seeing [the truth], both merit and sin [are destroyed]"— such is the drum-beat of the Vedas.

"Whatever he sees there"—that is, whatever object of enjoyment that Self perceives or beholds in that state, he remains unaccompanied by that visible object; that is to say, it does not follow him, but rather he himself passes on to another state. "Merit" means the happiness that is the fruit of merit, and "evil" means the suffering that is its fruit; the meaning is that he departs having merely seen them, without taking them along. || 12 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Establishing the stated point through scriptural authority (*śruti*), [the author] first cites two passages from the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* according to their meaning: "Whatever he sees there, he remains untouched by it, for this person is unattached" (*sa yattatra kiṃcit paśyaty-ananvāgatas tena bhavati asaṅgo hy ayaṃ puruṣaḥ*); and "Having rejoiced and wandered about in this state of serene clarity (*saṃprasāda*), and having seen both the auspicious and the inauspicious, he hastens back again according to his course, according to his origin" (*sa vā eṣa etasmin saṃprasāde ratvā caritvā dṛṣṭvaiva puṇyaṃ ca pāpaṃ ca punaḥ pratinyāyaṃ pratiyony ādravati*). Thus, these two statements.

"He reads: 'Whatever he sees there'—that is, that immutable Self which is the reflection of consciousness. There, in the state of dream, whatever dream-object he sees—that is, whatever object of enjoyment he perceives—he remains unattached to it; he does not become connected with it at all. Merit is its fruit, happiness; evil is its fruit, suffering. The rest is indeed clear. (12)
Rāma’s Commentary: He shows other scriptural passages dedicated to the discernment of the principle of the enjoyer:
"That which illumines the manifold world of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth..."
Having realized "I am that Brahman," one is liberated from all bonds.

Regarding the word "awake" (jāgrat): That Brahman, characterized by truth, knowledge, and bliss, which exists in the form of the witness (sākṣin), illumines—that is, makes manifest—the phenomenal world of waking and the other states. Having realized through scripture and personal experience that "I am that Brahman," and having ascertained that "I am not the intellect, the reflection of consciousness, and so forth," one is completely liberated from all bonds, such as the state of being a knower (pramātṛtva) and agency (kartṛtva); one is thoroughly released in every respect. || 13 ||
The commentary on verse 1a explains: Thus, he also cites the scriptural testimony from the *Kaivalyopaniṣad* of the Atharvaveda, beginning with the words "jāgrat" (while waking). By the word "etc.
(*ādi*), "samādhi" (deep meditative absorption) is included. The rest, however, is quite straightforward. || 13 ||
The Self should be understood as one and the same throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
For one who has transcended the three states, rebirth no longer exists.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 286.
[The commentary by Rāma on the *Tṛptidīpa*—regarding the word "one": One and the same Self is to be understood as persisting through the states of waking and so forth.
Thus, for the Self that has transcended the three locations and is distinct from the three states by means of discriminative knowledge, there is no further birth. This body—
The meaning is that immediately after falling, there is no attainment of another body. || 14 ||
a0 Commentary: Likewise, he also cites a mantra from the *Atharvaṇīya Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad*: "Eka eva" (He is indeed one).
This sentence, however, is already explained by the [authoritative] tradition (*nigada*). || 14 ||
That which is fit for the three abodes, as well as the enjoyer and the enjoyment that may exist therein.
Distinct from them, I am the witness, pure consciousness alone, the eternally auspicious Śiva. || 215 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Regarding the verse beginning with "In the three": that which is to be experienced (*bhogya*) in the three abodes—that is, in the three states—consisting of the gross, the subtle, and the infinite;

that which is the experiencer (*bhoktā*), consisting of the forms of Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña; and that which is the experience (*bhoga*), consisting of the perception thereof—from these [categories] such as the abodes and so forth, distinct is the Witness (*sākṣī*) whose nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). He is Sadāśiva, who is eternally blissful by virtue of being the nature of unsurpassed bliss.
The meaning is: "I am that Supreme Self which is wandering [as the individual soul]. || 215 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Again, he writes the very words of the *Kaivalya Upaniṣad*: "In the three... The meaning is: "in the abodes," that is, in the houses consisting of the gross body and so forth, delimited by the states of waking and the rest. The rest, however, has its meaning already revealed. Although here, in all three states such as waking, the triad known as the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), the enjoyed (*bhogya*), and enjoyment (*bhoga*) is explicitly mentioned in general terms, [it is said: "At the time of deep sleep, when everything has dissolved... [and so on].

"Overcome by that [ignorance], it attains the form of happiness; and again, through the connection with the karma of another birth, that very same individual soul sleeps and then awakens. Thus, the dissolution of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of the triad previously mentioned in the mantra appears contradictory. Nevertheless, because of the reflection upon waking—"I slept happily," "I slept painfully," or "I slept in a state of deep delusion"—the states of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) characterized as *sāttvika* and so forth, as established by the consensus of the learned and others, are proven.

Because of its threefold division, the earlier scripture (*śruti*) which teaches the dissolution of everything has the intention of referring to the *tāmasa* state and its subdivisions; whereas the [scripture] which generally asserts the existence of the "threefold group" (*tripuṭī*) in all three states has the intention of referring to the pleasure and so forth admitted in the two divisions beginning with the *sāttvika*. Therefore, the wise should contemplate this resolution. A detailed exposition, however, should be understood from my own work, *Ārabdhadhvāntasaṃhṛti*; this is the direction [of the argument]. (215)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: When the nature of the Self has thus been ascertained through discrimination, [the author] asks, "To whom then belongs the state of being an enjoyer? and answers:
"When the reality has been thus discriminated, that which is designated by the term 'consisting of consciousness'..."
That which is the modification of the reflection of consciousness—its state as an enjoyer remains. || 16 ||

"Thus" means that because the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), which is denoted by the word "consciousness," is subject to modification, it possesses the state of being an enjoyer (bhoktṛtva).
The commentary on this [verse] states the fruit of this analysis: "Thus," etc. (16).

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) is accepted as the enjoyer, then how would the previously stated words, 'To whom do desires belong?', not contradict the intended meaning of the absence of an enjoyer?
Anticipating this doubt, and intending to show that those words refer to the ultimate absence of an enjoyer, he establishes the falsity of the enjoyer, namely the reflection of consciousness:
This reflection of consciousness is illusory, according to both scripture and experience.
The world is said to be a magical illusion (indrajāla), since this [universe] is contained within it.

"Consisting of Māyā": this reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) is illusory, having a false nature, according to scripture; for scripture states, "By means of the reflection, it makes [the distinction] between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara). It is also so because of experience; that is to say, because it is experienced as existing within the triad beginning with the seer (draṣṭṛ).
