The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

Regarding the phrase "it is a magical illusion" (indrajāla): because this [dream] is included within the world, which is as false as a magical illusion, its falsity is likewise experienced by the wise—this is the implied sense. Since it falls within the world, it is therefore false; such is the construction of the meaning. || 117 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "Is this [world] real? He says, "It is illusory" (māyika). This means that it is so according to the Śruti, "He creates the Jīva and Īśvara by means of manifestation," and according to the experience of those who know Brahman. It is called "Indrajāla" because, as the Śruti states, it consists of Māyā, like a magician’s trick. || 17 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He states that this world is false also because its perishability is experienced, just like [the world] itself:
"For even its dissolution during deep sleep and so forth is indeed experienced by the Witness."
In this manner, he discerns his own true nature again and again. || 18 ||

"Even dissolution," etc.; the word "etc. (ādi) refers to fainting and so forth. To the question, "Granted that it is illusory, what follows from that? he says: "Such as this," etc. When the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), which is of the nature of māyā, is distinguished from the immutable (kūṭastha), then one repeatedly discriminates—that is, knows by distinguishing it from the immutable—this very nature and true essence (svatattva) of one's own as being of such an illusory character. || 18 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He also indicates another reason for the illusory nature (*māyikatva*) of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), stating: "even dissolution" (*vilayo’pi*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), fainting and so forth are included. Now, since the immutable Self (*kūṭastha*) is unattached, even the aforementioned discrimination must have the reflection of consciousness as its agent; if that is so, what is the fruit of this [discrimination] for it? To this he says: "of such a kind," etc. The implicit subject is "this reflection of consciousness. Of such a kind...
If it distinguishes its own intrinsic nature from the previously mentioned characteristics such as being illusory (māyika), [then it would be real]. 18.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
Having discerned and ascertained its destruction, one no longer desires enjoyment.
Who would desire marriage when lying on the ground, about to die? || 19 ||

Regarding the word "vivicya" (having discerned): he provides an illustration for the absence of desire for enjoyment when there is certainty of one's own destruction, stating: "like one about to die," etc. (Verse 19).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): "Then" (*tarhi*) means having analyzed and ascertained—even the destruction experienced by the witness in states such as deep sleep—and having determined it through discrimination alone; this is the meaning. "Again" (*punaḥ*) means immediately thereafter. It connects with the subsequent clause: "he desires the experience of enjoyment, such as garlands and the like.
In this regard, he provides a corroborative illustration (*arthāntaranyāsa*) with the half-verse beginning with "one who is about to die" (*mumūrṣu*). || 19 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Furthermore, he says that he even feels ashamed to engage in worldly activity by thinking, "I am the enjoyer," as he did before:
"And he feels ashamed to engage in worldly activity [thinking], 'I am the enjoyer,' as before."
Like one whose nose has been cut off, he is humiliated and experiences suffering while undertaking his work. || 220 ||
"He shames himself" (jiheti). If that is so, then how does he conduct his worldly affairs from the moment knowledge arises until the exhaustion of *prārabdha* (the momentum of past actions)?

To this, he says: "Chinna... (cut off). "Shamed" (*hīta*) means feeling abashed; thinking "even now my karma is not exhausted," and thus experiencing distress, he "enjoys the *prārabdha*"—meaning he experiences the fruit of the *prārabdha-karma*. || 220 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, even so, it must be stated that he must experience the fruits of his *prārabdha* karma; how is this possible? To this, he says: "He is ashamed" (*jihveti*). The connection is as follows: as before, from the perspective of the Witness (*sākṣin*), just as at the time of his own non-discrimination, he is ashamed—that is, feels abashed—to act as if "I am the enjoyer. For this very reason, [the text says] "cut off" (*chinna*). "Ashamed" (*hrītaḥ*) means feeling abashed. For this very reason, "afflicted" (*kli-*)...

The meaning is that even while being afflicted by suffering; "even the commenced"—that is, even the enjoyment of pleasure derived from a wife and other such things obtained through the force of past karma (*prārabdha*)—"he experiences" or "enjoys": such is the construction of the words. || 220 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, following the discussion on knowledge, he states that the absence of agency in the witness (sākṣin) is established by the logic of "how much more so" (kaimutikanyāya):
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya:
[The chapter titled] *Tṛptidīpa*.
When this [knower] even shrinks from conceiving of himself as an enjoyer, then...
What need is there for the futile talk that one should project this onto a witness? || 21 ||

Regarding the word "yadā" (when): when this reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) feels shame—that is, it is embarrassed—to consider even its own status as an enjoyer, thinking "I am the enjoyer," then it would falsely superimpose that inherent quality of being an enjoyer upon the Witness (*sākṣin*), who is free from attachment; thus, what kind of talk could be more futile and devoid of substance?
The meaning is: none at all. || 21 ||

Commentary (a0): By this, it is established by the principle of "how much more so" (*kaimutya*) that one does not superimpose the state of being an enjoyer upon the immutable Self as before; thus he says: "When... (verse 21).
Intending this, he challenges the enjoyer without hesitation.
For whom are these desires? Therefore, there is indeed no fever of affliction for the body.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): He establishes the aforementioned point by grounding it in scripture with the words "iti" (thus). This means: "To whose desires?"—this is the meaning of the Śruti.

Intending to show that there is no ultimate state of being an enjoyer for either the immutable (kūṭastha) or the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), he challenges—that is, refutes—the enjoyer without hesitation, meaning without any doubt. To the question, "Let this challenge to the enjoyer be so; what follows from it?", he says: "From that... [and] "not... (na).
For fever (jvara) is a burning sensation (jvaraṇa), a state of intense heat (saṃtāpa). || 22 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): To the question, "What follows from that for the exposition of the subject matter under discussion? he says: "Thus" (iti). The words "the scriptural statement" (śrutivākyam) are to be supplied as the remainder. He states the resulting conclusion with the words beginning with "therefore" (tataḥ). || 22 ||
The body is traditionally taught to be threefold: gross, subtle, and causal.
In each respective case, there is necessarily a threefold fever that is appropriate.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In order to demonstrate the absence of the "after-fever" of the body for one who knows reality, he shows the differentiation of the body and the presence of fever therein with the verse beginning "The gross... (23).
Commentary (a0): He elaborates further on the manner in which the body is freed from the after-fever [of worldly existence] through five verses beginning with "sthūlam" (gross).
The meaning is that because the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*)—from the root *śṛ*, "to decay"—is common to all three, there are three types [of bodies]. || 23 ||
Diseases born of wind, bile, and phlegm exist by the millions upon the body.
Likewise, there are foul odors, ugliness, burning, breaking, and so forth.
Rāma’s Commentary: Regarding that gross body, he first describes the fevers—beginning with "vāta" (verse 24).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding the word "vāta": *śleṣman* is phlegm (*kapha*). *Bhaṅga* refers to the breaking off of a limb or its dislocation. || 24 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He shows the afflictions within the subtle body:
Desire, anger, and so forth, as well as tranquility, self-control, and so forth, reside in the subtle body (liṅgadeha).
Fever afflicts a person in both ways—by attainment and by non-attainment—successively.

Regarding the word "kāma" (desire): he establishes that desire, tranquility, and so forth, possess the nature of a fever by stating, "In both cases. The meaning is that both types—being of two kinds—are respectively afflictive to a person through attainment and non-attainment; therefore, because they resemble a fever, they are called "fevers" (*ajvara*). || 25 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on verse 225: Regarding the word *kāma*, the ancient commentators (*prāñcaḥ*) hold that *dvaye'pi* means "in both kinds. Here, by virtue of the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original), the suffix *tayap* is considered present even before the vowel *ac*; thus, because it ends in *tayap*, it receives the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), and the form *dvaya* is grammatically correct. || 225 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He states that the fever residing in the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*) is described in the Chāndogya Śruti—[page 289].
Seventh Section.
Accompanied by two commentaries:
"The self does not perceive itself or another, as if destroyed within its cause."
And that it is the seed of future suffering—this has been shown by Indra. || 26 ||
Regarding 'one's own' and 'another': for indeed, one does not at this time know oneself thus, 'I am this,' nor does one know these beings;
one has merely gone to destruction. 'I see nothing here to be enjoyed'—by this statement, [it is shown that] there is an absence of knowledge regarding one's own self and others."

The meaning is that Indra, acting as a disciple, reported to his teacher Prajāpati the fact that [the world] was almost destroyed by ignorance and that it was the seed of future suffering to come on the following day. || 26 ||
Commentary on verse 26: "Himself and another... The mention of Indra is solely for the purpose of demonstrating the magnitude of the fever caused by [ignorance].

Thus it is recorded in the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Indeed, this one does not now know himself thus: 'I am this'; nor does he know these beings; he has gone to utter destruction. I see nothing here to enjoy," and so forth. This has been shown and stated. || 26 ||
Rāghavabhaṭṭa’s Commentary: Having thus described the fevers in all three bodies, he states their inevitability:
"These fevers are considered natural within the three bodies."
But upon separation, those very bodies do not even remain due to fevers.

"These" refers to the following: these fevers, being perceived in all three bodies, are considered inherent (*svābhāvika*) because they arise simultaneously with the bodies. He confirms this inherent nature by means of a negative argument (via *vyatireka*): "But in the case of separation. Because, when there is a separation of those bodies from these fevers, those bodies do not cease to exist; therefore, [the fevers] are inherent.
Such is the meaning. || 27 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, if it is argued that if fevers occur in all three bodies, they must simply be pacified by their respective remedies, the author says: "These... (27).
Just as a cloth might be separated from its threads, or a woolen blanket from its fibers.
Just as a jar is made from clay, so too is the body produced from fevers; let this be observed. (28)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In this regard, he provides an illustration with the words "of the thread," etc. (Verse 28).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): In this regard, the presentation of an illustration establishes that even for one who possesses a body, there is a single material cause (*ekopādānakatva*) for fever—namely, "of the thread," etc. "Viyujyet" means it would undergo separation; "viyujyeta" is indeed a corrupt reading. || 28 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, desiring to demonstrate the absence of fever in the immutable (kūṭastha) by means of the logic of "how much more so" (kaimutikanyāya), he first shows the absence of fever in the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa):
"In the reflection of consciousness, there is no fever whatsoever by its own nature, because it is [a reflection] of consciousness."
Only the nature of being solely luminosity is observed, and not anything else. || 29 ||

Regarding the term "intellectual reflection" (cidābhāsa): in the intellectual reflection, no fever exists apart from its own connection with the fevers residing in the three bodies. Why is this so? To this he says, "because" (yataḥ). The sense is that since the nature of consciousness as consisting solely of light is established by the experience of the wise, the same must be accepted for the reflection, which is the intellectual reflection. || 29 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, if this is so, then since it is an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*), one might suspect that even in the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), which possesses the three kinds of bodies, a fever might somehow occur; to this he says: "In the reflection of consciousness" (*cidābhāsa iti*). The reason for this is stated by the words beginning with "since" (*yataḥ*). || 29 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: He now demonstrates that for which the absence of fever in the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) was established—*“The cloth would not be separated from the threads,”* according to the reading of Acyutarāya.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [pages 290–290]
If such fevers are impossible even in the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), what need is there to mention them in the Witness (sākṣin)?
Even so, the reflection of consciousness indeed conceives of oneness through ignorance.

Regarding the phrase "even in the reflection of consciousness" (cidābhāse'pi): the sense is that if even in the reflection of consciousness fevers are not possible, then what need is there to say they are not possible in the Witness (sākṣin)? Now, one might ask: "In that case, what is the status of the experience 'I am feverish'? To this he says: "Even so, [it attains] oneness... (evamapyekatām). || 230 ||

Commentary (a0): And thus, since the absence of all fevers in the witness (sākṣin) is established by the logic of "how much more so" (kaimutya), he says, "Even in the reflection of consciousness" (cidābhāse’pi). Now, one might object: "If that is so, then what is the basis for the perception of fever such as 'I am happy'? Anticipating this, it is stated that [such perception] is rooted solely in non-discrimination (aviveka).

He resolves the objection regarding the perception of fever with the words "even so" (*evamapi*). The implicit meaning is "by that which is of the nature of an beginningless entity. The sense is that otherwise, consequences such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and contradiction (*vyāghāta*) would be unavoidable. For example: if ignorance (*avidyā*), being a conceptual construction, were produced, then—just as it has ignorance as its sole root—it too would have another ignorance as its sole root, resulting in infinite regress. Likewise, if ignorance is the absence of knowledge denoted by the term "vidyā," then what...?

Is this duality counter-correlative to knowledge in general, or is it counter-correlative to a specific instance of that [knowledge]? In the first case, if there exists a cognition having both the locus (*dharmī*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) as its objects, then the absence of that generality (*sāmānyābhāva*) cannot be established; if such a cognition does not exist, then since the cognition of the counter-correlate and so forth is a cause for the cognition of an absence, that [absence] remains unestablished—thus there is a contradiction. In the second case, the very cognition having as its object that which is intended to be the object of the ignorance is what is meant by "counter-correlate."

A specific nature of knowledge must be stated; otherwise, since ignorance regarding a jar is of the nature of absence (*abhāva*), knowledge regarding a cloth would also have to be its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). But that is untenable, because one does not observe co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between a counter-positive and its absence. For indeed, even at the same time as Devadatta possesses knowledge of a cloth, ignorance of a jar is perceived. And thus, that knowledge which has as its object the thing that is the subject of ignorance—and which serves as the counter-positive—[is what must be specified].

In your view, however, knowledge regarding two objects is necessarily of the nature of *anuvyavasāya* (reflective awareness). Consequently, without that [reflective awareness], the establishment of the absence [of ignorance] would be impossible; and if it exists, the counter-positive (the object of ignorance) is established by implication, and thus, because of its co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there can by no means be an establishment of ignorance—which is defined as the absence of a specific cognition—any more than there could be an establishment of the absence of a jar when a jar is present. Thus, the contradiction remains exactly as before. || 230 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He elaborates upon the meaning briefly stated as "he considered them as one":
"Having superimposed the reality of the Witness upon the three bodies endowed with His own [nature]..."
He considers all of that to be his own real nature.

Regarding the term "witness" (sākṣī): the meaning is that the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), having superimposed the quality of reality residing in the witness upon its own three bodies, considers all those three bodies—like a flame—to be its own true nature. || 31 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He elaborates upon the very manner of oneness [in the verse beginning] "The witness" (sākṣī) || 31 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Thus, he states what occurs when such erroneous cognition exists:
"At this time of delusion, while these bodies are feverish, one indeed thinks, 'I myself am feverish,' like a member of a family. (32)

Regarding the phrase "in this": the meaning is that this reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), at the time of this delusion, superimposes upon itself the fever residing in the body; in this regard, he provides an illustration: "like a householder. || 32 ||

The commentary on verse (a) states the conclusion: "In this [state]" refers to this reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*). "Like a householder" means that by way of this illustration, just as one thinks, "I myself am incomplete or complete," when one's sons, wife, and so forth are incomplete or complete; [so it is here].
The secret is that this also indicates the manner of other superimpositions, such as that of a son and so forth, mentioned in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*. || 32 ||
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.
Just as it would be in vain for one to think "I am performing penance" while one's children and wife are suffering.
In the same way, the person (puruṣa) likewise identifies with that reflection.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He clarifies the illustration with the verse beginning "In children and wives" (33).
291a0 Commentary: He clarifies the aforementioned illustration with the word "putra" (son). The meaning is: "in those [regarding] sons and wives. || 33 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus demonstrated the fever of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) through delusion during the state of non-discrimination, he now shows its absence during the state of discrimination:
"Having discriminated and abandoned delusion, always disregarding even himself..."
Why should one who perceives the Witness cause the body to suffer? || 34 ||

"Having discriminated": having distinguished the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) from the immutable Self (*kūṭastha*) and from the bodies by knowing them as distinct, one abandons the aforementioned delusion—the notion that all those things are one's own real nature—and, through the knowledge of one's own nature as being of the form of non-existence (unreality), ceasing to have regard even for oneself, one should always contemplate one's own innate nature as the Witness, free from fever and the like. Why then should one suffer after the body?
Why should he not himself burn with fever, following the body that is afflicted by fever? The meaning is: "He certainly would burn. || 34 ||

The commentary on the root text (a0 ṭīkā) states the subject at hand: "Having distinguished" (vivicya). This means having performed discrimination (*viveka*) according to the manner previously described;

that is to say, by not counting [the world] as being real in the sense of being other than the Immutable (*kūṭastha*). "Having abandoned" (*ujjhitvā*)—from the verbal root *ujjha*, meaning "to cast off"—means having relinquished. || 34 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He clarifies that erroneous cognition and knowledge of reality are the causes of fever and its absence respectively by showing an illustration:
"The cognition of a snake or the like where none exists is the cause for fleeing."
When the cognition of a snake is destroyed by the knowledge of the rope, one regrets even what has already been done [out of fear]. || 235 ||

Regarding the word *ayathā*: the cognition of a snake or the like imagined upon a rope and so forth becomes the cause for fleeing. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), a thief imagined upon a post is included. When the notion of a snake and the like ceases through the knowledge of the rope and so forth, one then regrets that very flight, meaning one feels remorse, thinking, "I have acted in vain. || 235 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): The reason for the absence of fever following the destruction of the body is stated as "ayathā" etc. The word should be divided as "a-hi". || 235 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: He clarifies the aforementioned point by means of an illustration, stating that [this is done] for the sake of establishing an expiation for the fault of making a false accusation: mithyābhiyogadoṣasya prāyaścittaprasiddhaye || 12 || [3.54] Just as a person who has made a false accusation undergoes penance to purify himself from the taint of that falsehood, so too must one perform penance for the sin of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) in order to attain purity. This is the meaning. (3.54) The word "sin" (*pātaka*) is used here to indicate the gravity of the offense. Just as one who has committed a great sin performs penance to become pure, so too one who has committed the sin of egoism should perform penance to attain purity. This is the sense. As if seeking forgiveness for himself, he took refuge in the Witness as his protector. || 36 ||

This is false. Just as in the world a person who makes a false accusation repeatedly seeks forgiveness from the accused in order to accomplish the atonement for that fault, so too this reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), for the sake of atoning for the fault of falsely accusing the Witness—the non-attached Self—by superimposing the state of being an enjoyer and so forth, has gone for refuge as if seeking forgiveness from the Witness-Self. 36.

Commentary (a0): Now, to the question "What does it do?", he says: "As false" (mithyā). The meaning is: [it is the cause] of the defect consisting in the superimposition of false agency and enjoyership, preceded by the superimposition of oneself as qualified by the three bodies which are themselves false, upon the Witness (sākṣin). The word "occurs" (bhavati) is to be supplied at the end. || 36 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In that very context, he states another illustration:
"Just as bathing and other such acts are repeated for the purpose of removing accumulated sins,"
Constantly devoted to the witness-consciousness, he was as if revolving in meditation.

Regarding the word "āvṛtti" (repetition): just as for a person who has committed a sin, [it is performed] for the sake of removing that committed sin— that is, for the purpose of dispelling the sin already practiced—
In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
titled *Tṛptidīpa*:

"Just as beneficial acts such as ritual bathing and other expiations (*prāyaścitta*) are repeated and performed again and again, so too this [realization] remains for a long time within the Witness (*sākṣin*), despite the state of being a transmigrator (*saṃsāritva*)."
As if transforming his meditation in order to avoid the fault of false attribution, he always remains intent upon the witness-consciousness. || 37 ||
Commentary (a0): To the question, "Is this taking refuge momentary? he replies: "āvṛtta... (verse 37).
A courtesan afflicted with elephantiasis feels no shame in her amorous dalliances.
Likewise, a manifestation appearing before one who knows [the truth] feels ashamed when its own nature is revealed.

Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus described the state of being dependent on a witness through various examples, he speaks of the bashfulness felt when proclaiming one's own virtues, along with an illustration: "Like a leper woman [who reveals her secret]... (38).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: what is this meditation (*dhyāna*) here—is it the contemplation of identity with the Witness (*sākṣin*) along with one's own self, or is it the continuous reflection (*anusaṃdhāna*) upon non-dual Brahman, which has been directly experienced as mere Consciousness (*prāgdṛṅmātratva*) following the previously established falsity of all visible phenomena? To this, [the author] replies that it is indeed the latter alternative, and clarifies it with an illustration: "upasthe... etc. The phrase "jānato'gre" (before the knower) connects with what precedes. || 38 ||
A Brāhmaṇa who has been captured by Mlecchas while performing penance [is released] again.
Bhāsa is not at all mixed with Mlecchas in the same way as those with inferior bodies.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, he provides an illustration for the absence of the delusion of identity with the body-triad once again, regarding the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) which has been distinguished from them: "Having been seized... (39).

The commentary clarifies, through two verses beginning with "gṛhīte," the very absence of self-manifestation by the agent that is the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), using two examples that indicate the non-confusion of the object of perception and the unity of vision. || 39 ||

— Rāghavendra’s Commentary — Not only is there recourse to witnesses for the sake of ceasing one's own transgressions, but also for the accomplishment of a great purpose; thus, he provides an illustration according to the maxim of the "lion's glance" (looking back while moving forward).
Established in the position of crown prince, the prince desired universal sovereignty.
Just as one becomes an imitator of the king, so too is this witness an object of imitation.

Regarding the term "yauvarājya" (the state of being crown prince): it means that he becomes an imitator of the king, possessing qualities such as pleasing the subjects, just like the king himself. ||240||
Commentary on a0: Regarding the term "yauvarājye" (in the state of crown prince), this refers to the aforementioned reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa). || 240 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "In the case of a crown prince following his king, the fruit of sovereignty is seen; however, this is not so when following a witness.
Therefore, how can one be motivated to follow him? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed"—thus says the Śruti.
Having heard that, with a one-pointed mind, one knows Brahman and nothing else.

Regarding the word "ya" (who): the meaning is that since the fruit consisting of becoming Brahman and so forth is heard in the Śruti—namely, "He who indeed knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself; in his family no one ignorant of Brahman is born; he crosses over sorrow, he crosses over evil; released from the knots of the heart, he becomes immortal"—it is proper to proceed toward following the witness by means of that which denotes such a fruit. || 41 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that even the state of being a witness is dependent upon an imagined witness; therefore, he says: "He who... These are the words of the Śruti: "He who indeed knows that Supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself. || 41 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If the state of being Brahman is attained through the knowledge of Brahman, then the nature of being a reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsatva) itself would perish;
therefore, how can one engage in action for the sake of one's own destruction? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The Seventh Chapter, together with the two commentaries. 293.
For just as those desiring divinity enter into fire and other elements, so it is here.
He desires his own destruction so that he may remain as a witness. || 42 ||

"Desiring divinity": just as in the world human beings desiring to attain divinity engage in such acts as entering the fires of Bhṛgu, entering the Prayāga fire, or entering the Gaṅgā, so too, because there exists a superior fruit characterized by abiding in the form of the Witness, engagement in the knowledge of Brahman—which is the cause for the removal of the state of being a reflection of consciousness—is indeed possible; this is the meaning. || 42 ||
— Objection: But surely, in the state of non-dual Brahman, there is one's own destruction; to this he replies with the verse beginning "devatva... (verse 42).
It is well known in the *Śaṅkaravijaya* that the venerable teacher Kumārila Bhaṭṭa entered a fire of camphor (*tupāgni*). || 42 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If the state of being a mere appearance (abhāsatva) is removed by the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), how can there be the worldly usage of 'living-ness' (jīvatva) for those who know the truth?
Anticipating this doubt, he provides an explanation for its persistence until the exhaustion of prārabdha-karma, along with an illustration:
"As long as his own body has not been consumed by fire, that man does not truly relinquish his human state."
As long as the body has been undertaken, there can be no liberation from the state of being a mere appearance.

The word "yāvat" (as long as) means that just as a person who has entered into fire or the like does not lose his human nature—his fitness for human designation—even until the destruction of his own body due to burning and so forth, in the same way, the empirical usage of being a reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) does not cease until the exhaustion of the *prārabdha* karma. This is the meaning. || 42 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): In that regard, he refutes the disparity with the illustrative example [of fire] on the grounds that there is no destruction of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) as long as the experience of *prārabdha* karma continues—stating, "as long as his own body... He refers to that person who has entered the fire. || 43 ||
Even when the rope is known, trembling and other such symptoms subside only gradually.
Furthermore, in the darkness of intoxication, that rope becomes a slithering serpent.

Rāma’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Since ignorance (ajñāna), which is the material cause of the delusion of being an enjoyer and so forth, has been sublated, how can there be a continuation of experience?
Or how can there be the contrary perception that 'I am mortal'? Anticipating this doubt, he makes this possible by showing an illustration: "In the knowledge of the rope," etc. (Verse 44).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection is raised: in a non-superimposed illusion such as that of silver in mother-of-pearl, the destruction of the ignorance regarding that object and its effects is experienced at the very moment of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Similarly, in the illusion of duality—which is manifested solely by beginningless ignorance regarding the substrate—a destruction of that ignorance and its pervasions must likewise occur simultaneously with the direct realization of it. How then can [ignorance] persist as long as the body initiated by past karma (*ārabdhadeha*) lasts? Or as long as...?

Anticipating the objection that "the liberation from the appearance of duality—such as the body and so forth—which arises for one engaged in commenced action, would not result in the destruction of the appearance of consciousness (cidābhāsa)," [the author] replies, "It is not so," by showing that even an unconditioned delusion is established by experience for a certain period in a particular body through another illustration. He first clarifies that illustration with the words: "Even upon the knowledge of the rope... and so on; "and so forth" includes fear. Now, let it be granted...
Regarding the fact that the cessation of trembling and so forth occurs gradually, yet the perception of the serpent never arises again, he says "again" (punar) [in the verse]. || 44 ||
In this way, even an undertaking that has begun gradually subsides, and not by force.
But at some time during the period of enjoyment, the thought "I am a mortal" may manifest.
Rāma’s Commentary: He applies this to the point of the analogy with the words "evam" (thus). || 245 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, is it said that the very person whose delusion regarding the snake has been pacified by that knowledge becomes a female serpent when the rope is playfully cast into dim darkness by him alone, or by someone else? It cannot be the first case, because for one whose latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that valid cognition is not lost, the aforementioned delusion cannot arise in that situation. Nor can it be the second case, because that same rope, cast into dim darkness by another, would—after some time—have its [snake-]form lost...

This very mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of the serpent, even though it has arisen as a veil within the midst of dense darkness, serves as the illustration for the ignorance that veils one's own true nature (*svarūpa*).
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya [known as the *Tṛptidīpa*]:

having raised the doubt that there is an inequality due to the impossibility of [the soul's] movement, the two examples written in the first and second halves of the preceding verse are applied respectively to the two subjects of the present verse.

He provides the resolution by connecting the two statements made in the first and second halves [of the verse], beginning with "In this way" (*evam*). Just as when the knowledge of the rope is present, the trembling and other such symptoms subside only gradually, so too the experience of the *ārabdha* (commenced) karma subsides only slowly. It does not subside—that is, it does not perish—at that very moment through the forceful application of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) or through the power of yoga and the like. Rather, just as when darkness is destroyed by a lamp or similar means, the perception of the rope [remains] for a while...

Just as a person who has lost the delusion of a snake because that cognition has been destroyed might still cast that very rope aside in dim darkness for lack of purpose, yet due to the force of time, it would appear as a serpent again to him precisely because of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that prior erroneous perception; so too, at the time of enjoyment—during the experience of pleasure and other fruits of *prārabdha* karma—it may occasionally reappear, but not at all times. And thus, generally at all times, [the realization remains]: "I am indeed Brahman; this duality is merely false."

The knower of the Self realizes through his own inquiry that this is merely like the blackness of the sky. The connection is as follows: at some time or on some occasion, the thought "I am mortal" appears. As for the established conclusion (siddhānta): because there is no other veiling factor due to the unity of ignorance, for those knowers of Brahman whose ignorance has been destroyed, just as a rope might appear as a snake when thrown into a dense darkness, so too, at some time during the period of experience, the thought "I am mortal" may appear.

Thus has the disparity between the illustrative examples been stated; that is indeed true, yet there is a certain secret here. It is as follows: "Liberation while living (jīvanmukti) exists because of its perception; and therein, the shadow of duality exists because of that perception.
There is a slight trace for the preservation of the shadow of duality; in that matter, one's own experience is the authority."
Thus, according to the words of the venerable lord of sages, Sarvajñātman, even when the root ignorance— which has as its sole object the non-duality of Brahman and the Self— is destroyed,

there remains that which causes the concealment of deep sleep and so forth, for the sake of the experience of the fruits of *prārabdha* karma; this exists by the maxim of Arjuna’s chariot, though burnt by the Brahmāstra.
It must necessarily be admitted that a fragment [of the soul] established by the Lord of all volitions (saṃkalpa) remains until the completion of the enjoyment of the aforementioned fruits.

That very fragment, having brought about the veil known as deep sleep (suṣupti), produces—like a dream—even for those liberated while living (jīvanmukta), such as Yājñavalkya and others, during the period of experiencing intense prārabdha-karma, a non-dual Brahman-conduct characterized by worldly dealings such as: "We bow to the most learned in Brahman; we are merely seekers of cows."

One should simply accomplish it for even a moment by means of forgetfulness; thus, there is not even the slightest trace of inequality here. And that [bondage] will perish of its own accord at the moment of the exhaustion of *prārabdha*. This very point has been stated in my *Bodhaikyasiddhi*:
Just as Arjuna’s chariot was consumed by the Brahmāstra weapon until the battle with Kṛṣṇa ended—
being the sole obstacle to his desire for combat— and he himself was destroyed; so too,
when the entire visible world is shattered by the single blow of knowledge, it continues to manifest only due to the bondage of *prārabdha*.
"Right at that moment, he thus brings about his own destruction; this is likewise [to be understood].
This direction [of interpretation] is to be seen in my very commentary on this [work], titled *Advaitātmaprabodha*. || 245 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that with the recurrence of human birth and the onset of old age, that knowledge of reality would be sublated; anticipating this, he says:
"The knowledge of reality is not destroyed by such a transgression."
The detailed account, however, is found in the *Jīvanmuktiviveka*; this is not a mere vow, but rather the actual state of reality.

"It is not merely this much. Why is it that the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) produced by the authority of scripture (*āgama-pramāṇa*) is not sublated by the mere arising of such a cognition as "I am sometimes mortal"? To this he says: "Regarding liberation while living" (*jīvanmukti*). This vow of liberation while living, characterized by the employment of the notion of mortality, is not something that must necessarily be practiced; rather, the cessation of erroneous cognition through right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is the very nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*). Therefore—
The sense is that even when the notion of mortality occasionally arises, it is subsequently sublated by another cognition of reality (tattvajñāna). || 46 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, an objection may be raised: "In this way, if at the time of enjoyment, there should occasionally arise the manifestation 'I am a mortal' preceded by the forgetting of the non-dual Brahman-Self, then—due to the sin and merit produced by the anger of the Lord and other such results arising from actions such as the *saṃdhyāvandana* performed during that specific period—this person would again fall into *saṃsāra*. Consequently, even though the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) has arisen for him, the fruit characterized as liberation..."
Accompanied by the two commentaries. Page 295.

[The Seventh Chapter] Regarding the point that [the self] would be destroyed by way of destruction, and thus would indeed be established in reality, he says: "Not merely this much. Now, it was stated just below here that it is not merely from the forgetfulness of reality that there is misfortune, but rather from its opposite; and so, when the misconception "I am mortal" occurs, how could there not be saṃsāra?

If it is argued that this implies the destruction of knowledge (*jñāna*), we say no. This is because the remainder of the cited passage—“there is no time for it to be subverted, for one who remembers [it] instantly”—and the word “sometimes” (*kadācit*) found in the present context—“but at some time during the period of experience, the thought ‘I am a mortal’ appears”—have not been taken into account; thus, there is room for such a doubt. For this very reason, it is said: “liberation while living” (*jīvanmukti*). Regarding the word “reality” (*vastu*): through the two states of being sublated and unsublated, duality and non-duality—
The meaning is that the establishment of objects is characterized by cognition. || 246 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: It may be granted that in cases such as the [illusion of a] snake in a rope, the effects of that [error], such as trembling, persist even after the erroneous cognition has been sublated;

however, one might object that in the present example, when the delusion is removed by the knowledge generated through inquiry into the statement "You are the tenth" during the counting of ten people, no persistence of its effects is observed.
Anticipating this objection, he says:
Even when struck on the head for the tenth time, he woke up and did not weep.
But a wound on the head heals slowly over a month; it does not heal then [immediately]. || 47 ||
"Even the tenth": when the realization "I am the tenth" arises, there ceases to be mere weeping preceded by the striking of one's head;
however, the wound produced by that striking continues to persist—this is the meaning. || 47 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "In the illustration of the rope-snake, even after the delusion—along with its ignorance and its material cause—is sublated by the knowledge of the substrate, there remains for some time a residue of its effects, such as fear and trembling. But what is that [residue] in the present case, the tenth illustration, which was accepted as the primary example of the seven states? To this, he says: "The tenth also... The phrase *śirastāḍam* is an adverbial modifier. [The head...]

The "taste" (rasa) is the beating; just as a beating occurs, so too does one cry out from the delusion of death born of ignorance, thinking, "I am indeed the tenth," even though [it is said] "you yourself are the tenth. Although, upon hearing the words of a trustworthy person—who counts up to nine and says, "You yourself are the tenth"—one realizes "I am indeed the tenth" and no longer weeps, nevertheless, the throbbing of the head subsides only gradually over the course of a month; it does not subside at all through the force of sudden remorse.
This is the logical connection (anvaya). || 247 ||
The joy born from attaining immortality dispelled the pain of his wounds.
In the same way, the attainment of liberation conceals the suffering caused by *prārabdha* karma.

Rāma’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Even if the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) continues after the attainment of knowledge, on what basis can the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) be considered a human goal (puruṣārtha)? Anticipating this doubt, he states—by means of an illustration—that it is indeed a human goal because the joy born from the acquisition of liberation exists as that which obscures the suffering [of worldly life]. This is expressed in verse 48, beginning with "daśama... Ānandagiri’s Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, if it is argued that even if the cycle of worldly existence continues after knowledge, that [liberation] would be utterly fruitless, [the author replies]: "If so, regarding the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta)..."
To show that it is not so because of the attainment of *kṛt* suffixes, he clarifies the aforementioned example with the verse beginning "daśamāmṛti" (248).
Since superimposition occurs even in the absence of a vow, let this be further investigated.
One who indulges in tastes eats again and again throughout the day, in whatever manner possible. || 49 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: It has been stated that this is not a "vow" (vrata) for one liberated while living. To the question, "What follows from its not being a vow? he says: "Due to the absence of a vow. He provides an illustration for the necessity of repeated inquiry: "Like one who consumes mercury. Just as a person consuming mercury eats again and again on a single day to ward off the affliction of hunger, so too is discrimination practiced repeatedly to bring about the cessation of superimposition.
The meaning is "her. || 49 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, even so, one might object that this is not the previously mentioned vow of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti-vrata*), because it lacks the status of a vow and thus cannot be constant; and if that were the case, how could the attainment of the goal be achieved? For it is not the case that something already obtained, such as a golden ornament on one's neck, needs to be attained again. To this, he says: "Due to the absence of a vow" (*vratabhāvāt*). *Rasa* means love (*prema*). || 249 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 296.
He pacifies it with medicine, just as the tenth [person] heals his own wound.
Having pacified this prārabdha-karma through experience by means of this work called the Tṛptidīpa, one is likewise liberated. || 250 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Raising the doubt as to how the fruit of *prārabdha* karma—which cannot be nullified by knowledge—is terminated, he states that it ceases only through experience, just as a wound caused by beating is healed by medicine, in the verse beginning with "śamayati" (250).
— Commentary (A0 Ṭīkā): Thus, regarding when even that *prārabdha* karma which has not been ceased by knowledge will come to an end, he says: "When... (verse 250).

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: By this verse beginning with "If one should know the Self as 'This am I'," [the Lord] declares these two states residing in the individual soul (jīva), namely, immediate knowledge and the cessation of sorrow. In this mantra—"If a person should know the Self as 'This am I,' desiring what, longing for what, would he suffer for the sake of the body?"—there are two states of the soul known as immediate knowledge and the cessation of sorrow.

It was stated [in the previous section] that [the Self] is denoted [by the word "Self"]. Now, having first recounted what has preceded, he begins to describe the seventh state of the individual soul (jīva), characterized by contentment, which was indicated by that very denotation:
"The liberation from sorrow, expressed in the passage beginning with 'Desiring what...'," has been proclaimed.
For this is the sixth state of manifestation; satisfaction is the seventh.

"What does he desire?"— the liberation from sorrow, which was indicated by the latter half of that verse, has been explained through this entire textual composition. He states that among the seven states of the individual soul (jīvāvasthā) mentioned in this verse— "this is ignorance, this is veiling, likewise distraction, indirect cognition, direct realization, liberation from sorrow, and unbridled contentment"— it is the sixth state, referring to "of the reflection" (ābhāsasya).
The seventh [verse] is being explained; this is the ellipsis. || 51 ||

Commentary (a0): Having thus stated the meaning of the scripture and enjoined [the disciple] to engage in the exposition of the mantra that was promised, he concludes with the words "kimicchannatīti" (desiring what?). This is the [section] known as the Liberation from Grief (śokamokṣa). 251.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He declares, preceded by the demonstration of its opposite, that the satisfaction born of immediate knowledge (aparokṣajñāna) is unrestrained:
"This satisfaction [derived] from objects is restrained; this [other] satisfaction is unrestrained."
Thinking, "What was to be done has been done; what was to be attained has been attained," he is thus satisfied. || 52 ||

Regarding the term *sāṃkuśā*: because satisfaction born from the acquisition of an object is blunted by the desire for another object, it is "with a goad" (*sāṃkuśa*); due to the absence of that [desire], it is "unrestrained" (*niraṅkuśa*). He demonstrates this very point with the words "It is done" (*kṛtam*). || 52 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: is this satisfaction, which is asserted as the seventh state, like the sense of "enough" (*alaṃbuddhi*) produced by obtaining desired objects such as sound and so forth—therefore limited by the fact that other things yet to be obtained will inevitably perish? To this, he says: "It is limited" (*sāṃkuśā*). He demonstrates its very lack of limitation through a dramatic illustration: "Enough! (*kṛtam*). || 252 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He establishes the very fact of having accomplished all that was to be done:
"For the attainment of the multitude of goals pertaining to this world and the next, and for the attainment of liberation."
Formerly he had much to do, but all of that has now been accomplished.

Regarding the term *aihika*: prior to the arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), this wise person performs agriculture, trade, and so forth in this world for the attainment of the desired and the removal of the undesired; he performs sacrifices, meditations, and so forth for the attainment of heaven and the like; and he performs hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth for the attainment of the knowledge that is the means to liberation. Thus [it is said].
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

Such was what had to be done [previously]. But now, due to the absence of desire for the fruits of worldly existence and because the direct realization of the bliss of Brahman has been accomplished, all those activities—such as agriculture, sacrifice, and Vedic study—have become as good as finished; the meaning is that there is nothing further remaining to be performed. || 53 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) on verse a0 shows the duty itself in brief: "In this world" (aihika), etc. Now, it states the absence of that [duty] with the remainder of the verse beginning with "that" (tat). || 253 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus established the state of having accomplished all that was to be done, he demonstrates the satisfaction that results from it:
"This very state of having accomplished all that was to be done is preceded by its counter-correlate."
Connecting [the teachings] in this very way, he is constantly satisfied.

Regarding the phrase "tadetad" (this very thing): in the manner about to be described, he is always satisfied precisely by being preceded by the counter-correlate—that is, by first bringing the counter-correlate to mind. || 54 ||
Commentary on the Aṃśa: Having thus described the nature of having accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtyatva*), he next declares his intention to explain the manner of its contemplation:
"This very [state]... (254).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He elaborates upon that very same contemplation:
"Let the ignorant, who suffer due to their attachment to sons and other such things, wander in saṃsāra as they please."
Filled with supreme bliss, why should I wander through the cycle of existence out of any desire?

By the passage beginning with "duḥkhino jñā" (the ignorant are suffering), and by the preceding section ending with "kṛtyakṛtyatayā tṛptaḥ prāptaprāpyatayā punaḥ," he first demonstrates his own distinction from those who seek worldly happiness—namely, "duḥkhinaḥ. || 255 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Having thus made his declaration, and wishing to demonstrate within himself—by means of seven [verses]—certain absences (*abhāva*) that characterize the non-existence of all duality, together with the various entities to be described hereafter as the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), he first declares his own lack of engagement in the worship of Gopāla for the sake of obtaining a son, who is known as the "secondary self" (*gauṇātmā*). He says, beginning with "duḥkhinaḥ": "Because they are ignorant, therefore [they desire] sons and so forth... (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the available portion.)

"Kṣaya" means the desire for a son and the wife and so forth who serve as the means to achieve that [son]; "parama" refers to the three words [in the compound], all of which form a *karmadhāraya* compound. || 255 ||
Let those who desire to go to the next world perform their duties.
Since I am the self of all the worlds, why should I perform anything, and how?
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the distinction [of the knower] from those who perform rituals for the sake of heaven and other such goals: "Let him perform... (16).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, he also demonstrates within himself the absence of engagement in the general practice of karma, saying "let them perform" and so forth.
Regarding "those desiring the next world": the meaning is those who desire to go to heaven and other such realms. || 256 ||
Let them expound the treatises or teach the Vedas.
"Those who are qualified for this are my [disciples], but I have no qualification because I am inactive. (57)
Rāghava’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even in the absence of activity for one's own sake, why should there not be activity for the sake of others?
Anticipating this, he states that such activity also does not exist due to the lack of qualification, saying: "Let them explain... (verse 17).

— A0 Commentary — He clarifies the absence of his status as a teacher as well with the words "let them explain" (*vyācakṣatām*). The meaning is "let them expound. By this, he indicates within himself that even in the absence of activity for his own sake, there is likewise an absence of activity for the sake of benefiting others. In reality, however, [the situation is as follows]:
Since even helping others is a cause of merit, it is implied that this too is indeed for one's own benefit. || 17 ||
I have no desire for sleep, alms, bathing, or purification, nor do I perform them.
If the perceivers are merely conceptualizing, what would it matter to me if they conceptualize otherwise? (58)
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya, with the commentary (*rā0 ṭīkā*) titled *Tṛptidīpa*:
Now, [an objection may be raised]: "For the sake of sustaining your own body, you perform acts such as begging for alms, and for the sake of the next world, you perform acts such as ritual bathing."

Anticipating the objection that since [the world] is perceived as being created, its lack of agency (akriyatva) is unproven, he says "nidrā" (sleep), etc., to show that even that [creation] does not exist from his own perspective, but is merely imagined by others. || 58 ||

— Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, it might be argued that the state of being actionless is indeed improper, because one is still an agent of actions such as sleeping, begging for food, and eating for the sake of maintaining one’s own body, as well as actions such as bathing and so forth for the sake of the next world; to this, he says: "Sleeping... (verse 18).
A heap of gunja berries and the like would not burn by means of a fire superimposed upon something else.
I do not thus worship those very phenomena of saṃsāra that have been superimposed as other [than what they are].

Rāma’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that there might still be sublation even through another conceptualization, he states an illustration for the absence of such [sublation]: "A cluster of gunja berries... (verse 59).
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He clarifies, with an illustration, the absence of any personal loss despite a specific attribution made by another—namely, "guñje" (the berry). || 19 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even if there is no desire for other fruits, let there be no performance of ritual acts; however, for the sake of the direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*), hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth must certainly be performed.
Anticipating this, he states that because ignorance and the like are absent, even the agency to perform hearing and so forth does not exist:
"Let those whose reality is unknown listen; knowing it, why should I listen?"
Let them entertain doubts; I do not consider myself to be without doubt.
"Let them hear": those whose true reality (*tattva*)—namely, the identity of Brahman and the Self—is unknown, being thus characterized, should perform hearing (*śravaṇa*);

those possessing doubt as to whether that reality is such or otherwise should perform reflection (*manana*). The meaning is: "Since I lack both of these, there is no engagement for me in either. || 260 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, even if this is so, one might argue that the internal means such as hearing (śravaṇa) must indeed be performed as long as the body lasts.

To this, he says "no," because they would be purposeless, in two verses beginning with "Let him hear" (śṛṇvatv). The words "knowing the non-dual Self" (jānann advaitātmānam) are to be supplied [to complete the sense]. ||260||
One who is deluded should practice meditative reflection; for what need is there for meditation when there is no delusion?
I never entertain the misconception that the body is the self. || 61 ||

Rāma’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): Lest it be argued that hearing and reflection are unnecessary, and that one must practice meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) for the sake of dispelling misconceptions, [the author] replies—anticipating this objection—that since there is an absence of the misconception characterized by the notion of selfhood with respect to the body and so forth, even that [contemplation] need not be performed. He says: "One who is deluded" (61). Ānandagiri’s Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): "One who is deluded" (*viparyasta*). This means one who possesses contrary mental impressions (*viparītabhāvanāvān*). || 61 ||
The conventional usage such as "I am a human being" and so forth occurs even without this [notion of self].
Error is conceived from the latent impressions (vāsanā) practiced for a long time. || 62 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection—"But if there is an absence of misconception (viparyaya), how can the conventional usage 'I am a human being' be accounted for?"—he states that it arises through the power of latent impressions (vāsanā): "I... (verse 62).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask, "In that case, how is it that there are such worldly transactions as 'I am a human' or 'this is a jar'? To this, he says: "I... (verse 62).

[The Seventh Chapter] Accompanied by Two Commentaries:
When the karma that has begun to bear fruit is exhausted, worldly activity ceases.
But as long as karma is not exhausted, it will certainly not be stilled even by a thousand meditations.
"Regarding the term *prārabdha* (commenced karma): || 63 ||"
299 a0 Commentary:

If that is so, then when does the cessation of the aforementioned worldly discourse occur? To this he says: "When the prārabdha... and "In meditation... According to the Vivaraṇa school, even in the case of Devahūti, Ṛṣabha-deva, and others, during asamprajñāta-samādhi—or during sleep—there is a nescient mental modification (avidyaka-vṛtti) in the form of pleasure and so forth.

Since it is accepted that even at that time there are subtle mental modifications (*sūkṣma-vṛtti*) such as "I am Brahman" belonging to those whose internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) have been transformed by the essence of *sattva*—as expressed in passages beginning with "the modifications of *sattva* [arise] through the discrimination of reality"—there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in that case; this is the general direction of the argument. || 63 ||
If you desire the pervasiveness of conventional usage, then let there be meditation for you.
Seeing worldly affairs to be harmful, why should I meditate upon them?
Rāma’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Even for worldly activity caused by *prārabdha*-karma, meditation must indeed be practiced in order to make that activity rare.
Anticipating this, [the author] states that meditation need not be performed for its cessation, because such activity is seen to be non-obstructive: "raritva" (rareness), verse 64.

Ānandagiri’s Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, if this is so according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), then after the dawn of knowledge, just as there is the worldly usage of "I am a human being" and so forth, there would likewise be the usage "I am Brahman"—[is this not a contradiction?]

Thus, although even the mental state consisting solely of extremely subtle and dense sattva is indeed merely conventional (vyavahāra), nevertheless—considering that the first [type] is to be abandoned because it causes suffering due to its extreme grossness and so forth, while the last is to be accepted because it bestows happiness due to its extreme subtlety and so forth, and because it brings about the rarity of the aforementioned suffering-inducing convention—the author anticipates this objection and provides the resolution with the words "rāralatvam" (the state of being rare). The meaning is: "for you"—that is, for those opponents or disciples of yours. || 64 ||
Since there is no distraction for me, therefore there is no meditative absorption for me.
Whether it be distraction or meditative concentration, these belong to the mind which is subject to transformation. (265)

Rāma’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): Anticipating the objection that even if meditation (dhyāna) is not to be performed, concentration (samādhi) must still be practiced to avoid distraction, he states—beginning with the verse "vikṣepa" (verse 269)—that since both distraction and its pacification are attributes of the mind, he has no authority over concentration, which merely serves to ward off distraction.
Commentary on the Verse (a0 ṭīkā): He establishes this very point by saying, "vikṣepa."

"Having concealed its own radiant form, [ignorance] falsely projects it through the forms of the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), and the world, by virtue of its association with the powers of concealment (āvaraṇa) and delusion (vibhrama), and by the force of being the locus and object of pure selfhood"— as stated in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*. Since the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), which is the source of such projection (*vikṣepa*), has been destroyed, in its absence, that which is opposed to it...

The intention is that because samādhi also lacks the distinction of being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*), it should not be accepted as equal [to the state of liberation]. The reason for this is stated: "or else there would be distraction" (*vikṣepo vā*). || 265 ||
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even so, the experience that is the fruit of samādhi must still be accomplished.
Anticipating this, he states that it need not be accomplished because it is his own essential nature:
"What separate experience could there be for me, who am of the nature of eternal experience?"
"What was to be done has been done; what was to be attained has been attained"—such is his certainty.
Regarding the word "eternal" (nitya): he concludes the established state of having accomplished what was to be done with the words, "what was to be done has been done. (66)
Commentary (a0): Now, even so, the venerable Patañjali, concerning *nirvikalpa-samādhi*, stated in two Yoga Sūtras:

"Then the seer abides in his own nature; otherwise, there is conformity with the mental modifications" (*tadā draṣṭuḥ svarūpe'vasthānam*, *vṛttisārūpyamitaratra*), and "In that state, wisdom is truth-bearing, having an object other than what is reached through scripture or inference" (*ṛtaṃbharā tatra prajñā śrutānumānābhyāmanyaviṣayā*).
Thus, since he has declared that the experience of one's own true nature is to be accomplished solely through *samādhi*, it must necessarily be practiced. To this, he says:

Regarding the word "eternal" (*nitya*): as for the two aphorisms (*sūtra*), their utility lies solely in the purification of the meaning of the term "thou" (*tvaṃpadārtha*) for certain specific qualified aspirants. Now, if this is so, what is your own settled conclusion? In response to this expectation, he summarizes it: "It is done" (*kṛtam*). || 66 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya [pages 300–300]

[In the commentary on the *Tṛptidīpa* by Rāma: Having raised the objection that if agency is not admitted in all cases, it would follow that there is no fixed course of action, he accepts the lack of a fixed course of action as it is obtained through the force of *prārabdha* (past karma).
Whether it be worldly convention, scriptural convention, or even otherwise.
"Let that which has been begun proceed for me, who am a non-doer and free from attachment. (67)

Regarding the term "worldly activity" (*vyavahāra*): it refers to mundane activities such as seeking alms for food, or scriptural activities such as recitation (*japa*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), or even otherwise prohibited actions such as violence. The meaning is: "May this worldly activity proceed without transgressing my *prārabdha* karma, for me who am devoid of agency and enjoyership. || 67 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): If this is so, then how is your worldly conduct (*vyavahāra*)? To the question "How?", he says, "Worldly conduct," meaning it is exactly as it has begun. The *laukika* (worldly) consists of sleep, begging, and so forth. The *śāstrīya* (scriptural) is that which, by being prescribed by the scriptures, brings about merit characterized by the grace of the Lord; otherwise, by being censured by them, it brings about sin characterized by the wrath of the Lord, such as [the curse] through the medium of a *śāpa* (curse) directed at Vidagdha Śākalya by Yājñavalkya.

The form of "pāta" (falling) is indeed well-known in the fifth chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. Furthermore, the phrase "api vā" and so forth expresses both option (*vikalpa*) and conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Now, one might object: "Previously, by the words 'sleep and begging,' 'bathing and purification,' and so on, you yourself stated only two types of worldly and other-worldly activity; now, however, this third type of activity is being described as something different. What is your intention in this matter? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the following resolution: "My..."

By such [statements] as these. "As it was begun" (yathārabdham): this is the intended meaning. For that which has been commenced (*prārabdha*) is exhausted solely in the bestowing of pleasure and pain, but not even in the accomplishment of activities characterized by worldly conduct (*vyavahāra*). That [commenced karma], however, depends entirely upon the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the existent and non-existent; this is indeed beyond dispute.

And thus, according to the analogy of a potter’s wheel spinning due to its initial momentum (*dakṣiṇāvarta*), my body and so forth—which have been commenced solely by the impressions of the existent for me, the knower of Brahman—function in that very same way.
Thus it should proceed. || 67 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus stated the true nature of reality, he speaks by way of a bold assertion (prauḍhavāda):
"Or rather, although his purpose is accomplished, out of a desire to favor the world..."
I proceed solely by the path prescribed by the scriptures; what loss is there for me? (68)
Alternatively: "Out of a desire to favor the world" means out of a wish to favor living beings. || 68 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, he himself reveals the hidden intention (gūḍhābhisaṃdhi) already stated, beginning with "Or else" (athavā). Regarding the verse beginning with "Loka":
"Just as the ignorant act while attached to action, O Bhārata, so should the wise man act without attachment, desiring the welfare of the world. (Gītā 3.25)
The words “because of the Smṛti” are to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 68 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that if one accepts engagement in the very path prescribed by the scriptures, then there might still be a mental modification (vikāra) caused by pride regarding that [engagement], he says:
"Let the body engage in the worship of deities, bathing, purification, begging for alms, and so forth."
Likewise, let her mutter the Tāra mantra and recite the Upanishads, the crest-ornaments of the Vedas.
By means of the two verses beginning with "devārcana" (the worship of the gods), [it is said]: "Tāra" is the Praṇava, the crest-jewel of the traditional Vedic scriptures, the Vedānta-śāstra. || 69 ||

Commentary (a0): Demonstrating that very path of his own—consisting of physical and other activities—as one who has renounced the world (*saṃnyāsī*), he maintains his state of non-attachment through two verses beginning with "devārcana" (worship of the gods). By means of a representative image (*pratīka*) of either Hari or Hara, known as the Śāligrāma or the Bāṇaliṅga, [he worships] the God of Gods—the self-luminous Self, which is well-known from such Vedic texts as, "The One God is hidden in all beings."...

The meaning is that his vision is devoid even of the scent of Tantra; his worship consists solely of the *praṇava* mantra and the application of Ganges water and ashes, and nothing else, even in his dreams.
[End of] the Seventh Chapter.
Accompanied by the two commentaries.
By "and so forth," sleep is included. The remainder, however, is quite clear. "The high *oṃkāra*. "According to tradition" (*āmnāya*) means, that is to say, according to the Upanishads.
This is an illustrative indication [applying] also to the Bhagavadgītā and the Brahmasūtra, which are included within the threefold path (prasthānatraya). || 69 ||
Let the intellect meditate upon Viṣṇu, or let it dissolve into the bliss of Brahman.
I myself shall not do anything at all in this matter, nor shall I cause it to be done.
Rāma’s Commentary—270.

Commentary (Ṭīkā): "Viṣṇum" [refers to the verse]. This is an illustrative reference to Śiva as well, based on the Vedic scripture: "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon, the bringer of auspiciousness. Here, the phrase "or else" (*yadvā*) is used because there is a lack of natural inclination toward regarding him as possessing attributes (*saguṇatva*). However, the other [point] is indeed not obscure. || 270 ||
And thus, where could conflict possibly arise for me, an agent of action?
Because their objects are distinct, like the eastern and western oceans. || 71 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the conclusion with the words "If this is so" (evaṃ ca). || 71 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) states the conclusion: "And thus" (evaṃ ca). The reason for this is given by the verse beginning with "vibhinna... along with an illustration. || 71 ||
The agent of action is bound by attachment to body, speech, and mind, but not to the Witness.
For the wise, there is insistence on being a witness and untainted, but not so for others.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He clarifies precisely this difference in subject matter with the verse beginning "vapuḥ" (the body). || 72 ||
Commentary (a0): He clarifies that very point regarding the difference in their objects with the verse beginning "vapuḥ" || 272 ||
And thus, being ignorant of each other's circumstances, they were like two deaf men.
Seeing those two disputing, the wise simply laugh.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Nevertheless, he says "And thus" (evam ca) [verse 73] to show that those two—the man of knowledge and the man of action—who engage in dispute, are objects of ridicule for the wise.

Commentary (a0): Now, if this is so, then why does a dispute arise between the Pūrva-mīmāṃsaka and the Uttara-mīmāṃsaka, who respectively consider themselves to be practitioners of ritual action (karmin) and possessors of knowledge (jñānin)? If you ask this, know simply that it is because of their outward-looking nature (*bahirmukhatva*) and their consequent ignorance of the true purport of the scriptures. He provides an illustration for this resolution: "And thus, with one another... Intelligent people [know]: "Having understood this, one becomes wise and has accomplished all that was to be done. (*etad buddhvā buddhimān syāt kṛtakṛtyaś ca*)
The meaning is "of the knower of Brahman," according to the traditional teaching (smṛti) that "Bhārata" [is used] in this sense. || 273 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question, "Why is there cause for derision? he states that it is because [the ignorant] engage in quarrels devoid of any real object:
"The knower of reality does not regard as a witness that which the agent of action does not know."
Let the state of being Brahmā be understood therein; what is lost for the performer of ritual action? || 74 ||

"Yam" (whom): the ritualist does not recognize that Witness—the inner Self who is distinct from the body, speech, and intellect required for the performance of rituals. When a knower of reality has realized His nature as Brahman, what is lost for the ritualist in the performance of his ritual duties? || 74 ||
Commentary on Verse 1: He elaborates upon the very fact of their mutual ignorance regarding each other's circumstances through two verses beginning with "yaṃ karmī" (74).
By virtue of their false understanding, the body, speech, and intellect have been abandoned by the knower.
Let the practitioner proceed with these; what is lost here for the one possessed of knowledge? || 275 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [page 302] 302.

[The commentary by Rāma on the *Tṛptidīpa*—regarding the verse beginning with "deha": What is lost for the knower (*jñānin*) in the performance of ritual action (*karmānuṣṭhāna*) through the body, speech, and intellect, which have been abandoned by him through the realization of their falsity? Therefore, the meaning is that those two who provoke a quarrel over a non-existent object are to be ridiculed. ||271||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): "Devāg" etc. "Tyaktāḥ" means disregarded. "Anṛtā" means by the power of the cognition of falsehood; this is the sense. "By these"—namely, by the body, speech, and intellect—"let [them] impel the soul"—this is the ellipsis. This implies: in the performance of sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma for the sake of heaven and so forth, in the recitation of the Vedas, and in the meditation upon various deities. This is a locative of purpose (*viṣayasaptamī*). The meaning is: "let them employ [the soul]. || 275 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: An objection is raised that since it lacks a purpose, the performance of ritual action is not accepted by the man of knowledge:
"If active engagement is of no use, then what use is withdrawal?"
The cause of awakening is the desire for cessation, and likewise the other [cause] is the desire for thorough knowledge. (76)
"—is activity. He offers a rebuttal, stating that "the absence of experience is the same even in the case of cessation," by saying: "cessation.

He raises an objection, suggesting that because cessation is a cause of knowledge, there is no lack of utility, by saying: "if cessation is indeed a cause of knowledge. In that case, activity too is [a cause of knowledge].
He says that it is useful because it is the cause of the desire to know: "vubhutsā" (desire to know). || 76 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, raising the objection that engagement in action is improper because it generates distraction, he resolves it by means of a counter-objection (*pratibandī*), saying "Engagement... Having raised the objection regarding the release from the counter-objection, he refutes it with another counter-objection, saying "Awakening... (verse 276).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised again—that since one who has already awakened lacks the desire to know, inquiry is useless for him:
"If he is awakened, he would not desire to know, nor would he awaken again."
Cognition would persist due to its lack of sublation, and not from any other means of proof.

"If [it is argued that] he is already a Buddha," then, since there is no further awakening for one who is already a Buddha, the cessation of its cause is likewise useless with respect to him; thus he says, "Nor even... Anticipating the objection that cessation is required for the sake of stabilizing the awakening that has arisen once, he says, "Because of non-sublation," meaning that stability depends on the absence of sublation and not on some other means. [This refers to] the knowledge produced by the authority of the Vedic statement being [overpowered] by a stronger...
The meaning is that because there is no obstruction due to pride (māna), there will certainly be continuity; therefore, no other means should be practiced for that purpose. || 77 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, an objection is raised: "In the previous verse, it was settled by means of a counter-objection that 'if cessation is not useful, where is activity useful? If cessation is the cause of awakening, then the other [activity] is so in the desire to know'; this is improper because awakening cannot coexist with the desire to know reality. Anticipating this, he settles the matter there as well by means of a counter-objection: "If [he is] awakened" (buddhaścediti). That is to say, if a person is "awakened," meaning one who possesses the realization of reality.

If you say that one should not desire to know—that is, one should not form the wish to understand—because awakening has already arisen, then the connection [of the argument] is this: for that very reason, he does not awaken again, nor does he even accomplish awakening. And thus, just as you state that further activity, which serves as the cause for the desire to know, is of no use for the knower of reality because awakening has already arisen, so too is cessation—which serves as the cause for awakening—useless for him for that same reason.
"This is to be understood as the reality. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Because it is uncontradicted" (avādhāt). || 277 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even if there is no sublation by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), could there not still be sublation by ignorance (*avidyā*) or by its effect, namely the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of agency?
Anticipating this, he says:
Neither ignorance nor its effect is able to sublate awakening.
For those two have already been sublated by the realization of reality. || 78 ||
"It is not ignorance. He states the reason for this: "As previously [stated]," etc. (78).
