Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if it is asked "Why is there indeed no sublation?", do you mean that the ignorance which is a remnant of the root-ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*), which causes states such as deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and so forth, and which—being pervaded by that [root-ignorance] and characterized by its connection with consciousness through the distinctions of the individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśvara*), and their difference—is the sublater of the knowledge of ignorance? Or do you mean its effect, the subtle body (*ākāra*)?
[Page 303]
The Seventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.
Having deliberated thus, beginning with "from that time onwards," he says "neither of the two" by means of the passage beginning with "not ignorance. The reason for this is stated as "even before.

This is the intended meaning: just as the waking state arises precisely subverting the sleep along with its dreams, so too the knowledge of reality arises and is perceived as subverting duality along with its very root; however, until the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma, that [knowledge] continues to appear like the memory of a dream and so forth. || 278 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that even if ignorance (*avidyā*) has been sublated, its effect—which is still being perceived—cannot possibly be sublated; therefore, the sublation of knowledge (*bodha*) would occur by means of that effect.

Anticipating this doubt, he states that since the effect is also sublated precisely through the cessation of its material cause (*upādāna*), it is not possible to suspect a sublation of knowledge by that effect either.
Let it be seen that [the object] is sublated by the senses; therefore, no sublation of that [sublation] is possible.
A living rat does not kill a cat; how could it kill one when dead? (79)
"It is sublated. In this regard, he provides an illustration: "While living," etc. "Ākhu" means a mouse. || 79 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): For this very reason, it is said "sublated" (*bādhita*). This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) as well; thus, by that sublated object of perception, the sublation of the awakening to reality (*tattvabodha*) is implied. In this regard, he states two corroborative examples (*arthāntaranyāsa*) with the half-verse beginning with "living" (*jīvan*), etc., for the sake of illustration. || 279 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: To strengthen the fact that the realization of reality cannot be sublated by the perception of duality, he provides a supporting illustration by means of a *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument:
"Even if he were pierced by the weapon of Paśupati, he did not die."
"What proof is there that one whose limbs have been pierced will perish when [the effort] is fruitless? (280)

"Moreover"—this means there is no proof for the following: if it is said that he who was pierced by the *pāśupata* weapon did not die because he was indeed invincible, then what is the authority for saying that he will perish, his body tormented by an arrow from Viṣṇu which is "barbed-less" (*niṣphala*) and thus lacks a shaft? There is no evidence; such is the meaning. || 280 ||
Commentary on verse a0: Regarding the word "api" (even/also). It refers to that living being (*jīva*), for according to the Vedic scripture, "The living being does not die. || 280 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He applies the matter established by the illustration to the subject of the illustration:
"In the beginning, by ignorance, which is deluded by its own various effects..."
Having fought, that consciousness was victorious; how can it, being so firmly established today, be overcome? ||81||

"At the beginning" means: at the outset, during the time of practicing knowledge, consciousness fought—that is, waged war—with ignorance, which was increasing as it manifested through various effects such as the states of being a knower (*pramātṛ*), an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), and an agent (*kartṛ*). It conquered that ignorance. That very same [consciousness], now firmly established through proficiency in practice, once ignorance has ceased, how could it be sublated by the pure reality or by its effects, namely, superimposition (*adhyāsa*)? It cannot be.
The meaning is that even that [other cognition] would be sublated. || 81 ||
Commentary: He further elaborates upon that very point through a simile, beginning with "In the beginning. [The state is] by means of the blossoming, i.e., the expanding [consciousness]. || 289 ||
Let the corpses of ignorance and its effects remain slain by awakening.
There is no fear for the sovereign of awakening; on the contrary, his fame arises from them.
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He expresses the established meaning through a metaphorical illustration (*rūpaka*) for the sake of facilitating the listener's comprehension, saying: "Let it be... (verse 82).
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, even a sublated cognition is indeed desired; this he expresses by means of a metaphor: "Let them stand... (282).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Let it be so; what relevance does this have to the present topic? To this, he says:
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya: he who is thus never separated from such exceedingly heroic awakening.
What does it matter to this [Self] whether there is activity or cessation pertaining to the body and so forth? (83)

"Who" refers to that person who, in the manner described, is never separated from such exceedingly heroic awakening—the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self—which destroys ignorance and its effects. For this person, what can be gained by activity or cessation directed toward the body and so forth? The meaning is: nothing at all, whether desirable or undesirable. || 83 ||
The commentary on verse a states the conclusion: "He who thus... Regarding the word *deha* (body), it includes the sense organs and so forth by the use of the term "and so on" (*ādi*). || 283 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Then, one might object that it is not appropriate for even an ignorant person to have such insistence on worldly activity as a knower does; anticipating this, he says:
"Insistence on activity is entirely proper for one devoid of realization."
Therefore, men must strive for the sake of heaven or for liberation.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of engagement," he states the reason for it there: "for the sake of heaven. || 84 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): If that is so, for whose sake is activity desired? To this he says: "In [the pursuit of] activity. According to Amara, *mokṣa* means *apavarga*;
thus, the meaning is "for the sake of *apavarga*, that is, for the sake of *kaivalya* (isolation). || 84 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: It has been stated that persistence on the part of the wise man is not appropriate; [the author] now says what must be done by him while remaining among those who perform ritual actions:
"If the wise man should remain in the midst of such people, he should do so out of consideration for them."
One indeed performs all actions through body, mind, and speech. || 285 ||

"If he is a knower" (vidvān cet): if the knower should remain among such ritualists (karmiṇaḥ), then out of consideration for them—that is, in accordance with them—he indeed performs all actions through his body and so forth. The meaning is that he should not restrain those ritualists. || 285 ||

Commentary (a0): Thus, when the question arises as to what one who knows the Truth ought to do, [the Lord] says—in the two verses beginning with "vidvāṃścet" (if he is a man of knowledge)—that while both engagement and withdrawal may occur in the presence of various types of qualified persons solely for the sake of their grace, there is in reality nothing at all that remains to be done by him, because he has already achieved his purpose. This is stated in such passages as "even considering the maintenance of the world, you ought to act."

This means that all duties prescribed solely by the Śāstras—devoid of anything optional or prohibited, accompanied by their respective expiations, untouched even by the slightest trace of Tantric influence, appropriate to one's own caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama), complete in their nature as daily obligatory rites (nitya) and so forth, and having the sole fruit of pleasing the Supreme Self—he performs.

Here it is said "he indeed performs" (karoty eva), and not "he must perform" (kuryād eva). By this, his natural inclination toward the welfare of the world is established, rather than [the force of] an injunction.
And the action is indicated. || 285 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He describes the duty of this very person while situated among those who desire to know the truth:
"When he stands again in the midst of those who desire to know..."
May he himself abandon all actions that corrupt their enlightenment.

Regarding the word "this": when this wise man stands among those who desire to know, then, for the sake of awakening those seekers—that is, for the generation of the knowledge of reality—he should abandon even those very actions while censuring them. || 86 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): "This" refers to the fact that [the Lord] refutes [other paths] by means of thousands of scriptural passages such as the Taittirīya Śruti—"Neither by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone some have attained immortality"—as well as hundreds of Smṛti texts such as "Renouncing all duties, come to Me alone for refuge. This is the implied meaning. || 86 ||
[The Commentator asks: Why must it be done in this way?
He says: [Page 305] The Seventh Chapter.
Accompanied by two commentaries:
"The conduct of a Buddha is appropriate according to the perspective of the ignorant."
For the father conducts himself according to the wishes of his suckling child. || 87 ||

Regarding "avidvat" (the ignorant): the sense is that it is appropriate for the wise to act in accordance with the ignorant, because of their compassion and because those [ignorant ones] are to be pitied.
To show that this is indeed observed in the world, he says "stanaṃdhaya" etc. "Stanaṃdhayāḥ" refers to infants who perform the act of sucking at the breast.
This is the meaning. || 87 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "Even for the wise man who has accomplished all that was to be done, why should he continue to act in accordance with the ignorant? This is true; however, it is because of his status as a *jīvanmukta* (liberated while living) that he is regarded as the father of the world. With this in mind—and considering the scriptural texts such as, "In me alone everything is born," and "His sons inherit the estate, his friends the meritorious deeds, and his enemies the sinful deeds"—he [the Lord] uses the very example of a father.
He clarifies this with two verses beginning with "avidvat" (87).
Then his own father was either reviled or beaten by the child.
One should not be afflicted nor should one become angry; instead, one should cherish the fool. || 88 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He demonstrates that the father follows the child who is still nursing: "When reproached," etc. (88).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): "Adhikṣipta" means spoken to in an improper manner. In this regard, a suckling infant—one whose age is prior to the ceremony of naming and tonsure—does not suffer, that is, does not become distressed at all. || 88 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He applies this to the subject at hand:
"Whether reviled or praised by the ignorant, the wise man does not revile them."
He does not praise them, but rather acts in such a way that they may attain awakening.

Regarding the word "niṃdita" (blamed): whether blamed or praised by the ignorant, the wise man neither blames nor praises himself; rather, he should act in such a way that awakening arises in those ignorant people. || 89 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Since a child possesses only a portion of the state of youth characterized by the age mentioned, let there be insults and the like directed toward his own father; however, for a knower of Brahman, it is simply impossible for insults and such to be committed by an ignorant person. This is not so, because even in that case, such a possibility exists. To explain: when this [knower] stands among those who are still subject to worldly objects, then, according to the method previously stated, everything is indeed virtuous action (*sat-karman*).

However, when he stands among those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), he then censures all action—whether good or bad—and abandons it himself; this was stated immediately following [the previous verse]. Therefore, seeing him in such a state, censure directed toward the agent of sense-objects is indeed possible. Thus, it is narrated in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata* in the context of the "Song of the Mendicant" (*bhikṣugīta*), and likewise in the *Vāyavīya Māgha-māhātmya*, by the chaste wife (*pativratā*)— [The text continues with the verses. ...therefore, even though the mendicant is not at fault, the reproach of the people arises from their own delusion. Just as in the case of a virtuous wife who, upon seeing her husband intent on another woman, becomes angry and reproaches him, so too, when one sees a mendicant who has renounced all actions, the reproach of the people arises out of their own ignorance. For the mendicant is not at fault in this matter; rather, the fault lies in the people themselves, who, being deluded, censure him. As it is said: "When the sun rises, the lotuses bloom and the lilies close; when the moon rises, the lilies bloom and the lotuses close. But the sun does not blame the lilies for closing, nor do the lilies blame the sun for rising. In the same way, the mendicant does not blame the people for their reproach, nor do the people blame the mendicant for his renunciation. Therefore, the reproach of the people is merely a product of their own delusion. It is said: "Just as a mirror does not become stained by the impurities of the face reflected in it, so the mendicant is not stained by the reproach of the people. Thus, the reproach of the people is not a cause for the mendicant's downfall, but rather a sign of their own spiritual blindness. Therefore, one should remain indifferent to such reproach and continue on the path of liberation. As it is said: "The wise man should disregard the reproach of the ignorant, just as one disregards the noise of the crowd while walking on a road. Thus ends the discussion.

With the intention of providing a detailed account—including the story of Māṇḍavya’s impalement on a stake as a consequence of his adherence to truth—the author briefly summarizes even that definition of a sage well-known in the *Smṛtis*, namely "one who is indifferent to praise and blame," which is to be grasped by the discerning observer, using the words beginning with "niṃdita" (blamed). The phrase "being praised by those seeking liberation" is to be understood as implied. To the question "What then does he do?", he replies with the remainder of the verse beginning with "kiṃtu" (but rather): "he should practice"—that is, he indeed practices.
Such is the meaning. || 89 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the reason for acting in this manner:
"That by which he is understood here through his performance—that alone is the task."
For one who knows this, there is no task to be performed other than the awakening of ignorance.

Regarding the word "yena" (by which): this ignorant person in this world understands—that is, realizes the truth—by means of whatever kind of acting or conduct; that conduct must indeed be performed by him. [An objection is raised: "In that case, other duties would also necessarily follow as being required. To this, he says: 39.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 306] 303.
"It is known as the *Tṛptidīpa* (The Lamp of Contentment).

Since those who know the truth in this world understand it thus, there is no other duty remaining once the ignorant have been awakened; therefore, the meaning is that one should bring about the awakening to reality by following this [work]. || 290 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "Even for one who has accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtya*), what is the purpose in instructing the ignorant? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says: "Indeed, travelers running toward the water of a mirage in the desert at midday in summer, driven by excessive thirst with the thought that it is a real river, do not [stop] even before [reaching it].

Rather, they are first made aware of the midday light—[an awareness] produced by the visual perception (*cakṣuḥ-pratyakṣa*) assisted by the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the presence of trees and so forth."

Then, having returned from that place known as the saline wasteland (*ūṣaradharaṇī*), the man is not awakened [with the words]: "This is merely a mirage; it is perceived as water due to the conjunction of the midday sunlight with the saline wasteland, so do not run toward it. Therefore, even though there is no actual practical purpose [in his case], there is the destruction of the ignorance of other ignorant people through compassion for the suffering caused by their own remembered ignorance, by means of whatever physical or other activities [are appropriate].

He provides the resolution with the words "yenāyam" (by which this...), stating that [the ignorant person] is devoted to those very things because he does them by nature. Here, "this one" refers to the ignorant person (*ajñajana*). Through the word "acting" (*naṭana*), the unreality of the actions of the learned is suggested. "Only what ought to be done" means only that which is fit to be performed. Here, because the particle *eva* (only) is connected with the action, it suggests an absolute exclusion of non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*)—just as in the expression "a lotus is indeed blue"—regarding the engagement of the knower of Brahman in instructing ignorant people. Thus, out of compassion...

Since even the seizure of wealth and other possessions from those who are worldly-minded may be accomplished by a knower of Brahman through service to a master and the like, he says: "By the ignorant" (verse 290).

Rāma’s Commentary: He states the purport of what has been said and what is yet to be said: "Satisfied by having accomplished all that was to be done, and again, satisfied by having attained all that was to be attained."
Being thus satisfied, he constantly thinks this in his own mind: || 91 ||

"I am one who has accomplished what was to be done" (*kṛtakṛtya*). This wise person, being satisfied by the state of having accomplished all duties (*kṛtakṛtyatā*)— that is, by the condition of one for whom the entire collection of tasks (*kṛtyajāta*) has been completed— and having attained that which was to be attained in the manner about to be described— that is, by one for whom that which was to be reached (*prāpya*) has been reached— [he remains thus].
Being satisfied—that is, becoming content—by that state of being which is to be attained, he thinks thus in his own mind without interruption: || 91 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "Granted that there is such outward performance of one's own duties and so forth for the sake of awakening the ignorant, how does he find satisfaction within? In response to this expectation, he declares the manner of describing his experience: "By virtue of having accomplished all that was to be done" (*kṛtakṛtyatayā*). This refers to the one established in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭha*). || 299 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question "What do you think? he says:
"I am blessed, I am blessed; I know my own Self directly and eternally."
Blessed am I, blessed am I! The bliss of Brahman shines clearly before me. ||92||

"Fortunate am I, fortunate am I," and so forth. "Fortunate" (*dhanya*) means one who has accomplished his purpose; the repetition (*vīpsā*) is for the sake of emphasis. Because I always—without interruption—directly and immediately know my own self (*svātmānam*), that is, my own innate form (*svarūpam*) which is the inner self (*pratyagātman*) unconditioned by space and other such factors, therefore I am fortunate. Having thus described the satisfaction arising from the attainment of the knowledge of the Self, he shows the satisfaction arising from the attainment of its fruit with the word "fortunate."
The bliss of Brahman, the bliss of those who have become Brahman, shines clearly to me; the meaning is that it manifests in such a way as to be perfectly clear. || 92 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, he elaborates upon the restatement of the manner of the experience of the knower of reality as previously promised, by means of two Anuṣṭubh verses characterized by four Upagīti lines beginning with "Blessed am I, blessed am I, eternally" (*dhanyo'haṃ dhanyo'haṃ nityam*). This repetition is solely for the sake of expressing extreme reverence. The reason for this is stated by the words "eternally" (*nityam*) and so forth. "Eternally" means at all times, and not merely for a moment. By this, even non-dual valid cognition (*advaitapramā*), being a mental modification (*vṛtti*), is delimited [in time].

Even though it lasts for only three moments, its permanence is illuminated precisely because there is no possibility of forgetting it, owing to its being an indestructible, self-luminous, and singular object; or alternatively, "eternal" (*nityam*) is indeed a qualification of its own nature, according to such scriptural passages as "Eternal, pure," and so forth. By this, limitation by time is excluded; the exclusion of limitations by space and substance, however, is already implied by the specific qualifications themselves. For example: "Eternal" means pervading the three periods of time.

Even such a thing as this is to be meditated upon as one's own self (*svātmānam*). Here, it is indeed a *karmadhāraya* compound. And thus, by the word "own" (*sva*), that which is characterized by witness-consciousness is indicated.
[Page 307] Seventh Chapter.
Accompanied by two commentaries:

Only the pure, immutable consciousness (*pratyak-kuṭastha-cinmātra*), which is the purified meaning of the term *tat* (That), is indicated as the referent (*lakṣya*) by the word "Self" (*ātman*), according to such passages as "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone."
This is established by the Tāreya Śruti, by the Taittirīya Śruti stating "From the Self, space was produced," and so forth, and by the Smṛti:

"O Guḍākeśa, I am the Self dwelling within the hearts of all beings; I am the beginning, the middle, and indeed the end of all beings," as well as: "That which one attains, that which one takes, that which one eats here of sense objects, and that which is one's continuous state—therefore [it is called Ātman]."
"It is called 'ātman'."

Thus, according to the Smṛti as well, that which is called Brahman—characterized by existence, consciousness, infinity, and bliss—is indicated as being of the nature of the purified referent of the word *tat*, which is opposed to the non-existent, the insentient, the finite, suffering, and duality. By this, the exclusion of spatial limitation is indicated; furthermore, through the use of a *karmadhāraya* compound for these two [attributes], the exclusion of all-pervasive, real limitation is also implied. Even so, it is directly and immediately perceived: "I know the Reality taught by the venerable Guru" (*tattvamasi*).

The meaning is: "I know [this] from the inquiry into the great sentences (mahāvākya). And thus, by implication, the falsity of duality is illuminated. To the objection that even if satisfaction arises from the attainment of the knowledge of Brahman, that [satisfaction] resulting from the attainment of liberation-in-life (jīvanmukti)—which is its fruit—might not occur due to obstacles, he says in response with the three and a half verses beginning with "Blessed am I, blessed am I, I am Brahman" and so forth. || 292 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus described contentment through the attainment of the desired, he says that one also finds satisfaction through the cessation of the undesired:
"Blessed am I, blessed am I; today I no longer behold the suffering of worldly existence."
"Blessed am I! Blessed am I! My own ignorance has fled somewhere. (93)
"I am blessed!"—now at this moment, I do not behold, that is, I do not see, suffering or the nature of saṃsāra; therefore, my purpose is fulfilled.

He states the reason for the non-perception of suffering: "I am blessed!"—the meaning is that the net of ignorance consisting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of manifold actions has fled, that is, it has perished. || 93 ||

Commentary (a0): Having thus described liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), which consists in the attainment of happiness, he now describes that same state as consisting in the destruction of suffering along with its seeds—“I am blessed, I am blessed! (293).

Rāma’s Commentary: He demonstrates the fruit of the cessation of ignorance—namely, the state of having accomplished all that was to be done and having attained all that was to be attained—with the words:
"Blessed am I! Blessed am I! There remains nothing whatsoever for me to do."
I am blessed, I am blessed! Everything that was to be attained has been accomplished today.
"Blessed! || 94 ||

Commentary (a0): Thus, he reveals her who is the very nature of one who has accomplished all that was to be done and who has attained all that was to be attained, by means of the verse beginning with "Blessed am I, blessed am I; there is nothing more to be done by me," and so forth. || 294 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, with the words "I have accomplished my purpose" and so forth, he describes the unsurpassed nature of the satisfaction that has arisen:
"Blessed am I, blessed am I; may there be no comparison for my satisfaction in this world."
Blessed am I, blessed am I; blessed, blessed again and again. || 295 ||
"Fortunate!"—this shows that, since no further speech is seen after this point, only satisfaction radiates forth; thus he says, "Fortunate! (295).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): For this very reason, he reveals the incomparability of the aforementioned satisfaction through its unrestrained nature: "Blessed am I, blessed am I, by this satisfaction. Thus, "Blessed am I," and so forth. || 299 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Recalling the ripening of the mass of merit that has become the cause of all this, he says that [the Lord] rejoices:
"Oh, what merit! Oh, what merit! It has truly borne fruit, it has firmly borne fruit!"
"By the attainment of this merit, oh, we! Oh, we! (96)
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 308.
"Ah, what merit! This is the *Tṛptidīpa*. Thus, remembering himself as the one who has produced such a work, he rejoices; "of him," so it is said. ||96||

And so, since all this fruit arises solely from the merit consisting of the Lord’s satisfaction, he says, "O, what merit! (aho puṇyam), contemplating that very merit as something marvelous. Here, the repetition (*vīpsā*) throughout is intended to express an excess of wonder. The reason for this is stated by the words beginning with "of this" (*asya*). The plural form "we" (*vayam*) is used because of the intense self-regard produced by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*). [The fruit] consists of the non-duality of Brahman and liberation (*kaivalya*).
The meaning is: "We have become perfected. The indeclinable *aho* expresses wonder (*āścarya*). The remainder, however, is quite clear. || 296 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, having recollected the scripture which is the means for perfect knowledge and its teacher, the preceptor, he rejoices:
"O, the scripture! O, the scripture! O, the preceptor! O, the preceptor!"
Oh, what knowledge! Oh, what knowledge! Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss! (97)
"Aho! The scripture! Thus, recollecting again the knowledge born of the scripture and the bliss thereof, he is satisfied: "Aho! Knowledge! || 97 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, having recollected even the three means such as the scriptures, which are more internal [than the previous ones], he speaks in praise of their satisfaction, stating that he is fully gratified even by that wonder: "Aho śāstram" (Oh, the scripture!). Likewise, he states with "Aho sukham" (Oh, the happiness! and so forth that even the bliss of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) is of an exceedingly wonderful nature. Indeed, it is heard and recorded in the scriptures thus: "He beholds it as a marvel... (*āścaryavat paśyati*).
"Someone speaks of him as a marvel, and another likewise; yet another hears of him as a marvel," and so forth. (97)
Those wise ones who constantly contemplate this Lamp of Satisfaction, [attain liberation].
Immersed in the bliss of Brahman, they remain eternally satisfied.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Lamp of Contentment" (*Tṛptidīpa*), in the *Pañcadaśī* composed by the venerable Śrī Madhusūdana Sarasvatī.
He states the fruit of practicing this work: "The Lamp of Satisfaction" (Tṛptidīpa). || 298 ||

Thus ends the commentary on the *Tṛptidīpa* of the *Pañcadaśī*, composed by the scholar named Rāmakṛṣṇa, a servant of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Bhāratītīrtha Vidyāraṇya Muni. 7.

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, the venerable teacher Bhāratītīrtha, having concluded his commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad mantra beginning with "If one knows the Self" (*ātmānaṃ cet*), along with the seven stages of inquiry that arose in its context— culminating in the seventh stage named "Unrestricted Satisfaction" (*niraṅkuśatṛpti*)— and having also proclaimed the name of the present work by that very title, briefly describes the fruit of its practice for the sake of engaging wise seekers of liberation.
Thus—"satisfaction. Now, was it not previously stated by you:
"Since the individual soul (*jīva*) is accessible through perception and other means of knowledge, how can scripture [be its authority]?
This second obstacle here regarding the soul consists in the claim that it possesses the status of being known through those [means]."

Thus, by means of this Āryā verse, having presented the second obstacle—namely, the impossibility of valid cognition regarding the understanding of the meaning of the word "jīva" as being pure—the [truth] becomes clear from the commentary on the Śruti passage, "If one knows the Self as the seventh. Furthermore, by another Āryā verse beginning with "rasajñānām," the primary consistency (*samanvaya*) with respect to the *jīva* is stated; how then can this seventh chapter, titled *Tṛptidīpa*, be a sublater (*bādhaka*) of that?

If it is argued that [this] is possible, we say no; for by explaining the purport of this very section, the aforementioned contradiction and sublation of the stated meaning are implied, and because the indicative marks (liṅgas) found in the beginning and elsewhere concerning that subject are explained through the commentary on the Śruti text "If one knows the Self" (ātmānaṃ cet), as has been explicitly stated [by the author]. Thus all is auspicious. || 298 ||

I bow to that glorious Narasiṃha, my non-dual Guru who is eternal bliss, by whom—under the guise of a dream—there was given to me on the day of Jayantī a most beautiful white pen, a beautiful ink-pot, and likewise a full vessel; thus did Speech, the woman, manifest this pair of limbs through such a pretext.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the Tṛptidīpaprakāśa, of the commentary on the Pañcadaśī by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrīmad Advaitasaccidānanda. 7.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter, titled *Kūṭasthadīpa* (The Lamp of the Immutable Self).
Rāma’s Commentary: Having bowed to the venerable Bhāratītīrtha and Vidyāraṇya, the lords of sages, [I shall compose this work].
I compose the *Tātparyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Kūṭasthadīpa*.

In this context, since the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the self— which is the means to liberation for one desiring liberation— must be preceded by the purification of the referent of the term *tvam*, the Teacher, commencing this work titled *Kūṭasthadīpa* (The Lamp of the Immutable) which is devoted to that purification, intends to establish its status as a Vedāntic treatise through its very subject matter and other characteristics.

He therefore points out, with an illustration, the distinction between the immutable (*kūṭastha*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), which are respectively the indicated (*lakṣya*) and the denoted (*vācya*) meanings of the term *tvam*.
Just as a wall illuminated by the sun is [seen] like a wall illuminated by the sun in a mirror.
The body, though illumined by the immutable [Self], is illumined by the individual soul (jīva) residing in the intellect (dhī). || 1 ||

Regarding the phrase "khāditya": *khāditya* refers to the sun (*āditya*) illuminated by the ether (*kha*); thus, it means the well-known sun. By that term, its associated light is indicated. Illuminated—that is, made manifest—by that [light] upon the wall, just as in the case of the reflection of the sun’s light in mirrors, the wall is illuminated by the solar rays which strike the mirrors, turn back, and then connect with the wall; this is like being illumined by the immutable (*kūṭastha*), which is unchanging consciousness (*caitanya*).

The body has been described as illuminated; it is illumined and made manifest by the "living being residing in the intellect" (dhīstha-jīva), that is, by the reflection of consciousness situated in the intellect (buddhistha-cidābhāsa).

By this, it is asserted that there exists a twofold consciousness that illuminates the body, just as there is a twofold light—the sun and its illumination—that reveals a wall, both in general and in particular. || 1 ||
I bow to the Supreme Brahman, who is non-dual bliss, existence, consciousness, all-pervading, and eternally pure;
who, though the abode of the illusory spectacle of duality arising from delusion, remains as the immutable essence; who is the self-luminous crest-jewel of the Vedas;
and who is the ornament of the Raghu dynasty, the true Guru established in Brahman, along with all the foremost teachers.
I bow to my own guru, known as Śrīmannārāyaṇa, who is also named Mahādeva. || 1 ||
Having honored Jīvañjīvā, Vidyāraṇya, and Bhāratītīrtha,
I illuminate the *Kaumudī* through the light of the *Kūṭasthadīpa*, like the moonlight [illuminating] the king of mountains.

Then, the Blessed One, the teacher named Bhāratītīrtha, having observed the inquiry of his disciple— who, having heard that in the seventh preceding chapter of the *Pañcadaśī* titled the *Tṛptidīpa*, it was stated that the seven states beginning with ignorance and ending with unrestrained satisfaction belong only to the *cidābhāsa* (the reflection of consciousness) and not to the *kūṭastha* (the immutable)— and who specifically desired to know "Who is the *kūṭastha*? [proceeded] by way of the object of illumination known as the body...

He clarifies the distinction between the immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-cit*) and its reflection (*cidābhāsa*) through their respective roles as illuminators of the universal and the particular—expressed by the phrase "as the sun [in the sky]" (*khāditya*). This means illuminated by the sun situated in the atmosphere. "In such a wall" (*kuḍye*): according to Amara’s lexicon, *bhittiḥ* (wall) is feminine and *kuḍyam* is neuter; thus, it refers to a wall made of mud and other materials. "As in a mirror" (*darpaṇa*): this means like the solar radiance reflected in a looking-glass. This is an illustrative example (*upalakṣaṇa*), including reflections in water and so forth.

This is also the case with the sun. Having thus stated the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), he states the application (*dāṣṭantika*)—namely, "the immutable" (*kūṭastha*). Here, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The gross body, being illumined solely by the immutable witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), is manifested by the individual soul (*jīva*) known as the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), which takes the form of a reflection within the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). Alternatively, it is manifested by both the original and the reflection. This is because it is manifested by a qualified [consciousness]. It is like a wall illumined by the sun, which is reflected in a mirror and thereby illumined by that [reflection].

"Like the instruction [of a teacher]" (deśavad iti). Here, the benediction (*maṅgala*) consisting of the contemplation of the immutable Self (*kūṭasthātman*), which serves the purpose of a well-known means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is established; furthermore, because this is a treatise (*prakaraṇa*) on the non-dualistic scripture (*advaita-śāstra*), the excellence of the fourfold connection (*anubandha-catuṣṭaya*)—having that [Self] as its sole subject matter and so forth—is also suggested by the second half of the verse. || 1 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, having raised the objection that in that case the light of the sun in the sky is not perceived apart from the light of the mirror and the sun itself, he demonstrates that light by distinguishing it from those two: * *tatraivaṃ sati yadā darpaṇe mukhapratibimbaṃ dṛśyate tadā darpaṇagataprabhāmaṇḍalena sahaiva mukhapratibimbaṃ cakṣuṣā gṛhyate | na tu darpaṇaprabhāmaṇḍalaṃ parityajya pṛthag mukhapratibimbaṃ nāma kiñcid upalabhyate | tathāpi darpaṇaprabhāmaṇḍalāt pṛthakkṛtyaiva mukhapratibimbaṃ vyavahriyate loke | evam ādityaprabhāmaṇḍalād api pṛthakkṛtyaiva khādityaprabhā vyavahriyate | tasmād darpaṇādityaprabhāmaṇḍalavyatirekeṇa khādityaprabhā nopalabhyata iti na vaktavyam ||* In this regard, when the reflection of a face is seen in a mirror, the reflection of the face is grasped by the eye together with the circle of light residing in the mirror. However, no such thing as a "reflection of the face" is perceived separately, setting aside the circle of light in the mirror. Nevertheless, in common worldly usage, the reflection of the face is treated as if it were distinct from the circle of light in the mirror. Similarly, the light of the sun in the sky is treated as if it were distinct from the circle of the sun's light. Therefore, one should not say that the light of the sun in the sky is not perceived apart from the circles of light of the mirror and the sun.
In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[the following occurs] in the many joints of the radiance of numerous mirrors and suns.
The one called the immovable lamp (kūṭasthadīpa) is manifested by the others; even in their absence, it shines forth. || 2 ||

Regarding the word "anekā" (manifold): those various circular forms of light seen here and there on the wall produced by many mirrors—within their junction, that is, in their midst, another light in the form of a general illumination, which is the light of the sky and the sun, is manifested, meaning it is perceived;
and in the absence of those mirror-produced lights—due to the removal of the mirrors and so forth—and when they are present, it shines by itself everywhere. || 2 ||

Commentary (a0): Thus, providing an exposition of the meaning of the treatise as formulated in the aphorism, and wishing first to rectify the "unestablished reason" (*hetvasiddhi*), he clarifies the specific luminosity of the illustration by stating "aneka... and so forth. For just as a wall standing before one, though already illuminated by the sun, is specifically illuminated by the reflections of the sun's light in mirrors within a mirror-house according to the delimitation of each respective spot—and in the junctions between those [reflections], others [are seen]—so it is here.

The meaning is this: the solar light is indeed directly perceived; likewise, even in the absence of the solar rays reflected in a mirror, the solar rays that generally illuminate the wall are directly present upon the wall itself. || 2 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He applies the matter established by the illustration to the subject at hand:
"In the same way, this [Self] is the substrate for the manifold cognitions qualified by the reflection of consciousness."
Let it be discerned as that which illuminates both the connection of cognitions and their absence. || 3 ||

Regarding the term *cidābhāsa*: in that same manner, illuminating— that is, making manifest— the junction (*saṃdhi*), which is the interval between various mental modifications (*buddhivṛtti*)— designated by such terms as "cognition of a jar"— which are characterized by the reflection of consciousness (*citpratibimba*),
and also illuminating the absence of those very same mental modifications during states such as deep sleep, this immutable one (*kūṭastha*) should be discerned, known as distinct from them.
The meaning is "her. || 3 ||

— Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He elucidates the aforementioned point with respect to the subject at hand as well, beginning with the words "cidābhāsa" and "aneka. The meaning of "aneka" is: of the countless mental modifications (*vṛtti*) whose objects are jars, cloths, and so forth.

The *saṃdhi* (the junction) is defined by the statement in the *Laghuvākyavṛtti*: "As long as the preceding conceptualization has not dissolved and another has not yet arisen, non-conceptual consciousness shines forth clearly. Thus, it refers implicitly to that very interval of time delimited by states such as waking. In this way, regarding the aforementioned cognitions—

The meaning is: "only of those cognitions that have become the cause of the mental states" (*vṛtti*). This plural number is used for the sake of establishing [the principle] through the experience of all living beings. "And non-existence" means even dissolution delimited by deep sleep. Thus, while illuminating—that is, making manifest—in the manner of the previously mentioned examples, this immutable one (*kūṭastha*) should be discerned, made the object of profound inquiry; such is the syntactical connection. The words "by those seeking liberation" (*mumukṣubhiḥ*) are to be supplied as the ellipsis. Therefore, wherever... in the qualified [state]—

The intended meaning is as follows: the pervasion (vyāpti) here is that "being illumined" consists in being illumined by both the original object (bimba) and its reflection (pratibimba). Just as on a wall illumined by the sun, there is illumination by the solar radiance reflected in many mirrors, so too, even in the case of the subject called the body (deha), there exists both being illumined by the immutable (kūṭastha) which has become the original object, and being illumined by the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) which has become its reflection. Therefore, the reason [in the inference] does not suffer from defects such as being unestablished in its own nature (svarūpāsiddhi). || 3 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, in order to demonstrate the distinction between the immutable self (kūṭastha) and the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) within the body, he shows how the reflection of consciousness and Brahman are also distinguished outside the body:
"The consciousness residing in a cognition that has the form of a jar would illuminate only the jar."
The cognizedness of the jar is manifested by the consciousness of Brahman. || 4 ||
"Construe [the compound] as follows": that consciousness which has the form of a single jar—that is, whose form is like the single form of a jar—is "that which has the form of a single jar.

The reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) residing in such a cognition would illuminate only the jar. The property called "knownness" (jñātatā) belonging to that jar—[is what is meant by the term *ghaṭa*].
The Eighth Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

The meaning is that that which serves as the cause for the conventional usage "it is known" shines forth—that is, it is manifested—by means of the Brahman-consciousness, which is the substratum for the conceptualization of the jar and functions as the instrument. || 4 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Having thus demonstrated the distinction between the immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-cit*) and the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) within the body for the purpose of purifying the meaning of the term "Thou" (*tvaṃpadārtha*), he now demonstrates the distinction between Brahman and the reflection of consciousness outside the body for the purpose of purifying the meaning of the term "That" (*tatpadārtha*): "The intellect which has the form of a single jar... [etc. That intellect which possesses a form like that of a single jar—and not of anything else—exists therein as a reflection.

"Thus" (tīti) means "so indeed" (tatheti). The meaning is: such consciousness (saṃvit) which has the nature of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa). [Objection: Let this be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "of the jar" (ghaṭasya). The implied meaning is that the "cognizedness" (jñātatā) of the jar—which serves as the cause for the linguistic usage (vyavahāra) such as "the jar is known"—is due to the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) of the conceptualization (kalpanā) of the jar. By such [consciousness]. The words "Brahman," etc., have been explained by the literal reading (nigadavyākhyāta). And thus, in the cognition "this is a jar," the jar-consciousness—

The point is that the distinction between these two is perfectly clear: in the cognition "the pot is known," it is known as something manifested by the light [of the intellect]; however, in the cognition "this [pot]," it is manifested by the Brahman-consciousness which serves as the substratum for the superimposition of the pot. Thus, there is a distinct difference between the two. || 4 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Since the cognition of a jar is possible through the very consciousness that manifests its 'knownness' (jñātatā), what is the purpose of the intellect (buddhi)?
Anticipating this, he states that the intellect exists for the sake of establishing distinctions such as the jar's being "unknown" or "known":
"Before the emergence of the intellect, this jar was known as 'unknown'."
But this distinction [between them] is due to the fact that [the object] is known by Brahman alone from above.

Regarding the phrase "as being unknown": the meaning is that before the arising of the intellect (*buddhi*), this pot is manifested by Brahman alone as being unknown; once the intellect has arisen, it is manifested by Brahman alone as being known. This is the only difference, and no other. || 5 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if this is so, one might object: "In that case, even prior to the arising of the cognition in the form of a jar, let the manifestation of the jar occur by the very Brahman-consciousness that serves as its substrate. To this he replies, "By way of being unknown" (*ajñātatvena*), meaning that it indeed exists in that manner [as the substrate]. If this is so, what then is the fruit of the cognition?
To this he says, "But later on" (*upariṣṭāttu*). *Bhidā* means difference (*bheda*). || 5 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, having raised the doubt—“How can a single pot possess a dual nature characterized by both being known and being unknown?”—the author first demonstrates the essential nature of knowledge and ignorance, which are the causes of being known and being unknown, in order to clarify that point:
“Knowledge is a mental modification (vṛtti) ending in the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), just as a sword [is contained] within its sheath.”
—Inertness is ignorance; a jar pervaded by these two is said to be of two kinds. || 6 ||

Regarding the term *cidābhāsā*: a mental modification (*dhīvṛtti*) in which there is an internal reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*)—that is, a reflection of consciousness (*cit-pratibimba*)—is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*), because the Teachers have stated that "the intellect is kindled by awakening" (*bodheddhā buddhiḥ*). In this regard, the illustration is "like an iron needle within iron.
Inertia (*jāḍya*) is defined as being devoid of self-luminosity, which is called ignorance (*ajñāna*). Pervaded on all sides by these two in alternation—
The bound jar is said to be twofold; the meaning is that it is called both "known" and "unknown. || 6 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, it may be granted that a jar conditioned by being unknown and so forth is illumined by Brahman; likewise, according to the established doctrine of the Vivaraṇa, all this is illumined by the Witness (sākṣin) through its states of being known and unknown. Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the intention to describe Brahman as the Witness precisely because it is the illuminator by virtue of [the objects'] being unknown and so forth. Nevertheless, what is intended first here is the very nature of that knowledge and ignorance which constitute its basis?

In response to this inquiry, he summarizes it with the words "ending in the reflection of consciousness" (*cidābhāsāntā*). The meaning is: that whose end—that is, its foremost part—is the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), which is entirely false, is thus [described]. Such is precisely the mental modification (*dhīvṛtti*). Regarding the word "iron" (*loha*): it refers to a spear (*kuṇta*) whose end—the foremost part—is made of iron, consisting of that [iron]; it is like that. The grammatical connection is: "knowledge arises. Just as a certain bamboo...
If that very staff is fashioned with an iron-pointed barb, it is known by the other name *bhuśuṇḍī*, commonly called *bhālā* in Maharashtra.
The *Pañcadaśī* (The Fifteen Chapters) composed by Vidyāraṇya,
titled "The Lamp of the Immutable" (*Kūṭasthadīpa*).

The meaning is that just as a specific weapon exists [in the hand], so too the mental modification (*mativṛtti*) accompanied by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) is itself knowledge (*jñāna*). Having thus defined the nature of knowledge, he also states the nature of ignorance (*ajñāna*): "Inertness" (*jāḍyam*). According to the scriptural statement, "That which is inert and of the nature of delusion," the meaning is that it is an indefinable (*anirvacanīya*) entity, beginningless, positive in nature, and opposed to manifestation. Such is ignorance—that is to say, there exists that which is denoted by the term "ignorance."
He states the conclusion with the remainder of the verse beginning "By these two": the meaning is that it is known in two ways—as known and as unknown. || 6 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "While it may be that an unknown jar is illumined by Brahman because it is pervaded by ignorance, how can a known jar—which is pervaded by knowledge—be illumined by the consciousness of Brahman? Anticipating this, [the author] states that just as ignorance is exhausted merely by producing the state of being unknown, so too knowledge is exhausted merely by producing the state of being known; therefore, like an unknown jar, even a known jar is illumined by Brahman. Thus he says:
If the effulgence is unknown by Brahmā, why is the jar likewise not known?
By the very production of the state of being known, the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) is completely exhausted. || 7 ||
Regarding the phrase "unknown": just as an unknown jar is manifested by Brahman, why should a known jar not likewise be manifested by Brahman?
Indeed, it certainly is. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of being known," etc. (Verse 7).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Unknown" (ajñāta). Now, it may be argued: "But a known jar is clearly perceived as being manifested solely by the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa)"; this is true.
However, both the intellect (buddhi) and the reflection of consciousness residing within it pervade the jar.

Regarding this, he says "jñātatva" (the state of being known), because its purpose is fulfilled merely by the production of knowledge, according to the statement: "There, ignorance would be destroyed by cognition, and the jar would manifest through its appearance.
Just as "stick-ness" is nothing other than the stick itself, so too "known-ness" is nothing other than the knowledge itself. || 7 ||
By an intellect deficient in illumination, the state of being known is never produced.
What distinction could there be for such a cognition regarding clay and other things that are subject to transformation? (8)

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Just as ignorance is sufficient to produce the state of being unknown, so too the intellect alone should be sufficient to produce the state of being known; what is the need for this reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa)?

Anticipating this doubt, he states that for the intellect devoid of the reflection of consciousness, the production of the state of being known is impossible because it would be non-luminous in nature, like a jar or other objects—thus: "Ābhāsa... (verse 8).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Let cognition in the form of 'knownness' be produced by the intellect (buddhi) itself; what need is there for it to be produced by the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa)? To this he replies with the word "ābhāsa" (reflection). The reason for this is given by the word "tādṛk" (of such a kind). || 8 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He clarifies the absence of "knownness" in a jar that is pervaded by the intellect (buddhi) devoid of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) by means of an illustration:
"A jar smeared with clay is never said to be 'known' anywhere."
In the same way, the cognizedness of the jar pervaded by cognition is not admitted [as being produced]. || 9 ||

Regarding the phrase "is known": just as in the world a jar that has been smeared—that is, coated—with clay of either white or black color is not said to be "known," so too, the state of being known is not admitted for a jar, even if it is pervaded by the intellect devoid of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa). This is the intended meaning. || 9 ||
Commentary (ṭīkā): Regarding that, he states the supporting argument: "It is known," and so forth. || 9 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary— He states the conclusion:
[page 313] Eighth Chapter.
Accompanied by two commentaries: "The state of being known" refers, therefore, to the arising of the fruit which is the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) within the jar.
Brahman-consciousness is not the fruit [of knowledge], because it exists even prior to the means of valid cognition.

Regarding the term "cognizedness" (*jñātatva*): since bare consciousness alone is incapable of producing cognizedness, it follows that what is commonly known as "cognizedness" is simply the production of a result characterized by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) within the jar; this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "Even so, the reflection of consciousness need not be postulated, because the result exists as the very consciousness of Brahman. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The result is not [Brahman]. The consciousness of Brahman is not the result [of the cognition] of a jar and so forth.

"It does not become an instrument of knowledge (raṇa). Why? To this he says: "Because of [the existence of] the means (māna). The sense is that since the result exists even prior to the operation of the means of knowledge, whereas it is necessarily restricted to occurring at a time subsequent to that [operation]. || 10 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on verse a0: He concludes with the words "jñātatvam" (the state of being known) and "cidābhāsa" (the reflection of consciousness). The meaning is that the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) itself is the result, which is the fruit of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); this is what is meant by its "arising. Now, one might object: let the Brahman-consciousness itself, as the substrate of the jar, be the result. To this he replies with the words beginning with "na" (not), etc. The reason for this is stated in the remainder of the verse, beginning with "mānāt" (from the means of knowledge). || 10 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that this contradicts Sureśvara’s Vārttika, which begins with the words "parāgarthaprameyeṣu," he resolves it by showing that this challenge arises from a failure to understand the intended meaning of that text:
"In the case of objects external to oneself which are to be known, that [consciousness] which is accepted as the fruit..."
According to the authority of the Upanishadic teachings, consciousness alone is the object to be known here.

Regarding the phrase "parāgarthe" (in external objects): its meaning is as follows. While external objects such as jars and the like exist as objects of knowledge (*prameya*), that consciousness (*saṃvit*) which is accepted as the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-phala*) regarding those objects, is itself the object to be known (*meyo 'rthaḥ*) here in this Vedānta system, by means of the authority of the Vedāntic teachings—that is, by the means of valid cognition characterized by the statements of the Vedānta. || 11 ||

— Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, if it is argued that, in this way, the result is indeed the consciousness-reflection (cidābhāsa-caitanya) manifested by the modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti) produced by the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), and not the Brahman-consciousness itself as the result, then [the following is said] to demonstrate the contradiction with the venerable Vārttika of Sureśvara:

He recites that *Vārttika*: "parāg... etc. The meaning is as follows: "parāg" refers to all non-self objects (*anātmapadārtha*) distinct from the Self which has become the "inner object" (*pratyagarthībhūta*), such as jars and the like.
Their "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) are those objects of knowledge (*prameya*) fit to be the objects of valid cognition (*pramā*), namely, the consciousness delimited by unknown jars and so forth.

That consciousness (*saṃvit*) or cognition (*cit*) which exists as the result (*phala*)—characterized by "knownness" (*jñātatva*)—and which is accepted as the consciousness that is the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphalacaitanya*), is honored by all the learned.

That is the meaning. That very consciousness (*saṃvit*) is what is meant here in this non-dualistic scripture (*advaita-śāstra*). By "Vedānta," it means that which arises solely from the valid cognitive function (*pramāṇavṛtti*) produced by the great Upaniṣadic statements (*mahāvākya*), such as "This Self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*). "The object of knowledge" (*meyah*) means that which is to be made the object of valid cognition (*pramiti*). "In the matter" (*arthe*) refers to the matter characterized as non-dual Brahman.

The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as an implied ellipsis to complete the connection. As it has been stated in the *Siddhāntabindu*: "The method here is as follows: [He] resides within the body..."

Pervading the entire body, consisting primarily of *sattva* and composed of the subtle five elements, this transformation (*vivarta*) of ignorance called the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is extremely transparent like a mirror.

Having emerged through the doors of the eyes and other senses, it pervades suitable objects such as jars and assumes their respective forms, like molten copper. Its contraction and expansion occur instantaneously, just like sunlight. And because it possesses parts, it undergoes modification within the body.

Having completely pervaded the interior [of the body] as well as objects such as a jar, it remains undivided even between the body and the jar, like the eye. In that context, the portion of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) delimited by the body, called the ego (ahaṃkāra), is termed the "agent" (kartṛ). That portion of it which extends like a staff between the body and the object is termed the "action" (kriyā), known as the functional cognition (vṛttijñāna). The portion of it that pervades the object brings about the status of being the object of cognition for that object; this is the manifestation (abhivyakti).

It is said that [the mind] possesses the fitness for such reflection. And because that tripartite internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is extremely transparent, consciousness (*caitanya*) is manifested therein.

Although that manifested consciousness is one, it receives a threefold designation due to the distinctions among the parts of the manifesting internal organ: the aspect of consciousness delimited by the agent-part is the knower (*pramātā*); the aspect of consciousness delimited by the activity-part is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); and [the aspect delimited by] the manifestation residing in the object—

The aspect of consciousness delimited by the portion consisting of fitness (*yogyatva*) is valid cognition (*pramiti*). As for the object of knowledge (*prameya*), it is indeed the Brahman-consciousness residing in the object, which is [veiled by] ignorance (*ajñāna*). That very same [consciousness]...
[page 314]
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[the section titled] "The Lamp of the Immutable" (Kūṭasthadīpa).

And it is known that the fruit is the "known" (*jñāta*). Thus, because it is the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the Brahman-consciousness residing in the object itself, being conditioned by the state of being known, constitutes the fruit;

this indeed is beyond dispute. Accordingly, when a disciple is commanded by his teacher with the words "Bring the cow," even if he brings a white cow, why would he not be reproached by the teacher for bringing a "white cow"? Therefore, the maxim holds: "the qualified is not distinct from the pure."

It bears fruit. Therefore, the intention is that this Vārttika has been composed out of a desire to favor those who seek to know, because the intellect of one desiring to know cannot enter into the pure Brahman, which is inaccessible to speech and mind. || 11 ||
Thus, the author of the Vārttika intends to express a similarity to consciousness.
For the distinction between the fruit of the *brahman* and the *cit* is renowned in the *Sahasrī*. || 12 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: By this Vārtika, the intended meaning is that the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), which resembles the consciousness of Brahman, is what is meant by the "fruit of the means of knowledge" (pramāṇaphala), and not the consciousness of Brahman itself. Having raised the doubt as to how such an intention of the authors of the Vārtikas is understood, [the author] states that it is because their teacher, the venerable Ācārya, established the distinction between the consciousness of Brahman and the reflection of consciousness in the *Upadeśasāhasrī*.

He says this: "brahmacit" [means] "Brahman-consciousness. The analysis of the compound is as follows: "brahmacit" and "phala" (fruit) constitute "brahmacitphale," and [the phrase refers to] those two. || 12 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, when the present Vārtika has been cited in order to demonstrate the contradiction for a proponent who—being ignorant of the secret of the feet of the illustrious author of the Vārtika—maintains a doctrine of difference between the Brahman-consciousness and the fruit-consciousness on the grounds that they are respectively pure and characterized by some attributes, the author of the Siddhānta states its intended meaning with the half-verse beginning with "iti. The meaning is: "in this present Vārtika."

Regarding the term *vārtika*: here, the reading ending in the genitive plural (*vārtikānām*) alone is more appropriate, because it results in a simpler syntactic connection (*anvaya*). The plural number is used solely for the sake of showing great respect. The reading ending in the instrumental singular (*vārtikena*), however, is indeed a corrupt reading (*apapāṭha*), as it would lead to a strained or difficult construction. Regarding "cittvena" and so forth: by the very fact of being consciousness (*cittva*), there is a similarity—meaning an equality—between the consciousness that is Brahman and the consciousness that is the fruit of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-phala-caitanya*); this is what is intended to be expressed.

This is the construction [of the sentence]. If it is asked, "From where is this known?", he says—referring to the words "brahmacit" and so on—that it is because the venerable author of the *Bhāṣya* (Śaṅkara), in his *Upadeśasāhasrī*, has stated that very distinction between those two.
"Brahmacit" means both Brahman-consciousness and the previously mentioned fruit-consciousness (*phalacaitanya*); the meaning is "of those two.
This has been stated in the fourteenth chapter of the *Upadeśasāhasrī*: [The relevant verse from the Upadeśasāhasrī follows here.]

“Since all intellects in all bodies are illuminated by me through the light of pure consciousness (cinmātra-jyotis), therefore I am the Self of all. The instrument, the action, the agent, the activity, and the fruit in a dream—as well as these in the waking state—are seen [as such]; therefore, the Seer is other than that. Here, only as much of Rāmatīrtha’s commentary as is useful is summarized: “Therefore, the Seer is the Self...”

The meaning is that [the Self] is other than the intellect (*buddhi*), being of a different nature—namely, real and of an indivisible, single essence. Thus, the point is that by the words "pure consciousness" (*cinmātra*) and so forth, as well as "the Seer" (*draṣṭṛ*) and so forth, the distinction between the fruit-consciousness (*phala-caitanya*) and the Brahman-Self-consciousness is indeed clear. Now, even so, in the *Vedāntakalpalatā*, the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī has described this Vārtika as referring solely to the consciousness of Brahman; and thus, once again—
This leads to the very same state of contradiction. For instance, regarding that Brahman, it has been stated in the context of the pervasion by the mental mode (*vṛtti*):
"The fact that [Brahman] is to be pervaded by the fruit has indeed been rejected by the authors of the scriptures;
however, the pervasion by the mental mode is required for the destruction of ignorance regarding Brahman."

Because it has been stated thus, some say that being "objectified by the fruit" (*phala-vyāpyatva*) alone is what entails insentience (*jaḍatva*); but that is not correct. For in the scriptures, it is consciousness manifested through the modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ produced by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that is designated as the "fruit. If being objectified by that [consciousness] were the cause of insentience, then objects revealed by the Witness (*sākṣin*), like Brahman itself, would not be insentient. However, being an object of consciousness (*caitanya-karmatā*) exists everywhere, delimited by the fact of being distinct from consciousness; therefore, that alone is what constitutes insentience.

[She is] the motivator (*prayojikā*). It should also be understood that in the cited verse, the word "fruit" (*phala*) refers exclusively to pure consciousness (*caitanyamātra*). Now, an objection may be raised: since the mental modification (*vṛtti*) has [the object] as its domain, it is necessarily the case that consciousness colored by that [modification] also has it as its domain; for a mental modification arises only as containing the form of consciousness. As it has been said: "The filling of space occurs due to the very nature of the substance space itself, not from an external agent, just as in the production of a jar..."

Accompanied by two commentaries.

"Just as [the self-luminous nature] belongs to the seer, so too for cognitions: the state of being composed of pleasure, pain, and so forth belongs to cognition due to causes such as merit (*dharma*); whereas the pervasion by the awareness of an object established in itself arises from conformity to the reality [of that object]. Thus, because it has consciousness as its object, insentience (*jaḍatva*) is indeed unavoidable. [Reply: No; since consciousness as qualified by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) is itself of the nature of consciousness, it is not pervaded by that [modification]. For there is no occurrence of another fruit within a fruit. As for those things distinct from it, they lack intrinsic manifestation.

Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever in necessarily accepting that its pervasion [extends] to those [objects]. As it has been said: "Among objects of knowledge that are external (parāg), that which is accepted as the fruit is consciousness itself; by the authority of the statements of the Vedānta, that very consciousness is the object to be known here. And thus, according to the *Upadeśasāhasrī* of the author of the root text (*mūlakṛt*), the word "fruit" (*phala*) in this *Vārtika* is intended to mean the supreme Brahman-consciousness. Otherwise, [the meaning would conflict with] what is stated in the *Upadeśasāhasrī*.

Furthermore, the distinction between the Brahman-consciousness and the fruit-consciousness stated by you would be contradicted; for in the aforementioned *Kalpalatikā* text, their non-difference becomes quite clear—this is indeed true. Moreover, in the *Kalpalatikā*, in the passage immediately preceding the one cited: "Alternatively, it is only the state of being an object of [pure] consciousness that everywhere brings about insentience, and not even the state of being an object of a mental modification (*vṛtti*). For [the Upaniṣads say], 'from which words turn back,' and—"

It has been stated that [Brahman] is grasped neither by the eye nor by speech, according to both types of scriptural passages such as, "I ask you about that person known through the Upaniṣads," "One who does not know the Veda does not perceive that Great One," and "That which is to be known is known only through the Veda. Therefore, it is beyond dispute that even in the investigation of mental modifications (*vṛtti*), the object is indeed pure Brahman. Consequently, in this Siddhānta text, regarding the phrase "of the consciousness colored by the modification" (*vṛttyuparaktacaitanyasya*) and so forth, the word *vṛtti*— [The sentence appears to be cut off here.]

Having established that the Brahman-self-consciousness—which is colored by the final non-dual mental modification (*akhaṇḍākāra-caramavṛtti*) of the form "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*), produced by sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) after their meaning has been investigated, and which appears as if connected [to the world] through the destruction of root-ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*)—cannot be the object of that [modification] because it is itself of the nature of consciousness, this *Vārttika* beginning with "parārtha" is cited there as authoritative support. In that context, those objects external to oneself (*parāgartha*) such as jars and so forth, which are of the nature of the non-self (*anātmarūpa*)— [The rest of the sentence continues: ...are not the objects of that [consciousness]. This is the sense. The word "etc. (*ādi*) implies the inclusion of the body, senses, and so forth. The phrase "in the state of being the object" (*viṣayatve sati*) indicates that even though they are objects, they are not the objects of that [consciousness]; thus, the intended meaning is that they are not the objects of that [consciousness] precisely because they are not its objects. The word "therefore" (*ata eva*) means for this very reason. The phrase "the Self is not an object" (*nātmā viṣayaḥ*) means that the Self is not an object of that [consciousness], because it is of the nature of consciousness.
