Regarding the definitions of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), that consciousness which is the cognition of them—delimited by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by the eyes and other senses—is accepted as the result (*phala*) because, according to the scriptures, it is precisely the Consciousness manifested by the internal organ’s modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) produced by the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that is designated as the result; for this very reason, the previously stated definition of Consciousness is intended here. As it is said: "The instrument, the object, the agent, the action, and the result—all these are consciousness in a dream."

"Since it is seen even while one is awake," thus is the intended meaning of the venerable author of the Bhāṣya. However, according to the authority of the Vedāntic statements, the object of knowledge—which is characterized by the non-duality of Brahman and the Self—is the ultimate human goal (*puruṣārtha*). That [knowledge] itself constitutes the fruit; there is no need for a separate consciousness called "resultant-consciousness" (*phala-caitanya*) for the purpose of manifesting insentient objects such as jars. This is because that [consciousness] itself is unmanifested; such is the meaning according to my own understanding.

It shines. And thus, it should be understood that this use of the particle *eva* has been applied by me—following the author of the *Kalpalatā*—in the sense that the object is indeed the cognized thing (*meyārtha*), and not as something merely fabricated from one's own imagination (*kapola-kalpita*). Furthermore, in the root text, after stating: "What is called 'cognizedness' (*jñātatva*) in a jar is the arising of the fruit consisting of the reflection of Consciousness (*cidābhāsa*); the fruit is not the Brahman-consciousness itself, because [Brahman] exists even prior to the means of knowledge (*māna*)," [the text proceeds] to an investigation of the cognitive modification (*pramāṇavṛtti*) having the form of a jar and so forth, wherein the fruit-consciousness is [identified with] Brahman.

For one like you, who—unable to tolerate the clear distinction between those two—seizes upon the statement in the aforementioned Vārtika that "it is that very [consciousness]," and thus fails to grasp the literal meaning, the author of the *Vārtika* himself, after citing that very passage for the purpose of explaining the determination of objects such as jars (*ghaṭa*) and so forth, subsequently demonstrated the natural consistency of the passage beginning with "that which is accepted as the fruit" by providing reasons, starting with: "Thus, according to the authors of the *Vārtika*, what is intended is a similarity to consciousness (*citsādṛśya*). What room is there here for the *Mūlakalpalatā*?

There is not even a scent of contradiction between the supported (the object) and the supporter (consciousness). Although pure consciousness is non-dual, its sixfold differentiation according to specific limitations within the framework of the "determination according to each object" (*pratikarmavyavasthā*) has been clearly elucidated by me, along with supporting illustrations, in the *Bodhaikyasiddhi*.
The Self is pure like a lamp placed within a crystal palace rich in joints;

by virtue of that state, it becomes the Witness. When conditioned by those [states], it is the cognizer, just as before. The means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, the act of knowing, and its fruit are merely the manifestation of that [Self] shining outwardly.
"Just as [the breath] from the Kumbha to the end, so too does the non-dual [Self], though ignited by the movement of the instruments, vibrate."
The detailed exposition of this, however, is to be understood from my own commentary (*ṭīkā*) alone; may there be auspiciousness! || 12 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Since this is so, what follows for the subject at hand? To this he says:
From that, the reflection (ābhāsa) arises and produces the state of being known (jñātatva) in the jar. *The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, titled "The Lamp of the Immutable" (Kūṭasthadīpa)*.
Furthermore, that Brahman is indeed to be manifested by [the teacher], just like the state of being unknown. (13)

Regarding the term "appearance" (ābhāsa): since the distinction between Brahman and the fruit of cognition is well-known, therefore, the appearance—the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa)—which has arisen or been produced from that [Brahman], possesses the state of being known (jñātatva) within that jar; furthermore, this state of being known is manifested by Brahman alone, just as the state of being unknown is. This is indeed the established meaning. Commentary on Verse 13: Now, one might ask: "Let it be so; what does that have to do with the subject at hand? To this, he says: "Appearance," etc. "Ā-" [is the beginning of the word].

The phrase "in the mental modification (buddhivṛtti) having the form of a jar" is to be understood as being in proximity to the eye assisted by the world. "Ābhāsa" means the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa). "Has arisen" means that at the very same time [the jar arises], it has come into being like the space within a jar (ghaṭākāśa). The rest, however, is straightforward. || 13 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus established the difference between Brahman and the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), he clarifies it by demonstrating the distinction in their respective objects: "The aggregate of mental modifications, reflections, and jars is illumined by Consciousness."
Because it is the fruit of the measure of the jar, that one [consciousness] shines forth as a manifestation. || 14 ||

"By the movement of the intellect" (dhīvṛttyā) means by consciousness (cit), that is, by the Brahman-consciousness. Since the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) has the nature of a result residing solely within the jar, the meaning is that by that reflection, that very jar alone shines forth as manifest. || 14 ||
— Commentary (A0): Having thus established the difference between the consciousness of Brahman and the consciousness that is the fruit, he states another argument for its validity:

"dhīvṛtti... etc. The mental modification (*dhīvṛtti*) produced by a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which is called the manifestation (*ābhāsa*) and the fruit of the means of knowledge, contains within it the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*). [This is like] a jar...

The term *dviṣaya* is a *dvandva* compound meaning "the two objects" (*ghaṭaśca iti*). *Saṃghaḥ* means a collection. *Citā* means by the Brahman-consciousness which has become the substratum of the jar; this is the meaning. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "merely the jar. Thus, the point is that even due to the difference in objects, there is a distinction between the consciousness of Brahman and the consciousness that is the fruit [of cognition]. || 14 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: He states the evidence for the jar being illumined by both the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) and Brahman: "Therefore, consciousness is twofold in the jar, manifesting as the state of being known."
Others say that this, as has been described, is what is called reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya).

Regarding the term *caitanya*: therefore, because the jar is illumined by both Brahman-consciousness (*brahma-caitanya*) and the individual consciousness (*vidābhāsa*), a twofold consciousness shines forth in the pot as its "known-ness" (*jñātatva*). He states that this very consciousness which illumines the "known-ness" of the jar is what the logicians (*tārkika*) refer to under another name—namely, "another cognition called *anuvyavasāya*. As has been stated, other logicians call this very same Brahman-consciousness a distinct cognition known as *anuvyavasāya*.
Thus is the construction [of the sentence]. || 15 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Granted that the three—the mental modification (*dhīvṛtti*), the reflection (*ābhāsa*), and the jar (*kuṃbha*)—are all equally illumined by the consciousness of Brahman (*brahmacaitanya*);

nevertheless, what is the proof for the claim made here that the jar alone is illumined by the reflection of consciousness known as the 'fruit' (*phala*)? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the answer while suggesting that it is indeed an inference based on the mark of the effect (*kāryaliṅgaka-anumāna*): "Consciousness... [He continues: "Because, among the mental modification, the reflection, and the jar, the jar..."

The intention is as follows: when it flashes forth either as "the jar alone is known by me as an object of knowledge" or "I am the knower of the jar," there appears a twofold manifestation regarding the jar—namely, "the jar is consciousness-doubled" (i.e., the jar plus consciousness) and "the jar is known by me. However, this does not apply to the mental modification (*dhīvṛtti*) and the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) separately. In that regard, although in the initial cognition "this is the jar" the mental modification, the reflection, and the jar appear as common objects of perception (*dṛśyatva*), [the jar alone is what is truly perceived].

Because the operation of the means of knowledge called "the mother's eye" (the internal organ) functions for the purpose of cognizing an object merely as large as a jar, and because both the mental modification (*vṛtti*) and its reflection are not themselves objects of that [operation], they are manifested solely by the witness (*sākṣin*).

Now, one might object: just as in the initial cognition "this is a jar," the witness, the mental modification, and so forth—all three—are made objects by the witness, so too in the second cognition in the form "the jar is known," those same factors are made objects by the witness known as Brahman-consciousness alone; thus, in this single case...

The eighth chapter: Why [is it] "only the pot"? Since terms such as *jñāna* (knowledge), *bhāna* (manifestation), *sphuraṇa* (vibration), *saṃvit* (consciousness), *cit* (thought), and *caitanya* (sentience) do not denote different things, there would be a doubling of sentience.

If it is argued that [the subsequent cognition] is accepted [as valid], then certainly so; for since the initial cognition alone possesses the status of a means of valid knowledge (*pramā*), at that time it has only the jar as its object. Thus, only that [jar]— *Vyākhyādvayasametā*, 317.

If it is said that [the subsequent cognition] is accepted [as valid], then certainly so. Since the initial cognition alone possesses the status of a means of valid knowledge (*pramā*), because it has only the jar as its object, at that time only that—

This is because that [pot] alone is manifested [by the mental modification], and since the mental modification and the reflection of consciousness delimited by it are manifested by the knowledge consisting of the witness itself;

furthermore, in the case of a cognition whose form is "the pot is known" and which has the knowledge of the pot as its object, the witness itself simultaneously takes as its objects both the pot and the knowledge—which consists of the valid modification directed toward that object—as well as the reflection of consciousness delimited by that [knowledge]. Thus, it is indeed logical that there is a twofold nature of consciousness with respect to the pot.

The statement of the negative-only inference (*kevalavyatirekin*). Herein is the formal argument: Among the pot, the manifestation of the mental modification (*dhīvṛtti*), and the light of consciousness (*caitanyābhāsa*) which are appearing in the cognition "this is a pot," the very pot under dispute possesses a duality of consciousness; because, while being an object of valid knowledge (*pramiti*), it is also an object of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi*), whereas that which is not so [dual] is not an object of the witness-consciousness despite being an object of valid knowledge, as in the case of the [mental modification] itself. Since all things that are objects of valid knowledge are equal to the subject (*pakṣasama*) and thus there is no positive instance (*anvaya-dṛṣṭānta*), this is indeed a purely negative inference. Now, let it be so—

If it is argued that this is merely a technical convention (*paribhāṣā*) because we do not observe any other Tīrthikas accepting a doubling of cognition (*jñāna-dvaiguṇya*) regarding an object already cognized by other means, we say:

no. This is because the Logicians (*tārkika*) themselves accept what we have stated—that the "subsequent cognition" (*anuvyavasāya*) is precisely the witnessing cognition (*sākṣijñāna*) directed toward the [primary] cognition of the object.
With this intention, he says: "others. "Others" refers to the Logicians. "As stated" means as properly established by us.

This refers to the *rityārthika* [cognition]. The meaning is that it is the manifestation as knowledge (*jñānatvena*) of an object already cognized by this [primary cognition]. It is called *anuvyavasāya*, though it does not bear that name [in the strict sense].
The connection [of the words] is with the verb "they say" (*āhuḥ*). || 15 ||
This statement, "this is a jar," arises through the grace of the manifestation.
The statement "the jar is known" occurs through the grace of Brahman. || 16 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): He states that the distinction between the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) and Brahman must also be understood from the difference in linguistic usage, such as "this is a jar"—"ghaṭo'yam" || 16 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, he causes the very meaning already stated to ascend to the intellect by means of what is common to all experience, [saying]: "This is a jar—this [is it]. "Of the manifestation" (ābhāsasya) means of the reflection of consciousness delimited by the cognition [of the object]. "Brahman" means by the Brahman-consciousness that serves as the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) of the jar. || 16 ||
Just as the appearance of Brahman is discerned as being outside the body, [so too is the Self].
In the same way, one should distinguish between that which appears and the immutable reality even within the body.

Rāma’s Commentary: Just as the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) and Brahman are distinguished from outside the body, so too must the reflection of consciousness and the immutable witness (kūṭastha) be distinguished within the body; thus he says: "The reflection... (verse 17).

Commentary (a0): Thus, for the purpose of purifying the meaning of the word *tat* (*that*), fire, Brahman, and the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) have been distinguished from the body; and by means of that illustration, he now prescribes the discrimination between the immutable (*kūṭastha*) and the reflection (*ābhāsa*) for the purpose of purifying the meaning of the word *tvam* (*you*), which was introduced at the very beginning—stating "the reflection... One should not object that since this discrimination was already performed at the outset, it is redundant to prescribe it again; for [this is necessary] because of the fivefold [superimposition of] the body and so forth...

In brief, since it is precisely the non-discrimination of that [Self] from the body and so forth, through superimposition (*adhyāsa*), that serves as the cause for all practical purposes, there is a need for greater firmness specifically in the discrimination of them in order to eliminate that [superimposition]. || 17 ||
The reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) resides in the function of the ego (ahaṃvṛtti) as well as in desire, anger, and the like.
It exists pervading [the body], just as fire exists within heated iron. || 18 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary:

Now, an objection may be raised: "Since there is no mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward internal objects—unlike the modification in the form of a jar which extends outward from the body and is pervaded by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*)—how can a reflection of consciousness that pervades such [internal] objects be admitted? Anticipating this, [the author replies: even in the absence of a modification directed toward an external object, there is the modification consisting of the "I-sense" (*ahaṃ-vṛtti*), etc.
Since it exists, its pervader, the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), can be accepted; thus he states an illustrative example: "I" (aham). || 18 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, it has been stated that for the purpose of determining the meaning of the term *tvaṃ* (the "Thou"), both the reflected image (*ābhāsa*) and the immutable witness (*kūṭastha*) must be distinguished within the body as well.
Vidyāraṇya’s *Pañcadaśī*,
titled *Kūṭasthadīpa* (The Lamp of the Immutable),

summarizes its method through the four verses beginning with "In the mental modification of 'I'" (*ahaṃvṛttau*), as an expansion upon what was briefly indicated in the opening aphorism. Regarding the word "desire" (*kāma*)— it refers to a mental modification (*vṛtti*).
The word "in them" (sviṣu) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the verse]. In that regard, the illustration is provided by the remainder of the verse beginning with "heated" (tapta). || 18 ||
Heated iron illuminates only itself and never anything else.
Thus, the mental modifications, accompanied by their respective appearances, are self-luminous. || 19 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: He clarifies that it is only the mental modifications (vṛttis) such as "I" and so forth that are illumined by the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), by means of an elaboration of examples—beginning with "svamātram" (verse 19).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He clarifies the aforementioned illustration itself with the words "svamātram" (nothing but itself). He applies that [illustration] to the subject of the analogy with the word "evam" (thus). || 19 ||
All mental modifications arise, being successively interrupted one after another.
All of them also dissolve away during sleep, fainting, and meditative absorption.

Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus explained the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), he now shows the occasion for the absence of mental modification (vṛttyabhāva), which is useful for explaining the nature of the immutable (kūṭastha), with the words "In succession" (kramāt). || 20 ||

Commentary (a0): Having thus described, by means of two [verses], the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*)—which is distinct from them—within the internal body during the functions of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth, the author now intends to describe the *kūṭastha* (the immutable witness). To show the occasion for that manifestation, namely the absence of mental modifications (*vṛtti*), he describes their arising and dissolution with the words "In succession" (*kramāt*). By this, that which was previously indicated in the aphorisms as "the junction of thoughts" (*saṃdhi*) and "the absence of the intellect" (*dhiyām abhāvam*) is also explained. Here, in this state of *samādhi*:

Layayoga, for its part, is indeed the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) transformed into the forms of wealth and living beings along with their mental modifications; it is not, however, the state-knowledge (avasthājñāna) as transformed into the form of the quality of intense darkness (tamas), as occurs in states such as deep sleep. || 20 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Let it be so that there is a dissolution of mental modifications (vṛtti) during samādhi and the like; however, how is it understood by this [text] that [the Self] is immutable (kūṭastha)?
Anticipating this doubt, he states that it is understood as the witness (sākṣin) of the absence of modifications:
"The junctions and the absences of all mental modifications are manifested [by Him]."
Because it is changeless, it is called "immovable" (kūṭastha). || 21 ||

Regarding the phrase "junctions of the aggregate" (saṃghaya): the meaning is that the immutable (kūṭastha) should be understood as that consciousness by which both the junctions of the mental modes (vṛtti-saṃdhi) and the absences of those modes are manifested. || 21 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, having distinguished the immutable (*kūṭastha*), he expands upon it with the words "saṃdhaya" (the joints). The phrase "by the changeless one" (*nirvikāreṇa*) is a causal qualification intended to indicate the figure of speech *parikara* and to demonstrate the etymological analysis (*vigraha*) of that term: "one who stands like a peak (*kūṭa*)—that is, changelessly—is called the immutable (*kūṭastha*). The particle "ca" (and) is used for emphasis. The connection is: "This very one is called the immutable. || 21 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Such being the case, what is the resulting conclusion? To this he says:
"Just as there is a twofold consciousness in the external jar, so it is within."
Furthermore, in the case of the secondary functions (vṛttis) as well, there is a greater clarity therein due to their connection [with the primary function].

Regarding the term "jar" (*ghaṭa*): just as in the case of an external jar there is a twofold consciousness—namely, the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) which manifests the jar itself, and the Brahman-consciousness which manifests the "knownness" (*jñātatā*) of the jar—likewise, in internal modifications (*vṛtti*) such as the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), there exists a twofold consciousness consisting of the immutable consciousness (*kūṭasthacaitanya*) and the reflection of consciousness that manifests the modification. He states the justification for this with the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*): because this twofold consciousness exists, it is therefore [the object] is joined [with consciousness].
The remainder is that, among those functions, greater clarity is observed in the case of the *saṃdhis*. || 22 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, let it be so; yet that which is changeless, which illumines the internal mental states, their conjunctions, and their absence—that is the Immutable (Kūṭastha).
[Page 319] Eighth Chapter.
[This is] accompanied by two commentaries.

Although [the word "pot"] denotes a thing established externally, nevertheless, regarding a pot existing internally—such as one occurring in a dream, a mental construction, or a memory—it possesses a twofold consciousness (*caitanya*).

"Is there [such a defect] or not? In the first case (if there is), there would be the consequence of its being merely empirical (*vyāvahārika*). In the latter case (if there is not), there would be the consequence that the clarity of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) and so forth would not be attained. Anticipating this objection, he clarifies—by means of the first half of the verse beginning with "the jar"—that the first position alone is acceptable; for even though a lack of double-consciousness (*caitanyadvaiguṇya*) exists in the case of a magician’s jar and the like, we do not observe the status of being empirical, which is defined as "not being sublated by anything other than the knowledge of Brahman. He states this point as a proof, following the method to be explained later, even regarding internal mental states (*antaravṛtti*).

He extends [the rule] to the modifications as well, stating: "In the modifications (vṛttiṣvapi) also. Now, even so, do the internal mental modifications (buddhivṛttis) possess the same quality of consciousness (caitanya) as that [Self], or do they lack it? Not the first, because then they would result in being as clear (vaiśadya) as the conjunction of those [two]. Nor the second, because when the term "modifications" (vṛtti-pada) is understood to refer to the modifications of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa-vṛttis) as delimited by the class-characteristic of being a modification (vṛttitva), ignorance (ajñāna) is destroyed by them; this is according to the authoritative statement (pramāṇa-vṛtti) found in the final quarter of the subsequent verse.

If it is argued that this contradicts the apprehension of mere existence (*astitva-mātra*), and that out of fear of such a contradiction, if one were to accept the function of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) alone in that regard, then—as in the case of "I see a jar with my eyes"—those [functions] would result in being external; hear here the secret: in this context, because of the contradiction with the concluding passage where the term "function" (*vṛtti*) was used, one must understand the functions of the means of knowledge alone as being internal, which serve to destroy ignorance. And it is not correct to say that, if that were so, there would be the aforementioned consequence of their being external; for the function of the means of knowledge—

Because internality is possible even in the case of a cognition (*pramiti*), for example: "I remember Kāśī," and so forth. Even though memory has as its object something that already exists [in the past], it must necessarily be admitted to be a functioning of valid cognition (*pramāṇavṛtti*) precisely because it is uncontradicted (*abādha*). In the same way, the inference consisting of reflection—such as "The subject of dispute is false, because it is perceptible, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell"—is a functioning of valid cognition in the form of an inference (*anumityātmikā*), even though it is internal to the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) at the time of contemplation (*manana*). It is the same with regard to meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*).

Even the *kālika* [knowledge] such as "I am Brahman" is so; for it is said: "Everything is born in Me alone, everything is established in Me; everything goes to dissolution in Me—that non-dual Brahman I am. Although the mental state (*vṛtti*) consisting of the contemplation of the identity between the purified referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam* is internal, it possesses the status of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like a continuous stream of cognition (*dhārāvāhika-vṛtti*), precisely because it is unsublated. Likewise, this applies to that which consists of hearing and so forth regarding objects such as mantras perceived in a dream.

Even though this mental modification (*vṛtti*) is internal, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) remains entirely intact. This has been stated in the *Siddhāntabindu* itself: "In this way, there is the attainment of mantras and so forth in a dream;

[this occurs] from the waking state within a dream. By this, the fact that a mental modification is a valid means of knowledge—even when it is internal—is explained in cases such as "I am one who has perceived a mantra in a dream," where the modification is internal with respect to the time delimited by the subsequent perception of such a mantra. In the same way, the example of a daydream (*manorājya*) is also to be understood.

In all these cases, although they function internally, their validity is established by the fact that they are generally uncontradicted; however, as for their being the remover of ignorance, that should be understood according to the specific circumstances. He states the conclusion with the remainder of the verse beginning with "tataḥ" (therefore). || 22 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "In this case as well, why not accept that the immutable (kūṭastha) is the illuminator of both the known and the unknown, just as it is with jars and other objects?

Anticipating this, he states that there is no such thing as being known or unknown in the case of the internal functions, precisely because "the states of being known and unknown do not exist anywhere in the functions, as they do in jars."
Because it is not grasped by itself through itself, and because ignorance is destroyed by those [means]. || 23 ||

Regarding the term "known-ness" (*jñātatā*): he states the reasoning for this with the words "of its own. Known-ness and unknown-ness arise through the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of knowledge and ignorance respectively.

However, because mental modifications (*vṛtti*) are self-luminous, there is no pervasion by knowledge; nor is there pervasion by ignorance, because that ignorance regarding their own objects is removed by those very modifications at the mere moment of their own arising. This is the intended meaning. || 23 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if this were so, then just as with an external or internal pot, even in the case of external and internal mental modifications (*vṛtti*), there would arise a twofold consciousness—consisting of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) and the consciousness consisting of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*)—as they are objects to be illumined by that [witness-consciousness]. Consequently, just as with a pot, both "known-ness" (*jñātatā*) and "unknown-ness" (*ajñātatā*) would necessarily apply to those modifications as well. And thus, there would result the undesirable consequence of such experiences as, "I have the knowledge of the knowledge of the pot," or "That [knowledge] did not exist for all this time. Anticipating this objection, he provides the following resolution:

He maintains this by stating "jñātatā" (the state of being known). He states the reasons for this in sequence with the third and subsequent quarters of the verse, beginning with "svasya" (of itself), etc. Regarding the modification (*vṛtti*) of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) directed toward a jar, one must ask: is it said that this modification is known by that very [modification], or by the Witness (*sākṣin*)? It cannot be the latter; for the statement "the jar is known" would have to arise from the experience of Brahman, and since that was already established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) previously, its production [by the Witness] is now impossible.

Because of existence; nor can the first [alternative] be maintained, as it would entail the consequence of climbing onto one's own shoulders—this he states with the words "of itself," etc. Herein, consciousness is self-luminous...
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya— specifically the section titled *Kūṭasthadīpa*,

which contains refutations of the Mīmāṃsaka (Prābhākara) and other schools— should be understood from its original source itself; it is not presented here because it is not particularly essential and for fear of excessive prolixity.

"Is being destroyed"—this is the direction [of the argument]. Thus, just as light and darkness are mutually exclusive, so too, due to the opposition between knowledge (*jñāna*) and ignorance (*ajñāna*), it is not possible for those cognitive states that consist of knowledge to possess "unknownness," which is defined as being veiled by ignorance. He says this with the words beginning "And by those... The particle *ca* is used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). The point is that since ignorance is destroyed precisely by those cognitive functions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavṛtti*), it is simply untenable for them to be "unknown. Regarding this, the ancient [author] has explained it as follows: ... [text fragment] ...the ancient [author] has explained it as follows: [The text continues with a commentary on the verse: "But the ancient [author] has explained it thus: [the verse begins] 'But by those very [means]... [The text continues. (Note: The provided source text ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the available portion.)

It is said: "But surely, here too, just as in the case of jars and other objects, why is the immutable (kūṭastha) not accepted as the illuminator of both the states of being known and being unknown even in the case of mental modifications (vṛttis)?"—anticipating this objection, he says "jñātatā" (the state of being known), [meaning] precisely because the state of being known and so forth does not exist there. He provides the reasoning for that with "svasya" (of itself): the states of being known and being unknown arise through the pervasion by knowledge and ignorance respectively. Since mental modifications are self-luminous, they lack the pervasion by [external] knowledge; therefore, by those modifications—

The sense is that because ignorance (*ajñāna*) is removed by the mere arising of [the mental modifications] through their own objective range, ignorance possesses no pervasion (*vyāpti*) at all. This is the point here: although even those mental modifications (*vṛtti*) which take the form of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) do not possess self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*)—since insentience (*jaḍatva*), defined as non-self-luminosity due to being distinct from the Self, pervades the entire duality—nevertheless, that aforementioned modification possesses self-luminosity, which is the opposite of its own insentience.

Just as, by means of the example of mirrors introduced at the outset—namely, that within a single mirror there are the reflections of many sunbeams—all those mirrors, through their respective reflections, generally appear for a moment to be self-luminous from the perspective of worldly perception;
and just as they, like the sun, dazzle the eyes of the observer and dispel all darkness, so too [the Self] effects the destruction of each respective ignorance. Thus it is concluded.

In that context, self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) is indeed intended from the perspective of one who desires to know; therefore, even together with that [opposing] text, there is not even a scent of disagreement. Let those who are foremost among the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*) understand this for themselves; enough of this prolixity. || 23 ||
When consciousness is doubled through the experience of birth and destruction, [it becomes the Great Principle].
But that which is other than it is not immutable; however, [the Self] is immutable because of its changelessness. || 24 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection may be raised: since both the immutable consciousness (kūṭastha-cit) and the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) are equally of the nature of consciousness, on what basis is one called immutable while the other is called non-immutable? Anticipating this doubt, he states that the reflection of consciousness is non-immutable because birth and death are experienced as residing in it, whereas the other is immutable because there is no evidence for its being subject to modification. Thus he says: "The two-fold... (verse 24).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "Even though both the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) and the witness (*sākṣin*) are equal in their self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), what is the reason for one being non-eternal (*akūṭastha*) and the other being eternal (*kūṭastha*)? To this, he says: "In that which has doubled its qualities" (*dviguṇīkṛta*). The meaning is: in that reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) by which consciousness has been doubled through the delimitation of objects such as jars, in the manner previously described. [This occurs] even in deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

The sense is as follows: due to the absence of the cognitive modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) known as the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), which serves as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no emergence of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*); thus, only the witnessing-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) exists as one.

However, with respect to the limitation of the dream state and so forth, because the aforementioned modifications such as the ego-sense exist, the reflection of consciousness emerges along with them; therefore, the state of being "consciousness doubled" (*dviguṇīkṛta-caitanyatva*) is quite evident therein.
Indeed, this predicate, by the aforementioned etymological derivation, contains the reason [for the state of being a dream] and should be understood as indicating the poetic figure *parikara-aṅkura*.

Regarding the word "birth" (*janma*): it means that birth is experienced in dreams and the like, while destruction is experienced in deep sleep and the like. That [birth] belongs to the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa-caitanya*). The meaning is that it is non-eternal and subject to modification (*vikārin*). Having thus stated the reason for the reflector of consciousness being subject to modification, he states that the Witness (*sākṣin*) lacks such [modification] by saying "other than that" (*tadanya*). The word "but" (*tu*) is intended to indicate its distinction from that. "Unchanging" (*avikāritaḥ*) is a nominative expression where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary sense; [it means] "unchanging."
"Tvā" means "this. || 24 ||

Rāmatīrtha’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that the acceptance of a changeless reality (kūṭastha) distinct from the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) is merely a fabrication of one's own imagination,
the Teacher states— by demonstrating the existence of the changeless reality in various ways in passages such as "the witness of the internal organ and its modifications"— that this is not so.
The immutable (kūṭastha) alone is determined by the former teachers to be present everywhere. || 25 ||
The Eighth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

Regarding the phrase "the internal organ" (antaḥkaraṇa): the meaning is as in such passages as, "The witness of the internal organ and its modifications, whose form is consciousness, whose nature is bliss, and who is real—being thus, why do you not take refuge in the Self? || 25 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that accepting a "pure consciousness" (*kūṭacaitanya*) distinct from the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) is contrary to tradition. To this, he says: "The internal organ... and so on. The meaning is as follows: when the previous mental modification (*vṛtti*) has ceased and until another modification arises, the internal organ remains like water placed in a vessel in a windless spot—without having undergone transformation, and with the *sattva* portion of the five unevolved great elements (*apañcīkṛta-pañcamahābhūta*) as its constituent material. Its modifications (*vṛttayaḥ*) are egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and the rest.
These [words] are indeed well-known. For this is the very statement from the *Bṛhadvākyavṛtti* of the venerable author of the Bhāṣya:

"O you who are the witness of the internal organ and its modifications, whose form is consciousness, whose nature is bliss, and who are real—why do you not realize yourself? The rest is quite clear. || 29 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states that they have also described the reflection of consciousness as distinct from the immutable Self:
"And those reflections of the Self are just like the reflections of a face which depend upon [a surface]."
It is understood through scripture and reasoning; thus, the semblance [of an argument] has been described. || 26 ||
Regarding the term *ātmābhāsāśrayāḥ*: it is a *dvandva* compound consisting of "the self (*ātman*)," "the reflection (*ābhāsa*)," and "the substratum (*āśraya*).

The same applies to the phrase "the substrata of the reflection of the face (*mukhābhāsāśrayāḥ*). Just as these three—the well-known face, its reflection (the image of the face), and the substratum (such as a mirror)—are perceived through direct perception, so too [in this case] are there three: the immutable Self (*ātman*), the reflection (the reflection of consciousness, *cidābhāsa*), and the substratum (the internal organ, etc.).

The meaning is that [the Self] is understood through both scripture (*śāstra*) and reasoning (*yukti*). Here, the intention is that by the word "reflection" (*ābhāsa*), the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) distinct from the immutable (*kūṭastha*) is described. The scripture that establishes the immutable as the witness of the mind and the witness of the intellect—such as "He became the counterpart of every form" (*rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva*)—establishes the reflection of consciousness; and the reasoning concerning the nature of being subject to modification or not, and so forth, has already been stated.
Such is the meaning. || 26 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Granted that the description of the *kūṭastha* (the immutable) has been provided by the Teacher, yet the *cidābhāsa* (the reflection of consciousness) remains merely a technical term. To this he says: "The Self" (*ātma*). The meaning is as follows: the Self (*ātman*), the reflection (*ābhāsa*), and the substratum (*āśraya*)—namely, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth, which is characterized as the reflection of the aforementioned Self—and these constitute the *cidābhāsa*. Thus it is. Likewise, in the eighteenth chapter of the *Upadeśasāhasrī*, titled "That Thou Art" (*tattvamasi*), there is this verse:
By whom was this stated? However, the final quarter [of that verse] is as follows: "And the non-existence of appearances," etc. (26).
Rāma’s Commentary: In that regard, he introduces the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa):
"The immutable one (kūṭastha), delimited by the intellect, undergoes coming and going to other worlds."
Tell me, can it act through its reflection, like the space within a jar? 27.

Regarding the term "intellect" (buddhi): the very immutable (kūṭastha) Self, delimited by the intellect as it is imagined within itself, is capable of performing coming and going to other worlds through the medium of the intellect—just as the space within a jar (ghaṭākāśa) does through the medium of the jar. Therefore, the sense is that there is unnecessary complexity (gaurava) in postulating a reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa). ||27||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, the traditional status of the reflection (*ābhāsa*) having been established, the proponent of the theory of limitation (*avacchinnavādī*), who follows the view of the venerable Vācaspati, raises an objection: "By the limitation of the intellect" (*buddhyavacchinna*). Nor is it correct to argue that the departure to another world and so forth would not be possible through the mere limitation by the intellect alone without the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), because such a consequence has already been addressed; for in the theory of reflection (*pratibimbavāda*), [the reflection] is slightly inferior to that [consciousness].

Since this is equally applicable even in the theory of reflection (*ābhāsavāda*), if its possibility there is through the medium of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), then it is likewise unassailable in this present position as well;
with this intention, he says: "In another world," etc. There, establishing the authority of scripture (*śruti*) and clarifying the illustration, he says: "Like the space within a jar," etc.
Thus, the followers of the Atharva Veda declare: "Just as when a jar containing space is being carried, the jar is carried but not the space..."

"Just as space [is], so too is the individual soul (jīva) comparable to the sky. He concludes the aforementioned argument with the remainder of the verse beginning with "by means of the manifestation" (ābhāsena).
The detailed exposition of this, however, should be understood from my own works, such as the *Bodhaikyasiddhi*. || 27 ||
In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
one hears that by the mere cessation of attachment, one does not indeed become the individual soul (*jīva*).
[This is the chapter] titled "The Immutable Lamp.
Otherwise, there would be the state of being a *jīva* for that which is delimited by jars, walls, and so forth. (28)

Rāma’s Commentary: He refutes the objection that the status of being a *jīva* cannot belong to the immutable (*kūṭastha*) Self—which is by nature unattached—merely through its limitation by the intellect (*buddhi*), as otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), with the words: "Hear, O unattached one... (28).

— Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) offers a resolution according to the view of the venerable Vitaraṇācārya, beginning with the address "Listen" (*śṛṇu*). He demonstrates the impossibility of the [opponent's] position otherwise by the word "anyathā" (otherwise). || 28 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He raises an objection regarding the disparity between the intellect and a wall based on their transparency and lack thereof:
"If it is argued that the intellect is not like a wall because of its transparency, so be it."
Granted that there may be such a delimitation, what power of independence could you possibly possess? (29)
He says "no. He states that the aforementioned transparency is not the cause of delimitation: "Let it be so. (29)

Commentary (Ṭīkā): An opponent raises an objection regarding the difference between your intellect and objects such as pots or walls, on the grounds of its transparency, using the words "not a wall," etc. Then, the proponent, having conceded this point, considers that even with such an admission there is no benefit for you in the present context, and rather, it leads to an undesirable consequence; thus, he rebuts him with the words "in that case," etc. (Verse 29).
Not indeed with a wooden vessel, nor with one made of bronze.
The specific measure of the rice and other goods to be sold by the vendor is distinguished [by the rules]. || 30 ||

Rāma’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): He clarifies the aforementioned point by means of an illustration: "By the *prastha*. The meaning is that when two *prasthas*—one made of wood and one made of bell-metal—are present, their respective transparency and lack of transparency become the causes for a difference in quantity, such that the measure of rice in one is less and in the other more. || 30 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "Since the intellect is transparent, why is there no distinction [in its perception] when it perceives the Self?
To this, he says: "By means of a prastha... (30).
Even though there is no difference in size, the reflection is distinguished [from the original].
If that were so, then even in the case of cognition, an appearance would necessarily arise by force.

Rāma’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that although there is no excess in the quantity of rice when placed in a bronze vessel, there is nevertheless an excess characterized by its reflection, he says—“if there is no difference in dimension”—to show that, in that case, you yourself would have to admit the existence of a reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) even within the intellect. || 31 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Having thus accepted the opponent’s position regarding the non-distinction between transformations as stated by the proponent, [the opponent] says that in a bronze vessel, due to its clarity, the reflection itself is distinguished by the small amount of rice and so forth—this is expressed by the words "parimāṇa" etc. If this is so, then the theory of reflection (ābhāsavāda) is established. To this, the proponent replies with the remainder of the passage beginning with "yadi" and so on. The essential point therein is as follows:
Just as this sunlight, by virtue of reflection alone, may produce fire from a lens but not elsewhere despite being equally present as a means of cognition, so too the Supreme Self,
when distinguished within the intellect and other faculties, becomes the agent of measurement (cognition), but not otherwise, even though it is all-pervading.
"Therefore, the theory of limitation (avacchedavāda) is to be abandoned, and the theory of reflection (ābhāsavāda) is to be accepted by the best of the wise. || 31 ||

Just as the reflection of a face is not distinct from the face, so too the reflection of consciousness is not distinct from consciousness. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, since the reflection of the intellect is the reflection of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), it is called the "reflection of the ego-sense. Since the reflection of the ego-sense is the reflection of the mind (manas), it is called the "reflection of the mind. The eighth chapter, together with the two commentaries:
"Ābhāsa" (appearance) is a slight manifestation; a reflection is of that same nature.
Being devoid of power and characteristics, he indeed shines as one possessed of wisdom.

Regarding the word "īṣat" (slightly): having raised the doubt as to how the reflection possesses the nature of an appearance (*ābhāsa*), he states that it is because it possesses the defining characteristics of an appearance—namely, "the defining characteristics of the original object.
For this reason, since the reflection appears devoid of distinct characteristics and manifests as the original object (*bimba*), it is called an "appearance of the original object" (*bimbābhāsa*).
Such is the meaning. || 32 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Stating the reason for this, and in order to declare that the reflection-theory (*pratibimba-vāda*) and the appearance-theory (*ābhāsa-vāda*)—which are both accepted by the *Vivaraṇa* and the *Vārtika*—are in fact identical in their result, he defines their essential natures in reverse order [of their usual sequence], beginning with "īṣat" (slightly). || 32 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He clarifies precisely the possession of the characteristics of a reflection:
"The absence of the characteristics of a prototype due to [the presence of] association and modification."
The wise know that its nature as a manifestation is its appearance like a reflection.

"Having become associated" (saṃsaṃgatya): the meaning is that this reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), by virtue of its association and its mutability, is devoid of the characteristics of consciousness—which is essentially free from association and change—and consists instead of the nature of mere manifestation and the appearance of the universe. Just as "fallacious reasons" (hetvābhāsa) are defined as those lacking the characteristics of a valid reason yet appearing as if they were reasons, so it is here. || 33 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on a0: Establishing that [point], he concludes with the words "sasaṅgatva" etc. The phrase "the ancient teachers who perceive the unity of the purport of non-duality" is the required ellipsis (*śeṣa*). This summary of the section of the treatise has been stated in the *Vodhaikyasiddhi*, following the demonstration of the possibility of a formless reflection: "Thus, having first described the immutable (*kūṭastha*) as being like the sun in the sky in the *Kūṭasthadīpa*..."

"Then, since the individual soul (jīva) has the brilliance of one's own mirror, why not let the soul be the very same as the original [Self]?"—anticipating this objection, it is said: "If the Self were to become the individual soul merely through limitation, then like a wall, even the pure mind would become just like that [limited] bell-metal vessel. (33)

Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus refuted the argument that the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) is not a causal factor, he now states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in order to establish its existence as distinct from the intellect (*buddhi*):
"Indeed, because it exists only when the intellect exists, the reflection does not exist apart from the intellect."
If this is argued, then it has been said very little; for in this same way, the intellect [is distinct] from one's own body.

"Not indeed" (na hi): the sense is that just as a jar exists only when clay exists and is not distinct from the clay, so it is in this case. He refutes [the objection] by means of a counter-reductio (*prativandī*), saying "alpa" (insignificant), [arguing]: "If that were so, then even the intellect (*dhī*) distinct from the body would not be established. || 34 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, the proponent of the theory of limitation (avacchinnavādī) again raises an objection through another argument, beginning with "na hi" (not indeed). The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), refuting that very objection with a mocking retort while repeating its substance, answers by means of a counter-objection (prati-baṃdī), beginning with "iti cet" (if this is said). [He says] "sva" (one's own), meaning from the habitual notion "I am a Brāhmaṇa. || 34 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He raises an objection by way of a counter-argument: "Even when the body has died, the desire for liberation exists according to the scriptures; such being the case [what is the point of the practice]?"
A reflection of consciousness distinct from the intellect is heard of in the scriptures concerning "entry. (35)

Regarding the phrase "the body has died": the sense is that because the intellect (*buddhi*) is distinct from the body—this being established by such scriptural passages as "he becomes possessed of consciousness" (*savijñāno bhavati*)—it does not [cease to exist] upon death. Now, if one accepts the existence of an intellect distinct from the body on the strength of scripture, then one must likewise accept a reflection of the Self (*cidābhāsa*) distinct from the intellect on the strength of the scriptural passage concerning "entry" (*praveśa*). To this he says: "That being so... (verse 35).
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 324.

[The commentary on the chapter titled *Kūṭasthadīpa*—Then, having anticipated the opponent's objection regarding the release from the counter-argument he himself stated, he once again establishes the theory of reflection (*ābhāsavāda*) by means of that very method of release: "The body... (verse 35).]
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "But it is only for that which has the intellect as its limiting adjunct (upādhi) that entry is logical, not for any other. To this he replies:
"If it is argued that entry belongs only to that joined with the intellect, [we say] no, because in the Aitareya [Upaniṣad], the intellect is mentioned separately."
The Self, having formed the intention of entering, is said to have entered. || 36 ||

Regarding the phrase "of one endowed with glory": he refutes [the objection] that this cannot be so because the Aitareya Śruti mentions entry only for that which is distinct from growth—thus, "In the Aitareya," etc. (36).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, [the opponent] might argue that since the scriptures speak of the Self’s entry into the body and so forth as being qualified by the intellect (dhī), this must be understood as an entry of the pure Self because an entry of the pure Self is otherwise impossible; having thus restated his position, [the author] sets out to refute it with the words "of that which is joined with the intellect" (dhīyuktasya) and so on.

In this regard, he clarifies the reason while explaining the meaning of the scriptural passage concerning the "entry" found in the *Aitareya Upaniṣad*, using the remainder of the verse beginning with "In the Aitareya... (aitareye). || 36 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He recites that Śruti in its sense:
"How indeed could this body, along with its senses, exist without me?"—from such reasoning [it follows].
Having split open the boundaries of the skull, it enters and wanders through this [body]. || 37 ||

"O Mūka, how indeed [could it be]?"—having reflected thus: "How indeed could this entire collection of insentient things—the supreme Self together with the eyes, the body, and the vital breaths of the body—exist without me, the great Consciousness? It could not function at all," he considered.

The meaning is that, having pierced the boundary—the middle region between the three skull-hemispheres—by its mere presence, it enters and transmigrates, experiencing the states of waking and so forth. || 37 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might object that since an insentient Self lacks the capacity for the volition of entry, such an interpretation of the Śruti is impossible. Anticipating this, the author provides a resolution by restating that very Śruti in its essential meaning and stating the reason for the previously mentioned point, beginning with "How indeed did this... It is heard in the *Aitareya* [Upaniṣad]: "He reflected: 'How indeed may this become great for me? The word "sākṣā" [means] the senses (*akṣāṇi*) and the bodies (*dehāḥ*).

The meaning is "distinguished by that. It is of such a nature. This is directly perceived by me, the witness; that is to say, it is the visible world along with its beginning. How could it exist for one who is great—that is, without me? The meaning is: in the absence of the light whose essence is my existence, how could it function? He explains how it entered [the body] with the words "having split open": this too is stated in that very same passage: "He, having split open this very suture, entered through this door. Here, the first half [of the verse] [is explained].
The intention is that the resolve to enter and the actual entry by another [deity] have been taught in succession. || 37 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that even the "entry" of the unattached Self is illogical; thus he raises the doubt:
"If it is unattached, how has it entered? Or else, tell me, how could there be creation for it?"
The illusory nature of both is equal, and the destruction of both is likewise the same. || 38 ||

"How did he enter?"—this objection is equally applicable to the process of creation as well; thus he says, "creation. Anticipating the argument that there is no fault because the creator of creation is illusory (māyika), he states this rebuttal: "illusoriness" applies equally to the questioner as well. He states that the reason for the illusoriness of these two is the same: "destruction. || 38 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding this, he raises an objection with the words "How? and so forth. He resolves it by means of a counter-objection (prati-baṇḍyā) with the words "Or, creation... and so forth. The reason for that is "illusoriness" (māyikatva). [This refers to] those two: entry and creation. || 38 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He cites the scriptural text which establishes that the form conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is perishable: "Consisting of nothing but pure consciousness, having arisen from these elements, one perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death."
The Eighth Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.
Having arisen from these elements, it perishes following them alone.
"For it is clear," Yājñavalkya said indeed to Maitreyī. (39)

"Having arisen": this Self, which is a mass of pure consciousness, having arisen from these limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the body, senses, and so forth—which are effects of the five elements and serve as causal conditions—and having attained the conceit of being a living individual (*jīva*), perishes along with those very bodies and so forth.

As those [elements] perish, one abandons the conceit of being a living being produced by them. The meaning is that Yājñavalkya spoke thus to Maitreyī regarding the perishability of the form characterized by limiting adjuncts (upādhi). || 39 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask, "How can there be the destruction of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is a reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*)? To this he says: "Having arisen... He spoke thus; that is to say, the Śruti declares: "Consisting of pure intelligence alone, having arisen from these elements, one perishes after them. || 39 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: By the scriptural statement, "Verily, O amiable one, this Self is indestructible, its nature is not subject to annihilation," the immutable (kūṭastha) is shown to be distinct from that [destruction]; thus he says:
"This Self is indestructible; thus the immutable has been clearly distinguished."
"Because of the mention of non-attachment in the phrase 'contact with the elements' (mātrāsaṃsarga).

Regarding the word "indestructible" (avināśī): he says "mātrā" etc., explaining that the scripture has stated non-attachment as the reason for its indestructibility in the passage, "But contact with the elements occurs for this [Self]. The meaning is: "elements" (mātrā) refers to the body and so forth because they are measured; the sense is that there is no contact of this Self with them. 40.

Commentary (a0): Having thus cited scripture regarding the appearance, he speaks regarding the immutable (kūṭastha) as well: "O Maitreyī, this Self is indeed imperishable, its nature is indestructible" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.14), and "But there occurs for it a connection with a series [of bodies]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.8). Such is the scriptural testimony of the Kāṇva and Mādhyandina recensions respectively. || 40 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might raise the objection that the scripture, stating "Verily, this [body] dies when deprived of the living soul; the living soul does not die," establishes the indestructibility of even this conditioned self.
Anticipating this, he states that this scriptural passage concerns the attainment of another body and does not intend to deny absolute destruction.
"Indeed, it is the body bereft of the living soul that dies; he [the soul] does not die."
In this context, "liberation" (vimokṣa) does not mean release, but rather movement to another world. || 41 ||
"Deprived of life" means devoid of life, that is to say, abandoned by the living principle (jīva). The meaning is that the living principle itself does not die. || 41 ||

Commentary (a0): Thus, he also brings the scriptural passage of that [text], "Verily, it is when devoid of the living self (jīva) that this dies; the living self does not die," into conformity with his own position—[stating] "the living self" (jīva). || 41 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "If the individual soul (jīva) were perishable, then the knowledge of identity with the imperishable Brahmana—namely, 'I am Brahman'—would not be possible. To this, he replies: "It is not so; for it would not perceive itself as 'I am not Brahman,' because it is perishable. This is not the case.
For grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is possible even when there is sublation [of one of the meanings]. || 42 ||

"If [it is argued]: 'I am not [Brahman]'—that perishable individual soul (jīva) would not perceive or know itself as Brahman in the form of Brahman, because there is a contradiction between the perishable and the imperishable being one"—[the author] replies: "Not that... (verse 42). Even in the absence of primary grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), coreferentiality is possible through sublation (bādhā); thus, by the sublation of the state of being an individual soul, the state of being Brahman can be understood. This is what he says: "Not that... (verse 42).
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [pages 326–326]
[The commentary on the *Kūṭasthadīpa*, verse 42: Even though this has been stated, fearing that non-difference remains unestablished, he provides the resolution: "No."]

Rāma’s Commentary: The author of the Vārttika has stated, along with an illustration, the manner in which the meaning of a sentence is understood through co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); he demonstrates this point by citing that very statement:
"This which is a post is a man, just as the cognition of a post [is sublated] by the cognition of a man."
By the cognition "I am Brahman," even the residual notion of "I" is sublated. || 43 ||
Just as in the sentence "This is a post," the notion of being a post is sublated by the cognition of it being a person— namely, "This post is a person"—
so too, by the realization "I am Brahman," the entire notion of "I" (the ego-sense), which takes the form "I am the agent" and so forth, is sublated. || 43 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, let it be granted that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible in the case of sublation (*bādhā*). However, in reality, how could the possibility of such coreferentiality—which is defined as the expression of a single meaning while possessing a single case-ending—be logically tenable in the case of sublation?

Even if it were somehow logically tenable, this would not be in accordance with our tradition (*sāṃpradāyika*), as seen in examples such as "This is that Devadatta" and "That art thou" (*tattvamasi*).

To pacify the doubt that all previous teachers have stated that non-difference alone constitutes grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in sentences, he cites and explains the words of the venerable Sureśvarācārya from the second chapter of the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi* using two verses beginning with "yo'yam" (this which...). [The verse reads: "By the cognition 'I am Brahman'... This refers to the statement of a reliable person (*āpta*), such as: "This which you call a post is indeed a person."

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: just as a post is sublated by the cognition of a man through a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇaka-puṃdhiyā*), so too the entire notion of "I" (*ahaṃbuddhi*), along with its very root, is sublated by the cognition "I am Brahman" (*brahmāsmi iti dhiyā*).

And thus, just as there is the aforementioned grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two words in the sentence "This is a man who is a post," there is likewise coreferentiality between the two words in the sentence "I am Brahman," provided that the sublation of the objective notion of "I" (*saviṣayakāhaṃdhīvādhā*) has indeed occurred through the cognition of Brahman. Only when this occurs is [the identity of] the person...
The sense is that it occurs as if there were a sublation of the cognition of a post by means of [the cognition of] a person. || 43 ||
This has also been clearly stated by the Teachers in the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi*.
Therefore, let it be that grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) has sublation as its meaning. || 44 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: "By Naiṣkarmya... and so forth. In this manner, as stated by the teachers, the authors of the Vārtikas, in the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi*, it has been clearly declared that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) has the sense of sublation (*bādha*). He states the conclusion: "Therefore, let that be so. For this reason, in the sentence "I am Brahman," let that coreferentiality have the sense of sublation; such is the meaning. || 44 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding the word *naiṣkarmya*: the meaning is that even by the venerable author of the Vārttika, whose characteristics are described in the statement of the Teachers (*ācāryas*): “He who gathers the meaning of the scriptures, establishes others in right conduct, and practices it himself—he is remembered as an *ācārya*. The particle *api* serves to include agreement with his own previous statements. He concludes with the remainder of the verse beginning with *ataḥ*. That...
It has been stated that grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) occurs in the sense of contradiction. || 44 ||

"Just as there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the world and 'All is Brahman,' so too would there be grammatical coreferentiality between the individual soul (*jīva*) and 'I am Brahman. (45)
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that even so, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) based on sublation (*bādha*) is never observed in the Śrutis.
Anticipating this doubt, he says—"All this is Brahman"—pointing out that since coreferentiality based on sublation is indeed observed in that passage, it will likewise occur here. || 45 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Granted that such may be the case according to the view of the Vārtikakāra, who maintains the theory of appearance (ābhāsa); however, this is not accepted in the view of the venerable Bhagavatpāda, the author of the Bhāṣya. In response to this expectation, [the author] cites the Māṇḍūkya Śruti: "All this is indeed Brahman," and so forth. All this which exists... [[page 327-to-327]]
The Eighth Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.

He provides the resolution—“All is Brahman”—stating that this must necessarily be accepted even by them, because in the *Kāṇva* Śruti, [the self] is described as having no other destination (*gatyaṃtararāhityena*). The word “in the sense of sublation” (*bādhāyām*) is to be supplied. || 45 ||
The view that grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) has the purpose of sublation (bādha) has been refuted.
This is stated with effort in the commentary, with the intention of explaining the immutable one. || 46 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: "In that case, why did the teachers of the Vivaraṇa reject the co-referentiality with the sublated [object]?
Anticipating this doubt, he says—referring to the phrase "of the co-referentiality"—that it is because the teachers intended the immutable (kūṭastha) by the word "I. || 46 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): [Objection: Even so, the contradiction with the *Vivaraṇa* text remains as it was, for in that work, the view that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) signifies sublation (*bādha*) has been diligently refuted through an extensive discussion. [Reply: This is not so; because in the sentence "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*), the Master of the *Vivaraṇa* intends only the state of being the immutable witness (*kūṭasthatva*) in the inner self (*pratīci*), which is the referent of the word "I" (*ahaṃpadārtha*) once purified as the individual soul (*jīva*) and characterized by witness-hood.

Since it is appropriate for those who maintain the theory of reflection (*pratibimba*) that [the relationship] is indeed one of suchness (*tathātva*), and since the non-contradiction between the theories of appearance (*ābhāsa*) and reflection has already been established in the thirty-third verse, the author indicates this by saying "of the grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyasya*). The literal meaning of the words, however, is quite clear. || 46 ||
