That which is the purified meaning of the term "thou" (tvaṃpada), the immutable, attains the nature of Brahman.
Regarding its explanation, it has been stated thus in that [work] and elsewhere as well. || 45 ||

"Refined" (śodhita) means that which is the referent of the term *tvaṃ* (thou), distinguished from the intellect and so forth, and which is the immutable (*kūṭastha*) whose characteristics will be described hereafter.

The meaning is that, in order to declare its identity with Brahman—that is, its identity with Brahman characterized by truth and so on—the primary co-referentiality (*mukhya-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) has been stated in the *Vivaraṇa* and other works, preceded by the refutation of co-referentiality based on sublation (*bādhā-sāmānādhikaraṇya*). || 47 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Clarifying that very point and extending the method of resolving the contradiction mentioned to other texts such as the *Bhāmatī*, he says: "purified," etc. (47).
The commentary (Rāmatīrtha) states the purpose: now, in order to make possible the identity of the *kūṭastha* with Brahman, that which is intended by the term *kūṭastha* is described:
"Of the illusory appearance of the individual soul (*jīvābhāsa-bhrama*), which is associated with the body, senses, and so forth..."
This very consciousness as the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna-citi) is intended here as the immutably stable (kūṭastha). || 48 ||

"Deha" (body), etc.; by the word "etcetera," the mind and so forth are included. Thus, the meaning is that the foundational consciousness—the underlying reality (*adhiṣṭhāna-caitanya*)—of the illusory appearance of the individual soul (*jīvābhāsa-bhrama*), which consists of the illusory appearance of consciousness (*cidābhāsa-rūpa-bhrama*) and is associated with the body, senses, and so forth, as well as the two bodies, is what is intended here in the Vedāntas as the "immutable" (*kūṭastha*). || 48 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, even if there is no contradiction with this view, one might ask: "In this present context of the theory of reflection (ābhāsavāda), what kind of entity is intended by the terms 'immutable' (kūṭastha) and 'Brahman'? To this, he replies with two verses in sequence beginning with "dehendriya... (verse 48).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the meaning of the word "Brahman":
"That which is declared to be the substratum of the entire illusion of the world."
Therefore, in this context within the Vedāntas, that which is intended by the word "Brahman" would be that very thing. (49)

Regarding the word "jagat": the meaning is that the consciousness which has been described in the Vedāntas as the substratum for the conceptualization of the entire universe is what is intended here by the term "Brahman. || 49 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 328.
[The commentary on the verse titled *Kūṭasthadīpa*]:

Regarding the phrase "of the world-tree" (*jagadrūpasya*), the mention of "the three Vedas" (*tryanteṣu*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes all the Upaniṣads investigated within the *Śārīraka[-mīmāṃsā]*. As for those [Upaniṣads] not so investigated, their purpose is fulfilled precisely through the method of inquiry set forth therein; such is the general direction. || 49 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that it is untenable to say that consciousness is the immutable substratum of the individual soul's delusion, because the superimposed nature of the individual soul has not been established.
Anticipating this doubt, he establishes its status as a superimposition by means of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) logic:
And when the world is superimposed upon this very consciousness, [it appears].
At that time, what need is there to speak of its single part, the reflection of the individual soul? || 50 ||

Regarding the phrase "in this": the fact that [the Self] constitutes a single part of the world is established by such scriptural passages as "having entered with this living self" (jīvenānupraviśya). || 10 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that even if this were so in reality, the identity of consciousness (*cidaikya*) stated in such passages as "That thou art" would not be tenable due to the distinctions between the respective superimposed objects (*āropya*). Anticipating this doubt, he provides the resolution: "In this very [one]" (*etasminneva*). The meaning is: in the previously mentioned Brahman-consciousness. || 50 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection may be raised: since the consciousness that is the substratum of the universe is one, there is no difference between the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam*;
thus, the two terms would be redundant. Anticipating this, he states that while their difference is due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), their identity is real:
"The world is a part of That [the Self], owing to the distinction of the superimposed."
The referents of the words "That" and "Thou" are distinct, yet in reality, there is oneness of consciousness.
"Jagat" (the world). That which has the designations "the world" and "a part thereof" as its superimposed [object] is thus described. The singular number is used in the sense of a class (*jāti*). 51.
Commentary (Ṭīkā): He states the conclusion: "The world," etc. (Verse 51).

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Since the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) is not observed to possess the attributes of both the substratum and the superimposed object—unlike the case of silver in mother-of-pearl and similar examples—how can it be considered a superimposition?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The attributes of the intellect, such as agency and the rest, as well as the nature of the Self known as 'manifestation' (sphūrti)..."
Because an appearance manifests before one while [the object] is being held, there may arise an illusion. || 52 ||

"Agent-hood and so forth" means that [the Self], while bestowing its own nature—which is characterized by pure luminosity—upon agent-hood, enjoyer-hood, knower-hood, and the like, which are superimposed through the medium of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as growth, shines clearly before one and appears manifest; therefore, the meaning is that the "appearance" is imagined (*kalpita*). || 52 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that it is untenable to state that the individual soul (*jīva*), which is a reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) and constitutes a single part of the universe, possesses the nature of being superimposed (*adhyasta*); for in that case, the appearance of a conflation between a real and an unreal entity would be impossible. To this, he says: "agency and so forth.
By the word "before" (*purataḥ*), its perceptibility by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi*) is indicated. || 52 ||
To the question, "What is the cause of this delusion? he says [in the Rāmatīrtha commentary]: "It is the lack of thorough knowledge of the true nature of the intellect (buddhi) and so forth."
What is the intellect? What is this appearance? Or what is the self? And how does the world exist?
Thus, from this lack of ascertainment comes delusion; this very thing is what is intended by the term "saṃsāra. || 53 ||
"What is this intellect? To show that it must be eliminated because it is a cause of misfortune, he says: "This very [intellect]... (13).
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, even if this is so, one might ask: what is the root of this currently experienced saṃsāra? To this, he says: "What is the intellect? (verse 53).
He who discriminates the true nature of intellect and the other faculties is a knower of reality.
"He alone is liberated"—this is the definitive conclusion in the Vedāntas. || 54 ||
The Eighth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

329 Rāghavendra Ṭīkā: In response to the inquiry as to what is the means of turning [the mind] away from this [bondage], the author intends to show that the very discernment of the true nature of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other faculties is the means of cessation.
He states that one who possesses such discernment is indeed a man of knowledge (*jñānī*), and from that alone follows the cessation of all misfortune: "Of the intellect... (verse 14).
Commentary (a0ṭīkā): If this is so, then how is the abandonment of this saṃsāra achieved? In response to this expectation, he summarizes the means for that:
"of the intellect and the rest" (buddhyādīnām) || 54 ||
And this being the case, such fallacious arguments as "To whom would there be bondage? and so forth [would arise].
This mockery must be firmly shattered by means of refutations and arguments.

Rāma’s Commentary (rā0 ṭī0): Since bondage and liberation are thus rooted in non-discrimination (*aviveka*), the specific derisive remarks made by logicians (*tārkika*)—such as "In the doctrine of non-duality (*advaitavāda*), whose is bondage, or whose is liberation?"—which are based on fallacious reasoning, must be refuted by demonstrating their logical untenability through the arguments stated in the *Khaṇḍana*. Thus he says: "In this way... (verse 55).
Commentary (a0): Now, even so, it is indeed beyond dispute that the appearance (*ābhāsa*) consists of a confluence of two entities, the real and the unreal.

If that were the case, because it would possess reality by virtue of its real component, it could not be entirely false; consequently, this would result in the doctrine of reflection (*pratibimbavāda*). To avoid that [conclusion], [the following is stated].
"In delusions, only that which is superimposed manifests, and nothing else manifests in any way whatsoever;
for the nature of a rope, a piece of mother-of-pearl, or the earthiness of a mirage is not perceived [as such] due to [the perception of] oneness and so forth"—
according to the manner stated in this verse from the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*, one must accept that even the manifestation appearing as delimited by its own substrate is indeed false (*mithyā*).

If you argue that there would be a contradiction with the definition of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) indicated in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*—namely, "having coupled together the real and the unreal"—then, wishing to quell the doubt of the student, [the author] states that the derisive remarks made by bad logicians (such as: "Since bondage itself does not exist in the non-dualist view, for whose sake should the scripture be commenced for the purpose of liberation through the knowledge of reality? must be refuted by the very arguments stated by the author of the *Khaṇḍana*, the venerable Harṣamiśra.

To this he says: "And thus," etc. There, one who speaks as follows—"the doctrine of non-duality," and so forth—must be refuted by the opponent in this way: "As for you who ask [this question]. If it is asked, "Why?", [the answer is: because from your own perspective alone, duality appears due to the impossibility of explaining the question otherwise. From my perspective, however: "There is no teacher, no scripture, no disciple, no instruction, neither you, nor I, nor this phenomenal world; there is only the realization of one's true nature, which cannot tolerate conceptual construction."
"Only Śiva remains; I am the Absolute"—such is the intended meaning of the *Daśaślokī*. The detailed exposition, however, is found in the *Khaṇḍana* itself. || 55 ||
It abides as the witness of both the mental modification and the prior non-existence of that modification.
Likewise, when there is a desire to know, there is the appearance "I am ignorant," which is the object of ignorance. || 56 ||

Rāma’s Commentary (rā0 ṭī0): Having thus distinguished the immutable Self from the intellect and other faculties through both scripture and reasoning, he states—in the three verses beginning with "vṛtteḥ"—that this same discrimination has also been established in the Purāṇas. When modifications such as desire arise, He is their witness; prior to the emergence of those modifications, He is the witness of their antecedent non-existence; when there is a desire to know, He is the witness of that inquiry; and prior to that, He is the witness of the thought "I am ignorant."
And by being the witness of the ignorance that is thus being experienced, Śiva alone remains. || 56 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): To show that this immutable one (*kūṭastha*) is established not only in the Śrutis and other scriptures, but is also well-known in the Purāṇas, he cites three verses from the *Śaiva Purāṇa*, beginning with "vṛtteḥ" and so forth. Regarding the word "vṛtti":

here, by the term "prior non-existence of modification" (*vṛttiprāgabhāva*), what is indicated is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) itself, which is the material cause (*upādāna*) of modifications. The phrase "ajño'smi" (I am ignorant) is the division [of the verse]. Thus is the experience—

Such is the meaning. Regarding the word "ābhāsa" (appearance): it refers to that entity called ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is qualified by appearance and manifests through the relation of objectivity (*viṣayatā-sambandha*).
The term "as witness" (*sākṣitayā*) is to be connected with every instance [in the preceding verses]. || 56 ||
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
titled "The Lamp of the Immutable" (*Kūṭasthadīpa*).
For one who is entirely insentient, however, there is no truth at all, even in the act of bowing.
He is of the nature of consciousness as the means of accomplishment, because he is eternally the object of love. || 57 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: And He is real because He is the substratum and the locus of this unreal world; He is of the nature of consciousness because He is the illuminator that brings about the manifestation of everything insentient; and He is of the nature of bliss because He is eternally the object of love. || 17 ||
Commentary on verse a0: "Asatyā" (unreal) and so forth; "always love," etc., connects with what follows. || 17 ||
He is of the nature of bliss, by virtue of being the accomplisher of all goals.
He who possesses all relationships is complete and is designated as Śiva. || 58 ||

Rāma’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Because He illuminates all objects and is thus connected with everything, He is called "Complete" (saṃpūrṇa). Here, this is the intended meaning: Śiva, who is the subject of dispute, is distinct from mental modifications (vṛtti) and the like, because He is the witness (sākṣin) of those modifications and so forth; for whatever is not distinct from mental modifications and the like is not the witness of those modifications and the like, just as the modifications themselves are. Furthermore, Śiva must be real, because He is the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) of that which is illusory, whereas that which is unreal—such as the silver [mistaken for mother-of-pearl]—is not [the substratum].

Like mother-of-pearl as the substratum [of silver]. The subject under dispute is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), because it is the illuminator of that which is purely insentient (*jaḍamātra*); for whatever is not of the nature of consciousness does not illuminate the insentient, such as a jar or the like. The subject under dispute is of the nature of supreme bliss (*paramānandarūpa*), because it is the object of supreme love; for whatever is not of the nature of supreme bliss is not the object of supreme love, such as a jar or the like. The subject under dispute is all-pervasive (*paripūrṇa*), because it is related to everything, like space.

And its being related to everything is disputed because it accomplishes all objects. [Thesis: It possesses relations with everything, because it illuminates everything. [Reason: Whatever does not possess relations with everything is not an illuminator of everything, such as a lamp or similar objects. || 58 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): It gladdens (ānandeti). For this very reason, it was stated at the very beginning of the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*: "It has a nature opposed to the unreal and the inert; it is not limited by space, time, or object; and it is opposed to bondage and suffering," and so forth. || 18 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the purport of the cited Purāṇic passage:
"Thus, in the Śaiva Purāṇas, the immutable (kūṭastha) has been clearly discerned."
Śiva is devoid of being the soul, the lord, and so forth; he is absolute and self-luminous.

Regarding the word *iti*: the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: in this manner—in such works as the *Sutasamhitā* and other Purāṇas—the immutable Śiva, who is devoid of conceptual constructions such as being the individual soul (*jīva*) or the Lord (*īśvara*), who is absolute, non-dual, self-luminous, self-manifesting, and of the nature of consciousness, has been discerned. ||59||

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on A0: He concludes the aforementioned point with the word "iti" (thus). Regarding the term "śaiva": these are the *Skanda-sūta-saṃhitā*, the *Vāyu-purāṇa*, and others, which are "śaiva" because they establish Śiva as the preeminent principle. The word "iti" and so forth serve the purpose of concluding the section. || 59 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Anticipating the question of why [the Self] is devoid of being the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśa), and so forth, he states that this is because scripture demonstrates that those two are products of Māyā:
"Because of the scriptural statement: 'By the manifestation of Māyā, He creates the individual soul and the Lord.'"
The individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) are indeed both illusory; they are like a crystal jar [reflecting the light of the sun].

Regarding the term "māyā": the sense is that the scripture stating, "Māyā and Avidyā become [the cause] by means of the manifestation as the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa)," establishes the illusory nature (māyikatva) of the two consciousness-reflections (cidābhāsa) that are dependent upon Māyā and Avidyā. Anticipating the objection that if these two were illusory, there would be no distinction between them and the body and so forth, [the author replies: just as there is a distinction between a glass jar and other jars despite the lack of difference in their being composed of earth, such a distinction may exist for these two as well.
To this he says: "Because they are pure" (svacchau). || 60 ||
Commentary (a0): The reason for the absence of the nature of being the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśa), and so forth, is "Māyā" (illusion). || 60 ||
The Eighth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
Just as the mind arises from the body through food, so too are those two.
Even though they are illusory, they have attained greater clarity than everything else.

331. Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Now, an objection may be raised: "It is appropriate that there be a difference between the jar and the potter due to the difference between the two specific types of clay used in their production; however, since Māyā—the cause of the distinction between the world, the individual soul (jīva), and the Lord (īśvara)—is one, it is inappropriate for there to be such a distinction between those two [the soul and the Lord] regarding the world. Anticipating this, [the author] says: "Just as in the case of the body and the mind, which are both produced..."
He states that it is likewise characterized by distinctness with the words "anyeti" (61).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: since those two [the intellect and the mind] are illusory and appear as beginningless, how can they possess clarity? To this, he says: "In this" (anneti). The meaning is that they are fully nourished by the connection with food, according to the Chāndogya Upaniṣad scripture: "For, my dear, the mind consists of food" (anna-mayaṃ hi somya manaḥ). || 61 ||
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Let it be that [the Self] possesses transparency like glass and so forth; but from what source does its consciousness (cittva) arise?
Anticipating this objection, he says—on the basis of experience—that its nature as consciousness is to be admitted, because it manifests precisely as consciousness.
For Māyā, which possesses the power to conceive all things, there is nothing indeed that is difficult to accomplish.

Regarding the phrase "of the nature of consciousness" (*cidrūpa*): having raised the doubt that even manifestation as the nature of consciousness is impossible for the two [Māyā and Śuddhavidyā] which are illusory (*māyika*), he states—beginning with "all"—that it is possible because [the Power of Māyā] performs what is difficult to accomplish (*durghaṭakāritva*). || 62 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, even if this is so, how can those two possess the nature of consciousness? To this he says: "But the nature of consciousness... Even so, the reason is: "all... (verse 62).
Even our sleep creates the individual soul and the Lord, both sentient, moving through the sky.
"Mahāmāyā creates these two; what is there to wonder at in this for you? (63)
Rāma’s Commentary: He strengthens the stated point by means of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) logic—“asmad... || 63 ||
He establishes this with the commentary: "Our... (63).

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that if Īśvara were also of the nature of māyā, he would be subject to non-omniscience and other such defects just like the individual soul (jīva), [the author] states that even omniscience and the rest will be merely projected by māyā:
"Having projected omniscience and the rest in the Lord, it manifests them."
If she must postulate a substratum (dharmin), what burden is there in postulating a property (dharma)? (64)
Regarding the term "omniscience," he states the proof for it there: "the substratum" (dharmiṇam) || 64 ||
— Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, if it is the case that Māyā alone is the fashioner of the Lord, then she too, like the individual soul (jīva), would be subject to delusion;
to this he replies: "And omniscience, etc. By "etc.," omnipotence is included. The word "and" (ca) serves to aggregate what was stated previously.

Now, one might object: "Since scripture states that *māyā* is of the nature of darkness (*tamas*) and so forth, how can the attribution of omniscience and other qualities be possible for the Lord, who possesses her as his own nature which is essentially veiling?
To this, he says: "The substratum... (verse 64).
— Rāghavendra’s Commentary — Now, one might raise the objection: "But would it not follow that the immutable (kūṭastha) is also illusory, just like the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)?
To this he replies: "If you think there should be such an excessive doubt regarding the immutable, let no such doubt be entertained."
But there is indeed no evidence for its being immutable or illusory. (35)
Regarding the claim that [the self] is "immutable" (kūṭastha), he refutes it by stating that such is not the case due to a lack of authoritative evidence—lest this be over-exaggerated. || 65 ||
Commentary (a0): Nor should it be argued that, in that case, she alone might imagine even the immutable (kūṭastha); for there is a lack of authoritative evidence (prāmāṇyābhāvāt).
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, Part 1:
[The Section Entitled] Kūṭasthadīpa (The Lamp of the Immutable)

But since the assumption of a *jīva* and so forth is stated by the Śruti itself, he says: "Even in the case of the *kūṭastha*. The particle *hi* is used for emphasis. The syntactical connection is: "there is simply no means of valid knowledge [for such an assumption]. || 65 ||
All the Vedantas proclaim its reality.
In this world, there is no other object that rivals the nature of a rival.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that although the immutable (kūṭastha) is real, no means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) is found for it, he states that all the Vedas (śrutis) indeed constitute such a means: "The state of being the Reality" (vastutvam). The meaning here is that when the ultimate reality of the immutable is established, it does not tolerate any other entity as its opposite. || 66 ||

On the contrary, all the Vedāntas establish that its ultimate reality alone is true, while everything else distinct from it—namely, the entire range of the perceptible—is sublated; thus he says: "The state of being a real entity," etc. "With a rival," etc.; the meaning is that it acts as an enemy to the establishment of the true nature of the immutable (kūṭastha).
We clarify the meaning of the Śruti; we do not rely on anything whatsoever derived from mere logic.
Tell me, what occasion is there here for the doubts of logicians? (67)

Rāma’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "In establishing the reality of the immutable Self (kūṭastha) and the unreality of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), only the scriptures (śrutis) are cited;

nothing at all is established by means of reasoning (tarka). Anticipating this doubt, he states—beginning with the words "the meaning of the scripture"—that there is no introduction of reasoning because his purpose is to clarify the meaning of the scriptures for those seeking liberation (mumukṣus). || 67 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, it has been stated that all the Vedāntas, being inherently unable to tolerate any duality whatsoever that contradicts the realization of non-dual, immutable consciousness, teach that [truth] in such a manner to those seeking liberation. This is incorrect; for the aforementioned teaching itself depends upon the duality of teacher and disciple, and even after the teaching has occurred, as long as the *ārabdha* (projected karma) remains in the case of the doctrine of *jīvanmukti*, duality persists for Śuka and others even in their state of liberation.

Anticipating the objection that non-duality is perceived as perfectly stable by those such as Śamada and others, he provides the resolution with the words "the meaning of the scripture" (śrutyartha). The connection [of the sentence] is: "We do not clarify even the slightest thing whatsoever through reasoning. In this context, the reading "vacmi" (I speak) is indeed a corruption. || 67 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
Therefore, having abandoned fallacious reasoning, one who desires liberation should take refuge in the Śruti.
In the Śruti, however, it is demonstrated that Māyā creates both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa). || 68 ||

"Therefore" [is said]. He explains what kind of meaning of the Śruti those seeking liberation (mumukṣu) should contemplate: "In the Śruti," and so forth. In the Śrutis, the illusory nature (māyikatva) of both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) [is taught]. 68.
Commentary (a0ṭīkā): Let this be the resolution for the opponent; but how is it for one seeking liberation?
To that he says, beginning with "Therefore" (tasmāt), etc. || 68 ||
The creation, beginning with the act of looking and ending with the entry [into the egg], is performed by the Lord.
The cycle of worldly existence, beginning with the waking state and ending with liberation, has the individual soul as its agent.

Rāma’s Commentary: The Lord is the agent of the creation beginning with the act of seeing and ending with the entry [of the soul]; the individual soul (jīva) is the agent of the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra), characterized by waking, dreaming, deep sleep, bondage, and liberation. || 69 ||
Commentary on verse a0: "Īkṣaṇādi" (beginning with seeing) and so forth; this has already been explained previously. || 69 ||
He is indeed unattached and immutable; at all times, nothing whatsoever belongs to him.
"Therefore, let this excellence be considered as residing in the mind alone. (70)
1. "Let it be so," is the reading of Acyutarāya.
[Page 333] Eighth Chapter.
Accompanied by two commentaries.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Because the immutable (kūṭastha) is unattached and so forth, the entire collection of worldly transactions characterized by birth, death, and the like is non-existent.
And since this has been established, the intention is that one who desires liberation should always reflect upon this matter. || 70 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): "He is indeed without attachment" (asaṅga eva) up to "there arises an excellence" (bhavatyatiśayaḥ)—this is how it is to be construed as stated in the Śruti. He states the conclusion with the remainder of the verse beginning with "Therefore" (tena). || 70 ||
There is neither cessation nor arising, neither one who is bound nor one who practices for liberation.
Neither one who desires liberation nor one who is liberated—this is the ultimate truth.

Rāmānuja’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Anticipating the question, "From what is it understood that the immutable (kūṭastha) lacks such distinctions as birth and so forth?", and intending to show that it is from a scriptural statement, he recites that passage: "There is no cessation," and so on. || 71 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): What is to be investigated? He states this with the words beginning "No," etc., according to the Śruti itself. || 71 ||
The Śruti always seeks to make known that which is beyond the reach of speech and mind.
One should awaken [the disciple] by taking recourse either to the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśa), or even the universe (jagat). || 72 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: "In that case, for what purpose is the nature of the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), and so forth, set forth here and there in the Śrutis?
Anticipating this, he says—beginning with "Beyond speech and mind"—that it is for the sake of awakening [the understanding] of the Self, which is beyond the reach of speech and mind. || 72 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): If this is so, then why was it stated by you that [the Self] is "living" (jīva) and so forth? To this he says: "Beyond speech and mind" (avāṅmanasā).
He awakens—that is, he causes to understand—that which is of the aforementioned nature, the immutable (kūṭastha). || 72 ||
By whatever means there may arise in men an understanding of the inner self (pratyagātman).
"That very same process here would be correct," so it was stated by the Teacher. (73)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If the Reality is of a single nature and is to be understood through the Śrutis, why is contradiction seen among the Śrutis?

Anticipating this doubt, he says—beginning with the words *yayā yayā* (verse 73)—that there is no contradiction regarding the Reality itself; rather, the difference lies in the manner of its comprehension, which follows the diversity in the mental dispositions of the persons to be enlightened, as stated by Sureśvarācārya.
One.

Ghaṭa-a0 Ṭīkā: Now, if it is argued that the Śruti resorts to the duality of the individual soul (jīva) and so forth merely to awaken one to the fact that the immutable (kūṭastha) alone—which is beyond the reach of speech and mind—is ultimately real, let that be so according to the maxim of "the moon by way of its branch"; however, why is it that the Śruti itself does not establish its identity with that [immutable reality]?

It is not so stated; for instance, in the passage, "He creates through the appearance (*ābhāsa*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)," the doctrine of appearance (*ābhāsavāda*) is presented. As it is said: "Just as this one Sun, the light-soul, entering into various waters, appears divided in many forms according to its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), so too does this unborn, divine Self appear divided among the various fields (*kṣetra*). For the single Self of all beings is established in every being; though one, it is seen as manifold. Thus, it is indeed one.

"They are like the moon in water," and "He became the counterpart of every form"—in such passages, there is the theory of reflection (*pratibimbavāda*). "Just as when a jar is moved, the space enclosed within it is moved, yet the space [itself] is not moved; so too is the individual soul (*jīva*) comparable to space"—in this passage, there is the theory of limitation (*avacchinnavāda*). Since the Śruti itself contradicts itself in many ways through various statements such as these, which doctrine should one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) rely upon?

If it is asked, "What is to be accepted and what is to be rejected?"—the answer is no; for since the cognitions of individual souls (*jīva-buddhi*) are obstructed by various latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), each philosophical system (*vāda*) was taught in the Śruti in accordance with the respective intellect of those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). To illuminate that this is the intended meaning of the Śruti, as described by the venerable feet of Śrī Sureśvarācārya himself, he provides the resolution by reciting his *Vārttika*: "By whichever [method]... This refers to men who are seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*). The phrase "by whichever method" (*yayā yayā prakriyayā*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

"Pratyak" means that which shines forth exactly as it is by the very obstruction of duality. Furthermore, it is called the *ātman* because it attains (*āpnoti*), it takes up (*ādatte*), and it consumes (*atti*) objects here;
and because its existence is continuous (*saṃtata*), it is therefore termed the *ātman*.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 334.

Because of the statement "called the immovable lamp" (*kūṭasthadīpa*), it means that the object is non-dual Brahman, which is the purified referent of the word *tat* and is identical with the purified referent of the word *tvam*, characterized as the witness (*sākṣin*) and known as the "immovable" (*kūṭastha*). "Firm proficiency" (*vyutpatti*) means familiarity through indirect valid cognition (*parokṣapramā*). That very thing is the method (*prakriyā*).

The meaning is that in this non-dualistic (advaita) system, she is "virtuous" (*sādhvī*), in the sense that she is beneficial toward each respective qualified seeker (*adhikārī*). Thus, it means that this has been determined by the venerable feet of the teacher, the illustrious Vārtikācārya. Therefore, the intention is that there is not even a trace of any defect arising from a difference in methodological procedure (*prakriyābheda*) here. || 73 ||
Without having understood the entire purport of the Vedas, the dull-witted person wanders in delusion.
But the one possessed of discernment, having understood everything, abides in the ocean of bliss. || 74 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Having raised the objection—“If the meaning of the Śruti is of a single uniform nature, why is there disagreement among those who propound it?”—he states that disagreement exists only for those devoid of an understanding of the Śruti’s purport, but not for those who know it: “The purport of the Śruti... (verse 74).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "Even if the meaning of the Śruti is uniform in this way, why is there disagreement here among the dualists who themselves accept its authority? To this, he says: "The Śruti... and so on. Thus, the intention is that their extreme dullness of intellect, caused by the unseen impressions (*adṛṣṭa*) from previous births, is the very cause for their failure to understand the complete purport of the Śruti, and consequently, for their wandering in the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). By that merit accumulated over infinite births...

He briefly summarizes the distinction of the non-dualists (*advaitins*)—who are favored by the Lord, who follow the pure Vedic path, and who subsist upon the doctrine of the venerable teacher Śrī Bhagavatpāda—for the sake of the engagement of discerning seekers of liberation: "But the discerning one... The word *tu* ("but") indicates this distinction. The term *vivekin* ("the discerning one") suggests that discernment alone is the root of all spiritual means. The singular number serves to indicate the rarity of such qualified aspirants. [The ocean...]
By this word, his resemblance to Śrīkānta (the Beloved of Lakṣmī) is suggested. || 74 ||
Just as this cloud of illusion rains down the water of the world, so it is.
The established state is that for the space of consciousness there is neither loss nor gain. || 72 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Then, in response to the inquiry as to what the conviction of the discriminating person is like, he says: "Illusion... (verse 75).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "How can there be such internal certainty for the living-liberated (jīvanmukta) of the aforementioned nature—who possesses a bliss equal to that of the Beloved of Lakṣmī—even while the appearance of duality persists as long as prārabdha karma lasts? In response to this expectation, he summarizes that [certainty] by means of the metaphor of *māyā*. The word *iti* refers to the aforementioned form. The implicit meaning is that such a state—the established condition (*sthiti*)—of the living-liberated exists. || 75 ||
He who continuously contemplates this immovable lamp [of consciousness], [attains liberation].
He shines by himself, eternally, in the form of the immutable.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Lamp of the Immutable" (Kūṭasthadīpa), in the Pañcadaśī composed by the venerable Vidyāraṇya.
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the fruit of studying this work: "This... (verse 76).
Thus ends the *Kūṭasthadīpatātparyadīpikā*, composed by the scholar named Rāmakṛṣṇa, a servant of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Bhāratītīrtha Vidyāraṇya Muni. 8.

— Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, he describes the fruit of studying this work, beginning with the words "imam" (this). The meaning is that it "shines," that is, it is revealed. The rest, however, is quite straightforward. [Objection: But you stated at the outset: "If the Self is pure consciousness, then all means of knowledge such as perception..."

"...it would be cut asunder. Furthermore, by the verse beginning with "There is no such logical connection; this third obstacle here concerns the living self," the third obstacle called *prameyāsaṃbhāvanā* (the impossibility of the object of knowledge) regarding the knowledge of the meaning of the term *tattvamasi* as purified has been stated. Likewise, by the verse beginning with "Through various reasonings, non-contradiction has indeed been stated based on the discrimination of the purified living self; therefore, even in the eighth [chapter], why should there not be a focus on that [non-duality] through other means of knowledge?"—it is established.
The Eighth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

If it is asked how it is possible that even the destruction of the obstruction of doubt (*ruktapratibandhapradhvaṃsakatva*) is stated in this eighth chapter, titled "The Immutable Lamp" (*kūṭasthadīpa*), consider this:

by means of the indicators such as the introduction (*upakrama*) and so forth, this chapter [establishes] the removal of the impossibility regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*) concerning the purified meanings of the words *tattvamasi*.

Because of this [reason]. For example, here—beginning with: “Just as the sun’s light is reflected upon a wall illuminated by the sun, so the Lord, though eternally self-luminous, is illumined by the *jīva* residing in the intellect,” and concluding with “My *māyā* today,” etc.—therein, having pointed out the immutable (*kūṭastha*), attributeless Supreme Self (*paramātman*) itself as the illuminator of all duality indicated by the body, [the text] refers to that which has been purified by the term *cidākāśa*.

By reflecting upon [the Self] as non-different from the object and stating that "this world is my Māyā" and so forth—thereby declaring His status as the cause of the illusory universe—the Teacher has established that there is no contradiction with other means of valid cognition such as perception; thus, the removal of doubt regarding the impossibility of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is clearly accomplished. As it is said:
"Just as the reflection and Brahman are distinguished from the body externally, so too should the reflection and the immutable witness (*kūṭastha*) be distinguished within the physical form."
Thus: "The junctions and the absences of all mental modifications are manifested by that which is changeless; therefore, it is called the 'immutable' (kūṭastha).

In various contexts throughout the treatise, there is such repeated mention of the immutable. Likewise: "If it is argued that 'I am not Brahman' because [the self] is subject to destruction, that is not so; for grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is possible even when there is sublation [of the apparent meaning]. This refers to the pure individual soul known as the immutable.

The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—as in "the post is a man" (*sthāṇuḥ puruṣaḥ*)—is intended for the purpose of sublation (*bādha*) of the specific individual soul (*jīva*) known as the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), so that Brahman alone remains; this constitutes its novelty (*apūrvatā*). The result is that [the Self] is indeed unattached and immutable (*kūṭastha*), and so forth. The passage beginning with "The Self, having conceived the entry, is said to have entered" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). [And: "Because birth and death are experienced by the consciousness that has been doubled [by the intellect], that [intellect] is non-immutable, while the other [the Self] is different."
"The [Self] is that immutable and unchanging one," and so forth; such is the logical justification. Thus, there are six types of indicative marks. || 76 ||
Vam.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Lamp of the Immutable" (Kūṭasthadīpa), from the commentary on the *Pañcadaśī* by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Śrīmad-Vedavyāsa-Sarasvatī, known as Śrīmad-Dvaita-Saccidānanda-Bhāratī-Tīrtha-Mahāsvāmī.
This eighth [chapter] is complete. || 8 ||
This Kūṭastha-dvīpa is completed.
Now begins the ninth chapter of the Śrī Pañcadaśī, titled Dhyānadīpa.
Rāma’s Commentary: Having bowed to the lords of sages, Śrī Bhāratītīrtha and Vidyāraṇya;
I shall provide a concise commentary on the *Dhyānadīpa*.

In this Vedānta scripture, it has been established that for one who is endowed with the fourfold means— beginning with the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities— and who practices hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), liberation characterized by the state of Brahman arises through the immediate knowledge of the meaning of the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*), preceded by the discernment of the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam*. In that regard, even for one who has heard the Upaniṣads, due to some obstacle such as dullness of intellect or the like—
Desiring to demonstrate the meditations (*upāsanā*) that have liberation as their fruit by means of producing direct valid cognition regarding the object consisting of one's own self,
[the author] first asserts— along with an illustration— that liberation occurs even through meditation on the reality of Brahman:
"One is liberated even by meditation on the reality of Brahman, like a concordant error (*saṃvādibhrama*)."
Therefore, in the subsequent Tāpanīya [Upaniṣads], meditations based on scriptural revelation are presented in manifold ways.

"Consistent" (*saṃvādī*) means that just as one who acts upon a consistent error attains the intended object, so too through the meditation on the reality of Brahman, liberation characterized by the state of Brahman—which is the desired goal—is attained. To the question "What is the proof for this?", he says:
"In the subsequent [section]. Since liberation exists even through meditation, the meditation on the reality of Brahman is heard of in various ways in the *Tāpanīya Upaniṣad*.
The meaning is "having been spoken. || 1 ||
I bow to the Supreme Brahman, who is non-dual bliss, existence, consciousness, all-pervading, and eternally pure;
who, though the abode of the illusory net of duality arising from delusion, remains as the immutable essence and the self-luminous crest-jewel of the Vedas;
and to the assembly of all excellent teachers, the true Guru, the ornament of the Raghu dynasty, who is firmly established in Brahman.
I bow to my own guru, known as Śrīmannārāyaṇa, who is also named Mahādeva. || 1 ||
Having honored Jīvañjīva, Vidyāraṇya, and Bhāratītīrtha,
I shall clarify this *Dhyānadīpa* (Lamp of Meditation) by means of the *Ahni-prakāśa* commentary on the *Kaumudī*.

Now, the venerable teacher named Bhāratītīrtha, in the eighth chapter of the *Pañcadaśī* titled *Kūṭasthadīpa*, at the conclusion of the preceding section, stated with the verse: "He who constantly contemplates this *Kūṭasthadīpa* shines himself perpetually in the form of the immutable (*kūṭastha*)," thus declaring that for one possessed of constant contemplation of Brahman, the fruit in the form of liberation (*kaivalya*) is indeed attained.

Having first cultivated the fourfold means beginning with the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal, one approaches a teacher who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭha*). Then, having thoroughly practiced the Uttara-Mīmāṃsā consisting of four chapters— preceded by the *Bhāṣya* and its commentaries composed by the venerable Bhagavatpāda— through the processes of hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), and being freed from the five-fold obstacles, one attains through the great sentences (*mahāvākya*) such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) a most firm immediate realization (*aparokṣapramā*) born of inquiry.

Even though all duality has been sublated through the destruction of root ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*), as long as the *prārabdha* karma remains, it continues to appear like a mirage; however, after that [sublation],

it would be better than that to dwell in solitude and meditate upon one of the Saguna Brahman forms, such as Hari or Hara, during the time remaining after the performance of the duties of one’s own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*), preceded by the renunciation of all attachments until the fall of the body— having observed this thought of a certain disciple, he [the teacher]...

Desiring to compose this chapter entitled *Dhyānadīpa*, which primarily concerns the worship of the attributeless Self (*nirguṇa-ahaṃ-graha*), and wishing to indicate the auspiciousness consisting of the contemplation of the identity of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikya-anusaṃdhāna*)—which serves as both a well-known authority and a purpose—he [the author] indicates the subject matter as "the reality of Brahman. Although this is a chapter belonging to the non-dualistic (*advaita*) scriptures, the subject matter—the identity of Brahman and the Self—is presented specifically through its being known as the object of worship; and likewise, through the maturation of that worship of the liberated one, characterized by immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*), [he indicates] the body...
At the very moment of falling—
[page 337]— the ninth chapter.
Accompanied by two commentaries: "He for whom there is no ripened meditation here [in this life] is liberated after death or in the world of Brahmā, having realized the Reality."
Based on this statement, as well as the two Yoga Sūtras— "then the seer abides in his own nature" and "therein, wisdom is truth-bearing"—
one attains immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*), which consists in the destruction of ignorance along with its effects, through the direct realization (*aparokṣajñāna*) that "I am Brahman."

By stating that "one is liberated even through worship characterized by application" (*yojanatayopāstyā*), [the author] suggests—thereby indicating the relationship of the subject-matter and the expositor between the present context and the reality of Brahman as the Self delimited by the object of worship—and likewise illuminating the qualified seeker who desires liberation as previously described, he asserts with an illustration that liberation is attained through the aforementioned worship: "It is corroborated" (*saṃvādī*). In this regard, he establishes the necessity of this conclusion by citing scriptural authority itself: "In the subsequent [text]" (*uttara*).
The meaning is that this refers to the portion of the Upaniṣad known as the Nṛsiṃhottaratāpanīya. || 1 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To elaborate on what was stated as "like a consistent error," he recites the Vārttika that establishes the nature of a consistent error:
"For two people who run toward the light of a jewel and the light of a lamp, respectively, perceiving them both as jewels..."
Even though there is no distinction between false cognitions, there is a distinction with respect to their causal efficacy. (2)

Regarding the phrase "maṇipradīpe" (in the gem and the lamp): the analysis of the compound is as follows—*maṇiśca pradīpaśca maṇipradīpau*, [meaning] "the gem and the lamp"; *tayoḥ prabhe* [means] "the two lusters of those two," hence *maṇipradīpaprabhe*.

The cognition of a gem that occurs with respect to the luster of a gem and the luster of a lamp is indeed false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), because it is a cognition of something as being that which it is not.

Nevertheless, the cognition of a gem that occurs with respect to the luster of a gem is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāriṇī*), for a person who runs toward the object with the thought that it is a gem [obtains the gem].
The meaning is that there is a disparity in causal efficiency (arthakriyā), in that gain occurs for one [of the two] but not for the other. || 2 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that the aforementioned example for the term "concordant error" (*saṃvādibhrama*) has never been heard before; therefore, he clarifies it by means of the very Vārttika verse beginning with "maṇipradīpa... (verse 2).
Rāmānuja’s Commentary (Ṭīkā) explains the Vārtika: "The lamp exists within the inner chamber, while its light is outside."
Just as it is seen elsewhere at the door, so too is the luster of the gem observed.

By means of these three verses beginning with "A lamp within a chamber," [it is explained as follows]: In a certain mansion, a lamp stands within a chamber; its radiance is perceived outside at the doorway like a gem, appearing circular. Likewise, in another mansion, the radiance of a gem situated within a chamber is perceived outside at the doorway like the radiance of a lamp, yet it is not perceived as being equal to the gem itself. || 3 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) on verse a0 explains the aforementioned Vārtika with the three verses beginning with "dīpa": In a royal palace, two lamps are placed by the hundreds in a specific vessel known as a *jālī*— so called from the etymology "that which covers" (*apavṛṇoti*)— which is made of fine meshed silver or other materials, shaped like a jackfruit (*panasa*), and well-known in the Marathi language as *jālīdāra phāṇasa* or *jālīdāra kaṃdīla*, for the purpose of pacifying disturbances such as moths and the like.

This is well known among royal people. Therefore, "outside the door" (tatprabhā bahirdvāri) means in the area outside the doorway. It is seen; that is to say, by some person who is unaware [of its presence] at night due to the force of fate, it is perceived as if it were a self-luminous jewel, because its light has emerged through a particular opening in the lattice-work of the circular window mentioned earlier. Then, immediately thereafter, in another place such as a forest or a mine, the same applies to the radiance of that jewel, which is a gem possessing its own light.
Because it was surrounded by creepers and other growth, it appeared perfectly circular; yet, by chance, it was seen by a certain forest-dweller who had heard the story of his own radiant jewel.
Seeing them from afar exerting their power, he ran toward them, perceiving them to be jewels.
In the case of the luster [of a gem], however, the notion that it is a jewel is a false cognition for both parties. (4)

Rāma’s Commentary: Regarding the word "dūre" (from afar): having seen such a pair of radiance from a distance, two men run forward with the cognition, "This is a gem; this is a gem. The knowledge of the gem arising in both of them regarding that radiance is indeed merely erroneous. || 4 ||
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya, [the commentary on the chapter titled] *Dhyānadīpa*,
verse 4: "From afar" (*dūrāt*) means from a great distance.
The jewel cannot be obtained by one who runs toward the light of a lamp.
By running toward the light, the jewel of the gem will certainly be found.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Nevertheless, just as a man running after the light of a lamp while thinking it to be a gem does not find the gem, one who runs after the light of a gem while thinking it to be the gem would certainly find the gem. || 5 ||
a0 Commentary: "Not" [is the answer]; it should be construed as "in the light of the gem. || 5 ||
Rāmatīrtha’s Commentary: Let it be so; what relevance does this have to the present subject? To this he says:
"The error of mistaking a gem for the light of a lamp is known as a non-corresponding delusion (visaṃvādibhrama)."
The error consisting of the mistaken perception of a jewel in the luster of a jewel is called a "corresponding error" (saṃvādibhrama).
Regarding "lamp-light": that error which occurs when lamp-light is mistaken for a gem is known by the learned as a "non-corresponding error" (*visaṃvādibhrama*).

However, the cognition of a gem that occurs regarding the luster of a gem is called a "corresponding error" (*saṃvādibhrama*), because it possesses the causal efficacy characterized by the acquisition of the gem. This is the meaning. || 6 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, he states the resultant nature of erroneous cognition (*bhrānti*) that is either non-concordant (*visaṃvādin*) or concordant (*saṃvādin*), beginning with the words "dīpa" and so forth. The analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is: "the error of [perceiving] a gem in the light of a lamp," and so on. || 6 ||
He demonstrates this:
[Rāmānuja’s Commentary]— having thus shown a concordant error regarding the object of perception, he now shows it regarding the object of inference as well.
Having perceived the vapor as smoke, one infers the presence of embers therein.
Fire obtained by chance is considered a "concordant error" (saṃvādibhrama). || 7 ||

Regarding the term "vapour": suppose a person, standing in a certain place, mistakes vapour for smoke; having inferred that the region at its source possesses fire because of the presence of smoke—namely, "this region has fire because it has smoke"—and proceeds toward it, if by chance fire is indeed perceived there, then the cognition of smoke regarding what was actually vapour is considered a "concordant error" (*saṃvādibhrama*). || 7 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, having described [the case of] perceptual error that is subsequently confirmed, he speaks of similar cases regarding inference and scripture as well, by means of the three verses beginning with "vāṣpam" (steam). In the winter season and so forth, the steam perceived in the morning upon a body of water is well known as "vāṣpa," a term established in common usage.
This is an illustrative instance; it also includes a mass of dust which causes the delusion of smoke. "Yadṛcchayā" means accidentally or unexpectedly. || 7 ||

Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: He also shows that [the same applies] regarding the subject of sacred scriptures: "Considering the water of the Godāvarī to be the water of the Gaṅgā for the sake of purification..."
Having been sprinkled with water, it attains purity; this is considered a "corresponding error" (saṃvādibhrama). || 8 ||

Regarding the phrase "the water of the Godāvarī": the fact that even the water of the Godāvarī is a cause of purification is established by scripture; therefore, purification certainly occurs through sprinkling it as well.
Nevertheless, the notion that the water of the Godāvarī is the water of the Gaṅgā is nothing but an error. || 8 ||
Commentary (ṭīkā): Regarding the word "Godāvarī," the phrase "having considered [it] from the Purāṇas" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 8 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states another illustration:
"One who has fallen into a life-threatening fever, remembering Nārāyaṇa through delusion..."
One who dies [there] attains heaven; this is considered a "corresponding error" (saṃvādibhrama).
The Ninth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

"Attained by fever": a person who has reached a state of *sannipāta* (a critical derangement of the humors) may, even without the knowledge that "this remembrance of Nārāyaṇa is the means for my attainment of heaven," remember Nārāyaṇa as an ordinary person— just like a physician or others— under the influence of the delusion induced by the *sannipāta*, and thus die.

From such statements in the Purāṇas as, "One certainly attains heaven [by remembering Him]," "Hari removes sins even when remembered by those whose minds are merely directed toward Him," and "When Ajāmila, though a sinner, called out 'Nārāyaṇa' at the time of death while addressing his son, he attained liberation," it is clear that even here, the knowledge that the name Nārāyaṇa was the name of one's son is nothing but delusion. || 9 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding the phrase "by fever" (jvareṇa): since he had fallen into a state of *saṃnipāta* (a critical derangement of the humors), the connection is that it was "due to delusion" (*bhrāntyā*). "Remembering" (*smaran*) means reciting [the name].

For this very reason, he went to heaven (*svarga*), but not to Vaikuṇṭha. By this, it is illuminated that even though one remembers the Saguna-Nārāyaṇa with full attention at the time of death—as per such Smṛti texts as "remembering Nārāyaṇa at the end"—one indeed goes to Vaikuṇṭha. This too is merely an illustration, because [the attainment of Vaikuṇṭha] is accessible through the Śāstra alone. || 9 ||
Within the domain of perception, inference, and likewise scripture, [there is no contradiction].
Indeed, by the logic already stated, there are millions of concordant errors (saṃvādibhrama). || 10 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Thus, by means of these three examples of concordant error, he states the established conclusion: "Of perception," etc. (10).
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He extends this [principle] to other examples as well with the words "of perception" (pratyakṣasya). || 10 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He strengthens the stated point by demonstrating a sublation in the case of the opposite view:
"Otherwise, how could clay, wood, and stone be deities?"
Or else, how could women and the like be objects of worship through the cognition of them as fire and so forth? (11)

"Otherwise" means that, in the absence of a concordant error (*saṃvādibhrama*), clay and other such materials would not be worshipped as deities for the sake of attaining results, because they lack deityhood by their own nature. He states another objection: "Because of being fire," etc. In the *Pañcāgnividyā*, it is said:
"Woman, O Gautama, is indeed fire; man, O Gautama, is indeed fire; earth, O Gautama, is indeed fire; Parjanya, O Gautama, is indeed fire... [and so forth].

The meaning is that meditations such as those expressed in the passage beginning, "The heavenly world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire," which consist of viewing the woman, the man, the earth, the rain-cloud, and the heavenly world as fires, would not have the attainment of the world of Brahman as their fruit. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), passages such as "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" and "The sun is the instruction of Brahman" are included. || 11 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Therein, he establishes presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) as a means of valid cognition with the words "otherwise... and "clay...". "Deities" refers to the gods residing within the specific forms of earthen objects such as the Jagannātha Liṅga and the Śālagrāma. This is well-known from the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, in passages such as, "Woman, O Gautama, is indeed fire. || 11 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, for the sake of ease of understanding, he demonstrates concisely the "corresponding error" (saṃvādibhrama) established through many treatises:
"From a cognition that does not correspond to reality, the desired fruit is obtained."
This is called a "concordant error" (saṃvādibhrama), occurring by chance, like the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit.

"Non-conformity with reality" (ayathāvastu) means as follows: because of a cognition that does not correspond to reality—whether it be a prescribed or an unprescribed cognition—that is, a contrary cognition—the desired or longed-for result is obtained by chance, through the course of destiny; this is the meaning of "concordant error" (saṃvādibhrama). || 12 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, concluding the discussion on veridical error thus established, the author provides a concise definition for the sake of intellectual ease: "ayathā... (not as it is). The meaning is: "even from knowledge consisting of error. The absence of the *saṃdhi* (euphonic combination) in the phrase "labhyeta īpsitam" is intended by the author himself. || 12 ||
1. "labhyeta" is the reading of Acyutarāya.
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
titled "The Lamp of Meditation" (*Dhyānadīpa*),
shows how even one's own delusion, when it accords with reality, yields the perfect fruit.
Likewise, even the meditation upon the reality of Brahman bestows the fruit of liberation.

Rāma’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "How can the meditation on Brahman—which has as its object that which is not the actual state of reality—bestow the fruit of liberation, which is to be accomplished through perfect knowledge?
Anticipating this doubt, he says, "Itself an error," just like a concordant delusion (saṃvādibhrama). || 13 ||
Now, the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* commentary: Having thus established the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), he applies it to the subject of the proposition (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "himself" (*svayam*).
[This refers to the state] of one liberated by means of numerous scriptural passages such as: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey. And so forth.

If it is argued that since [liberation] is achievable solely through the knowledge of the non-dual Self (*advaitātma-jñāna*), how can it be said in the cited illustration that it is achievable through meditation (*upāsanā*) in the interim? We say no, because of a failure to understand the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of that passage; for by that very example, it is clearly demonstrated that [meditation] effects the desired goal by means of knowledge. Indeed, one who runs toward the luster of a gem with the thought that it is the gem itself does not obtain the gem simply by reaching its vicinity if the gem is absent there. Therefore, [the goal is] the Nirguṇa...

The sense is that it is entirely logical that even through the worship of the "I-grasping" (nāhaṃgraha-upāsanā), which consists of the constant contemplation "I am Brahman," one whose all obstacles have been removed thereby attains from that very Great Saying (mahāvākya) the immediate, direct realization of the non-dual Self; and thus he attains liberation in the form of the instantaneous destruction of ignorance along with its entire sphere of effects. || 13 ||

1. Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Now, an objection is raised: Is meditation performed after knowing the reality of Brahman, or without knowing it? In the first case, meditation is redundant, since the knowledge that is the means to liberation already exists. In the second case, because the object is not fully understood, meditation itself is not possible. Thus [the objection stands].
What did he say?
From the Vedāntas [he learned] that the reality of Brahman consists of an undivided, single-flavored essence.
Having understood this indirectly, they worship it with the thought, "I am this. || 14 ||

"From the Vedāntas," etc. This is the intended meaning: since the direct realization (*aparokṣajñāna*) of the identity of Brahman and the Self—which is the means to liberation—has not yet arisen, meditation is not useless; for Brahman, though known through the scriptures only as something indirect (*parokṣa*), remains an object of meditation. || 14 ||
Commentary (a0): He elaborates on this very point with the words "From the Vedāntas," and so forth. "They worship" means that those desiring immediate liberation contemplate [it]. || 14 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In response to the inquiry as to what the nature of that indirect knowledge (parokṣajñāna) is, which has as its object the reality of Brahman to be meditated upon, he says:
"Without delineating the inner individual self (pratyagvyakti), [it arises] from the scripture, like the forms of Viṣṇu and others."
The cognition "it exists" is a general knowledge; here, it is a mediate cognition. || 15 ||

"Pratyak" (the inward-facing): the meaning is that here, in this meditation (*upāsanā*), what is intended by "indirect cognition" (*parokṣadhī*) or indirect knowledge is the knowledge arising from the scriptures—specifically from the collection of statements such as "Being, Consciousness, etc. (*satyajñānādi*)—in a general form, namely "Brahman exists," without delineating or making an object of the inward-facing individual, the witness of the intellect and so forth, who is the Self consisting of bliss (*ānandātman*). In this regard, there is an illustration: "Viṣṇu, etc."—[referring to] the representation of the forms of Viṣṇu and others.
The meaning is: "like the knowledge produced by the scriptures. || 15 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, in response to the inquiry as to why this required indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) must come first, [it is said]:
"It exists..."

He summarizes that very definition, well-known from the Taittirīya Śruti passage, "If one knows him as Brahman, then they know him as the Truly Existent," with the words "the inner witness" (pratyaksākṣī). || 15 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Since the scriptures convey specific attributes such as the four-armed form of Viṣṇu and others, how can the knowledge of Him also be considered indirect (parokṣa)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even when there is a cognition of the four-armed form and so forth, [the Lord] does not appear as a physical form."
At that time, those who possess indirect knowledge through the subtle elements do not behold Viṣṇu.
