accompanied by the two commentaries.

Even when a specific attribute such as having four arms is understood through scripture, a person who does not perceive the form of Viṣṇu or others with their eyes and other senses remains one whose knowledge is merely indirect (*parokṣajñānī*). He states the reasoning for this: "Not at that time," etc. At that time, during the period of meditation, Viṣṇu is the object of worship.
"He does not look" means that he does not make [them] objects of the senses. || 16 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): To clarify first the nature of the mediacy (*parokṣatva*) of the knowledge concerning forms such as Viṣṇu—which was cited as an example for the aforementioned mediacy—he says: "caturbhujādi... ("four-armed, etc."). The word "from scripture" (*śāstrāt*) is to be supplied [as the source]. "Of Viṣṇu" is implied. Even when there is an understanding of the four-armed form and so on, Devadatta, not having brought the form to mind (*anullikhann*), is indeed one possessing mediately perceived knowledge; therefore, at the time of meditation, by the senses— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]
The grammatical connection is that one does not see Viṣṇu with the sense organs such as the eyes, nor indeed does one perceive him directly. || 16 ||

Rāghava’s Commentary: Now, one might object that knowledge whose object is Viṣṇu and others must be erroneous because it lacks the manifestation of individual particulars; anticipating this, he states that it is not erroneous because it is produced by a valid means of knowledge:
"Due to the fault of being indirect (parokṣatva), there would be no cognition of reality."
Because the one whose form is existence is manifested by the scripture itself, which is the very means of valid cognition. || 17 ||

Regarding the phrase "due to being beyond the senses" (*parokṣatve*): the state of being indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñānatva*) is not the cause of erroneous cognition (*bhrāntijñānatva*); rather, it is the unreality of the object.

However, in this case, because the true form of Viṣṇu and others is manifested by the scripture itself, which serves as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no delusion (*bhrama*). This is the meaning. || 17 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, if this is so, how can there be validity (*prāmāṇya*) in indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*)? To this, he says: "In the case of being indirect...

(verse 17). Commentary (rā0): Now, one might object: "How can the knowledge of the reality of Brahman—which arises from the scriptures and which manifests the individuality of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*)—be indirect?
Anticipating this, he states that it is because of the absence of the manifestation of inner subjectivity (*pratyaktva*), which is the necessary condition for immediacy (*aparokṣatva*).
Even when the nature of reality—as being, consciousness, and bliss—is revealed through the scriptures, it remains unmanifested [in the mind].
But that Brahman does not directly perceive the witness who is turned inward.

"Sat-cit-ānanda" means: although Brahman, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss—as established by such scriptural passages as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," "Eternal, pure, awakened, true, free, and stainless," and "All this is Being; that is Being"—is manifest, one who does not delineate the inner witness (pratyak-sākṣin) and thus does not know Brahman’s identity with the inner self (pratyagātman) does not directly perceive, indeed does not see, that Brahman. ||18||

— Commentary (A0 Ṭīkā): Regarding the phrase "saccidānanda" in the context of indirect knowledge of the subject matter (*dārṣṭāntika*); the meaning is that it is of the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānandarūpa*). Not delineating the innermost Self (*pratyañcam ātmānam*), the witness (*sākṣiṇam*), one does not, for that very reason, directly perceive (*sākṣāt*) Brahman as immediate (*pratyakṣam*).
This is the connection [of the verse]. || 18 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: How then can knowledge whose object is such a Brahman be considered "knowledge of reality" (tattvajñāna)?
Anticipating this question, he states that it is because it is produced by the authority of scripture:
"Because of the certain realization of Being-Consciousness-Bliss through the very path taught in the scriptures."
Even though that knowledge is indirect, it is knowledge of reality and not an error. || 19 ||

Regarding the word "śāstra": although that knowledge is indirect (parokṣa), because it determines Brahman’s nature as existence, consciousness, and bliss precisely according to the method taught in the scriptures, it is indeed right knowledge (samyag-jñāna) and not an error; this is the meaning. || 19 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, he states that this [scripture] also possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramātva*) just as before: "The scripture... (verse 19).

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection might be raised: "Since the nature of Brahman as being existence, consciousness, and bliss is indeed understood through statements such as 'That art thou' (*tat tvam asi*), its nature as the inner self (*pratyag-rūpa*) is also taught by those very same statements; therefore, because the knowledge produced by the scriptures also refers to the individual inner self, it must be immediate (*aparokṣa*) itself.
Anticipating this, he says:
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 342.
Although Brahman, known as the lamp of meditation, is described in the scriptures solely as the inner self (pratyak),...
Nevertheless, this remains difficult to understand for one who does not engage in inquiry, even by means of the great sayings (mahāvākyas).

"Brahman. Although in the Vedāntas Brahman is taught through the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) precisely as the inner self (pratyagātman), nevertheless, this nature of the inner self is difficult to understand—and indeed impossible to comprehend—for one who lacks discrimination between the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam* by means of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). Therefore, the meaning is that immediate, direct knowledge (aparokṣajñāna) does not arise from the sentence alone. || 20 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that based on the Vārttika passage—"The reality that is neither excluded from nor followed by anything else is called Brahman; the meaning of 'Brahman' is difficult to find here when there exists a second entity"—the very notion of indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) of Brahman is untenable. To this, he says: "Brahman... (Verse 20).

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Since right knowledge is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the nature of the object (*vastu*), and since the means of valid cognition exists in the form of statements such as 'That thou art' (*tattvamasi*), and the object exists in the form of the identity of Brahman and the Self, why is it difficult to understand without inquiry?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
While the delusion that the body and so forth are the self remains awake, a person cannot [attain liberation] by force.
Because of his dull intellect, he is unable to realize [the Self] as being identical with Brahman. || 21 ||

Regarding the phrase "dehādi" (the body, etc.): the meaning is that inquiry is required for the sake of removing the delusion of identifying with the body, senses, and so forth—an error that is contrary to the direct realization of the non-duality of Brahman and the Self and which is to be dispelled by inquiry. || 21 ||
In that regard, he explains the reason [for this] with the verse beginning "dehādi" (21).

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "In that case, since the delusion of duality—which has the body, senses, and so forth as its object—actually exists, even indirect knowledge (parokṣajñāna) regarding non-dual Brahman would not arise.

Anticipating this, he states that for a person endowed with faith, indirect knowledge indeed arises from the scriptures, because indirect knowledge of duality is not contradictory to indirect knowledge of non-duality.
Brahman alone is easily known by one who possesses faith and has insight into the scriptures.
The direct cognition of duality prevents the indirect cognition of non-duality.

Regarding the phrase "brahmamātram" (nothing but Brahman): the construction is that since the direct perception of duality is preceded by the indirect perception of non-duality, "nothing but Brahman" is easily understood. || 22 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection may be raised: "Just as for one of dull intellect, due to the absence of a sharp intellect capable of discerning the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*), the immediate (*aparokṣa*) knowledge whose object is the non-dual identity of Brahman and the Self does not arise; likewise, even while the immediate perception of duality persists here—just like the notion that the body and so forth are the Self—how could there be even a mediate (*parokṣa*) knowledge of Brahman during the waking state? To this, he says: "Brahman alone" (*brahmamātram*). The reason for this is stated: "Immediate" (*aparokṣa*). It is not...

Even the non-perceptual knowledge that "the tenth exists" contradicts the perceptual knowledge produced by the words of a reliable person; therefore, it is indeed appropriate that what was stated in the present context is correct—this is the intended meaning. || 22 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To illustrate that immediate delusion is not contradicted by mediate right knowledge, he says:
"The immediate cognition of a stone does not dispel the mediate [cognition] of God."
Who indeed would disagree that Viṣṇu resides in images and such? || 23 ||
Regarding the term "aparokṣā" (direct perception): he demonstrates the absence of contradiction by providing an illustration—namely, "in images and so forth. || 23 ||

The commentary explains that very point with the words "aparokṣa" and so on. The phrase "in Śālagrāma, Cāṇaliṅga, and the like" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Furthermore, it states a specific distinction regarding those with the words "in images and so forth. || 23 ||
The Ninth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that some are observed to hold contrary views, he says:
"One who lacks faith and is devoid of conviction does not deserve to be cited as an example."
For only one who possesses faith has the qualification for all Vedic matters. || 24 ||

Regarding the phrase "for one who lacks faith": why is this so? To this he says, "only for one who has faith. The meaning is that only one who possesses faith—that is, one who is faithful—has the qualification for all the practices prescribed in the Vedas. || 24 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that even there, a lack of faith is indeed observed in some; therefore, he says: "of the faithless" (aśraddhālōḥ).

Faith (śraddhā) is the conviction of trustworthiness regarding the words of a reliable authority (āpta); its effect is indeed the certainty of the inevitable attainment of the fruit, which is confidence (viśvāsa). This is the distinction between the two. || 24 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To the question, "What follows from this regarding indirect knowledge (parokṣajñāna)? he says:
"Indirect knowledge may arise from a single instruction received from a trustworthy authority."
For the designation of Viṣṇu’s form indeed does not depend upon Mīmāṃsā. || 25 ||
Regarding the phrase "attained once": he confirms the stated point through common worldly experience with the words "in the form of Viṣṇu" (viṣṇumūrti). || 25 ||

Commentary (a0): Let it be so; what follows from this in relation to the subject at hand? To this he says: "sakṛt" (once). He supports that very point by means of an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a different instance): "viṣṇumūrti" (the form of Viṣṇu) and so forth. || 25 ||
— Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: "If that is so, why are investigations conducted in the scriptures?

Anticipating this doubt, he states that investigations are conducted to resolve uncertainties regarding the two things to be practiced—namely, ritual action (*karma*) and spiritual practice (*upāsana*).
Action and meditation are investigated here because it has not yet been determined which of them is to be practiced.
Who among men is capable of determining that which is scattered across many branches? || 26 ||
Regarding the phrase "rites and meditations," he explains how doubt actually arises: "having many branches.

What man such as ourselves is capable—that is, competent—to determine by collecting together the rites or meditations enjoined here and there across numerous branches? The meaning is: none at all. || 26 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): If this is so, then treatises such as the *Dvādaśalakṣaṇī* that investigate ritual action (*karman*) and the like would be useless; therefore, he says: "Karma... (verse 26).
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that if this is so, it follows that ritual action (*karman*) and meditation (*upāsanā*) are simply not to be performed; anticipating this, he says:
"The meaning has been determined and composed by the *Kalpasūtras*; what [is gained] by that much?"
Even without deliberation, he is capable of performing [the rite] correctly.

"Decided" (*nirṇīta*) means an object determined by former teachers such as Jaimini and others. The method of performance is already summarized in the *Kalpasūtras*; therefore, a person who has confidence in them simply because they have been composed by those [authorities] is indeed able to perform the ritual correctly even without further deliberation. || 27 ||
Commentary (a0): If that is so, how can action and meditation be determined as practices to be performed by people such as ourselves, given the lack of certainty? To this, he says:
"It has been determined. *Añjasā* means quickly. || 27 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that since there is no discussion of meditative worship (*upāsanā*) therein, its performance would not be possible; anticipating this, he says:
"The performance of meditations is described in the works of the sages."
And mortals who are incapable of critical inquiry, having heard that, worship [it] from the teacher. || 28 ||

[Regarding the phrase "of the meditations known as the lamp of dhyāna":

In the *ārṣa* (sage-authored) texts, such as the *Brahmavāsiṣṭha-mantrakalpa* and others, the method of meditation (*upāsanā*) is described. The sense is that humans who are incapable of independent inquiry learn that meditation as taught in the *kalpas* from the mouth of a teacher and then practice it. || 28 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, one might ask, "Where is the determination of the performance of these meditations (*upāstis*) found? To this, he says: "Of the meditations...

The ancient commentators say, "In the *Āgamas*, that is, in the *Mantrakalpas* of Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Vāsiṣṭha, and so forth"; however, the correct view is that they are found "in the Purāṇas and other such texts," according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "One should augment the meaning of the Vedas by means of the *Itihāsas* and Purāṇas. || 28 ||
People who desire to determine the meaning of Vedic statements should engage in inquiry (mīmāṃsā).
For indeed, the performance [of the rite] can only be possible through the instruction of a trustworthy authority alone. || 29 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection—"But why do even the authors of treatises belonging to that same period engage in an investigation of Vedic sentences?"—he replies with the verse beginning "Veda... (29), stating that they do so merely for the satisfaction of their own intellects, and not for the sake of establishing a practical application.
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): If that is so, then who has the authority in the Pūrvamīmāṃsā, and who is the one for whose sake its injunctions are to be performed? To this, he says: "The Veda... (29).
But for human beings, the direct realization of Brahman cannot occur without such inquiry.
It is not possible anywhere through the mere instruction of a trustworthy person alone. || 30 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Why should the direct realization of Brahman not be accomplished through mere instruction, just as the meditation on Brahman is?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Brahman... (Verse 30).
But in the case of the knowledge of Brahman, it is not so; thus he says: "Brahman... (Verse 30).

Rāma’s Commentary: It has been stated that through the mere instruction of a trustworthy person (āpta), indirect knowledge (parokṣajñāna) conducive to the practice of meditation arises, whereas direct knowledge (aparokṣajñāna) does not arise without inquiry; he states the reason for this as follows:
Lack of faith obstructs knowledge of the imperceptible, and nothing else does.
Non-investigation (avicāra) is the obstacle to immediate (aparokṣa) knowledge. || 31 ||

Regarding the term "indirect" (*parokṣa*): since it is precisely lack of conviction (*aviśvāsa*) that obstructs indirect knowledge, and not a lack of inquiry (*avicāra*), it is possible for indirect knowledge to arise from a single instruction once that [lack of conviction] has been removed. However, as for immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), which is obstructed by a lack of inquiry, its production is not possible without the removal of that obstruction through the means of inquiry. Therefore, the sense is that inquiry must be performed. || 31 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): If that is so, then what are the obstacles to indirect (parokṣa) and direct (aparokṣa) knowledge? To this, he says: "Indirect... (verse 31).
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: "Even when inquiry has been performed, if immediate realization (aparokṣajñāna) does not arise, what should be done?
To this he says:
"If, even after inquiring, one does not know the Brahman-Self through immediate realization..."
Because it culminates in direct perception, one should investigate again and again. || 32 ||

"Even after investigating" (vicāryāpi): The sense is that even if one has properly investigated the meanings of the terms *tattva* and *padārtha*, if one still does not know the meaning of the sentence—the oneness of Brahman and the Self—through direct perception (*aparokṣatayā*), then one must investigate again and again, because there is no other cause for direct knowledge. Commentary on Verse 32: Now, it may be argued that investigation (*vicāra*) is indeed required to eliminate the lack of investigation which acts as an obstacle to direct knowledge; however, [the Advaita] scripture...

Anticipating the doubt as to whether [the inquiry] into the Self should be performed once or repeatedly, he provides the resolution: "Even after having inquired" (vicāryāpi), etc. [The phrase] "until direct realization" (āparokṣyeṇa) has "of the inquiry" (vicārasya) as its ellipsis. || 32 ||
The Ninth Chapter:
Accompanied by Two Explanations.
If, while investigating until death, one does not find the self at all;
When obstacles have been destroyed, one will certainly obtain [the fruit] in another birth. || 33 ||
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that if direct realization does not arise despite repeated inquiry, then such inquiry would be useless;
anticipating this doubt, he says: "Inquiring... (verse 33).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might fear that even if inquiry into Brahman is conducted throughout one's life, if the direct realization (*aparokṣapramā*) of it does not arise, then the passing away of life would be in vain; thus, the author consoles such a person with the verse beginning "vicārayan" (while inquiring). || 33 ||
"Whether here or in the next world, it is knowledge"—thus has it been declared by the author of the Sūtras.
"Even though many hear it here, they do not understand"—so says the Śruti.

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the doubt as to how this is known, [the author] states "either here or in the hereafter," because the author of the Brahma-sūtras, Vyāsa, declared in the sūtra *aihikamapyaprastutapratibandhe taddarśanāt* that even knowledge pertaining to this life arises when there is no obstruction. He cites scripture regarding the non-arising of knowledge in this birth when an obstruction exists: "Though they hear... (34).
— Commentary (A0 Ṭīkā):
Now, if it is asked what the proof for this is, he provides the answer along with its authority: "Or in this life" (iha vā).
Thus, this is the Sūtra of the Śārīraka: "Even that which belongs to this life [occurs] when there is no obstruction of what is relevant, because that is seen. This is its meaning: "Ā—"

By the preceding sūtra, "vṛttirasakṛdupadeśāt," it is established that through the repeated practice of inquiry— based on the nine-fold instruction given by Śuddhālaka to Śvetaketu in the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad— the immediate realization of the non-dual identity of Brahman and the Self arises when there is no present obstacle,

provided that the obstacles to be mentioned later are absent; furthermore, such realization may even occur in this very life (aihika), meaning within this current body, and not merely in the next birth, but immediately.

It is so; the reason for this is "because it is seen [in scripture]. Thusness (*tathātva*) has been stated in the *Śruti* in the case of Śvetaketu and others regarding knowledge pertaining to this world, and in the *Smṛti* in the case of Arjuna and others.
However, regarding knowledge pertaining to the next world, it is seen in the *Śruti* in the case of Vāmadeva while still in the womb, and in the *Smṛti* in the case of Madālasā’s children and others.
In that regard, he also cites the *Śruti*: "Even for one who hears... The reading of the *Śruti* is: "He who is not attained even by many through hearing..."
"It is possible that even while listening, many do not understand. || 34 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: To show that for one who performs hearing and other means in this life, direct realization (*aparokṣajñāna*) occurs even in another birth, he recites in substance the following scriptural passage: "While still lying in the womb, Vāmadeva realized: 'I have known the births of all the gods,'" and so forth—stating that while lying in the womb, Vāmadeva attained awakening.
Through reflection practiced previously, [there arises] that [insight] regarding study and so forth. || 35 ||
—Regarding the word "garbhe" (in the womb): he provides an illustration for the knowledge produced in this life arising at another time with the words "just as" (yadvat). || 35 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, while still in the womb, this Śyāvāśva Vāmadeva spoke thus: "I was Manu and I was the Sun.
He cites another scriptural passage here as well—namely, "while still in the womb"—and clarifies the illustration therein with the words "just as... (35).
If, even after studying many times, it does not come back then, [one should continue].
On the following day, even without studying, a person may remember what was previously studied.
Rāma’s Commentary — He explains the illustration [with the verse beginning] "bahuvāram" (many times). || 36 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He explains that [verse] with the words "many times" (bahuvāram). || 36 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: By means of the word “etcetera,” he states other examples included therein:
"Just as the products of agriculture, such as grain and the like, ripen in due time."
In the same way, the inquiry into the Self also ripens gradually over time. || 37 ||
Vidyāraṇya’s *Pañcadaśī* [states]: "By time... He applies this to the illustrative instance [of the dream] with the words: "In the same way" (tadvat). || 37 ||
[Commentary on the *Dhyānadīpa*, verse 37]—In this regard, he states the conclusion preceded by another illustration: "By time... (verse 37).
Even when investigating again and again, [this occurs] due to three kinds of obstacles.
"It does not know the reality"—this has been correctly stated in the Vārtika. || 38 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Even when the reality has been investigated many times, direct realization does not arise due to the force of obstacles;
this has also been established by the author of the Vārttika, as he says: "Again and again... (38).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding this, the three obstacles beginning with *bhūta* have been described in the Vārttika; thus he says: "Again and again" (*punaḥ punar*). || 38 ||

Rāghavānanda’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): He cites those very Vārtikas, beginning with "Whence that knowledge? and ending with "by Bharata through three births. Therein, he first asks for the cause of the arising of knowledge at this present time, which had not arisen previously.
If it is asked, "From where does that knowledge arise?", [the answer is: for that indeed arises from the complete destruction of bondage.
And that [being] is either past, or future, or indeed present. (39)
Why is this? He provides the answer: "For that is bondage. The meaning is: because of the complete destruction of that bondage, which is an obstruction.
He further states that this obstruction is threefold—past, future, and present—with the words: "This [obstruction]... (39).
a0 Commentary: He recites those very Vārttikas beginning with "kutaḥ" (from what?). "Bandhaḥ" means obstruction. || 39 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Let it be so that there are these three kinds of obstacles; what follows from that? To this he says:
"Even one who has studied the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas is not liberated for this very reason."
Indeed, this very point has been demonstrated through the analogy of a hidden treasure of gold and other such examples.

"Because it has been studied"—this means precisely because the obstruction exists. When an obstruction exists, knowledge does not arise; as this very Śruti declares: "Just as those who do not know the location of a buried treasure of gold might pass over it again and again without perceiving it, even so all these creatures go day after day to the world of Brahman, yet they do not find that world of Brahman, for they are obstructed by untruth. By this [scriptural passage],...
He says that this has been shown: "By gold," etc. (40).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Regarding the phrases "having studied" (*adhīta*) and "treasure of gold" (*hiraṇyanidhi*); the meaning is that this refers to what is well-known from the eighth chapter of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, beginning with the words "Just as, for example, a treasure of gold... (40).
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection that it is not observed for a past thing to act as an obstacle, he says:
"Because there was an obstruction even by the past affection for his buffalo-cow."
"A monk does not know reality"—thus is a verse sung in the world. || 45 ||

Regarding the phrase "in the past": this is the meaning. A certain ascetic, having previously formed an attachment to a particular queen during his stage as a householder, later engaged in *śravaṇa* (listening to the scriptures) after renunciation; yet, due to the obstruction produced by that very attachment, he did not understand the reality even though it was taught by his guru.
Such verses are sung in the world, but they are not recited in the Purāṇas and similar texts—this is the meaning. || 41 ||
Commentary (a0): Regarding that, he states what has occurred: "even by the past," etc. According to Amara, *mahiṣī* means "one who has been consecrated" (*kṛtābhiṣekā*). ||41||
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: If that is so, how did knowledge arise in him who was of such a nature? To this he says:
"The Guru, following his affection for the queen, spoke the Truth."
Then, according to his word, through the complete destruction of this obstruction, || 42 ||
The Ninth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

Regarding the word *anusṛtya* ("having followed"): the guru, who is the instructor of truth (*tattva*) for him, having followed his affection for that queen, taught the Truth—that is, Brahman conditioned by that very queen—to her. Then, through the removal of the obstacle characterized by affection for the queen, he too [attained it] from the guru—
The meaning is that he has understood the taught reality exactly as it is, according to the method prescribed in the scriptures. || 42 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): If this is so, then why is it that the arising of knowledge does not occur in that very birth? To this he says: "Having followed" (*anusṛtya*). The word "of him" (*tasya*) is to be supplied from the context. "In the queen" means in the royal wife previously enjoyed by him. "Affection" (*sneham*)—because it resides in the heart—means his own love, as it were, which had been communicated in private by that renunciant. "Having followed" means having [listened] with truthful narration.

The Guru, who is supremely compassionate, being pleased, spoke the Truth to Mahiṣī—that very queen of the aforementioned description—by means of explaining the discrimination regarding the five sheaths (pañcakośa) and so forth; such is the syntactical connection. || 42 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus demonstrated the past obstacle, he now shows the present one:
"The present obstacle is characterized by attachment to sense objects."
Dullness of wisdom, fallacious reasoning, and stubborn adherence to error; || 43 ||

Regarding the term "obstacle" (*pratibandha*): the present obstacle consists of the mind’s attachment to sense objects; the dullness of insight (*prajñāmāndya*), which is the absence of sharpness in the intellect (*buddhi*); fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*), which is the misinterpretation of the meaning of the scriptures due to being a dry logician; and dogmatic adherence to error (*viparyayadurāgraha*), which is an irrational insistence on the misconception that the Self is characterized by attributes such as agency. Even the presence of any one of these [is an obstacle].
The meaning is that knowledge does not arise in a sentient being. || 43 ||
Commentary (a0): Having thus described the past obstruction, he now describes the present one: "Obstruction" (pratibandha) ||43||
Rāma’s Commentary: To the question, "By what means is this obstacle removed?", he says:
"Through tranquility and the like, and through hearing and the like, as appropriate in each case, [the obstacle] comes to an end."
Therefore, when this obstacle has been removed, he attains his own true nature as Brahman.

Regarding the phrase "by means of tranquility and so forth": "tranquility and so forth" refers to those qualities mentioned in the Śruti—*śānto dānta uparatastitikṣuḥ samāhito bhūtvā* ("having become tranquil, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated")—and "listening and so forth" refers to those prescribed by the Śruti as *śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ* ("one must listen, reflect, and meditate"). When, through these appropriate and suitable means, each respective obstacle has been removed, brought to exhaustion, and destroyed; [then...]
When [this ignorance] exists, then by the very removal of this obstruction, one attains the state of Brahman for oneself, that is, for the inner self (pratyagātman); such is the meaning. || 44 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "What is the means for the pacification of these fourfold [defects]? To this, he says: "By means of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth," and so on, in due order. Thus, through tranquility and the other [means], there is the destruction of attachment to sense objects; through hearing (*śravaṇa*), the dullness of wisdom (*prajñāmāndya*); through reflection (*manana*), fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*); and through meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), the irrational pride characterized by the stubborn adherence to the erroneous notions of the self's agency and the reality of the world.

[The opponent] says: "But surely you yourself explained that [ignorance] as being fivefold at the outset. [The author] replies: True. However, based on the natural sense of the words *viparyaya* (error) and *durāgraha* (perversity) found in the present Vārtika, and because Śrī Madhusūdana Ācārya himself stated in his commentary on the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* that he intended by the word *viparyaya* the cultivation of the opposite of the means (*sādhana-viparīta-bhāvanā*) and by the word *durāgraha* the cultivation of the opposite of the result (*phala-viparīta-bhāvanā*), whereas here [in our own text], we follow the ancient commentaries alone.
And because of the statement regarding its fourfold nature. || 44 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now he shows the future obstacle: "And the future obstacle is declared to exist in Vāmadeva."
It was exhausted by Bharata in one birth, whereas it would have taken three births [for others]. || 45 ||

"Āgāmī" means the obstruction of future [births], which is the cause for another birth; the meaning is that it is the remainder of *prārabdha* (commenced karma). And of that, there is experience—[[page 348-to-348]] 348.
In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[in the chapter titled] *Dhyānadīpa*, he states—

by means of the verse beginning with "ekena"— that because there is no cessation [of ignorance] through any other means, there is no fixed rule regarding time for its cessation: "And that [ignorance] is destroyed in a single birth."
The word "of Vāmadeva" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. It is connected [to the previous verse] with the phrase "exhausted by the three births of Bharata. || 45 ||
Commentary (A0 Ṭīkā): Thus, he explains that future [result] as well, with an illustration, by means of nine verses beginning with "āgāmī" (45).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection, "But by saying 'with one [birth] or with three births,' you yourself have stated that there is a fixed time limit," he says:
"For one fallen from yoga, according to the Gītā, after many past births..."
The destruction of obstacles has been declared [as the means]; even inquiry is not useless. || 46 ||

Regarding the term "yoga": one who has fallen from yoga means one who is devoid of inquiry until the point of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of reality. Anticipating the objection that inquiry into reality would then be fruitless, he says: "nor even inquiry. The sense is that the fruit characterized by immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) exists immediately after the removal of obstacles. || 46 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might object: "If the certainty [of liberation] after one birth or the like occurs upon the destruction of obstacles, then that is better. To this, he says: "By yoga... (verse 46).
Having attained the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds through the investigation of the reality of the self.
One is born with longing in the home of the pure and the prosperous. || 47 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary—He demonstrates the meaning propounded in the Gītā with the passage beginning with "Having attained" and ending with "then he goes to the supreme goal. Regarding "having attained": one who has fallen from yoga, by the power of investigating the reality of the Self alone, attains the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds—that is, specific regions of heaven—and having experienced happiness there for a long time, at the conclusion of that enjoyment, if he still possesses desire, then in this world, among the pure... [the sons] of mothers... [and so forth].
From that, those who are pure on both the mother's and father's sides are born into a most illustrious family. || 47 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might ask, "How is it that inquiry is not rendered useless? To this, he replies by explaining the meaning of the Gītā verse beginning with "prāpya" (having attained). || 47 ||
Rāghava’s Commentary: He states another alternative:
"Or else, he is born into a family of wise yogis themselves."
Free from desire, through the investigation of the reality of Brahman—indeed, that is difficult to attain. (48)

Alternatively: if one is free from desire and personally deeply dispassionate, then by the mere inquiry into the reality of Brahman, one is born—meaning one takes birth—in the family of those yogins who possess a one-pointed mind and have investigated the determination of the self-reality through the inquiry into the reality of Brahman. To the question, "What is the distinction from the previous position?
he says: "For that... (taddhi). For (hi) because of that reason, birth in such a family of yogins is difficult to attain (durlabha), meaning it cannot be obtained by those with little merit. || 48 ||
Commentary (ṭīkā): He summarizes the distinction regarding that which is beyond verbal expression with the words "Alternatively" (athavā). || 48 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He establishes its rarity:
"In that state, he obtains that same connection with the intellect belonging to his previous body."
And from that point he strives even more; therefore, this indeed is difficult to attain. || 49 ||

Regarding the word "therein" (tatra): for this reason, in that birth, he quickly regains—that is, obtains—that connection with the intellect (*buddhi-saṃyoga*) pertaining to his previous body, which consists of an intellectual engagement with the sphere of inquiry into reality. It is not merely the recovery of the connection with the intellect;
rather, from that previous effort, he exerts himself further—that is, he makes a greater effort. Therefore, the meaning is that such a birth is difficult to attain. || 49 ||
Commentary (ṭīkā): What follows from that? He says: "In that case" (tatra). || 49 ||
The Ninth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the reason for further practice:
"For by that very previous practice, he is carried away even against his will."
Having attained perfection through many births, he then goes to the supreme goal.
"By the former" means that even one who has fallen from yoga—though he is helpless and lacks self-control—is nevertheless drawn or pulled back by that very former practice.

Thus, through the effort of many births' well-performed deeds, he becomes fully perfected and endowed with the knowledge of reality; then, from that knowledge of reality, he attains the supreme goal, which is liberation.
The meaning is that he attains [it]. || 50 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): For this very reason—“as previously [stated]” || 50 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He shows another future obstacle:
"Having completely restrained the desire for the world of Brahmā, which is fully present..."
He who reflects upon the self does not, however, directly realize it. || 51 ||

Regarding the phrase "in the world of Brahmā" (brahmaloke): the meaning is that when there is a firm desire to attain the world of Brahmā, if one suppresses that [desire] and investigates the Self, the direct realization of it does not arise at all. || 51 ||
— Commentary (A0): Thus he states that fourth [state] as well: "Brahman," etc. This is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) of Vaikuṇṭha and other such realms. || 51 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection that in that case liberation would never occur for him, he says:
"Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the realization of Vedānta"—that is, from the scriptures.
In the world of Brahmā, at the end of the kalpa, he is liberated along with Brahmā.

Regarding the term *vedānta*: by virtue of such scriptural passages as, “Those who have well-ascertained the meaning through the knowledge of Vedānta, who are self-controlled, whose being is purified by the yoga of renunciation— they all, having become supreme immortals at the time of the final end, are liberated in the world of Brahman,” and “When the dissolution arrives, all those perfected souls enter the supreme state along with Brahman at the end of the highest [cycle],” it follows that after attaining the world of Brahman, the reality [is realized].
The meaning is that liberation will occur after having directly realized [Brahman] together with Brahman. || 52 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask, "In that case, what is his destiny? To this, he says: "Vedānta...
[The text continues with the phrase] "Vedānta-vi-".

The meaning is as stated in the *Taittirīya Śruti*: "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through knowledge, who have exerted themselves in the yoga of renunciation, and whose being is purified—they all, at the time of the final end, are liberated from the supreme nectar in the world of Brahman"; and as stated in the *Smṛti*: "When the dissolution arrives, all those who have perfected their selves enter the supreme state along with Brahman at the end of the highest [cycle]. || 52 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus stated that when the investigation of reality is being conducted, direct realization does not arise here due to the force of obstacles, he now says that for those who are intense sinners, even such investigation is difficult to attain:
For some, even that investigation is obstructed by karma.
For it is stated in the scripture: "He who is not obtained even for hearing by many. (53)

Regarding the phrase "of some": he states the authority for this there—namely, "for hearing. The meaning is that the Supreme Self is difficult to attain, such that even by many persons He is not obtained even for the purpose of hearing. || 53 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): These obstacles do not exist only for knowledge itself; rather, they also exist in the investigation that brings about that knowledge, characterized by a specific lack of far-sightedness. Thus he says: "Of some... He provides the proof for this: "Even for the sake of hearing... This is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) [of other obstacles as well]. There is also an obstacle to the fruit of knowledge known as liberation while living (jīvanmukti); the detailed exposition of that will be found in the *Jīvanmukti-viveka*.
"We shall indeed act with singular brilliance"—this is the direction [of our intent]. 53.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 350.

[The commentary by Rāma, titled *Dhyānadīpa*: Having thus stated that as long as obstacles exist, neither the direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*) nor the inquiry (*vicāra*) which serves as its means can occur, there now arises the expectation: "What should be done by a person seeking the human goal who is incapable of inquiry? In response to this, [the text says]: "For mortals incapable of inquiry—" ]
Having heard that, they worship the Guru; thus he establishes what was previously promised:
"Either due to extreme dullness of intellect, or because of the impossibility of the [necessary] totality of conditions..."
He who does not find fault with anyone should worship Brahman incessantly.

Regarding the word "atyanta" (extreme): the impossibility of the totality [of conditions] means the non-existence of the teacher who instructs it, or the non-existence of the spiritual scripture (*adhyātmaśāstra*), or of the place, time, and so forth;
the meaning is "because of that. || 54 ||
Commentary on Verse 11:

Having thus set forth the entire procedure for the removal of obstacles as stated in the Vārtika, he now establishes the connection with what was previously promised in the verse: "And the gods, incapable of inquiry, having heard that [instruction], worship the Guru. This is done by the words beginning with "atyanta" (extreme).
The meaning is: "of the totality consisting of the teacher and the scripture. || 54 ||
For it is not impossible to meditate upon the reality of Brahman as devoid of qualities.
For here, as in the case of the Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahman), the repetition of the mental application (pratyayāvṛtti) is possible. || 55 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object that since the reality of Brahman devoid of attributes (nirguṇa-brahmatattva) is free from qualities, its worship is not possible.

Anticipating this doubt, he states—beginning with "nirguṇa"—that because worship consists of the repetition of mental impressions (pratyayāvṛtti), it is possible even for the attribute-less Brahman, just as it is for the Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahman). || 15 ||
Commentary (a0): To the question, "How can there be worship of that which is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa)? he replies: "Nirguṇa... (verse 15).
If it is argued that because it is inaccessible to speech and mind, it cannot be an object of meditation; then:
Furthermore, the cognition of that which is inaccessible to speech and mind would not be possible.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection that the attributeless Brahman cannot be an object of worship because it is beyond the reach of speech and mind, he states—anticipating that this same defect applies equally to the position of mere knowledge—that [Brahman] is "beyond speech and mind. (56)
Commentary (a0): Now, one might object that since Brahman is inaccessible to speech and mind, meditation—characterized by the repetition of mental impressions—is not possible there at all.
Anticipating this, he provides a solution by way of a counter-objection: "Avāk... (16).
If he knows it thus: "It has a form that is beyond the range of speech and the other senses."
One should meditate upon it as having a form that is beyond the reach of speech and other [senses]; why not? || 57 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection that Brahman cannot be known as "beyond the reach of speech and mind," he says "vāgādi... (verse 17) to show that it can indeed be worshipped in this very manner.
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, he replies with an equal counter-objection even regarding the release from the impasse, beginning with the words "vāgādi" (speech, etc.). ||17||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that Brahman would necessarily possess attributes (saguṇatva) if it were an object of worship, [the author] states that it would likewise possess attributes if it were an object of knowledge:
"If [Brahman has] the state of possessing attributes because of being an object of worship, then it would have that [state] even because of being an object of knowledge."
If that which is to be known is characterized by the function of its defining marks, let it be worshipped. || 58 ||

"Being endowed with qualities" (saguṇatvam) means that it possesses qualities. Now, one might object: "Since we rely on the function of indication (lakṣaṇā), there is no consequence of [Brahman] being endowed with qualities even if it is an object of knowledge. Anticipating this, he says, "If it were an object of knowledge," [meaning]: let meditation also be performed in exactly the same way. || 58 ||
— Commentary (A0):

Having thus raised the objection that [Brahman] possesses attributes (*saguṇatva*) because it is an object of worship, he resolves it by means of a counter-objection (*pratibandī*): "If it possesses attributes...
He anticipates a similar counter-objection regarding the subject at hand and pacifies it with an equalizing argument: "And if it were an object of knowledge... (58).
The Ninth Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised that the status of Brahman as an object of worship is negated by scripture:
"Know that you are indeed That [Brahman], and not this which they worship."
If, according to this scripture, the status of Brahman as an object of meditation were thus prohibited; || 59 ||
“Know that as Brahman,” [he said]. “That which the mind does not perceive, that by which they say the mind is perceived— know that alone to be Brahman, and not this [which is perceived].”

The meaning is that the Śruti passage, "They worship this," negates that the object of worship is Brahman. The construction is as follows: "Know that which is beyond the reach of speech and mind—that alone is Brahman; but know that which persons worship as 'this' is not [Brahman]. || 59 ||

The commentary on verse a0 raises an objection: that the status of being an object of worship is prohibited in the case of Brahman by scripture—namely, the *Taittirīya Upaniṣad*: "Know that alone to be Brahman, not this which they worship here. || 59 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Since the negation of its being unknowable is equal to the negation of its being an object of worship, he says:
"It is certainly other than the known"; thus, according to the Śruti, this [Brahman] is not an object of knowledge.
If that which is to be known is to be known through scripture alone, then it should likewise be meditated upon through scripture.

Regarding the phrase "from the known": the meaning is that the scripture [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26], by stating "That indeed is different from the known, and also from the unknown," precludes even the knowability of Brahman. "From the known" means from that which is cognized; "from the unknown" means from that which is not cognized. If it is argued that the scripture establishes that Brahman is other than both the known and the unknown, and one should therefore understand it in that very way, then [the author] says the following, anticipating the objection that this same logic applies to meditative worship (upāsana) as well:
"As follows" || 60 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): "That is indeed other than the known, and furthermore other than the unknown"—by this very scriptural statement, even the state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) therein is negated. He resolves [the objection] by means of a counter-objection (*pratibandī*), beginning with "viditāt" (than the known). He states the established conclusion (*phalita*) with "yathā": the meaning is that it is seen by the intellect (*buddhi*) in its pure form, as expressed in such passages as "But it is seen by the subtle intellect. "Tathā" (so too) means: by the scriptural injunction "one should cultivate wisdom" (*prajñāṃ kurvīta*). || 60 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, having raised the objection that knowability does not belong to Brahman as a reality, he says that its being an object of meditation is likewise [not real]:
"If knowability is unreal, why is it not the same with respect to being an object of meditation?"
If it is argued that "knowability" consists in being pervaded by a mental modification (vṛtti), then that is equally true even in the case of an object of meditation (upāsya). || 61 ||

Regarding the term "unreal": one might object that while the mental modification (*vṛtti*) possesses the form of Brahman in the case of direct realization (*vedana*), this is not the case for meditative worship (*upāsana*). Anticipating this doubt, he states "the modification" (*vṛtti*) [in verse 61], asserting that by the power of the words [of scripture], the possession of that form is equal in both cases.

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He states that in the context of worship (*upāsana*), the lack of reality and so forth is equal to [the lack of reality] in mere knowledge (*vedana*): "It is unreal" (*avāstavī*). || 61 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He states that a censure devoid of reasoning is equally applicable to your own position as well:
"If you have devotion toward worship, then tell me, what is your aversion toward that [other form]?"
The absence of pride should not be predicated of this [state], because it is observed in many scriptural passages. || 62 ||

"What is that? [The opponent asks. Anticipating the objection that there is no authoritative evidence for the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa), he says "There is no proof" (mānābhāvaḥ) to show that this is not so, because such [meditation] is found in numerous Śrutis. || 62 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, if it is asked, "Why do you have this love specifically for the worship of the attributeless (nirguṇa) *ahaṃgraha*?", he replies, "What is your devotion? [implying that your own aversion here must likewise have a root]. Anticipating the objection that there is no evidence for such devotion, he counters with, "Respect... (verse 62).
Rāma’s Commentary: He explains the meaning stated as "because it is seen in many scriptural texts" (bahuśrutiṣu darśanāt) on page 352.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[based on] the Uttara-tāpanīya, the Śaivyapraśna, and the Kaṭhaka.
In the Māṇḍūkya and other such texts, meditation known as the "lamp of dhyāna" is everywhere declared to be the worship of the attributeless (nirguṇa).

Regarding the phrase "in the latter": in the *Tāpanīya Upaniṣad*, meditation on the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) is taught in various ways, beginning with, "The gods indeed said to Prajāpati: 'Explain to us this Self, which is subtler than the subtle, as the syllable Om.

Furthermore, in the fifth question of the *Praśna Upaniṣad*, within the section concerning Śvetaketu, it is stated: "But he who meditates upon that supreme Puruṣa by means of this very syllable 'Om' consisting of three measures..."

Thus, in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad (the Kaṭhavallī), beginning with "That goal which all the Vedas proclaim," and continuing with "This very syllable is Brahman; this is the supreme support," and so forth, the meditation on the Praṇava is taught. In the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, by the passage beginning "The syllable 'Om'—this whole world is this," and so forth, it is precisely the meditation on the fourth state (turīya), which transcends the [other] states, that is described; this is the meaning. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the Taittirīya...
The Muṇḍakas and others are included. || 63 ||

Commentary (a0): In that regard, he states the names of certain scriptural passages—beginning with the words "In the latter" (*uttarasmin*). As it is said in the *Nṛsiṃhottaratāpanīya*: "The gods indeed said to Prajāpati: 'Explain this Self, which is subtler than the subtle, as the syllable Om (*oṃkāra*)'" and so forth. Likewise, in the *Praśnopaniṣad*, in the question of Śaibya: "But he who, by means of this very syllable 'Om' consisting of three measures, [meditates upon] the Supreme Person... and so on.
Thus it is said: "He meditates upon that. Similarly, in the Kaṭhavallī, beginning with "That goal which all the Vedas proclaim," it concludes:
"I shall tell you that goal in brief: Om. Likewise, in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad as well, starting with "Om, this syllable is all this," and so forth;
by the phrase "and so forth," [are included] such passages as "Om is Brahman; Om is all this" from the Taittirīyaka and other texts. 63.
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might ask, "How is the worship of the Nirguṇa Brahman to be performed?
To this he says: "The method for its performance is declared to be Pañcīkaraṇa."
If it is argued that this is not a means for attaining knowledge, who has ever prohibited it? (64)

Regarding the word "anuṣṭhāna" (practice): one might object that this meditation is merely a means to knowledge (*jñāna*) and not a means to liberation (*mukti*). Anticipating this, he says, "It is a means to knowledge," which is favorable to our position—that one is liberated even by meditating upon the reality of Brahman. || 64 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Granted that its authoritative status is thus established here, where, then, is the method of its practice described?

To this he replies with the words "anuṣṭhāna" (practice). If it is argued, "But surely the aforementioned meditation is merely a means to knowledge," he says "no," and explains why no one can say so by stating "jñāna" (knowledge). || 64 ||
If someone does not practice this, let them not practice it.
Does worship become defiled by the fault of the person? || 65 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection that everyone performs only the meditation on the qualified (saguṇa) Brahman and not the meditation on the unqualified (nirguṇa), [the author] states—“He does not perform [it]”—in order to show that it is improper to deny that which is established by authoritative evidence. || 65 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, one might object that almost no one in the world performs this practice; to this, he says: "He does not perform it. || 65 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He provides an illustration for the fact that what is established by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) must not be abandoned because it cannot be practiced:
"For this reason as well, considering them to be even more excellent than these, [one should not abandon] mantras that effect subjugation and so forth."
Let the deluded perform recitation; let those even more deluded than them attend to agriculture.

"From this also"—this is the intended meaning. Just as when fools, perceiving that mantras capable of producing subjugation (*vaśya*) and so forth grant results in this life (*aihika*), are inclined toward the recitation (*japa*) and other rites of those mantras over meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsana*) which yield results at a later time, the discerning (*vivekin*) [do not follow suit].
[Page 353]
The Ninth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

The meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa) is not abandoned. Just as, for example, even though the most ignorant might engage in agriculture and the like—considering them to require less discipline than those mantras which depend upon the performance of observances (niyama)—their practice of those mantras is nevertheless not abandoned; so too, although those desiring worldly fruits do not perform the meditation on the attributeless, the seekers of liberation (mumukṣu) do not abandon the meditation on the attributeless. || 66 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, raising the objection—"What is the fault of a person if they do not perform the aforementioned meditation?"—the author, with the intention that it is indeed a lack of discrimination (*aviveka*), censures such a non-discriminating person through indifference, providing an illustration, beginning with the words "ito'pi" (even from this). The meaning is: "even from the meditation on the attributeless *ahaṃgraha* (I-am-Brahman), which bestows liberation by means of knowledge. [The ignorant person thinks] out of their own mere whim: "What is the use of liberation, which is devoid of the pleasures of sense objects such as the dalliances of children? etc.

"Having resolved" means up to that point. "Mantras" refers to the Śrīvidyā and other mantras. That very fifteen-syllable mantra, consisting of three *kūṭas*, is designated as the "Fifteenth" (*pañcadaśī*) by the Śāktas;

however, by the insertion of another seed-syllable (*bīja*), it is conventionally called the "Sixteenth" (*ṣoḍaśī*). Disregarding that [convention], for the sake of investigating the reality that directly bestows liberation, these two most compassionate teachers have presented this Fifteenth [mantra] along with the *Jīvanmuktiviveka*, and the Sixteenth [mantra] for those desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*).
The secret is that this was done out of a desire to favor Kṣveḍa.
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus concluded the incidental discussion, he returns to the subject at hand: "Let the deluded remain aside; the meditation on the Nirguṇa is now being described."
Because the knowledge is one and the same, one should collect the qualities found in all the Vedic branches here.

"Let it be so. By the logic already stated—that there is a single cognition of Brahman across all Vedāntas due to the non-difference of the injunctions and other factors—the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa) Brahman is one;

therefore, he says "knowledge" (vidyā), meaning that one should perform the meditation by collecting together in one place the various qualities of the object of worship mentioned in those various recensions (śākhās). ||67||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Having thus disregarded the fools, he follows the subject at hand with the words "Let it be" (tiṣṭhatu). He states the manner of that [subject] as follows:
"Knowledge" (vidyā) || 67 ||
The withdrawal of the aggregate of qualities, such as bliss and the rest, which are to be enjoined.
In this sūtra, "Ānanda and others," [the matter] has been described by Vyāsa. (68)

Rāmānuja’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Furthermore, those qualities are of two kinds: those to be affirmed and those to be negated. Among these, regarding the qualities to be affirmed—such as "Brahman is bliss," "Brahman is knowledge and bliss," "He is eternal, pure, awakened, true, free, stainless, all-pervading, non-dual, bliss, the supreme, and of one essence with the inner self"—their synthesis is established in the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with "Bliss and the rest [belong to the Principal]."
He states the answer, beginning with "of bliss and so forth" (ānandādeḥ). || 68 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Dispelling the doubt that this is not according to tradition and asking what those qualities are, he states them through injunctions and prohibitions along with scriptural authority in two verses beginning with "ānandādeḥ. In the Sūtra: "Bliss and so forth belong to the Principal [Brahman].
In the locative case. || 68 ||
The withdrawal of the collection of qualities, such as "not gross" and so forth, which are the objects of negation.
Likewise, it has been stated by Vyāsa in this Sūtra: "But [the rule] regarding the cognitions of the syllables... (Brahma-sūtra 3.3.1).

Rāmatīrtha’s Commentary: Regarding those qualities to be negated which are heard here and there in various scriptural passages—such as "neither gross nor subtle," "that which is neither short nor long," "the invisible, the ungraspable, the soundless, the touchless, the formless, the imperishable," and so forth—their subsumption (upasaṃhāra) under the cognition of the Imperishable (akṣara), by virtue of their commonality and their presence [in all Upaniṣads], is stated in this section [of the Brahma Sūtras] beginning with "But the restriction of the cognitions of the Imperishable is due to their commonality and their presence, as in the case of the Upasad rites; so it has been said. Thus he says: "Of the 'not-gross' and so forth. (69)

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding the phrase "of 'not gross' and so forth"—the meaning is that this refers to the section in the Sūtras beginning with: "But there is no contradiction regarding the cognitions of the Imperishable, on account of the commonality and the presence therein, as in the case of the Aupasadās; that has been stated. However, the literal meaning [of the Sūtra] should be understood from the *Brahmāmṛtavarṣiṇī* commentary on that very work. ||69||
In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya, this is the "Withdrawal of Attributes" (*Guṇasaṃhṛti*) within the knowledge of the reality of the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇabrahmatattva*).
"The objection that 'this [treatise] called Dhyānadīpa would not be appropriate' was directed at Vyāsa alone, and not at me. (70)
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "In the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇabrahmavidyā*), the inclusion of attributes (*guṇopasaṃhāra*) is not appropriate.

Anticipating this objection—that since the Sūtrakāra himself has stated that it is the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman, our own assertion of such an inclusion does not contradict him—we respond as follows.
He says that this is appropriate: "nirguṇa" (devoid of qualities), etc. || 70 ||
In that regard as well, he mocks [the opponent] by raising an objection and then resolving it: "Nirguṇa... (Verse 70).
Because the forms beginning with Sūrya are not mentioned as having golden beards.
If you argue that being devoid of qualities (nirguṇatva) is not contradictory [to this], then let yourself be satisfied with that.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: If it is argued that because there is no mention of forms characterized by qualities such as having golden hair and beard, this must be an meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa) [Brahman], then he says "hiraṇya... to show that there is no contradiction. Regarding the forms of Hiraṇyaśmaśru, Sūrya, and others:
one whose beard is made of gold is "Hiraṇyaśmaśru"; the Sun is of that nature; and those for whom the Sun with the golden beard is the first are the "Hiraṇyaśmaśru-sūryādi" [forms].

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "those [beings] beginning with Brahmā" refers to their forms; "the forms of Hiraṇyaśmaśru, Sūrya, and so forth" refers to those very forms. Thus is the grammatical construction. || 71 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Having understood the intention behind the mockery, he approves of it in a favorable manner: "Gold," etc. (71).
Because qualities serve as indicators, there is no actual entry [into the object] in reality.
If this is so, let the reality of Brahman be meditated upon in exactly this way.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (rā0 ṭī0): Now, an objection is raised: "Since qualities such as bliss (ānanda) and those such as 'not gross' (asthūla) do not enter into the reality that is the object of meditation, how can Brahman be the object of meditation as qualified by those qualities? Anticipating this doubt, he states—beginning with the verse "guṇānām"—that even though they do not enter into the interior of that reality, it is possible for them to function as indicators (lakṣaka), and thus Brahman indicated by them is the object of meditation. || 72 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection may be raised: "Since the enjoined qualities such as bliss (*ānanda*) mentioned in the aforementioned sūtras, and the negated qualities such as 'not gross' (*asthūla*), serve as indicators of the true nature [of Brahman], they have no place therein; therefore, it is improper to say that the meditation on Brahman qualified by those [qualities]—which is the subject under discussion—can be accomplished without them. This is true. However, [the author] says, "Of the qualities" (*guṇānām*), etc., to show that Brahman is indeed to be meditated upon as indicated by the aforementioned qualities. || 72 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He demonstrates the very manner of worship in this way:
"In this context, the Self is indicated by [the qualities] beginning with bliss and those beginning with 'not gross'."
They worship in this manner: "I am He, the indivisible single essence."

Regarding the phrase "by Ānanda and others": the ellipsis here is that those seeking liberation (mumukṣavas) meditate thus: "I am that very Self which is indicated by these qualities such as bliss (ānanda) and the like, as well as by qualities such as 'not gross' (asthūla) and so forth, as the one indivisible essence (akhaṇḍaikarasa) in these scriptural passages. || 73 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): And so, how does the form of worship conclude? To this he says: "By bliss and the rest.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "those seeking liberation meditate upon [Him], that is, they contemplate Him continuously. || 73 ||
If it is asked what the distinction is between enlightenment and worship, listen as it is explained.
In reality, awakening is dependent on the object, whereas worship is dependent on the agent.

Rāghavabhaṭṭa’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: "If this is so, what is the distinction between knowledge (vidyā) and meditation (upāsanā)? Anticipating this, he states that the distinction lies in their being based on reality (vastu-tantra) versus being based on ritual action (kartṛ-tantra):
"Of knowledge and meditation... (verse 74).

Commentary (a0): Now, having raised the doubt—"In that case, what is the difference between knowledge (*bodha*) and worship (*upāsanā*)?"—he provides the resolution with the verse beginning "of knowledge and worship" (*bodhopāstyoḥ*). || 74 ||
The Ninth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
Rāma’s Commentary: To establish another distinction, he shows the cause and other factors of awakening:
"Awakening arises from inquiry; no desire can turn it back."
Merely by its own arising, it burns away the entire reality of saṃsāra. || 75 ||
By the two verses beginning with "From inquiry it is born" (355), [it is said]: "From inquiry"—that is, from inquiry into the true nature of reality (*vastutattva*), knowledge (*bodha*) arises.
Furthermore, regarding the knowledge arising from inquiry, one does not turn back [from it] by thinking, "May this knowledge that is arising not be an undesired knowledge."
And awakening, as it arises, would prevent [the world]; by its mere birth, it burns away—that is, destroys—the reality of the entire phenomenal universe within saṃsāra. ||75||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, he explains the distinction between awakening (*bodha*) and meditation (*upāsti*) as formulated in the aphorism, beginning with "from inquiry" (*vicārāt*). "Indifference" (*anicchā*) means lack of interest. The point is that since even a lover in separation perceives the knowledge of the moon and other objects despite having no desire for them, awakening is entirely dependent upon the object as presented by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). He states the difference of the realization of Brahman from worldly realization with the word "own" (*sva*): [it is] the destruction of the fundamental ignorance regarding its own object.
The phrase "sanadvāre" is implied. || 75 ||
Having thus accomplished his purpose, he nevertheless attained a state of insatiability.
Having attained liberation while living, one awaits the exhaustion of the prārabdha karma.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: By that much—meaning merely by the arising of the knowledge of reality—one attains unsurpassed happiness; such is the meaning. || 76 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He states that its fruit is indeed immediate by saying "tāvatā" (by that much). "Īkṣate" means he perceives it as a witness, seeing it being exhausted moment by moment through experience. || 76 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To establish another distinction between meditation (*upāsanā*) and knowledge (*bodha*), he demonstrates it as follows:
"Trusting the instruction of a reliable authority, one who does not investigate..."
One should contemplate it through other mental impressions that arise without interruption. || 77 ||

Regarding the word "āpta" (the authoritative one): having attended upon the instruction of an authoritative teacher, and having placed full trust in the collection of statements that establish the true nature [of reality], one should investigate it. One should contemplate that reality through mental states (*vṛtti*) that are uninterrupted—that is, not separated—by other cognitions whose objects are heterogeneous things such as jars. || 77 ||
Commentary (a0): Having thus described the cause and effect of awakening, he now describes those [factors] of meditation (*upāsti*), beginning with "āpta" (the authoritative).

The syntactical connection is as follows: one should contemplate "I am Brahman" by means of mental states that are uninterrupted—that is, devoid of the separation caused by the aforementioned misconceptions—and which are distinct from other heterogeneous factors. || 77 ||
As long as the conceit of one's own nature as consciousness arises.
Having reflected upon it for that long, one should thereafter maintain it in that very same way until death.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question of for how long one should meditate, he says: "As long as... (verse 78).
Commentary (a0): Now, one might ask, "For how long should one contemplate in this manner? To this, he says: "As long as... (78).
The Rāma-Ṭīkā clarifies the lay follower’s (upāsaka) identification with that [divine] nature by means of an illustration:
"A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), while begging for alms, was endowed with the Saṃvarga-vidyā."
Having fixed the nature of the universal absorber within his mind, he indeed made this request.

Regarding the term *brahmacārī*: a certain celibate student (*brahmacārī*), a worshipper of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) distinguished by the quality of being the "absorber" (*saṃvarga*), having arrived for the purpose of collecting alms, stood before the king named Abhipratārin and [recited]: "The one God, the protector of the world, has swallowed the four great ones; who is he? [Kāpeya...
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[the section] titled "The Lamp of Meditation" (*Dhyānadīpa*).

The meaning is that it is heard in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad that [the sage] manifested the state of his own self as the *saṃvarga* (the absorber) by means of the mantra: "O Abhipratārin, those mortals who do not perceive you dwelling in many ways... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.1.2). || 79 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Even when a momentary sense of identification with the nature of the object of worship has arisen within oneself, he explains the maintenance of that very state until death through an illustration, beginning with the words "brahmacārī. A certain celibate student (*brahmacārī*), who was a meditator identifying himself with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as characterized by the quality of being the "absorber" (*saṃvarga*), while wandering for alms—performing even the act of begging for food due to his prior impressions (*saṃskāra*) just like bathing and purification—[was instructed] by means of the Saṃvarga-vidyā from the Chāndogya...

[He was] endowed with the aforementioned meditation on *prāṇa*, as is well known from the scriptures. For this very reason, the passage beginning with "the absorber" (*saṃvarga*) and so forth should be applied.

Once, having gone to the palace of a king named Abhipratārin for the sake of alms, [he spoke] by means of the Chāndogya mantra: "The one God, the protector of the world, has swallowed the four great ones;
O Kāpeya, O Abhipratārin, mortals do not perceive Him who dwells in many forms. Thus, by this mantra...

By reciting [the mantra], he manifested within his own mind the identity with the vital breath (prāṇa) of the aforementioned form that he had held toward Him; thus it is recorded in that very [text]: "He has swallowed [it] and He is awake. "Gopāḥ" means the protector. "Kāpeya" means O you who are born of the Kapi lineage. || 79 ||

In the *Rāma-ṭīkā*, showing the cause for maintaining [the state] until death, he states the distinction from the nature of awakening (bodhadharma) mentioned in the passage "one should not turn back due to lack of desire": I rā0 ṭīkā—showing the cause for maintaining [the state] until death, he states the distinction from the nature of awakening (bodhadharma) mentioned in the passage "one should not turn back due to lack of desire": [he says]:
According to the will of a person, [it is possible] to act, not to act, or to act otherwise.
Therefore, one should always perform worship that is possible to carry out, thereby creating a continuous stream of conviction.

Regarding the phrase "of the person": worship can be performed, not performed, or performed in another manner according to the will of the person who is the worshipper; therefore, because it is dependent on the person's will, the meaning is that one should perform the worship at all times. || 80 ||
Commentary: To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Of the person," etc. (80).
Rāma’s Commentary: To the question, "What happens when one contemplates thus constantly? he says:
"For one who studies the Vedas remains vigilant; through that constant mental impression (*adhivāsa*), he continues to study even in his dreams."
Just as one who has recited [the mantra] indeed continues to recite it, so too one who has meditated upon it causes [the deity] to dwell [within].
"Vedādhyāyī" means one who is vigilant in the study of the Vedas, always habituated to recitation, and a perpetual practitioner of *japa*.

By virtue of firm latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he performs recitation or *japa* even during dreams and so forth; likewise, the practitioner (*upāsaka*) should meditate (*dhyāyet*) even during dreams and the like, as long as those impressions persist. || 81 ||

— Commentary (A0 Ṭīkā) — In that regard, he provides two worldly examples as well, beginning with "vedādhyāyī" (one who studies the Vedas). "Vāsitaḥ" means refined or cultivated. He then establishes the resulting fruit by means of the remainder of the verse, beginning with "tathā" (so too), and so forth. || 81 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the reason for continuing meditation even during one's own speech and other activities:
"Having abandoned contrary cognitions, one should cultivate [the object] without interruption."
Through the influence of latent impressions (vāsanā), one experiences mental cultivation even in dreams and similar states. || 82 ||
Regarding the term "contradictory": it refers to meditation (*bhāvanā*), which arises from the influence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the intensity of mental formations (*saṃskāra*). || 82 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one who is distressed by the thought that it is extremely difficult to accomplish the cultivation of states up to the status of a meditator—even in dreams and the like—by means of examples such as the student and so forth, is consoled with the verse beginning "virodhī" (verse 82).
Even while enjoying [the fruits of his actions], he constantly persists in his own undertaking with extraordinary intensity.
One who is addicted to sensual objects is undoubtedly unable to meditate. || 83 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "How can the perfection of constant contemplation be achieved for one who, under the influence of *prārabdha* karma, continues to experience sense objects?
[End of page 357] Ninth Chapter.

Anticipating this objection, he says "bhuñjānaḥ" (while enjoying), meaning that when there is an excess of firm resolve, the perfection of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) will occur, just as in the case of one who is addicted to a sensual object. || 83 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "How can there be uninterrupted meditation for one who experiences hundreds of pleasures and pains produced by prārabdha-karma through contact with sense objects? To this, he says: "Even while enjoying... He clarifies the illustration therein with the verse beginning: "viṣaya... (Verse 83).
A woman who is devoted to another man remains distracted even while engaged in her household duties.
He alone internally relishes that elixir of union with the Supreme.
Rāmānuja’s commentary explains the illustration: "One who is devoted to another's misfortune" (verse 84).
He illustrates that with the verse beginning "para" (verse 84). The commentary says: "He illustrates that. || 84 ||
Even while she relishes the company of another, that domestic duty of hers remains undone.
This [intellect] may indeed become dull, yet it continues to function by its very onset alone. || 85 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that indulging in the company of others might lead to the neglect of household duties, he says: "parasaṅgam" (the company of others). || 85 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, one might ask: "If she thus tastes the elixir of union with another, how could there be household duties for her? To this, he says:
"Union with another... (verse 85).
Just as one who is devoted to household duties performs them properly.
One who is devoted to another's misfortune does not do that at all, under any circumstances. || 86 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He explains the meaning of what was stated—that he exists merely by outward appearance—with the verse beginning "gṛhakṛtya" (verse 86).
Commentary (a0): He explains that the mere turning around is the housework by means of a negative example (vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta), [stating]: "gṛhakṛtya... (verse 86).
Thus, even one who is solely intent upon meditation may, as a minor undertaking, engage in worldly activity.
One should properly practice worldly conduct, for it is not in contradiction with being a knower of reality.

Rāma’s Commentary: He applies this to the subject at hand [the simile]: "In this way, through meditation... Now, one might ask: does even a knower of reality engage in worldly activity only slightly, or does he do so fully?
