Since the engagement with objects is not contradictory to the knowledge of reality, he says, "The knower of reality," [implying that he engages fully]. || 87 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He clarifies the aforementioned point in the practical application (dārṣṭantika) with the half-verse beginning with "evam" (thus). He summarizes the distinction of one established in Brahman (brahmaniṣṭha) from that [ordinary person] with the verse beginning with "tattvavit" (the knower of reality). || 87 ||
This phenomenal world is composed of illusion (māyā), while the Self (ātman) possesses the nature of pure consciousness (caitanya).
Thus, what contradiction is there for one who engages in worldly affairs regarding this awakening? || 88 ||
He demonstrates the very fact of non-contradiction with the words: "consisting of illusion" (māyāmaya). || 88 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) on verse a0 elucidates the very manner of non-contradiction: "Illusion" (māyā), etc. || 88 ||
Conventional discourse does not depend upon the reality of the phenomenal world.
Nor is there any innate dullness in her; rather, she simply desires the means of accomplishment.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He elaborates on the very absence of contradiction with the verse beginning "apekṣate" (89).
The commentary (ṭīkā) on a0 explains that very lack of contradiction: "It depends," [verse 89].
In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya, [in the chapter titled] *Dhyānadīpa*, the commentary (*rā0 ṭīkā*) asks:
"What are those means for worldly transaction? and therefore says:
The mind, speech, body, and their respective objects are the means of accomplishment; these [are what one should understand].
One who knows reality does not destroy [the world]; why then would conventional practice not belong to him? || 90 ||

Regarding the phrase "mind and speech": external objects such as houses, fields, and so forth—since the knower of reality does not restrain the mind and the other [faculties] toward those [objects], how could there be no worldly activity for this knower? The meaning is that it certainly does exist. || 90 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "Apart from the reality of the world, what other means are there for worldly transaction (*vyavahṛti*)? To this he replies with the verse beginning with "the mind" (*mana*). One might further object: "Even so, for the knower of truth (*tattvavit*), all these—mind and the rest—are indeed illusory; therefore, how can he engage in transaction by means of them? To this he replies with the remainder of the verse beginning with "those" (*tān*). Here, "sublation" (*upamardana*) refers strictly to destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and not to sublation in the sense of cognitive invalidation (*bādha*); and thus, [it is] sublated...
The meaning is that his conventional usage would indeed be sublated by those [arguments], just like the conventional usage involving a stone-son (śilāputraka) performed by a young girl. || 90 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection that even if objects are not suppressed, the knower of truth must still suppress the mind, [the author] says that if he were to do so, he would no longer be a knower of truth:
"If he were to suppress the mind, he would be a yogi, but not a knower of truth."
One who suppresses the intellect is not seen to be a knower of the true nature of the jar.
"Upamṛdvāti" (he crushes). Now, one might object that it is not observed that the mind is crushed by a knower of reality; anticipating this doubt, he says: "Not the intellect" (na buddhim).

The meaning is that a person who, while knowing—that is, cognizing—the reality of a jar, crushes or afflicts the intellect by failing to maintain one-pointedness, has never been seen or perceived. || 91 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings; attached to sense objects it leads to bondage, while free from sense objects it is known to lead to liberation. According to this scripture, how can the mind become free from sense objects without its destruction? To this he says: "He crushes [it]," etc. In that regard, he provides a corroborative illustration (arthāntaranyāsa): "Not the intellect," etc. (91).
By the mere occurrence of a single cognition, it always appears as a jar.
This self is self-luminous; why does it not shine forth like a jar? (92)

Rāma’s Commentary: Raising the objection that because a jar is gross and thus manifest, no mental effort is required to perceive it, whereas Brahman is not so, and therefore such effort is required for its knowledge—the author replies that since Brahman is self-luminous and thus even clearer than a jar, the restraint of the mind is not required at all; this he states in the verse beginning with "sakṛt" (once). || 92 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection is raised: "But the example of the jar here is indeed dissimilar, because it is cognizable by a single [simultaneous] cognition. Anticipating this, he provides the resolution with the verse beginning with "sakṛt" (once). || 92 ||
Since it is self-luminous, what need have you for a cognition of it to be the knowledge of reality?
The objection that growth and momentary destruction [apply] is equally valid for jars and other such things. || 93 ||

Rāma’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Even though Brahman is self-luminous, since only the mental modification (buddhivṛtti) directed toward it constitutes the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), and because that modification is momentary, it must repeatedly abide in Brahman. Anticipating this objection, he states that this same difficulty applies equally to objects such as jars, saying:
"By virtue of being self-luminous" (svaprakāśatayā). || 93 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, it may be argued that the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of Brahman is irrelevant, because even while Brahman exists, there is the experience of the existence of beginningless positive ignorance (*bhāvarūpānādyavidyā*) within it. Rather, your established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that only the cognition whose object is the non-difference of the Self from That—generated by the investigation of the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*)—is the bestower of liberation in the form of the destruction of ignorance. Furthermore, it is agreed upon by all who accept the reality of the three times (*sarvāstika*) that such a cognition lasts for only three moments; therefore, when that [cognition] dissolves—
The Ninth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

An objection may be raised: "Just as a jar is obscured by darkness when the lamp is extinguished, or by that same darkness which has returned once more, so too, because an obscuration of the reality of the non-dual Brahman-Self occurs at every moment through that very [ignorance], it is necessary to bring about the modification of the intellect (*buddhi*) into the form of that [Brahman] until the destruction of *prārabdha* karma, in order to prevent such obscuration. Anticipating this, [the author provides] a rebuttal:
And he establishes this very point: "by virtue of its self-luminosity. || 93 ||
When a jar or the like has been ascertained, the cognition [of it] perishes as soon as the jar [is no longer present].
If it is argued that [the self] can then be led as desired, that is equally true of the internal [self].

Rāma’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that even if the cognition of a jar or similar object is momentary, it is still possible to employ that jar at all times once it has been ascertained a single time—therefore making the attainment of steadiness of mind therein purposeless—he states, "In the case of the jar, etc.," showing that this [objection] applies equally to the Self as well. || 94 ||

Commentary (ṭīkā): Now, having raised the objection regarding the "releasing of the counter-example" (pratibandīmocana), he pacifies that as well by means of the very same parity of the counter-example:
"In the case of a jar, etc. (94).
When one has ascertained the self once and for all, at that very moment there is no further dependence upon it.
For indeed, the knower of reality is able to speak, deliberate, and likewise meditate.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He explains the meaning of what was stated as "equally toward oneself" with the verse beginning "having resolved. || 99 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Just as for a person who has once ascertained a jar, even after the cognition of that object has perished, there may still be a need for it—for instance, for the purpose of fetching water from the Gaṅgā—so too, after the destruction of the cognition of the Self, [the need for it] would not be impossible, since according to the method already established, its repeated recurrence is possible. This is not so; for in the view that there is a single ignorance (*ekājñānapakṣa*), through the destruction of the power of concealment by means of one's own cognition (*svabuddhyavacchedena*), the various forms of ignorance and the fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) [are destroyed].

With the intention that there is no disparity—since the destruction of the ignorance regarding the sprout and the non-acceptance of its being a veil over the identity of Brahman and the Self preclude any further veiling of the Self, whereas darkness is accepted as merely receding from the space occupied by light—he says: "Having ascertained" (niścitya). Thus, it should be understood that the similarity with the cognition of a jar exists even in the case of the cognition of Brahman. || 95 ||
If, like a lay devotee, one were to meditate and forget the mundane world.
She seemed to forget due to her meditation; it was a lapse of memory, not a lapse of feeling.
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even a knower of reality is seen to be devoid of concern for the world, just like a practitioner (upāsaka), due to his constant contemplation of the Self.

Anticipating this doubt, he states [verse 96]: "The practitioner..."—thereby showing that such an absence of concern is caused by meditative absorption (dhyāna) and not by the realization of truth (vedana).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, if it is argued that even worldly forgetfulness is observed in some who know the truth, such as Ṛṣabha and others, due to their meditation—let it be so; however, since that [forgetfulness] is an effect of meditation, it is not produced by knowledge. With this intention, he says: "Like a devotee" (upāsaka iva). ||96||
But for him, meditative absorption is optional, because liberation is accomplished through knowledge alone.
"But liberation comes from knowledge alone"—this is the drum-beat proclaimed in the scriptures. (97)

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even by a knower of reality, meditation on Brahman must be performed for the sake of attaining liberation. Anticipating this, [the author] states that meditation need not be performed for the sake of liberation, because of the existence of such scriptural passages as: "Liberation is attained through knowledge alone, by which one is released"; "Only by knowing Him does one go beyond death; there is no other path"; and "By knowing the God, one is freed from all sins. Thus, meditation is not required for liberation.
Ha— meditation. || 97 ||
The commentary on the *Yanāya* states the conclusion: "But meditation... (verse 97).
If one who knows reality does not meditate, then [the mind] would proceed outward.
Let this proceed with ease; what obstacle could there be to its proceeding? (98)
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [pages 360–360]
[The commentary on the *Dhyānadīpa* by Rāma:]—Now, one might object: "If the knower of reality does not accept meditation (*dhyāna*), would he not always be engaged in external activity?
Anticipating this, the author states that such activity is accepted precisely because it acts as a sublater [of ignorance], saying: "The knower of reality... (verse 98).

Commentary (a0): Anticipating the objection that there might be a fault in the absence of meditation for such a person, he replies by conceding the point with the words "tattvavid yadi" (if the knower of reality...). ||98||
If you say this leads to an over-extension, then first state the unwanted consequence.
If it is argued that the scriptural injunctions apply by way of logical consequence, that is not so with respect to one who knows reality.

Rāma’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Anticipating the objection that "if external activity were admitted, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga)," he refutes it by stating, "it is not so," on the grounds that such an over-extension is difficult to establish. If it is argued that the over-extension is not difficult to establish because the word "over-extension" (prasaṅga) is intended here to refer to the scriptural injunctions (vidhiśāstra), [the author] replies: "No; for that [injunction] pertains to those who lack knowledge, and thus does not apply to one who knows the reality. He states this with the words, "The over-extension (prasaṅga)."
The term "injunctional scripture" (vidhiśāstra) is an elliptical expression that includes the prohibitive scripture (niṣedhaśāstra) as well. || 99 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Anticipating an over-extension of the argument, he asks about the logical consequence and refutes it with the verse beginning "Ati... (99).
He who possesses the conceit of caste, stage of life, and state of age;
And all prohibitions as well as injunctions pertain to that very [Self]. || 100 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He demonstrates that the ritualistic scripture (*vidhi-śāstra*) has as its subject matter only those who are not enlightened (*avidvat*), with the verse beginning "varṇa... (100).
The castes, stages of life, and so forth, are imagined within the body by means of māyā.
"Of the Self, which is of the nature of consciousness"—such was his firm conviction.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that even for a knower of reality, there exists the conceit of caste, stage of life, and so forth, due to the fact that he still wears a body; anticipating this, he says: "Caste, stage of life," etc. (Verse 1).
The reason for this is stated in the two verses beginning with "varṇa" (100–101).
Whether one practices meditative concentration or performs actions, or whether one does not perform them at all.
With all attachments cast off by the heart, one of supreme disposition is indeed liberated. || 2 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Let the determination of reality stand for now; however, the scripture teaches that there is a duty to be performed by him.
Anticipating this, he says "samādhim" (meditative absorption) to show that even that [scripture] indicates the very absence of any duty for him. He who, with his heart and intellect—

One whose every kind of attachment has been entirely abandoned is such [a person]. For this very reason, he is one of "exalted disposition" (*uttamāśaya*), meaning one whose intention (*abhiprāya*) or pure knowledge is supreme; he is indeed liberated. Therefore, the syntactical connection is: "then, for him, both meditative absorption and actions... (2).
Regarding this, he states the proof: "Samādhim" (concentration). This is from the *Vāsiṣṭhasāra*. || 102 ||
His goal is achieved through renunciation; his goal is not attained by ritual actions.
For one whose mind is not free from latent impressions through meditative concentration and the recitation of prayers, [there is no liberation].
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To show that there is nothing further to be done by the man of realization, he cites another scriptural statement:

"By means of *naiṣkarmya*," etc. *Naiṣkarmya* is the state of being free from action; the meaning is "by the renunciation of action. *Samādhāna* is meditative absorption (*samādhi*). *Japya* is silent recitation (*japa*). || 3 ||
— Commentary (A0 Ṭīkā): Thus, he cites two other passages from that same work as authority here, beginning with the words "naiṣkarmyeṇa" (by means of actionlessness).

*Naiṣkarmya* is renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). *Samādhāna* is meditative absorption (*samādhi*). *Japya* refers to the collection of mantras such as the *praṇava*. *Nirvāsana* is the absence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). ... [and so forth].
That indeed is the refinement of the sacrificial essence. || 103 ||
The Ninth Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.
The Self is attachment; that which is other than it is indeed a magical illusion, for it is illusory.
Thus, when the mind has been determined to be immovable, whence can there be any latent impression?

361 Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Now, raising the objection that even the knower (*vidvan*) must practice meditation (*dhyāna*) for the cessation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), [the author] states—beginning with the word "ātma"—that for one who possesses perfect knowledge, no such latent impression exists at all. || 4 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): "The Self is unattached. Whatever is illusory (*māyika*)—that is, the visible world consisting of *māyā* and its effects—is indeed a magical illusion (*indrajāla*), meaning it is nothing but a falsehood. || 104 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Let it be so; what relevance does this have to the present subject? To this he says:
"In this way, even the [undesirable] contingency does not exist; how then can there be an over-extension of this [objection]?"
The charge of an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) should be raised only against one for whom such an over-extension is possible.
"Thus [it is]. To the question, "Whose [consequence] then is this over-extension (atiprasaṅga)? he says: "The consequence (prasaṅga). || 105 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Stating the result, he applies it to the present subject with the words "evam" (thus). || 105 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question "Where has this been seen?", he says:
"Because of the absence of an injunction, the over-extension [of the rule] is not observed in the case of a child."
How could there be such an over-extension for this [injunction], given that it is equally absent in the case of a positive injunction?
"Because of the absence of an injunction. He applies this to the subject of the illustration: "It might be," etc. (6).
a0 Commentary: Thus, he clarifies this very point with an illustration: "Because of the absence of an injunction" (vidhyabhāvāt). || 106 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that while ignorance is the cause for the absence of injunctions in the case of a child, it is not so for the knower, he states that even though the knower lacks such ignorance, there exists something else—the omniscient reality—which serves as the cause for the absence of injunctions:
"If the child knows nothing at all, the knower of truth knows everything indeed."
All injunctions apply only to one who possesses little knowledge, and not to the other two.
"Nothing at all. Then, raising the doubt as to whose qualification for the injunction it might be, he says: "Of one who possesses little knowledge. ||7||

— Commentary (A0 Ṭīkā): There, refuting the example, he raises an objection with the words "not at all" (*na kiñcit*). For that person who is subject to injunctions is ignorant and possesses little knowledge; however, the Supreme Lord is not ignorant in every respect, nor is a child or the like entirely ignorant. Therefore, for this [Lord], Brahman...

Since everything that is perceived has its existence dependent solely upon the substratum because it is superimposed thereon, it is utterly void when separated from that [substratum]. Thus, there certainly exists a knowledge whose object is the entirety [of reality] by virtue of its falsity. For this very reason, the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* states, "By which the unheard becomes heard," and so forth, asserting through the knowledge of one thing the knowledge of all things. Therefore, he says that for the knower (*jñānin*), there is indeed an absence of ritual obligation (*vidhi-kaiṅkarya*): "All... [the text continues].
And so forth. He states the refutation: "alpa... (verse 107).

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Only he who possesses the power to curse and bless, like Vyāsa and others, is a knower of reality, and no other. To this, he replies: "If it were so, then the power to curse and bless would not be the fruit of his austerity, since [the true goal] is that from which [liberation arises]. (8)
[The opponent] says, "By a curse. [The author] refutes this, saying, "That is not so. He states the reason for that: "Because of the efficacy of the curse and so forth. (8)

Commentary (a0): Even so, one might object: "Since he lacks the power to curse or grace others, how can his status as a knower of reality be trusted? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the following resolution: "Śāpa... (verse 108).
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya—[the commentary by Rāma called *Dhyānadīpa*]:
Now, one might raise the objection that even for those who know reality, such as Vyāsa and others, the power to bestow curses and so forth is observed. Anticipating this:
He states that for them, even the fruit of knowledge of reality is not the result of knowledge, but rather the result of austerity:
"The power of Vyāsa and others is also seen through the force of austerity."
Apart from causes such as a curse, austerity is the cause of knowledge.

Regarding the phrase "of Vyāsa and others": one might object that, according to the scriptural injunction, "Seek to know Brahman through austerity" (*tapasā brahma vijijñāsasva*), even the knowledge of reality would be impossible for one devoid of austerity. Anticipating this objection, he states "by a curse, etc. (*śāpa...*) to show that this is not the case, since there exists another form of austerity [in their instance] caused by a curse or similar circumstances. ||9||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): If this is so, then how is it that even Vyāsa and others—who are teachers possessing such knowledge—are seen to have the power to exercise restraint and so forth?
To this he says: "Even of Vyāsa and others. The meaning is: "by force alone. Now, one might object: "In that case, [the scripture] says, 'One should seek to know Brahman through austerity'..."

Regarding the Taittirīya Śruti statement, "Sva...," which suggests that even for knowledge (*jñāna*) the cause is indeed austerity (*tapas*), he says: "From a curse, etc. For there are two verbal roots, *tap* meaning "to contemplate" and *tap* meaning "to torment"; therefore, the intended meaning is that their respective causes for knowledge and for a curse are indeed distinct. || 109 ||
Only for one who possesses both [the object and the means] is there the arising of the knowledge of capacity.
But by performing each one of those [acts] individually, one obtains the fruit of each one individually. || 10 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Then, one might ask, how is it that those such as Vyāsa and others are seen to possess knowledge of reality while also being the cause of curses and the like?
Anticipating this, he says "dvayam" (the pair), because both kinds of austerity exist [in them]. || 10 ||
— Commentary (Ṭīkā): For this very reason, it is said "the two. And thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. || 110 ||
If he is devoid of capability, censurable, and shunned by the practitioners according to the rules;
It is led away incessantly by others who are intent on enjoyment, even though one strives [to restrain it].

— Rāghavendra’s Commentary — Now, one might object: "Surely, even for one who lacks the power to curse others and so forth, there would be censure from those who perform prescribed duties, even in the absence of a scriptural injunction.
Anticipating this, he says, "One devoid of capacity," [verse 11], meaning that even such persons would be censured by those who are addicted to sense objects.

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, [the author] states that the lack of power to curse and so forth on the part of a knower of Brahman constitutes a censurable defect for one engaged in ritual action—namely, "sāmarthya... (verse 11).
If these [monks] were to protect their alms-bowl, robes, and so forth for the sake of satisfaction in enjoyment, [they would be at fault].
Oh, how their asceticism is slowed by the weight of dispassion!

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that these [ascetics] might also strive to acquire sense objects for the sake of contentment through enjoyment, he mocks them with the intent that, in such a case, their very status as ascetics would be lost: "Alms... (verse 12).
Commentary (a0): Now, [the author] answers with a joke the objection that ascetics should be prevented from accepting alms and so forth by laypeople through censure—[he says]: "Alms... (verse 12).

If it is said that fools devoted to caste and stage of life are "led away," then those who possess the notion that the body is the self, even if they are enlightened, are led away while merely imagining themselves to be in a [spiritual] stage of life.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: If it is argued that there is no loss for cultured (śiṣṭa) people devoted to ritual action due to the censure uttered by vulgar folk who are greedy for sense objects, then [the author] says—starting with the verse beginning "varṇāśrama"—that even for a knower of reality, there is no loss due to the censure uttered by those devoted to ritual action who identify with the body. || 13 ||
The Ninth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

363a0 Commentary: If it is asked, "What loss is there for those devoted to their caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama) through the censure directed at their specific objects? [the author] replies with the verse beginning "varṇa... (verse 13), stating that the absence of loss even for a knower of Brahman (brahmavid) due to the censure directed at ritualists (karmaṭha) is exactly the same.
Thus, in this way, because the means of knowledge do not subvert the realization of reality.
A knower of reality is able to properly carry out worldly affairs such as kingship and the like.

Rāma’s Commentary: Having concluded the incidental discussion, he returns to the subject at hand with the words, "Therefore, thus. For that reason, when the knowledge of reality has arisen in this manner described, because there is no destruction of the means [of worldly action]—that is, because the mind and other faculties, which are the instruments of worldly activity, are not dissolved—the knower is able to properly perform worldly activities such as kingship or the governance of a kingdom.
The meaning is "how" (katham). || 14 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, with the latter half of the eighty-seventh verse, he concludes what was stated in the words, "One who knows reality should practice correctly that which is not opposed to it and is beyond the world" (*tattvavittvavirodhitvālaukikaṃ samyagācaret*). He does so by saying, "Therefore, in this manner" (*tadittham*). The word *ācaritum* (to practice) is the required grammatical division. The phrase "like Janaka and others" is implied. || 14 ||
If there is no desire for that because of the perception of it as false, then let it not be [desired].
Or else, let him dwell as he has begun, either meditating or engaging in worldly affairs.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Since the knower of reality perceives the world as illusory through his knowledge of its falsity, no desire for it should arise at all.
To this, he says: "mithyātve... (verse 15), implying that [the knower] may continue to act according to the force of his own past karma.

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "In the case of Bṛhadratha, as well-known from the Maitrāyaṇīya Upaniṣad, would it not generally be impossible for a knower to have the notion of falsity regarding his kingdom? Anticipating this, the author accepts [the point] with the words "mithyātva" (falsity). The meaning is: "as it has begun," that is, in such a way as not to transgress the momentum of the prārabdha karma, such as its intense force and so forth. || 115 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now he shows the difference between this [state] and that of the practitioner (upāsaka):
"But the practitioner should dwell constantly engaged in meditation alone, because..."
His status as Brahmā was produced by meditation alone, just like his status as Viṣṇu and others.

Regarding the term "lay follower" (upāsaka), he states the reason for it with the words "because" (yataḥ). The meaning is that since his status as Brahman was established solely through meditation and not measured by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), therefore a meditator must always practice meditation. In this regard, there is an illustration: "like Viṣṇu-hood and so forth.
Just as Viṣṇu-hood and the like, which are produced within oneself through meditation, do not possess ultimate reality, so too [is the case here].
This is the meaning. || 16 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, while discussing the nature of the lay practitioner (*upāsaka*), [the author] prescribes the continuity of meditation by stating "The lay practitioner, however," and so forth. Therein, he clarifies the reason with an illustration using the remainder of the verse beginning with "Since," and so on. || 16 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that what is produced through meditation might nonetheless be ultimately real,
he says "not so," because it is observed that qualities such as being a "cow of speech" (vāgdhenu) produced by meditation disappear when the meditation ceases.
That which is derived from meditative absorption dissolves in the absence of meditative absorption.
True Brahmanhood does not dissolve in the absence of knowledge. || 17 ||

Regarding the phrase "by meditation": he states its distinction from the state of being Brahman as revealed by knowledge with the word "real" (*vāstavī*). This is a qualifying attribute containing a reason: since the state of being Brahman is real, it does not dissolve even in the absence of the knowledge that makes it known. || 17 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [page 364] 364.
[Commentary on the *Dhyānadīpa*, verse 17]:

In this regard, he states the reasoning composed of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth with the words "In meditation... (*dhyāna*). He establishes its distinction from the fruit of knowledge by means of its being uncreated (*akṛtakatva*), stating: "...is real" (*vāstavī*). || 17 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Precisely because it is real, this [Self] does not produce knowledge; thus he says:
"Therefore, this [Self], being the knower, does not produce eternal knowledge."
For truth does not vanish merely through the absence of a means of cognition. || 18 ||

Regarding the word "tataḥ" (therefore): since that state of Brahman-hood is eternal, knowledge is merely its indicator (*abhijñāpaka*) or revealer (*avabodhaka*), not its producer; this is the meaning. He states the supporting argument there by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "jñāpaka... (as an indicator). The intention is as follows: if the state of Brahman-hood were produced by knowledge, then upon the destruction of that knowledge, it would itself vanish. But it does not vanish. Therefore, it is not produced; this is the meaning. || 18 ||
Commentary on Sūtra 1
— The reason for this is stated as "tataḥ" (from that). Because this aforementioned knowledge has become its own object—
The connection is as follows: since non-dual Brahman is eternal, it does not produce [anything]; therefore, it is merely indicative and informative, but not a causal agent.

He supports this very point through an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle) with the words "jñāpaka" and so on. The sense is that this is quite evident in the case of the beauty of a mirror and similar instances. || 18 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "But surely, even for the worshiper, the state of being Brahman is indeed real.
To this, he says: "If it be argued that the worshiper also possesses a real state of being Brahman..."
Is the true nature of Brahman not also present in commoners and even in animals? 19.
"It certainly exists. With the intention that this which has been said is far too little, he says: "Of the common folk," etc. (Verse 19).
Commentary (a0): Now, one might object: "In the Siddhānta, does even the worshipper not possess actual Brahman-hood?
To this he replies, "It certainly exists," and then resolves that objection with the words beginning "pāmarāṇām" (of the ignorant). || 19 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that although the state of being Brahman exists even in commoners and others, it is not conducive to human purpose because it is unknown, he states that the lack of conduciveness to human purpose due to ignorance is equal for the meditator as well:
"Due to ignorance, the lack of being the supreme human goal is the same in both cases."
Just as alms-seeking is superior to fasting, so too is meditation superior to other practices.

"Out of ignorance. Now, one might ask: "In that case, for what purpose is meditation (upāsana) being described? Anticipating this, he says—with the intention of showing its superiority over other practices—by means of an illustration: "From fasting," etc. (20).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object that ignorance exists even among common folk; therefore, he says "due to ignorance. If that is so, then why is there such excellence for the ritualist (*karmī*) and the worshipper (*upāsaka*) in the scripture? To this, he says "from fasting" (*upavāsāt*). || 120 ||
The performance of ritual actions and so forth is better than the conduct of the ignorant.
After that comes the meditation on the qualified (saguṇa), and after that, the meditation on the unqualified (nirguṇa).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He demonstrates the very superiority [of this practice] over other observances with the verse beginning "pāmarāṇām" (21).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Therein, he states the sequence of internal gradations: "Of the common folk" (*pāmarāṇām*). "Worldly activity" (*vyavahṛteḥ*) refers to agriculture, trade, service, and so forth. "Ritual action and the like" (*karmādi*); by the word "and the like," the recitation of the names of either Hari or Hara and so on are included. "With attributes" (*saguṇā*); for that [worship] is of two kinds, distinguished as *pratīka-upāsanā* (meditation on a symbol) and *ahaṃgraha-upāsanā* (meditation identifying the self with the object). That too is twofold, through the distinction between meditation on a particular symbol (*yatkicit-pratīka*) and meditation on the universal symbol (*sarva-pratīka*). Among these—

For example, the first type is: "One should meditate [on Brahman] as Name-Brahman. The latter type is also exemplified by: "All this, indeed, is Brahman. In this same way, the *ahaṃgraha* (the method of grasping the Self as the object) regarding the Saguna [Brahman] is twofold: "I am Viṣṇu" and "All this and I am Vāsudeva. Regarding the Nirguṇa [Brahman], it has already been stated below. || 21 ||
The Ninth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the reason for the progressive excellence:
"As long as there is proximity to perfect knowledge, so long does excellence increase."
For the sake of your knowledge of Brahman, I shall gradually provide you with direct instruction on the worship of the attributeless (Nirguṇa).
Regarding the phrase "as far as": he states the reason for the sandals being supreme among all things—namely, that they are "for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman. || 22 ||
The reason for this is stated: "As long as... (a0 ṭīkā). || 22 ||
Just as a non-erroneous illusion is recognized as valid cognition at the time of its result.
In the same way, meditation becomes manifest at the time of liberation due to its complete ripening.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He confirms the stated point by presenting an illustration, beginning with the words "yathā" (just as). || 23 ||
Commentary (a0): He recalls an illustration for the fact that meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa) leads gradually to the knowledge of Brahman: "Just as... (yathā). || 23 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "A concordant error is not itself valid knowledge; rather, when a person acts upon it, valid knowledge arises from the contact of their own sense organ with its object. To this, he raises the following doubt: "For a person who has acted upon a concordant error, [knowledge arises] from another means of cognition."
If it is argued that this is valid knowledge, then let such worship be directed toward me as the cause within the heart. || 24 ||

[Objection: "Let it be so. [Response: Then even meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇopāsana), being of the nature of profound reflection (nididhyāsana), will become a cause for the immediate knowledge (aparokṣajñāna) produced by the Great Saying (mahāvākya). To this he says: "In the same way" (tathā). || 24 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, an objection may be raised: when meditation in the form of the apprehension of the Self as "I am the attributeless" (nirguṇāhaṃgraha) eventually transforms into the nature of non-dual Brahman, the illustrative example of a "concordant error" (saṃvādi-bhrama) is indeed inappropriate. This is because, in that case, proximity to a real object serves as the cause only for a direct perception (pratyakṣa) regarding that [real] object; furthermore, the aforementioned error lacks the transformation into a direct perception whose object is the actual reality under discussion. Anticipating this, he resolves the issue by accepting the consequence (iṣṭāpatti): "saṃ-"...
"The proponent" (vādī) [is defined as follows]. || 24 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, if this is so, one might object that even the meditation on a form and the like would become a means for immediate realization by way of producing one-pointedness of mind; to this he replies, "That too is accepted," stating:
"If [it is argued] that meditation on a form, mantras, and so forth are also causes..."
Granted that this may be so, nevertheless, proximity (pratyāsatti) is distinguished here [as the determining factor]. || 25 ||

Regarding the word "mūrti" (the form): if that is so, what is the excellence in the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa)? To this he says, "tathāpi" (even so). "Pratyāsatti" means proximity; the ellipsis is that it is proximity to knowledge. || 25 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, if it is the case that there is such regard for the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa) [Brahman] because it is the means to the knowledge of Brahman, then let it be granted that the meditation on forms such as the four-armed [Viṣṇu], as well as the Gāyatrī mantra and the six-syllabled (ṣaḍakṣara) mantra, and even the utterance of the name of either Hari or Hara, may likewise be causes for the knowledge of Brahman through indirect connection. Furthermore, regarding the statement "And there is a need for all [works], because of the scriptural texts concerning sacrifices and so forth," etc.— [End of fragment]
He says—“of the meditation on the form”—because, by virtue of that very [chapter], all actions not opposed to the Vedas are likewise accepted. || 125 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He demonstrates the very manner of proximity:
"When the worship of the attributeless (nirguṇa) has matured, from that, samādhi will gradually arise."
That concentration which is called cessation is obtained without effort. || 26 ||
Regarding the term "nirguṇa": when the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa) becomes mature, then there arises the samādhi with mental constructs (savikalpaka-samādhi);
from that—[[page 366-to-366]] 368.
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya:
"That cause is to be attained through Sāṃkhya and Yoga; such indeed is the Śruti."
However, that which contradicts the Śruti is a mere semblance of Sāṃkhya and Yoga. || 35 ||

Regarding the phrase "that is the cause": one might object that since both Sāṃkhya and Yoga are accepted as means to liberation by way of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the principles (*tattvas*) propounded in those respective scriptures would also have to be accepted. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But he who... The meaning is that the appearance is sublated. || 35 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): In this regard, he also corroborates it with the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, saying "That" (tad). [Objection: But if that is so, then [the Smṛti says]—

If it be argued that this leads to the fault of leaving no room for other [scriptures], we say no, because that would lead to the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis. By these two sections, [the Sūtrakāra] refutes Yoga as well.
To explain why the venerable Teacher Bādarāyaṇa and others performed such a refutation, he says:
"But that which... This implies: "That portion of Sāṃkhya and Yoga which is contrary to Śruti is merely a semblance (ābhāsa). It is not the true knowledge (samyak-khyāti).

This is because of the traditional rule that the root *khyā* means "to declare," and based on the etymological derivation that it is so called because by it the Self is made known (*jñāpyate*) through the excellence (*prakarpa*) of its nature as non-dual Brahman.
Likewise: "Having rendered the mind free from fluctuations and having unified the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) with the Supreme Self, one is liberated; this is declared to be the primary yoga."

And because of this traditional teaching (*smṛti*), since the terms "Sāṃkhya" and "Yoga" are intended solely for the single valid cognition whose object is the non-dual identity of the Self, and because [the other systems] are sublated, the meaning is that Sāṃkhya and the rest are merely semblances (*ābhāsa*). || 135 ||
He for whom there is no neglect of spiritual practice in this world [will find it] in the next.
Whether at death or in the world of Brahmā, one who has realized the reality is liberated. || 36 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection that liberation might not be attained if death occurs before the realization of truth for one who is practicing meditation, he says: "Meditation... (verse 36).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might raise the objection: "If the span of one's life comes to an end even before the knowledge of the Self—which arises from the ripening of the practice of the formless (*nirguṇa*) *ahaṃgraha* meditation—is attained, what is the destination? Anticipating this, he provides the resolution with the words "Upāsanam" (The Meditation). He who, in this present birth, has practiced the formless meditation but it has not reached full maturity to bear the fruit of the realization of Truth—he, for his part, is born according to such [scriptural statements] as: "One fallen from Yoga is born into the house of the pure and the prosperous."

The syntactical connection is as follows: having realized the truth through memory in a previous birth, one is liberated; or, at the time of death when the ripening [of karma] has occurred and only the latent impression (vāsanā) of dwelling in the world of Brahmā remains, one realizes the truth in the world of Brahmā and is liberated. || 136 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the authoritative proof for attaining liberation through knowledge on the day of death:
"Whatever state of being one remembers when they finally cast off the body..."
"He goes to whatever he thinks of; by that [thought] he goes," according to the scripture. (37)

Regarding the phrase "whichever [world] he intends": the meaning is that by whatever state of mind one possesses, by that very state the vital breath (prāṇa) follows; and according to the scriptural statement, "the vital breath, joined with heat (tejas), together with the self (ātman), leads him to the world as it has been conceived," this is the sense. || 37 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding death, he cites the statement from the Gītā beginning with "yaṃ yaṃ... as the authoritative proof for the knowledge of reality arising from the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa).

He also cites the Śruti that serves as its source, beginning with "yat...": "By whatever [object] the mind is set, by that the vital breath (prāṇa) follows; the vital breath, joined with heat (tejas), together with the self (ātman), leads him to the world as it has been conceived. This is according to the Kaṇva recension of the Śruti. The word "is liberated" (mucyate) connects with what precedes.
The connection [is as follows]. || 37 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, having raised the objection that the previously cited scriptural and traditional texts describe a future birth arising from the final thought-moment, [the author] concedes that point explicitly, while maintaining that liberation arises from knowledge:
[Page 367]
The Ninth Chapter,
together with the two commentaries:
"If that were the case, future birth would certainly [arise] from the final cognition."
Even the cognition of the attributeless may occur during the meditation on the qualified, just as [in the case of the previous example]. || 38 ||

Regarding the phrase "from the final cognition" (antyapratyayataḥ): one might ask, "How then is liberation attained through knowledge at the time of death? Anticipating this, he says "tathā sati" (that being so), meaning: that being so, when the future birth is determined by the final cognition.

Just as for one who meditates on Brahman with attributes (saguṇa), at the time of death a cognition in the form of the qualified Brahman arises by the force of prior practice, so too for one who meditates on the attributeless (nirguṇa) Brahman, a cognition having the attributeless Brahman as its object arises—or will arise; this is the meaning. || 38 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): To the question, "What follows from that in the present context?", he says: "The last," etc. (Verse 38).

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "By the power of practicing the contemplation of the attributeless (nirguṇa), there may indeed be the attainment of the attributeless Brahman, but that is not liberation.
Anticipating this doubt, he states that there is a difference between the attainment of Brahman and liberation only in name, not in actual fact:
"Let that which is eternally of an attributeless nature be sung by its mere name."
In its actual meaning, this is considered to be liberation itself, like a consistent error.

Regarding the phrase "eternally devoid of qualities" (*nityanirguṇa*): the sense is that while that Brahman may be called "eternal" in name only, in reality this is liberation itself, since liberation is defined as abiding in one's own true nature (*svarūpāvasthiti*). To illustrate this, he provides an example: "consistent with reality" (*saṃvādī*). Just as an "apparent error" (*saṃvādibhrama*) is called an "error" in name only, whereas in fact it is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), so it is here. || 39 ||

— Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He states that liberation is indeed the state of being the attributeless Brahman (nirguṇabrahmatva) with the words "eternal" (nityam). In this regard, he provides an illustration with the word "corresponding" (saṃvādī). The meaning is: just as that [cognition] is called an error by name alone, whereas in reality it is a valid cognition (pramā), so it is here. || 39 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that it is contradictory to state that the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa), which consists of mental activity, is a means to liberation.
Anticipating this, he says that there is no contradiction because what is stated as the means to liberation is the knowledge produced by that meditation:
"By its power, there arises an intellect that brings about the cessation of root ignorance."
By means of worshiping Avimukta, it is like the realization of the Tāraka Brahman. || 40 ||

Regarding that, he provides an illustration: "In Avimukta. The meaning is that just as the knowledge of the *tāraka* Brahman arises through the power of meditating upon the *saguṇa* (qualified) Brahman in Avimukta, so too does the knowledge of the *nirguṇa* (unqualified) Brahman arise from meditation upon the *nirguṇa* Brahman. || 40 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might ask, "How can there be liberation without knowledge? To this, he says: "That" (tad). He provides an illustration for that: "Avimukta... This is well known in the *Laghu-Jābāla Upaniṣad*. || 140 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, raising the doubt as to what authority there is for the claim that liberation is the fruit of the meditation on the Nirguṇa [Brahman], he says:
"He is desireless and free from desire; indeed, he is bodiless and devoid of sense organs."
For it is heard in the Tāpanīya [Upaniṣad] that the fruit [of knowledge] is liberation, characterized by fearlessness. (41)

"He is without desire. He is without desire, free from desire, one whose desires are fulfilled, one whose desire is the Self; his vital breaths (*prāṇas*) do not depart, but are absorbed right here. Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman. Indeed, being bodiless, devoid of sense organs, without vital breath, and without mind, he becomes pure existence, consciousness, and bliss—the self-ruling Lord (*svasvarāj*). This is for one who knows thus. For this *Oṃkāra* is composed of consciousness, and all this is composed of consciousness; therefore, the Supreme Lord alone is the One.

The meaning is that in the *Tāpanīya Upaniṣad*, through such statements as "That becomes this; it is the immortal, it is the fearless; this is Brahman; indeed, he who knows thus becomes the fearless Brahman," it is heard that liberation is the fruit of the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa) [Brahman]. || 41 ||

Commentary (a0): For it has been stated there that, by meditating upon Īśvara as delimited by the union and separation of the eyebrows and the nose, at the end, the realization of Brahman as the Tāraka arises; likewise, in the present context, he states the authorities regarding how the worship of the Nirguṇa produces the fruit of liberation through the gateway of non-dual knowledge—47.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [pages 368–368] 370.

"He is without desire," and so forth, with six verses beginning with that [phrase], titled *Dhyānadīpa*. In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*: "He is without desire, free from desire, desiring the Self, his desires fulfilled; his vital breaths do not depart; they are absorbed right here. Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman. He is bodiless and devoid of sense organs.

"Indeed, the Prāṇa, being mindless and consisting solely of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, becomes the Svar (the Self-luminous) for one who knows thus. For this Oṃkāra is composed of Consciousness, and all this is composed of Consciousness;

therefore, the Supreme Lord alone is each and every one of these. This is the Immortal, this is the Fearless, this is Brahman; for indeed, he who knows thus becomes the fearless Brahman"—thus it is stated in the *Nṛsiṃhottaratāpanīya Upaniṣad*, beginning with the words "This is the secret," and so forth. 41.
From the power of such meditation, the arising of knowledge then occurs.
For thus the scripture stating "there is no other path" is not at all contradicted. || 42 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that if liberation were attained through meditation (*upāsanā*), it would contradict the scriptural statement, "There is no other path for going. Anticipating this doubt, he says—beginning with "of meditation"—that there is no contradiction, because it is stated that [meditation] bestows liberation by means of intervening knowledge (*vidyā*). || 42 ||

Commentary on verse a0: Regarding the phrase "of worship" (*upāsanasya*) and "none other" (*nānyaḥ*). The sense is that even when taken together with the Śruti passage, "Only by knowing Him thus does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey," there is no contradiction. || 42 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Regarding the stated point that one is liberated by realizing the Truth either at the time of death or in the world of Brahmā, he cites scripture as authority:
"Liberation through desireless meditation is proclaimed in the Tāpanīya [Upaniṣad]."
The world of Brahmā is declared for one who still possesses desire in the *Śaivyapraśna*.
Regarding the term "free from desire" (niṣkāma): the passage from the *Tāpanīya* beginning with "He is without desire" has already been cited previously. || 43 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā) on verse a0: Regarding the phrase "niṣkāma" (desireless), the Tāpanīya Śruti passage beginning with "He who is desireless is indeed desireless" has already been cited.

However, for one who meditates on the attributeless Brahman (nirguṇopāsaka) while still possessing desire (sakāma), the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka) is attained. He states this, citing the question of Śaibya in the Praśnopaniṣad: "The world of Brahmā. || 43 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now he recites the statement from the Śvetāśvatara and Praśna Upaniṣads according to its meaning:
"He who meditates by means of the three measures is led to the world of Brahman."
He beholds the Supreme Person beyond this mass of life. || 44 ||

Regarding the phrase "he who meditates": "Furthermore, he who meditates upon the Supreme Person by means of this very syllable *Om* consisting of three morae (*trimātra*), having become united with the radiant sun, is liberated from evil just as a snake is freed from its slough; indeed, he is led up by the Sāmans to the world of Brahman, and from this living body, he beholds the Person dwelling within the city. Thus [is described] the world of Brahman for one who possesses desire.

The meaning is that the attainment [of Brahman] is heard [in scripture]. Now, one might object: "In the case of Śvetaketu, who possessed desire, only the reaching of the world of Brahman (brahmaloka) is perceived"; anticipating this doubt, he states—beginning with "sa etasmāt"—that the direct realization of reality is also heard there. Having gone to the world of Brahman, that worshipper [goes] from this "mass of living beings" (jīvadhana), which is the aggregate of individual souls, to the Supreme Person (puruṣa) who is superior to Hiraṇyagarbha, the unconditioned Supreme Self in the form of pure consciousness.
When [the obstacle] has been destroyed, one realizes [it directly]. || 44 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He recites that very scripture according to its meaning: "He who meditates... and so forth. "But he who meditates upon this supreme Puruṣa by means of this very syllable 'Om' consisting of three measures—he, having reached the sun in its radiance, is liberated from evil just as a snake is freed from its slough; indeed, he is led up by the Sāman chants to the world of Brahman. From this mass of living beings—"

For this is the scriptural passage from the *Praśnopaniṣad*, in the inquiry of Śaibya, which serves as the root source [for this teaching]: "He beholds the Person dwelling in the city, who is higher than the high.
This concludes the ninth section.
Accompanied by two commentaries.

Thus [it is said]. That one is the *upāsaka* (worshiper). This is because of the commonality of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) with this [universal aggregate], as perceived by direct observation (*sākṣipratyakṣa*). "In the living" (*jīve*) means in Hiraṇyagarbha, who is the nature of the aggregate of individual souls (*jīvasamaṣṭi*). The rest, however, is quite clear. 44.
In the section concerning the absence of means (apratīkādhikaraṇa), the principle of "as was his intention" (tatkratu-nyāya) was stated.
Therefore, it is described that for one who possesses desire, the fruit is the world of Brahmā. || 145 ||

Rāma’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Furthermore, in the sūtras “Bādarāyaṇa [holds that the one who does not rely on symbols] leads [him to Brahman]” and “Because there is no fault in either case, and because of his resolve,” it was established that the attainment of results occurs according to one's desires; therefore, he states—beginning with "apratīke" (sūtra 45)—that for one who possesses desire, there is access to the world of Brahmā.

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, he states the agreement with the Sūtra regarding the attainment of the world of Brahmā by one who possesses desire but meditates on the Nirguṇa Brahman—with the words "apratīka... and so forth. This refers to the section [of the Sūtras] beginning with "He leads those who do not rely on symbols," according to Bādarāyaṇa. "The principle of *tatkratu*" means the principle stated as "In both cases there is a defect, therefore [the result depends on] his resolve" (*Brahma-sūtra* 4.3.15). What is meant here?
Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the Sūtra," he says: "Brahman. However, the literal meaning of the words should be understood from the *Brahmāmṛtavarṣiṇī* itself. || 149 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Then, raising the objection as to how one who possesses desire can attain knowledge of reality, he says:
"By the power of the worship of the Nirguṇa [Brahman], one perceives reality therein."
This one does not return again, and is liberated even at the end of the kalpa.
Regarding the term *nirguṇā*: because of the existence of such scriptural and traditional texts as, “He does not return to this human whirlpool; he does not return again;
he does not return again,” and “Together with Brahmā, all of them [attain liberation],” there is no further attainment of saṃsāra for him, but rather liberation.
Revatī said: "He returns again. || 46 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): If this is so, then how can one who possesses desire (sakāma) possess knowledge therein? To this, he says: "nirguṇa" (devoid of qualities). || 46 ||
The meditations on the *praṇava* found in the Vedas are for the most part devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*).
For it has indeed been stated that the meditation on the Praṇava may also possess attributes.
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, in connection with the meditation on the Praṇava, he shows its two-fold nature as it arises in the mind: "Praṇava... (verse 47).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): And thus, he states that there are two kinds of meditations on the Praṇava: "Praṇava... (verse 47).
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the authority for this twofold nature:
"The syllable Om, in the form of the higher and lower Brahman, was described by the sage Pippalāda to Satyakāma, who questioned him. (48)

Regarding the phrase "the higher and the lower": the meaning is that its dual nature has been established by the passage, "O Satyakāma, this syllable Om is indeed the higher and the lower Brahman; therefore, the wise man, by means of this very support, attains one or the other. (48)

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Regarding this, he states the proof: "pareti. It is heard in the *Praśnopaniṣad*: "O Satyakāma, this syllable Om is indeed the higher and the lower Brahman" (Praśna Upaniṣad 5.2). || 48 ||
Having understood this objective support, whatever anyone desires, that belongs to him.
Thus it was spoken by Yama even to Naciketas, who questioned him.
Rāma’s Commentary: He states that even Yama, in the Kaṭhavallī, spoke of this twofold nature by saying, "Having known this support," and so forth—namely, "This support" (verse 49).
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya [pages 370–370] 372.

[In the commentary on the chapter titled *Dhyānadīpa*, verse 49: He states that the practice of both the worship of the attributeless (*nirguṇa*)—by means of delimiting it through the *praṇava* (Om)—and the worship of the qualified (*saguṇa*), has been described by Yama to Naciketas in the *Kaṭhavallī*: "This... (verse 49).
Whether he dies here, or in the world of Brahmā, his state shall be such.
The direct realization of Brahman belongs to one who correctly meditates upon the attributeless [Brahman]. (150)
Rāma’s Commentary: He concludes the aforementioned point with the verse beginning "iha vā" (150).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Let it be so; nevertheless, he concludes that the fruit of the worship of the Nirguṇa [Brahman], through the progressive stages of its maturation and by means of the knowledge of Brahman, is indeed liberation alone—thus: "iha vā" (or here). || 150 ||
This meaning has also been clearly expressed in the *Ātmagītā*.
"One who is incapable of reflection should constantly worship the Self. (51)

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states that this matter—that one who is incapable of attaining the knowledge of reality through inquiry has the qualification for meditation on the attributeless Brahman—is correctly set forth in the *Ātmagītā*: "This is the meaning," etc. (51).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that the practice of the formless (nirguṇa) meditation is generally not well-known in the Smṛtis and other texts as it is in the Śruti; therefore, he says:
"This is the meaning" (verse 51).
Even if one is unable to realize [this directly], one should contemplate me without hesitation.
In due time, may I surely become one who has ascended to direct experience and borne fruit. || 52 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He cites the very words of the Ātmagītā—beginning with "sākṣāt" (directly)—in verse 52.
Commentary (a0): He recites those very statements in three verses beginning with "sākṣātkartum" (to realize directly). || 52 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He provides an illustration regarding how meditation serves as a means to perfect knowledge:
"Just as there is no means for obtaining a deep-seated treasure-store other than digging."
Likewise, even when a wrestler is unavailable, there is no other [means] except for one's own self-consciousness.
"Yathā" (as): he applies this to the subject of the illustration—namely, "the acquisition of a wrestler. || 13 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): He clarifies the illustration regarding how meditation is the means for the direct realization of the non-dual Self with the words "Just as" (yathā).
Regarding the word "agādha" (bottomless): it means [a place] where a vast accumulation of gold and other treasures has been deposited in a very deep spot. || 53 ||
Having again removed the stone of the body by means of the spade of the intellect,
Having dug up the god of love, a man should take me back as his treasure. || 54 ||
Rāma’s Commentary (rā0 ṭikā): He states the meaning already expressed by way of negation (vyatireka) by way of affirmation (anvaya)—“the body-stone” (dehopala). || 64 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): In that regard, he states the locus, the means of proof, and the result of the connection by means of a metaphor: "The body," etc. This is also an illustration for the five sheaths (pañcakośas). || 54 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To show that one who is incapable of [attaining] knowledge has the qualification for meditation, he cites another statement:
"Even in the absence of direct experience, let 'I am Brahman' alone be meditated upon."
If even that which is non-existent can be attained through meditation, how much more so Brahman, which is eternally attained? || 155 ||

Regarding the phrase "from experience": he states the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument concerning the attainment of Brahman through meditation with the word "even. This concludes the ninth section on the meditator.
Accompanied by two commentaries:

It is said that even divinity and the like, though previously non-existent, are attained through meditation; for Brahman, which is the self of all and eternally attained as one's own essential nature, is meditated upon—
The meaning is: what need is there to say that [it] is not attained? || 159 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): In that regard, he provides another scriptural authority for the statement that one who is incapable of action should perform knowledge alone:

"Of experience" (anubhūteḥ). Therein, he states the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument: "Even the non-existent" (apyasad iti). According to the Vedic text, "Having become a god, he goes even to the gods," [even] godhood and the like, though non-existent (*asad*) or not currently present, [are attained through knowledge]. || 155 ||
The daily fruit of meditation and the other practices is the weakening of the notion of self.
If one does not meditate even while seeing, who else is more of a beast than he? (56)
Rāma’s Commentary: He states that meditation must be practiced because the fruit of meditating on Brahman is established through direct perception: "The non-Self... (Verse 56).

Commentary (a0): Clarifying that the fruit of meditating on Brahman is seen daily even here [in this world], he censures those who are averse to it with the verse beginning "anātma... (not the Self). Therefore, the intention is that a seeker of liberation who is clever in inquiry should always practice the meditation on the attributeless Brahman (nirguṇa-brahma) alone. || 56 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, he demonstrates the meaning established above in summary:
"Having destroyed the identification with the body, through meditation [one realizes] the non-dual Self."
Seeing [it], the mortal becomes immortal and indeed attains Brahman here. || 57 ||

Regarding the phrase "the conceit of the body": by abandoning the conceit of "I" with respect to the perishable body, one becomes immortal oneself and, even in this very body, attains one's own innate form—Brahman, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss. || 17 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Although the fruit of that [meditation] has already been stated three times—namely, "in this world," "at death," or "in the world of Brahmā"—according to the gradations of the ripening of one's practice, he now summarizes it once more for the sake of showing great respect for it: "deha" (the body), etc. For those with intense spiritual urgency (*tīvrasaṃvega*), the attainment of wisdom (*prajñālābha*) is imminent. || 57 ||
The person who correctly contemplates this lamp of meditation,
Free from all doubt, he meditates upon Brahman continuously. || 58 ||
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Lamp of Meditation, in the *Pañcadaśī* composed by the venerable sage Vidyāraṇya. 9.
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the fruit of following the Dhyānadīpa (The Lamp of Meditation) in the verse beginning with "dhyānadīpam" || 18 ||
Thus ends the commentary on the *Dhyānadīpa*, composed by the scholar named Śrī Rāmakṛṣṇa, a servant of the illustrious Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Bhāratītīrtha Vidyāraṇya Muni. 9.

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Regarding this, he states that the thorough investigation of this very treatise is the cause for attaining proficiency in the aforementioned meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa), saying:

"The Lamp of Meditation" (dhyānadīpa). Now, at the outset, you stated regarding this ninth treatise: "Liberation is attained through right meditation, action, and knowledge; or by meditation, or by the pure knowledge that has arisen; or by purity—this is the fourth obstacle here in the living being."

Thus, by means of this [work], the *Dhyānadīpa* acts as a sublater of the fourth obstacle, which consists of the expression of contrary notions regarding the means for determining the true nature of the individual soul (*jīva*)—the referent of the term *tvaṃpada*—as purified [of adjuncts].
For it has been stated that "one becomes enlightened only when the obstacles have been destroyed by either meditation (*dhyāna*) or inquiry (*vicāra*). Therefore, it is devoted to that [purpose].

That [point] is clearly determined in the ninth [chapter] by the verse beginning with “...is established,” as stated in the Āryā; if you ask how that is so, listen. For here, having begun with the statement that one is liberated even through the meditation on the reality of Brahman—as in the case of a concordant delusion—it concludes with “having destroyed the conceit of the body,” and so forth. Therefore, by the word “even” (*api*) in the phrase “even through the meditation on the reality of Brahman,” it is implied that one is liberated through knowledge (*jñāna*) by means of inquiry (*vicāra*) alone; whereas in the event of an inability for that, there is meditation on the reality of Brahman.

Having determined the intention of the conclusion— that even by means of the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman (described in the *Dhyānadīpa*) one removes the obstacles to knowledge and is liberated through that very knowledge— [Vidyāraṇya] composed the *Pañcadaśī*.

The identity of these two must be understood. Likewise, the signs such as practice (*abhyāsa*) and so forth are also evident there, as in: "Having understood from the Vedāntas that the reality of Brahman consists of an indivisible, single-flavored essence, they meditate upon it [with the thought], 'I am this'. This is clearly stated in the *Vasiṣṭha*: "O Rāghava, there are two paths for the destruction of the mind: Yoga and Knowledge. Yoga is the restraint of its fluctuations; Knowledge is [the realization of] the Truth."

"Observation: for some, yoga is not achievable; for others, the ascertainment of reality. Therefore, the supreme deity Śiva spoke of these two modes. Thus, there is not even the slightest room here for any contradiction regarding the means of accomplishment. May there be auspiciousness! 58.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Dhyānadīpaprakāśa, of the commentary on the Pañcadaśī by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Śrīmad Vidyāraṇya, known as Śrīmad Advaitasaccidānanda.
May there be constant offering at the lotus feet of the venerable Śrīmad Advaita Saccidānanda Guruvarya, the venerable Śrīmat Svarūpānanda Guruvarya, and the venerable Śrīman Nārāyaṇa Guruvarya.

1. Those known as Śrī Raghunātha Bhaṭṭa, who served as assistants in the contemplation of the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā). 2. Those designated as Mahādeva Buvā, who were the preceptors of the great five-syllabled mantra of Śiva (śivapañcākṣarī) and held the yogic seat (yogapaṭṭa) of Svarūpānanda Āśrama. 3. The teachers (ācāryas) who taught the four systems of philosophy (catuḥśāstra), bearing the surname Sāṭhe.
Now begins the tenth chapter, entitled *Nāṭakadīpa*, on the fifteenth [day].
Rāma’s Commentary: Having bowed to the lords of sages, Śrī Bhāratītīrtha and Vidyāraṇya, the meaning of the *Nāṭakadīpa* will be stated by me in brief. (1)

Performing an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) characterized by the recollection of the true nature of the chosen deity for the sake of completing the work he intends to compose without obstacle, and in order to achieve for students of duller faculties the realization of the non-dual Brahman-self without effort, [the author] follows the maxim: "The sequence devised by those who know reality—'through superimposition and negation, the non-dual is elaborated for the sake of establishing the understanding of disciples'. Thus: *adhyāropāpavādābhyāṃ niṣprapañcaṃ prapañcyate |* *śiṣyāṇāṃ bodhasiddhyarthaṃ tattvajñaiḥ kalpitaḥ kramaḥ ||* ...following this principle, he begins: (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the portion available.)
First, he states the superimposition upon the Self: "The Supreme Self, who is full of non-dual bliss, formerly [projected] through His own Māyā..."
Having himself become the world, he entered it in the form of the individual soul (jīva). || 1 ||

Regarding the term "Supreme Self" (*paramātman*): prior to creation, He is the Supreme Self—full of non-dual bliss, as established by such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, O dear one, this was Being alone, one only without a second," and "Brahman is consciousness and bliss; that is full, this is full. Devoid of internal or other distinctions, consisting of supreme bliss, and perfectly complete, He [manifests] through His own *māyā*, according to the scripture: "One should know *māyā* as nature (*prakṛti*) and the Great Lord as the wielder of *māyā*."

By its own inherent power of *māyā*, having itself become the world, it made itself its own self—according to the Śruti: "It became both the existent (*sat*) and the non-existent (*tyat*). Having itself attained the form of the world, it entered by way of the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*). The meaning is that it entered in the form of the individual soul, as stated in such Śruti passages as: "Having entered with this living self," and "Having created that, it entered into that very thing. || 1 ||

I bow to the one whose form is the immutable Supreme Brahman—non-dual bliss, existence, consciousness, all-pervading, and stainless; who, though the abode where the net of duality born of delusion dissolves, is the self-luminous crest-jewel of the Vedas; and to all the foremost teachers, the ornament of Raghu’s lineage, the true Guru established in Brahman. a0 ṭīkā - Advaitānandasaccidvibhu-vimala-parabrahma-kūṭastha-rūpam, mohādvaiteṃdrajālālayam api, śrutīnāṃ tilakam, svaprakāśam; sarvān ca ācāryavaryān, raghukula-tilakam, sadgurum brahmaniṣṭham.
I bow to my own guru, known as Śrīmannārāyaṇa, who is also named Mahādeva. || 1 ||
Having honored Jīvajīva, Vidyāraṇya, and Bhāratītīrtha;
Now, by means of the illumination of the quarters provided by the Kaumudī, I shall clarify the Nāṭakadīpa.

Then, the venerable Bhāratītīrtha Ācārya, in his own work, the fifteenth chapter of the *Pañcadaśī* titled *Dhyānadīpa*, while discussing the fruit of that contemplation, stated: "This one, with all doubt dispelled, meditates upon Brahman continuously. [A disciple then asked: "How can someone like me—who am exceedingly dull-witted and intensely craving for sense objects—become one whose doubts are entirely dispelled without great effort and with only a small amount of text?"

Thinking, "May I be able to meditate upon Brahman continuously," and having determined through the withering of his face and other signs that he was deeply anxious, [the author], desiring to favor him, begins the tenth chapter of the *Pañcadaśī*, titled *Nāṭakadīpa*. Performing the auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) characterized by the contemplation of the Supreme Self—which serves as a well-known means for attaining valid knowledge—he thereby also implicitly establishes the connection of this work with its subject matter, purpose, and so forth, beginning with the words: "The Supreme Self."

Regarding the term *advaya*: it is that wherein no duality—that is, no dualistic form of the visible object—exists; that which is such and is also bliss (*ānanda*) is thus [described]. The analysis of the compound *paramātman* is likewise: he who measures (*mimīte*) the supreme objects (*parān*), namely the visible entities, by manifesting them as a witness (*sākṣitvena*) is *parama*; and that which is such and is also the self (*ātman*) is [the *paramātman*], following the same method as before, as a *karmadhāraya* compound. By this, the pure meaning of the term *tat* (That), characterized as the witness, is indicated through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

By the words "thus non-dual" (*evamadvaya*) and so forth, the pure meaning of the word *tat* (That), characterized as Brahman—truth, knowledge, infinite, bliss, and non-dual—is illuminated. By the word "full" (*pūrṇa*), the non-difference between those two [the subject and the object] and the meaning of the word *asi* (you are)—which is the partless, single essence—are indicated. Thus, by these three words, the entire purport of the Advaita scriptures is summarized. That very [meaning]...
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[the section titled] "The Lamp of the Drama" (*Nāṭakadīpa*).

The subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*) of this treatise (*prakaraṇa*), like those of the Śāstra itself, are established respectively through the states of being known and unknown. Since, in this Siddhānta, only the *bhāgatyāga-lakṣaṇā* (the type of indication where parts of the primary meaning are abandoned while others are retained) is accepted, the relationship between the Śāstra and its subject matter is well-known as that of the indicator (*lakṣaka*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*). As for the qualified seeker (*adhikārī*), he has already been indicated below; such a seeker of knowledge is intended for whom this treatise is commenced.
[End of section] Now, for the sake of establishing the realization of the meaning already stated:
"Through superimposition and negation, the worldless [reality] is elaborated;
this sequence has been devised by the knowers of truth for the purpose of establishing the realization of their disciples."

Based on the statement of the ancients (*prācām vacanāt*), he first describes superimposition (*adhyāropa*) with the words beginning "previously" (*pūrvam*). "Previously" refers to the state prior to the commencement of creation.

The meaning is: "by means of the limitation of time such as moments, characterized by the connection with the Self through beginningless positive ignorance (*avidyā*). Regarding the word "its own" (*sva*): it means by means of that ignorance which consists primarily of pure *sattva*, which is beginningless and positive in nature, and which possesses a connection with the Self alone, being imagined as having its existence dependent solely upon the Self. Regarding the phrase "by itself alone" (*svayameva*):

by this, the exclusion of any other causal complex (*sāmagrī*)—other than the aforementioned *māyā*—which has attained identity with the Self, is indicated. Consequently, because the theory of illusory transformation (*vivartavāda*) is accepted, [theories] such as the doctrine of new production (*ārambhavāda*)...

The absence [of duality] has been indicated; that is to say, the world is non-dual from the beginning. Having become [thus], it is called "jīva" (the individual soul), as per the Taittirīya Śruti: "The one unborn female, red, white, and black, produces many offspring similar to herself; one unborn male lies by her, enjoying her, while another unborn male leaves her after she has provided him with enjoyment. Likewise: "Know both Prakṛti and Puruṣa to be indeed beginningless."

The meaning is that [the Lord] is the primordial collective individual self (*samaṣṭijīvātman*), as established by the statement of the learned: "The individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśa*), pure consciousness (*viśuddhā cit*), the difference between the individual soul and the Lord, ignorance (*avidyā*), and the connection between that [ignorance] and consciousness—these six are beginningless for us. Whether by way of being conditioned (*upahitatva*), limited (*avacchinnatva*), reflected (*prativimbatva*), or appearing (*ābhāsatva*), He is like the solar light delimited by the desert appearing as the mirage-water imagined by itself, due to its own identity with it.

The syntactical connection is with the word *viśat* (entered). And thus say the Śruti texts: “In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone”; “In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second”; “Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite”; “One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā; by His limbs, this entire world is pervaded”; and “Truth and untruth both became Truth.”
Namely: "Whatever there is," "Having created that, He entered into it," and "Having entered by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms. || 1 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "If the single Supreme Self alone has entered into all bodies, then the relationship of worshiper and worshipped, as well as the distinction between superior and inferior perceived [in the world], would be contradicted. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Having entered the supreme bodies of Viṣṇu and others, one becomes a deity.
Abiding within inferior bodies such as those of mortals, it partakes of mortality. ||2||

Regarding the word "viṣu": the sense is that this distinction between superior and inferior is not inherent, but rather is dependent upon the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the body; therefore, there is no contradiction. || 2 ||
