Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if it is thus the non-dual Self alone that has entered into this world of the aforementioned nature by the power of *māyā*, then—given its entry into the common form of individual souls (*jīvas*) such as reflections and the like, and given the possibility of a distinction between consciousness and insentience through the states of being the "seer" and the "seen"—how could there be a distinction between the relationship of the served and the server? To this, he says: "Viṣṇu, etc. Nor, in this way, does Viṣṇu and the others become mere individual souls (*jīvas*).
[Objection: This is undesirable. [Reply: It is not, for we accept this as our position. For instance, in the *Advaitasiddhi*, at the very beginning of the maṅgala, it is stated:
"The locus of the illusory manifold of duality, whose face is the agency imagined through māyā..."

Viṣṇu, whose nature consists of truth, knowledge, and bliss, who is the object of the indivisible cognition arising from the crest of the Vedas, and who is free from all conceptual constructs, reigns supreme as if having himself attained liberation— which consists solely of supreme bliss through the shaking off of false bondage.
The Tenth Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

Thus, having first indicated that Viṣṇu alone possesses the status of the primary *jīva* according to his own preferred doctrine of the "one soul in many bodies" (*aneka-śarīra-eka-jīva-vāda*), he subsequently establishes the identity of the *jīva* through extensive textual exposition within the doctrine of the "single soul" (*eka-jīva-vāda*). Nor is it the case that [this contradicts] the Śrutis which teach omniscience, universal agency, and so forth.

It must not be argued that [the Lord] cannot be the object [of knowledge], because ignorance is absent in pure consciousness (*śuddhacaitanya*), and because there is no Lord distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), since the omniscience of the *jīva* is contradicted by experience. This is incorrect, because we accept that the *jīva* who identifies with the collective totality (*samaṣṭyabhimānin*) possesses omniscience and universal agency. Nor is there a contradiction with experience; for, through the power of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of non-difference between the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the Self, both the experience of that [omniscience] and its opposite experience are possible. [This applies to] the one who identifies with all...

However, there certainly exists the conceit of omniscience [in Viṣṇu]. For this very reason, the experience of the Blessed Lord himself has been cited as an illustration, based on the logical consistency of such statements as: "I know all those things, but you do not know them, O scorcher of the foe. Therefore, it is entirely appropriate that Viṣṇu possesses the nature of a *jīva* (individual soul). To this, it is replied: Is this nature of Viṣṇu as a *jīva* asserted because the root texts would otherwise be inexplicable, or is it based on the intended meaning of the previously cited *Advaitasiddhi* text? It is not the former.

[This is] because you yourself have not understood its intended meaning (*tātparya*). For instance, it is quite clear that in that [previous] verse, the manifestation of the illusory Brahman (*māyībrahman*) in the form of the world by its power, as well as its entry [into that world] in the form of the beginningless collective individual soul (*samaṣṭijīva*) through the nature of a reflection (*pratibimba*) and so forth, were stated.

If that entry was stated in a general sense, then how is the relationship between the worshiped and the worshiper (*pūjyapūjakabhāva*), which is perceived at the beginning of the scripture, to be explained? [Thus arises the question.]

The verse beginning with "kṣāyāmeva viṣṇvādīti" has been introduced. Thus, Viṣṇu and the others—well-known from the Śrutis and other sources—are all the supreme Lord’s playful incarnations (līlā-vigrahas), who are the most excellent and most powerful among those individual souls (jīvas) well-known as the distributive selves (vyaṣṭy-ātmaka) such as Indra and the rest; for the analysis of the compound as "in their bodies"—referring to those physical forms (kāyas) well-known from the Śrutis and other sources as "the thunderbolt-handed one," "the destroyer of cities," and so forth—is indeed the natural and primary meaning.

It must necessarily be stated that [the word] is intended by the author in its technical sense (*ācāryavivakṣitatva*). Otherwise, since it would be improper to employ the word *devatā*—which is well-known in lexicons as a common term for gods, as in "those who have entered [the body], being gods (*devatāḥ*), became [such]" (where *vṛndāraka*, *daivata*, and *puṃsi vā devatāḥ striyām* are established)—one could equally say, "But the Lord (*īśvara*) entered and became [them]. Nor, if this were the case, would Viṣṇu and the others be the supreme [deities] for people like us in their manifest form (*vigraha*).

It is not at all agreed upon by the scriptures that all dogs are *līlāvigrahas* (sportive incarnations) and thus superior to all, such that Indra and the other gods alone should be accepted [as such].

This is because it is well-known from the beginning of the scriptures that, compared to humans and others, the gods generally possess a greater degree of knowledge (*jñānādhikya*). It is precisely with the intention of expressing the gradations in the possession of knowledge that [the scripture states]: "Of the gods, whosoever awakened to that [Brahman], he indeed became that; likewise among the ṛṣis, and likewise among men... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2].

And because the sequence is stated in the Śruti: "Of those who are thirsty... If that is so, then in the case of the term *martyādi* as well, this analysis must be stated as a genitive *tatpuruṣa* preceded by a *bahuvrīhi*. Otherwise, there would be the fault of inconsistency (*vairūpya*). If you say this is not so, [we reply]: *martyādayaḥ*—by the word "etc. (*ādi*), those such as animals and the lower classes are included, who are extremely insignificant due to their abundance of suffering; [the compound refers] to those seekers who, through the ripening of their previous merit, are qualified for devotion (*bhakti*).

Because it is intended that [the term "in them"] refers to those very bodies; otherwise, there would be an inconsistency with the subsequent text: "He worships the deity as established in another way. For it is well known that not all humans and others worship the gods, such as Indra, with the thought that they are the Supreme Lord, merely by performing the Śrauta and Smārta rites appropriate to their respective varṇas and āśramas. And thus, within the entire insentient universe—which is superimposed through Māyā upon the collective totality of infinite individual souls (jīvasamaṣṭi) and is [thereby] bestowed by Himself—...

Because it is the manifestation of that [Supreme Reality], it is figuratively said to have entered into what is non-different from itself through *māyā*. In this regard, it should be understood that even among the infinite individual souls (*jīvas*) known as the "dividuals" (*vyaṣṭi*), only some attain the state of being worshipped or being a worshipper, and this occurs solely according to the gradations of their accumulated merit (*sukṛta*), not all of them. Nor is the latter case [the attainment of such status] possible for everyone, because that [attainment] is a specific counter-action whose sole fruit is the awakening of a particular distinction within the youth. [This is the view] of the venerable Madhusūdana Ācāryas.
And because there is no intended meaning (tātparya) for that [interpretation] therein; otherwise, if Viṣṇu were the aggregate of individual souls (jīva-samaṣṭi), [the following would be impossible]:
"From Him whose hands are adorned with the flute, who has the luster of a fresh rain-cloud, who wears yellow garments, and whose lower lip is like a ripe, reddish bimba fruit..."

"From Kṛṣṇa, whose face is as beautiful as the full moon and whose eyes are like lotuses, I know no reality whatsoever that is superior"—this statement of theirs, found within their own text, would be contradicted [by your position]. Nor should it be argued that this refers only to the collective individual soul (*samaṣṭijīva*), for that would violate the natural force of words such as "any" (*kimapi*). Furthermore, it is precisely the non-dual Brahman that is described in such a manner due to the intensity of their devotion. It is exactly thus that they [have stated]:
His own intention has been indicated in the auspicious verse of the commentary on the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*:
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya:
Having approached a Guru [who has realized] that Brahman which is truth, knowledge, infinite, non-dual bliss, and...

"I bow to the one with eyes like lotuses, whose moon-like beautiful face plays the flute in Vṛndāvana for the joy of all— He who was manifested through the power of His own blissful penance for the sake of liberation, and who was directly realized by the best of sages who had attained meditative absorption."
[Regarding the work titled *Nāṭakadīpa*:

"If that is so, then how is it that in the *Siddhāntabindu*, these very same views from the *Vārttika* and other sources are presented? [Namely: 'The Lord (Īśvara) is consciousness conditioned by ignorance (*ajñāna*); the individual soul (*jīva*) is consciousness reflected in ignorance; and pure consciousness is that which is unconditioned by ignorance.'"...]

"Or else, the Lord [is the primary reality], while the individual soul (*jīva*) is that which is conditioned by ignorance (*ajñāna*); this is the principal Vedāntic doctrine known as *ekajīvavāda* (the theory of the single soul). And they call this very system *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda* (the theory that creation is perception). Thus, according to the intention of the word 'principal' here, it must be said that this alone is the doctrine accepted by them.

And so, based on the natural consistency of the unity of their two texts, if it is argued that Viṣṇu alone possesses the status of the aforementioned collective soul (*samaṣṭijīva*)—that is what they accept—[we reply]: No."

In the *Siddhāntabindu*, the author who has realized Brahman highly esteems this theory of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*); this is understood from the *Anubhūtiprakāśa* to mean that he intends it as his own accepted view. Therefore, in this context, only the doctrine of a single body and a single soul (*ekaśarīraikajīvavāda*) is approved by him, and not even the doctrine of a single soul with multiple bodies (*anekaśarīraikajīvavāda*), which is set forth in the *Advaitasiddhi* for the purpose of instructing specific types of qualified seekers. For this very reason, there is no use here of the term "universal soul" (*samaṣṭijīva*). Thus, everything—
The wise should meditate upon that which is pure white. || 2 ||
He demonstrates this—
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus briefly shown the superimposition upon the Self, he now briefly presents its negation along with its means.
Due to having undergone many births, he desires to perform self-investigation.
When Māyā has been destroyed by investigation, the Self alone remains. || 3 ||

"Aneka" means: because of "bhajanāt"—that is, from the act of offering up (samarpaṇa) those karmas performed throughout "aneka-janma," or many births, unto Brahman; he "cikīrṣati," meaning he desires to perform "svavicāram," which is the means for the knowledge of his own self (ātman) as being of the nature of Brahman, such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth.
Then, through "svavicāreṇa"—that is, by the knowledge produced by that inquiry—he [removes] ignorance (ajñāna) regarding Māyā, which is the concealer of his own non-dual blissful nature.
When that which is denoted by the word "dyā" (the duality) has perished and ceased to exist, the Supreme Self alone remains, Himself full of non-dual bliss. || 3 ||

Commentary (a0): Having thus described superimposition upon the non-dual Self, he explains its removal (apavāda) along with its means, beginning with the verse "aneka-". Devotion has already been explained below in the passage: "Abiding in inferior bodies such as those of mortals, one worships the deity. (3)

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Since such scriptural passages as 'Having known that Brahman as "I am," one is liberated from all bonds' declare that liberation, characterized by the cessation of bondage, is the fruit of knowledge, it is inconsistent to state that the result is the remaining of the Supreme Self alone.
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
And she is the companion of that whose nature is non-dual bliss, even while being subject to suffering.
Bondage is said to be existence by way of one's own nature; liberation is declared to be abiding [in that same nature]. || 4 ||

Regarding the term *advayānanda*: since in non-dual Brahman neither bondage nor liberation can be established as real, bondage is merely the delusion of suffering and so forth, while liberation is simply the cessation of that [delusion], characterized by abiding in one's own true nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, there is no contradiction with the scriptures; this is the intended meaning. || 4 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Granted that Māyā, characterized as root-ignorance, may perish through inquiry; nevertheless, what bondage was created by her, and upon her destruction, what kind of liberation is attained? In response to this expectation, he summarizes the definitions of those two [bondage and liberation] in the verse beginning with *advaya* (verse 4).

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: since the Smṛti states, "Indeed, Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone," it is understood that liberation has action as its means;
therefore, what is the use of this knowledge produced by inquiry? To this, he says:
[page 377]
The tenth chapter:
Bondage, produced by a lack of inquiry, is removed by inquiry.
Therefore, one should always investigate the individual soul and the supreme Self. || 5 ||

It does not investigate. For the bondage produced by ignorance—characterized by the prior absence of investigation—cannot logically cease through knowledge born of investigation. Furthermore, in the cited Smṛti passage, the word "perfection" (*saṃsiddhi*) denotes only the purification of the mind, not liberation.

[The word] *bhāvaḥ* [indicates the end of the previous section]. It has been stated that the cessation of bondage occurs through inquiry; however, one might ask: "What is the object of this inquiry? To this, he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is that one should practice inquiry at all times until the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*) is attained. || 5 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: even if Māyā is destroyed through inquiry in the manner previously described, how is bondage destroyed?
To this, he says: "By non-inquiry... (Verse 5).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In that regard, he first defines the nature of the individual soul (jīva):
"That which conceives 'I' is the agent; it is the instrument of that [agency]."
The two functions of that mind—its internal and external activities—arise in succession.

"I" (aham). The meaning is this: that ego (ahaṃkāra), characterized by the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), which during the state of empirical transaction identifies with the body and so forth as "I," is the agent; it is the individual soul (jīva) distinguished by attributes such as agency and the like. In response to the inquiry, "What is its instrument? he says: "Of that" (tasya).

The mind (manas) is that portion of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) possessing modifications (vṛtti) such as desire and the rest. Since an instrument is pervaded by action, he demonstrates its function: "Of that... [and so on].
"Action" (kriyā). || 6 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Even so, in response to the expectation of how the aforementioned inquiry is to be conducted, [the author] first states the inquiry into the nature of the *jīva* in general—namely, that the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) which identifies itself through the superimposition of identity upon the body qualified by the caste of "Brāhmaṇahood" and so forth is indeed the *jīva*, distinct from the body—by saying, "I am... Now, if agency belongs only to the aforementioned identifier, then...

To the question of what its instrument (*karaṇa*) might be, he says "of that" and so forth. Just as the action of a staff is the whirling of a wheel, so too must the action of this [mind] be stated; therefore he says "of that. "Successively" (*krama*) means produced in succession. || 6 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having distinguished their essential natures and objects, he demonstrates them:
"This inward-turned mental modification, 'I', delineates the agent."
When directed outward, this [cognition] delineates an external object as "this."

Regarding the term *antarmukhā*: the phrase "this" (*idam*) and "such-and-such" (*eṣā*) are gestures representing the nature of outward-directed activity. By what remains [of the verse], there is the indication of the object; the meaning is that one should delineate—that is, make into an object—the thing existing outside the body which is pointed out as "this. || 7 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He describes the form and the activity of the internal and external functions that arise in succession, which consist of both etymological derivation (nirukta) and action (kriyā)—beginning with the word "antar" (internal). "The agent" refers to the reflection in the intellect, which is the appearance of the immutable consciousness characterized by witnesshood; the meaning is that it "should delineate," i.e., should take as its object. Regarding the word "bahiḥ" (external): here, internality and externality are relative only to the body. [External] refers to what is outside the body—
This means that one should delineate this existing object—the collection of entities such as a jar—as "this," and thereby take as an object the "this-portion" (idamaṃśa) residing therein. || 7 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that if all worldly transactions were established by the mind alone, it would follow that the eyes and other senses are useless; anticipating this, he says:
"Those specific qualities of this [world], such as smell, form, taste, and so forth..."
One should distinguish those five sense organs, beginning with the ear, without confusion.

Regarding the phrase "this": by the mind, only the generality "this" is grasped, but not its specific qualities such as odor and so forth; therefore, the sense organs such as the nose are employed for the apprehension of those [specifics]. This is the meaning. || 8 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [page 378] 380.

[Commentary on the *Nāṭakadīpa*, Chapter 1]: Now, one might object: "Let this 'this-ness' (*idamaṃśa*) be the object of a mental modification (*manovṛtti*) in its general form, while sound and the other objects are its particularities; why then are they not grasped by that [mental modification] alone?
To this he says: "This... and so forth. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), sound and touch are included. And by the second "etcetera"—
Their tongues, ears, and skin are like razors. || 8 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus described the nature of the individual soul (jīva) along with its adjuncts, he now describes the Supreme Self (paramātman):
"The agent, the action, and the objects distinct from those two."
He who manifests by a single effort is the witness here, whose form is consciousness.

Regarding the phrase "the agent" (*kartāram*): he who, being of the very nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), simultaneously and with a single effort, may manifest—that is, illumine—the previously mentioned agent in the form of egoity (*ahaṃkāra*), as well as action in the form of mental fluctuations consisting of "I" and "this," and even objects such as smell which are distinct from one another, mutually different, and perceivable by the senses starting with the nose; he, while remaining pure consciousness, is called the "Witness" (*sākṣin*) in this Vedānta scripture. This is the meaning. || 9 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Having thus described the nature of the individual soul (jīva) along with its adjuncts, he now describes the nature of the Supreme Self (paramātman) as introduced at the outset—beginning with the words "the agent" (kartāram). Regarding the phrase "distinct" (vyāvṛtta): the meaning is that even those objects which are mutually different. This is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) including the internal and external organs. "Sphorayet" means he would manifest or illuminate [them]. || 9 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Demonstrating by means of dramatic action how the Witness-consciousness (sākṣin) illuminates everything through a single effort, he says:
"I see, I hear, I smell, I taste, and I touch."
Thus it illuminates everything, like a lamp situated within a dance hall. || 10 ||
"I see," "I hear"—in such ways as "I see a form, I perceive it," the Self illumines simultaneously with a single effort this triad characterized by the seer, the act of seeing, and the object seen;

the same should be applied to "I hear" and so forth. To illustrate its capacity for simultaneous manifestation without undergoing modification, he says: "like a lamp situated in a dance hall. || 10 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) elaborates on that very point: "I see" (īkṣe). The meaning is "I am looking. He provides an illustration for this: "As in dancing," etc. || 10 ||
The commentary on Rāmānuja clarifies the illustration:
"A lamp situated in a dance hall [illuminates] the master, the audience, and the dancer."
One should kindle it without distinction; even in its absence, it shines forth.
"Dance" means: without distinction—that is, without undergoing modifications such as *vṛddhi* (increment) and so forth—in order to manifest the specific objects of the Lord and others. || 11 ||
The commentary clarifies that very point: "the hall of dance" (nṛtyaśālā). || 11 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He applies this to the subject at hand:
"The Witness may illumine the ego, the intellect, and even the objects."
Even in the absence of egoism and the like, it shines forth by itself just as before.
"—the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). The meaning is that even in states such as deep sleep, where the ego-sense and so forth are absent, it nevertheless shines forth as their witness. ||12||

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on verse a0: He clarifies this even in the case of the subject matter at hand with the words "the ego-sense" (ahaṃkāram). Now, an objection may be raised: while it is acceptable that the ego-sense and the intellect—occupying the positions of the master and the dancer respectively—are directly perceived by the Witness, who occupies the position of the audience, how can the direct perception of objects by the Witness be justified? For objects appear to the knower, who is the reflection of consciousness delimited by the ego-sense, through the medium of the senses such as hearing; they do not appear directly. To this, the answer is: true.

By this very same lack of logical consistency, the view of "creation-as-perception" (dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda) belonging to our teacher— which was previously cited from the *Siddhāntabindu* under the name of the doctrine of "one body and one soul"— is [refuted].
[Chapter Ten]
Accompanied by two commentaries, [it is said]:
"381 ...is understood as being intended. In that very state, since even the entirety of the perceptible world is illusory like a dream, the objects themselves are directly—"
The sense is that it is entirely appropriate for [the object] to be manifested by a witness-consciousness. || 12 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Since the intellect (buddhi), which is of the nature of light, is itself capable of illuminating all things such as the ego (ahaṃkāra) and so forth, what is the purpose of postulating a witness (sākṣin) distinct from it?
Anticipating this, he says: "In the immutable (kūṭastha) which shines incessantly by virtue of its nature as pure consciousness..."
Illuminated by its light, this intellect dances in manifold ways. || 13 ||

Regarding the word "constantly" (*niraṃtaram*): while the immutable, changeless Witness (*sākṣin*) shines constantly by virtue of being self-luminous consciousness in the form of pure awareness (*jñapti*), this intellect—always flashing forth—is manifested and illumined by His light, that is, by the consciousness that is the very nature of that Witness. Thus, it dances—that is, undergoes modification—in manifold ways through the forms of cognitions such as "this is a jar," "this is a cloth," and so forth. This is the intended meaning: since...
Because the intellect is insentient due to its mutability, it lacks self-luminosity; therefore, one must admit a witness distinct from it that illumines everything. || 13 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: since it is possible for the intellect (*buddhi*)—which is dominated by the quality of *sattva*—to be the illuminator of all things, according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) that "from *sattva* knowledge is born," what is the need for a witness (*sākṣin*)? To this, he says: "constantly" (*niraṃtaram*). Regarding "cognition" (*jñapti*): the meaning is "because its nature is consciousness" (*cidrūpatvāt*).
Regarding "that" (*tat*): thus, because the intellect is insentient (*jaḍa*) and lacks self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), its status as the direct illuminator of all things is not possible.
Such is the meaning. || 13 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He describes the aforementioned subject matter in the form of a drama for the ease of the listeners' understanding:
"The ego is the lord; the sense objects are the members of the assembly; the intellect is the dancer."
The sense organs hold the palm-leaf and other objects; the lamp is the witness that illuminates them. || 14 ||

Regarding the term *ahaṃkāra* (the ego-maker): because it is characterized by joy and dejection induced by the conceit of either possessing all objects of enjoyment or lacking them, the ego-maker is like a master who presides over a dance. Although the objects of sense are situated in its vicinity, they lack that [conceited] quality; thus, they are comparable to the members of the audience. Because it possesses various modifications (*vikāra*), the intellect (*dhī*) is like a female dancer. Because it possesses activities conducive to the modifications of the intellect, it is similar to one who holds the cymbals and other instruments.
It should be understood that because it illuminates all these [faculties], the Witness (sākṣin) possesses a resemblance to a lamp. || 14 ||
Commentary (a0): Thus, having summarized all the points stated, he describes the matter through a metaphor: "Egoism" (ahaṃkāra), etc.

"The senses" (akṣāṇi) refers to the organs. Regarding "the cymbals" (tālādi)—the sense is that it is entirely appropriate for those who play musical instruments such as cymbals to be eunuchs, as they serve as attendants to the female dancers. || 14 ||
Just as a lamp situated in its own place illuminates everything on all sides.
Stable, enduring, and likewise a witness, he illuminates both the external and the internal.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that if the Witness (sākṣin) also manifests the ego and so forth, it would follow that it possesses modifications consisting of the departure and arrival of those respective associations. Anticipating this, he says: "svasthāne" (in its own place). Just as a lamp, remaining in its own location and devoid of modifications such as movement, illuminates all objects situated near it, so too is the Witness; this is the intended meaning. || 15 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object that the illustration of the lamp is inappropriate; for while the witness (sākṣin) is changeless, the lamp—due to the necessity of accounting for the gradual decrease of its oil and wick—is subject to the transformation of new flames at every moment. Furthermore, the recognition "this is that same lamp-flame" is based merely on extreme similarity. To this we reply: "Quite so. However, it is intended that the lamp serves as an illustration only insofar as it possesses empirical self-luminosity (vyāvahārika-svaprakāśatva). With this in mind, [the author] proceeds to reconcile...

He maintains [the state]—“in its own place,” meaning without performing movement and so forth. The application to the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*) is by means of the words “stable” and so on. In that regard, stable...
In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya, regarding the title *Nāṭakadīpa*:

if one were to analyze it as a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both a lamp (*dīpa*) and stable (*sthāyī*)," the fault of tautology (*paunaruktya*) would arise; therefore, it is [interpreted] with the stable [Self], according to the teaching: "These two persons exist in the world, the perishable (*kṣara*) and the imperishable (*akṣara*)."

And likewise: as in the *Gītā-bhāṣya* on the verse, "The perishable consists of all beings; the immutable is called the imperishable," where the term *kūṭastha* (the immovable) refers to ignorance (*ajñāna*), so too here, by necessity, the word "stable" (*sthira*) refers to ignorance itself through its quality of remaining unshaken in the absence of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Thus, the meaning is that [the Self] is stable by means of ignorance and possesses the nature of being a witness (*sākṣitva*)—defined as the state of being the seer (*dṛk*) with respect to the visible (*dṛśya*) objects caused by that [ignorance]; but in the absence of that [ignorance], it is merely pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
The terms "external" and "internal" are used solely with reference to the body. || 15 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection may be raised: the description of the Witness as that which illumines both the external and the internal is untenable, because the Śruti declares, “Without what is before, without what is after, without what is within, without what is without,” thereby stating that there is no distinction between the external and the internal for It. Anticipating this, he says:
This distinction between the external and the internal is with respect to the body; it does not exist in the Witness.
The objects of the senses reside in external regions, while the ego resides within the body.
Regarding the word "external": to the question of what is external and what is internal, he says: "The objects" (viṣayāḥ). || 16 ||
He states that very point: "Externally and internally," etc. (Verse 16). The commentary says: He states that very point—“externally and internally,” etc. (16).

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "The statement that the unchanging Being—being stable, enduring, and a witness—illuminates both the internal and the external is improper. For in the experience "I see the jar," there is first an illumination as the witness of the internal ego (the "I"), and subsequently, there is the experience of going outwards in the form of the manifestation of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form of the jar, in the manner of "I see the jar. Thus [the objection stands].
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"The internal intellect goes out again and again toward external objects together with the senses."
The flickering restlessness residing in the intellect is vainly attributed to the Witness. || 17 ||

Regarding the phrase "within" (*antaḥ*): the intellect (*buddhi*), which resides within another body as the perceiver of objects, repeatedly goes out through the doors of the eyes and other senses in order to grasp forms and so forth.

Consequently, the flickering instability inherent in that [intellect] is superimposed upon its illuminator, the Witness (*sākṣin*). Thus, the point is that the Witness does not possess actual instability. || 17 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might raise this objection: "Even within the body, the Witness shines as the illuminator of the ego; likewise, even outside [the body], He shines as the illuminator of objects such as jars. Since He thus clearly manifests, does He too, like the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), undergo coming and going along with the intellect?
To quell this doubt, he says: "Existing within" (antaḥstha). "By the senses" (akṣaiḥ) means by the organs of perception. || 17 ||
A small amount of sunlight entering within the house remains motionless through the window-lattice.
In that case, when the hand is being made to dance, it is as if the heat itself were dancing.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question, "Where has the attribution of flickeringness to the moon been observed?", he says: "Having entered within the house" (gṛhāntaragata).

A small patch of sunlight that has entered within a house through a window remains indeed motionless; yet, when a person moves that sunlight here and there with his hand, just as the sunlight appears to dance or move, though in reality it does not move—this is the meaning. || 18 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) clarifies that very point by means of an illustration: "gṛhya" etc. (verse 18).
The witness, stationed in its own place, [observes] the coming and going within and without.
Due to the fickleness of the intellect, one acts as if performing [actions] in various ways.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the application to the subject at hand: "In its own place," etc. (19).

The commentary (ṭīkā) applies this to the subject at hand (dāṣṭantika): "nijeti" (by one's own). The meaning is: He resides in that Brahman which is the locus (adhiṣṭhāna), the substratum, of one's own primal ignorance (mūlājñāna), which is the cause of its being the witness (sākṣitva). || 19 ||
The Tenth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
383 Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 ṭīkā): By the phrase "situated in its own place," does he mean that it is located in an external region or the like? No; he says:
"The Witness is neither external nor internal, for both of those are regions of the intellect."
When all mental constructions, such as cognition and the like, have completely subsided, that [Reality] shines forth; it exists there.

"Not external. He states the reason for this: "of the intellect" (*buddheḥ*). Then, what is intended? To this he says: "by the intellect, etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the sense organs and so forth are included; by the word "subsidence" (*saṃśānti*), the cessation of the cognition thereof is intended. || 20 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) on verse a0 states the conclusion: "Not [so]," etc. The reason for this is given by the words beginning with "of the intellect" (buddheḥ). If that is so, then where does the Witness (sākṣin) reside? To this, he says: "intellect and so forth" (buddhyādi). In Brahman alone—which is inaccessible to speech and mind—the conventional usage "Witness" arises due to ignorance, which is the cause for designating something as a Witness; therefore, the meaning is that He resides in that very place. || 20 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection—"If all worldly activity has ceased, then space itself is not perceived; how then can its being the locus [of that cessation] be asserted?"—he reveals his own intention:
"If no space whatsoever were to appear, then let it be that [the cessation] does not reside in space."
Omnipresence exists solely through its manifestation in all places, but not inherently by itself. || 21 ||

Regarding the word "deśa" (place): the sense is that the substratum for the conceptualization of place and so forth has no requirement for a place distinct from itself. Now, one might object: if there is no such thing as place and so forth, would not the scriptural statements regarding its being all-pervasive and the witness of all be contradicted? To this he says: "sarvadeśa... (in all places). Why should it not be natural [to it]? To this he says: "na tu svataḥ" (but not by itself). The sense is that this is because it is non-dual and unconditioned. || 21 ||

— Commentary (A0 Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "If this is so, then no location whatsoever would appear to that Witness. Anticipating this, he refutes it by accepting the consequence, stating: "Location," etc. [The opponent asks: "But then, how is it that the Śruti says, 'He is omnipresent and eternal like space'? Regarding His omnipresence...

Because it has been stated that [the object] has gone [there], he says: "of all places" (*sarvadeśa*). The meaning is that, due to ignorance regarding those [places], they are merely constructed—that is, imagined—just as waves of water in a mirage appear within the sunlight. || 21 ||
Whether internal or external, whatever place one may conceive of, [it is all the same].
A witness who has gone to that place should likewise apply [the same criteria] to material objects. || 22 ||
Rāma’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): He states that, like omnipresence, being the witness of all is also not real—“inside and outside” (antarbahiriti).

Ānandagiri’s Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Just as the Self’s omnipresence is merely a conceptualization based on all locations, so too its being the witness of all is merely a conceptualization based on being the witness of everything;
thus he says “inside” (antariti). Whether it be the internal intellect, the external, or everything—the interior space or the exterior space, or all space—[the Self is the witness].

The meaning is "he knows. Such a place as this he would "imagine"—that is to say, through ignorance, he would superimpose it upon the non-dual Self (*advaitātman*)—by virtue of being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the witness (*sākṣin*).
Being the illuminator, like a self-luminous jewel, of the fire superimposed upon itself, the non-dual Self, while residing in that place, joins together the things in such a way:

"this internal thing is the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth; this external thing is the jar and so forth; all this is a thing delimited by the state of being an object of perception (*dṛśyapadaśakyatva*)."
The syntactical connection is that one should cause the direction to be revealed. || 22 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He elaborates on this point—“likewise, one should apply [the Self] to objects”—as follows:
“Whatever form or other quality may be conceived by the intellect, illuminating each of those...”
Of each and every [state], there is a witness, which is self-evident and beyond the reach of speech and intellect. || 23 ||
Regarding the phrase "whatever...": if one asks, "In that case, what is its own inherent form?", he says: "by itself" (svataḥ). || 23 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) on the conclusion states: "Whatever... and so forth. By the word "etc. (ādi), names and other such attributes are included. The syntactical connection is as follows: even though the Self is by its very nature beyond the reach of speech and the intellect, it becomes the witness of each and every one of those [objects]. || 23 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [pages 382–382] 384.
[In the commentary on the *Nāṭakadīpa* by Rāma: He raises an objection— that if [Brahman] is beyond the reach of speech and mind, it would not be grasped by one seeking liberation.
If you ask, "How can such a thing be grasped by me?", then let it not be grasped at all.
When all planetary afflictions have been pacified, it remains by itself.

"How so? [The author] says, "It is indeed intended that it is ungraspable," beginning with "Not so. Now, one might object: if the Self is ungraspable, then when Māyā has been destroyed through inquiry, it would be stated that "He remains by Himself"; thus, the remaining of the Supreme Self (paramātman) would not be established. To this, he says: "i-sarvagra... [the rest of the verse].

Thus: the meaning is that, through the certainty of the falsity of duality—which is distinct from one's own self—when the perception of that [duality] subsides, one's own self alone remains as the truth. || 24 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might raise the objection: "If the Self is thus inaccessible to speech and mind, how can it be grasped by me, a seeker of liberation? Anticipating this, he replies with the phrase "How [is it grasped]?"—accepting the objection as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*). One might further object: "If the Self is thus ungraspable, then the inquiry into the Supreme Self previously enjoined—based on the premise that bondage caused by non-inquiry is removed by inquiry—would be rendered devoid of an object. This is not so; for when Māyā has been destroyed through inquiry, [the Self] remains.

He says "himself" (*svayam*) because, by the very method previously described, for one who has performed inquiry into the Supreme Self, there remains only the self-luminous non-dual Supreme Self—just as when a royal swan drinks milk, only the nectar remains after the destruction of the water; this is due to the dissolution of *māyā*. He says "all" (*sarva*): the meaning is that when all duality, consisting of name and form, is sublated by knowledge denoted by the word "grasping" (*graha*). || 24 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Although, by the aforementioned reasoning, one’s own Self remains as the sole residue, nevertheless, for the sake of its direct realization (aparokṣya), some means of knowledge (pramāṇa) is required; therefore, he says: "In that regard, there is no need for a means of knowledge, because [the Self] has the nature of self-luminosity."
If you require such an etymological derivation, then recite the scripture from the mouth of your teacher.

"Not there," he says. He states the reason for this: "self-luminous" (*svaprakāśa*). Now, one might object: since the Self is self-luminous, it does not require a means of knowledge (*māna*) for its own manifestation; yet, a means of knowledge is required for the sake of establishing [its nature] through linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*). Anticipating this doubt, he states that scripture itself is the authority here:
"such" (*tādṛg*). || 25 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Granted that through such inquiry the non-dual Self remains once duality has been sublated, nevertheless, a means of knowledge is still required for the sake of its direct realization. To this he says: "Not there" (*na tatra*). Furthermore, one might argue: "Even so, a means of knowledge is certainly required for the purpose of establishing that the Self is self-luminous. To this he says: "Of such a kind" (*tādṛg*). || 25 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus described the means for self-realization for the superior aspirant, he now shows it for the dull-witted aspirant:
"If the renunciation of all objects of perception is impossible, then take refuge in the intellect."
Let it be experienced that this [world], both internally and externally, is dependent upon Him as its refuge. || 26 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Lamp of Drama" (*Nāṭakadīpa*), in the *Pañcadaśī* composed by the venerable sage Vidyāraṇya. 20.

Regarding the word "yadi" (if): [the author] asks, "What is the fruit in taking refuge in the intellect? and answers with the words "tadadhīna" (dependent on that). The meaning is: whatever—whether external or internal—is conceptualized by the intellect, let the Supreme Self, being the witness of each and every one of those things, be experienced as such, for He is dependent upon that [intellect]. || 26 ||

The commentary on the tenth chapter, *Nāṭakadīpa*, within the *Pañcadaśī* treatise, composed by the scholar named Rāmakṛṣṇa, a servant of the venerable Śrīmad-Vidyāraṇya Muni, is hereby completed. 10.
The Tenth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

Commentary: Thus, for the highest type of qualified seeker (*uttamādhikārī*), through the investigation characterized by reflection—which is reinforced by the logic of refutation (*khaṇḍana-yukti*) that supports the sublation of the visible world as established in such scriptural passages as "This Self is 'not this, not this' (*neti neti*)"—and which results in the sublation of duality, there remains only the non-dual, self-luminous Self; this is the definition.

Having thus taught the means [of liberation] for those of superior capacity, he then speaks regarding those of even duller capacity with the words "If... (yadi). Regarding the phrase "devoid of that" (taddhīna):

the implicit meaning is "by virtue of being the illuminator of the intellect" (buddhyavabhāsakatvena). The meaning is: this Supreme Self (paramātman), characterized as the Witness (sākṣin) in the form described above, who is self-luminous non-dual Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda). "Within the body" (antar-dehe) means by way of being the illuminator of the intellect consisting of the mental modification of "I" (ahaṃ-vṛtti); or "outside the body" (dehāt bahiḥ) refers to the eyes and so forth.

This means by way of being the illuminator of mental modifications (*buddhi-vṛtti*) that take on the forms of jars and so forth through two doors [the eyes]. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "let it be experienced as having the nature of self-luminosity.
Now, you have begun with this much:
"Because of non-duality in liberation, even the experience of the bliss of Brahman would not exist."
"O Śiva, O Śiva! How then could this fifth obstacle arise here regarding the individual soul?

Having thus, by means of an Āryā verse, described the fifth obstacle called *viparīta-bhāvanā* (contrary conception) concerning the awakening to the true nature of the individual soul—which is the purified meaning of the term *tvaṃ-pada*—he proceeds further: "In the tenth [chapter], it is said that the Self, like a lamp, is the illuminator of everything and is of a single essence; it is the singular water of self-luminous bliss..."

Regarding the statement "Dhīr means devotion through the description of the fruit," and so forth: if it is asked how it is justified that this tenth chapter of the fifteenth [section] of the work titled *Nāṭakadīpa*—which speaks of the removal of obstacles by way of describing the fruit characterized as being a single ocean of the nectar of non-dual, partless, one-flavored Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda) which is self-luminous, even though the nature of the Self is non-dual like a pearl—is explained, it is said: first, at the beginning here...

Having stated at the beginning, "The Self is Ramā, non-dual bliss, and full," and concluding with, "Let the Self, which is infinite bliss and self-luminous, be experienced," there is a uniformity between the opening and the conclusion; this constitutes one mark (*liṅga*) indicating that the subject matter is the aforementioned fruit. Likewise, in the fourth verse, [it says] "of the nature of non-dual bliss";

in the ninth verse, "the witness here is the body of consciousness" (*cidvapuḥ*); and in the thirteenth, "in the immutable (*kūṭastha*) which shines incessantly, as the form of pure awareness" (*jñaptirūpatā*), and so forth.

Practice [is required]. Therein, because its nature is self-luminous, there is no dependence on any means of knowledge; this is the "novelty" (apūrvatā) in the twenty-fifth [verse]. "When all grasping has ceased, it remains by itself alone"—this is the fruit in the twenty-fourth [verse]. "Like a lamp situated in a dance hall," and so forth, is the corroborative statement (arthavāda) in the eleventh [verse]. "The small amount of sunlight that has entered the interior of a house through a window remains motionless," and so forth, is the logical justification (upapatti) in the eighteenth and subsequent verses. Thus, the marks (liṅgas) are sixfold. Therefore—
In this regard, there is not even a trace of disagreement concerning the nature of liberation as the fruit, which has been thus defined; may there be auspiciousness! (26)

Thus ends the fifth chapter in the work titled *Pūrṇānandendukaumudī*, composed by the student Acyuta Śarmā, whose mind moves like a royal swan among the lotus feet of Śrī Nārāyaṇa Śāstrī— whose name is the sixth [in the lineage] of the venerable Advaitavidyendirāramaṇa, who sports in the milk-ocean of the venerable Padavākya-pramāṇa, and who is the disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakācārya, Śrī Madvaita Saccidānandendra Sarasvatī.
In the *Candrikā* commentary on the *Daśarūpaka*, the tenth chapter, "The Illumination of the Lamp of Drama" (*Nāṭakadīpaprakāśa*), is complete. 10.
Now begins the eleventh chapter of the fifteenth [section].
In this [work], the first chapter, titled "The Bliss of Yoga," within the *Brahmānanda*, [the author] says:
Having bowed to the venerable masters Bhāratītīrtha and Vidyāraṇya.
I shall comment upon the work titled Brahmānanda for the sake of attaining enlightenment.

Performing the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) consisting of the contemplation of the true nature of the chosen deity for the sake of completing the work he intends to compose without obstacle and for the removal of obstructing impurities, and revealing the subject matter along with its purpose to ensure the engagement of the listeners, he declares the commencement of the book:
"I shall proclaim the bliss of Brahman; when that is known in its entirety," [all suffering ceases].
Having abandoned the multitude of misfortunes pertaining to this world and the next, one finds happiness. || 1 ||
Regarding the phrase "the bliss of Brahman":
"Those dull-witted ones who are unable to directly realize the supreme Brahman devoid of distinctions are shown compassion through descriptions of Brahman with attributes."

Thus, because the reality (*tattva*) of the deities who possess specific attributes (*saviśeṣa*) is declared to be the nature of Brahman devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*), and because Brahman is declared by such scriptural passages as "Bliss is Brahman" (*ānando brahma*) to be of the nature of bliss (*ānandarūpa*), the expression "Brahmānanda" employs a term denoting Brahman as the embodiment of bliss;

and according to the principle stated in the scripture, "Whatever one meditates upon with the mind, that one expresses with speech," this constitutes the characteristic mark of the contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*) of Brahman.

The auspicious invocation is established. Since Brahman is that which is propounded by all the Vedāntas, the subject matter (*viṣaya*) of this work—which takes the form of a treatise upon Him—is likewise that very same Brahman;

thus, by the employment of the word "Brahman," the subject matter is also indicated. By the second half of the verse beginning with *aihika*, the two-fold purpose (*prayojana*)—consisting of the cessation of the undesirable and the attainment of the desirable—is stated explicitly. "Brahmānanda" means that which is both Brahman and bliss (*ānanda*); it is the bliss that is Brahman, or the Brahman that is bliss. [Regarding] the expressed and the...

Because of the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) between the two wheels [of the body], the treatise that explains them is also called *Brahmānanda*. Thus, [the author says] "I shall expound that. When that *Brahmānanda*—consisting of both the subject to be explained and the means of explanation—is known and understood, there occurs the destruction of the multitude of misfortunes pertaining to this world and the next. "Pertaining to this world" (*aihika*) refers to those things arising in this life, such as the egoism and possessiveness (*ahaṃ-mama-abhimāna*) directed toward the body, sons, and so forth, as well as the internal and other torments (*ādhyātmika-ādi-tāpa*). "Pertaining to the next world" (*āmuṣmika*) refers to those things arising in the hereafter...

Having abandoned—that is, completely relinquished—without remainder that multitude, that collection of those various misfortunes, he becomes happy; that is, he becomes Brahman itself, which is of the nature of bliss. || 1 ||
I bow to the Supreme Brahman, the immutable essence of non-dual bliss, existence, consciousness, and omnipresence, which is the pure pinnacle of the Vedas;
though it is the abode of the illusory net of duality due to delusion, it is its own self-luminous ornament.
I also bow to all the preeminent teachers, and especially to my true Guru, the jewel of the Raghu dynasty, who is firmly established in Brahman.
I bow to my own guru, known as Śrīmannārāyaṇa, who is also named Mahādeva. || 1 ||
Having paid homage to Jīvajīva, Vidyāraṇya, Bhāratītīrtha,
and Yogānanda, I shall now clearly explain [this work] through the light of Śiva, like the Kaumudī commentary.
Then the Blessed One, the teacher Bhāratītīrtha, concluded his tenth chapter, titled *Nāṭakadīpa*, in the work *Pañcadaśī* that he himself had composed:
"If the abandonment of all attachments is possible, then resort to the intellect."
Let this Vaiṣṇava refuge, which is dependent upon Him, be experienced both internally and externally.
[End of Chapter Eleven]
Accompanied by the two commentaries.

Having observed a certain disciple who was intent on investigating the mental modifications arising from hearing his own words, [the Teacher], out of a desire to favor him, here—[in this Brahman-sūtra]—proceeds...

Now, commencing the first section, titled *Yogānanda*, which is the eleventh among the fifteen chapters of the work known as the *Pañcadaśī*—the latter consisting of five chapters divided into three parts—the author performs an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) that possesses both well-known authority and purpose; this invocation consists of the contemplation of the non-dual Brahman-Self, which is the subject matter of the present section. He proceeds to explain, through five sections each, the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam* respectively within the aforementioned *Pañcadaśī*, which comprises five chapters.

Since the two parts were taught as distinct based on their predominance, [the author], in order to teach that the subject matter of the five treatises—which is constituted by non-difference—is indeed predominant, gives them the single collective name "Brahmānanda. By thus indicating its primary subject matter, he declares the composition of these works for the sake of engaging wise seekers of liberation, saying: "Brahmānanda. Herein, the excellence [of this bliss] will be...

Let it be that this is the very definition of the perception of a *māna-yogin*; nevertheless, when one considers what the purpose of that [definition] is, he elaborates upon it in the three quarters beginning with "jñāte" (when known). The term "aśeṣataḥ" (without remainder) connects with both the preceding and the following according to the "middle gem" (*madhyamaṇi*) maxim. By this, the exclusion of momentary pleasure and the like arising from occasional hearing is indicated. Worldly misfortunes, such as mental anguish and physical disease, are indeed well-known. Ā- (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.)

Furthermore, O Indra, the specific types of torment consisting of the [Buddha's] teachings that are enacted in the hells by Yama and Bhairava are also accessible through the scriptures alone, being delimited by the respective qualifications of those [who undergo them].

One who desires this [liberation] is the qualified person (*adhikārī*) here. Moreover, the relationship between this work and its subject matter is that of the expounder and the expounded (*pratipādaka-pratipādya-bhāva*). || 1 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Desiring to demonstrate that there are many scriptural and traditional (śruti-smṛti) statements serving as evidence for the fact that the knowledge of Brahman is the cause of the cessation of the undesired and the attainment of the desired, [the author] first cites: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), and "It has indeed been heard thus from the Blessed One... (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.22).

He recites two statements from the text in substance: "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow," and "I am such, O Venerable One; I am in sorrow; may the Venerable One carry me across to the further shore of sorrow.
[He summarizes: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme, and the knower of the Self crosses over sorrow."
Having obtained the essence of Brahman, one becomes blissful; it is not otherwise.

Regarding the term *brahmavit*: one who knows Brahman (*brahmavit*) attains the supreme, most excellent Brahman, which is of the nature of bliss. One who knows the Self (*ātmavit*) knows the Self, which is denoted by the word "Bhūman" and is devoid of limitations of space, time, or substance. As for "grief" (*śoka*): it is called grief because it causes the person with whom it is associated to grieve; it is the cycle of transmigratory existence rooted in ignorance (*tamas*). One crosses over—that is, transcends—that [grief]. Now, in the cited passage from the Taittirīyaka Upaniṣad...

Anticipating the objection that the knowledge of Brahman appears only as the cause for attaining the Supreme (liberation) and not as the cause for attaining bliss, [the author] recites in substance that very statement of his own—"He is indeed Rasa; for having obtained Rasa, one becomes blissful"—which is intended to establish it as the cause for attaining bliss: "Rasa...
[and so on]. [This follows] from such scriptural passages as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite" and "From this very Self, space was produced."

The meaning is that the Self which is denoted by the words "Brahman" and "Atman" in the context of the battle and so forth is *rasa*, the essence, whose nature is bliss (*ānanda-rūpa*). Having attained Brahman, whose nature is *rasa* and bliss—having reached it through the knowledge "I am Brahman"—one becomes blissful; that is, one comes to possess unlimited and unsurpassed happiness.
He confirms the stated point by demonstrating its converse: "Not otherwise. That is, [it cannot be attained] otherwise than by abandoning the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Atman.
The meaning is that one does not become blissful through the performance of other means of accomplishment. || 2 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, demonstrating the purpose—which consists in the attainment of unsurpassed bliss preceded by the cessation of all suffering—through the unimpeded direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the non-duality of Brahman and the Self arising from the inquiry into the present treatise, and summarizing a multitude of Vedic texts, [the author] first cites the well-known verse from the *Taittirīya* and *Chāndogya Upaniṣads*: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. (*brahmavidāpnoti param*)

Thus, he recites the two statements—"He who knows the Self crosses over sorrow"—in terms of their meaning as "the knower of Brahman. Now, one might object: from the definition of the essential nature of Brahman, "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," it is understood from that very statement that for the knower of Brahman—characterized by truth and the rest—there is only the attainment of the supreme reality denoted by the word "para" (the Highest), but not the attainment of the aforementioned bliss; therefore, [he cites] the Taittirīyaka itself: "That indeed is the essence (rasa). Having obtained that very essence..."
The phrase "there is joy" also contradicts the meaning of the sentence, as it says: "it is flavor. || 2 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 386] 388.

[The commentary by Rāmānuja on the *Yogānanda*—having thus presented the statements intended to establish the attainment of the desired and the cessation of the undesired by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he now presents the statement intended to demonstrate the cessation of misfortune through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): "For when, indeed, this one [is established] in that which is invisible, bodiless, indefinable... ]

"He finds a secure foundation in his own abode and then becomes free from fear; for when he perceives even a slight difference in this [Self], then fear comes to him"—thus the author summarizes the meaning of these two scriptural passages: "When he finds a secure foundation within himself, then he is free from fear."
If one creates an interval in this, then fear shall arise for him.

"Pratiṣṭhām" (the firm foundation). This is its meaning: "When"—that is, at which time—"hi" is a particle intended to indicate what is well-known among the wise; it serves to establish the restriction that this alone is the means for the cessation of suffering, and no other. This seeker of liberation, in this [Reality] which is accessible through the experience of the wise, which is invisible (adṛśya) and beyond the range of the senses, which is without a self (anātmya) and without anything belonging to a self (anātmīya), being devoid of ownership by virtue of its own nature, and which is indefinable (anirukta)—for "nirukta" refers to a definition... [text continues].

That which cannot be designated by any word is "anirukta" (undefined). In that "anilayana"—wherein no *nilayana* exists, for *nilayana* means a support (*ādhāra*) in the sense that "one rests within it"—He resides by His own majesty; this is the meaning. It is "fearless" and "non-dual," for according to the Vedic scripture, "From duality, indeed, fear arises. Here, by the word "fear," its cause, namely "duality," is indicated. Thus, He exists in such a way that fear—that is, duality—does not exist.

"Pratiṣṭhā" is a firm standing, a state of abiding as "I am Brahman," free from doubt and error; he finds that—having performed hearing and so forth by approaching a teacher—he attains it. Then, at that very moment, he who knows thus reaches—that is, attains—the fearless, non-dual Brahman which is liberation, according to the Vedic scripture: "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself. When—at that very time—
This time refers to that aforementioned Brahman, which is non-different from the inner self (pratyagātman) and possesses qualities such as invisibility. The particle *api* has the sense of "even.

Even if one perceives—since verbal roots have multiple meanings—only a slight interval (*aram*) or distinction (*antaram*) characterized by the relationship of the object of worship and the worshiper, then at that very moment, fear—the suffering caused by transmigratory existence—arises for that perceiver of difference. || 3 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Likewise, there are two statements composed of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that bring about the cessation of the aforementioned suffering, belonging to that very [text]:

"For when he finds fearless support in this which is invisible, incorporeal, indefinable, and without abode, then he becomes free from fear; but when he perceives even the slightest difference in this, then fear comes to him. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7).
He summarizes the meaning: "The foundation. || 3 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To strengthen the point that fear arises for those who perceive duality, he recites in substance the mantra beginning with "From fear of Him the wind blows," which demonstrates the fear experienced by Vāyu and others who lack the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self.
Vāyu, Sūrya, Vahni, Indra, and Mṛtyu [are the presiding deities] in one birth after another.
Even those who understand the Dharma act out of fear of this very thing.

Regarding the word "Vāyu": the five deities, beginning with Vāyu, who are well known as the governors of the universe—even though they understood the Dharma characterized by sacrifice (*iṣṭā*) and public works (*pūrta*) in their previous birth and performed it with prior knowledge—nevertheless, having created a distinction between themselves and the inner Brahman (*pratyag-brahman*), they move within this birth as Vāyu and the others, always engaging in their respective functions out of fear of this Brahman. By the word "hi" (for/indeed), [it is meant that] out of fear...

"The fire burns out of fear; the sun burns out of fear; out of fear the mountains and the wind [burn]; and death indeed is the fifth"—thus he shows the well-known tradition spoken by Yama in the Kaṭha Śruti. || 4 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): In response to the inquiry, "Where has fear been seen by one who perceives such difference?", he provides the answer through the meaning of the scriptural statement: "From fear of Him the wind blows; from fear the sun rises; from fear of Him Agni, Indra, and Death as the fifth run on" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8).
He does so by means of the word "vāyuḥ" (the wind). This applies even to one who possesses specific knowledge, characterized by the performance of duties in accordance with that realization.
The Eleventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

"Even though they know"—the meaning is "even though they perceive through the natures of cause and effect. "From this," meaning from this Inner Controller (antaryāmin). "They move" means that they indeed proceed toward their respective functions. || 4 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that in the scriptural passages cited, such as "The knower of the Self transcends sorrow," the fact that the knowledge of Brahman-bliss is the cause for the cessation of evil does not appear clearly.
Anticipating this doubt, he cites a verse intended to establish that point:
"One who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing whatsoever."
For her, this very anxiety born from the fire of karma has been extinguished by penance alone. || 5 ||

"Bliss" (ānanda): The designation of difference, such as "the head of Rāhu," is merely figurative. A person who knows—that is, who realizes through direct perception—the bliss that constitutes the very nature of Brahman, does not fear anything whatsoever; he does not encounter fear from any cause of worldly fear, such as a tiger, nor from any cause of otherworldly fear, such as sin. Now, one might ask: how is it known that there is no fear of sin and the like for the knower of reality?
Anticipating the doubt as to how this is understood, he recites in substance the passage that establishes it—"This indeed does not burn him: 'Why did I not do what is good?

Why did I do what is evil?'"—with the words "this" (etam). The fire produced by action is action itself, consisting of merit and demerit; for, like fire, it is the cause of torment through both non-performance and performance. By that [action] is produced this [state], namely, the heavenly world (*nāka*) of merit.

"Why did he utter such a sinful cry? Why indeed?"—such is the nature of his anxiety. He alone, who knows the truth, would not torment or cause distress to another who is ignorant; however, the meaning is that he himself is constantly tormented by that very anxiety. || 5 ||

Commentary (A0): Thus, he cites that very statement of his own regarding the attainment of fearlessness: "One who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing from anywhere" (*ānandaṃ brahmaṇo vidvān na bibheti kutaścana*). In the phrase "of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ*), the genitive case is figurative (*aupacārika*), as in expressions such as "the head of Rāhu."

[The phrase] "from whatever" means from anything pertaining to this world, such as the maintenance of the body, as well as from merit performed for the sake of the next world and from sin committed [therein].
For this very reason, it is said: "This indeed does not afflict him: 'Why did I not do what is good? Why did I commit sin?

He states the meaning of that passage: "This very... This refers to what is about to be described. Regarding "action": action alone is the fire; action consisting of both merit and sin is itself the fire.
Because it is neither "done" nor "not done," and because it causes torment, it is fire; by that [fire], it is "saṃbhṛtā," meaning fully nourished. It would not burn, nor would it consume. || 5 ||
Knowing this, one should abandon both types of action and always remember the Self.
And when the action has been performed, he perceives it as being of the very nature of his own self.

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: To demonstrate the reason why merit and demerit do not cause distress, he recites in substance the two scriptural passages—"He who knows thus protects these two selves"—and "For he indeed protects both these selves"—with the words "Thus...
He who is any person whatsoever, in the manner described, [realizes] by the method expressed in "That which is here in the person and that which is yonder in the sun are one."

The learned one, knowing [this], proceeds; the ellipsis here is "having abandoned these merits and demerits. He "satisfies" (spṛṇute)—that is, delights—the Self, which is non-different from Brahman and is the inner witness; the meaning is that he should constantly remember it. Since the abandonment of merit and demerit has been accomplished through the contemplation of their falsity, there is no thought regarding them at all. The intention is: how could there be suffering caused by them? Furthermore, this learned one [realizes] these two previously mentioned...

The meaning is that one perceives—that is, knows—both types of action, consisting of merit and demerit, which are produced through the activity of the body, senses, and so forth, as being entirely conformable to one's own Self, according to the manner stated in such scriptural passages as "All this is what this Self is. Therefore, the sense is that because [the Self] is non-different from one's own Self, it does not cause affliction. || 6 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: for what reason is it said that even at the outset, the knower of Brahman does not experience distress caused by the anxiety over the fire of karma? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the answer by reciting the meaning of the previously cited remainder of the scriptural passage—"He who knows thus protects these selves; for he indeed protects both these selves"—beginning with the words "Thus knowing" (*evaṃ vidvān*). Two...

It is of two kinds, consisting of the form of *ṇya* and so forth; the meaning is that one should abandon or renounce [them], or else discard them as being false. Now, after the knowledge of the Self—[[page 388-to-388]] 390...
In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya, [in the section titled] *Yogānanda*, it is stated:
"Let this arrangement of the two [types of karma] be thus; nevertheless, regarding those two known as 'accumulated' (*saṃcita*), which exist prior to that [present action]—"
To the objection that [the soul] has a destination, he says: "And when [the body] has been made" (kṛte ca). || 6 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, an objection may be raised: since there exist scriptural authorities such as, "Karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of kalpas unless it has been experienced," and since in this beginningless saṃsāra there are innumerable karmas characterized by merit and demerit acquired over many births—which, being unknown, are unfit for identification as one's own—how could there not be anxiety regarding them? Anticipating this, [the author] states that for those [karmas] along with their causes, through the knowledge of reality...

With the intention that [the Self], being imperishable, cannot be a cause for anxiety, he recites the passage found in the *Muṇḍaka* and other Upaniṣads, which aims at the cessation of the knots of the heart and so forth:
"The knot of the heart is severed; all doubts are rent asunder."
And his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.

Regarding the word *bhidyate*: since even the "higher" (*para*) states, such as that of Hiraṇyagarbha, are "lower" (*avara*)—meaning inferior—compared to it, therefore, when the Supreme Self is seen, that is, directly realized, the "knot" of this one who possesses such realization—the knot consisting of the heart (the intellect), the self (the conscious soul), and their mutual superimposition—is "pierced," meaning it is torn asunder and destroyed. All doubts [regarding the question] whether the Self is distinct from the body and so forth [are resolved].

Whether [the individual soul] is distinct [from Brahman], or even if not distinct, whether it possesses attributes such as agency; or even if it lacks agency, whether there is any difference between that [soul] and Brahman;

or even if there is no difference, whether the knowledge of That, accompanied by ritual action and so forth, is the means to liberation, or whether it is [knowledge] alone—such doubts are "cut asunder," meaning they are split in two. The sense is that an object realized in its true nature is never seen to be the domain of doubt or error. As for "accumulated actions" (*saṃcitakarmāṇi*)...
The characteristics of merit and demerit perish; they are destroyed by the destruction of the ignorance that is their own cause. || 7 ||
Commentary on Sūtra 1.1:
Now, one might object: "How is it appropriate to contemplate infinite, accumulated, and imperceptible karmas as being identical with the Self?

Out of this dissatisfaction, [the author] provides the *Muṇḍaka-upaniṣad* as an illustration demonstrating their destruction immediately after the moment of realizing the Truth—just as the snake itself destroys its own previous state of being a Brahmin-slaughter or a horse-sacrifice.

He cites the scripture itself: "It is split. The meaning of this is stated in the *Anubhūtiprakāśa* as follows: "Since the supreme unmanifest is inferior to the conscious Self (cidātman), when that [Self] is seen, the knot between the ego (ahaṃkāra) and consciousness is split. Māyā creates a firm knot between those two by superimposing the agency of the ego onto consciousness, and likewise the manifestation of consciousness onto the ego. When that knot is split through discernment, doubts..."

"Those who have reached the reality of Brahman; there shall be the cutting away [of bondage] and likewise the destruction of the karma that causes future births. In this very same way, the Bhagavad Gītā also states:

"Just as a well-kindled fire reduces wood to ashes, O Arjuna, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all karmas to ashes. Regarding this, Madhusūdana’s commentary (*Ṭīkā*) says: "Just as wood—that is, pieces of timber—[is reduced]; a well-kindled fire—that is, one that has been set ablaze—reduces it to ashes."

It reduces them to ashes. O Arjuna, the fire of knowledge completely reduces all actions—both sins and merits, especially those distinct from the fruits already commenced—to ashes; the meaning is that it destroys them by annihilating the ignorance that is their cause. And so says the Śruti:

"The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away, and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen. And in the Sūtra: "Upon the attainment of That, there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior [karmas], because of the scriptural declaration thereof; and for the other [the remaining karma] as well, there is likewise non-clinging upon death. Regarding the fact that merit and demerit whose effects have not yet begun are indeed destroyed, the Sūtra states: "But only those whose effects have not yet begun..."

Regarding the phrase "prior to that limit": for those who have initiated the body that produces knowledge, their destruction occurs at the very end of that body, according to the Śruti: "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be united. And from the Sūtra: "But having exhausted the others through experience, he becomes [united]. However, in the case of those holding office (ādhikārika), the very same elements that initiated the body which produced knowledge also initiate subsequent bodies.

As in the case of Vasiṣṭha, Avāntaratama, and others. And so says the Sūtra: "The persistence of those who hold office lasts as long as their office. Here, "office" (adhikāra) refers to powerful karma that has begun to bear fruit and which necessitates the commencement of multiple bodies. This [karma] belongs only to those who are practitioners of meditation (upāsakas), not to others. Karma whose fruit has not yet begun perishes, but that whose fruit has begun persists until the completion of its experience. And that experience occurs through a single body—
