There is no distinction as to whether [the fruit] is obtained by one means or another; however, the detailed account should be seen in the original source (*ākara*). Here, the qualification "distinct from those whose fruits have already begun" applied to all actions by the venerable teacher Sarasvatīpāda was made solely in accordance with the perspective of limited vision, such as our own. For this very reason—

In the *Anubhūtiprakāśa*, it is stated that there is likewise the destruction of karma which is the cause of future births. For those [karmas] whose fruits have already begun (*prārabdha-phala*), they lack the very nature of being "karma" by virtue of having already become its fruit. Indeed, even when rice is undergoing transformation into the state of a sprout and so forth, the quality of being "rice" (*vrīhitva*) is not seen in that sprout; nor is cotton, once it has attained the state of thread, still designated as "cotton. Otherwise, if Devadatta were commanded, "Bring earth for the sake of the sacrificial altar," he would [bring the earth].

One should also bring the *pālā* and other such items. Therefore, our preceptor’s sons, the Pūrṇāyuṣas, the disciples of Pāṇḍuraṅga, maintain that those aforementioned qualifications do not apply to them by virtue of their own preference. Furthermore, the statement that this [practice] is for the devotees alone and not for others is spoken only with reference to those of dull intellect;
otherwise—“He who beholds the Lord on the full moon day of Kārttika in conjunction with the Kṛttikā constellation shall become a wealthy Brāhmaṇa for seven births.”

According to the *Smṛti* text, "He who has mastered the Vedas," in former times a certain person had a vision of the Lord Skanda on Śrīśaila during such a yoga. By the merit of that, following his death, he was by destiny born here as a wealthy man. Having first studied his own Vedic branch—characterized by the word "Veda"—he [performed] his duties appropriate to his own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), which were free from all desire-driven and prohibited acts, devoid of even a trace of ritualistic formalism, and characterized by total self-surrender to the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) accumulated through countless previous births.

When, through the performance of obligatory rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, the mind has attained purity, one should study grammar, logic, and Mīmāṃsā as much as necessary out of a desire to know the eternal and the non-eternal.

Having thereby developed a distaste for all worldly objects—both those of this life and others—through the discrimination between the permanent and the impermanent, and having acquired the six means beginning with tranquility (śama), one should take refuge in a preeminent teacher who possesses the aforementioned characteristics, is learned in the Vedas (śrotriya), and is firmly established in Brahman; and then, with an intense desire to know Brahman, one should engage in inquiry.

If he—having attained the direct realization of the non-duality of Brahman and the Self through the great Mahāvākya of his own Vedic branch as interpreted by the venerable teacher Advaitācārya Bhagavatpāda, thereby removing the fourfold obstacles characterized by the impossibility of [the Self being] a valid means of knowledge and so forth; and having destroyed the root ignorance, thereby achieving the sublation of all duality as a necessary consequence; and remaining a *jīvanmukta* who, like one who has renounced all worldly ties, continues to dwell while experiencing the fruits of *prārabdha* karma—then for him:

Among the enjoyment of the fruits of merit (*puṇyāpūrva*)—which consists of the satisfaction of the Lord resulting from the sight of the Master, as described in the passage concerning the seven births characterized by wealth and so forth—this enjoyment occurring in a single birth has already been accomplished. Consequently, the remaining six births would necessarily belong to that person even without practicing [further], due to their state of *jīvanmukti*, just like Vasiṣṭha and others; such being the case, what is the solution? Nor can it be argued that this applies only to those of the present day who, by chance...

It is now argued that for those Brahmins who know Brahman as Consciousness (*cidbrahman*), there arises an extreme state of suffering due to the uncertainty regarding the possibility of two or more future births, based on the expectation of attaining Brahminhood through the vision of their Master according to the etymological derivation (*nirukti*). However, this is not the case; for if they possess the aforementioned qualities such as wealth and so forth, then the desired outcome is achieved.

Furthermore, even the suffering associated with the possible occurrence of two to seven births is rendered as insignificant as a blade of grass by the bliss of *jīvanmukti*; moreover, this occurs without even the need for formal meditative worship (*upāsanā*).

Furthermore, even across many lifetimes, as in the case of Vasiṣṭha and others, it is only the excellence of contentment and the abundance of bliss resulting from the play of liberation-in-life (*jīvanmukti*) that is truly possible. However, in this most wretched Kali age, for Brahmins today, even mere wealth is extremely difficult to obtain; even if that exists in some cases, mastery of the Vedas is far more difficult to find; and even if both of those exist, true knowledge of Brahman in the manner described is exceedingly rare.

This is indeed true. But even so, after two or three years, the aforementioned conjunction (*yoga*) certainly recurs; and at that time, thousands of men indeed behold Lord Skanda at Śrīpauṇḍarīka, yet they all die.

Why is it that not even one of them is found in this land of Bharata for seven births thereafter as a wealthy man who has mastered the Vedas? Furthermore, why are there not hundreds of others endowed with the knowledge of Brahman, established by the very impossibility of otherwise accounting for their mastery of the Vedas?

If it be argued that this is not so, we reply: no, because the aforementioned Smṛti does not state a restrictive rule such as, "In this very life, immediately following [the realization], one shall become a Brahmin after seven births. Even if such a rule were to be inferred—as one might infer from statements like "one desiring heaven should sacrifice"—the relative strength or weakness of karma remains difficult for anyone who is not omniscient to discern. For instance, even after attaining the vision of the Lord (Svāmī), if death occurs in Kāśī, or if any one of the great sins (mahāpātaka) such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa or the drinking of liquor should occur, there would still arise, in due order, both the destruction of those [sins] and the obstacles thereto.

And because it is possible [otherwise]. Therefore, it is indeed logical that for those who know Brahman—even if they are not practitioners (*anupāsaka*)—the possibility of conceiving the fruits of karma to be experienced over many births exists only when there is the state of being a knower of Brahman distinguished by wealth and mastery of the Vedas. Since the practice here is exclusively Vedic, everything is entirely clear. || 7 ||

[The commentary by Rāghavendra on the passage titled *Yogānanda*]:

Now, one might object: "Performing actions alone in this world, one should desire to live a hundred years; thus it is for you, and not otherwise than this—action does not cling to a man. He who knows both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) together, by means of ignorance [he overcomes] death... [Isa Upanishad 2].

Having crossed over by means of knowledge, one partakes of immortality—so says the Śruti. And from the Smṛti: "Indeed, Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone," and "Just as food joined with honey, or honey joined with food, so too austerity and knowledge, when combined, constitute a great medicine. Anticipating the objection that action—either independently or in combination with knowledge—might be the cause of liberation, [the author] cites the following passage: ...of the words contained in the cited statement:

Furthermore, because the word *tapas* refers to the cessation of evil, the prefix *ā-* refers to the non-cessation of evil, the word *saṃsiddhi* denotes the purity of mind which is the means for knowledge, and the word *vidyā* intends to express meditative worship (*upāsanā*), it is with the intention that ritual actions are not the means to liberation that the following text, aimed at negating other means, is stated: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8)
Thus he recites the words of the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad according to their meaning:
"Only by knowing Him does one transcend death; there is no other path."
Having known the Lord, there is the destruction of the bonds; with the afflictions exhausted, one no longer undergoes birth.

"Only him": only one who knows that aforementioned Supreme Self transcends death, which is to say, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). No other path—whether consisting of a combination [of knowledge and action] or consisting of action alone—exists as a means to liberation; indeed, such a path does not exist at all. Now, one might object: "In the scriptural passages cited, through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it appears that primarily the cessation of undesirable things pertaining to this world is intended, and not those pertaining to the next world. Anticipating this, [the author says: "The next world..."

Since an undesirable future birth must be preceded by its cause, [the author] recites in substance the statement from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad—"Upon knowing God, there is the casting off of all bonds; with afflictions destroyed, there is the abandonment of birth and death"—which establishes the absence of that [birth] along with its cause: "Having known" (jñātvā). Having known—that is, having experienced through direct realization—the God who is self-luminous Brahman non-different from the inner self, for one who remains thus, there is the [casting off] of all bonds such as desire, anger, and the rest.

There is a falling away by means of those afflictions—passion and the rest—which are designated by the word "fetter" (pāśa); the meaning is that when these have been exhausted and destroyed, one does not reach [rebirth] there because of the impossibility of initiating karma that is the cause for future birth. || 8 ||
25. Commentary on Verse 25:
Now, an objection may be raised based on the Vedic scripture: "Performing actions alone here, one should desire to live for a hundred years."

Furthermore, because of the Smṛti passage, "Indeed, Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone," and because the attainment of complete happiness preceded by the cessation of all suffering is possible through action alone, the aforementioned Śrutis are merely praises of knowledge; as stated in the Śruti, "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together...
and so forth, "Just as the flight of birds is achieved by means of both wings, even so is [liberation] attained through both knowledge and action."

Anticipating the objection that—on account of the Smṛti stating "the eternal state"—the attainment of the aforementioned human goal may occur only through the performance of the combination of knowledge and action (jñāna-karma-samuccaya), he recites the verse from the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* in substance to resolve this by means of Śruti itself: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey. He says:
"tameva" (only Him). Only by knowing that very Self, which is of the nature of non-dual Brahman, does one [pass beyond] death.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: having sublated—by means of uncontradicted immediate knowledge in the form "I am Brahman"—the entire network of visible objects which consists of the effects of that [Brahman] and is pervaded by it, as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) which is its cause, one attains liberation characterized by the true nature of the Self as described above. Regarding the force of the particle *eva* (in the phrase *viditvaiva*), he states the authoritative proof with the words beginning "the path" (*panthā*). Therein, his own [text] establishes the cessation of all suffering pertaining to this world and the next.

Next, regarding *dāna*, he summarizes the meaning of the statement, "Having known God, there is the falling away of all bonds; with the afflictions (*kleśa*) exhausted, there is the abandonment of birth and death," as follows: "Having known" (*jñātvā*). This means having known God, who is self-luminous and the non-dual Self (*advaitātman*). According to the saying, "Compassion (*ghṛṇā*), doubt (*śaṅkā*), fear (*bhaya*), shame (*lajjā*), and disgust (*jugupsā*) as the fifth, along with lineage (*kula*), caste (*jāti*), and character (*śīla*)—these eight are proclaimed as the bonds (*pāśa*)," compassion (*karuṇā*) [is included].

The sense is that it is indeed appropriate for *ghṛṇā* (compassion) and the like—referred to by the word *ghṛṇā* according to the statement of Amara—to be considered "nooses," since their binding nature is well-established in the works of Bharata and others. The afflictions (*kleśas*), however, were stated by Patañjali himself: "Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are the five afflictions.
Here, *asmitā* is subtle egoism; it is said to be the very same as the principle of *mahat*. || 8 ||
The Eleventh Chapter [pages 391–391]
Accompanied by two commentaries.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Now, it may be argued that although the fruit of crossing over grief and so forth is indeed heard in scripture, it is not actually experienced even by the wise, since they still encounter desirable and undesirable objects.

Anticipating the objection that activity is observed for the sake of avoiding sin, the author quotes the *Kaṭha Upaniṣad*—intended to demonstrate the absence of such activity in those possessing firm immediate knowledge—in its sense: "Having known the Divine through the attainment of the yoga of the inner self, the wise man abandons both joy and sorrow. He recites it as follows:
"Having known the Divine, the steadfast one here itself abandons joy and sorrow."
Neither merit nor demerit, whether performed or unperformed, ever causes this one to suffer.

Regarding the word *devam*: one who is steadfast and endowed with the means such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*), having realized—that is, understood—the Divine characterized by consciousness, bliss, and so forth, abandons both joy and sorrow in this very life. To specifically illustrate the meaning of what was stated in the passage, "He alone should practice austerity; this anxiety produced by the fire of karma does not [affect him]," the author recites in substance the statement from the Yājñavalkya-brāhmaṇa: "Neither what is done nor what is left undone afflicts him."

Regarding the phrase "not this": it was previously stated that for one who knows reality (*tattvavit*), merit not yet performed and sin already committed do not become causes of affliction; however, the distinction here is that it is stated that such merit or sin—whether performed or unperformed—is likewise not an affliction. For affliction (*tāpa*) is a specific modification of the mind (*cittavikāra-viśeṣa*). Merit, when performed, produces a modification characterized by joy, while when unperformed, it produces dejection; sin, on the other hand, is the opposite of that.

That which is not done does not produce joy, and that which is done does not produce dejection; however, for one who knows reality, neither of these two kinds of causes for modification ever arise, because of the knowledge of the nature of Brahman as changeless—this is the intended meaning. || 9 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Even that which is stated in the Śrutis regarding the crossing over grief and so forth is not being experienced. To this, he recites in substance the statement from the Kaṭhavallī: "Having known the Divine through the attainment of the yoga of the Self, the wise man abandons both joy and grief," using the words "the Divine" (devam).
Furthermore, although it was previously stated that merit and the like do not affect him, this is specified by the Kāṇva Śruti: "Neither what has been done nor what has not been done afflicts him."
— "Not this," he says. Merit performed brings joy; sin brings sorrow. Merit not performed brings sorrow; sin not performed brings joy.
The meaning is that for one who knows the truth, neither of these two result in the heat of suffering characterized by such dual modifications. || 9 ||
He says:
"No," [as stated in] Rāghavendra’s Commentary: "Is it not the case that only these many sentences are authoritative?
To this he replies: "Such numerous Śruti texts, together with the Purāṇas and Smṛtis," and so forth.
They proclaimed that in the knowledge of Brahman there is the destruction of misfortune and also bliss.

"Such scriptural passages as these," and so forth. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the following are included]: "If one has known this here, then there is truth; if one has not known this here, there is great ruin"; "Those who know this become immortal, while others enter only into suffering"; "Whosoever among the gods... and so on.

The meaning is that scriptural passages such as, “He awakened and became that very thing,” and “Having perceived Him, one is released from the jaws of death,” are to be understood along with the authoritative statements of the Purāṇas and Smṛtis, such as: “He who perceives the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self is indeed a sacrificer to the Self and attains self-sovereignty; through the knowledge of the Self, the purification of the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña) is considered supreme. These constitute the means of valid knowledge.
He states the purport of all the cited passages from the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas in the verse beginning with "brahmajñāne" (regarding the knowledge of Brahman). || 10 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): He concludes with the words "ityādi" (and so forth). By the word "ādi," [the author includes such passages as] "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself. ||10||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, since the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) in the phrase "the bliss of Brahman" (*brahmānanda*) is qualified by the word "Brahman," it is understood that there exists another kind of bliss.

In response to the inquiry as to how many types of such bliss there are and what their nature is, the author undertakes an investigation into the bliss of Brahman by first demonstrating its various divisions:
Bliss is threefold: the bliss of Brahman and likewise the happiness of knowledge.
In the passage beginning with "the bliss of sense objects" (viṣayānanda), the bliss of Brahman (brahmānanda) is being distinguished.
Regarding "bliss" (ānanda): bliss is threefold in this manner—namely, the bliss of Brahman (brahmānanda), the bliss of knowledge (vidyānanda), and the bliss of sense objects (viṣayānanda).
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[the section] titled *Yogānanda*.
The meaning is that since the other two types of bliss have their root in the bliss of Brahman, the bliss of Brahman is first demonstrated by way of division through the first three chapters.

Commentary (a0): Thus, in this work consisting of five chapters—which forms the final portion of the *Pañcadaśī* titled *Brahmānanda*—the purpose (*prayojana*) is characterized by the attainment of unsurpassed happiness preceded by the cessation of all suffering. This is established through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by means of a cognition whose object is the identity of Brahman and the Self, which is the object of knowledge (*prameya*). Here, because the word "Bliss" (*ānanda*) is qualified by the word "Brahman," there is the presence of another term [to distinguish it from worldly bliss].
When this [bliss] has been established, in order to dispel the inquiry as to how many kinds it possesses, he prescribes its threefold nature with the words "Bliss" (*ānanda*).

By this, it is indicated that the bliss of objects (*viṣayānanda*) alone includes the others, such as the bliss of latent impressions (*vāsanānanda*) and so forth. One might ask: "Let it be so; what does that have to do with the subject at hand? To this he replies: "Brahman. Thus, within all five chapters, there are the bliss of yoga (*yogānanda*), the bliss of the self (*ātmānanda*), the bliss of non-duality (*advaitānanda*), and the bliss of knowledge (*vidyānanda*).

It is implied that among the pleasures of sense objects, the primary subjects to be expounded are, in sequence: the discrimination between the meanings of the words *tat* and *tvam*, the realization of their identity, the resulting perpetual happiness, and the means for its constant contemplation. || 11 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: First, with the intention of showing that Brahman is understood to be of the nature of bliss through an examination of the Taittirīya Śruti, he briefly presents the meaning of the Bhṛguvallī:
"Bhṛgu, the son, having heard from his father Varuṇa the definition of Brahman..."
Having abandoned food, vital breath, mind, and intellect, he realized bliss.

Regarding the word *bhṛgu*: the son named Bhṛgu received from his father, Varuṇa, the definition of Brahman in the form of the scriptural text: "That from which indeed these beings are born, that by which, once born, they live, and that into which they enter at death—desire to know that; that is Brahman. Thus he heard.

Having determined that those [sheaths] beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*) are not Brahman because the defining characteristics of Brahman are impossible therein, he understood—by applying the definition of Brahman—that the Bliss (*ānanda*), which is heard in the scripture as "Brahman is the tail, the support" (*brahmapucchaṃ pratiṣṭhā*) and exists as the fifth constituent within the sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), is indeed Brahman. This is the meaning. || 12 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding that analysis of Brahman-bliss which was proposed, [the author] establishes, by means of the *Bhṛguvallī*, that Brahman alone is the primary form of bliss—thus: "Bhṛgu... (Verse 12).

Rāma’s Commentary: Anticipating the question, "How did he apply that definition to bliss? and intending to demonstrate the manner of that application, he recites the following passage according to its meaning: "Verily, from bliss alone these beings are born; by bliss, once born, they live; towards bliss they proceed and merge."
From bliss alone all beings are born; by it they live.
Their dissolution occurs therein; therefore, there is no doubt that it is the bliss of Brahman.
"From bliss," it is said. It is from bliss alone, caused by worldly sexual intercourse (*grāmyadharma*), that living beings (*prāṇinaḥ*) are born;

they obtain their livelihood through that bliss caused by the enjoyment of sense objects and the like. Furthermore, the dissolution (*laya*) of those living beings occurs in that very bliss which constitutes their own true nature during deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Since in deep sleep there is no experience of anything other than bliss, bliss is indeed Brahman itself.
The sense is that, because this is established by the experience of everyone, no doubt should be entertained in this matter. || 13 ||
The reason for this is stated: "Because of bliss alone" (ānandādeva). || 13 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus demonstrated that Brahman is of the nature of bliss through a critical examination of the Taittirīya Śruti, and desiring to show the same through a critical examination of the Chāndogya Śruti as well, [the author cites] the passage from the seventh chapter—which takes the form of a dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Nārada and establishes Brahman as the Infinite (bhūman): "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else, that is the Infinite."
He states the meaning of the aforementioned passage in brief:
[Page 393] Chapter Eleven.
Accompanied by two commentaries:
Prior to the origin of the elements, there is plenitude (*bhūman*), because of the absence of the duality of the threefold circle.
Indeed, at the time of dissolution, there is no triad consisting of the knower, the act of knowing, and the object known.

"Because of the arising of the elements" (bhūtotpatti): because prior to the arising of the elements—space and so forth—and their effects, such as those born from a womb or an egg, there is the absence of duality consisting of the threefold set; that is, the "triplicate set" (tripuṭī) is the collection of the three "compartments" (puṭa)—the forms consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge—and that itself is duality. Its [absence].

"Varjana" means non-existence; therefore, the Supreme Self is devoid of limitation by place, time, or substance because it is "plenty" (bhūman). According to the maxim, "the bringing of a substance [is implied] when there is a mention of its absence," the word "was" (*āsīt*) is supplied, meaning "there was only plenty. He establishes that very exclusion of duality with the words "knower, knowledge, etc.

By employing the particle *hi* ("for"), he indicates that it is a universally accepted principle of all Vedānta that the triad consisting of the knower and so forth—which will be described later—does not exist at the time of dissolution.
This may be the intended meaning. || 14 ||
Commentary (a0): The meaning is "prior to the manifestation of the five great elements. The reason for this is stated as "by the knower" (jñātrā). || 14 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now he demonstrates the nature of the knower and so forth: "The knower is born as consisting of consciousness; knowledge consists of the mind."
Sound and the other [objects] are to be known; these three do not exist prior to their production.

Regarding the phrase "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*): the individual soul (*jīva*), which has arisen from the Supreme Self and is conditioned by the intellect (*buddhi*), is "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) as the knower. That which is reflected in the mind is called "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*); this refers to consciousness as knowledge. Sound, touch, and so forth are well known as the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). The meaning is that these three—knower, knowledge, and object—being effects, do not exist prior to their production apart from their cause. || 15 ||

He establishes this with the commentary: "vijñāna" etc. The word "sheath" (kośa) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. "Sound" etc.; by the word "etcetera," touch, form, taste, and smell are included. || 15 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the conclusion:
"But in the absence of the triad, the non-dual is experienced as truly full."
He is likewise full during deep sleep, fainting, and before the creation of the universe. || 16 ||

"Regarding the word 'traya' (triad): in the absence of the triad beginning with the knower (*jñātṛ*), the Self, which is devoid of duality and non-duality, is experienced as truly full. To show that it is experienced by the *kula* (the spiritual community), he says: 'In samādhi...'. The mention of *samādhi* is for the purpose of demonstrating the experience of the wise, while the citation of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and fainting (*mūrchā*) is for the sake of illuminating the experience of all. [This is because] the non-perception and subsequent recollection of duality by one who has arisen from deep sleep and so forth would otherwise be inexplicable; thus, the non-dual nature of that experiencer is established."

This is the intended meaning. [The opponent might object: "Let the establishment of non-duality (*advaita*) hold true in states such as deep sleep; what relevance does this have to the present subject? To this, he says: "Complete" (*pūrṇa*).
Just as it is complete in deep sleep and so forth due to the absence of any limiting factors (*paricchedaka*), so too it is complete prior to creation because of that same absence. || 16 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) states the conclusion: "By the three" and "in samādhi. The word "by the witness" (sākṣiṇā) is to be understood as implicit. || 16 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection, "Granted that Brahman is fullness, what follows regarding its being of the nature of bliss?", he sequentially restates the meaning of the passage, "That which is the Full (bhūmā) is bliss; there is no bliss in the small," which is intended to demonstrate through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) that the Full is of the nature of happiness.
That which is plenitude is happiness; there is no happiness in the small, which is divided into three parts.
Sanatkumāra spoke thus to the deeply grieving Nārada.

"Regarding the phrase 'that which is the Infinite' (*bhūman*): that which was previously described as the Infinite is of the very nature of bliss (*sukha*), because in the non-dual state there is an absence of any cause for suffering.
Regarding the 'limited' (*alpa*)—which is explained as being divided threefold—the qualifying term "dividing into three" contains a reason; the meaning is that bliss does not exist therein.
To the question of by whom and to whom this was thus stated, he says: "Sanatkumāra. [This refers to] the reason for Nārada’s status as a disciple.

Vidyāraṇya’s *Pañcadaśī* [in the section titled *Yogānanda*, he says "to one who is excessively sorrowful" (*atiśokine*). One who possesses excessive—that is, superior—sorrow is an "excessively sorrowful" person; to him. || 17 ||

A0. Let it be so that the Self is non-dual at the beginning of dissolution; what follows from that in relation to the subject at hand? To this, he states the meaning of the Śruti—"That which is plenitude (bhūman) is bliss; there is no bliss in the small"—with the word "ya" (that which). Thus, he also cites the Sanatkumāra-vidyā found in the seventh chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad as authoritative evidence with the words "bhūta" etc. [The term *bhūta*] refers to the threefold limitation by space, time, and substance.
This is the meaning: "in the manifold," meaning in that which possesses differentiation; "in the small," meaning in duality. || 17 ||
The five Vedas along with their ancillaries, and various treatises as well.
Even though he knew this, Nārada, due to his lack of self-knowledge, grieved exceedingly.

Rāma’s Commentary: He states the reason for his extreme grief with the words "together with the Purāṇas. Nārada, though he had mastered the five Vedas along with the Purāṇas (thus being "with the Purāṇas") as well as various other scriptures, attained excessive grief due to being devoid of self-knowledge. || 18 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Anticipating the doubt as to whether Nārada’s grief was due to a lack of study, he says "no" with the words "sapurāṇān" (along with the Purāṇas).
All of this is well known; however, for fear of prolixity, it is not elaborated upon here. This is the general direction. || 18 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: since knowledge concerning the Vedas and Śāstras is well known to remove sorrow, how can it be a cause of excessive sorrow? To this he says:
"Before the study of the Vedas, one was sorrowful merely due to the threefold affliction."
But later, it is afflicted by lack of practice, forgetfulness, interruption, and pride. (19)

Regarding the phrase "from the study of the Vedas": the word *śokī* means one who possesses sorrow (*śoka*)—that is, one characterized by the threefold suffering consisting of the internal (*ādhyātmika*) and so forth; the state of being such is *śokitā*, and this is to be supplied as the predicate (*tattā āsīt*). The word "but" (*tu*) in the phrase "afterwards, however" (*paścāttu*) is intended to indicate a distinction. "Study" (*abhyāsa*) refers to the repetition of recitation and so forth. "Forgetfulness" (*vismāra*) is the loss of what has been studied. "Defeat" (*bhaṅga*) is being overwhelmed by one who is superior to oneself. "Pride" (*garva*) [is being overcome] by one who is inferior... [text fragment].
The notion of one's own superiority arises from seeing [the faults of others]. Through these causes, there is sorrowfulness. || 19 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): He states the reason for this with the word "vedet" (knows). The threefold suffering, consisting of the physical (ādhibhautika) and so forth, is indeed well known. || 19 ||
Therefore, O learned one, I grieve; lead me across to the further shore of this sorrow.
Thus addressed, the sage declared, "Happiness itself is its further shore. || 20 ||

Rāmatīrtha’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: "How is it known that even Nārada, who is omniscient, became exceedingly sorrowful? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] intends to show that this was understood from Nārada's own words, namely, "O Venerable One, I am sorrowful. Then, when he asked for the means to end that sorrow by saying, "May the Venerable One carry me across to the further shore of sorrow," Sanatkumāra [taught] that which is denoted by the word *bhūman*.

He states—“So, I [am that]”—that in the sequence of the subsequent text beginning with “Bliss indeed is to be sought to be known,” he has declared that Brahman itself, when known as the nature of bliss, is the means for the cessation of sorrow. || 20 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, when even his mastery of grammar was [insufficient], what did Nārada, overwhelmed by grief, do? To this he says: "So'ham" (Thus am I). The sage Sanatkumāra. || 20 ||
Sensual pleasure is indeed [not true happiness], because it is enveloped by thousands of sorrows.
Thinking that it is indeed suffering, he said: "There is no happiness in what is small. (21)
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that since there are many pleasures produced by birds and other such things, the statement that "there is no pleasure in what is small" is untenable.
[Page 395] This is the eleventh section.

If it is argued that this is not so because of the two commentaries, we say no; for the Sage intended that those sacrificial implements, such as the ladles (*sruk*), are essentially of the nature of great suffering due to their association with pain, like food mixed with poison.
Thus he says: "Happiness. || 21 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He says "pleasure" to show that it is not that [pleasure] which pertains to sense objects. || 21 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having accepted that there is an absence of happiness in duality, he now raises the doubt regarding non-duality as well:
"But surely, even if there be no happiness in duality, there is no happiness for us in non-duality either."
If it were to exist, it would be perceived; and in that case, there would be a threefold division.

Regarding the word "nanu": he establishes the non-perception of reality by saying, "If it exists... The meaning is this: if happiness existed in non-duality (advaita), then it would be perceived just like sensory pleasure and the like; since it is not perceived, it does not exist. Anticipating the objection that "it is indeed perceived," he replies with "tathā" (so too). The implication is that because experience necessarily depends upon an experiencer and an object of experience, non-duality would be lost. || 22 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): In this regard, he raises an objection with "nanu" (but surely). He establishes his own non-perception as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with "asti ced" (if it exists). He counters [the objection] by showing that otherwise the desired conclusion would be untenable, with "tathā ca" (and so it is). || 22 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) accepts the negation of non-duality being the locus of happiness:
"Let there be no happiness in non-duality; rather, non-duality itself is indeed happiness."
If it is asked, "What is its means of valid cognition? there is no requirement for a means of valid cognition in that which is self-luminous.

"Let it not be so. He states the reason for this with the words "But rather... (*kiṃ tu*). For (*hi*), because non-duality alone is happiness, therefore [the senses] are not the instruments for producing happiness; this is the meaning. Anticipating the doubt, "What is the proof that non-duality is happiness?", he says "What is the means of knowledge? (*kiṃ mānam*)—stating that, since it is self-luminous, the very question regarding a means of knowledge is untenable. || 23 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, having accepted the doubt raised by the opponent, he provides the resolution: "Let it not be so" (*māstu*). The particle *hi* is used for the purpose of indicating what is well-known from the scriptures (*śruti*). Thinking that [the objection] does not apply there because non-duality (*advaitatva*) is not destroyed—either through functions such as power (*śakti*) and the like, or through the attainment of being an object of the valid cognition produced by itself—he raises a doubt: "Why? [This is because] the non-dual Self-bliss is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), and thus... all...
He provides the resolution with the remainder of the verse beginning with "it does not exist," stating that it is simply a lack of dependence on pride. || 23 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection, "Even if it is self-luminous, what is the proof for that?", he says: "Your own word is the authority for its being self-luminous, because you yourself have stated this."
Having accepted non-duality, he says that there is no happiness in this [world]. || 24 ||

Regarding the phrase "being self-luminous" (*svaprabhatva*): he establishes this by saying "because" (*yasmāt*). Since you, having accepted non-duality independently of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), easily raise an objection [against it], the meaning is that [non-duality] is therefore self-luminous. || 24 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): If you should still have doubt even in that regard, he says "born from yourself" with the intention that you should ask your own self;
the reason for this is given by the remainder of the verse beginning with "because," etc. || 24 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He raises an objection, suggesting that no proof of his own position is established by this, as he does not accept duality, but rather refutes non-duality (advaita) merely by restating what you have said:
"I do not accept non-duality; I am merely offering a refutation by restating your words."
If you say, "I speak," then tell me: what existed prior to this duality?
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [pages 396–396] 398.

[Thinking that the non-acceptance of non-duality is untenable because it cannot withstand critical analysis, he asks— starting with "Then"— that he does not accept what is called the bliss of yoga. 25.
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Even there, the proponent, suspecting a particular intention [of the opponent], raises an objection with "No" (na). || 25 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He shows the alternative suggested by the word "what" (kiṃ):
"Is it non-duality, or duality, or some other final alternative?"
The second [alternative] is not established because it has not arisen; therefore, the first remains. || 26 ||

"What is non-duality? He refutes the third position with the words "the last," meaning that a form distinct from both duality and non-duality is not observed in the world. He refutes the second position with the words "not the second," stating the reason for this:
"because of its non-arising," meaning that at that time, duality has not yet arisen. Therefore, the first position remains as the only alternative.
To this he says: "It is taught" (śiṣyate). || 26 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, having revealed his own underlying intention to the opponent who does not understand the question he himself posed in a general manner, [the author] sets forth three alternatives and, by refuting two positions in reverse order, establishes the first one as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by elimination: "What is non-duality (*advaita*)? By this, [he refers to] the Śruti: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second."

It is illuminated that [the world] is also favored [by this realization]. Or rather, non-duality alone remains as the ultimate reality by virtue of being the limit of sublation; whereas duality, because it is sublated, is false. || 26 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Non-duality is established by reasoning alone in the manner described, not through experience. To this he says:
"If you say that the establishment of non-duality is by reasoning alone and not through experience..."
Whether with examples or without examples, there is no other alternative in this mantra.

Regarding the word "advaita": thinking that the statement "the proof of non-duality is by means of reasoning alone" is untenable because it cannot withstand logical alternatives (*vikalpa*), the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) analyzes that reasoning with the words "vadet" (he might say). He dispels the deficiency of the alternative by stating "another alternative" (*koṭyantaram*). || 27 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Even there, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvavādī*) raises an objection with the words "Advaita... The proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) asks, posing alternatives, by means of the remainder of the passage beginning with "If it be said... Is that reasoning—which brings about the proof of non-duality (*advaita*) and which we have set forth as having the nature of an inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumiti*)—without an example (*nirdṛṣṭāntā*), taking all duality as its subject (*pakṣa*) in the form "The subject of dispute is false because it is distinct," and thus having the entirety of duality itself as the subject, [or] is it with an example? [End of fragment]

The intention of the alternative questions is as follows: [Is the world] devoid [of reality], like a fallacious reason (*anupasaṃhārī hetvābhāsa*)? Or is this empirical duality false, because it is not perceived when its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) cease, like a mango tree created by a magician? These two are accompanied by examples; the meaning is that they concern the arguments I have set forth. "Any other" refers to a third possibility (*tṛtīya-koṭi*). || 27 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He refutes the first position with derision:
"Neither experience nor an illustrative example exists; thus, the argument lacks luster."
But if you maintain the position that there must be an illustrative example, then provide me with an example according to your own view.

"Not experience" means: for one who asserts that the proof of non-duality is established by reasoning alone, experience (*anubhūti*) is not accepted; yet reasoning accomplishes nothing without the presentation of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Therefore, the statement "there is no example" is improper—this is the sense. Regarding the second alternative, he says "with an example," meaning that an example agreed upon by both disputants must be stated. || 28 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He refutes the first of the two alternatives thus stated by means of ridicule alone—“It is not an experience” (nānubhūtiḥ). Even in a dream, the observation of one’s own head being severed and so forth is not unreal despite the absence of an external object; rather, it is merely delusive and not authoritative (prāmāṇika).
The Eleventh Chapter, together with the two commentaries. 399.

He states [the answer] spontaneously: "There is no example. And thus, even in the absence of an example, the reality remains the same. Its seed, however, is precisely its being composed of the aforementioned fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). Nor should it be argued that there is no lack of pervasion (*anupasamhāritva*) because there exists a negative example (*vyatirekadṛṣṭānta*) such as "like Brahman" in the case of the negative concomitance;
for you yourself have stated, "I do not accept non-duality. This is the truth. Only the position of *arthāpatti* (presumption) remains, and therein lies the example accepted by oneself.
He asks: "Is it with an illustration? (28)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Then the proponent of the prima facie view raises an objection, intending to establish non-duality by means of an illustration itself:
"Dissolution is non-dual because of the non-perception of duality, as in deep sleep."
If you say this, then provide an illustration for the statement that "sleep is non-duality. (29)

"Non-duality" (advaita): Dissolution must be devoid of duality because it possesses the non-perception of duality; for whatever possesses the non-perception of duality is devoid of duality, just as deep sleep (svāpa). Now, in proving this, do you take your own sleep as the example or the sleep of another? If the former, since that is unestablished for another person, you would have to state another example to establish it; thus he says: "Deep sleep," etc. (29).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, regarding the proof of non-duality existing prior to creation, the opponent clarifies the example asked by the proponent—namely, "non-duality" (advaita). Thereupon, the proponent asks for an example in that regard as well—namely, "sleep" (supti). || 29 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, anticipating the second alternative—that the illustration is indeed the deep sleep of another—he says:
"If the illustration is the deep sleep of another, oh, how great is your skill!"
He who does not know his own sleep—what then can be said of the sleep of another?

Regarding the term "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*): since the sleep of another is unestablished for you, it is illogical for you to employ it as an example. Thus, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) says with derision, "Oh! The sense is: for you—who, by not accepting that sleep is accessible through experience, do not even know your own sleep—what talk can there be of the sleep of another? It goes without saying that there is no knowledge of another's sleep. || 30 ||
Commentary (a0): There, suspecting that the "sleep of another" has been made into an illustration, he mocks it with the verse beginning "dṛṣṭānta" (the illustration). || 30 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, he raises an objection, suggesting that the existence of another person in deep sleep is established through inference:
"If it be argued that the other is in deep sleep because of his lack of movement, just as I am."
Because the proponent himself is in a state of deep sleep, his own self-luminosity would be established by force. || 31 ||

"Motionless" (*niśceṣṭa*): the meaning is that the opponent's argument is based on the inference: "The other [the Self] must exist during deep sleep, because while possessing breath and so forth, it is motionless, just like me. To this, the proponent says—"In that case," etc.—pointing out that if this were so, the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of deep sleep would be established for you by force, since you are citing deep sleep as an example for yourself when you say, "At that time, for me... [referring to the state of one who cites deep sleep]. Thus, the self-luminosity of deep sleep remains established.
It would follow [that it is so] precisely by virtue of the capacity of the example. || 31 ||

Commentary (a0): If you intend to establish the state of deep sleep (*parasupti*) by means of inference using the state of dreaming itself as an illustration, then by the very force of that witness [within you], self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) would necessarily follow; thus he says: "Because of the absence of movement" (*niśceṣṭatvāt*). || 32 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question, "How does it happen by force?", he says:
"Neither the senses nor an illustrative example [can prove it], yet you still accept that [agency]."
This alone is self-luminosity: that manifestation which occurs without means of proof.

Regarding the phrase "the sense organs": the sense organs that perceive deep sleep do not exist, because they have dissolved into their own causes; furthermore, there is no commonly accepted illustrative example [for this], as it has been stated that another person's deep sleep is unestablished (*aprasiddha*). Nevertheless, you still accept that state of deep sleep. This being the case, the meaning is as follows: "self-luminosity" (*svaprakāśatva*) refers to this very manifestation or illumination (*bhāna*) which occurs even without means—that is, even in the absence of the instruments of knowledge—by means of deep sleep. *Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment from a philosophical commentary (likely Advaita Vedānta) discussing the nature of consciousness during deep sleep.*

400 I. *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā* with the Commentary *Bhāṣya* by Śrī Śaṅkarācārya. Chapter Fifteen: The Yoga of the Supreme Self (*Puruṣottama-yoga*). Arjuna said: 1. O mighty-armed one, what is that Brahman? What is Adhyātma? And what is Karma? What is said to be Adhibhūta? And what is Adhidaiva? 2. And who is Adhiyajña here in this body, and how? And at the time of death, how are You to be known by the self-controlled? The Blessed Lord said: 3. Brahman is the Immutable; Adhyātma is the source of beings; Karma is said to be action. Adhibhūta is all perishable things, and Adhidaiva is the Puruṣa. 4. And I am Adhiyajña here in this body, O best of bodies; and at the time of death, I alone am to be known by the self-controlled through the practice of yoga. 5. And he who departs, thinking of Me alone at the end, enters My very being; of this there is no doubt. 6. Whatever state of being one thinks of at the end, giving up the body, to that state alone does he go, O son of Kuntī, ever permeated by that state. 7. Therefore, at all times, think of Me and fight; with mind and intellect dedicated to Me, you shall surely come to Me, having no doubt. 8. If, however, you are unable to fix your mind steadily on Me, then seek to reach Me by the yoga of constant practice (abhyāsa-yoga). 9. If you are not capable even of constant practice, then perform actions for Me; even performing actions for My sake, you will attain perfection. 10. If you are unable to do even this, then resort to the yoga of renunciation (sannyāsa-yoga); with self controlled, having surrendered the mind and intellect to Me, take refuge in Me alone. 11. The mind is indeed difficult to control and fickle; yet it may be subdued by constant practice and dispassion. 12. For one who is not self-controlled, yoga is difficult to attain; but for one whose mind is disciplined, O mighty-armed one, it is possible to attain through the method of repeated effort. 13. He who, with his thoughts free from attachment, controls the senses moving among sense-objects, and rejoices in the Self with the self, he attains peace. 14. But for him who dwells on sense-objects with the senses attached to them, passion arises; from passion comes desire, and from desire arises anger. 15. From anger comes delusion; from delusion, the loss of memory; from the loss of memory, the destruction of discrimination; and from the destruction of discrimination, he perishes. 16. But the self-controlled man, moving among sense-objects with senses free from attraction and aversion, brought under the control of the mind, attains serenity. 17. In serenity, all his miseries are destroyed; for the mind of one whose heart is serene soon becomes steady. 18. One who has attained steadiness is neither grieved nor desirous; indifferent to all objects, he attains supreme bliss through the knowledge of the Self. 19. This supreme bliss belongs to one whose mind is absorbed in the Self, who is sinless, and who has become Brahman; who, having tasted that bliss, finds nothing else superior to it, and who, established therein, is not moved from that state. 20. Those sages who have conquered their minds, whose sins are destroyed, and who are absorbed in the Self, attain that infinite bliss which is beyond the reach of the senses and is perceived only by the intellect. 21. That which is imperceptible, unmanifest, and immutable, which the senses cannot grasp and which is beyond the reach of thought, that alone one should know as the subject of the field (kṣetra), and Him who is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). 22. And that which is the beginningless supreme Brahman, which is called neither being nor non-being, that is My own nature as the field (kṣetra); and I am the Knower of the Field in all fields. 23. Know that the distinction between matter and spirit, the three qualities, and the source of birth, death, and old age—all this is to be understood through the science of the Self. 24. I shall now declare to you that science of the Self, by knowing which all sages have attained the highest perfection from this world, having become liberated from the jaws of death. 25. The Supreme Spirit (Puruṣa) is distinct from these; He is called the Immutable; He is the Supreme Lord who, pervading the three states of existence, sustains this entire world. 26. Since He transcends the three states and is eternal, therefore, though dwelling in the body, He neither acts nor causes anyone to act. 27. As the all-pervading ether, due to its subtlety, is not tainted because of its contact with gross objects, so the Self, though dwelling in the body, is not tainted. 28. As the single sun illumines this entire world, so the Knower of the Field illumines the entire field, O Bharata. 29. Those who, by the eye of wisdom, perceive the distinction between matter and spirit, and the deliverance from the three qualities, they go to the supreme goal. 30. "This is the Supreme Spirit," thus they speak of Him who is free from birth and death, decay and growth, who is eternal, all-pervading, stable, and ancient, and who is both the internal witness and the external. 31. And those who, having abandoned all desires, are freed from the pairs of opposites, and are devoted to the welfare of all beings, they attain that supreme goal. 32. Those who are free from pride and delusion, who have conquered the evil of attachment, who are ever established in purity, and who have realized the Self within themselves, they attain that supreme goal. 33. Those who are indifferent to the pairs of opposites, who are firm in their vows, who have renounced hope, who are without possessions, and who are devoted to the welfare of all beings, they attain that supreme goal. 34. Those who look upon an enemy and a friend, pleasure and pain, earth, stone, and gold as equal, and who are the same in praise and blame, they attain that supreme goal. 35. Those who are the same in honor and dishonor, the same toward cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and who are free from attachment, and to whom praise and blame are equal, they attain that supreme goal. 36. Those who are content with whatever comes, who are self-reliant, who possess wisdom, who are focused on the Self, and who have subdued their minds and senses, they attain that supreme goal. 37. Those who dwell in secluded places, who are disciplined in body, speech, and mind, who are free from expectations, who have renounced egoism, and who are full of compassion for all beings, they attain that supreme goal. 38. Those who have no sense of "mine" regarding their home, who are free from the desire for progeny, wealth, and territory, and who have renounced the enjoyments of this world and the next, they attain that supreme goal. 39. Those who have no attachment anywhere, who are free from affection for son, wife, home, and kin, and who have no longing for anything whatsoever, they attain that supreme goal. 40. Those who have no attachment to any possession, whether it be a clod of earth, a stone, or gold, and who look upon a lump of earth, a stone, and gold as equal, they attain that supreme goal. 41. Those who are the same toward pleasant and unpleasant things, who have conquered their senses, who are balanced in mind whether they obtain or do not obtain, and who are unperturbed, they attain that supreme goal. 42. Those who are free from the egoism of "I" and "mine," who are pure, skillful, and free from the notion of "I" and "mine," who are patient and concentrated in mind, they attain that supreme goal. 43. Those who have renounced all undertakings, who are free from the dualities of likes and dislikes, who are wise, and who have subdued their minds and senses, they attain that supreme goal. 44. Those who perceive the Supreme Spirit as existing in all beings, and who, seeing everything as the same, worship Him, they, being established in the Supreme Spirit, attain the supreme goal. 45. Those who, through the yoga of devotion, perceive Me as existing in all beings, and who, worshipping Me with a single-minded devotion, are in Me, they too attain Me. 46. The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya: [Regarding the section titled] "Yogānanda," this is the formal argument (*prayoga*). The subject under dispute is deep sleep; it is self-luminous because it is manifest even when the instruments of cognition are absent. According to the Sāṃkhyas—
The meaning is: like the self as conceived by our own school, like the cognition as maintained by the Prābhākaras, and like one's own self as maintained by the Śākyas. || 32 ||
The reason for this is stated there: "No. (32)

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Having thus established that deep sleep—cited as an illustration of dissolution—is non-dual and self-luminous, [the author] raises the expectation of the opponent in order to establish the presence of bliss therein: "Granted that it is non-dual and self-luminous; tell me, how can there be bliss in sleep?"
Listen: at that time there is no suffering; therefore, only happiness remains for you.
"Let them be. Since suffering, which is the opposite of happiness, is absent at that time, only happiness remains;
thus he says, "Listen. The point is that because happiness and suffering are mutually exclusive like light and darkness, happiness must necessarily be admitted when suffering is absent. || 33 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, the opponent, having accepted that non-duality and so forth exist even during sleep, asks about happiness, saying "Let them be" (stām), which means "let both [happiness and misery] exist. He answers by way of elimination—that it is indeed [happiness]—due to the absence of misery during sleep, saying: "Listen" (śṛṇu). || 33 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the inquiry as to what constitutes the proof for the absence of suffering during sleep, he states that it is both scripture and experience:
"Though blind, one becomes non-blind; though pierced, unpierced; and though diseased, healthy."
The Veda declares, "He is free from disease," and all people know this to be so.

Regarding the passage beginning with "He becomes blind": "Therefore, having crossed this bridge, even though he was blind, he becomes non-blind; even though he was pierced, he becomes unpierced; even though he was afflicted, he becomes unafflicted. Therefore, O Venerable One, even if this body is blind, he becomes non-blind," and so forth. This Śruti negates defects such as blindness, which are caused by the identification with the body, during deep sleep (*suṣupti*); for even one who is tormented by disease and the like does not experience that suffering during sleep.
The meaning is that it is well known to all people that "existence does not exist. || 34 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) on verse a0 states: "In this regard, it cites the Chāndogya Upaniṣad text—"Being blind, he becomes non-blind; being pierced, he becomes unpierced; being afflicted, he becomes unafflicted"—as well as direct experience as proof, [expressed by the words] 'aṃdha' (blind), etc. || 34 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that the claim "where there is an absence of suffering, there is happiness" lacks pervasion and is contradicted by examples such as desired objects; thus he raises this doubt:
"Happiness does not exist merely through the absence of suffering, as seen in clods of earth, stones, and the like."
If it is argued that this is because the non-existence of the duality has been seen, that statement is inconsistent. || 35 ||

"It is not [that there is] suffering. The meaning is that it is impossible to conceive of pleasure merely through the absence of suffering, because one observes the absence of both pleasure and suffering in things such as clods of earth and stones, where both are absent. He refutes this by stating "The example is dissimilar," on the grounds that the example and the thing illustrated (the *dṛṣṭānta* and *dāṣṭāntika*) are unequal. The meaning is that the statement regarding the example is "dissimilar" (*viṣama*), in that it does not conform to the thing being illustrated. || 35 ||
— Commentary (Ṭīkā): Anticipating an over-extension of this argument in that context, he pacifies it with the words "not suffering" (na duḥkha). || 135 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He establishes the very lack of conformity of the illustration [with the case at hand]:
"The inference of another's suffering or happiness occurs through the contraction or expansion of the face;
since such contraction and so forth are absent in a clod of earth, the inference of suffering therein is impossible. (36)
Regarding the phrase "mukhena": the inference of pleasure and pain residing in another must be performed respectively by means of the two signs of facial expansion and dejection.
The meaning is: "This person is suffering because his face is dejected, like a recognized sufferer; this person is happy because his face is serene, like a recognized happy person."
The Eleventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

"Let it be so; what follows from this regarding the subject at hand in the world? To this he says: "By dejection," and so forth. Since signs such as dejection of the face are absent in a clod of earth and the like, even the inference of pleasure and pain is impossible. Therefore, the meaning is that even the absence of suffering cannot be determined there. || 36 ||
The reason for this is stated as: "The mouth," etc. (36).
— Rāma’s Commentary — Now he demonstrates the disparity between one's own pleasure and pain and those of another:
"But one's own pleasure and pain are not to be envied; therefore, [one should remain indifferent] to those two."
An entity exists solely through its being experienced; its existence does not arise from anything else.

Regarding the phrase "in one's own": since pleasure and pain residing within oneself are established by direct experience (*anubhava*), they are not objects of inference. Therefore, the existence (*sadbhāva*) of those two—pleasure and pain—is to be known through experience alone and is apprehended by perception; likewise, their non-existence (*tadabhāva*), that is, the absence of those two, pleasure and pain, is also not apprehended from another source such as inference, but rather by perception alone. This is the meaning. || 37 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Having thus demonstrated the manner of perceiving the suffering and other states belonging to another, [the author] says "In one's own... (svakīye) [verse 37], asserting that the existence and non-existence of one's own suffering and so forth are to be known solely through the experience characterized by the self-luminous Witness (sākṣin).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the conclusion:
"That being so, the absence of suffering during one's own sleep is established through direct experience."
Because it is devoid of the suffering that opposes it, let happiness be understood as being free from obstacles. || 38 ||

"So be it. This being the case, since one's own pleasure and so forth are accessible through experience, the absence of suffering existing even during one's own sleep is established by experience itself. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Because of the contradiction. Since there is an absence of suffering—which is the opposite of pleasure—during sleep, let pleasure be accepted as being unimpeded and free from sublation. || 38 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now he states the conclusion: "That being so" (tathā sati). || 38 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states that even by the fact that the preparation of means such as a bed and so forth would otherwise be inexplicable, it is understood that there is happiness in sleep:
"By means of great effort, one prepares soft beds and other such implements."
From what is pleasure produced during sleep, if it were not present there? (39)

Regarding the word *mahattareti*: if there were no happiness in that sleep, for what reason (*kutaḥ*)—that is, from what cause (*kasmāt kāraṇāt*)—would one procure through great effort, such as the expenditure of various kinds of wealth and the infliction of bodily pain, soft bedding and the like, or cushions, couches, and other means of comfort? The meaning is: for no reason at all. || 39 ||

The reason for this is stated as "mahattarā" (greater). By this, it should be understood that pleasure during sleep is established solely through the principle of *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility of being otherwise). || 39 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He raises the objection that there may be another way to account for this presumptive testimony (arthāpatti):
"If it be argued that this [scripture] is solely for the purpose of destroying suffering, just as in the case of a collection of diseases..."
But let it be known for certain that this [remedy] is for the very happiness of those who are free from disease. || 40 ||

Regarding the term "suffering" (*duḥkha*): he refutes [the opponent's view] by stating "of the sick," [meaning] that the procurement of means such as a bed and so forth, which has the cessation of suffering as its fruit, is not necessarily so.

The meaning is that when suffering from disease and the like exists, let there be such procurement for the sake of its cessation; however, in its absence, since the suffering to be removed does not exist, it is understood that the procurement of those means leads only to pleasure. || 40 ||

The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya—[Commentary on the chapter titled *Yogānanda*: Anticipating the objection that [the self] is delimited, and accepting those specific delimiting attributes, he refutes it in general terms: *pañcadaśī* [yogānandākhyaṃ a0 ṭīkā — tadvighaṭanamāśaṅkyāvacchedakaviśeṣaṇatadaṅgīkṛtya sāmānyatastatkhaṇḍayati—] [The commentary on the chapter titled *Yogānanda* within the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya: Anticipating the objection that [the self] is delimited, and accepting those specific delimiting attributes, he refutes it in general terms.]
"Regarding 'suffering' (duḥkha): 140."
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "If the bliss of deep sleep were produced by such means as a bed and so forth, its nature as the very essence of the Self would be contradicted.
To this, he replies: "In that case, because it is produced by means, that bliss would be merely sensual (vaiṣayika)."
Let there indeed be here, prior to sleep, that which arises from lying down, sitting, and so forth. (41)

"So be it. Having raised the alternative—whether it is being asserted that the state prior to the onset of sleep is produced by the object, or whether it is the state simultaneous with sleep—he accepts the first: "Let it be so. || 41 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Anticipating an objection even there, he provides a resolution with the two verses beginning with "tathāpi" (41).
Rāma’s Commentary: He refutes the second [position]:
"But as for the pleasure that arises in sleep, by what cause is it produced?"
First, one whose intellect is directed toward happiness should subsequently immerse oneself in the supreme bliss.

Regarding the phrase "in sleep": the point is that since there is no recollection (*anusaṃdhāna*) of the bed or other such things during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), its being produced by them is impossible.
Now, one might object: "If there is pleasure unproduced in sleep, then why is it not experienced like the pleasure derived from an object?

Anticipating this, he says "pleasure" (*sukha*) with the intention that because the experiencer is then immersed in that [state], it is not experienced in the same way as the pleasure of an object—at the very beginning of sleep.

In former times, the individual soul (jīva) possesses an intellect directed toward pleasure—that is, an intellect whose orientation is toward the pleasure produced by beds and such things—and being of such a nature, it subsequently sinks—that is, becomes dissolved—in the supreme, excellent happiness of its own essential nature (svarūpa-sukha) during the time of sleep. || 42 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, having accepted—by way of implication—that the pleasure derived from objects such as a comfortable bed prior to sleep is non-ultimate because it is produced by external means, and having intended that the pleasure during sleep is ultimate because it is of the nature of the Self (ātman), the proponent asks about the causal complex that produces it: "But in sleep... In the absence of a response from the opponent, he himself [proceeds].

With the desire to favor those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), he summarizes all the established rules with the word "mukha" (face): "One whose intellect is one-pointedly directed toward the face [of the Guru] produced by the pleasure of the bed and so forth—such a person, being thus at the beginning, should subsequently immerse himself in the supreme face, the ocean of the bliss of Brahman. This is the construction. The term "living being" (*jīva*) is to be understood as implied. 42.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He elaborates upon the meaning briefly stated by means of three verses:
"Having become tranquil through the cessation of waking states, and having then rested from their opposites..."
Having withdrawn [the senses], one whose mind is composed should experience happiness in the sense objects. || 43 ||

By the phrase "by the cessation of waking states," etc.: the individual soul (*jīva*), exhausted by the specific activities performed during the waking state (*jāgaravyāvṛttibhiḥ*), having rested and lain down upon a soft bed, and subsequently, when the suffering produced by opposing activities has been removed or warded off, becomes one whose mind is composed and whose heart is undisturbed, and thus experiences the pleasure arising from objects such as the bed.
One should realize it directly. || 43 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, regarding the bliss of sense-objects produced by lying on a bed and so forth, as well as the state of mental focus immediately preceding sleep, he states the reasons for their perishability; and regarding the bliss of deep sleep, he states the reason for its permanence—successively, by means of the three verses beginning with "jāgrat" (while awake). || 43 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In response to the inquiry as to what the nature of sensual pleasure is, he demonstrates its true character and shows that even in its experience there is effort, by virtue of its being the cause for immersion in a higher happiness: The pleasures of sense objects are like a drop of water on the tip of a blade of grass, while the pleasure of liberation is like the ocean; therefore, O wise one, abandon the former and resort to the latter. (2.53) The pleasure derived from sense objects is momentary and arises from contact with external things; it is like a drop of water on the tip of a blade of grass. Liberation (*mokṣa*), however, is the cessation of all suffering and the attainment of supreme bliss; its pleasure is like the vastness of the ocean. Therefore, O wise one, abandon the former and resort to the latter. This is the meaning. Furthermore, this [sensual] pleasure is not merely momentary, but is also accompanied by pain. As it is said: "Pleasure is preceded by pain, and pain follows pleasure. Moreover, because it is dependent upon external objects, it is impermanent and leads to rebirth. On the other hand, the pleasure of liberation is eternal, independent of external causes, and free from all fear. Thus, the wise man should strive for the latter alone. Moreover, the pursuit of sensual pleasure involves great exertion and results in exhaustion. Just as a person seeking water in a mirage undergoes toil without finding it, so too does one who pursues sense objects suffer without attaining lasting satisfaction. Therefore, having understood the true nature of both, one should turn away from the transient and seek the eternal. Thus, the verse indicates that while the experience of sensual pleasure exists, it is ultimately characterized by effort and leads to further bondage, whereas the joy of liberation is effortless and infinite. Hence, the seeker of truth must renounce the former and immerse himself in the latter.
In the mental modification directed toward the Self, one's own bliss is reflected.
Having experienced this even here, one would incur exhaustion through the threefold division (tripuṭī).

Regarding "the Self": having experienced suffering through the pursuit of future objects and the like, the intellect of one lying upon a soft bed and so forth becomes inward-turned for the sake of its cessation; and within that mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*), the bliss that constitutes one's own true nature appears, just as a face appears in a mirror facing oneself.

It reflects [the Self]. For this is the bliss of the objects (*viṣayānanda*). Even here, at this very moment, by experiencing this bliss of the objects, one would incur exhaustion through the "triplicity" (*tripuṭī*) characterized by the experiencer, the experience, and the object of experience. || 44 ||
Commentary (a0): "The self" (ātman)—the meaning is that it reflects like a face in a mirror facing the face. || 44 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: To this he says—what follows from that?—"In order to dispel that fatigue, the individual soul (jīva) should run toward the Supreme Self."
Having attained oneness with that, the bliss of Brahman residing therein becomes manifest of itself. || 45 ||

Regarding the phrase "of that fatigue": for the sake of dispelling that fatigue produced by the perception of the triad (tripuṭī), that very individual soul (jīva) should quickly go to the Supreme Self, to Brahman whose nature is bliss; and having gone there, having attained identity (*tādātmya*) and oneness with that Brahman—according to the Vedic scripture, "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being"—he himself, remaining therein during that deep sleep (*suṣupti*), becomes the bliss of Brahman. ||45||
Commentary on a0: Regarding the phrase "of that exertion," the term "pertaining to that" (*tattvya*) is the reason for emerging from meditative absorption (*vyutthāna*). || 145 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having established this, he states that there are many examples mentioned in the Śruti regarding the bliss of deep sleep, such as the bird, the hawk, the child, and the great king: "The examples are the bird, the hawk, the child, and the great king."
O Great Brāhmaṇa, these are declared in the Śruti as the bliss of deep sleep.

Regarding the "examples": by means of the five examples beginning with the bird, the view that there is no happiness therein was refuted through the demonstration that bliss exists for one who is asleep. || 46 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Granted that this is the manner of your own system, nevertheless, since there is no mental modification (*vṛtti*) therein, what is the proof for the existence of the experience of the bliss of the attributeless Brahman? Anticipating this doubt and thinking, "This is not so, because out of compassion for a sophist such as yourself, it is by the Śruti itself, through five illustrations, that inference alone has been presented," he addresses them with the words: "The illustrations" (*dṛṣṭāntāḥ*). || 46 ||

Rāmatīrtha’s Commentary: In this regard, just as a bird bound by a string, having flown in every direction and finding no other place of rest, takes refuge in its very bond; even so, my dear, that mind, having flown in every direction and finding no other abode, takes refuge in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone—this is the illustration and the thing illustrated for the statement, "For the mind, my dear, is bound by the vital breath."
He briefly demonstrates the meaning of the passage from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad concerning one intent on the feet [of Brahman] with these two verses:
"A bird, while bound by a string, having flown about in all directions, finds rest..."
If he cannot find a place of confinement, he should resort to supports such as his own hands or a pillar.

Regarding the term "bird" (śakuni): suppose a bird is tied by a tethering string to some support such as a hand; in order to catch food and so forth, it exerts itself in various directions, such as the east and so on. Failing to find a place of rest—that is, a support where it might rest—it returns to its very point of attachment, such as the hand. || 47 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Regarding this, first [the text says]: "Just as a bird tied by a string, having flown in every direction and finding no other place of rest, settles back upon its bond; even so, my dear, that mind, having flown in every direction and finding no other place of rest—" [[page 402-to-402]]
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, titled Yogānanda.

Not finding that [resting place], it takes refuge in the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—this is the statement from the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* beginning with "For the mind, my dear, is fastened to the vital breath" (*prāṇabandhanaṃ hi somya manaḥ*), which establishes the analogy of the bird and so forth; he recites it according to its meaning in two verses beginning with "The bird" (*śakuniḥ*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), a staff is included. (47)
The mind, which is the limiting adjunct of the individual soul, exists for the sake of attaining the fruits of merit and demerit.
Having wandered through both dream and waking states, it dissolves when its karma is exhausted.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Likewise, the mind, which serves as the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva), wanders here and there through the states of dreaming and waking for the experience of pleasure and pain—the fruits of merit and demerit. When the karma that grants such enjoyment is exhausted, the mind dissolves into its own material cause, which is ignorance (ajñāna).
And when that [ignorance] is destroyed, the individual soul, being conditioned by it, becomes the Supreme Self itself; this is the meaning. || 48 ||
Commentary (a0): "The adjunct of the individual soul" (jīvopādhi). This means that it dissolves into Brahman as delimited by the ignorance of deep sleep (sauṣuptājñāna). ||48||
