Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, regarding the elaboration of the illustration of the hawk from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad—"Just as in this space a hawk or a falcon, having flown about and become weary, folds its wings and is borne toward its own nest; even so this person hastens toward that bliss where, when asleep, he desires no desire and sees no dream"—the following is said: The *rā0 ṭīkā* (Rāghavendra’s commentary) continues: "Now, for one who is intent upon expanding the illustration of the hawk, [there is the passage]: 'Just as in this space a hawk or a falcon, having flown about and become weary, folds its wings and is borne toward its own nest, even so this person hastens toward that bliss where, when asleep, he desires no desire and sees no dream. This is from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka... [The commentary proceeds to explain this passage].
Summarizing the meaning of the verse, he says:
"Like a hawk, solely intent on its nest, one should go with speed to lie down."
Thus, the individual soul, solely intent upon the bliss of Brahman, should hasten toward deep sleep.

Regarding the term "hawk" (*śyena*): Just as a bird named hawk, moving everywhere in the sky, would go swiftly—intent solely on its nest—to make a bed, that is, to lie down, in order to dispel the fatigue caused by its movement through the air; in the very same way, the individual soul (*jīva*), which is a reflection of consciousness conditioned by the mind (*manas*), being desirous solely of the bliss of Brahman, goes swiftly to the space of the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*) for the sake of sleep.
This is the remainder [of the sentence]. || 49 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, he cites the Kāṇva Śruti itself, beginning with the illustration of the hawk, as follows: "Just as in this sky a hawk or a falcon, having flown about and become weary, folds its wings and remains for the sake of alighting, even so this person hastens toward that end where, having slept, he desires no desire whatsoever and sees no dream whatsoever"—thus [he cites] the hawk.
Thus; "to lie down" means to sleep. || 49 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He explains with three verses the statement found in the Bālāki-Brāhmaṇa, which aims to present the three examples of the prince, the great king, and the great Brahmin— namely, "Just as a young boy, or a great king, or a great Brahmin, having gone to the height of supreme bliss, might lie down, even so does he now lie down."
The very young child, having drunk from the breast, lay upon a soft bed and laughed.
Because passion, hatred, and the like do not arise, it partakes of the singular nature of bliss.

• By the words "ativāla" and so forth: Just as an infant at the breast, having been made to drink from the breast up to the throat and being laid upon a soft bed, remains as a mere embodiment of bliss—devoid of passion and the like due to his lack of knowledge regarding "self" and so on, and because of his possession of qualities such as softness. || 50 ||

Commentary (a0): Thus, with the three verses beginning with "ativāla," he summarizes in substance the Kāṇva Śruti passage concerning the remaining three illustrations: "Just as a young boy, or a great king, or a great Brāhmaṇa, having gone to [a place of] extreme bliss, lies down, even so does he lie here. || 150 ||
The universal monarch, the great king, was fully satisfied with all enjoyments.
Having reached the limit of human bliss, he became the very embodiment of pure bliss. || 51 ||
The Eleventh Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.

405 Rāja-Ṭīkā: Or, just as a sovereign emperor, although his intellect may not be entirely clear, remains a very embodiment of bliss—free from passion and the like—because he is sought after by all human beings and lacks any sense of personal longing. || 51 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding the words "O Great King" and "human": the meaning is the pinnacle of human bliss as established in the Taittirīya Śruti, namely, "That is one measure of human bliss. || 51 ||
The great Brahmin, the knower of Brahman, [attains] the state characterized by having accomplished all that was to be done.
Having attained the supreme limit of the bliss of knowledge, he remains established therein. || 52 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Just as a great sage—a great Brahmin who has realized the non-dual Brahman within himself—having attained the supreme limit of the bliss of knowledge, namely the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), remains established in the very nature of supreme bliss, thinking "I have accomplished all that was to be done," so too does one remain in the form of bliss even while asleep; this is the sense. || 52 ||
Commentary on verse a0: "O great Brahmin" (mahāvipra). "Brahmavedī" means one who possesses direct realization of Brahman. || 52 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: "Why have only these three—the boy and the others—been chosen as examples, and not others?
Anticipating this doubt, he states the intended meaning behind the presentation of these three examples:
"In the world, the state of being essentially happy is well-established for those of dull intellect and those of superior intellect."
But others among those mentioned are suffering and do not consist of happiness. || 53 ||

Regarding the word *mugdha*: the meaning is that those who are devoid of discrimination are illustrated as examples; among them, the very young are happy; among those possessing discrimination, the sovereign (the emperor) is happy; and among those possessing supreme discrimination, only one who has realized the Self as bliss is truly happy, whereas others are always unhappy due to being possessed by passion and other afflictions. || 53 ||
The commentary on the result states: "Mugdha," etc. This means [the state] of children, universal emperors, and knowers of Brahman. || 53 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection, "Let these [others] be happy; what relevance does this have to the present case?", he states the purport of the scriptural passage concerning the subject at hand:
"Just like Kumāra and others, this one is solely intent upon the bliss of Brahman."
O you whose body was embraced by a woman, there is neither external nor internal [suffering]. 54.

"Like a youth, etc. (kumārādi): Just as those beginning with the youth are partakers of bliss (*ānandabhāj*), so too this [person] in deep sleep is solely intent upon the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*) and is a partaker of that very bliss of Brahman; this is the meaning. The following passage, "Just as one embraced by a beloved wife knows nothing external nor internal, even so this person, embraced by the conscious Self (*prājña ātmā*), knows nothing external... is intended to demonstrate the reasoning for this exclusive intent toward the bliss of Brahman.
The passage from the *Jyotirbrāhmaṇa*, "He knows nothing within or without," is restated here in substance as "embraced by a woman.
Just as in the world a lover embraced by his beloved becomes an embodiment of bliss due to being devoid of knowledge of external or internal objects,

so too the individual soul (*jīva*), having attained oneness with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) during deep sleep, exists solely as the nature of bliss (*ānanda-rūpa*) because of the absence of knowledge regarding external and other objects.
...is present. || 54 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) concludes with two verses beginning with "kumāra," based on the very meaning of the Kāṇva Śruti: "Just as a man embraced by his beloved wife knows nothing external nor internal, even so this person, embraced by the conscious Self (prājña ātmā), knows nothing external nor internal. (54)

Rāma’s Commentary: Here, he sequentially demonstrates the intended meaning of the words "external" (bāhya) and "internal" (abhyaṃtara) as they occur in the illustrative example and the subject of the illustration.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[the section titled] Yogānanda.
The external conduct, such as [behavior on] the streets and so forth, as well as domestic duties, according to one's capacity.
Likewise, waking is external, while dreaming, situated within the channels (nāḍīs), is internal.

Regarding the term "external": "vṛtta" means "occurrence. The phenomenal world perceived within the channels (nāḍīs) due to the latent impressions (vāsanā) of the waking state residing in the channels is called "dream. || 55 ||

Commentary on verse a0: Regarding the word "external" (*bāhya*), he states the application to the subject at hand with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). Here, the distinction between "external" and so forth is made solely in relation to the body. || 155 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Regarding the statement that the individual soul (jīva) exists during deep sleep in the very form of the bliss of Brahman, he states the purport of the scriptural passage beginning with “In this state, the father becomes no father,” which is intended to demonstrate the underlying reasoning.
For even in cases such as "the father is also sleeping," there is the exclusion of being alive.
In deep sleep, there is only Brahman and not the individual soul (jīva), because the state of being a transmigrating subject is not perceived.

Regarding the word "father": here, since the superimposed attributes of the individual soul (jīva), such as fatherhood and so forth, have been negated by the scripture itself, the sense is that when the state of being a jīva is no longer perceived, only the nature of Brahman remains. || 16 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, regarding the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) of one who has fallen asleep, [the author] maintains his own established doctrine that the individual soul (*jīva*) remains in the very form of the bliss of Brahman—which is its own essential nature and is conditioned by it. To pacify the doubt raised by fallacious logicians (*kutārkika*) concerning the absence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and following the maxim that "a ghost must be awakened by speaking in the language of ghosts," he indicates inference itself as the authoritative proof against that opponent who relies primarily on inference, and then proceeds against the Mīmāṃsaka.

To indicate that even the presumption based on what has been heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) applies there in that same manner, [the text says]: "In this state, the father becomes a non-father, the mother a non-mother; worlds become non-worlds, gods non-gods, and the Vedas non-Vedas. In this state, a thief becomes a non-thief, a killer of an embryo a non-killer of an embryo, a Cāṇḍāla a non-Cāṇḍāla, a Paulkasa a non-Paulkasa, an ascetic a non-ascetic, and a mendicant a non-mendicant. He is untouched by merit and untouched by evil, for he has crossed over."
Then, he summarizes the meaning of the scriptural passage, "He becomes the heart of all forms," in brief by means of two verses beginning with "Even the father," etc. (56).
For that conceit of being a father and so forth is indeed the source of pleasure and pain.
When that has departed, he becomes one who has crossed over all sorrows. || 57 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, one might object: even in the absence of the conceit of being a father and so forth, why should the transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) consisting of happiness and the like not still persist? Anticipating this, and considering that transmigratory existence is rooted in the conceit of the body—such that it ceases when that conceit ceases—the author explains, by way of its purport, the immediately following scriptural passage which establishes this: “For then he has crossed beyond all the sorrows of the heart,” beginning with the word *pitṛtva* (fatherhood).
[He] shines. || 17 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding the phrase "due to fatherhood, etc."—the ellipsis is to be supplied as "sorrows, which are the sufferings associated with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). || 97 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that in the scriptural passages cited, the attainment of happiness is not explicitly stated as the primary subject.
Anticipating this, he recites a verse from the *Kaivalya-śruti* which, though primarily concerned with the description of that state, implies the attainment of bliss:
"At the time of deep sleep, when all [mental modifications] have dissolved and one is enveloped by darkness..."
For the Atharvaṇa Śruti declares that one attains the nature of bliss. || 58 ||

Regarding the term "deep sleep" (suṣupti): when the entire phenomenal world characterized by the waking state and so forth has dissolved and has reached its absorption into primordial matter (prakṛti), which consists of darkness (tamas) as its own material cause, the individual soul (jīva), covered and veiled by that dark primordial matter, attains Brahman whose nature is bliss; such is the meaning of that scriptural passage. || 98 ||
The Tenth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

407 a0 Commentary: Now, one might object: "Why do you state here that [the Self] remains in the form of Brahman as conditioned by that [state], since in the aforementioned scriptures no conditioning by deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is perceived? To this, he says: "In deep sleep... and so forth; thus, in the *Kaivalya Upaniṣad*—

It is recorded in scripture: "At the time of deep sleep, when everything has dissolved, one overcome by darkness attains the nature of bliss. The ancients explain "everything" (*sakala*) as the phenomenal world characterized by the waking state and so forth; however, that is intended according to the theory of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi* (the creation of the world upon perception). But according to the theory of *sṛṣṭidṛṣṭi* (the perception of the already created), the meaning is "in the mind in its entirety," that is, in all its parts. || 58 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He states that this meaning is not only well-known from the scriptures, but is also established by universal experience:
"I slept happily here; indeed, I was not aware of anything at all."
Thus, having awakened, one reflects upon the blissful ignorance [experienced] while asleep. || 59 ||

Regarding the word "happiness": a person who has arisen from deep sleep reflects upon—that is, remembers—the happiness and ignorance pertaining to the time of sleep, thinking, "For such a long time I slept happily; I was not aware of anything. From this as well, it is understood that there is happiness in deep sleep. ||59||
Commentary on the *Aṃśa*: Therein, he also provides proof based on the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the reflection of one who has emerged [from meditation], stating "the face.
Those two are mentioned in the Śruti. || 19 ||

— Rāma’s Commentary — Now, raising the objection: "Since the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), how can the establishment of pleasure (*sukha*) result from its force?"—
the author says the following with the intention that even though it is not a valid means of knowledge, its establishment occurs by the force of the experience (*anubhava*) which is its root:
Since there is recollection (parāmarśa) regarding what was experienced, there must have been an experience at that time.
Because its nature is consciousness, bliss shines forth by itself; therefore, it is not dependent on ignorance or the intellect.
Regarding the term "parāmarśa" (recollection): recollection is a memory-cognition that occurs only with respect to an object already experienced, not with respect to an unexperienced object.

For this reason, it is understood that there was an experience during sleep. Now, one might raise the objection: since the instruments of cognition along with the mind have dissolved during sleep, how can the existence of experience be established? To this, one must ask: is it being said that there is no means for the experience of pleasure, or is it that there is no means for the experience of ignorance?

Not the first, because if bliss is of the nature of self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśacidrūpa*), it would not depend upon any instrument (of cognition). Not the second; with the intention that the realization of the ignorance obscuring that [bliss] is established by the power of self-luminous bliss itself, he says: "the conscious Self" (*cidātma*). Therefore, from that self-luminous bliss, there arises the cognition of ignorance—the realization of ignorance. || 60 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): What follows from that? He says: "Subsequent reflection" (parāmarśa). || 160 ||
"Brahman is consciousness and bliss," so say the Vājasaneyins.
Therefore, it is read that bliss is Brahman alone, which is self-luminous, and nothing else.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even if the pleasure of deep sleep (*sauṣupta-sukha*) is self-luminous pleasure, it cannot be the case that Brahman-bliss (*brahmānanda*) is itself [that pleasure], because its being of the nature of Brahman is impossible due to a lack of evidence. Anticipating this doubt, he says, "Brahman is consciousness," etc., asserting that this is not so, since there exists the scriptural passage from the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* beginning with "Consciousness, Bliss... (VI.3.28). || 61 ||
Commentary (a0): In that regard, he cites the scriptural authority, "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," with the words: "Brahman" || 61 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, an objection may be raised: since there is a rule that experience and recollection must have the same substratum, and since the deep-sleep bliss and ignorance are recollected by the individual soul (jīva) denoted by the term "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*)—as in the statements "I slept happily" and "I was not aware of anything"—it must be asserted that this very soul is the experiencer of that bliss and so forth.
Anticipating this, [the author] states that this is not so, because the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), namely the consciousness which is an effect of ignorance, has dissolved into ignorance.
As it is said: "In that ignorance wherein they are dissolved are those two—the intellect (vijñāna) and the mind-made (manomaya)."
For sleep and ignorance are indeed the state of dissolution of those two.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [pages 406–406] 408.
Regarding the phrase "that ignorance called *yogānanda*": there exists an ignorance that is inferred because the recollection "I knew nothing at all" would otherwise be inexplicable.

In that ignorance, those two—the *vijñānamaya* and the *manomaya*, which are well-known as the subject (*pramātṛ*) and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—are dissolved; they abandon their forms as consciousness and so forth.

The sense is that, since they remain in the form of their cause [during sleep], that which is conditioned by them does not possess the status of an experiencer. He states the reasoning for this with the words "of those two. For (*hi*) because the state of dissolution of those two—the intellect (*vijñāna*) and the mind (*manas*)—is called "sleep" (*nidrā*), as it is designated as "the cessation of consciousness" (*vijñānavirati*). Anticipating the objection that one must then say they are dissolved only in sleep, he says: "ignorance" (*ajñāna*). That very [state]...
The meaning is that sleep is designated as "ignorance" by the wise. || 62 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if this were so, liberation would result from sleep alone; therefore, he says: "That ignorance... (verse 62).

Rāmatīrtha’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If that is so, then since the *vijñānamaya* (consisting of consciousness) is non-existent at the time of experiencing the bliss of deep sleep (*sauṣupta-sukha*), how can it be the rememberer of that upon awakening? Anticipating this doubt, he says—with the intention that even in the state of dissolution there is no destruction of its essential nature, and thus it is possible for a single entity to be the experiencer in the form of the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss) characterized by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the state of dissolution, and the rememberer through possessing the limiting adjunct of condensation denoted by the word *vijñāna*: ... [the text continues] ...he says: "The Self, having entered the heart, remains in the space within the heart. Here, "heart" refers to the lotus-like cavity of the heart; "space" is the ether (*ākāśa*) located therein. "Having entered" means having reached that space. "Remains" means dwells. By this, the following is shown: the Self, which is the witness of the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, is not subject to birth, death, or other modifications; rather, it is eternal, pure, and free from all attributes. This is because, as stated in the scripture: "The Self is neither born nor does it die" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.18), and "This great, unborn Self is undecaying, immortal, and fearless Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.25). Furthermore, it is taught that the Self is the witness of the three states: "He who is awake in those who sleep, whose form is never seen, but who perceives dreams—He is the Self, and He is immortal; everything else is perishable" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.5.8). Thus, the Self is established as the witness of all states. Therefore, it is concluded that the Self is eternally free from all attributes. This is the meaning. Now, the question arises: if the Self is indeed the witness of the three states, then why is it not perceived? To answer this, he says: "It is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech, nor by other senses; it is not perceived by the mind, nor is it attained by the intellect. Here, "eye" stands for all the sense organs. "Speech" stands for all the organs of action. "Other senses" refers to the internal organs such as the mind. "Not grasped" means not perceived. "Mind" refers to the faculty of thought. "Intellect" refers to the faculty of determination. "Not perceived" means not known. "Attained" means realized. The sense is that the Self cannot be grasped by the external senses, nor by the internal organs such as the mind or intellect. Why? Because the Self is devoid of form, sound, and other qualities, and is beyond the reach of the senses. As the scripture says: "It is not seen by the eye, nor grasped by speech, nor perceived by the other senses; it is subtle, beyond thought, and unattainable by the intellect" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.8). Therefore, the Self is not an object of perception. However, it is said: "When it is seen by the sharp and subtle intellect, the highest peace is attained. How is this? It is explained: when the intellect, purified by the practice of yoga and the like, becomes sharp and subtle—that is, free from the impurities of passion and the like, and capable of perceiving the most subtle objects—it then perceives the Self. As the scripture says: "But when the intellect is perfected by yoga, it sees the Self dwelling within itself" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.13). Therefore, the Self is perceived by the intellect alone. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the Self is not perceived by the senses, then how is it known? To answer this, he says: "It is known by him by whom it is not known; by whom it is known, by him it is not known. It is not known by those who know, and it is known by those who do not know. Here, "by whom it is not known" refers to those whose intellect has not been purified by the practice of yoga and the like. "By whom it is known" refers to those whose intellect has been purified. "By those who know" refers to those who think they have understood the Self through mere intellectual speculation. "By those who do not know" refers to those who have abandoned all mental constructs through the grace of a teacher and the practice of meditation. The sense is that the Self is not known by those who rely on the intellect, but it is known by those who have transcended the intellect. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the Self is not an object of the intellect, then what is its nature? To answer this, he says: "It is the unseen seer, the unheard hearer, the unthought thinker, and the unknown knower. There is no other seer than this, no other hearer than this, no other thinker than this, and no other knower than this. Here, "unseen seer" means that while it is the seer of all, it is itself not seen by anyone. Similarly, it is the "unheard hearer," the "unthought thinker," and the "unknown knower. "There is no other seer than this" means that apart from this Self, there is no other agent of seeing. The same applies to hearing, thinking, and knowing. The sense is that the Self is the witness of all activities, yet it is itself devoid of activity. As the scripture says: "There is no other seer but He, no other hearer but He, no other thinker but He, no other knower but He. By Him, O Maitreyī, this whole world is known" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23). Therefore, the Self is the supreme reality, the witness of all, and the source of all knowledge. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the Self is the witness of all states, then why does it appear to undergo various transformations? To answer this, he says: "The Self, having entered the heart, remains in the space within the heart. Thence, emerging, it moves about among the deities, and thence, departing, it enters into the elements. Here, "having entered the heart" means having reached the heart-cavity. "Space within the heart" is the ether located there. "Remains" means dwells. "Thence, emerging" means rising from that state. "Moves about among the deities" means experiences the waking state, where it perceives the various gods such as Indra and Agni. "Thence, departing" means leaving that state. "Enters into the elements" means experiences the state of deep sleep, where it merges with the causal ignorance (*māyā*). The sense is that although the Self is eternally changeless, it appears to undergo various states due to the influence of the limiting adjuncts of the body and the senses. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the Self is the witness of these states, then what is the relationship between the Self and the states? To answer this, he says: "The Self is the creator of the worlds, the lord of all, and the protector of all. It is the bridge, the support, and the imperishable Brahman. Here, "creator of the worlds" means the cause of the manifestation of the universe. "Lord of all" means the sovereign ruler of everything. "Protector of all" means the sustainer of all beings. "Bridge" means the support of the world. "Support" means the foundation of all things. "Imperishable Brahman" means the eternal, undecaying reality. The sense is that the Self is the ultimate cause and support of the entire universe. This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the Self is the creator of the worlds, then how is it that the world appears to be separate from the Self? To answer this, he says: "In the beginning, this was only the Existent, one without a second. It thought: 'May I be many, may I grow forth. It created fire. Here, "in the beginning" means before creation. "Only the Existent" means the reality that is pure consciousness. "One without a second" means devoid of any other object. "It thought" means it willed. "May I be many" means "may I manifest as many diverse forms. "May I grow forth" means "may I expand. "It created fire" means it first brought forth the element of fire. The sense is that the Self, being the sole reality, manifests the universe through its own power of illusion (*māyā*). This is the meaning. Now, one might ask: if the Self is the creator of the universe, then how is liberation possible? To answer this, he says: "He who knows this as
Afterwards, like melted clarified butter, one becomes a solid mass consisting of pure consciousness.
The state of dissolution is expressed by the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya). || 63 ||

Regarding the term "dissolved" (*vilīna*): Just as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) that has been melted by contact with fire and so forth later becomes solid again through the influence of contact with air and other factors, even so, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which had dissolved into the form of sleep due to the exhaustion of the karma that bestows experience during the waking state and other conditions, becomes solidified again in the form of consciousness (*vijñāna*) upon awakening, under the influence of karma that again bestows experience. Therefore, the Self (*ātman*) conditioned by that [internal organ] would also become dense and consist of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*); this very same [Self] was previously...
Being conditioned by the state of dissolution, he is called "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya). || 63 ||
Commentary (a0): He states the reasoning for that—namely, "in the state of dissolution. Thus he explains the *ānandamaya* as "in the state of dissolution" (vilīnāvastha). || 63 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He clarifies the very point already stated—that the state of dissolution is *ānandamaya*—with the following verse:
"The mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) which, at the moment preceding sleep, is permeated by happiness..."
That very [consciousness], joined with that manifestation, then becomes composed of the bliss of absorption.

Regarding the word "supteḥ" (of sleep): in the immediate preceding moment of sleep, there occurs an inward-turned modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) which is endowed with the reflection of the bliss that constitutes its own nature; immediately thereafter, that very same modification, accompanied by that reflection, having dissolved into the form of sleep, is designated as "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*). || 64 ||

— Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): The reason for this is "supti" (sleep). Regarding "sukha": the meaning is that it is so called because in it the reflection (viva) and counter-reflection (prativiva) of happiness have arisen. For that reason [it is so]. || 64 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus demonstrated the nature of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), he now establishes the experience of happiness at that time for the sake of proving its status as the rememberer in the form of the one consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) during the state of awakening:
"The one consisting of bliss, who is inward-turned, [experiences] that bliss of Brahman then."
He experiences [the results] through modes of existence born of ignorance that are devoid of consciousness. || 65 ||

Regarding the term "introverted" (*antarmukha*): during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*)—which has as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) ignorance accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the inward-turned mental modification (*vṛtti*) associated with the reflection of happiness—experiences or enjoys the bliss of Brahman, which is his own essential nature (*svarūpa*), through modifications (*vṛtti*) that are specific transformations of *sattva* arising from ignorance; these modifications have as their objects happiness and the like, and are accompanied by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*). || 65 ||
The Eleventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, regarding the experience of Brahman within deep sleep, he describes the bliss of the *ānandamaya*—the subtle state of the individual soul (*jīva*)—by means of the very modes of ignorance (*ajñānavṛtti*) in the form of the witness-consciousness of bliss, as explained in the *Vivaraṇa*: "With the face turned inward" (*antarmukha*). || 165 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: "In that case, why does the conceit 'I am experiencing happiness now' not arise as it does during waking?
Anticipating this, he says—with the intention that the functions of ignorance lack the clarity of the functions of the intellect:
"The functions of ignorance are subtle; the functions of the intellect are distinct."
Thus indeed do those who have reached the further shore of the Vedānta siddhānta declare.
Regarding the phrase "the functions of ignorance": from what is this understood? To this he says: "Thus" (iti). || 66 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if it is the case that in deep sleep the individual soul (*jīva*), in its subtle state, experiences the bliss of Brahman through the modifications (*vṛtti*) of ignorance (*ajñāna*), then why does the reflection "I am happy" not arise there for it, as it does during the waking state and so forth? To this, he says: "The modifications of ignorance. Anticipating the objection, "What is the proof for this?", he provides the resolution with the intention that it is indeed the statement of the teacher Vivaraṇācārya: "Thus... (iti).

This has been stated by Brahmānanda Sarasvatī in the *Nyāyaratnāvalī*, a commentary on the *Siddhāntabindu*: "In deep sleep, three non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) modifications of ignorance arise, having as their forms the nature of the witness (*sākṣi*), the nature of bliss (*sukha*), and the nature of ignorance (*ajñāna*). This is accepted in the *Vivaraṇa*. || 66 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: what is the proof that the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) experiences the bliss of Brahman through subtle modifications of ignorance?
To this, he says:
"This is very clear in the Māṇḍūkya, Tāpanīya, and other Śrutis."
The state of being the enjoyer belongs to that which consists of bliss, while the state of being the object of enjoyment resides in the bliss of Brahman.
Regarding the word "Māṇḍūkya," he states its very meaning as "Ānanda" [and so forth]. || 67 ||

— Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Regarding the point that some Śruti which is the root of that [statement] must be cited, he says: "Māṇḍūkya," etc. By the word "etc.," [he refers to] Kaivalya Upaniṣad 15: "That which is to be enjoyed, the enjoyer, and the act of enjoyment, which exist in the three abodes. To what does this refer? He says:
"Consisting of bliss. || 67 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, he recites in substance the passage from the *Māṇḍūkya* and other Upaniṣads—“In the state of deep sleep, having become one, he is indeed a mass of consciousness, consisting of bliss, enjoying bliss, and having the mind as his mouth”—as follows:
“Established in deep sleep, having become one, he has attained the state of being a mass of consciousness.”
Consisting of bliss and enjoying bliss through the modifications of the mind.

"Ekībhūtaḥ" (become one): "suṣuptaḥ" means deep sleep; he who stays therein is "suṣuptasthaḥ," meaning one who identifies with deep sleep. "Ānandamayaḥ" means abounding in bliss; "ānandabhuk" means one who enjoys the bliss that constitutes his own nature. "Cetomayavṛttibhiḥ": "cetas" is consciousness; "tanmayyaḥ" means abundant in that, i.e., accompanied by the reflection of the conscious principle. These are the "cetomayavṛttayaḥ"—those which are both those [consciousnesses] and modifications (vṛttis). They...
The construction is: "one who experiences bliss. 68.

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Regarding this, he recites the *Māṇḍūkya* passage—“In that state of deep sleep, [the Self] has become one, a mass of pure consciousness, consisting of bliss, enjoying bliss, and having the mind as its gateway”—in accordance with its meaning: “become one” (*ekībhūta*) and “the mind” (*cetaḥ*). The meaning is: by means of the modifications of ignorance (*avidyāvṛtti*) which abound with the reflections of consciousness (*citpratibimba*). || 68 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He explains the meaning of the word "become one" (*ekībhūta*) found in that statement:
"He who was previously endowed with forms primarily consisting of consciousness has now attained oneness through dissolution, like rice flour [formed from many grains]. (69)

The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya, titled *Yogānanda*: "That Self which previously, in the waking state, was primarily composed of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*)... [Thus begins the passage: "sa vā ayam ātmā..."]

The Self (ātman), which was previously endowed with specific forms and characteristics as described in such scriptural passages as "consisting of knowledge, consisting of mind, consisting of breath, consisting of sight, consisting of hearing, consisting of earth, consisting of water, consisting of air,

consisting of ether, consisting of light, consisting of darkness, consisting of desire, consisting of non-desire, consisting of anger, consisting of non-anger," has now, through dissolution— that is, through the dissolution of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as knowledge and mind— attained oneness and uniformity.
[The state of] having gone [to that condition] occurs. Regarding this, he states an illustration: "like fire," meaning like flour produced from many grains of rice. || 69 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, he clarifies the word *ekībhūta* ("become one") occurring in the aforementioned scripture with the words *vijñānamaya* etc. The meaning is:

by means of the various forms described in the Kaṇva-śruti, beginning with, "This very Self is Brahman, consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), consisting of mind (*manomaya*)," and so forth. || 69 ||
In former times, he was Prajñāna, and then he became Dhana, the activity of the intellect.
Just as there is solidity in a region of snow and ice, so it is here.

— Rāma’s Commentary — Now, he states the meaning of the term *prajñānaghana*: “*Prajñānāni*,” etc. Previously, during the waking state and so forth, there were mental modifications (*buddhivṛttayaḥ*) denoted by the word *prajñāna*, which had objects such as jars as their domain; then, at the time of deep sleep, when objects such as jars are absent, [those modifications cease].
He became one with the nature of consciousness; regarding this, he provides an illustration: "solidity," etc. (verse 70).
Commentary (a0): In this way, he also clarifies the very term *prajñānaghana* found there: "The cognitions... (170).
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, in the context of defining the meaning of the term "forest of wisdom" (*prajñāvana*), he states something that has arisen [in this connection]:
"They declare that state of density to be the state of being a witness and the absence of suffering."
The worldly logicians [act] up until the destruction of the occurrence of suffering. (71)

Regarding the phrase "that state of being a solid mass" (*taddhanatvam*): that which is designated in the Vedāntas as the "solid mass of consciousness" (*prajñānaghana*) as the Witness (*sākṣin*), that very thing worldly people—those logicians such as the Vaiśeṣikas and others who lack the refinement of scriptural study, as well as learned scholars—describe as the "absence of suffering"; they say it is the absence of suffering.
Why? To this he says: "As many as... That is, [they describe it as such] because of the cessation of all those various modifications of suffering (*duḥkhavṛtti*).
This is the meaning. || 71 ||

And so, during the waking state, all the reflections of consciousness delimited by their respective mental modifications (vṛtti) merge back into the intellect (buddhi), which is the root of their own limiting adjuncts (upādhi). Thus, in deep sleep, they attain a state of dissolution within the witness (sākṣin).

The common people and the logicians (Tārkikas) speak of the absence of that [intellect] precisely because of the non-perception of suffering, asserting that its nature is one of ignorance; thus he says: "tadvantatva... (the state of possessing that).
Thus [it is said]. || 71 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He explains the meaning of the word "mouth" (*mukha*) occurring in the scriptural passage cited previously: "Consciousness, when veiled by ignorance, becomes the mouth for the enjoyment of bliss."
Having abandoned the liberated bliss of Brahman, he then goes outward by means of karma.

Regarding "ignorance": in the enjoyment of bliss—that is, in the tasting of the bliss of Brahman during deep sleep—the mouth is the instrument; it would be the consciousness (cit) manifested through ignorance, which is reflected within the modification of ignorance. Now, one might object: if the individual soul (jīva) enjoys the face of Brahman in the form of bliss during deep sleep, then why, having abandoned that, does it subsequently return to the waking state, which is an abode of suffering? To this, he says: "It has been enjoyed."

Because it is bound by the fetters of meritorious and non-meritorious karma, the individual soul (jīva), impelled by that [karma], abandons even the bliss of Brahman that has been directly realized and then goes outward; the meaning is that it undergoes waking and so forth. 72.

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, he states the meaning of the term "ceto-mukha" (the gateway of the mind) with the verse beginning "ajñāna... (ignorance...). An objection is raised: "In that case, it would be improper for the individual soul (jīva) to emerge from that state once it has tasted the bliss of Brahman. To this, he replies: "muktam" (liberated). || 72 ||
The Eleventh Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
That karma which existed in another birth is experienced again through its connection [with the present].
Thus, in the Kaivalya branch, awakening born of karma has been described. || 73 ||

411 Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Anticipating the objection, "How is this known?", and considering the statement from the *Kaivalya-śruti*, "Furthermore, due to the connection with the karma of another birth, that very same living being sleeps and then awakens," he recites that scriptural passage in substance and explains its intended meaning:
He says: "Karma" || 73 ||
— Commentary (Ṭīkā):

He states the proof for that [identity] in the verse beginning with "karma": "And again, due to the connection with the karma of another birth, that very same living being sleeps and then awakens. This is the scriptural authority (tac-chruti) for that. || 73 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He provides a further sign that the bliss of Brahman is experienced during sleep:
"For some time, the latent impression (vāsanā) of the bliss of Brahman remains for one who has awakened."
Therefore, one should follow [this path], remaining silent, free from sense-objects, and happy.

Regarding the phrase "someone": even for one who has awakened—that is, one who has attained wakefulness—the latent impression (*vāsanā-saṃskāra*) of the bliss of Brahman experienced during sleep persists for some time, that is, for a short duration. Why is this understood? To this he says: "Because.

Because, at the beginning of awakening and so forth, even though one is devoid of objects—meaning lacking the experience of sense-objects—one remains silent while being happy; therefore, it is understood.
The meaning is "become tranquil. || 74 ||
In that regard, he also states the reasoning: "Something," etc. The reason for this is: "Since," etc. ||74||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: If that is so, why does one not remain silent? To this he says:
"Driven by past actions, one subsequently contemplates various miseries."
All these people forget the bliss of Brahman. || 75 ||
Regarding the phrase "by actions": impelled by the aforementioned actions, every living being subsequently undergoes various kinds of sufferings and gradually forgets the bliss of Brahman. || 75 ||
Commentary (a0): To the question, "If that is so, why does he not remain in that very state? he replies with the words "by means of karmas" (karmabhiḥ). || 175 ||
Even before and after sleep, there is a daily inclination of men toward the bliss of Brahman; therefore, what wise person would dispute this? (73)

Rāma’s Commentary: For this reason as well, he states "prāk" (before) and so forth, to show that a misconception regarding the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*) should be dispelled. Every day, for human beings, there is an attachment to the bliss of Brahman both before and after sleep—namely, at the commencement of sleep and at its conclusion.
This is because they prepare a soft bed and such at the beginning of sleep, and at its end, being unable to abandon it, they remain silent; for that reason, in this [bliss]—
"Who would find [this]? means that no one at all would find it, O Nanda. || 73 ||
Commentary (a0): Thus, having established the existence of the aforementioned experience of Brahman during sleep, he states yet another argument, beginning with "prāk" (before).
The meaning is: by the experience of inward-turned mental modifications before sleep, and by the experience of the bliss of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) after [waking]. || 76 ||
Rāmānanda’s commentary raises an objection: "But surely, if the bliss of Brahman shines forth while remaining silent, then why do worldly people [not experience it]?"
If they were already languid and had already achieved their purpose, what would be the use here of a teacher or a scripture? (77)

Regarding the word "nanu": the meaning is that if the experience of the bliss of Brahman—which is obtainable through service to the guru and so forth—were obtainable merely by remaining silent, then hearing [the scriptures] preceded by service to the guru and so forth would be in vain. || 77 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 410] 412.

[Commentary on the chapter titled *Yogānanda*: Now, one might object: "If this is so, then even worldly people who lack the refinement of scriptural training and are indolent would achieve their goal.
Thus he raises this objection with the word "nanu" (now/if this be so). 77.

Rāma’s Commentary: When it is known that "this is the bliss of Brahman," one certainly becomes fulfilled; yet, that very knowledge does not arise without service to the Guru and so forth. Thus he says:
"If they should know, 'This indeed is Brahman,' they would be fulfilled by that alone."
Without the teacher’s instruction, who can know the exceedingly profound Brahman? (78)

"Certainly. [The meaning is: Who could know Brahman—which is exceedingly profound, difficult to fathom, inaccessible to speech and mind, omniscient, the innermost of all, and the very form of the self of all—by any means other than a teacher and the scriptures? No one at all; such is the sense. || 78 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), having partially accepted the aforementioned doubt, replies to the charge of the futility of the Guru and others with the word "bāḍham" (certainly). The syntactical connection is as follows: "If they [the disciples] should know [the truth], then by that alone they become ones who have accomplished their purpose. || 78 ||
I know from your words today; why then have I not attained my purpose?
Listen here to the account of another person who considered himself wise, such as yourself. (79)

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, anticipating the objection—"From your words alone, I who know the bliss of Brahman do not attain the state of having fulfilled my purpose"—he offers a reply accompanied by derision, beginning with the statement "I know": || 79 ||
Commentary (a0): Even there, he mocks the objector by recounting a worldly anecdote: "I know" (verse 79).
Commentary (rā0): He illustrates that very anecdote:
"Hearing that 'it should be given to one who knows the four Vedas,' he said..."
"I know that there are four Vedas; therefore, let wealth be given to me. (80)

Regarding the phrase "caturveda": suppose someone, having heard a statement such as "this great wealth must be given to one who knows the four Vedas," says, "I know [them] precisely from this very statement that 'the Vedas are four'; therefore, let it be given to me. The meaning is that you are acting in exactly that same way. (80)
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): To the question "What is this account?", he states it [in the verse beginning] with "caturveda... || 180 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "He who knows that 'the Vedas are four' knows only the number contained within the Vedas, but not their actual nature.
To this, he replies: "He knows only the number, but not the Vedas in their entirety."
If, then, you likewise do not know Brahman entirely in its destruction, indeed— (81)

Regarding the word "saṃkhyām" (number): he resolves this by saying "tat" (that). Thus, like another [ignorant person], you too do not know—that is, you do not at all understand—the Brahman in its entirety, that is, in its complete perfection. || 81 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): There too, he [the opponent] raises an objection, saying "only number. Now, the proponent (siddhāntin), having restated that doubt of his, rejects it by means of a counter-objection (pratibandī), completing the sentence with the words "If...". Thus, "If... is the necessary supplement. || 81 ||
In the bliss of the indivisible single essence, which is devoid of māyā and its effects.
What occasion is there even for discussion regarding whether it is without remainder or with remainder? 82.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "In Brahman—which is partless and one, like the nature of the Vedas which is distinct from their number, and which is of the nature of bliss devoid of internal divisions and the like—there is no unmanifested portion; therefore, the reproach that [the Lord] possesses incomplete knowledge is untenable. To this, he raises the objection with the verse beginning "akhaṇḍaika...
(verse 82).
[The Eleventh Chapter] Accompanied by Two Commentaries.
Commentary on Verse 82: Even in that regard, the proponent of the prima facie view raises an objection, beginning with the words "akhaṇḍa" (indivisible).

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā) on verse 413: In order to demonstrate that even in the knowledge of Brahman there is a state of being "without remainder" and so forth, he questions one who says "I know Brahman," by means of a dilemma:
Do you merely recite the words, or do you also perceive their meaning?
The understanding of the meaning from the recitation of the words is enjoined as that which is to be accomplished. || 83 ||

"Regarding the words 'śabdān' (words): do you merely recite the words themselves, such as 'the partless, single-flavored, non-dual reality whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss,' and so forth; or rather, do you perceive the meaning of those words—such as their being devoid of internal distinctions and the like? The sense of the alternative is: 'Do you know [them]? In the first case..."
In this regard, he demonstrates that there remains something further to be said with the words: "the recitation of the word. (83)
Regarding that, the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) mocks them as well: "Only words...
(83). The commentary on verse 83 states: "In that regard, the proponent of the final view mocks [the opponent] with the words 'only words'."
Rāma’s Commentary: He shows that [this] is also the case in the second [verse]: "When the object has been understood through grammar, direct realization remains."
O friend, as long as the thought that your purpose has been fulfilled persists, so long should you attend upon the Guru.

Regarding the word "artha" (meaning/purpose): the mention of "grammar" (*vyākaraṇa*) is an elliptical expression for the Vedas (*nigama*) and so forth. Once indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) has been produced through grammar and other means, what remains is its realization as direct perception (*aparokṣīkaraṇa*) by means of the removal of doubt and the like. Then, anticipating the question of when that knowledge reaches completion, he shows its limit with the words "it would be" (*syāt*). The meaning is that when the cognition of having achieved one's purpose (*kṛtārthatva*) arises, then the completeness of knowledge is to be understood. 84

The commentary (ṭīkā) on verse a0 states: "The meaning, however, is indeed understood from grammar"; thus he says, "the meaning. If that is so, how then can there be direct realization (sākṣātkāra)? To this he says, "it may be" (syāt). || 84 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus concluded this incidental discussion, he returns to the subject at hand:
Let this matter rest; wherever there may be happiness, it occurs without sense objects.
Know that in all those instances, this is the latent impression (vāsanā) of the bliss of Brahman. || 85 ||

"Let it be so. The meaning is that wherever and at whatever time—such as during silence and the like—happiness arises without the experience of sense objects, there, because that happiness is not produced by sense objects and because it is veiled by the general ego-sense (*sāmānyāhaṃkāra*), it should be understood as the bliss of latent impressions (*vāsanānanda*). || 85 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Then, perceiving through gestures that he had come for refuge, thinking "You alone are my guru," [the author], desiring to favor him, generally explains the *brahmānandavāsanā* to him with the words: "Let it be... (85).

Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus demonstrated the bliss of Brahman and the bliss of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he now reiterates the previously mentioned object-bliss (*viṣayānanda*)—which was stated in the verse beginning with "when the mental modification is turned toward the Self"—in order to define the threefold nature of bliss:
"Even when objects have been obtained, [bliss arises] upon the cessation of the desire for them."
Bliss is reflected in the inward-turned activity of the mind.

"Even regarding sense objects": whenever the cessation of desire for objects such as garlands and the like occurs due to their attainment, and at that time the mind becomes inward-turned, the bliss of one's own self which is reflected therein is what is meant by "the bliss of sense objects. || 86 ||
— Commentary (A0):

Having thus explained the bliss of Brahman and the bliss of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), [the author] now reiterates the previously mentioned objective bliss (*viṣayānanda*) for the sake of enumeration, stating "In objects... and so forth. [This occurs] when [an object] is obtained.
The meaning is: when they have met according to their desire. || 86 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 412] 414.
[The commentary by Rāma, titled *Yogānanda*, states the conclusion: "Brahman-bliss, mental impression (*vāsanā*), and reflection— these three [are the nature of the Self]."
Without him, there is no joy whatsoever in this world.

Regarding "Brahmānanda": That which is Brahman-bliss, manifesting in deep sleep by way of self-luminosity according to the manner described; and that which is the bliss of latent impressions (*vāsanānanda*), perceived during silent stillness without the experience of external objects; and also that which [arises] from the attainment of a desired object when the mind is turned inward—

The bliss of sense objects reflected in the mind—apart from these three, there is no other bliss whatsoever in this world. Now, it may be argued that bliss is said to be threefold in this manner: "Brahman-bliss, the happiness of knowledge, and likewise the bliss of sense objects"; however, what is being stated now is a different threefold division of bliss, namely: Brahman-bliss, latent impression (*vāsanā*), and reflection (*pratibimba*). Therefore, the former—

There is no contradiction. Furthermore, it is said: “To the extent that the ego is forgotten through the yoga of practice, to that same extent the bliss of the one who perceives the subtle is inferred. Thus, even during the state of neutrality (*udāsīna*), such a person, setting aside the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of bliss, contemplates the primary bliss (*mukhyānanda*) alone, being intent upon it.
Therefore, by these two aforementioned methods, *nijānanda* (intrinsic bliss) and *mukhyānanda* (primary bliss) are designated as distinct from [the other] two types. Likewise, in the second chapter—

"One should awaken the seeker of dull intellect through the bliss of the Self (ātmānanda). Thus, the bliss of the Self is mentioned as distinct from that [previously mentioned]. In the passage beginning "The bliss of yoga (yogānanda) which was previously described," the bliss of yoga also appears to be something distinct. It is taught in the third chapter of the work titled *Brahmānanda* that it would indeed be the bliss of non-duality (advaitānanda); thus, we understand the bliss of non-duality to be yet another. Therefore, there is no bliss in this world apart from these.

If it be argued that the statement "anyone" would be contradicted, it is not so. This is because the bliss of knowledge (*vidyānanda*), like the bliss of objects (*viṣayānanda*), is intended to be included within the bliss of objects by virtue of being a particular modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti-viśeṣa*); for it will be stated later that, like the bliss of objects, the bliss of knowledge consists of a modification of the intellect (*dhīvṛttirūpa*).

Furthermore, as for the bliss of the self (*nijānanda*), the primary bliss (*mukhyānanda*), the bliss of the Self (*ātmānanda*), the bliss of union (*yogānanda*), and the bliss of non-duality (*advaitānanda*), they are not distinct from the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*). Thus...

For, in the verse beginning with "Indeed, as long as there is the notion of 'I'," the innate bliss (*nijānanda*)—which is intended to be the bliss of yoga because it is accessible through the means characterized by yoga—is designated as the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*) in the very following verse: "Where neither duality appears nor sleep, that which is happiness, he, the Blessed One, declared to Arjuna, is the bliss of Brahman. Thus, innate bliss does not differ from the bliss of Brahman.

The primary bliss (*mukhyānanda*) is indeed Brahman-bliss (*brahmānanda*) itself. Thus, in the verse stating that "Brahman-bliss, self-luminous, remains generating these two—sensory bliss (*viṣayānanda*) and the bliss of latent impressions (*vāsanānanda*)"—it is precisely Brahman-bliss, which is designated as the generator of the two secondary forms of bliss (sensory and impression-based) that are produced, which is illustrated by the phrase "even during the state of indifference" (*udāsīnakāle’pi*). [This] refers to the primary bliss, setting aside the bliss of latent impressions.

He indeed meditates [on this]. Because it is designated as "supreme" (*tatpara*), it is called the primary bliss; however, both self-bliss (*ātmānanda*) and non-dual bliss (*advaitānanda*) constitute the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*).

At the beginning of the third chapter, following the statement in the first chapter—"Let that which was previously described as the bliss of yoga be understood as self-bliss"—the author, after restating the very bliss of Brahman intended there as the "bliss of yoga" and designating it as self-bliss, asks: "How does this possess the nature of Brahman?"

This is to be understood from the demonstration of the non-dual nature of Brahman—beginning with the phrase "if [it be argued] 'of the two-fold reality'" and continuing through "from space down to the body"—which is preceded by a question. Therefore, the threefold classification stated as "the bliss of Brahman, the latent impression (*vāsanā*), and the reflection" is well-established. Now, an objection might be raised: "In that case, regarding the statement, 'Thus the yogi should know his own bliss (*nijānanda*) as distinct from the bliss of latent impressions and the bliss of Brahman,' how is it that this *nijānanda* [is distinct] from the bliss of Brahman and the bliss of latent impressions?"

It should not be suspected that a distinct designation [of two forms] is untenable; for it is logical to designate a single Brahman-bliss (brahmānanda) as distinct based on the difference between its association with and dissociation from the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of being the cause of the world. To illustrate: at the point of defining Brahman-bliss, by stating "from bliss alone these beings are born," and so forth, one understands the omnipresence of Brahman-bliss through the declaration of its status as the cause of the world.

They [are not illusory], because it is logically untenable for that which is devoid of illusion (*nirmāya*) to be the cause of the world. Furthermore, even at the time of defining *nijānanda* (intrinsic bliss), since the dissolution of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) along with its causes is established by the passage beginning with "to whatever extent there is egoism," the non-illusory nature of *nijānanda* is proven; thus, everything is without fault. || 87 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā):
To that, he says what follows—"Brahmānanda. The reflection is the bliss of sense objects (viṣayānanda).
The Eleventh Chapter.

This is the meaning, accompanied by two commentaries. Now, it may be asked: "In the past, bliss was said to be threefold—Brahman-bliss, the bliss of knowledge, and likewise the bliss of objects; thus there is a threefold division."

Thus it was stated: "To the extent that the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is forgotten through the yoga of practice, to that same extent the innate bliss (*nijānanda*) is inferred by one of subtle vision. And: "Therefore, even during the state of neutrality, a person who is intent upon it abandons the latent impression of [ordinary] bliss and indeed cultivates the primary bliss (*mukhyānanda*). Thus, both the innate bliss and the primary bliss are mentioned. Likewise, in the second chapter: "But for one of dull intellect, there is the desire to know..."

"One should awaken [the self] through the bliss of the Self"—this refers to the *ātmānanda*. "The bliss of yoga which was previously mentioned"—this refers to the *yogānanda* as well. "In the work titled *Brahmānanda*, that which is declared in the third chapter shall indeed be the *advaitānanda*"—this refers to the *advaitānanda* as well. Thus, although the eightfold bliss ending with *advaitānanda* appears to be difficult to reconcile with the aforementioned *vāsanānanda*, how then can it be called *brahmānanda*?

If it is argued that there is no bliss whatsoever in this world apart from these three—objective experience (*vāsanā*), reflection (*pratibimba*), and [the third], then we say no, because of a failure to understand the intended meaning (*tātparya*). For instance, since the subsequent text states that the bliss of knowledge (*vidyānanda*) is of the nature of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), just like the bliss of objects, it is beyond dispute that both the bliss of objects and the bliss of knowledge are effects of the bliss of latent impressions (*vāsanānanda*), which consists of specific residual traces (*saṃskāra*). As for the bliss of the self (*ātmānanda*), which is the primary bliss of one's own nature (*nijānanda*)— [The text continues: ...[it is] not an effect. Therefore, the statement "there is no bliss" refers only to those forms of bliss that are effects; it does not exclude the bliss of the Self, which is eternal and non-produced. Thus, there is no contradiction with the scriptural texts. Furthermore, the word "any" (*kaścana*) is used in the sense of "all," as in the phrase "there is no jar anywhere. Moreover, the term *vāsanā* here denotes the bliss of the Self, which is the cause of all other types of bliss. This is because the bliss of the Self is the very essence of all bliss, and because the bliss of the Self is the cause of the bliss of objects and the bliss of knowledge. This is established by the fact that the bliss of the Self is the cause of the bliss of objects and the bliss of knowledge, while the bliss of the Self itself is not an effect. Therefore, the statement "there is no bliss" is made with reference to the bliss of the Self, which is the cause of all other blisses. Consequently, there is no contradiction with the scriptures. Furthermore, the bliss of the Self is not an object of perception, because it is devoid of the attributes of being an agent, an instrument, and an action. Nor is it an object of inference, because it lacks any inferential mark (*liṅga*). Nor is it an object of verbal testimony, because it is not denoted by any word. Nor is it an object of comparison, because there is no similarity to anything else. Nor is it an object of presumption (*arthāpatti*), because there is no unaccountable anomaly (*anupapatti*). Nor is it an object of negation (*abhāva*), because it is a positive entity. Therefore, the bliss of the Self is known through the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) alone, which is purified by the grace of the Guru and the practice of meditation. Indeed, the five types of bliss—consisting of the bliss of song (*gānānanda*), non-dual bliss (*advaitānanda*), and the bliss of the self (*ātmānanda*)—are non-different from the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*), which is characterized as the cause of the triad beginning with the bliss of objects (*viṣayānanda*). For, in the verse cited beginning with "To whatever extent the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*)," it is shown that the innate bliss (*nijānanda*) itself is the "bliss of yoga" (*yogānanda*) because it is accessible through the means of yoga; and regarding that [innate bliss], the subsequent verse states: "Where neither duality appears nor sleep exists, that happiness is the bliss of Brahman."

The Blessed One said this to Arjuna: "In this context, because the bliss of yoga (*yogānanda*) and innate bliss (*nijānanda*) are stated to be the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*); and likewise, [it is said] right before that: 'Thus, the self-luminous bliss of Brahman exists, generating these two—sensory bliss (*viṣayānanda*) and the bliss of latent impressions (*vāsanānanda*)'—in comparison to the secondary blisses of sensory objects and latent impressions which are produced, [the text says]: 'Such a person, even during a state of indifference (*udāsīnakāla*), having disregarded the impression of bliss... [he attains] the primary [bliss]."

Because the primary bliss (*ānanda*), which is stated as the cause in the passage, "He, being intent upon that, meditates on bliss alone," is established as being the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*).

Thus, having stated in the third chapter that the previously mentioned "bliss of yoga" (*yogānanda*) is indeed the "bliss of the Self" (*ātmānanda*), [the text] raises the question: "How can this [bliss], which possesses duality, be Brahman? and proceeds from the ether (*ākāśa*) up to the body.

By such statements, since duality does not exceed existence (*sattā*) and is thus merely Being (*sanmātra*), it follows by implication that both the non-dual bliss of the Self (*ātmānanda*) and [other forms of bliss] are indeed the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*).

Nor is it correct to object: "But if this is so, then the statement that 'the yogi should know his own bliss (*nijānanda*) as distinct from the bliss of latent impressions (*vāsanānanda*) and even from the bliss of Brahman' would contradict [your position] by implying that *nijānanda* is different from the bliss of Brahman. This is not so, because the bliss of Brahman is the cause and is all-pervasive, whereas *nijānanda*—[is the effect].

And because it is free from illusion (*nirmāya*), that very threefold nature of bliss—which was described through the distinctions of cause, effect, and so forth—is merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*).
In reality, however, Brahman-bliss (*brahmānanda*) alone is the ultimate truth (*pāramārthika*); such is the general direction [of the teaching]. || 87 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, one might object that since the investigation of the bliss of Brahman alone is the subject at hand in this chapter, the presentation of the other two types of bliss is irrelevant to the topic.
Anticipating this objection, he says—with the intention that they are not irrelevant to the subject because they are produced from the bliss of Brahman and are thus useful for its realization:
And thus, there is the bliss of sense objects and the bliss of latent impressions.
The self-luminous bliss of Brahman remains, generating joy.

"So be it. And thus, since there are these three kinds of bliss, the meaning is that the self-luminous bliss which produces both the bliss of sense objects and the bliss of latent impressions (vāsanā) is to be known as the bliss of Brahman. || 88 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): For this very reason—it is said, "and thus. || 88 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having first summarized what has already occurred, he introduces the subsequent portion of the work:
"In that which is of the nature of self-luminous consciousness, [established] through scripture, reasoning, and experience..."
When the bliss of Brahman is realized during deep sleep, listen further to what occurs at other times. || 89 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 414] 416.

[Regarding the statement] "It is called *yogānanda* (the bliss of yoga) according to scripture": by the scriptural passages cited, such as "When all has dissolved at the time of deep sleep, one, overcome by darkness,

attains the nature of bliss," and by the logical arguments (*yukti*) such as the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the retrospective reflection "I slept happily," as well as by direct experience (*anubhūti*).

Thus, by means of the experience of deep sleep as established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the self-luminous bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*) has been proven during the state of deep sleep. Hereafter, listen to that other means for realizing the bliss of Brahman which will be described even during the waking state at other times. || 89 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, following the restatement of what has been said, he promises to describe the bliss of Brahman even in other states: "śruti... (verse 89).

Rāma’s Commentary: To demonstrate the very means for realizing the bliss of Brahman as promised, he shows—by way of its preliminary—the attainment of the two states of the individual soul (jīva) along with their causes:
"He who, during deep sleep, [attains] the nature of the Self consisting of consciousness and bliss..."
Having gone there, one attains either sleep or awakening according to the distinction of the place. || 90 ||

Regarding the word "ya" (he): that which was described as the *ānandamaya*— existing in a state of dissolution during deep sleep (*suṣupti*)— is that very same *ānandamaya* which, having attained the state of being *vijñānamaya* by virtue of possessing the intellect (*buddhi*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), will be described according to its different locations.
Through the application of specific states of pride, one goes to either sleep or wakefulness according to one's karma. || 90 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) on that very point says: "He who... (90).
Rāma’s Commentary: Now he shows the locations associated with the states of waking and so forth:
"Waking occurs in the eyes; sleep occurs spontaneously in the throat and in the heart-lotus."
The conscious principle remains awake, pervading the body from the feet to the head.

Regarding the word *netra*: intending that the term *netra* (eye) serves as an indicator for the entire body, he states the meaning of the portion "awakening in the eyes" with the words "from the feet... and so forth. The conscious one is the *jīva*. || 91 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): He states the locations—namely, "in the eyes"—[verse 91].
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He clarifies the intended meaning of the phrase "pervading the body" by means of an illustration:
"Having attained identity with the body, like a heated iron ball."
Having thus determined, "I am a human being," he remains fixed in that very conviction.

"Identity with the body. Regarding this, he states the proof: "Therefore," etc. Since one has attained identity with a body possessing the genus of humanity and so forth, one therefore remains having ascertained "I am a human being" and having grasped this through a cognition free from doubt and the like. || 92 ||
The commentary on verse a0 states the manner of that [attainment]: "deha" (the body), etc. || 92 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He demonstrates that the other states arise solely from the cause of the false identification with the body:
"This [Self] attains three states—being indifferent, happy, or miserable.
Happiness and misery are the effects of karma, whereas indifference is its natural state. (93)

Regarding the term "indifferent" (*udāsīna*): therein, in order to demonstrate that happiness and suffering—which serve as qualifiers for the purpose of knowing that being happy or miserable is produced by karma—he shows that happiness and suffering have those [past actions] as their cause, [stating]: "Happiness... (verse 93).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, he describes three intermediate states even within dreaming and waking, due to the identification with the illusory (*prātibhāsika*) and empirical (*vyāvahārika*) bodies respectively—beginning with "the indifferent" (*udāsīna*). He states the result of that: "happiness" (*sukha*). || 93 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states that these two, pleasure and pain, are of two kinds due to the difference in their causes—
[Chapter Eleven].
Accompanied by two commentaries:
External enjoyments and the kingdom of the mind—pleasure and pain are considered to be of two kinds.
In the intervals between pleasure and pain, there should be a state of remaining silent.

Regarding the word "external": if one asks when neutrality (*audāsīnya*) might then occur, he says "happiness" (*sukha*). The plural number is used with the intention of referring to different individual instances. || 94 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He further states the twofold nature of both the aforementioned pleasure and so forth—beginning with "external" (bāhya). He states their purpose—beginning with "pleasure" (sukha)—in verse 94.
Rāma’s Commentary: He now demonstrates the purpose for which the states of waking and so forth were introduced—saying, "I have no anxiety whatsoever today; may I remain in happiness."
Every person speaks of the manifestation of innate bliss in a state of indifference.
"None at all. This means that everyone [now] says, "I have no concern whatsoever regarding my home or other worldly objects;

therefore, I remain as I am, in whatever way brings me happiness. By speaking thus, he describes the manifestation of the bliss of one's true nature (*svarūpānanda*) during a state of indifference (*audāsīnya*). Therefore, the intended meaning is that it should be understood that the manifestation of one's own bliss exists even in the waking state (*jāgaraṇāvasthā*). || 95 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): What follows from that? He says: "None whatsoever. By the word "entire" (akhila), it is indicated that there is no room here for dispute. || 99 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that if that which appears in the state of indifference is indeed self-bliss (*nijānanda*), then because it would be the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*), it could not be the previously mentioned "bliss of latent impressions" (*vāsanānanda*).
Anticipating this, he resolves the objection by stating that it is not the bliss of Brahman because it is veiled by the general sense of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*):
"Because it is covered by the general egoism [expressed as] 'I am'."
This self-bliss is not the primary reality; rather, it is merely its latent impression (vāsanā).

"I am" (ahamasmīti). The meaning is that this [ego-sense] is not primary because it is veiled by a general ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra-sāmānya*) of the form "I am," which is devoid of specific attributes such as "I am Devadatta. To the question, "What then is its nature? he says: "But this... (96).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if it is argued that if one's own bliss (*nijānanda*) manifests during the state of indifference (*audāsīnya*), then by the method previously stated, that is indeed the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*); and thus, as was said before: "The latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the bliss of Brahman experienced for some time follows [the practitioner], whereby he remains silent, free from objects, and happy"—then regarding that form of happiness which appears during the period of indifference defined by the aforementioned state...
To the objection that there would be no perpetual bliss, he says: "I am. (96)
Rāma’s Commentary: An illustration for the existence of the bliss of latent impressions (vāsanānanda) distinct from the primary bliss [of Brahman]:
"The coolness on the outside of a vessel filled with water is not that water itself."
Rather, by that [quality], the state of being devoid of taste (nīrasattā) is inferred as a quality of water. || 97 ||
"But as for 'water'":

that which is perceived by touching the outer surface of a jar filled with water is not, first of all, water, because liquidity is not perceived there. What then is it? To this he says: "But rather... How is its status as a quality of water understood?
To this he says: "By that [reasoning]. The disputed coldness perceived in a jar must be produced by water, because it is coldness, like the coldness perceived in water. || 97 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): In this regard, he provides an illustration: "nīra... (verse 97).
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: One might object, "Let it be so that coldness is an indicator of water; what does this have to do with the present case?
Anticipating this doubt, he states that, similarly, the bliss of latent impressions (vāsanānanda) also functions as an indicator of the primary bliss (mukhyānanda).
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 416] 418.
[As long as the ego-sense is forgotten through the yoga of practice, so long does that which is called the bliss of union persist.]
To that same extent, through subtle vision, one's own innate bliss is inferred.

Regarding the phrase "as far as" (*yāvad*): through the yoga of repeated practice, one should restrain the knowledge within the Great Self (*mahat*), and restrain that [Great Self] within the Peaceful Self (*śānta ātman*)—according to the yoga of the practice of *nirodha-samādhi* as declared in the Śruti. It is inferred that to the extent that the dissolution of mental modifications such as "I" (*ahaṃ*) and so forth occurs, and the subtlety of consciousness (*cit*) arises, to that same extent the manifestation of one's own bliss (*nijānanda*) comes about. Herein is the formal argument (*prayoga*): [the state characterized by specific degrees of contraction of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*)...]

In these [moments], the second and subsequent moments constitute the position (pakṣa); they possess the manifestation of their own bliss greater than the preceding moment and are endowed with a specific contraction of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), because they are moments characterized by the contraction of the ego-sense, just like the first moment which is endowed with the contraction of the ego-sense. || 98 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): He states the application of the analogy (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "as much as... and "through practice (*abhyāsa*).

Regarding this, the *Laghuvākyavṛtti* states: "When a previous conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has dissolved, until another arises, the non-conceptual consciousness (*nirvikalpakacaitanya*) shines forth clearly. Thus, the cessation of conceptual construction should be practiced daily and gradually for two or three moments by those who desire the experience of Brahman."

The meaning is: "because of the reason that it has been enjoined for you. Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): Among the moments characterized by the dissolution of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), the second and subsequent moments are the subject (*pakṣa*). They possess greater happiness than the preceding ones, because they are times characterized by the dissolution of the ego-sense, just like the first moment characterized by that same dissolution. (98) Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: In response to the inquiry as to what the limit of the subtlety of the intellect (*buddhi*) is, he states that direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) is the limit.
Having been completely forgotten, it attains supreme subtlety.
