Because there is no shrinking back, there is no hatred; therefore, even the body shall not fall away.

"Everything"—if that were so, it would simply be sleep; therefore, he says "unmerged. Even when all mental modifications (*vṛtti*) have dissolved, because there is no dissolution of the essential nature of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), this is not sleep. This is because the Teachers have stated that deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is the state of the intellect (*buddhi*) abiding in its causal form. He provides the evidence for the absence of dissolution of the essential nature of the internal organ with the word "thence" (*tataḥ*). Where there is dissolution of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), as in deep sleep and so forth, there [is the persistence of] the body...
Since it was seen here in the morning, its absence now implies that it has not perished. || 99 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): What follows from that? He says: "All... [etc.]. Now, one might object: "If that were so, it would be sleep"; to this he says: "Because of non-dissolution" (*alīnatvāt*). The word "of the mind" (*manasaḥ*) is to be supplied. Therefore they say: "For it dissolves in deep sleep; when restrained, it does not dissolve. He also states the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for that: "From that... [verse 99].
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the conclusion:
"Neither does duality appear, nor is there sleep therein; that which is bliss [is liberation]."
The Blessed One said to Arjuna: "That is the bliss of Brahman. (100)

"Not duality. The meaning is that the bliss which is experienced at that time when there is no appearance of duality and even sleep has not arrived, that is the bliss of Brahman (brahmānanda). Raising the objection, "How is it known that this is the bliss of Brahman? he says, "Thus," because of the words of Kṛṣṇa; the remainder is that this is from the sixth chapter of the Gītā. || 100 ||
A0 Commentary: One might ask, "What does this have to do with the present inquiry into the bliss of Brahman? To this, he says: "There is no duality. (100)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question of by which verses he spoke on that matter, he recites those verses according to the sequence of their meaning:
"One should gradually come to rest through the intellect held with firmness."
Having established the mind within the Self, one should not think of anything at all.

"Gradually"—this is the meaning. By means of an intellect (*buddhi*) characterized by fortitude (*dhṛti*) and serving as the instrument, one should gradually, not all at once, bring the mind to rest; that is, one should effect its cessation. To the question "To what extent? he says: "The Self. [The mind] should be established in the Self.
The Eleventh Chapter, together with the two commentaries, page 419.

"Established in the Self" means one whose firm abiding is in the Self alone, having realized that "all this is indeed the Self; there is nothing whatsoever other than That. Having made [the mind] such as this—established in the Self—one should not think of anything at all; this is the supreme limit of Yoga. || 1 ||
In response to the question "By which statements?", he recites those very words beginning with "Gradually, gradually," and so forth.
By this, *yama*, *niyama*, *āsana*, and *prāṇāyāma* are taught in their proper sequence. (101)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question of what a yogi engaged in accomplishing this should first do, he says:
"From whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away..."
Having restrained it from this and that, one should bring it under control within the self alone. || 2 ||

Regarding the word "yataḥ": when the mind— which is fickle due to its inherent defect, unstable, and thus fixed upon no single object— rushes out or goes forth from this or that cause, such as sound and so forth, then from each of those causes, such as sound and so forth, it must be restrained by perceiving the defects of those sounds and others, such as their falsity, thereby rendering them mere appearances, preceded by the cultivation of dispassion (*vairāgya*).

Having restrained this mind, one should bring it under control within the Self alone; that is, one should cause it to attain the state of being subject to the Self. For one who thus practices yoga, the mind becomes tranquil within the Self alone by the power of practice.
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now he describes withdrawal (pratyāhāra) with the words "yato yataḥ" (whencever). The rest is straightforward. || 102 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To explain what occurs when the mind is tranquil, he says:
"For this yogi whose mind is tranquil, there is supreme bliss."
He approaches the one who has become Brahman, free from stain and with passion stilled. || 3 ||

"Tranquil" (praśānta): [He approaches] that supreme yogin who has quieted the *rajas*—that is, whose dust of afflictions such as delusion (*moha*) and the like has been destroyed—and for that very reason whose mind is profoundly tranquil, being entirely free from distraction; who has become Brahman (*brahmabhūta*), possessing the certainty that "all this is indeed Brahman," and is thus liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*); and who is stainless (*akalmaṣa*), being devoid of unrighteousness and other such taints. He approaches—that is, he attains—the bliss of such a one, which is free from defects such as perishability and comparability. ||3||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now follows the internal limb of yoga known as *saṃyama*—consisting of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*—which occurs in its proper sequence.

Since this triad is practiced together with the inquiry into the identity of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikya-vicāra*)—as described in the present section of one hundred verses and culminating in the verses spoken in the *Bhagavad Gītā*—all obstacles are destroyed. Consequently, at the time of practicing these three stages beginning with *dhāraṇā*, [the practitioner realizes] "I am Brahman," from that which was contemplated...

When ignorance has been destroyed solely by the direct (aparokṣa) knowledge arising from the Great Saying (*mahāvākya*)—namely, "I am Brahman" (*ahamasmi brahma*)—it describes that which is characterized as liberation-in-life (*jīvanmukti*), known by the synonym of "non-cognitive absorption" (*asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*) or "thought-free absorption" (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*), with the words "tranquil" (*praśānta*). Thus, the meaning is: one whose mind possesses preeminent tranquility through the practice of the five limbs of yoga ending with withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). It is for this very reason that such a state is called "tranquil" (*śānta*). Tranquility is...

The meaning is: he is one by whom the multitude of cravings for objects such as sound and the like—which have become intensified through the quality of *rajas* (passion) and extend as far as the world of Brahmā—is [subdued] by means of *dhāraṇā* characterized by the consciousness of the meaning of the aforementioned statement, restricted to specific locations such as the *brahmarandhra*. For this very reason, because his impurities have been dispelled by such *dhāraṇā* according to the scriptural injunction, "One should burn away sin with breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and evil with *dhāraṇās*," there is the realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self.

"Endowed with the continuity of cultivation" (bhāvanasātatyaśālinam) means possessing constant practice; by this, meditation (*dhyāna*) is implied. The particle *hi* is used for emphasis. It refers specifically to the yogin distinguished by the two aforementioned qualifications, because of the traditional teaching that "yoga is samādhi"; thus, it refers to one who is concentrated (*samāhitam*), possessing one-pointedness of mind directed toward the object of the identity of Brahman and the Self. Toward this practitioner, [the Lord speaks of] the "Supreme" (*uttamam*), according to the Smṛti: "But the Supreme Person is another," meaning one who is unsurpassed due to being distinct from objects and the like.

[The word] *śayam* [is used]. For this very reason, it is "become Brahman," meaning it has the nature of Brahman. Such bliss means non-dual bliss of the Self (*advaitātmasukha*). By this, the state of *unmanī* is manifested. The connection is that [the yogi] "approaches" (upaity), i.e., it becomes manifest. || 103 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He recites those very verses of his which are intent upon elaborating the summarized meaning:
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
wherein the mind is restrained through the practice of yoga according to the non-dual (Advaita) view.
And by means of the yantra called Yogānanda, seeing the Self by the self within the self, one finds contentment.

"Wherein"— that is, at which time the mind, having been withdrawn from all objects through the practice of yoga, that is, the performance of yoga, becomes stilled, meaning it attains cessation; and furthermore, at which time [the self] by means of the self, that is, by the internal organ purified by samādhi—

Perceiving and experiencing himself and the Supreme as the light whose nature is consciousness, he finds satisfaction and attains contentment within himself alone, not in sense objects; this is the meaning. || 4 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): For this very reason, in order to illuminate that this yoga was previously presented by the Blessed One as having great fruit, he recites those four verses beginning with "yatnoparamate" and so forth. Here, according to the rule that "a *kālapaka* consists of four [verses]," the word "taṃ" (him/that) from the fourth verse serves as the correlative for all six instances of the word "yat" (which/whom) found within the three verses beginning with "yatra."

The connection with the words is as follows: "by the practice of yoga," that is, by the cultivation of yoga; "it ceases" means it becomes tranquil. "By the mind itself which has ceased" means by the very mind that has become stilled.

"The Self" refers to the non-dual Supreme Self itself. "Beholding" means realizing through direct experience that "I am Brahman"; the implied sense is that one becomes the immutable (kūṭastha). "In the Self" refers to the subject matter of the aforementioned true nature. || 104 ||
That which is absolute bliss is graspable by the intellect and beyond the senses.
Wherein he knows [the Self], and being established therein, he does not deviate from reality. || 105 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Furthermore, at whatever time this yogi, established in the Self, experiences—that is, perceives through direct experience—such a happiness as is absolute (meaning it exists eternally), infinite, graspable by the intellect (being apprehended by the intellect independently of the senses), beyond the senses (transcending the range of the senses), and not produced by sense objects; furthermore, he, being established in the Self, [perceives it] in its true nature.
Therefore, it does not waver from nor deviate from its own essential nature. || 105 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding the word "bliss" (*sukham*): the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the realization that can indeed be attained through the very valid knowledge (*pramā*) concerning the meaning of the term *tattva*, which has been purified by [the practice of] *tadbuddhi*. And the connection is that once this qualified seeker is established therein, he does not waver from it in reality. || 105 ||
Having obtained which, one considers no other gain to be superior to it.
Established in which, one is not shaken even by heavy suffering.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Furthermore, having attained—that is, having reached—this Self, one does not consider any other gain to be superior to it, in accordance with the Smṛti text: "There is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self. Moreover, established in this reality of the Self, one is not shaken even by great suffering characterized by such things as wounds from weapons, just like Prahlāda. || 6 ||

Commentary on verse a0: "Having obtained which" (yaṃ labdhvā). Even by the Guru, with great difficulty—that is, even by the suffering arising from being impaled upon a stake, as in the case of Māṇḍavya and others—[he did not abandon it]. This is the meaning. || 106 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now he concludes the yoga that has been explained:
"One should know that [state] called yoga to be the disjunction from the conjunction with suffering."
This yoga must be practiced with determination by one whose mind is free from despondency.

"One should know that" means: one should know—that is, understand—that particular state of the self characterized by the qualifiers beginning with "gradually" (śanaiḥ śanaiḥ) and ending with [the verse], which was called "yoga"; that disjunction from the conjunction with suffering (duḥkhasaṃyogaviyoga)—where "conjunction with suffering" (duḥkhasaṃyoga) is the union with sufferings, and "disjunction" is the separation from that—[which is] designated as "yoga" through figurative indication (viparītalakṣaṇā), meaning that which has the name "yoga"—one should know that yoga of such a kind.

Regarding this matter, he states a specific duty to be performed: "He, with resolve" (verse 7). That previously mentioned yoga should be practiced—that is, performed—with resolve, which is to say with determination and with a mind free from despondency (*anirviṇṇa-cetas*), devoid of world-weariness. || 7 ||
The Eleventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.
Commentary on verse 421:

"That" (tam) means that which is free from connection with suffering; that is to say, devoid of suffering. There is a word-break at "anirviṇṇa" (undiscouraged), meaning one who possesses an excess of zeal. || 107 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now he concludes the matter just explained:
"Thus constantly yoking the self, the yogi, freed from taint..."
Through that bliss, he experiences the touch of Brahman, which is ultimate happiness.

"Yuñjan" (while practicing yoga): the yogi, whose impurities have vanished, whose sins have departed, and who is free from obstacles to yoga, while always thus practicing—that is, maintaining continuous connection—with the Self in the manner described, easily—that is, without effort—attains, that is, reaches, the "touch of Brahman" (*brahmasaṃsparśam*); this means that bliss which has contact with Brahman, or rather, which consists of the very nature of Brahman. He attains an exceedingly imperishable and unsurpassed happiness. || 8 ||
The commentary concludes with the verse beginning "guñjan" (humming). It states the fruit of that practice with the words "sukhena" (with ease). Regarding the word "brahma":
it is of the nature of the object consisting of non-dual unity. || 108 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To show that the practice of yoga, when performed without despondency, leads to its fruition, he states this with an illustration:
"Just as the emptying of the ocean by a single drop from the tip of a blade of kusha grass..."
The restraint of the mind consists in that very absence of weariness.

Regarding the term "overflowing" (*utseka*): it refers to the overflowing of the ocean caused by a single drop raised by the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass. Just as water, having been drawn out and sprinkled outside, will eventually overflow the ocean in the absence of exhaustion, so too the restraint of the mind, when practiced without weariness, will achieve perfection in the course of time. This was stated with the story of the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird in mind. || 9 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Even so, since it is possible to take the literal meaning of the phrase *anirviṇṇacetasā* as 'one whose mind is detached'—which is consistent with the context—why do you insist on providing the meaning 'one who possesses intense devotion' by resorting to the elision of the vowel *a* (*a-nirviṇṇa*)? [The answer is: Because this is the consensus of the tradition (*sāṃpradāyika*), and because yoga practiced for a long time, without interruption, and with reverence...

Indicating that this is the intention of the Sūtra by the phrase "the firm ground" (*ḍhabhūmi*), [the author] cites the very words of the teacher Gauḍapāda with great reverence: "Like the overflowing... etc. Of the ocean—that is, the sea—just as by a single drop on the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass, according to the well-known worldly maxim of the story of the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird, even in this very life; "the other"—meaning, by the mere absence of distress over its non-attainment—it would indeed have ceased to exist; in the same way, the restraint of the mind would also come to pass.
The construction is "he knows. || 109 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Not only is this meaning stated in the Gītā, but it is also found in the Maitrāyaṇīya Śākhā; thus he says:
"To the royal sage Bṛhadratha, the sage Śākāyanya [taught] happiness..."
He spoke thus in the branch known as Maitra, preceded by a formal agreement.

Regarding the phrase "of Bṛhadratha": in a specific branch of the Yajurveda known as the Maitrāyaṇīya, a certain sage named Śākāyanya spoke of the bliss of Brahman to the royal seer (rājarṣi) called Bṛhadratha, who had approached him as his disciple, by means of what is termed meditative absorption (samādhi). || 110 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, while citing the Maitrāyaṇīya Śruti as well regarding the aforementioned yoga, he introduces the dialogue found therein with the words "of Bṛhadratha. || 110 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question of in what manner he spoke, [the author] recites his own mantras that establish that point:
"Just as a fire without fuel is extinguished in its own source..."
Likewise, through the destruction of its activity, the mind subsides into its own source. || 11 ||

From the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya, the section titled "Yogānanda": Just as a fire, having consumed its fuel and being without wood, subsides into its own source— its own cause— which is pure light (*tejomātra*), so too does the mind subside.

Just as [the sun] remains in the form of pure light after abandoning its specific forms such as [the appearance of] *lā* and so forth, in that very same manner, the mind—the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—also becomes tranquil within its own cause, which is pure *sattva*, through the dissolution of all modifications (*vṛtti*) by means of the practice of cessation-meditation (*nirodha-samādhi*), due to the destruction of all Rajasic and other modifications; the meaning is that it becomes characterized by the residue of pure *sattva* alone. || 11 ||
He recites those very [verses] beginning with "yathā": "In its own source," that is, in its own cause, the subtle fire (*sūkṣmatejas*).
"In its own source" means in its own cause, which consists of the fivefold portion of sattva predominant among the five great unevolved elements (*apañcīkṛta-pañcamahābhūta*). || 11 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: What follows from this? To this he says:
"For one whose mind is pacified in its own source and who desires the Truth..."
For one who is deluded regarding the objects of the senses, [these] false [perceptions] follow the power of karma.

"In its own source" (*svayonau*): one who has desire for the object that is the true Self is "one whose desire is for the True" (*satyakāmī*). For that very reason, because it is pacified in its own source, the mind—being pacified, deluded regarding the objects of the senses (such as sound and so forth), turned away from them, and devoid of knowledge—follows the power of karma; thus they are called "followers of the power of karma. These [states] such as pleasure and so forth, along with their means, are unreal and illusory (*māyika*).
The meaning is that they would be false by virtue of the knowledge of their being so. || 12 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): What follows from that? He says: "His own" (sva), etc.; "truthful" (satya), etc. This means one who possesses an intense longing (*utkaṇṭhā*) for the attainment of the Brahman-Self, which is uncontradicted by time. For such a mind, which has become tranquil within its own source (*svayoni*);
for this very reason: "by the senses," etc., meaning devoid of the cognition of sound and other objects sought by the senses; for this very reason: "from latent impressions" (*saṃskārataḥ*).

"Even for one who has emerged from [that state]," refers to "karma. The meaning is that such things as the face of meditative absorption follow the individual soul (jīva) under the influence of karma.
The construction is: they are "unreal" (anṛtāḥ), meaning they are false because they are fashioned by one's own ignorance (avidyā). || 12 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that it is illogical to say that the world becomes illusory upon the subsidence of the mind, because the world does not have the mind as its material cause; anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The mind alone is indeed saṃsāra; therefore, one should purify it with effort."
Whatever the mind of a mortal is focused upon, he becomes that; this is an eternal secret. || 13 ||

"It is mind alone. Although the world is not, in its own nature, derived from the mind as its material cause, nevertheless, its capacity [to appear] has the mind as its very cause; this is what the word "alone" (eva) here intends to establish by citing universal experience as proof, since enjoyment is not observed when the mind is dissolved in states such as deep sleep. Since transmigratory existence consists of the mind, therefore one should purify that very mind through effort characterized by practice, dispassion, and so forth. Rāja-... [text truncated]

One should make the mind one-pointed by means of the absence of dullness (*stama*). Now, one might object: for the liberation of the Self, it is the Self alone that must be purified, not the mind. Anticipating this, he says: "He whose mind... The term "mortal" is an *upalakṣaṇa* (a figure of speech) for any embodied being (*dehin*). Whatever a person’s mind is directed toward—whatever object such as a son or other thing he possesses in his mind—he becomes identified with that, consisting of that very thing, because he superimposes upon himself the entirety or the deficiency of that object. This is eternal...

The secret, the mystery, is established through reflection and so forth. This is what is meant: because the self, which is pure by its very nature, possesses the state of transmigratoriness solely due to contact with the mind—according to the Vedic scripture, "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were"—therefore, the cessation of the self's transmigratory state occurs through the purification of the mind. || 13 ||
The reason for this is stated as "the mind alone" (cittameva). This is intended solely according to the doctrine of the creation of perception (dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda). || 11 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might raise the objection: "Since merit and demerit—which bestow pleasure and pain—have been accumulated through a beginningless succession of births, how can the cessation of the self's worldly existence (saṃsāra) occur even through the purification of the mind? Anticipating this, he refutes it by stating that such is not the case, because the destruction of all karma is possible through the contemplation of Brahman characterized by the clarity of the mind.
The Eleventh Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
"For by the serenity of the mind, one destroys both auspicious and inauspicious karma."
With a serene self, abiding in the Self, one enjoys imperishable happiness. || 14 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the mind": by the word *hi* (for/indeed), he indicates the well-known authority of Śruti and Smṛti, such as: "Just as a tuft of cotton-wool thrown into a fire is consumed, even so all his evils are consumed," and "In the case of all minor offenses and great sins, one should enter for a quarter of the night and practice meditation on Brahman. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "the self is serene" (*prasanna ātmā*). The self is serene.

He whose mind is thus described is called "one of such a mind. Abiding in the Self—which is his own essential nature, characterized as non-dual bliss, and which is Brahman—and having abandoned the entire realm of the visible through the firm conviction "I am that very [Brahman]," he remains in the form of pure consciousness and experiences that inexhaustible, imperishable happiness which constitutes his own true nature. || 14 ||

Commentary on verse a0: "For this very reason" [is stated]. Regarding the phrase "of the mind" (cittasya): the particle *hi* is used for emphasis. "By clarity" (*prasādena*) means by the supreme, stainless transformation consisting of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). || 14 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He confirms the very point already stated—that "one whose self is serene, abiding in the Self"—by means of an illustration:
"Just as the mind of a living being is intensely attached to the sphere of sense objects..."
If it were thus with Brahman, who would not be liberated from bondage? || 115 ||
Regarding the phrase "completely attached": the mind of a living being is naturally and perfectly attached to its objects—that is, to the field of sensory activity.

If that very same mind were thus attached to Brahman, the Supreme Self non-different from the inner self (pratyagātman), then who would not be liberated from saṃsāra? The meaning is that everyone would indeed be liberated. || 115 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): What, then, is the means for this serenity? To this he says: "attached" (samāsaktam), etc.; "to an object" (viṣaye) means to an object that binds. || 115 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To provide further detail on the subject already mentioned, he states the internal subdivisions of the mind:
"The mind is indeed said to be of two kinds: pure and impure."
It is impure due to contact with desire; it is pure when free from desire. || 16 ||
Regarding the word "mind" (manaḥ), he states the reason for it: "it is impure. The term "desire" (kāma) is illustrative, as it includes anger and other such states as well. || 16 ||
The reason for that as well is stated: "For the mind... (verse 16).
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings.
Attached to sense objects, it leads to bondage; free from sense objects, it is known to lead to liberation. || 17 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He demonstrates how that very same [mind], being of two kinds, is respectively the cause of worldly existence and liberation—“The mind alone,” etc. (17).

The commentary on the aphorism states the conclusion: "The mind alone," etc. This means that it is devoid of objects because, through the knowledge of reality, its objects have been discarded as being illusory. || 17 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: The Śruti itself elaborates upon the very meaning already stated in the verse, "The one whose self is serene, abiding in the Self, enjoys imperishable bliss."
The bliss that arises when the mind, its impurities shaken off by meditative concentration, is established in the Self.
It cannot be described by speech; at that time, it is grasped by one's own inner faculty.
Regarding "samādhi": for one who has been established in the self, which is of the nature of direct perception, and whose impurities have been shaken off by *samādhi*, by means of that *samādhi*—

The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya: [the section] titled *Yogānanda*, concerning the mind whose impurities have been shaken off through the repetition of the cognition that has as its object the identity of renunciation and Brahman, and whose stains of *rajas* and *tamas* have been entirely removed.

The meaning is that the bliss which arises in that samādhi cannot be described by words or speech because it is a supramundane bliss; rather, that bliss, being its very nature, is apprehended within by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) alone. || 18 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): For this very reason, [it says] "in samādhi. The meaning is: in the inner self (pratīci), which is of the nature of Brahman through its non-duality with the Self. || 18 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection that since this very samādhi is difficult for men to attain, how can the certainty of the bliss of Brahman arise through it, he says:
"Even though this samādhi is difficult for men to attain for a long period of time..."
Nevertheless, this momentary [state] causes one to ascertain the bliss of Brahman. || 19 ||

The phrase "even though" means that although this [state of] continuous concentration is impossible, because its momentary form is possible, this bliss can indeed be determined by that very [momentary state]. || 19 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: since the aforementioned Yoga Sūtra prescribes that long-term practice is required for the attainment of samādhi, it is exceedingly difficult for us—whose lifespans consist of but a few moments—to achieve it. To this, he says: "Even though... Even this momentary samādhi ascertains—that is, brings about the certain realization of—the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*), which is the very nature of non-dual Brahman (*advaita-svarūpa*), the immediate reality that is the object of supreme love. This is the syntactical connection. ||19||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even though some engage in hearing and other practices for the sake of realizing the Self, they remain extroverted and devoid of certainty regarding bliss.
Anticipating this, he states that although such is the case for those lacking faith and other virtues, for those possessing faith and the rest, certainty indeed arises.
One who is full of faith and intent upon his goal will certainly determine everything in every way.
But once that has been ascertained, he trusts it even at other times. (120)

"Faithful" (*śraddhālu*) means one who possesses the persistence (*vyasana*)—the resolve that "I shall accomplish this in every way"—regarding this samādhi; here, it means "in every way" or "certainly. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "But when it is certain" (*niścite tu*). When this bliss of Brahman has been ascertained even once—that is, at some time during a momentary samādhi—this person, possessing that single instance of certainty, trusts that "bliss exists" at other times as well.
He utters a breath. || 20 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if this is so, why is it that not all who have performed the hearing (*śravaṇa*) are nevertheless turned outward?

To this, he says: "The faithful" (*śraddhāluḥ*). Faith (*śraddhā*) is intense trust in the teacher and the scriptures, consisting of the certainty that the results they describe will necessarily occur; one whose character is defined by that is the meaning. That without which there is no stability while awake is one's addiction (*vyasana*); or rather, it is the nature of practicing the other limbs of yoga.

The word "va" means "as much as. This refers to the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) who possesses the certainty of the bliss of Brahman once and for all, and is intent upon yoga; the meaning is that at all other times as well, he indeed attains conviction—that is, he gains confidence—regarding the experience of the bliss of Brahman. This is the sense of the verse. || 20 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
Such a person, even during the state of indifference, [possesses] the latent impression of bliss.
Having set aside the primary bliss, he meditates upon that [state] alone, being intent upon it.

"Such a person" means: such a man, preceded by faith and other virtues, possessing firm conviction even once, disregards the previously mentioned latent impression of bliss which is perceived even in a state of indifference; becoming intent upon it—that is, having his primary focus on the supreme bliss—he contemplates that alone.
(Chapter 21, Commentary) — For this very reason: "such a person" means one who possesses the aforementioned confidence. (21)
A woman who is devoted to another man remains distracted even while engaged in her household duties.
He relishes within himself that very elixir of union with the Supreme.
The Eleventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.
425 Rāma-Ṭīkā: Thus, even during the time of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*), he contemplates his own bliss; regarding this, he provides an illustration with the verse beginning "pare" (22). A0-Ṭīkā:
He reveals an illustration for contemplating that [bliss] with total absorption through the verse beginning "pare" (22).
Thus, the steadfast one has attained rest in the supreme, pure reality.
Even while engaging in external and internal activities, he relishes that very [bliss] within.
Rāma’s Commentary: He applies this to the subject of the illustration with the words "evam" (thus). || 23 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): He clarifies the application of the analogy with the words "evam" (thus). "In others" means in those who are devoid of ignorance and its effects;

"pure" means free from the stain of mediacy (*parokṣatva*). "The steadfast one" (*dhīraḥ*) refers to one possessing the fortitude characterized as follows: "Steadfastness is the continuous stream of recollection of the reality of the awakened truth. "Rest" (*viśrāntim*) means liberation (*mukham*). || 23 ||
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: He states the meaning of the word "dhīra" (steadfast): "Steadfastness [is the state] even when the senses are powerful, due to the desire for the savoring of bliss."
Having set aside all the senses, its engagement is directed toward that consciousness.

Regarding "steadfastness" (dhīratvam): although the senses possess the power to attract a person toward their respective objects, steadfastness means the state of setting aside all the senses through the desire to contemplate the bliss of one's own true nature, and thus proceeding solely in the contemplation of that bliss. || 24 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): He clarifies the meaning of the word *dhīra* (steadfast) by stating "steadfastness" (*dhīratvam*). The word "of oneself" (*svasya*) is to be understood as implicit. ||24||
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the intended meaning of the word "rest" (viśrānti) along with an illustration:
"A bearer of a load, having set down the burden from his head, sits having attained rest."
When one abandons engagement with saṃsāra, such an understanding is indeed rest. || 125 ||

Regarding the term "bearer of a burden": just as in the world a man carrying a load becomes free from fatigue by discarding the burden situated upon his head which was the cause of his weariness, so too, when the activities of saṃsāra have been abandoned, the realization that arises—"I am now free from fatigue"—is what is expressed by the word *viśrama* (rest). This is the meaning. || 125 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, he also explains the meaning of the state of rest (*viśrānti*) with the words "the bearer of the burden" (*bhāravāhī*) and "in saṃsāra. The phrase "by way of falsehood" (*mithyātvena*) is to be understood as the implicit sense. || 125 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now he states the resulting meaning:
"Having attained supreme rest in equanimity, in whatever manner that may be,"
And even in states of pleasure or pain, he was solely intent upon that bliss.

Regarding the word "rest" (*viśrāntim*): the meaning is that a person who has attained the supreme, unsurpassed rest characterized as described above becomes intent upon relishing his own supreme bliss even in the state of his own indifference; likewise, even at the time of encountering the causes of pleasure and pain, he abandons the pursuit of them and remains intent solely upon relishing his innate bliss. || 26 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): What follows from that? To this he says: "Viśrāntim" (rest). Regarding "sukha": the word "ca" (and) has the sense of "api" (also). Regarding "tat":

the meaning is that he is intent upon the savoring of the bliss of the identity of Brahman and Ātman alone—which was previously contemplated by first disregarding the bliss of the latent impressions (vāsanā) mentioned during the state of indifference (audāsīnya). || 26 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Granted that there is no desire to pursue suffering because it is disagreeable, why should there not be a desire to pursue sensual pleasure, since it is agreeable and sought after by people? Anticipating this doubt, [the author states] its procurement from objects and so forth...
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [pages 424–424] 426.

[He says, preceded by the presentation of an illustration, that even the desire for worldly pleasure—known as *yogānanda*—does not arise in the discerning person, because it produces extreme outward-directedness and is thus opposed to the contemplation of one's own innate bliss: "Even the desire for pleasure born of yoga does not arise in the discerning person, just as a man who has awakened from sleep does not desire the objects he saw in a dream. (1.20) The word "even" (*api*) implies that other desires do not arise; how much less so the desire for the pleasures of sense objects! This is because such desire is incompatible with the contemplation of one's own innate bliss. To explain this, he provides an illustration: "Just as a man who has awakened from sleep does not desire the objects he saw in a dream. For example, when a man falls asleep and sees various objects in a dream, upon waking he does not desire those objects, because they were merely mental constructs and not real. Similarly, the discerning person, having awakened from the deep sleep of ignorance, does not desire the pleasures born of yoga, which are likewise unreal. Therefore, since there is no desire for them, there is no engagement in their pursuit. Thus, the discerning person remains established solely in the contemplation of his own innate bliss.]
The state of mind regarding the cause for entering the fire is exactly like that which exists in the aesthetic sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra).
In the case of a wise person, [this] arises when there is an obstruction to the continuous contemplation of the object. || 27 ||

"Agni" (Fire). The meaning is this: when there is a very firm desire for the swift release from the body, just as a sense of distaste arises in one who is about to enter fire toward ornaments and other things that cause delay, so too does it arise in a discerning person endowed with the means such as detachment toward the pleasure of sense objects, which is opposed to the contemplation of Brahman. || 27 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: even during states such as pleasure, if there is a contemplation of the Self, is there no manifestation of that pleasure and so forth? To this he replies with the verse beginning "In fire" (agnau). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "as they burn the body of the dead or sleeping husband. Regarding "contemplation": the meaning is that which is contrary to the contemplation of the non-dual Self. || 27 ||
The intellect [is fixed] on non-conflicting happiness, and there is coming and going within one's own bliss.
As she was performing these [rites], this [power] moved here and there in succession, like the eye of a crow.

Rāma’s Commentary: Lest it be argued that while there may be no desire for pleasure regarding an object that is antagonistic, why should it not arise regarding an object that is non-antagonistic—which, by its ease of attainment without effort, serves as a cause for the outward-turning of the mind? To this he says: "Non-antagonistic," etc. (Verse 28).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, let it be granted that there may be an awareness of the aforementioned worthlessness regarding pleasures produced by women, sandalwood, and the like—which are opposed to spiritual inquiry—but how can such an awareness arise regarding pleasures produced by eating and so forth, which are not opposed to it? To this, he says: "Not opposed," etc. (28).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He explains the illustration:
"The gaze of a crow is indeed one and the same for both its left and right eyes."
Thus, the mind of the knower of reality moves back and forth between these two states of bliss.

"There is but one sight. Just as the eye—the instrument of seeing, defined as that by which the sight of a crow is seen—is indeed one, yet performs the coming and going alternately between the two eyeballs of the left and right eyes; in the same way, the intellect (*buddhi*) of the discriminating person likewise moves between the two states of bliss.
This is the meaning. || 29 ||

Commentary (a0): Regarding the fact that the mental state (*vṛtti*) of a yogi—though one and the same—performs both going and coming between the bliss of sense-objects and the bliss of Brahman, which are not incompatible with the contemplation of non-dual Brahman-bliss (*advaita-brahmānanda*), due to the difference in time, the author clarifies the analogy of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣidṛṣṭānta*) as follows: "One and the same... (verse 29).
Rāma’s Commentary: He elaborates on the application of the principle—the person who knows reality experiences both the bliss of sense objects and the bliss of Brahman.
One should know that both the worldly and the Vedic [traditions] are like one who is proficient in two languages. || 130 ||

Regarding the phrase "while enjoying": the knower of reality, while enjoying sense objects, should understand both the bliss of sense objects arising from them and the bliss of Brahman known through the Upaniṣadic statements—both the worldly and the Vedic bliss of sense objects and the bliss of Brahman—just like one who knows both languages. || 130 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): He clarifies the application of the principle with the words "bhuñjānaḥ" (while enjoying). The word "ānandau" (two joys) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

Here, the truth is that there is no contradiction between the worldly joy derived from sense objects and the Vedic bliss of Brahman precisely because they are both duties pertaining to one's own stage of life (āśrama-dharma). || 130 ||
The Eleventh Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

427. Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If there is agitation at the time of experiencing suffering, how can there be the experience of one's own bliss? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"When suffering is encountered, there is no agitation as before, because [the yogi] possesses the twofold vision."
Just as for a man whose body is half-immersed in the Gaṅgā, there is the dual potency of cold and heat.

Regarding the word "duḥkha" (suffering): because he is a *vivekin*—one who possesses the two-fold vision and is a knower of both worldly and Vedic conduct—therefore, even upon the occurrence of suffering, he experiences no agitation as he did previously during the state of ignorance (*ajñāna*). Since he is being awakened by means of discrimination (*viveka*) at every moment, the meaning is that even at the time of experiencing suffering, his contemplation of his own innate bliss (*nijānanda*) is not contradicted. An illustration for the simultaneous contemplation of both is provided: [The example follows: Just as a person who has mastered the science of archery, while shooting an arrow, does not experience any mental distraction or agitation regarding the target even though he perceives the pain in his hand caused by the bowstring, so too, one who has attained the knowledge of the Self remains undisturbed even when undergoing physical suffering. This is because, through the power of discrimination, he simultaneously perceives both the pain and his own true nature. Thus, there is no contradiction between the experience of suffering and the realization of bliss.
He said to her: "O Gaṅgā," [verse 31].

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, even so, one might ask how it is that there is no agitation when suffering is encountered; to this he says—"suffering" (duḥkha). Why is there no agitation for him as before? To this he says—"since" (yataḥ). He provides an illustration for this: "the Gaṅgā" (gaṅgā) || 31 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the conclusion:
"In this way, for the knower of reality, there is always the bliss of Brahman during wakefulness."
Just as that [object] appears in a dream produced by its latent impressions (vāsanā), so too does it appear [in the waking state]. || 32 ||

"Thus" (ittham) means: during the state of constantly experiencing pleasure and pain, as well as in the state of remaining silent [in meditation]. He states that its manifestation occurs not only in the waking state but also in the dream state by saying "its latent impression" (tadvāsanā). This is an attributive qualification containing a reason, because a dream is produced by the latent impressions of the waking state. Even there, that face of Brahman shines forth in the same manner as it does in the waking state; this is the meaning. || 32 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): What follows from that? He says: "In this way" (ittham). || 32 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If the dream is produced by the latent impressions (vāsanā) of the experience of bliss, then it is bliss itself that appears.
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Since the latent impression of ignorance also exists, [it arises] from that impression.
In a dream, he perceives pleasure and pain just like a fool.

Regarding the term *avidyā*: it arises not only by the power of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of bliss, but also by the power of the latent impressions of ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, because it is produced from those impressions, the experience of pleasure and so forth occurs there just as it does for an ignorant person; this is the meaning. || 33 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, raising the objection that joy, sorrow, and so forth might still arise due to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), he replies with the verse beginning "avidyā" (verse 33).
Rāma’s Commentary: With this much of the textual composition, he concludes the subject matter already stated: "In the work titled *Brahmānanda*, [this is] the illumination of Brahman-bliss."
Yogic perception has been explained in this first chapter. || 134 ||
Thus ends the first chapter, named "The Bliss of Yoga," in the *Brahmānanda*.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Pañcadaśī composed by the venerable sage Vidyāraṇya. 11.

"Brahmānanda" means: in this work consisting of five chapters titled *Brahmānanda*, it is stated in the first chapter that there is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—in the form of the experience of a qualified practitioner—which reveals the self-luminous bliss of Brahman (*svaprakāśacidrūpabrahmānanda*) during the state of deep sleep, even at times of indifference, as well as during the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and in states of pleasure and pain. This is also an illustration for scripture (*āgama*) and other means of knowledge, which are likewise shown here.
Because it is the reality. || 134 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [pages 426–426] 428.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Bliss of Yoga" (*yogānanda*), in the *Brahmānanda* composed by the scholar named Pṛṇā, a servant of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Bhāratītīrtha Vidyāraṇya Muni. 1.
Śrī Rāmakṛṣṇa’s Commentary (A0 Ṭīkā): Concluding this first chapter, he states its essential purport: "Brahmānanda," etc. Now, one might object:

at the commencement of the commentary on this work titled *Pañcadaśī*, it was said: "In the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), where indeed are sense-objects, teachers, scriptures, gardens, rivers, and holy fords?"

Having stated the first obstacle known as the latent impression (*vāsanā*) regarding sense objects in the verse beginning with "Thus, agitation in the mind is the first obstacle even in [the state of] oneness" (*iti vihvalatā citte pratibandhaḥ prathama eṣa aikye’pi*), and having stated in the eleventh [chapter] that the unsurpassed nature of the bliss of yoga is realized through knowledge— that its devotion to that [bliss] must be determined as the supreme human goal even when there is no external object— the author has stated in this extensive section that this very work serves as the sublater (*bādhaka*) of the aforementioned obstacles. This is what was said.

If it is asked how this is so, it is said in reply: Here, having commenced with "I shall now proclaim the bliss of Brahman" (*brahmānandaṃ pravakṣyāmi*), the work concludes by stating that the manifestation of the bliss of Brahman is the direct perception of the yogi.

Thus, because its primary intent is the unsurpassed happiness found in the experience of non-dual bliss (*advaitānanda*), its first indicative mark (*liṅga*) is its sublation of the mere semblance of pleasure derived from perceptible objects.
Likewise, the nine verses beginning with "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (*brahmavid paramāpnoti*) and those following them throughout the text likewise [establish this].

The repetition [of the mantra] is indeed clear. By this very [explanation], the fourfold set of indicators—namely, novelty (*apūrvatā*), the fruit (*phala*), the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and logical consistency (*upapatti*)—is also explained; for they have been made manifest there quite explicitly. This is the general direction [of the argument]. || 134 ||

Thus ends the *Yogānandaprakāśa*, composed by the student Acyuta Śarman, surnamed Moḍaka, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa, the illustrious Dvaitasaccidānandendra Sarasvatī, and pupil of the venerable Padavākyapramāṇapārāvārapārīṇa, the one bearing the surname Paṣṭhi, the venerable Nārāyaṇa Śāstrī. 11.
Now begins the twelfth chapter on the fifteenth [day];
therein is the second section, titled "Bliss in Brahman," concerning the bliss of the Self.
Indeed, in this way, it is different from both the bliss of latent impressions (vāsanānanda) and the bliss of Brahman (brahmānanda).
The yogi should experience his own innate bliss; what recourse is there for the deluded person in this matter?
Rāma’s Commentary: Now he begins the second chapter, named Ātmānanda, which is contained within the Brahmānanda.

Thus, having demonstrated in the first chapter the manner in which a discriminating person experiences his own bliss through yoga, he introduces the question of the disciple in order to demonstrate the manner in which an ignorant seeker of knowledge may experience the bliss of Brahman by means of analyzing the meaning of words—specifically, to show how that very bliss is denoted by the term "Ātmānanda. He says: "But surely..."
Thus [it is said]. || 1 ||

I bow to the Supreme Brahman, who is non-dual bliss, existence, consciousness, all-pervading, and eternally pure; who, though the abode of the illusory net of duality arising from delusion, is the crest-jewel of the Vedas and self-luminous; and to all the best of teachers, the ornament of Raghu’s lineage, my true Guru, who is firmly established in Brahman. a0 ṭīkā - I bow to the Supreme Brahman, who is non-dual bliss, existence, consciousness, all-pervading, and eternally pure;
who, though the abode of the illusory net of duality arising from delusion, is the crest-jewel of the Vedas and self-luminous;
and to all the best of teachers, the ornament of Raghu’s lineage, my true Guru, who is firmly established in Brahman.
I bow to my own guru, known by the name Śrīmannārāyaṇa, who is also designated as Mahādeva. || 1 ||
Having honored Jīvañjīvaka, Vidyāraṇya, and Bhāratītīrtha,
I now clarify Ātmānanda with this Kaumudī, like the light of the sun.

Now, the Blessed One, the teacher Bhāratītīrtha, in the first of his own compositions on the *Pañcadaśī*, namely in the first chapter called *Yogānanda*— which constitutes one-third of the five chapters of the *Brahmānandī*— stated as follows: "In the work titled *Brahmānanda*, that which illuminates the bliss of Brahman..."

Having thus concluded that "the perception of the yogi has been described in this first chapter," and now commencing the twelfth chapter— named *Ātmānanda* and belonging to the second book— with the desire to favor those of duller intellect, the author performs an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) by means of the term *brahmānanda*, which signifies the well-known purpose of the valid means of knowledge and denotes the identity of Brahman and the Self; and by that very [invocation], he [establishes] the subject matter of the present treatise.

Indicating the fourfold connection (anubandha) such as the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and so forth, [the author] himself restates the student’s doubt with the words "Now then" (*nanu*). The bliss of latent impressions (*vāsanānanda*) is a particular kind of happiness experienced for a short time by one who has awakened from sleep due to residual impressions (*saṃskāra*). The bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*) is that which occurs during deep sleep;
it too was explained in detail in the preceding section. Likewise, the innate bliss (*nijānanda*) is also [described]: "To the extent that the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is forgotten through practice..."
"By means of yoga, to that same extent, one's own bliss is inferred by one of subtle vision," and so forth, according to the process of yogic perception. || 1 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Thus questioned by the disciple, the Guru says that for one who is utterly deluded, there is no qualification for knowledge at all:
"Under the influence of merit and demerit, this [individual] is born and also dies."
Furthermore, tell us out of courtesy: what is the use of millions of bodies again and again? || 2 ||

"Dharma" means: this extremely deluded one, due to the power of the good and evil deeds performed in past births throughout beginningless saṃsāra, having assumed various kinds of bodies, is born and dies again and again—this is the meaning. || 2 ||

Commentary (a0): To this question thus posed, the proponent answers with an air of indifference: "Dharma... etc. The meaning is: out of courtesy—that is, through an insistence on the capacity to enlighten all ignorant people. || 2 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [pages 428–428] 430.
[Regarding that which is called Ātmānanda—Rāma’s Commentary]: Because he is the benefactor of all, the disciple says that the Teacher must also describe some destination for him:
"Is there a purpose for your compassion, since you desire to favor me?"
Tell me, was he a fool, or one seeking knowledge, or perhaps one who had turned his face away? || 3 ||

"It exists. [The word] *anujighṛkṣutvāt* means "because of the desire to favor (*anugrahītum icchavaḥ*) you," that is, because of the state of being those who wish to favor you. Therefore, the meaning is that there is a purpose characterized by rescuing him, due to his being endowed with the desire to uplift the disciple and out of courtesy. Having heard the disciple's words in this way, the teacher, having reflected upon him, asks: "If some course must be told for the deluded one, then [is he] the deluded one?"
Tell me, are you one possessed by passion or one free from passion? || 3 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, once again, the disciple states its purpose, beginning with "It exists. Thereupon, the teacher questions him by means of an alternative analysis, beginning with "In that case," and so forth. || 3 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: If he is one possessed of passion (*rāgī*), then his action or meditation must be taught in accordance with that passion; thus, he states the first resolution:
Or one may describe the ritual of worship or the action as appropriate to one who has turned away from it.
But one who is of dull intellect yet desirous of knowledge should be awakened by means of the bliss of the Self.

—Regarding the term "upāstim" (meditation): it means for one who is "vimukha," that is, averse to the knowledge of reality or outward-looking. "Yathocitam" (as is appropriate) means according to what is fitting;

the meaning is that if [the disciple] desires the world of Brahmā and so forth, one should teach meditation, whereas if he desires heaven and so forth, one should teach ritual action (*karman*). Even if he is desirous of knowledge (*jijñāsu*), he—

Having considered the alternatives—that one might be either highly discriminating (*ativivekī*) or of dull intellect (*mandaprajña*)—and having intended that the highly discriminating person attains the direct realization of Brahman through yoga in the manner described in the preceding chapter, he now states the means for the vision [of Truth] for the person of dull intellect: "The dull... (verse 4). He who is of dull intellect—meaning one whose intellect (*prajñā*) or understanding (*buddhi*) is dull or inert—is called *mandaprajña*.

Desiring to know him (*jijñāsu*), one should instruct that person of dull intellect by means of the bliss of the Self (*ātmānanda*), specifically through the method of discerning the Self from bliss. || 4 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding the first [type of aspirant], he states the means according to the gradations of their respective capacities—“Upāstim” (meditation), etc. This means: when there is some degree of subtlety of intellect, one should practice the worship of the attributeless Self through the “I-grasping” (ahaṃgraha) and other methods described in the Dhyānadīpa; but in its absence, one should perform obligatory rites and the like, free from desire for fruits, with the understanding that they please the Lord. Regarding the second [type of aspirant], he says: “Manda,” etc. (Verse 4).
Rāma’s Commentary: Thus, to the question "By whom was whom enlightened?", he says:
Yājñavalkya enlightened his own beloved Maitreyī.
"Or rather, O Maitreyī, it is not that the husband is dear for the sake of the husband," so he said. (5)

"Bodhayāmāsa" means: a certain sage named Yājñavalkya, the founder of a specific branch of the Yajurveda, while "uttering"—that is, speaking—to his own beloved wife named Maitreyī in such a manner as, "Verily, O dear one, the husband is not dear for the sake of the husband," and "Verily, O dear one, the husband does not become dear for the sake of desire for the husband," etc., "enlightened her"—that is, he caused her to realize [the truth]. ||5||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Who indeed is this bliss that is non-different from the Self by virtue of its simplicity? And what is the method for awakening to it, as well as the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and the traditional lineage (sampradāya)?
To this, he says: "He caused [them] to awaken," and so forth. || 5 ||

Rāma’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Desiring to establish that the Self is of the nature of supreme bliss by means of the reason that it is the object of supreme love—through the statement, "Let it be accepted as supreme bliss because it is the object of supreme love"—the author first intends to show that the cited sentence is illustrative in nature.
With this in mind, he states the purport of all the synonymous statements found in that context, in order to first substantiate the reason that the Self is the object of supreme love.
Husband, wife, sons, wealth, cattle, Brahmins, and those born of the arms (Kshatriyas).
The worlds, the gods, the Vedas, and all beings are dear for the sake of the Self.
The Twelfth Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

Regarding the term "husband": the meaning is that the category of objects of enjoyment, such as husband, wife, and so forth, is dear only through its connection to the enjoyer because it exists for his sake (*śeṣatva*), and not by its own nature. || 6 ||
Commentary (a0): He summarizes the categories mentioned therein with the word "Lord" (pati). || 6 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, having analyzed the purport of the previously cited statement—"Verily, not for the sake of the husband is the husband dear, but for the sake of the Self the husband is dear"—he demonstrates it as follows:
"When the wife has a desire for her husband, then she bestows affection upon him."
At that time, due to hunger, the performance of religious duties, illness, and so forth, her husband does not desire it.

Regarding the word "patyau": when, at whatever time, there arises a desire or longing in the husband—that is, toward the wife's husband—then that wife feels affection and love for her husband; but when that husband is possessed by causes such as hunger that result in the absence of desire, then she does not desire him nor does she long for him. || 7 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): He explains them in sequence, beginning with "In the husband," and so forth. Regarding "hunger" (kṣud): it refers to that time when the wife is in a state of pleasure. || 7 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Since this is so, what is the resulting conclusion? To this he says:
"That love is not for the sake of the husband; she performs it solely for her own sake."
And the husband [acts] solely for his own sake, never for the sake of his wife.

"Not for the sake of the husband. The pleasure that is produced by the wife is not for the sake of the husband—that is, not for his purpose—but rather the wife produces that pleasure in the husband solely for her own sake, for her own purpose. As it is said: "Verily, it is not out of love for the wife that the wife is dear, but out of love for the Self that the wife is dear," and so forth; "Verily, it is not out of love for everything that everything is dear."

He demonstrates the purport of the series of statements ending with "but everything becomes dear for the sake of the self" by dividing them in order, beginning with "And the husband... The meaning is that even a husband, as a maintainer, feels affection for his wife solely for his own purpose, and not for the sake of the wife's pleasure. || 8 ||
I. Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): "Not so. Regarding the object (*arthe*), that is, with respect to the purpose; he extends this [rule] to the husband and others as well—“and the husband” (patiśca).

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): Now, if one engages in activity through the desire for each [partner] individually, let the pleasure be for one's own sake; but what of engaging simultaneously with the desire for both?
Anticipating the objection that, in the case of worldly activity (*vṛtti*), pleasure would serve both purposes [of the self and the senses], he says:
"Even in the case of mutual instigation, there is likewise engagement solely by one's own will. (9)

"Mutually" (anyonya): the remainder [of the sentence] is that, in the manner thus described, the engagement of both occurs solely by their own will—that is, solely through the desire to fulfill their respective wishes. || 9 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object that by chance, for a certain period of time, even the favorability of both [fate and human effort] is observed; therefore, he says—by means of the half-verse alone beginning with "anyonya" (mutual)—as follows: || 9 ||
The commentary by Rāmānuja shows the very same proceeding according to one's own will:
"When a child cries because his beard is pierced by a thorn, his father..."
That is not truly affection; it merely kisses [the child], for that is merely self-interest for the sake of one's own purpose.

Regarding the phrase "the beard-thorn": the kissing of the son’s face and so forth performed by the father is not for the sake of the son's pleasure, because [the child] causes weeping due to being pricked by the "beard-thorns"; therefore, it should be understood that this is solely for the father's own satisfaction. This is the meaning. || 10 || [page 430]
Thus, regarding the son as well, he says "the beard-thorn," and so forth. (Pañcadaśī, Aṣṭama Adhikaraṇa, Commentary by Vidyāraṇya, verse 10)
Even while desiring nothing, one should protect wealth such as jewels and other possessions with diligent effort.
He produces joy known as the bliss of the self; he does not doubt the attainment of wealth for his own sake. || 11 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Since a doubt may arise regarding whether the affection shown toward sentient beings—such as husband, wife, and son—is for one's own sake or for the sake of another, [the text] intends to show that such a doubt cannot even exist regarding wealth, which is insentient and devoid of desire;
thus, the purport of the statement, "Verily, wealth is not dear for the sake of wealth, but wealth is dear for the sake of the Self," is as follows.
"Even without desiring it," [he said]. || 11 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Having thus spoken regarding wealth, he says "even though desireless" (*niricchamapi*). Regarding the word "pleasure" (*prītim*): Devadatta is the petitioner. In that context, whatever pleasure he produces is directed solely toward his own purpose—namely, the purpose of wearing it on his neck or elsewhere—since even now no one has suspected that there is any value in it as a jewel; this is the connection [of the sentence], having supplied the ellipsis. || 11 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Even though [oxen] possess consciousness, he states the intended meaning of the sentence "Not indeed of oxen" (na vā are paśūnām), which refers to oxen that lack the desire to carry loads and so forth: "When a bull does not wish to marry, it is made to marry by force."
That pleasure is for the sake of the merchant alone; how could it be for the sake of the oxen? (12)

"Anicchanti" means: even when the ox (*anaḍuh*)—that is, the draft animal—is unwilling, that is, does not desire to carry the burden, [the owner] nevertheless desires to make it carry it by force; in that case, the pleasure regarding the act of carrying belongs solely to the merchant's purpose and not to the desire of the ox. || 12 ||

The commentary (*ṭīkā*) clarifies this even regarding an animal with the words "even though it does not desire" (*anicchati*). Thus, the meaning is: even when the ox (*balīvarda*), the bull, does not desire—that is, has no wish—to bear the burden; nevertheless, the merchant, by means of grass, food, drink, and so forth, compels it to exert its strength—this is the sense of the ablative case used here with the elision of the suffix *lyap* (meaning "having [compelled]"). He causes it to be wedded (*vivāhayiṣate*), that is, he specifically makes it take upon itself the burden of his own grain and other goods through its wife.
The meaning is that he wishes to sacrifice. The remainder, however, is indeed clear. || 12 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the purport of the sentence, "But indeed, O dear one, there are no desires for Brahman":
"One is satisfied by worship [thinking], 'I am a Brāhmaṇa; I am worthy of honor.'"
Satisfaction at the birth of that which is insentient belongs to the person alone.
Regarding the term "brahminhood": the meaning is that one is satisfied only by the conceit "I am a brahmin" through worship based on the cause of brahminhood, and not by a dull, inert caste. || 13 ||
Commentary (a0): Thus, he speaks regarding the genus of Brahminhood as well: "Brahminhood" [is the cause].

(13) Commentary (rā0): He states the purport of the passage beginning with "Verily, not by the Kṣatriya..."—namely, that in the thought "I am a Kṣatriya; therefore I rule the kingdom," it is kingship [that is the cause].
This was not stated for the purpose of applying [the term] to the caste of Vaiśyas and so forth. || 14 ||

Regarding the term "kṣatriya": the meaning is that the happiness caused by the enjoyment of sovereignty belongs only to one who possesses the *kṣatriya* caste, and not to the *kṣatriya* caste itself. He states—“in the case of the Vaiśya caste and so forth”—to indicate that this example of the Kṣatriya is intended to include the Vaiśyas and others as well. || 14 ||
The commentary (*ṭīkā*) explains that this is also an illustration for the caste of the Kṣatriya: "I am a Kṣatriya. (14)
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the purport of the passage beginning with "Not indeed for the sake of the worlds" (na vā are lokānāṃ kāmāya) in the twelfth chapter.
Accompanied by two commentaries:
"May the worlds of heaven and Brahmā be mine"—such is my longing.
It is of no benefit to the two worlds, serving only for one's own enjoyment. || 15 ||

Regarding the phrase "the heavenly world": the mention of these two worlds is intended to represent all worlds that are to be attained through the two means characterized by ritual action (*karma*) and meditative worship (*upāsana*). || 15 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He states this even regarding the worlds such as heaven—“svarga... etc. Let them both be so. || 15 ||
Gods such as Īśa and Viṣṇu are worshipped for the destruction of sin.
It is not for the sake of making that [other] sinless, but rather it is employed for one's own purpose. || 16 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Furthermore: "Īśa, Viṣṇu, and others... The phrase "for the destruction of sin" means for the cessation of sin.

That worship is not for the sake of sinless gods—that is, for the purpose of gods who are inherently free from sin—but rather for one's own sake, for the purpose of the person performing the worship. || 16 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, he speaks regarding the gods as well—beginning with "Īśa" (the Lord). By the word "etc. (ādi), Gaṇeśa and others are included. || 16 ||
For the Rigveda and the others are studied for the sake of not failing to attain the status of a true Brahmin.
That which is attached to the Vedas does not attach itself to human beings. || 17 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Furthermore, [the verse begins with] "The Ṛg and so forth. "Degraded Brahminhood" (*durbrāhmaṇyam*) means the state of being a *vrātya*.

And that degraded Brahminhood, which consists of a sub-species within the genus of humanity among human beings, does not apply to the Vedas, as they are devoid of that [humanity]. This is the meaning. || 17 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) on this also states in the Vedas: "For the Ṛgveda and so forth... Regarding the term *durbrāhmaṇya* (the state of being a bad Brāhmaṇa):

it means for the sake of avoiding the condition of being a wicked Brāhmaṇa. Since, in the Kali age, those among humans who possess the aforementioned characteristics of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas are not found today, the meaning is "among human Brāhmaṇas. Thus, in the absence of the study of one's own Vedic branch (*svaśākhā*)—which is what is intended by the word "Veda"—there must be the study of that [branch] for the purpose of avoiding the status of a bad Brāhmaṇa.
The meaning is that those alone are human brāhmaṇas, whereas those distinct from them are indeed animal brāhmaṇas. || 17 ||
The five elements, beginning with earth, [are characterized] by supporting, ripening, and drying.
They desire these [beings] through causes or by providing space; yet these are not [the beings'] own causes.

Rāma’s Commentary: Furthermore: "Earth and so forth. All living beings desire—that is, depend upon—the five elements, beginning with earth, for specific reasons or causes known as providing a place, warding off grass, cooking, drying moisture, and providing light.
However, these elements, such as earth and the rest, do not possess the causes or motives such as the desire for a place; therefore, they do not desire [anything] on their own.
Such is the meaning. || 18 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Having thus [discussed] the five elements, he says regarding them as well—beginning with "earth" (bhūmyādi)—verse 18.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now he states the purport of the sentence, "Or rather, it is not for the sake of all that [the world] loves":
"Everyone, such as masters, servants, and so forth, desires [others] for their own benefit."
But no benefit whatsoever has been rendered by this or that [individual] to him. || 19 ||
"Master," etc.: all people, such as servants and others, desire everything, such as a master and so forth, for their own benefit or for their own purpose;
likewise, the master and others [desire their subordinates] in the same way. || 19 ||

Commentary on A0: Regarding the master and so forth, the author likewise states this for all terms in the root text—beginning with "the master" (svāmī). By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the house and other such things are included. || 19 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: for what purpose has such a display of numerous examples been made in the Śruti? Anticipating this, he says:
Thus, one should reflect in this manner upon such [a Self] in all worldly activities, as composed by Vidyāraṇya in the *Pañcadaśī*.
[One should establish one's own mind by means of that abundance of examples known as the bliss of the Self. (20)

"In all worldly dealings" (sarvavyavahṛtiṣu) means in all activities preceded by desire, such as eating and so forth. The remainder of the sense is that, in order to reflect—according to the manner stated in the passage "but everything is dear for the sake of the Self"—this abundance of examples consisting of the demonstration of affection toward husband, wife, and others has been set forth. For that reason, one should dwell upon one's own mind or intellect (mati) which pertains to oneself.
The meaning is that one should act with the realization of one's own self as being most dear, by understanding that everything else is subordinate to it. || 20 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He states the conclusion—“all,” etc. The meaning is that one should cause [the mind] to dwell [there], that is, one should refine it through discernment (viveka). || 20 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that the statement that the Self is the dearest of all because everything is dear as being subordinate to the Self is untenable;

for when one analyzes the nature of affection (*prīti*), affection itself is difficult to define. With this intention, he asks about the essential nature of affection: "Now, what indeed is this affection that is heard of with respect to one's own Self?"
Passion (rāga) is directed toward objects such as a bride; faith (śraddhā) is directed toward rituals such as sacrifice.
Devotion (bhakti) is [the inclination] toward the guru, the deity, and so forth; whereas desire (icchā) is [the inclination] toward an object not yet attained.
Regarding the word "atha" (now/then): the word *atha* signifies a question. What is this love (*prīti*) that is heard to exist toward one's own Self?

Is it of the nature of passion (*rāga*), or of the nature of faith (*śraddhā*), or of the nature of devotion (*bhakti*), or perhaps of the nature of desire (*icchā*)? Regarding the meaning of the word "kiṃ" (what), he states—beginning with "rāga"—that in all four of these positions, it is impossible for love to have everything as its object. [Love] would exist only toward women, wealth, and so forth, and not [toward the Self].

If faith were directed toward sacrifices and the like, it would exist only toward sacrifices and the like, and not toward one's wife and so forth; if devotion were directed toward gurus and the like, it would exist only toward gurus and the like, and not toward others; and if desire were directed only toward objects already attained, it would not have other things as its object. Therefore, the meaning is that affection does not have everything as its object. || 21 ||
Commentary on the half-verse: || 21 ||
— Now, having raised a doubt for the purpose of determining the true nature of *prīti*, he asks: "Now," and so forth.
[Sāra-ṭīkā] — He provides the answer by adopting a position that is distinct from the four aforementioned alternatives: "He says... and so forth.
In that case, let there be a sattvic disposition that follows after happiness.
Even when it is attained or lost, because its true existence persists, it is distinct from desire. || 22 ||

"Let it be so. If that is the case, since joy (*prīti*) cannot possibly consist of passion (*rāga*) and the like, let there be a modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—a modification consisting of the transformation of the quality of *sattva*—which follows after pleasure alone; that is to say, by following pleasure itself, which is "pleasure-only," its object is exclusively pleasure. This is the meaning. [Objection: But then, is not that joy merely desire? Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it: "attained... (as follows).

Thus: desire (*icchā*) has as its object merely pleasure and so forth that have not yet been attained; this [thirst], however, has all things as its object, because it persists even when pleasure and so forth have been attained or have perished. Therefore, it is distinguished—that is, differentiated—from desire. ||22||

Commentary on verse a0: Regarding the word "devotion" (*bhakti*). Thus, since not even one among passion (*rāga*), faith (*śraddhā*), devotion (*bhakti*), or desire (*icchā*) is seen to be capable of being denoted by the term "affection" (*prīti*), he says [in response]: "That" (*sā*). To exclude passion and desire, he specifies it as "pure" (*sāttvikī*). According to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), liberation is the cessation of ignorance (*avidyāstamaya*); for, according to the *Vārttika*, that [liberation], which consists in the destruction of the beginningless superimposed ignorance, has the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) as its [ultimate] nature.

Since the individual self (ātman) is not distinct from the Supreme Brahman, His will is indeed the Self’s own will; and because there is no lack of attainment for that which belongs to the Universal Self, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding His will. To exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to valid knowledge (*pramā*), the term "pleasurable" (*sukha*) is used. By the suffix *-mātra*, pleasures produced by the embrace of a beloved and the like are excluded. Thus, the definition of pleasure (*prīti*) results as: being a modification of the *sāttvika* mind, while having pleasure-in-general as its object. In that regard also—
The intention [of using the term] "citta" is for the purpose of excluding the mental modification of ignorance (avidyāvṛtti) pertaining to deep sleep. || 22 ||
The Twelfth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

435 Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised that since one observes affection for the self just as one does for food and other things which are means to happiness, the self too must be a means to happiness, like food and such.
Food, drink, and so forth are dear because they are the means for attaining pleasure; this is due to the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being a means to happiness. || 23 ||

"Is it happiness? [The answer is: Just as food, drink, and so forth are perceived as dear through the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being means to happiness, the Self also—because it is dear due to its conduciveness—would be equal to food and drink, meaning it would be a means to happiness like food, drink, and the like. || 23 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Even so, in order to refute the desire for pleasure, he himself says: "attained," etc. Now, one might object that food and other such things are indeed objects of affection; to this he replies: "pleasure," etc. || 23 ||
If food and such were equal [to liberation] by virtue of being favorable to the self, then what would be the point of this [spiritual practice] here?
It would have to be made favorable; there can be no single agent for both the action and its subject.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Here, the following inference is indicated: "The self under dispute must be an instrument of happiness because it is dear, like food and so forth. With the intention of refuting this by pointing out that "being an object of enjoyment" (bhogyatva) is the limiting condition (upādhi) in the case of food, drink, and the like, he replies with the words "by this":
"In this world, who could be made agreeable by this agreeable thing [the self] as an instrument of happiness? None at all; for there is nothing other than the self [that could be so made]."
