The meaning is: "because of the absence of an enjoyer. Now, one might object that [the self] should be the one who benefits itself; to this he says: "not in one" (naikasmin).
The meaning is that two properties—being the beneficiary and being the benefactor—are contradictory in the case of a single self at the same time. || 24 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): [The opponent] raises a doubt even in that regard through the inference: "The self is similar to food and so forth, because it is favorable [to the experiencer], like a tiger and such. To this, the proponent asks in order to resolve that doubt as well, beginning with the words "By this...
and so on. That is to say: by this self, which is favorable like food and so forth due to being a means of happiness, who else is there to be made favorable as the enjoyer?

The meaning is that no one at all should be one who is to be gratified. Now, [an objection is raised]: "But surely the enjoyer is also the Self, just as the sun is to its light"; to this he says: "No. || 24 ||
In sensual pleasure there is merely delight, but the Self is exceedingly dear.
This [consciousness] deviates with respect to pleasure, but it does not deviate with respect to the Self.
Rāmatīrtha’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Even if it is not a means to happiness like food and so forth, it could still be subordinate to the enjoyer, just as happiness is.
Anticipating this, he refutes it by stating that the Self is the object of unsurpassed love, and thus it is not so: "In happiness...

In the case of sensual happiness—that which is produced by sense objects—there is merely affection, not unsurpassed love. The Self, however, is exceedingly dear and is the object of unsurpassed love. Therefore, [it is not subordinate].
The meaning is that it is equivalent to the pleasure produced by sense objects. He then states the justification for both cases: "It deviates with respect to pleasure.
This joy arising in relation to sensual pleasure (*vaiṣayika-sukha*) is subject to deviation; sometimes it moves toward another pleasure and does not remain fixed exclusively in that one.
However, the joy existing in the Self (*ātman*) is not subject to deviation; it does not go toward other objects. Therefore, [it is eternal].
The meaning is that it is superior by way of excellence. || 25 ||

Furthermore, he states that there is also a disparity between the pleasure derived from sense objects and self-satisfaction—namely, "In pleasure... The reason for this is: "because it deviates in the case of pleasure. (25)
Having abandoned one thing, it always takes up another sensual pleasure.

"The Self is neither to be abandoned nor to be acquired; how could one deviate from it? (26) Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He demonstrates the deviation of affection directed toward objects of pleasure with the verse beginning "One... (ekaṃ). He shows the absence of such [deviation] regarding the Self with the verse beginning "The Self...
(nātmā). The meaning is that [the Self] is unfit [for such fluctuation]. He states the conclusion with the words "In that... (tasmin). (26)
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya [with the commentary named *Ātmānanda*:
explaining both of those in sequence, beginning with "one," such as "the pleasure of Devadatta"].
The purposeful [is established]. || 26 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: One might raise the objection: "Even if the Self is devoid of being an object of rejection or acquisition, why could it not be an object of indifference, like grass and such?"—this is the doubt expressed in:
"If there is indifference toward this [Self] which is devoid of rejection and acquisition, as toward grass and the like..."
Because equanimity is the very nature of the one who is equanimous, the self cannot be an object of equanimity.

"Abandonment" (*hāna*) means relinquishment; "appropriation" (*ādāna*) means acceptance; "indifference" (*upekṣā*) means neutrality. With the intention that, just as the Self is not an object of abandonment and so forth, it is also impossible for it to be an object of indifference because it is unfit [for such treatment], he refutes [the objection] with the words: "of the one who is indifferent" (*upekṣituḥ*).
For the innate Self—the imperishable nature—of the one who is indifferent, the one who performs indifference, since it is his very own nature, is distinct from himself...
The ellipsis implies that there is no state of being worthy of indifference, nor the status of being an object of indifference, as in the case of empty grass and the like. || 27 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Even there, he raises an objection with the words "hāna" (loss), etc., and provides the resolution with the words "upekṣituḥ" (of the indifferent one). || 27 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "It was stated that the Self is not an object of abandonment, but this is untenable because we observe that it is sometimes abandoned out of hatred.
He anticipates this by stating: "In some cases, the desire for death is observed among those overcome by disease and anger."
If it is argued that the self must therefore be abandoned due to hatred, that is not so.

Regarding the word "disease": the remainder of the argument is that if it were said, "Since a desire for death is observed, then because hatred toward the self arises from that, the self too should be abandoned—just like a scorpion or similar [creature]," he refutes this by stating, "That is not so," because such abandonment has as its object the body, which is distinct from the self. || 28 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Even there, he raises an objection with the words "roga" (disease) etc. "Mumūrṣā" means the desire to die. The proponent refutes that [objection] along with its restatement by means of the remainder of the verse beginning with "iti" etc. || 28 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Regarding the phrase "to abandon"—the body, which is fit and appropriate to be abandoned or cast off, does not possess the nature of the Self.
To the question, "To whom then does that [nature] belong?", he says:
"The body, which is fit to be abandoned, does not have the nature of the Self; rather, it belongs to the abandoner alone."
Hatred does not reside in the one who abandons; rather, what harm is there in the object that is to be abandoned? || 29 ||

Regarding the term *tyaktuḥ*: the meaning is that for the *jīva*—who is distinct from the body and is the agent of abandoning the body—that [body] is the self (*ātmatā*). One might object: "Let it be that the abandoner is the self; what follows from this? To this he says: "Not of the abandoner. The intention is that, therefore, the self cannot be something to be abandoned. Anticipating the objection that while there may be no hatred toward the self, it is certainly perceived in the body, he says: "In the abandonable," etc. In the abandonable...
Even if there is hatred toward the body as an object of experience, what loss is there for me, who maintains that the self does not perish? This is the implied meaning. || 29 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) explains that: "It has been abandoned" || 29 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Thus, having demonstrated that the Self is the most beloved by examining the purport of the scriptural passage beginning with "Verily, not for the sake of the husband" and ending with "but for the sake of the Self everything is dear," he now demonstrates it through reasoning as well:
"Because everything exists for the sake of the Self, and because all affection is directed toward it, the Self is indeed supremely dear."
Just as a son is dearer than other sons and friends, so too is Siddha. || 30 ||
"Self": because everything accompanied by pleasure, as well as the collection of its means such as husband, wife, and so forth, exists for the sake of the self.
[Page 435] Chapter Twelve.
Accompanied by two commentaries:
Since pleasure is dear because it is an agent [of satisfaction], it is established that the self is itself the recipient of benefit and is exceedingly dear. This very point—

He clarifies this by demonstrating an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as). Just as in the world, from a person such as Yajñadatta—who is an object of affection for a father like Viṣṇudatta through his son, who is himself a friend to that father—the son, such as Devadatta, becomes even more beloved than him because he is an object of affection without any mediation; in the same way, [the Self] is itself more beloved than everything else that is an object of affection by virtue of being related to oneself.
The meaning is that it comes to be. || 30 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) concludes the established conclusion with the words "the Self" (ātmeti). Therein, it clarifies the illustration with the remainder of the verse beginning with "just as" (yathā). || 30 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Thus, having established through scripture and reasoning this unsurpassed love for the Self, he confirms it by demonstrating his own experience:
"May I not cease to exist, but rather may I continue to be forever."
Since the fulfillment of every wish is observed, joy is directly perceived within oneself.

"May I not cease to be"—that is, "may it not be that I do not exist"; let there be no absence of my self-existence anywhere, but rather, "may I always be, may my existence always persist. Such a benediction or prayer is observed to belong to every class of living beings;
the meaning is that everyone prays in this very way. He states the conclusion: "Because it is thus prayed for by all, therefore [with regard to] the Self..."
The meaning is that unsurpassed joy is established through direct perception. || 31 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) on a0: It demonstrates that very state of extreme endearment through dramatic gesture (sābhinaya), saying "May I not cease to exist," which is a prayerful desire (āśī-manoratha). It concludes with the words beginning with "iti" and so forth. || 31 ||
Rāmānuja’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Preceded by a recapitulation of what has occurred, he restates another view in order to refute it, with the words:
"When [devotion] has been thus established in the Self through these three verses beginning with 'ityādi'..."
Some have asserted that the self exists as subordinate to one's sons, wife, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "by these and so forth": the word *iti* refers to direct experience (*anubhava*). The word *ādi* (and so forth) includes reasoning (*yukti*) and scripture (*śruti*).

Thus, by means of these three authorities—namely, experience, reasoning, and scripture—in the manner described, although love for the Self has been established, some who are ignorant of the intended meaning of the scriptures and other sources have asserted that the Self is subordinate to one's son, wife, and others, and that one is merely an accessory (*upasarjana*) in relation to them.
Beneficial. || 32 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): What follows from that? He says: "By these [verses]," referring to the three beginning with "ityādibhiḥ. Because such scriptural passages as, "Indeed, O Maitreyī, it is not for the sake of the husband that the husband is dear, but for the sake of the Self that the husband is dear," are established through reasoning, there exists a twofold means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consisting of both scripture (*śruti*) and reasoning (*yukti*), like the confluence of the waters of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā at Prayāga—the king of holy places (*tīrtharāja*). Furthermore, there is the third, namely, direct experience (*anubhūti*), which was mentioned in the preceding verse.
The meaning is: by means of the three combined measures of knowledge. || 32 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: From what is this understood? To this he says:
"With this intention, the status of being the primary self was declared by the Śruti with regard to the son."
"The self indeed is called 'son'"; this is clearly stated in the Upanishad. (33)

"Regarding this [statement]: 'This'—the meaning is that with the very intention of expressing this, certain [teachers] have interpreted it; and with the aim of making this manifest through such scriptural passages as "The self (ātman), indeed, is the name of the son," the status of the son as the primary self has been declared.

Furthermore, the remainder [of the sentence] implies that this primary status of the son as the self is clearly and explicitly stated in the Upaniṣads, such as the Aitareya Upaniṣad and others. || 33 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 436] 438.

[Regarding the commentary on the verse titled *Ātmānanda*: Now, one might ask: how can the subordination of the self to sons and others—which contradicts the three aforementioned means of valid knowledge—be asserted by them? To this, he says: "This... The meaning is: with the desire to restate the opinion of certain thinkers who have been introduced. This is declared in the Śruti: "The self, indeed, was named 'son' (*putra*). (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.2).

The ellipsis implies that this has been stated by such scriptural passages as these. The meaning is that it is made clear in the Upaniṣad; that is, it is elaborated upon in the Aitareya Upaniṣad. || 33 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In response to the inquiry as to by which statement [this is said], he recites that statement according to its meaning:
"This self of his is assigned for the sake of meritorious deeds."
Then his other self, having accomplished its purpose, passes away.

Regarding the phrase "so 'sya" (that belongs to him): in the beginning of the context—specifically in the passage, "This person, indeed, becomes an embryo in his father"—it is stated that he exists as an embryo within the person, that is, the body. Furthermore, in the passage, "He, even before [birth], brings the boy to existence at the very outset of birth," it is stated that the Self in the form of a son, who is to be protected with special care, is placed as a representative for the performance of meritorious deeds (*puṇya-karman*). He is established as a substitute for those meritorious actions.

"He is being burned," is the ellipsis. Then, immediately after that, this other [person]—distinct from the son and currently visible before one's eyes—the father’s self in the form of a father, seized by old age, having himself accomplished all duties (*kṛtakṛtya*) and completed the multitude of tasks to be performed, "passes away," meaning he dies. || 34 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, he briefly summarizes the meaning of the aforementioned Upaniṣadic statement: "So 'syāyam" (This is his...).

The meaning is that this person, who was previously introduced in the passage, "Verily, from the very beginning, this [soul] becomes an embryo in the father," is "this" one perceived directly in the form of a son. He is placed as a representative for the sake of meritorious deeds—that is, for the performance of good works—acting as a deputy in the matter of their execution.

That is to say, it is so ordained. Then, immediately thereafter, this perceptible other self of his, consisting of the body, having fulfilled its purpose and having fully experienced the fruits of the karma already commenced, passes away—that is to say, dies. || 34 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: To strengthen the aforementioned point, he states the meaning of the sentence "There is no world for one without a son," which demonstrates the absence of the next world for one who lacks a son:
"Even though the Self exists, there is no world for one without a son; therefore indeed [this is so]."
The wise declare that only a son who has been duly instructed is truly of this world. || 35 ||

"Even though [he exists]" means: since the son possesses the primary nature of the self (*ātmatva*), therefore, even though the self—one's own—is present and existing, the world—the next world—does not belong to a father who is sonless, i.e., devoid of a son; for this is well-known in the *Purāṇas* and other texts.

He states the meaning of the sentence, "They say a son who has been instructed is conducive to the world," which establishes through the method of agreement (*anvaya*) the same point that was stated by way of contrast (*vyatireka*).

Regarding the word *anuśiṣṭam*: the wise (*manīṣiṇaḥ*), those who are proficient in the meaning of the scriptures, say that the son who has been instructed—that is, taught by means of the mantras to be mentioned hereafter, beginning with "Thou art Brahman"—is *lokya*, meaning beneficial for the world, a means for attaining the next world. This is the sense. || 35 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He connects by way of meaning even that Vedic scripture which supports the aforementioned favoring [of the son], namely, "There is no world for one who has no son" (*nāputrasya loko'sti*). Furthermore, he corroborates here the statement from the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa*, "They say that a son who has been thus instructed is worthy of the world" (*anuśiṣṭam... lokyam āhuḥ*), with the words "instructed" (*anuśiṣṭam*). || 35 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, with the intent of demonstrating that even worldly happiness has its cause in a son, he recites in substance the Vedic statement: "This world of men is to be conquered by a son alone, and not by any other ritual act.
manuṣyaloko jayyaḥ syātputreṇaivetareṇa no |
One who is about to die should address his son with the mantras beginning with "You are Brahman."

Regarding "the world of men": the happiness of the human world can only be won and accomplished through a son; it cannot be achieved by any other means such as ritual acts (*karma*) and the like. The sense is that for one who is childless, even the means of happiness, such as wealth and so forth, become sources of disillusionment.
The Twelfth Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

In the verse beginning with "the son instructed for the sake of the world" (*anuśiṣṭaṃ putraṃ lokyam*), the instruction of the son has been stated; now, [the author] shows the occasion for that and its mantras by saying "one about to die" (*mumūrṣuḥ*).

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the two mantras "Thou art the sacrifice, thou art the world" (*tvaṃ yajñastvaṃ lokaḥ*) are included. The meaning is that at the time of death, the father, being about to die, should address the son with these three mantras beginning with "Thou art Brahman" (*ebhistvaṃ brahmetyādibhiḥ*); that is, he should perform the instruction of the son. || 36 ||
Commentary (a0): Similarly, this world of humans is to be conquered by a son alone; thus he cites the Kaṇva Śruti as well—beginning with "manuṣya...

In the preceding verse, the instruction for the son was mentioned; he now prescribes the manner of that [instruction] with the words "mumūrṣuḥ" (one about to die). By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the two mantras "tvaṃ yajñaḥ" and "tvaṃ lokaḥ" are included. || 36 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He concludes the stated point with the words "ityādi":
Thus, the Śrutis declare that [the self] is subordinate to the son, wife, and so forth.
Even worldly people acknowledge the preeminence of a son. || 37 ||
Regarding the phrase "and so forth": he states that this matter is not only established by scripture but is also well-known in the world, saying: "The worldly people... (verse 37).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): He concludes with the words "ityādi" (and so forth). By the word "ādi," [the author includes] such passages as "with offspring for the ancestors.

Regarding "wife and so forth": it is established by scripture that "this wife is indeed half of one's own self. Here too, by the word "ādi," [the author includes] the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so on. 37.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He establishes that very point:
"Just as even when one has died, a son or other relative may live by means of wealth and so forth,"
In that very same way, the principal sons and others then exert effort.

Regarding the phrase "in oneself": by the first "self," one's father and others are included; by the second, the wife and others are meant. He states the reason for this: "they are primary. Because one endures personal exertion even to provide the means of livelihood for one's son and others, therefore they—the son and others—are "primary," meaning they are the most important. || 38 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): For this very reason—"in oneself"—the words "Devadatta acts" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. The proponent of the previous argument states the conclusion with the words beginning "primary," and so forth. || 38 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Thus, he acknowledges the primacy of sons and others as demonstrated by both worldly custom and scriptural authority:
"Certainly; yet even by this much, the Self does not become subordinate to anything else."
This self is threefold, through the distinctions of the secondary, the false, and the primary. (39)
"So be it. Anticipating the objection that this would contradict the demonstration of the Self's status as the "remnant" (śeṣin), he says: "By this much...

He means: by this much—that there is a certain primacy in the son and so forth—it is not established by mere assertion; rather, in whatever worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) the selfhood of whichever thing is intended to be expressed, that very thing is seen to possess primacy therein.

As an introduction to the main subject, he states the threefold nature of the self—beginning with the word "gauṇa": The self is threefold, consisting of the secondary self (gauṇātman), the illusory self (mithyātman), and the primary self (mukhyātman). || 39 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), in order to provide a resolution, partially accepts [the opponent's position] by saying "Certainly" (vāḍham). "The remainder" (śeṣa) is the subordinate element (upasarjana). He explains its nature with the words beginning "gauṇa" (secondary), etc. || 39 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: In that regard, in order to demonstrate the figurative nature of the selfhood attributed to sons and the like, he cites a figurative usage found in common worldly experience:
"This Devadatta is a lion"—the identity between these two is figurative because their difference is clearly perceived; likewise is the selfhood attributed to sons and the like. (40)
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [page 438] 440.

[The example is] "Devadatta, who is called Ātmānanda. As for this identity between Devadatta and a lion—namely, "This Devadatta is a lion"—that is secondary (gauṇa) or metaphorical (aupacārika). He states the reason for that with the words "of these two" (etayoḥ). He applies this to the case under discussion (the *dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "of the son, etc. (putrādeḥ). || 40 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "Granted that the self is thus threefold—primary, secondary (gauṇa), and so forth—but what follows from this in the present context? To this he says: "But Devadatta... [and so on]. "Secondary" means produced by qualities such as cruelty. The meaning is: "of these two," namely, Devadatta and the lion mentioned in the sentence under discussion. As for the question "Why is it not primary?", he replies with the words beginning "Because of the difference... He applies this to the subject at hand with the words "Of the son, etc."
By the word "etcetera," the wife [is included]. || 40 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Next, he demonstrates the false self:
"There is a distinction within the five sheaths, yet that Witness does not appear as such."
Therefore, the sheaths are of a false nature, just as the trunk [is falsely perceived] as being a man.

Regarding the word "difference": although a difference exists between the Witness and the five sheaths—ranging from the *ānandamaya* at the beginning to the *annamaya* at the end—that difference does not manifest; thus, their nature is false. To illustrate this falsity, he provides an example: "of the trunk... [as in the verse].
Thus, the meaning is that just as the nature of being a thief in a post—which is actually terrified by a thief—is false, so it is in this case. || 41 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, he describes the false self (*mithyātmā*) which follows in sequence, beginning with the words "the distinction" (*bheda*). The connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: for the aforementioned reasons, even the five [entities] beginning with the body—which are grasped by the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of a Brahmin who repeatedly performs *prāṇāyāma* upon the sheaths (*kośa*), thinking "I am happy"—possess only the nature of a false self. He provides an illustration for this with the remainder of the verse, beginning with "of the post" (*sthāṇoḥ*). || 41 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus established the secondary and false selves, he now establishes that the Witness is the primary Self:
"No difference appears, nor does it exist, for the Witness has no counter-correlate."
Because it is the innermost of all, that alone is accepted as the primary Self. || 42 ||

"It does not appear as distinct": why does no distinction from anything whatsoever appear for the Witness—the Self whose nature is witnessing—just as [no distinction appears] from the secondary self such as a son? Furthermore, there is no distinction from false selves such as the body; the reason for both cases is "because it has no counter-correlate" (*apratiyoginaḥ*). This is a qualifying attribute containing a reason: because of its state of having no counter-correlate, whereas for things such as a son or a body, one's own self exists as their counter-correlate, but for the Reality itself, this is not so.

The sense is that there exists no real entity (*bhūta*) that could serve as a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), because everything, including the body and so forth, is superimposed. Now, one might object: "Granted that the Witness (*sākṣin*) may not possess secondary or illusory falsity due to the absence of difference, but from what source does its primary status as the Self (*ātmatva*) arise? To this he says: "Because of being internal to all. Because the innermost Self (*pratīc*), the Witness of all, is perceived as being more internal than everything—such as the body, son, and so forth—it is the Witness alone whose status as the Self is primary and absolute.

The term *pacārika* means that it is intended or accepted. Here, the following inference is indicated: "The witness under discussion must be the primary Self (mukhyātman), because he is the innermost of all (*sarvāntaratvāt*). Whatever is not the primary Self is not the innermost of all, such as the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth.
This is a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekī*). || 42 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if it is argued that the primary Self (mukhyātman) must likewise be described, [the author replies: although it has been indicated immediately following [the previous verse], it is not understood by the deluded; therefore, he establishes it explicitly with the words "it does not appear" (na bhāti). The connection is as follows: in the Witness (sākṣin), just as in Devadatta [there is no distinction from the lion], even the empirical (vyāvahārika) difference of any object does not appear, nor is there [such a difference] as exists between the five sheaths (pañcakośa). In this regard, the reason is...

While speaking of that [non-difference], he qualifies it as "non-apprehension" (*apratīti*). This is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of "being the correlate" (*anuyogitva*). Thus, if all things such as jars and the like—this duality (*dvaita*)—were to appear as distinct from the self-luminous Witness (*sākṣin*), then a difference having that [duality] as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) might indeed appear in the Witness, who is the correlate (*anuyogin*);

likewise, a difference having the Witness as its counter-correlate might appear even in that visible object (*dṛśya*) which is the correlate. However, because that [difference] is imagined (*kalpita*) like silver and so forth, it is non-existent.

The sense is that, just as in the case of [an abstract noun] ending in *ktvā* and so forth, there is no manifestation or the like as something distinct from the witness (*sākṣin*) which serves as its substrate; thus, this [object] is simply non-existent as a counter-correlate (*apratiyogin*).
[End of] the Twelfth Chapter.
He states the conclusion:
"All," etc. Accordingly, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The subject under dispute is the Witness alone as the primary Self, because He is the innermost of all.
The intention is that, because of the absence [of the probans] in all things that are perceptible, it is a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*). || 42 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Let it be that there are three types of self; however, what follows from this regarding the statement that the son and others are the "residuum" (śeṣin)? To this he says:
"While this is so, in whatever worldly transactions a particular thing is appropriately regarded as the 'self'..."
Among those, that alone is the principal (śeṣin), while everything else is subordinate (śeṣa). || 43 ||

"Even so," it is said. Even though this threefold nature of the Self exists, among those specific worldly and Vedic activities—such as protecting, nourishing, and the contemplation of the identity with Brahman—it is appropriate that the status of the Self belongs to whichever is the case: the son and so forth, the body and so forth, or the Witness.

Among those [activities], that son and so forth, the body and so forth, or the Witness possesses the status of the "residue" (śeṣin), meaning primacy; while everything else distinct from that possesses the status of being the "subsidiary" (śeṣa).
The ellipsis is that it becomes subordinate (pāratantrya). || 43 ||
a0 ṭī0—What follows from that? He says: "This being so," etc. *Śeṣitva* means the state of being the principal (*aṅgin*); *śeṣatva* means the state of being a subordinate member (*aṅga*). ||43||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He elaborates on this very point:
For one desiring to die, the secondary self alone is useful for protecting the house and so forth.
Therefore, the son is neither the primary self nor the false self; he is the residual self. || 44 ||

By means of the five verses beginning with "of one about to die" (*mumūrṣoḥ*), [the author] explains that in specific rituals such as the protection of the household, it is only the secondary self (*gauṇātman*)—in the form of sons, wife, and so forth—that is employed, that is, becomes useful. The meaning is that this is because of the desire to live (*jijīviṣutva*) for the sake of what follows. The primary self (*mukhyātman*) is not employed because it is changeless (*avikāritva*); nor is the illusory self (*mithyātman*) employed because it is oriented toward death. This is the intended sense. He states the conclusion: "The son," etc.
This is clear. || 44 ||
a0 Commentary: He states that very arrangement with the words "of one about to die," and so forth. || 44 ||
Rāghava’s Commentary: Although the aforementioned worldly practices such as guarding one's home exist, he provides an illustration regarding the acceptance of sons and others within oneself:
"In the case of 'the student is fire,' the fire, though present, is not grasped."
Because of its lack of fitness, it is precisely the opposite of fitness that is understood here. || 45 ||

"Let him study" (*adhyetu*). In this usage, "Let him study the fire" (*vahnim adhyetu*), although the actual fire exists in its own form, it is not grasped as the meaning of the word "fire," because it is impossible for fire to be a student. Rather, the meaning is that only the boy (*baṭu*) or youth (*māṇavaka*), who is fit for the state of being a student, is grasped here as the meaning of the word "fire" due to his fitness (*yogyatva*). || 45 ||

Commentary (a0): "Let him study..."—the intention is that this serves as an illustration for the inclusion of the son known as the *nirukta-gauṇātman* (the figurative self derived from verbal derivation). || 45 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Having thus illustrated the instance where the secondary self (the body) is predominant, he now illustrates the instance where the false self is predominant:
"I am thin; I shall become nourished"—in such cases, the identification of the body with the self is appropriate.
In this matter, he does not appoint his son to the consumption of food intended for nourishment.

Regarding the phrase "I am emaciated": in worldly discourse such as, "I have become emaciated; therefore, I shall achieve nourishment by eating food and so forth," it is appropriate to grasp the body—which is fit for consuming food—as the self. He strengthens the aforementioned point by demonstrating worldly usage with the words "not the son" (na putram). || 46 ||
— Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): "I am emaciated. || 46 ||
In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[in the section titled] *Ātmānanda*, it is appropriate to regard the agent as the Self in such [thoughts] as, "By means of austerity, I shall attain heaven," and so forth.
Then, disregarding his body and its enjoyments, he should perform the Kṛcchra and other such penances.

Rāghava’s Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the verse beginning with "tapasā" (by austerity): when one engages in such worldly discourse as "I shall attain heaven by performing austerity," then it is appropriate that the nature of the self belongs only to the "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*), which is denoted by the term "agent," and not to the body and so forth. He establishes this very point with the word "anapekṣya" (without dependence): since it is not appropriate for the body to be the self, therefore, preceded by the renunciation of bodily enjoyments—
The meaning is that he performs the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such penances which are beneficial to the agent. || 47 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding the words "tapasā" and "vapuḥ": the meaning is the enjoyment of the body by means of garlands, sandalwood paste, women, and so forth. || 47 ||
At that time, the person is rightly characterized as having consciousness as their very self in the thought, "I shall be liberated."
One knows that through the teacher and the scriptures, yet one does not desire to do anything at all.

Rāma’s Commentary: Furthermore: "I shall be liberated. When a person, having cultivated tranquility and the other [disciplines], forms the thought, "I shall attain liberation," then—through the immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) produced by the investigation into the meaning of the words of the teacher's instruction, which arises from both the Guru and the Śāstra—he realizes the conscious Self (*cidātmā*) thus:

"I am not the agent and so forth; I am Brahman, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*). For such a one, it is only appropriate that he be of the nature of the conscious Self, not [the nature of the non-conscious].

The meaning is that [the Self] possesses the nature of being the agent and so forth in that context; however, this is not so, because of such scriptural passages as: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," "Brahman is Consciousness and Bliss," and "Without interior or exterior, the whole is a mass of pure consciousness alone. || 48 ||
a0 ṭī0 – "I shall be liberated" (mokṣye'ham). "Consciousness" (ciditi) means the state of being the primary Self known as the self-luminous witness (sākṣin).
rā0 ṭīkā – He provides an illustration for the predominance of the three types of selves mentioned above, established according to their specific functions in various worldly dealings:
Just as Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others [perform] the Bṛhaspatisava and other such rites.
Likewise, the secondary, the false, and the primary [meanings] abide as is appropriate. (49)
Regarding the term *vipra*: just as in the injunction "A Brāhmaṇa shall sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," only a Brāhmaṇa has the qualification (*adhikāra*), not a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya;

and in "A King shall sacrifice with the Rājasūya," only a King has the qualification, not a Brāhmaṇa or a Vaiśya; and in "A Vaiśya shall sacrifice with the Vaiśyastoma," only a Vaiśya has the qualification, not the others—likewise, for the selves (ātman) which are distinguished as primary and secondary or real and false, [the qualification] is according to what is appropriate for each.
The sense is that [this] holds primacy among conventional usages. || 49 ||

The commentary on verse a concludes by stating: "He fears," etc. The meaning is that this is based on such Vedic injunctions as, "A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," and "A King should sacrifice with the Rājasūya. The word "himself" (ātmanaḥ) is to be supplied. || 49 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the conclusion:
"In each of those appropriate cases, there is an exceeding love for the Self alone."
But when that [pleasure] remains in what is not-self, there is joy; elsewhere, neither exists. || 50 ||

Regarding the phrase "there, there": in whichever transaction whatever self is appropriate, in each such transaction, toward that very self which is appropriate—that is, primary by virtue of its utility—there is an excessive, surpassing affection (*prīti*). Toward what remains of it—that is, toward the non-self, the remaining entity distinct from that self—there is merely affection; the meaning is that it is not an unsurpassed love.
The meaning is that elsewhere—in any object other than the Self or what pertains to the Self—there is neither [of these two], nor even both kinds of love. || 50 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, he establishes even such affection as is appropriate, stating "there, there" (*tatra tatra*). "In that" means in the Self—the primary Self alone—which is the remainder of that [affection]; thus, it refers to the aforementioned worldly activities such as protecting the house, which are its limbs. The construction is: both types of affection and so forth exist in those two cases, but they do not exist at all—indeed, they are absent—in other cases, namely where the status of being the principal member (*aṅgin*) and so on is lacking. || 50 ||
The Twelfth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Regarding the phrase "elsewhere neither," he states the internal subdivisions of the meaning of the word "elsewhere" as previously mentioned:
"The other is twofold—negligible and hateful, such as road-grass and the like."
That which is to be disregarded, such as tigers, snakes, and so forth, and that which is to be hated—thus [the objects of the senses] are of four kinds. 51.

Regarding the term "to be disregarded" (*upekṣyam*): any other object that has become indifferent is the object of disregard (*upekṣā-viṣaya*), while that which is hateful is the object of hatred (*dveṣa-viṣaya*). Thus, it is of two kinds. He illustrates both of these with the verse beginning "On the path" (*mārga*). The meaning is that grass, clods of earth, and so forth encountered on the path are objects of disregard, whereas a tiger or similar creature that causes one's own affliction is an object of hatred. He states the conclusion with the word "Thus" (*evam*). || 11 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: what is that other thing which is devoid of agency (*aṅgitva*) and so forth, and is the non-self (*anātman*)? To this he says: "It is to be disregarded" (*upekṣyam*). He concludes with the remainder of the verse beginning with "thus" (*evam*); the meaning is "the entire collection of objects. || 51 ||
The commentary on Rāma (Rā0 ṭīkā) demonstrates this very fourfold nature:
"The self, the remainder, that which is to be disregarded, and that which is to be hated—thus among these four..."
There is no restriction to specific individuals; rather, it occurs in such and such a manner according to their respective effects.
[The opponent asks: "But is the state of being most dear and so forth fixed for all four, beginning with the self? [The author] says "No"—"even among the four.
The meaning is that there is no fixed rule such as, "this alone is the most dear," "this alone is dear," "this alone is to be neglected," or "this alone is to be hated, and nothing else.
If one asks, "What then? he says: "But rather..."—that is, in such and such a way, according to those specific effects consisting of assistance and so forth.
The meaning is: "having the form of the beloved and so forth. || 52 ||

1. Commentary: He clarifies this with the words "The Self," etc. Now, one might object: "Granted that this is so, yet since the Witness (sākṣin) is the innermost of all, it is the primary Self and thus the most beloved; however, is there a fixed rule regarding the manifestation of the limbs and so forth for the remaining three? Is it that this one alone is the limb and this one alone is the secondary part? [End of fragment]
To show that this [person] is to be hated as a specific individual, he says "iti" and so forth in the remainder of the verse. || 52 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: To demonstrate the absence of such a restrictive rule even in the case of a well-known object of hatred, namely a tiger, he says: "A tiger may indeed be hateful when facing one, but it is to be desired when turned away."
And because it is favorable for nurturing, it is understood that its purpose is for amusement; this is the remainder [of the sense]. || 53 ||

It may be so. When a tiger approaches face-to-face to devour him, he becomes an object of hatred; when that same tiger turns its back and departs, he becomes an object of indifference; and if that very same tiger becomes favorable through being petted, then it becomes a means of diversion—meaning, as a supplement to the verse, it attains the state of being dear due to its utility to oneself. Such is the general sense. 53.

The commentary (ṭīkā) provides an illustration of that with the words "syāt" (it may be). [It refers to] the state of being a subordinate member (śeṣatām), that is, the state of being an auxiliary (aṅgatām). || 53 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that if a single entity is admitted to possess all three attributes—dearness and so forth—there would be no systematic order in worldly transactions; anticipating this, he says:
"Let there be no restriction regarding individual instances, but there is a fixed rule concerning their definitions."
Favorability, unfavorability, and the absence of both are the defining characteristics. || 54 ||
"Of individuals" means that even in the absence of a restriction regarding specific individuals, a determination will occur by virtue of their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
When the question arises as to what that characteristic is, he states its definition: "Favorability. Favorableness is the characteristic—that is, the distinguishing attribute—of one who is dear;
unfavorableness is the characteristic of one who is hateful; and the absence of both favorableness and unfavorableness is the characteristic of one who is indifferent.
This is the meaning. || 54 ||
