[The commentary on the *Ātmānanda* (A0 Ṭīkā) states: Having accepted this, he asks about the characteristics of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) and so forth—namely, "of individuals. He summarizes that: "favourability," etc.; by implication, this refers to those who are respectively "to be served" (*śeṣa*), "hated" (*dveṣya*), and "indifferent" (*upekṣya*). (54)
— Rāghavendra’s Commentary — Having established the meaning through this much of the textual context, he states it concisely for the sake of intellectual clarity:
"The Self is the most beloved; everything else is dear as being subordinate to It; aversion and indifference pertain to those other than these."
Thus is the world established, and such is the doctrine of Yājñavalkya.

"Self" (ātman): the Self is the inward bliss (pratyagānanda). "Dearest" (preyān) means exceedingly dear. "Remnant" (śeṣa) refers to an object that has become subordinate to oneself; this is "dear. Regarding the two others—namely, those other than the Self and the remnant—there arise, respectively, aversion and indifference toward things such as a tiger and grass encountered on the path. Thus, the world is established and reaches its settled state through these fourfold categories. [This concludes] the fourfold manner described above.
The intention is that nothing exists apart from this. This is the meaning. He says, "O Yājñavalkya," to show that even what is intended by the Śruti is so;

the meaning is that whatever constitutes the state of being most dear and so forth regarding the Self and other things, that is the view of Yājñavalkya, and it is also approved by Yājñavalkya himself. || 55 ||
The commentary on verse a0 states the conclusion: "The Self," etc. || 55 ||

Rāmatīrtha’s Commentary: With the intention of showing that the self's status as the dearest is not stated only in the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa, but also in the Puruṣavidha-brāhmaṇa, he summarizes the meaning of that passage:
"Elsewhere too, the Śruti declares [the self to be dearer] than sons, wealth, and likewise other things."
This very reality is more intimate than everything else; let it be desired as dearer than all else.

"In another place as well": the meaning is that by the statement, "This Self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than everything else—this Self which is more internal," the fact that the reality of the Self is the most beloved of all things, including sons, wealth, and so forth, because it is more internal, has been declared. || 56 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, in order to state that the fact of the Self being the object of supreme love has been declared even in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad itself—specifically in the passage: "This very Self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than everything else, for it is more internal"—the author summarizes that very statement according to its meaning with the words: "In another place also... (56).
Rāma’s Commentary: Let it be that this is stated in the Śruti; what relevance does this have to the present topic? To this he says:
"By the scriptural perspective of inquiry, this Self is indeed the Witness, and not anything else."
Having analyzed the five sheaths, the vision of the inner reality is discernment.

Regarding the term "śrautyā" (based on scripture): the meaning is that through the perspective of inquiry, which consists of reflecting upon the meaning of the scriptures, the status of being the primary Self belongs to the Witness alone, and not to others such as sons and so forth. He states the nature of what was described as the "perspective of inquiry" with the words "the sheaths": having distinguished the five sheaths—beginning with the one consisting of food—from the Self according to the method taught in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, the experience of the Self abiding within is [the result of] inquiry.
The meaning is "no. || 57 ||
Commentary (a0): What follows from that? He says: "By the Vedic [text]," etc. (57).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He now describes the very manner in which an object situated within is perceived:
"The appearance of the coming and going of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep."
For this very reason, this Self consists of self-luminous consciousness. || 58 ||

By the words beginning with "jāgara" (waking), the meaning is as follows: since the manifestation of the attainment of each successive state and the cessation of each preceding state among the states such as waking occurs from the Witness, whose nature is eternal consciousness, that Self is of the nature of self-luminous consciousness. || 58 ||
The Twelfth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

Commentary on 445a: Now, let it be granted that through the discrimination of the five sheaths (pañcakośaviveka), by means of the vision of inquiry born of scripture characterized by the perception of the inner reality, there is a determination of extreme affection for the witnessing Self alone; nevertheless, what is this very [Self]? To this he says: "In waking... (jāgareti). || 58 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He elaborates upon the meaning of the Vedic text stated in brief:
"The remaining [objects], beginning with the vital breath (prāṇa) and ending with wealth (vitta), are proximate according to their relative gradation."
Likewise, a gradation of joy is observed among all of them. || 59 ||

"Regarding the word 'the rest' (*śeṣā*): the objects yet to be mentioned, beginning with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and ending with wealth (*vitta*), which are distinct from the witness (*sākṣin*), exist in proximity to the Self according to their relative degree of closeness. He states the reasoning for this: "affection" (*prīti*). Just as there is a gradation of degrees [of proximity], so too, because of that very gradation among those [objects] such as the vital breath and so on, affection is experienced by everyone; this is the implied meaning. (59)
Commentary (a0): Even so, who are those remaining? To this he says: "The remaining ones. This means those who are near or close by. ||59||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He clarifies the experience of affection according to its degrees:
"A son is dearer than wealth; a grandson is dearer than a son; and likewise, a sense organ is dearer than a grandson."
The vital breath is dearer than the senses, and the Supreme Self is dearer than the vital breath.

"From wealth," etc. "Piṇḍa" refers to the body composed of food. This is the underlying idea: for the sake of averting calamities such as those befalling sons and others, living beings spend their wealth; sometimes even a son or other relative is given away for the protection of one's own body; to prevent the destruction of the senses, physical pain through beating and the like is endured; and when death is imminent, to avoid it, even the impairment of the senses is accepted. Therefore...

That each subsequent thing is more dear than the preceding one is established by the experience of everyone; however, that the Self is the object of unsurpassed love is established by the experience of the wise. || 60 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) on that very point says: "From wealth," etc. (verse 60).

Rāma’s Commentary: Although the fact that the Self is the dearest of all is thus established by proof, the author states that the Vedic scripture has shown the disagreement between the enlightened and the ignorant in order to dispel their conflicting views:
"This being the case, there is a dispute here between the awakened and the deluded."
In that regard, the scripture has declared the conclusion: "The Self alone is to be cherished. (61)
Thus it stands. Regarding that, he states the conclusion: "In that regard, [it is] the Self. The meaning is: because the fact that the Self is the dearest has already been established. || 61 ||

Commentary (a0): Having thus presented the dispute between the knower and the non-knower by means of the Śruti itself, they state that the Self alone has been shown to be the most beloved: "Thus," etc. (61).
The knower of reality says that the witness itself is dearer than any other object of perception.
The person of deluded intellect thinks that his son or other beloved ones alone are the witnesses to enjoy this [world]. || 62 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states that very same contradiction: "The witness," etc. (62).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): In this regard, which is the position of the knower of reality according to the aforementioned Bṛhadāraṇyaka Śruti?
To this he says: "The Witness alone" (sākṣyeva). What then is the position of the ignorant opponent here? To that as well, he says: "More dear than... (preyān iti) || 62 ||
Rāma’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): In order to provide a detailed answer to one who maintains that there is something dearer than the Self, he analyzes that very proponent and speaks as follows:
[page 444]
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[the section titled] "Bliss of the Self" (*Ātmānanda*).
Both the disciple and the opponent declare someone other than themselves to be dear.
His reply shall bring about awakening and a curse for those two respectively.

Regarding the word "ātmanaḥ" (of oneself): he states the manner of the subsequent expression as "tasyottaram" (the answer to that). The meaning is that one should, in due order, produce the answer—that is, a statement in the form of a reply—to that speech belonging to both the disciple and the opponent, making it either of the nature of enlightenment or of the nature of a curse. || 63 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): For this very reason, regarding the phrase "of the Self," one might ask: what answer should be given there by the proponent who knows reality? To this, he says: "Of that" (tasya). || 63 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: He recites the meaning of the immediately following scriptural passage, which takes the form of a reply: "He who says to another person who speaks what is dear to himself, 'It will cause you pain'—"
The knower of reality speaks this reply: "He will obstruct you, though you are dear to him."
Through discernment, the disciple understands the wickedness of that which he himself has spoken as dear to him. || 64 ||
"Dear one, you... [The teacher] speaks this reply in the manner described: "O disciple, O opponent—both of you who are seekers of truth—hear this:

that which is dear to you, such as a son or other objects of affection, will cause you, whether disciple or opponent, to weep by means of its own destruction. This single statement is addressed to both the disciple and the opponent alike.

Anticipating the question, "How did the answer arise?", he first provides the response to the disciple with four and a half verses beginning with "Of that which is dear as spoken by oneself" and ending with "he gazes upon it day and night. Regarding the phrase "of that which is dear as spoken by oneself": the disciple understands the defectiveness—that is, the corruption—of that object of affection, such as a son or the like, which was mentioned by himself, through discernment (*viveka*), namely, by means of the investigation of the faults to be described hereafter.
...desires. || 64 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, he recites that very same scriptural passage for the purpose of addressing one who speaks of something other than the Self as being dear, saying, "The dear will perish for you. He states what happens to the disciple thereafter: "svokteti" (by his own statement). || 64 ||
A son who cannot be obtained causes his parents long-lasting distress.
Even when obtained, it causes distress through miscarriage and childbirth. || 65 ||
For one who is born, there are planetary afflictions, diseases, and the like; for a youth, there is ignorance.
Even when brought near, there is ignorance [of him], and for the wise man, there is no marriage.
For the youth, there is the pursuit of another's wife and the like; for the householder, there is poverty.
There is no end to the suffering of one's parents if they are deprived of wealth. || 67 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He demonstrates the very method of investigating defects with three verses (65, 66, and 67), beginning with the words "alabhyamāne" (when not being obtained).

The commentary (ṭīkā) on that very wickedness elaborates [upon it] with the three verses beginning with "alabhyamāne" (when not being obtained). Regarding "of one who has been born": a "graha" (seizing spirit) refers to well-known spirits such as those that afflict children (*bālagraha*). Regarding "and of a youth": the phrase "accompanied by his son" is to be understood as implied. 65, 66, 67.
Having thus discriminated and abandoned attachment toward one's son and others, [one should fix it] upon one's own self.
Having ascertained this, she gazes upon him day and night with supreme joy.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Thus, the description of the defects pertaining to the son is intended to serve as an illustration for all objects of sense, beginning with the wife.
"Having thus discriminated" means: having distinguished and understood the existing defects in the category of objects such as sons and so forth, by the manner already described.
The Twelfth Chapter,
together with the two commentaries.

Having abandoned attachment to one's own [limited] self, and having resolved upon supreme, unsurpassed love for the inner Self as the Witness, he beholds—that is to say, he constantly contemplates—that inner Self day and night at all times. || 68 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): What follows from this? He says: "Thus" (*evam*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the wife is also included. An analysis of that suffering has been stated by way of illustration in the *Prabodhasudhākara*: "A wife devoid of beauty causes distress to the minds of men; if, by fate, she is beautiful, she is captivated by other men. The meaning of "he observes" (*vīkṣate*) is that he reflects upon it. || 68 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He reveals that this very statement, "He will obstruct you who are dear [to me]," takes the form of a curse directed at the opponent:
"Of one who does not abandon this position, even out of obstinacy or hatred for Brahman..."
For the proponent, hell is declared as the result, along with rebirth in many wombs due to his faults. || 69 ||

"Because of obstinacy": because of the obstinacy consisting of the thought "I shall by no means abandon the stated affection for sons and so forth," and because of the hatred of Brahman consisting of the thought "I shall refute what has been said by him"— for the opponent who does not relinquish his position, which consists of asserting that sons and so forth alone are dear, there is the attainment of hell, as well as the suffering in many births among various wombs such as those of animals, characterized by separation from beloved ones like sons and wives, and the occurrence of the undesired.
It was stated by the Knower—namely, by Jñānin—that "attainment in the form of [this state] will obstruct you, O dear one. This is the implied sense. || 69 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might object: "Let this be so for the disciple; but what would happen to the opponent? To this, he says: "Because of obstinacy" (āgrahāt). The meaning is: "of one who does not relinquish," that is, "who does not abandon [it]. || 69 ||
Because he is the knower of Brahman and possesses the nature of Brahman, he is the Lord; thus it has been described by him.
Whatever [is asserted] by the disciple and the opponent, that very thing shall be exactly so.

Rāmānuja’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "How can a single statement uttered by a knower possess these two contradictory forms—being an instruction toward a disciple and a curse toward an opponent? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] considers that since the speaker is of the nature of the Lord (Īśvara), both will occur according to his intention; thus, the purport of the immediately following sentence, "The Lord indeed would be exactly so," is to establish that possibility.

The author says: "The knower of Brahman" (*brahmavit*). Since the knower of Brahman possesses lordship (*īśvaratva*) due to his experience of his own nature as Brahman, whatever—whether desired or undesired—is spoken by him to a disciple or anyone else, that very thing shall necessarily come to pass exactly so for both that disciple and the opponent; that is, the desired or the undesired will certainly occur for them. || 70 ||

The reason for this is stated as "one who knows Brahman" (brahmavit). Now, one might object: how can a single statement, "Pleasure will overwhelm you," serve successively as the cause for both the disciple’s discernment and the opponent’s descent into hell? This is not so, because the difference in results arises from the difference in qualification (adhikāra).
Just as the same water is sweeter in a grape and more bitter in a mirage, such is the truth of the matter. || 70 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: He recites the meaning of the immediately following passage—which establishes by way of affirmation (anvaya) the same point that was stated by way of negation (vyatireka)—namely: "One should meditate on the Self alone as dear;

he who meditates on the Self alone as dear, his dear ones do not perish here. The translation of the Sanskrit passage is: "One should meditate on the Self alone as dear; he who meditates on the Self alone as dear, his dear ones do not perish here."
But he who serves himself as a witness, which is the highest of dear things—
This beloved Self of his is never destroyed at any time. || 71 ||

Regarding the phrase "But he who... (*yas tv iti*): the word "but" (*tu*) is intended to highlight the distinction from what has been stated previously. As for that disciple who, unlike one who asserts that things other than the Self are dear, always serves the Self alone as the supreme, the most beloved, and the object of unsurpassed love—constantly remembering the Self—that Self, which is held by such a disciple to be the dearest (*preyān*), never perishes, unlike the "dear" thing asserted by the opponent; rather, it...
The meaning is that he appears as one whose very nature is the bliss of giving. || 71 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 446] 448.
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Then he states the conclusion: "But he who... (verse 71).
[The commentary by Rāma, titled *Yogānanda*: Having thus established the reason why the Self is the object of supreme love, he now states the resulting conclusion:
"By virtue of being the object of supreme love, [the Self] consists of supreme bliss."
The increase of happiness upon the increase of joy is heard [to occur] among the universal monarchs and others. (72)

Regarding the phrase "supreme love" (*paraprema*): here is the formal argument (*prayoga*). The Self (*ātman*) is of the nature of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), because it is the object of unsurpassed love (*niratiśayapremaviṣayatvāt*).

Whatever is not of the nature of supreme bliss is not the object of unsurpassed love, just like a jar (*ghaṭa*) or other such things. This is a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekī*), intended to demonstrate the capacity of the reason—being the locus of supreme love—to establish that the Self is of the nature of supreme bliss; for this purpose, he cites the increase of happiness (*sukhavṛddhi*) as the increase of affection (*prītivṛddhi*).

Regarding the phrase "the increase of the threefold happiness": since it is stated in both the Taittirīya and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Śrutis that wherever joy increases among the various specific stations—beginning with that of a sovereign ruler of the earth and culminating in the state of Hiraṇyagarbha—therein lies an increase of happiness; therefore, the sense is that when joy is unsurpassed, it can be understood that bliss (*ānanda*) is likewise unsurpassed. || 72 ||
The reason for this is stated as "para" (the other). And thus, the sense is that for him there arises only the excellence of the bliss of liberation while living (jīvanmukti). || 72 ||
If pleasure, like consciousness, were the inherent nature of this conscious self, [then it would always be perceived].
One should conform to all mental modifications just as consciousness does.

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised: "The nature of the Self as supreme bliss is untenable; for if that were so, it would follow that bliss—which is its very essence—would persist in all mental modifications (dhīvṛtti), just as consciousness does. This is expressed in the verse beginning with *caitanyavat*. (73)
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Here, an objection is raised: "Like consciousness" (caitanyavat). || 73 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Although both consciousness (cit) and bliss (ānanda) are of the very nature of the Self, consciousness alone persists during mental modifications (vṛtti), whereas bliss does not; he resolves this by means of an illustration:
"It is not so; a lamp consists of heat and light, and its radiance [persists] in the house."
In the same way, heat does not pervade [the object]; it is merely a following of the consciousness itself.
"Not so," [it is said]. Just as of a lamp whose nature consists of both heat and light, it is only the light that follows into the house and so forth, and not the heat;
in the same way, the meaning is that it is consciousness alone that persists, and not bliss. || 74 ||
In this regard, he provides a resolution with an illustration: "It is not so," [verse 74].

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If consciousness (cit) and bliss (ānanda) are non-different, then the manifestation of bliss should necessarily occur whenever there is a mental modification (dhī-vṛtti) that manifests consciousness.
Anticipating this, he provides an example to show that such a rule does not hold:
"Just as [the qualities] of smell, form, taste, and touch, though all present, [are perceived] separately..."
By means of a single sense organ, only one object is grasped, and not another in that same way. (75)

Regarding the word "gandha" (smell): just as among the four qualities—smell and the rest—which reside in a single substance, only one quality such as smell is perceived by a single sense organ like the nose and not the others, so too, between consciousness and bliss, it is consciousness alone that is manifested; this is the meaning. || 75 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, one might raise the objection: "Granted that there is such persistence of consciousness alone, why is it that bliss—which is non-different from it—does not likewise persist within the mental modifications? He dispels this doubt by means of an illustration itself, beginning with the word *gandha*. The phrase "in a substance such as a mango fruit" is to be supplied. "By a single eye" means by a single sense organ, such as the nose; "only one" refers to each individual quality, such as fragrance and so on. Likewise, in that same manner, generally in the mental modification—

The meaning is that it is precisely this consciousness; for bliss is also manifested through mental modifications (vṛtti) such as the cognition of one's own desired objects, like a beautiful woman and so forth. || 75 ||
The Twelfth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He raises an objection regarding the disparity between the illustration and the illustrated:
"Consciousness and bliss are not distinct at all, whereas smell and the other qualities are indeed different."
If this is argued, then tell me: is that non-difference [of the cognition] in the witness-consciousness (sākṣin) or elsewhere? (76)

"Cit and Ānanda" means they are of different characteristics (*vilakṣaṇā*), that is, distinct. To resolve the aforementioned disparity, he raises the alternative as to whether the non-difference (*abheda*) between consciousness (*cit*) and bliss (*ānanda*) in the case of the subject under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*) is natural (*svābhāvika*) or conditional (*aupādhika*). "That non-difference" (*tadabheda*) means the non-difference or unity of those two—consciousness and bliss—is [located] either in the Witness who is the nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*), or elsewhere in the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) which serve as their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). || 76 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He raises an objection regarding the disparity in the aforementioned illustration with the words "Consciousness and Bliss" (cidānandau). To that, the proponent (siddhāntin) replies by first restating the opponent's doubt and then questioning him through a series of alternatives, beginning with "If it be so" (iti cet), and so forth. || 76 ||
In the first case, he states the similarity between the illustration and the illustrated:
"In the first [case], fragrance and so forth are likewise non-different from that which resides in the flower."
If their difference were due to a difference in the sense organs, then the distinction between those two would arise from a difference in their functions. (77)

Regarding the phrase "in the first": in the first case, which holds that there is no difference between consciousness (*cit*) and bliss (*ānanda*) as the witness (*sākṣin*), the meaning is that even qualities such as fragrance residing in a flower are non-different from consciousness and bliss themselves, being devoid of mutual distinction; for it is impossible to apprehend one while excluding the others. Regarding the second case as well, he states their equality with the words "by the senses" (*akṣa*): by the difference of the senses—the sense organs such as the nose and so forth, which perceive fragrance and the rest—there is a difference in those [qualities].

The meaning is that if one accepts a distinction among those [qualities] such as fragrance and so forth, then just as in their case, due to the distinction between the rajasic and sattvic mental modifications (vṛtti) which are the causes for the manifestation of consciousness (cit) and bliss (ānanda), a distinction—that is, a difference—will arise between those two, consciousness and bliss. || 77 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He answers the first [objection] with equanimity: "The flower," etc. The meanings of smell, color, taste, and touch residing in flowers such as the *mālatī* are indeed non-different; they are not perceived as distinct from one another—this is the meaning. Anticipating the objection that their difference arises from the difference in the cognitions of those objects due to the difference in the sense organs (*indriya*), he provides an answer based on the same principle of parity: "By the difference of the senses" (*akṣa*), etc. By the difference of the senses—that is, by the difference of the sense organs. If there is a difference in those [cognitions]...

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: since a distinction between these [qualities] such as fragrance and so forth must necessarily be stated, even in the present case, due to the difference in mental states (*vṛttibheda*), there arises a distinction—that is, a division—between those two entities, consciousness (*cit*) and bliss (*ānanda*), precisely because of the aforementioned difference in mental states delimited by the relationship of generality and particularity. || 77 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might ask, "In what then is the identity of consciousness (cit) and bliss (ānanda) perceived? Anticipating this, he says:
"The identity of consciousness and bliss occurs in the modification of the quality of goodness (sattva), because that modification is pure."
But because of the impurity arising from the activity of passion (rajas), the portion of happiness here is obscured.

Regarding the phrase "in the function of *sattva*": when there is a function of *sattva*—that is, a function of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) established by virtuous action and consisting of the transformation of the quality of *sattva*—the unity of consciousness and bliss, the unity of *cit* and *ānanda*, shines forth; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. He states the justification for that: "of that function" (*tad-vṛtteḥ*). But then, from where does the appearance of difference arise? To this he says: "of the function of *rajas*" (*rajo-vṛtteḥ*). || 78 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: how can this distinction of mental states (vṛttibheda) be the regulator for the manifestation of consciousness, bliss, and so forth? To this, he says: "And that...
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He provides an illustration for the obscuration of even an existing element of pleasure:
"When a tamarind fruit, which is sour, is combined with salt..."
Then, due to the suppression of the sourness, it becomes slightly sour, just so.

Regarding the word *tiṃtiṇī*: just as the extreme acidity of a *tiṃtiṇī* fruit is concealed by the addition of salt, in the same way, bliss (*ānanda*) is concealed within the function of the intellect (*vṛtti*). This is the meaning. || 79 ||
In this regard, the author provides an illustration: "The Tamarind," etc. (Verse 79). This concludes the commentary on the fifteenth chapter of the Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He raises a doubt regarding the hidden intention:
"But surely, because the Self is the most beloved, it possesses supreme bliss."
If it is possible to discern that which is called the bliss of the Self in this way, what would happen without yoga? (80)

Regarding the word "nanu": [The opponent objects: "Granted that, by the method already stated, the nature of the Self as supreme bliss can indeed be distinguished—discerned and known—from the secondary, false selves consisting of the beloved, the indifferent, and the hateful, on the grounds of being the object of supreme love; nevertheless, this discernment is not the means to liberation, because yoga, which is the cause of liberation through the medium of immediate realization (aparokṣajñāna), has been taught. This is the hidden intention. 80.

Commentary (a0): Now, an objection is raised with a hidden intention: "But surely," it is argued. Even when such an investigation is conducted regarding the beloved, the indifferent, and the hated, and even when there is the discernment that the Self alone is of the nature of supreme bliss because it is the object of unqualified love, the immediate realization (*aparokṣapramā*) will not be accomplished without the practice of yoga. Thus he asks: "But surely... (80).
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: With a hidden intention, he gives the answer:
"We say that by means of which yoga that very [yoga] exists for the sake of attaining knowledge."
Yoga has been declared to be discernment; why then does knowledge not arise? || 81 ||

Regarding the phrase "by means of yoga": just as yoga possesses the quality of being a cause for direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), so too does discriminative discernment (*viveka*); this is the hidden intention (*gūḍhābhisaṃdhi*) here as well. Now, he reveals the underlying intention behind both the objection and its resolution with the words "knowledge" (*jñāna*). Just as yoga was previously taught in the preceding chapter as a means to indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), so too in this chapter [discriminative discernment is taught] by way of the discernment of the self from the secondary selves (*gauṇādyātmatva-viveka*) as taught herein.
The meaning is that knowledge indeed arises even through the discernment of the five sheaths. || 81 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding your statement that immediate realization (*aparokṣajñāna*) arises through yoga, the proponent (*siddhāntin*), with a hidden intention, replies—“That very thing may also arise through inquiry”—using the words beginning with “yat. To this, the opponent raises an objection with the words beginning with “jñāna. Thereupon, the proponent provides a reply accompanied by a refutation, using the remainder of the verse starting with “vivekena. || 81 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question, "What is the proof for that? he says:
"The state which is attained by the followers of Sāṃkhya is also reached by the followers of Yoga."
Thus is declared the unity of the fruit for both yogins and those possessed of discernment. 82.

Regarding the phrase "that which by the Sāṃkhyas": that state in the form of liberation which is attained—that is, reached—by the Sāṃkhyas who distinguish between the Self and the non-Self, is also reached and attained by the Yogis through Yoga. By this, it is stated that there is a unity of fruit for both the Yogis and the discriminators; the meaning is that there is a single fruit characterized as liberation, mediated by knowledge. || 82 ||

Commentary (a0): Even though both paths—investigation (*vicāra*) and so forth—contribute to the attainment of liberation by means of the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*), [the author] cites scripture as authority: "That which by the Sāṃkhyas... etc. They correctly explain—that is, they declare through the Upaniṣads and other sources—that the identity of Brahman and the Self is the intended meaning, by way of the falsity of duality. Thus [ends verse 82].
For some, yoga is unattainable; for others, the certainty of knowledge.
Having reflected thus, the Supreme Lord declared two paths. || 83 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If the fruit of discrimination (*viveka*) and yoga (*yoga*) is indeed one and the same, then it would be appropriate for only one of these two to be taught in the scriptures, not both.
Anticipating this doubt, with the intention of showing that the teaching of both is justified due to the diversity of qualified aspirants (*adhikārī*), he says:
"Asādhya" (verse 83).
The Twelfth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
451a0 Commentary: Now, one might ask: "If the fruits of Viveka (discrimination) and Yoga are equal, why does the scripture not prescribe only one of the two?

Anticipating this objection, [the author] intends to show that both are necessary due to the difference in the qualifications (*adhikārin*) of the practitioners, and thus states: "There are two methods for the dissolution of the mind: Yoga..."

He provides the resolution through a passage from the *Bṛhadyogavāsiṣṭha*: "O Rāghava, knowledge is [the means], while yoga is the restraint of its fluctuations; knowledge is correct discernment. Yoga is unattainable for some, while the certainty of knowledge is unattainable for others; therefore, the supreme Lord Śiva declared two methods.
Thus he concludes with the words "asādhya" (unattainable). || 83 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might raise the objection that the superiority of Yoga—which is accomplished through extreme exertion—over Viveka (discrimination), which is easily obtained without effort, must be stated.

Anticipating this, one might wonder whether this superiority is asserted because Yoga produces immediate intuitive knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), or because it is the cause for the cessation of attachment, aversion, and so forth, or because it is the cause for the non-perception of duality. Having thus raised these alternatives, he states that in the first case, the result is the same: rā0 ṭīkā — nanvatyaṃtāyāsasādhyasya yogasya nirāyāsasulabhādvivekādatiśayo va-ktavya ityāśaṃkya so'tiśayaḥ kimaparokṣajñānajanakatvāducyate, uta rāgadveṣādinivṛttihetutvāt, atha vā dvaitānupalavdhikāraṇatvāditi vikalpya prathamapakṣe phalasāmyamityāha— Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might raise the objection that the superiority of Yoga—which is accomplished through extreme exertion—over Viveka (discrimination), which is easily obtained without effort, must be stated. Anticipating this, one might wonder whether this superiority is asserted because Yoga produces immediate intuitive knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), or because it is the cause for the cessation of attachment, aversion, and so forth, or because it is the cause for the non-perception of duality. Having thus raised these alternatives, he states that in the first case, the result is the same:
What excellence is there here in yoga? Knowledge has been declared to be equal for both.
Furthermore, the absence of passion, hatred, and the like is equal for both the yogin and the man of discernment. (84)

Regarding the word "yoga": since the fruit characterized by knowledge has been declared to be equal for both—the discrimination (*viveka*) and the yoga—by the Sāṃkhyas in the passage beginning with "that which [is attained] by the Sāṃkhyas," the meaning is that there is no superiority whatsoever in your yoga. To the second [objection], he replies: "attachment and aversion" (verse 84).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "In the case of Yoga, which is accomplished through great effort, what is the superiority over Viveka, which is accomplished without effort?

Having raised this doubt, the author considers the alternatives—whether it is the production of immediate (aparokṣa) knowledge, or the mere absence of passion and so forth, or the non-perception of duality—and refutes the first by stating:
"Yoga... The capacity to produce immediate knowledge is common to both Yoga and Viveka, as evidenced by the aforementioned statement of the Lord.
The meaning is that this has already been stated. Regarding the second [point], he says: "rāga... (verse 84).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He establishes the absence of passion and other afflictions in the discerning person:
"For one who knows that there is no beloved object of affection greater than the Self, [passion does not exist toward objects of pleasure]."
Whence can there be passion or whence hatred for one who perceives no opposition? (85)
"Not attachment" means this: for a person who knows that the self is dearer—that the self is the most beloved—there is first of all no attachment toward sense objects;

therefore, passion does not arise toward them, because of the absence of the knowledge of favorability, which is the cause of passion. Nor does aversion arise, because of the absence of the knowledge of unfavorability, which is the cause of aversion. This is the meaning. || 85 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) explains this: "Not [so]. The connection with the preceding is: "Therefore, whence could there be attachment? Similarly, the construction is:
for one who, through such constant contemplation of the Self, perceives no hostility toward anything, whence could even hatred arise? || 85 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that even for a person of discrimination (*vivekin*), aversion toward things that cause affliction such as the body is observed during the state of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*).
Anticipating this, he resolves the objection by stating that at that time, such aversion is equal for both the yogi and the person of discrimination:
"Aversion toward things adverse to the body and so forth is equal for both."
If a practitioner of yoga were to harbor hatred, he would be just like one who lacks discernment.

Regarding the phrase "of the body and so forth": if you do not admit that one who feels aversion toward hostile things such as scorpions and the like possesses the state of a yogin, then we likewise do not admit that such a person possesses discernment (*viveka*). Thus he says: "aversion. The meaning is that such a person who harbors aversion is neither non-discerning nor discerning. || 86 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, if it is argued that even for a person of discrimination (*vivekin*), aversion toward those who cause pain to the body, senses, and so forth is indeed observed in worldly conduct (*vyavahāra*), [the author] replies that this is exactly the same for the yogi as well—thus he says "of the body, etc. If it is further argued that one who hates what is adverse cannot truly possess the state of a yogi, [the author] replies that such a person would likewise not possess the state of a person of discrimination—thus he says "aversion" (*dveṣam*). || 86 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [pages 450–450] 452.

[Regarding the one called *Ātmānanda*, Rāma’s Commentary (*Rā0 Ṭīkā*) says: Now, an objection may be raised: "While the perception of duality exists for the one possessed of discrimination (*vivekin*), it does not exist for the yogi; thus, in the third alternative, there will be a distinction in favor of the yogi.
Anticipating this, [the author] asks: Is that perception of duality by the one possessed of discrimination spoken of in the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra-daśā*), or—
Having raised this alternative, he states that it applies equally even to the yogi:
"But the appearance of duality is the same for both in worldly transaction."
If it is argued that [this is not so] in the case of meditative absorption (samādhi), then it is likewise not so for one who discriminates non-duality. || 87 ||

Regarding the phrase "of duality": he raises a second objection with the words "in meditative absorption" (*samādhau*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "If it is said that for the yogi there is no perception of duality at the time of meditative absorption. He refutes this by saying "likewise," meaning that for the person of discrimination (*vivekin*) as well, the non-perception of duality during the state of discrimination is equal [to that of the yogi]. Just as for the yogi in the state of absorption, so too for the one who discriminates non-duality, there is a discernment of the reality of non-duality through both scripture and reasoning.
The meaning is that even while acting at that time, there is no perception of duality. || 87 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, if the third position is that the very fact that duality does not appear to the yogin constitutes the excellence of discernment (viveka) in yoga, then one must consider whether that appearance [of duality] occurs in worldly activity (vyavahāra) or in meditative absorption (samādhi). Regarding the first alternative, the appearance of duality is exactly the same for both [the ordinary person and the yogin] in worldly activity; otherwise, worldly activity itself would not be possible. Thus he says: "Of duality... Then, having raised the second alternative, he refutes it:

Regarding the phrase "in samādhi": the connection is that, likewise, even for one who discriminates non-duality like a yogi, there is no appearance of duality whatsoever during the state of discursive samādhi (vaicārika-samādhi). || 87 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question of how that absence [of duality] occurs, he states that it will be demonstrated in the subsequent chapter:
"That shall be explained by us in the work titled *Advaitānanda*."
Therefore, everything in this third chapter is also exceedingly auspicious.
"It is intended to be said. He concludes the point already stated with the words "all of it" (sarvam api). || 88 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "How is it logically established that for one who discriminates non-duality within that meditative absorption (samādhi), there is no appearance of duality?
To this, he says: "It is intended [to be shown]" (*vivakṣyate*). He concludes with the remainder of the verse beginning with "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). || 88 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might raise the objection: "Surely, one who possesses the vision of the Self accompanied by the non-perception of duality will indeed be a yogi. To this he says:
"Always seeing his own bliss, not seeing the entire world..."
If you say it is because of its meaning, then may you, who are satisfied with that, prosper! (89)
Regarding the phrase "always seeing," he refutes it by accepting the consequence: "then [it would follow that... || 89 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Since duality, consisting of name, form, and so forth, is imagined upon the non-dual Self which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss, if it is separated from that [Self] whose nature is pure Being, it is immediately reduced to the state of a sky-flower; therefore, only one who possesses such real discrimination is a truly realized yogi. To this, the author expresses approval, saying "sadā" (always), as this is indeed a desired conclusion. || 89 ||
In this work titled Brahmānanda, for the sake of bestowing grace upon the dull-witted;
In this second chapter, the bliss of the Self has been analyzed. || 90 ||
Thus ends the second chapter, named "Bliss of Brahman" and "Bliss of the Self," in the Śrī [text]. 2.
Rāma’s Commentary: He shows the purport of the chapter in brief—“Brahmānanda,” etc. (90).

"Just as the meaning of unity is constructed by dualists according to their own views, so too by others. With this verse, the second obstacle—namely, the lack of conviction regarding the identity between the pure individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, known as the "impossibility of proof"—was presented. Likewise: "In the case of the non-dualistic unity, the perfect systematic correlation (*samanvaya*) of the *Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa* and other passages has been stated; therefore, their orientation toward that [unity] should be understood even in the twelfth [chapter]."

If it is asked how the statement made in another Āryā verse—that this twelfth chapter, named *Ātmānanda*, sublates that [previous view]—is justified, it is replied as follows: For here, the very passages such as the *Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa* culminate naturally in the primordial unity of the pure consciousness characterized as the individual soul (*jīvatva*) with the pure consciousness characterized as Brahman; thus, it extends up to the point where the punishment of a curse serves as the limit of refutation.

Since the teaching is preceded by a dialectical discourse of those who maintain difference (*bhedavādin*), why should the aforementioned doubt—which concerns the unity established by etymology (*nirukta*) and is rooted in the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—not act as a sublater of the stated obstacle consisting of a lack of faith? If the teachers had not here presented the demonstration of the unity of the Self preceded by the citation of the etymological passage, then perhaps there would be room for the doubt you have expressed. Even according to the Śruti: "Indeed, O Maitreyī, he... [and so forth].

[This is] by such passages as, "Everything becomes dear for the sake of desire for the Self; but everything becomes dear for the sake of desire for the Self," and likewise by such passages as, "This very Self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than everything else, for this Self is more internal. By these means, [the texts] directly teach that Brahman, which is of the nature of unsurpassed bliss, is indeed the Self. And if this were not accepted, [there would be a distinction] from the proponents of duality (bhedavādins).

It should be understood that by her speaking even the pronouncement of a curse through the mouth of a knower of Brahman, and by her describing what is experienced by all the worlds, the obstacle consisting of the aforementioned doubt is overcome. || 90 ||

Thus [ends the work] by Śrī Nārāyaṇa Śāstrī, whose feet are like lotus-kings for the royal swan that is [this author], who bears the secondary name Paṣṭha; who is the delight of Goddess Advaitavidyā; who sports in the milk-ocean of the Padas, Vākyas, and Pramāṇas; and who is a disciple of the venerable Advaitasaccidānandendra Sarasvatī, the preceptor of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakācāryas.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Self-Bliss," in the commentary on the *Pañcadaśī* entitled *Pūrṇānandendukaumudī*, composed by Acyutaśarman, known by the name Mānasamoda, while he was a student. 12.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Pañcadaśī* composed by the venerable Vidyāraṇya. || 12 ||

May that which shines solely through the mass of pollen from the lotus feet of the venerable and illustrious Guru Śaṅkara be ever resplendent in the highest degree. May the Vedic prosperity, which nourishes the desires of all the hosts of cows and Brahmins, be uninterrupted. He is the One, the Non-dual; the Fourth (Turiya) through the dissolution of the triad;
the Knower of the Five Sheaths; the Essence of the Six Shastras; the Self established on the Seventh Stage; and yet the Eightfold Formed (Aṣṭamūrti). 1.
Thus ends this Āryā verse from the *Advaitāmṛtamañjarī* composed by Acyuta, which succinctly indicates the essential truth of all the Vedas.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter on the fifteenth [day];
therein, in the *Brahmānanda*, is the third section titled "The Bliss of the Absorbed" (*adhyātmananda*).

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection may be raised: "In the first chapter, after proposing that there are three kinds of bliss—namely, the bliss of Brahman, the happiness of knowledge, and the bliss of sense objects—it is inconsistent to define a 'bliss of the Self' distinct from those in the second chapter.
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
That which was previously described as the bliss of yoga should be understood as the bliss of the Self (ātmananda).
If you ask how this Being possesses the nature of Brahman, listen.

Regarding the term *yogānanda*: the sense is that just as the very Brahman-bliss previously promised is designated as *yogānanda* because it is the object of direct realization born of yoga, and as it is designated as *nijānanda* (intrinsic bliss) due to its being free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), so too is it called *ātmānanda* (self-bliss) with the intention of making it understood through the discrimination between the secondary, false, and primary selves. Now, [one might ask]: from the secondary self consisting of those of the same class, such as son, wife, and so forth—

He raises an objection, asking "How so?", on the grounds that for one's own self—which is distinct from heterogeneous things such as the body and so forth, and from the dualistic bliss of the Self—the nature of the bliss of the second yoga mentioned in the first chapter cannot possibly exist. This is because the secondary self (gauṇātman), such as a son and the like, which is considered to be of the same class [as the primary self], and the false self (mithyātman), such as the body and so forth, are included within the world as described in the Taittirīya Śruti; and since the world, including space and so forth, is the Self—
Because he is non-existent due to the excess of bliss, his nature as the non-dual Brahman is established; thus, with great respect, he gives the reply: "Listen! (verse 1).
Commentary (a0): [I bow to] that which is the immutable form of the Supreme Brahman—non-dual bliss, existence, consciousness, all-pervading, and stainless;
though it is the abode of the illusory net of duality arising from delusion, it is the crest-jewel of the Vedas and self-luminous.
I bow to all the preeminent teachers, to my true guru, the ornament of the lineage of Atri who is established in Brahman and named Śrī Nārāyaṇa, and also to my own teacher known as Mahādeva. || 1 ||
Having honored Jīvañjīva, Vidyāraṇya, and Bhāratītīrtha.
O Bliss of Non-duality, through the light of remembrance, I illuminate [the world] with the moonlight of your splendor. || 2 ||

Now, the venerable sage Bhāratītīrtha, at the conclusion of the second chapter titled *Ātmānanda*—which constitutes the third part of his own work, the *Pañcadaśī*, and forms the second section within the five-chapter work *Brahmānanda*—establishes the connection with the third chapter, titled *Advaitānanda*, by means of what was stated therein:
"In this second chapter, *Ātmānanda*, has been investigated. With that [connection], he begins the third...

Indicating the purpose of the authoritative means of knowledge for the thirteen chapters of this treatise, while contemplating the auspiciousness characterized by the investigation of reality as intimated by the term "Ātmananda," and further manifesting both the subject matter and the purpose of the present chapter, [the author] also illuminates the qualifications of the seeker and so forth; thus, having drawn in the disciple to ensure his attention, he addresses him with the words "Yogānanda. || 1 ||
From space down to one's own body, as proclaimed in the Taittirīya Śruti.
There is no other world than bliss; therefore, it is the state of non-dual Brahman.

Rāma’s Commentary: Regarding the phrase "ākāśādi" (ether, etc.): The intention is that since the world—declared by the Taittirīya Śruti in such passages as "From this very Self, ether was produced"—is not other than or separate from the Self-bliss which constitutes its own cause, for that reason, that Self-bliss is non-dual (advitīya). || 2 ||
The Thirteenth Chapter.
Accompanied by two commentaries.
Commentary on the Text (a0 ṭīkā): He states this with the words "ākāśādi" (beginning with space). And thus it is recorded there in the *Brahmavallī*:
From that very Self, indeed, space was produced—beginning thus and ending with, "This person, verily, consists of the essence of food. (2)
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "In the scriptural passage cited, it is the Self that is heard to be the cause, not Bliss.
Anticipating this, he recites in substance that very statement of his [the Upaniṣad] which establishes that point:
"From Bliss alone was that born; in Bliss alone does it abide."
Since it is said that bliss alone is dissolved [in Brahman], how can it be separate from bliss? (3)
"From bliss alone"—this has been explained. He states the conclusion: "Thus it has been said. Here, the following inference is indicated:

the world under dispute does not differ from bliss, because it is its effect; whatever is an effect does not differ from that [cause], just as a jar or other effects of clay do not differ from clay. || 3 ||
The reason for this is stated as "from bliss alone" (ānandādeva). This is also heard in that very [text]:
"Verily, from bliss alone these beings are born; by bliss, once born, they live; toward bliss they depart and merge.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that the reason [adduced] is inconclusive because a jar produced from a potter is seen to be distinct from him, he says—“Let it not be suspected that a jar is produced from a potter and yet is different [from him]”—because the potter is merely the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), whereas here bliss is established as the material cause (*upādāna*). Thus, it is not so.
In this case, clay and so forth are the material cause (*upādāna*), not the efficient cause (*nimitta*) as in the case of a potter. (4)

Regarding the phrase "from the potter": this Self is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) like clay—for instance, as clay is to a jar—but it does not become the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), like a potter. || 4 ||

Commentary—Having stated the doubt of the logicians (*tārkika*) regarding that point, they refute it with the words "from the potter" (*kulālāt*). The reason for this is given as "like clay" (*mṛdvat*).

"Just as, my dear, by means of a single clod of clay, everything made of clay would be known—the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while the reality is simply 'clay'"—for such is the Sāma-śruti. 4.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might ask, "Why does the potter not also possess the status of material cause? Anticipating this doubt, he states that it is because the definition of material causality—consisting in being the substratum of both persistence and dissolution—is absent [in the case of the potter].
Stability and dissolution do not exist at all within the potter's wheel.
Just as those two are seen in clay, so too would they have that [clay] as their material cause, because of the scriptural statement.

Regarding the term "sthitih" (subsistence): for the reason that the subsistence and dissolution of a jar do not have the potter as their support, therefore [the potter] lacks the status of being the material cause (*upādānatva*); this is the sense of the remainder [of the argument]. To the question "In what, then, do those two reside?", he says: "dṛṣṭau" (are seen). Those two—the subsistence and dissolution of the jar—are seen, that is, perceived by direct observation, in the clay alone which constitutes its material cause. To the question "Let it be so; what does this have to do with the subject at hand?", he says:

To that, [the author] replies: "Just as clay is the material cause (upādāna) of a jar, so too bliss (ānanda) must be the material cause of the world. The reason for this is stated: "Of those two" (tayoḥ).
This means that because the Śruti, in such passages as "From bliss alone," declares that the maintenance and dissolution of the world have bliss as their cause. || 5 ||
a0 Commentary—He states the proof for that: "The stability... (verse 5).
Rāma’s Commentary: In order to state his own view regarding bliss being the material cause of the universe, he describes its intermediate subdivisions:
*Note:
This is the opening of the commentary on verse 456.*

In the Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, the material cause (upādāna) is divided into three types: the illusory transformation (vivarti), the transformative modification (pariṇāmi), and [the third type].
The two [factors] called Advaitānanda and Ārambhaka are not applicable to you in the case of that which is partless.

Regarding "appropriation" (*upādāna*): therein, in order to set aside the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), he refutes the other two positions with the words "therein. The theories of final origination (*antyārambha*) and transformation (*pariṇāma*) find no place—that is, they have no scope—within a reality that is partless and devoid of components. (6)
— Commentary (A0 Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Even so, just as there is the cognition of clay in a jar, would there not likewise result the cognition of bliss (*ānanda*) in duality?

Anticipating this, in order to explain its status, the author first declares the threefold nature of material causes (*upādāna*). Then, regarding the present context, he refutes the latter two positions—the views of the Sāṃkhya and the Logicians (*Tārkika*)—on the grounds that [the primordial matter] is partless (*niraṃśatvāt*), and thus [those views] are not tenable.
He states his opinion: "The material cause" (upādāna). "Possessing space" means having space; the word "wings" (pakṣau) is to be supplied as the remainder. || 6 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In order to demonstrate that those two [theories] lack any scope, he first restates the view of the proponents of the theory of origination (ārambhavādins):
The proponents of origination have declared that one thing arises from another.
Indeed, because of the production of something other than that [thread], the thread and the cloth are distinct.

Regarding the term "ārambha" (commencement): the Vaiśeṣikas and others are proponents of commencement (ārambhavādinaḥ). They have asserted—that is, they have stated—the production of one thing from another cause with respect to its effect, and the production of another effect from another cause with respect to that cause. To the question, "Why do they speak thus? he says: "From the threads," etc. The words "because [their] production—that is, origination—is observed" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. To the question, "How is the difference between cause and effect established by this much? [the answer follows:]
"Divided" means that they possess contradictory transformations and perform contradictory purposeful actions; this is the intended sense. || 7 ||
He says—[in the] commentary on verse 1—he briefly defines *ārambha* (origination) as desired by the logicians, along with an example: "Ārambha...
The definition of that [origination] is: that which possesses an existence distinct from its cause. || 7 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now he describes the nature of transformation:
"The state of being subject to transformation is the attainment of another state by that which is one."
It may be milk, curd, an earthen pot, or a golden earring, as the case may be.
"State" (avasthā): The meaning is that transformation (*pariṇāma*) is the attainment of another state by a single entity itself, preceded by the relinquishing of its previous state.

He illustrates this with the word "syāt": for example, when milk, clay, gold, and so forth, having abandoned their suitability for the conventional usage of "milk" and so on, attain suitability for the conventional usage of "curd" and so on. || 8 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, he also states the theory of transformation (*pariṇāma*) with the words "avasthā" and so on. The two examples of clay and the like are intended solely for the purpose of refuting the Logicians (*Tārkika*). Since a different state (*avasthāntara*) exists even in the case of a cloth, just as it does in curds, there is no such thing as a new beginning (*ārambha*). || 8 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now he states the definition of illusory manifestation (vivarta):
"Illusory manifestation, however, is the appearance of another state, like a snake in a rope."

Even though space is partless, this [delusion] exists due to the conceptualization of its surface and impurity.

Regarding the phrase "in another state" (*avasthāntare*): the word *tu* (but) is intended to highlight the distinction of this [view] from the two preceding positions. *Vivarta* (illusory manifestation) is the appearance of another state without abandoning the previous state. He illustrates this with the example: "as in the case of a rope" (*rajjviti*). Just as the appearance of a substance existing in the form of a rope as being in the form of a snake is *vivarta*. Now, one might object: since we observe that things undergoing illusory manifestation, such as ropes, possess parts (*sāṃśatva*), how could it apply to that which is partless (*niraṃśa*)?

Anticipating the objection that this is not possible, he says, "Even in the partless," meaning: even in the case of the sky and other such things which lack parts, such phenomena are observed; therefore, it is not so [that the analogy fails]. This refers to the illusory transformation (*vivarta*): the appearance of a surface (*talatva*) and the likeness of a downward-facing sapphire bowl (*indranīlakaṭāha*), as well as turbidity and blueness. The meaning is that these are superimposed by those who are ignorant of the true nature of space. || 9 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Likewise, he describes transformation (*vivarta*) with the words "in another state" (*avasthāntare*). He applies that very principle to the subject at hand with the words "even though partless" (*niraṃśe’pi*). According to tradition, the phrase "the surface of the downward-facing sapphire vessel" (*talamadhomukhendranīlakaṭāha*) refers to the base [of the world]. || 9 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the conclusion:
"Therefore, let the world be considered a vivarta (illusory manifestation) within partless bliss."
The power of illusion (māyā-śakti) is that which effects conceptual construction, like the power of a magician. || 10 ||

Regarding the word "tataḥ" (therefore): the meaning is that since a phenomenal appearance (*vivarta*) is possible even in that which is partless, one must accept that the world is a phenomenal appearance superimposed upon the partless Bliss. Now, one might object: "The conceptualization of the world within non-dual Bliss is untenable because of the absence of a cause for such conceptualization. Anticipating this, he says "māyā" (illusion). To the question, "Where has the power [of Māyā] been seen to act as a creator of conceptualizations? he replies with "aiṃdrajālika" (the magician). Just as [the power of illusion] residing in a magician...

The meaning is that it is just like the power of illusion (māyā-śakti), consisting of gems, mantras, and so forth, which brings about the conceptualization of things such as a city of Gandharvas. || 10 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): What follows from that in the present context? He states it with the words "tataḥ" (therefore). || 10 ||
Power does not exist apart from the possessor of power; likewise, there is no difference [between them] as perceived by experience.
Since an obstruction is observed, to what would it apply in the absence of power?

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that if Māyā is admitted to exist as something distinct from the Self which is Bliss (ānandātman), it would result in the fallacy of duality (dvaitāpatti). Anticipating this, the author demonstrates—in order to state her unreality due to her being indefinable—that the worldly power of fire and so forth, which will be discussed later, cannot be defined as either different or non-different [from its substrate]. He says: "Power" (śakti). Power residing in fire and the like, which produces bursting [of wood] and other effects...

It does not exist as something distinct or separate from the nature of fire and so forth. Why? To this he says: "tadvat" (like that). This means that, just like that, its non-existence through distinction is observed; that is, because it is not perceived apart from the nature of fire and so forth. Nor is power merely the nature of fire and so forth; he says: "na ca" (nor). "Abhidā" means non-difference, and this is also not the case. He provides the reason for this as well: "pratibandhasya" (of the connection).

The intention is that since an obstruction to the effect of power (śakti)—such as the bursting of a seed—is observed through the use of gems, mantras, and so forth, a power distinct from the essential nature [of the object] must be admitted.

To the objection, "Let there be the observation of obstruction; let there be no distinction of power; what is the fault in that?", he replies: "In the absence of power. Since it is impossible for the nature of fire and such things—which is established by perception—to be obstructed, if one does not admit a power distinct from that [nature], then even the phenomenon of obstruction would be without an object.
Such is the intended meaning. || 11 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask, "What is the proof for postulating such a power (*śakti*)? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that if its existence were separate from the possessor of the power, then even in the case of worldly powers such as those of fire and so forth, your desire for proof would not be possible;

thus he says: "Power" (*śakti*). "Like that" (*tadvat*): this is a reference where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary meaning, as in the argument: "The jar is denotable because it is cognizable."

The phrase "just as" (tadvaditi) means that in the case of a purely positive inference (*kevalānvayin*), the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) has its power residing in the universal (*jāti*) alone—this being the view of the Mīmāṃsakas due to parsimony (*lāghava*) and the absence of any specification of a particular instance—just like the power of the word "cow" (*go*) in such commands as "bring [the cow]" (*ānaya*). Therefore, the mention of the word "jar" and so forth is primarily intended to denote the state of being (*bhāva-pradhāna*). Likewise, in the present case as well, since the state of being (*tathātva*) which is the referent of the word "that-like" (*tadvat*) is observed, and since its power is observed in words such as "this" (*idam*), the meaning is established. Thus, he says [the following] because, in the absence of a distinction in power, there would be the consequence of non-difference (*abhedāpatti*):

"Nor [is it the case that there is no proof]," he says. The reason for this is stated as "of the obstruction" (*pratibandhasya*). This means: of the obstruction to the power of burning residing in the fire produced by a magnet-stone (*maṇi*) and so forth.

With this much, he indicates that the *arthāpatti* (presumption) is established even in the absence of the non-difference of the power, by means of the remainder of the passage beginning with "But if there were no power" (*śaktyabhāve tu*). However, if there were no [power] distinct from the capable [fire], then to what would that obstruction belong—that is, the suppression of effects such as burning caused by the magnet-stone and so forth—even when the fire exists? For its effect, namely burning, [would not occur].

The cessation of laughter caused by a jewel or similar object is perceived through direct perception; that [cessation] would not occur [if the power were non-existent]. Therefore, the implication is that it is also improper to say that "power is non-different from the possessor of power" on the grounds that such a phenomenon would otherwise be inexplicable. || 11 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection—"How can the obstruction of a power that is beyond the senses be understood?"—he says:

That which is called non-dual bliss is the obstruction to what is not an effect, because Śakti is inferred from its effects.
If there is no burning by a blazing fire, it must be due to the obstruction caused by mantras and the like.

Regarding the phrase "of power" (*śakteḥ*): although power is beyond the senses, since it is to be known through the mark of its effect, it follows that when an effect does not arise despite the presence of its cause—i.e., when there is an obstruction—the obstruction is understood; this is the implied meaning. He clarifies the stated point by showing an example:
"of a burning [fire]" (*jvalataḥ*). In the world, when an effect characterized by burning and so forth does not arise from a fire that is burning in its own nature, [the obstruction is inferred].
The meaning is that there would be an obstruction of mantras and so forth; that is, mantras and the like would possess the quality of obstructing [their own] power. || 12 ||
Commentary (a0): Now, one might ask: "In this way, how can even the obstruction of a power that is indefinable and beyond the senses be understood?

To this, he says: "Of the power... and so forth. Regarding "by mantras, etc.": the connection is that the state of being obstructed—the state of having its power hindered—of even a blazing fire would occur when there is no burning caused by it, due to [obstruction] by means of mantras, gems, medicinal herbs, and the like. || 12 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus presented the worldly power (*laukika-śakti*) both in terms of its essential nature and its means of proof, he now recites, in accordance with the meaning, the passage from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad regarding the existence of the power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*): "Those who have entered into the yoga of meditation beheld the divine power of the Self, hidden by its own qualities."
The sages have known the divine power of the Self, concealed by its own qualities.
His supreme power is manifold, consisting of action, knowledge, and strength.

"Of the Divine Self" (*devātman*): The sages, having perceived the defects in the theories of time, inherent nature (*svabhāva*), and other such causes, and being qualified aspirants who have resorted to the yoga of meditation with the desire to know the cause of the universe, [perceive] the power of the Divine Self—the power of Brahman, which is the shining, self-luminous conscious Self, non-different from the inner witness (*pratyagātman*), and whose form is *māyā*. This power is hidden by its own qualities, namely its effects in the form of gross and subtle bodies; it is "thoroughly hidden" (*nigūḍhā*).

The meaning is that they did not perceive, but rather directly realized [it]. In that very Upaniṣad, he recites another passage by way of its meaning: “*parā'sya śaktivividhaiva śrūyate svābhāvikī jñānabalakriyā ca*” (His supreme power is heard to be manifold indeed, consisting of innate knowledge, strength, and action). He explains this with the words “*parā'sya*”: of this Brahman, the supreme—that is, the most excellent—power which is the cause of the universe is heard to be manifold; such is the remainder of the sentence. He states its manifold nature as follows:

Regarding the word *kriyā*: when action (*kriyā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) are established, power (*bala*) is the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), because it accompanies the powers of knowledge and action. That whose nature (*svarūpa*) consists of the powers of action and so forth is "that which has action, knowledge, and power as its essence" (*kriyā-jñāna-bala-ātmikā*). || 13 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, since the existence of the aforementioned power follows from the very existence of the Self, he cites the following scriptural authorities—“Those who have attained the yoga of meditation beheld the divine power of the Self, hidden by its own qualities” and “His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, consisting of knowledge, strength, and action, and it is inherent”—by using the word “divine” (deva). “Hidden” (nigūḍhā) means pervaded. || 13 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question of where these two statements originate, he says:
"Thus spoke the Vedic word, and Vasiṣṭha likewise declared."
The Supreme Brahman possesses all powers; it is eternal, ever-full, and non-dual.
—Thus [it is said]. Not only is the power of *māyā* well-known from the *Śruti*, but it is also well-known from the *Smṛti*; thus he says:
"Vasiṣṭha. Just as the *Śruti* has described the manifold power of *māyā*, Vasiṣṭha likewise described it in the work titled *Vāsiṣṭha*.

The word "text" (*grantha*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. He recites the very verses from the *Vāsiṣṭha* that set forth *māyā*: "All... etc. "Eternal, ever-full, non-dual" describes the ultimate nature of Brahman; "possessing all powers" describes its nature when it has adjuncts (*sopādhika*). || 14 ||
Commentary: Thus, he states that the words of Vasiṣṭha are likewise present here, saying "iti" (thus). He recites those very words beginning with "sarva... (all...). 14.
