By which power he shines, he attains manifestation.
O Rāma, the power of consciousness (cic-chakti) of Brahman is perceived within bodies.

459 Rāghavānanda’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): That Supreme Brahman, when—by whichever power of *māyā*—it shines forth, unfolds, or manifests itself, then that very power attains illumination, that is, it reaches manifestation. Now, [the author] describes that very manifestation:

He elaborates on this [nature] with two verses beginning with "The power of consciousness" (cicchakti): "In bodies characterized as gods, animals, humans, and so forth, the power of consciousness is perceived—that is, seen—as the cause for the conventional usage of 'sentience'. (19)
Commentary (a0): This is that power (śakti). "In bodies" means by way of the delimitation of the physical body. || 15 ||
The power of movement resides in the winds, and likewise, the power of solidity resides in stones.
Likewise, the power of fluidity resides in water, and the power of burning resides in fire.

Rāma’s Commentary: By the statement that the power of vibration (*spandaśakti*), which is the cause of movement, attains manifestation, the existence of the universe within Brahman is shown even during its unmanifested state. || 16 ||
Commentary on verse 16.
Likewise, the power of emptiness resides in space, and the power of destruction resides in that which is perishable.
Just as there is no great serpent within a rope, so there is no world within the Self.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He provides an illustration for the existence of that which is unmanifest by saying, "Just as an egg," etc. (17).
Commentary: || 17 ||
It possessed fruits, leaves, creepers, flowers, branches, twigs, and roots.
Is it not the case that, just as a tree exists within a seed, so too does this [universe] abide within Brahman? (18)
Rāma’s Commentary: To provide an illustration for the existence of that [unmanifest] even though it is variegated, he says: "Like a seed," etc. (18).
Commentary on verse 18.
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: why do all the powers not manifest simultaneously?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Therefore, certain powers arise at certain times and in certain places."
Due to the diversity of place and time, they are like rice plants on the surface of the earth. || 19 ||

Regarding the phrase "in some places" (*kvacid*): in certain specific locations and at certain specific times, particular powers (*śakti*) and so forth [manifest]. He provides an illustration for their non-simultaneous manifestation with the words "from the surface of the earth" (*kṣmātala*): just as among all seeds situated in the ground, sprouts arise from only some seeds in a particular place and at a particular time, and not from all of them—such is the meaning. || 19 ||
Commentary on verse 19.
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, in order to demonstrate that the world consists of mere imagination, he first shows the nature of the mind that performs that imagining:
"O Rāma, that Self is all-pervading and possesses an eternally manifest, great form."
That which holds the power of even slight reflection is called the mind (manas). || 20 ||
"He" refers to the one whose great body is eternally risen— that is, whose vast form is perpetually manifest and free from the limitations of space, time, and so forth.
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya:

[He whose essential nature (*svarūpa*) is a body devoid of suffering, called *Advaitānanda*; if, at this time, even slightly, he possesses the power of reflection consisting of the realization of both self and other...]
When it assumes and maintains forms that are transformations of Māyā, at those times it is called the mind (manas). || 20 ||
The collective mind of the commentators. || 20 ||
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Now he describes the manner of conceptualization:
"First, the mind and the two views regarding its bondage and liberation; afterwards, the construction of the manifold world, which is called the universe."
This state of affairs, beginning with these words, has indeed attained firm establishment, like a narrative recounted by a child of fortunate disposition. || 21 ||

"At the beginning" means: first, through the manifestation of the power of thought (*manana-śakti*), the mind (*manas*) comes into being; immediately thereafter, the notions of bondage and liberation—the conceptualization of bondage and liberation—arise; and subsequently, within the very notion of bondage itself, that which is called "the world" (*bhuvana*)—that is, she whose designation is "the world"—namely, the construction and conceptualization of the phenomenal universe (*prapañca*) consisting of mountains, cities, rivers, oceans, and so forth, comes into being.

"Beginning with 'tyādi' (and so forth): this condition of the world is of such a nature; it has attained and reached stability and firmness. To provide an illustration for the perception of reality even in that which is imagined, he says 'ākhyāyikā' (a narrative): just as a story told to children reaches the status of being perceived as real, so too is this world. || 21 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā) on verse 21: "Subhagā" means a princess. || 21 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He relates that very story from the Vāsiṣṭha:
"For the amusement of a child, a nurse tells a pleasant tale."
"O mighty-armed one, are there three auspicious princes? [22]
Two were not born, and likewise one did not even remain in the womb.
Those endowed with righteousness dwell there, even though the city is utterly non-existent.
Having emerged from their own empty city, those of pure intention—
As they were traveling through the sky, they saw trees laden with fruit.
In that future city, all three of those princes shall also exist.
"O son, those engaged in the practice of hunting are now dwelling happily today. (25)
O Rāma, this auspicious narrative concerning the boy has thus been told by Dhātrī.
That boy reached a firm conviction through his non-discerning intellect.
By the words "of the child," etc. (vv. 22–26).
Commentary on the Āgama (A0 Ṭīkā): He clarifies the aforementioned illustration itself with the verse beginning "of the child" (v. 22). 22, 23, 24.
This is the construction of saṃsāra for those whose minds are devoid of inquiry.
Thus, this narrative concerning the boy has reached its conclusion.
Rāma’s Commentary: He applies the point established by the illustration to the subject of the illustration—“This,” etc. (27).
The commentary applies this to the subject at hand: "This," etc. (27).
Rāma’s Commentary— He concludes what was stated by Vasiṣṭha:
[Chapter Thirteen]
Through these and other such narratives, the expansion of the power of *māyā* [is explained] along with the two commentaries.
Vasiṣṭha spoke: "That very Śakti is now being defined. || 28 ||

Regarding the phrase "by these and others": having thus presented the evidence for the existence of Māyā, he makes a formal declaration (pratijñā) to state its indeterminability (anirvacanīyatva): "That very [Māyā] is Śakti. || 28 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Having concluded the statement of Vasiṣṭha, he introduces the subject at hand with the words "ityādibhiḥ" (by these [verses], etc.). ||28||
This power would be distinct [from its cause] both in terms of its effect and its substratum.
When sparks and embers are seen, power is inferred therein. || 29 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Regarding the phrase "from its effect" (*kāryāt*): this power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*) must be of a different nature—that is, of a contrary character—both from the world, which is its own effect (*svakārya*), and from Brahman, which is its substratum (*svāśraya*). [This is because] the power of illusion differs from its effect and its substratum...

He clarifies its distinctness by means of an illustration: "The crackling sound and the charcoal. The crackling sound (*sphoṭa*), which is the effect-form of the power residing in fire, and the charcoal, which is its substratum-form, are both accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Power (*śakti*), however, is to be inferred from its effects (*kāryānumeya*). Therefore, the meaning is that it is of a different nature (*vilakṣaṇa*) than those two. || 29 ||
a0 Commentary: He elaborates upon what has already been asserted, beginning with the words "from the effect" (kāryāt). In that regard, he provides an example:
"the bursting forth" (sphoṭa), etc. || 29 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He applies the aforementioned principle even to the power of clay:
"In this case, the jar—which has the form of a broad base and a belly—is the effect, and the clay is [the cause]."
Power (śakti), though not of that same nature, is endowed with the five qualities beginning with sound.

Regarding the phrase "pṛthubudhna" (broad-based): that which has the form of a broad-based belly—meaning a pot whose base (*budhna*) is broad, thick, and round, and whose belly (*udara*) is likewise—is what should be produced. Clay, endowed with the five qualities known as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, is the material cause (*āśraya*). However, *śakti* (the causal power) is distinct from both of these; this is the meaning. || 30 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He provides another illustration of the two [types of causes] with the verse beginning "pṛthu. The meaning is: that which has a form such that its base (*budhna*) is broad (*pṛthu*) and its belly (*udara*) is round—that is the kind of pot; it is to be produced, meaning it is to be fashioned by a potter using a rod and other tools. In this context, the cause called "pot" is endowed with the five qualities, such as sound and so forth, whereas the power (*śakti*), however, is not of that same nature.
The logical connection is that it becomes distinct from [the states of] dreaming and so forth. || 30 ||
Rāma’s commentary states the very distinction:
"It is neither earth and so forth, nor sound and so forth; it is a reality that exists in the form of power (śakti), just as it is."
For this very reason, she is inconceivable and does not admit of definition. || 31 ||

"It is not [like] earth and so forth. This means that in *śakti* (potency), there is no effect-property such as "broadness" (*pṛthutva*), nor is it found in the substratum-property such as sound and so forth; therefore, it is of a different character (*vilakṣaṇā*). If one asks, "Then what is it like?", he says: "Let it be... He clarifies the very meaning already stated with the words "in whatever way": "For this very reason... Since it is distinct from both the effect and the substratum, for this very reason it is inconceivable (*acintya*). It is... inconceivable.
"It is impossible to describe. Anticipating the objection that its essential nature must therefore be simply inconceivability, he says: "It is not definable.
The meaning is that it cannot be defined by any form whatsoever—whether as distinct, as non-distinct, as inconceivable, or otherwise. || 31 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) says: He states that very point with the words beginning "no," and so forth. He states the resulting conclusion with the remainder of the first half-verse, beginning with "let it be," and so forth. He asks what follows from that and replies with "for this very reason. || 31 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 460–460, verse 462.

[Advaitānanda-nāma-rāghava-ṭīkā: Now, one might object: "If there exists a power (śakti) distinct from the nature of the cause, then why does it not manifest like the nature of the cause itself? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Prior to the arising of the effect, the power remains hidden, situated within the clay.
With the assistance of the potter and others, it undergoes the state of having a modified form. || 32 ||

Regarding the phrase "from the arising of the effect": the meaning is that the power of the clay exists latent within the clay prior to the arising of effects such as a jar; therefore, it does not manifest. Anticipating the objection that if it were latent, there could be no manifestation of it even subsequently, he says "the potter, etc."—meaning that just as butter and the like, though unmanifest, are manifested through churning and so forth, so too its manifestation occurs through the activity of the potter and others.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the staff, the wheel, and so forth are included. || 32 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) explains that [point] with the verse beginning "kārya" and so forth. || 32 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If the effect exists as something distinct from its cause, why does the difference between cause and effect not manifest?
Anticipating this, he states that it is due to the absence of inquiry—which is the cause for perceiving such a difference:
"The expansion and other modifications, as well as the touch and so forth, [are all perceived] in the clay."
People who lack discernment speak of a "pot" by treating these [elements] as a single unity. || 33 ||

Regarding the phrase "due to its broadness, etc.": undiscriminating people, failing to investigate, conflate the effect—consisting of the form of a broad base and so forth—with the cause, the clay, which consists of qualities such as sound and touch, and thus they call it a "jar. || 33 ||

Commentary (a0): If that is so, what then is the form of the jar? To this he says: "pṛthutvādi" (broadness, etc.). This refers to the modification characterized by broadness and so forth, which was mentioned previously. The reading "pṛthutvādivikārāntam" is indeed a corruption. || 33 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question, "Why is this conventional usage regarding the jar rooted in a lack of inquiry? he says:
"Whatever portion [of the clay] existed prior to the potter's activity, that was not our 'jar'."
But subsequently, when it possesses a broad base and so forth, its status as a jar is indeed logical. (34)

Regarding the term *kulāla* (potter): the point is that because the portion of clay existing prior to the potter’s activity is conventionally designated as a "jar," such usage is rooted in a lack of critical inquiry. To the question, "To what, then, does 'jar-ness' belong? he replies with the word "subsequently" (*paścāt*).

It is appropriate that the status of being denotable by the word "jar" belongs only to that which possesses the form of a broad base and belly, appearing after the potter’s activity; for it is observed that the word "jar" is employed only immediately following its production.
This is the intended meaning. || 34 ||
a0 Commentary: He states the reasoning for that [point] as "kulālādi" (like a potter, etc.). || 34 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection that it is illogical for an ultimately real pot to be the effect of an indeterminable power, he states that the ultimate reality of the pot itself is unestablished:
"That pot is not different from the clay, because it is not perceived when [the clay] is separated."
Nor is it non-different [from the body], because it was not perceived even previously during the state of being a physical mass. || 35 ||

Regarding the statement "that is the jar": because it is impossible to perceive the jar as something separate from the clay, it is not different from the clay; yet it is not identical to the clay either, because it is not perceived during the state of being a lump of clay. || 35 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): What follows from that? He says: "He" (saḥ). The word "from clay" (mṛdaḥ) is to be supplied here as well, following the ablative case [of the previous verse]. Thus, the meaning is: because of the non-perception—that is, the non-observation—of the jar when it has been separated from its source, the clay. || 35 ||
*Regarding that modification such as broadness and so forth, this is the reading of Acyutarāya.

Accompanied by two commentaries:
therefore, this [world] is indefinable; like a power, it is born from that power.
In its unmanifest state, she is said to be power (śakti); in its manifest state, she bears the name of the jar (ghaṭā).
Rāghava’s Commentary (Ṭīkā) on Verse 463:

Therefore, like the power (*śakti*), the jar (*ghaṭa*) is indeed indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*). He states the conclusion with the words "by that" (*tena*). Now, if both the power and its effect are equally indeterminable, from what source does the conventional distinction between them—as "power" and as "effect"—arise? To this, he says:
Regarding the state of being unmanifest: || 36 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) on the conclusion states: "Therefore" (ataḥ). "Inexpressible" (anirvacanīyaḥ) means incapable of being defined in terms of either difference from or identity with the cause. || 36 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection that it is not well-known how the power of *māyā*, which was previously unmanifest, becomes manifest later—thus failing to establish the true nature of *māyā*—he says:
"Even the *māyā* residing in a magician is not manifested beforehand."
Afterwards, he shall manifest in the form of Gandharvasena and others.
"An illusionist" (aiṃdrajālika) means: prior to the application of jewels, mantras, and so forth. || 37 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask: "Where in the world has this definition of *māyā*—which culminates in the state of being manifest as an effect while previously unmanifest and non-existent through both difference and non-difference from its own substratum—been observed? To clarify this, he says: "By the magician... (verse 37).

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: It is stated even in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad that the effect of power, such as a jar and so forth, is unreal, while the substratum of that power, such as clay and so forth, is real; thus he says:
"In this way, by virtue of being composed of māyā, the modification has the nature of unreality."
And the Śruti has declared that the clay substance, which is the substratum of the modification, is real. || 38 ||

"Thus" means: because they consist of illusion—that is, because they are effects of illusion—the unreal nature (mṛṣātva) of modifications such as jars, which are products, has been stated by the Śruti: "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is true," and so forth, thereby declaring the reality of the clay which serves as the substratum for those modifications like jars. || 38 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Stating the conclusion, he cites scripture as authority there with the words "evam" (thus). "Anṛta" means the state of being false or illusory in nature. || 38 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, he recites in substance the passage beginning with "a mere beginning in speech" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4): "The modification, which is to be produced by speech, is a mere name; it has no reality."
But pure clay alone is real, though it possesses qualities such as touch and the rest. || 39 ||

"Produced by speech" means that which is to be uttered by the organ of speech is merely a name; for this jar and so forth, reality consists only in the name. There is no ultimate form existing apart from the name; rather, the meaning is that only the clay, which serves as its substrate, is real. || 39 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He recites, according to its meaning, that very Śruti passage found in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad—"The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth"—beginning with the words "vāk" (speech). || 39 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the reason for the unreality of both power and its effects, as well as the reality of their substratum:
"The manifest and the unmanifest, and their substratum"—thus, among these three, [the first two are unreal].
The third, however, follows as a transformation through the distinction of time. || 40 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [page 462] 464.
[Regarding the phrase "the one called Advaitānanda has manifested":
The manifest is the effect characterized by the banyan tree and so forth; the unmanifest is the power that constitutes its cause.
Between these three—the manifest, the unmanifest, and the earth which is their substratum (the support of those two)—in the case of the first two mentioned at the outset:

Because there exists a distinction between the two times associated with the power (*śakti*) and the effect (*kārya*), there is a succession (*paryāya*), which is their occurrence in sequence. However, the substrate (*ādhāra*), such as clay and so forth, persists through both; it continues to exist in both states. This is the meaning: since the power and the effect are occasional, they are unreal (*anṛta*); but since the substrate persists throughout the three periods of time, it is real (*satya*). 40.

Commentary (a0): Thus, how could both the power (*śakti*) and its effect be false? To this he says: "Manifested" (*vyakta*), etc. It "follows" (*anugacchati*), meaning it persists through both the manifested and the unmanifested. || 40 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now he states three reasons for the unreality of the transformation itself:
"The manifest, which appears while being devoid of reality, is subject to birth and destruction."
Upon its arising, its name is produced by speech through the vocal organs. || 41 ||

"Without reality" (nistattva): the manifest (vyakta)—the effects such as jars and the like denoted by the word "manifest"—appears while being non-existent in its own nature; likewise, it is perceived as having origination and destruction, and immediately after its origination, it is designated through speech as consisting of names produced by the organ of speech. ||41||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Thus, although both the excluded [object] and the unmanifest-unmanifest are equally false, one might ask: what is the distinction regarding the manifest? Anticipating this, he states that its very nature is being produced: "nistattvam" (it is devoid of reality). || 41 ||
Even when the individual has perished, this name continues to persist in the mouths of men.
Because it is defined by that name, its form is said to be unmanifest (avyakta). || 42 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Furthermore, [it is said] "the manifest" (*vyakta*). Even when the manifest, which is the nature of the effect, has perished, this name—which is non-different from that effect—persists in the mouths (*nṛvaktreṣu*) of men (*nṛ*), that is, of those who employ speech. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "By that" (*tena*).
Because the manifest effect is defined (*nirūpyatvāt*) by that name or word being uttered (*vācā vyavanhiyamāṇena*), it is of the nature of that [name].
The meaning is that its very form is the form of that name; thus, it is said to consist of the nature of the name. This is the underlying intention:
the pot under dispute must consist of the word "pot," because it is designated by the word "pot," just like the word itself. || 42 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, he establishes the state of being a mere verbal handle (*vācāraṃbhaṇatva*) as declared in the Śruti—beginning with the words "vyakte" (in the manifest). That form is the form of a mere verbal handle. || 42 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Having thus established the three reasons, he now indicates the manner of formulating the inference:
"Because of being devoid of reality, because of perishability, and because it is a name based on mere speech."
But that form of the manifest is not real in any way, like [the form of] clay and so forth. (43)

"Because it is devoid of reality (*nistattvatvāt*). This means that whatever form the manifest effect—such as a jar or the like—possesses, such as its specific shape and so forth, none of that is in any way real. It is "devoid of reality" (*nistattva*) because its *tattva*, its true or essential nature, has departed from it;

the state of being thus is "devoidness of reality. Furthermore, because it is perishable—that is, because it stands in the relation of being subject to destruction only when the clay exists—it is a mere verbal handle (*vācārambhaṇa*).

Since the clay [in the example] consists merely of sound produced by the organ of speech, it serves as a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) for all three reasons, just like the clay itself. Here the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "An effect such as a jar must be unreal because it lacks reality (*nistattvatvāt*); whatever is not unreal does not lack reality, just as the clay which is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the jar. This is a purely negative inference (*kevala-vyatirekī*). The same logic should be applied to the other two reasons as well. || 43 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): For this very reason. "Because of being devoid of reality" (nistattvatvāt) means "because of being sublated. The reason for that is: "and because of being speech" (vāceti). The reason for even that is: "because of perishability" (vināśitvāt). || 43 ||
The Thirteenth Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā) on Verse 465: Having thus established the unreality of the modification, he now establishes the reality of the clay, which is the substratum of that modification.
Therefore, prior to and even after the time of manifestation, it possesses a single uniform nature.
That which is eternal and indestructible is called the truth; that which is perishable is said to be falsehood. || 44 ||

Regarding the term "manifest" (*vyakta*): [it exists] during the time of manifestation, during the time of its persistence, prior to that—that is, before the manifestation arises—and also after, even at the time following the destruction of the manifest. That which possesses a single form (*ekarūpa*), which exists as a single aspect (*ekākāra*), and which is "endowed with reality" (*satattva*)—meaning it exists together with reality (*tattvena*) in its true, essential nature (*vāstava-rūpa*)—is indestructible; that clay-substance which is devoid of destruction along with its modifications is called "real" (*satya*). Herein lies this inference: [The text continues: ...the clay-substance is real because it persists through its own modifications, just like the self (*ātman*). This is the reason (*hetu*). It is not unproven (*asiddha*), for it is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of knowledge. Nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), for it is observed in similar instances (*sapakṣa*). Nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), for there is no other category of things that could serve as a counter-example (*vipakṣa*). Furthermore, since the clay-substance is perceived as persisting through its various states such as being a lump, a jar, or shards, it is established that it is real. If it were unreal, it would follow that it is non-existent, like a sky-flower. But this is not accepted. Therefore, the clay-substance is real. Thus, the clay-substance is real because it persists through its own modifications, just like the self. This is the inference. Furthermore, the clay-substance is real because it is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of its effects, just like the threads of a cloth. This is the reason. It is not unproven, for it is established by perception and other means of knowledge. Nor is it contradictory, for it is observed in similar instances. But this is not accepted. Therefore, the clay-substance is real. Thus, the clay-substance is real because it is the material cause of its effects, just like the threads of a cloth. This is the inference. Furthermore, the clay-substance is real because it is the object of the notion of "clay," just like the self. This is the reason. Thus, the clay-substance is real because it is the object of the notion of "clay," just like the self. This is the inference. Furthermore, the clay-substance is real because it is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of its qualities, just like the self. This is the reason. It is not unproven, for it is established by perception and other means of knowledge. Nor is it contradictory, for it is observed in similar instances. Nor is it inconclusive, for there is no other category of things that could serve as a counter-example. Moreover, since the clay-substance is perceived as the substratum of its qualities, it is established that it is real. If it were unreal, it would follow that it is non-existent, like a sky-flower. But this is not accepted. Therefore, the clay-substance is real. Thus, the clay-substance is real because it is the substratum of its qualities, just like the self. This is the inference. Furthermore, the clay-substance is real because it is the agent of its own actions, just like the self. This is the reason. It is not unproven, for it is established by perception and other means of knowledge. Nor is it contradictory, for it is observed in similar instances. Moreover, since the clay-substance is perceived as the enjoyer of its fruits, it is established that it is real. If it were unreal, it would follow that it is non-existent, like a sky-flower. But this is not accepted. Therefore, the clay-substance is real. Thus, the clay-substance is real because it is the enjoyer of its fruits, just like the self. This is the inference. Furthermore, the clay-substance is real because it is the knower (*jñātṛ*) of objects, just like the self. This is the reason. It is not unproven, for it is established by perception and other means of knowledge. Nor is it contradictory, for it is observed in similar instances. Nor is it inconclusive, for there is no other category of things that could serve as a counter-example. Moreover, since the clay-substance is perceived as the knower of objects, it is established that it is real. If it were unreal, it would follow that it is non-existent, like a sky-flower. But this is not accepted. Therefore, the clay-substance is real. Thus, the clay-substance is real because it is the knower of objects, just like the self. This is the inference. Furthermore, the clay-substance is real because it is the object of the notion of "existence," just like the self. This is the reason. It is not unproven, for it is established by perception and other means of knowledge. Nor is it contradictory, for it is observed in similar instances. Nor is it inconclusive, for there is no other category of things that could serve as a counter-example. Moreover, since the clay-substance is perceived as the object of the notion of "existence," it is established that it is real. If it were unreal, it would follow that it is non-existent, like a sky-flower. But this is not accepted. Therefore, the clay-substance is real. Thus, the clay-substance is real because it is the object of the notion of "existence," just like the self. This is the inference. Furthermore, the clay-substance is real because it is the object of the notion of "substance," just like the self. This is the reason. It is not unproven, for it is established by perception and other means of knowledge. Nor is it contradictory, for it is observed in similar instances. Nor is it inconclusive, for there is no other category of things that could serve as a counter-example. Moreover, since the clay-substance is perceived as the object of the notion of "substance," it is established that it is real. If it were unreal, it would follow that it is non-existent, like a sky-flower. But this is not accepted. Therefore, the clay-substance is real. Thus, the clay-substance is real because it is the object of the notion of "substance," just like the self. This is the inference. Furthermore, the clay-substance is real because it is the object of the notion of "earth," just like the self. This is the reason. It is not unproven, for it is established by perception and other means of knowledge. Nor is it contradictory, for it is observed in similar instances. Nor is it inconclusive, for there is no other category of things that could serve as a counter-example. Moreover, since the clay-substance is perceived as the object of the notion of "earth," it is established that it is real. If it were unreal, it would follow that it is non-existent, like a sky-flower. But this is not accepted. Therefore, the clay-substance is real. Thus, the clay-substance is real because it is the object of the notion of "earth," just like the self. This is the inference. Furthermore, the clay-substance is real because it is the object of the notion of "cause," just like the self. This is the reason. It is not unproven, for it is established by perception and other means of knowledge. Nor is it contradictory, for it is observed in similar instances. Nor is it inconclusive
The opinion that "the subtle entity must be real because it possesses intrinsic nature, like the self," and so forth, should be applied [as a formal argument]. || 44 ||

Commentary (a0): He states the specific characteristic regarding clay: "vyakta" (manifest), etc. "Satattvam" means accompanied by its true nature—that is, accompanied by its essence as clay even at the time of its manifestation and so forth. By this, the statement "only 'clay' is real" is explained. || 44 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "If the entire class of effects, such as a jar, is unreal, then like superimposed silver, it would be removable by the knowledge of its substratum. To this he raises the following doubt:
"It is clearly expressed by these names—'jar', 'modification', and so forth—"
If the object were unreal, why would it not cease upon the cognition of clay? (45)

"Manifest" (vyakta), etc.: the meaning is that if it is accepted that the object denoted by the three words beginning with "manifest"—which is of the nature of an effect—does not exist apart from its cause, then why would there not be the cessation [of the effect] upon the cognition of the cause characterized as clay? || 45 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): In this regard, he raises an objection: "The manifest... (verse 45).
For it is precisely because [the mind] has ceased that your cognition has reached the state of being endowed with that.
In this context, such a cessation itself is the manifestation of the state of being born of awakening.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He dismisses the objection with the words "this is an admitted consequence" (*iṣṭāpatti*) by stating "he has ceased" (*nivṛtta*).

He provides the reasoning for this with the words "because" (*yasmāt*): the meaning is that since your cognition regarding the reality of objects such as jars has perished, therefore he has indeed ceased [to exist as such].

Anticipating the objection—"But what is actually perceived is the non-perception of the superimposed form of silver and so forth, not the disappearance of the cognition of reality"—he states that this [cognition] is without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*).
"Let it be so because it is a non-delusory error; however, in the case of an error with an adjunct (*sopādhika-bhrama*), cessation must consist precisely in the removal of the cognition of reality.

With this intention, he says "of such a kind" (*īdṛk*). Here, in the context of an error with an adjunct, cessation—which arises from knowledge (*bodhajā*) produced by the realization of the true nature of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-yāthātmya-jñāna*)—must be accepted as being of this very nature, namely the removal of the cognition of reality; it does not mean non-appearance, nor does it mean a state of non-perception of the essential form (*svarūpa*). || 46 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) resolves [the objection] with the words: "It has indeed ceased" (nivṛtta eva). || 46 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question "Where has this been seen?", he says:
"Even though a man appears with his face downward in water, he does not exist in reality."
Like a bystander or a mortal, no one has any attachment whatsoever to that [body].

Regarding the term "pumān" (the man): although a man appears in the water with his face turned downwards, he does not exist in reality. He states the reasoning for this with the word "taṭasthasya": for no one—whether a person of discrimination or one lacking it—ever possesses the conceit of its reality in that downward-facing person at any place or time, just as they do toward a person standing on the bank. || 47 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He establishes that point with the words "The person" (pumān). For when the eyes are directed downward into water—[[page 464-to-464]]—the person [perceives].
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
[the section titled] *Advaitānanda*.

The intention is that the *raṇas* grasp the universe precisely by turning back and having their heads downward and so forth; however, the rest should be understood from my *Siddhāntaratnaśuddhānta*. || 47 ||
The proponents of non-duality (Advaitavādins) maintain that such realization constitutes the ultimate goal of human existence.
Because it does not abandon its nature as clay, the state of being earth persists in the jar. (48)

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that the mere knowledge of the unreality of what has been superimposed does not result in the attainment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Anticipating this, he says: "In this manner" (*īdṛk*). The intention is that when, through the doctrine of non-duality (*advaitavāda*), there is the certainty that everything other than the bliss of the Self is false, the human goal—characterized by the manifestation of non-dual bliss—is accomplished. [Objection: But surely, if it is established that the jar is a transformation (*vivarta*) of clay, then from the knowledge of that [clay], the reality of the jar [would follow]...
Fearing that it might be objected that "the intellect does not cease, and this is not established at present," he says: "of the nature of clay" (mṛdrūpasya) || 48 ||

The commentary on verse a states the conclusion: "Such is [the case]" (īdṛk). The reason for this is given as "clay" (mṛt). The intention is that the dualist logician, the Lord of Disputants, has been refuted. || 48 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection—“Even if there is no abandonment of the nature of clay in the jar, why should the jar not be a transformation of clay?”—he says:
“In a transformation, the previous form must be abandoned, just like the form of milk.”
The clay and the gold do not cease to exist when they become a jar or an earring.

Regarding the term "transformation" (*pariṇāma*): the meaning is that where transformation is admitted, as in the case of milk and the like, there the abandonment of the prior form—the state of being milk—is observed. Now, raising the objection, "In what instance is the non-abandonment of the prior form seen in the case of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*)? he replies, "In clay and gold," stating that it is seen in the illusory manifestations of clay and gold. Even when jars, bowls, earrings, and bracelets have been produced from their respective causes, the clay and gold—[which serve as the material basis]—remain.
—They do not turn back from form; this is indeed well-established, such is the meaning. || 49 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He states the distinction regarding transformation (*pariṇāma*)—namely, "transformation" (*pariṇāma*). He clarifies its difference from the initial stage of commencement (*ārambha*) and so forth by means of the example: "clay" (*mṛd*). || 49 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that it is untenable for the jar to be a transformation (vivarta) of clay, because when the jar is destroyed, the clay is not observed again; thus he raises this doubt:
"When the jar is broken, there is no state of clay, because only shards are perceived."
"Do not say so; in this powder there is the form of silver, but the form of gold is very clear. (50)

Regarding the term "pot": he states the reason for the absence of the state of clay with the words "of the potsherds. He refutes the objection that "if the potsherds were also destroyed, the state of clay would be perceived" by saying "it is not so. He states that this objection has no place in the case of gold with the words "gold. || 50 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Anticipating an objection even there, he provides a resolution with the words "the jar" (ghaṭa iti). The meaning is that when the powdering of the potsherds is also performed by grinding them down, it is called "powder" (cūrṇa). The detailed exposition, however, is found in the original source itself; this is the direction [for further study]. || 10 ||
Let there be transformation in milk and so forth, because that [original] state is subsequently abandoned.
By this much, the status of clay and the other examples as illustrations is not lost. || 51 ||

Rāmānuja’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection is raised: "If, among milk, clay, gold, and so forth—which were cited as examples for transformation (*pariṇāma*)—clay and gold are accepted as examples of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), then by that same logic, milk too would have to be such [an example]. Anticipating this, he says: "In the case of milk, etc. [Objection: "In that case, since they undergo another state just like milk, clay and gold could not serve as examples of illusory manifestation. Anticipating this, he says: *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The full passage from the commentary continues:* "...Anticipating this, he says: 'In the case of milk, etc. [Objection: 'In that case, since they undergo another state just like milk, clay and gold could not serve as examples of illusory manifestation. Anticipating this, he says: 'But in the case of clay and gold, etc. [He explains: "The word 'but' (*tu*) is used to remove the doubt. Clay and gold do not undergo another state merely by being transformed into jars or ornaments; rather, they undergo another state through the removal of their previous form and the production of a new form. Therefore, because they are examples of illusory manifestation, there is no contradiction with the scriptural statement that 'the effect is non-different from the cause' (*kāryakāraṇābheda*). *Note: This translation reflects the standard interpretation of the *Śrībhāṣya* on BS 2.1.14, where Rāmānuja distinguishes between *pariṇāma* (transformation) and *vivarta* (illusory manifestation), arguing that while milk truly transforms into curd, clay and gold appear to transform into pots and ornaments only through the removal of a prior state and the imposition of a new one, which constitutes *vivarta*.*
The Thirteenth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.

467 ha—“By this much” means that by this much—the fact that milk and the like undergo transformation (pariṇāma)—the status of clay and gold as examples of illusory manifestation (vivarta) is neither lost nor destroyed. This is the intended meaning: that milk, preceded by the abandonment of its prior form, enters into another state...

Because of the actual existence of attainment, there is indeed transformation (*pariṇāma*). However, in the case of clay and gold, although there is the occurrence of the assumption of another state, because there is no abandonment of the previous form, there is also illusory manifestation (*vivarta*). || 51 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection is raised: "But clay and the like, well-known from the Śruti, are unfit to serve as examples for *vivarta* (illusory manifestation), because they are subject to transformation (*pariṇāma*), like milk. Anticipating this, the author accepts the example and refutes the point at issue (the *dārṣṭāntika*). [He says: "In the case of milk and so forth... Supplying the word "in the doctrine of *vivarta*," the construction is: "the status of being an example is not lost. || 51 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Why not also accept the theory of origination (ārambhavāda) for clay and gold, just as one accepts transformation (pariṇāma) and illusory manifestation (vivarta)?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"For the proponent of origination, the doubling of the clay would result in the effect."
Form, touch, and the rest are said to be distinct in both the effect and the cause.

Regarding the phrase "for the proponent of origination" (*ārambhavādina*): in the view of the proponent of origination, in the case of an effect such as a jar, there would result a doubling of the substance, such as clay or earth, by way of both its causal form and its effect-form. The implication is that if this were so, there would also result a doubling of properties such as weight. Anticipating the question "Why is this so?", he says: "form," etc.; [it is because] there is a distinction between the cause and the effect regarding qualities such as form and the rest.
The sense is that this has been accepted by those very [opponents] themselves. || 52 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, he refutes the theory of origination (*ārambhavāda*) with the words "the proponents of origination" (*ārambhavādinaḥ*). The mention of "clay" (*mṛdaḥ*) is illustrative; it includes gold and other materials as well. The reason for this is given by the word "form" (*rūpa*); for the logicians maintain that the qualities of the cause originate the qualities of the effect.

If transformation (*pariṇāma*) were also included under the category of "effect" by means of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) and so forth, then there would be a doubling of the cause—namely, the gold—in the bracelet and other effects; this is the implication for those who maintain the theory of new production (*ārambhavāda*). || 52 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: "Are both clay and gold alone intended as examples for illusory transformation (vivarta)? No; he says:
"Clay and gold, and [the ether]," thus Āruṇi provides three examples.
Therefore, one should cause falsehood to dwell within all things.

"Clay," etc. The meaning is that a certain sage named Uddālaka, the son of Aruṇa, beginning with the words "Just as, my dear, by a single lump of clay... and ending with "...the iron [is real]," stated three examples—clay, gold, and iron—in that sequence of sentences regarding the unreality of the effect (*kārya*). Having raised the question, "For what purpose did he state these three examples?", he says: "Therefore," etc. Since, in this way, among many [clays]...

The meaning is that since the falsity of effects has been observed in things such as clay, one should therefore instill the notion of the falsity of effects regarding entities consisting of the primary elements and their derivatives. || 53 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might ask, "Where has the status of clay and so forth as an illustration for *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) been stated? To this he says: "Clay," etc.

In the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, in the sixth chapter, Aruṇa’s son Uddālaka, beginning with the words "O dear one, by means of a single lump of clay... and ending with "...that which is made of iron is truly real," establishes through this series of statements that the doctrine of *vivarta* applies to clay, gold, and so on; this is the implicit meaning (*ārthika*). Thus.

The connection is that he states three examples. To the question "What follows from that?", he replies with the remainder of the verse beginning with "ataḥ" (therefore). "Therefore," for this reason, "in all things. "Kārya-" refers to the falsity of the effect. "Vāsayet" means one should practice; completing the ellipsis, the construction is: "the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) should cultivate his own intellect so as to instill the falsity of the effect with respect to every object. || 53 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might ask: for what purpose was the contemplation of the unreality of the effect also stated?
Anticipating this doubt, he says—with the intention that the knowledge of the effect is established through the knowledge of the cause:
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 466] 468.
He also spoke of the knowledge of the effect derived from the knowledge of the cause, which is called Advaitānanda.
How can the cognition of the unreal occur here in the presence of the cognition of the real? || 54 ||

Regarding the term *kāraṇa*: the meaning is that [the Teacher] stated that through the knowledge of the cause—such as clay and so forth—there is also knowledge of the entire collection of effects—such as jars and so forth—as expressed in a series of passages beginning with, "O dear one, by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay would be known. Now, an objection is raised: it is untenable that there can be knowledge of an effect such as a jar, which is of a different nature from its cause, based on the knowledge of an ultimate cause such as clay or gold.
"In truth," [it is said]. || 54 ||

The reason for this is stated as "the cause" (kāraṇa). The intended meaning is that if the aforementioned subliminal impression (*saṃskāra*) of the falsity of the effect did not exist, then the knowledge of the effect could not possibly arise from the knowledge of the cause. To this, an objection is raised: "If [it were] real" (*satya*). ||54||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Since an effect consists of two parts, the real and the unreal, he says— with the intention that knowledge of the cause results in knowledge of the real part within the effect—
that "from the worldly perspective, every modification is an effect."
In this case, the real clay-portion [of the pot] is understood through the understanding of its cause. || 55 ||

"Of the clay" (samṛtkasya): the meaning is that it is well-known in the world that the "state of being an effect"—the referent of the word "effect"—belongs to a modification such as a jar, which is superimposed and accompanied by the clay that serves as its substrate. One might object: "Even if this be so, how has the challenge been answered—that the knowledge of the effect does not follow from the knowledge of the cause? Anticipating this, [the author] states that even in the absence of knowledge regarding the unreal portion belonging to the effect, [there is knowledge] regarding its real portion...
He provides a rebuttal with the words "vāstava" (real): "In this effect, there exists a real portion of clay;
the cognition—that is, the knowledge—of this real portion arises from the knowledge of the cause. This is the meaning. || 55 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He provides the resolution with two verses beginning with "samṛtkasya" (of that which consists of clay). The meaning is: "of the modification," such as a jar, etc., which is established as being inseparable from the clay (*mṛd-avinābhāva-siddha*). || 55 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Just as the element of truth pertaining to the effect must be understood, so too must the element of untruth be understood. Anticipating this, he says, "It is not so, because there is no purpose in understanding it": *amṛtāṃśo na boddhavyastadbodhānupayogataḥ*. (The element of untruth is not to be understood, because its comprehension is of no use.)
Knowledge of reality leads to the goal of man; it is not the comprehension of false portions.

Regarding the phrase "the unreal portion" (*anṛtāṃśa*): he demonstrates the very absence of purpose [in knowing it] with the words "knowledge of reality" (*tattvajñāna*). A *bahuvrīhi* compound is used here: that which has as its purpose (*pumartha*)—meaning the goal or aim (*artha*)—of the person (*puṃsaḥ*), i.e., the knower (*jñātuḥ*), is "that which has the person's purpose" (*pumartham*). The meaning is that the comprehension of the unreal portion, which is a modification (*vikāra*), does not possess a purpose. || 56 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Regarding the phrase "anṛtāṃśa" (the portion of untruth), the meaning is that it is the goal of man (pumartha) because it bestows liberation, which is the ultimate goal of man. || 16 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "The statement that 'knowledge of the effect arises from knowledge of the cause' was spoken with the intention that it would serve as a source of wonder for the increase of the listener's wisdom; however, this is not possible. Thus he raises the doubt:
"If it is asserted that knowledge of the effect comes from knowledge of the cause..."
Since it is perceived as clay due to its clay-nature, it would be called "clay-cognition"; what wonder is there in this? || 57 ||

"Thus [it is said]. When it is stated that from the knowledge of the cause, such as clay, there arises knowledge of the real constituent part (satyāṃśa) of clay residing in the effect, it amounts to saying that from the knowledge of clay comes the knowledge of clay. And this being the case, the wonder lies merely in the words, not in the meaning—this is the sense. || 57 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Even there, he raises an objection with the words "tahiṃ" (then). || 57 ||
The Thirteenth Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

Rāghavānanda’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā) on Verse 469: Even though those possessing such discrimination are free from wonder, he provides a rebuttal by showing that for those devoid of it, wonder will certainly arise.
For one who knows that in all effects, the constituent part of the object is the very nature of the cause, truth [is realized].
Let there be no wonder for one who is ignorant; by whom can such wonder be prevented? || 58 ||

"It is true. The meaning is that while those who know that the real constituent part existing within effects such as jars is none other than the very nature of the cause—let them not be struck with wonder—it is impossible to prevent the astonishment arising in others who are devoid of knowledge of reality. || 58 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Accepting [the objection] and resolving it by means of another intention, he says: "True" (satyam). || 58 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He elaborates on the very point already stated—that wonder would arise in the ignorant—[with the verse]:
"The one who initiates action, the one who undergoes transformation, and the worldly person [all exist] in a single cause."
Having heard everything known by Sarvamati, he indeed experienced astonishment. || 59 ||

"Ārambhī" (the proponent of origination): "Origination" (ārambha) refers to the production of an effect that is distinct from its causes—namely, the inherent (samavāyi), non-inherent (asamavāyi), and instrumental (nimitta) causes. One who asserts this is called an Ārambhī. One who asserts transformation (pariṇāma)—characterized by the attainment of another form through the relinquishing of a prior form—is called a Pariṇāmī. One who is ignorant of these two systems and is concerned solely with worldly convention is called a Laukika (worldly person).
The meaning is that upon hearing the statement, "From the knowledge of a single cause among these three, there arises the cognition of many effects," astonishment would surely occur. || 59 ||
a0 Commentary: He cites an example of that: "The initiator," etc. (59).

Now, one might ask: "What is the reason for abandoning the meaning exactly as it was heard and explaining it in this way? Anticipating this doubt, he says that it is because the scripture has no such intention there: "In order to bring about realization of non-duality, [the scripture] speaks here of the awakening to the One."
There is no cognition of all things in scripture, because of the intention to express diversity.

Regarding the term "non-duality" (advaita): the intention is that in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, the knowledge of this single cause was taught for the sake of making the disciple face toward the realization of non-duality, and not for the purpose of establishing the knowledge of many individual effects.
The commentary on verse 60 states its purpose: "Regarding non-duality"—the underlying thought is that, therefore, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, having first explained the meaning of the statement "Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay becomes known," which is intended to demonstrate the illustration of knowing all through the knowledge of one,

[the author] proceeds to explain the meaning of the statement "Tell me, then, that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known," which is intended to present the application of that illustration to the subject at hand.
He states the result [of the argument]: "Just as from the cognition of a single clay lump, there arises the cognition of everything made of clay."
In the same way, let the world be perceived as being awakened through the awakening of the one Brahman. || 61 ||

"By means of a single lump of clay," etc. The meaning is that just as from the understanding of a single lump of clay—the material cause of jars, bowls, and so forth—there arises an understanding of all its modifications such as jars and the like, so too it should be understood that from the understanding of Brahman, the single material cause of everything, there arises an understanding of the entire world, which is its effect. || 61 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, [the author provides] a passage intended to direct [the mind] toward the non-duality already mentioned, such as: "O dear one, by means of a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay [is known]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4–6).

Vidyāraṇya’s *Pañcadaśī* [in the chapter titled *Advaitānanda*] quotes the meaning of such scriptural passages as "the world consisting of consciousness shall be known," beginning with the word "one" (*eka*). Let the definition of the superimposed (*adhyasta*) be contemplated.

That is to say, since the effect possesses no existence apart from its substratum, it should be subsumed under the investigation solely as having the reality of pure Being, which constitutes that substratum. || 61 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that if the true nature of Brahman and the world is not understood, it cannot be comprehended that knowledge of the world arises from the knowledge of Brahman.
Anticipating this doubt, he shows the nature of both in order to facilitate that understanding:
"Brahman consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss; the world consists of name and form."
In the Tāpanīya [Upaniṣad], Brahman is heard of as being characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.

Regarding the phrase "saccit" (Being-Consciousness): raising the doubt as to what authority there is for Brahman’s nature as Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda), the author states "in the Tāpanīya," intending to show that the *Tāpanīya* and other Upaniṣads constitute the authority. The meaning is that in the latter *Tāpanīya*, according to the followers of the Atharva Veda, Brahman’s nature as Being-Consciousness-Bliss is declared in such passages as "All this is indeed Brahman, consisting solely of Being-Consciousness-Bliss. || 62 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): To establish that, he states the nature of Brahman and the world in succession, beginning with "Being-Consciousness" (saccit).

Regarding the first of these, he cites the authority in the passage beginning with "In the Tāpanīya," etc.: "All this is indeed Brahman, consisting solely of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss"—thus it is stated in the *Nṛsiṃhottara*. (62)
Rāmānuja’s Commentary: By the word "etcetera," he shows other scriptural passages intended [by the author]:
"The form of Being (sat-rūpa), Āruṇi declared; Prajñāna-Brahman, the Bahvṛca."
"O Sanatkumāra, let us go elsewhere from this place of bliss. || 63 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the nature of Being" (*sad-rūpam*): In the *Chāndogya-śruti*, Uddālaka, the son of Aruṇa, defines Brahman as being of the nature of Being through such passages as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sad eva somyedam agra āsīt*). Likewise, the Bahvṛcas—those who study the *Ṛg-veda* branch—in the *Aitareya-upaniṣad* demonstrate that Brahman is of the nature of consciousness (*prajñāna*), stating, "Consciousness is the foundation; consciousness is Brahman. Similarly, in the very same *Chāndogya-śruti* cited previously, the one named Sanatkumāra...

The meaning is that the Guru, having begun with the words "The Infinite (bhūman) indeed must be sought to be known" addressed to his disciple named Nārada, stated that Brahman—which is denoted by the word 'bhūman'—is of the nature of bliss, saying, "That which is the Infinite is bliss. He extends this same principle to other cases as well with the word "thus":
in other scriptural texts such as the Taittirīyaka, through passages like "He understood that Bliss is Brahman," [Brahman] is shown to be of the nature of bliss.
The meaning is that it should be understood as having been stated in general terms. || 63 ||

Commentary (a0): He states that even there, the state of being of a single form is taught in the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad—namely, "of the nature of Being" (*sadrūpa*). This is based on the Śruti passage: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second. It should be understood that Āruṇi Uddālaka spoke of it as "of the nature of Being," while those belonging to the Vājasaneyi branch understand it as "Brahman is consciousness" (*prajñānaṃ brahma*), and so forth. || 63 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He shows that there is scriptural authority for names and forms as well, just as there is for existence, consciousness, and bliss:
"Having discerned all forms and having created names, he remains."
"I shall designate these names and forms," according to the Śruti.

Regarding the word "having discerned" (*vicitya*): the meaning is that the two aspects of name and form residing in the world—the object to be fashioned—are shown by the Śruti in the passages, "Having discerned all forms, the Wise One, having made names, abides calling them forth," and "Entering with this living self, let me manifest names and forms. (64)

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Having thus stated the proofs for Brahman’s nature as existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), he now states those same proofs regarding the world’s nature as name and form (*nāmarūpa*), beginning with the verse "Having discerned... (*vicitya*). Accordingly, it is declared in the Śruti: "The Wise One, having discerned all forms...
[page 469].

"Having made names, he remains addressing them," so it is said in the Puruṣasūkta. Likewise: "Entering with this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms," so it is said in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. And similarly: "In the beginning, this was indeed unmanifest; it was manifested by means of name and form—'He has such a name, this has such a form,'" so it is said in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. (64)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In that very context, he cites another scriptural passage:
"Prior to creation it was undifferentiated; thereafter, it is differentiated into two."
This is the inconceivable power of Māyā, designated as the unmanifest (avyākṛta) within Brahman.

Regarding the term "undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*): in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, it is stated, "In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated; it was differentiated by name and form alone, as 'this is such a name' and 'this is such a form. The meaning is that the nature of the created world is shown to consist of name and form. Prior to creation, this world existed as undifferentiated, having an unmanifest nature of name and form; subsequently, at the time of creation, it became differentiated into two ways, through the relationship of the signifier and the signified.

The meaning is that it has been made manifest. Now, regarding the phrase "this was then unmanifest" (*tadvedaṃ tarhyavyākṛtamāsīt*), he states the meaning of the word "unmanifest" (*avyākṛta*): "inconceivable," etc. The meaning is that this Māyā, which is the inconceivable power (*aciṃtyaśakti*) residing in Brahman, is designated by the word "unmanifest" in this passage. || 65 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus he states the category of the indeterminate (avyākṛta) as "inconceivable" (aciṃtya). || 65 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the meaning of the phrase "it was differentiated by name and form" as follows:
"That which rests in the changeless Brahman undergoes manifold transformation."
One should know Māyā as Prakṛti, and the Great Lord (Maheśvara) as the wielder of Māyā.

Regarding the term "unchanging" (*avikriya*): although it resides in the unchanging Brahman, that [Māyā] undergoes manifold modifications and transformations in the form of the diverse world of beings and their physical bodies.
He provides the scriptural authority for the statement that Māyā resides in Brahman with the words, "But one should know Māyā...
One should know—that is, understand—the aforementioned Māyā as *prakṛti*, meaning the material cause (the source from which things are produced). And [one should know] the *māyin*, its...

The phrase "one should know Maheśvara as possessing that [power], as its substratum, and as the controller of Māyā" is understood to carry over [from the previous verse]. In both cases, however, the word *tu* (but/however) is intended to highlight their mutual distinction. || 66 ||

The commentary on a0 explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "by name and form alone" with the words "without modification. In that regard, it also provides corroboration from another scriptural text (śruti) with the verse "But [the Lord projected] māyā... (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10). || 66 ||
7:44 Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now he describes the first effect of Brahman as conditioned by Māyā:
"The first modification is space; it exists, it shines, and it is dear."
Space is its form; that [space] is false, but not those three.

Regarding the word "the first": he states its threefold nature derived from its cause with the words "it exists" (*so'sti*). The meaning is that it consists of the nature of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss (*saccidānanda*). He states its individual nature with the word "space" (*avakāśa*). He states its distinction from the previous triad of natures with the words "that is false" (*tanmithyā*); the meaning is that the triad of natures beginning with Being is real. || 67 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, he elaborates—beginning with the verse "ādye" and so forth—upon how these [categories] such as Being (sat) and the rest are woven through as the substratum, while the universe, consisting of name and so on, is imagined and thus possesses counter-correlatives such as prior non-existence (prāgabhāva). || 67 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the reason for the falsity of that fourth form:
"It does not exist prior to manifestation, nor even after, because of its destruction."
That which does not exist in the beginning and at the end likewise does not exist in the present.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 470] 472.

"[It is called Advaitānanda, not because of its manifestation. Now, one might object: "How can that which is perceived during the interval between origination and destruction be non-existent? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the beginning... (68).]
The reason for this is given as "not from manifestation" (na vyakteḥ). The meaning is "because of its appearance" (āvirbhāvāt). || 68 ||
Beings have an unmanifest beginning, O Bhārata, and a manifest middle state.
"Indeed, they have their dissolution in the unmanifest," Kṛṣṇa said to Arjuna. (69)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He cites the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa as proof for the stated meaning: "The unmanifested is the beginning... (6.69).
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): In that regard, he also cites Smṛti as an authority: "The unmanifest and so forth" (avyaktādīni) || 69 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Anticipating the question, "What is the proof for the existence of the three forms beginning with 'Being' (sat) as the underlying substratum? he states that experience itself is the proof:
"The qualities of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss always follow [the object] during its manifestation."
In the absence of space, there is the experience of existence and so forth within one's own self.

"Like clay" (mṛdvat): the phrase "like clay" is an illustration intended for demonstration. Just as clay persists throughout the three periods of time in jars and other objects, so too the three forms beginning with "Being" (sat) are always inherent; this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "Excluding space, how can the three forms beginning with 'Being' be experienced? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "without space" (nirākāśa). || 70 ||

The commentary concludes with the words "mṛdvat" (like clay). Herein is the formal argument (*prayoga*): The Self, whose nature is existence and so forth, is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), because it is the underlying continuity, just like clay. He demonstrates this accordingly with the words "nirākāśa" (without space); this is an epithet of the Self. || 70 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He establishes that very point as follows:
"Now, tell me, when the space has been forgotten, what appears there to you?"
If it is argued that it is indeed empty, let it be so; for it certainly appears in such a manner.

Regarding the term "space" (*avakāśa*): he restates the objection of the proponent (*pūrvavādin*) with the word "void" (*śūnya*). Having accepted [the objection], he states the rebuttal: "Let it be so. He says that although it is void in terms of its verbal expression, in terms of its actual meaning, one must admit that there exists something perceived as the substantive (*viśeṣya*) of the qualifying attribute "absence of space"; thus he says "of such a kind" (*tādṛk*). The particle *hi* is intended to indicate what is well-known in the world. || 71 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "When is the self devoid of space? On the contrary, by the very scripture stating, 'And like space, both are omnipresent and eternal,' its omnipresence and other qualities are declared. To this, he says: "Space... Anticipating the answer to that, he refutes it even while conceding the point: "It is indeed void (*śūnya*). The particle *hi* is used for emphasis. "Void" refers to its space...

Even if one were to grant that a thing qualified by the absence of other things has an unimagined name, nevertheless, such a thing shines forth by its own nature; this is the logical connection (*anvaya*). || 71 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the objection, "Let it be so; what does this have to do with the present case?", he states that the nature of that which is perceived as the substantive must be accepted:
"Precisely because it is such, its existence is [established]; through indifference, that is its happiness."
That which is devoid of both favorability and unfavorability is one's own innate happiness.

"Because it is such" (tādṛktvāt). He states that its nature is bliss (*sukhasvarūpatva*) by means of the phrase "by way of indifference" (*audāsīnyena*). The meaning is that its nature is bliss because it is the object of indifference. Anticipating the objection—"How can that which is devoid of favorability (*anukūlatva*) have the nature of bliss?"—he says: "By favorability... (72).

together with the two commentaries.
473a0 Commentary:
To this he says, "Precisely because it is such" (*tādṛktvād eva*). And thus, by the phrase "it shines forth indeed," its nature as consciousness (*cit*) is established;

likewise, precisely because it is such, its existence (*sat*) is established; and similarly, through its indifference (*audāsīnyena*), its bliss (*ānanda*) also exists. Thus, the nature of the Self as Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānandarūpatva*) is affirmed.
The connection is that it is indeed established by existence alone. || 72 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He establishes that very point:
"In the case of favorability, there would be the cognition of joy; but in the case of unfavorability, the cognition of suffering."
In the absence of compassion, there is no personal bliss, nor indeed is there any end to one's own suffering.

Regarding the term "conformity" (*ānukūlya*): one might object, "Could one's own suffering not be like one's own bliss? Anticipating this doubt, he says, "one's own suffering," to show that such is not the case because suffering lacks the establishment of one's true nature. || 73 ||
Commentary (a0): He establishes that one's own happiness exists even when it is devoid of such favorability and so forth—starting with the words "ānukūlye" (in favorability).

Now, one might object: "If that were the case, then one's own suffering should also exist [as a source of happiness]. Anticipating this, he says "nijaṃ duḥkhaṃ tu" (but one's own suffering... and so on, concluding with the remainder of the verse, to show that this is not so because it is never actually experienced. || 73 ||
When one is established in innate bliss, joy and sorrow undergo an instantaneous reversal.
Since the mind is momentary, let it be accepted that those two are mental [perceptions]. (74)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, one might object that since one's own bliss (*nijānanda*) is eternally blissful, there should always be joy and never sorrow.

Anticipating this doubt, he states [verse 74]—beginning with "nijānande"—that although that bliss is eternal, because the mind that perceives it is momentary, both of those mental states (joy and sorrow) are likewise momentary.

The commentary (Ṭīkā) on verse a0 states the conclusion: "nijeti" (one's own). The meaning is that the very Self, denoted by the word *nija*, is a specific modification of the mind (*cittavṛtti*) characterized by the form "I am bliss. "When stable" means when it is unmoving. "Reversal" means becoming void in every respect. The construction is:
"it would occur in a mere moment, from one instant alone. He then asks what follows from that and says: "of the mind... [verse 74].
Rāma’s Commentary: He applies the point established in the illustration to the subject of the illustration:
"In the same way, bliss exists even in space; for its existence and manifestation are indeed accepted."
In this manner, let it be contemplated within all things, from the element of air up to the body itself. || 75 ||

"Even in space" means: in this way, within one's own self, according to the manner already described. The meaning is that since existence (*sattā*) and manifestation (*bhāna*) are admitted even by you, they do not require further proof. He states that the point established regarding space must be accepted for all things from air up to the body—namely, "air and so forth"—in verse 75.

The commentary concludes: "In space also it is thus. Regarding that, there is no disagreement at all concerning the persistence of existence (*sattā*) and so forth; otherwise, space itself would incur the status of being a mere flower [of fancy]. Thus he says: "Existence" (*sattā*). He extends the aforementioned analysis to other cases as well: "Wind and so forth" (*vāyvādi*). || 75 ||
The touch of movement is the form of air; burning and illumination belong to fire.
The determination is that liquidity belongs to water and solidity to earth. || 76 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In that regard, he demonstrates the specific attributes of air and the other elements with the two verses beginning "motion and touch" (verse 76).
The commentary (ṭīkā) summarizes that manifestation as follows: "The states of existence" (gatīti) || 76 ||
In the *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
it is stated that even in plants, food, and bodies, there exists a unique form.
In this manner, one should contemplate with the mind each respective form as appropriate, namely that which is called non-dual bliss. (77)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: "Asādhāraṇa" (uncommon). || 77 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): He states the specific characteristic of space with the words "asādhāraṇa" (uncommon). He concludes the aforementioned analysis with the word "evam" (thus). || 77 ||
And though names and forms are divided in many ways, [it remains] as one.
It abides as existence-consciousness-bliss; there is no contradiction for anyone.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He states the conclusion: "In many ways" (verse 78).
The commentary (ṭīkā) on the conclusion states: "He says 'aneka' etc. || 78 ||
Name and form are devoid of reality, and they are both joined with birth and destruction.
Behold [the world] within Brahman through immersion, like bubbles in the ocean. || 79 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Then, raising the objection as to what is the status of name and form which are perceived, he states that their status is precisely being imagined (kalpitatva), saying "nistattve" (devoid of reality). The reason for their being imagined is "janma" (origination) || 79 ||
He illustrates that [point] with the words "nistaraṅga" (waveless). He provides an example for this with the word "samudra" (ocean).
This too is intended to establish the theory of illusory transformation (*vivarta*), as previously argued in the *Ghaṇṭā*. || 79 ||
When this perfect Brahman, whose nature is truth, consciousness, and bliss, is beheld;
He himself gradually comes to disregard name-and-form. || 80 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Existence-Consciousness-Bliss... (verse 80).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): He states the conclusion: "Saccit... (80).
To whatever extent there may be contempt, to that same extent there is the initiation into it.
To whatever extent one observes [the world], to that same extent one should abandon both.

Rāma’s Commentary: Since the firmness of the knowledge of Brahman is preceded by the disregard for duality, just as it is with hearing and other means of realization, one must also practice the disregard for duality;
thus he says: "As long as... (81).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He states that between those two—observation (*vīkṣaṇa*) and disregard (*avajñā*)—there is a state of mutual causality: "As much as... and so forth. Both [refer to] name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). || 81 ||
Through the practice of that, once knowledge is firmly established, this person—
One may become liberated even while living; let the body be as it may.
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the fruit of practicing both [meditation and action] with the words, "By the practice of that... (82).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, he states the fruit of the practice of contemplating the reality of the Self—which is non-dual Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda) and pervading all—preceded by a disregard for the duality consisting of name and form (nāmarūpa), with the words "by that practice" (tadabhyāsena). The meaning is: when [the contemplation] is well-established, it becomes capable of bestowing liberation while living (jīvanmukti) by subverting the obstacles characterized by the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of contrary conceptions (viparītabhāvanā). || 82 ||

that contemplation, that discourse, and their mutual awakening to one another.
