Rāghavānanda’s Commentary (Rā0 Ṭīkā): Now he describes the nature of the practice of Brahman: "That contemplation... (verse 83).
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He clarifies the etymological derivation and the practice thereof with the words "taccintanam" (the contemplation of That). This has already been explained below [in verse 83].
Latent impressions (vāsanā) span many times, being continuous over a long duration.
And when practiced with reverence, it is entirely and completely eliminated. || 84 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might raise the objection: "How can this duality, which has been manifesting since beginningless time, ever be removed by some practice of knowledge? Anticipating this, he states that it is indeed removed by practice cultivated with long duration, continuity, and devotion: "Vāsanā... (Verse 84).

The commentary (ṭīkā) on that point provides the reason: "It is *vāsanā*. Regarding "long" (*dīrghā*): it is because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is beginningless. This power (*śakti*) is *Kālī*, which serves as the substratum for all time. According to the multi-meaning lexicon (*nānārtha*), the word *inaḥ* means "the sun," "the lord," or "the king"; thus, she is the one who governs like a sovereign. She is both "long" (*dīrghā*) and "of the nature of Kālī" (*kālīnā*), and thus the compound is grammatically correct. For this very reason, [she is] "long" (*dī-*)...
Thus, Patañjali states that only long duration, uninterrupted practice, and devotion are necessary. || 84 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection that it is illogical for the one Brahman to be the cause of a world with manifold forms, he states that it is indeed logical because of its power:
"Like the power of clay, the power of Brahman creates many unreal things."
Alternatively, the illustration here is sleep and dreaming as they occur in a living being. || 85 ||

"Like the power of clay" means that [the world] consists of unreal effects. Anticipating the objection that this is an unequal analogy because the power of clay is real and possesses multiple causes, he states another alternative: "Or else... (verse 85).

Commentary (a0 ṭī0): Now, one might object: "Let it be so that Brahman, when practiced for a long time, without interruption, and with devotion through meditation and other means, bestows the bliss of *jīvanmukti* by destroying the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of contrary notions; yet, how can that non-dual [Brahman] be the originator of this manifold world from the very beginning?
To this, he says: "Like the power of clay" (*mṛcchaktivat*). But surely, the example of clay and the like was already given at the outset?

Because the knowledge of the mere existence of the cause (the Self) brings about the realization of all effects—which are otherwise inexplicable appearances—thereby leading the listeners toward non-duality and, through the direct perception of reality, culminating in the ultimate purport of being solely the immortal essence of non-dual Being-Consciousness-Bliss; how then could the worldly order be established by the analogy of that [magical] power? Due to this lack of conviction, he says "Or else" (*yadvā*). The illustration is as follows: in the causal principle known as *māyā*, which has the other name *avidyā*...
The meaning is that there exists an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) regarding both the characteristic and the effect. || 85 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He clarifies the illustration:
Just as the power of sleep, though residing in the individual soul (jīva), brings about impossible dreams;
This Māyā, which effects creation, preservation, and destruction, is established in Brahman.
[The verse] says "sleeps. He states the application [of this analogy] with the words "in Brahman" (brahmaṇi). || 86 ||
The commentary (ṭīkā) applies this to the subject at hand: "Sleep," etc. (86).
One may see in a dream the act of traveling through the sky, or likewise the cutting off of one's own head.
In a single moment, there is a flood of years, and again, the death of one's children and so forth. (87)

Rāma’s Commentary: He demonstrates the very fact of performing what is difficult to accomplish with the verse beginning "In a dream" (87).

In this state known as non-dual bliss,
the distinction that "this is right" and "this is not" is difficult to find.
In whatever manner and as whatever [object] is perceived, it is joined with that very [nature] in that very manner.
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the reason for the difficulty of [the dream] occurring: "This... (verse 88).

When such greatness was seen of the power of sleep, then—

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He clarifies the aforementioned point by means of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) logic: "Such as this," etc. (89).

Commentary (Ṭīkā) on verse a0: Having thus clarified how the power of sleep accomplishes the impossible, he now demonstrates its establishment in the present context by way of a *kaimutya* argument (the principle of "how much more so"): "Of such a kind... (verse 89).
While a person is lying down, sleep creates manifold dreams.
Thus, he imagines modifications within Brahman itself, which is changeless.

Rāma’s Commentary: He provides an illustration for how Māyā, which is not itself striving for the state of Brahman, serves as the cause of the world—beginning with the verse "śayānaḥ" (lying down). || 90 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He clarifies that very point through the illustration and the illustrated by saying "lying down" (śayānaḥ). This refers to Māyā. || 90 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He shows the objects created by Māyā:
ether, air, fire, water, earth, the worlds, living beings, stones, and so forth.
The modifications within the vital breaths are reflected as the shadow of consciousness.

"Digged," he says. Anticipating the objection—"Even though there is equality in being composed of the five elements (pāñcabhautika), why is some [matter] sentient while other [matter] is insentient?"—he replies with the word "prāṇi. The meaning is that within the bodies of living beings (prāṇin) and within their internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa), there is sentience due to the reflection of consciousness (caitanya); elsewhere, there is insentience because of the absence of that reflection. || 91 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He states those very modifications (*vikāra*), their nature as accepted by himself, and so forth—beginning with the word "kh" (ether). "Lokas" refers to the worlds, such as Satya-loka and others; by the word "ādi" (and so forth), trees and other things are included. "Prāṇi" refers to the intellects (*buddhi*) of living beings (*jīva*). The word "antar" (within) is used to exclude the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) delimited by mental modifications (*vṛtti*) such as valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, [the ether] is reflected in the reflections of consciousness that are reflected within all the intellects of living beings, which are themselves undifferentiated from the immutable (*kūṭastha*).

This is the meaning. Here, "inexplicability" (durghaṭatva) consists precisely in the absence of a locus (*viṣva*). By this, the view of the *Bhāmatī* school—that for each individual soul there is a distinct phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—is indicated here. || 91 ||
Among these conscious and unconscious things, [He] is characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
The Brahman is one and the same, yet name and form are divided separately and distinctly.
Rāghava’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Why should the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious not be created by Brahman, whose nature is consciousness?
Anticipating this doubt, he says "consciousness... (verse 92), meaning that this cannot be so, because Brahman, as the material cause of everything, is equal toward all things.

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, setting aside the duality consisting of name and form as being merely imagined, the author elaborates upon the contemplation of the Self as Brahman—which is the substratum and consists of non-dual existence, consciousness, and bliss—beginning with the verse starting "cetana" (92).

accompanied by two commentaries.
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the reason for Brahman being common to both the conscious and the insentient: "These names and forms reside in Brahman like a painting on a canvas."
Having disregarded both name-and-form, one’s intellect should become fixed upon Being, Consciousness, and Bliss. || 93 ||

Regarding the term "in Brahman": the meaning is that Brahman is omnipresent because it is the substratum of all conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*). To the question, "How is this understood? he says, "having disregarded," [meaning] that when the superimposed name and form are set aside, Brahman is understood as the underlying substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). || 93 ||

In the commentary (ṭīkā) on verse a0, [the author] illuminates the reason for the difference in name and form despite the equality of existence, consciousness, and bliss—namely, the characteristic of being imagined—and establishes that through an illustration with the words "In Brahman" (brahmaṇi). He then states what follows from that: "Therefore, by indifference" (upekṣayā) || 93 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: To illustrate the point already stated, he provides an example:
"Even when one's own body is seen in the sky reflected in water and turned upside down, one disregards it."
Just as one remains on the shore, so too should one maintain focused intent toward one's own body.

Regarding the phrase "standing in water": the meaning is that just as one might disregard the body seen submerged face-down in water and instead maintain a sense of ownership (*mamatva*) toward one's own body standing on the bank—which is its opposite—so it is here. || 94 ||

Commentary (a0): By means of the illustration of a painting, the reason for equanimity (*upekṣā*) is established: that even a person may sometimes experience great attachment toward a most beautiful painting, which is proven by one's own experience. To clarify this with another illustration, he says: "situated in water" (*jalastha*). Here, the cause for seeing a reflection facing downwards is the reflection of the face and so forth of the original object (*bimba*), due to the turning back of the visual rays—which are unable to penetrate through the mirror or other clear substances that are directly in front.

When perception occurs upon seeing Devadatta standing before one in ordinary life, the observer's right eye connects with his left limbs simultaneously, and the left [eye] with his right [limbs]; therefore, even though they have become distinct through that refinement (*saṃskāra*), they appear in that very same way. Just as the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) situated on the left shoulder appears in a mirror as being on the right shoulder, so too, when observing a reflection in water, the observer first looks downward.

It becomes milk; thus, even the rays of his eye perceive him as being with his head downward and feet upward—everything is now clear. For a detailed account, one should consult my own *Siddhāntaratnaśuddhānta*; this is the direction [for further study]. || 94 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He states the consistency of this treatise with the present work consisting of five chapters, as well as the fruit of its study, beginning with the words "Brahmānanda. Now, an objection may be raised: was it not stated by you at the outset—"Whether [the creation] be the individual soul (jīva) or the Lord (īśa), how could either of these possibly exist here at the end of a kalpa?"?
And no logical argument (*tarka*) is seen here; this third obstacle exists even in the case of identity (*aikya*).

Having thus stated, by means of this *āryā* verse, the obstacle known as the "impossibility of the object of knowledge" (*prameyāsaṃbhāvanā*) regarding the purified identity of the individual soul and Brahman (*jīvabrahmaikya*), [the author] says:
"And in the thirteenth [chapter], the non-dual identity was also explained through various types of reasoning."

If it is asked: "How is it possible for this thirteenth chapter, named *Advaitānanda*, to be a sublater of that [previous position], given the other Āryā verse which states: 'Its predominance, however, is to be understood as being based on mere conceptual esteem (*saṃbhāvana*)'?"

Listen! For here, by means of the illustration of the clay and the jar, it is indeed beyond dispute that the reality of the cause—known as the material cause (*upādāna*)—is established because it persists through all states, whereas the unreality (falsity) of the effect—known as the modification (*vikāra*), such as the jar—is established because it does not so persist. And thus, from the scriptural text: "This individual soul (*jīva*) has the effect as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); the Lord (*īśvara*) has the cause as its limiting adjunct," the falsity of the effect is established as a necessary corollary (*nāntarīyakasiddha*) to the fact that the individual soul has the effect as its limiting adjunct.

Due to falsity (*mithyātva*), even though identity with the Lord— who is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the cause— is impossible for that pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) characterized by it, [the reflection] exists in the cause. [[page 478-to-478]] 480.

Since the nature of being a cause is defined solely by its relation to an effect, and since that effect is illusory, the inseparable connection (avinābhāva) of this [causality] is also established as illusory;

therefore, what contradiction could there be in its identity with pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) as indicated by it? For when the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the pot is destroyed, there is no inherent contradiction in the identity of the space within the pot with the great space (*mahākāśa*).

Once this is established, no learned person would dissent. Thus, by means of this very example of sleep and dreaming, the falsity of the entire duality consisting of cause and effect is easily demonstrated; likewise, the ultimate non-dual unity of Brahman—the pure consciousness that serves as the substratum and is indicated by that duality—is also easily established.
Therefore, it should be understood by the wise that it is entirely appropriate for this treatise to serve as a sublater of the aforementioned obstacles. 105.
