When the self has been determined within this individual soul (jīvātman) according to the method stated [above],...
There is no enjoyer whatsoever here in this body; so how can there be fever?

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): Then, since the nature of the individual self (jīvātman) has been ascertained—according to the method stated in the preceding chapter—as being non-attached and immutable pure consciousness, it is said that due to the absence of a desirer, there is no connection with fever and the like: "The Self-bliss... (verse 11).
a0 Commentary: "The Self" (ātman)—this too, like the previously mentioned falsity of the object of enjoyment, serves to establish the falsity of the enjoyer.
rā0 Commentary: Now he shows the fever pertaining to the next world:
"Anxiety regarding merit and demerit constitutes the suffering of the next world."
It was stated in the very first chapter that anxiety shall not afflict him.
Regarding the word "puṇya": he states that its non-existence was established in the first chapter—thus, "in the first [chapter]. || 12 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Having thus described the absence of suffering in this world, he first summarizes its opposite in order to speak of that [suffering] pertaining to the next world—beginning with the word "puṇya" (merit). He reminds us of the very absence of that [suffering] which was mentioned previously, using the words "prathama" (first) and so on. This is indeed stated in his own fifth verse: "For one who practices this very austerity, this anxiety produced by the fire of karma does not exist. || 12 ||
Just as there is no clinging of water to this lotus leaf, so it is [with the self].
After feeling, there is no further clinging to future karma for the wise one. (13)

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object: "Granted that the knower may have no anxiety regarding karma already commenced, there will surely remain anxiety regarding future karma. Anticipating this, [the author] states "yathā" (just as), asserting that even anxiety regarding future karma does not exist for the knower, because the connection with future karma has been refuted by the scriptural text beginning with "tadyathā puṣkaraparṇe" (Just as on a lotus leaf...). || 13 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "Let that statement refer only to what has already been accumulated; however, the present action itself must surely be an obstacle.
To this, he says: "Just as... The scriptural passage beginning with "Just as a lotus leaf" is indeed well known. || 13 ||
Just as the burning of reeds, grass, or cotton by fire occurs in an instant;
Likewise, his accumulated karma becomes burnt through this realization.

Rāma’s Commentary: Relying on the scriptural authority of the passage, “Just as a tuft of cotton-wool thrown into a fire is consumed, even so all his evils are consumed,” he states that for the knower, there is no concern even regarding accumulated karma—thus, “ipīka” etc. (verse 14).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, he recites in substance even the following Śruti text: "Just as a tuft of reed-grass thrown into a fire would be consumed, even so all his evils are consumed"—expressing this with the words "iṣīka" etc. || 14 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, [pages 482–482] 484.
Just as a kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna.
Just so, the fire of knowledge called Vidyānanda reduces all karmas to ashes. || 15 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He also cites the words of the Lord as authoritative evidence for the stated meaning: "Just as [the fire consumes] pieces of wood," etc. (15).
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): In that regard, he also corroborates this with a traditional authority (smṛti), beginning with the words "yathā" (as it is said). || 15 ||
He whose state of being is not characterized by egoism, and whose intellect is not defiled;
Even having slain these worlds, he does not kill, nor is he bound.
Rāma’s commentary: "Of whom there is no 'I'... || 16 ||

Commentary on Verse 16: Regarding the phrase "of whom" (yasya): *bhāva* refers to the Self (*ātman*) whose nature is pure existence (*sanmātra*). *Ahaṃkṛtaḥ* means that which is established through identification with the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).
He is one for whom such [identification] does not exist. For this very reason, the text says "the intellect," and so forth.
"Him," even having slain—meaning having struck down—these worlds, that is, living beings within the range of perception; he remains. The rest is indeed clear. || 16 ||
The killing of mother and father, theft, the destruction of an embryo, and other such acts [are grave offenses].
Liberation does not destroy sin, nor does the radiance of the face perish.

Rāma’s Commentary: On this very point, he recites in substance the sentence from the Kauṣītaki Śruti—"Neither by the killing of a mother, nor by the killing of a father, nor by theft, nor by the slaying of an embryo—no sin at all adheres to the face of one who has committed [these acts]"—reading it as "mātāpitroḥ" etc. Here, "canā" is a single word, and "nīlam" means luster. || 17 ||

The commentary on this root text cites, by way of its meaning, the Kauṣītaki Śruti which serves as its source: "Neither by the killing of a mother, nor by the killing of a father, nor by theft, nor by the slaying of an embryo, does any evil appear on the face of one who has committed [these acts]. This is quoted as: "Mātā... etc.

The meaning of this is stated in the *Anubhūtiprakāśa*: "Even if one performs such acts as the murder of a mother through speech or mind, nevertheless, the liberation of the knower is not obstructed by these. Even for one who has committed sin, there is indeed no loss of joy on his face; for according to the scriptures, the certainty is that 'liberation does not perish,'" and so forth. (17)
Just as the absence of suffering [is attained], the attainment of all desires is declared for him;
for it is said that having attained all desires, he indeed became immortal. || 18 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Among the four types mentioned, he states the second kind with the words "duḥkha" (suffering), etc. The word "by the Śruti" is to be understood as the ellipsis for "is declared. Regarding this matter, he recites the statement of the Aitareya Śruti according to its meaning: "sarvān" (all), etc. || 18 ||

— Commentary (A0 Ṭīkā): Now, he also describes the attainment of happiness which follows in sequence, beginning with the words "duḥkha" (suffering). The phrase "it has been stated" implies that this was declared by the aforementioned Śruti. He restates that very Śruti in its essential meaning: "sarvān" (all), etc. Having attained all desires, one becomes immortal.
"He became [the universe]," according to the statement of the Aitareya Upaniṣad. || 18 ||
Eating, playing, and attaining delight with women, by means of vehicles and other such things.
The vital breath does not remember the body; by means of action, it sustains that [body].

Rāmānuja’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): He recites the meaning of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad passage, "Eating, playing, sporting—whether with women, or with vehicles, or with those possessing knowledge, or with those lacking knowledge, or with companions—he does not remember this body as having been born," by quoting the verse beginning with "jakṣan. || 19 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Thus, in this very context, he also summarizes by way of its meaning the *Chāndogya* Śruti—“eating, playing, and delighting with women, or with vehicles, or with kinsmen, not remembering the production [of this body], thinking ‘this is the body, this is the body’”—in the words “jakṣan” and so forth. This has been explained [on page 483].
Accompanied by Two Commentaries | Chapter Fourteen [485]

In the light of the experience of speech, while eating various kinds of food and the like in the bodies of Indra, kings, and others, he sometimes laughs with children and sports with women; indeed, he rejoices in vehicles and in the company of his kinsmen. He never remembers that this body was once near other people. Previously, there was suffering due to the delusion of identity with this body; now, with the dawn of discrimination and the disappearance of that delusion, that suffering no longer exists.

It is observed that there was no identity [of the Self] with the bodies of Indra, kings, and others even in the past; therefore, not even a suspicion of suffering from such bodies exists for this [Self].

The Witness observes all the pleasures residing in those bodies. Being one who identifies with the nature of the Witness, the Knower (jñānin) regards them as his own. The Witness likewise observes sufferings as well; nevertheless, the knower of reality does not adopt identification with these sufferings because they are illusory (māyika). And—

The fragments of bliss arising from sense objects are themselves [mere] pleasures; therefore, those who know reality possess an attachment toward these. Another Vedic scripture declares: "One attains merit alone through this, for one possessed of sin does not go to the gods; thus it speaks of the happiness of one who perceives the Self in all.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In that very context, he recites the statement of the Taittirīya Śruti according to its meaning:
"He attains all desires simultaneously, unlike others who do so through successive births and actions."
Enjoyments exist simultaneously and without succession for one learned in the Vedas. || 20 ||

"Of all" (sarvān). Now, one might object: "If the enjoyment of the fruits of karma is admitted, would it not follow that rebirth must also occur? Anticipating this, he says: "Not like others" (nānyavat). The meaning is that because accumulated karmas have been burnt by knowledge, there is no rebirth as there is for the ignorant. || 20 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Likewise, summarizing the meaning of the Taittirīya Śruti passage beginning with "Thus he enjoys all desires together with the omniscient Brahman," he says "all" and so forth in four and a half verses. || 20 ||
He is youthful, handsome, learned, free from disease, and firm of mind.
Accompanied by his army, he protected the entire earth, which was filled with wealth.
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, he recites the passage from the Taittirīyaka and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣads, summarizing its meaning: "You two... (21).
Commentary on verse a0: "Young" (yuvā) and "firm" (dṛḍha)—by these two, the absence of subjection to the mind is suggested. || 21 ||
Endowed with all human enjoyments, the lord of the earth was fully satisfied.
One attains the bliss of Yama and reaches the highest state of one who knows Brahman.

Rāma’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): Now, one might object: "How can the blisses residing in the individual souls (jīvas)—ranging from that of a sovereign emperor up to that of Hiraṇyagarbha—be possible in a person of knowledge?
Anticipating this doubt, he states that they are indeed possible because all such blisses are portions of the venerable Brahman within the knower, saying:
"By all... (verse 22). Ātreya’s Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Regarding the word "sarvaiḥ" (by all): in the compound "tṛpta" (satisfied), a *karmadhāraya* is intended. || 22 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, an objection is raised:
"In the enjoyment of mortal pleasures, there is no desire for the two [of them] that is equal to satisfaction; therefore, they are alike."
For one person, there is detachment from enjoyments; for another, it arises through discernment. || 23 ||

Raising the objection as to how there can be equality of bliss when there is no equality in the attainment of objects for the universal sovereign (*sārvabhauma*) and the Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), [the author] states "by me" (*mayā*), asserting that there is equality of satisfaction due to equality in their lack of dependence. He states the reason for this equality of satisfaction: "from enjoyment" (*bhogāt*).
Commentary on Verse 23: "Martya... etc. Regarding the two—the universal sovereign and the Vedic scholar—there is the enjoyment of mortals, meaning the enjoyment of the world of men.
This is the meaning. || 23 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He explains the meaning stated by the word "through discrimination" (vivekataḥ) as follows:
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya observes the defects of the Lord [in the world] through the Vedic scriptures due to his status as a learned priest (*śrotriya*).
King Bṛhadratha, known as Vidyānanda, illustrated those faults with verses: || 24 ||

Regarding the phrase "because of being a *śrotriya*": having raised the doubt as to in which branch (*śākhā*) and by whom the defects of sense objects (*viṣayadoṣa*) were described, he states—beginning with the word "The King"—that they were spoken in verse (*gāthā*) by Bṛhadratha in the branch known as the Maitrāyaṇīya. || 24 ||

Commentary on verse a0: Regarding the phrase "because of being a *śrotriya*," he says—by means of the half-verse beginning with "O King"—that there are defects in the enjoyment of sense objects within the Veda.
This refers to the Maitrāyaṇīya Śruti beginning with, "There was indeed a king named Bṛhadratha... [24]
The defects of the body, the defects of the mind, and the manifold defects of objects of enjoyment—these [arise from the defects of ignorance].
Just as a dog has no desire for vomited milk-rice, so it is with the man of discrimination.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He provides an illustration regarding the non-arising of desires in the case of a person of discrimination: "guṇa... (verse 25).
The commentary (ṭīkā) condenses those very points: "deha" || 25 ||
Even though there is equality here in the king's lack of desire regarding the accumulation of the means of accomplishment.
There was suffering because of the impending destruction, and great fear in following [the path]. || 26 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the superiority of the Śrotriya over the sovereign emperor—“In the state of desirelessness,” etc. (26).

Commentary (a0): Now, by the maxim of the lion’s backward glance, the author states another distinction between the previously mentioned universal monarch and the Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), despite their equality, beginning with the words "niṣkāmatve" (in the state of desirelessness). The phrase "duḥkhamāsīt" (there was suffering) connects back to what preceded. || 26 ||
Neither of these two belongs to the Vedic scholar; therefore, his bliss is greater than that of the other.
The Gandharvas desire the king, but not the discerning man.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: The meaning is that since there are two defects—namely, that sovereignty over the whole earth is to be achieved through effort and that there is subsequently the fear of its destruction—the Śrotriya possesses superiority because both of these are absent in his case. He states another reason for the Śrotriya’s superiority with the verse beginning "gandharva... (27).
Commentary on verse a0: "Neither both" means neither of the two, namely, the pair consisting of suffering and fear. || 27 ||
In this kalpa, being a human being, by virtue of the specific ripening of his merit, he attained this state.
Having attained the state of a gandharva, he is called a mortal gandharva. || 28 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, in order to demonstrate the twofold nature of the Gandharvas, he states the divisions of the Gandharvas in two verses, beginning with "In this... (28).
Commentary on a0: "In this" means, by implication, "in another kalpa. || 28 ||
If, due to merit performed in a previous kalpa, one should come into existence at the very beginning of that kalpa;
Such a state here is called being a Gandharva among the divine Gandharvas. || 29 ||
Rāma’s commentary: "As before" || 29 ||

Commentary on verse a0: Regarding the phrase "at the beginning of the previous [kalpa]," the distinction from the preceding case is that here, Gandharvahood is attained at the very start of the kalpa.

In contrast, in the latter case, for one who has performed meritorious deeds while delimited by a human body in this very kalpa, the attainment of Gandharvahood occurs only after the fall of that body, due to the specific ripening of that merit; this is the distinction. || 29 ||
In this world, the Agniṣvātta and other ancestors are those who have resided for a long time.
Those who have attained divinity at the very beginning of the kalpa are the *ājāna-devatās*.
The Fourteenth Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): To demonstrate the joy of the ancestors residing in the eternal world (ciraloka), he mentions those ancestors: "the Agniṣvāttas and others.
To provide knowledge of the threefold nature of the joy of the gods, he states the divisions of the gods: "at the beginning of the kalpa," and so forth. || 30 ||
Commentary on verse 30: "In Agni" means in the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka). || 30 ||
In this kalpa, having performed rituals such as the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), one attains the great state.
Having attained [this state], those who are worshiped by the *ājānadevas* are the *karmadevas*.
Rāma’s Commentary: "In this kalpa," [etc. || 31 ||
Commentary (a0): "In this kalpa" means by those who have attained the status of gods at the very beginning of the kalpa—namely, the *ājāna-devas*. || 31 ||
The gods Yama and Agnimukhya, as well as Indra and Bṛhaspati, are to be known [as the presiding deities].
Prajāpati is declared to be Virāṭ, while Brahmā is named Sūtrātman.
Rāma’s Commentary: Regarding the phrase "Yamānī," it means Indra and Bṛhaspati are well-known [by those names]. || 32 ||

Commentary on verse 32: Regarding the word "yamān" (those who restrain), by the primary term [of the verse], Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, and others are intended. They are "jñātāḥ," meaning well-known. ||32||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: In order to indicate that those ranging from the universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*) up to the knower of the Vedas (*sūtrānta*) are inferior to the *śrotriya*, he says:
"Those from the universal monarch up to the knower of the Vedas desire each subsequent [state]."
This bliss of the Self is beyond speech and mind; it is superior even to that.
Regarding the phrase "the universal monarch and so forth": he declares that the bliss [of Brahman] is superior to all these by saying "beyond speech and mind.
The meaning is that since this bliss of the Self is inaccessible to speech and mind, it is therefore superior to all of them. || 33 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, the author declares the distinction of the bliss of non-dual Brahman—which is attained by a learned Śrotriya endowed with tranquility and other virtues, even over the blisses beginning with that of a universal sovereign and ending with that of the Sūtra-author—by stating "sārvabhaumādi" (beginning with the universal sovereign). The phrase "uttarottara" (each subsequent one) is a qualifying attribute containing a reason for their being inferior. Thus, it is quite clear that in the case of the bliss of the Self described as "avāk" (inexpressible) and so forth, each preceding one is subordinate to the succeeding one. || 33 ||
For by means of those various [means], the one learned in the Vedas attains all the pleasures desired therein.
Being free from desire for them, all those joys belong to him.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, [the author] states that all joys exist in the learned Śrotriya because he is free from desire for them, with the verse beginning "taistaiḥ" (34).
Commentary (a0): Thus, since the Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) possesses the reality of bliss as defined, he states that desirelessness alone is the cause: "By those various... (34).
Rāma’s Commentary: He summarizes the point established: "The attainment of all desires is said to occur when [the Self] is realized as the conscious witness-Self."
One regards the enjoyments in all bodies as being like those in one's own body. || 65 ||

"Of all"—now he states another alternative with "or else. The meaning is that just as there is the state of being blissful (ānanditva) in one's own body by virtue of being the witness to the intellect whose form is bliss, so it is likewise in other bodies as well. || 35 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Having thus concluded the attainment of all desires as previously stated, he speaks of another such attainment with the words "sarva... etc. The meaning is that he perceives [all things] through non-cognition; for according to the established doctrine, everything is manifested by the Witness (sākṣin), and thus he reflects upon it as being unknown. || 35 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 486–486] 488.
[The commentary by Rāma, known as the Vidyānanda-ṭīkā—

Now, having raised the doubt that even an ignorant person might attain all bliss in the manner described, he says "not so," because such a person lacks the knowledge: "I am the witness of all cognitions in all things."]
Even for the ignorant this exists, yet there is no satisfaction because of their lack of awakening.
"He who knows it attains all desires"—thus the Śruti has declared. || 36 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the ignorant," he cites the Taittirīya Śruti as authority for the stated meaning: "He who knows... The construction is: "He who knows the Brahman hidden in the cave, he enjoys [it]. || 36 ||
Anticipating an objection even there, he provides the resolution: "Even for the ignorant," etc. He cites scripture as authority in this regard: "He who knows," etc. (36)
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now he states the third method:
"Or else, he always sings of his own state as the Self of all through the Sāman."
"I am the food, and likewise the eater of food"—thus indeed is the Sāman studied. || 37 ||
Or else, the meaning is: "wandering through these worlds and desires, assuming forms at will," and so forth. || 37 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, since the aforementioned scripture—namely, "All other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss"—states that the attainment of all desires occurs precisely through the nature of Brahman as the Self, [the author], finding this unsatisfactory, states it in another way with the words "Or else" (yadvā). ||37||

The absence of suffering and the attainment of desires—these two are thus defined as the state of having accomplished all that was to be done and the attainment of all that was to be attained for those who perceive [the truth]. (38)
Rāma’s Commentary: Summarizing the meaning established by the preceding text, he says: "Suffering," etc. (38).

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Having concluded the discussion on the absence of suffering and so forth as previously stated, [the author] says "duḥkha... (verse 38), indicating that even the state of having accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtyatva*) and other matters will be examined exactly as described in the *Tṛptidīpa*.
For both [of these] have been correctly set forth by us in the *Tṛptidīpa*.
Those very verses should be reflected upon here for the purification of the intellect. (39)

Rāma’s Commentary: He states "ta eva" (they alone) to indicate that both the remaining state of having accomplished all that was to be done and the state of having attained all that was to be attained are to be understood from the *Tṛptidīpa*. || 39 ||

The commentary (ṭīkā) on verse a0: Since the state of having accomplished all that was to be done (kṛtakṛtyatva) and so forth has already been elaborated upon by us in the *Tṛptidīpa*, one should simply reflect upon that here as well; thus he says: "Both" (ubhayam). || 39 ||
For the accomplishment of the multitude of goals pertaining to this world and the next, and for the attainment of liberation.
Formerly he had many duties to perform; all of those have now been accomplished.
This state of having accomplished all that was to be done is preceded by its counter-correlate.
Continuing in this very manner, he is eternally satisfied.
Let those who are ignorant and suffering wander at will through saṃsāra out of attachment to sons and the like.
Filled with supreme bliss, why should I wander through the cycle of existence out of desire?
Rāmadīkṣita—verses 40, 41, and 42.
Commentary on the Verses 40, 41, and 42 —
The Fourteenth Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.
Let those who desire to go to the next world perform their duties.
Since I am the self of all the worlds, why should I perform anything, and how?
Let them expound the treatises or teach the Vedas.
But those for whom I am the authority have no authority [over me], because I am beyond action.
I have no desire for sleep or alms, nor do I perform bathing or purification.
If the perceivers are merely conceptualizing, what would it matter to me if they conceptualize something else? (45)
A heap of gunja berries and the like would not be burned by a fire superimposed upon something else.
I do not worship these phenomena of saṃsāra as anything other than superimpositions.
Let those who do not know the truth listen; why should I, who already knows it, listen?
Let those who have fallen into doubt think so; I, however, am without doubt.
One who is subject to error should practice profound reflection; for what need is there for meditation when there is no error?
I never at any time indulge in the misconception that the body is the self. ||48||
The conventional usage such as "I am a human" and so forth occurs even without this [self].
Error is conceived from the latencies of long-practiced habituation. || 49 ||
When the karma that has been initiated is exhausted, worldly activity ceases.
However, as long as karma is not exhausted, this [suffering] will certainly not cease even through a thousand meditations. || 50 ||
If you desire that the practice of worldly convention be universal, then let your meditation be upon that.
Seeing worldly activity to be non-obstructive, why should I engage in meditation? (51)
Since there is no distraction for me, therefore there is no meditative absorption for me.
Whether it be distraction or concentration, both belong to the mind which is subject to modification.
For one whose nature is eternal experience, what separate experience could there be for me here?
"What was to be done has been done; that which was to be attained has been attained"—such is his certainty. || 53 ||
Whether it be worldly, scriptural, or otherwise, such is conventional usage.
Let that which has been commenced proceed for me, who am a non-doer and free from attachment. || 54 ||
Alternatively, even though my purpose is accomplished, I shall proceed by the very path prescribed by the scriptures out of a desire to favor the world; what loss is there for me? (56)
Let the body be engaged in the worship of the gods, bathing, purification, begging for alms, and so forth.
Let the voice chant the Tāra mantra and likewise recite the crest of the sacred tradition (Āmnāya).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary—verses 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48, 49, and 50.
Commentary on verses 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48, 49, and 50.
May the intellect meditate upon Viṣṇu, known as Vidyānanda, composed by Vidyāraṇya; or may it dissolve into the bliss of Brahman.
I myself bear witness that I do not perform even the slightest thing here, nor do I cause it to be performed.
Satisfied by having accomplished what was to be done, and again because he has attained that which was to be attained.
Being thus satisfied, he constantly thinks this within his own mind: || 58 ||
Blessed am I, blessed am I, for I constantly and directly know my own Self.
Blessed am I, blessed am I; the bliss of Brahman shines clearly before me. ||59||
Blessed am I, blessed am I; today I no longer behold the suffering of saṃsāra.
Blessed am I, blessed am I! My own ignorance has fled somewhere.
I am blessed, I am blessed; there is nothing further for me to do.
I am blessed, I am blessed! Everything that was to be attained has been accomplished today.
Blessed am I, blessed am I; my satisfaction shall have no equal in the world.
I am blessed, I am blessed; blessed, blessed again and again. || 62 ||
Oh, what merit! Oh, what merit! It has truly borne fruit, it has borne firm fruit!
"By the attainment of this merit, oh! we [are truly] fortunate; oh! we [are truly] fortunate! (63)
Oh, what a scripture! Oh, what a scripture! Oh, what a teacher! Oh, what a teacher!
Oh, what wisdom! Oh, what wisdom! Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!
Rāma’s Commentary—verses 57, 58, 59, 60, 61, and 62.
Commentary on verses 57, 58, 59, 60, 61, and 62.
The fourth chapter has been described in the work titled Brahmānanda.
Let it be understood that practice consists of the bliss of knowledge, extending up until its full realization. || 65 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter, named "The Bliss of Knowledge," in the *Brahmānanda* of the *Pañcadaśī*. 4.
Rāma’s Commentary: He concludes the meaning of this chapter with the verse beginning "brahmānandābhidha" (65).
Thus ends the fourth chapter, named "The Bliss of Knowledge" (Vidyānanda), in the *Brahmānanda* commentary on the *Śrī Pañcadaśī*. 14.

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He states the connection between the book and its specific section with the words "Brahmānanda," etc. Now, he prescribes the necessity for the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) to practice tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, as well as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, for a long duration, without interruption, and with devotion, until the manifestation [of knowledge] occurs, by means of the remainder of the verse beginning with "tadutpatti" (the arising of that). An objection: At the outset, you stated that even regarding knowledge, liberation exists only after the fall of the body.

From duality; or [it is] by means of the seventh stage—this is the fourth obstacle. By the verse beginning with "Even in unity," the composition of the fourth obstacle concerning the identity of the purified referents of the terms *tattva* and *pada* is established. Likewise, in the fourteenth [chapter], by the verse beginning with "Because liberation for one whose body is the non-dual Self occurs through knowledge alone; since this has been stated, how could its intent not be even more clear?", the intent of this fourteenth section, titled *Vidyānanda*, is established.

If you ask how that [the former] can be sublated by that [the latter], consider this: for here, in the bliss of Brahman, there occurs an immediate valid cognition (*aparokṣapramā*) whose object is the identity of Brahman and the Self.
[End of] the Fourteenth Chapter.

Accompanied by these two commentaries, it has been demonstrated by those very authors that the state characterized by abiding in the Self alone—which is non-dual Being, Consciousness, and Bliss—is attained through the sublation of the visible world, which consists of residual ignorance, its pervasive influence, and its effects; thus, there is not even a scent of disagreement here, so enough of this prolixity. || 65 ||
"Liberation is clear"— thus [ends] the work of Śrīmat Padavākyapramāṇajña... disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakācārya Śrīmad Advaitasaccidānandasarasvatī.

This concludes the section on *Vidyānanda* within the commentary on the *Pañcadaśī* entitled *Pūrṇānandendukaumudī*, composed by the student Acyuta Śarman, surnamed Moḍaka, whose mind sports like a royal swan at the lotus feet of the venerable Nārāyaṇa Śāstrin— the one who bears the sixth name "Śrī" and who delights in the Goddess of Non-dual Knowledge (Advaitavidyā) that ranges over the ocean of the nectar of pride. This work consists of five chapters known as the *Brahmānanda*, which form the third part of the entire treatise.
The fourteenth illumination of the fourteenth chapter of the fourth book of [the work of] Dha is complete. || 14 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter. 14.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter on the fifteenth day.
Therein lies the fifth chapter, titled "The Bliss of Objects," within the *Brahmānanda*.
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the subject matter to be expounded in the fifth chapter:
Now, here, the bliss of sense objects partakes of the nature of a portion of the bliss of Brahman.
It is examined as being the gateway; the Śruti has declared its state of being a constituent part.

Regarding the word "atha" (now): An objection might be raised that since the bliss of sense objects (*viṣayānanda*) is worldly, its description in a treatise on liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*) is inappropriate. Anticipating this, the author states "dvāra" (the door) to show that although it is well-known in the world, it is appropriate [to discuss it here] because it is a portion of the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*) and is thus useful for the knowledge of Brahman. Anticipating the question of what proof there is for its being a portion of the bliss of Brahman, he says "tadaṃśatvam" (its being a part of that). || 1 ||
I bow to the one whose form is the immutable Supreme Brahman—non-dual bliss, existence, consciousness, all-pervading, and stainless;
who, through delusion, appears as the dissolution of the magician’s trick of duality, yet remains the self-luminous crest-jewel of the Vedas;
who is the foremost of all teachers, the ornament of Raghu’s lineage, the true Guru established in Brahman.
I bow to my own guru, known as Śrīmannārāyaṇa, who is also named Mahādeva. || 1 ||
Having honored Jīva-jīvaka, Vidyāraṇya, and Bhāratītīrtha,
I shall illuminate the *Viṣayānanda* from the *Tithiprakāśa*, like moonlight [illuminating] the Kaumudī festival.

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, the venerable Bhāratītīrtha, the best of sages, wishing to compose the fifteenth chapter—entitled *Viṣayānanda*—within the fifth book (*adhyāya*) called *Brahmānanda*, which consists of five chapters and forms the third part of the *Pañcadaśī*, performs an auspicious invocation characterized by the contemplation of Brahman, for which the means of knowledge and the purpose have already been established. While stating the subject matter (*abhidheya*) of the present chapter, he [also] states its scope (*viṣaya*).

The [author] illuminates the fourfold connection beginning with "yojana" by means of the three quarters of the verse beginning with "atha. Regarding the term "dvāra," the sense is "for the attainment of Brahman-bliss. He declares the proof for the aforementioned nature of being a part (aṃśa) by means of the final quarter of the verse beginning with "tat. || 1 ||
This is his supreme bliss, which consists of an undivided, single flavor.
Other beings subsist on only a fraction of this [body]. || 2 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He recites that very same scripture according to its meaning: "This... (verse 2).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Those very [passages], namely, "This is his supreme bliss" and "Of this very bliss, other [blisses are...]"—
And the scripture, "The beings subsist upon a portion [of Him]," connects these meanings in sequence; this is summarized as follows: "This... (verse 2).

Rāmānuja’s Commentary: Now, in order to demonstrate that the bliss derived from sense objects is but a mere fragment of the bliss of Brahman, he analyzes the modifications of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which serve as its limiting adjuncts:
"The modifications of the mind are threefold: peaceful, terrible, and deluded."
Dispassion, forbearance, magnanimity, and so forth are the peaceful modes of conduct.
Thirst, affection, passion, greed, and so forth—these are of terrible conduct.
Delusion, fear, and so forth are said to be the functions of the deluded state. || 4 ||
Fifteenth Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.
493. "Peaceful" (*śāntāḥ*): these are the *sāttvika* mental modifications (*vṛtti*). "Terrible" (*ghorāḥ*): these are the *rājasa* ones. "Deluded" (*mūḍhāḥ*): these are the *tāmasa* ones.
He demonstrates those very peaceful and other modifications by means of the passage beginning with "detachment" (*vairāgyam*) and so forth. (Verses 3–4).

Commentary (a0): Thus, having proposed with supporting evidence that the bliss of sense objects (*viṣayānanda*) is a partial manifestation of the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*), [the author] now seeks to establish this by first distinguishing those mental modifications (*cittavṛtti*) generally into three types—since the bliss of sense objects is specifically a particular mental modification—for their utility in that regard. He does so with the words "The tranquil" (*śāntā*). Now, one might object: "Granted that this is so due to the distinction between the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva* and the rest; nevertheless, why is it that the determination of those very qualities is not made first?"

To this he says, beginning with "detachment" (vairāgyam) and so forth, in one and a half verses. Patience (*kṣānti*) is the endurance of suffering through discernment. By the first word [of the compound], non-hostility, humility, fearlessness, and so forth are included. Regarding "thirst" (*tṛṣṇā*): thirst is the longing for sense objects; affection (*sneha*) is love directed toward sentient beings; that same [affection] when cultivated with long duration, continuity, and intensity is passion (*rāga*). Likewise, greed (*lobha*) is the attachment to wealth; thus it is a sub-variety of that [passion]. Here too, by the first word...
Hypocrisy and the like; delusion and fear are indeed well-known. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), laziness and other such qualities are included. || 3 || 4 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He states that even among all these various functions (vṛtti) cited, the nature of Brahman as consciousness shines forth:
"In all these functions, the nature of Brahman is consciousness."
It reflects in those who are peaceful, and it reflects happiness as well. || 5 ||

Regarding the phrase "in the [other] fluctuations": he states the distinction regarding the peaceful ones with the words "in the peaceful ones. The word "ca" (and) serves to include the two [remaining types] not explicitly mentioned. || 5 ||

Commentary (a0): What follows from that? He says: "In the modifications" (*vṛttiṣu*). He states the distinction regarding the peaceful modifications: "In the peaceful ones" (*śāntāsu*). The word "also" (*ca*) has the sense of "even. In this regard, the determining factor is that while the reflection of the sun's light occurs in all perfectly pure substances, it is only in the sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*) that heat is also obtained; thus, it is indeed the extent of purity [that matters]. || 5 ||
"He became form after form; such is the Vedic revelation."
The author of the aphorisms composed the sūtra beginning with "upamā sūryaka... and so forth.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary (Ṭīkā): He recites a scriptural statement (*śrutivākya*) in accordance with the meaning of what has been stated: "The form... In that very context, he recites a portion of Vyāsa’s Sūtras: "The comparison... This is the first part of the Sūtra beginning with "And for this very reason" (*ata eva ca*). || 6 ||

— Commentary (Ṭīkā): He states the authority for the reflection even of that which is devoid of qualities: “Form, form” (rūpaṃ rūpam). This refers to the Śruti passage beginning with, “He became the counter-form of every form” (rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva). Likewise, he cites the Sūtra as authority: “The comparison” (upamā). For this very reason...

The aphorism states that the analogy is like that of the sun and so forth. For it is said: "Just as this luminous self, Vivasvat, though one, enters into many different waters; so too is this unborn Self, the God, made to appear as diverse in various fields (kṣetra) through limiting adjuncts (upādhi). Thus indeed is that [taught].
The concluding statement. || 6 ||
Commentary (ṭīkā): Here he cites the very scripture—“He is indeed one” (eka eva)—[verse 7].
For the single Self of all beings is indeed established within every being.
He is seen as one and indeed as many, like the moon reflected in water.
Rāma’s Commentary: Regarding how that which is one by its very nature appears as manifold through contact with limiting adjuncts (upādhi), he cites the scripture: "One alone... (verse 7).
Commentary on Verse a0: Here, Śrutipriyā says: "He is indeed one alone. (7)

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, one might object that it is illogical to make such a distinction—wherein Brahman, being partless, appears as pure consciousness in one place and as consciousness-bliss in another. Anticipating this doubt, he resolves it by means of the analogy of the moon.
The *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
titled "The Joy of Objects" (*Viṣayānanda*).
This moon has entered the water; it is indistinct in the turbid water.
Just as [a reflection] is clear in a stainless [mirror], so too is Brahmā, the Creator, clearly manifest within the mental modifications (vṛttis).
"Having entered the water": he applies the stated meaning to the subject at hand with the words "in the same way. (8)

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Clarifying the very example of the moon mentioned in the Śruti, [the author] explains the distinction between the reflection of consciousness alone (*cit-pratibimba*) and the reflection of both consciousness and bliss (*citsukha-ubhayapratibimba*) within the mental states (*vṛtti*). He says: "In water... Thus, just as the moon appears indistinct due to the limitation of turbid water and thus only the aspect of light is reflected, whereas due to the limitation of pure water it appears distinct and generates both light and the capacity for bliss—so too [is the case with the mind].

The sense is that the reflection of both [the individual soul and the intellect] occurs in the aforementioned functions; likewise, the arrangement of the reflection of consciousness and so forth within Brahman must also be understood. || 8 ||
In the states of terrible delusion, due to impurity, even the portion of bliss is obscured.
From your slightly stainless [nature], there is the reflection of the gods of consciousness.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He establishes that very point with the verse beginning "ghora" (9).
The commentary on the aphorism applies this to the subject at hand: "ghora... (verse 9).
Or rather, it is like the transmission of the heat of fire into pure water.
In that same way, there would be no such manifestation for light, nor indeed for the emergence of pure consciousness alone. || 10 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, an objection may be raised: while the partial manifestation [of the moon] is logical because the limiting adjunct (upādhi), namely water, is twofold, in the present case it is illogical for there to be a partial manifestation because the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which serves as the limiting adjunct, is one. Anticipating this doubt, he states another illustration: "Or else... (yadvāpi). || 10 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, an objection might be raised that since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is an effect of the pure essence (*sattvamātra*) of the five unquintuplicated great elements (*apañcīkṛta-pañcamahābhūta*), the analogy of muddy water and the like is inappropriate. To avoid this awkwardness, he offers another illustration with the words "Or else" (*yadvāpi*). "Of fire" means of a fire located in a vessel or elsewhere, separated [from the observer] merely by a container. Thus, when the internal organ—which is an effect solely of *sattva*—is in contact with Brahman through its *sāttvika* and peaceful modifications (*vṛtti*), there is an absence of any intervening obstacle.

The intention here is that both consciousness (*cit*) and bliss (*ānanda*) are reflected therein [in the *sattva* aspect]; however, in other states such as the *ghora* (terrible) and so forth, because they are slightly obscured by impurity through the intervention of the quality of passion (*rajas*), the reflection of pure consciousness alone is entirely appropriate, just like the heat of fire. || 10 ||
Just as heat and light both arise from wood when it is ignited.
In those tranquil states, bliss and consciousness likewise attain manifestation.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Now, regarding the perception of consciousness and bliss when the mental modifications have subsided, he states another illustration:
"But in wood... (verse 11).
He clarifies that very point by means of an illustration: "But in wood... (11). The commentary on verse a0 states: He clarifies that very point by means of an illustration—“But in wood... (11).
However, based on the intrinsic nature of things, the formal establishment of both [the conventional and the ultimate] is the same.
For that which determines [the object] is indeed postulated in accordance with experience.

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question, "But from what authority is such an arrangement established?", he says: "The thing... He anticipates the further question, "What is the regulating factor there? and says: "...experience... (Verse 12).
A0 Ṭīkā: Now, what is the proof for the aforementioned established order? To this he says: "The nature of things" (vastusvabhāvam).

If that is so, why is there no doctrine of inherent nature (svabhāvavāda) in the present context? To this he says: "Because of experience" (anubhūti). Thus, the intention is that here the proof is precisely the impossibility of explaining experience otherwise; however, since it can be explained otherwise in the case of the doctrine of inherent nature, that doctrine does not apply here. || 12 ||
The Fifteenth Chapter,
accompanied by the two commentaries.
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: He demonstrates this very experience:
"Neither in the terrible states nor in the deluded states is the experience of happiness observed."
Let it be observed that even in states of tranquility, some [individuals] experience an excellence of pleasure in certain instances. || 13 ||

Regarding the phrase "not in the terrible ones": even in the peaceful states there is the manifestation of bliss; he says "in the peaceful ones" to indicate that even there, a certain degree of excellence of happiness occurs in some instances. || 13 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): He states the experience itself: "Not even in the terrible... [etc.]. Now, if this is so, does the reflection of happiness exist in the same form even during peaceful states, or not? To this he says: "Even in the peaceful... [etc. || 13 ||
When desire arises regarding such matters as houses, fields, and so forth, then—
Because this passion of a king is terrible, we find no happiness therein.

Rāma’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): By means of dramatic representation (*abhinīya*), he demonstrates the very absence of happiness within the previously mentioned terrible and deluded states of existence—beginning with the verse "House, field...
(14). Ānandagiri’s Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He establishes that same point by means of the passage beginning with "House... (14).
There is suffering whether it succeeds or not; if it fails, that suffering increases.
If there is an obstacle, there may arise anger or hatred due to its being contrary [to one's will]. || 15 ||
Rāghava’s Commentary: When happiness is not established, suffering increases; when happiness is obstructed, however, anger arises.
He states another reason for the absence of happiness: "or hatred. This means that in such a state, there is the presence of disagreeable suffering. || 19 ||
Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): "Whether it will succeed or not"—this is the meaning of a doubt of such a nature. "That suffering" means: when there is an obstacle. || 15 ||
If a remedy is impossible, despondency would be of the nature of tamas.
In anger and such states, there is great suffering; even the suspicion of happiness is far removed.
When desired gains are obtained, your state of joy is tranquil; that is great happiness for you.
Indeed, when one is attached to gain, the attachment to enjoyments is even greater. || 17 ||
But the greatest [joy] is said by him to be in the bliss of knowledge regarding detachment.
In this way, patience and magnanimity likewise [are established] through the warding off of anger and greed. || 18 ||

Rāghavendra’s Commentary: When avoidance is impossible, despondency arises. Since that too is characterized by *tamas*, there is no happiness therein; thus he says: "When it is impossible," and so forth. The terms beginning with "anger" and the rest have their meanings evident. (16, 17, 18)

Commentary (Ṭīkā): "Impossible" (aśakya) means that a remedy—namely, the removal of obstacles and the like—is not possible. "Despair" (viṣāda) means excessive distress. Having thus established that in states such as the "terrible" (ghora), which have results such as suffering, there persists only the aspect of consciousness (cidaṃśa), he now elaborates upon how both consciousness and bliss manifest in the sattvic, peaceful states, beginning with the verse starting "kāmya. [Objection: But what if there is the occurrence of obtaining what is desired?

Because one who desires a son experiences happiness upon seeing his own wife’s conception of a fetus, [the author] asks what that [happiness] is like and says: "Lābha... (The gain...). Now, even so, where is the greatest happiness? To this he says: "Mahattamam" (The greatest). When there is the expectation of what that is like, he reminds us of it: "Vidyā" (Knowledge). He extends this analogy elsewhere as well: "Evam" (Thus). 16, 17, 18.
Whatever happiness there may be, that is Brahman itself, due to its being a reflection.
In the inward-turned mental modifications (vṛttis), there is its reflection without obstruction.
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya, page 494–494, verse 496.

[Regarding the one called *viṣayānanda*—Rāghavendra’s Commentary (*rā. ṭīkā*) states: "Thus, he declares that patience and the other virtues are established, saying 'in the mental modifications' (*vṛttiṣu*). || 19 ||
Commentary on verse a0: He states the conclusion with the words "yadyat" (whatever). This refers to this Brahman. || 19 ||
Existence, consciousness, and bliss are the three inherent natures of Brahman.
In clay, stone, and so forth, only existence (sattā) is manifested, not the other two.

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, in order to demonstrate the experience of the nature of Brahman everywhere, he recalls its essential nature with the words "Being" (sattā). The meaning is that in clay, stone, and so forth, there is only pure Being. || 20 ||

Commentary (a0): Now, one might object: "Let this arrangement of the reflection of consciousness and bliss be so; nevertheless, where is the reflection of existence (sattā)? To this, he says, beginning with the word "existence" (sattā). || 20 ||
The two states of existence, consciousness and manifestation, are evident in the two functions of the intellect: the terrible and the deluded.
In the state of peaceful conduct, these three are manifest; thus is Brahman described as being mixed.

Rāma’s Commentary: In the two states of the terrible (ghora) and the deluded (mūḍha), there are two—existence (sat) and consciousness (cit); in the peaceful state (śāntavṛtti), all three—existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda)—are manifest.
Thus, he says "mixed" (miśra) to declare that Brahman has been described along with its phenomenal expansion (saprapañca). || 21 ||
Commentary (Ṭīkā): Even so, one might ask, "Where is there the manifestation of two, such as existence (*sattā*), or of three? To this he says: "Existence," etc.
He concludes with the remainder of the verse beginning with "mixed" (*miśra*). || 21 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question, "How is it known that [this path] is unmixed? he says:
"It is unmixed because of the two paths of knowledge and yoga, and these two have been described previously."
In the first chapter there is reflection on yoga; in the [next] two chapters there is knowledge.

"Unmixed" (amiśram). The meaning is that those two—knowledge (*jñāna*) and yoga (*yoga*)—have already been explained. Anticipating the question "Where were they explained?", he says "In the first [chapter]" (*ādye*), indicating that yoga was taught in the first chapter. He then says "Knowledge" (*jñānam*), indicating that knowledge was taught in the two immediately preceding chapters. Commentary on Verse 22: Now, if Brahman is indeed unmixed, how then is it known? To this, he says: "Unmixed... and so forth. Ta-...
He states the two parts: "the first," etc. || 22 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: Now, raising the objection—"If existence, consciousness, and bliss are the nature of Brahman, what then is the nature of Māyā?"—he says:
"Non-existence, insentience, and misery—these indeed are the threefold nature of Māyā."
Non-existence [is perceived] in such things as a human horn, and insentience in wood, stone, and the like. (23)
Regarding "non-existence": the distinction is that non-existence pertains to things such as a human horn, while insentience pertains to things such as clay or stone. || 23 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, even if this is so, what then is the form of Māyā that is woven through everything? To this he says: "Non-existence" (asattā). Non-existence, as well as the two—insentience (jāḍya) and suffering (duḥkha)—where insentience is the state of being opposed to consciousness (cit) and suffering is the state of being opposed to happiness (sukha); the connection is that these three combined constitute the nature of Māyā. He illustrates them: "Non-existence," etc. (verse 23).
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Anticipating the question "Where is there suffering?", he says:
"In this way, Māyā, having unfolded, brings about only suffering for those of terrible and deluded intellect."
Because of its identity with mental modifications such as tranquility and so forth, Brahman is celebrated as "mixed" (miśra). || 24 ||

Regarding the phrase "ghoramūḍhā" (the terrible and the deluded): he says "evam" (thus) to show that in this way, Māyā appears everywhere. To the question, "What is the cause for the mixture of Brahman within the states such as the peaceful (śānta) and so forth? he replies with "śāntādīti. || 24 ||
The Fifteenth Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

497a0 Commentary: Regarding the word "ghora" (terrible), one might object: "If it is the case that Brahman, which is full and consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), is reflected in peaceful mental states (*śāntavṛtti*), then why is it said here—in the passage beginning with 'in that peaceful state'—that Brahman is described as being thus mixed (*miśra*)? This is not so, because of the [nature of] the mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*).
He says "in the tranquil ones" (śāntāsu) [to show] that it is precisely because of that identity (tādātmya). || 24 ||
Rāghavānanda’s Commentary: Anticipating the question of what the purpose of this description is, he states that it is for the sake of meditating upon Brahman:
"In this situation, whatever man here desires to meditate upon Brahman," and so forth.
One should disregard the wicked, the horned beasts, and so forth, and meditate upon the disciplined as is appropriate.
"Thus. He says "human horns, etc. to state that one should perform meditation on Brahman elsewhere, setting aside [unrealities] such as human horns and the like. || 25 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Having concluded [the discussion], he prescribes the means for meditating upon Brahman with the words "Thus" (evam). By the word "etc. (ādi), insentience (jāḍya) and suffering (duḥkha) are included. || 25 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: To the question, "It was said 'elsewhere'; where and how is it to be meditated upon?", he says:
"Having abandoned both name and form in a stone and so forth, one should contemplate pure Being alone."
Having abandoned the terrible suffering of those with deluded intellects, one should contemplate existence, consciousness, and bliss.

Regarding the phrase "in stone, etc.": he says "having abandoned" [verse 26] to indicate that one should abandon suffering and practice contemplation upon the two forms of Being (sat) and Consciousness (cit) in those whose intellects are fierce or deluded.

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): He clarifies the very method of meditation just described with the words "on stone, etc. and "terrible, etc. The meaning is: of the mental states previously mentioned as rājasa and tāmasa. || 26 ||
Rāghavendra’s Commentary: Regarding the sattvic states, he says that all three—Being, Consciousness, and Bliss—should be meditated upon:
"In the peaceful [states], one should likewise contemplate these three: Being, Consciousness, and Bliss."
These three types of altars—inferior, middling, and superior—are respectively as follows. || 27 ||
Regarding the phrase "in the peaceful ones": he asks what the similarity among these meditations is, and answers that it is not [as previously thought]—stating, "the youngest," etc. (27).

Commentary (Ṭīkā): Now, among the sattvic mental states known as "the peaceful" (*śāntā*), which follow in sequence, [the author] prescribes their contemplation without explicitly mentioning the abandonment of those [other states], because by the mere reflection upon that [peaceful state], the dullness consisting of name and form inherent in the mental states dissolves of its own accord, due to the reflection of the very Brahman who is full and whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
He says: "In the peaceful... etc. Furthermore, he describes the gradation of the aforementioned contemplations: "The lowest... etc. (27).
Even for one who is dull-witted, there is reflection upon the mixed Brahman even during worldly activity.
In this context, the bliss of sense objects is said to be the most excellent.

Rāma’s Commentary: Now, with the intention that those who are not qualified for the meditation on the attributeless Brahman (nirguṇa-brahma) may be favored by being granted qualification for the meditation on the mixed Brahman (miśra-brahma), he says: "Of the dull-witted," etc. (28).
Commentary (Ṭīkā): He states this purpose with the words "of the dull-witted" (*mandasya*). The term "qualified person" (*adhikāriṇaḥ*) is implied. Regarding the word "mixed" (*miśra*):
the meaning is that its object is Brahman as conditioned by the visible world (*dṛśya*). || 28 ||
But in the case of indifference, because of the slackening of the mental modification, it is the highest of the high.
Meditation on the bliss of latent impressions is said to be of four kinds. || 29 ||

— Rāghavānanda’s Commentary — Having thus described the three types of meditation (*dhyāna*) accompanied by mental fluctuations (*savṛttika*), he describes the meditation without fluctuations (*avṛttika*) with the words "But in equanimity" (*audāsīnye tu*).
The meaning is that it is superior to these aforementioned meditations. He concludes the discussion with the word "meditation" (*dhyānam*). || 29 ||
The Pañcadaśī composed by Vidyāraṇya. [Page 496] 498.

[Commentary on the *Viṣayānanda* chapter: Having thus described the three forms of meditation (*dhyāna*)— characterized by the contemplation of Brahman through the limitation of the three states beginning with the peaceful (*śānta*), and accompanied by mental modifications (*savṛttika*)— the author now describes the fourth meditation for such a qualified aspirant, which is called *Vāsanānanda*, is devoid of mental modifications (*nirvṛttika*), and is the most excellent of all.]
He states [the name] with the three quarters beginning "But in the case of indifference" (*audāsīnye tu*), etc.; he concludes with "meditation" (*dhyānam*). || 29 ||
It is not meditation through the practice of knowledge and yoga; rather, it is indeed the knowledge of Brahman itself.
When the mind has attained one-pointedness through meditation, knowledge becomes firm. || 30 ||

Rāma’s Commentary (rā0 ṭīkā): He asks whether this is a sub-division of meditation (*dhyāna*) or not, and says: "It is not meditation. Then, suspecting what it might be, he says: "It is the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). Suspecting how this knowledge of Brahman arose, he says: "By means of meditation" (30). Ānandagiri’s Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Now, if this were meditation, then the position of Patañjali would follow; therefore, he says: "No."

Regarding the word "jñāna": it means by the knowledge taught in the *Ātmanandādvaitānanda* and by the yoga taught in the *Yogānanda*. If this is so, one might ask what kind of meditation (*dhyāna*) is appropriate here;
therefore, he says "by meditation" (*dhyānena*). This means steady—that is, capable of subduing ignorance and the like due to the absence of doubt and error.
[One attains] the state of the Self as the indivisible single essence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss within that knowledge.
Having attained [this state], they shine without distinction, due to the abandonment of the limiting adjuncts that cause differentiation. || 31 ||
Rāma’s Commentary: He states the reason for this being knowledge (vidyā) in the verse beginning with "vidyāyām" || 31 ||
Commentary (a0): What follows from that? He says: "In the case of knowledge" (vidyāyām), etc. || 31 ||
The peaceful, the terrible, and those beginning with the stone are considered to be limiting adjuncts (upādhis) that produce differentiation.
Through yoga and through discernment, there is indeed the removal of these limiting adjuncts (upādhis). || 32 ||

Rāma’s Commentary: It was stated that this occurs "by abandoning the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) that cause differentiation"; he now enumerates those very adjuncts that cause differentiation with the words "the tranquil ones" (śāntāḥ).
Anticipating the question, "By what means is their removal achieved?", he says: "through yoga" (yogāt). || 32 ||

Commentary (Ṭīkā): To the question, "What are the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) that cause differentiation, and how are they to be abandoned?", he says: "Peaceful" (śāntāḥ), etc., and "Firm" (śilā), etc. This [mention of the peaceful] is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) for deluded states of being (mūḍhavṛtti). Alternatively, the word "terrible" (ghora) itself is the indicator for those; such is the summary. || 32 ||

When the unconditioned reality of Brahman, self-luminous and non-dual, shines forth, the triad [of knower, known, and knowing] does not exist; therefore, it is called the bliss of plenitude (bhūmānanda).

Rāma’s Commentary: He states the conclusion: "Nirupādhi" (without limiting adjuncts). The meaning is that because of the absence of the manifestation of the threefold division [of knower, known, and knowing], it is called the bliss of plenitude (*bhūmānanda*). || 33 ||

66 - Commentary on the Verse (a0 ṭīkā): He states the conclusion: "nirupādhi" (without limiting adjuncts). By the word "svayam" (itself), the exclusion of mental modification (vṛtti) is intended. By the word "bhūma" (the Infinite).

"In that [state] one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūman); the Infinite alone is bliss; there is no bliss in the finite"—thus it is heard in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. || 33 ||
The fifth chapter has been declared in the treatise titled Brahmānanda.
Let the bliss of the sense-objects enter within through this very gateway.
Rāma’s Commentary: He concludes the work with the verse beginning "Brahmānanda. It is not explained here because it is self-evident. || 34 ||

Commentary (a0 ṭīkā): Having thus established the bliss of the vast state of liberation— which consists of the non-dual identity with Brahman as Existence-Consciousness-Bliss, characterized by the destruction of all duality that constitutes the ultimate purport of the entire Advaita scripture and its various treatises— the author now presents the connection between this fifth chapter, titled *Viṣayānanda*, and the fifteen-chapter work (*Pañcadaśī*) as a whole, specifically its final third portion consisting of five chapters.
Fifteenth Chapter,
accompanied by two commentaries.

He describes the nature of the door and the one who possesses the door with the words "Brahmānanda" and so forth. It should be understood that even at the time of the manifestation of objects, because the non-dual, self-luminous, inner bliss-consciousness is established by first setting aside those [objects] through their falsity, this [bliss] has the appropriate designation "viṣayānanda" (object-bliss). ||34||
May Hari-Hara always be pleased by this bliss of Brahman.
And he protected all living beings who had taken refuge in him, their minds being pure. || 35 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Bliss of Objects," in the *Pañcadaśī* composed by the venerable sage Vidyāraṇya, within the section on the Bliss of Brahman.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Fifteen [Discourses]. || 15 ||
Rāma’s commentary: "May he be pleased. || 35 ||

Thus ends the commentary on the subjects contained within the *Brahmānanda*, composed by the scholar named Śrī Rāmakṛṣṇa, a servant of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Bhāratītīrtha Vidyāraṇya Muni. 15.

Commentary (a0): Now, at the conclusion of his own work, the Teacher, wishing to ensure that the benedictory verse—which is characterized by a prayer for blessings—is fruitful, offers this very non-dual Self as a prayer to the Supreme Lord.

For the sake of favoring His devotees, the Lord has manifested the form of Hari on His left side and the form of Hara on His right side; He is the Supreme Lord delimited by a specific playful body composed of Māyā.
Praying thus, he offers this aforementioned work as a dedication of a single foot to Him alone, with the words: "May [He] be pleased."

In this context, the word "always" (*sarvadā*) connects with both verbs, "may he be pleased" (*prīyāt*) and "may he protect" (*pāyāt*), according to the maxim of the central gem in a necklace. The same applies to the phrase "by means of the bliss of Brahman" (*brahmānandena*). Consequently, the protection of all living beings by Him is accomplished through that very bliss—as the Śruti declares: "Upon this bliss alone do other beings subsist as they eat"—specifically by delimiting it as desired sound and so forth. However, for His own devotees, those designated as "supported by Him," protection is achieved solely by bestowing the devotion characterized by constant, supreme attachment.

Thus, it is the truth that for those seeking liberation whose minds are purified, liberation occurs precisely through the aforementioned [realization]. Now, you may object: at the outset, you stated according to the *gīti*: "Even in the singular flavor of nectar, the bliss of the couple exists indeed as the witness of one's own nature; even in this unity, there is this fifth obstacle, like the obstruction caused by the rays of one's own light. By this verse, you described the fifth obstacle called "contrary contemplation of the fruit," which concerns the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman as refined [by inquiry].

Having set this aside: if it is asked, "How is it possible for this fifteenth chapter to be a sublater [of the previous teachings], given that its extensive statement—'Indeed, the fifteenth [chapter] speaks of the non-dual, self-luminous, and infinite bliss which is devoid of all parts, objects of manifestation, and subjects'—is intent upon that [very same reality]? The answer is:

True. However, even though the non-dual Self is self-luminous, it exists as the subject of its own manifestations, just as the sun, while being self-luminous, is the illuminator of its own reflected light (*vyāvahārika-sārvaryava*). Thus, [the distinction between subject and object remains].

If this doubt—that the status of being a witness to its own nature (*svarūpasākṣitva*) could apply to Brahman, which is partless and devoid of qualities—were to arise, it simply cannot occur at any time throughout the three periods of time; thus, it is stated here in the *Viṣayānanda* that there is only the instruction for meditating upon Brahman as characterized by the visible world. To explain: in this section, having begun with the instruction for the continuous contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*) of non-dual Brahman as Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), which is characterized by the qualities denoted by terms such as "tranquil" (*śānta*) and so forth, [the text concludes] at the end with: "a..."

"In duality there is no triad; therefore, the bliss of plenitude (bhūmānanda) is spoken of"— thus, under the guise of a conclusion, it is taught beyond dispute that the reality of the Self as Brahman— which is attributeless, partless, non-dual, the bliss of plenitude, and self-luminous— is indeed realized only through the sublation of all objects of perception.
"Indeed it is so; everything is entirely irreproachable; it is auspicious. || 35 ||
May the two feet of the venerable Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Teachers, protect us; may there be non-duality in the pair of feet of the most excellent True Guru, who is Śrī Saccitsukha.
Likewise, from that Ācārya, the bestower of the supreme boon of devotion to Śiva, [may there be] Śrī Viraṃ... [the rest of the verse is incomplete].
This work is most capable of being well-preserved and is also sufficient for its renown. || 1 ||
May the Lord, the Witness, whose limiting adjunct is beginningless existence-ignorance (*anādibhāvāvidyopādhi*), who is the Self consisting of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*),

protect us— He who, though the Self, appears as the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) manifested in the intellect that identifies with these effects, [and thus constitutes] the individual souls (*jīvas*).
In this *Pañcadaśī* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
through its purification, one who knows it becomes liberated by the destruction of that ignorance.
Beholding this duality, which is his own mental construction and yet has begun as a result of past karma, he sees it as a mirage.

Having prostrated again and again before the venerable Kapāleśvara, Rāma, Lakṣmī, Prāṇeśa, and Godā, I request this [work] for the sake of easily attaining the incomparable tradition of non-dual knowledge. || 3 ||

O best of the twice-born, may you quickly become the king here over infinite realms; protecting and instructing the worlds through your own duties as if they were your own offspring, may even the Lord of the Gods grant the desired abundance of rain, and may there be great happiness for the Brahmins and the cows. ||4||

Purifying their own bliss through the Vedāntas, with minds purified by their own dharma offered solely to the Lord of Śrī, these twice-born ones—delighting in the state of tranquility and other virtues, dispassionate, and devoted to liberation in the infinite, sweet consciousness of their own non-duality—[attain the goal]. || 5 ||
May people, always devoted to their own duty through love for the Supreme Brahman who is the most excellent Guru, become ever more fulfilled by both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
and may they dispel the heat of their hearts by obtaining the power of the Guru’s compassion.
With his face full of the nectar of the Guru’s words, he beheld this Kaumudī, born from the moon of perfect bliss.
These [verses], numbering one hundred and twenty-five, were illuminated from the *Pūrṇānandadukaumudī* by the grace of the feet of my Guru in the *Śrīpañcadaśī*. (7)
Where am I, named Acyuta, a mere seeker of knowledge, and where is the manifestation of the Fifteenth [Tithi]?
Nevertheless, it has been acquired through the rays of the toenails of the venerable Gurus.

In the year reckoned as one thousand seven hundred and fifty-one of the illustrious Śālivāhana Śaka era, on the fifteenth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, this Kaumudī festival indeed took place at Pañcavaṭī, graced by the banks of the Godāvarī, during the observance of the Lalitā-vrata under the constellation of Bhārgava (Venus). || 9 ||
I am the son of Nārāyaṇa; I am the disciple of the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa;
I am one who has taken refuge in Nārāyaṇa; may I become Nārāyaṇa himself. 10.
May the venerable Śrī Pāṇḍuraṅgaśāstrī, the son of my guru, be long-lived forever;
O Lord, grant me the non-dual Self through wealth, sons, grandsons, learning, and incomparable righteousness. 11.

Thus ends [the work] *Pūrṇānandadukaumudī*, composed by the student Acyuta Śarmā, known by the surname Moḍaka, whose mind resembles a royal swan dwelling at the lotus feet of Śrī Nārāyaṇa Śāstrī— who bears the sixth name (*ṣaṣṭhyupanāmaka*)— the lover of the Goddess of Non-dual Knowledge (*dvaitavidyā*), who sports in the milk-ocean of the authoritative words and sentences (*padavākya-pramāṇa*), and who is the disciple of Śrī Dvaitasaccidānandendra Sarasvatī, the venerable wandering ascetic teacher (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya*).
In the commentary on the *Pañcadaśī*, this fifteenth chapter is complete. 15.
May this work be offered at the lotus feet of the venerable teacher Śrī Śaṅkara; may it grant all desires, and may there be prosperity!
And thus this Pañcadaśī, together with its two commentaries, is completed.
